content:
Names like Nobnocket are the surest sign you’re in New England, and the Nobnocket Boutique Inn isn’t about to let you forget it. Located on Martha’s Vineyard, a short walk uphill from the dock on a on a bluff above Vineyard Haven, this 1908 Arts & Crafts-style house was once the home of the island’s doctor. The new owners overhauled the place, knocking down walls to create open living areas, polishing the hardwood floors, installing large picture windows to maximize the sweeping garden views. Floral wallpaper and bric-a-brac, be gone: these days, the Nobnocket is practically a showcase of modern design and art, featuring works by the likes of Marcel Wanders and Philippe Starck.  

We don’t need to tell you that they haven’t skimped on details inside the guest rooms, either. The aesthetic is elegant but minimalist — think parquet floors, natural light, and fine materials in crisp white, slate gray, and bold pops of color from ruby red to tangerine. Frette linens and towels, check. Large, sparkling bathrooms lined with glass, marble, and tile, complete with walk-in showers, check. Flat-screen TVs, personal sound systems, free wi-fi, obviously, check. Splash out on a Luxury Grand room and you’ll get a fireplace, a freestanding soaking tub, a Nespresso machine, and possibly even a window seat.

Public spaces include a light-filled sunroom where you can linger over a breakfast of house-baked pastries and farm-fresh eggs. Or they’ll bring it to your room — but act decisively. The Nobnocket might be a boutique inn, but breakfast, in old-fashioned B&B style, is served for exactly one hour. Luckily for overtired travelers, good coffee is available 24/7, and regardless of what time you rise, the village is just steps away.

Please note: Nobnocket Boutique Inn is a small property with only 7 rooms. Book early; rooms sell out quick.

content: It’s an unusual name, but it certainly paints a picture. You and the Sea pretty well sums up the experience at this stylish apartment-style boutique hotel, set within walking distance of Praia do Sul beach, in the Portuguese surf mecca of Ericeira. Sure, it’s not just you — but from within one of its 36 fully serviced apartments, which range from generously sized studios all the way up to sprawling five-bedroom family apartments, it’s not at all hard to forget about the rest of the world. You’ll find some traditional hotel services, like a spa with a pair of massage rooms, a heated indoor pool, an aromatherapy steam room and a contrast shower. The restaurant, Jangada, is a sibling of a well-known Lisbon eatery called Infame, and serves an inventive menu that’s focused on local ingredients, including ultra-fresh seafood along with wood-fired pizza. But for the most part it really is just you — and your traveling companions — and the sea. Ericeira is a fantastic place to learn to surf, with breaks that are suitable for any skill level, and the town is a charmingly evolved fishing village, less than an hour’s drive from Lisbon.

content:
There’s more to Barcelona, architecturally speaking, than just Gaudí. Hotel Bagués is a fine example, a nineteenth-century edifice in the Romantic Classical style, an aesthetic that’s as eclectic as its contradictory name would suggest. In its current incarnation it’s a luxury boutique in a style that’ll be somewhat familiar to old Barcelona hands — a little bit Gothic, a little bit minimalist, with high-end fixtures and furnishings and a dark, rich color scheme, the better to balance that blazing Spanish midday sun.

We mean “rich” literally as well as metaphorically; that dark hardwood is Madagascar ebony, and the accents are in gold leaf. That’s not to say the look is Emirates-style bling, though — there’s a subtle restraint to the design which only accentuates the richness of the materials. The better rooms look out over the Ramblas and the Jewel Suites, on the sixth floor, open onto private terraces.

The restaurant, El Regulador, is named for the building’s former incarnation, and serves three meals a day plus cocktails, in an elegant double-height space. A single meeting room hosts small conferences, making the Bagués a reasonable option for business travel — and it’s the rest of Barcelona, from the Gothic Quarter on out, that makes it a magnet for leisure travel as well.

content:
Elounda Peninsula All Suite Hotel is less a hotel than a small village dedicated to leisure, each of its rooms in fact an airy multi-room suite defined by breathtaking views of the Aegean Sea. The most modest of these feature jetted tubs, private sundecks and heated salt-water pools, while the more lavish also provide landscaped gardens, and close-up beach access.

Most of us, quite frankly, will have to make do with the relatively humbler suites — if you’re in the market for the Peninsula Palace, it’s probably your assistant’s assistant who’s reading this right now. But life at the low end of the Elounda Peninsula is still pretty high-end. Calypso restaurant offers ample opportunity for sea-gazing over haute cuisine, with wide windows opening over the Aegean and a wine cellar that doubles as a tasting venue, pouring glasses from the hotel’s massive collection. Right at the water's edge sits Sumosan, pairing Asian-inspired plates with equally sumptuous views; it's joined by the self-explanatory Il Borro Tuscan Bistro.

A serious draw is the Six Senses spa, which draws on every spa culture from North Africa to the Far East. More active pursuits include tennis, golf, and all manner of water sports, from a dip on the private beach to a fully serviced yacht excursion. And while the atmosphere is relentlessly upscale, it’s kid-friendly as well — childcare is provided, and includes kids-only pools and recreational programs.

How to get there:
Crete can be easily reached by plane. Flight time from Athens to Heraklion is approximately 50 minutes. Direct flights to Heraklion can also be found from several major cities, including: Paris (3.5 hours),  Berlin (3 hours) and London (4 hours). Ferry services from several islands are also available.  Ferries from Santorini Thira to Heraklion port take approximately 2 hours. Elounda is approximately 1 hour by car from Heraklion airport and Heraklion port.

content:
Japan has no shortage of charming ryokans, or traditional inns. But people pay extra attention when Adrian Zecha, the founder of Aman Resorts, puts his name behind one. Azumi Setoda, located on the remote island of Ikuchijima in the Japanese Inland Sea, is the first property in the Indonesian hotelier’s Azumi line. Zecha lived in Tokyo for a time, and his fondness for Japanese aesthetics is obvious here. So is his respect for the place, once an important port on an island known for its citrus fruits — instead of designing something new, Zecha chose to revitalize a 140-year-old estate long owned by a prominent merchant family.

The Kyoto-based architect Shiro Miura handled the restoration with an eye to creating calm, light-filled guest rooms as well as appealing shared spaces. The result is a boutique ryokan with many perfectly executed elements — minimalist interiors, exposed beams, clean lines, low-rise furniture, pale wood and washi paper, huge glass panes revealing views of a peaceful courtyard garden — and a few exclusive features, like an open-plan restaurant where local and seasonal ingredients are prepared with French techniques. The atmosphere is low-key but socially oriented; unless otherwise requested, meals are served communally, and the traditional bathhouse across the street hosts both locals and hotel guests.

For private soaking, each room comes with a cypress tub. All are sleek and sanctuary-like, with granite floors, bespoke blonde-wood furnishings, and sliding screens opening to private stone-lined gardens. Some have balconies, and a few feature two floors with tatami rooms and private patios with daybeds. Azumi Setoda emphasizes community, and there’s an island to explore just outside, but the rooms alone are reason enough to choose this hotel for a peaceful retreat.

content:
The Club House name on its own is a rather large understatement; this lodging, in the Chianti hills a half-hour from Siena, is the smaller, more exclusive (and adults-only) sister to the Hotel Le Fontanelle, with which it shares not just its location but its lavish Tuscan style and its atmosphere of splendid seclusion. 

In terms of style, The Club House isn’t big on modern architecture or edgy contemporary design; its spaces, both public and private, are classic in their inspiration — not antique, exactly, but continuous with centuries of local tradition. The Club House’s 12 rooms and three suites are up-to-date in their comforts, however, and each one is blessed with a slightly different view of the estate and the Chianti hillsides.

The Club House’s leisure facilities include an outdoor infinity pool, a gym and yoga studio, and an impressive spa, known as The Wellness Sanctuary. Meanwhile The Club House has two restaurants, Osteria Il Tuscanico and the fine-dining Il Visibìlio; the first serves a comfort food–focused menu of Tuscan specialties, the second a blind tasting menu crafted by the award-winning chef Daniele Canella.

Please note: The Club House operates seasonally, from April through October.

content: On the relatively sleepy west coast of the island of Paros, close to the capital but comfortably secluded above a picturesque little bay, is Andronis Minois, a 44-room boutique hotel in a style that’s equal parts modern minimalism and Cycladic tradition. It’s less a party hotel and more a luxurious little enclave, but that doesn’t mean it’s any less glamorous — its buildings combine a contemporary take on Greek architecture with a vibrant mix of Western Mediterranean influences, from the Italian Riviera to France, Spain, and even Morocco, all unified by the confident hand of its Athens-based designers.\n\nMany of the rooms and suites come with private plunge pools, and all of them have terraces or patios, some with more or less direct views out to sea. And the in-room décor feels unique, for good reason — many of the fixtures and furnishings are custom-designed. There’s a luxe little spa as well as a lovely swimming pool that serves as the center of the hotel’s daytime social life. Meanwhile Olvo, the terrace restaurant, is an impressive one, serving modern Mediterranean flavors under the direction of chef Anastasios Tsantilas.

content:
It’s a long way, both literally and figuratively, from Rhode Island to Hawaii. But the sequel to the original Wayfinder in Newport finds itself in Honolulu, a city which, for all its charms, hasn’t seen a hotel this hip in half a century or more. Wayfinder Waikiki is set on the canal side of the Waikiki Beach strip, a short walk from the beach itself, in a midcentury building that used to house a more conventional hotel.

What’s inside, of course, is far from conventional. Waikiki Wayfinder’s interiors, by local design firm The Vanguard Theory, are warmer and more organic than the quasi-Brutalist building might lead you to suspect. And while the style is unusual and eclectic, it’s perfectly tailored to the location, and feels authentically Hawaiian in a fresh and cliché-free way.

And there’s more to Honolulu than just the beach. This city is a crossroads of cultures, and is home to some remarkable food as a result — and the Wayfinder is correspondingly home to some impressive flavors, from the B-Side Coffee Bar to Redfish, a very fine poke restaurant; Lost + Found, the speakeasy-style lounge and pool bar, is coming soon.

content:
The fact that Asterion Suites & Spa takes its name from a mythical king of Crete is some indication of the level of hospitality that it aspires to. It’s set on the island’s scenic northwest coast, a short enough distance from Chania to make access easy, but far enough for a pleasant measure of beachside seclusion. And what you’ll find inside its 66 rooms and suites is the very picture of the modern luxury boutique hotel: no stucco or other faux-rustic touches, just a polished minimalist aesthetic, a palette of warm neutrals, and a mixture of subtly organic textures.

Most of the rooms and suites can accommodate up to three or four guests, thanks to some strategically deployed sofa beds. Some suites offer swim-up pool access, others come with their own private pools, and the top-level suite has a rooftop plunge pool with a view out to sea; at all levels you’ll find luxe details like Marshall speakers and Nespresso machines.

The spa is an impressive one, and features a seaside pavilion as well as a gym and a yoga studio. And the cuisine is impressively developed as well — there’s a fine-dining restaurant, a second, more casual eatery, and a pair of bars, one in the lobby and one by the pool.

content:
Six Senses has some experience with this sort of thing, but even by their lofty standards, this is a special one. Six Senses Kanuhura is spread across three private islands in the Maldives, accessible by seaplane from Malé or speedboat from the Lhaviyani Atoll. Some may remember the original Kanuhura resort; the Six Senses era is marked not just by a substantial refurbishment but an expansion of the facilities and a general upgrade to what was already a thoroughly luxurious experience — all while preserving the integrity and the beauty of Kanuhura Island.

The accommodations range from couples-sized beachfront villas to larger “retreats” and “reserves,” many of them family-sized. And the water villas, with their thatched roofs and attached plunge pools, offer an overwater experience that’s as close to the ocean as you can get and still stay dry. At all levels they’re stylish in an understated tropical way, and they’re exquisitely comfortable and well-equipped.

One of the outlying islands is used for a private beach picnic, while the other is home to Drift, a restaurant specializing in grilled seafood. Back on Kanuhura Island you’ll find a few more restaurants, from the eclectic and versatile Market to the Italian-inspired Bottega. In classic Six Senses style the spa program is almost absurdly extensive, ranging from massages and manicures to yoga classes, private training, and the Biohacking Recovery Lounge. And the sea life of the Maldives is perhaps the ultimate attraction — the lagoon is paradise for diving and other water sports.

content: Family-owned for over a hundred years, what’s now the Auberge du Bon Laboureur is more than twice as old as that; what began as a coaching inn in the year 1786 is now a beautiful little boutique hotel, combining the personable atmosphere of a private residence with the style and service of a professional lodging. The location, in Chenonceaux, a lovely Loire Valley village, is splendid — the chateau, a few minutes’ walk from your door, is a local highlight. And the auberge’s restaurant, under the direction of chef and proprietor Antoine Jeudi, is highly regarded for its classic seasonal French fare.\n\nThe hotel has grown over the years, adding a handful of additional houses to the original coaching inn. The rooms, across all of the buildings, combine antique charm with contemporary focus, and the comforts are subtly upscale. There’s a heated swimming pool as well as a tranquil little wellness area, and a bar for a pre-dinner apéritif or an after-dinner nightcap. There’s also a vegetable garden where much of the restaurant’s produce is grown — and from this location, the best of the Loire valley, from chateaux to wineries to nature reserves, is right at your feet.

content: It’s hard to imagine a more picture-perfect introduction to the Provençal-style good life than Coquillade Provence, a village-style resort surrounded by the panorama of the Luberon Regional Nature Park. With 69 rooms and suites it’s a substantial operation, complete with a vast spa and wellness center as well as an extensive cycling center, offering rentals and tours. The accommodations are lovely in that characteristic Provençal farmhouse style, but they’re modern in their comforts and subtly quite luxurious. Restaurants range from the gastronomic Avelan to the bistro-style Les Vignes, which opens onto a tranquil garden.

content:
Long Island contains multitudes, from Brooklyn and Queens (technically) to the Hamptons, and beyond. The relatively sleepy North Fork certainly qualifies as beyond — Greenport, once a fishing village, is now an upscale haven for travelers from the city, and the heart of the Long Island wine country. It’s also, as you’ll have noticed, home to the Menhaden, a stylish and self-assured 16-room boutique hotel, set right on Front Street, at one end of Greenport’s compact main drag.

The look is almost totally monochrome, with a bit of hardwood and some carefully curated plant life serving as accents. Furnishings come from Restoration Hardware, and the bathrooms are lavish and modern, with walk-in showers and in some cases deep soaking tubs. And space is plentiful, both in-room and outside — there’s a charming rooftop deck, the highest point in town, and each floor has a galley stocked with drinks and snacks.

Meanwhile the ground floor is home to the most significant public space: the restaurant, Bunker Bar, and The General Store Café. For getting around, there’s a fleet of loaner bikes, as well as a Moke electric car. And perhaps most convenient of all — the hotel is just two blocks from the end of the Long Island Railroad.

Smaller hotels like The Menhaden fill up quickly. If you can’t find what you’re looking for, contact us and we can help.

content:
Split between Peru and Bolivia, the magnificent Lake Titicaca, considered by Incas to be the sacred birthplace of human civilization, is one of the largest, deepest, and highest bodies of water on the globe. Backpackers have long made the pilgrimage to the water’s edge; this, by contrast, is a high-end luxury boutique hotel that’s set to bring a whole new audience to these shores. 

Despite the uncluttered design and contemporary amenities — heated floors, black-out curtains, and wireless internet — Titilaka isn’t a generic five-star. The simple structure, standing solitary on the grassy edge of the lake, is a forward-looking and eco-friendly hotel, with 18 plush suites decorated in earthy hues. The high-end linens, handcrafted bath products, and oversized tubs are pleasant, to be sure, but the real attraction is the jaw-dropping view of the deep blue water through the huge picture windows. It’s fitting, as nearly every activity at Titilaka centers around the lake — cocktail hour on the waterfront terrace, kayak excursions, gourmet dinners of freshly caught trout. 

It’s worth noting that the indulgent service is half the fun: a private tour guide and driver meet guests at the airport, escorting you by Land Rover and speedboat to the secluded hotel. The star treatment continues during your stay, with personalized options ranging from breakfast in bed to customized archaeological tours of the region. It’s lavishly equipped, it’s contemporary, but at its heart, Titilaka is appealing in a down-to-earth way that’s faithful to its natural environment.


How to get there:
From the Juliaca airport or Puno Train Station, a Land Rover or similar transports guests for an hour and a half to a picturesque wharf, bypassing the congestion of Puno. The half hour approach via private speedboat is completely serene, a fitting beginning for an authentic Titicaca experience. Titilaka can also be reached in about five hours by car or train from Cusco, and six hours by car from Arequipa. It is also possible to arrive at Titilaka via Bolivia.

content: The Comporta Peninsula, an hour and a half to the south of Lisbon, is known for its endless expanse of idyllic Atlantic-facing beach. Less well traveled is the village of Comporta itself — but that’s where you’ll find AlmaLusa Comporta, the country cousin of the capital’s stylish AlmaLusa Baixa/Chiado. And in a region almost exclusively known for high-end luxury hospitality, AlmaLusa Comporta is remarkable for its ability to deliver a stylish and thoroughly relaxing experience at a price that doesn’t exclude the vast majority of travelers who might be in the market for such a thing.\n\nIt’s set not on the beach but by the side of the Sado River; guests gather by the poolside, or in the rooftop bar. Of the hotel’s 53 rooms, 31 are suites, and even the smallest single room is eminently livable, with all the essential comforts, high-tech and low. And at all levels they’re attractive spaces, minimalist in their broad outline but full of organic textures and natural materials. A café, a breakfast room, and a pair of bars keep guests restored throughout the day, and there are more to be found in town within a few minutes’ walk. Meanwhile the beach is also close by — as tempting as AlmaLusa may be, this coastline is something special indeed.

content: Italian farmhouse hotels come in a variety of styles, from the classic pastel Tuscan variety to something like the Masseria Fontana di Vite, its sun-bleached stone exteriors exhibiting an almost Moorish profile against the rough landscape of Basilicata. It’s set in the hills outside Matera, the famous cave city, and its name, which translates as something like “Fountain of Life,” refers to a legendary nearby spring — precious indeed in these dry latitudes. The original building dates back to the 18th century, with expansions in the very early 20th, but it’s only after a 2014 renovation that Fontana di Vite became the luxury boutique hotel you see here today. In classic Italian style its interiors mix modern and antique elements with no regard for consistency; ultra-modern bathrooms are attached to bedrooms that lie beneath weathered stone vaults. Some are set in the original farmhouse, others in outlying village houses. And the hotel’s restaurant, beneath its own vaulted ceilings, is a thoroughly contemporary affair. Here at the border of Basilicata and Puglia it’s got a wealth of Southern Italian culinary tradition to draw from, and the spirit is one of abundance — which goes not just for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, but for aperitivi and local Southern wines as well.

content:
So plentiful are mainland Italy’s charms that it’s easy enough to overlook Sardinia. But to do so is to risk missing out on some truly spectacular natural beauty. The Costa Smeralda is not only surrounded by wild, unspoiled landscapes but it’s also home to some of Europe’s most extravagant luxury resorts. Against this opulent backdrop, a place like the CPH | Pevero Hotel feels downright restrained, even with its five swimming pools, relaxing wellness center, and its seemingly endless outdoor terraces.

In the guest rooms you’ll find soft, soothing shades, beamed ceilings and traditional tile floors, and stunning views whether you’re in a superior room or presidential suite. The service is ultra-discreet and ultra-capable, and the two restaurants serve a generous spread of Sardinian cuisine, which understandably leans in the direction of fresh Mediterranean seafood. All this, and the town of Porto Cervo, the heart of the Costa Smeralda, is just minutes away.

content:
Funny as it sounds, there really is a Zanzibar less traveled: its less-developed southeastern shore, to be specific, some distance from Stone Town and the more established tourist industry. It’s hardly undeveloped — the resorts have been gaining ground for some time — but they tend to have more than enough breathing room, and perhaps more importantly, beaches of their own. Such is Zanzibar White Sand Luxury Villas & Spa, a name which squeezes all its attractions into one delicious mouthful.

Let’s take them in order. The sands are indeed white, gradually transitioning to lush tropicalia as one proceeds inland, passing eleven roomy villas along the way. Size and privacy are the keywords here, enough that a freestanding outdoor tub and a private pool can be comfortably concealed. Then there's the spa, which takes full advantage of locally sourced products, incorporating seaweed, coconut, and Zanzibar’s renowned spices into its treatment offerings. 

It’s a safe bet those figure large in the cuisine as well: Doors to Zanzibar plates poolside Tanzanian fusion with delectable emphasis on the hotel’s own organic fruits and vegetables. The bars present a narrative of sorts — start with cocktails and snacks on the beach, transition to the lounge bar for a second act, then perch yourself at the rooftop champagne bar for a sunset to write home about. Or take advantage of the dedicated butler service. Come sunrise, an impressive slew of complimentary activities awaits including yoga classes, guided tours, and Swahili lessons, and there's the hotel’s own watersports center, Zanzibar Kite Paradise, a subtle nod to the region’s ideal kitesurfing conditions. 

How to get there: Zanzibar White Sand Luxury Villas & Spa is just over an hour's drive from Zanzibar International Airport.

Please note: Zanzibar White Sand Luxury Villas & Spa is a small property with 21 rooms.

content: The Myconian Collection is a smallish, homegrown, locally owned hotel chain, and fully a third of its hotels happen to be located in the hills above Elia Beach, which ought to tell you something about how spectacular this place is. The Myconian Avaton Resort is the highest of the three, with the panoramic views and the relative seclusion that that implies. And its rooms, suites and villas are among the group’s most luxurious — though, to be fair, that’s drawing the distinctions pretty finely, as the others are not exactly rough.\n\nThe look is contemporary, full of contrasting black and white and vivid pops of color, a welcome departure from the white-and-Aegean-blue standard. Many of the villas and suites have direct sea views, plunge pools, outdoor jacuzzis, or some combination of the three. And even the standard rooms spread out over 27 square meters, with the full complement of up-to-date modern comforts. Meanwhile, you’ll dine on the terrace with that grand view unfurled in front of you, and you’ll pass many a daytime hour on the pool deck or in the capacious Sanctuary Spa. Mykonos is perhaps the most familiar of Greek island destinations, but that shouldn’t count against it: its pleasures, after all, are timeless.

content:
The Willard is the capital’s most elegant and old-fashioned hotel, and it’s still the unofficial center of Washington. Every president since the middle of the 19th century has been a guest, along with countless foreign diplomats and heads of state, and all manner of American legislators, lobbyists and assorted bigwigs have curried favor and struck deals with one another in this grand old hotel’s lounges and executive suites.

Its 14 signature suites are now named after some of the historical figures who have played a role in the hotel’s story, with design elements inspired by each character blended with classic early 20th century details such as hardwood flooring, decorative moldings and crystal chandeliers. The guest rooms have been imagined more in the style of an upmarket private apartment with classic neutral shades and highlights of soft blue giving each a timeless finish. The best rooms look out onto Pennsylvania Avenue with views of the Capitol.

Politics is at bottom a business like any other, and the Willard’s business facilities are world-class with plenty of meeting space and a capable business desk in the guest rooms. The location is absolutely central, two blocks from the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue and it’s a short walk to the monuments and museums of the National Mall.

More informal business is transacted in the Café du Parc restaurant and the Round Robin bar — the former serving contemporary French cuisine, and the latter the kind of classic clubby bar where deals are made over cocktails. Legend holds that the mint julep, hitherto a simple country cocktail, was introduced to Washington high society from behind this very bar.

content:
The mythical hydra has many heads, but the island of the same name has only one sandy beach — and it’s on this idyllic stretch of sand that you’ll find the Mandraki Beach Resort, a modern luxury resort built on the site of a 19th-century naval fortification. It’s this curious history that explains the aesthetic; one part weathered stone and one part crisp, contemporary minimalism, it’s a look that conveys plenty of character without feeling heavy or overbearing.

It’s a fitting aesthetic for this low-key, bohemian destination. While Mandraki offers what is unmistakably a luxurious experience, it’s an unpretentious one, and the tranquil vibe is helped along by the solidity of the construction and the spaciousness of the interiors. There’s nothing here smaller than a 22-square-meter suite, and at the upper end of the range they come with luxe extras like private pools, and the suite in the old watchtower adds extra space and a far-ranging sea view.

Meanwhile Mandraki’s beach is lined with orderly rows of loungers, and guests are served by the Captain M restaurant, whose menu ranges from Mediterranean classics to bao buns and sushi — and whose atmosphere ranges from sunny beach-bar ease to casual glamour in the evenings.

content:
St. Edward State Park is an unusual thing: more than 300 acres of lakeside forest, feeling for all the world like a far-flung rural escape, yet situated very much within the greater Seattle metropolitan area. And the Lodge at St. Edward State Park is equally unusual: a one-time seminary designed by an eminent local architect, now renovated and transformed into a historically aware and uniquely atmospheric luxury boutique hotel.

The rooms come decorated with murals based on the original architectural blueprints, as well as nature photographs and furnishings that are a stylistic nod to — and a substantial upgrade from — the building’s monastic past. The rooms are quite literally twice the size of the old quarters, each one combining a pair of seminary students’ bedrooms. And the views are almost uniformly pastoral, looking out into the park’s plentiful green space.

There’s a proper hotel spa, and the on-site activities range from miles of hiking and biking trails to an in-house art gallery. And the common spaces are no less impressive than the rooms, from Father Mulligan’s Heritage Bar and the subterranean Tonsorium Bar, occupying the seminary’s old barbershop, to Cedar + Elm, serving seasonal Pacific Northwest fare in a sunny and grand double-height dining room.

content:
Stuck out on a promontory in the middle of Narragansett Bay, the old Agassiz Mansion’s location was ideal for its original owner, a Harvard marine biologist. Which means it’s equally well suited for its present purpose, as the Castle Hill Inn and Resort. A short drive from Newport, it’s possibly the most impressive location on the Rhode Island coast. Which, by the transitive property of real estate, means the Castle Hill is one of the coast’s top lodgings.

It spreads out over forty acres of land along a private beach, overlooking the picturesque waters of the bay. The bedrooms in the 19th-century main house are the most atmospheric, but the outlying beach houses and cottages are scarcely less stylish, with a bit more space thrown in in the bargain. In all rooms you’ll find crisp, well-maintained classic New England style, and a full complement of contemporary comforts.

As with most historical properties in New England, the ultimate result is somewhere between the quirky charm of a family-owned bed and breakfast and the smooth polish of a modern luxury hotel, incorporating elements of both. Fine food and top-notch service ensure that the experience is anything but rough, while the Northeastern nautical atmosphere contributes an air of romance that the dull corporate hotels can’t hope to match.


How to get there:
Castle Hill Inn and Resort is approximately a 40-minute drive from Newport State Airport (NPT).

content:
Monasteries and convents make great hotels. For while their ultimate purposes — one otherworldly, the other earthly — could scarcely be more at odds, in terms of day-to-day operation they’re actually quite similar. Both require a room with a bit of peace and quiet, a setting that inspires contemplation, and some places to gather, whether in worship or simply over a meal. Cartagena’s Santa Teresa has followed more or less this exact formula from its seventeenth-century founding to the present day, in its incarnation as the Charleston Santa Teresa Cartagena.

The rooms are contemporary in style, if somewhat conservatively so, and there’s a decided focus on physical comfort, with 600-thread linens and marble-clad baths. The Santa Teresa is a luxury hotel through and through, and the architecture of the colonial and 20th-century wings only adds to the hotel’s personality. The city itself, of course, isn’t exactly short of personality either, and the old-town location doesn’t hurt the Santa Teresa’s case one bit — whether your room faces out to sea or back over the town, there isn’t a bad view in the house. The best view, though, takes in 360 degrees: it’s the dramatic, atmospheric rooftop pool that’s the Santa Teresa’s ace in the hole.

How to get there:
Charleston Santa Teresa Cartagena is located 1.5km (10-15 min) from the Cartagena Airport. Transfers can be organized for approximately USD20 for up to 3 guests, USD35 for 4-7 guests in a van, or USD42 for up to 2 guests in a Cadillac SUV, all prices per segment.

content: Among the most unique hospitality concerns in Lisbon is the Almaria group, which transforms unusual historical structures into stylish and modern apartment-style quasi-hotels. For Almaria Officina Real the raw material is a handsome building in Baixa-Chiado which was once used as a pewter workshop for the Royal House — one imagines the pewter needs of a royal family were rather greater in those days than they are today. The loss of this workshop is a gain for Lisbon’s hospitality world, however; Almaria Officina Real adds 10 attractive and characterful apartments to the city’s stock of lodging.\n\nThe apartments retain plenty of historical character by virtue of some well-preserved architectural elements, as well as decorative choices that echo the building’s historical use. But the style is more contemporary than classic, even if it’s a warm and inviting variety of contemporary. The top-floor apartments come with mezzanines and plenty of natural light; others, on the lower floors, offer views of the neighborhood’s colorful thoroughfares. Kitchenettes are universal, and breakfast is supplied on a daily basis by your hosts; after that, you’re on your own, though surrounded by no end of options for restaurants and more.

content: As the name might suggest, Dusit Thani is indeed a Thai hospitality brand, and Dusit Thani Kyoto does indeed bring a touch of Thai aesthetics and culture to this most traditional of Japanese cities. (It’s hard to imagine a much more fruitful collaboration from the perspective of service.) The rooms and suites are stylish in a soothing way, with visual nods to both cultures; the spa draws on both Japanese and Thai traditions. And the restaurants, rather than attempt a hybrid experience, choose to specialize: Ayatana in a vibrant and contemporary Thai cuisine, and Kōyō in a concept that respects the 24 “micro-seasons” of Kyoto.

content: That’s a capital A, not just the indefinite article “a” — A Hotel Mykonos certainly isn’t just any hotel. It’s set in the hills above Mykonos’s port and old town, making it a private enclave in what can at times be a busy destination. And if there’s one common thread that elevates it over other boutique-sized Greek island escapes, it’s the sense of tastefulness that pervades its rooms, suites, and common spaces; the classic minimalist white-on-white look that’s typical of the region is brought to life by well-crafted accents in rough-hewn wood or hand-made ceramics.\n\nStyle aside, above all it’s a comfortable and a relaxing place to be — breakfast is served by the pool, which remains the focus of the hotel’s social life during the day, helped along by cocktails from the poolside bar. There’s a well-equipped spa and fitness center, and the beaches, of course, are easy enough to reach. A restaurant serves simple yet upscale Greek dishes for lunch and dinner seven days a week — though the town is close by, if you’re not in the mood for exploration, A Hotel Mykonos can provide a totally self-sufficient resort-style experience.

content: If you know any French at all you can see L’Eautel Toulon Port’s maritime theme coming from a thousand miles away, but as always, it’s not the concept that matters so much as the execution — and here the nautical color scheme and the graphic wave motif are applied with a light touch, lending an air of whimsical fun to this 62-room boutique hotel in Toulon, on the Mediterranean coast between Marseille and St. Tropez. This is a working port city, not an idle beach town; L’Eautel is set on the edge of the old town center, right across from the maritime museum and the Arsenal Toulon naval base. \n\nThe hotel’s rooms are bright and breezy, most of them typical double rooms; others, the “crew rooms,” are designed in a dorm-style layout with enough bunks for up to eight guests. And while they’re nautical in style, they’re more spacious and comfortable than ship cabins, with the full complement of no-nonsense contemporary comforts. L’Équerre, the restaurant, is open from breakfast into the night, and occupies a colorful space beneath a 19th-century glass atrium ceiling believed to have come from the Eiffel workshops.

content:
The Garden Island of Kaua‘i is wild enough to have featured as a filming location for TV’s Lost and various Jurassic Park films, but what’s perhaps most appealing about it is that its unspoiled landscapes and seascapes aren’t all that hard to reach. Timbers Kaua‘i is a case in point; here you’re surrounded by impossible vistas, pressed right up against the water’s edge, and yet you’re minutes from Lihue, the island’s largest settlement (and, crucially, the home of its commercial airport). 

More important than convenience, however, is the fact that Timbers, set in Hōkūala on 450 acres of prime oceanfront land, is as ambitious as they come — sister to the Sebastian in Vail and Casali di Casole in Tuscany, it’s a similarly state-of-the-art luxury resort. Safe to say you’ll lack for nothing here in terms of comfort — the rest is just details.

That’s not to say the details aren’t of interest. No mere rooms or suites, the accommodations at Timbers Kaua‘i are residences, spanning two, three, or even four bedrooms. Some feature plunge pools, others lanais that extend to the water’s edge, and all are positioned for impressive views.

In addition to an impressive farm-to-table restaurant, you’ll have access to two swimming pools, a fully equipped fitness center, and a concierge service to arrange activities like surf lessons. Not to mention, the Jack Nicklaus–designed Ocean Course is among the resort’s standout amenities — if you’re a golfer, that’ll be all the inducement you need.

content:
It’s not the closest hotel to the ruins at Machu Picchu, but Inkaterra boasts a location that’s special in another way: this 85-room eco-lodge is surrounded by twelve acres of high-mountain forest filled with all kinds of flora and fauna, wild birds and exotic orchids. It’s at the edge of the town of Machu Picchu Pueblo, which used to be called Aguas Calientes — there are bars and restaurants here, if you’re in the mood to explore.

But there are so many reasons to stay in. 85 rooms and suites decorated in a classic Spanish Colonial style are spread about the property, all outfitted with local craftsman-made furnishings and alpaca blankets on the beds. Slippers are made from recycled material, the bath products are environmentally friendly, and despite the wood-burning fireplaces, Inkaterra as a whole is fully carbon-neutral.

A restaurant serving upscale Andean cuisine and a full-service spa drive home the point that this is a luxury hotel, however rustic and earth-friendly. Ultimately the hotel, though, is only part of the story: you’re at Machu Picchu to see the citadel, which is a half-day trip from Inkaterra, complete with an expertly guided tour.

How to get there:
Inkaterra Machu Picchu is 70 miles from Cusco.
Cusco City is 4 hours away by train. The hotel recommends traveling by car to Ollantaytambo and then continuing by train for the last one and a half hours.

content:
Like its neighbors on the Amalfi Coast, Sorrento at its best is a destination that promises tranquil seclusion with a bit of drama — the cliffside setting of Sant’Agnello in particular makes for extraordinary views out to sea, as well as some memorably unusual topography. And the Hotel Mediterraneo Sorrento benefits from both — its terrace looks out across the Bay of Naples at the distant peak of Mt. Vesuvius. 

This century-old structure has been a family-owned hotel for more than 60 years, and a thorough renovation preserves its historical character while preparing it for 21st-century guests. Its 61 rooms and suites are today decked out in a style that combines the finest elements of classic and modern design — elegant parquet floors, Deco-influenced details, and a tightly focused color scheme of blues and whites, echoing the panoramas outside.

There’s an outdoor swimming pool surrounded by a garden and a citrus grove, as well as a small spa; an elevator connects guests with the beach club at the bottom of the cliff. A poolside lounge and a cocktail bar add to the atmosphere, and the most dramatic common spaces have to be the Vista Sky Bar and the sea-facing terrace of the Vesuvio Restaurant.

The hotel is temporarily closed for renovation.

A good boutique hotel strikes a balance between upending certain expectations while thoroughly fulfilling others. And a Venetian hotelier must be tempted to reject the whole ornate package of Gothic/Renaissance glamour that’s characteristic of the city. Eight Venezia, however, chooses a route that’s more difficult, but ultimately more rewarding — crafting an atmosphere that’s thoroughly, recognizably Venetian, but with an unusual depth of character.

It begins with a 15th-century palazzo tucked between the canal and the Santa Maria Formosa square. Heroically preserved, both inside and out, it’s rich with period detail and an authenticity that can’t be faked. Visit the rooms, though, and you’ll find these antique touches comfortably coexisting with modern comforts and more than a little bit of contemporary design. As always there’s a premium placed on a view of the canal, but there’s no angle on this city that’s less than picturesque.

The hotel’s Marea Wellness spa makes much of Venice’s association with the seas. Meanwhile the daily breakfast service is a surprisingly artful affair; for lunch, dinner, and drinks there’s the Peacock Bar, named for a creature that symbolizes love, vanity, and rebirth.

content: Montreal is perhaps best known for its picturesque historic district, its cobblestone streets lined with heritage buildings, including the 18th-century structure that conceals the thoroughly contemporary Hotel Gault. For a follow-up, the Gault’s owners have decided to play even more against Montreal’s type with the towering, ultra-modern Hotel Monville, a hotel that’s drawn nearly as much attention for its forward-looking architecture as for its futuristic amenities — specifically, its robot room service.\n\nYes, you read that right. Room service is delivered by a sort of anthropomorphic Roomba, whose retro styling makes the experience less bizarre than it might otherwise be. Meanwhile the rooms are minimalistic, largely monochrome, but warm and bright thanks to their touchable organic textures and their vast full-length windows. Space is at something of a premium, at least until you get into the suites, but comforts like espresso machines and king beds ensure comfort doesn’t suffer unduly. If, come mealtime, you’d rather not wait for the robot, you’ll find a restaurant with a menu that takes liberal inspiration from multicultural Montreal, as well as a café and lounge that does double duty as a co-working space, and a stylish cocktail bar to cap things off.

content:
For a long time Bali was the only island you needed to know in Indonesia, but as it’s built up, that secluded island feeling is getting harder and harder to find. An hour to the east, however, the island of Sumba remains far more wild, and it’s here that you’ll find the extraordinary Nihi Sumba. It’s been called the best hotel in the world — and while we would hesitate to go quite that far, it’s fair to say there’s a strong case to be made.

It’s set on hundreds of acres of waterfront land, between a glorious private beach and the edge of a truly untamed jungle. And while in its present incarnation it’s fantastically luxurious — its villas are the very picture of contemporary luxury elegance — it grew slowly from what was once a secluded surf shack, and there’s still something unpretentious about the atmosphere as a result.

It’s worth reiterating, of course, that it’s a surf shack no more; private infinity pools and butler service pretty much rule that out, as does the spa with its open-air treatment pavilions. Three restaurants serve everything from sushi to wood-fired pizza, and the dry-land activities range from yoga classes to horseback tours and mountain biking. The essential attraction, however, remains the ocean — fishing, diving, and paddle-boarding are all on offer, as is the surf break, Occy’s Left, that put this spot on the map in the first place.

How to get there:

Daily flights depart from Bali’s Ngurah Rai International Airport in Denpasar (DPS) to Sumba Island’s Tambolaka Airport (TMC). There are additional routes to Sumba Island from Jakarta (CGK) and Surabaya (SUB) international airports, both on Java, flying through Kupang (East Nusa Tenggara); all in Indonesia.

content:
If you know Cappadocia, in east-central Turkey, it’s because of the caves — here in the soft volcanic rocks lie any number of man-made spaces, from the humblest dwellings to the most ornate underground churches, frescoes and all. In this far-flung region the town of Ürgüp stands out as an oasis of modern civilization (and decent nightlife); and in Ürgüp the Sacred House stands out as an example of the best tendencies of the high-end boutique hotel world.

Some of the development in Ürgüp has been a bit on the hasty side, but the Sacred House is anything but. The mansion is two and a half centuries old, and was for a time a Christian church, as the name may well have led you to guess. Inside are just ten rooms, each one unique, all of them in a style that it’s not entirely unfair to call “maximalist.”

Though it was restored from near-ruin within living memory by its present owners, at times Sacred House feels authentically medieval — antiques abound, and bare stone walls go a long way in setting a mood. It’s the best of both worlds: the ancient ambience of the caves, along with the convenience of Ürgüp’s modern infrastructure.

How to get there:
Sacred House hotel is approximately a 1¼–hour drive from Erkilet International Airport (ASR).

content:
Zakynthos may not be quite as highly touted a destination as some other Greek islands, but it’s certainly not because it lacks any of the attributes that are essential to the form. Spectacular, impossibly blue seascapes are all you need, with distant islands looming on the horizon. Infinity pools certainly help, and if you’re in the mood for romance — or just quiet contemplation — it also doesn’t hurt a bit that Lesante Blu Exclusive Beach Resort is an adults-only hotel.

With 92 suites, it’s bigger than it feels, but it’s never crowded — again, thank that adults-only policy. The exteriors and interiors make liberal use of classic Greek-isle white and cream — why abandon a successful formula? Even the entry-level suites are plenty comfortable, with balconies and direct views of the Ionian Sea, and from there you can add a jacuzzi or even a plunge pool.

An absolutely stunning spa and a vast infinity pool provide ample opportunity for relaxation, as does the hotel’s small but lovely beach club. Meanwhile a trio of restaurants — Melia, the fine-dining option, Gaia, the more casual, and Ostria, the all-day poolside restaurant and bar — see to guests’ gustatory needs, while the Almyra Beach Bar and the Panorama Champagne Bar hardly need elaboration.

content:
When we catch ourselves asking why the Portuguese hotel world seems to be so generously endowed with first-rate contemporary design, we forget there’s actually a totally straightforward answer: much of it is the work of designer Nini Andrade Silva, whose elegant, modernist-inspired style sets the tone for many a luxury boutique hotel on the mainland — and on the island of Madeira as well, home not only to Silva herself but to the Saccharum Resort.

The name is a reference to the site’s former use as a sugar mill, now converted into a seaside resort, many of whose 243 rooms and suites look straight out at the endless expanse of the Atlantic. And though they’re not quite extravagant, they’re luxurious, with a balcony and some interior lounge space to stretch out as well.

Downstairs, the Saccharum Spa features everything from traditional massage and spa treatments to a lovely mosaic-tile indoor pool. And you’ll find no fewer than two restaurants and five bars — an encouraging ratio, we’d say — everywhere from poolside to the beach to the eighth floor with a view out to sea. All of this less than an hour’s drive from the airport, and less than half an hour from Funchal, the island’s capital.

content: There’s visiting the Yucatán, and then there’s fully immersing yourself in it. Boca de Agua Bacalar offers an experience that falls firmly in the latter camp, plopping you right on the banks of the Bacalar lagoon and its outrageously clear turquoise waters. Rooms come treehouse style, lifted on stilts to minimize their footprint while also affording sweeping vistas of the jungle — and, if you’re lucky, a spider monkey or an iguana. It’s a winning recipe: a tranquil hideaway, central to a rich selection of nature excursions, neighbors with Mayan ruins, all mercifully free of the spring-break set. Your hardest choice will be: swim some more or snooze in the hammock?

content: The Maldives comprise some 1,190 islands, and it only seems as though there are 1,190 luxury resorts — few of them, however, are on the level of the Soneva hotel group, whose Soneva Fushi is among the most rarefied luxury resorts in the world. And the newest one, Soneva Jani, is eminently worthy of the name. It’s hard to compare them in terms of extravagance, but where Fushi is known for its dry-land beachfront villas, Jani is comprised mostly of overwater villas, the sine qua non of Maldivian luxury hospitality. You’d think space would be at a premium, but apparently not — the one-bedroom “water retreats” are enormous, spanning some four thousand square feet, including plunge pools, roof decks, and vast amounts of lounge space. A small upgrade earns you a waterslide from the second-floor deck, and larger villas add second, third, or fourth bedrooms, as well as, at the top end, extras like personal gyms and en-suite wine cellars. There’s a spa, of course, as well as a dive center, and the activities include some unique offerings, from dolphin cruises to guided astronomy sessions in the hotel’s own observatory. The restaurants are as extravagant as the accommodations, though the atmosphere remains elegently casual. And the most exclusive restaurant concept features a series of dinners by a rotating cast of chefs, all of them from Michelin-starred restaurants, serving small groups of guests — a destination dining concept in the most extraordinary setting.

content:
Lake Lugano crosses the borders of Switzerland and Italy several times, and the region is a predictably complex mix of Swiss and Italian culture. That goes for Swiss Diamond Hotel Lugano as well. Situated near the southern end of the city of Lugano’s peninsula, right on the shores of the lake, it’s a rich blend of quasi-tropical lakeside luxury and hardier Alpine escapism. And in terms of style, it’s a hybrid as well; the building is modernist, its exterior maximizing its exposure to views of the lake, but on the inside, the rooms and suites are as classic as they come, with furnishings and details that wouldn’t look far out of place in a Renaissance-era villa.

And because this is Switzerland, the tactile comforts are even more extravagant than the visual ones. Top-quality mattresses, encyclopedic pillow menus, bathrooms that could double as day spas — people have been flocking to Switzerland’s lakes for some physical restoration since time immemorial, and they’ve built up a substantial amount of expertise.

To that end the wellness offerings go beyond an impressive spa with multiple pools, saunas and steam rooms, and venture into “aesthetic medicine.” Or you can improve yourself the hard way with a hike, a swim, a bike tour, or an hour or two in the Swiss Diamond’s well-equipped gym. Meanwhile the restaurants make good use of both Swiss and Italian traditions in order to fuel you for the next day’s adventure.

How to get there:
Lugano is less than an hour’s drive from Milan. A shuttle connects Swiss Diamond with Lugano’s city center.

content: Even in Fès, the city that invented and perfected the riad form, Karawan Riad somehow manages to distinguish itself. That may be due to its former incarnation as a 17th-century Maqfia harem-palace, the illustrated picture of otherworldly Ottoman elegance. Yet even though we’d never blame such an establishment for resting on its Andalous-Quarter laurels, a decade of renovations has proven that this jewel rests in the hands of forward-thinking proprietors. This is a textbook case of translating a classic formula for the 21st century without sacrificing an ounce of grandeur. The neighborhood certainly helps — here, you’re far enough from the tourist glut to actually breathe and get your bearings, and that selfsame space is grounds for a bracing mix of antique gravity and urban rejuvenation. Karawan Riad is of a piece with its setting, executing its singularly haute-palatial caravanserai with an obsessive eye for even the smallest high-end details. That means complimentary wi-fi and sound-system docking stations, but also cedar writing nooks with views framed in wrought-iron filigree. Or black marble bathrooms with stone vessel sinks, but also underfloor heating, Italian rain showers, and Les Sens de Marrakech bath products. The surfaces, in particular, nearly beggar description, ranging from artfully carved plaster wall treatments to exquisite zellije tilework flooring. Of course, some aspects won’t ever need a neon sheen to stay relevant. Nothing says opulence like extra space, and these seven lavish suites have it in spades. The open-plan layouts reveal their treasures at a leisurely, anything-but crowded pace, typically ending with patio doors opening onto lush, private terraces. Suffice it to say that you won’t forget you’re in Fez — ritualistically adorned lanterns, opulent silk brocade, rich damask cushions, and hand-painted calligraphy make sure of that. Everywhere, expertly placed mirrors reflect the brilliant North African light without communicating its oppressive heat. For the most privacy, and the finest views, the rooftop suite comes second to none, boasting a rose-bedecked terrace, vertical garden, and a swank embedded bathtub. Tough though it may be to quit your sanctuary, the commanding stone courtyard doesn’t disappoint; it sings with desert cosmopolitanism, criss-crossed with minuscule water conduits and featuring a step-down lounge and cozy tea rooms with Mariage Frères products. The gourmet restaurant plates French-Fassi specialties, foregrounding succulent seafood prepared with tantalizing spices. From there, it isn’t too far to wend your way past keyhole arches, one-of-a-kind curios, and vaulted passageways to the hammam and salons for a rejuvenation of your own

content:
Don’t let the names mislead you. Seehotel Ambach, designed by architect Otmar Barth, lies on the Italian side of the border, in the Alpine province of South Tyrol. It’s a modernist classic from the Seventies, a decade whose style is only now being appreciated for its utopian spirit. And if this retreat on the shores of Lake Caldaro isn’t utopia, we don’t know what is — the gentle arch of the building allows for panoramic views from its terraces and sunlight-filled rooms, providing a remarkably close connection between the interiors and the landscape.

The original 1973-vintage design is still very much in evidence, but it looks brand new — not only is it well preserved, but it’s been supplemented over the years by new contemporary furniture in the same distinctive warm colors. Many of the details in the rooms are by Barth as well, alongside lamps, chairs, and bathrooms by other Italian modernist designers.

Also a new addition is the spectacular Badehaus, a low-slung modernist spa pavilion built from wood and walled entirely in glass. In this part of Italy you can expect a full-featured wellness experience — and you can also expect an extravagant dining experience, mixing Alpine abundance with Italian indulgence, all overseen by chef Albin Widmann, a South Tyrol native.

content:
It’s fair to say it’s been a while since Bali was truly uncharted territory, but while parts of the island are indeed feeling the strain of development, you can trust COMO to deliver that all-important seclusion. The location, in Canggu, is where the busy south coast begins to give way to greener pastures, and the immediate setting of COMO Uma Canggu leaves you perched right above a beautiful black-sand beach, with nothing at all to distract you from the views of the surf. (Speaking of which, this stretch of beach also happens to have breaks for both novice and experienced surfers, and COMO has Tropicsurf instructors on hand to provide an introduction or a little brush-up.)

The resort itself was designed by designers Paola Navone and Koichiro Ikebuchi, and you’ll spot both Japanese and Milanese influences in these luxe, visually striking rooms, suites, and residences. They’re luxurious, one and all, starting out with king beds and plenty of space, and adding balconies, outdoor showers, and kitchenettes as you ascend the range — culminating in the penthouses, with their spectacular arched construction and their private rooftop pools.

COMO Beach Club is the restaurant, an upscale version of the traditional beach shack, serving grilled fish and cocktails with a front-row sea view. And the typically lavish COMO Shambhala Spa is present as well, offering everything from beauty treatments and massage to meditation, yoga, and pilates — we can’t guarantee a life-changing experience, but you’ll certainly be given all the necessary tools.

content:
How many perfect places can there be? And isn’t it a bit suspicious that so many of them seem to bear the COMO name? At this high level there’s very little to separate one purveyor of high-end perfection from another, save a personal preference for one brand’s aesthetic over another. At COMO Maalifushi, on yet another speck of an island in the Maldives, you’re made to feel as if bodily wellness and spiritual relaxation are the most fashionable things on the planet — and come to think of it, maybe they are.

The dry-land offerings are diverse, all of them mixing high polish and hand-made rough edges in perfect measure; the simple Garden Rooms are, let’s face it, quite luxe enough for most mortal couples. To upgrade to one of the Beach Suites or Villas, to say nothing of the Beach House, is to vastly increase one’s living space, and the COMO Residence, a two-story, four-bedroom affair, is practically a resort unto itself.

Also practically a resort unto itself is Maalifushi’s selection of overwater offerings. Suites and villas alike come with private pools, for those moments when wading directly into the Indian Ocean is, for whatever reason, not in the cards. And the overwater COMO Villas add to their expansive spaces the added convenience of butler service (also available in the top-end on-land offerings).

The key to it all, though, as with any COMO property, is the Shambhala spa, part of a family that’s quite rightly regarded as among the world’s finest. Add three restaurants which are frankly better than they need to be, along with a whole raft (no pun intended) of waterborne activities and excursions, and you’ve got yourself an island escape that you won’t soon forget.

How to get there: Seaplane transfers are required for stays at COMO Maalifushi. You will be met at Malé International Airport and transferred to the resort. Round-trip transfer costs are as follows, inclusive of taxes, not included in room/package rates: $750 for adults, $375 for children aged 2–11, free of charge for infants under 2 years of age.

content: Montecarmo 12 is more than a stylish boutique hotel. Occupying a quaint corner in the neighborhood of Príncipe Real, the building is a piece of Lisbon’s history, and it’s been thoughtfully transformed by one of the country’s most prominent architecture firms. The Portuguese brothers behind Aires Mateus are known for their exploration of light, geometric lines, and empty spaces. Their minimalist, less-is-more philosophy is on display here, from the choice of fine materials — local limestone, traditional tiles, rich blonde wood — to the simple, elegant guest rooms flooded with sunshine and perfumed with natural fragrances crafted from hand-picked lavender and rosemary. \n\nQuiet luxury is a guiding principle throughout the hotel, starting with the sleek open kitchen on the ground level, where a leisurely vegetarian brunch is served every morning around a large oak table. Afternoon tea is available on request in the quiet reading room or on the patio. Upstairs, guest rooms have high ceilings and windows, pale parquet flooring, and luxurious beds on custom wooden platforms. Bathrooms are surprisingly spacious, lined with iridescent pearl-like tiles and featuring ultra-modern double vanities and standalone soaking tubs. French doors open onto tiny wrought-iron balconies or, in the case of the best rooms, more sizeable terraces with views over the Tagus River and the city’s red rooftops.

content:
Among Caribbean island destinations, Guadeloupe is one of the less traveled — and for a hotel like La Toubana Hotel and Spa, that’s entirely the point. The French Caribbean in general is known for its slightly rarefied air, and at La Toubana you’re free from the crowds that beset many an island destination. It’s set on a rocky cliffside just above a sheltered private beach, which makes for the best of both worlds: panoramic, elevated views as well as immediate access to the sea a few steps below.

The fact that all of its 44 units are either bungalows, suites, or villas also contributes to the sense of seclusion; the spaces are generously sized and exceedingly private, and come with, at minimum, a king bed and an Italian shower — some add freestanding bathtubs or even plunge pools. 

There’s a small but beautiful spa, and by the poolside there’s Le Grand Bleu, serving upscale Creole cuisine as well as what the French call an American breakfast. There’s also Toubana La Plage, serving drinks and light fare down by the beach. And the setting, on the edge of the fishing village of Sainte-Anne, also places you within walking distance of a more expansive public beach.

content:
Mixing old and new is standard practice in the sphere of boutique-hotel design. But the concept takes on new dimension at Alegra Boutique Hotel. This is a place that’s old — not just because it’s in Jerusalem, one of the oldest cities in the world, but because it’s located in Ein Kerem, one of the oldest sections of the metropolitan area. And the idea of a boutique hotel is a new one around here. Several hotels in Jerusalem call themselves boutiques, but Alegra Boutique Hotel is one of the first in Jerusalem with a legitimate claim.

The building itself, a romantic-looking villa with thick stone walls and arched windows, isn’t ancient. But it has the feeling of an old-fashioned retreat from the city. Indeed, it’s a short drive away from the busy center, located in Ein Kerem, a forested valley famous for its pilgrimage site — according to Christian tradition, it’s the place where Elizabeth, mother of John the Baptist, experienced an immaculate conception, and where a pregnant Mary drank from the village well. Those same waters, still considered sacred, feed the verdant orchards and that surround the hotel, the tall trees that shade its courtyards, the creeping vines that climb up the stone walls. It’s just as lovely inside. There are thirteen memorable guest rooms and suites; all feature gorgeous exposed stone walls, free-standing marble baths, and Eastern design elements. Four are in the standard Deluxe category, offering king-sized beds with Egyptian cotton linens, espresso machines, iPod docks hooked up to in-room stereo systems, and complimentary minibars. Five Studio Suites are spacious, with large work tables and separate living areas — some also have private terraces. The real show-stoppers at Allegra are a pair of lavish Signature Suites. The aesthetic here, with dramatic vaulted ceilings, and heavy on Oriental rugs and lived-in leather, is supposedly modeled after the look of a modern home in Jerusalem. (If that’s the case, we’d like to take a peek inside some of the private houses in the neighborhood.)

Alegra Boutique Hotel’s public spaces are a delight, grand in structure but thoughtfully illuminated and warmly decorated with original artwork and rich fabrics. There’s a small but charming outdoor swimming pool, and plenty of space to relax with a book or a cup of tea under the trees. An elaborate breakfast, traditionally Israeli and put together with products from Jerusalem’s markets, is served in the cozy ground-level restaurant. Stick around later for more of a cutting-edge local dining experience: the hotel’s chef, up-and-comer Amir Na’or, offers an intimate Chef’s Table-style dinner on reservation. Afterward, head up to the hotel’s terrace for a nightcap with views over Ein Kerem. Considering Alegra is a pioneer on this particular scene, it’s safe to say they’ve nailed it: this is what a boutique hotel should look like in Jerusalem.

content:
There are a multitude of ways to experience the coast of Maine, but it’d be hard to find a better introduction than this one, just a few minutes from Portland, in Cape Elizabeth: the Inn by the Sea. It’s contemporary-classic in style but as crisp and fresh as a new build, and its rooms and suites are luxurious, but unpretentiously so. You’ll find gas fireplaces and/or heated floors, both of which are quite useful in the winter. And air conditioning is present as a matter of course, though the plentiful sea breeze is an essential part of the experience.

The look is stylish, but the atmosphere is exceedingly relaxed, not to mention thoroughly kid- and pet-friendly. And not only is the Inn luxe and tranquil, but it’s green to the core as well. The garden is fertilized with compost from the food service, and hotel’s energy needs are entirely satisfied by a solar farm, right down to the heated pool and the EV charging stations. They even plant a tree for every guest visit. So as you’re loafing about the grounds, dining al fresco on seasonal fare at Sea Glass, even taking the occasional spa treatment, you’re doing your part to keep the beach, the surf, and the surrounding wildlife habitats in tip-top shape.

How to Get There: Inn by the Sea is located on scenic Route 77 (Bowery Beach Road), approximately 15 minutes from Portland International Jetport (PWM). Daily direct flights service Portland from most major cities in the Northeast as well as Chicago and Atlanta. By car, Inn by the Sea is approximately 2 hours north of Boston.

content:
Tucked away high in the mountain state of Vorarlberg, Austria’s westernmost state, is the resort village of Lech am Arlberg, which is that most unusual variety of ski town: it’s actually a proper town, founded not during the 20th-century ski boom but by Swiss migrants during the 14th century. And here you’ll find a most unusual resort inn, the Walch's Rote Wand — a classic centuries-old Alpine inn, which beneath its absolutely traditional surface has been cleverly modernized, renovated in a light, contemporary style.

Instead of heavy timbers the rooms are minimalist, in white Austrian maple, simply furnished and well-lit by the sun. The 1,500-square-meter spa is a new addition, offering a Finnish-style outdoor sauna, a steam grotto, and an indoor-outdoor pool — even in winter the water is warm enough for an outdoor swim. There’s a fitness center, to suit the Rote Wand’s active clientele, and massage, just the thing to recover from a day on the slopes.

The restaurant, open during the winter, serves a fresh and modern Austrian cuisine. Along with its sister resort of Zürs, Lech offers some of the finest skiing in Europe — and in the summer this bucolic landscape, dotted with grazing cows, is about as picturesque as it gets.

content: The Loire Valley is home to some of France’s most impressive châteaux, many of which have been turned into museums. A few function as hotels, like La Borde en Sologne, an elegant 17th-century estate that’s been in the same family for generations. Its current custodians are a couple of youthful Parisians who’ve wisely left the property’s best features alone: French and English gardens, a private lake, a working farm, and the stone castle’s original hand-painted murals and grand fireplaces. Modern additions, like a pair of swimming pools, a MyBlend & Alaena spa, and tennis courts designed by French tennis champ Guy Forget, add to the appeal without diminishing the old-world charm.\n\nRooms and suites are spacious and refined, with high ceilings and herringbone parquet floors. No two are alike; some have rich wood paneling and others floral wallpaper, but they all feature a mix of antique and designer pieces and large, modern bathrooms with walk-in showers or marble tubs. One suite, constructed in the estate's old stables, has an equestrian theme, and family suites feature exposed wood beams and lofted sleeping areas. Breakfast is served on Restaurant Mémoire's picturesque terrace or in its palatial dining room, which is also the venue for gourmet French comfort food at lunch and dinnertime. Walking trails lead from the château through the forest that surrounds it, and bicycles are provided free of charge.

content:
Châteaux come in a variety of shapes and sizes, but few are as photogenically castle-like as the Château de Belet, a 15th-century relic in the Périgord, which comes complete with battlements and towers, like something from a fairy tale. One half expects to find its surrounding woodlands inhabited by mythological creatures. This is the setting for what is, in the present day, a thoroughly unique lodging: a seven-room bed and breakfast whose throwback opulence is complemented by modern luxuries and contemporary hotel-style service.

Its rooms are named after artists of the caliber of Matisse and Monet; the latter is housed in the castle’s tower, and features rough-hewn stonework in the bedroom and an ultra-luxe spa-like bathroom beneath its well-worn timbers. All of them make use of this vibrant contrast between old and new, combining the comforts of a modern hotel with an atmosphere befitting a 15th-century château.

And though there’s no permanent restaurant per se, Château de Belet’s open-plan kitchen capably handles a daily breakfast for guests, and is available to host a variety of specially prepared meals, from a private bistro-style lunch to an elaborate gastronomic experience featuring a visiting chef.

content: Beacon Grand, the hotel formerly known as the Sir Francis Drake is back in business after a very thorough renovation. It’s a welcome return to a city that just doesn’t feel complete without a proper grand hotel presiding over the corner of Powell and Sutter. And while the updates are significant, they haven’t papered over the details that connect this hotel with San Francisco’s history — the lobby is as ornate as ever, the top-floor bar and lounge, Starlite, still offers its famous panoramic view of San Francisco’s hills, and there are still some Prohibition-era secrets if you know where to look.\n\nIn the guest rooms you’ll find a style that threads the needle between contemporary and classic; plentiful tribute is paid to the era of the hotel’s original opening, but there’s nothing at all dated about it; a large proportion of them have impressive views of Union Square or the surrounding city. The Post Room, in the mezzanine above the lobby, is a restaurant and bar that features live music on Friday and Saturday nights. And beyond that, you’re lucky to find yourself in one of the finest restaurant towns in America; the Beacon Grand’s “Social Hosts” are at your service with recommendations and reservations.

content:
If a hotel in Surlej, Switzerland wanted to indulge its quaint side, all the ingredients are in place: the alpine village is nestled in the picturesque Engadin Valley, offering an unobstructed view down the mountain pass to Lake Silvaplana. Here, the sun is shining almost every day of the year, the climate is dry and pleasant, and hardy pleasure-seekers put skis to slopes in winter and bikes to trails in summer. Thankfully, Nira Alpina eschews chalet kitsch in favor of modern construction defined by glass and locally sourced timber. After all, Surlej is just a few minutes’ drive from St. Moritz, the next lake up the road — presumably its visitors are no strangers to contemporary architecture and design.

The five-story structure is appealingly low-slung, and its seventy guest rooms have all been designed in service of the mighty views helpfully provided by the valley. Each room boasts its own terrace or balcony, and the abundance of floor-to-ceiling windows ensure that you’re never far from the panorama. Clean-lined furniture and a preponderance of blond wood chase away any lingering folksiness from the village, while deep baths and waterfall showers make each bathroom a sleek yet welcoming haven. There isn’t a whole lot of aesthetic variation between the rooms, but the junior suites practically double the living space.

While one of Nira Alpina’s three restaurants is all about cheese, fondue and regional beers served among vintage local décor, the rest of the public spaces feel curiously urban-inspired. At the rooftop bar, guests snack on Asian fusion dishes around the glass cube of a fireplace. The same goes for the spa, which makes elements like an underwater relaxation bed and color-changing fountain feel like après-ski classics. 

How to get there: Nira Alpina is 2 hours and 30 minutes away by car from Zurich.

content:
Not long ago the original Experimental Cocktail Club took Paris by storm, and what began as a liquor-fueled labor of love soon snowballed into bars, restaurants, even hotels — a full-spectrum hospitality brand. Now the Experimental Group’s urban hotels — two in Paris and one in London — are joined by the Experimental Chalet, in the Swiss Alpine village of Verbier.

Frankly, if you can make it in the hippest quarters of London and Paris, you can make it in the Alps. The Experimental Chalet is stylistically miles ahead of the vast majority of ski hotels (to say nothing of its nightlife). The interiors, by Milanese architect Fabrizio Casiraghi, pay homage to the modernist styles that were current during the postwar ski boom, and the light, minimalist look is a refreshing departure from the old Alpine standard.

The Chalet’s lobby bar is, as you’d expect, an impressive one, and it’s joined by the Farm Club downstairs, an upscale nightclub that’s among the village’s hottest tickets. There’s also a farm-to-table restaurant, serving sustainably sourced fare by the Parisian chef Gregory Marchand. And if you can spare a moment for a bit of skiing, you’ve got easy access to the vast network of lifts and slopes that makes up the Quatre Vallées.

content:
You might be prepared for a hotel venture from a famed nightclub group to rather emphasize nightlife at the expense of old-fashioned hospitality and in-room luxury and comfort. Prepare to be enlightened. The first of what’s intended to be a series of Buddha Bar hotels has opened in Prague, not far from the Charles Bridge and everything that’s historic in the old town. What’s surprising is that inside you’ll find not just the next installment of the Buddha Bar nightlife franchise, but thirty-nine very stylish and exceedingly luxe rooms and suites as well.

The décor is the expected mod-Orientalism of the Buddha Bar concept, certainly a departure for Prague, and the rooms have some substance beneath that style — massive tubs, occasional jacuzzis, rain showers, and a few classic luxury-hotel touches, such as a complimentary shoeshine service and the increasingly rare bit of chocolate on the pillow at turndown. A small gym and spa balance the decadent nightlife with a bit of daytime rejuvenation, and the Siddhartha Café serves an eclectic international cuisine at more or less all hours, to suit the eccentric schedules of the Buddha Bar’s globe-trotting, nightclubbing clientele. This is one of those cases where the execution almost transcends the concept — one can even imagine greatly enjoying the Buddha-Bar Hotel without ever setting foot in the Buddha Bar itself.
