content:
Ergon means “vocation,” and in this case, the profession is one of a culinary nature. The Ergon brand is responsible for dozens of high-end Mediterranean food shops and restaurants, including two food-oriented boutique hotels in Athens. Ergon Beach House is the latest addition to the collection. Eating well is a major focus here, and there’s no question the oceanfront restaurant and bar deliver on that promise. But the hotel is noteworthy on its own, not only for its location, on the Halkidiki peninsula’s Nikiti Beach, but for its glamping-style lodgings and inclusive, no-need-to-leave setup, where everything from morning yoga classes to open-air film screenings has already been thought of and provided.

Right on the sand is a picturesque beach club with neat rows of sunbeds and thatched umbrellas; set slightly back from the water, amid olive and pine trees, are tents, cabanas, suites, and villas that blend easily into the coastal landscape. No one’s roughing it here — even the simplest tent features air-conditioning, a large TV, a Marshall speaker, an espresso machine, a minibar with Ergon goodies, and an open-air shower. All tents have a private patio, garden, or pool, as do the larger cabanas, suites, and villas. The interiors are down-to-earth, outfitted in crisp whites and natural materials like linen and raffia.

The gourmet food bar turns out first-rate salads, sandwiches, iced coffee, and craft cocktails to guests lounging by the beach or relaxing under rustic pergolas, and a more formal restaurant handles evening meals, which are served communally at big wooden tables in the garden. Between eating and drinking, there’s little to do but doze, swim, and sunbathe, though an outdoor gym and playground await those with energy to spare. Under the stars at night, an open-air cinema shows classic films paired with Greek wines and savory snacks.

content: Family-owned for over 80 years, Relais & Châteaux member for more than 40 — you might imagine the Post Lech Arlberg would be a rather traditional sort of place, and you would be entirely correct. But you don’t get to stay at the top of the hospitality business, especially in a place as well-traveled as the Alpine resort of Lech, by staying completely frozen in time. Here you’ll find lavish, classically-styled rooms, complete with ornate carved-wood furniture, but in suspiciously fine condition — Gasthof Post is so well-maintained it looks like it was built a hundred years ago but never used.\n\nThe single and double rooms are impressive enough, but the apartments and suites are from another world — a more classic example of Alpine elegance you’re unlikely to find. And impressive in another way is the Post’s spa. Here, modern comfort takes precedence over classic style, resulting in a space that’s not just as thoroughly equipped with restorative treatments as any we’ve seen, but is unapologetically modernist in aspect as well. Meanwhile a handful of restaurants and bars return to classic Alpine atmosphere, and serve a predictably hearty spread for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. All the better to fuel you for your various outdoor pursuits, for Lech is an equally inspired setting for winter and summer alike.

content:
About two hours to the south of Mexico City is the valley town of Tepoztlán, a place whose volcanic landscape and historic ruins make it a popular choice for a city break for residents of the Distrito Federal, whether as a part of a tour of the Franciscan, Dominican and Augustinian monasteries, or a trip to Tepoztlán’s own pyramid temple. If mythology is your specialty, you’ll know this town as the purported birthplace of no less a luminary than Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent deity of the pre-Columbian Nahua people; if you’re more the luxury-travel type, you’ll know it as the site of a delightful boutique hotel by the name of Casa Fernanda.

Why not both? The charming house, largely constructed of that familiar volcanic stone, had been given a contemporary makeover, and its suites combine a bit of classic colonial-era charm with a healthy dose of modernist-inspired contemporary design (as well as a very focused color palette). Check out the Master Suite if the idea of a terrace with a Jacuzzi appeals to you. And in any case, there’s a splendid little spa featuring hydrotherapy, massage, and a beautiful mosaic pool, as well as a restaurant that specializes in the cuisine of the Baja California. 

Please note: Casa Fernanda Hotel Boutique is a small property with only 14 rooms. Book early as rooms sell out quick.

content: Taj hotels have established themselves as urban mainstays for the business-class bon vivant, absolutely, but they’ve also made room — under the Taj umbrella — for the sweetly indolent resort-goer. Taj Bekal Resort and Spa, Kerala fits this model to a tee, sprawling languorously over 26 acres on the palm- and coconut-bedecked shore of the Arabian Sea. It’s a sinuous, almost whimsical family of rooms and villas, each a swoopy-yet-solid architectural statement in plaster, wooden beams, pillars, and flared thatch roofing. Kappil Beach is the primary attraction, seamlessly melding into the resort’s orderly lawns and meticulously landscaped gardens; its influence can be felt in the airy, white-on-wood interiors of the rooms, whose décor blends elements of the regional houseboat tradition, illustrated palm-leaf manuscript patterns called chitra pothi, and mythic laterite sculpture. Not that they’ve abandoned the present day altogether — interactive LCD flatscreens, sumptuous bathrooms, and king beds with pillow menus make sure of that. Rather, an ageless ambience predominates as ceiling fans inscribe lazy breezes and tropical pastels reflect and amplify the copious sunlight. The best part? All rooms come encircled and embellished by lush vegetation, affording the experience priceless beauty and privacy. Oh, and a furnished balcony or terrace certainly doesn’t hurt. When the mood strikes, saunter down to Latitude for all-day South Indian fine dining with river views. Or, if the water’s the point, sample the excellent Keralan seafood at By the Bay or comfort barbecue right from the pool. You can’t miss Ivory Bar’s massive underlie dome — nor, for that matter, its garden moat — retire here for a bartender’s choice cocktail and prime stargazing potential. Pro tip: put in a timely word with the concierge to arrange for a romantic meal right on the river in the hotel’s pontoon.

content: Bloom House intends its name to be taken quite literally — this 10th arrondissement boutique hotel, set mere blocks from both the Gare de l’Est and the Gare du Nord, is full of floral textures, live greenery, and warm-toned organic materials. Lovely enough on its own, it’s a particularly stark contrast to the stations themselves, and provides arriving travelers with a total aesthetic reset.\n\nIts 91 rooms are characteristically economical with their space; some open onto substantial balconies with far-ranging views. All are stylish in a fun and eclectic way; the specter of minimalism is allowed no purchase here. The Bloomy Spa, with its 18-meter indoor pool, follow’s through on the hotel’s mission of restoration. Nor is restauration neglected — Bloom Garden serves Mediterranean-accented fare by the poolside, and the Bloom Bar pursues excellence in both coffee and cocktails.

content:
Many of Medellin’s best hotels are housed in modern high-rises, a fact that makes Hotel Quinta Ladera especially notable. While it’s close by to the museums, this sustainably built 20-room boutique hotel feels like an urban oasis — calm, light-filled, and neatly tucked away from the busy city streets. Lush greenery frames the petite property, with its verdant courtyard gardens and trees illuminated with twinkling lights after dark; thanks to the hotel’s thoughtful design, the indoor-outdoor flow is seamless, creating a treehouse-like atmosphere in garden-facing guest rooms. 

In addition to being full of natural light, the interiors are elegant, cozy, and full of character with terracotta-tiled floors and white wood-beamed ceilings. A team of Colombian artists and artisans is responsible for many of the hotel’s charming details, from decorative woven baskets and handmade ceramics to delicate framed watercolors and large-scale oil paintings. Guest rooms have tangerine or olive green accent walls, potted plants, and modern bathrooms stocked with organic products and artisan-made towels. Some have French doors opening onto private tree-shaded patios with luxurious stone tubs.

There’s a French flavor to the hotel’s all-day café and restaurant, as well, though several traditional Colombian dishes are also on offer for breakfast, alongside freshly baked almond croissants. Many of Medellin’s cultural attractions are an easy stroll away, and after a day of sightseeing, there’s no better place to relax than a hammock suspended by the hotel’s reflecting pool.

content:
Toronto’s SoHo Hotel & Residences is an example of what’s probably the most significant secondary effect of the boutique-hotel revolution: now, thanks to eccentric small operators, the luxury market is moving in a more design-forward direction. This is the sort of hotel that, a decade or two ago, might have been content to sacrifice style for comfort — but the SoHo, as it exists today, makes no such concessions.

Witness the crisp lines, the neutral tones, the stylish modernist furniture, and the riotously colorful glass sculpture by Dale Chihuly. And the pleasures, naturally, are more than just visual — the bathrooms, for example, feature soaking tubs, elaborately functional shower stalls, and Molton Brown bath products.

The SoHo’s city-center location is essentially Toronto’s version of midtown Manhattan, convenient for business travelers, shoppers and theatre-goers alike. As such it needs to appeal not just to boutique diehards but also to more casual travelers as well, and its particular brand of stylishness is an understated, accessible one. It’s not the sort of place where your sense of hospitality will be aggressively challenged — unless being chauffeured in the hotel’s luxury sedan is your idea of a challenge.


How to get there:
SoHo Hotel & Residences is located 2.5 miles (15 min) from Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport and 27.5 miles (35 min) from the Toronto Pearson International Airport. Transfers can be organized from Bishop for CAD60 and from Pearson for CAD125.

content: What was the second hotel to open on the island of St. Barth is back after a thorough renovation, and the result is barely recognizable. Le Tropical Hotel St. Barth aims for nothing less than to bring the spirit of the French Riviera to the Caribbean, and it’s perhaps more Saint-Tropez than Cannes, set back a few steps from the beach in a lush garden setting. The look is self-consciously retro, in an effort to recapture the glamour of the island as it was nearly a century ago. And the restaurant, in another departure from the regional norm, is neither Caribbean nor French but Indonesian.

content:
Mashpi is, first of all, a private nature reserve spanning some 3,000 acres in the cloud forest of Ecuador’s interior, a research and conservation project dedicated to preserving one of the world’s most biodiverse landscapes. In this spectacular setting you’d be happy with just about any old hotel, but Mashpi Lodge is not that — this is a very modern and very luxurious lodge, and one with a remarkably small ecological footprint. 

Glass walls are a crowd-pleasing choice in a place like this, and the rooms and suites make the most of them, offering guests front-row views of the forest floor and the tree canopy. The interiors are modern and more than a little bit luxe, though with rustic accents that refer to the local and indigenous methods of building. 

The cuisine, naturally, is hyper-local, and there’s an exceedingly tranquil spa that manages to feel both private and open to its surroundings. As pleasant as it is, however, you’ll want to spend more time out and about — Mashpi Lodge offers a wide variety of rainforest explorations, from walking tours to the Dragonfly, an aerial gondola system for observing the forest canopy with a bird’s-eye view.

content:
As short-haul travel once again becomes the norm, places close to New York City are experiencing a renaissance — among them Asbury Park, New Jersey, a beach town that’s right in the heart of the Jersey Shore. A hotel like the Asbury Ocean Club would have been unthinkable a decade or two earlier, but today it’s a breath of fresh air, a light and stylish luxury hotel that’s set right on Ocean Avenue, steps from the boardwalk and the beach.

The clearest departure from the Asbury Park of old is in the aesthetics; this ultra-modern structure wouldn’t look out of place in a major metropolitan area. Meanwhile the accommodations themselves come decked out in a style that mixes elements of laid-back seaside shacks and glossy urban loft living. They’re light-filled and full of boutique-hotel comforts, and more stylish than just about anything else in town.

A spa and an expansive fitness center are among the wellness offerings, alongside a rooftop pool and a garden terrace, complete with a poolside bar. Meanwhile the Drawing Room restaurant and bar make up the social heart of the hotel — and while the vibe is lively, it’s substantially more restrained than many of the nightspots in this often-raucous town.

content:
Before they turned it into a hotel, owners Nabil and Zoe Debs lived in this spectacular house in Beirut’s vibrant, bohemian Gemmayze neighborhood — it’s been in the family for generations, but it’s a bit much for one couple, frankly, spread out as it is across four distinct buildings (and incorporating some Roman ruins). Now it’s a high-end boutique hotel, and the Arthaus name isn’t bestowed lightly; the hotel’s permanent collection is an impressive one, and exhibitions and art-world events are regular features here.

As for the interiors, the buildings’ historical Ottoman style is made contemporary by its proprietors’ excellent design sense, and its rooms and suites effortlessly span the centuries, with rough-hewn stone walls alongside vintage furnishings, contemporary artworks, and modern boutique-hotel comforts.

In spite of Arthaus’s smallish size and residential atmosphere, it offers moments of indulgence, like a gym and a mini-spa featuring a hot tub and a steam room as well as a lovely little pool. Arthaus Kitchen, an informal yet upscale restaurant, is joined by the impressive Lounge Bar, while across the garden the Cocktail Bar serves impressively creative cocktails, and features DJs and live performances.

Roughly equidistant from Siem Reap’s busy city center, the temple complex at Angkor Wat, and Siem Reap International Airport, Anjali by Syphon benefits both from convenience — distances are best measured in minutes — and from a more tranquil setting than the city’s more urban hotels and resorts. It’s the perfect place for a hotel whose mission is to offer a transformative experience: a small, stylish, contemporary boutique eco-resort whose meditative modernist architecture wraps around a green oasis of a central pool courtyard.

Modestly sized at 29 rooms and suites, Anjali never feels crowded, and even the entry-level rooms are large, spanning some 35 square meters plus a private balcony. An upgrade earns you a room that opens onto the pool deck, and the top floor is reserved for even more lavish suites with peaked roofs and freestanding soaking tubs. 

The Anjali Spa offers further opportunities for relaxation, while Hunkaar Table & Lounge serves refined Khmer and Western dishes made from market-fresh produce. And when it’s time to break the spell of restful seclusion, there’s a free tuk-tuk service connecting you with downtown Siem Reap — and the temple complex is only a few minutes farther away in the other direction.

content:
In keeping with its Sanlitun environs — Adidas and Apple maintain international flagships here, to give you an idea — CHAO Hotel aspires to deliver every conceivable luxe-lifestyle experience in one hyper-curated swoop. Dining, networking, entertainment, fitness, and the arts all have something urgent to say, often interrupting one another to do so. Context helps here: in a landscape dominated by skyscraping excess, naked hospitality needs to wear a statement to stand any chance of success. And with patronage heavily skewed towards contemporary entrepreneurs and business travelers, it’s hardly a surprise that they’ve chosen to resolve the classic dichotomy between expert focus and genial adaptability. In any case, “hotel” is unequivocally just one of CHAO’s many names, and as long as that aspect doesn’t get snowed under, we’re more than game to see just how far the concept can go.

Quite some ways, naturally. This place is huge, though never without that crucial veneer of seamless, effortless luxury. Rooms don’t rock the design boat, preferring instead to emphasize the sunlight through floor-to-ceiling windows (occasional smog notwithstanding) and the human touch in handworked leather, walnut furnishings, and plenty of hardwood. To be sure, some megahotel gloss creeps in with the recessed neon lighting, but it finds balance against the warmth and subtlety of the earthy color scheme. The sheer breadth of freebies also warrants mention — tea service, Nespresso machines, bluetooth multimedia systems, wi-fi, snacks, and a surprisingly robust bar with all the fixings.

Tempting as it may be, don’t limit yourself to just the room. All guests obtain clubhouse access, an innocuously phrased amenity that means much, much more here than one might expect. Among the work-hard/play-hard offerings are a bleeding-edge gym, a swank barbershop, a functional library (we hate to have to clarify the term), future-chic workshare facilities, and a spectacular fleet of event spaces that nearly beggar description, all geometric and tracklit and underscored in softly lit wood. You’re unlikely to see the entire hotel in just one visit, in other words, especially when accounting for the multiple dining and nightlife outlets. A fine reason for a return visit, if you ask us.

content:
For connoisseurs of Asia’s villa hotels, the concept is the thing: small-scale luxury, physically up to international standards, yet painstakingly localized. That last bit is important when you’re talking about a destination like Siem Reap, a place where the city’s cultural inheritance is practically as palpable as the 400-thread linens or the deep soaking tubs. A 39-room villa resort in a contemporary Khmer style, Anantara Angkor Resort is set a few miles from Angkor Wat, one of the great cultural wonders of the world — a setting that, to say the least, sets a rather high standard.

Of course a little bit of restraint is in order, given the gravity of the location, and the Anantara is less a monument than an inward-looking compound. The rooms are all immersive privacy, laid out like studio apartments, and the suites, all with butler service, are self-contained — the Queen Suites feel sequestered, designed for romance, while the grander King Suites feel geared toward entertaining. Either way you’re in a world all your own; it’s a short drive into town or to the temples, but with a very fine spa and a stunning Khmer-French restaurant it’s easy to imagine days and nights spent in.

Anantara Angkor Resort is a 45-minute drive from Siem Reap Angkor International Airport, offering domestic and international flights. Airport shuttle service is available for USD 100 per vehicle (one-way and up to 3 people).

content: Scenic landscapes have long drawn travelers to the Polish resort of Szklarska Poręba, and the region’s best hotels are strategically positioned to make the most of them. Case in point: Jaskółka Dom i Spa, perched on a high mountain slope, its verandas facing an expanse of pine forests and snowcapped peaks. The landmark inn opened in 1894 and served a variety of purposes over the years — the building functioned as a convent and, later, in the 1960s, was put to use by the government — before undergoing extensive renovations and reopening as a luxury boutique accommodation. \n\nThe interiors are just as impressive as the views, especially on the ground level, where the elegant living and drawing rooms feature high coffered ceilings, an ornate Viennese chandelier, and original woodwork, and the inn’s old porches, furnished with rocking chairs, are framed by decorative stained glass panels. Rooms are more modern, though each has period elements like hand-carved wainscoting or an antique writing desk. Apartment-style rooms are light-filled and earthy, with pale linen and exposed beams, while suites are sultrier, outfitted in moody shades of midnight blue and charcoal gray. All have stylish stone bathrooms with freestanding soaking tubs, and a few have private patios with mountain views. Breakfast is served on a sunny terrace when weather permits, and an outdoor fire pit and cozy pub-style bar are especially inviting after cross-country skiing or hiking to nearby waterfalls.

content: There’s a lot more to Baja California Sur than Cabo excess. Just an hour or so north is the pueblo mágico of Todos Santos, an artsy town that marries a keen visual sense to laid-back Pacific coastal vibes. The Todos Santos Boutique Hotel, as the name implies, distills the locale’s timeless Jesuit heritage down to an intimate, ten-room affair just off the main drag. Ivy-wreathed brickwork defines the public spaces, giving way in the rooms to an ornate vision in dark wood and gilt-framed mirrors. Each of them even boasts a unique, full-wall mural of a frozen-in-time colonial scene.

content:
An hour into the countryside from Bucharest, set on more than 1500 acres of forest and parkland, is a place where rural living and luxury hospitality come together: Singureni Manor Equestrian Retreat. It’s not the only European hunting lodge to have evolved into a country hotel, but it may be the one that remains most dedicated to the traditions upon which it was founded — here you’ll find the deer and stags still roaming the forest, as well as an equestrian program that encompasses everything from casual rides to dressage lessons and Saturday afternoon Arabian horse shows.

The accommodations are divided between two distinct sites; Paul’s Lodge, the 13-room hunting lodge that was the original residence on this property, and Paul’s Horses, the 19-room inn that opens directly onto the stables, so that guests have Arabian horses as their neighbors. Throughout, the rooms are decorated in a contemporary reconstruction of an antique hunting-lodge style, and outfitted with modern luxury-hotel comforts. 

Along with a diverse array of outdoor experiences, Singureni Manor is known for culinary excellence, thanks to chef Alexandru Dumitru and the fine-dining La Hambar restaurant, serving modern Romanian cuisine from farm-fresh produce. And on Saturday nights the hotel offers a Chef Experience dinner, followed by an informal gathering around the campfire.

content: That’s the Professional Golfers’ Association, in case you were wondering — which goes a long way towards explaining why the PGA National Resort, in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, has not one or two but six championship golf courses. Of course, if that were all there was to it, you wouldn’t be reading about it here. But it just so happens that this 339-room luxury resort takes its hospitality as seriously as it does its golf, adding a 40,000-square-foot spa, a generous handful of restaurants and bars, and a very substantial racquet club to its offerings.\n\nThe rooms, suites, and cottages are perhaps surprisingly stylish, full of graphic motifs and decorated in a style that feels subtly Parisian. The comforts, naturally, are first-rate, and include lavish spa-like bathrooms, and nine pools dot the property, from the enormous central pool to the satellite pools surrounding the spa. And the restaurants go far beyond ordinary country-club fare, ranging from the Butcher’s Club, a midcentury-style steakhouse, to the Southern-style Honeybelle and the nostalgic Birdie’s Diner — plus a chocolate shop, and a fast-casual market and café.

content: The Western Mediterranean and the Greek side of the Aegean Sea are justifiably famous, but often overlooked is Turkey’s Bodrum Peninsula, home to landscapes and seascapes that are every bit the equal of their western neighbors. It’s a matter of local pride, and of course within Turkey this place is rated extremely highly — Allium Bodrum Resort & Spa, in the harborside town of Yalikavak, joins a dizzying array of ultra-luxe resort developments. What sets this one apart isn’t so much the location or the concept but the execution: Allium exhibits a tastefulness and a thoughtfulness that’s far beyond the norm.\n\nIts architecture is impressive without being ostentatious, its interiors luxurious without opulence. And while the comforts are certainly first-rate, there’s plenty of old-fashioned coziness on offer as well, thanks to surfaces in rustic warm wood and textiles with a handmade quality. With their direct views of the Aegean — that’s every room — these are top-shelf luxury rooms, but in the local context the look reads as charmingly “shabby-chic.” There’s a pier offering swimmers access to the sea, a spectacular heated outdoor infinity pool (seasonal), and an elaborate spa and wellness complex, naturally.

content:
Underrated among Far East megacities is Kuala Lumpur, the Malaysian capital, perhaps best known either for its iconic Petronas Towers or for its out-of-this-world street-food scene. For hotel fans, however, it’s perhaps even better known as a place where extravagant heights of luxury are available at prices that, for foreign travelers, are a fraction of what they’d expect. All of which is the long way around to saying that the RuMa Hotel and Residences, despite its relatively modest price tag — and its memorable style, of which more in a moment — offers an unmistakably high-end experience.

It’s part of the same Urban Resort Concepts family as the PuXuan in Beijing and the PuLi in Shanghai, both highly impressive hotels in their own right. The name is a play on the Malay word for “home,” and the brand’s concept is “hostmanship,” which is URC’s name for human-centered, relationship-based hospitality that prizes personal connection over mere physical comfort.

The RuMa does, of course, have a surplus of physical comforts, as well as a style that’s contemporary, yet clearly influenced by Malaysian culture and heritage. They range from the 43-square-meter Deluxe Room all the way up to the two-bedroom Ruma Suite, and at all levels they include indulgences like automated blackout blinds and full-size bathtubs with separate rain showers.

ATAS, the restaurant, serves high-end Malaysian fare, while SEVEN is the lobby bar and lounge, and SANTAI the poolside option for lighter fare or a sunset cocktail. Meanwhile the UR Spa will see to it that your bodily needs are well taken care of.

content:
Perhaps no one other than GHM Hotels, the management company behind the Chedi hotel brand, would put Montenegro on the same list of high-end destinations as Switzerland, Bali, and Oman. But Montenegro is already home to several top-flight luxury resorts, and Luštica Bay, a purpose-built marina village on the Bay of Kotor, aims to outdo them all, with no fewer than seven hotels in the works. And with a blank canvas to work with, the Chedi Luštica Bay has a free hand to enact its singature variety of all-encompassing luxury.

It’s styled as something of a village unto itself, its 111 rooms and suites set on a hillside overlooking the Adriatic Sea, giving most rooms a view from their private balconies. The style is contemporary-luxe, equal parts calming minimalism, vibrant colors, and far-East inspiration, and the comforts and amenities throughout are state-of-the-art. There isn’t a room in the house that’s anything less than luxe, and the heights scaled by the suites are truly dizzying.

A formal restaurant and a casual seaside eatery are joined by a lobby bar and another on the beach, and the Chedi’s spa is predictably elaborate. Meanwhile the spa’s indoor pool is paired with an outdoor infinity pool, and the waters of the Adriatic are close at hand, along with all the seafaring fun the Chedi’s marina setting implies.

content: There’s no place quite like Cappadocia, the region in central Turkey that’s known for its unique rock formations and its inimitable cave dwellings. (Of particular note is the local tradition of hot-air ballooning, the best way to see these unforgettable landscapes.) And while there are more than a few boutique hotels carved into these stone hillsides, there’s room for many more — our appetite is far from sated. Part modernist structures, part traditional cave dwellings, Ariana Sustainable Luxury Lodge goes perhaps heavier on contemporary design and lighter on heavy stone architecture than many other Cappadocian hotels, and its eleven rooms and suites are among the finest in the region.\n\nThe Cave Rooms are exactly what they sound like, cut directly into the rock, but with modern comforts like espresso machines, wi-fi, and curvy contemporary furniture. And of the suites, some are cave dwellings, while others are above ground, but all are spacious, stylish, and similarly luxe. Many come with gas fireplaces or onyx bathtubs, and those that aren’t subterranean boast impressive views. Of particular note is the restaurant, which isn’t just a glorious glass structure with an extraordinary view but also has its own gardens and vineyard, and serves impeccably farm-fresh Mediterranean fare.

content: Most of Saint-Tropez’s best hotels are in town, but a few are farther afield, like the Hôtel La Tartane Saint-Tropez. Located midway between the port and the peaceful beaches of Plage Les Salins, it’s an idyllic retreat modeled after a Provençal hamlet. A collection of traditional stucco houses, each named after a prominent figure in the French Riviera’s 1920s scene — Ernest, Peggy, Pablo, Gabrielle, Sara, and Scott — contain the guest rooms and suites. They’re framed by fragrant citrus trees and Mediterranean gardens, and all are within easy reach of an inviting outdoor pool on a wooden deck lined with colorful daybeds.\n\nRooms are rustic-chic and quaintly cottage-like, inspired by the look of a French family vacation home on the Côte d’Azur. Many have exposed timber beams, mustard-yellow flooring, vintage mirrors, and king-sized beds with rattan headboards, while larger duplex suites feature living rooms with striped sofas and spacious bathrooms with marble vanities and soaking tubs. Nearly all rooms and suites have private patios or terraces shaded by olive trees. Lavender and rosemary are plucked from the herb gardens for cocktails at the cheerful pool bar, and lunch on the terrace at the Saint-Amour, La Tartane’s restaurant, feels like dining at an elegant beach club. It makes sense: though you can’t see it from the hotel, the ocean is only a few minutes away by car.

content:
There aren’t many high-end hotels in the far-flung surfers’ enclave of Itacaré, Brazil. Offering a sophisticated alternative to the region’s traditional inns is Barracuda Hotel & Villas, set on a palm tree-framed clifftop, its wide infinity pool and wooden terraces open to the sea, sky, and jungle. The atmosphere and aesthetics bring together laid-back Bahian charm and Scandinavian minimalism, both in an authentic way — the original owners are, in fact, Brazilian and Swedish. 

The main building houses 17 suites with clean architectural lines, polished concrete floors, wood-paneled ceilings, and furnishings built by local carpenters. Most have private verandas facing the water; all have floor-to-ceiling white drapery that flutters romantically in the breeze. The hotel’s freestanding villas, meanwhile, provide extra space, plus kitchens and private infinity pools. 

Freshly caught seafood and potent cachaça-infused cocktails are served at a restaurant and bar that spills onto the pool deck — though it’s hard to beat the views from the smaller rooftop bar, especially with a caipirinha in hand at sunset. Meanwhile the hotel’s staff happily arranges surfing, hiking, and canoeing nearby, while Barracuda’s indoor-outdoor wellness space features a picturesque yoga deck.

content: We do love a good independent one-off boutique hotel, but we’re not above acknowledging when one of the big hospitality chains is doing extraordinary work. That’s very much the case with India’s massive Taj group at the moment, and Taj Rishikesh Resort & Spa, Uttarakhand is yet another stunning new opening — this one at a bend in the Ganges river in the foothills of the Himalayas, offering astounding views of the river and the mountains in every direction.\n\nIt’s set several miles upriver from Rishikesh proper, a location that gives it an outsize cultural significance, and which also positions it for some extraordinary rafting and trekking opportunities. Of course, it’s also a fine place for more sedentary pursuits as well — the Jiva spa offers blissful escape as usual, and the rooms, with their first-rate comforts and sedate, minimalist design, are perfectly situated for some riverside rejuvenation. All of them have views of the river, the valley, or both, and many have balconies for an added measure of immersion in nature. And the same goes for Rock Flour, Taj Rishikesh’s all-day restaurant — this double-height space is ringed with windows, and, weather permitting, offers al fresco seating for its farm-fresh dishes.

content:
Most people’s vision of a Balinese hotel doesn’t involve a modern red-brick structure that soars higher than the tree line. But as you might guess from the name, Potato Head Suites & Studios is not a typical Balinese hotel. More than just a hotel, Desa Potato Head is a “creative village” that also serves as a gathering and events space for the local community, designed by architect Rem Koolhaas’s OMA.

This explains the architecture, which finds a fertile middle ground between neo-Brutalism and Indonesian tradition. It also explains such interior-design flourishes as Le Corbusier’s Thonet No. B9 Chair, the Pendant lamp ph5 1958 by Louis Poulsen and the Lampe Gras 1921 by Bernard- Albin Gras. Situated in separate wings, the Suites are the high-end option, while the Studios come in at a more attainable price point, though there’s considerable overlap between the two ranges. All of them feature king beds and custom-made organic bath products, and all are cut from the same crisp and contemporary stylistic cloth.

Thanks to Desa Potato Head’s substantial scale, guests benefit from a resort-like array of amenities, from the Sanctuary Wellness Centre to multiple restaurants, including one entirely plant-based option. There’s always the beach, of course, as well as the by now somewhat legendary Potato Head Beach Club.

content:
Any way you look at it — population, economy, cultural footprint — Dallas is a major city. To put it bluntly, it’s long past time it had a hotel scene to match. That’s the last we’ll say of the city’s surfeit of ordinary corporate hotels, because we’re here to focus on something entirely different: Canvas Hotel Dallas. The name is a reference not just to any old fabric, but to a painter’s canvas — this hotel is as devoted to local contemporary art as some hotels are to beige carpet (sorry, we said we’d stop).

The location, in the Cedars district, could hardly be more perfect — it’s a one-time industrial area that’s been home to Dallas artists for decades. And like many artists’ districts, it’s become a dining and nightlife hotspot as well. Canvas Hotel is a perfect match for that scene as well, with Gallery, its rooftop cocktail lounge, and Chef’s Palette, an eclectic space with a creative menu.

And the rooms don’t just feature a painting or two — they’re patterned after authentic artists’ lofts in every way, from the 12-foot ceilings to the concrete floors, the exposed brickwork, and the oversized windows. Safe to say there’s not a chance you’ll mistake it for a convention-center hotel (though, ironically, the convention center is close at hand.)

content:
If the name Savoy Palace doesn’t sound glamorous enough on its own, consider the idea of an exclusive hotel-within-a-hotel occupying the penthouse level — a place with a private rooftop pool and personal assistants on hand around the clock to attend to guests’ every need. This is The Reserve, a luxurious boutique hotel located on the uppermost six floors of Funchal’s towering waterfront landmark. 

Every room in the building overlooks Madeira’s coastline, but the very best views are reserved for the top, accessible by a private elevator from street level. Guests are welcome to use any of the Palace’s pools, bars, and restaurants, but most stick to the quiet luxury of the Jacarandá Club, the Reserve’s chic all-day lounge and bar, which leads to a wide palm tree-dotted sun deck and a gorgeous infinity pool. No need to battle a crowd for poolside cocktails or a good spot in the shade. 

Sleek white and ivory-hued rooms and suites are laid out like luxury apartments, with distinct living areas, palatial marble bathrooms, and furnished outdoor spaces with ocean views. Corner suites have beautiful wraparound balconies, and pool suites have turquoise-tiled plunge pools. All come with a dedicated personal assistant to handle complimentary unpacking service, book a table at the hotel’s upscale Japanese restaurant, or arrange for treatments at the spa, an ethereal space inspired by the island’s ancient forests. Turndown service includes a bottle of Madeira and traditional honey cake, a charming nod to the region’s history.

content:
Australian hotels do a lot of things well, but perhaps nothing lies more squarely within the national expertise than this sort of laid-back, effortlessly chic seaside escape. Bask & Stow is set in coastal New South Wales, a few minutes’ walk from the main drag of the beach town of Byron Bay. The neighborhood provides the low-key, residential vibe, and Bask & Stow is nowhere near large enough to spoil it, with just five suites and a stand-alone three-bedroom cottage.

The style reads as Scandinavian to some, but architect Harley Graham was inspired by Palm Springs modernism and the Bauhaus movement; the result, all clean lines, blond wood, and minimalist white, is stylish by any name. Most suites come with bathtubs, and all have kitchenettes, as well as easy access to the property’s gardens and plunge pool.

It’s possible to order breakfast in, but that’s the extent of Bask & Stow’s culinary program. This is no great hardship, of course; the very fine Top Shop Café, known for its breakfast and burgers, is right around the corner, and a few blocks away in the other direction is Jonson Street, the town center, and a wealth of excellent restaurants.

content:
There are palaces and then there are palaces. By which we mean, there’s no shortage in India of palace-style hotels, whose entire object is to convey the illusion that you’re an aristocrat’s guest. But Umaid Bhawan, as it happens, is still occupied by what remains of Jodphur’s old royal family.

You won’t find the Maharaja himself taking drink orders, however. The palace’s hotel wing is under the direction of a little hotel concern called Taj. In this wing you’ll find sixty-four rooms and suites, which, though only a fraction of the larger palace, proves to be quite enough space. And where some palace hotels come off a bit stagy, attempting to stand in for some Platonic idea of an Indian palace, Umaid Bhawan has a character all its own — it’s of a more recent vintage than many of its counterparts, and seventy years on it’s staying true to its Art Deco self.

As for the luxury of the place, it’s got as much of whatever they award stars for as any of India’s other top hotels — meaning, quite a lot. The difference is personality. If you’re a box-ticker and a square-foot-counter then you’ve probably got your own formula, but if it’s romance that floats your boat then this place has to be somewhere near the top of the list.

content:
Deep in the heart of northern Laos, along the banks of the Mekong, is the old royal capital of Luang Prabang, one of the better places in Southeast Asia if you’re looking to get away from the crowds and the bright lights of the established tourist destinations. And roughly two kilometers outside of town is La Résidence Phou Vao, a French colonial classic with sweeping views of the forested mountains surrounding this photogenic town.

It’s been updated since its previous life as the Pansea hotel, but not updated too much — despite a fresh coat of paint and a certain paring down of the décor, plenty of the original colonial charm of the place shines through. With just thirty-four rooms and suites it’s intimate by nature, an effect intensified by the lush green of the gardens and the twists and turns of the historic property.

Each room features a private terrace or balcony, complete with day beds and views of the gardens or the mountains, as well as luxurious oversized terrazzo baths. As for facilities there’s not much more than a pool, a spa, and a cocktail lounge and restaurant serving upscale Laotian and European fare — which, actually, might be all you need for this kind of elegant escape.

content:
With Vail’s established luxury names getting a little too comfortable, there’s a pronounced need for a place like The Sebastian - Vail, a hotel that, luxe as it is, manages to bring some youthful energy to this classic Colorado ski town. The Vail Village location is prime real estate, if perhaps less rarefied than the ski-in ski-out frontage at the mountain’s base, and with a dedicated slopeside ski concierge, and close proximity to all Vail’s dining and nightlife, The Sebastian is an immediate contender.

A fair proportion of Vail’s dining and nightlife, it must be said, takes place within the Sebastian itself. Leonora, the flagship restaurant, wears its Alpine bistro influence on its sleeve, proof of a newly cosmopolitan Colorado ski scene, and Frost, the cocktail bar, mixes high-design theatrics with casual Mountain West cool. And for a quiet drink over a book or a board game there’s the warm and sophisticated Library.

The rooms and executive suites are more than spacious, designed in a crisp, contemporary style that’s miles from Alpine-lodge kitsch or traditional luxury-hotel fussiness. It’s in the residential suites, naturally enough, that the Sebastian spreads its wings, with full kitchens, large, luxurious bathrooms and space ranging all the way up to four bedrooms. 

Meanwhile the Base Camp and its staff of ski valets means that your morning commute is negligible. Bloom spa and fitness center offers a multitude of ways to recover from a hard day spent on skis, and the pool terrace, with its view of the mountain, is an option for all seasons. Vail might be best known for winter, but it’s scarcely less appealing in summer, and the same goes for The Sebastian.

content:
The South Tyrol spa town of Merano has been a luxury travel destination for longer than the phrase “luxury travel destination” has existed; even against this backdrop, the aptly named Villa Eden stands out for its extraordinarily restorative atmosphere. Its setting, in an ornate Art Nouveau villa, feels like something out of a fairy tale, and its spa is no mere massage operation, but an intensively health-focused medical establishment specializing not just in relaxation but in longevity as well.

Its modest size — a mere 25 suites — contributes to this mission of restoration, and its adults-only policy helps as well. Even the so-called Petite suites spread out over 35 square meters, and the largest ones range from 70 to 100. And at all sizes they’re extraordinarily comfortable, with particularly lavish bathrooms.

The spa offers everything from beauty treatments to fitness and recreation to medical analyses and therapies. And the cuisine, as flavorful as it is, is designed to support Villa Eden’s health-conscious approach. The Eden’s Park restaurant serves artfully prepared dishes crafted from traditional Tyrolean ingredients, with an unusual variety of vegetarian, vegan, or detox options. All this surrounded by one of the most spectacular valleys in the region — you can see why they call it Eden.

content: Dwarika’s is named for its late founder, who established this one-of-a-kind hotel in an effort to preserve the arts, crafts, and culture of Kathmandu in a way that keeps them alive and accessible to curious visitors to Nepal. The result is something like a museum that you can sleep in — and, in case it’s not clear, one of the most memorable hotels we’ve ever come across. It’s also a rather luxurious one, with expansive suites, three distinctive restaurants, and a pool and Ayurvedic spa, complete with yoga classes. As long as it stands, travelers have a direct line to Kathmandu’s past.

content:
Grenada’s two-mile-long Grand Anse Beach is grand indeed. And Spice Island Beach Resort, spanning some eight acres of beachfront real estate, isn’t too shabby either. This family-owned resort was rebuilt after a hurricane a little more than a decade ago, and in the process it was reborn as something rather more high-end — a quietly contemporary, subtly luxurious all-inclusive, all-suite escape.

The 64 suites open onto breezy terraces facing the gardens or, in the best case, the beach; some, set back from the beach, center around private plunge pools instead. All are outfitted in a contemporary style with clear Caribbean-colonial roots, but all studiously avoid floral-print kitsch or seashell cutesiness — it’s a sober, dignified look from top to bottom, and the tactile comforts are more than up to the task.

Oliver’s combines Caribbean fine dining with a lively Grenadian atmosphere, to the sound of steel drums, while the Sea and Surf Terrace & Bar is a touch more casual. Safe to say it’s several steps up from ordinary Caribbean hotel fare, making good on the all-inclusive promise, kids’ club, tennis courts, and all. St. George may not be quite the marquee name that some other Caribbean destinations are — but that’s entirely to Spice Island’s benefit.

content:
Located in Melbourne’s Central Business District, Ovolo is as much a business hotel as anything — and yet, where the typical business hotel is drab and sterile and entirely unappealing for anything more than a quick passing-through, Ovolo’s apartment-style rooms invite as long a stay as you like. The mood is a homey one in the style of Australia’s creative capital, where it seems perfectly plausible that living like a local means having a sunny, open-plan apartment full of bold, brightly colored art. Some of the rooms are tiny while others are vast penthouses with amenities like a hot tub on the private rooftop patio, but all share a rare blend of whimsy and livability. 

If you keep an eye out, you’ll notice quirky touches like a recurring shiny-silver-ball motif, repeated in the metal globules floating across the lobby like mercury loosed in outer space, in the futuristic metal tchotchkes in the fruit basket, and, if you’ve got the right penthouse suite, in the pinballs clanging around that in-room pinball machine. The point is they’ve put some effort into the design, though it’s sufficiently reined in that you’re more likely to let it all wash over than to dissect all their clever ideas. And fortunately, Ovolo is as thoughtful as it is clever: free minibars, Apple TVs, black-out curtains. In the better rooms, where full-size kitchens and room to entertain come standard, it’s easy to feel at home even if you’re away for work. 

One of the trade-offs of a hotel that’s closer to an apartment than a resort is that you won’t be swimming in on-site amenities like spas and restaurants. If you want a feeling of complete escape to Vacationland, of pampering, this might not be the place; but if it’s enough to be taken care of, to have your laundry done and to walk out your door to a nearby restaurant like the rest of Melbourne’s hip polloi, you won’t be disappointed by Ovolo.

content:
South Andros is less traveled than some other Bahamian islands; it’s no wonder Caerula Mar Club drew some attention when it opened in 2020, as it was the first new opening on the island in decades. And there’s no question that the property’s present-day iteration is stylish — clean lines, earthy hues, bright white umbrellas around a sparking aquamarine pool with sweeping views of the Caribbean just beyond.

Caerula Mar Club sits on an idyllic white sand beach, and the vibe is barefoot luxury, with perhaps slight emphasis on the latter. Rooms feature supple white oak flooring, marble stone accents, and open-plan layouts with huge glass doors opening onto private decks with ocean views. Some have four-poster beds and oversized walk-in showers, while others feature vaulted white ceilings and midcentury modern furnishings. Spacious villas, shaped from the old hotel’s cottages, come with charming wooden porches and multiple bedrooms. 

Breakfast is served at a casual but chic café and smoothie bar, or in the more formal Lusca, with views of the pool and the sea. But the airy beach bar is a highlight throughout the day, perfect for a lunch break on the sand or sunset cocktails following an afternoon out bonefishing, sailing, or snorkeling.

content:
Right in the center of the city of Mérida a 19th-century mansion has been put to new use as a luxury boutique hotel whose design pays the maximum possible tribute to local tradition. Hotel CIGNO is not a strictly historically correct recreation of the grand Yucatecan residential style, but a contemporary interpretation, full of details inspired by both the colonial and indigenous traditions. 

Its French-style façade remains as ornate as ever, but once inside it’s clear this house is a perfect example of a Spanish-inspired courtyard house. Many suites come with balconies, some come with plunge pools, and a couple of them open directly onto the rooftop terrace. And the interiors are roughly equal parts antique and contemporary, with timbered ceilings, tile floors, and modern built-in storage that feels cut from the same cloth as the colonial-style décor.

Life here is slow, in the best possible way, but that doesn’t mean dull; Cigno offers a multitude of activities to guests, from yoga and massage to cooking classes, kayak tours, and even cenote dives. Of particular note is the hotel’s restaurant that crafts modern dishes from traditional local flavors.

content: If Greek-island luxury hospitality sometimes feels formulaic, it’s because the formula is just about perfect: luxe accommodations, ocean views, Mediterranean flavors, and an atmosphere that’s laid all the way back. The best hotels in the genre excel because of the details, and in the case of Domes White Coast Milos it might be the modernist simplicity of the design that sets it apart, above all else; it looks fantastic, and it’s got everything else taken care of, from the private pools that come with each unit to the open-air restaurant on the terrace overlooking the ever-impressive Aegean seascape.\n\nThe views here are nothing short of extraordinary; the Sea View units look out over a 180-degree coastal panorama, and the public spaces are similarly well endowed. The en-suite plunge pools are supplemented by a central swimming pool, and the beach lies just a few minutes’ walk away. Meanwhile the restaurant is sister to the highly regarded Makris Athens.

content:
The baroque city of Valletta, capital of the island nation of Malta, is becoming a hot destination, thanks to its mid-Mediterranean location, its distinctive visual language, and a surfeit of excellent hotels. Among these is Palazzo Consiglia, a 13-room boutique hotel right on the edge of the old town — a hotel that’s both better equipped and rather more opulent than its small size might prepare you to expect.

Every room is different, but they’re uniformly luxurious, and all combine historic architectural elements with contemporary interventions in a fantastic, borderline whimsical style. Stone walls and timbers could feel heavy, but not against pastel colors and wall-sized murals depicting nature scenes. Meanwhile 40-inch televisions, Bluetooth sound systems, and USB outlets are present as a matter of course.

To all this the hotel adds a rooftop terrace lounge with a plunge pool, as well as a well-equipped spa hidden away in the villa’s old cellar. A hotel of this size can’t quite justify a restaurant, beyond its satisfying breakfast service, but given the location — within a few minutes’ walk of just about anything in old-town Valletta — you’re never short of satisfying options.

content:
The Cugó Gran Macina Malta is housed in a massive centuries-old stone building, once part of the harborside fortifications in the Maltese city of Senglea, designed to lift entire ships out of the water with a large crane. Its sturdy structure and grand scale translate particularly well, after extensive renovations, into a one-of-a-kind luxury hotel. 

The result is nothing if not dramatic, a high-contrast marriage of antique architecture  — parts of the building date back to the 16th century — and ultra-modern interior design. High vaulted ceilings and soaring limestone archways lend a dramatic cathedral-like beauty to guest rooms and public spaces alike. Suites are spacious and sleek, with cool slate floors, king-sized beds, and seating areas with stylish Italian furniture; some face the water, others the exterior walls of the ancient structure. 

A rooftop terrace is the place to be at sunset, with a swimming pool offering magnificent views of the old fortress and the harbor. Meanwhile, the modern Mediterranean restaurant serves a menu whose flavors are informed by Malta’s unique position at the crossroads of the Lebanese, Arab, and Latin cultures, paired with wines from the hotel’s expansive cellar.

content:
Though it flies a bit under the radar, anyone who’s been knows that the Peruvian capital is gritty, sprawling, and fully alive. The second largest city in the Americas — bigger even than Mexico City — Lima’s sheer size and bustling streets can be overwhelming to even the most seasoned traveler. The best way to explore the city, to really get to know it, is with the help of someone who knows the lay of the land, who can uncover hidden treasures within its millennia of history — because once you get this intoxicating place into your bloodstream, you’ll want to learn all its secrets. Atemporal is that gracious refuge in the midst of the sprawl. 

It’s presented as the home of an imaginary globetrotting photographer, one who’s left you full access to his 1940s Tudor-style mansion in the Miraflores neighborhood, his car, and his staff, with instructions to anticipate and meet your every need. And he wants you to love Lima as much as he does. It’s a nice little idea, but in fact, Atemporal is nearly as close to a private home as a boutique hotel gets: Only guests staying in the hotelito’s nine rooms have access to the property. The guestrooms are small but comfortable, dressed in a modern decor that still matches the European, colonial vibe so much of Lima presents. 

You might even forget for a minute that you’re in the heart of a major Latin American metropolis. But once you’re ready to rejoin the hustle and bustle, bicycles are freely available, as is a house car with a private chauffeur who can take you to nearby hotspots and holes in the wall alike. Many visitors come to Lima for the food — this is a city at the top of its gastronomy game. Your breakfast is included with your stay, and there is fresh, locally sourced food available for room service 24/7, but know this: you’re within short walking distance of some of the city’s best restaurants, including the famed Astrid y Gastón and Osaka.

content: There are a lot of hotels on the Riviera Maya. Very few of them make it into the pages of Architectural Digest. Casa Malca, a new boutique hotel boldly imagined and brought to life by prominent New York gallerist Lio Malca, made the cut. It’s not hard to see why. The main house itself isn’t new: it’s a simple stucco structure, rustic, traditional. It sat empty on the sand for years before Malca snapped it up and redesigned it, knocking down walls to create open spaces, adding new buildings to house additional guest rooms, putting up Keith Haring prints like wallpaper, and furnishing the airy spaces with retro furniture and key pieces from his own art collection. Casa Malca sits on a quiet section of the white-sand beach; nearly all rooms and suites have ocean views. Nine rooms are located inside the original house, including the lavish Malca suite with a private rooftop terrace. 26 other rooms, located in the newer buildings, are scattered around the property. No two are quite alike: some have private patios set amid tropical gardens, while others open directly to the swimming pool or beach. What’s standard are the floor-to-ceiling windows, sustainable bamboo linens by Kassatex, and original artworks. Casa Malca has two restaurants, both specializing on lighter takes on Mexican dishes — think gourmet grilled fish tacos — prepared with locally sourced ingredients. Sleep in, lounge by the pool, doze in a hammock, go for a walk on the beach, forget what time it is for awhile. When it comes to good food and culture, Casa Malca has you covered: it’s a stylish urbanite’s getaway. It’s a place that helps you relax, not disconnect entirely.

content:
Set amid rocky cliffs overlooking the sea, the Nest Resort is an elegant refuge on Crete’s northern coast. It’s not as flashy as some of the island’s other resorts; there’s no private beach or fine-dining restaurant. But the guest rooms and villas, each with a private pool, are the embodiment of quiet luxury.  

The architectural style is modern with cubist-inspired wood, glass, and concrete buildings neatly built into terraced gardens on the hillside. The color palette is earthy inside and out: lots of blonde wood, pale stone, and bright white. Accommodations are evenly divided, with nine rooms in varying categories and nine private villas. All are light-filled and refreshingly minimalist, though artisan-crafted objects, vintage pieces, and colorful bathroom tiles add character. Most have water views. Villas have two to four bedrooms, open-plan kitchens, and spacious terraces with their own pools. 

The resort’s main pool, with its sweeping views of the Aegean and an all-day bar and café offering poolside dining, is a highlight; an ethereal indoor pool, dramatically illuminated and framed by botanical murals, awaits at the spa.

content:
In planning their Greek island escape, many overseas travelers skip straight to the Aegean side of the country, and thus risk missing out on the island of Zakynthos. It’s here, just up the coast from the capital, that you’ll find Tsilivi Beach, and the adjacent town of Planos. And just off the west end of the beach is the reason for this geography lesson: Contessina Hotel, one of two hotels in town doing business under the Contessina name. (The other, the equally fine Contessina Suites & Spa, is smaller, and admits adults only.)

It’s visually impressive from the start, a modern, somewhat minimalist affair — and it’s a proper luxury boutique hotel as well, complete with its own spa and wellness center, as well as a substantial central swimming pool. A few of the garden suites add plunge pools of their own, and there’s a separate kids’ pool in addition to a playground and garden.

Even the restaurant, Veggera, features a thoughtful sub-menu just for children’s palates; adults, meanwhile, enjoy a menu that draws heavily from produce grown on site. Vedema, meanwhile, offers a more adult atmosphere, in the open air on the roof terrace overlooking the central pool.

content:
The Six Senses resorts are nothing if not restorative, but wellness, until now, has been just one component of the brand’s ultra-luxe approach. At Six Senses Vana, however, wellness is the primary focus. This retreat, in the outskirts of Dehradun, the capital of Uttarakhand, sits at the foot of the Himalayas, in a remarkably contemporary structure surrounded by woodland — a more meditative setting would be difficult to imagine.

Its style is minimalist and modern, but its accommodations certainly don’t lack warmth — they’re just as painstakingly tailored to their surroundings as any traditionally styled resort. In classic Six Senses style they’re extremely plush, but tasteful rather than opulent, and there’s a hint of Zen tranquility to the careful arrangement of the objects and spaces.

And that’s before you’ve taken into account the wellness component of your stay, which is a substantial one: personalized nutrition plans, consultations on sleep issues or weight management, and programs centered around detox, yoga, and Ayurvedic or Tibetan medicine. It’s a transformational experience no matter how you measure it — for some of us, an ultra-luxe minimalist resort serving carefully considered Indian cuisine — especially under the Six Senses banner — is a wellness journey unto itself.

content: Having a whole hotel floor to yourself is a luxury that’s usually reserved for the high-rollers in the penthouse suite. Not at One96 in Hong Kong. At this super-sleek boutique hotel, housed in an eye-catching modernist building that’s midway between the Central and Sheung Wan districts, the glass exterior mimics the texture of undulating waves – every suite occupies a whole level. So you don’t have to share those panoramic city skyline views with the adjacent room. And you won’t have to hear the neighbor’s sound system through the bedroom wall. And you don’t have to endure that awkward wait for the elevator with perfect strangers — no, you’ll summon the lift from your private “lift lobby.” \n\nSpace is luxury, indeed, especially in Hong Kong, only one of the most densely populated places in the world. And Norman Chan, a designer-architect who earned his stripes at RISD and Columbia before returning to his native Hong Kong, has taken full advantage of the floor space on offer here. Each suite is cool and sophisticated, and filled with natural light, thanks to the floor-to-ceiling windows. Features include a lounge and dining area furnished with bespoke sofas, a bedroom outfitted with Simmons mattresses and Frette linens, and a chic kitchenette equipped with a Nespresso machine.

content:
If you’ve made it to Santorini in the first place then the evidence suggests you’re seizing the day quite firmly as it is. But if you really want to grab the thing by the scruff of the neck and never let go, a visit to Carpe Diem is probably in order. Nothing says pure in-the-now hedonism like an infinity pool with a view of the volcanic caldera — except, perhaps, an exceedingly private suite with its own pool, its own outdoor terrace, and its own corresponding view.

Needless to say Carpe Diem is a hotel that sees its fair share of honeymoon business. It’s very much a couples sort of place, and it feels even more secluded thanks to its high elevation — what its views lack in dramatic front-row spectacle, compared to the more coastal hotels, they make up for in sheer wide-ranging panorama. The owner is the architect, which means the interiors, however subtle, are always thoughtful.

With just ten suites the vibe is always low-key, and the sleepy medieval town of Pyrgos is charming yet undemanding. Room service breakfast goes practically without saying, and you’ll only see your fellow guests at dinner, or in the bar — a sundown cocktail, with the caldera to the west, is a matter of course.

Please note: Carpe Diem cannot accommodate children under the age of thirteen. Carpe Diem is a seasonal property and is open from April through October.

content: All of Cortona’s best hotels are located inside landmark buildings — palaces in town, country estates set amid vineyards — and the Monastero di Cortona Hotel & Spa is no exception. Indeed, this 15th-century monastery, with its gorgeous original frescoes, high vaulted ceilings, and breathtaking hilltop vantage point, may be the most impressive of them all. The imposing stone building was thoughtfully restored and transformed into a luxury boutique hotel in 2019, and it remains one of the most elegant lodgings in this corner of Tuscany.\n\nRooms and suites, almost entirely outfitted in shades of cream and white, are all unique. Attic rooms have wooden flooring, quaint beamed ceilings, marble bathrooms, and views of the monastery’s cloisters, while larger suites feature travertine tile floors and French doors leading onto private terraces. The friars’ former garden is now home to a wide, sun-drenched terrace with a small swimming pool and views over the surrounding landscapes; the spa’s luminous indoor pool, framed by old stone archways, is even more striking. The house negroni — a custom blend inspired by the original, a proudly Tuscan invention — is served on the rooftop garden with views over Cortona’s rooftops and the hills beyond.

content:
A prime waterfront location in the Financial District is the only natural site for the InterContinental group’s grand entry into Boston, given the demographics of its likely audience — the fact that it’s pretty much the exact site of no less historic an occurrence than the Boston Tea Party is just a bonus.

This is big-time modern luxury hospitality the way it’s supposed to be done: from the building itself, a monument in blue glass and polished granite, to the interiors, sleek and minimal but not too stark, right down to the most minor of details, such as flat-panel televisions mounted on swivels for maximum visibility.

With 424 rooms it’s not exactly intimate, but an army of staffers see to it that you’re never without help. And a hotel of this size can afford some big amenities: the InterContinental’s spa is enormous, 6,600 square feet, with a 24-hour gym and a 45-foot indoor pool.

Cocktail hour can be enjoyed at Bar Fellini or the Loyall Counting Room before heading to restaurant Matria, which specializes in dishes from Piedmont and the Italian Riviera. Weather permitting, we’d advise you to take a seat outside on the waterfront terrace for a view of the Seaport. Not the sort of thing you’re likely to run across in the average business hotel.

content:
We’ll forgive you for failing to imagine that Western Australia would have a luxury hotel of the highest caliber, but such a prejudice would make your entry to Perth’s COMO The Treasury all the more surprising and delightful. Not only is this 48-room hotel housed in a truly grand space — a series of restored 19th-century state buildings, all soaring arches and stately white columns — but the guest rooms are outfitted in a manner that’s lavish by any standard. Did we mention there’s a pair of chic restaurants, a cocktail bar, and a signature spa? It’s enough to make you want to stay in the City of Light (no, not that City of Light, the other City of Light, so nicknamed when Perth’s citizens turned all the lights on as astronaut John Glenn passed overhead in 1962) for another day or two.

Rooms and suites are cool, quiet, and light-filled, designed in pale earth tones by architect Kerry Hill, the man whose stamp is all over the Pacific Rim’s small luxury resorts. Standard amenities include king-sized beds with Grand Posture mattresses and Egyptian cotton sheets, complimentary minibars, LED TVs, Illy coffee machines, and remote-controlled blackout curtains. The real luxury is in the bathroom — almost always true in a good hotel — with heated stone floors and towel racks, walk-in showers, German-made freestanding oval bathtubs, and custom products by COMO Shambhala at Home. Yes, the very same you’ll find at the hotel’s spa, or rather, its Urban Escape, which is also where you’ll find the fitness center and an indoor swimming pool.

COMO The Treasury has a range of high-end suites with features like fireplaces and views of  Swan River, and bathrooms bordering on palatial. If you can’t see any boats from your bathtub, though, just head up to Wildflower, the hotel’s rooftop restaurant. There’s also Post, serving French-inspired cuisine, on the ground level. Both employ Western Australia’s produce — avocados, mandarins, and passionfruit all figure in heavily. Sitting high above Perth, sipping Chenin Blanc produced in the Swan Valley, you’ll almost forget you’re a thousand miles from the next big city. Or not: but a hotel this thoughtfully executed would be a pleasure to stay in, in Perth or anywhere else.

content:
As the growth in the Bodrum Peninsula has surged over the past decade, this port city has found its legacy of cultural significance to be nothing but an asset. Bodrum Castle beckons visitors back to the 15th Century, and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus dates back to 350 BC. For the modern luxury traveler, of course, Halicarnassus is not the primary concern: the history simply adds an extra dimension of depth to the experience. Much more immediately pressing is the matter of the peninsula’s aquatic surroundings, the maritime idyll of the Aegean Sea — a setting to which the Doria Hotel Bodrum, not entirely incidentally, provides a front-row view.

The Turkish version of the Aegean seaside hotel is perhaps unsurprisingly reminiscent of the Greek, though with some subtle differences. The décor makes use of aged wood, perhaps recalling driftwood, to tone down the white-on-whiteness, as well as mellow accents in sea foam green. The Doria’s look is very contemporary but very understated and unpretentious, tasteful above all else. And while the in-room comforts are quite up to snuff, it’s the common spaces that impress the most: the spa, the stylish Blu restaurant, and the seafront cabanas, perched on stilts above the water.

Please note: Doria Beach is a five-minute drive from the hotel via a free shuttle bus; contact reception to arrange transportation.

Guests can learn the art of cheesemaking, dine on seasonal farm-to-table dishes, or simply unwind amid the rhythms of country life - an authentic escape in the heart of the Var.

content: The 16th-century Monastery of Santa Scolastica, once a treasure trove of beautiful frescoes and stained glass panels on a hilltop in Tuscany, has been altered and abandoned many times over the course of its history. Following years of painstaking restoration involving a team of historians, architects, and art conservators, the convent reopened as La Monastica Resort & Spa in 2024. The results are nothing short of spectacular: the original chapel has been transformed into an atmospheric restaurant, the old stone terraces now feature tiered gardens and swimming pools fringed by lemon trees, and the nuns’ humble quarters have been shaped into elegant rooms and suites with sweeping views over the valley below. \n\nRooms highlight the monastery’s finest assets, including high wood-beamed ceilings, exposed stone walls, and an abundance of natural light, thanks to the elevated position. Simpler rooms are charming and cloister-like, with wooden writing desks and shuttered windows opening to the gardens, while suites are more opulent, with extras like seating areas, kitchenettes, and spacious bathrooms with freestanding tubs. Elsewhere on the property, the one-of-a-kind spa has an ethereal indoor-outdoor pool built into natural rock walls, the old cellar hosts wine tastings, and the peaceful citrus grove is the perfect place to relax with a cappuccino or a spritz.

content:
New Orleans might just have more character than any other city in the United States. Not every hotel in town lives up to the city’s legendary reputation, but the Henrietta has personality to spare. It’s a new build, and a strikingly modern one at that, at least from the outside — but look closer and you’ll see it’s packed with references to classic NOLA architecture, from the arched colonnade on the ground floor to the galleries on the upper floors.

Inside it’s a similarly heady mix of old and new; the reception features richly veined marble and a parquet floor that happens to be on the ceiling. And the rooms are a little bit mid-century modern, a little bit Art Deco, and a little bit Belle Époque, and are provided with up-to-date boutique-hotel details like Tivoli radios and Le Labo bath products.

There’s art everywhere, from vintage pieces to works by contemporary local artists. And while there’s not quite a restaurant, there’s Avenue Room Coffee, which serves as a café and bagel shop in the morning and segues into cocktails and light bites later in the day.

content:
Right on the main square in the village of Lagrasse, this centuries-old stone building was once a popular bakery. While a French family sold baguettes from the storefront in 1944, they were also secretly housing a Jewish couple from German militia; the nearly year-long effort ended happily, and put the building on the map. Today, it’s home to Bouquerie Lagrasse, an elegant small hotel that pays homage to the property’s culinary history. Instead of a traditional restaurant, the hotel’s first floor features a state-of-the-art kitchen workshop where visiting chefs offer seasonal tasting menus and guests are invited to join in hands-on cooking classes devoted to regional cuisine. 

Eating well is a priority here, and five of the hotel's six apartment-style accommodations have sleek modern kitchens equipped with appliances by Miele and Vipp. The aesthetic is Scandinavian-inspired: rooms are filled with natural light and feature pale wood flooring, minimalist decor, high beamed ceilings, leather chairs, and colorful framed artwork. All have luxurious king-sized beds and most have a private balcony or terrace, ideal for sipping café au lait or a glass of wine. 

A generous breakfast is served for a leisurely three hours every morning, either in the courtyard when weather permits or in the airy kitchen and open dining area. Of note is Bouquerie Lagrasse’s collection of modern sculptures and paintings, especially impressive for a hotel so focused on food. There's a museum-like quality to the lounge spaces on the ground level, and the owner happily accompanies guests to the wine cellar to choose the perfect bottle to uncork while relaxing and soaking up the art-filled atmosphere.

content:
It’s an unusual name, but it pretty well sums up the vibe; Beach Enclave is not one but three enclaves in three distinct sections of the east side of the island of Providenciales: North Shore, Grace Bay, and Long Bay. In each of the locations, you’ll find a selection of villas, all of them vast, ultra-modern, and ultra-luxe, featuring a small army of service staff and a level of privacy and seclusion that’s just about unparalleled.

They range from three to seven bedrooms, and come with everything you need for a self-contained stay, from private pools to full open kitchens and a surplus of common lounge space, so that even at full occupancy they never feel crowded. Fixtures and finishes are first-rate, and the style is quietly contemporary, a sort of chic island-casual that never approaches tropical kitsch.

Private beaches offer ample opportunity for any mode of recreation you can imagine, and private chefs are on hand to take care of the catering. From the enclaves the rest of Providenciales is easily accessible, but more than a few guests will likely opt to remain on-site for the duration of their stay — with comforts like these, they’re not missing out on much.

content:
Ask an Argentinean where to go for an experience that combines rural customs with the conveniences of urban living, and one likely answer is Salta. This mid-sized city in the northwest corner of Argentina boasts a wealth of neoclassical architecture and a tradition of local craftsmanship that retains some of the region’s Incan influence. A twenty-minute walk from downtown Salta brings you to the quiet foothills neighborhood of Tres Cerritos, home of the family-owned, bed-and-breakfast–style Kkala Boutique Hotel.  

Kkala’s exterior evokes an Andalucian manor, with its Spanish tile roof, stucco walls, and stone pathways. Inside, however, the Argentine influence asserts itself, in the form of striking red wall hangings with an indigenous flair and an abundance of local handmade crafts that haunt the rustic wooden furnishings. The ten rooms vary in size, with all but two offering the unforgettable luxury of a personal jacuzzi set into a deck-style hardwood floor, next to an enormous window overlooking the edge of Salta where the city meets the hills. We can imagine plenty of guests spending a little too long in their tubs, emerging pickled and sheepish after skipping the day’s sightseeing entirely.

The guest experience at Kkala includes breakfast, of course, delivered right to your door, unless you’d prefer to enjoy it in the sun-splashed solarium. And unlike some skimpier, over-literal interpretations of “bed and breakfast,” Kkala provides a more complete package, including an outdoor garden, pool, and library. Dinner can be prepared upon request, though an abundance of nearby restaurants means you’re never short of options. 

Please note: Kkala Hotel Boutique can only accommodate guests over the age of 10.

content: Increasingly, it takes something special to stand out among Phuket’s crop of luxury boutique hotels. Part of what sets Noku Phuket quite literally apart from the competition is its inland setting, on a hilltop overlooking Chalong Bay, near the island’s southern extremity. It gives up direct beach access for a unique elevated infinity pool, as well as a number of private pools attached to the larger units. And for many guests — think of Ubud in Bali — the forest is a fine substitute for a view of the sea.\n\nEven the entry-level Lofts come with private balconies and oversized bathrooms with soaking tubs; some add outdoor whirlpools to the equation. And the larger Villas are where you’ll find private pools, some with far-ranging views over the island and others encircled by lush greenery. There’s a substantial wellness center in the main pavilion, next to the central swimming pool; the Embrace restaurant and Terrace cocktail bar both take plentiful advantage of the property’s elevated view.
