content:
Located in the city's stylish Thong Lo district, MUU Bangkok comprises both a boutique hotel and high-end residences; some people live here, and the thoughtful design reflects that reality — the name, after all, is the Thai word for “community.” While rooms have all the amenities one would expect at a luxury hotel, they’re also well-suited to longer stays, and the common areas, from the pool deck to the sophisticated cocktail lounge, encourage socializing.

There’s a time and place for everything, of course, and it’s tempting to retreat to one’s own space after an afternoon exploring Bangkok. Rooms and suites are elegant with a touch of glamour, featuring timber flooring, king-sized beds, marble bathrooms with tubs and rain showers, and twenties-inspired decor, from jewel-toned headboards and vintage alarm clocks to gilded detailing and velvet divans. Larger apartment-like suites are more minimalist in style, with multiple bedrooms, fully equipped kitchens, and furnished terraces. 

Double infinity-edge swimming pools set amid attractive landscaping serve as a cool oasis on the hotel’s eleventh floor. Adjacent are a lively pool bar and a restaurant specializing in Mediterranean cuisine; elsewhere onsite are a café and bakery, a modern fitness center, a spa suite, and a speakeasy-style cocktail bar. For more options, MUU is connected to Eight Thonglor, an upscale shopping area, and the surrounding neighborhood is filled with boutiques, bars, galleries, and restaurants.

content:
Beachy chic is a vibe that’s somewhat rare in England, but at the Gallivant, in the East Sussex seaside town of Camber, it’s in plentiful supply. The Gallivant is now a remarkably swanky boutique hotel. And while it’s inspired by an idealized vision of the Hamptons, its interpretation is a unique one, studiously avoiding transatlantic clichés in favor of a look that’s roughly equal parts casual surf shack and stylish country inn.

The bedrooms incorporate splashes of bold color alongside sober, soothing neutrals, and contrast elegant touches like custom headboards with home-style elements like well-stocked bookshelves and quirky vintage artworks. Some open onto the garden, others onto private decks; all feature more lounge space, and more comfort than you’d expect.

Also far beyond is the Gallivant’s culinary program; which includes their recently relaunched restaurant, Harry's. The chef prepares a thoughtful breakfast as well as a seasonal menu of locally sourced fare for lunch and dinner, accompanied by an extensive wine list. 

And if you’d prefer a picnic lunch, they’re happy to pack a basket for you, complete with to-go cocktails and a blanket for the beach.

content: A nearby alternative to busy Mykonos is the island of Tinos, practically undiscovered in mass-travel terms. And while Pnoēs Tinos will raise the island’s profile, it’s not likely to disturb the local tranquility — this ultra-stylish retreat comprises a mere three villas. They’re the work of the Greek firm Aristides Dallas Architects, and they’re a very modern evolution of the classic Cycladic white-on-white look, providing shelter from the midday sun and generous amplification of the morning and evening light. Each villa is a self-contained luxury experience, complete with private pool; common spaces are minimal, but there’s plenty to do nearby.

content:
All the major global players have Maldivian resorts, but there’s space, still, for a homegrown brand: THE OZEN COLLECTION is a small group, entirely focused on the Maldives, and its flagship, OOZEN RESERVE BOLIFUSHI, belongs in the top tier along with all the more familiar names. As you’d expect, it occupies its own private island and lagoon in the South Malé Atoll. And on this island — and on stilts in the shallow water that surrounds it — are a collection of suites, villas, pavilions, and “reserves” to rival anything in the region.

At all sizes, the accommodations are spacious, tasteful, and finely finished. Many of the overwater units come with waterslides to deliver guests directly into the Indian Ocean; they also feature plunge pools, while many of the on-land units come with L-shaped lap pools.

The plan is all-inclusive, and begins with an airport transfer via private catamaran. An expansive spa features its own overwater treatment pavilions, and there’s an on-site dive center to prepare guests for underwater adventures. And given the remoteness of the location — there’s no popping off to town for a quick bite — OZEN RESERVE BOLIFUSHI sensibly divides its culinary attention across five separate venues, plus the possibility of a private meal in a setting of your choice.

content:
Almost all of Malta’s impressive crop of luxury boutique hotels have been built in and around Valletta, the capital city. But this island has charms that are capable of tempting you away from the crowd. And while we’re not certain that’s why it’s called Lure Hotel & Spa, the upshot is the same: a compelling hospitality reason to venture into the island’s north, to the picturesque village of Mellieħa.

And if the word “village” leads you to expect something rustic, prepare to be surprised. The rooms and suites are nothing if not glamorous, combining Art Deco elegance with modernist furnishings and fixtures. The smallest rooms spread out over 35 square meters, with plenty of space for oversized four-poster beds, while the suites grow to twice that size or more. 

The vibe throughout is refined, owing perhaps to the adults-only policy; the spa, in particular, is a tranquil oasis, as is the small but extremely stylish indoor pool. And while there’s plenty in the way of restaurants in the surrounding area, there’s not much as artfully crafted as what you’ll find at Lure’s table — whether in the dining room or outside on the terrace.

content: The colonial district of Santo Domingo is thick with historical atmosphere, and for good reason — it’s the Americas' oldest continuously populated European settlement. So a hotel like the Billini can get away with taking some liberties with the centuries-old style. It’s housed in a 16th-century convent, and proudly displays certain well-preserved architectural elements. But on the whole, the Billini is, if anything, reminiscent of certain Italian hotels for the way it confidently grafts a superstructure of avant-garde modern design onto a solid base of 450-year-old brick and stone. When you’ve got this much historical depth you don’t have to be precious about it.\n\nThe suites, in fact, go quite a bit heavier on modernist furniture and 20th-century fashion photography than on architectural preservation. And the comforts within are pure 21st-century luxury hotel, right down to the Bang & Olufsen sound systems and the L’Occitane bath products in the rain showers. The main restaurant, Castil, serves Dominican fare in a space that’s dominated by original stone columns, and the Moon Restaurant & Bar makes the most of its rooftop setting, overlooking the rooftops of the Zona Colonial. All in all, it’s an oasis of modern calm in this hectic throwback of a town.

content:
Johannesburg is a bit off the travel radar, for such a large city; whether it's geography (on a high plain, nowhere near a body of water) or much-publicized social issues (there are still neighborhoods that are not quite safe for tourists), no one can say for sure. But travelers who do brave the arid plains and find themselves in this gold rush town, there are a number of sleek and stylish hotels.

One of these, and probably the most intimate and stylish, is Ten Bompas, named for its Sandton/Rosebank location, at Number Ten, Bompas Road. There are only ten suites here, but they vary widely, having been created by ten different designers, in ten different styles, from African tribal to haute couture. All have separate lounges and bedrooms, fireplace and steam bath, and outdoor access via patio or balcony.

Don't worry, there's space to meet and mingle at Winehouse, a contemporary-continental restaurant with robust French specialties and a penchant for showcasing the hotel's own organic produce. And, yes, a plethora of South African wines: delicious, inexpensive, and the perfect accompaniment to the dining room's fireplace or, weather permitting, the terrace and poolside garden.

How to get there: Ten Bompas is approximately a 30 minute drive from Johannesburg International Airport. Taxis wait opposite Terminal A at the airport and should cost approximately R400 (40 USD) for a one way transfer. Taxi fares should be agreed upon before departing the airport.

content:
The dream for any city-center luxury hotel is a location that’s at once surrounded by attractions and yet comfortably sequestered; here, on a side street in the 8th arrondissement’s famed Golden Triangle, the Hôtel San Régis manages to have it all. Nor does it suffer in the style department, with interiors by Pierre-Yves Rochon, whose work is practically synonymous with Parisian luxury hospitality.

What sets the San Régis apart from many of its peers, however, is its very slight edge of eccentricity — it feels in some ways more like a 42-room house than like a planned and designed luxury hotel. Every room is different, and all throughout are the gradually deposited traces of a history that goes back more than a hundred years.

In this corner of town you’re by no means hard up for something to eat, but the San Régis, perhaps unusually for a hotel of its size, offers a restaurant of its own, the versatile and elegant Les Confidences, serving hotel guests and Parisian diners in a verdant winter-garden setting.

content:
Right around the corner from the slightly larger Contessina Hotel, and a block from the west end of Tsilivi Beach, is the more intimate and more luxurious — and, crucially, adults-only — Contessina Suites & Spa. Its style is modern and rather minimal, with not a hint of island kitsch; in fact it’s sophisticated enough to feel quite urban, even while its compound-like design makes it feel like something of a world unto itself.

Luxe touches are everywhere: some suites have freestanding baths, others have hot tubs, and many either come with their own plunge pool or share one with their neighbor.

Of particular note is the spa, with its curvaceous grotto-like pool. Another pair of open-air pools are on hand for guests who didn’t book pool villas. And the Ionian Sea, of course, is a scant 250 meters from the hotel’s door. As are several worthwhile restaurants — but the hotel’s own offerings run from a classic Greek breakfast and a poolside snack bar to Lentika, the ground-floor restaurant surrounded by gardens, and Nobile, the rooftop fine-dining venue with a view of the pool.

content: The Inn at Thorn Hill, a luxury hotel and spa in the woods of northern New Hampshire, is nothing if not relaxing. Each of the suites and rooms of the main building has its own unique style and layout, but all feature two-person whirlpool bathtubs and gas fireplaces. Guests in need of more space and privacy may also choose from a pair of charming independent cottages, while a larger group may prefer the historic carriage house, adjacent to the main building, whose six rooms can accommodate up to twelve guests. content: An “albergo diffuso,” or “distributed hotel,” is an Italian hospitality form that takes not a single building but an entire village as its raw material. In the case of Torre Del Nera Albergo Diffuso Spa the village in question is the staggeringly picturesque Scheggino, a triangle-shaped hamlet built around a medieval fortress in Umbria. The hotel occupies a cluster of beautifully restored historic buildings in the heart of the village, down a cobblestoned lane that's only accessible on foot, the interiors thoughtfully transformed into peaceful rooms and suites. \n\nThe aesthetic is elegant and timeless: terra cotta or exposed stone walls, wood-beamed ceilings, and parquet flooring. Each room features one-of-a-kind antiques, from hand-painted headboards to decorative armoires, as well as modern details, like modern bathrooms and sophisticated lighting systems. Some rooms have private balconies or small sitting rooms, and larger suites are apartment-like with wood-burning fireplaces and cozy kitchenettes. Torre Del Nera’s expansive spa, with its pool  framed by old stone archways and facing views over the terraced gardens outside, is a particular highlight, as is the atmospheric restaurant specializing in Umbrian cuisine.

content: Castiglioncello del Trinoro, a medieval village perched on a hilltop in Tuscany’s Val d’Orcia, was all but abandoned after the Second World War. Decades later, a vacationing American attorney fell in love with the place and started snapping up property, later tapping the Rome-based architect Ilaria Miani to turn a collection of old houses into a luxury boutique hotel. Today, Monteverdi Tuscany is part of the village, with ancient cobblestoned streets leading between guest rooms, a stone-walled swimming pool set, beautiful gardens, a spa and wellness center, a library, a terrace bar, an art gallery with rotating exhibitions from contemporary artists, a culinary academy, and a 14th-century church used as a concert venue.\n\nAfter careful restorations, the rooms are charming and character-filled: rustic wood-beamed ceilings, heated floors, custom four-poster beds draped in hand-dyed Italian linens, hand-crafted furnishings, and modern bathrooms with rainfall showers and locally made bath products. Some suites have travertine soaking tubs and views over the vineyards below, and spacious village houses, with two to six bedrooms, come with generous common areas, well-equipped kitchens, and a private garden furnished for outdoor dining. Breakfast is served at Zita (designed by Foster + Partners), located right in the center of the village, and the surrounding labyrinth of streets is a pleasure to explore on foot before venturing into the UNESCO-protected countryside just down the hill.

content: By this point an Aman hotel hardly needs vetting, true, but it remains a pleasure to detail their ongoing success story. They’ve hit photogenic gold again here in Lijiang, jewel of China’s Yunnan province, an astoundingly well-preserved repository for the region’s heritage and peerless natural beauty. Amandayan overlooks the impossibly ancient Old Town, a rich lattice of irreplaceable artifacts and architecture with a whimsical penchant for bridges and cobblestone streets. Here in the Land of Eternal Spring, so-called for its clement weather, it’s the snow-mantled Jade Dragon Snow Mountain that gets highest billing, in every sense — presiding over Yunnan’s limestone heights and untamed rivers, its lordly presence elevates many room views from that’s nice to must have. Good thing these all-suite accommodations recognize that fact, and even better that they pair it with flawless interiors in the time-tested Nakhi tradition. The universal luxury signifiers are here in the clean lines and lofty ceilings, of course, but the specifics will astound you: pagoda roofs, courtyard-core, and expertly carved screens and ornaments in local pine and elm. The affect is open, soothing, and softly lit throughout, extending into the bathrooms with freestanding tubs for the requisite soak. Technology, though state-of-the-art, is kept supremely discreet; you’ll enjoy the flat-screens, the sound system, and the underfloor heating, we’re sure, but they won’t obtrude. And tempting though it may be to cocoon yourself in your room, you’ll be glad for the restaurant when hunger strikes. Serving a balance of Yunnan and Cantonese fare, it centers on mountain-foraged plates, with global dishes available nearby in the lounge. There’s also a tea house, oriented towards some of the resort’s best views, with both traditional and Western varieties on offer. And it wouldn’t be Aman without a wellness suite, here emphasizing Chinese medicinal herbs and massage, augmented by a lengthy heated outdoor pool, a fully equipped gym, yoga classes on request, and multiple treatment rooms. How to get there: Amandayan is a 40-minute drive from Lijiang Airport.

content:
In an area as overrun with contemporary luxury resorts as Seminyak, it’s refreshing to find a place that’s still in touch with Indonesia’s more traditional side. The BK Village’s architecture is based on the design of the joglo, the teak houses traditional to the island of Java — though it is, in fact, on Bali, a short drive from the international airport via the resort’s complimentary shuttle.

Unlike some of the highest-end resorts, The BK Village is not located on the beachfront, but in the nearby residential neighborhood of Umalas. Not that you’re likely to care once you’re floating on your back in your very own clover-shaped swimming pool. It’s but one of the many elegant amenities on offer inside the three-bedroom Villa Kalua. With three bedrooms, it’s the smallest of the resort’s three free-standing houses, but that’s not saying much: each of the villas looks like the size of small hotel.

Comprised of interconnecting teak buildings, the Kalua features a large garden, a lotus pond, and a fully equipped kitchen. Each of the three bedrooms has its own refrigerator and outdoor shower, and one has a plunge pool — it’s Balinese-style indoor-outdoor living at its finest. Nearby, the four-bedroom Kayu Villa has even more to offer: an even bigger garden, this one laid out according to the principles of feng shui, and striking natural stone accents around the swimming pool and inside the villa’s series of bathrooms. The top-of-the-line Ka Villa has five bedrooms, ornate wood statues, and so much gorgeous lounge space that you won’t know what to do first: go for a swim, recline on a luxuriant pile of silk cushions, or sip tea and just stare at the Eden-like garden.

A little paradise, indeed. You’re minutes away from the trendy shopping district and expat-happy cocktail bars of Seminyak, but don’t be surprised if you leave Bali without ever laying eyes on those.

Please note: The BK Village requires a two-night minimum stay from November to December.

content: A seaside town in northern Poland might not be the first place you’d look for a storybook castle. But Zamek Łeba’s off-the-beaten-path location, tucked between the shoreline of the blue Baltic Sea and the shifting dunes of Słowiński National Park, is part of what makes it magical. The castle dates back to the 1900s, and functioned as a wellness retreat for decades before it became a luxury hotel. There’s still an unmistakably old-world air to the place, and many details feel charmingly redolent of the past: an elevator was never installed, bathrooms have vintage-looking tubs instead of modern walk-in showers, and Polish classics like smoked sturgeon and red borscht are served in the restaurant.\n\nRooms display a period character, too, though they’ve undergone a significant refresh. All are individually decorated with a mix of antiques and midcentury modern pieces; some have bold floral wallpaper and velvet sofas, and others have crystal chandeliers, lilac accent walls, and geometric headboards. A handful of larger suites feature private balconies or terraces overlooking the sea. Also facing the water are an outdoor pool, open in warmer weather, and the spa’s outdoor Jacuzzi. The quiet beach in front of the hotel awaits in all seasons — though lovely in summer, it’s nothing short of otherworldly in winter, when the staff builds bonfires on the snow-covered sand.

content: There are plenty of glamping options near Zion National Park, but none as luxurious as Open Sky Zion, featuring safari-style canvas tents crafted in South Africa, an upscale restaurant, and 80 acres of wilderness to explore. Located near the park’s far west border, the resort is accessible via a long dirt road, its camps dwarfed by a spectacular landscape of red rocky cliffs, canyons, and plateaus. Zion’s entrance is a 25-minute drive away, but there are five miles of hiking trails to enjoy without leaving the property, plus easy access to Guacamole Trail, one of the best mountain-biking routes in the region.\n\nA dozen tents are generously spaced out on the property, each built on an elevated platform to optimize the views from their private decks. Amenities vary — the top-of-the-line Star Seeker camp has a glass-ceilinged stargazing lounge and a clawfoot soaking tub with views, while the family-friendly Milky Way camp contains two spacious bedrooms — but all have king-sized beds with fine linens, cozy fireplaces, and patios with fire pits. En-suite bathrooms are modern and comfortable with filtered running water and heated floors, and all but the smallest camp have both indoor and outdoor showers. A complimentary breakfast is available in the lobby each morning. After the day’s outdoor adventures, s'mores fixings are provided, and the hotel’s destination restaurant Black Sage serves dinner with locally sourced ingredients and scenic views.

content:
Following the success of La Fiermontina, a gem of a boutique hotel in the Puglian city of Lecce, the owners opened a second hotel in Paris. La Fiermontina Ocean, on Morocco’s northern shore, is the third addition to the collection. Like the original, it has an elegant, worldly air inspired by the short but romantic life of Antonia Fiermonte, a painter and musician who modeled at Villa Medici, regularly attended Parisian salons, and traveled extensively in Morocco. And like its Italian counterpart, La Fiermontina Ocean is in an off-the-beaten-path place with few luxury hotels — it’s tucked away in a natural park near the fishing port of Larache, which is about an hour’s drive from Tangier. 

The hotel’s remote location, hugging a sloping hillside overlooking the ocean, is a major part of its appeal, and its low-lying stone buildings, surrounded by windswept sand dunes and scenic olive trees, make the most of the landscape. Part of the complex overlaps with the rural village of Dchier, and guests can choose to stay there in traditional houses built according to ancestral techniques — vaulted ceilings, woven rugs, small antique windows — or in more contemporary lodgings closer to reception. Pool suites are outfitted in all-natural materials and hues, with cool stone flooring and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking private gardens and infinity pools. Larger pool villas also have spacious kitchens and dedicated staff. 

In the village, the hotel’s gorgeous hammam offers traditional treatments, and back on the main property, a restaurant serves Italian and Moroccan cuisine with a view. 

A short shuttle ride or a 20-minute stroll down the hill leads to the beach club, where it’s all too easy to while away the day sipping mint tea or cocktails in a white-canopied cabana.

content:
While L’Assiette Champenoise is best known for its extraordinary restaurant, the attached hotel is notable in its own right. It's one of the only luxury hotels in a region, Champagne, that sees plenty of affluent travelers — and while dining on site is practically obligatory, these stylish family-run lodgings also serve as a practical option for those road-tripping through the wine regions of northeastern France. 

From the outside, the stately mansion looks like many others in the Reims suburbs; inside, the interiors are surprisingly modern, characterized by clean lines, geometric shapes, and a moody color palette. On the ground level are various lounge areas with fireplaces, contemporary art, and modular sofas, plus a beautiful glass-walled indoor pool with floor-to-ceiling windows revealing views of the surrounding gardens. Upstairs, rooms and suites are simple but sophisticated, with colorful accent walls, sleek furniture, and lamps that glow at just the right tone for reading in bed after a day of wine tasting. Suites have extras like separate lounge space, balconies, and the largest suite has its own hammam and private garden. 

It’s a quick trip downstairs to Arnaud Lallement’s famed restaurant, and an elegant breakfast buffet is served overlooking the gardens. At any time of day, guests are welcome to sip Champagne — included with every room, naturally — on a lovely pergola-shaded patio or, in winter, by a crackling fire in one of several inviting living rooms.

content:
The Austrian Alps are home to no end of traditional mountain lodges, many of them very fine indeed. But other forms are possible, even in these storied landscapes. The Mariazellerland, in northern Styria, roughly equidistant from Vienna and Graz, is as spectacular as any region in the Alps — and in the Hideaway Hotel Montestyria Mariazell Chalets & Suiten it’s got a hotel that dares to depart from the Alpine-lodge norm, to impressive results.

As its full name suggests, the hotel is made up of a small collection of chalets, six in number, plus an additional two suites in the main house. Their modern construction leaves them free to explore modern interiors, and inside you’ll find a hybrid of boutique-influenced contemporary design and classic Alpine materials — crisp, clean lines and minimalist colors, but also warm textures of knotted pine.

The chalets come with kitchens, and breakfast is delivered; there is, however, a central restaurant and bar where guests gather. A heated pool offers relaxation, as does the bathing jetty, which offers access to the lake. And while you’re immersed in nature — hikes and ski tours begin right at your doorstep — you’re right on the edge of the picturesque town of Mariazell, within walking distance of all the sights.

content:
Though there’s still more than a hint of colonial history about the place — the FCC group is named for the Foreign Correspondents Club in Phnom Penh, and this chapter, in Siem Reap, is housed in the old French Governor’s residence — the FCC Angkor is anything but fixated on the past. Behind the walls of this Indochina Art Deco mansion is a sophisticated high-design boutique hotel, made of simple modern materials and decorated in a sedate contemporary-Eastern style, far indeed from the conventional picture of the colonial luxury hotel.

Guest rooms look out over either the orderly gardens of the old French mansion or the hotel’s stunning centerpiece, a black-bottomed salt-water swimming pool. Interiors are dark and masculine, minimal, outfitted in hardwoods and Cambodian silks, with palatial bathrooms built around heavy stone tubs. Flat-screen televisions and high-speed internet access are standard, another sign of progress since the colonial days.

There’s an excellent modern-Cambodian restaurant, a stylish cocktail bar complete with billiards table, and even a small spa offering massages and bath treatments. And there’s plenty to do outside the hotel’s doors — the location is central for exploring Siem Reap, and should all this modern minimalism get you down, the temple at Angkor Wat is close by enough for an easy day trip.

content: Between Narbonne and the Mediterranean Sea, in a lesser-visited part of the south of France, there’s a natural area full of vineyards and lagoons. It’s here, on an expansive estate with no neighbors in sight, that you’ll find Château l’Hospitalet Wine Resort. A rarity in a region where the land is protected and the vast majority of hotels are located in the city or on the beach, its existence is justified by its historic status. Château l’Hospitalet, once an 11th-century hospital, is now a boutique hotel with a vineyard-framed swimming pool, a spa, a high-end restaurant, a working winery, and scenic grounds to explore, glass in hand. \n\nSome rooms and suites are housed in the original château, and the rest are in adjacent buildings fashioned out of the remains of an ancient winery. The aesthetic is elegant and minimalist, the sun-bathed interiors done up in an earthy color palette with crisp white cotton linens, wood furnishings, and parquet or travertine marble flooring. Modern bathrooms have walk-in showers and organic products, and in suites, feature freestanding tubs and oversized double vanities. Suites in the newer buildings also come with large private terraces overlooking the vineyards or the sea. Touring the winery is a must, as is a tasting in the cellar, though another of Château l’Hospitalet’s highlights is off the property — the luxurious beach club, open seasonally, just a few miles down the road.

content:
Tucked away amid scenic rice paddies on the outskirts of town, Kappa Senses Ubud is both literally and figuratively immersed in Balinese culture. The resort, like several others in the area, embraces an eco-friendly philosophy while delivering unabashed luxury — the kind of place with a strict recycling program and an ultra-modern spa, solar paneling and private infinity pools, and a vast organic garden and farm that sources ingredients for the hotel’s gourmet restaurants and bars, which are unironically referred to as Epicurean Nests. 

Suites and villas embody the same mix of high-end and down-to-earth, with airy indoor-outdoor layouts and built-in four-poster beds made of locally sourced wood and draped in elegant white mosquito netting. The comforts grow increasingly lavish in higher-level villas with freestanding tubs, private pools, and wide outdoor daybeds, but all rooms have soothing views over the surrounding rice fields or the jungle.

The resort’s two pools are pleasingly contrasting, with one featuring an infinity edge and the other lazy river-style with a poolside bungalow serving cocktails. It’s one of several venues where guests are invited to sip drinks and graze on creative Balinese dishes throughout the day and evening. The sleek spa complex, with a fitness center, hammam, yoga deck, and relaxation lounge with tea service, is a five-star attraction; unsurprisingly, many of the spa’s essential oils were made with the garden’s herbs. But what sets this hotel apart is its integration with the local community. Kappa Senses Ubud is more than a place to stay: the resort offers a wide range of cultural experiences both on- and off-site, from farm tours to temple visits to market trips and Balinese cooking classes. And the resort’s relationship with the place isn’t just for show — half of the garden’s bounty is given directly to families in the village.

content:
The word “agora,” before it came to denote the sort of place where ideas are exchanged, once simply meant “market” — a place where the exchange was a bit more literal. Similarly, the building that houses Agora Hotel was once Pano Lefkara’s central market — though the Danish creators of this chic adults-only boutique hotel won’t mind if that loftier connotation comes to mind as well.

Its owners were also its designers, which is impressive given that they came to the project from other professions. It would be reductive to call the resulting style a Danish-Mediterranean hybrid, but it also wouldn’t be far from the truth — what elevates it from this formulaic description is the uniqueness of the design decisions, and the care taken with every detail.

With just fifteen rooms and three suites, it’s not a large hotel, but it’s substantial enough to feel lively and convivial. Guests gather at Novél, the hotel’s all-day Mediterranea bistro, and the adjoining bar; in the daytime, they also lounge around the salt-water courtyard pool. From here the whole of the village, famous for its lace and for its photogenic blue doors, is no more than a few minutes away on foot.

content: You wouldn’t guess it at first — this triangular Haussmannian-style building in the 8th arrondissement dates back to the early 1900s, and the wrought-iron marquise framing the entry is a reminder of days gone by — but the Hôtel Florida is almost entirely new inside. The Parisian architecture firm Liautard and the Queen worked hard to strike the perfect balance between vintage charm and modern glamour, revitalizing the landmark’s interiors with walnut wood paneling, Art Deco furnishings, and fanciful tropical-print wallpaper. Rooms are cool and quirky, with retro carpets and animal print armchairs, and bathrooms have olive-green or chocolate-brown tile, marble fittings, and products by Maison Dyptique. A chic restaurant and wine bar add an air of liveliness that’s well-suited to the central location: the Champs-Elysées and the Louvre are just a short stroll away.

content: In Lisbon’s oldest neighborhood, a medieval arch connects the riverfront square Campo das Cebolas and the busy blocks around the cathedral. Built by ancient Romans, the passageway is even older than the surrounding building, a 12th-century landmark with a cheerful yellow Pombaline-style façade — and all of it, after extensive restorations, is part of AlmaLusa Alfama. This boutique hotel is the third offering from Almalusa, a Portuguese brand devoted to rescuing historic structures and turning them into stylish contemporary hotels. \n\nGreat care was taken to preserve the building’s old-world charm, especially on the ground level, with its curving glass panels, original woodwork, and the all-day Delfina Café, featuring pale exposed-brick walls, rustic beamed ceilings, and tables that spill out onto the plaza. Rooms are light-filled and modern, outfitted in white and earth tones with delicate botanical murals, while sleek bathrooms are tiled in black and white. Nearly every detail, from high-end mattresses and luxurious cotton linens to fragrant Benamôr bath products, is Portuguese-made. Smaller rooms face the cathedral or an interior courtyard, while suites have views over the Tagus River. There’s no pool or spa, but you won’t miss it; when it comes to exploring Lisbon’s quaint side streets, shops, and cafés, it’s hard to beat the perfect location.

content:
The Napa and Sonoma valleys are iconic travel destinations, and for good reason. Santa Rosa is a different side of the California wine country, presenting a more urban aspect, but with access to all the phenomenal wineries and restaurants that make the Sonoma Valley what it is. The Astro Motel is an authentic 1963 motor lodge, with its finest mid-century attributes still in place; like so many great American motels, it’s since been renovated into something much more than its original incarnation.

This means not just preserving or restoring its existing mid-century Modernist aspects, but adding more period-specific furnishings and artworks, as well as contemporary pieces that fit the aesthetic. In its comforts, it’s an upgrade from the motel days as well, a proper boutique hotel; much of the original parking lot is now a garden, while the rooms range more widely in size than ordinary motel rooms, and conveniences like kitchenettes are welcome additions.

A fleet of bikes makes getting around Santa Rosa and its surrounding trails a breeze. And while the Astro lacks an on-site restaurant, its owners are also responsible for the nearby Spinster Sisters, a highly regarded New American eatery.

content:
The village of Eressos, on the Greek island of Lesvos, is most famous for having been the birthplace of the poet Sappho. Tourism, here, is perhaps of less concern than it is in, say, the Cyclades. But the Eressian Hotel & Hammam Spa is every bit the equal of its counterparts elsewhere in the Aegean; from design to setting to comforts, it’s an extraordinary hotel offering a first-rate experience.

It’s set in an 1850s mansion, one whose style is rather more classical and colorful than the Greek-island norm, and whose windows look out over the ruggedly beautiful landscapes of the southwestern corner of the island. With just two rooms and two suites it feels more like a private residence than a boutique hotel; the pool deck, with its pint-sized swimming pool, never feels busy — the whole villa can be booked by a single party, and sleeps up to ten.

For such a small hotel, it’s got a fairly elaborate spa program, with offerings ranging from self-directed baths to full-scale hammam and massage treatments. Breakfast is the extent of the in-house food and beverage program, but it’s an impressive one, and for lunch and dinner Eressos’s restaurants are at your disposal.

content:
It’s been a long time since the storied seaside town of Asbury Park was as uncomplicatedly pleasant as it is today, and the Asbury Hotel, a block from the famous boardwalk, aims to weave together the Jersey Shore’s Victorian-era history, its more recent rock-and-roll reputation, and the straightforward beachy fun that any seaside town aspires to. 

The building is a distinctive one, a red brick 1950s structure that once housed the Salvation Army. A mid-century modernist-inspired graphic sensibility marks its interiors, from the typical double rooms all the way up to its Quad and Octo floor plans, for families, rock bands, and/or entourages. The comforts are simple but modern and more than adequate, and the artwork throughout is an homage to the 20th-century heyday of the Jersey Shore.

Meanwhile the Asbury’s Soundbooth bar also operates as a café and a music venue, and one of its two rooftop lounges doubles as an open-air cinema — and, in the warmer months, look for a beer garden and food trucks. Next door, the Asbury Lanes bowling alley comes complete with its own classic diner, and it probably goes without saying that Asbury Park is home to no end of other dining and drinking options.

content: On its face, Trancoso isn’t very different from any of the other charming coastal villages in the northeastern state of Bahia, Brazil. It just happens to be the one that A-list celebrities have heard about. Beyoncé, Leonardo di Caprio, and Diane von Furstenberg, to name just a few, have all vacationed here in recent years, but the village still feels surprisingly traditional. A tiny church sits on the central quadrado, on a cliff high above the ocean. By day, it’s quiet, save for a few kids kicking around a soccer ball; a wooded path leads downhill to the beaches, where you’ll find Hotel Villas de Trancoso. Like the village itself, it retains a thoroughly relaxed, low-key feel — a quality that predates, and will surely survive, the current parade of actresses and rock stars who name Trancoso as a favorite getaway. In fact, to understand the appeal of the place, it’s better to forget about the celebrities altogether and consider what makes this part of Brazil so appealing in the first place. Hotel Villas de Trancoso, like the town itself, is secluded, down-to-earth, effortlessly stylish. Unlike some of the competition, it’s outside of town, close to the white sandy beaches for which Bahia is famous. Though there are a handful of suites, most of the hotel’s guest rooms are housed within independent villas. The aesthetic might be called tropical Brazilian chic: high wood-beamed ceilings, four-poster beds with romantic (and practical) mosquito netting, white drapery, verandas facing lush green gardens. Standard amenities include 42-inch flatscreen TVs, bathrooms with waterfall showers and products by L’Occitane, iPhone docks, and hammocks. Villas also feature two-story layouts, skylights, Jacuzzis, and separate dining areas. Not that you’ll need your own dining space when such a world-class breakfast is served each morning in the open-air restaurant. Here’s another thing northeastern Brazil is famous for: lavish but laid-back breakfast spreads featuring exotic fresh-squeezed fruit juices and a variety of freshly baked pastries and savory regional dishes. As the day rolls on, the same space doubles as a beach bar, and later, a fine dining venue. You can also order lunch (or a couple of caipirinhas) while lying in a lounge chair on the hotel’s exquisite private beach, or relaxing beside the white marble swimming pool, a family of monkeys playing in the treetops overhead. At night, thousands of tiny lights illuminate the tropical foliage, adding extra magic to an already memorable seaside landscape. It’s an idyllic place, regardless of who’s in town — and part of the charm here is that you won’t know, or much care, who else might be around. How to get there: Hotel Villas de Trancoso is located approximately 71 km by car from Porto Seguro Airport via BR-367 and Estr. Trancoso. Please note: Hotel Villas de Trancoso has a 4 night minimum stay requirement.

Local materials and bespoke furnishings immerse guests in a rich visual language, where every surface reflects the soul of the Pacific, grounded in place and purpose.

content: Named after the patron saint of wine, this boutique bolthole sits amid Tuscany's vineyards with panoramic views that hypnotize. The former 18th-century farmstead houses rooms cleverly named after bottle sizes, from Jeroboam studios to the sprawling Nebuchadnezzar suite. Cypress-shaded poolside loungers invite languorous afternoons after cycling to nearby wineries or exploring medieval Montepulciano's cobbled streets. Days here are filled with long vineyard lunches and sunset toasts with a glass of Vino Nobile in hand.

content:
There’s still much to love about Bali, but in some ways the Indonesian island of Sumba feels like turning back the clock — this island paradise is hardly developed at all, compared to its more famous sibling, which lends it a diamond-in-the-rough quality and makes its finest hotels all the more impressive. Among them is Cap Karoso, a truly inspired boutique-style resort created by a French couple who fell in love with the place and decided to settle there permanently.

Its modernist architecture sets a stylish tone, and it’s harmoniously contrasted with indigenous Sumbanese design and construction. In fact the whole operation seamlessly (and respectfully) blends an international sensibility and a strong contemporary design sense with local crafts, culture, and excursions. The studios and suites are chic and spacious, and the villas are downright palatial, and come complete with private pools.

The cooking is French, as is chef Antoine LeVacon, but it’s local as well — the hotel’s own farm supplies many of the ingredients. And the hotel’s smaller restaurant, Julang, is something special: an ever-evolving program that brings top French chefs to the island for a short residency and a series of chef’s table–style dinners.

content: The Austrian alpine resort town of Bad Gastein was once among Europe’s most exclusive destinations — and after a period out of the limelight it’s in the middle of a kind of renaissance. Emblematic of this new era is the Cōmodo, a mid-century hotel refurbished for a hip new generation of mountain travelers, taking its stylistic inspiration from Sixties modernism and classic Art Deco. The spa puts the local spring water to therapeutic use, and the restaurant and bar will be familiar to visitors accustomed to urban boutique hotels: farm-to-table cooking, small-batch wines, and inventive craft cocktails.

content:
There are flashier Caribbean destinations, but the tranquil charms of Grenada are perfectly embodied in this family-owned and -operated hotel. When its current owners took over in 1987, Calabash was already, in some ways, a luxury boutique hotel, even before the world had the phrase to describe the concept. And now, some decades on, it’s evolved with the times, but gently; it might be more accurate to say that the rest of the world has caught on to the idea of luxury hospitality on a modest, human scale.

In practical terms this means a mere 30 suites, spanning at least 565 square feet and furnished with comforts both high-tech and low, from Amazon Echo smart speakers to Elemis bath products. Some have plunge pools, some have hot tubs, and many have views of the sea. And the style is subtle, but noteworthy: it’s clearly Caribbean in the colonial lineage, with no pretensions to urban minimalism, but it steers equally clear of island kitsch. In a word: tasteful.

In fact, that might be the word that best sums up Calabash’s appeal. There’s a spa, a gym, and a yoga program, as well as an infinity pool in the garden, and the white sand beach is just yards away. The beach is home to one of the casual restaurants, the other being poolside — and in the evening, the more formal Rhodes restaurant and piano lounge is a charming throwback, complete with dress code.

content:
The house at 21 Broad Street has always stood out, a lively, ornate Victorian in a town that’s dominated by a slightly austere Federal style. But now, 21 Broad is even better known for its interiors, which update this 19th-century inn for 21st-century travelers who’ve grown to expect a healthy dose of modern design.

That involved much more than just a fresh coat of paint. The restoration was entirely historically correct, architecturally speaking, right down to the plasterwork, which followed the original 19th-century recipe. But the interior design, by the Boston-based Rachel Reider, is contemporary, overlaying a modernist influence on the old house’s Victorian vibe.

There’s also more than a little bit of maritime atmosphere, which is fitting, given the setting. The rooms are fairly cozy, as you’d expect from an inn of 21 Broad’s heritage, but the comforts are high-end. And while breakfast is the extent of the hotel’s food service, it’s a fine one — and thanks to a location right in the heart of town, you’ve got no shortage of options for lunch and dinner.

content: Perfectly positioned midway between two of Florence’s iconic landmarks — the Duomo and the Basilica of Santa Maria Novella — Casa G Firenze is a gem of a boutique hotel housed in a restored 18th-century palazzo. It was once the home of Carlo Lorenzini, author of Pinocchio, and plenty of period character remains in the villa’s beautifully restored frescoes, white stucco ceilings, and original wood flooring. Rooms are cozy and elegant with vintage pieces like writing desks and old-fashioned bathtubs, while high-ceilinged suites, occupying the former dining room and ballroom, offer two levels of living space. Guests have round-the-clock access to various living rooms, including one with a marble honesty bar and plush armchairs, and a pair of plant-filled patios.

content:
The name doesn’t quite do justice to a hotel that takes an unusual late-modernist structure in Fiorano Modenese — the home of Ferrari, among other attractions in Italy’s so-called Motor Valley — and transforms it into an ultra-stylish, ultra-contemporary boutique hospitality experience. Executive Spa Hotel’s 1980s silhouette seems built for speed, but inside, it’s a state-of-the-art hotel whose 64 rooms showcase the finest fixtures and furnishings from today’s top Italian makers.

Its interior design and its art collection evoke an idealized vision of modernism’s Fifties heyday, though viewed through a contemporary lens — the finishes and materials are substantial, even serious, while the colors, though subtle, are unmistakably 21st-century. The rooms aren’t vast, but are spacious enough, and are efficiently laid out and supplied with plentiful natural light. Suites, on the other hand, do spread out, and the largest ones feature walk-in closets and balconies.

The spa lives up to its billing, and is accompanied by a gym that includes yoga, Pilates, and personal training. Exé, the restaurant, serves the sort of artful contemporary Italian cuisine that you have every right to expect, when in Emilia-Romagna; Alto, meanwhile, serves lighter fare on the rooftop with an impressively far-ranging view.

content:
Ovolo Nishi occupies three floors of the mixed-use Nishi building, which is by some distance the most memorable landmark in Canberra’s emerging cultural district of New Acton. The building is also home to an impressive contemporary art gallery, a bike shop, a pilates studio, a spa, and an art-house cinema — which is the long way of saying it’s the perfect location for what has to be the hippest hotel in town.

The rooms go all-in on organic warmth, full of reclaimed wood, roughly textured concrete, and restored vintage furniture. And though they don’t beat you over the head with ostentatious opulence, they’re luxurious as well — plush beds, proper linens, Aesop products in the bathrooms. The hotel’s social life is a lively one, taking advantage of all of Nishi’s attractions, which include a café, a couple of bars, and a small handful of restaurants. We’d go so far as to say every city could use something like this — and if you’re still thinking of Canberra as a sleepy government town, this will be the hotel that changes your mind.

content:
The regal corner building that houses the Amauris Vienna, with its scrubbed white facade, cheerful red roof, and perfectly symmetrical rows of windows, looks more than a little bit like a Wes Anderson production. This impeccable exterior is well-suited to a city where appearances matter, especially at an address as prominent as this one, just around the corner from the opera on the busy Ringstrasse. 

The refined interiors live up to the exterior impression. Once a noble residence, this 19th-century building retains much of its historical grandeur — high ceilings and hardwood flooring, coffered walls and glittering chandeliers — but recent updates have given the place a breath of fresh air, stripping back heavier materials and colors in favor of sleek marble, jewel-toned velvet, and a modern, mostly monochromatic palette of slate gray and bright white. Even the simplest room, an attic-like single overlooking the quiet courtyard, features heated floors, high-end Italian linens, a marble bathroom, and an Illy espresso machine. On the upper end of the spectrum, ultra-spacious suites are more like luxury apartments, sumptuously outfitted in Viennese style, with marble busts and artwork in gilded frames, chic lounge space, and extras like walk-in closets and well-stocked bars. 

A ride down the quaint original elevator leads to a serene spa with a glass-roofed swimming pool. Also on the ground level is a sophisticated but whimsical bar and bistro with emerald-green banquettes and Austrian sparkling wines served in delicate glassware. A more formal restaurant provides another dining option, but on a sunny day — including in winter, when outdoor heaters warm up the space — it’s hard to beat the people-watching from the bistro’s sidewalk tables.

content:
For proof that the boutique-hotel revolution has conquered the world, you need look no further than this: a proper luxury boutique hotel in the Azerbaijani capital, the Merchant Baku makes its home in a stately 19th-century building that was once the headquarters of the Caspian Shipping Company, at the heart of the city’s historic district and just a couple of streets over from Baku Boulevard, the seaside promenade.

Guest rooms are genuinely spacious, with high ceilings, plentiful sunlight, and the full complement of modern hotel comforts, from rain showers and separate bathtubs to digital newspapers via Press Reader. Suites add balconies with city views, and in all categories the style is a handsome one, unmistakably Azerbaijani but thoroughly contemporary.

The Merchant’s restaurant makes much of the city’s Silk Road associations, and serves a modern local cuisine informed by disparate influences from both East and West, while the bar features a thoughtfully composed cocktail menu and an expert staff of bartenders; in summer, the bar’s terrace just might be the hotel’s most pleasant space. And while the immediate neighborhood, the UNESCO-listed Old Town, is rich with history, you’re never far from the ultra-modern side (and the ultra-modern skyline) of this thriving regional capital.

content: Since its 2017 opening the Loren at Pink Beach has raised the bar for glamorous, contemporary luxury hospitality in Bermuda. Its modernist-inspired interiors invite comparisons with Miami Beach, but it’s got Pink Beach all to itself, and its surroundings are anything but urban. The suites and villas are stylish and substantial, with private terraces, Sferra linens, and freestanding tubs alongside walk-in rain showers. Similarly modern are the restaurants, from the seafood-focused Pink Beach Club to Marée, the elegant cocktail lounge. A Sisley spa and a capacious fitness center are complemented by two heated pools, one for families and one for toddlers — and the beach itself lies just beyond.

content: If there’s one place on earth where Divine Cave Experience is an entirely straightforward name for a hotel, it’s Santorini. In fact this hotel, set in Imerovigli on the island’s inner curve, goes even a bit further than most in pursuit of the archetypal underground lifestyle. Each of the hotel’s ten suites is carved directly into the rock, and frames a unique view of the caldera at Santorini’s center; some add Jacuzzis, either on an open-air terrace or at the opening of the cave. Another subterranean space is given over to the wellness area, while the restaurant and bar venture out onto the rooftop terrace, for the most wide-ranging views.

content: Le Fucine isn’t a typical wine-country getaway — but then again, Friuli, tucked away in Italy’s northeast near the borders of Austria and Slovenia, isn’t a typical wine region. Known as a producer of some of the country’s finest white wines, it’s little-visited compared to Tuscany or Piedmont, though it does have a handful of stylish new hotels — including the ultra-modern Le Fucine, in the vineyard-dotted hills of Buttrio.  \n\nLocated just off the highway to Udine, the property was once the site of a gas station, and the hotel’s sleek, low-lying buildings vaguely resemble an avant-garde service area. Inside, it’s more like a design museum, mixing sixties glamour with Scandinavian simplicity and alpine chalet-inspired elements. Rooms and suites are minimalist with floor-to-ceiling windows, pale wood floors, white walls, built-in bookshelves, and eye-catching lamps by Artemide. Pieces by Italian designers and artists appear throughout the hotel, including in the retro lounge, with its conical fireplace and wraparound conversation pit, and in the airy, light-filled restaurant, a destination in itself.

content: While only about an hour’s drive from Cabo San Lucas, Kimpton Mas Olas feels like it’s in the middle of nowhere. Wedged between the desert and the sea, this boutique resort sits on a large waterfront property on Baja’s coastline, its beautifully landscaped gardens stretching out toward the sand dunes and the dramatic silhouette of the Sierra de la Laguna mountain range. Indoor-outdoor living is the ideal in a setting as spectacular as this — and with its breezy design and gorgeous open-air spaces, the adults-only Kimpton Mas Olas nails the assignment.\n\nThe architecture is inspired by local tradition, with whitewashed, low-lying adobe buildings housing rooms and suites. Inside, they’re modern but down-to-earth, furnished with locally sourced materials including handmade ceramic tiles, native wood, and colorful textiles. Every room has a private terrace with a daybed, and while a few face the gardens, the majority offer sea views. Many have outdoor showers, private plunge pools, and roof decks, and villas come with larger infinity pools and firepits. With every amenity provided — four outdoor pools, a huge spa, three restaurants, a coffee shop, and an oceanfront bar — there’s no need to leave, and that’s precisely the idea.

content:
The Catskills aren’t what they used to be — neither the family-friendly summer resorts of their midcentury heyday or the near-forgotten version of a decade or two ago. These days, the Catskills, like many places in the Hudson Valley, are increasingly the playground of young New Yorkers anxious to get out of town for a few nights. And Scribner’s Catskill Lodge is ready to receive them, and anyone else who’s in the mood for a little fresh air and farm-to-table cuisine.

The lodge, which dates from 1966, was originally the passion project of an artist owner intent on creating a playful getaway. After extensive restorations, Scribner’s still has some of that retro charm. But the aesthetic and amenities are distinctly 21st-century: the Lodge’s 38 guest rooms, with built-in furniture and high vaulted wood ceilings painted bright white, feel more like urban lofts than cabins. Indeed, some have lofted sleeping spaces. All are lined with dark maple floors, made cozier by woven rugs, with terracotta tiles in the bathroom, in addition to rain showers and artisanal bath products. Some have fireplaces, too, a feature that’s especially desirable in ski season, as Scribner’s Catskill Lodge is within easy proximity of Hunter Mountain.

The Rounds, meanwhile, are an even more upscale option: a cluster of 11 luxury cabins a ten-minute walk from the Lodge, each one with a spacious circular living room, an outdoor soaking tub, and an oculus for stargazing.

To add to the appeal, Scribner’s Catskill Lodge is also within easy driving distance of New York City. That’s more or less the point. It’s easy to get to, but you’ll feel far enough away when you’re sunbathing or sipping cocktails on the cedar deck, or dining on Alpine-inspired cuisine — made with locally sourced meat and produce — in the hotel’s gourmet restaurant, where floor-to-ceiling windows showcased the forest-fringed hikes beyond. Scribner’s Catskill Lodge is your base camp for the weekend: from here, you can hike or ski, kayak or cycle, or just drink in the mountain views.

content:
Hōm Santorini calls itself a summerhouse, which is a rather modest term for this stylish twelve-suite hotel built right into the island’s cliffs. With a laid-back, footwear-optional, drinks-anytime vibe, it certainly embodies the homey charm of a friend’s vacation home. But the sleek design and panoramic ocean views from every room are a step above what a houseguest might reasonably expect — not to mention the striking swimming pool and a menu of modern Greek dishes, delicately portioned and exquisitely presented on stone plates.

The look mixes the elegance of ancient Greek architecture with a clean, contemporary aesthetic, the décor rendered in curving shapes and earthy hues inspired by sky and sea. Like many Santorini hotels, Hōm tumbles down a steep hillside, and the building’s form is somewhat dictated by the landscape. As a result, the hotel’s physical spaces are compact, including rooms and terraces that hug the cliffs and jut out over the water. Options run the range from double rooms with built-in wood furnishings and smooth concrete floors to the lavish master suite with its oversized marble bathroom and a spiral staircase leading to a private terrace with a plunge pool. Of particular note is the cave suite; as the name suggests, it’s carved into volcanic rock, and the room opens onto a small private patio with a hot tub. All rooms and suites have king-sized beds, Nespresso machines, eco-friendly Greek toiletries, sculptural lamps, and art objects that evoke Mediterranean antiquities. 

On a terrace facing the sea, gourmet Greek cuisine is served al fresco for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Some tables are set between an infinity pool and the ocean, perhaps disrupting the view for swimmers but offering diners the illusion of being suspended between two serene bodies of water. It’s a matter of personal preference whether the pool or an outdoor table is a superior venue for cocktails during the spectacular Santorini sunset.

content:
The West Midlands village of Hampton-in-Arden, a comfortable half-hour from Birmingham, is the setting for Hampton Manor, a stately Victorian-era house that once belonged to the family of Sir Robert Peel. Its exteriors remain lovingly preserved, while its interiors are a tribute to the Arts and Crafts Movement of the house’s early years; rather than keep it to themselves, Hampton Manor’s current family owners have opened it to paying guests as a country house hotel and a pair of noteworthy restaurants.

Many of the rooms and suites are set in the main house, including the most lavish suites; all are decorated with a thoughtful mix of antiques and complementary modern pieces. Meanwhile a stylistic counterpoint is provided by the Walled Garden suites, set on the site of the estate’s old timber yard. With their neutral colors, cast concrete baths, and floor-to-ceiling windows they’re possessed of a sort of chic coziness that’s almost Scandinavian in its simplicity — and guests in these suites are offered a chef-led tour of the gardens.

On that note: one fine restaurant is typically enough for a hotel like this, but Hampton Manor has two. The One-MICHELIN-Star Grace & Savour serves a seasonal tasting menu that celebrates impeccably sourced British cooking, and next door is the less formal and more rustic Kynd.

content:
Aman has roots in Thailand: the company’s very first property was a resort on Phuket. Now, more than three decades later, the brand offers a presence in Bangkok: like its urban counterparts in Tokyo and Venice, Aman Nai Lert Bangkok is every bit as lavish as the ultra-luxurious resorts that first put the brand on the map, with an extra measure of city-center chic. 

The location, for starters, is unbeatable: Aman Nai Lert occupies the first 19 stories of a 36-story tower rising above Nai Lert Park, one of the largest green spaces in the city’s busy downtown. The futuristic building features open-air terraces, a gorgeous infinity pool, and airy rooms with wraparound floor-to-ceiling windows revealing views of tropical gardens and the city skyline. 

Famed architect and designer Jean-Michel Gathy, the creative mind behind Aman New York and the Four Seasons Bangkok, oversaw the hotel’s designs, blending elements of traditional Thai style with Aman’s dramatic but minimalist aesthetic. From the sleek, spacious suites and state-of-the-art spa to a sultry jazz bar and several high-end restaurants, there’s plenty here to tempt resort-goers to spend time in the big city.

content: For nearly two centuries, Chania’s historic tanneries processed leather on a stretch of rocky shoreline outside town, far enough away that the smell wouldn’t bother the city’s residents. The old stone factories were largely abandoned after World War II, and though the district of Tabakaria is considered an architectural monument, it looked like a ghost town for years — until the Tanneries Hotel and Spa moved in. Seeing potential in the secluded waterfront location and its heritage-protected buildings, the owners transformed four connected tanneries into an industrial-chic boutique hotel with all rooms overlooking the Aegean Sea.\n\nPlenty of the buildings’ original character remains: their red roof tiles, high ceilings, exposed stone walls, and vaulted wood beams hold up particularly well. An antique  well is visible through a glass panel on the restaurant floor, and the old dyeing pits were converted into an outdoor pool and Jacuzzi. The interiors are minimalist, featuring lots of concrete and glass, blonde wood, and — of course — leather. Suites are quietly luxurious with built-in modular furnishings and travertine bathrooms. The main thing, whether in rooms with small balconies or two-level suites with fireplaces, Jacuzzis, and terraces, is the unobstructed ocean view. The same is true at the striking spa and at Periplous Seaside, the hotel’s stylish restaurant, where modern Cretan cuisine is served on a picturesque open-air terrace.

content:
The Singapore-based COMO Hotels and Resorts has been a global force in luxury hospitality since its first hotel, London’s Halkin, opened in 1991. But it would be more than three decades before the COMO name would hang above the door of a Singaporean hotel. With the COMO Orchard development, however, they’re making up for lost time — this 19-story tower gathers all of the COMO brands under one roof, from fashion retail to wellness to dining and, of course, luxury hospitality, in the form of COMO Metropolitan Singapore.

11 floors are given over to the hotel’s 156 rooms and suites, all of which are clean-lined and contemporary, furnished with high-end Italian furniture by Giorgetti. The designers are an international dream team: architect Paola Navone and interior designers Koichiro Ikebuchi and Preeti Sriratana. Their work, both in the accommodations and in the public spaces, lends the Metropolitan a cosmopolitan stylishness that places it among Singapore’s most attractive hotels.

It helps, of course, that it’s also the site of a COMO Shambhala spa, whose wellness offerings are first-rate. Two floors are reserved for Club 21, the fashion retailer whose selection includes a who’s-who of women’s wear and menswear brands. And among the restaurants on site is COTE Singapore, an outpost of Simon Kim’s Korean steakhouse, whose New York and Miami locations have been recognized with Michelin stars.

content:
In a place as pleasant as Mykonos, a hotel doesn’t need to confound expectations with some radically new form of hospitality. All it takes is a beachfront location, a keen eye for modern luxury, and a bit of tastefully forward-thinking design sense. It’s not as easy as it might sound, of course, but Mykonos Ammos is proof that it can be done — and that the result is a fine hotel indeed.

Here a series of low-slung whitewashed structures contain some 41 rooms and 9 suites, many of which look out over an orderly little beach at the waters of a sheltered bay. All of them are decorated in a soothingly minimalist monochrome style, and even the standard double rooms come with luxuries like Nespresso machines and 55-inch televisions. The suites come with extra space, naturally, both indoors and outdoors, and the most lavish of them are equipped with private hot tubs.

There’s a spa and a fitness center, as well as a fully serviced private beach club. And despite its smallish size, Mykonos Ammos is amply blessed in the restaurant department — here you’ll find an upscale Greek restaurant as well as an Italian trattoria, and with its sister hotel, the neighboring Mykonos Blanc, it shares Pasaji, a specializing in a fusion of Greek, Italian, and Asian flavors.

content:
The idea of a minimalist, modernist luxury resort in some idyllic Asian coastal locale isn’t a new one. But the success of a hotel like The Balé Phnom Penh depends less on the element of surprise and more on pure execution. And on that score this one, like its older sister in Bali, is just about faultless; the design achieves the Zen simplicity it’s aiming for, and the physical comforts of the place ensure that you’re never shaken out of the blissful state that the architecture has induced.

It starts from the dramatic arrival, over a stone walkway that seems to float above a black-bottomed pool. And it carries on in the suites, each of which spans a palatial 100 square meters, with views over a central courtyard or the waters of the Mekong River. Inside, the design is restrained, elegant, the focus on tactile pleasures and such prosaic charms as butler service and in-room espresso machines.

The restaurant provides contemporary updates on classic Khmer dishes, and they’re happy to share their knowledge — cooking classes begin with a trip to the local market followed by an intensive session back at The Balé. Meanwhile the spa and wellness center offer everything from traditional Khmer massage to personal-training sessions in the gym. And while you’re nominally in Phnom Penh, which makes travel a snap, the location, well outside the center of town, gives you a taste of a secluded idyll by the side of the Mekong river.

content:
Piedmont has plenty of attractive lodgings with vineyard views, but few on the level of Le Marne Relais. Set on the grounds of a winery in the UNESCO-listed landscape of Langhe and Monferrato, it’s made up of just fourteen rooms — some named for contemporary artworks, others for Piedmontese poets, while the treehouse-like Suspended House offers elevated views of the vineyards and the estate. 

The Beauty Exists suite, for example, references a poem by Gianmaria Testa, and has supple acacia wood floors, a freestanding soaking tub, and wraparound windows overlooking the rolling hills; the Stay Close suite, taking a cue from Alessandra Scandella’s fanciful Mother Nature illustrations, features a walk-in shower facing a lush private garden. 

The spa and wellness area features a 25-meter indoor pool, and food and wine are an area of particular focus: Radici, the restaurant, serves painstakingly locally sourced fare in the vault of the vineyard’s cellar, and wines from the estate’s Mura Mura label are in plentiful supply.

content:
Staying near Playa Guiones, one of Costa Rica’s most prized beaches, usually means checking into a traditional hotel or self-catering at a house rental. Silvestre Nosara Hotel & Residences offers the advantages of both, filling a gap identified by one of its British co-owners during an extended stay in the area a few years ago. This sustainably built boutique hotel is set slightly back from the beach, and each of its nine suites feels like a small house, with two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a fully equipped kitchen with a stocked refrigerator, and furnished outdoor space. 

But apart from slicing a mango for fruit salad or running a load of beach towels through the washer-dryer after a surfing class, guests don’t have to lift a finger. Silvestre Nosara has all the services of a hotel, from a delicious al fresco breakfast and a cool cocktail bar to an open-air gym and a rooftop infinity pool.

Inside and out, the look is modern and tropical, a mix of high-end and artisan-made: think luxurious modular sofas, woven hammocks, cheerful greenery, Marshall speakers, colorful artwork, creative light fixtures, and coffee tables crafted out of driftwood. The largest residence has a private garden with a dining table and a barbecue, but the others have spacious balconies, and it’s not uncommon to spot toucans in the trees from the residences’ airy living rooms. 

The Jim Banks high-performance surfboards included with each residence are not just for show: the hotel is near one of the best surf breaks in the country, and lessons can be booked via the surf concierge. Afterwards, retire to the rooftop for a swim and a smoothie, or venture down the street, where a range of bars, shops, and restaurants await.

content: Not far from Gallipoli, on the Salentine Peninsula, stands a 19th-century estate that’s now a luxury boutique hotel by the name of Il Giardino Grande - Dimora in Salento. There’s artwork everywhere, and each of the six rooms and suites marries period details like typically Puglian vaulted ceilings with modern Italian luxury design. The house is surrounded by gardens which contain a lovely swimming pool, next to which is a bar serving drinks and light fare.

content: On a remote stretch of land framed by ancient citrus and olive groves, not far from Sicily’s southern tip in the UNESCO-honored Val di Noto, a grandly appointed luxury hotel stands out from the region’s many agriturismi. Il San Corrado di Noto occupies a sprawling estate that was once a nobleman’s residence, and although painstaking renovation efforts have been made, the place still has a regal air, from the decorative entrance gates to the ivory-walled architecture to a pair of oversized aquamarine pools encircled by palm trees and generously spaced-out sunbeds. \n\nLow-lying buildings house Il San Corrado di Noto’s suites, all featuring polished hardwood floors, modern four-poster beds, and palatial bathrooms lined in travertine marble. Luxurious details include Frette linens, walk-in closets, custom furniture and doors crafted by local artisans, and plush indoor and outdoor seating areas. Private patios face one of the two pools, and a few suites have private pools, as do a collection of larger villas. A lavish Sicilian-style breakfast can be delivered to rooms or served in the hotel’s signature restaurant, Il Principe di Belludia, and a more casual osteria and bar offer additional options for lunch and spritzes by the pool. Rounding out the offerings are a state-of-the-art spa, complimentary bicycles, and a shuttle service to the private beach club, located about a 15-minute drive away, and open from June to September.

content:
Providenciales is no stranger to luxury hospitality, and Rock House fits in perfectly. A sister hotel to the well-loved Grace Bay, Rock House is named for its setting atop a 25-foot limestone cliff along the island’s North Shore. It’s a luxury boutique resort with a pronounced European accent — its white stone construction is reminiscent of certain Greek islands, and elsewhere the vibe recalls the Côte d’Azur or the Amalfi Coast.

The site spans 14 oceanfront acres, and includes a 350-foot stretch of idyllic beach as well as a jetty that extends 100 feet out to sea. Meanwhile the suites and villas line the ridge, and while they vary in size they’re uniformly both luxurious and stylish in a palette of light neutrals.

Some of the suites and all of the villas feature private pools, though the resort’s main pool is unsurpassed — to say nothing of the fully serviced beach club. Vita Restaurant is the resort’s culinary centerpiece, serving Italian fare with a Caribbean influence; more casual options are available by the poolside or on the beach. And the Cave Bar, with its stone walls and live DJ, is joined by the Sunset Bar, a quieter venue set atop the cliffside with views out into the Atlantic.

content:
Straight across Bellport Bay from the east end of Fire Island, 65 miles from Manhattan, is Bellport Village, a charming seaside town that’s home to — perhaps a theme is becoming apparent — the Bellport Inn. This lovely little estate is, in some ways, both a hotel and a vacation rental; in July and August the Main House, the adjoining Garden Suite, and the detached Cottage are each rented in their entirety, while during the rest of the year the Main House’s rooms are available individually.

In any permutation, the units are stylish, bright and bold, with an antique vibe enlivened by a contemporary sensibility, and comforts that you’ll recognize from your boutique-hotel travels. The outdoor spaces are a large part of the Inn’s appeal, from the main patio to the various gardens and lawns, furnished with fire pits and sun loungers.

Self-serve snacks are available, as is a selection of beers, wines, and spirits, all from local makers. There are bikes available to explore the town, and one of the best things about Bellport Village is actually a brief ferry ride across the sound — Ho Hum Beach, on Fire Island, is a gem, and is jealously guarded by Bellport residents during the height of the summer season.

content: CityCentre — a pedestrian-friendly district with high-end shopping, dining, and residences — is a twenty-minute drive to the west of downtown Houston. Its centerpiece, at least from a hospitality point of view, is the Moran Citycentre, a modern luxury hotel with an airy terrace bar and a spacious pool deck overlooking the community’s central park. \n\nRooms are sleek and tech-forward with parquet floors, sophisticated lighting systems, custom bar carts stocked with spirits made in Texas, and floor-to-ceiling windows; some face sweeping views of Houston’s skyline, others look out over open-air plazas and tree-shaded walkways. The on-site fitness center is state-of-the-art, and the hotel’s stylish café is popular for breakfast. Still, the idea here is that everything’s walkable: everything from a great cappuccino to a perfect margarita is a short stroll away in the neighborhood.

content:
“Backwater” is typically meant as a metaphor, and not a particularly kind one. But the Kerala backwaters are among the world’s minor natural wonders — this network of inland waterways along the southwest Indian coast makes for, if nothing else, a marvelous place to get lost. It’s here, on the shores of the eponymous lake, that the Malabar House group, the South Indian boutique concern with a predilection for small hotels named for abstract concepts, has opened Purity at Lake Vembanad.

Or reopened, perhaps. This strange white Italianate villa, backing up directly onto the lake’s shores, is only about a decade old, but it’s been given a thorough renovation by Malabar House. It’s split into four rooms and two suites, one of the latter comprising the villa’s whole upstairs floor — and if your Indian expedition is a large one, Purity is available in its entirety as a villa rental.

Backwater certainly doesn’t mean backwards. Purity comes equipped with wi-fi, flat-screen televisions, spa treatments, swimming pool and teaching kitchen. But the most memorable aspect of the Purity experience is bound to be the most low-tech one — by boat or by beach, the water is the main attraction, and dinner with the backwater as a backdrop is an experience you won’t soon forget.

How to get there: Purity at Lake Vembanad is located only 70 km from Cochin International airport and 8 km from the Alleppey railway station (on the mainline route between Trivandrum and Mumbai).

content:
Come summer, South American society types and European jetsetters flock to Punta del Este, the glitzy resort and mini-city by the sea where yachts outnumber fishing boats. But if for some reason rubbing shoulders with Argentine twentysomethings in designer swimwear isn’t your thing, don’t fret: you can experience the region’s natural glory from nearby Jose Ignacio, a relaxed beach village that’s home to a handful of cool restaurants and inns. The most desirable of the selection (at least judging by its popularity — the place is always booked months ahead of time) is La Posada del Faro. The twelve-room boutique, perched on a quiet stretch of sand, radiates laid-back sophistication and beachhouse-style warmth.

Three categories of guest rooms feature hardwood floors and minimalist décor in nature-inspired hues of cream, beige, and aquamarine. Though no two rooms are alike, standard accommodations offer garden views and wireless internet, while ‘Special’ rooms come with private terraces, fireplaces, and plush armchairs ideal for a post-swim siesta. Rattan furniture and wood-beamed ceilings lend a rustic quality to the beach getaway.

The hotel’s outdoor attractions include a self-serve pool bar — there’s no time like the present to perfect the art of mixing your own martini — and access to the gorgeous Playa La Mansa beach. You’ll want to venture off the property if you’re in the mood to explore the local beaches and dining scene. Posada del Faro, after all, serves a simple function — the hotel provides fashionable accommodations just far enough away from the bustle of Punta, meaning guests can take part in the area’s famed nightlife without sacrificing a little peace on the beach the morning after.
