content: Spain is well known for its wine, sherry, and cava, but the northwest coast, as it happens, is cider country. Set on a picturesque road that leads past apple orchards and cider mills, Hotel ARTIEM Asturias is a sophisticated escape just outside Gijón. It’s the first luxury-hotel offering from ARTIEM, a Spanish hospitality group that honed its style — a hybrid of healthy, high-end living and environmentally friendly practices — on Menorca. The formula works well here; the hotel doubles as a spa and wellness retreat with a state-of-the-art hydrotherapy circuit and an extensive menu of treatments for body and mind. \n\nThe design, with its clean lines and plentiful wood and glass, is both modern and classic. The sleek, airy lobby has high vaulted ceilings, cozy leather sofas, and huge picture windows overlooking the gardens and the Asturian countryside. Rooms and suites are elegant, silent, and designed for relaxation. The simplest have blonde wood floors, blackout blinds, wide beds made up in luxury linens, and stone-lined bathrooms with walk-in rainfall showers. Suites come with extras like private terraces and separate living areas, while attic rooms, though smaller, are especially charming with sloping timber ceilings. A health-conscious breakfast spread highlights local produce, and the hotel’s lounge, with its gleaming grand piano and glass-encased fireplace, is an inviting place to return to after a day out exploring beaches and cider houses.

content: Rethymno, on the north coast of Crete, is a small city, but it’s large enough to lend Nautilux something of a dual aspect: this is a proper beach resort with direct access to the Aegean, but it’s also a quick walk from the vibrant little town center. The spiral-shaped building puts to rest any concern that the hotel’s name wouldn’t be explored for all it’s worth. And in fact the architecture is distinctive beyond this broad shell-shaped gesture — inside and out it’s a lively mix of modern lines and warm textures, and feels authentically Greek without resorting to cliché.\n\nWith 118 rooms and suites, Nautilux is a proper resort, and offers a wide range of accommodations, from standard rooms, which are substantial enough, to expansive suites and even two-level Maisonettes, which come with hot tubs and direct sea views. There’s a well-equipped spa and fitness center which is no less impressively modern in its style, and the hotel’s beach club is augmented by a pair of picturesque outdoor swimming pools. And while the town has its share of restaurants and nightspots, Nautilux gives guests plenty of reasons to stay in, from the daytime pool bar and the main Spiral Bar to Ulivo, the hotel’s modern Greek eatery.

content:
There’s probably a dissertation to be written about Sri Lanka’s surfeit of sleek, modernist hotels and villas, but our instinct is to not inquire too deeply, lest we distract ourselves from the vital task of appreciating them. And Villa Sielen Diva, in the coastal village of Talpe, just outside Galle, is worth appreciating: a seven-room hotel built in an uncompromising modernist style but decorated by its family owners in a manner that evokes endless warmth and vibrance from its crisp edges and concrete surfaces.

Initially intended as a private home, it turned out to be too stunning not to share, and it now features a professional staff, as well as rooms and suites that combine the best aspects of a small luxury hotel and a personal residence. All seven units face out to sea, and though elevations and views vary, the full-length windows provide total immersion. Modern electronics and lavish bathrooms complete the package — though it’s visually restrained, this is an unapologetically luxe experience.

Public spaces include a 17-meter infinity pool surrounded by loungers and overlooked by a sun terrace, as well as a dining room that features dishes prepared by the hotel’s chefs from local produce and seafood. It’s another feather in the cap of a coastline that’s already amply blessed.

content: Not far outside Marrakech, on the road leading to the Atlas Mountains, an elegant Indo-Moorish villa rises up behind a row of palm trees. Keyhole-shaped doors lead past the coral-hued facade into a labyrinth of terracotta-lined passageways, cozy fireplace-warmed lounges, mosaic-lined dining rooms, and open-air courtyards — and then to magnificent gardens with a large olive tree-framed swimming pool and a pond dotted with floating water lilies. \n\nWhen Palais Hassoun isn’t rented out in its entirety, it’s possible to snag one of its nine rooms or suites for an overnight. Each is uniquely decorated with artisan-made details including carved wooden doors, ornamental lanterns, and colorful handcrafted rugs. Bathrooms are lined in rich green marble, each with a luxurious soaking tub, and many have large windows overlooking the grounds. A handful of suites, located directly off the hotel’s upper-level terrace, have wraparound nature views, decorative antique furniture, and private patios. The oasis-like central garden is the place to be during the day, preferably on a chaise longue by the pool, while the rooftop is the best spot to catch the sunset. But even on a rainy day, there’s much to explore and appreciate without leaving the property, including the palace’s impressive art collection and a library filled with travel books.

content: An abandoned tannery in a remote French village might not sound like the most obvious setting for a boutique hotel. But thanks to its location on the famous Santiago de Compostela pilgrimage route, the place was discovered by a pair of Parisians who spent four years overseeing its transformation into the elegant La Manufacture Royale de Lectoure. One part of the property is the Pilgrim Cottage, with simple accommodations for hikers, while the main hotel has five chic rooms characterized by sophisticated but subtle details. Co-owner Christèle, formerly a decorator and set designer, collaborated with colorists to design custom paint shades for the lime-washed walls, and rooms feature designer furnishings, vintage pieces, writing desks, and spacious bathrooms with tubs. Downstairs, the common spaces and gardens are just as aesthetically pleasing, and local delicacies are served for breakfast on ceramic dishes handmade in town.

content:
Le Domaine des Prés Verts & Spa started out with a single room, a treehouse-style suite overlooking the hills of Burgundy. In a little over a decade, this unusual luxury hotel has expanded to include an eclectic collection of lodgings across four locations in wine country. The owner is a youthful hotelier who studied at the Ecole Hôtelière de Paris before purchasing a large plot of land in Pochey to develop his passion project, going on to personally design all of the hotel’s indoor and outdoor spaces with a focus on relaxation and harmony with nature.

Pochey is still home to the original treehouse, which now features a terrace with a covered Jacuzzi that’s heated year-round — an amenity included in all of Le Domaine des Prés Verts & Spa’s rooms, alongside minibars stocked with organic treats and bath products made with pinot noir extracts — and as a handful of other suites, the spacious Le Studio with its own garden and wine cellar, and the hotel’s Le Cube spa. 

Across the board, the look is modern and rustic-chic with lots of exposed brick, natural stone, and local wood. In nearby Allerey is Le Refuge, a freestanding caravan-inspired suite surrounded by a quiet rural landscape. A few more luxurious suites are across the road in the medieval village of Châteauneuf, which is also where the hotel’s bistro and boutique are located; the northernmost site, Mont-Saint-Jean, is home to another sophisticated treehouse suite. And though there’s no single central gathering place in a hotel as spread out as this, it’s a fair trade for the uncommon degree of privacy.

content:
Set not on an island but on the Greek mainland, THE DANAI nevertheless offers everything you’d want from an Aegean holiday escape, set in Nikiti, on the Sithonian peninsula, just over an hour by car from Thessaloniki. The style, as you might expect, is rather more refined than what you’d find on the islands, and space is more plentiful here, which allows Danai Beach’s rooms, suites, and villas to spread out to exceedingly comfortable dimensions.

Suites, in fact, make up the bulk of the accommodations, and with comforts like Bulgari bath products and Nespresso machines — as well as outdoor terraces, marble bathrooms, and a minimum of 35 square meters of indoor space — they’re unmistakably high-end. The best ones feel like self-contained residences, and have direct views out to sea — but really there’s not a subpar room in the house.

There’s an impressive outdoor pool, and a second indoor pool in the spa; there’s also a private beach just a few steps down from the hotel’s terraces, furnished with loungers and umbrellas. Three restaurants range from the high-end French-Mediterranean Squirrel to the more expansive Andromeda and the casual Anithos Restaurant, and they’re joined by a truly vast wine cellar and the Philosophy Seaside Bar, named in tribute to Aristotle, who was born nearby but somehow found the discipline to turn from the idyllic beach to the life of the mind….

content:
Its Art Deco façade is as grand and elegant as can be, but from the moment you arrive at reception, flanked by bins full of comically oversized pencils, it’s clear that the Collège Hotel intends to go all the way with its back-to-school theme. Fortunately it’s handled with charm — and, lobby aside, a sense of subtlety and proportion — and the hotel’s location, in the stunning Vieux Lyon district, is just about perfect.

The public spaces are all warm, weathered comfort, with surfaces in worn wood and leather; rooms contrast starkly, in a minimalist, monochrome scheme. They’re simply furnished, but substantially more luxe than the student digs they’re meant to remind you of, with well-chosen design pieces — the version of modernism on display here is less stark and more humanistic and comfortable.

For many of us, the best thing about our school days was the abundance of social life. The Collège Hotel features plenty of spaces for guests to mingle, including a garden terrace and a number of meeting rooms and co-working spaces. Meanwhile Le Cantine serves a hearty breakfast, while Baràgones, a South American and Caribbean-inspired tapas bar, handles both drinks and dinner.

content: The Greek islands are deservedly popular for their luxurious waterfront hotels, but Amethyst Selene proves that equally appealing options exist on the mainland. Sophisticated but understated, with sweeping views of the Ionian Sea, the boutique hotel is located in a quiet village on the western coast. It takes its name from a gemstone known for its calming and healing properties, which is fitting: the architecture is characterized by clean lines, geometric shapes, and the use of organic materials, including local wood and stone. Floor-to-ceiling glass lets in abundant sunshine and panoramas of the surrounding seascape, green hills, and olive groves. And silence is golden — no children are allowed.\n\nEvery suite features a private ocean-facing terrace with an infinity plunge pool, plus outdoor steps leading down through landscaped gardens to a private spot on the beach below. Inside, they’re modern, minimalist, and outfitted in earth tones. Each has a teakwood bed with a natural mattress, a walk-in rain shower and a separate soaking tub, and a stocked kitchenette with a Nespresso machine. A lavish continental breakfast showcasing produce from the hotel’s own farm is served in-room each morning and ideally enjoyed poolside. Down by the marina, the owners also run a restaurant, the Yacht Club at Paleros Bay, that’s perhaps best appreciated at sunset.

content: Many Puglian masserie, or traditional fortified farmhouses, have been converted into hotels, and Secolario Masseria del Viverbene is among the finest examples. It’s set amid ancient olive groves in the Salento countryside, a region known for its production of cold-pressed olive oil. There’s a quiet sobriety to the property’s thick-walled limestone buildings, and they’ve been smartly refreshed inside, with their best features, from high vaulted ceilings to exposed wood beams, enhanced by elegant white and earth tones. In addition to custom stonework by the Portuguese architect Álvaro Siza, the gallery-like common spaces feature installations by an impressive array of international artists like Hidetoshi Nagasawa and Michelangelo Pistoletto.\n\nThe best rooms are ground-level suites with sliding glass doors opening directly into the surrounding gardens. But even the simplest rooms are silent and sophisticated with cool stone flooring, king-sized platform beds made up with cream-colored linens, artisan-made furnishings, and spacious bathrooms with oversized walk-in showers. Outside, local wines and olives are served beneath the shade of centuries-old trees, and fresh vegetables and herbs, grown in the nearby greenhouse, are the basis for Puglian dishes at the hotel’s restaurant, Volivo. The outdoor pool is particularly inviting after hiking or wine tasting nearby, and the hotel arranges boat trips departing from Otranto, a short drive away.

content:
86 Cannon Historic Inn is just about everything you could ask from a boutique hotel in Charleston, South Carolina: a well-preserved 1860s house updated with impeccably chic contemporary interiors (and a bit of a French accent), with a genteel residential calm that’s only fortified by its adults-only policy. The result is a lodging with all the amiable charm of a classic bed and breakfast and all the style of a proper luxury boutique hotel.

The rooms themselves differ in layout and details, though all are richly detailed and impressively plush, from the Loft King under the eaves of the old house to the Cottage Suite in the adjoining building. There’s no restaurant on site, but nor is there any shortage of food and drink — guests arrive to a champagne toast, there’s a daily happy hour featuring wine and cheese, and locally sourced breakfast items and snacks are available in the café and library.

Meanwhile the rest of the town is chock full of restaurants, bars, and other attractions — the neighborhood is close to the city center, and the fleet of loaner bikes make the city’s sights (and flavors) eminently accessible. (There’s also a daily wine-and-cheese hour, and a thoughtful breakfast is served in the house’s café.)

content:
The Modernist Thessaloniki takes its inspiration not from the classical world but from its immediate setting, a Twenties landmark close to the central Aristotelous Square. Inside you’ll find elements of the evolution of modernist design, from its precursors in Art Deco on through to Bauhaus and all the way to the present day.

Of course, this is no museum exhibit — what matters is how well it hangs together for guests, and the answer is: very well indeed. Rooms occupy a range of sensibly named categories, from Small on up through Extra Large to Family; all are chic in near-monochromes with occasional thoughtful (if sober) accents of color. And all, regardless of square footage, come with up-to-date comforts like espresso machines and Marshall Bluetooth speakers.

Breakfast is served amid the greenery of the rooftop garden, and there’s a small shop showcasing branded lifestyle products, as well as an informal art gallery. 

Just next door is a café serving light bites and lunch, and beyond that you’re at the mercy of the city — no hardship, given the Modernist’s position at the heart of urban Thessaloniki.

content:
Kahanda Kanda came first, a delightful little boutique hotel occupying a tea plantation by the side of Kogalla Lake, not far from the southern city of Galle. And KK Beach, while it’s certainly capable of standing on its own, is perhaps best thought of as a part of a pair — just fifteen minutes’ drive from Kahanda Kanda, KK Beach sits on the Indian Ocean seaside, overlooking a spectacular stretch of beach less than a half-hour from Galle Fort.

Like its sister, KK Beach is pocket-sized, weighing in at a mere ten rooms and suites. They range from a pair of spacious Deluxe Doubles, with impressive ocean views, to a pair of Penthouse Suites, spanning nearly a hundred square meters. At any size they’re stylishly contemporary even as they’re invitingly traditional, and the comforts are more than up to the task.

KK Beach and Kahanda Kanda are linked by a shuttle service, so you’re welcome to swap hotels for lunch or dinner — both have fine little restaurants serving Sri Lankan fare with a Thai influence. And while both hotels are well placed for tours of Galle Fort or the surrounding countryside, KK Beach’s main draw is (sensibly enough) the beach, as well as the surfing, diving, and sailing opportunities it entails.

content:
Think of a Mykonos luxury boutique hotel and it’s likely what you’re imagining bears a strong resemblance to the Mykonos Blanc Hotel. Set at one end of the picturesque south-facing Ornos Beach — a short walk from its sister hotel, the beachfront Mykonos Ammos Hotel — it’s a picture-perfect slice of Cycladic hospitality, a terraced village of whitewashed villas containing 42 minimalist-chic rooms and suites.

Many of them face out to sea, some more directly than others, but all partake in the same atmosphere of untroubled seaside tranquility. All come with outdoor space, whether it’s a balcony, a private patio, a plunge pool, or an outdoor hot tub. And while the honeymoon suites and the Blanc suites are the top of the line, even the relatively double standard rooms are swanky, stylish, and more than comfortable enough.

A spa, a boutique, and a gym round out the creature comforts, along with a swimming pool with a view of the beach. On site is Pasaji, a restaurant serving a fusion of Greek, Italian, and Asian cuisines; at the neighboring Mykonos Ammos you’ll find the upscale Mediterranean restaurant called Kuzina, as well as Farina, an Italian trattoria.

content:
Though it’s named, in a roundabout way, for Gothenburg itself — the city’s Swedish, Göteborg, simply means “the city by the Göta river” — the Hotel Riverton knows better than to try to represent the whole of the city all at once. Instead, like all the best boutique hotels, this family-owned gem presents a singular point of view, and offers an angle on the city that other hotels can’t match — both figuratively and quite literally, thanks to its waterfront setting.

The building is an unmistakably modern one, though certainly not without warmth, thanks to its red-brick industrial style. And the rooms and suites are even warmer, dressed in the rich textures of figured wood, faux fur, and velour. The tactile comforts are equally enticing, from the Dux beds to the Rituals bath products. And as you work your way up, your view gets bigger and bigger, culminating in the harbor panorama visible from the top-floor penthouse.

Of course it’s the open-air Skybar, on the 12th floor, that offers the finest view; despite it’s name it’s not just a bar but a restaurant as well. It’s joined by a ground-floor restaurant called One, as well as the lobby-adjacent Livingroom bar, and a spa and fitness center that wouldn’t look out of place in a much larger luxury hotel.

content:
This secluded corner of Halkidiki, on the Greek mainland, is home to Avaton Luxury Hotel & Villas, a surprisingly contemporary high-end boutique hotel on a hill above a stunning north-facing beach. The vibe is postmodern ultra-luxe, mixing clean lines and modern colors with ornate, classic French-style furniture, the ultimate upscale signifier. The rooms and suites are spacious and extremely well-equipped; some even come with private pools. 

A hotel doesn’t get to wear the Relais & Châteaux fleur de lis without a pretty impressive kitchen; here Avaton benefits from the work of chef Panos Papadopoulos, whose two restaurants put an artful spin on the bountiful classics of traditional Greek cooking. Meanwhile, the Champagne Bar awaits; there’s no better venue for an al fresco drink as the sun sets behind the peninsula.

Just a bit farther down the peninsula and you reach Mount Athos, a UNESCO World Heritage site, an Orthodox holy place, and a quasi-sovereign territory that, surprising as it may sound, admits only male visitors — all the more reason for a hotel like Avaton to offer a lavishly equipped wellness center for anyone left behind, as well as the option of a yacht cruise offering a less restrictive look at the monasteries.

content:
The region of Matarraña, in the countryside of eastern Aragon, is sometimes said to be Spain’s answer to Tuscany. You can see why, then, a luxury boutique hotel crafted from a 200-year-old farmhouse would be a great success here. Mas de la Costa is surrounded by gardens and groves of olives and almonds; in the distance, the peaks of the Els Ports de Beceite, along the border with Catalonia.

The rooms are a lively mix of antique elements — suites feature fireplaces, stone walls, and timbered ceilings, and all the bathrooms are finished with tiles hand-made in Granada — and contemporary touches, like modern furniture and Frette linens. There’s a salt-water pool for guests’ use during the summer, and a sauna and steam bath for colder seasons; and the surrounding countryside offers plenty of outdoor adventure, including some very fine biking and hiking as well as tours of the vineyards and villages of the Matarraña.

Another Italian connection: Mas de la Costa’s fine-dining restaurant is organized along Slow Food principles, and serves a modern and eclectic Mediterranean cuisine. There’s an honesty bar as well, set in the wine cellar and surrounded by bottles from Spain, France, Italy, and Argentina.

content: Just outside the village of Stowe on the edge of picturesque Cady Hill Forest, AWOL Stowe is a stylish addition to the mountain resort’s growing boutique hotel scene. It’s unabashedly hip, the kind of place with an artisanal toast bar, tabletop s’mores service, and a cold plunge pool, though noticeably livelier after dark — thanks to the location, it empties out during the day, with guests out skiing, hiking, or trying to photograph the region’s famously dazzling fall foliage.\n\nRooms are quiet, minimalist, and outfitted in natural materials and earthy hues. The simplest suites have king-sized platform beds, cozy living rooms, private patios facing the woods, and thoughtful amenities from plush throw blankets and La Bottega bath products to proper wine glasses. Larger suites feature wood-burning fireplaces and fully equipped kitchens, while wooden A-frame cabins, with knotty pine walls and private porches, have a rustic-chic feel. While there’s no formal restaurant, AWOL serves craft cocktails and charcuterie boards all day, and inviting communal spaces include a library, open-air fire pits, and a courtyard terrace with a cedar hot tub that’s ideal for a post-adventure soak.

content:
Set neither in the coastal hotel zone nor the busy town center, Muaré Tulum makes its home in the hip, largely residential district of La Veleta. From within its grounds, however, you might as well be deep in the jungle — the setting is lush and verdant, and the grounds are dotted with plunge pools in addition to a winding, lagoon-like main pool.

Muaré’s structures, meanwhile, are crafted in a style that marries modern design and traditional Mayan architecture, and the materials throughout are low-tech and organic, lending a hand-crafted warmth to the hotel’s clean lines. Every villa opens onto a private garden with its own plunge pool.

Gaudea, the restaurant, marries Mediterranean and Mexican flavors, and the bar takes an inventive approach to the classic local spirits. And despite the hotel’s relatively sedate setting, it’s close enough to the beaches, the ruins, and everything else you came to Tulum to see.

content: On the outskirts of Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, discreetly hidden amid 37 acres of parkland and lush gardens, is a 16th-century bastide that’s been transformed into a small and luxurious 19-room escape. That alone is tempting enough, but it’s made more so by some of the names involved: Domaine de Chalamon is the work of Les Domaines de Fontenille, the group responsible for at least half a dozen of France’s finest country hotels. And the architect, Alexandre Lafourcade, has a personal connection to the old bastide — not only did his father, also an architect, work on a previous renovation, but his mother designed the extraordinary 15 acres of gardens.\n\nIt’s a labor of love, clearly, which is evident in the smallest details. The rooms are marked by a contemporary simplicity and a classic atmosphere, and combine the charm of a bedroom in a historical residence with the comfort of a modern hotel room. There’s a heated outdoor pool as well as a tennis court, and the grounds invite lounging and rambling. And while there’s no restaurant on site, a daily breakfast is served, as are the Domaine’s wines; meanwhile all of Saint-Rémy-de-Provence lies mere minutes away.

content: Eco-hotels may be most at home in the countryside, but the future of urban hotels is green as well. The Hotel Britomart, on the Auckland waterfront, shows the way: its handmade bricks and salvaged wood aren’t just sustainable but radiate organic warmth, and the interior style may be understated, but it never feels austere. Nor is there any sense of deprivation involved in minimizing the hotel’s environmental footprint — this is a properly luxurious boutique hotel, and one that’s rich with memorable detail.\n\nThe rooms, therefore, are as luxe as they are stylish, and the suites can rightly be described as lavish. The waterfront location makes for impressive views of both the skyline and the harbor. Meanwhile the hotel’s public spaces, as elegant as they are, feel delightfully lived-in, from the collection of rooms known as The Libraries for lounging or private dining to kingi, an all-day restaurant with a focus on sustainability, housed in a beautiful industrial-style space.

content: Ideally located midway between Bolzano and the Alpe di Siusi, Presulis Hideaway Apartments & Restaurant is peaceful, sophisticated, and surrounded by beautiful landscapes — just what you’d want on a getaway to Italy’s South Tyrol. It’s the passion project of a local couple who turned an old farmhouse into an elegant boutique hotel focused on the art of slow living. There’s easy access to hiking and skiing, and it’s a pleasure returning to the alpine chalet with its sunny gardens, an infinity pool heated year-round, and a restaurant with panoramic views of nearby Prösels Castle. Pale wood-lined rooms are more like apartments, with well-equipped kitchens, living rooms, and private patios, many facing the Dolomites.

content: You can find anything your heart desires in Bangkok’s diverse Sukhumvit neighborhood:  Korean restaurants, Indian tea shops, Cuban bars, even British-style boutique hotels. To be fair, chicken satay is served by the saltwater pool, and Thai DJs spin records on weekends at Public House Bangkok; but the social atmosphere and mid-century modern aesthetic feel remarkably like London or New York. Rooms and suites are compact and cool with parquet floors, eclectic modern art, Nespresso machines, and vintage-styled bathrooms lined in subway tile. But as the name suggests, it’s the hotel’s hip common spaces that set it apart, including a colorful co-working area, a podcast lounge, an all-day café and bar serving comfort food from an open kitchen, and a lively rooftop bar with views of the city skyline.

content: Strategically located in the Mediterranean, Menorca has a rich military history, and in recent years, some of the island’s castles and fortresses have been turned into hotels. Cap Menorca Relais & Chateaux is a rare example of a hotel built on a former military base. High on a cliff over the sea, on a remote, pine-forested stretch of Menorca’s southern coastline, the setting is spectacular — and the hotel’s designers have transformed the place into an idyllic getaway, turning the dusty grounds into tropical gardens and the old military buildings into luxury suites with private saltwater pools.\n\nInside and out, the look is inspired by the simplicity of the island’s whitewashed villages. The interiors are airy, high-ceilinged, and charmingly rustic-chic, furnished with natural and local materials including terracotta, marble, teak, and leather. Each has a spacious, sun-drenched bathroom lined with emerald-green tile, and suites open onto private stone-walled gardens with pools. Not plunge pools, either, but pools large enough to swim in, bordered by native plants and olive trees, with small decks, chaise longues, and sun umbrellas. Breakfast, dinner, and everything in between can be served poolside or in the hotel’s restaurant. Horseback riding on the cliffs, or cruising the coast on one of Cap Menorca’s yachts, are both worth the effort of venturing off the property.

content: Just inside the ancient city walls that encircle Antalya’s old town, Casa Sur is a beautifully realized retro-modern boutique hotel. Each of its fourteen rooms blends contemporary colors and design with antique elements and one-of-a-kind objects.The result is unique in the most literal sense of the word, but is also notable for the way it prizes character and personality above the ostentatious luxury you’ll find in so many of the region’s bigger, brasher hotels.\n\nEvery room is different; in some, rough-hewn stone walls dominate, while others are sleeker and more urban in inspiration. All are a heady blend of modern and classic, and all of them, however eclectic, feel carefully considered, down to the smallest detail. Breakfast and cocktails are both served (presumably at distinct hours of the day) in a lush, tranquil garden with a view of no less significant a Roman-era landmark than Hadrian’s Gate itself.

content:
One of the more interesting hotels to open on the Athenian Riviera, a quickly revitalizing stretch of coastline south of the Greek capital, offers a stylish twist on glamping near the beach. 91 Athens Riviera is an offshoot of the popular Domes hotel line, and features a collection of luxurious canvas tents, designed with a similarly keen eye for design.

Each unit is outfitted with plush king-sized beds, spacious bathrooms with walk-in showers, and furnished decks. Some feature private plunge pools and multiple bedrooms, and all come with Marshall speakers, Nespresso machines, and a host of other self-care amenities, from foam rollers and bespoke sleep masks to white-noise machines.

Both the swimming pool and the hotel’s beach club invite lounging and sunbathing, while a tennis club includes eight courts and an instruction program. A spa is present as a matter of course, and the chic restaurant is an outpost of the Paros-based Barbarossa.

content: The Domaines de Fontenille collection of small, high-end hotels has grown across France and beyond, but it’s perhaps most at home in Provence, where it was born. Bastide du Mourre is perfectly true to form for these purveyors of south-of-France luxury; here in the Lubéron you’ll find a charmingly weathered 17th-century farmhouse and cottages whose rustic charm remains intact even as it’s been updated with stylish modern interventions.\n\nAs luxurious as it is, however, it remains delighfully low-key, connected to its landscape and the agricultural tradition. There’s a small and stylish spa featuring products made from local botanicals, and a guided hike or a tour of the Lubéron gets you right in touch with nature. Meanwhile the hotel’s table makes the most of the local bounty, not to mention an impressive selection of Domaines de Fontenille wines.

content:
In Indian hospitality there’s no more important name than Taj; the homegrown hospitality behemoth operates nearly a hundred hotels all across the country, from urban business hotels under the flagship banner to more exclusive, immersive luxury resorts like the Taj Exotica Resort & Spa, Goa. Here, on the spectacular white-sand Benaulim Beach in South Goa, you’ll find the living is extraordinarily easy.

A central building houses 32 rooms and six suites, while outlying villas contain the rest. They vary in size and plan, but all are classic-contemporary in style, and border on the extravagant in comfort — you won’t just have a pillow menu, you’ll have the option of firmer or softer mattresses, as well as Mohandas Arjundas bedding, Forest Essentials Ayurvedic bath products, and round-the-clock service.

The straightforwardly named Lobster Shack serves fresh seafood by the beach, while Miguel Arcanjo is the fine-dining restaurant, a tribute to the legendary local chef of the same name. Save some time for the Jiva spa, in between stretches by the pool or on the beach — or indulge in a near-comical list of sporting offerings, from a nine-hole golf course to tennis courts, badminton facilities, and even a cricket ground.

content: It’s not easy to stand out in Mexico City’s hippest neighborhood, but Casona Roma Norte is a modern classic that’s as striking from the street as it is inside. This rose-pink Belle Époque mansion dates back to the 1920s, and though its grand interiors have been stripped back and outfitted with minimalist décor and modern art, the place still radiates old-world magic. \n\nRooms are bohemian-chic with wooden floors, handmade Oaxacan rugs, marble bathrooms and luxurious beds made up in organic cotton linens; many have romantic writing desks, and a few feature private balconies. The hotel’s popular all-day restaurant serves elevated Mexican comfort food, and there’s also an agave tasting lounge and a great Japanese tea room on-site, though the undisputed crowning glory is the leafy rooftop terrace — perfect for cold drinks after a day out exploring the neighborhood's shops and galleries.

content: After sitting vacant for nearly two decades on a prime piece of oceanfront real estate, a landmark hotel in Palm Beach underwent extensive renovations and reopened as Palm House. Many of this Mediterranean-style property’s best features were preserved, from the coral-hued facade to the elegant pool deck framed by palm trees in the central courtyard. But as the first property to open in the US as part of the London-based L+R Hotels’ Iconic Luxury Hotels collection, it's been updated accordingly. Refreshed rooms are bright and cheerful with sixties-inspired decor — decorative mirrored wall panels, mod table lamps, king-sized beds with retro-looking upholstered headboards, Juliet balconies, and huge marble bathrooms with soaking tubs. Suites are palatial with curving modular sofas and Art Deco details; one has an Alaskan king bed rumored to be the largest in town. The fanciful Palm bar, with glamorous pink Murano glass chandeliers suspended from high vaulting ceilings, is worth the trip on its own.

content: The reference to Bali here is a state of mind — this is Panama, and the villas in question stand over the waters of the Caribbean, constructed on stilts in the manner pioneered by certain South Pacific resorts and designed by architect Andres Brenes in a style that’s unmistakably local and thoroughly modern. Bocas Bali’s private-island setting means it’s a blissfully private escape, and the experience, in its low-tech immediacy, is just what the modern traveler needs. The local coral reefs are a natural treasure; swimming, snorkeling, kayaking, and other waterborne diversions make up the lion’s share of the activities.

content: The charming old “Albergo Lorelei Londres” sign still stands atop this bright red Liberty-style edifice, but what’s inside has seen a thorough update. The present-day Hotel Lorelei Londres is a contemporary luxury boutique hotel through and through, a cliffside escape offering sensational sea views and near-monochrome minimalist-luxe rooms and suites, dressed entirely in white save for accents in ocean blue. Meanwhile, back up at clifftop level, the MICHELIN-Starred Lorelei serves a contemporary take on traditional Campanian flavors.

content: It’s quiet luxury all the way at Malibu Beach Inn, a swanky seaside hotel where every room faces the ocean. With a front door on the Pacific Coast Highway and a back door that opens onto the so-called Billionaire’s Beach, it feels like the private beach house of a wealthy friend who splurged on high-end Italian linens and already knows your drink order. Light-filled rooms are simply but finely outfitted with pale wood paneling, slate-bordered fireplaces, custom white oak furnishings, and spacious balconies overlooking the sea. Modern bathrooms are comparatively futuristic with remote-controlled Toto toilets. Wait staff attend umbrella-shaded chaises on the beach, and everything from early-morning avocado toast to late-night espresso martinis — with ingredients sourced from local farmers markets, of course — is served on a wide waterfront terrace with dazzling sunset views.

content: Once the workers’ cottages on a 19th-century agricultural estate, Casas da Quinta de Cima has been reimagined by the same family five generations on. Each of the nine suites pairs high wicker ceilings and terracotta floors with marble baths, wood-burning stoves, and vintage touches in wool and cotton. Private terraces look onto groves of orange and avocado, with the sea just beyond. The estate’s farm-to-table culinary approach is a particular highlight, as is the generally tranquil and low-tech atmosphere. This is heritage made habitable, rooted in memory, and carried forward with intent.

content: You’d be hard-pressed to find a boutique hotel with more Flemish flair than Quay 17. Located in a centuries-old stone building that previously housed a textile factory and a brewery, it’s right on a quiet canal near Bruges’ historic heart, and several of its rooms, with their high wood-beamed ceilings and tall windows, overlook the boats floating by. Bathrooms are ultra-modern, with oversized walk-in showers, and a pair of suites have soaking tubs. Downstairs, in keeping with tradition, the hotel’s house beer flows freely on an open-air terrace — also a prime spot for an al fresco breakfast, traditionally Belgian — and inside the glass-walled winter garden.

content: The old ranch town of Paso Robles, once a nondescript exit off Highway 101 on the trip between San Francisco and Los Angeles, has emerged as an up-and-coming wine country destination with hotels and restaurants to match. One of the standouts, River Lodge, is equally well suited for a leisurely stay as it is a short stopover — visible from the freeway, it was originally a 1940s-era motor lodge. The mid-century modern design has been smartly preserved, from the retro façade to the postcard-like pool surrounded by potted greenery and sunbeds. But guest rooms were thoroughly upgraded with bespoke furnishings, stylish work spaces, and private porches or yards, some with Bolivian hammocks or firepits. Complimentary Linus bikes and a poolside cocktail bar add to the appeal.

content: Of the many islands off the coast of Cartagena de Indias, Tierra Bomba is nearest to the mainland, just twenty minutes away by boat — convenient to reach, yet far enough to feel like a tropical escape. It’s a popular day-trip destination, but a handful of hotels, like the stylish and sustainable Blue Apple Beach on the southwest coast, make it easier to enjoy the island’s idyllic white sand beaches at a leisurely pace. This boutique hotel takes inspiration from beach clubs in the south of France, where the owner used to live: rosé flows freely and DJs spin afro-latino beats at the chic open-air restaurant and bar, which faces a turquoise-tiled pool framed by sunbeds. \n\nThe pool party quiets down after dark, when Blue Apple Beach feels more like a quiet retreat for the lucky few who get to stick around. There are just eleven rooms, all spacious and colorful with cheerful stripes and patterns in oceanic hues, artisan-crafted wood furnishings, stone-lined bathrooms with walk-in showers, and private terraces, many with hammocks and plunge pools. Larger cabaña-style bungalows have outdoor showers, king-sized daybeds, and sea views. Elsewhere on the grounds, a large palapa shades a yoga deck that doubles as an outdoor cinema at night. The hotel provides stand-up paddleboarding equipment down on the beach, and it has its own PADI scuba center, with a nearby coral reef a short swim away.

content:
For many travelers, the name Nikki Beach instantly conjures up images of a glamorous coastal lifestyle: champagne and house music by the infinity pool, pop-up fashion shows at the Cannes Film Festival, lavish white parties to kick off the season. Indeed, the hotel component is only part of the brand — Nikki Beach is, first and foremost, a luxury beach club concept, born in Miami Beach and continually branching out to seaside locales in places like Monte Carlo, Saint-Tropez, and Ibiza. 

The outpost on Greece’s northeastern Peloponnese coast follows in the same festive tradition. Open only when the weather is warm, Nikki Beach Resort & Spa Porto Heli feels like a stylish, buzzy beach club that happens to have a hotel attached. The lodgings are every bit as chic as the club, of course, outfitted with smooth parquet flooring and modern décor in shades of white and blue. All rooms come with sultry mood lighting, futuristic in-room entertainment systems, customizable minibars, and floor-to-ceiling glass windows overlooking the bay; bathrooms are especially luxurious, with spacious walk-in showers and oversized tubs. Most have private patios or terraces, and higher-end suites have private pools. 

At Nikki Beach, though, it’s all about the scene outside. Resident DJs and live performers enliven frequent parties and the brand’s signature Sunday brunch, and around every corner is another inviting spot to relax with a mimosa, from white daybeds on the sand to chaises partially submerged in the pool’s aquamarine water. There’s a rooftop bar and restaurant open for sunsets and beyond. And for the conscientious partygoer, a 24-hour gym awaits, plus an open-air spa and an all-day café, ideal for recovering from the revelry of the night before.

content: London is home to some cutting-edge hospitality experiments, but traditionalists take heart: it’s also got its share of perfectly judged contemporary classics. The Adria is a 19th-century townhouse in South Kensington, a quick walk from the Natural History Museum, the Victoria & Albert, and the bottom of Brompton Road. Inside are 24 rooms and suites, all renovated in a traditional-meets-modern style with luxe extras like underfloor heating and marble bathrooms. The Adria’s ambitions don’t quite extend to a full-service restaurant, though the breakfast is a substantial one, and the afternoon tea is a suitably elegant affair. The hotel has managed to squeeze in small wellness area, however, with a sauna and a range of treatments available to pre-book including massages, physiotherapy, and reflexology.

content: It’s a remarkable fact about Cartagena’s hotel scene that, however picturesque the old city center may be, its hoteliers aren’t afraid to balance its historical charm with some unapologetically contemporary design. Casona del Colegio is a fine example. This colonial-style building’s 13 rooms and suites contain visual echoes of Colombian history and tradition — the suites in particular are notable for their brick arches and timbered ceilings.\n\nArchitectural flourishes aside, though, the accommodations are unmistakably 21st-century in style, featuring modern and contemporary furnishings and up-to-date comforts. No less dramatic is the space that contains the Restaurant Costa, a Caribbean-inspired eatery with a focus on seafood. Additional enticements include a spa as well as a swimming pool complete with a poolside bar.

content:
Tucked away on an atmospheric side street in the Cretan village of Archanes, Manili Boutique Suites & Villas is perhaps a more modern and stylish luxury boutique hotel than you’d expect to find in this corner of the island, a little less than half an hour inland from the city of Heraklion. 

A cluster of whitewashed buildings house rooms with exposed stone walls, minimalist décor in earth hues, handy kitchenettes, and bathrooms with walk-in showers. Some overlook the sunny central courtyard with an aquamarine-tiled swimming pool and lounge chairs, while others face the bistro’s terrace. Multi-level suites and villas benefit from extra space, and some feature private open-air hot tubs with sweeping views of the nearby mountains.

Though there are plenty of reasons to stay in, from the accommodations to the pool to the Manili Bistro, there’s also much to do around the island, and from here the whole of the north-central coast is close at hand.

content: Phuket has more than its fair share of high-end resorts, but Anantara Mai Khao Phuket Villas feels especially luxurious. It’s partly the secluded location, tucked away between the Andaman Sea and a mangrove forest near the island’s northernmost point, part of the protected Sirinat National Park, and pleasantly removed from the busy port of Phuket Town. It’s also the fact that most rooms are airy Thai-style villas with private pools, and that the lagoon-like main pool stretches out along the coastline, dotted with double sunbeds elevated on platforms above the water — and that famed landscape artist Bill Bensley designed the grounds to resemble a tropical paradise with wooden catwalks leading across ponds with floating magenta lotus blooms.\n\nThroughout the resort, the look mixes modern elegance with Thai tradition: high ceilings, rich teak furniture, crisp white linens, decorative woodwork, and pieces by local artists. Suites are relatively simple with vibrant botanical-inspired murals, floor-to-ceiling windows, kitchenettes, and private balconies, though some have multiple bedrooms or private pools. An array of villas feature perks like sunken outdoor tubs, free-standing pavilions for poolside dining, and direct beach access. Boating, diving, fishing, and various other activities are easy to access. But with so much available onsite, from a beautiful spa to yoga and Muay Thai classes, from a treehouse omakase experience to a swim-up bar and a range of sophisticated dining venues, no one would blame you for staying put.

content:
To call Guanajuato an old mining town hardly does it justice. It's perhaps better described as the one-time location of the world’s largest silver extraction site, a town founded and made fabulously wealthy after the Spanish struck gold and silver in the early 16th century. Nueve 25 Hotel Boutique is one of a handful of luxury hotels in the UNESCO-honored historic center, the name a reference to the precious metal — a composition of at least 92.5% pure silver is required for the denomination of sterling silver — that put Guanajuato on the map.

Housed in a historic building with high beamed ceilings and exposed stone walls, but refreshed with a sleek, contemporary sensibility, the hotel’s look mixes historic and modern. The courtyard-style lobby is elegant and airy with old-world details like pale checkered tile floors, high arching doorways, wrought iron railings, and greenery spilling over the first-story balconies. Rooms and suites are simpler but just as stylish. Some feature original stone walls and whimsically tiled bathrooms, while others have high beamed ceilings from which striking bedside lamps are dramatically suspended. All feature espresso machines, Egyptian cotton sheets, and bath products by L’Occitane. 

The hotel offers a small spa and a wine cellar, stocked with wines produced nearby, located in the building’s old cisterns. But the crowning glory is the rooftop terrace with its spectacular view of the neigborhood's antique churches and bell towers. Its open-air bar and restaurant serve a mix of local and international cuisine; at sunset, when the basilica is romantically silhouetted against the surrounding hills, one can’t go wrong with a locally produced tequila on the rocks.

content:
To call Six Senses Southern Dunes, The Red Sea a destination resort might be stating the obvious; very few of us are going to find ourselves just passing through this expanse of desert in search of a room for the night. No, like any Six Senses, you come to Southern Dunes for top-flight luxury in a spectacular setting — here, an oasis-like collection of rooms, suites, and villas, set under tent-like roofs in an otherworldly landscape of rolling dunes, with the Hijaz Mountains in the distance.

Stylistically, the accommodations strike a remarkable balance, feeling fresh and novel but also warm and traditionally inspired. The rooms and suites spread out over 60 square meters, and come with terraces that double as outdoor living rooms. The villas, meanwhile, add plenty of extra space as well as private pools; the largest of them contain three- and even four-bedroom varieties, and feel like private resorts unto themselves.

And to say the Six Senses Spa is a highlight of the experience is a bit of an understatement — it spans nearly 4,000 square feet over two floors, with six treatment rooms, a gym, two pools, and a pool bar. Beyond the spa, activities include everything from cooking classes to fishing tours on the waters of the Red Sea. And the resort’s restaurants offer plenty of variety, from a gelato parlor to the fine-dining Al Sarab.

content:
The Island Lodge makes its home not just on any old island, but on the Mekong Delta’s Unicorn Island, an auspicious setting if ever there was one. Here, a short distance from Ho Chi Minh City, is one of the most relaxing hotels in Vietnam, a place whose sense of tranquility belies its relatively convenient location. And if it’s not the flashiest boutique hotel in the world, that’s to be expected — here it’s charm and character, not eye-popping luxury or design fireworks, that keeps guests coming back.

Its modest size also keeps it mellow — 12 rooms is small by any standard, and with eight in the main lodge and four in a pair of outlying pavilions, the Island Lodge is anything but crowded. The style is classic, featuring plenty of traditional craftsmanship as well as modern necessities like flat screens and (crucially) air conditioning.

The Mekong delta isn’t exactly urban, but it’s certainly settled, and you’re free to wander the local markets and explore by bicycle, either at your own pace or on a guided tour. And while a bit of Vietnamese cooking is always appreciated, it’s even better when accompanied by French fare, as is the case at Le comptoir de Marthe et Edouard, named for the hotelier’s grandparents.

content:
There are beach hotels that blend into the landscape — streamlined interiors in shades of sand and seashell, the separation between indoor and outdoor, and between water and sky, almost seamless. And then there are beach hotels that swing the other way. Take one look at Hotel Tugu Lombok, and the giant rooster sculpture, visible from miles away, proudly perched atop a towering, dramatically lit open-air restaurant, and you know that this resort falls firmly into the latter category.

The Tugu Lombok is over-the-top, to be sure, but the aesthetic is firmly rooted in the region’s rich pre-colonial history, most particularly the ancient Majapahit era, when a prosperous Hindu kingdom ruled the island. The palm-fringed property is located on the northwest coast of Lombok. It’s just a hop, skip, and a jump away from Bali, its hugely popular sister island, but feels like a world apart, devoid, as it is, of nightclubs, high-end shopping and namedrop-worthy resorts. What Tugu Lombok does have is an opulent 200-year-old temple, a pristine white-sand beach, a huge freshwater swimming pool, yoga classes, a state-of-the-art indoor-outdoor spa, a wine cellar, bike rental — you get the picture.

Guests receive a complimentary foot and shoulder massage on arrival, just the ticket to loosen you up for further relaxation in your private villa, suite or bungalow. The colonial-style Bhagavat Gita suites are dreamily romantic, with high thatched ceilings, flower-strewn beds beneath filmy white canopies, bathtubs carved out of massive boulders, and private oceanfront plunge pools. Flat-screen TVs with home theatres, rain showers, and private lotus ponds are standard amenities across the board.

Higher up on the food chain, a night in the exquisite Villa Puri Dadap Merah feels like sleeping inside a luxurious archaeological museum, if such a thing exists: based on the architectual structure of an ancient temple and packed with antiques from the Indonesian islands, the villa has a private rooftop terrace where you can lounge or dine under the stars. That is, if you’ve already experienced a meal beneath the big rooster, and seafood on the beach beneath the glow of bamboo torches, and drinks at the old teak bar at Lara Djonggrang, a cocktail venue modeled after the look of a traditional Balinese hut. Leave Bali to the crowds — you can have Lombok all to yourself.

content: Viceroy at Ombria Algarve enjoys a privileged position in the lush, rolling Algarve hills, on a pristine estate sequestered far from the crush of the beach crowd. A decadent spa is complemented by four pools with private cabanas and tableside service; the hotel’s 18-hole GEO-certified golf course is a major attraction in its own right.

content:
Harbor Court Hotel is the rare San Francisco hotel that evokes the the colorful, slightly gritty history of the Embarcadero. This stately Spanish Colonial Revival-style structure, built in 1926 across the street from the Ferry Building, was formerly an Army-Navy residence. Today the landmark is a stylish boutique hotel, but a range of details are reminders of its past, from the red-brick facade to the cheerful maritime-inspired color scheme.

Rooms are light-filled and modern, outfitted in crisp white, charcoal gray, and royal blue. All feature Frette linens, Soundfreaq sound systems, spacious workstations, and white subway-tile bathrooms. Some look over an interior courtyard or face the city skyline, but the best come with sweeping views of the San Francisco Bay and the Bay Bridge — including the apartment-like penthouse suite, with a Chesterfield sofa serving as a comfortable lookout point over the water below. 

Included amenities are plentiful and practical: a complimentary continental breakfast, an evening wine hour, loaner bicycles, and access to the on-site YMCA fitness center. Also conveniently connected to the hotel is the sushi restaurant Ozumo, and countless other restaurants and bars are within blocks of the front door.

content: Thailand is no stranger to architecturally modern villa hotels, but this one, by the award-wining architect Duangrit Bunnag, is exceptional. There’s an Olympic-sized swimming pool serving all guests, along with a large and lavish spa. The larger of the two restaurants stretches out alongisde the main pool, while the Sky Lounge offers what might be the resort’s most impressive elevated views.

content: The region of Cappadocia is famous for its ancient cave dwellings, some of which have been turned into guest lodgings. The striking Tafoni Houses Cave Hotel, located in the village of Ortahisar, is one of the best. The name refers to the bird nests that form at the tops of the region’s naturally occurring rock pillars, and the hotel takes inspiration from the concept — though with its sweeping terraces, art gallery, and fine dining, Tafoni Houses feels more grand than cozy.\n\nFashioned out of the site’s rock caves and the original housing built into them, the hotel’s suites are each named after a different bird’s nest. No two are alike, though all have large windows, stone archways, and colorful tiled floors. Some feature details that were uncovered during excavations of the old dwellings, like iron window grates, old-fashioned fireplaces, and interior doors painted charming shades of blue. Others are more luxurious with custom chandeliers and marble Jacuzzis. The best suites are almost museum-like, displaying carefully restored antiques and decorative art objects, and their palatial bathrooms are show-stoppers, crafted from marble and stone brought in from all over Türkiye.

content: Staying anywhere on Madrid’s Gran Vía is a treat, but the new Brach Madrid, a five-star hotel designed by Philippe Starck, offers next-level luxury. The building itself, of course, isn’t new: part of the avenue’s dazzling architectural showcase, it was completed in 1922, initially housing a stylish café-bar on the street level and various designer ateliers on the upper floors. Rich material for Starck’s artistic reimaginings — and he’s made the most of the building’s history, borrowing inspiration from its original style and function to create a hotel that’s glamorous and modern.\n\nA Parisian-style pastry shop, separated from pedestrian traffic by large picture windows, enlivens the entrance, the aromas of freshly baked croissants filling a lobby lined with traditional terracotta tile. The hotel’s elegant restaurant is modeled after the city’s twenties-era cafés, but with a sleek open kitchen, and a leafy rooftop terrace looks out over the romantic silhouettes and decorative facades of downtown. Rooms and suites are more theatrical, in typical Starck fashion, with sultry lighting, deep red walls, parquet floors, leather headboards, eclectic design pieces, and palatial bathrooms.

content:
Most visitors to the Galapagos sleep on boats, moving quickly from one island to another. Finch Bay Galapagos Hotel, located on the beach on the southern shore of Santa Cruz Island, offers a slower pace, and the chance to wake up in the same place each day, wading out into the water at dawn and relaxing on the sand at sunset. This luxury hotel’s design is built around the natural landscape, with a terrace facing the sea and wooden walkways threading past volcanic rocks and tropical foliage. 

The rooms and suites are sunny and bright, and constructed with natural materials, from dark stone to native wood; modern and contemporary furnishings are accompanied by whimsical tortoise artwork, modern glass-encased showers, and blackout curtains. The suites all have private balconies with direct ocean views, while the rooms open onto shared porches or balconies equipped with hammocks.

There’s a spa as lavish as many a luxury hotel, and a stylish pool just yards from the beach. Also within walking distance is Las Grietas, home to some of the finest snorkeling in the Galapagos. Tortuga Bay Beach and the Charles Darwin Research Center are both an easy drive away, as are the Santa Cruz highlands and their giant tortoise reserve. Meanwhile, Finch Bay’s restaurant employs organic ingredients from the hotel’s garden.

content: The Hudson Valley has long served as a weekend getaway for New Yorkers, and the minds behind the most sought-after lodgings understand the assignment, providing an outdoorsy escape without sacrificing style. The Hasbrouck House is a prime example. The 18th-century Dutch Colonial mansion, set on a park-like estate with a private lake in Stone Ridge, about a two-hour drive from the city, was once the country home of a wealthy family. The New York-based Akiva Reich & Co. oversaw its transformation into a luxury boutique hotel, turning the carriage house and stables into elegant guest quarters, installing a chic farm-to-table restaurant, Butterfield, on the ground level of the main house, and modernizing the 100-year-old swimming pool.\n\nRooms are understated and charming, with period details like brick fireplace facades and steeply pitched ceilings. No two are alike, but all are bright and elegant with hardwood floors, hand-woven rugs, cozy beds made up with Frette linens and down comforters, and a mix of modern and antique pieces. Suites in the carriage house are particularly inviting, with extra features like in-room soaking tubs, kitchenettes, and gas fireplaces, and a freestanding cottage on the property offers more space and privacy, plus a spacious eat-in kitchen and a bathroom lined in Carrara marble. An après-ski-inspired outdoor lounge is a fanciful spot for cocktails after hiking or wandering around the grounds, and in summer, the hotel sets up a big screen on the lawn for its outdoor film series.

content:
Almost exactly a century after the opening of Madeira’s original Savoy hotel in 1918, the Savoy Palace was unveiled on the same spot on Funchal’s waterfront. Though it’s not a remodel — the old hotel was demolished — the new version channels the glamour and sophistication that drew aristocratic travelers from around Europe. There’s plenty of old-world allure here, from the swish marble lobby with romantic staircases to the gleaming grand piano and lavish floral arrangements in the bar. But the Savoy Palace is strikingly modern, too; instead of traditional chandeliers, the reception area features a massive suspended light installation, three stories tall and crafted from miles of matte metal chain. 

The building itself is extraordinary in both size and shape, its wave-like silhouette rising 16 stories above the sea. But it’s the interiors, overseen by the celebrated designer (and Madeira native) Nini Andrade Silva, that command the most attention. Floral and botanical themes are consistent throughout, a nod to the island’s natural landscape — think larger-than-life flower sculptures in common spaces and carved wooden blossom panels beside beds. Rooms and suites are spacious and luxurious but simple, with walnut wood furnishings, spa-like bathrooms, and an ivory, gold, and champagne color palette. All but the most standard rooms feature private balconies with water views, and the best suites have private plunge pools and large wraparound terraces.

Apart from nearly a dozen stylish restaurants, lounges, and bars, the Savoy Palace is home to the largest spa in Portugal, connected to an indoor-outdoor pool complex with waterfalls. Both are ethereal, their look inspired by the island’s laurel forests and unique topography. A pair of rooftop infinity pools, one of which is for the exclusive use of suite guests, offer high-elevation sunbathing with spectacular views over the Atlantic. On the same level is the Galáxia bar and restaurant: in a nostalgic throwback, it borrows the name of the original hotel’s nightclub.

content:
Mykonos has, loosely speaking, two hospitality modes: there’s the legendary party destination, and there’s the setting for a luxe and tranqil retreat. Once in Mykonos Luxury Resort sets a scene that’s as stylishly sedate as anything on the island, a minimalist heaven of clean lines and shades of white. But it aims for something more social — not just by virtue of its location, a short walk from Ornos Beach and a short drive from Mykonos Town, but by virtue of its casual, convivial atmosphere as well.

An adults-only policy keeps “casual” from crossing over into “cacophonous” — the daytime vibe at the central swimming pool is thus suitably restful. As for the accommodations, every room and suite comes with at least a partial sea view, and many of them come with plunge pools. They start out quite large enough, and are equipped with sensible, if not extravagant, modern conveniences; the largest suite is practically a private villa unto itself.

By night the scene grows rather more lively, as the poolside Infinity Restaurant switches over from lunch to dinner and then late-night cocktails. There’s a substantial spa along with a gym and facilities for outdoor yoga, and excursions can be arranged by land or by sea.

content:
The first luxury hotel in Goa is still at it, under the banner of India’s most famous luxury-hotel brand: Taj Fort Aguada Resort & Spa, Goa. There’s no beating its setting, on over 40 acres of lush hillside gardens, overlooking both Sinquerim Beach and the ramparts of the 16th-century Portuguese-built Fort Aguada. And while the Taj shows plentiful Portuguese influence of its own — a stylistic thread that’s inseparable from Goan architecture — it’s far more elegant, even delicate, than the word “fort” might imply.

The bulk of the rooms occupy the main building of this low-slung compound, with others contained in outlying cottages and villas. They come in a wide range of sizes and layouts, but they’re uniformly spacious, comfortable, and perhaps more stylish than you might predict, each one decorated in a single saturated color, with antique-style furniture and modern-style amenities.

No Taj hotel would be content only to offer luxe accommodations, of course. This one adds a gym, a spa, a stunning infinity pool, and facilities for both tennis and squash. Meanwhile three restaurants specialize in seafood, pan-Indian cuisine, and Italian fare, and there’s a seaside lounge as well as a martini bar. If there’s another way to see Goa in such high style, we’d love to hear about it.

content:
Just up the coast from the artsy village of Todos Santos, about an hour’s drive to the north of Cabo San Lucas, a string of stylish boutique hotels line the beach road. The intimately sized Casa Blanco Madera is one of the finest. Run by a Mexican couple who fell in love with the region on a road trip through the Baja California Peninsula, it’s made up of just three rooms housed in a low-lying whitewashed building surrounded by desert gardens. 

All are alike in style, modern and mostly white with pale wood furnishings, king-sized beds, spacious bathrooms with walk-in rain showers, and staircases that lead up to private rooftop terraces with sea views. Each has a well-equipped kitchenette and sliding glass doors that open onto the oasis-like grounds, a plum spot for café con leche amid picturesque cacti and palm trees.

There’s no pool on the premises, though the beach is a short stroll away, as are the many stylish shops, restaurants, and art galleries in town. After dark, it’s hard to think of a better place to be than the hotel’s open-air fire pit: laid in concrete and perfectly circular, it’s a cool conversation pit under the stars.

content: The first part of the story is a familiar one: a pair of New Yorkers set out for Alentejo in search of their dream home. What brings it to our attention is the fact that, after they found it on a forested hillside near the beach, they didn’t keep it all to themselves. This is Quinta Camarena, a sustainability-focused boutique hotel that doubles as a laid-back retreat for surfers and yoga enthusiasts. Just two hours from Lisbon, it’s a convenient weekend getaway, though the owners encourage longer stays — billed as not-so-serious yoga, not-so-serious fitness, etc. — that bridge the gap between wellness and pleasure, between green juice–fueled guided meditations and convivial dinners with free-flowing wine.\n\nThe hotel comprises several traditional country houses connected by steep trails on the terraced landscape. Some rooms are located in the main house, with easy access to the outdoor pool and yoga deck, while others are a short hike uphill, enveloped by native trees and offering elevated views over the surrounding nature. All are quiet and filled with light, featuring locally crafted furnishings, high-end Portuguese linens, and organic bath products. Some are duplexes with large private terraces, others have clawfoot tubs and cozy reading rooms, and the largest is a freestanding four-bedroom villa with a kitchen and a patio with a grill. Breakfast and dinner, featuring seasonal dishes made with local ingredients are served in an open-air setting by the pool and gardens, and the nearby village of Cercal do Alentejo is a short stroll away.

content:
Turning a prison into a luxury hotel is no small task. It helps that Offenburg’s former penal institution, which comprises a pair of simple but elegant brick buildings that date back to the mid-19th century, was somewhat aesthetically pleasing — and it’s essential, too, that the hotel’s designers were interested in preserving some of the prison’s character instead of completely overhauling the place. After careful planning and renovations, the sleek Hotel Liberty opened in 2017.

A new glass-walled addition, now housing the reception and restaurant, joins the two original buildings. Some of the prison’s hallmark features remain, like the curving exposed brick ceilings, bars on the windows, and a gray color palette that feels both stylish and tongue-in-cheek. In the same vein, the buildings’ once-bleak hallways are still dark, but now in a way that feels dramatic and glamorous; the industrial atmosphere remains, but now it’s industrial-chic, the sandstone cellar transformed into a stylish wine bar. 

Onetime jail cells are now stylish guest rooms with parquet floors, bespoke furnishings, and modern decor in white, black, and charcoal. Suites feature freestanding tubs and skylights for stargazing, and the rooftop suite highlights the prison’s original timber beams and has its own dining area and library. And downstairs an open-air cocktail lounge occupies what was once the prison yard.

content: Sri Lanka’s hospitality scene is blessed with plenty of variety in both landscape and style — longtime readers will know that it’s got some very fine modernist beachfront boutique hotels, but it’s also got something close to the polar opposite. W15 Hanthana Estate Kandy is set in the mountainous interior of the island, surrounded by verdant hillsides and tea plantations, and aesthetically it’s as pure an example of colonial-style elegance as you’re likely to experience, its bungalow-style buildings wrapped in verandas and columns, its guests ferried from the rail station to the estate in a robin’s-egg-blue vintage Land Rover.\n\nThe accommodations themselves similarly prize the familiar trappings of colonial country-house life, from the stately and solid wooden furnishings to the tactile comforts, including indulgent tiled bathrooms. This being tea country, you’re never more than arm’s length from a cup, and the cuisine, from breakfast on through to dinner, encompasses both Sri Lankan and English traditions. And while there’s nothing stopping you from simply lounging about the estate all day, you’re also welcome to explore the surrounding landscapes on foot, by bicycle, or on a motorized safari-style tour.

content:
Like many mid-sized American cities, Downtown El Paso, Texas has experienced a resurgence in the last few years, and the newly opened Stanton House is another symbol of that revival. Housed in a renovated 100-year-old, four-story building that was formerly a furniture store, it’s been transformed into a boutique hotel that blends rich local history with elegant, art-focused interiors — from the lobby to the guest rooms, every space is filled with artworks from renowned and up-and-coming Mexican, European, and local artists.

Stanton House’s 42 rooms and suites range from 330 to 700 square feet, and though luxe, there’s a touch of minimalism to the décor — the art is always the focus. The artworks on display in the rooms are for sale, and in some rooms, visitors will notice a small reading area with a window overlooking the hotel’s four-story Light-Well, which showcases a mobile light sculpture that illuminates the Taft-Díaz restaurant on the ground floor.

Speaking of which, head chef Oscar Herrera is well known in Juárez, just across the border, for his facility with traditional Mexican flavors and exciting, contemporary ingredients. Nearly 70 tons of steel were used to make the giant atrium-like structure that rises over restaurant, which was named for another cross-border collaboration: the historic 1909 meeting between U.S. President William Taft and Mexico President Porfirio Díaz in El Paso.

content:
When the Taj group uses the word “palace,” it’s best to take them seriously, we always say (and it says something about their selection that we actually do say it rather a lot). Taj Usha Kiran Palace, Gwalior, for example, is more than just an awfully luxurious hotel, though it certainly is that. First built as a guest house in preparation for a visit from a future King of England, it later became a residence for Gwalior’s ruling family — just the sort of institutional heritage the Taj hotels dine out on.

The building, needless to say, is an architectural treasure, and the nine acres of gardens certainly don’t hurt the mood. Rooms and suites are typically luxe, with the sort of interior character only a historic building can give you. The décor is clean and sparse in the rooms, more opulent in the suites, always tending towards antiques, and no corners are cut when it comes to physical comfort, especially in the self-contained villas ringing the pool. 

A spa sees to guests’ bodily needs, and a fine Marathi/Nepalese restaurant to their gustatory ones. But as always, the cherry on top is the service — the staff at Usha Kiran, as in any Taj palace hotel, are impeccably schooled and anticipate guests’ needs with eerie precision.

How to get there: Conveniently located, the hotel is just 25 kms from the Gwalior Airport (GWL) and 3 kms from the railway station.

content: On the quiet island of Vis - once a naval base closed to foreigners for nearly 50 years - Pomâlo Inn offers a rare glimpse into Dalmatia as it once was. An 1810 Brač stone house just steps from the harbor, this ten-room retreat brings together laid-back design and contemporary minimalism. Lamps resemble traditional fishing traps, walls are lined with fine art photography, and a vintage 1958 Dr. Pepper machine stands stocked with Croatian sodas. With just ten rooms and suites, the vibe is relaxed, reflective, and unmistakably local. “Pomâlo” means to take it slow, and here, you truly do.

content: Tucked between the snow-capped Andes and the mirror-like expanse of Nahuel Huapi Lake in the deep reaches of Argentine Patagonia, far-flung Villa La Angostura is one of the most scenic destinations in the country. And its most luxurious hotel, Las Balsas, housed in an elegant wooden lodge right on the lakefront, looks straight out of a fairytale — its facade painted a cheerful cobalt-blue, a quaint private dock jutting out into the water, the whole scene dwarfed by native evergreen trees and the mountains beyond. The hotel, impressively, is just as lovely inside. The look evokes alpine chalet-style elegance with exposed wooden beams, fireplaces built with native stone, and cozy seating areas beside huge windows revealing postcard-like views of the great outdoors. \n\nEvery room faces the lake, from light-filled suites in the main building to a newer collection of stilted freestanding villas. All are airy and rustic-chic, featuring high vaulted ceilings, parquet floors, fluffy white duvets, Illy machines, and spacious bathrooms with separate showers and tubs. Las Balsas’ indoor-outdoor hot tub and infinity pool are heated year-round, and walking trails invite a stroll through the woods. A traditional afternoon tea includes an array of gourmet jams, cakes, and pastries, and elevated Patagonian cuisine is served for lunch and dinner. Sailing, hiking, horseback riding, fly fishing, mountain biking, and kayaking are easily arranged onsite.

content: Mid-century style runs deep at the Foundry, a hip boutique hotel in Athens’s historic Psirri district — the building, constructed in 1930, originally served as a type foundry, and later as a printing house and a cultural center. Today, it’s home to a collection of industrial-chic suites with wood or terrazzo floors, high ceilings, large steel-framed windows, exposed stone walls, and a mix of vintage and modern furnishings. No two are the same, but all are apartment-like with open floor plans and features like fully equipped kitchens, built-in workspaces, and marble-lined bathrooms. Ground-floor units open onto private garden areas, while loft suites have two levels of living space connected by a floating staircase. Up on the lushly planted rooftop terrace, gourmet pizzas and Greek wines are served with a striking view of the Acropolis.

Today it mixes heritage glamour with contemporary cool, filling the rooms with high-end modern comforts and adding enticements like a spa, a sauna, and a seasonal outdoor pool. Farm-to-table cooking is a major point of emphasis, as are Prince Edward County’s local wines.

content: One of the great French dramatists, Pierre Corneille, regularly retreated from Paris to his sister’s home in the Norman countryside. The elegant 16th-century estate has since been converted into a luxurious boutique hotel, Les Manoirs des Portes de Deauville. Many of the property’s best assets remain intact: a collection of smartly renovated cottages frame the historic manor house with its original stone fireplace, and the surrounding park, with its pear and apple trees, is wildly picturesque. \n\nA handful of rooms and suites are located in the main building, featuring light oak flooring, exposed wood beams, pale linen-upholstered furnishings, and modern bathrooms lined in white tile. But most are in the cottages nearby, where ground-level suites have double doors opening directly onto the garden. Across the board, the look is light and bright, with cozy throw rugs, velvet armchairs, and antique pieces adding warmth and character. A trio of private cottages offer extra space and privacy, with floating staircases connecting kitchen and living areas to the bedroom upstairs. There’s no restaurant at the hotel, though you’re unlikely to miss it with the chic village of Deauville just minutes away, and an honesty bar is open around the clock. A pretty swimming pool bordered by sun umbrellas and chaise longues invites late afternoon lounging.

content:
Perched on the cliffs above Agios Stefanos beach and the port, Bard De Sol is intimately sized, with just 13 rooms and suites spread across three levels. And unlike many of the island’s other hotels, there’s almost nothing rustic about it: apart from the Cycladic-style stone exteriors and whitewashed patios, Bard De Sol is thoroughly modern, even glamorous, with sleek, urban-looking interiors. 

All rooms have furnished balconies or patios with sea views, minimalist décor in shades of white, ivory, beige, and black, wide work desks, minibars with Nespresso machines, and artfully illuminated bathrooms with walk-in rain showers. With the exception of the simplest deluxe rooms, which open onto a shared pool area, most rooms have private outdoor pools or hot tubs overlooking the Aegean. The largest suites feature spacious terraces with built-in furniture both inside and out — daybeds by the pool, a conversation pit–style sectional sofa in the living room, and sharing the same space, a stylish island with stools in the fully equipped kitchen. 

There’s a large infinity pool for communal use, plus an attractive wood- and stone-lined fitness center and sauna. Fresh, colorful Mediterranean dishes are served al fresco for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and a range of other dining options are nearby, as are Little Venice and the beach.
