content:
West Hollywood’s Design District is a unique corner of Los Angeles, a little triangular oasis surrounded by some of the best shops, restaurants, and nightlife in the city. Le Parc at Melrose is set on a residential street between Melrose and Santa Monica Boulevard, and occupies a relatively unassuming converted apartment building. Inside, however, are suites that marry residential spaciousness and comforts with boutique-hotel good looks.

Kitchenettes come equipped with Keurig coffee makers, turntables and fireplaces are universal, and each suite has a private balcony in addition to plentiful indoor lounge space. The look is glamorous, but in the kind of low-key way that’s suited to an extended stay, informed by Hollywood’s Art Deco heritage and the modernist influence of the Design District.

Knoll, the hotel’s restaurant, serves French-influenced farm-to-table fare in an elegant dining room, while more casual fare is available on the rooftop by the poolside. This roof deck, incidentally, is one of Le Parc’s highlights, a semi-private refuge by day and a lively but secluded nightspot after dark — a welcome counterpoint to the high-intensity nightlife of the Sunset Strip and West Hollywood’s busier corners.

content:
Hotel standards are elevated on Koh Samui, home to several of Thailand’s most luxurious resorts. Santiburi Koh Samui is set apart from many of its rivals by one of the island’s largest swimming pools, its only full-size golf course, a secluded half-moon-shaped beach on the island’s north shore, and a degree of dedication to landscaping that puts some botanic gardens to shame.

The super-sized circular pool sits right in the middle of the tropical foliage, surrounded by cheerful red umbrellas, white lounge chairs, and scenic palm trees, notably separate from the beach. Steps away are the reception building and paths that lead to villas and suites. In both architecture and interior design, Santiburi forgoes the modern but bland aesthetics of chain resorts in favor of traditional Thai elegance: fine woods, jewel-toned silk, exotic floral arrangements, decorative art objects, and softly glowing lamps. All rooms are duplex-style with two levels of sleeping and living space, French doors opening to private balconies or terraces, and spacious bathrooms with rainfall showers and upscale Thai bath products. Some villas have gardens and plunge pools; a few are set right on the beach, with hammocks strung between trees just above the sea. 

Down on the sand, beach butlers serve cold drinks and ice cream to sunbathers at thoughtfully spaced-out sunbeds, and kayaks and standup paddleboards are free for the taking. The beachside bar and restaurant is just one of Santiburi’s five dining venues, and the resort also has a peaceful spa, a state-of-the-art fitness center, and tennis courts. Best of all, perhaps, is the nature trail that winds through the gardens and out to the beach, providing a picturesque overview of the resort’s assets.

content:
Set in the beautifully named South Tyrolean village of San Candido, just a few miles from the Austrian border, is Post Hotel - Tradition & Lifestyle, a 1926-vintage inn that was extensively renovated in 2014 and now stands as a fine example of Italy’s modern generation of Alpine luxury boutique hotels. It’s an adults-only hotel, which certainly aids in its efforts to provide a tranquil atmosphere, while its location offers endless opportunities for adventure, from downhill and Nordic skiing to summertime hiking and biking.

Most of the rooms and suites retain just one element of the traditional lodge aesthetic, and that’s the wood flooring; otherwise, they’re decorated in a contemporary Italian luxury style, some more subtly stylish and others decked out in bold graphic murals. (The “classic” rooms contain more traditional wooden furnishings.) Some have views of the village rooftops, others, the mountain peaks.

The spa and wellness center is perhaps Post Hotel’s most visually striking space; it’s connected to the outdoor Secret Garden. Meanwhile the P-Lounge is a contemporary-luxe evolution of the classic après-ski bar, and the Ristorante Post Hotel serves a sophisticated modern menu of high-end Tyrolean classics.

content: Santorini is full of romantic hotels, but the highest concentration might well be found in Imerovigli. Maybe it’s the location, on the highest point of the island with sweeping views over the caldera; perhaps it’s the breathtaking sunset over the water; maybe it’s the quaint village itself, with its whitewashed buildings and quiet lanes. Or it could be the fact that the hotels that have staked their claim here have been in the business for decades, like Astra Suites, a luxurious boutique hotel that’s been perfecting the sun, sip, and swim experience since first opening in the early nineties. The formula works: in short, every room is a stylish sea-facing suite with a private terrace.\n\nThe simplest suites are anything but. Designed in a loft style, with a domed ceiling over the sleeping area and an open-plan living and dining space, they’re bright white with colorful tiled floors resembling opalescent sea glass. Higher-end suites are lavishly appointed with spacious living rooms and open-air hot tubs or plunge pools; a few have in-bedroom showers. The larger pool offers a sleek all-white bar and striking views over the Aegean, and the lookout from the restaurant’s terrace is just as marvelous, especially in the late afternoon as the sun goes down.

content:
It’s back to basics at The Well, northern Europe’s largest spa: phones aren’t permitted, and swimwear isn’t allowed in saunas and steam baths, where a “natural nudity” policy prevails. Luckily, it’s easy to go with the flow here, joining relaxation-seeking Norwegians as they stream from pools to waterfalls to meditation rooms, a Japanese-style bathhouse, and a Turkish hammam  — and you can wear whatever you want in the privacy of your room. 

Though the location is just outside Oslo, the wooded setting feels pleasingly remote. Rooms and suites are appealing in their silence, simplicity, and Scandinavian style. Each has parquet floors, locally produced Wonderland beds and Høie linens, modern bathrooms with walk-in showers, and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the forest. There are no screens around — digital detox is a key component of the spa’s philosophy — but Marshall speakers and Nespresso machines are welcome amenities. 

Even when staying in the most luxurious suite, with its oversized tub and its double shower, guests are unlikely to spend much time in their rooms, given that the Well Spa is open practically around the clock. Other notable features include a poolside bar, a pair of restaurants — including one that’s bathrobe-friendly — as well as Norway’s largest private art collection (with pieces by Herb Ritts and Robert Mapplethorpe), a sculpture forest, and a network of hiking and cross-country skiing trails.

content: The Maldives comprise more than a thousand islands, the vast majority of which are uninhabited. In recent years, the sustainability-driven lifestyle brand JOALI has claimed two of them, building a pair of luxury resorts in Raa Atoll. The secluded Muravandhoo Island is home to JOALI Maldives, billed as the archipelago’s first art-immersive resort — and indeed, it’s art and design that separate this hotel from its rivals. Art installations and interactive exhibits are everywhere, an artist-in-residence runs creative workshops, and one-of-a-kind artworks are displayed in the resort’s sophisticated over-water bungalows and thatched-roof beach villas. \n\nThe indoor-outdoor design is striking: spacious, high-ceilinged villas are airy and opulent, featuring white marble, dark carved-wood panels, futuristic lighting and sound systems, Art Deco–style bars for mixing a drink, and spa-like bathrooms with freestanding tubs. All come with private infinity pools, outdoor rain showers, and round-the-clock butler service. Outside, the resort has everything you’d expect and then some, including several high-end restaurants and bars, a spa with glass-walled treatment rooms and a floating yoga pavilion, and an impressive main pool with dazzling sunset views.

content: For a destination that attracts so many outdoor adventurers, Peru was a late adopter of the luxury camping trend. But Puqio, the first tented camp in the country, doesn’t disappoint — in fact, when it opened in 2024, this stylish safari-style hotel quickly became one of the most buzzed-about places to stay in the Colca Valley. There’s stiff competition in the region, a trekkers’ paradise known as the gateway to one of the world’s deepest canyons, but elegant Puqio, set outside the village of Yanque, offers something special.\n\nThe hotel centers around a cozy, light-filled lodge where gourmet meals, prepared with local ingredients and cooked over open fires, are served family-style. Accommodations are in canvas tents or round adobe cottages, all featuring wood-burning stoves, heated walls, and private terraces. Cottages have wood-beamed ceilings and clawfoot tubs, while tents have open-air soaking tubs as well as indoor and outdoor showers. The look is rustic-chic throughout, with wooden writing desks, antique lamps, and natural linen and leather accents. Puqio’s knowledgeable guides lead guests through the surrounding wilderness, and closer to camp, it’s common to spot Andean hummingbirds and alpacas around the property — and, if you’re lucky, a condor flying high overhead.

content: Georgia is home to, among other things, the earliest evidence of wine production anywhere in the world. And against the backdrop of an 8,000-year-old wine culture, the Vazisubani Estate, established in 1891, is a relative newcomer. Still, the 19th-century grandeur of this splendidly restored house lends an enormous amount of character to its 19 rooms and suites, which have been redesigned by a team of Georgian and British architects and designers, and outfitted with a unique collection of authentic English-made, Victorian-era antique furniture, resulting in an atmosphere quite unlike any other.\n\nThe house is surrounded by a substantial expanse of parkland, perfectly suited for a midday picnic or an afternoon ramble. And beyond that are the vineyards, responsible for producing the grapes which are turned into wine using the ancient Qvevri method. These wines, naturally, feature in the selection available in the hotel’s restaurant, where chef Keti Bakradze crafts creative interpretations of traditional Georgian dishes in a classic farm-to-table style, using many ingredients grown right here on the grounds of the estate. The result of it all: an experience that showcases a side of Georgia that’s rarely seen by visitors.

Located in the historic heart of the city, Vanoro is a modern, stylish boutique hotels, a model of subtlety and restraint in a near-monochrome palette with generous helpings of mid-century modernist influence.

content: Though it’s barely an hour’s drive up Sri Lanka’s west coast from Colombo, and mere minutes from the city of Negombo, Wattura Resort and Spa feels quite convincingly secluded. The immediate setting, with a sunset-facing beach on one side of the property and the peaceful Gin Oya river on the other, certainly contributes to the idyllic atmosphere. And if you’re familiar with Sri Lanka’s tropical modernist architectural tradition, you know there’s something uniquely calming about the clean geometries of the forms and interiors, as well as the juxtaposition of polished concrete and stone with richly figured wood and traditional craftsmanship.\n\nThe humblest of the suites stretches out over nearly 800 square feet, and comes complete with butler service and a view of either the lagoon or the river. From there they double in size, and double again, adding extravagances like jacuzzis, plunge pools, even, in the case of the Wattura Residence, a rooftop infinity pool. And there’s always the hotel’s central infinity pool — and by the poolside, Pappali, the hotel’s restaurant, with its tucked-away booths and its contemporary Sri Lankan cuisine. Excursions include everything from whale-watching to rainforest walks to the country’s first elephant orphanage — safe to say the experience has all the makings of a memorable one.

content: Athita The Hidden Court Chiang Saen Boutique Hotel enjoys an unusual distinction in the ancient walled city. It’s not just located beside Wat Athi Ton Kaeo, one of the best-preserved temples in town — the hotel is in direct conversation with its neighbor, almost like an extension of the 500-year-old landmark. The architects borrowed heavily from regional traditions, working with local artisans and technicians to build a modern complex out of teak wood and handmade bricks. The result is a boutique hotel that’s both contemporary and steeped in the cultural heritage of northern Thailand.\n\nThe L-shaped, two-story main building is set back from the street, with a peaceful courtyard garden serving as a meditative space between the hotel and the temple. On one edge is a beautiful rectangular-shaped pool partially enclosed by brick walls lined with greenery, and on the other, the restaurant and café, strikingly situated on a wide wooden terrace that’s open to the courtyard. Rooms are tranquil and high-ceilinged, their bright white Egyptian cotton sheets contrasting with the dark wood floors and walls. Some have private gardens and others have temple views. A pair of freestanding villas nearby, set apart from the hotel but still part of the property, offer multiple bedrooms and well-equipped kitchens.

content:
According to its 16th-century literary origins, utopia is an imaginary place: peaceful, organized, architecturally uniform, and equally pleasurable for all. Naxian Utopia, a boutique hotel on the Greek island of Naxos, delivers on that promise — but with the distinct advantage of actually existing. It’s quiet and somewhat remote, located on a hill overlooking the salt lake of Agios Prokopios and within easy walking distance of the beach. 

The hotel’s small collection of Cycladic-style suites and villas all feature spacious private terraces with plunge pools, and though layouts vary — some suites have outdoor Jacuzzis and villas have fully equipped kitchens — they’re all modern and luxurious, with all-white furnishings, gleaming concrete floors, Coco-mat beds, tadelakt tubs, and walk-in rain showers.

There’s another pool on the rooftop with an all-day bar and lovely views over the island’s landscapes. Nearby is a fitness center and a spa that offers treatments featuring organic Greek products. A simple breakfast is served daily at a communal table, and it’s a quick taxi ride into town and a range of restaurants, cafés, and bars.

content:
At the time of this Hertfordshire estate’s founding, it took rather longer to travel the 18 miles from London. Today the splendid Georgian house that is The Grove — along with its attractive contemporary addition — offers all the charms of a country-house luxury hotel, an absurdly short ride from the capital. And we mean all the charms: not just afternoon tea and a wander in the garden, but everything from nature trails and spa treatments to golf, tennis, even archery.

The Mansion’s rooms and suites are a touch more historical in style than those in the much more recent West Wing, but the difference is one of degree, not of kind. Regular renovations have kept them all looking sharp, and the comforts are unobtrusively modern. And The Grove is family-friendly to a remarkable degree — not only do many units comfortably house families, but the kids’ club keeps them effortlessly entertained.

The Grove’s championship golf course and its Sequoia spa account for a large part of its appeal. Summertime sees a wealth of activities added to the menu at the Walled Garden, with its outdoor pool, landlocked beach, and outdoor cinema. And year-round, three permanent restaurants serve Grove guests; additional pop-ups and special dinners, some of them seasonal, augment the offering.

content:
Elegant whitewashed architecture, a sparkling pool, sweeping views of the Aegean Sea; Rocabella Mykonos has everything you’d expect at a luxury hotel on one of Greece’s most visited islands. But this boutique resort pulls off the Grecian paradise aesthetic with more style and sophistication than most. It’s partly a question of size. Though the grounds are expansive, the hotel has just 26 rooms and one villa, so there’s no crowding by the pool. With relatively few guests, the staff can be especially attentive, whether taking drink orders directly from chaises or spritzing custom fragrances during turndown service.

The hotel’s design mimics the look and feel of a Greek village, with winding staircases and cool, shadowy pathways leading through the hillside property and opening onto sun-dappled stone terraces overlooking the sea. Housed in low-lying white buildings, rooms and suites embody a modern Cycladic aesthetic, outfitted in bright whites, earth tones, and natural materials like wood, stone, and straw. Nearly all feature ocean views, and many come with private outdoor plunge pools, but even the simplest room option has a private outdoor patio. Amenities like Nespresso machines, stocked minibars, Marshall speakers, fluffy bathrobes, and organic bath products are standard.

A focal point of Rocabella Mykonos is the pool, surrounded by shaded white daybeds partially submerged in turquoise water, and its picturesque pool bar. An à la carte breakfast is served poolside, as are cocktails and Greek small plates throughout the day. A brand-new fitness center and yoga pavilion, both glass-encased and facing the sea, are spacious and state-of-the-art, and a spa offers a range of massages. Agios Stefanos Beach is just a short walk down the hill. It’s also possible to reach the ferry port, if not the town, on foot: luckily, the hotel offers free shuttle service until midnight.

Small-scale, retro-chic, and environmentally friendly, Numo Mykonos is a refreshing antidote to the island’s more party-focused hotels. Housed in a beautifully restored historic building on a gently sloping hill above Kalafati Beach, it’s the work of a boutique hotel group that runs the popular Numo Ierapetra, on the island of Crete. 

Numo Mykonos, like its sister hotel, embodies barefoot luxury — in this case, adding a minimalist Cycladic twist and vintage ’60s- and ’70s-inspired glamour, with elegant stone archways opening onto a garden-framed pool area with striped chaises and woven straw umbrellas. 

Rooms have mid-century charm, featuring curving upholstered headboards, built-in seating areas, geometric artwork, and private outdoor spaces, some with pools and sea views. A spa and fitness center are present as a matter of course, as is a Mediterranean restaurant called Anemoessa and Màre-Màre, a chic poolside bar and lounge.

content: Once a quiet tropical island off the coast of the Yucatán Peninsula, Isla Holbox is now a stylish hotspot with hundreds of hotels to choose from. Only a handful are right on the beach, though — among them is Awa Holbox, a modern boutique hotel that’s a 10-minute golf cart ride from the ferry terminal. The design is contemporary, with low-rise buildings made of locally sourced wood and stone, but the hotel channels the island’s laid-back spirit: thatched-roof cabanas provide shade by the pool, fish tacos are served at wooden tables on the sand, and glowing wicker lamps illuminate the indoor-outdoor bar after dark.\n\nAll suites have private outdoor spaces facing the water. Some feature balconies with open-air tubs and elevated views over the Caribbean, while ground-level rooms open directly onto the pool deck. Inside, the look is sleek but down-to-earth, with poured concrete flooring, exposed wooden beams, gauzy white curtains, and handwoven rugs in natural hues. The master suite has its own rooftop terrace with a stone tub and a daybed ideal for afternoon siestas. For everyone else, there’s Viento, the adults-only, open-all-day rooftop bar and café, and a festive, boho-chic beach club and restaurant, family-friendly and located just steps from the crashing waves.

content:
Cars aren’t allowed on the island of Gili Air — hardly an inconvenience, as it spans less than two square miles. Part of an archipelago off the coast of Lombok, it’s a laid-back tropical getaway best explored on a bicycle, and Villa Tokay, easily one of the most luxurious places to stay, gladly provides them. 

This eco-friendly, design-forward hotel is tucked away on a lushly landscaped property near the island’s west coast. Instead of traditional rooms and suites, there’s a small collection of freestanding villas, each a striking example of local craftsmanship and indoor-outdoor architecture. Bamboo takes the starring role here: both practical and decorative, it’s used as the primary material for the villas’ sweeping staircases and high, curving ceilings, and it’s bundled together to form soaring pillars that support lofted sleeping areas. Each villa is one-of-a-kind, but all have dreamy gardens with colorful foliage, whimsically shaped private pools, and fanciful treehouse-like details. One has an open kitchen at the poolside and a copper tub in the garden, while another has an open-air Art Deco-style shower and a private yoga deck. The largest, which sleeps ten, features four bedrooms and an infinity pool.

It’s hard to leave the confines of such a thoughtfully planned private paradise, so it’s fitting that breakfast is delivered directly to each villa’s dining area. When the urge arrives to venture further afield, the hotel is a great jumping-off point to discover the island. In addition to offering complimentary bicycles, Villa Tokay lends out its snorkeling gear, and the front gate is just a stone’s throw from the island’s lovely beaches.

content: The southernmost island in Greece’s Sporades archipelago is also its least-visited. A world apart from cruise ship crowds and tourists in pursuit of the perfect photo op, bohemian Skyros is comparatively rugged and remote — and ALERÓ Seaside Skyros Resort, elegantly secluded and low-key, is very much of its place. This seaside boutique hotel takes its name from the Greek words for salt (álas) and water (neró). Separated from the water only by picturesque sand dunes, it’s just a short stroll down to a sandy beach where guests recline beneath picturesque white umbrellas and waitstaff take orders for iced coffees and spritzes. Forget about claiming a chaise with a strategically placed towel: there are just twelve suites at this intimately sized resort, so there’s always more than enough room for everyone.\n\nBack on the other side of the dunes, the hotel’s suites offer a similar level of space and privacy. Simply furnished in earth tones, all feature wood paneling and speckled tile flooring, linen sofas and hanging plants. Filled with natural light, they’re quietly luxurious, and each has a private outdoor space with a plunge pool. A number of suites are duplex-style, comfortably accommodating families or small groups, and all come with desirable extras like modern kitchenettes, outdoor dining spaces, or sea views.

content: There doesn’t have to be a trade-off between historical atmosphere and contemporary boutique hospitality — the tiny nine-room Casa Antonieta, in the historic center of Oaxaca City, offers an abundance of both. It’s set in a colonial-style building that dates back to 1529, old even by local standards, and while its original architecture is proudly displayed, its rooms effortlessly mix weathered stone walls with contemporary furniture and artworks, locally made crafts, and luxe, modern hotel comforts. \n\nThe rooftop terrace is a particular delight, and the inner courtyard makes for a welcome refuge from the city by day. A continental breakfast is served in-house, and for lunch and dinner you’re left to explore the streets of what might be Mexico’s most celebrated culinary city.

content:
Built as a private residence in 1534 and completely rebuilt in 1924, the three-story Renaissance-style Casa Gangotena honors its history through lovingly restored painted ceilings, wooden paneling, oil paintings, murals, and friezes. It’s set in a prominent corner of Quito’s Old Town, itself a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and is, if not exactly typical of the city’s lodgings, certainly a fine introduction to the Ecuadoran capital.

It remained a private residence all the way up to the mid-2000s, which means its residential atmosphere remains intact. All rooms have gorgeous high ceilings, towering full-length windows, and beautiful Art Deco furniture, while some suites feature museum-quality murals, spacious balconies and Neoclassical stucco columns. The vibe is decidedly retro — nothing minimalist about it — though the comforts are just as definitively modern.

There’s a proper spa, as befits a luxury hotel of Casa Gangotena’s stature, and the hotel’s award-winning restaurant showcases Ecuador’s rich culinary tradition through traditional techniques and locally sourced ingredients. “Café Quiteño,” the local equivalent of high tea, is a mid-afternoon highlight as well, as are the quiet garden lounge and the cozy, clubby cocktail bar. Meanwhile the hotel’s rooftop terrace features impressive panoramic views of the city and its immediate surroundings.

content: Travelers from all over the world come to Uttar Pradesh with one goal in mind: passing through the grand marble gates of the Taj Mahal. Far from the camera-snapping crowds of Agra, however, another destination awaits, one that’s relatively undiscovered by tourists. Lucknow, the capital, doesn’t have one must-see landmark. What it offers is the chance to step into the past — to wander through glittering sultan’s palaces, to view the faded grandeur of the British Raj, to live out their Passage to India-style fantasy in relative solitude. Stay under the Forsterian spell by checking into Lebua Lucknow. The historic hotel, located inside an Art Deco-style bungalow and surrounded by manicured green lawns and reflecting pools, is rich with turn-of-the-century charm. Guest rooms, featuring details like hand-carved headboards, antique wooden chairs, and cushions covered with traditional Chikan embroidery, open onto colorfully tiled patios and terraces. Breezy passageways, framed by wooden latticework, lead between candlelit courtyards. It’s seamless indoor-outdoor living, as it always has been in this part of India, but with elegant updates and modern in-room amenities like flat-screen TVs and free wi-fi. Awadhi, Hyderabadi, and Rajasthani cuisines are all represented at Azrak, the hotel’s signature restaurant. Lined with bright blue tile and dark wooden paneling, it’s encased with glass windows that look out over Lebua Lucknow’s lush gardens. There’s also 1936 for al fresco dining: strange as it may seem to feast on Italian cuisine while traveling in India, remember that Lucknow is a cultural crossroads as you belly up to the hotel bar. Perched atop a decorative wooden stool, sipping scotch out of a crystal glass and bathing in the soft glow of the chandelier overhead, you’ll feel transported to English colonial days. In the morning, venture out into the fabulously photogenic streets of Lucknow. There’s even a spectacular pair of mausoleums — and you won’t have to wait in any lines to see them.

content: Wymara Resort & Villas, Turks + Caicos makes its home on Providenciales, on a stunning stretch of sand, looking straight out at that big empty blue sea — and the combination of unspoiled natural beauty and the clean-lined contemporary-luxe Wymara is a powerful one indeed. The look is more reminiscent of stylish Miami Beach than the Caribbean norm — the rooms are crisp and contemporary, not aggressively modern or minimal, though mostly monochrome, the better to keep the attention focused on the sun, surf and sand outside. Many of the rooms, and all of the suites, face out to sea, but even if you’re overlooking the garden, you won’t leave here without getting a good close look at the ocean — the fishing, diving, and snorkeling, if you want to get that close, are extraordinary. Whether or not you go that far, you’re certain to spend some time at the beach club or the pool — rent a beach bed at the former, or an “island pod” at the latter, for all your private-in-public sunbathing needs. Two bustling restaurants and a spa with the latest in group fitness offerings complete the city-by-the-sea package — though mellower than Miami Beach, there’s still a bit of an urban party vibe to be found here. Wymara Resort & Villas, Turks + Caicos is a ten-minute drive from Providenciales International Airport.

content: The Honduran island of Roatán is perhaps most famous for its proximity to the world’s second-largest barrier reef and the world-class snorkeling and diving that that implies. Kimpton Grand Roatán Resort & Spa applies the Kimpton brand’s decades of high-end boutique-hotel experience to this island idyll, with impressive results. Accommodations range widely across categories, from rooms and suites to bungalows and condos; the design is vibrant and modern and the comforts are plentiful. The indigenous-inspired Kao Kamasa Spa is a major attraction, as are the excursions, both on land and sea; the Kimpton signature social hour is a daily highlight.

content:
At the southern end of the Atacama Desert, among the driest places on earth, is the remarkably verdant Elqui Valley. It’s here, surrounded by gardens and greenery, that you’ll find CasaMolle, a 12-room luxury boutique hotel whose expansive grounds and absolute seclusion offer something of a resort experience, albeit a small-scale one.

After all, not many boutique hotels of CasaMolle’s size can claim a nine-hole par 3 golf course among their attractions. Three pools and six outdoor hot tubs are available for aquatic relaxation, as is a full-service spa and health club. There’s a thoughtfully designed kids’ program to keep children entertained, and at night guests are treated to some of the darkest skies — and the finest stargazing — anywhere in the world.

As for the rooms themselves, they’re clean-lined and modern, but decorated in rustic local colors and textures. All are spacious and comfortable, and are roughly equal in sizes and layouts, with some variations. Meanwhile the hotel’s restaurant operates on an all-inclusive basis, and uses local ingredients and produce — much grown in CasaMolle’s own gardens — to create a menu that’s both artful and dedicated to the flavors of the region.

content: Swinton Park is impressive enough: a beautifully picturesque 18th-century castle surrounded by some 200 acres of lake-dotted parkland. But that’s only the core of the greater Swinton Estate, which expands to an eye-watering 20,000 acres and encompasses a number of freestanding cottages as well as Swinton Bivouac, a collection of lodges and yurts providing an uncommonly rustic glamping experience. \n\nIt’s a rare hotel that can offer everything from a castle turret suite to a yurt, from a hydrotherapy spa to a “Druid’s Temple.” Activities include semi-wild country-house diversions like archery and falconry, and extend to some fairly distant rambles, thanks to the sheer size and wildness of the estate. Nor are the culinary arts neglected; Swinton Estate offers everything from fine dining and afternoon tea to cookery classes and the casual camp-side Bivouac Café.

content: After successful launches in Jackson Hole and Mammoth Lakes, Outbound Hotels turned eastward to one of New England’s top mountain resorts. For all of Stowe’s considerable charm, it’s a destination somewhat short on modern boutique hotels, and the youthful, nature-oriented Outbound Stowe fills the gap nicely. On a wooded property a few miles outside of town, with direct access to Stowe’s popular Recreation Path, it’s a hybrid of glamping and hipster summer camp complete with communal fire pits surrounded by Adirondack chairs, a stylish all-day eatery, and one of the largest outdoor swimming pools in the area. \n\nStandard rooms and two-level loft suites, all cozy and colorfully furnished, are housed in the main buildings, while Scandinavian-inspired A-frame cabins come with handy kitchenettes and floor-to-ceiling windows facing the forest. Offering extra space and privacy is a shabby-chic three-bedroom cottage with a full kitchen and fireplace. At the end of the day, though, Outbound Stowe is a social place, its beautifully illuminated pool and patio ideal for hanging out and sipping maple-infused craft cocktails under the stars after a day out skiing, hiking, or mountain biking.

Just across from Oxford University’s photogenic and exclusive Balliol College is a hotel that doesn’t suffer from the comparison: The Store Oxford makes its home in the building that previously housed the famous Boswells department store. Hence the name. In its current incarnation it’s a thoroughly contemporary luxury hotel, one with style to spare and a level of comfort that places it at the top end of the local hospitality scene. 

Behind its handsome façade The Store is confidently, quietly modern in its style, in a way that particularly stands out in contrast with the traditional look that’s more typical around town. The accommodations, in particular, are full of references to the building’s history, even while the overall impression is one of stylish contemporary luxury.

A subterranean spa is among the hotel’s charms, while its most unexpected attraction is a rooftop bar and terrace with a panoramic view of Oxford’s distinguished rooftops. Treadwell, the restaurant, serves seasonal and sustainable modern British fare; the ground-floor bar, which opens onto Broad Street, keeps the hotel connected with the city’s daily social life.

content:
Torre Virreyes, one of the last works of the celebrated architect Teodoro González de León, looks like the tallest building in Mexico City. It isn’t; in fact it’s not even close. But looming high over the Bosque de Chapultepec, one of the largest urban parks in the Americas, this trapezoid-shaped skyscraper — home to the Alexander Hotel — dwarfs everything around it. 

Needless to say, Alexander offers spectacular views over the park and the city skyline, not least of all because the design is airy and modern, all high ceilings and massive glass panes that stay miraculously pristine and smudge-free. Unlike many of the city’s luxury hotels, Alexander isn’t loyal to Mexican tradition of any kind. The custom-made furniture is Italian, the high-end bath products are Swedish, and the caviar bar is the only one of its kind in the city. Indeed, the list of in-room amenities reads like a who’s-who of international luxury brands: sound systems by Bang & Olufsen, lighting by Lutron, Dyson hairdryers, Nespresso machines, and so on. The best of everything, in other words, to befit the hotel’s spacious suites with their spa-like marble bathrooms and treetop vistas.

Alexander’s sleek Caviar Bar is a place for Mexico City’s elite to see and be seen, but it’s also a fanciful spot to sip craft cocktails and enjoy the view. The hotel also has a restaurant specializing in elevated Mexican cuisine, a European-style spa, and personal trainers on call. It’s equally rewarding, however, to borrow an e-bike and take a spin through the sprawling park that spreads out before the hotel, a seemingly neverending expanse of greenery just waiting to be explored.

content: Chattanooga’s Terminal Station was once a symbol of the golden age of rail travel. But the stately Beaux Arts–style building, home of the famous Chattanooga Choo Choo, barely escaped demolition in the 1970s. Newly protected as a historic site, it functioned as a Hilton hotel for decades. In its latest iteration as the Hotel Chalet, the landmark’s original grandeur has been fully restored — sunshine pours through dome-like skylights, classic cocktails are served through the window of a refurbished caboose, and the interiors, illuminated by antique lamps, exude old-world charm. \n\nThere’s extra novelty, and a special reverence for history, in the guest rooms that are housed in renovated Pullman carriages. Some are Victorian, with original Tiffany Glass pendants and bentwood dining chairs, and others are midcentury modern, with custom wall coverings, plush sleeper sofas, and scalloped king beds. Designer Jenny Bukovec brings the same retro nostalgia to rooms in the main building, which feature wall-to-wall patterned carpeting, Italian linens, and rich wood paneling. With old-school wet bars and powder rooms, suites feel out of another era, save for the updated sound systems and Toto bathroom fixtures. French-Belgian dishes with an Appalachian twist are served at Elsie’s Daughter, the name a reference to the terminal’s architect, and outdoor highlights include a romantic courtyard bar and a pool surrounded by striped chaises.

content:
Wrapped in ten acres of its own private estate with 360° views including Koggala Lake to the west and distant views of the Indian Ocean to the south, the regal Tekanda Lodge has just six rooms. The estate is sometimes rented out for exclusive use, but even for those occupying a single suite, the refined eco-lodge offers plenty in the way of privacy and luxury. The place was once a tea and coconut plantation, and some organic crops are still grown on the grounds, including cinnamon, which is pleasingly aromatic when it catches on the morning breeze.

The main lodge houses four rooms, all set around a traditional courtyard and featuring private verandas with views of the surrounding landscape. The look mixes colonial charm with safari chic: beds draped with breezy white mosquito netting, handmade wooden furniture, antique-looking writing desks, and light-flooded bathrooms, two of which come with freestanding tubs. A pair of cabanas, set slightly apart from the lodge, are especially striking, with high, vaulting wood-beamed ceilings, four-poster beds, and lounge space with built-in daybeds. 

Served on the lodge’s main deck or in rooms on request is a lavish breakfast with tropical fruits and Sri Lankan dishes. Most guests are out exploring during the day, but a gorgeous infinity pool, reflecting the silhouette of palm trees and bordered by a spacious stone deck, is a perfect place to cool off afterward. Later, banana leaf–wrapped fish and other local specialties are prepared for a communal-style open-air dinner, and drinks — many incorporating tea and other ingredients grown on the grounds — flow freely under the stars.

content:
Most of the Domaines de Fontenille hotels have sprouted on French soil, but the Chianti wine country of Tuscany is a sensible place for this wine-focused brand to establish an Italian satellite. Pieve Aldine is, like its French cousins, an absolutely classic rural escape — in this case, a beautifully historic 10th-century residence and agricultural estate surrounded by picture-perfect Tuscan hillsides.

The 22 rooms and suites combine antique architecture and contemporary design, mixing rustic textures with 16th-century frescoes and a modern graphic sensibility. The accommodations are luxurious, but quietly so — not just soothingly simple in their visual style, but uncluttered and free of ostentatious ornament. Each unit is different, owing to the peculiarities of the historic floor plan, and many of the views are nothing short of extraordinary.

Wellness offerings include a spa and an outdoor swimming pool, as well as paths that crisscross the estate and continue out into the countryside. Le Rondini, the hotel’s bistro, serves modern Tuscan fare alongside wines from Chianti and beyond; L’Enoteca, the more casual option, is a vision of Fifties glamour that opens onto the property’s gardens.

content: A few minutes up the coast from Punta del Este, the natural setting is no less spectacular, and the atmosphere is a good deal more tranquil. It’s here, in the seaside town of La Barra, that you’ll find Casa Flor, tucked between the forest and the sea, in a residential neighborhood a block from the beach at Playa Montoya. This is about as low-key as a boutique hotel can get — it’s got the atmosphere of an exquisitely designed private home, and with just nine rooms and suites it’s not easy to imagine it ever feeling busy.\n\nThe units themselves are decked out in heavenly white-on-white, and are decorated with surf-inspired paintings by the local artist Nicolás Caubarrere. The style is a little bit modern and a little bit rustic, polished but not too polished; same goes for the comforts, which are substantial but far from ostentatious. And if you can get the Master Suite it’s worth splashing out; there’s a private terrace facing the hotel’s outdoor pool and an ocean view. The restaurants and nightlife of La Barra are just a few blocks away — Casa Flor itself remains a quiet, private refuge.

content: Nearly a century after a seed factory took up residence in an industrial building in Washington’s Union Market district, the landmark was reborn as the stylish Hotel Nell. A connection to the past is an essential part of this boutique hotel’s ethos: it’s named after Nell Bolgiano, matriarch of the Bolgiano Seed Company. A horticultural theme endures, with lush shades of green enlivening the lofty interiors and live foliage framing the Treehouse bar on the uppermost level. Sustainability matters too, naturally — a nearby farmers market provides tomatoes and berries for the breakfast menu, and green roofs help keep the building cool in summer. Rooms are modern and cozy with exposed beams, minimalist décor, and colorful pieces by local artists.

content: What’s now Landhotel Voshövel has been in the family since 1872, though you’d never guess it from the looks of the contemporary luxury hotel that today occupies the estate. Just as important is the spa, with its pools, saunas, and fitness equipment — and some of the region’s finest cycling and hiking routes are availble just outside. Also of note: the property’s old barn, now redesigned, houses a pop-up restaurant, just one of several culinary offerings in-house.

content: It’s hard to believe that bears, tigers, and monkeys once lived in the Granger Building, an elegant Romanesque-style landmark in the Gaslamp Quarter. This five-story building was originally a bank, and its basement served as a temporary residence for animals before the 1916 opening of the San Diego Zoo; more than a century later, the building was reborn as the design-forward Granger Hotel. \n\nMany of its charming original features remain, like the tin ceilings, high arching windows, and grand hallways, and whimsical references to the building’s past, including a custom mural with wildlife motifs, were integrated into its sophisticated updates. Rooms are outfitted in shades of navy blue and espresso with a mix of modern and vintage-inspired pieces, including Art Deco-style armoires, quirky antiques, plush flower-shaped headboards, and custom leather sofas. There’s no restaurant, but breakfast is served in the greenery-framed lobby lounge, and the low-lit Parlor Room is an irresistible spot for a nightcap.

content:
The proprietors of Monsieur Didot rightly call it a residence, rather than a hotel; this elegant neoclassical townhouse in the heart of Athens is more like an aristocratic pied-à-terre than anything else. And its French name is as clear a sign as any that this is no ordinary lodging; it’s inspired by, and named for, the type designer Firmin Didot.

The charming house positively overflows with just-so details: think spiral staircases, gilt mirrors, pastel shutters, and riotously verdant houseplants. Six individually decorated rooms and suites nod to that literary heritage, with built-in bookshelves alongside plush linens, framed wall art, and invigorating city views.

At this size, a restaurant is too much to ask, but Monsieur Didot serves a thoughtful in-room breakfast; its staff, meanwhile, can confidently recommend any number of local restaurants, bars, and attractions.

content:
Based on a quick description of the place — a small and stylish lodge on a private tropical island, accessible only by boat — it would be easy to get the wrong idea about Jicaro Island Ecolodge. Because the hotel isn’t located on the kind of island you’re picturing. It’s not on the ocean, for starters, but on the freshwater Lake Nicaragua, the largest lake in Central America. The island is one of 365 small islets formed by a long-ago eruption of the nearby Mombacho volcano. It’s tropical, yes, but forget about clear blue water and white sand: this landscape, thick with lush vegetation and home to a wide range of exotic birds and monkeys, feels more like a river delta or bayou.

Jicaro consists of just nine casitas, free-standing bungalows, tucked into the forested island like quiet treehouses. Each has two stories: on the ground level is an airy living room, and up the floating staircase, a bedroom with a king-sized bed. As you’d expect of an ecolodge, the look is chic and minimal, all natural wood, earth hues, and romantic yet practical mosquito nets. And as you’d expect of an ecolodge, there’s no air-conditioning; thanks to smart architectural design and the surrounding trees’ deep shade, you’re unlikely to miss it. Each casita has a private terrace overlooking the lake.

Rates include breakfast, lunch, and dinner, a particular treat in a corner of Central America that’s renowned for its spectacular produce and seafood. Menus change seasonally, but highlights include fresh ceviche, coconut shrimp, watermelon salad with feta, and cocktails like the rum-based “Caipinica,” the Nicaraguan twist on a Brazilian caipirinha. No one would blame you if you just want to hang around the island, sipping fresh juices, partaking of Jicaro’s complimentary yoga classes, or swinging in a hammock all afternoon. We hear they're quite generous with the kayaks and paddleboards, as well. Topping it all off, there's a lakefront spa with open-air treatment rooms.

But that’s another thing you wouldn’t expect of a private tropical island: it’s pretty easy to get to. An island on Lake Nicaragua sounds remote, but that depends on your definition — should you wish to venture to the mainland, its a short boat ride (arranged by Jicaro) back to the pretty colonial city of Granada, Nicaragua, and the volcanoes, artisan markets, and crater lakes that surround it. (Not to mention, an hour’s drive later, Managua’s international airport.)

How to get there: Jicaro Island Ecolodge may only be accessed via a 15-minute boat ride from Asese Port outside Granada, which is just over an hour's drive from Managua International Airport.

content: The Greek islands have never been more popular with travelers, but there’s a downside to the surging tourism numbers. One hotel that’s dedicated to offsetting the environmental impact is Laguna Coast Resort, on the west coast of Naxos, part of the largest regeneration project in the Cyclades. This luxury hotel is intimately sized, especially in comparison to the protected reserve it sits on — spanning some 480 acres of wetlands, an offshore reef and islet, and a mile of private coastline, this wildly beautiful landscape is a natural habitat for flamingos and rare birds. \n\nAfter a tour of the reserve on horseback or e-bike, the resort’s sleek cedar-lined villas and suites, outfitted in modern earth-toned decor and featuring private pools or Jacuzzis, offer sophisticated retreats from the sun. As the sun goes down, lanterns and twinkling lights illuminate the chic open-air restaurant and bistro.

content: Only a handful of historic buildings survived the fire that swept through the Greek castle town of Ioannina in 1820. One of these, a handsome stone mansion near the castle walls, is now home to Kamares Boutique Hotel. Much of its old-world grandeur remains — heavy wooden doors, brick archways, ornate fireplaces, sumptuous antiques, and original tile flooring. Rooms exude period charm, too, with exposed stone or brick walls, decorative bedframes, and vaulting wood-beamed ceilings. \n\nDespite its retro atmosphere, though, Kamares is up to date where it counts. Alongside the rooms’ antique velvet loveseats and hand-painted wall panels you’ll find Nespresso machines and modern bathrooms with Jacuzzis. The hotel’s Bodrum Spa, meanwhile, offers some intensive relaxation; the historic town center’s restaurants, shops, and museums are all a short stroll away.

content: This 17th-century convent became a hotel in the 1960s, but it was only during its 2020 closure that Palazzo Ripetta found its present form — a family-owned luxury hotel with a strong visual identity (and an enviable collection of art). The location, two streets to the south of the Piazza del Popolo, could hardly be more auspicious, and the 78 rooms and suites are the very picture of modern Roman elegance. Piazzetta Ripetta is open all day for drinks and light snacks while restaurant San Baylon serves classic Roman dishes. Up on the rooftop locals and visitors alike gather over unique cocktails with a view of the city.

content: Aria Retreat & Spa is a hotel within a hotel — a luxury boutique enclave within the larger Parco San Marco resort, set right on the shores of northern Italy’s Lake Lugano. The greater property spans some 60 acres of park, with spectacular views of the water and the mountains on the Swiss side of the lake. And while the resort is family-oriented, Aria Retreat reserves its spaces for guests 16 and up, which ensures a certain measure of genteel tranquility.\n\nIt’s appropriately sized for its purpose, a mere 15 suites, each of which is the very picture of contemporary Italian luxury; all of them face the lake, and are furnished with the full complement of modern comforts. The adults-only spa is an expansive one, and guests who venture beyond Aria’s confines enjoy the Parco San Marco’s multiple pools, a second family-oriented spa, and even a water park. Meanwhile the two hotels between them are served by no fewer than nine restaurants and bars, from the casual poolside pizzeria to Aria’s own Dolce Vita Lounge.

content: Arriving at Cali Mykonos is a slow reveal - an ancient olive tree, whitewashed walls, and then the Aegean stretching endlessly below. Carved into a cliff above Kalafatis Beach, it is a quieter, more refined take on Mykonos, where muted tones and contemporary Greek design set a soothing scene. A 130-meter infinity pool curves along the edge, a private beach awaits below, and days unfold between Pilates, yacht excursions, and freshly-caught seafood. A rare moment of stillness on an island known for its energy.
name: Cali Mykonos
policy: Cali is not just a place to stay—it is a place to live, better than home, better than anywhere. Born from a family’s love for summers spent in Greece, Cali stand on ten acres of Mykonos' southern coast. It is a village comprised of forty stone-built suites and villas, each its own refuge. A 130-meter infinity pool stretches toward the horizon, a private sand beach, three places to eat and drink, a padel court, outdoor gym, spa, and more. Two boats stand ready to carry guests to Nammos, Scorpios, and other beach clubs. The northern beaches—Alemagou, Principote—are only a short drive away. And when the lights of Mykonos Town call, a shuttle moves back and forth through the night.• The hotel welcomes guests 4 months old and older. Guests 13 and older are considered adults.

content: Named for the only town on the island of Rapa Nui — Easter Island — Nayara Hangaroa is a luxury hotel built to blend into the environment. The design was inspired by indigenous tradition, comprising a village-like cluster of low-lying buildings with grass roofs and native wood beams. Guest rooms feature locally sourced materials, from volcanic stone to cypress wood, as well as handmade clay soaking tubs and private terraces overlooking the ocean. There’s a cool geometric swimming pool — the island’s largest — plus a spa and two restaurants specializing in fresh seafood. You’re here for the island’s main attractions, of course, to see the famous moai statues, beaches, and archaeological sites, and the staff can arrange it. But the hotel, located just a few minutes’ stroll from the harbor, is a wonderful refuge to return to at the end of the day.

Just a short stroll from the city center, it is a great way to see a new side of Cork.

content: The ancient Greeks used the term “asty” to denote the center of a town or city. The new Asty Mykonos Hotel & Spa borrows the name, in reference not so much to its exact location — the hotel isn’t in Mykonos Town, but on a hillside overlooking it — as to its sophisticated style. Like many others in the area, the hotel is characterized by Cycladic architecture, but there’s a modern twist here: bold elements punctuate the white facade and its tiered terraces, from chaise longues upholstered in black to striking metallic light fixtures and a swimming pool lined in moody, dark-hued tiles.  \n\nThe interiors are a departure from the island’s white-on-white standard, as well. Rooms have earth-toned decor, boho-chic details, and bathrooms lined in deep green marble. Even the simplest room has a private terrace with a jetted tub or Jacuzzi, while suites, many facing the sea, feature private terraces with plunge pools. Loft-style maisonette suites come with two levels of living space, and the master suite has a private infinity pool and fitness room. Down by the main pool, macrame sun umbrellas offer shade on the sun-baked terrace and creative cocktails are served with dreamy water views; a great selection of restaurants and bars are a short drive or an easy walk away.

content: Lodgings in Lima’s popular oceanfront neighborhood of Miraflores run the range from luxury chain hotels with rooftop pools to small inns with local character and personalized service. Fausto falls squarely into the latter category: the boutique guesthouse has just five rooms. Housed in an elegant 1920s townhouse on a tree-lined street just a block from the coastal promenade, the hotel is sophisticated but casual, like staying in the home of a stylish friend. A sleek kitchen is open to guests, the fridge is full of complimentary snacks, and an honesty bar is stocked around the clock. Communal spaces include the sala, a cozy ground-level living room that opens onto a pretty tiled patio, and the open-air terrace on the top floor.\n\nInstead of knocking down walls or reconfiguring the layout, Fausto’s owners have let things be; the house's original bedrooms still serve their original function. These days, they’re modern and simply furnished, divided into three categories. The minimalist Pequeña room is large enough to fit a double bed, desk, and chair, but not much else, while the Mediana room features a high-arching doorway that leads onto a luminous private patio. The Grande room is a standout with its four-poster bed, sitting area, and freestanding soaking tub. At any rate, Fausto is a social spot — not the kind of place to hole up in the room. Friendly staff are on hand to offer recommendations or mix the perfect pisco sour, but the hotel’s location near the neighborhood’s clifftop park makes it an ideal base for independent exploring.

content: Zulal isn’t just another ultra-luxe Qatari resort, though it certainly is that — it’s the first wellness retreat in the Middle East by the Thailand-based Chiva-Som concern. From a detox point of view it’s significant that there’s no alcohol; maybe even more so that there’s no internet. \n\nThe resort’s low-slung buildings cluster around the twists and turns of the lagoon-style pools, just yards from a natural beach. Its wellness center is no mere spa but a holistic health center informed by Traditional Arabic & Islamic Medicine, and the restaurants’ offerings serve this health-centered focus as well.

content: Bangkok-based Centara Hotels & Resorts has dozens of hotels around Thailand. But Centara Reserve Samui, set on a secluded stretch of Koh Samui’s idyllic Chaweng Beach, represents the brand’s first foray into the ultra-luxury sphere. It’s more exclusive than its sister hotels on the island, with a stunning pair of waterfront swimming pools — a vast, turquoise-tiled infinity pool with a swim-up bar and chaise longues partly submerged in cool water, and a quieter pool for adults only — a light-filled spa, a slew of upscale indoor-outdoor restaurants, and a sophisticated gin bar. \n\nRooms are outfitted in modern Thai decor with sliding glass doors opening onto spacious furnished terraces and glamorous details like decorative wooden screens and elegant marble-topped bars equipped with cocktail shakers and martini glasses. The pièce de résistance is a collection of lavishly appointed suites with private pools and round-the-clock butler service.

content: It’s hard to say which of Cayo Exclusive Resort & Spa’s assets is most impressive. There’s the privileged location in the Cretan village of Plaka on the island’s northeastern coast — overlooking Elounda Bay, the hotel offers unparalleled views of picturesque Spinalonga Island. There’s the striking and eco-friendly architectural design, with six tiers of modern stone structures built into the steep hillside and connected by funicular trains. Then there are the rooms themselves, all with private pools and sea views, the interiors elegant and contemporary with custom-made beds, marble bathrooms, and sophisticated lighting systems. Completing the picture are three large infinity pools, a 24-hour fitness center, an array of high-end restaurants and bars, a private beach club, and an open-air waterfront amphitheater for live entertainment under the stars.

A modern spa occupies the estate’s onetime dovecote, and an outdoor pool is set amid the gorgeous surrounding park. Adding to the storybook charm is an elegant afternoon tea served on fine china.

Highfield, a country house in the scenic Yorkshire Wolds, has long been imbued with a romantic atmosphere. The original owner, who oversaw its construction in 1864, dedicated this country house to his wife; another husband-and-wife duo restored and reopened it in 2022 as a luxury boutique hotel. These days, with its mix of classic and contemporary offerings — think afternoon tea and Sunday roasts as well as a creative cocktail program and a locally sourced breakfast — Highfield still makes a cozy escape for couples or for families.

There are just eight suites, all uniquely decorated, and some flamboyantly so. One is inspired by the look of an antique train carriage, another is fashioned as a pale pink boudoir; an attic-like room in the old servants’ lodgings features mounted deer heads and woodland fairy artwork, and in the old master's quarters, there’s a dark, whimsical suite with Batman logos incorporated into the designer wallpaper, an homage to the owners’ son. All come with bespoke mattresses, all-natural bath products made in the British countryside, and complimentary “maxi bars” stocked with local snacks and drinks, while some feature freestanding vintage tubs and four-poster beds. 

Downstairs, the charming chandelier-lit Library Bar is open all day, with tables spilling onto the adjacent open-air terrace in warmer weather. The 1864 restaurant, located in Highfield’s original dining room, is focused on foraging and sourcing ingredients from the kitchen gardens and the local farms.

content:
A 39-story skyscraper hotel might not be what you expect from a luxury hotel in the Cambodian capital, but the Rosewood Phnom Penh is nothing if not surprising. This isn’t just a pied-à-terre from which to explore the city, but a part of its urban life; its variety of high-end restaurants make it a fixture on the capital’s social scene, as does Sora, the spectacular rooftop bar. 

The rooms and suites are modern and luxurious, clean-lined and contemporary but with plenty of tastefully applied local character, and the elevated views over this low-rise city are like nothing else in town. Even the entry-level rooms span some 50 square meters, while the signature suites are proper residences, complete with dining rooms and kitchens.

Sense, the spa, draws its inspiration from traditional Khmer practices and ingredients; it’s accompanied by a full-featured fitness center and a 22-meter lap pool on the 33rd floor. As for restaurants and bars, the Rosewood’s guests are spoiled for choice: from French comfort food at Brasserie Louis to Chinese cooking at Zhan Liang and Sora, the open-air cocktails-and-tapas venue on its vertiginous cantilevered terrace.

content:
What began as a small boarding house, founded by Marie Lorain in 1945, has grown and evolved over the years into something quite extraordinary: today La Côte Saint-Jacques is a highly regarded restaurant and an exquisitely refined small hotel, overseen all along the way by subsequent generations of the Lorain family. The experience is a luxurious one, to be sure, but it’s one with plenty of personal touches and residential character, offering the pleasing impression of staying in the home of well-heeled French hosts. 

Its rooms and suites, like the restaurant’s famous dining room and terrace, overlook the river Yonne and the forested hills on the other side. Many have private patios to make the most of the bucolic Burgundy landscape. The design, by Karine Lorain, employs luxurious materials and bright yet harmonous colors to great effect, alongside large-format wildlife photographs by Jean-Michel.

The restaurant, under the direction of Jean-Michel Lorain and Alexandre Bondoux, has been recognizes with a pair of MICHELIN Stars. Breakfast is elegantly presented in a riverside setting, or brought to one’s room or balcony; cooking classes may be arranged on request. Meanwhile a light-filled two-level spa with a hammam and heated indoor pool is a relaxed place to recover from vineyard visits and multi-course meals.

content: Brick is a relatively uncommon building material in California, but this (amply reinforced) 1888-vintage brick building, once Oceanside’s first hardware store, is an eye-catching exception. The Brick Hotel isn’t large — just ten rooms — but for boutique-hotel fans it plays an outsized role in a hospitality scene that’s in the middle of something of a renaissance.\n\nThe rooms themselves are stylish, with a bit of an urban edge that’s a welcome departure for sunny San Diego County. And the location is as central as can be, right in the heart of Oceanside’s compact downtown, and a short walk from the pier and the beach. There are reasons to stay in, though; The Brick Hotel itself is home to a rooftop bar called Cococabana and a lobby-level tiki bar, both popular among guests and locals alike.

content:
Arriving at Sonora Resort is an adventure, whether you coast over Desolation Sound on a seaplane or glide past seal colonies on the boat journey from Campbell River. Open seasonally from May 1 - October 15, Sonora Resort is the only resort on Sonora Island. on Sonora Island, part of a remote archipelago on Canada’s west coast. And while most make the trip here to see humpback whales and black bears in the wild, the fishing lodge-turned-luxury resort, with outdoor mineral pools, fly-fishing ponds, and a gorgeous spa, is a destination in itself. 

A collection of timber buildings, each with common lounges featuring stone fireplaces and open-air hot tubs, house rooms lined in cedar and stone. All are outfitted in calming earth tones and feature large picture windows overlooking the sea, while a few freestanding lodge suites and villas, dramatically positioned on rocks over the water, offer more peace and privacy. Organic produce and locally caught seafood figure prominently on the restaurant’s menu, and it’s not uncommon to catch sight of a bald eagle from the resort’s ocean-facing dining room.

How to get there:
Sonora Resort is accessible by air or water. Regular scheduled flights (by helicopter and seaplane) operate between Vancouver and Sonora Resort. Private charter flights are also available from various locations in the PNW. Scheduled seaplane service is available from Seattle to Sonora Resort. Daily water taxi service is available from Campbell River on Vancouver Island. Please see the Need to Know section for more information.

content: Tucked away between the taco bars and boot shops of South Congress Avenue, Frame Hotel is a minimalist oasis in one of Austin’s liveliest neighborhoods. There’s no front desk, no elevator, and no pool or restaurant, just a collection of calm, elegant suites set around a lush courtyard garden with a koi pond, fountain, and custom-made lounge chairs and café tables. Sliding glass doors open onto each suite’s private wood-lined veranda. Framed by greenery, they’re tranquil spots for sipping coffee or taking a mid-afternoon break from shopping, sightseeing, or sipping cocktails on SoCo.

content: There’s something pleasingly symmetrical, even geometrical, about the design-focused boutique hotel Alpenloge. It’s located at the junction of four countries — Germany, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, and Austria — and each of its nine rooms is named after the cardinal direction it faces, some overlooking dazzling alpine landscapes and others a scenic mountain village. The architecture is loosely modeled after the Bavarian schoolhouse that once stood in its place, with a wood-shingled roof and high-ceilinged rooms bathed in natural light. But the interiors are more modern than traditional: the owners went to great lengths to outfit the interiors with the finest furnishings available in Europe, from king-sized beds by the renowned German manufacturer Schramm to chairs by Danish brands like Nor11 and Fredericia.

content: At the southernmost tip of mainland Greece, the secluded Mani Peninsula is home to quiet beaches and quaint hill towns. The fishing village of Gerolimenas is located on a small inlet where rugged cliffs wrap around a sheltered bay, and here, a historic landmark has been cleverly converted from a bustling grocery store into the sophisticated KaSeas Boutique Hotel. Like many of the older buildings in town, it’s sturdily built of native stone. But unlike most, the hotel enjoys privileged waterfront access: across the street from the entrance, KaSeas has a private beach club-style setup, with an open-air bar and a row of umbrellas and chaises right on the village’s natural harbor. \n\nMost rooms have dazzling sea views, too, save for a handful that overlook an interior garden. With exposed stone walls, vaulted wooden beams, and poured concrete flooring, they’re atmospheric and dramatically illuminated. King-sized beds, Nespresso machines, and marble bathrooms are standard features. A few loft suites come with large furnished terraces, and other suites have open-air hot tubs or ocean-facing balconies. The hotel’s indoor-outdoor restaurant, set across the building’s stone terraces and especially inviting when candlelit after dark, is popular with locals; by day, guests enjoy trips around the coastline’s caves and crystal-clear waters on the hotel’s boat.

content: There’s nothing but fir trees and quiet mountain trails around MANNA Arcadia, tucked away in the highlands of Greece’s central Peloponnese. The high-altitude location was specifically chosen for its healing properties: opened in the late 1920s, this building first served as a sanatorium for soldiers. After the introduction of penicillin, the solitary stone lodge sat abandoned for decades until it was acquired by a Greek entrepreneur, who worked with a team of archaeologists to carefully restore the landmark and transform it into a luxury hotel.\n\nThe property’s original function — a peaceful escape immersed in nature — remains largely the same, so minimal intervention was key to the overhaul. The interiors are modern, light-filled, and lined in pale wood. Rooms have king-sized beds with raw linen duvets, heated floors, sustainably crafted bath products, and views of the surrounding forest. Most have private balconies; suites feature built-in sofas and large wooden decks, and a few have freestanding copper bathtubs. A major highlight is, naturally, the wellness area with its cave pool, hammam, outdoor forest sauna and fireplace-warmed yoga room. Hiking, skiing, horseback riding, truffle hunting and other activities are all easily arranged nearby. Before and after the day’s outdoor adventures, MANNA’s cozy all-day restaurant serves creative Greek cuisine made with local and seasonal ingredients, which can be followed by a movie in summer at one of the hotel’s open-air cinema nights.
name: MANNA Arcadia
policy:
• The hotel welcomes guests 11 and older.

MANNA: Surrounded by a landscape that has been considered an earthly paradise since antiquity and situated within a historically preserved building, MANNA is a newly opened luxury mountain retreat in Arcadia, Greece. Replete with outdoor yoga, multiple cozy fireplaces, a serene wellness hub, an architectural concept and entirely bespoke furnishings by K-Studio, and farm-to-table cuisine conceived by award-winning Greek chef Athinagoras Kostakos, the hotel offers a place to refresh, reset, and reengage with one’s mind, body, soul, and earthly surroundings.

Located in Arcadia, in the heart of Peloponnese just two hours from Athens, at an altitude of 1,200 meters and surrounded by virgin fir forest, MANNA is a mountain retreat ripe for rejuvenation and reconnection. This year-round destination unfolds across a landmarked sanatorium constructed between 1927 and 1929. Straying from the neoclassical architecture typical in Greece at the time, the building—which welcomed patients suffering from tuberculosis from its opening until 1938, when penicillin became widely accessible—has a design that reflects characteristics more closely related to Central Europe. After standing in a state of abandonment for over eight decades, a medley of old and new elements now come together to create a property where visitors feel the weight of history while enjoying contemporary luxuries and natural surroundings; while slowing down and embracing the moment; while nourishing relationships with other humans, nature, and oneself. “Manna,” after all, means a sudden and unexpected source of gratification or pleasure—and here guests will find just that, nestled amongst an almost untouched landscape.

Around the corner from Ioannina Castle, an old stone archway leads into the elegant Stoes Boutique Hotel. This mansion dates back to the late 19th century, and much of its old-world character has been preserved, but the hotel’s aesthetic is clean and contemporary — high ceilings, whitewashed walls, gleaming black-and-white tiled floors, a well-placed chandelier. 

The simplest rooms are refined but austere, quiet and cloister-like with exposed stone walls, parquet floors, dark wood furniture, and minimalist bathrooms with walk-in showers; some also have balconies or striking modern fireplaces. Upper-level suites feature spacious living rooms with Chesterfield sofas and lavish bathrooms lined in decorative tile.

Among its public spaces are a sunny terrace as well as an all-day restaurant and a bar; the whole of historic Ioannina, meanwhile, is close at hand, and offers no end of complementary options.

content: Connected to Mykonos by a narrow isthmus, Aleomandra is almost like a separate island — remote, exclusive, and home to some of the area’s most opulent private villas. The Cycladic-chic Enigma Hideaway Suites Mykonos feels especially far-flung and private, thanks to its location near the very tip of the peninsula. This luxury boutique hotel is made up of just four rooms, each sumptuously outfitted in modern earth-toned décor with king-sized beds and stone-walled terraces overlooking the sea. Sleek and spacious bathrooms, filled with natural light, have walk-in rain showers. Two are suites with separate living rooms, and a few come with private outdoor pools.\n\nEven more appealing is the hotel’s sparkling infinity pool, with its dazzling views of the Aegean. Lined in aquamarine tile, it features a row of stylish sunbeds elevated on platforms above the water’s edge, a long canopied pool bar running along one side. On the other side is The Harper, Enigma’s sophisticated open-air restaurant. It’s an idyllic spot for an al fresco breakfast, which can also be served in one’s suite: for those with a private pool, on a picturesque floating tray. The calm and off-the-beaten-path Glyfadi Beach, a short stroll away, is one of the best spots on the island to catch the sunset.

content:
Adler Lodge Ritten occupies a wooded Alpine glade just outside Bolzano, Italy, where Italian and German cultures intermingle freely in the shadow of the Dolomites. The concept is a timeless one, as is the execution; the style blends the region’s typical warmth with confident contemporary design. It’s a winning formula, with storybook vistas that can be seen from all over the property, including the all-season infinity pool and the extensive wellness complex. 

The hotel’s accommodations come in two flavors — lodge suite or freestanding chalet — with both offering décor that’s marked by Alpine wood, warm textiles, and roomy private balconies. Meanwhile the cuisine is both hearty and healthful, as you’d expect from a hotel of this caliber in this particular corner of the world. In summer, hiking and biking feature prominently; in winter, Ritten’s ski area is one among many.

It is a destination designed for total relaxation: the property offers only all-inclusive rates, which cover full board, beverages, and a rich program of indoor and outdoor activities.

Not far from the hotel runs the Renon train, which regularly connects the two main villages of the Renon, Collalbo and Soprabolzano, from where the cable car descends directly to Bolzano.

content:
A member of one of the better-known mini-chains in Greek luxury boutique hospitality, Domes Noruz Kassandra is an upscale adults-only hideaway in Halkidiki, a place where tranquility can’t always be taken for granted. It calls itself “a beach club with rooms,” which is a phrase that certainly does justice to the seaside setting and to the lively nightlife.

None of which, though, should be taken to imply there’s anything secondary about the hotel’s 154 rooms and suites, all of which are decorated in heavenly white and cream and outfitted with tasteful high-end comforts. Units are divided by their proximity to either the “Vibrant” or the “Secret” pool; the difference in atmosphere follows logically from there.

The Soma Spa is a touch livelier than the typical wellness offering, though its mission remains one of relaxation; meanwhile Topos, the restaurant, is a seafood-focused Greek eatery.

content: It’s nowhere near the ocean, but the laid-back, West Coast–inspired vibes are unmistakable at Drift Nashville. Indeed, this boutique hotel may have more in common with its stylish sister properties in California — midcentury modern architecture, a cool coastal aesthetic, breezy indoor-outdoor lounge space — than with its Music City neighbors. \n\nFor their debut in the American South, the Drift group revamped a sixties-era hotel in the East Bank and tapped into local talent and tradition, stripping back the interiors to create minimalist spaces that showcase the work of Nashville-based creators. A nearby woodworking studio nearby designed the rooms’ custom walnut beds, and the rooms display work by local artists. Other highlights include a retro cocktail bar and a penthouse suite with a standalone tub and a golden toilet — the latter an homage to Elvis, the original hotel’s most notable guest.

content:
The lovely waterside Park Hotel Kenmare is a Victorian-era gem, a fixture on Ireland’s luxury-hotel scene for well over a century. In its place, some hotels might go all in on nostalgia, but not this one. Its current owners are devoted to keeping it up to date, and after a renovation by the Kenmare-raised hospitality designer Bryan O’Sullivan, it’s neither a modern experiment nor a strict period piece, but something altogether timeless.

This means luxurious rooms and suites decorated in a style that feels contemporary, but still pays generous tribute to the 19th century. Each one is different, and all are equipped with state-of-the-art comforts, handled as unobtrusively as possible. Some face lovely gardens, others the sublime Kenmare River and Caha Mountains. And every unit is stocked with Blue Bottle coffee, Barry’s Irish tea, and sencha for green tea devotees — as perfect a morning trifecta as we’ve ever seen.

Nor are the accommodations the whole of the story. SÁMAS, the spa, is key to the Park Hotel Kenmare’s appeal. The hotel’s art collection is noteworthy in its own right, and is the subject of daily tours. The surrounding mountains and waterways offer no end of possibilities for recreation, while the Kenmore Golf Club lies just next door. And food and drink are by no means neglected — Landline, the restaurant, is joined by an elegant cocktail bar, a handful of lounges and terraces, and a wide variety of wines and whiskeys.

How to get there:
Park Hotel Kenmare is approximately a 1 1/2 hour drive from Cork Airport, 50 minutes from Kerry Airport and a 40 minute drive from the town of Killarney.

content: It’s been generations since the Catskills were as popular an escape as they are now, and the Leeway in Mount Tremper is one of the many stylish hotels taking advantage. It isn’t entirely new: opened as a motel in the 1950s, this creekside property got a kitschy makeover in 2004 by Kate Pierson, frontwoman of the B-52s. After extensive renovations at the hands of its new owners, it was reborn as a boutique inn with rustic-chic interiors, locally roasted coffee, sustainable landscaping, Apotheke bath products, and countless other details carefully chosen to help Brooklynites feel right at home. \n\nRooms feel like cool custom-made cabins with eat-in kitchens, bespoke wood furnishings, designer carpeting, and leather butterfly chairs. Adding warmth are artisan-made elements like ethically handcrafted rugs and colorful throw blankets, and standard amenities include Marshall speakers, Brooklinen bedding, and sleek portable coolers and lanterns. Many rooms also feature extras like gas fireplaces, front porches, or private terraces with river views. Cozy as these lodgings are, some of the Leeway’s highlights are outside: fireside gatherings on the river’s edge are especially popular, camping-style grills are set up for DIY barbecues, and hammocks swing between the trees, inviting a late afternoon nap after hiking, swimming, or fly-fishing in the beautiful surrounding landscape.
