content: Located at the foot of the Hardenberg castle ruins, a thousand-year-old clifftop monument that rises up majestically in the Palatinate Forest, Relais & Châteaux Hardenberg BurgHotel has a privileged location on the grounds of an ancient estate. The noble family abandoned the castle in the 18th century, around the same time the hotel was built — but the old distillery, tavern, and castle park are still in operation, and Hardenberg BurgHotel is the perfect base from which to enjoy them. With its red-shingled roof and half-timbered gables, the beautifully restored building exudes fairytale charm, and inside, it’s refined but cozy, with native wood flooring, exposed stone walls, and antique furnishings.\n\nMost rooms and suites are housed in the main house, with several others in the renovated mill next door. They’re all spacious and elegant with coffered walls, original artwork, bathrooms with tubs, and private balconies or terraces. Some face the castle, others the courtyard or the riding grounds, and all have large sitting areas ideal for sipping a Nespresso or complimentary spirits from the estate’s distillery. Downstairs, the modern BurgSpa has a fireplace and whirlpools with castle views.The generous breakfast buffet features regional and organic products, including homemade jams and eggs provided by a nearby farmer. Novalis, the hotel’s restaurant, follows suit with seasonal dishes crafted from locally caught fish and game. When the weather cooperates, relaxing or dining outside on one the hotel’s pretty wood-lined terraces is especially appealing, and guests are invited on a free guided tour of the castle ruins on Sundays.

content: Les Domaines de Fontenille may be best known for their fine little Provençal farmhouse hotels, but that’s changing as the brand expands across France and beyond. Les Hauts Mers lies off the west coast, on the dramatic Île d’Yeu, within walking distance of the island’s main port; and yet from here, on a parcel of land that looks straight out over the Atlantic, the sensation is one of pure seaside seclusion.\n\nWith 17 rooms and suites Les Hauts Mers is right in the sweet spot where a small and intimate escape can justify a bit of infrastructure. Here that means Vent Debout, a very fine seafood-focused restaurant, as well as a lovely little heated outdoor pool. Like all of the Fontenille establishments, there’s nothing ostentatious about it — this is a subtle and self-assured sort of luxury living.

content: Milan isn’t just the center of modern Italian fashion and design — it’s also home to the Gothic marvel that is the Duomo di Milano, or Milan Cathedral. Both of these sides of the city’s character are represented in this hotel: The Street Milano Duomo stands quite literally right around the corner from the spectacular church, and while its interiors are adorned with large-scale images of the cathedral and historical Milan, they’re otherwise decorated in a colorful, contemporary style that pays liberal tribute to the Italian designers of the modern era.\n\nThe Street Milano Duomo, though it may not operate on the palatial scale of some of Milan’s bigger hotels, is more than luxurious enough. Its rooms and suites are not just stylish but full of top-shelf comforts; meanwhile the hotel’s bar and its elevated terrace are more or less the extent of the public spaces. In so central a location, of course, you’ll be faced with no shortage of options for dining and nightlife, and the hotel’s concierge is happy to help you sort the local favorites from the tourist traps. As for shopping, The Street is also right around the corner from the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, which is likely the most aesthetically pleasing shopping mall in the Western world; not far in another direction are the high-end retailers of the Quadrilatero d’Oro.

content:
Though Montenegro’s Adriatic coast is only a fraction as long as those of its neighboring states, it’s every bit as picturesque. Increasingly, too, the Montenegrin coast is home to luxury resorts that rival anything else on the Mediterranean. Among them is the Dukley Hotel & Resort, in the seaside town of Budva: a luxe compound made up of a series of modern stone-and-glass buildings cascading down the hillside, ending in a sunset-facing private beach.

Within these buildings you’ll find a wide range of accommodations, from a compact-yet-stylish Superior room with a single king bed to a variety of suites (or “Residences”) and a handful of Penthouses. Many are sized for families; the largest fits up to eight adults and one child. And at all levels they’re handsome and modern, decorated in a stylish maritime palette and chic contemporary furniture.

Dukley’s location places it directly between public beaches at Budva and Bečići, to which the resort’s own private beach is a most welcome alternative. Also on offer are a variety of water sports as well as diving excursions and tours by land and sea; meanwhile the resort’s bars and restaurants place a decided emphasis on the flavors of the Italian peninsula.

content:
Though not as famous as the French Riviera, the Côte d’Argent, or Silver Coast, has its own considerable charms: long stretches of quiet coastline, untouched pine and oak forests, and the highest sand dunes in Europe, to name a few. 70 Hectares… & l’Océan is one of three connected resorts under the banner of Les Domaines de Fontenille — a luxury collection of hotels in France and Spain — and like its sister hotels, it’s modern and elegant. 

The name, however unusual, is straightforwardly descriptive: the resort sits on a 70-hectare (173-acre) golf course overlooking the sea, its green and white exterior partly obscured by the wooded setting. The three-story building houses sun-filled rooms and suites with large bay windows, cheerful plants, and whimsical yet sophisticated decor. There’s light and color everywhere — pale wood floors, crisp white linens, pastel details, bold, deep turquoise wall paneling — and eye-catching original artwork, from lithographs to photography to quirky sculptures, add visual interest. Bathrooms have tiled walk-in showers and organic products. Many rooms have private balconies or patios with views of the golf course, forest, or the Atlantic Ocean. 

On the ground level, a wide open-air terrace is a picturesque venue for breakfast, cocktails, and everything in between. Just beyond is a swimming pool, its deck pleasantly shaded by tall trees and rows of umbrellas. It’s a short stroll down to the water’s edge, and some of the region’s best surf breaks are located nearby; 70 Hectares gladly arranges surf lessons, bike rentals, and sailboat rides.

content:
Quaint timber and stone chalets line the streets of Livigno, an alpine village near the Swiss border. Some are lodges catering to skiers and cyclists, like Eco & Wellness Boutique Hotel Sonne, a stylish inn that’s been run by the same family for half a century. There’s plenty of tradition here — the interiors feature oak and Swiss pine, crackling fireplaces, and picture windows facing views of the snowy mountains nearby — but this boutique hotel has a modern air and eco-friendly updates to match.

Rooms are cozy and rustic-chic with pale wood flooring, crisp white linens, leather and flannel details, and balconies overlooking the slopes; attic-like suites on the uppermost level are especially charming. Adding to the appeal are a small spa with a Turkish steam bath, a gourmet breakfast spread with freshly squeezed juices and homemade cakes, and easy access to the ski lift, just a short stroll from the front door.

content: The Rusty Parrot is a longtime Jackson Hole institution, and in its newest incarnation as the Rusty Parrot Lodge & Spa it’s the sort of unpretentiously upscale luxury boutique hotel that the destination demands. It’s still family-owned and -operated, and the service is as personal as ever. But the interiors now blend Rocky Mountain ruggedness with crisp contemporary style, and the rooms and suites add high-end comforts like soaking tubs and custom-made Italian linens. content: Located in Cuenca’s UNESCO-protected historic center, Hotel Cruz del Vado offers a glimpse of the city’s past grandeur. The opulent French-inspired façade is made entirely of locally mined pink marble, while exposed brick archways frame the lobby, the doors are made of rich wood carved into relief sculpture, and the windows feature colorful stained glass. Standing on the tiers of wrought-iron balconies encircling an elegant interior courtyard, it’s easy to imagine reporters and secretaries rushing around below: the building was once the headquarters of the city’s first newspaper. In recent years, the property was restored by a local architecture firm and acquired by Art Hotels Ecuador, a family-run hospitality brand with a small collection of boutique hotels located in historic buildings.\n\nThe rooms and suites are lavishly appointed, the thick bahreque walls a nod to indigenous tradition and the hand-carved headboards crafted by local artisans. The look is dark and theatrical, with rich brocade, framed oil paintings, and suspended lamps glowing romantically at bedsides. Even the bathrooms have black marble countertops, plus walk-in rainfall showers and organic Ecuadorian bath products. All rooms come with custom Simmons mattresses and coffee stations with locally sourced and roasted beans, and the largest rooms have Jacuzzis and views of the Tomebamba River. Breakfast is included in the third-floor restaurant with big picture windows overlooking the blue domes of Cuenca’s cathedral, and panoramic vistas of the Andes and the city are even more impressive from the hotel’s marvelous rooftop bar.

content:
As the name suggests, it’s luxury all the way at King Jason Zante, an exclusive adults-only getaway overlooking the Ionian Sea on the Greek island of Zakynthos. The hotel embraces a philosophy of slow living — priorities include a restful atmosphere, leisurely meals, and down-to-earth activities like meditation walks and bread baking — and while “slowness coaches” are available to help guests unwind, they’re not strictly necessary in these surroundings.

King Jason Zante is like an island on an island: water covers nearly half of the sprawling hilltop property, with idyllic swimming pools stretching out toward the sea from nearly every angle. Swim-up suites have private terraces at the pools’ edges, and the highest-end options have private pools, but every suite has water views.

The sophisticated interiors mimic the island landscape, too, simply and beautifully outfitted in neutral tones and natural materials like wood and stone. Suites are cool and quiet, like the rest of the resort, including a state-of-the-art spa and fitness center, a poolside bar, and several restaurants. One has a walk-in cave for wine and olive oil tastings, and picnics can be arranged amid the olive groves on request.

content:
The city of Siem Reap is best known to overseas travelers as the gateway to Angkor. Thrilling as it is exploring ancient temples in the jungle, it’s important to consider where to recharge after a day of sightseeing in a tropical climate — and it stands to reason that the area’s best hotels are more like resorts. Hotel Vellita Siem Reap, set just outside of town, is no exception. This boutique hotel’s central feature is a generously sized free-form swimming pool surrounded by banana and palm trees, and its two open-air bars are strategically positioned, one poolside and the other on the rooftop, for refreshing post-tour cocktails.

Inside, Hotel Vellita’s rooms and suites are cool and spacious, with a sophisticated gray-and-white color palette, decorative tile floors, dark wood furniture, and original artwork by Cambodian artists. Suites come with comforts like private patios and four-poster canopy beds. The junior suite, notably, has a rare feature: a freestanding, egg-shaped tub at the foot of the bed, adjacent to built-in window seating overlooking views of the pool and gardens.

Traditional Khmer massages are on offer at the hotel’s spa, and the elegant, light-filled restaurant makes on-site dining effortless. All told, this hotel is designed for relaxation, and the all-local staff provide a particularly warm atmosphere. Come and go as often as you’d like from the nearby archaeological sites: they’re prepared with chilled towels and welcome drinks every time a guest sets foot inside the front door.

content: Among the new hotels giving Palm Springs’ historic lodgings a run for their money is Drift, a stylish boutique in a surprisingly quiet location just off the main drag. Some face mountains and palm trees, others overlook a swimming pool bordered by cheerful yellow sun umbrellas and chaise longues. An all-day indoor-outdoor eatery serves Bajan dishes and mezcal, and all of Palm Springs’ main attractions are a short stroll or ride away on one of Drift’s complimentary bikes.

content:
It’s not easy to find a quiet beach on Phuket, but count on Anantara Resorts to claim one of the few that remain. Anantara Layan Phuket Resort has a privileged location, to be sure, right on Layan Beach, a section of the northwestern coast that’s relatively secluded, shaded by coconut trees and facing a calm, shallow bay. 

A row of waterfront villas are lavishly appointed with private pools, outdoor dining areas, and direct beach access, and those that face away from the sea feel like tropical hideaways with their lush interior gardens and indoor-outdoor showers. Even the simplest room feels palatial with its high vaulted ceilings, terrazzo-tiled tub, and elegant teak paneling, and all feature locally crafted textiles and original artwork by Thai artists. 

Elsewhere at the resort, there’s a state-of-the-art spa, a sophisticated Japanese eatery, a beachhouse-style restaurant with a rooftop bar, and an observatory deck for stargazing over cocktails. A large infinity pool stretches out along the length of the mostly empty beach: few day-trippers make it to these white sands, which are unofficially reserved for resort guests.

content: Located in bustling Bukit Bintang, almost exactly in the center of Kuala Lumpur’s Golden Triangle, Bintang Collectionz Hotel is something of a rarity. In a Times Square–like neighborhood known for its skyscrapers and entertainment complexes, including one of the world’s largest shopping malls and Malaysia’s biggest indoor theme park, this relatively small-scale hotel embraces its connection to the past. After decades of operating as a simple family-run hotel in a quickly developing area, the property was snapped up and restored by youthful new owners in 2022. The lower levels of the building’s pre-colonial façade were deep-cleaned and placed behind protective glass, their decorative panels and antique wooden shutters illuminated by the glow of LED lights. \n\nThe updated interiors still feature architectural details and artifacts from days gone by. But the once-dated corridors were transformed into curving hallways painted a sultry deep red, the old carpets were pulled back and replaced with sleek wood flooring, and the lobby level features a striking exposed brick ceiling, black leather sofas, and contemporary art installations. Rooms and suites are simple and modern with built-in wood furnishings, sophisticated lighting systems, and bathrooms lined in charcoal-gray terrazzo tile. A handful of hipster-friendly fast food-style eateries on the ground level — one serving Malaysian food, the other Japanese — are convenient, and everything else one could wish to eat, drink, or buy is available within a few blocks’ walk.

content:
Though the vast majority of travelers visit Otavalo on day trips from Quito, staying overnight has its benefits, from exploring the nearby crater lakes and waterfalls to delving more deeply into the indigenous craft traditions represented at the town’s famous market. There are some lovely lodges in the surrounding area, but the stylish Hotel Otavalo is the finest option in town. Located in a Spanish colonial landmark that dates back to the 1930s, this hotel was acquired and restored by Art Hotels Ecuador, reopening in 2018 as a luxury boutique hotel.

The current iteration is faithful to its roots — the building’s best features have been preserved, from its charming brick archways and exposed stone walls to light-filled courtyards and heavy wooden doors inlaid with intricate relief sculpture. New additions lean into the theme, including furnishings made by local artisans and wide-ranging programs that enthusiastically introduce guests to Ecuadorian music, art, and cocktails.

Art objects and antiques add character to rooms and suites. All have exposed brick or stone walls, hardwood floors, custom Simmons beds with hand-carved headboards, and coffee stations stocked with locally grown and roasted beans. Modern bathrooms, outfitted in speckled marble and white tile, have walk-in rainfall showers and organic bath products. The highest-end rooms also feature Jacuzzis and private balconies. Downstairs, breakfast is included at the cavernous restaurant, which specializes in dishes inspired by ancestral traditions, and upstairs, a rooftop bar offers sweeping views of Otavalo’s rooftops and the Andes just beyond.

content: The Moorings benefits from a prominent location on Jersey’s Gorey Pier, overlooking the beach below Mont Orgueil Castle. content: Visitors to Denver are no doubt familiar with the downtown-adjacent districts, but there’s another secondary city center a few minutes’ drive to the south and east. Cherry Creek North, surrounded by upscale residential neighborhoods, is home to some fine shopping and nightlife, as well as — to give it its full name — Halcyon, a hotel in Cherry Creek. Here all of Denver’s aspirational threads are woven together: glamorous but unpretentious design, a low-key and welcoming atmosphere, a couple of ambitious restaurants, plus a selection of activity-focused services and a rooftop pool with a view of the Rocky Mountains.\n\nThe rooms and suites are luxurious and loft-like, with full-length windows that admit more than enough of Colorado’s plentiful sunshine. Lavazza coffee makers and Jonathan Adler bath products are among the luxe details. Halcyon’s own in-house gym is augmented by guest passes to local yoga, barre, and cycling studios. The Gear Garage is stocked with sleds, snowshoes, skateboards, scooters, and New Belgium cruiser bikes. And to the already substantial Cherry Creek North restaurant scene Halcyon adds three options: the bistro-style Local Jones, the rooftop Rare Bird, and the perfectly self-explanatory Quality Italian.

content:
Ideally located for lovers of ancient monuments, Anthology of Athens stands between the Acropolis and what remains of the Temple of Olympian Zeus; many rooms, in fact, look directly out over the columns and toppled stones of the latter site. It takes some confident contemporary architecture to stand confidently in such company, but this five-story structure is up to the task.

It’s not unimpressive inside, either; the central atrium is home to a cascading vertical garden, and clean-lined contemporary furniture cuts a sleek figure alongside polished stone that recalls the ancient sites. Meanwhile the elegant rooms and suites, decked out in an earthy palette of sage and ivory, feature parquet floors, king-sized beds, and sleek marble bathrooms; the aptly named Zeus Presidential Suite features an ivy-framed Jacuzzi with its own dazzling view.

An all-day bistro occupies the atrium space, while the rooftop fine-dining restaurant features its own ornamental gardens and its own impressive elevated views.

content: In an effort to protect Mexico City’s architectural heritage, local designers and developers are increasingly looking to restore existing structures instead of defaulting to new construction. The results are inspiring, perhaps most especially in Condesa, where a handful of mid-century buildings have been transformed into stylish hotels. Hotel Dama is a prime example: architects Paulina Herrera Chain and Patricio Galindo Chain cleverly converted this 1950s-era apartment complex into a boutique hotel with retro Mexican flair. \n\nSome of its best assets aren’t original, but rather inspired by the past, like the sunken library lounge with mod built-in sofas and a rare collection of pre-Hispanic artwork — and others, like the jacaranda-shaded rooftop terrace lined with white sun umbrellas and an all-day café, are timeless. Rooms have a crisp vintage look with checkered marble flooring, bespoke wooden furnishings, and sliding glass doors opening onto private balconies or patios.

content: Tulum has no shortage of stylish lodgings, but Chiringuito Tulum has a distinct look from many others lining the beachfront. Instead of embracing the bohemian-chic aesthetic that’s so popular in the area, this boutique hotel is modern and Mediterranean-inspired. Airy suites have polished cement flooring and minimalist decor, some of it built-in, and wide furnished terraces, many with ocean views and private pools. In-room details like Nespresso machines and Bose sound systems invite hiding away with a good book, though the lagoon-like swimming pool and open-air eatery are just as appealing. Pathways thickly shaded by palm trees lead down to the hotel’s beach club and kitesurfing school, an adventurous alternative to the yoga studios and meditation decks offered at most hotels nearby.

content: Even in a neighborhood as saturated with stylish lodgings as Mexico City’s Colonia Condesa, Casa Cuenca offers something special. Iván Esqueda oversaw the transformation of an elegant 1930s mansion into a sleek ten-room boutique hotel with a gorgeous courtyard patio and a popular farm-to-table bistro, Maleza. The interiors pay homage to modernist Mexican design with custom built-in furnishings, handmade tiles, colorful woven rugs, and original artwork. Some rooms have private terraces and tubs, and the sun-drenched Presidencial suite features a chic living room and large windows overlooking the pretty patio below. The bar pours top-shelf artisanal mezcal, ideal for sipping in the garden, and countless cafés, bars, and restaurants are within easy walking distance.

content: Greenhills Country House Hotel has everything you’d wish for on an escape to the English countryside: a quiet rural setting, historic architecture, afternoon tea in the gardens. Never mind the fact that Greenhills is on Jersey, which isn’t technically part of England, or even the United Kingdom — the shared regional character is responsible for a large part of the hotel’s charm. Not far from the island’s northern beaches, it’s conveniently positioned on the Green Lanes, an idyllic network of country roads connecting Jersey’s farms and forests.\n\nThe 17th-century stone villa, though fully restored inside, adheres to the aesthetic of a traditional English inn. Rooms feature period decor like patterned floral wallpaper and elegant drapery, plus cozy details like down duvets, plaid throw blankets, plush bathrobes, and tea stations with homemade biscuits. Most rooms overlook the gardens, and larger rooms have bathrooms with tubs and walk-in showers. A seasonal outdoor pool and al fresco dining are delightful in warmer weather; the ground-level bar and lounge, with wood-beamed ceilings and a rustic stone fireplace, is appealing year-round. The island’s famous landscapes, not far from the hotel, are just a stroll or a bike ride away along country roads and coastal paths.

content:
Colonial heritage infused with a contemporary sensibility — this is the combination that defines The Prestige Hotel, a chic lodging in Penang’s Georgetown neighborhood (which is itself a UNESCO World Heritage Site). The building suits the district’s Victorian architecture to a tee, but once you’re inside you’ll see the liberties that have been taken with the hotel’s 19th-century inspiration.

There are six types of accommodations, all with the latest technology and a soft, soothing design. The look is modern, but with Victorian bones — the near-monochrome palette is livened by gentle pastels and highlights in brass, and while the style isn’t exactly traditional, it is extremely tasteful. After a busy day of exploring the area’s rich cultural treasures — most within walking distance — guests rest and relax at the rooftop saltwater pool with views overlooking the Straits of Malacca or with a wellness-focused treatment at the spa.

content: Once a bustling Spanish colonial capital, San Miguel de Allende emptied out after the Mexican Revolution and a flu epidemic, leaving its colorful houses and cobblestoned streets nearly abandoned for decades. Many of its historic buildings have since been turned into hotels, and even more recently built properties, like Real de Minas, take inspiration from the past. Set just outside of the historic center, the hotel is modeled after a countryside hacienda, complete with decorative stucco buildings, stone archways, beautifully landscaped gardens, a large pool, even a lienzo charro, or Spanish-style bullring. \n\nThe theme is n’t subtle, but that’s part of the fun. Real de Minas San Miguel de Allende is the kind of place with two-for-one margaritas by the pool and children running around a playground while a mariachi band plays at a family wedding on the grassy lawn nearby. Rooms are simple and traditional, outfitted with wooden furniture and decorated in earthy shades of ocher, yellow, and chocolate brown. Some have ceramic floor tiles and private balconies overlooking the pool. A lively bar and restaurant serves up hearty breakfasts in the morning and mezcal on the rocks in the afternoon, and a wide range of other dining options are an easy stroll away in downtown San Miguel de Allende.

content: While the thought of Borneo conjures up images of beaches and rainforests, the world’s third-largest island has some sizeable cities, too. Kota Kinabalu, part of Malaysian Borneo, is one of them, and the recently opened Luma Hotel is among the top hotels in town. Located in a recycled office building in the city center, the hotel, named after the native Sama-Bajau word for “home,” has a modern, distinctly urban feel. But the sleek interiors are warmed up by abundant greenery, colorful modular furniture, and floors inlaid with white stone mosaics.\n\nWhile the ground level’s interior design takes inspiration from the region’s lush landscapes and cultural traditions — the lobby features a striking spiral staircase made of Sabahan wood, and a soundtrack put together by local musicians plays in the background  — guest rooms are simpler. The most standard option is compact and minimalist with curving wood-paneled walls, an earthy color palette, oak flooring, raffia headboards, and Japanese-style etched glass doors opening to bathrooms lined in polished deep-green tile. Larger rooms have writing desks and separate seating areas. Amenities include a fitness center, a stylish all-day coffee shop supported by a local roastery, and an elegant bar and Asian fusion restaurant with terrace seating.

content: The clifftop village of Ravello, as the old saying goes, is closer to heaven than the sea. And while the views over the Amalfi Coast are fantastic from anywhere in town, they’re especially astonishing from the 11th-century Hotel Villa Cimbrone. Its famous Terrazza dell’Infinito, or Terrace of Infinity, overlooks the Bay of Sorrento, as do many of the luxury hotel’s rooms and suites. \n\nInside, they’re bright and ornately decorated with frescoed ceilings, stone fireplaces, and antique majolica tile floors; many have private terraces or balconies facing the sea. Despite the museum-like interiors, the hotel’s real draw is outside — and while some of the grounds are open to admission-paying tourists by day, the best parts are exclusively for guest use, including private English gardens and a gorgeous pool framed by avocado trees. A collection of glamorous restaurants and bars, including the one-MICHELIN-Star Il Flauto di Pan, adds to the old-world grandeur.

content: After years of working in New York for brands like Ralph Lauren and Tommy Hilfiger, designer Shannon Maldonado returned to her native Philadelphia and opened a modern homewares boutique. Her carefully curated gift shop was a hit, and it wasn’t long before the business expanded into a larger corner space complete with a stylish café and a 13-room hotel in Queen Village. Yowie Hotel, occupying a pair of former rowhouses on South Street, has a classic-looking brick exterior, but inside, it exudes Maldonado’s signature style: minimalist, eclectic, and colorful. There’s no traditional reception area — guests are invited to check in independently, which feels like letting yourself into the hip studio apartment you never had. \n\nEach suite is uniquely decorated to showcase the work of emerging artists and established designers. Some have lime-green accent walls and bespoke coffee tables, others have oversized bay windows, kitchens with artisan-made tableware, and vintage-inspired bathrooms lined in cheerful yellow tile. Nearly every piece is available for purchase, just like the ceramics, accessories, and art objects in the ground-level shop. Also on the street level is Forin, Yowie’s sunny all-day café, and Philly’s historic center is a stroll away, as are many of the recommended venues featured in the owner’s custom city guide.

content: The Bassin d’Arcachon is one of France’s most unique places, a seaside idyll on the Atlantic coast. At the opening of the bay, looking straight across at Cap Ferret, is the village of Le Moulleau, and a small hotel with an unassuming name: the Villa du Moulleau. Here in the heart of the village, this classic Arcachon-style villa has been thoroughly renovated — its architecture remains a perfect example of the characteristic local manner of building, while its rooms and suites have been brought functionally up to date and redesigned in a style that’s chic and contemporary without losing touch with its roots.\n\nIts historical floor plan dictates some unusual spaces, like the Mezzanine rooms, perfect for families of four. Others open onto the hotel’s pleasant gardens, some with their own loggias or balconies. And while it’s set a mere two blocks from the beach, it’s also home to a lovely outdoor pool; the villa also maintains a pair of boats available for day trips within the Bay of Arcachon.

content: Even judging by the elevated standards of one of the ritziest ski resorts in the Alps, No.14 Verbier is a luxurious place to stay. This elegant wood-and-stone lodge — available for up to 26 guests on an exclusive-use basis — is sometimes referred to as the world’s greatest chalet, thanks not only to its design but also to its dedicated team of private chefs, drivers, and hosts who are ready to attend to your every need. The distinction feels especially earned when you’re watching the snow fall by the 360-degree fireplace, enjoying a personalized breakfast prepared by a private chef, or sipping après-ski cocktails on a wide terrace with a Jacuzzi and a fire pit facing the mountains.\n\nWith such a socially oriented setup, the rooms could easily feel like an afterthought — but with their modern alpine design, bespoke furnishings, and bathrooms lined in Italian stone, they’re more than worthy of a solo retreat. Other perks include a sleek spa with a sauna, pool, and hammam, a cinema room, a lavish afternoon tea service, and a fully stocked bar with champagne on ice around the clock.

content: A ninety-minute drive southeast of Porto, deep in a pocket of the countryside little visited by tourists, the village of Santar is home to about a thousand residents — and a gorgeous Relais & Châteaux hotel that’s very much worth the detour. Formerly a royal residence, Valverde Santar Hotel & Spa is grand and historic, surrounded by picturesque gardens and centuries-old vineyards. A regal air remains in the hotel’s formal sitting rooms with their gilded chandeliers, original oil paintings, antique loveseats, and original hand-carved woodwork. But rooms and suites are smartly updated, both modern and quaint. The old winery was transformed into a state-of-the-art spa with a spacious indoor pool and a Turkish bath, and the mansion’s original library now serves as an atmospheric breakfast room.

content: Before Crete became part of Greece, the island was Ottoman-ruled, its capital city home to a range of European embassies. Today, some historic buildings in Chania’s former diplomatic quarter have been converted into hotels, including Domus Blanc Boutique Hotel. It’s located in the elegant former residence of the French consul, with many of its best features — the neoclassical facade, original parquet flooring, high ceilings, exposed wooden beams, even the kitchen’s old wood-fired oven — carefully preserved. \n\nSuites are sophisticated and light-filled with designer furnishings and large windows overlooking the garden. Attic rooms with skylights have a Parisian air, while suites with flower-framed terraces and outdoor hot tubs are particularly luxurious. The swimming pool is tucked into a stone-walled courtyard, and the airy ground-level bistro is open all day. Relaxing on a rosy velvet banquette, champagne coupe in hand, it’s easy to imagine the room’s former iteration as an aristocratic gathering spot.

content:
Atlanta’s historic Old Fourth Ward is more of a culinary hotspot than a place to stay the night; most of the city’s luxury hotels are located in Downtown or Midtown. A notable exception, the hip Forth Hotel, is a creation of the same team that converted the nearby Ponce City Market from an old Sears building into a vibrant food hall. 

The hotel’s strikingly geometric glass and concrete facade gives away two key facts: the design by Morris Adjmi Architects is thoroughly modern, and every room has floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the city park below. Inside, the aesthetic mixes minimalist and romantic with bold floral wallpaper, dark wood furnishings, and sleek bathrooms stocked with Le Labo products. Terrace suites have spacious private patios, some with outdoor fireplaces, and larger apartment-style suites feature multiple bedrooms and smartly equipped kitchens. 

Other highlights include a gorgeous outdoor pool on the fourth floor, a state-of-the-art spa and fitness center, and a lively rooftop bar with sunset views unmatched in Atlanta.

content: Who says there’s nothing stylish to be found in staid old D.C.? The Hotel Washington is taking its design insurrection straight to the heart of the city. It would be next door to the White House if not for that pesky Treasury building, and this is a neighborhood that, let’s be frank, needed a bit of after-work life. You’ll find plenty of it here — in fact the trademark funky interiors and youth-culture borrowings may prove to be a bit much for some of Washington’s more traditional hotel guests. It’s their loss. \n\nTo be fair, the Hotel Washington pays plenty of homage to the history of what used to be, and its interiors preserve quite a lot of its Beaux-Arts grandeur, underneath a welcome gloss of contemporary color. The rooms are eye-catchingly modern and more than a little bit luxurious; many of the suites take in unparalleled views of the Washington Monument. And no less impressive are the public spaces, from the handsome restaurant and the seasonal Patio to VUE, a rooftop bar offering views that are dramatic enough to worry the Secret Service.

content: It’s hard to picture a historic landmark better suited to hospitality use than the 16th-century Universidad de Santa Catalina de Alejandría in the medieval city of Soria, Spain. A place of learning for nearly 300 years, this stately building is now home to Castilla Termal Burgo de Osma, the classrooms and offices transformed into luxurious rooms with original exposed stone walls and wood beams. \n\nThe parquet floors, bold wallpaper, and modern bathrooms with walk-in showers are all new, and cloister-like suites feature details like fireplaces and soaking tubs. The hotel’s true highlights, however, are its stylish common spaces. The university was built around a large central courtyard framed by two levels of elegant archways; it’s now topped by a striking glass ceiling, bathing the bar and restaurant below in natural light. Down a staircase, the dramatically lit subterranean spa, with its Romanesque frescoes and thermal pools fed by a nearby spring, is a quiet and ethereal refuge.

content: Located on a busy block in the hillside neighborhood of Mets, Monastik Living in Athina is unassuming from the street. Once inside, it’s another story. Designed by the Athens-based architectural duo George Gavalas and Giannis Mourikis, this eleven-suite boutique hotel is a modernist escape showcasing a thoughtfully curated collection of Greek artwork and ephemera. \n\nEach glass-walled room is bathed in natural light, and many face breathtaking views of the Acropolis or the Parthenon. Standard amenities include luxe king-sized beds, mood lighting, Marshall speakers, cozy sofas, kitchenettes with Nespresso machines, and welcome baskets filled with local delicacies; a few suites also have stylish private patios. A larger rooftop terrace with a plunge pool is open to all, a refreshing spot for a morning coffee — and especially impressive after dark, when the Acropolis is majestically illuminated in the distance.

content: In the heart of Kaat Benahid, one of the oldest quarters of the medina, Dar Al Dall, or “House of Shadows”, offers five digital detox suites shaped for intentional living. Part of the This Time Tomorrow brand, the riad is rich with hand-chiseled tilework, carved plaster, and archways that throw soft patterns across the courtyard. There is a rooftop for lingering, a hammam for reset, and an open kitchen where couscous is made the proper way. Between the curated workshops, textured design, and shaded calm, this is a stay that favors presence over plans, while rewarding the pause.

content: It’s a hotel best known as the highest spot in the city for sunset cocktails: Mai The Sky Bar serves up Spanish tapas and 360-degree views from a pair of rooftop bars connected by a striking glass walkway. But Meliá Chiang Mai has plenty more to recommend it, starting with its location on the banks of the Ping River, with one of the city’s busiest night bazaars at its doorstep. A modernist podium building houses the sleek breakfast area, spa and fitness center, and a resort-style pool, while the rooms are located in the adjacent 22-floor tower. With parquet floors, crisp white linens, and rainfall showers, they start out more than comfortable enough. But higher up, in the exclusive hotel-within-a-hotel Level area, suites feature chic sofas built-in along the windows, traditional Thai patterns and art objects, and lavishly appointed bathrooms with freestanding tubs.

content: Steps from the white sand on Kuta Beach, MAMAKA by Ovolo is a luxury hotel with a youthful spirit. So youthful, in fact, that the list of complimentary amenities — self-service laundry, morning coffee, happy-hour drinks — might remind you of the nicest hostel you stayed at on your last backpacking trip. While there’s no doubt the destination attracts a fresh-faced crowd intent on surfing all day and sipping tropical drinks all night, the hotel’s traveler-friendly offerings are standard across the Ovolo brand, and the sociable, why-not-stay-a-while vibe works particularly well at the group’s Bali outpost.\n\nRooms and suites are colorful and modern, cheerfully decorated in a beachy palette of white, navy, and aquamarine, with raffia rugs and lamp shades, framed black and white photography, and floor-to-ceiling windows facing the sea or an interior garden planted with palm trees. Some have private furnished terraces and espresso machines, and spacious two-bedroom suites come with bathtubs and cocktail bars. A lively beachfront eatery serves Asian street food-inspired dishes, and the rooftop, lined with white daybeds on one side, features a gorgeous blue tile-lined infinity pool overlooking the water. It’s a short trip down to the shoreline and the chance to catch a wave with MAMAKA’s Rip Curl-sponsored surf school.
name: MAMAKA by Ovolo

content: On an island filled with glamorous hotels, Canaves Oia Suites is in the top tier. Maybe it’s the spectacular setting high over the Aegean Sea, or the sleek, spacious suites with designer furnishings, each with a private pool; maybe it’s the intimate scale and the air of exclusivity. Run by the Chaidemenos family, who practically invented the concept of luxury lodgings on Santorini — they’ve been turning centuries-old cave dwellings into modern guest rooms since the 1980s — the hotel is part of the Canaves Collection. It’s built right into volcanic cliffs in the village of Oia, and each of its suites, as well as its infinity pool, indoor-outdoor spa, and restaurant, features a sweeping view over the caldera.\n\nThe look is modern Cycladic, with whitewashed walls, clean lines, and gently curving archways framing the sea and the sky. All suites have an open-plan layout with airy living areas and large, sunny terraces with plunge pools or, in the case of some of the top-level suites, infinity-edge pools. The decor is sophisticated but simple, with a down-to-earth color palette and lots of wood, stone, and glass. Some suites have built-in sofas positioned in front of huge picture windows, and others have freestanding tubs with water views. All feature modern bathrooms with walk-in rainfall showers, custom bath products, and high-quality terry robes. Breakfasts and candlelit dinners can be arranged on the suites’ private terraces or enjoyed in the gorgeous clifftop restaurant, one of the island’s finest sunset spots.

content: Instead of Berlin or Munich, FREIgeist chose a few off-the-beaten-path locations, like the historic university town of Göttingen, for its first boutique hotels. The brand’s name is German for “free spirit,” and that’s exactly who the FREIgeist Göttingen Innenstadt aims to attract with its eclectic mix of modern design, creative influences, and laid-back atmosphere. The elegant brick building by Hannover-based architecture firm Ahrens & Grabenhorst Architekten is sleek and understated, but inside, the interiors by Frank Kassner are full of vibrant, unexpected details like Basquiat-inspired street art, colorful Moroccan tiles, and bespoke carpets by the Barcelona-based Nani Marquina.\n\nThe Nordic-style rooms are comparatively pared down, with pale oak flooring and custom-built furnishings, including upcycled pieces, like luggage racks made of reclaimed wood. Soundproofed floor-to-ceiling windows reveal views of the park below, and amenities include Danish sound systems and airy bathrooms stocked with natural products by L:a Bruket. Top-level suites feature extras like freestanding Vallone tubs and espresso machines. A spacious rooftop terrace with hammocks and lounge furniture opens to the indoor fitness center and sauna; downstairs, the Herbarium bar offers signature drinks made with ingredients from the vertical garden on the back wall, and the adjacent restaurant, INTUU, specializes in Japanese–South American fusion dishes. In keeping with the free-spirited ethos, the breakfast buffet stays open until two in the afternoon on weekends.

content: Bulgaria’s capital city is having a moment, and Junó Hotel, on a quiet side street in Sofia’s historic center, may be a sign of things to come. This boutique hotel is modern and minimalist, yet grounded in its place, featuring locally made custom furnishings, original oil paintings by the Bulgarian artist Tatiana Harizanova, and a stylish restaurant and bar focused on contemporary Balkan cuisine and wines. The angular six-story corner building is unmistakably modern, but carefully designed to complement its historic neighbors.\n\nEvery room has floor-to-ceiling windows and French doors that open onto a private balcony or terrace; especially appealing are the corner rooms, with a curving row of windows revealing views over Sofia’s streets, and the top-floor loft and penthouse suites with large wraparound verandas. All rooms have elegant parquet flooring, Nespresso machines, Bang & Olufsen sound systems, and spacious marble bathrooms, most with freestanding tubs. Downstairs, Junó’s designers decided against a formal reception area in favor of a sleek lobby lounge that flows seamlessly into the art-filled wine bar and farm-to-table restaurant. Sofia's many attractions, both old and new, are practically just outside the front door.

content: The name is first of all meant literally; The Pinnacle Athens occupies a distinctive Seventies tower in the city’s Commercial Triangle, constructed in the Seventies in an Athenian Modernist style. A high-rise hotel in a low-rise city, it affords its guests an unusual high-angle perspective on the city’s landmarks and rooftops. And inside it’s as modern as can be, filled with an ever-evolving collection of contemporary artworks and design elements. With just 16 suites it’s an intimate experience by design, and its Roof Garden is a magical space, serving breakfast or a sunset cocktail with an unparalleled view.\n\n

content: Fresh air and great wine are reasons enough to escape to South Tyrol. The Weinegg Wellviva Resort has all that covered, and then some: surrounded by snow-capped peaks and scenic vineyards, the luxury hotel features a sprawling, state-of-the-art spa that’s a destination in itself with an indoor-outdoor infinity pool, Finnish saunas, and a snow room stocked with fresh powder sourced in the Dolomites. Luminous rooms have parquet floors, native wood paneling, and French doors opening onto private balconies with nature views, while suites have their own mini spas with private saunas and freestanding soaking tubs. Gourmet regional dishes and locally produced wines are served in the resort’s elegant restaurant, and the open-air bar is a requisite stop after a day out skiing, hiking, cycling, or wine tasting.

content: Few hotels anywhere are as aptly named as the Hôtel Splendide Royal Paris. Its neighborhood places it close to some major landmarks, as well as some of the city’s most luxurious palace hotels. But this is less a palace than an ultra-discreet semi-private residence, whose emerald-green façade conceals a mere 12 suites in a style that takes its inspiration not from boutique hotels but from an idealized vision of classic Parisian luxury.\n\nAnd while at this size it may not have space for certain grand-hotel facilities, the Splendide Royal’s service is cut from the same cloth as the palace hotels — as are the in-room comforts, from the junior suites on up to the 105-square meter family suites. Downstairs is Tosca, an upscale Mediterranean restaurant that’s also home to the cozy Loggia Bar, where guests sip drinks in front of the fireplace.

content: Some of the best hotels on Corsica aren’t on the beach, but tucked into the hills that rise up along the coastline. Take Les Regalia, set on a wooded estate overlooking the sea. There’s much to admire about the elegant family-run hotel, from the sustainable design employing local stone and recycled wood to a secret garden-style cocktail bar framed by olive groves. But with a location like this, it’s all about sweeping water views — from the restaurant’s terrace and the striking infinity-edge pool, and of course, from many rooms. \n\nThe best suites have glass-walled terraces, postcard-like bay vistas, and spa-like bathrooms with sculptural soaking tubs designed by Philippe Starck, but even the simplest rooms are luxurious, with floor-to-ceiling windows and private balconies facing Mediterranean gardens. It’s just a quick stroll down to sea level and the hotel’s private beach club, and a slightly longer walk into the harbor town of Porto-Vecchio.

content: Even before ancient Romans popularized Montegrotto as a wellness retreat, the region’s thermal waters were renowned for their healing properties. Spas are still the star attraction here, and Esplanade Tergesteo has a particularly impressive one. Two separate spa areas, one indoor and one rooftop, comprise facilities such as Finnish saunas, a Turkish bath, hammam, an infrared cabin and numerous pools, including a magnesium and potassium pool, a refreshing plunge pool and on the rooftop, an adults-only saltwater pool, built around a sleek outdoor fireplace and overlooking panoramic views of the surrounding hills. And that’s all in addition to the wide-ranging menu of beauty treatments. Guest rooms are elegant and peaceful with large windows, pale wood paneling, minimalist furnishings, and custom lighting that casts a warm glow throughout; spa suites have their own saunas and fireplaces, plus private decks with plunge pools.

content: Stepping into Villaggio Albergo i Dammusi di Borgo Cala Creta feels like slipping quietly into another time. Scattered gently across Lampedusa’s windswept landscape, these traditional stone cottages (dammusi), built in classic Arab-influenced style, stand with white domes, dry-stone walls, and slender windows. Life here moves softly, from shaded patios to private gardens; guests sip coffee, explore the on-site art gallery, or wander toward the turquoise shallows of Guitgia Cove. It is tranquil, understated, and perfectly matched to an island that remains refreshingly untouched.

content: Not all Brazilian beaches were created equal, which stands to reason — it’s one of the longest coastlines in the world. But lots of locals say the best ones are in the northeast. That’s where you’ll find Hotel Vila Selvagem, an elegant but down-to-earth boutique hotel in the fishing village of Pontal de Maceió. \n\nThere’s nothing between the art-filled lobby and the dreamy white-sand beach, save for tropical gardens and a pair of palm tree-framed swimming pools, and nothing to do but relax. Low-lying bungalows house airy rooms and suites with native wood detailing, king-sized beds, and private porches with artisan-woven hammocks. Kitesurfing and horseback riding are easily arranged, but it’s hard to resist the simple pleasure of reclining under a palapa, sipping a caipirinha while watching local fishermen bring in the daily catch, destined for your dinner plate.

content: Germany is home to multiple climate-neutral hotels, but Naturresort & Spa Schindelbruch, opened in 2009, was the very first. This wellness-focused luxury resort was constructed on the foundations of an old hunting lodge in the Harz Mountains, now part of a large biosphere reserve popular with cyclists and hikers. A natural spring nearby underpins the resort’s water supply, sourcing a large thermal pool and a series of saunas and steam baths, and the restaurant serves seasonal cuisine paired with wines from ecologically responsible wineries. \n\nRooms in the original building are bright and elegant, with large windows facing the surrounding beech forest, while those in the newer addition next door are more lavishly appointed with private terraces, extra-spacious modern bathrooms, and custom-made art installations.

content: High on a wooded hilltop overlooking the medieval village of Stolberg, a German shipping magnate built an elegant half-timbered villa to use as a summer residence. More than a century later, this historic property was converted into the Hotel & Spa Suiten FreiWerk, a luxury retreat with easy access to the hiking and cycling trails of the surrounding Harz Mountains. \n\nSome rooms in the main building are modern and sleek with monochromatic murals, white marble bathrooms, and panoramic windows facing the treetops, while others, like the charmingly wood-paneled tower room or the cozy attic suite in the restored coachman’s house next door, have historic character. Sustainably built two-story spa suites, each one with its own Finnish sauna and open-air whirlpool tub, offer extra space and privacy. Breakfast is served in the light-filled restaurant, and self-guided mountain biking itineraries leave right from the front door.

content: Just a few minutes up the coast from Elounda, on a hillside just outside of the village of Plaka, Phāea Blue marries timeless Cretan hospitality with glamorous, globetrotting elegance. Breezy, tranquil rooms, suites, and bungalows blend eggshell and nautical tones with locally crafted art objects, marble bathrooms, and private, furnished balconies. There’s also a freestanding, full-service villa, available in two- and three-bedroom orientations, for a more private and more luxurious experience.\n\nThere’s much to be said for remaining on site, thanks to the lovely swimming pool, the Anthós restaurant, and the more casual Blue Door Taverna. But to do so would be to miss out on a large part of Phāea Blue’s appeal. This is a hotel that specializes in experiential travel — be it a cooking lesson, an island-hopping sailing excursion, or a jaunt in a classic car, the concierge will arrange it all. Of particular note is the Phāea Farmers Feast, where guests pick fresh ingredients alongside the hotel’s chef before dining on a meal served around a communal table.

content: A few dozen miles off Korea’s east coast is Ulleungdo, a volcanic island rich in natural grandeur and steep, breathtaking views. Kosmos Ulleungdo is planted like a docked spaceship on the edge of these cliffs, the vision of architect Kim Chan Jung made real in ambitious curves, spirals, and futuristic domes. Its accommodations are spread across three villas, named Terre, Sommet, and Kosmos. \n\nEach one follows its own distinct style, both inside and out; across all three, the interiors are modern and the experience is luxe. La ULL, the restaurant, is a modern take on boyang, or “revitalizing food,” sourced with care for seasonality and presented as artfully as the hotel’s architecture. Le FLOT is the hotel’s wellness offering, a unique “stone therapy” experience, while the infinity pool is an amenity that needs no explanation.

content: Though just a fifteen-minute ferry ride away from Mykonos, the island of Tinos, considered one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Greece, feels like a world apart. It’s a place for quiet hikes and dozing by the sea, and the boutique resort Ela Tinos, located near the island’s southernmost point, matches the Tinos’s wavelength with a collection of elegant suites overlooking the Aegean. \n\nUnderstated luxury is a guiding principle around the spacious pool deck framed by fringed parasols and sunbeds draped in billowing white cotton. Rooms are similarly stylish but laid-back, outfitted in minimalist decor and natural materials like native wood and raw linen. Some have private terraces with pools or hot tubs, and all are modern but down-to-earth, with little to distract from the dizzyingly beautiful surroundings. A petite fitness center and spa add to the appeal, and the beach is minutes away.

content:
It would be easy to mistake Castilla Termal Brihuega, housed as it is in a circular-shaped structure in the Spanish countryside outside Madrid, for a bullring. But this eye-catching 18th-century landmark was once a textile factory, and its unusual layout, with two concentric rings built around a central courtyard, lends itself surprisingly well to its latest iteration as a wellness-focused luxury hotel. 

Beautifully restored stonework and original wooden beams are on prominent display in high-ceilinged rooms, and upper-level attic rooms and treehouse-like suites look out over lush, Versailles-inspired gardens. But the true showstoppers here are the common spaces, especially the airy all-day eatery La Redonda, which features a round dining room topped with a magnificent glass dome and illuminated by glowing lanterns at night. Coming in a close second is the stone-walled spa with its low-lit thermal baths, and, in season, the outdoor infinity pool facing views over the surrounding landscapes.

content: Sly Berlin stakes out a corner of Friedrichshain that’s rapidly evolving, and is, if not exactly uncharted territory, certainly outside the established borders of the boutique-hotel world. But the way these things go, that won’t be the case forever; for now, this spot, closer to Volkspark Friedrichshain than to the Spree, is close to the heart of all that’s cool in the so-called New East.\n\nThe 150 rooms are as stylish as you’d expect, and perhaps warmer and more richly figured; parquet floors and classic design pieces share space with Marshall bluetooth speakers and Nespresso coffee makers. Rather than in-room minibars, the hotel features a Späti, or the Berlin version of an all-night convenience store. And some more luxurious amenities are on offer as well, including a thoughtful little fitness studio and a rooftop wellness area with a sauna. Meanwhile, though Friedrichshain’s nightlife will likely tempt you outside, the hotel makes a case for staying in, via the Asian-inspired restaurant and the swanky cocktail bar and lounge.

content: The vast majority of hotels in Florianópolis could be described as beachy or boho-chic. Fuso Concept Hotel, occupying a modern glass and wood building on Santa Catarina Island’s northern coast, stands out in stark contrast, proving that proximity to the ocean needn’t dictate a conventional aesthetic. content: Named after its late founder, a businessman and art collector devoted to the preservation of Nepal’s cultural heritage, Dwarika’s Hotels is best known for its flagship property in Kathmandu — a one-of-a-kind luxury hotel showcasing a museum-worthy collection of antique woodwork. Following along similar lines is the newer Dwarika’s Resort, a wellness escape located on a hillside in Dhulikhel, with sweeping views of the Himalayas. Like its sister hotel, this resort pays homage to regional tradition in both style and spirit. Its architecture is inspired by the building techniques of the native Newar, constructed using local materials like wood, earth, and stone, with an infrastructure underpinned by age-old practices from rainwater harvesting to solar energy.\n\nThe atmosphere is sanctuary-like with a series of yoga decks, an Ayurvedic spa, a Himalayan salt room, a meditation maze, and chakra sound chambers alongside more conventional resort offerings like an infinity pool, a gourmet farm-to-table restaurant, and a glass-walled lounge with sunset views. Suites are spacious, silent, and furnished in all-natural materials: wood-beamed ceilings, parquet floors, Nepalese rugs, and handcrafted textiles. Bathrooms are luxuriously appointed with separate tubs and showers, and stocked with organic bath products made in-house. All open onto outdoor terraces — most private, but some shared — with plush daybeds, and the Royal Suite comes with an outdoor hot tub and a private chef. Even in the simplest room, which includes access to all of the resort’s activities and amenities, peace and well-being feel within easy reach.

content:
Oaxaca City’s Hotel Sin Nombre may be the “hotel with no name,” but it’s certainly got an identity — an elusive, somewhat mysterious one, but an identity all the same. It’s the creation of a local artist, the California-born Elliott Coon, and the Portuguese architect João Boto Caeiro, who transformed this 17th-century house into a contemporary boutique hotel with a singular point of view.

The interiors may be sparse to the point of minimalism, but this isn’t a simple case of grafting contemporary design onto a historical structure; the decoration and restoration of this building went hand in hand, and the economy of ornament serves to accentuate the shapes and the materials of the original house. As a courtyard building, it lends itself to some North African influence as well, and the rooms and corridors are livened by large-scale monochrome photos by the Mexican artist Alberto Ibañez.

A location just off Oaxaca City’s main square places the best of the city right at your feet, but there’s plenty to do within the hotel’s walls; the courtyard patio serves breakfast and drinks, while a little library invites contemplation and a rooftop pool provides a view of the city. Of particular note: Restaurante Sin Nombre, for vegan variations on classic Oaxacan cuisine, as well as artisanal mezcal by Gem&Bolt, the proprietors’ own brand.

content: An old army barracks later turned into a school is an unlikely setting for a luxury hotel, but Hotel La Mission pulls off the transformation with panache. It’s located on L’Île d’Yeu, a laid-back island just off the west coast of France, with seven low-lying buildings arranged like a cloister around a central garden — once a schoolyard — with a century-old plane tree and a heated swimming pool. \n\nThere’s a nostalgic air to the rooms and suites, with pale wainscoting, cheerful patterns, and antique pieces that channel the owners’ childhood. Kid-friendly details like bunk beds are fun for families, and the grounds feature pétanque courts and in July and August, a food truck specializing in crêpes. After pedaling down to the beach on one of the hotel’s rental bikes, climb up to the retro-styled rooftop bar for apéritifs with views of the nearby Saint-Sauveur bell tower.

content: Sitting around 2,200 meters high in Austria’s Ötztal Alps, Hotel Riml is perfectly positioned for guests to either ski out directly onto the slopes or take in the fantastic Alpine views with a cocktail in hand from the large outdoor terrace, or one of the poolside indoor sun loungers. There’s even a massive indoor golf facility — one of Europe’s largest, in fact. The restaurant is complemented by two bars, where the specialty to try is the homemade stone pine schnapps. Rooms put a contemporary twist on alpine style with blonde wood, clean lines and an understandable focus on the majestic mountain backdrop through a wall of windows.

content:
A luxury resort in one of Mexico’s coastal enclaves would be nothing new, but a hacienda-style hotel in the heart of a historic city center is far from commonplace. The Rosewood San Miguel de Allende is a departure for the Hong Kong–based luxury brand, a detailed reproduction of a grand colonial-style residence, surrounding a lovely central courtyard in the city’s UNESCO-listed old town. And while a lesser hotelier might have been tempted to import their own characteristic aesthetic, here Rosewood wisely opts for a purely local style, leaving its own contributions to the (still essential) areas of comfort, service, and programming.

This means rooms and suites that look like they’re straight out of the 19th century, even as they’re furnished with modern bathrooms, deep soaking tubs, and state-of-the-art entertainment systems — as well as low-tech luxuries like fireplaces and Rivolta Carmignani linens. Views vary according to the rooms’ and suites’ height and orientation, but the best ones have terraces with far-ranging vistas of the city’s rooftops.

The flagship 1826 Restaurant and the associated tequila bar are the culinary main events, though there’s also the Agua poolside restaurant and bar, as well as Luna, the rooftop tapas bar, with the best views in the house, if not in all of San Miguel de Allende. Also on the top floor is Sense, the Rosewood spa — and the associated recreation offerings include a gym, a pair of tennis courts, and no fewer than three swimming pools.

content:
The iconic Saint-Germain-des-Prés district is home to a chic little 23-room boutique hotel owned and operated by the same family responsible for the Right Bank’s famous Grand Hôtel du Palais Royal. The contrast is dramatic; the Prince de Conti is nothing if not intimate, hidden away behind the doors of a 17th-century residential building.

Each of the rooms and suites is different, thanks to the building’s period architecture, and a few come with balconies or patios. Some face the inner courtyard, others rue Guénégaud outside, and the suites come with lounges, living rooms or, in one case, an expansive elevated terrace.

Luxe touches like Diptyque bath products establish the Prince de Conti’s boutique bona fides. Meanwhile breakfast and an honesty bar are the extent of the food and beverage service; thankfully there are few neighborhoods better prepared to fill these needs than Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

content:
Playa Guiones, on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica, is a legendary surf spot, and a destination for plenty else besides, from yoga retreats to wildlife tours and beyond. Just a few minutes up the hillside from Guiones is Tierra Magnifica, a boutique hotel whose views alone justify the extravagance of its name.

Guiones and Nosara are well-kept secrets no more, but Tierra Magnifica takes advantage of its seclusion, offering a degree of tranquility that’s impossible to find in town. Its 13 rooms and suites are tasteful, a touch minimalist in their visual style, and luxurious, in a laid-back sort of way.

Every space is as open as possible to the environment, from the breeze that flows through the rooms and suites to the views from the yoga pavilion and the terrace at Huacas, the restaurant, where artful (and healthful) Costa Rican fare is served alongside creative cocktails.

content:
The family-owned Hotel Granbaita Dolomites shows off the region at its best no matter the season. Located in the centre of Selva di Val Gardena, the hotel looks across picturesque views of the Dolomites mountains from its collection of rooms and suites, which put a modern spin on classic chalet style with contemporary furnishings, sleek black lighting and wood paneled walls engraved with clean geometric lines. 

Granbaita Gourmet Restaurant serves both tasting and à la carte menus that combine the region’s traditional cuisine and seasonal produce with international flavors, accompanied by a choice of more than 400 local wines from the stone vaulted cellars. Bar & Lounge Granbaita is open from morning coffee to après-ski drinks, and there’s a large terrace in summer. 

The vast spa is a real highlight, with an indoor and outdoor swimming pool, both heated to 32°C, numerous saunas and steam baths, a salt grotto and a fitness room. If you can tear yourself away from the comfort of the spa then the all-weather activities range from spring and summer hiking and mountain biking to winter skiing.

content:
Right on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, nearly a mile above sea level, is one of the region’s best-kept secrets. The Swag started its life as a private home, but gradually evolved into an inn; now, after the addition of a second lodge and a handful of outlying cabins, it’s something more akin to a luxury boutique resort.

The main house was built in the 20th century out of reclaimed wood, some of it dating back as far as 1785. Today, six rooms remain in the original house, and they’re the most historically minded of the accommodations. But the rooms in the newer Chestnut Lodge are in no way second-class — the look here and in the cabins is perhaps more contemporary, but still full of visual interest and authentic details.

There’s no restaurant in the traditional sense, but three meals a day are part of the rate: a hearty breakfast, a packed picnic lunch, and dinner back at the Swag House, an artful yet unpretentious affair that is, in some ways, a metaphor for the whole Swag experience.

content: It’s not easy to find a more spectacular corner of the Appalachians than this 825-acre expanse at the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park. And while Cataloochee Ranch has been in operation for close to a century, it’s only in recent years that it’s been upgraded to its current high level of luxury. The property remains crisscrossed with 12 miles of trails for hiking and horseback riding, but it’s now also home to a restaurant, Switchback, that serves High Country classics reimagined by a French-trained chef.\n\nThe cabins and suites have gone accordingly upscale as well. The look is decidedly modern-rustic, and impressively stylish, combining antique decorative elements with first-rate modern comforts. 2026 will see the opening of Cataloochee Ranch’s spa, as well as an outdoor swimming pool; outdoor activities are near-limitless, and in winter include the neighboring Cataloochee Ski Area.

content: Few hotels anywhere have an origin story quite like La Reserve 1785. Mademoiselle Henriette Reboul, friend of Cézanne, acquaintance of Chanel and Picasso, and self-described love priestess, once lived here with her Dutch-governor companion. The current owner, an architect who first encountered Henriette as a student in Aix-en-Provence, has transformed it into an adults-only hotel where comic-book characters share wall space with East Timorese textiles, and tomb-like spa rooms sit behind an imposing golden door.\n\nIt’s the sort of hotel that makes its near neighbors look bland by comparison. The high-ceilinged suites find space for canopy beds, and some open onto balconies or plunge pools. Meanwhile Le Café Rouge serves a local take on French and Mediterranean classics just off the courtyard herb garden.

content: Sultan Cave Suites isn’t the only cave hotel in Cappadocia, but that doesn’t limit its appeal — this form of hospitality is one of the world’s treasures, and there’s room in the region for plenty of variations on the theme. This one is built into the terraced hillside above the village of Göreme, which means that even as its 35 bedrooms burrow into the limestone, its windows and balconies take in views of the iconic Cappadocian landscape and its balloon-dotted skies.\n\nHere the accommodations feel more built than discovered, their arches and columns crafted from hefty blocks of stone. They range in size from classic double rooms to the capacious Pasha and Sultan suites, the latter finding space for a roll-top copper tub and a freestanding Jacuzzi, respectively. Seten, the restaurant, serves classic Anatolian fare in an atmospheric indoor-outdoor space; tours of the region, by land or by air, can be arranged with the help of the staff.

content: It’s not quite an urban boutique hotel, but for Costa Rica, it’s close: Santarena Hotel makes its home not on some isolated hillside or some purpose-built resort compound, but in the car-free center of the town of Las Catalinas, on the Pacific coast. The signature Mediterranean restaurant opens onto a ground-floor terrace, and is joined by a lobby bar and a second, more casual restaurant and bakery. It’s a remarkably self-sufficient stay, but there’s also plenty of opportunity to get out and about: the town, the beach, and the surrounding countryside all call....

content: Moroccan hospitality is more or less synonymous with riad hotels, but there’s more under the sun, especially in the rarefied air of Rabat’s largely residential embassy district. STORY Rabat is a substantial piece of contemporary architecture, and what’s inside is no mere guest house, but a full-fledged luxury boutique hotel, one whose compound-like layout lends it something of a resort-like quality.\n\nIts rooms and suites are contemporary-classic in aspect, marrying modern visual simplicity with historically inspired décor. Suites add balconies or terraces, and the Emiri Villa spans some 2,000 square feet, and comes with its own hammam and private pool. The main pool and the neighboring spa and fitness center comprise STORY’s leisure facilities; an upscale Moroccan restaurant and a cocktail bar round out the offerings.

content:
The Duncombe Arms describes itself — factually, but with characteristic British understatement — as “a pub with rooms,” a phrase that risks underselling the quality of the hospitality on offer. The rooms are ten in number, for one thing, plus a freestanding cottage and a converted barn for larger parties or longer stays. And while the pub itself is recognizably an example of the venerable public-house tradition, the quality of its food and drink defies expectation.

Stylistically the Walnut House, where the ten rooms are located, is one part rustic and one part refined, landing squarely in luxury boutique hotel territory, though with more variety in size and layout than you’d expect from a ten-room hotel. The Garden Cottage is within walking distance, while the Old Barn is a few minutes’ drive away; once part of the Calwich Estate, it sits on the same grounds where Handel, Rousseau, and Erasmus Darwin were guests in earlier centuries. 

And the Duncombe Arms pub is quite naturally the heart of the whole operation, serving modern British cuisine ranging from pub classics to artful experiments, with all ingredients sourced from local Staffordshire farmers and purveyors.

content:
Riverside hotels are rare in Rome, but The First Musica stands on the right bank of the Tiber, in Prati, a district curiously underserved by Roman hoteliers. It’s sister to The First Arte, the visual arts–focused luxury boutique hotel across the river; The First Musica, as you might guess, is a tribute to the art of music, with each room and suite dedicated to a different composer or performer.

It’s also a living example of the art of hospitality; architects Studio Marincola transformed this handsome mid-20th-century palazzo into a bastion of contemporary-luxe elegance; it’s as much a feast for fans of high-end modern Italian design as for music aficionados. With just 24 rooms and suites it maintains a discreet and private atmosphere, with service that’s both professional and personal.

Alto, the restaurant, takes up three floors at the top of the hotel, including an open-air rooftop space with direct views over the river.

content:
One of Chile’s most highly regarded wineries, Viña Santa Rita stands on nearly 100 acres of parkland less than an hour’s drive from Santiago. And it’s more than just fertile ground for growing grapes. It was established in the late 19th century, and the mansion at its heart, the former summer residence of the winery’s founder, is a beautifully preserved National Monument. Today, of course, it’s no private residence, but a luxury boutique hotel: the Hotel Casa Real Viña Santa Rita.

Here “boutique hotel” is most definitely not synonymous with “design hotel.” The public spaces remain resplendent in their 19th-century finery, and while the 16 rooms and suites do feature some judicious contemporary interventions, their style is consistent with the rest of the house. Additions, meanwhile, include an outdoor pool.

Even as a stand-alone hotel, it would be a stunner, but the benefit of being on the Santa Rita wine estate is that the hotel doesn’t have to stand alone — on the grounds you’ll find a working winery as well as a spectacular 19th-century chapel and the Restaurante Doña Paula.

content: Cartagena’s historic center is home to an unusual number of remarkable boutique hotels; among the most impressive is Cinco Quintas, whose 21 rooms and suites combine historic colonial architecture with stylish modern design. Inside the walled city, compound-like residences are the norm, and Cinco Quintas is oriented around a central courtyard whose quiet belies its central location.\n\nEven the humblest double rooms come with king beds and high ceilings, and spread out to nearly 300 square feet, while at the top end are suites that sleep up to six, including the Master Suite with its private swimming pool. The rooftop terrace bar is for everyone, and offers extraordinary elevated views of the city, while downstairs a gastronomic restaurant presents its own elevated take on modern Colombian cooking.

content:
South Americans know it well, but the rest of us might need some introduction: Carmelo, Uruguay is on the banks of the Rio de la Plata, three hours by car (or a negligible plane flight) up the river from Buenos Aires, and not much farther from Montevideo. And Carmelo Resort & Spa presents a pretty strong inducement for making the trip — suddenly Punta del Este seems positively run-of-the-mill, by comparison.

To call it small would do it no disservice. With just 24 suites and 20 freestanding bungalows it certainly doesn’t give off that big-resort vibe. The feeling is one of immersion in the forest setting, and the six bungalows that overlook the river are a special treat. And the design, while not exactly avant-garde, is a good deal more eclectic than the usual luxury fare, incorporating elements from as far afield as China and Indonesia.

This part of the world is tipped to see a bit more high-end hospitality traffic in coming years, but for now Carmelo Resort & Spa is ahead of the game. Golfers may be aware that there’s a first-class course right there on the premises, and the rest of us are content with the spa, the tennis club, the gym and pool, and perhaps a bit of biking, riding or boating.

content: Kéa is one of the less traveled Cycladic islands, a fact we mention not as a judgment but as a reason it’s worth a second look — as other more famous islands grow ever more densely developed, Kéa, close to the Greek mainland, looks more and more appealing. And its case is only strengthened by a hotel like Ydor Hotel & Spa, a villa-style luxury boutique hotel in the seaside village of Vourkari.\n\nIts two dozen rooms and suites are decorated in tranquil neutral tones and combine traditional Greek decorative elements with modern and contemporary elements. Balconies or terraces open the accommodations to the environment, and many of the units feature impressive sea views. The promised spa is a lovely one, as is the restaurant, Mizu, serving a hybrid Japanese-Mediterranean cuisine.

content: Located in Cais do Sodré, near the city’s waterfront, Corpo Santo Lisbon Historical Hotel adds 75 stylish and luxurious rooms and suites to a city that’s quickly moved into the top league of boutique hospitality. It’s set in an 18th-century building just downhill from Chiado and the Bairro Alto, in a lively neighborhood that provides a vibrant contrast to the hotel’s sedate and private atmosphere.\n\nThe accommodations vary in size and layout, following the twists and turns of the historical structure; all of them are sunny and soothing, and come equipped with the full complement of contemporary high-end boutique-hotel comforts. The Sense Spa is a compelling offer, and food and drink play a large role as well — the hotel’s restaurant is a fixture on the local scene, and cooking classes and wine tastings are available as well. And within the hotel’s structure is a hidden curiosity: a section of the city’s old medieval wall, uncovered during renovation and carefully preserved.

content: In Roma Norte an unassuming name marks a discreet but seriously impressive boutique hotel. Casa Seis Siete is a former private mansion that, even now, feels much more like a residence than like a traditional hotel. Each of its five rooms and suites is styled like a chic modern apartment, blending period architecture with contemporary art and design. One suite features a kitchenette, making it ideal for longer stays, while another spans the entire top floor and comes with an outdoor terrace with a dining table and lounge area.\n\nBreakfast is served daily in a convivial, guest-house-like environment, and the hotel’s staff knows the neighborhood well — while there’s no room for a restaurant here, Roma Norte is amply supplied with a wealth of worthy options.
