content: Though it’s named like a country house hotel, Stanwell House is no manor, but a boutique hotel in a prominent location in Lymington, the port town where the New Forest meets the Solent. Long a hotel, it’s only recently been upgraded to its current form: a luxurious contemporary-classic boutique whose décor brilliantly complements the building’s authentic Georgian style.\n\nThe rooms and suites vary in size and layout, lending each one a unique charm. They’re divided between the original house and a later addition, but the latter are no less appealing. The comforts are substantial but not ostentatious — though one suite does open onto a private roof terrace — and the style is antique but not old-fashioned. And holding it all together is a trio of social spaces: Samphire, a modern British restaurant with diverse influences, the Orangery for afternoon tea and evening cocktails, and Salt Bar, where hotel guests and Lymington locals mingle over drinks.

content:
At the southern end of Phu Quoc Island is the relatively more sedate Khem Beach, home to a handful of upscale resorts — one of which is New World Phu Quoc Resort, an independent and luxurious enclave that stands out even in a region that’s no stranger to high-end hospitality.

With 366 villas it’s certainly not small, but each one is spacious and remarkably private, set in its own tropical garden complete with a private pool. The interiors are quietly contemporary, warmed by indigenous materials and local crafts. And the physical comforts are substantial, but tasteful; kitchenettes and dining areas make them practically self-sufficient.

Not that anything is missing from New World Phu Quoc when it comes to shared facilities. In addition to a substantial stretch of beach it comes with a spa and a well-equipped fitness center, as well as a kids’ club complete with its own pool; restaurants range from a poolside bar to Italian, pan-Asian, and Indo-Arabic options.

content:
Despite its perch on the outskirts of the French Quarter, The Windsor Court isn't exactly full of Creole charm. Forget fluffy beignets and the strains of a saxophone wafting through the humid air; think instead of afternoon tea with blackcurrant scones and smartly dressed maids straightening 300-threadcount cotton sheets. Indeed, as the name suggests, The Windsor Court has a distinctly British feel that matches New Orleans’ old-world appeal, if not its colorful sensuousness.

Cordial, impeccably turned-out bellhops lead guests into a classically furnished lobby proudly displaying original oil paintings of royal figures like King George V and Queen Mary. Similarly valuable works by British masters like Gainsborough grace the hotel’s public spaces and the Presidential Suite.

The museum-like ambience relaxes a bit in the cream and beige-hued guest rooms and luxury suites, where sunshine streams through huge bay windows, gourmet chocolates punctuate fluffy feather pillows, and lightly fragranced Diptyque products stock Italian marble bathrooms. Top-end accommodations offer private balconies overlooking the Mississippi River, and even further up, the two penthouses feature perfectly manicured garden terraces.

Before wandering down to nearby Bourbon Street, prolong the British holiday a few moments longer with port wine or cognac in the The Polo Club, where equestrian-themed artwork and a shiny grand piano complete the genteel scene. Traditional New Orleans it may not be, but top-notch hotel it most certainly is. Though not exactly stuffy, the Windsor’s grand airs are best breathed by those with some appreciation for fine horses and powdered wigs.

content: In Devon, a short distance from Dartmoor National Park, a Victorian farmhouse and barns have been carefully restored and transformed into something special: a modern and luxurious boutique hotel operating within a functioning regenerative farm. Fowlescombe Farm’s interiors avoid both historical reenactment and country-house kitsch, opting instead for a quietly luxe contemporary look that suits these buildings’ old bones to a tee.\n\nWith just ten suites, the atmosphere is an intimate one; many of the suites come with kitchens, making them very nearly self-sufficient. Guests will want to get out and about, though; they share the 500-acre estate with animals that range across its fields, pastures, woodlands and gardens. Naturally, the kitchen is supplied by the seasonal products of this expansive farm — The Refectory serves thoughtful farm-to-table fare to Fowlescombe Farm guests and a limited number of outsiders. And the rate is all-inclusive, which means the meals are integrated into the experience in a seamless way. Nearly as close as Dartmoor is the South Devon Coast; both are tempting sites for day trips and guided activities.

content: Costa Rica’s trio of Nayara resorts are all remarkable in their own ways, but none more so than Nayara Tented Camp, which brings safari-inspired glamping to the lower slopes of the Arenal Volcano National Park. And as in the finest tented camps the world over, the only things less than solid about these accommodations are their tented roofs. They’re more than up to the task of keeping the weather out, of course, and the result is that guests sleep just a little bit closer to nature than they otherwise might.\n\nNayara Tented Camp shares a spa and a small and diverse handful of restaurants with its sister properties, located on the same parcel of land at the foot of the volcano. And while the sum of all three is a remarkably complete resort experience, this is a place you’re meant to leave on a daily basis — excursions into Nayara’s spectacular natural surroundings are plentiful, whether by river, by suspension bridge, by zipline, on horseback or on foot.

They’re certainly comfortable, but much of the day’s activity will take place outside them: spa treatments, zipline tours, volcano treks, river rafting, and much more. Meanwhile multiple restaurants serve a range of cuisines, from upscale local flavors to Asian-inspired dishes.

content: LOISIUM Wine & Spa Hotel Champagne brings a fresh perspective to the vineyard-covered hills outside Épernay. Perched onto the slopes of Mutigny, near the Montagne de Reims Regional Natural Park, the hotel’s curved wooden exterior recalls the staves of wine barrels while sitting comfortably in its natural surroundings. Inside, 101 rooms frame vineyard and forest views through floor-to-ceiling windows, with soft textures and a natural palette. The spa is extensive, the Champagne list impressive, and the on-site restaurant focuses on seasonal French cooking. It is a dreamily modern stay shaped by its setting, and its wine.

content: Oregon’s Willamette Valley wine country is well on its way to being the Northwest’s answer to California’s Napa and Sonoma valleys, and a significant milestone on this journey is the opening of the region’s first proper luxury resort. The Allison Inn & Spa is set amid 35 acres of vineyards and woodland, less than an hour’s drive from downtown Portland. And while its architecture and interior design shows some European influence — this is pinot noir country, after all — the style is inimitably Pacific Northwest.\n\nWith 85 rooms and suites it’s substantial in size, and each unit is in turn generously sized, starting at nearly 500 square feet. Luxe touches like soaking tubs, gas fireplaces, and balconies or terraces are universal, and works by Pacific Northwest artists are plentiful, both in room and in the public spaces. Meanwhile the hotel’s spa is among the region’s finest, and the restaurant, JORY, serves modern Northwestern fare accompanied by wines from the Willamette Valley’s hundreds of producers.

content:
Hacienda Xcanatun Angsana Heritage sits just a 25-minute drive away from Mérida, yet feels a world away from the buzz of the Yucatán Peninsula’s cultural capital. The 18th century hacienda was once key in Yucatán’s henequen agricultural boom, a plant native to the peninsula, and still sits surrounded by lush private gardens home to natural flora and fauna. Now restored to its former glory, it’s home to 54 spacious suites – there are no guest rooms – which open up onto a mix of private balconies, terraces, hot tubs, pools and green garden views.
 
The main restaurant is for gathering any time of day over classic Mexican dishes crafted with local ingredients, but there’s also the choice of the laidback pool club, which sits by one of the hotel’s three pools, and the bar for tacos, snacks, and cocktails. For more special occasions, private dinners can be held in front of the hacienda’s chapel. The spa makes the most of the hotel’s natural surroundings to further connect guests with nature; yoga sessions take place on the open-air pavilion and indoor treatment rooms are crafted from natural stone and look out onto verdant palms.

content: Monza’s Hotel de la Ville could hardly occupy a more prominent position — it stands opposite the Villa Reale, the 18th-century palace that was once home to the House of Savoy. By comparison, the Hotel de la Ville feels intimate, almost residential, and it is, by luxury-hotel standards. It’s belonged to the same family for generations, and while it’s been continually updated over the years, its style remains classic, with artworks and furnishings that reach as far back as the 17th century.\n\nIn fact its interiors are directly inspired by the old summer residence of the House of Savoy. In classic European style the rooms range from cozy-but-luxe single rooms to extravagant two-bedroom suites. And despite the urban setting, the hotel’s interior atmosphere is suggestive of a rural escape. The restaurant, Derby Grille, maintains an English interior style, even as the cuisine is decidedly Italian; it’s joined by the swanky Derby Bar.

content:
Panama City’s old town is unmistakably an urban setting, but you’d be hard pressed to feel the city’s presence from within the walls of Hotel la Compañia Casco Antiguo. It’s built from three historic structures that surround a substantial central garden courtyard: a Spanish Colonial wing, a French Colonial wing built by Jesuit priests, and an American wing built at the dawn of the 20th century.

All three have been carefully restored, and now contain some 88 contemporary-classic rooms and suites. Modern in function and antique in atmosphere, they’re remarkably stylish, and are designed to express the individuality of the buildings that contain them. Even the humblest double rooms are spacious and thoughtfully equipped, and the suites spread out, some over two levels.

Modern additions like a spa and a rooftop pool are welcome interventions, and many of the buildings’ larger spaces have been recast as gathering spaces; the upscale French restaurant 1739 was formerly a Jesuit chapel, and El Santuario serves a Panamanian and Spanish beneath the double-height stone walls of an old monastery.

content:
The Zetter group’s townhouse hotels occupy an unusual niche in London’s hospitality scene: though residential in their style and atmosphere, they’re fully serviced, like proper luxury boutique hotels, and correspondingly come with lively, club-like social spaces. The Zetter Bloomsbury is emblematic: a row of Georgian townhouses (a moment’s walk from the British Museum) combined and updated in an eclectic, retro-influenced contemporary-classic style.

Designer James Thurstan Waterworth has experience with high-end hospitality and high-end members’ clubs, and it pays off here; these spaces feel not just well-designed but well-curated, incorporating as they do a varied selection of antique and modern elements. Each room and suite is unique, if subtly so, thanks to the individuality of the original houses, but all sustain a high standard of comfort and a consistent visual style, a look that’s not quite like anything else in London.

The Parlour is the Zetter Bloomsbury’s cozy indoor social space, serving drinks and small plates, while the Orangery is more expansive, offering breakfast and afternoon tea with a view of the hotel’s gardens.

content:
Myanmar is already well off the beaten path for a great many travelers, to say nothing of a private island in the Myeik Archipelago. It’s three hours by boat from the mainland to Wa Ale Island, home to Wa Ale Resort, an escape that is quite unlike anything else in this part of the world.

Here conservation comes first. The island itself is publicly owned, and the resort operates a foundation dedicated to preserving it. And with a mere 15 units — 14 villas divided between sites on the beach and in the forest canopy, as well as the four-bedroom Beach House — the resort keeps a modest profile.

The accommodations are luxurious, but laid-back, classic examples of barefoot luxury. And if it’s a touch less lavish than the phrase “private island resort” might suggest, it’s by design — one thing Wa Ale will never be is overbuilt. At the same time, every luxe must-have is present, from the spa and yoga pavilion to the open-air Burmese restaurant. And the focus, as always, is on the environment, with activities designed to maximize contact with the forest, the sea, and the local wildlife.

content:
Set mere minutes from Kos’s town center, Theros All Suite Hotel is proof that you can establish an atmosphere of luxe tranquility without a far-flung, isolated location. With 88 suites, Theros isn’t unusually small, either — but its adults-only policy and its generous indoor and outdoor spaces mean it never feels busy or crowded.

Its visual style, too, is soothing, and stylish as well — modern but organic, minimalist but warm. The suites come with furnished outdoor terraces at the very least, and some add roof decks or even private pools.

Meanwhile a pair of swimming pools serve as the hotel’s daytime heart, with the Ef-Zin spa offering an even more relaxing escape. And while there’s no shortage of nightlife around town, plenty of guests opt for a night in at one of Theros’s two restaurants, each of which features its own bar.

content: Dolkhar Resort might be located in Tukcha’s main town of Leh, a former stop on the silk road, but you’ll still feel like you’re in the heart of the Himalayan wilderness thanks to the natural setting of verdant foliage and mountain views. A respect for this nature underpins the resort, starting with the seven villas that have been sustainably crafted from local woods by local artisans and dressed with handwoven wool rugs and textiles weaved in nearby villages. Restaurant Tsas is set withing Dolkhar’s apple and apricot orchard and follows the same principles, serving a hyper seasonal menu that highlights produce from the resort’s own kitchen garden. Similarly, the spa eschews the usual beauty and anti-aging treatments in favour of deeper relaxation through practices such as meditation and treatments that are rooted in indigenous ingredients and traditions.

content: A 19th-century house on a noble estate in northwestern Sicily is the setting for what’s now a perfect little slice of boutique hospitality: Tenute Baglio Passofondo. It’s a working agricultural estate, growing olives and multiple varieties of grapes, including Sicily’s native Alcamo Bianco. And within the house are ten suites, each one a handsome blend of antique farmhouse architecture and high-end contemporary Italian design.\n\nLuxe details like eye-catching gas fireplaces are universal; some units come with Jacuzzi tubs, while all feature modern spa-like bathrooms. A wellness area features baths and a treatment room, and Sicilian cooking features prominently in the Baglio Passofondo experience — from cooking classes to gourmet dinners and tastings of local wines.

content: Long one of Saint Barthélemy’s best-loved and most luxurious small hotels, Le Toiny makes its home on the quiet east end of the island, a setting that provides it with an extra measure of privacy and tranquility, both of which aid in providing a singular sense of laid-back glamour. And while it’s been renovated over the years, today’s Le Toiny is still the chic little gem that’s been a favorite among in-the-know travelers since 1992.\n\nIts suites dot the hillside above Anse de Toiny, and while their interiors have been brought subtly up to date, there remains an air of timelessness about its blend of Caribbean rusticity and French sophistication. Your neighbors might be Hollywood royalty, but you’d never know it, so discreet is the service (and so self-contained are the suites). All of them come with private pools, though you’ll mingle with other guests by the side of the main pool. La Table, the more formal restaurant, is supplemented by the ultra-casual Beach Club.

content:
Hotel Biaclyn Hakodate is truly unique: this unusual red brick building was constructed in 1908 as a consulate serving the pre-Revolution Russian Empire. The historic house is now the Consulate Wing, joined by the very modern Wellness Wing; together they form a luxury boutique hotel whose singular aesthetic is backed up by the first-rate virtues of classic Japanese hospitality.

The two suites in the Consulate Wing display some period architectural details that are absent in the Wellness Wing, but all of the units are cut from the same contemporary-luxe cloth — textures are rich, colors are deep, and the tactile elements are immensely comfortable. The bathrooms are indulgently spa-like, and every suite comes with a private sauna.

Meanwhile a common wellness space serves all guests, complete with a jacuzzi, a plunge pool and both dry and mist saunas, for a self-directed relaxation experience. Nor is the cuisine neglected; Biacya, the restaurant, serves artful French fare under the direction of a chef who studied under Bernard Loiseau and M.O.F. Jacques Maximin. Meanwhile Sushi-dokoro Funami prepares exquisite local seafood, and Bar Hakodadi is an elegant and intimate cocktail venue.

content: Unlike some of Europe’s spa towns, Bad Füssing and its Lower Bavarian neighbors are relative newcomers, whose hot springs were discovered well into the 20th century. Das Mühlbach, by contrast, first existed as a tavern in the 19th century — but the advent of the thermal waters changed its fortunes forever. Today it’s a luxury hotel and spa retreat after the classic German model, where no aspect of wellness is overlooked, whether that means a pleasant dip in a spring-fed pool or an intensive medical intervention.\n\nHere, of course, health and pleasure go hand in hand. The rooms and suites are as stylish as they are comfortable, equal parts modern and rustic, with first-rate comforts and bathrooms that verge on the spa-like. And the cuisine is proof that health and flavor need not be in opposition — options include the Bavarian Kirchawirt and the fine-dining Mühlbach Restaurant. Meanwhile the spa and wellness offerings are comprehensive, comprising a wide array of pools, saunas, and other treatment facilities.

Some rooms come with balconies, others with outdoor hot tubs, and some suites go so far as to add plunge pools in their outdoor living spaces. The main pool is a luxe little haven in its own right, and the property contains multiple intimate little lounges as well as a cocktail bar.

content:
Santorini is one of just a few destinations that truly needs no introduction; its hotels are variations on the compelling theme of tranquil contemplation with astonishing views. Valsamo Suites distinguishes itself by going just a little bit further in pursuit of peace and quiet.

The property itself keeps a low profile — it’s not a single structure, but a small handful of village buildings whose classic Cycladic architecture remains intact, even as the interiors have been brought up to modern boutique-hotel standard. The suites come with sea-facing terraces or patios, some with private hot tubs. And all are handsome in the classic Greek island fashion, in a palette of cream and white with judiciously chosen accent colors.

In terms of service, the suites are meant to be self-sufficient; breakfast is served daily, and each suite is equipped with its own kitchenette. A small spa offers massages and treatments, and your hosts can guide you to worthwhile restaurants as well as more ambitious excursions, from hikes to sailing expeditions and even wine tours.

content: Fort Lauderdale’s Pier Sixty-Six has been a local icon since the mid-sixties, and after an extremely thorough renovation it’s back to the height of its powers, combining the retro glamour of the era of its founding with the top-flight comforts of a 21st-century luxury hotel. Its situation, overlooking its own marina along Fort Lauderdale’s inland waterways, is unique, and places the beaches and the best of the city center within easy reach.\n\nPlenty of guests, however, will opt to remain on site for the duration of their stay. It helps that the rooms and suites are spacious and thoroughly well-equipped, and make use of floor-to-ceiling windows to provide far-ranging views. There’s plenty to do here, from the vast Zenova Spa to the correspondingly thoughtful Pier Explorers Kids’ Club. The marina itself is a strength; plenty of guests arrive via yacht, and all manner of excursions are available. And no fewer than 12 restaurants cater to guests’ needs, from a French-inspired breakfast to Pier Top, the revolving 17th-floor cocktail lounge.

content: Often the most understated names are reserved for the most impressive hotels. The Retreat Costa Rica is set in the inland mountains to the west of San Jose, Costa Rica, and is thus dedicated not to sand and surf but to relaxed contemplation with views of the rainforest. But peace and quiet are only part of the package; there’s a spa and an Ayurvedic center, as well as yoga instruction, a diverse fitness program, and more unconventional interventions, from IV therapy to detox protocols and “emotional healing.”\n\nAnd simply as a lodging it’s got plenty to recommend it. The Retreat’s accommodations range from spacious double rooms to a selection of luxury lofts and even a three-bedroom villa, the Residence at Santosha. Meanwhile the views range from idyllic to spectacular, thanks to the hotel’s position atop a forested mountainside. The restaurant serves locally sourced farm-to-table cuisine with a particular emphasis on health, though the bar is happy to pour wine, beer, and cocktails. And while a shut-in holiday is a perfectly viable option, excursions to a variety of natural and cultural destinations are offered as well.

content: There’s a feeling of stepping back in time at Palazzo Santa Maria. Hidden away in one of Hermoupolis’s labyrinthine streets, the boutique address is housed in an 1874 neoclassical mansion, which although renovated to offer modern travelers all the necessary comforts of today, still retains plenty of historic charm and grandeur. Guest rooms are dressed in noble shades such as royal blue and rich burgundy, while suites show off previously hidden frescoes and a mix of artworks and antiques that include marble lamps and vintage Lalique crystal lights from the owner’s personal collection. Mornings start over a traditional Greek breakfast of local homemade produce, and although there is no restaurant, the town’s tavernas, bars and main square are just a few minutes’ walk away.

content:
A Norman manor house has been restored with artistic sensitivity at Verneuil La Douce, a contemporary countryside retreat just two hours outside Paris. Owner Camille Agnès Omerin envisaged the hotel as being an artistic project as much as a place to rest and revive, and enlisted the talents of a group of French creatives to reimagine the 140-year-old property with soothing shades, layers of soft tactile materials and decorative frescoes across the 17 rooms and public spaces.

The large conservatory-style Glassroom, covered with hand-painted frescoes inspired by Greek mythological, serves a place to unwind over afternoon tea by day or cocktails by night. Drinks can be followed by dinner at restaurant Patiné, which celebrates Normandy’s rich cuisine and seasonal produce sourced by the chef himself from the local Verneuil market. The all-year-round indoor pool opens onto a terrace and verdant gardens, home to two-hundred-year-old plane trees and an outdoor pool, which itself has become a work of art with a spring-inspired mosaic hiding at the bottom of the water. Relaxation can also be found in the small wellness area, which comprises a sauna, steam room, and a soothing spa menu signed by holistic beauty brand Holidermie.

content: This family-owned and operated hotel in Alpine Liechtenstein is proof that in the right setting a hotelier with a light touch can achieve extraordinary results. This is classic hospitality in its timeless form — though the interior design is quietly contemporary, the values on display at Park Hotel Sonnenhof are the same that made for a first-class stay a century or more ago.\n\nRooms and suites are handsome and comfortable, and the mountain views are spectacular; the look is identifiably Alpine but highly refined and free from kitsch. The considerable physical comforts are supported by personable, professional service, a point of pride for this family establishment. The spa and wellness center features a spring-fed indoor swimming pool, and the mountains offer no end of recreation in all four seasons. Chef-owner Hubertus Real’s culinary artistry is on display at Marée, the hotel’s flagship restaurant.

content: No matter how many French castle hotels you’ve seen, you haven’t seen another quite like Domaine du Château des Pères. In large part, it’s what it sounds like: an estate with roots in the 12th century, and a castle that, in its current form, dates back to the 18th. But it’s the remainder that makes it truly unique — alongside its meticulously restored château is a vast sculpture park and a hotel whose pod-like rooms hang like bluebells from a towering central axis.\n\nThe Hotel L’EssenCiel features 42 essentially identical rooms, 36 of them elevated above the estate and another six at ground level. They’re decorated in a contemporary style — historical château-chic would be an odd fit for an igloo-shaped bedroom — but they’re warm and welcoming all the same, in a color palette that harmonizes with the natural surroundings. And to the hotel is added a state-of-the-art spa and a diverse selection of dining and drinking options, culminating in the One-MICHELIN-Star La Table des Pères.

content:
Originally an aristocratic residence in the heart of Marrakech’s 10th century medina, Riad Botanica now blends classic Moroccan design with a modern Australian aesthetic thanks to its cross-cultural owners Mohammed and Angela Mellak. The duo has set out to create more of a home than a hotel, with just six guest rooms that draw influences from their respective homelands, from the Moroccan arched doorways, handcrafted latticed cedar doors, and colorful tadelakt walls to the patterned wallpapers and textiles by Australian designer Florence Broadhurst. 

Outside, the courtyard sits center stage as per Morocco’s traditional architecture and is home to a blue zellige tiled pool surrounded by daybeds, Moroccan beni ourain cushions and shaded by an orange tree for poolside lazing. It’s also a relaxing al fresco spot for dining on the riad’s seasonal, market menu of tagines and Moroccan salads, and there’s a rooftop terrace with sun loungers and a bar for sunset mocktails. 

The team can also organize on-property activities such as mint tea masterclasses and storytelling soirées that continue a 1000-year-old Moroccan tradition, or ask them about balloon rides, shopping tours, or to open up their Marrakech address book for some insider recommendations.

content: In some places the phrase “B&B” puts one in mind of a guest room in a family home, often indifferent to design and light on facilities and services. B&B Itadaki is as far as a lodging can get from such a thing while still qualifying as a bed and breakfast. Yes, the family owners live next door, and a night in this mountain inn includes a carefully prepared breakfast. But everything about the stay is extraordinary, from the isolated (and spectacular) natural setting on the fringes of Shizuoka City to the stunning modern-rustic architecture and design to the creature comforts, which include a hot tub with a view of the forested hillsides. And while there’s no restaurant per se there’s breakfast, of course, as well as the option to book a private dinner — the owners come from a culinary family and the cuisine is as memorable as the setting.

Though it’s closer to the city of La Paz than to the resort towns of Los Cabos, Ámina Wind Resort feels secluded indeed. It’s placed here not for access to infrastructure, after all, but for the specific conditions that make it a perfect spot for pursuits involving the wind and the sea, from kite surfing and windfoiling to scuba diving and even spear fishing.

Here, being “off the grid” is a selling point, not a disadvantage. The vibe is more upscale adventure than five-star luxury, though with wi-fi and air conditioning it’s far from rough. The villas come with private patios or balconies, full kitchens, and in the case of the Beachfront Penthouse villas, rooftop Jacuzzis.

The activities on offer include hiking, mountain biking, padel, fishing, and “seafari” excursions, in addition to the aforementioned surf-adjacent sports. Cambujo, the restaurant, specializes in the local traditions of the Baja peninsula.

content: The Wakayama resort town of Shirahama lies within easy reach of Osaka, but feels a world apart. It’s known for its white-sand beaches and its geothermal springs, the latter of which are put to excellent use at Five Spring Resort The Shirahama. Suites feature kitchenettes and terraces, many equipped with outdoor Jacuzzis. A spring-fed lagoon-style swimming pool winds across the property, and a classic public bath supplements the in-room options. Meanwhile Wakayama’s varied attractions are close at hand, and the resort’s setting, surrounded by forested hillsides, makes for idyllic views.

content: Though it’s just ten minutes’ drive from the waterfall for which it’s named, Harmony Seljalandsfoss feels every bit as secluded as you would want a rural Icelandic escape to be — and the fact that it comprises a mere two lodges, placed almost comically far apart, only adds to the thoroughgoing sense of privacy. Each of them is a modern cottage, built mostly from glass, to maximize the views — and in the bedrooms that includes the ceiling, the better to glimpse the famous Northern Lights.\n\nEach one also comes with a private sauna and hot tub in a separate glassed-in outbuilding, so you never have to leave the view behind. What they don’t have is any kind of common space — no lobby, no reception, and certainly no restaurant. Anyone who’s made it this far is mobile, presumably, and their days will be spent exploring the South Coast of Iceland; you’ll bring what you need to supply your cottage’s kitchenette.

content: Deep in the Italian Alps, in the Udinese town of Malborghetto, is Hammerack, a modern luxury hotel with roots in the 15th century. It’s built for comfort and designed to reward attention — the look is not simply modern design-studio chic, but an eclectic mix of styles and eras. The philosophy, after all, is based on the timeless virtues of hospitality — of which visual appeal is only one.\n\nThus for every piece of contemporary design furniture there’s an antique flourish. The accommodations are typically Italian-Alpine, knotty pine and all, though they’re outfitted with first-rate modern comforts. An impressive modern spa boasts views of the surrounding peaks from its outdoor Jacuzzi and sun terrace, while guests are offered the choice between a semi-casual bistro and a more formal restaurant. All in all, a remarkably complete Alpine getaway, with a little something for travelers of any stylistic preference.

content:
In the middle of the 20th century, this Collins Avenue classic hosted every conceivable A-list celebrity in high Art Deco style. It was renovated in the 1950s by the legendary Miami Beach modernist architect Morris Lapidus, in the first of what would be a long series of updates — the latest of which leaves it in what might be its most impressive form, newly re-christened The Shelborne By Proper.

The building and its grounds have been treated with a respect bordering on reverence, which is as it should be. But the new interiors, thankfully, are no mid-century revival — the look is modernist-inspired, but fresh and contemporary, and while it looks native to its South Florida setting, it’s not like anything else in town.

That iconic Shelborne pool looks as fine as ever, and it’s joined by a fitness center that goes far beyond ordinary hotel-gym equipment — Peloton bikes, Pilates reformers, an Alo Yoga studio, and more. Meanwhile the restaurants and bars start with the all-day Pool Deck and range all the way up to Pauline, the signature restaurant, whose menu leans on South Florida’s vibrant Latin and Caribbean influences.

content: It takes some humility for a hotel as architecturally distinguished as Woods at Sasan to use its name to honor its setting rather than itself. But site-specificity is one of the cardinal virtues of modern architecture, and Woods at Sasan’s structures use floor-to-ceiling windows and plentiful indoor-outdoor spaces to blend the interior experience with that of its location, an 8-acre mango orchard at the edge of Gujarat’s Sasan Gir National Park, home to Asia’s last remaining lions.\n\nIts 38 units range from studios to pavilions, plus there is a private villa, each category gaining an extra level of space and privacy. But at all levels it’s an impressive place to stay, with warm contemporary interiors that play the perfect foil to the idyllic views. The restaurants and bar serve a variety of cuisines, from Gujarati to Italian, and the experiences take full advantage of the unique setting, encompassing anything from relaxing wellness treatments and outdoor yoga to a village visit and lion safaris.

content:
Just about every hotel of any ambition wishes to be seen as more than “just” a hotel; Hotel Saltus, set a thousand meters up in the Dolomites, has a strong case. It styles itself a “holistic health retreat,” and it’s fair to say guests don’t just end up here by accident. Rather, this spot in the mountains outside of Bolzano is sought out specifically for the healing effects of its natural environment — and for this stylish, high-design, luxurious mountain lodge.

The rooms and suites are modern and somewhat minimalistic in style, but that doesn’t mean blank or cold — the sparseness of the décor leaves space to appreciate the organic materials and rich textures. Even easier to appreciate are the views of the Dolomites or the surrounding forest through the floor-to-ceiling windows.

A full-featured spa offers everything from classic treatments to medical therapies, while outdoor options range from yoga to hiking and beyond. Snow sports are a big draw, in season, and year-round culinary options range from a bistro and cocktail bar to a gourmet restaurant.

content: Mere minutes outside of the city of Gdánsk, on Poland’s Baltic coast, is a remarkably pleasant seaside escape: Grano Hotel Solmarina is set on the edge of the Martwa Wisła river, and looks out across the marina and the river at Sobieszewska Island, home to a nature reserve and miles of soft, sandy beach. And the hotel itself combines the best of two worlds — the chic modern style of an urban boutique hotel along with the unhurried atmosphere and indulgent comfort of a seaside resort.\n\nIts accommodations are soothingly minimalist in their design, and range from classic hotel rooms to more elaborately serviced (and spacious) studios, apartments, and residences. Travelers with children find plenty to love here, from family-sized rooms to plentiful entertainment options for kids. And adults can’t help but love the hotel’s thoroughly well-equipped spa and wellness complex — to say nothing of the modern-Polish restaurant and the open-air Sunset Bar.

content: Sintra is one of the most picturesque places in Portugal; it’s a UNESCO World Heritage Site for a good reason. Here just about any hotel would immerse you in an atmosphere of historical splendor, but Casa da Estefânea goes a little bit farther. It’s a sight to behold in its own right, a century-old house restored in the 1990s and more recently transformed into a “pequeno hotel” — a nine-room gem whose atmosphere is memorably one-of-a-kind.\n\nIt’s the sort of hotel that makes apartment-shares look laughable by comparison. It’s owned by a Sintra resident, a hands-on host with hospitality experience who knows how to make guests feel like locals. But it’s serviced and furnished like a boutique hotel, with all the convenience that implies. A daily breakfast is followed up later in the day by wine and local pastries in the lounge or out on the terrace, and while there’s an enormous amount to see in town, your hosts are happy to help make sense of it all.

content: The boom in Portuguese tourism hasn’t just meant an increase in the number of lodgings, but a flowering of diversity as well. At the small but luxurious end of things we find Tarabel Lisbon, a 19th-century house in the upscale Lapa district, with a mere nine bedrooms and an atmosphere that’s pleasingly residential — plus views that are well worth the price of admission.\n\nInside are interiors that feel more carefully curated than the typical hotel, even the typical luxury boutique hotel; the style is eclectic but restrained, and seems to span a multitude of eras. Claw-foot tubs and separate rain showers are universal, while higher-end rooms and suites add balconies or terraces that take advantage of the hillside setting. A lovely little pool in the garden is the extent of the leisure facilities, and rather than a public restaurant there’s a dining room where the hotel’s chef serves classic Portuguese fare, local and seasonal, accompanied by Iberian wines.

content: Green isn’t the first color most travelers associate with Rajsasthan’s Thar Desert, but Maro Khet can rightly call itself an oasis. Before it was a hotel, it was a working farm, and still is — its restaurants serve only a small portion of what’s produced in its fields, gardens and orchards. To all of this Maro Khet adds just 10 cottages, each one a distinct variation on an eclectic style that includes traditional and contemporary influences and effortlessly combines hand-crafted décor with tastefully modern luxuries.\n\nEach comes with two outdoor decks, one oriented towards the sunrise and the other the sunset; inside there’s an open-air meditation courtyard, and the spa-like bathrooms are calming in their own way. Meanwhile the farm’s produce is the raw material for no fewer than three restaurants, if you define “restaurants” generously: there’s a poolside café, an all-day restaurant and bar, and an outdoor dining experience comprising nine courses served at a communal table in the guava orchard. All of this is accompanied by activities like cooking classes, walking tours, cultural performances, and more — safe to say there’s not much that’s ordinary here.

content: Just south of the city of Athens lies the Athens Riviera, a stretch of coastal idyll that’s returning to favor among Greek travelers as the islands grow ever more heavily traveled. One look at the Roc Club and you’ll wonder why anyone ever left the mainland. The coastal seascape is spectacular, as is nearby Astir Beach, and Lake Vouliagmeni, with its therapeutic thermal waters, is just a few minutes’ walk to the south.\n\nNor are the surroundings the only reason to visit. The Roc Club itself is a stylish, sunny, modernist-inspired hotel, a thorough reimagining of an existing mid-century property. The rooms and suites are tastefully luxurious, and the sparse lightness of their decoration lets the views speak for themselves. An outdoor pool feels more private than the nearby beaches and lake, and is served by a poolside bar; more formal meals are served at the Roc Veranda and the flagship Rocket Restaurant.

content:
Iceland has long had a small but vibrant boutique-hotel scene, but the island’s hoteliers were slower to embrace high-luxury hospitality. That’s changed now, but in this country luxury is always tempered by tasteful understatement — which is certainly the vibe at Black Sand Hotel, on Iceland’s south coast, 40 minutes’ drive from Reykjavík.

Lovers of austere natural beauty will be drawn to the black-sand beach from which the hotel takes its name, and architecture and design fans will appreciate the hotel’s low-profile structure and minimalist clean lines. Its sparsely decorated interiors are warmed by rich textures and by high-quality fixtures and furnishings, which include DUX beds dressed in Quagliotti linens.

The restaurant makes much of Iceland’s local ingredients — lamb, seafood, roots — and serves diners in front of floor-to-ceiling windows with direct views over the beach. And as magical as the setting is, it’s also a jumping-off point for excursions in Iceland’s south and beyond, to see attractions that range from waterfalls and geysers to the famous Northern Lights.

content: For many travelers South Tyrol is synonymous with mountain lodges, but the city of Bolzano has its urban (and urbane) side, too. Parkhotel Laurin dates back to 1910, and it looks it — the Art Nouveau façade is the very picture of grand-hotel splendor, and its interiors are no less impressive. And while its rooms and suites aren’t exactly historical reproductions, neither are they chasing after boutique-hotel cool; instead, they’re a handsome blend of original architectural features and subtle contemporary design.\n\nNor are the rooms and suites the whole story, in this or any other grand hotel. The hotel’s park and gardens are a fair-weather delight, and guests dine al fresco in the warmer months. There’s an outdoor pool in the English garden, with a Finnish sauna by its side. A bistro and bar strike a convivial note, and in the park’s old Art Nouveau greenhouse you’ll find Contanima, the hotel’s haute-cuisine restaurant.

content: The name is an unusual one for Emilia-Romagna, a fact that reflects an unusual history. This 1930s villa was founded in the ’40s by the silent film star Monty Banks — born Mario Bianchi — and much like Mr. Bianchi’s pseudonym, it shows a pronounced English influence. Lately it’s been restored with an eye towards historical preservation, but it’s not a strict thirties period piece; in the modern Italian style its century-old architecture contrasts vibrantly with clean contemporary decoration and tasteful high-tech interventions.\n\nRooms range from generously sized to quite large indeed, and come with plush comforts like marble bathrooms. There’s also plenty of space for a full-featured spa by the local company EFFE, and more unusually, the hotel is also home to the Technogym Glass Garden, an outdoor, heated glass pergola kitted out with Technogym equipment. The estate also includes an outdoor pool and a working farm, whose olives, fruits and vegetables are put to excellent use at L’Agrosteria, Villa Monty Banks’ restaurant.

content:
La Particulière is a boutique hotel in the true sense of the word: just eight guest rooms, eclectic design, and an intimate bar for a cozy cocktail hour. Each room has been given its own personality with a mish-mash of prints and colors; La Discrète, for example, is less discreet than its name thanks to a leopard-print headboard set against a backdrop of wallpaper inspired by Asian legends, while La Flèche takes its cues from Byzantine mosaics. There are thoughtful extras such as Clarins beauty products in the bathrooms, and some rooms come with their own private terrace. 

Breakfast is served in Le Damier, a private lounge where guests are also welcome to stop by for afternoon coffee, and in the evenings the 1824 bar shakes up signature cocktails alongside a carefully curated selection of spirits and rare bottles. Cocktail hour can be followed by dinner in one of the local restaurants that surround the hotel, and the central location also places guests within easy walking of some of Caen’s main attractions such as Place Saint-Sauveur, the Abbaye aux Hommes, and Caen Castle.

content: A scant few minutes inland from the busy Côte Fleurie town of Deauville stands an early-20th-century manor house that was built by the Gallimard family of publishers. Like many houses of its vintage, it lived a multitude of lives. The house was restored at the turn of the 21st century, and upgraded to its present form in 2025; today it’s a small luxury hotel known as the Maison Douce Époque.\n\nWith just 14 rooms and suites it still feels somewhat like a private residence. The accommodations are divided between the main house and the former stables; the spaces are generous, and the historical architecture is everywhere visible, while the décor displays a contemporary sensibility. And like any good country-house hotel, the bedrooms are only half the story — here guests benefit from the expansive gardens and grounds, the outdoor swimming pool, a spa in partnership with KOS Paris and Bellefontaine Switzerland, and a gastronomic restaurant called Le Romanesque.

content: From the street, this stately building in Lisbon’s picturesque Estrela district could almost pass as a proper grand hotel. But what’s inside is something much more subtle. The Verse is no high-touch luxury hotel, but a residential-style apartment hotel whose 15 units combine self-sufficient comforts with handsome, minimalist boutique-hotel aesthetics.\n\nThe apartments themselves range from compact and efficient lofts to more spacious units that open onto terraces or garden patios. Full kitchens are universal — you’re truly on your own for lunch and dinner, though a thoughtful room service breakfast is served daily. Whether you cook or not depends on how enticing you find the neighborhood’s restaurants; both groceries and meals out are in plentiful supply in this corner of town, and the hotel’s own cocktail bar is a fine, low-key alternative for an evening in.

content: A few minutes up the Basque Coast from Biarritz, Maison Chiberta is enviably positioned among Anglet’s resorts — surrounded by forests, just inland from the beaches, and right alongside the Chiberta golf club. It’s long been one of the best-known local stays, but it’s looking fresher than ever thanks to its new association with the Annie Famose hotel group.\n\nToday’s Maison Chiberta has been extensively renovated, but it retains its classic Basque Country character even as its details are brought up to 21st-century spec. The 58 rooms and suites combine contemporary clean lines with artisan-made crafts; some overlook the surrounding pine forest, others the golf course. At the hotel’s heart is an Andalusian-style courtyard; other attractions include a well-equipped spa in partnership with the Swedish brand L.A. Bruket and a restaurant that marries Basque and South American traditions.

content: Visiting some of the 300 or so chateaux that are dotted around the Loire Valley is one of the region’s main attractions, but Les Hayes also gives you the chance to spend the night in one. The 19th century castle has been reborn as a boutique hotel, home to 19 individually designed rooms which are split across the chateau or La Solognote, a historic property built in the region’s traditional style, and surrounded by a vast 180-hectare estate. Everyday guests can discover the French tradition of goûter, or teatime, with homemade crêpes and cakes, and the bar is open all day long from morning coffee to evening cocktails. Restaurant Le Cyprès cooks up seasonal, local cuisine from Wednesday to Sunday, and on Mondays and Tuesdays a simple set menu of homecooked hearty dishes is served around a communal rustic table for guests to dine together. By day there’s plenty of activities to choose from, and they’re all included in a stay, from forest laser games to free bike hire and astronomy nights.\n

content: Zeeland’s historic maritime academy was blessed with an extraordinary location right on Vlissingen’s seaside promenade — good news for apprentice sailors, but even better news for patrons of the building’s new occupant, the Hotel De Zevaartschool. The original structure is a national monument, and was thus carefully preserved, leaving the old students’ quarters compact and cozy. \n\nBut if there’s one nation we trust to make efficient use of space, it’s the Netherlands; here the smallest rooms feel spacious enough, and the family-friendly Quad rooms make clever use of a loft and a miller’s staircase. To its appealing accommodations the Hotel De Zevaartschool adds a versatile all-day restaurant as well as a bar with a sea-facing terrace. Outside, the beaches (and the cycling paths) beckon.

content: Portugal’s Atlantic-facing Vicentine Coast is spectacular enough; add a striking modernist luxury boutique hotel set on 500+ acres of protected woodland and you’re in for something extraordinary. Safe to say Praia do Canal Nature Retreat is a cut above the majority of the hotels that opened during Portugal’s most recent tourism boom — its low-profile, somewhat austere modernist architecture lends some extra gravity to this tranquil escape. Inside, the rooms and suites are rescued from minimalism by warm textures, natural materials, and colorful crafts and textiles. Some units come with balconies, others with terraces, rooftop lounges, or plunge pools, and all of them face out into the verdant landscape of the nature reserve. An extensive spa and fitness program is present as a matter of course, and the main infinity pool is a stunner. Azeitona, the main restaurant, is joined by a casual poolside option as well as a swanky cocktail bar. And the hotel’s surroundings invite exploration as well — both surfers and golfers find themselves well taken care of in this corner of Portugal.

content: In the hills above the city center, facing Funchal Bay and the Atlantic Ocean stands an 18th-century house that was home, during the Napoleonic Wars, to the British general William Carr Beresford. The rooms and suites are generously sized and look out over the property’s spectacular gardens; some also feature distant views of the valley, the city and the sea. The formal dining room is named for General Beresford, and is joined by the Colombo Bistro, a cocktail bar and a poolside bar.

content: Weighing in at 475 rooms and suites, The Apurva Kempinski Bali is no secret little boutique hotel. In fact its near-monumental scale is a large part of its appeal. Here on the cliffs above Nusa Dua Beach, guests enter a self-contained realm of luxury, where rooms, suites, and villas cascade down the hillside from the vast open-air building that contains the bulk of the public spaces. \n\nThe majority of the accommodations come with plunge pools, and all are decorated in an eminently tasteful modern-meets-classic style, with a near-monochrome color palette and a highly polished, even somewhat urban feel. Meanwhile all guests share access to an extravagant spa, a vast lagoon-style main pool, and a generous (and diverse) handful of restaurants and bars — including the extremely memorable Koral, whose dining room is set inside a vast aquarium.

content:
Earl’s Court isn’t the most central of central London neighborhoods, but this slight remove is how you get a setting as tranquil as Templeton Garden. Here a row of Victorian buildings conceals an expansive garden, whose verdant outdoor space is something no other London hotel can claim to match.

The hotel’s indoor spaces are impressive as well, especially the 156 rooms and suites, which are understated in their luxuriousness and which present a fresh and remarkably warm take on mid-century modern style. They vary unusually widely in both size and standard of service; the smallest rooms feature only “essential” service, with a housekeeping visit every other day, while the top of the range gets “the full works,” including a fully stocked complimentary minibar and daily turndown service.

Pippin’s is the versatile modern British restaurant, serving a classic Sunday roast and expanding its dining space into the garden, while Sprout is an intimate and irreverent cocktail bar. Earl’s Court Station connects guests to anywhere in London in a matter of minutes, and even on foot, quite a lot of the best of West London is within easy reach.

content: The Dorset town of Wareham grew up around this historic monastery on the banks of the River Frome, which explains its unique atmosphere: a country house mere steps from the town center. The Priory Wareham in its present form dates back to the 16th century and to the 1970s — the former date marking the current house’s construction, and the latter its establishment as a hotel.\n\nThus it was, in a way, a luxury boutique hotel before the phrase was coined; and as this family-owned hotel has been continuously updated over the years, it remains a fine example of modern country-house hospitality. Its rooms and suites, divided between the main house and the riverside boathouse, offer plenty of antique atmosphere, while the details of the décor show a contemporary designer’s touch. The restaurant, too, is in the contemporary-classic vein, helmed by a French-trained chef and serving dishes crafted from fresh, seasonal British ingredients.

content: Named after the Greek words for wind (anemos) and oblivion (lithi), Anemolethe Suites Hotel wants you to forget about it all when you check into its sea-facing guest rooms. The hotel sits perched on the rocky edge of Kimolos, one of the lesser-known Cyclades islands, with a sweeping view of the Aegean and the sound of nothing else but the sea breeze. The traditional whitewashed blocky buildings hide equally bright white minimalist rooms, all of which come with private terraces, and some with hot tubs and plunge pools. The main pool is also set to an idyllic backdrop of endless water, and while there is no restaurant or bar on site, the hotel sits just a 10-minute walk from Kimolos’ capital, Chorio.

content: Set on the Côte Vermeille just a few miles from the Spanish border, Collioure is French, but displays quite a bit of Catalan influence. And though it’s a paradise on the Mediterranean, it’s far less heavily traveled by overseas visitors than the Côte d’Azur. Only here, perhaps, could a place like Maison Nova remain a well-kept secret — this 13-room escape is stylish, luxurious, sustainable, and as private as can be.\n\nEach of Maison Nova’s rooms is decorated with original works by Catalan artists, the impact of which is heightened by the interiors’ spare, modernist visual style. A few come with a private Jacuzzi or an outdoor bathtub, and all guests benefit from the hotel’s Phytomer spa, as well as its sauna, hammam, and dazzling outdoor pool. Breakfast is served daily, and light fare is available later; for a proper restaurant, you’re no more than half a kilometer from the center of Collioure.

content:
The country counterpart to its sister hotel in Siem Reap, Shinta Mani Wild offers more than just a change of scenery. In order to preserve the indigenous forest, its 15 tented suites and all of its public spaces are built on elevated platforms. Some more elevated than others — as of this writing, Shinta Mani Wild is the only hotel we know of where guests have the option to arrive via zipline.

Like Shinta Mani Angkor, Shinta Mani Wild was conceived and designed by Bill Bensley, the California-born, Bangkok-based architect whose work set the tone for a generation of Southeast Asian luxury resorts. Here he’s in a particularly expressive mode, which means these tented suites are full of details that evoke various chapters in Cambodia’s history, with a particular focus on the glamorous 1960s. 

And though it’s a tented camp, with extraordinary measures taken to protect the local flora and fauna, no compromises are made in the area of comfort. The rate is truly all-inclusive, covering not just food and drink but also unlimited spa treatments — and it subsidizes the local conservation efforts, which not only make this experience possible, but aim to safeguard it for future generations.

content:
ROKI Collection Queenstown offers just fifteen suites overlooking Lake Wakatipu and The Remarkables, a setting that feels both discreet and indulgent — the address is Queenstown, but the neighborhood is quiet and hidden from prying eyes. 

Interiors use soft gray tones, textured throws, freestanding tubs, and fireplaces set beside wide glass doors that open onto the view. Even the (relatively) smaller suites feature walk-in wardrobes and spacious bathrooms, while larger residences add outdoor fireplaces, dining terraces, and balcony spas or saunas. Butler service and private chefs are available in the multi-bedroom suites, though all guests can rely on the house car for evening runs into town.

Essence, the signature restaurant, is joined by the less formal Terrace, with its far-ranging views, and the Library Bar, a cozy lounge serving light fare alongside cocktails and wines.

content: An 18th-century olive mill on the mainland-facing coast of southeastern Corfu, mere minutes down the coast from the city, is now The Olivar Suites, a luxurious and stylish boutique-style resort that offers a memorably cosmopolitan take on Greek island life. Its 120 suites surround the old mill in a village-like arrangement, affording the accommodations an extra measure of privacy; most of them come with plunge pools or small swimming pools, and all of them are decorated in a manner that avoids island kitsch and lets the setting speak for itself.\n\nThe beach lies just beyond the row of sea-facing suites, and a substantial swimming pool offers a freshwater option. There’s a spa for more intensive relaxation, and at the heart of the hotel are a pair of gathering places: Flya, the all-day restaurant, serves an upscale take on the local culinary tradition, and Olibar serves cocktails and wine surrounded by the machinery of the old mill.

content: It's hard to believe from its sleek modern exterior, but Maison Hotel Bangkok takes its inspiration from the classic Thai novel Plae Kao, a Romeo-and-Juliet-like novel set partly to the backdrop of 1930s Bangkok. To nod to this calmer Bangkok of the past, contemporary minimalist rooms have been designed to offer a sanctuary from the buzz of the modern-day Bangkok, while the verdant garden surrounding the poolside terrace nods to a slower way of Thai life found by the country’s historically significant canals. The four restaurants include Saan Somtum Bar for Thai street food, and Yardbird for all day coffee and pastries. Other facilities include a gym, yoga studio, and the Bulann Moonlight Spa, which is rooted in traditional Thai treatments and massage techniques. And if you’re traveling with children, the Kid’s Club is kitted out with ball pits and slides for supervised playtime.

content:
What was once a single California wine country is now one of the most prestigious names in luxury boutique hospitality, and when Auberge Resorts took over the Goldener Hirsch in 2021, the whole Park City hospitality scene got an upgrade. They did more than rename the inn, of course. Star Seattle architects Olson Kundig were brought in for a substantial expansion, and today’s Goldener Hirsch is a double act: the original Bavarian-style chalet is now joined by a striking modern addition.

It’s a matter of more than architecture. The Inn remains decorated in a heritage European style, featuring imported Austrian furniture, while the new Goldener’s interiors are contemporary, though cozier than the exterior might lead you to believe. In both wings the comforts are first-rate, as is the service throughout.

Two restaurants serve hearty and refined Alpine-influenced cooking, and the leisure facilities are boutique-sized, though no less impressive for it — massages are available en suite, while the rooftop is home to an infinity pool and a hot tub with an impressive view of the Wasatch Range. This is a proper ski hotel — Deer Valley’s Silver Lake Express lift is right outside — but like any mountain resort worth its salt, it’s an equally compelling destination in warmer months, offering access to no end of hiking, biking, and other dry-weather outdoor pursuits.

content: You might guess that a place called Windsor, Nova Scotia, along the banks of the Avon River, might be touched by just a tiny bit of influence from Great Britain. The August House, however, is notable for its Italian influence. Not only is this historic mansion, a survivor of the 1897 fire, constructed in the Italianate style, but its current owners undertook its restoration and its transformation into a boutique inn after a visit to Italy and a close-up look at the slow-living virtues embodied in the best Italian hospitality.\n\nAbsent, though, is any overt Italian style. The August House is as devoted to its particular locale as the finest Chianti farmhouse is to Tuscany — right down to the floorboards, proudly milled from Nova Scotian lumber. The rooms and suites are simply decorated, but far from minimalist, decorated with a keen eye for color and just the right amount of ornament, comfortable without feeling overly lavish. A house-made breakfast is served each morning, and while the house goes without a dedicated restaurant, your hosts are handy with detailed local recommendations.

content:
The lovely little town of Picton, in Ontario’s Prince Edward County, is maybe the most likely setting in all of Canada for a hotel like Merrill House. This red brick Gothic Revival mansion stands just off Main Street, a block from Picton Harbour, but feels quiet and quasi-rural all the same. And the style is unforgettable. Both inside and out, Merrill House is anglophilic even by Canadian standards — its owners live part-time in London, and the house’s décor wouldn’t look a whisker out of place there.

Each of the 14 rooms and suites is different, but all feature an eclectic and individual blend of the antique and the modern, including plenty of playful contemporary art. A few go to extremes — the Future Room is furnished on both floor and ceiling — and all are as subtly luxurious as they are overtly stylish.

A hotel like this could very reasonably go without a bar or a restaurant, but Merrill House has both; Bar Atlas makes its home in a riotously colorful conservatory space, and features a wide selection of local wines alongside Old World vintages, while Brasserie Alexandria is as classically French as the house’s second-floor Parisian Suite.

content: Stella Island isn’t an island, although it does sit on the coastline of Crete, but the collection of lagoon pools weaved around the adults-only resort might make you feel like you’re on one. The abundance of water means all the rooms have a blue pool view, and some, including the overwater bungalows and the villa, come with a swim up option for a private deck with direct pool access. When not swimming there are activities such as padel, cycling, and an outdoor gym. Post-work out the Anassa spa is just the tonic, home to a sauna, Jacuzzi, another pool, and Elemis beauty treatments. There's one bar, six restaurants, including a Greek-style taverna, a Mexican fusion cuisine and a steakhouse, and the option to go all-inclusive.

content:
At this late date it takes something special to stand out in boutique-hotel-saturated Tulum, but NABOA Hotel Tulum has what it takes. While many local lodgings have luxe aspirations, the experience here is authentically high-end. It’s also authentically local — architects Jaque Studio combined traditional materials and craftsmanship with contemporary clean lines and modernist-inspired simplicity.

The idea is slow living, Riviera Maya style. To that end, NABOA’s 10 suites are solidly built and exquisitely private, even though their spaces are open; some feature indoor-outdoor bathrooms, and all open onto the property’s lush gardens. The fixtures and furnishings are high-quality, proof that Tulum’s ideal bohemian-luxe vibe is achievable without compromising comfort.

Wellness offerings include massages as well as yoga and barre classes, and the hotel’s pool is a delightful one. And while the hotel’s location means both the town center and Tulum Beach are close by, LU_LO, the restaurant and cocktail bar, makes a compelling argument for a night in.

content:
There are certainly ways to visit Thailand in a spirit of devil-may-care decadence, but Chiva-Som Hua Hin is the opposite of all that. Guests check in here not only to get away, but to clean up and dry out, to relax and de-stress, to make major lifestyle adjustments.

Here the spa treatments and the health programs are the main attractions, with the beaches and restaurants playing second fiddle, and your fellow travelers out by the pool are more likely sipping carrot juice than cocktails. Despite the difference in purpose, however, Chiva-Som Hua Hin is every bit as stunning as the more typical luxury resorts. The location is the seaside town of Hua Hin, traditional getaway of Thai royalty, three hours south of the capital—not as removed from Bangkok’s bustle as Phuket, for example, but still anything but urban.

The resort sprawls over the rolling hills between the town and the coast, a collection of rooms and pavilions nestled amid landscaped gardens. Guest rooms are handsomely minimal, with a heavy traditional Thai influence, and all the expected charms, like hardwood floors, hefty modern beds, and spacious showers. Guest rooms in the main building have private balconies or terraces, and the pavilions scattered across the grounds offer an added measure of privacy.

As for the treatments, they range widely, from classic detox massages and an encyclopedic menu of Ayurvedic and Thai therapies, to physiotherapy or quasi-scientific treatments. Have your irises examined, if that’s your bag, but it doesn’t take a wellness specialist to point out that eating well, sleeping well and the occasional massage are bound to do some good.

content: With the advent of the Zhiwaling hotels, there’s now a Bhutanese alternative to the small handful of resorts that constitute the local high-end hospitality scene. Zhiwaling Heritage is set in the scenic Paro Valley, not far from the famous Tiger’s Nest Temple. And while it may be less precariously perched than the temple, the hotel, with its wealth of hand-painted detail and traditional architecture, is scarcely less picturesque.\n\nThe suites are spacious, sunny, and mix sparse design with intricate, lavish detailing. They’re divided among a number of outlying cottages, and all of them feature views of the resort’s unspoiled natural surroundings. Outdoor recreation is an area of particular focus, and the word “heritage” in the hotel’s name is no accident either — among the experiences are many cultural activities, with a tea house, a temple, and an archery range on site.

content: The golden sands and clear blue waters of a remote Greek island has long set the scene for romance, and so it makes sense that the tranquil, White Pebble Suites taps into Greece’s reputation as an escape for loved up couples and honeymooners. In fact, it has a love story all of its own: after three Greek Australian friends travelled to Milos to reconnect with their roots, they fell so hard for its charms that the trio made a more permanent commitment to island by opening the boutique hotel. The blocky whitewashed buildings take their design cues from a traditional Cycladic village and house just twelve couple-friendly suites, each with sea-view terraces and eight with private plunge pools. The well-connected team has access to a Rolodex full of local experts, from chefs and skippers to geologists and walking guides, who can lead various activities around the island and its waters. Alternatively, for doing nothing at all, there’s a spa with treatments based around the beneficial beauty properties of Greek olive oil and local plants. To enhance the intimate feel the usual hotel restaurant is replaced by private room service, and more relaxed and romantic al fresco poolside dining.\n

content:
Inland Bali is for escaping the crowds, and surrounded by sprawling gardens and a vast expanse of rice fields, Tanah Gajah, a Resort by Hadiprana certainly qualifies as an escape. Here, a mile or two outside of Ubud, you’re never far from civilization, but from within the confines of the estate the rest of the world might as well not exist at all.

The Club Suites get things started with ample space, spa-like bathrooms with indoor tubs and outdoor showers, all rendered in a luxe and richly textured contemporary style. The Pool Villas raise the stakes a bit, with private sundecks adjoining their ten-meter pools; some add saunas, cold-water plunge pools and outdoor tubs, while the two-bedroom Hadiprana Estate serves as something of a presidential suite, a self-contained luxury residence unto itself.

A massive central pool serves all hotel guests, as does The Spa at Tanah Gajah, and The Tempayan serves a broad range of cuisines from Bali and far beyond. All the luxe resort staples are present and accounted for — but given Tanah Gajah’s expansiveness, its elegance, and its generally genteel atmosphere, the atmosphere here is less like a typical island resort and more like the Balinese equivalent of a country-house hotel.

How to get there:
Tanah Gajah, a Resort by Hadiprana is located 35 kilometers (approximately 45–60 minutes by car) from the Ngurah Rai International Airport.

content:
What was once strictly a Parisian nightlife outfit has quickly developed into one of Europe’s most interesting hospitality brands. The Experimental Group follows the success of Experimental Chalet Verbier with another Alpine hotel, this one a little closer to home: Experimental Chalet Val d’Isère is further proof that ski hotels and boutique-hotel style belong together.

Here Experimental’s designer of choice Dorothée Meilichzon transformed an existing hotel — the group’s largest property to date — into a fresh and original take on the ski-hotel genre. The visual language is influenced as much by American national-park lodges as it is by Alpine tradition, and the sum total of the effect is a look that’s indelibly unique.

In a place like this, a spa is a must; this one features an indoor pool and a steam room and sauna alongside its treatment rooms. An in-house ski shop handles rentals in partnership with Ski Set, and the lifts are an easy walk from the hotel. Nor are food and drink neglected in any Experimental production; here a grand brasserie, l’Aigle d’Or, and the cheese-focused l’Aiglon are joined by the Experimental Cocktail Club Val d’Isère, an Alpine counterpart to the Parisian original.

content: The historical and spiritual gravity of the temples at Angkor don’t stop Shinta Mani from indulging its playful side — this Siem Reap luxury resort was designed by the California-born, Bangkok-based architect Bill Bensley, who is responsible for more than his fair share of Southeast Asia’s finest hotels and resorts. Here he’s at his most eclectic, leaving his stamp — and his artworks — all over the resort.\n\nBensley was first known for his landscape work, so it’s no surprise that Shinta Mani Angkor, despite its urban setting, is as verdant as can be. The accommodations come in three distinct flavors, with the Bensley Pool Villas at the top of the range. And along with a generous helping of style, Shinta Mani Angkor features substantial attractions, from the Khmer Tonics Spa to Kroya, a modern-classic Khmer restaurant.

content: Housed in the former Bordeaux Institute of Zoology, from which it takes its name, La Zoologie doubles down on its natural sciences beginnings with interiors inspired by biology, flora and fauna. The 40 guest rooms are split across three wings, named Geology, Zoology and Botanic, and blend a mix of Bordeaux stone and clay walls, original brickwork and half moon windows with natural, earthy shades and wallpapers depicting a mix of animals, verdant forests and maritime scenes. The wellness area offers massages with made in France products, a Jacuzzi, hammam, sauna, and an outdoor terrace shaded by leafy palms, although relaxation time comes at an extra charge for guests booking into a Classic room. Bistronomic restaurant La Zoologie serves a seasonal menu focused on market produce, a team of mixologists shake up the hotel’s signature cocktails in the bar,  and in summer, the rooftop terrace opens with panoramic views of Bordeaux.

content: The comically picturesque seaside town of Castellammare del Golfo provides the raw material for Costamante Suites & Spa: an 18th-century mansion restored in the inimitable modern-classic collage style perfected by Italian hoteliers and transformed into a seven-suite luxury boutique hotel. It’s a form perhaps less common in Sicily, where seaside resorts and farmhouse hotels predominate, but it’s one with much to recommend it.\n\nEach suite is different, all of them inspired by the twists and turns of the historical structure; all come with kitchens, for the added privacy of a self-sufficient stay. The spa is an impressive one, given the hotel’s small size, and a typically Sicilian breakfast is provided daily — for lunch and dinner the town of Castellammare fills the gap.

content: With rooms and suites spread across a patch of northern Crete’s rocky coastline, the adults-only Seaside A Lifestyle Resort feels more like a tiny Cretan village than a hotel resort. The soothing design blends traditional whitewashed walls with earthy neutral shades and layers of straw and wood that complement the mix of natural mountain, garden and sea views. In keeping with the village theme, you could almost eat somewhere new every night, from local cuisine at Minoan Cretan Taverna and seafood with sea views at Oceano to intimate private dinners in the heart of an olive grove at Eleonas. There’s just as many options for relaxation in the vast spa, including an indoor pool, a sauna and ice fountain, massages, shiatsu and acupuncture, and even a dedicated nail and hair salon to add the finishing touch.

content: You can just visit Corona Island for the day, but it would be hard to resist staying the night to wake up in paradise. The tiny Caribbean island is home only to the hotel, which is actually more of a collection of eco-friendly boat-shaped cabins, designed to maximize the sound of the waves and positioned to face the sunset views. The rest is dedicated to nature, with pristine beaches, lush forest, and a turtle zone which together are home to titi monkeys, parrots, macaws and several protected species. Completely disconnected, guests can immerse themselves in the slow pace of beach and island life with a yoga class, sunbathing, or reading in the library, or explore the waters with kayaking, snorkeling and stand up paddleboarding. The restaurant serves up the flavors of the Caribbean, and the Sunclub is the place to meet to catch the sunset and kick off the evening.

With 125 acres of land, sweeping sea views, beachside restaurants, and even its own watersports center, Carbis Bay Estate is home to many of the Cornish attractions that continue to pull tourists to the shores of St Ives. Sea view rooms and suites are split between the 19th century Main House and the beachside Beach Houses, Lodges and Suites, or for more privacy the charming stone Valley Cottages & Suites can be found tucked away in a wooded valley just a few minutes’ walk from the hotel.

And whilst the Cornish coastline is by nature family-friendly, the hotel also offers its own Kids’ Club to keep children entertained with beach games, film nights, pizza making and more.

content: Many American cities have tried to rejuvenate downtown districts with sporting venues, and in Denver the result has been a complete success. The Lower Downtown (or LoDo) district anchored by the Coors Field baseball stadium is now home to a vibrant dining, nightlife, and entertainment scene, and the mixed-use McGregor Square lies right at its heart. content: The cave hotels of Cappadocia are one of the travel world’s favorite stories, and it’s not hard to see why: subterranean suites, stone walls, and picturesque rock formations make for an irresistible setting, and the fact that the skies are dotted with hot air balloons is an unexpected bonus. Signature Cave Cappadocia combines the rough-hewn walls and hand-built construction of the classic cave hotel with an extra measure of elegance, from its fluted columns to its antique-inspired furnishings and ornate en-suite woodwork and carvings.\n\nIt’s an all-suite property, and many of the units come with luxe extras like fireplaces, jetted tubs, Turkish baths, or hammams. The restaurant, too, occupies a substantial underground space, possibly the hotel’s most refined environment, thanks to its columns, arches, and polished stone floors. There’s outdoor lounge space as well, for catching a glimpse of the sky, and tours of the region are available via horseback and hot air balloon.

content: Boutique hoteliers have rediscovered the Hudson Valley in a big way, but few of them have shown as much ambition as the proprietors of Pocketbook Hudson. First a textile mill, later a pocketbook factory, this red brick industrial structure has stood since the 1890s on a generous parcel of land just off Hudson, New York’s main drag. But it’s only after a 2025 re-imagining at the hands of Charlap Hyman & Herrero that it became what it is today: a proper luxury boutique hotel on a scale that sets it apart from the region’s farmhouse inns and modernized motor lodges.\n\nIts rooms and suites benefit from the contrasts between the brick-and-timber construction, the modern minimalist décor, and the pastoral small-town setting. And with capacity for close to 100 guests, Pocketbook draws enough of a crowd to justify some impressive services, including a café and bar, an art exhibition space, a grab-and-go market, and even a subterranean nightclub. The Baths, set in an adjacent building, open in late 2025, while Ambos Restaurant is already serving New Argentine fare cooked on an open fire from local and seasonal ingredients.

content: A not-too-hot climate plus a varied terrain of beaches, rivers, and natural lakes makes the fishing village of Fortim an ideal choice for active travelers. Hotel Jaguarindia Village encourages this adventurous spirit by organizing numerous outdoor experiences such as water skiing on the Jaguaribe River and buggy rides, horse riding, and kitesurfing on the nearby beach, tapping into Fortim’s reputation as one of the best kite spots in the state. Back at the hotel are yoga classes and a semi-Olympic sized pool, for swimming or lounging under the tall coconut palms, as well as a spa with treatments based around natural ingredients from the Brazilian Amazon.
name: Hotel Jaguarindia Village
