content: Situated on 4,000 acres just outside Park City, The Lodge at Blue Sky offers a remote, design-driven take on the mountain getaway. Accommodations range from creekside cabins to grass-roofed hillside suites and cliffside rooms with wide views of Alexander Canyon. The vibe is peaceful but active with horseback rides, high-alpine hikes, and seasonal meals that pull from the on-site farm. Adults can retreat to the Creek Houses, while families gravitate toward the spacious Sky Lodge suites. Every detail: stone, glass, wood, is placed to keep the landscape front and center.

content: Spa time is taken seriously at Koia All Suite Wellbeing Resort, where the wellness concept is rooted in the Hippocratic philosophy. Pared back rooms in shades of white and wood come with instantly calming Aegean Sea views, and in most cases a private pool. YDΩR SPA is of course the highlight, this is a wellbeing resort after all, with treatments based around the healing properties of water and herbs. There’s an indoor pool with more sea views, a steam room, a Hippocratic Tea Bar, and relaxing massages using the hotel’s own natural botanical oils. Restaurant Thyme complements the experience with nutritional dishes rooted in traditional Grecian cuisine, and cocktail bar Elixir and the Pool Bar & Restaurant serve a mix of herbal alcohol-free drinks and local wines.

The adults-only, riad-style hotel places beach view rooms around a central leafy courtyard, and each space is decorated with Moroccan-inspired wooden arches, motifs, and golden lanterns. The wellness offering comprises a varied mix of beach yoga sessions, Jiu Jitsu classes, ice baths, and sound healing, as well as relaxing massages.

content: The proprietors of downtown Charleston’s The Pinch chose Upper King Street, in Cannonborough, for the sequel. The Nickel Hotel is twice as large — a still boutique-sized 50 rooms and suites — and announces itself with just a touch more fanfare, thanks to a building by Morris Adjmi Architects whose façade, though unmistakably contemporary, pays tribute to the melting pot of historical styles that is Charleston. Once you’re in the central courtyard, though, ringed by three stories of wrought-iron balconies, you’ll likely do a double-take at the thoroughly immersive Victorian atmosphere.\n\nThe rest of the public spaces follow suit, while the rooms and suites pursue a hybrid contemporary-classic style. In them you’ll find residential comforts like full kitchens and washers and dryers, and many of them open onto courtyard-facing balconies. And at this size, The Nickel Hotel can sustain a pair of dining and drinking venues: Bar Daniel, a swanky second-floor cocktail lounge, and, from September 2025, a rooftop bar and lounge called Rosemary Rose.

content: It’s not often you find Victorian England architecture in Spain, but coming across the unique design of Angelats Hotels amongst the forest of the Catalan Pyrenees is even more of a surprise. The property was first built as a residence by Domingo Batlló, who wanted to be close to the waters of the Torrent d’Angelats and their supposed health benefits, before been finished by his son in the Victorian style. The original design has been retained and the building transformed from home to hotel, with 20 rooms looking over the historic courtyard or the sloping hills of the Pyrenees. Some can also be connected via the bathroom to create family-friendly accommodation. Restaurant La Santa is housed inside the stone wall and vaulted ceiling’s the former church and serves Catalan cuisine with meat cooked over a live fire. The outdoor swimming pool also has a prime location on top of one of the houses arched structures, offering a high up panoramic view of the Pyrenees. It this remote location in nature which makes the hotel an ideal spot for stargazing, or by day, exploring the surrounding forests and national parks.

content: Sitting in the heart of London’s Fitzrovia, The Newman takes its design cues from the neighbourhood’s distinct architecture, which blends Victorian design with Art Deco touches. The neutral palette of the guest rooms and suites is accessorized with softly curved furnishings and highlights of polished steel to add a 1920s edge to the contemporary design. The mix of Victorian and Art Deco elements also continues into the bathrooms, decorated with bespoke tiles and rounded stone-carved sinks. \n\nAfter dining on European cuisine at Brasserie Adalana guests can head underground to Gambit Bar, where the low-lit, intimate atmosphere brings to mind the days when Fitzrovia’s bohemian, literary crowd would gather together over drinks. Aside from drinking and dining there’s also a whole floor dedicated to wellness, with a comprehensive offering that includes a gym, hydrotherapy pool, salt therapy room, yoga classes and spa treatments.

content: There may be no historical building form better suited to a bout of luxe escapism than the monastery — and a Tuscan one offers additional charms that are specific to the region. Badia di Pomaio, in its original form, dates back to 1645, but it was only in 2019 that it underwent its transformation, becoming a stylish and tastefully luxurious boutique hotel.\n\nThe location, just a few miles outside of Arezzo, means it’s placed to enjoy the archetypal Tuscan countryside experience, from rolling verdant hills to a table that serves local fare from zero-kilometer ingredients. Meanwhile the rooms and suites retain enough historical character to convey an unmistakable sense of place, while the decoration moves in a decidedly contemporary-luxe direction. Experiences include everything you come to rural Tuscany for, from truffle hunting and wine tasting to hiking, biking, clay-court tennis and more. Meals are served in the dining room or on the terrace, and the indoor-outdoor bar sits under a glass roof.

content: It’s almost hard to believe that Le Dune Piscinas began life as a humble warehouse for mining materials, or that the golden dunes that surround it hide the remains of a 19th-century mine. After a radical transformation the property has been reborn as a luxuriously soothing retreat, which feels far from everything except the beach and the blue waters of the Mediterranean. The 28 rooms look across the dunes and the sea—you can even hear the waves at night—and some come with balconies and terraces to place guests even closer to the sands. Interiors nod to traditional Sardinian design, note the tonal bas relief walls and cast-iron beds, as well as the building’s mining history, with Orosei marble bathroom floors sourced from nearby quarries.\n\nThe American bar has also retained the spirit of the place with its exposed stone walls and grand stone fireplace, whilst the three restaurants, which include the beachside Maestrale, casual all day Ginepro, and fine dining at Rosso Tramonto, all champion local Sardinian produce. Other facilities include an outdoor pool, gym, and spa, a library filled with books on Sardinian culture, and more unusually, a silent cinema, where guests can browse films and listen through headphones to retain the hotel’s tranquil beachside ambience.

content: The Edison George Town brings fresh energy to a 1906 mansion just outside Penang’s UNESCO-listed core. Once a Hakka tycoon’s home, and later converted into a guesthouse, the building was fully restored in 2016, preserving its marble floors and cast-iron columns while restoring and updating its Art Deco-influenced colonial-era splendor. \n\nRooms are handsome, combining classic elements with a contemporary color sensibility. The pool sits in a leafy courtyard, with shaded cabanas for mid-afternoon escapes, and the Lounge is a versatile all-day space serving a grab-and-go menu. But the real action is right outside, where George Town’s temples, shophouses, and street food stalls wait in every direction. Heritage with bite, right in the middle of Malaysia’s most flavor-packed city.

content: There are four of Brown’s urban boutique hotels in the Greek capital, but none put you as close to the world-famous Acropolis as Villa Brown Ermou. The hotel sits just a 15-minute walk from Athen’s top attraction, and even closer to the main Syntagma Square and the shopping hotspot of Ermou Street, from which the hotel takes its name. There’s a stylish all-day bistro and a rooftop for drinks, plus the excellent location means the restaurants and bars of the Plaka neighborhood just strolling distance away.

content: About an hour to the south of Florence, just outside the medieval town of Radda in Chianti, stands Borgo Vescine, a Lombard-era fortification that slowly evolved into a village before achieving its current form as a smallish and thoroughly charming boutique hotel. It’s surrounded, as such villages often are, by vineyards and olive trees. And much of the village character has been retained, as the Borgo’s rooms are divided among a number of restored historical buildings. The village also retains its central piazza, which now serves as a gathering place for guests and a venue for a weekly “cena in piazza.” On other nights, dinner is served at La Terrazza del Borgo and Bistrot la Torre, accompanied by selected wines from the estate’s collection.

content: Set not in the city of Lecce but in the small town of Minervino di Lecce, Palazzo Ducale Venturi is a meticulous restoration of a 16th-century palazzo, brought back to life as one of Salento’s most luxurious lodgings. The restoration was guided by the local cultural authority, and the Palazzo’s antique atmosphere is thus as authentic as possible. Its rooms and suites sit beneath arched ceilings, some frescoed, some in raw stone; all exhibit an air of aristocratic refinement, from the ornate Ducal Suite all the way down to the garden-facing Classic Room.\n\nNor are contemporary luxuries overlooked. The spa and wellness area are a noteworthy inclusion, as is the outdoor pool. In addition to a gourmet restaurant, the Palazzo offers cooking classes as well as private dining experiences set in the palace’s garden. And the excursions and experiences range all over the region, from tours of Lecce’s artistic and culinary destinations to sailing excursions along the coast of Salento.

content: The Colle Alberti estate is unique even among its Tuscan neighbors; not only is it home to vineyards producing wines with the Chianti DOCG appellation, it’s also home to what was once the Medici family’s hunting estate. It’s also, as you might have guessed, home to the Colle Alberti Country House, a classic Tuscan villa whose interiors have been given a thoroughly, refreshingly contemporary makeover and now host the estate’s hospitality operation.\n\nInside the house and the nearby granary and barn are 15 rooms and three suites, a size that makes for a convivial atmosphere but never a crowded one. Each unit is a soothing blend of modern minimalism and antique architecture, and all are luxurious, though not ostentatious. Guests visit Colle Alberti not to impress but to live the good life, Italian style — lounging by the poolside, tasting wines from the capacious cellar, and dining on elevated Tuscan classics made from fresh local ingredients.

content: Cavo Tagoo, like most of the best hotels on Santorini, isn’t just a casual B&B at the beach. It’s a stunner of a resort, complete with dramatic whitewashed architecture, five-star amenities, a seductive open-air bar and restaurant that’s a destination in itself. The owners know what they’re doing. The flagship location of the Cavo Tagoo, just a hop, skip, and a jump away on the island chain, is considered one of the best hotels on Mykonos. They have a formula that works — Cycladic minimalism, to borrow their phrase, a killer cliffside location, an air of exclusivity, a preternaturally hip and youthful staff — and they’ve repeated it here. \n\nCavo Tagoo Santorini doesn’t have any standard guest rooms, only suites. And those suites deliver the wow factor. Even the most basic option is sleek and spacious, bathed in natural light and featuring a Jacuzzi and a private balcony or terrace. Note the French doors, the copper sink, the potted plants — there’s beauty in the details, which double as welcome reminders that you’re on a Mediterranean island, not somewhere in the Caribbean. Standard amenities include 43-inch flat-screen TVs and free wi-fi. Moving up the scale, the suites get downright lavish, with wide terraces and private plunge pools. The views over the caldera are equally enchanting from Ovac, the hotel’s signature restaurant, or from the daybeds at the open-all-day pool bar and lounge. You could see the sunset from anywhere on the island. But it looks even better from here.

Contemporary rooms and suites, all of which come with balconies, sit above the Mediterranean gardens with either a view of the sea or the greenery below. Six restaurants offer a variety of cuisines, from Mediterranean and traditional Cretan to Italian and Asian, and the three bars include rooftop bar The Spritzeria and Ammos, which sits just a few minutes away on the hotel’s own private shingle beach. If you’re here for some R&R then fitness training, sea view yoga sessions, and laps in the outdoor pool can be followed by downtime in the spa, which comprises an indoor pool, sauna, steam room, Jacuzzi, and soothing beauty treatments.

Firstly, the hotel has set itself away from the main attraction of Mykonos Old Town and boasts soothing sea viewz from most of its coastal whitewashed villas, which come dressed in calming neutral shades, and with the option of upgrading to extras such as a balcony, private Jacuzzi or pool. If you don’t manage to make it up in time for breakfast then restaurant Antonino’s serves brunch until lunchtime, and relaxed Italian plates by night. The highlight though is the Soma Spa “The Amuse”, which comes with an outdoor gym and yoga sessions, access to a personal trainer, and a mix of detoxing massages, CODAGE Paris facials, and more high tech treatments, which are ideal pre-party, such as LED therapy and microcurrent lifting.

content: Family-friendly Domes Novos Santorini has enough going on to keep the kids entertained, but is also stylish enough to feel like a grown-up retreat. Rooms for two feel serene with neutral creamy shades and layers of natural materials, whilst the Bungalows and Villas offer more space for traveling with children. Thessaloniki restaurant Maitr & Margarita has opened a second address on the hotel’s rooftop and serves its seasonal Greek cuisine alongside local Greek and Santorinian wines, with a particular focus on biodynamic bottles. Kids are welcome at the two outdoor pools, and can have some alone time of their own at the Kid’s Club. There’s also plenty of activities for everyone to enjoy including hiking, horseback riding, and boat trips.\n

content: It would be a stretch to call the Italian Riviera an underrated destination, but it’s a simple fact that tourism in Italy is more widely distributed than it was at the dawn of the 20th century. Grand Hotel Bristol, in Rapallo, on the Portofino Coast, is a throwback to that first golden age of travel. But this handsome Liberty-style monument is as relevant as it ever was, for guests in search of the modern equivalent of the classic grand-hotel experience.\n\nThis means professional service, top-flight comfort, a lively but discreet social life, and the full complement of in-house amenities. The views from the sea-facing rooms and suites are idyllic, topped only by the rooftop restaurant, Le Cupole. The Erre Spa Bristol is expansive, with a wide variety of offerings; it’s complemented by low-tech alternatives like the pool deck and the beach club. It’s no boutique hotel, but like the best of the grand hotels, it’s adapted to the times, reinventing itself for a new generation of travelers who prize personality and memorability above all else.

content: Doric Eco Boutique Resort & Spa is a Sicilian escape with a bit of a twist, one that’s hinted at by the first word of the name. (The remainder is straightforward, and accurate.) Doric is the architectural style displayed by the seven ruined structures of the UNESCO-listed Valley of the Temples, which stands on the outskirts of Agrigento, mere minutes away. And Doric Eco Boutique Resort & Spa, from whose rooms and suites the Temple of Juno is visible, offers stylish relaxation with this unique scene as a backdrop.\n\nThe rooms and suites are crisp and contemporary, and furnished with outdoor lounge space, featuring either plunge pools, hot tubs, or Jacuzzis. For those of a traditional bent, a 19th-century farmhouse is available as well, and sleeps up to 8. Among the resort amenities are a spa and wellness center and a gym with a view, as well as a shop selling agricultural products from the Doric farm. And the restaurant is a versatile one, serving everything from a hearty Sicilian breakfast to a dinner artfully composed from local ingredients.

content: The Florentine Renaissance painter Domenico Ghirlandaio was once the proprietor of this scenic Tuscan estate, mere minutes outside of Florence’s city center. And while plenty has changed since the days when a young Michelangelo passed through his workshop, the essential character of Dimora Ghirlandaio remains as appealing as it ever was: a Medici-style villa surrounded by picture-perfect Tuscan countryside, supplied with produce and wines from this legendary region.\n\nToday the estate’s bedrooms, divided amongst a number of villas, are equal parts antique and contemporary, retaining their historical character but furnished with up-to-date comforts. A spa, set under the brick barrel vault of the estate’s cellar, offers more intensive relaxation. And Dimora Ghirlandaio’s table, serving traditional Tuscan fare crafted from the estate’s own produce and olive oil, is open only to guests.

content: The conical structures known as trulli are among the most distinctive of Puglia’s traditional building forms, and it’s perhaps unsurprising that Leonardo Trulli Resort leans all the way in to the charm of these whitewashed stone buildings. It’s set on the outskirts of Locorotondo, an inland town midway between Bari and Brindisi, and it benefits from the pastoral tranquility of its rural setting.\n\nSurrounded by gardens and groves, the resort’s trulli are joined by a central farmhouse, which contains a few more rooms; those in the trulli themselves might be more atmospheric, but the masseria rooms are handsome in their own right, similarly whitewashed but a touch more polished. An expansive pool is the centerpiece of the daytime social life, while such diversions as yoga, padel, and massages are available. The restaurant serves classic Puglian fare crafted from ingredients grown in the resort’s own garden, and cooking classes are offered as well.

content: The most immediately arresting thing about Radio Hotel NYC has to be its location; this spot, in the corner of Washington Heights known as Little Dominican Republic, is at least 100 blocks uptown from the majority of Manhattan’s boutique hotels, which means it brings a much-needed dose of stylish hospitality to a part of the city that’s long gone without. The hotel itself is eye-catching as well, of course, its colorful structure towering above its surroundings, and its interiors decorated in an even more colorful contemporary style.\n\nRadio’s rooms are a touch more sedate than its public spaces, the bedrooms minimalist but still handsome in neutrals and warm wood, setting up a stark contrast with the bathrooms, which are clad in ultra-saturated indigo-blue subway tiles. The spaces are highly efficient thanks to their modular modern furniture, and the views over this largely low-rise district are expansive. Downstairs, Jalao NYC serves Dominican-inspired flavors in a lively space, which opens onto El Patio, a courtyard space that’s tailor-made for summer nights.

content:
Perched upon a hill right in the center of Chora, Anandes Hotel offers a best of both worlds location. It places you close enough to soak up the energy of Mykonos Town, but just far away enough to also feel like you've checked into a tranquil retreat, and one with very enviable sunset views across the whitewashed town and Aegean Sea. Minimalist rooms blend together soothing shades of greige with clean lines and tactile materials, think travertine stone, embossed pine wood, linen, and bronze highlights. All face the sea, and some come with the luxurious option of enjoying the view from a private Jacuzzi or infinity pool. 

The hotel’s main pool is the focal point, however. Not only does it come with those spectacular sea views but it’s also where you’ll find the only Greek outpost of the famed La Petite Maison (LPM). A bespoke menu created just for Anandes puts a Grecian riff on LPM’s usual French Riviera-style dishes, which are served al fresco alongside signature favorites such as the vanilla crème brûlée and Tomatini cocktail. If you’re looking for some downtime then as well as poolside lounging there’s also a gym, hammam, sauna, and a range of massages and beauty treatments.

content: Sometimes the word “castle” is open to interpretation, but Castel Hörtenberg means it in the most straightforward way. This Renaissance-era structure played a central role in the Tyrolean Rebellion of 1809; today, in quieter times, it’s been meticulously restored, uncovering centuries of history, and now stands as one of Bolzano’s most luxurious and unique lodgings.\n\nIts rooms and suites are nothing short of lavish, and while many incorporate original elements like timbered or coffered ceilings, what’s new is as new as can be — the fixtures and furnishings might look equally at home in an urban design hotel. The spa, perhaps surprisingly, feels thoroughly high-tech, almost futuristic, while the old dungeons, with their weathered stone walls and vaulted ceilings, now host Le Segrete, the hotel’s gastronomic restaurant.

content: What makes the Weisses Kreuz a rare find is not that it is still family-owned, but that it has been owned by the same family since 1871. These family ties have meant that the hotel has been carefully cared for over the years, growing from a humble village store to a local inn and now, a luxury adults-only retreat. A full facelift under the current generation has given the hotel a more modern youthful glow, with guest rooms that combine traditional Alpine wood paneling and rustic beams with minimalist furnishings and sober shades of grey.\n\nFine dining restaurant Mamesa serves up creative dishes that bring an Asian influence to the local produce, and with a view of the South Tyrolean Venosta Valley. The glass-fronted spa, which has been built from a local quartz rock, looks across the outdoor infinity pool and surrounding mountains and offers a complete wellbeing experience with an indoor pool, gym, yoga and meditation room, sauna, and treatments based around the relaxing properties of Alpine herbs.

content: In architectural terms it’s a palazzo, no doubt, but don’t let the word’s associations mislead you as to its size. The century-old Palazzo Piccinno contains a mere four rooms, and is thus just about as intimate as they come. In contrast with many pocket-sized Puglian hotels, it’s no farmhouse — it’s set in the small town of Parabita, a few miles inland from Gallipoli. Not a busy location, by any means, but one that allows a hotel to lean in to its residential aspect, depending on the town’s offerings for everything else, from restaurants to entertainment and cultural experiences.\n\nThe rooms are exquisite, each one unique, from the “cosy” Terra Rossa to the Oliveto suite, decorated in a tasteful modern style that brings out the contrast with the historical architecture. The lobby lounge makes for an intimate gathering space, its piano bench occasionally occupied by a local musician; by day, the garden swimming pool offers a respite of its own. A house-made breakfast is served daily, and after that the whole of Salento is at your feet.

content: Strictly speaking, it’s not one palace but two, a pair of neo-Baroque monuments that look across the Ringstrasse at the verdant Stadtpark. Behind its 19th-century façades, however, Almanac Palais Vienna is a collage of multiple eras and styles, from authentic antique architecture to contemporary furnishings and design, plus artworks from a number of eras, including an original Gustav Klimt. It all adds up to a remarkably self-assured luxury hotel, and a fine flagship for this Vienna-based brand.\nThe ratio of suites to rooms is an unusual 80 to 31, another hint at the hotel’s ambition; the rooms start out generously sized, while the largest suite expands to more than 2,000 square feet, and can be combined with three others, spanning an entire floor of the palace. At all levels they’re luxurious, but tastefully so, and nothing if not memorable. So is the spa, with its 14-meter indoor pool; meanwhile the restaurant, Donnersmarkt, serves a plant-forward menu. And to complement the hotel’s impressive art collection, every room key is also a pass to Belvedere 21, the contemporary art branch of Vienna’s Belvedere museum.

content:
About an hour inland from Naples and the Amalfi Coast, Campania’s wine country is booming. It’s here that you’ll find the Feudi di San Gregorio winery, an impressive piece of contemporary architecture by Hiraku Mori. And it’s also where you’ll find Borgo San Gregorio, the overnight hospitality component of the winery’s offering, split between three distinct structures distributed across the estate.

The first, Dimora Naturalia, is a 19th-century villa, beautifully restored; it’s joined by Dimora Botanica, a 20th-century addition covered in colorful graphic work by the Californian artists Fallen Fruit, as well as the Winemaker’s Suite, set alongside the Venice Biennale award-winning winery building. Though the architectural styles differ, the rooms and suites are all outfitted in a tasteful modern style, with up-to-date high-tech amenities as well as simple charms like views of the vineyards and the surrounding countryside.

The advantages of an on-site winery hardly need enumerating; it’s enough to say that wine is an integral part of the experience. As is Borgo San Gregorio’s restaurant, a venue that’s every bit as visually attractive as the winery, and does an admirable job of representing the local cuisine.

content: Finca Ca’n Beneït describes itself as a retreat rather than a hotel, and with its remote location perched up on a hill overlooking the peaks of the Serra de Tramuntana, it certainly does feel like a place to get away from it all. Just ten rooms are housed in the carefully restored 200-year-old former chapel, which sits surrounded by 70 hectares of organic gardens, orchards, and olive groves. A taste of this terroir can be found at Restaurant Mirabona, which takes a farm-to-table approach for its seasonal Mallorcan dishes; the olives are even pressed in the still working centuries-old olive mill. Guests can also enjoy relaxed al fresco dining on the poolside terrace with views of the Tramuntana. Spa time also takes place outdoors, either with one of the hotel’s treatments, a yoga class, or in the secluded open-air plunge pool.

content: Even more than most beachfront boutique hotels, Nerea takes water as its central inspiration. The name means “flow,” and the hotel stands mere yards from the waters of Tankah Bay, whose crystalline waters are supplemented by a lagoon-style swimming pool as well as a handful of plunge pools. It’s located just outside the established hotel zone, which makes for a slightly wilder setting as well as a slightly more tranquil atmosphere than the typical Tulum boutique; the city is easily reachable but pleasingly separate. The finest accommodations are the rooftop suites, the best of which directly face the water. And while the beach itself is a rocky one, a small pier serves as the launch for kayaking, stand-up paddling, and snorkeling, all included in the nightly rate.

content: In riverside Kuwana City, on the outskirts of greater Nagoya, next to the Shichiri no Watashi ferry crossing and its famous torii gate, is the historic Maruyo Hotel, built and operated by the fifth generation of a family whose lumber company once stood on this spot. Scarcely a hotel at all, the house is fully serviced, but is booked as a unit, sleeping up to four guests. Needless to say, it’s a labor of love, and displays a concern for artisanal craft that’s uncommon even among Japanese ryokan.\n\nWith a mere two bedrooms it’s clearly not meant to dominate the local hospitality scene, but to provide an experience without equal elsewhere. European and Japanese influences harmoniously coexist, and the decoration includes a number of noteworthy artworks and antiques. Meanwhile the bedrooms are complemented by a lounge, a library, and a dining room, as well as a courtyard. Breakfast is served by Maruyo’s staff, and dinner is available via room service from one of a number of highly regarded local restaurants. It’s not for high-maintenance luxury-hotel guests, perhaps, but the independent-minded traveler will find nothing else like it.

content: Whilst you can just visit the historic Chatsworth Estate as a day tripper, staying awhile at The Cavendish Hotel at Baslow allows some time for exploring more of the estate’s 30,000 plus acres, and for taking in the beauty of the Peak District. Guest rooms and suites all come with a verdant view of the estate and put a contemporary riff on its rich heritage with traditional four poster beds, stone fireplaces, and rustic beams mixed in with block colors and stripes for a fresh country chic style. To pay homage to the region’s craftsmanship, textiles have been locally woven in Derbyshire, and the glazed ceramic bedside lamps have made by a member of the Chatsworth team. \n\nSimilarly, the Gallery Restaurant celebrates the Derbyshire terroir and British tradition with a menu of elevated classics, afternoon tea, and Sunday roasts that highlight the region’s best produce, including meat and vegetables from the Chatsworth Estate. This is also where to find some of the best views of the seemingly never-ending rolling countryside, especially from the outdoor terrace, or cozy up in the 1950s-style bar. Guests are also welcome at Chatsworth Health Club, equipped with a gym, pool, and tennis and netball courts.

content: Right in the heart of El Nido town, The Funny Lion is a well-located base for exploring one of the Philippines’ most cinematic landscapes. The 50 rooms are smartly laid out, with locally sourced materials, clever lighting, and breezy balconies overlooking the pool and plenty of little comforts for downtime between adventures. The all-day restaurant takes design cues from the region’s limestone cliffs, and opens onto a terrace for al fresco dining, perhaps after an aperitif at the Poolside Bar. The locally sourced menu focuses on fresh seafood alongside a mix of Asian and Continental dishes, and on Friday nights the hotel fires up the grill for its weekly fire buffet. Other facilities include a gym and the Sea Tree Spa, where soothing treatments are based around natural local ingredients and traditional Filipino therapies.

content: You get the best of both worlds at Brij Paraiso, which sits surrounded by verdant forest whilst still being in the heart of Saligao and all of its city sights. The real highlight here though is the number of experiences on offer, which could be tastings of the local spirit Feni at the hotel, guided walks of Saligoa, or half- and full days out visiting and hiking around natural beauty spots such Khajjiar.

content: Rajasthan’s Pali district is some distance off the usual tourist trail, which suits the Brij hotel group just fine. They’ve made it their mission to bring travelers to India’s less visited corners, and in that task this 19th-century hunting lodge succeeds admirably. Brij Lakshman Sagar is made up of a mere 12 cottages, set on 32 acres of land; safe to say it never feels busy.\n\nThe style is authentic to the region, and the cottages are decorated with riotous colors, a fine complement to the austere beauty of the Rajasthan badlands. Plunge pools are universal, and the property’s shared pool is a delight. Meanwhile the activities range from hikes and safaris to local liquor and tobacco tastings; the cuisine of Rajasthan is on display at Mardana, the hotel’s slow food–inspired restaurant.

content: Like many boutique hotels now scattered across the Greek islands, Tella Terra takes a pared-back approach to design with neutral, muted shades, clean lines, minimalist interiors, and raw, unfinished textures. But it’s as much about sustainability as it is about style, with furnishings crafted by local Cretan artisans, and rooftop gardens sitting above each suite to help naturally control the temperature. Restaurant Anemoia is based around the same ethos, and serves up a seasonal menu of creative plates that put local ingredients at the forefront. In the spa, it's all about relaxing with traditional rather than high-tech methods, such as soaking in the magnesium-rich bath or booking a massage with handmade botanical oils. If you want to get moving you can also ask the team about booking a yoga session, or to point out where the nearest hiking trails are.

content: Perched on the edge of the iconic Côte de Granite Rose, Les Bassans has sat overlooking Trestignel beach since it opened in 1936 as Villa Le Sphinx, one of the first properties to be built on this stretch of Breton coastline. It’s now been renamed and restored as part of the Fontenille Collection, who have given the hotel a brand-new look inspired by the elegance of 1930s Art Deco ocean liners. The sandy shades of the 25 rooms and suites complement the blue sea views, which can be more closely observed using the in-room telescopes, and in the bathrooms, mosaics have been made from locally using the water’s marine sediments. \n\nRestaurant Les Bassans champions local produce and classic Breton dishes, from fresh seafood at its dedicated shellfish bar to favorites such as buckwheat galettes and butter-rich kouign-amann, while Bar des Bassans shakes up seaweed-infused spirits with local citrus fruits. In the spa, marine-based treatments are complemented with time in the steam room, sauna, Jacuzzi in the indoor pool with sweeping views of the Sept-Îles.

Eugene’s expansive trail network connects to the property, and the University of Oregon’s campus is just minutes away.

content: There’s no shortage of grande dame hotels in Switzerland, but not all offer the spectacular lakeside location of the Grand Hotel Villa Castagnolare. The hotel has sat on the shore of Lake Lugarno since 1880, when it was commissioned by a noble Russian family as their winter residence. They weren’t the only ones who had a keen eye for prime real estate, and just a few years later it was snapped up by a Swiss couple who decided to reopen the property as a guest house. It’s still family-owned now, although not by the same one, and has since grown into a complete luxury offering comprising three restaurant and two bars, a Clarins spa, a pool, a tennis court, and all of the outdoor Swiss excursions you could think of. The highlight is still the simple pleasure of sunbathing lakeside, which has now been made a tad more luxurious thanks to the hotel’s private summer terrace.

content:
The Potlatch Club was something of a mid-century celebrity haunt, a small and intimate escape on the island of Eleuthera where big names and other in-the-know travelers could enjoy the fruits of small-scale luxury hospitality. Its first golden age didn’t last forever — they rarely do — but in its new incarnation, under its new ownership, the Potlatch Club is poised to recapture the magic.

11 suites, cottages, and villas on 12 acres of land is, after all, a highly favorable ratio, and the atmosphere, as a result, can’t help but stay tranquil. The renovations have been uniformly stylish, preserving some of the old property’s best-loved features while updating the rest in a style that’s harmonious with the original. Kitchenettes or full kitchens are universal, but by no means necessary, as the Fig Tree restaurant serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner, and private meals are available en suite or on the beach.

There’s a spa featuring Natura Bissé products alongside a well-equipped gym, and the aquatic activities range from paddle boarding and kayaking to snorkelling, fishing, and sunset cruises. All this a mere 20-minute drive from Governor’s Harbour, with its international airport.

content: With a prominent location in Bukit Bintang, surrounded by restaurants, shops, and nightlife, WOLO Kuala Lumpur is squarely aimed at a young and vibrant clientele. The rooms are swanky enough, even the entry-level Copper rooms, compact as they are, while the high-end suites are spacious indeed. And all throughout, the look is far from minimalist — think mid-century modern with a hint of Art Deco ornament and a modern graphic sensibility. Services are minimal, but given the richness of the hotel’s surroundings, that’s no great drawback; this is more a stylish pied-à-terre than a self-contained oasis, and its guests wouldn’t have it any other way.

content:
It took more than 20 years for this boutique-hotel brand, with its beginnings in New York’s SoHo, to reach the nation’s capital: SIXTY DC makes its home not among the staid downtown luxury hotels, but on Dupont Circle, which, even if it’s not exactly D.C.’s SoHo, is certainly a neighborhood that’s as focused on nightlife and entertainment as it is on business, government or otherwise.

Behind a suitably glamorous façade you’ll find a hotel whose public spaces take playful liberties with D.C.’s signature style. Meanwhile the rooms display a more pronounced mid-century modern inspiration. Luxurious details abound, and the bathrooms are particularly swanky.

As is, in a different way, the hotel’s restaurant, Casamara, with a menu whose flavors range across Spain, France, Italy, and Greece. It’s joined by Reynold’s, a low-lit cocktail bar with a mid-century retro vibe, proof that you don’t need speakeasy styling to create an air of hushed secrecy.

content:
Though it’s less than an hour from Lisbon, Immerso feels like a properly secluded escape. It’s set on a hillside overlooking the Atlantic, just a mile from Ericeira, the first World Surfing Reserve in Europe. And while the famous breaks are a major draw, what Immerso immerses you in is not the sea, per se, but the easy life of a high-end, high-design luxury boutique hotel.

Immerso’s founders are designers themselves, and their fine taste is on display in every aspect of the hotel, from the clean and sustainable contemporary architecture to the minimalist-yet-warm interior design and the extraordinary collection of Portuguese artworks. Wraparound terraces provide direct access to the sea air, and some of the suites have deep soaking tubs with views.

For relaxation there’s a yoga deck, a pair of pools, and a spa; restaurants include a poolside bar and a pair of restaurants by an award-winning chef. There’s a beach within walking distance, and bikes are available as well — and aspiring surfers will benefit from a lesson with the Tiago Peres Surf School.

content: Set in the Palmeraïe, the vast palm grove that serves as the tranquil alternative to Marrakech’s busy medina, Palais Ronsard makes the most of its generously sized spaces. This is no oversized riad, but an expansive, extroverted sort of palace, wrapping around pools and gardens; an oasis within an oasis. The style is classic through and through, the interiors by Gil Dez complementing the palace’s grand colonial style.\n\nThis is true not just in the public spaces but in the rooms and suites as well, from the entry-level (but still palatial) Prestige Rooms on up to the Grand Pavillions, with their private gardens and pools. The Spa Ronsard marries the Moroccan hammam tradition with modern treatments and Sothys products; two restaurants, the gastronomic Jardin d’Hiver and the al fresco Le Verger du Poète, are joined by an elegant cocktail bar and the daytime Pool House.

content: Right next door to Berlin’s Wilmina Hotel, well loved for its serene warmth in spite of its history as a women’s prison, is something that shares an outlook, if not a visual aesthetic. Wilmina Apartments & Lofts occupies a modern building by Grüntuch Ernst Architects, and it’s connected to its sister via a courtyard garden. But inside you’ll find not conventional hotel rooms but loft-style apartments, decorated in a more decidedly modernist and minimalist style.\n\nNeedless to say, they’re an excellent fit for a hotel already known for its stylish good looks and its serene atmosphere. They sleep up to four, with ample space for lounging, and even for entertaining — and with full kitchens and en-suite laundry facilities, they’re completely self-sufficient. Not that they need to be; this corner of Charlottenburg is amply supplied with amenities and services. Many of them, of course, come from the neighboring Wilmina Hotel, which is home to a fine restaurant and bar, as well as a café and a bakery.

content: Lark Hospitality has plenty of experience with this sort of thing; The Madison Hotel dates back to 1929, and in its restored and renovated incarnation it’s a small, memorable, and rather luxurious boutique hotel. What’s unusual for this New England–born brand is that it’s not in the Northeast but in Oak Cliff’s Bishop Arts District, a particularly vibrant and creative corner of Dallas, Texas.\n\nIts 27 rooms vary in size and layout, keeping to the inherited floor plan; inside, they share a common design pattern, and are outfitted with modern comforts and retro furnishings. The Parlor is the hotel’s social space, and the social life spills out onto the back patio. For restaurants and bars, you’re at the mercy of the Bishop Arts District, which is abundantly supplied with them, and with plenty else to see and do besides.

content: It’s not often a hotel prides itself on education as much as hospitality, but then The Laurel Hotel & Spa does sit within one of America’s most historic college towns. In what it claims is a first of its kind, the hotel has teamed up with the Horst Schulze School of Hospitality Management at Auburn University to train the next generation of hoteliers and chefs outside of the limits of the classroom. This might not mean much for guests, but providing students with as many real-life settings as possible has resulted in an excellent choice of restaurants and bars, including the fine dining 1856, the summer terrace Walt's On The Roof, and the hotel’s own micro coffee roastery and microbrewery. There’s also an extensive spa menu complemented by a steam room, Himalayan Salt Room, and a healthy food and drinks menu so you can make a day of it.

content:
A quick drive from Mactan-Cebu Airport, this relaxed coastal retreat sits on the tip of the Punta Engaño peninsula with panoramic views of sky and sea. Dusit Thani is a long-established Thai luxury-hotel brand well known for its top-tier hospitality, and the concept travels well to the warm and welcoming Philippines.

A stylish Thai restaurant and breezy beachside bar complete the scene, all anchored by a lobby that feels more like a tropical stage set than a check-in desk. Meanwhile the infinity pool is one of the most impressive in the region.

content: Rising up on stilts along a steeply angled stretch of pine forest in South Tyrol, My Arbor is the largest treehouse hotel in the country. The Italian architect Gerhard Tauber is behind the striking design, a boxy modernist structure elevated on steel pillars resembling tree trunks, built in part from repurposed wood from the surrounding region. \n\nLuminous rooms, lined in reclaimed larch and fir with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the Dolomites and the valley below, range from quiet Nest Suites to luxurious Treetop Suites with spacious terraces and spa-like bathrooms featuring saunas and freestanding tubs. Five larger saunas await in the hotel’s lavish spa, not to mention an indoor-outdoor infinity pool, a heated open-air whirlpool, and cabana-style “cuddle nests” for cozying up in blankets by the water’s edge. Everything from early-morning cappuccino to a seven-course dinner is included, and the Plose skiing and hiking area is steps away from the front door.

content: Still family-owned, La Cheneaudière Hôtel & Spa has gone from strength to strength over the last half century. After opening in 1974 with just ten rooms, the once boutique property has since grown into a fully-fledged five-star hotel and spa, whilst retaining all the independent character that first drew guests upon its opening. Cozy rooms nod to the hotel’s countryside location in the heart of Alsace, with rich shades of blue, green and midnight black inspired by the nearby forest and Vosges mountains. The vast three-floor spa and its various pools, baths and saunas have elevated the hotel to a true R&R retreat, and classic French restaurant Le Chêne and one Michelin star at Le Feuillage are also putting it on the map for gastronomes.

content: You might not expect to find a Moroccan riad in one of Mexico’s trendiest beach towns. But in the case of Layla Tulum, a boutique hotel tucked away on one of downtown Tulum’s liveliest streets, the concept feels surprisingly natural. Stepping through its ornate arched doorway is like transporting yourself to Marrakech, the lush central courtyard framed by intricate tilework and illuminated by artisan-made lanterns. \n\nIts centerpiece is a palm tree-shaded pool lined with geometric turquoise tiles, and elegant poolside tables for two are the perfect spot for sipping mint tea. Or a margarita: you’re still in Mexico, and there’s another pool on the rooftop, this one more tropical in style with a lively mezcal bar and daybeds for lounging in the sun. Rooms are a mix of minimalist chic — poured concrete floors, floor-to-ceiling glass — and decorative Moroccan, with Moorish arches, hanging beds, and spectacular bathrooms covered from top to bottom in colorful patterned tiles. A Middle Eastern-Mexican fusion restaurant and access to a chic beach club, about a 20-minute ride away, add to the appeal.

content: Like many great hotels, Bethlen Estates Transylvania pushes the boundaries of the concept. No mere collection of rooms, it’s a reclamation project, a once-abandoned village whose centuries-old buildings have been restored by a family with deep local roots. Three of these buildings comprise the hospitality portion of the project: Depner House, the Caretaker’s House, and the Corner Barn.\n\nThe Corner Barn is divided into four bedrooms that are individually bookable; the two-bedroom Depner House and the four-bedroom Caretaker’s House are booked as units, for larger parties. The style throughout pays homage to the estate’s history, viewed through a contemporary lens; something similar might be said of the fine-dining restaurant, with its devotion to local sourcing. The local landscape and culture, meanwhile, are an essential part of the experience, from the nearby villages to the heights of the Carapathian Mountains.

content: A former garage for vintage cars might not sound like a beachside escape, until you see Le Garage. Originally built in the 1930s as a private garage for the neighboring Hôtel du Régina’s high-end guests, the building was later abandoned, then briefly taken over by street artists in 2018. Today, it is a striking 27-room boutique hotel just above Marimar Beach — and, crucially, operates under the banner of the ultra-hip Experimental group. Industrial bones remain, but the vibe is bold and bright: terrazzo floors, Art Deco curves, handwoven Ghanian lights. There is a garden pool where the gas pump once stood, and a low-key, surf-friendly pulse that feels perfectly Biarritz.

content: Set on a hillside above and overlooking the medina, Palais Faraj is no ordinary hotel — the word “palais” here is not aspirational but frankly descriptive. Built in the 19th century, during the period when Fes was Morocco’s capital, Bensouda Palace was the hub of a network of riads belonging to a prominent local family. Now, under its new name, Palais Faraj has been transformed by its new owners into one of the city’s most luxurious lodgings.\n\nWith 25 rooms and suites it’s substantially larger than a riad hotel, and though functionally up to date, the experience it offers is one of immersion in authentic Moroccan aesthetics and tradition. Meanwhile the Essencia Spa offers a classic hammam experience alongside more modern treatments, while the rooftop restaurant showcases the eclectic flavors of Fes in a garden atmosphere with a far-ranging view.

content: Glamping and cabin-style lodgings are popular around Guatapé, an Andean village famous for its spectacular landscapes. Tau House, a luxurious boutique hotel, offers something different in the region. It’s still immersed in nature — the modern wood and stone building is positioned on the shore of the turquoise Peñol-Guatapé Reservoir, with floor-to-ceiling windows revealing sweeping views of the surrounding mountains and forest — but the atmosphere is sophisticated and upscale. \n\nRooms and suites are calm and elegant, each with a private wooden deck or balcony, many of which feature open-air Jacuzzis. The best ones have high wood-beamed ceilings and water views. The airy indoor-outdoor restaurant faces the same dramatic scenery, and down by the reservoir, there’s a larger Jacuzzi and fire pit, a floating dock, and a fleet of kayaks and canoes for self-guided adventures.

content: The Art Nouveau façade of The Bristol Belgrade marks it out as one of the city’s original grand dames. Opened in 1912, this historic hotel was quite the hotspot during the Roaring Twenties and the Golden Age of the 1930s, when the likes of the Rockefellers and the British royal family came to stay. It’s now looking younger than its years (and its many nights of entertaining), thanks to a recent facelift — guest rooms have been refreshed with classic creamy shades, plush burgundy furnishings, and Art Deco-inspired accessories which nod to its heyday. The hotel’s bistro, The Dining Room, puts a contemporary twist on traditional Serbian dishes, and an elegant afternoon tea is served in The Courtyard and The Library. The complete spa experience offers a fitness room, hammam, and a range of treatments.

content: Though easily reached by ferry from Vancouver or Victoria, Salt Spring Island feels remote indeed. The artistic community of Ganges is a charming small town, and just a few minutes’ walk from the town center is Hastings House Country House Hotel, which feels for all the world like an English country-house luxury hotel transported to British Columbia’s Gulf Islands. \n\nIt stands on 22 acres of land with views over Ganges Harbour, and contains a mere 18 rooms and suites, which makes for a tranquil atmosphere. The accommodations range from substantial standard rooms to expansive suites, as well as the three-bedroom Churchill Family Cottage. Spa services are available inside a converted barn, and in the house’s restaurant a Swiss chef puts his European training to work on seasonal British Columbia ingredients.

content:
A wave of stylish new hotels have popped up in Oaxaca to accommodate the influx of travelers to one of Mexico’s most photogenic destinations. Even in a crowded cohort, Majagua Boutique Hotel stands out, in part for doing things a little differently. 

It’s housed in a restored 1950s Art Deco mansion, a rarity in the region, and is strictly adults-only, with complimentary craft cocktails served at check-in. It doesn’t hurt that the rooms are light-filled and design-forward, with modern bespoke furnishings, artisan-made textiles, and eclectic art objects from Asia and Africa. 

Elevated Oaxacan dishes are served on a treetop-framed terrace, and locally produced mezcal flows freely in the speakeasy-style bar. And, perhaps best of all, the hotel is right in the center of town, making it easy to come and go throughout the day and night.

content: In its highest incarnation, an English pub is more than a spot to grab a beer: it can also be a cozy place to spend the night. The Penny Bun, an old country inn turned into an elegant but down-to-earth boutique hotel in the North Yorkshire village of Askwith, epitomizes the concept. The focus here is on gourmet food and drink — mostly locally sourced, the name a reference to a mushroom that grows in the woods nearby — and the social experience of enjoying it by the glow of candlelight. Fittingly, the inn’s five rooms are free of screens and all other manner of distractions; calm and low-lit with sustainably built furnishings, they’re intended mostly for resting. Walking trails and bucolic rural landscapes await just outside the front door.

content: The high-elevation village of Grossarl is home to several luxurious lodges, but the Hotel Nesslerhof, considered one of the best spa hotels in the Austrian Alps, has an edge over its neighbors. The main draw is an expansive wellness area with connected indoor and outdoor pools, including a heated infinity pool overlooking the surrounding valley, a natural swimming pond, a series of saunas and steam baths, and a full spa with an open-air garden bar for post-treatment drinks. Rooms are luminous and modern with native wood paneling, crisp white linens, and private balconies with scenic views, while spacious suites come with extras like fireplaces and hot tubs. Yoga classes and guided hikes are included, and the hotel, located directly across from the Kieserlbahn ski lift, is a perfect base for hiking, skiing, and mountain biking.

content: Positioned in Pennsylvania’s Pocono Mountains, The Swiftwater makes an unforgettable first impression: soaring wood-and-stone architecture, floor-to-ceiling windows, and a setting that feels lifted from a dream. content: If you’re reading this then you’re well aware of the restorative effects of a comfortable night in a stylish suite, complete with luxe bathrooms and well-equipped kitchens. And of course the Restoration Charleston’s setting in the heart of the old downtown district places guests right in the thick of the city’s booming restauration scene. The fifteen suites deal in a contemporary urban-reclamation style, all exposed brick and original hardwood floors, adding a welcome industrial edge to Charleston’s classic elegance. Well-chosen antiques and artworks liven the spaces, and the creature comforts are legion, right down to washers, dryers and kitchens that probably rival what you’ve got at home. And while the feeling is residential, the Restoration comes with its share of services. Breakfast arrives in a picnic basket each morning, there’s an evening wine and cheese reception, and cookies and milk make an appearance a little later on. They’ll send out for groceries in case you’re planning on dining in, and the lobby is the site of a 24-hour coffee and tea service.

content: Asheville’s most famous landmark was a key inspiration for one of the city’s coolest boutique hotels. Structurally speaking, the Restoration Asheville may not seem to have much in common with the Biltmore Estate; the former is in a modern building downtown, the latter a French Renaissance–style chateau on the outskirts. But the hotel’s striking lobby, with its elegant archways and towering bookshelves, mirrors the work of the Spanish architect who designed the estate’s interiors in the 1890s, and the ethereal garden bar on the rooftop, with views over the Blue Ridge Mountains, resembles the Biltmore Conservatory. Rooms are light-filled and industrial-chic with exposed brick detailing, velvet loveseats, creative lighting, and bar carts stocked with craft spirits. Downstairs, an all-day café serves elevated southern fare, and a cozy basement bar features a bowling alley and local beers on tap.

content: With its secret garden-like pool and a speakeasy-style rosé bar, Fleur Noire Hotel offers a taste of France in Palm Springs. Indeed, its origin story began in the French countryside, where the owners purchased seeds from a roadside cart. The flowers bloomed black, providing the inspiration for this boutique hotel’s theme. Its modern, light-filled interiors feature moody floral wallpaper by designer Ellie Cashman, while Louise Jones’s larger-than-life botanical murals bloom across the hotel’s outdoor spaces, including a poolside courtyard with fire pits, Adirondack chairs, and lawn games. Casitas, bungalows, and suites have terracotta-tiled floors with woven throw rugs, midcentury-inspired bespoke furnishings, and more boldly painted flowers, and some come with kitchenettes and private patios. When the afternoon sun bears down, there’s no better place to be than beneath a fringed parasol by the pool, taking in a postcard-like view of the nearby mountains, framed by palm trees.

content: Its sisters Dunton Hot Springs and Dunton River Camp have long been regarded as some of Colorado’s finest and most singular outdoor luxury lodgings. Dunton Townhouse is more conventional, but it’s still far from ordinary. This five-bedroom guest house is set in Telluride, home of the famous film festival as well as some phenomenal skiing and summertime recreation. At this size, it’s bound to fill up far in advance — a party of ten can book the whole thing — but the well-deserved Dunton reputation is such that, if a room is available, it’s worth planning a trip around.

content: Hudson, New York’s boutique-hotel explosion continues in fine style with the Rivertown Lodge, a 1920s cinema — later a mid-century motor inn — that’s been transformed by its independent owners and the Brooklyn design firm Workstead into one of the city’s most stylish lodgings. The look is both modern and historic, incorporating Shaker influences alongside contemporary colors, and drawing on the work of craftspeople and manufacturers from Hudson and greater New York State.\n\nAt 27 rooms it’s smallish, but large enough to sustain a lively social life within its walls; the Rivertown Tavern serves dinner and drinks as well as a weekend brunch. Meanwhile the rooms and suites themselves are sparsely but thoughtfully furnished with high-quality basics, and as striking as they are, they’re equally full of warmth, helped along by local artworks and textiles. A memorable addition to the Hudson scene.

content: The upscale Atlanta district of Buckhead has long been a hotbed of hotel luxury, but Nobu Hotel Atlanta expands the scene in a new direction. What originally seemed like a one-off — an unlikely collaboration between the restaurateur Nobu Matsuhisa and the actor Robert De Niro — is now a global luxury-boutique phenomenon, whose signature cocktail of sharp, modernist-inspired design and Japanese-Peruvian cuisine is a welcome addition to the unofficial capital of the American South.\n\nInteriors are crisp and contemporary, but still warm and welcoming — hipper than the typical Atlanta luxury hotel, but never off-puttingly avant-garde. The comforts are first-rate, both in-room and out; the rooftop saltwater pool is a particular delight. A rooftop lounge serves cocktails by the poolside, while the main event is Nobu Atlanta, which imports Japanese aesthetics alongside a Japanese culinary philosophy, creating an experience that’s like nothing else in town.

content:
The Continentale hotel is a Lungarno Collection hotel, which means it's a Salvatore Ferragamo hotel. Why the chain of code names? Why not just come out and say it, Ferragamo in blinking neon, or at least radiant gold (a la Versace)? Why not at least take advantage of the opportunity to better position the brand, like Cerruti or Bulgari? 

Unlike those others, this is not a fashion concept hotel. And, to be fair, Ferragamo has been in the hotel game since 1955 — so this is clearly not an afterthought or a marketing scheme. Ferragamo, as Lungarno, is in this business with both feet (sorry), not just as some kind of co-branding experiment, but as a full-fledged business venture. Thus you will never see the Ferragamo name in your room, unless it is already attached to your footwear. 

Then why spend two paragraphs outlining the association? Because this is a hotel that is determined to win you over on its own, without coasting on a reputation earned in the fashion world. And it's a bit counter-intuitive at first, but consider this: as so many full-time hoteliers place visual flash above hospitality substance, here is a fashion hotel that prizes service over design. 

That said, the Continentale is not short on design. Architect/designer Michele Bonan went the (seemingly) safe route, with white predominating, but with unexpected accents of bubble-gum pink, intended to evoke the optimistic affluence of the Dolce Vita Fifties and Sixties. In fact you may catch La Dolce Vita playing on the monitor in the lobby. 

The service is the story, though; the look is secondary. Many hotels as attractive as this one would make do with flashy appearances and try to get away with a sneering, indifferent staff. Not so at the Continentale. Privacy and courtesy are the order of the day — this is not a place to be seen, but a place to stay, to get away. And the staff are hired, whenever possible, from outside the hospitality industry, so that they may be trained to Lungarno's exacting standards, without any bad habits to forget. 

Rooms are comfortable if not enormous (this is Florence, after all) and continue in the palette of choice, whimsical rather than minimal white. The rooftop bar La Terrazza, on the top floor overlooks the Arno River, the hills, and the city. There is no restaurant, just breakfast, but the neighboring Gallery Hotel Art (another Lungarno Collection hotel — there are five in Florence, all told) makes its restaurant available via  room service. And the White Iris Spa is a study in Florentine elegance.

It is an impressive hotel, one as stylish as any, and puts to shame the more tentative offerings of other fashion houses. In fact, staying at the Continentale, you may soon forget the Ferragamo connection altogether — and nothing would please the owners more.

content:
The opening of a new Bunkhouse hotel, by the Austin-based hotelier Liz Lambert, is news around Texas, naturally, but it’s also news beyond the borders of the erstwhile Republic — there are people, to be frank, for whom San Antonio has just become an option, now that the Hotel Havana is open. Our point isn’t to talk Texas down; the fact that there’s a network of quality small hotels spreading south and west is a testament to the sophistication of the Lone Star State.

In this town there’s no better location than the Riverwalk, and that’s where the Havana has stood, for close to a century. It was a bit of a landmark, and called for a sensitive approach for renovation — no stripping the place to the studs. The historical character of the building is still very much intact. And there’s a healthy dose of Cuban history as well — the Havana is shot through with a Hemingway-esque pre-Castro romance, especially in the cellar bar, long a notorious local nightspot.

Studio rooms start out smallish but as you move up the scale you quickly transition into borderline luxury territory, a feeling that’s only amplified by the hotel’s distinctive personality. And in the end it’s not the measurable quantities that matter so much as the character — which the Havana has in spades.

content:
The concept is a simple one, and is all the more powerful for it: 360° Boutique Hotel is named for the panoramic view made possible by its hilltop setting and its wraparound glass-walled construction. From here, fifteen minutes past the town of Selfoss, the view takes in mile after mile of wild southern Icelandic countryside, from forests and fields to distant waterways, mountains, and even, when the atmosphere cooperates, the Northern Lights.

This is a proper design hotel, and a fairly luxurious one at that, combining stylish modern furniture and a sort of plush-meets-industrial vibe with floor-to-ceiling windows. The most lavish comfort has to be the spa, with its thermal baths, fed by a mineral-rich spring a thousand feet below ground, as well as a cold-water pool and a sauna.

360°’s restaurant serves a daily three-course set menu for dinner, adapting Icelandic traditions to a modern palate; the ingredients are locally sourced, which makes for memorable flavors. You’ll want to have lunch out and about — the hotel’s location places any number of Iceland’s natural attractions close at hand, from waterfalls and glaciers to geysers, hot springs, and even the Eyjafjallajökull volcano.

content:
Prepare for a slight case of culture shock — the old Cox’s and King’s bank on the corner of Waterloo Place and Pall Mall, just around the corner from the Piccadilly Circus tube station, is now the place to go in London for a little taste of Paris. Today owned by the French Sofitel chain, it’s had a makeover courtesy of designer Pierre-Yves Rochon, and now sports a fine French brasserie.

Absent is the country-house look of the standard London luxury hotel — this one is contemporary and continental through and through. There is such a thing as five-star luxury without chintz and printed fabrics, and these rooms prove it, outfitted in smart, nearly monochrome color schemes with dark lacquered furniture against muted backgrounds, trading patterned wallpaper for black-and-white photographic prints.

Beneath the Art Deco surface you’ll find all the trappings of a state-of-the-art hotel, technological and otherwise: palatial bathrooms, flat-screen televisions, high-speed internet, spa and massage treatments and a full complement of business services. Wild Honey St James, the restaurant, has been recognized with a MICHELIN Star, and is complemented by the Bistrot Wild Honey and the swanky St James Bar.

content:
Everything you’d expect from a hotel called the Grand, including a dignified old-world exterior, a location in the heart of the historic city center, every imaginable service and amenity, and a guestbook that reads like a social register, including captains of industry, heads of state, and Mick Jagger. In its first life, around 1400 AD, this majestic building was a convent; a hundred years ago it was the town hall.

However historic the facade, the interiors are 20th-century through and through—rooms are decorated in a contemporary classic style, rather than an overtly historic one. Though you’ll find nods to the more distant past, the Jugendstil windows and Art Deco bathrooms are more representative. These are some of the largest hotel rooms in town, and probably the most luxurious, with plush fabrics and soft sofas and armchairs, as well as all the modern conveniences—must-haves like satellite TV, internet access and 24-hour room service, and such welcome details as Diptyque Bath products and full-length bathrobes.

The hotel’s apartments are suitably sprawling, and there are no fewer than three presidential suites, and three Royal Suites thrown in for good measure. A full-service spa and a fine restaurant are the norm for a hotel of this caliber, and it’s hard to imagine being disappointed by either one. And perhaps most incredibly, despite the rarefied air, you’re right in the heart of the city, with canals on either side and Dam Square and the red light district a short walk away.

content:
One of just a few hotels that uphold the tradition of the classic European grand hotel,  De L’Europe Amsterdam has been in business since 1896. And while it’s kept itself continually updated throughout the decades — most recently undergoing a thorough renovation in 2020 — the intent was never to reinvent the place, but to maintain the sense of timeless luxury that’s long been its signature. In fact a guest from a century ago might feel right at home here, once certain high-tech amenities had been adequately explained.

The rooms and suites come in a dizzying variety of plans and styles; all are rich with detail and rich with functionality, including an uncommon flexibility in connecting rooms for families and large parties. The ‘t Huys suites are particularly distinctive, each one the unique result of a collaboration with a different creative partner, all of them full of unique art and objects and uncharacteristically contemporary design.

Its position on the waters of the Amstel river makes the De L’Europe an unmistakable local landmark, as do its restaurants, which include a French brasserie, an Italian trattoria, and a Michelin-starred modern Dutch kitchen. A well-equipped spa and fitness center complete the package, and the hotel’s central location places it within easy reach of Amsterdam’s museums and the rest of the city center’s sights.

content:
It’s not quite on the level of the Stephansdom cathedral itself, but architecture buffs will want to set aside some time for the SO/ Vienna as well. Pritzker winner Jean Nouvel re-thought the typical hotel shape, changing the ho-hum rectangle into a celebration of geometry. Glass abounds, and the top-floor restaurant ceiling is clearly visible from street level, its riotous colors echoing the many-hued mosaics of the Stephansdom’s roof.

The room interiors stand up to a bit of ogling as well. Like its brethren SO properties around the world, this one is all minimalist polish, with more than a touch of distinctly Viennese elegance. Monochromatic grays play off the surrounding old city, full of steep arches and textured stone, the hotel’s clean look framing the city’s Gothic flourishes. Straight-backed chairs mimic the right-angled buildings, while the interior’s blacks and whites resemble an ever-present cup of coffee, the elixir at the heart of Viennese culture. You won’t likely forget you’re in Central Europe.   

Fine-dining restaurant, bar, meeting rooms, 24-hour room service, a just-opened spa — they’re all here, as you would expect. So are views of the Riesenrad, a giant Ferris wheel, and the Vienna Woods, where nature gently asserts its dominion over the city’s urbane sophistication.

content:
You wouldn’t know it by looking at the storybook-style mountain scenery, the adorably tiny ski cottages, or the steam trains chugging through the valley, but Andermatt was one Swiss ski resort in need of a facelift. The problem wasn’t aesthetic as much as historical: Andermatt is as pretty as any Alpine village, but it was also occupied by the military for a hundred years, complete with firing range and barracks to house 1,000 soldiers. Change isn’t easy. But sometimes an outsider — in this case, the Egyptian-born developer Samih Sawiris — is the right person to take on the challenge. The result is the sophisticated and ecologically friendly Chedi Andermatt resort, the first European hotel from the Chedi group, a luxury brand that’s well-established in Asia.
 
The resort development has doubled the size of the town — the soaring buildings dwarf the traditional chalets scattered around them. But that said, this is a resort that’s been carefully planned, employing a local staff, built using sustainable materials. Twin fireplaces lend the grand lobby a cozy atmosphere, despite the dimensions and the sleek Asian-inspired decor. 105 guest rooms and suites are strikingly outfitted in dark wood, natural stone and smooth leather, the picture windows positioned to offer expansive views of the Alps or of the village below. Many Deluxe Suites come with private balconies and outdoor fireplaces; the Furka Suite has a private kitchen and its own spa. For the rest of us, there’s the Chedi Andermatt’s state-of-the-art wellness center with an indoor swimming pool facing the mountainscape.
 
Elsewhere within the resort, The Restaurant features a towering cheese cellar and a menu of Swiss and international cuisine, while The Japanese Restaurant serves a modern omakase menu (and has earned two MICHELIN Stars). The low-lit Wine and Cigar Library has a walk-in humidor and channels the old-world charm of Andermatt. To truly appreciate that charm, though, you’ll have to hit the slopes and take in views of the village from the summit — this is some of the most exciting skiing around. After the journey down one of these legendary off-piste routes, join the beautiful people for après-ski around the indoor-outdoor fireplaces at The Bar and Living Room.

content: Marseille might not be quite the rough-and-tumble port city its reputation would have you believe, but it’s closer to that than it is to, say, Dubai. Which is bad news if you want an utterly typical skyscraper-bound five-star hotel, but good news if you’re in the market for a lodging with personality. This is a city that’s overflowing with local character, a point that’s underlined by the fact that the closest thing it’s got to a contemporary luxury hotel is the Sofitel Marseille Vieux Port. For this Sofitel is an odd duck, and if you know us, you know that’s praise, not criticism. It’s located not in some downtown district of office towers, but on a hill above the harbor, facing (if not technically within) the picturesque Old Port. It shares its building, a somewhat fortresslike mid-century structure, with its cousin the Novotel, but with a dedicated staff and a separate entrance it takes a keen eye to notice it. It goes without saying that the Sofitel’s rooms are the ones you want — clean-lined, contemporary, with a soft edge of luxury but nothing resembling gaudiness. This is the ultra-refined style for which the chain is so well loved. Les Trois Forts, the signature restaurant, is a slice of fine-dining sophistication with an elevated view; round out your dining schedule with Le Carré Bistromanie’s evolving bistro menu and custom libations at Dantès Skylounge Bar. If that all gets to be a bit much, restore yourself in perfect isolation at the spa; sometimes this bustling harbor town is best seen but not heard.

content: The very first MGallery resort on the Asian continent was VIE Hotel Bangkok. Elegant and practical, located steps from the BTS Skytrain near the downtown shopping district of Siam, it set the tone for Accor’s boutique hotel collection in Asia. The brand is French, and so is BOIFFILS Architectures, the firm behind the hotel’s modern design, consisting of two buildings — the first a boxy three-story structure, rising high on stilts with a striking infinity pool on the uppermost level, and behind it, a 26-story tower housing sleek rooms and suites with floor-to-ceiling windows. Light-filled and outfitted in calming neutrals, they’re surprisingly spacious; even the most standard room features a daybed, a generously sized workspace, and a bathroom with a separate rain shower and soaking tub. \n\nHighlights include the luxurious VIE Spa, a sushi restaurant with nightly omakase sessions, a lively piano bar, and a poolside bar serving tropical cocktails on the rooftop with views over the city’s skyline. And in an Art Deco–styled space on the 11th floor is the one-MICHELIN-Star Signature Bangkok by the French-born chef Thierry Drapeau.

content:
Number Sixteen is either the coziest boutique hotel in London, or the most luxurious bed and breakfast — we’re still not sure. The location, down a sleepy side street in South Kensington, is fairly well hidden; just a row of nineteenth-century Victorian townhouses without so much as a sign to show the way. As a member of Firmdale’s Townhouse Collection, it’s a more low-key experience than the bigger, more lively Ham Yard or Soho Hotel — Number Sixteen is notable for its intimate scale and its quiet charm.

Interiors avoid an excess of clichéd Englishness, mixing the usual antiques with modern artworks and muted contemporary colors. Rooms vary from typical London size (rather small) to surprisingly large, and all are luxuriously outfitted with big comfortable beds and top-quality linens. Some rooms come with balconies, and the views vary as well, looking over either Sumner Place or the meticulously kept gardens and conservatory around back. The conservatory is also the site of a restaurant that serves breakfast, lunch and dinner to guests and non-residents alike, and the social life spills over into the hotel’s library and drawing room, where travelers huddle round the fireplace or the honor bar, according to taste; meanwhile the Orangery serves afternoon tea in spring and summer.

Though Number Sixteen isn’t exactly nightlife central, there’s plenty to like about the geographic situation — the nearest underground station will connect you directly with Heathrow, the West End and the theater and financial districts. Within walking distance are Hyde Park, Harrods and the Knightsbridge shops, and the Natural History and Victoria & Albert museums are steps away. Swinging? Not quite, but for those who cringe at the very mention of that most tiresome word, this place is nearly perfect.

content:
There was a time when the Firmdale hotels were more or less synonymous with London. The group’s Crosby Street Hotel, however, changed all that. The setting, on the cobbled street for which it’s named, is a perfect one, both in the thick of SoHo and just removed enough from Broadway for a bit of privacy. Meanwhile the style is a fine fit for a neighborhood whose artistic residents transformed an old industrial district into an upscale residential and commercial one; behind those typically Firmdale metal-framed warehouse-style windows is the strong dose of English town-meets-country luxury that New York didn’t know it needed.

The arrival of Kit Kemp’s eclectic design eye, ultra-vivid color sense, and affinity for prints and patterns may in fact have been what put an end to the downtown Manhattan mania for minimalist, monochrome luxury-hotel spaces. The appeal runs deeper than visual panache, of course — the service is both personal and professional in the best sense, and the in-room comforts are luxurious without ever crossing over into gratuitous opulence.

Meanwhile the inviting public spaces are a large part of the draw for Crosby Street’s well-heeled, creative crowd. As in any Firmdale hotel there’s unusually eye-catching art practically everywhere you look, and a 107-seat cinema beneath the lobby makes the hotel a fixture for film-world events. And no less popular is the Crosby Bar, a versatile and capacious restaurant and bar where hotel guests and SoHo locals gather at the table or over a drink, in an atmosphere that feels both rarefied and welcoming at the same time.

About the Neighborhood:
With its cobblestone streets and cast-iron buildings, the historic district of SoHo is nothing if not distinctive. Once known for its affordable artists’ lofts made from disused manufacturing spaces, it’s now gone upscale, and is one of New York’s retail centers, with everything from mainstream chain shops to one-off boutiques. The location places you at what’s more or less the center of lower Manhattan, with everything from Union Square to the Financial District within easy reach. And it’s long been a hotbed for great boutique hotels as well, from the early days of the boutique-hotel movement right up to the present day.
