content:
Hotel history in the Americas doesn’t get much deeper than this; Hodelpa Nicolás de Ovando occupies three stone houses dating back to the year 1502, on Santo Domingo’s Calle las Damas, the oldest paved road in the New World. As you might imagine, it’s been updated over the years, and today combines colonial-era atmosphere with contemporary luxury-hotel comforts — some rooms contain original stone walls or rehabilitated timber ceilings, and all feature tile floors and other stylistic nods to the building’s heritage.

With just over a hundred rooms and suites it’s not a terribly large hotel, though the spaces feel oversized, and its courtyard-wall layout means it’s got plenty of interior space, including room for two restaurants, two bars, a swimming pool, and some shaded private nooks for lounging. You’re close to any number of restaurants and attractions in the picturesque Zona Colonial, including several museums and the seat of the Spanish Colonial government. The one thing Santo Domingo hasn’t got is the splendid beaches for which the Dominican Republic is known — but pair a visit to this historic city with a stay in Punta Cana or the Samaná Peninsula and you’ve got yourself a remarkably well-rounded island getaway.

How to get there: 
Hostal Nicolas de Ovando is located 30km (25 min) from the Santo Domingo Airport.  Transfers can be arranged for US$40 each way.

content:
Ask a Colombian about his country, and you can expect the conversation to quickly turn to the subject of Cartagena de Indias. The beautifully preserved colonial city is a jewel in Colombia’s crown, an UNESCO World Heritage site — a point of national pride, and with good reason. So if you’re going to the trouble to make the trip, you’ll want to do it right. Which, in this case, means staying in the heart of the old walled city in an elegant historic house like Hotel Casa San Agustin. 

There are three houses, in fact: the hotel’s designers have cleverly connected a trio of adjacent homes with traditional stucco exteriors. They’re centered around a peaceful courtyard, fringed with palm trees and containing a swimming pool and a unique historical feature — a 300-year-old aqueduct, a throwback to the city’s original irrigation system. And that’s not the only notable relic of the past at Casa San Agustin. The building’s stone gargoyles and traditional wood-beamed beings are original, as are the Renaissance-era oil paintings and dreamy frescoes, on display in the library. Suffice it to say, the Frette linens and artisanal Italian bath products, upstairs in each of the hotel’s 30 rooms and suites, are all brand-new. The stone floors, four-poster beds, and richly tiled bathrooms, though imagined by contemporary designers, certainly evoke the past, perhaps just a more comfortable version of it. That antique armoire is just for show: you’ll be unpacking your suitcase inside a spacious walk-in closet. 

Some guest rooms have traditional wooden balconies overlooking the street, ideal for people-watching, and the most lavish suites have private terraces with plunge pools. But some of the loveliest spots to unwind at Casa San Agustin are in the breezy indoor-outdoor public spaces, outfitted with daybeds and divans where guests can retreat during the hottest midday hours. At night, there’s Alma, the hotel’s hip bar and eatery, as well-respected for its craft cocktails as its ceviches. And, of course, the rest of the walled city of Cartagena, a magic place to be when the historic center is beautifully illuminated after dark.

content:
For over six centuries, Palazzo Gattini — overlooking the square of the majestic Cathedral — served as the residence of one of the city’s oldest and most prestigious families, as illustrated by the impressive family tree displayed inside. A careful restoration has preserved its historic charm while giving it new life: today, Palazzo Gattini is an elegant and welcoming hotel offering a type of hospitality quite different from the cave dwellings typical of the Sassi. Here, you don’t sleep in a grotto, but in an authentic noble residence where every room has a story to tell.

The suites are particularly dramatic, with vaulted ceilings and bathtubs reminiscent of Roman fountains; one of them even boasts a large private terrace with a pool.

Set aside some time to relax in the hotel’s atmospheric spa, carved into the palazzo’s ancient cisterns — a quiet, captivating space.

Dining options include the Le Bubbole restaurant, open from breakfast through dinner, a lively wine bar, and, in summer, a panoramic terrace overlooking Piazza San Pietro Caveoso and the Murgia Materana.

content:
We’ve been talking for years about how stylish a city Munich is, but even with that knowledge, Roomers Munich comes as something of a surprise. And while there’s a lot of loose talk about this being Germany’s most Mediterranean city, there really is something vaguely Italian in the way it combines luxe contemporary design and a touch of old-world elegance. To confound it all, its designers are Dutch, and its restaurant Japanese-Peruvian. Maybe “cosmopolitan” is the word we’re looking for.

In any case, the point is that Roomers Munich’s stylistic experimentation pays off. You just might forget that Berlin is supposed to be the hipster capital of Europe. The rooms are full of art, both serious and whimsical, and are stylish in a slightly retro way, and more than a little bit luxe. Some of the suites have unusual features like freestanding bathtubs in the bedrooms, and the lighting, often a bit of an Achilles heel in hotel rooms, is uniformly inventive and pleasant.

No less inspired are the public spaces, from Izakaya, the aforementioned Japanese-Peruvian restaurant, to the dark and dramatic Roomers Bar and the almost-secret RED, a whiskey bar that feels like a private club (without any speakeasy kitsch). The bottom line? There are “hip” hotels, and then there are hotels that are authentically hip — and it’s to the latter tendency that Roomers definitively belongs.

content:
It’s fitting, given Washington D.C.’s French heritage, that one of its top hotels would be a Sofitel. As the name may suggest, this fine 1920s Art Deco building is just off Lafayette Square, which is also bordered by the White House; it’s hard to imagine a more prestigious location, or one that’s more photogenically typical of the District of Columbia.

With a multilingual French-accented staff, the Sofitel’s Continental atmosphere goes deeper than just the surface. Art Deco is a style that renovates well — these rooms feel classic but not old-fashioned, and are modern where it matters, namely the duvet-topped king beds and the plasma-screen televisions, and marble bathrooms with separate tubs and showers.

In terms of luxuries, the Sofitel Lafayette Square measures up well against the District’s other high-end hotels. In this town, the fashionable crowd isn’t put off by a bit of luxury; you’ll find there’s plenty of life in the Opaline Bar & Brasserie.

content:
None of the Greek islands are particularly unsightly, but even among such gems, Corfu stands out. And equally easy on the eyes is Domes Miramare, a modernist hotel that was originally constructed in the Sixties for the Onassis family. And after a thorough yet sensitive renovation — its original mid-century style is perhaps more fashionable than ever — it’s back in business under Mariott’s Luxury Collection banner.

It’s also back to its status as one of Greece’s most prestigious hotels. Its adults-only policy goes a long way towards maintaining an atmosphere of refinement, and the new interiors, by designer Kristina Zanic, will have you reaching for your most flattering resort wear. The rooms, suites, and villas vary in size and in views but are uniformly extravagant — though they’re visually restrained, their comforts are second to none.

Domes Miramare has a rare private beach, a pair of pools with corresponding pool bars, and the Soma Spa, featuring products by Elemis and Codage Paris. A pair of restaurants, Makris and 1962, serve elevated Mediterranean and Corfiot fare under the guidance of the Michelin-starred chef Tassos Mantis. And while it won’t be easy to tear yourself away from the hotel’s comforts, the rest of Corfu awaits — you’re 20 minutes from town via the hotel’s own yacht....

content:
Tourism in Cambodia is booming, and nowhere more than in Siem Reap — this picturesque colonial city is the center of the local luxury travel industry, thanks in no small part to its proximity to Cambodia’s most famous attraction, the temple at Angkor Wat. And now one of the city’s classic hotels, the Hotel de la Paix, has been rebuilt, in a style that’s partly a modern homage to its Art Deco heritage and partly a tribute to Angkor Wat itself.

The focal point of the Park Hyatt Siem Reap is the central courtyard swimming pool and water garden, a stunning and sedate public space. The hotel’s 107 rooms ring the courtyard, and the pricier suites have garden terraces of their own, some including outdoor baths. Other rooms face outward, overlooking Siem Reap’s street life — inside, though, even these rooms are quiet and still, little Art Deco temples in black and white.

An excellent Khmer restaurant and the three-story Spa Indochine make the hotel something of a self-contained hospitality experience. It’s far from the only game in town, however — there’s plenty to see (and to eat) on the streets of the city, and of course just a few miles up the road is a certain ancient temple site you may have heard a bit about.

content:
Marrakech is famous for its pocket-sized riad houses, hidden away in the bustle of the city-center medina — but more or less the opposite approach is taken by the Fairmont Royal Palm Marrakech. With its 134 villas, suites, and rooms, it’s twenty times the size of a riad, and spread as it is over an estate that spans nearly a square mile, it offers the kind of tranquility that nothing in the old city can match.

That space includes an 18-hole golf course by the American architect Cabell Robinson, as well as a full-scale country club facility, with tennis and squash courts, a capacious spa, and a pair of swimming pools. Meanwhile another vast pool wraps around the main body of the resort, affording easy access for many of the rooms and suites.

The smallest of the accommodations spreads out over an extraordinary 72 square meters, while the suites start out in the 80s and climb well over 100. At all levels they’re faultlessly luxurious and handsomely stylish — Fairmont isn’t known for cutting-edge design experiments, but an eminently palatable attractiveness. And with four restaurants ranging from the poolside L’Olivier to the romantic Al Aïn, it’s got enough variety for a lengthy stay — though of course the city, just minutes away, offers attractions of its own.

content:
As the capital city of the United States it’s only natural that Washington D.C. should be home to a fair number of grand, historic luxury hotels. Not all of them are quite as old-world as they seem, though. The Jefferson certainly has all the opulence and historical atmosphere you’d expect from one of the original grand dames, and the fact that it’s mostly the result of a 2009 renovation is neither here nor there.

What’s important is that the Jefferson combines old-world aesthetics with boutique-era services, amenities, and personality. The rooms are classic in design, but modern in function, with iPads in every room and suite and charging stations in the desks. Premier and Deluxe rooms are lavish, and the First Lady and Presidential suites are positively opulent — the latter featuring no fewer than five balconies with extraordinary views of the city and its monuments.

To all that is added a restaurant, The Greenhouse, serving breakfast, lunch, dinner, and brunch under the hotel’s historic skylight, and Quill, an upscale cocktail bar and lounge. It’s a seemingly impossible blend, equal parts historical luxury hotel and contemporary boutique hotel, but The Jefferson carries it off.

content:
This century-old luxury hotel has seen Santa Monica change from bohemian beach town to upscale enclave; and though it’s just a few minutes’ walk from the beach itself, it’s even closer to the mall that is Downtown Santa Monica. No matter — a stay at the Fairmont Miramar Hotel & Bungalows is what you make of it, and can be as private as you want it to be. The grounds themselves are planted with lush gardens overlooking the Pacific; the hotel’s own private beach club is accessible via a shuttle.

The rooms and suites are handsome and rather understated, in typical Fairmont style, with just the right amount of local color and flavor — a surfboard on the wall would be a bit much for a hotel of the Miramar’s gravitas. The most unusual options are the bungalows mentioned in the hotel’s name — 31 colorful freestanding bungalows set amid the hotel’s gardens.

It wouldn’t be Santa Monica without a lavish spa and a gym featuring Peloton bikes and personal trainers. And the Fairmont Miramar’s food and beverage outlets range widely: from Dogtown Coffee and the Baja-style Bungalow lounge to modern Californian fare at FIG and an upscale sushi bar called Soko.

content:
Singapore’s Chinatown is one of the world’s most unique neighborhoods, and it’s here, in a row of five well-preserved 19th-century shophouses, that you’ll find an equally memorable hotel: Duxton Reserve, a spectacular French-accented boutique hotel with interiors by one of the originators of the boutique-hotel movement, the British designer and hotelier Anouska Hempel.

It’s won awards for its restoration, and inside, it’s just as impressive — decked out in elegant black, white, and gold, it’s both a retro fantasy and a thoroughly modern hospitality experience. And while it’s aesthetically unique, it draws on quite a lot of hard-earned expertise — it’s owned by the Garcha Group, a local luxury-hotel concern, and operated by Marriott under the Autograph Collection banner.

The result is something that’s playful and surprising yet thoroughly professional; the rooms and suites are theatrical and romantic, and equipped with all the modern must-haves, from British-made Naturalmat organic mattresses to Bose sound systems and Diptyque bath products. Meanwhile Duxton Reserve’s restaurant, Yellow Pot, serves modern Chinese cuisine with a healthful philosophy, and Anouska’s Bar takes its inspiration from the optimistic excesses of the ’70s and ’80s.

content:
There are plenty of other hotels for the Puerto Vallarta spring-break experience. Hotel Mousai is strictly reserved for the 18-and-over set. So while we can’t guarantee perfect silence by the poolside, your odds of achieving the peace and tranquility you’re after are significantly higher here than they’d otherwise be.

So what is it, exactly, that you’ll find in this child-free Mexican paradise? 74 sleek suites, a good Japanese restaurant, a rooftop infinity pool, an outdoor tennis court, multiple cocktail bars, a modern gym and spa, both with ocean views. Indeed, there are fabulous views from most of the rooms and terraces at Hotel Mousai: the boutique resort is perched high above the sea in Jalisco’s Garza Blanca Preserve. The decor is modern and seductive, perhaps more urban than you’d expect on the edge of a rainforest, but that’s Puerto Vallarta for you. The aesthetic works reasonably well, perhaps because there aren’t any five-year-olds climbing on the giant chess piece-shaped sculptures at the entrance or smearing their fingerprints all over the lobby’s glass and gold-plated surfaces.

There’s more glitz inside the suites, as well: gold-tiled bathtubs or plunge pools, large, glamorously illuminated mirrors, champagne on ice in silver engraved buckets. Amenities vary pretty widely across suite categories, but all feature terraces with hammocks, panoramic views over the water, ample lounge space furnished with plush jewel-toned sofas, and iPads that facilitate communication with the concierge (or your private butler, as the case may be) from the comfort of your king-sized bed. Many guests opt for the all-inclusive plan, but you can also go à la carte at the Hotel Mousai’s range of dining and drinking venues, which include a steakhouse with panoramic views of the bay, and of course, the glorious rooftop bar.

content:
Here’s an enticing formula for a hotel. An Art Deco building in Singapore’s up-and-coming Kampong Glam neighborhood, plus an illustrious French architect and interior designer. Indeed, there’s much to love about the Jacques Garcia–designed Vagabond Club. That’s partly because the sumptuous 41-room boutique looks like a lot more than a cool place to sleep. The hotel’s Whiskey Library and Jazz Club is home to a carefully curated selection of over 1,000 whiskies, and also features an Artist In Residence program, which brings writers, musicians, and visual artists from all over the globe to live, work, and socialize with guests in a Parisian salon-inspired space. 

Ambitious, yes, but no one ever made an impact, especially on a hotel scene as crowded as Singapore’s, by playing it safe. It feels like a special occasion when you step into the hotel. The interiors are dark and romantic, channeling the old-world glamour of Garcia’s native Paris — red velvet banquettes, Dalí-esque paintings, bouquets of roses — as much as the Far-East flair of the neighborhood itself. You’re close to Singapore’s Little India, and it feels like it: glittering, larger-than-life sculptures of an elephant and a rhinoceros grace the lobby, a golden baboon stares back at you as you order a martini, a magnificent golden tree soaring up past the bar, the gilded branches seemingly woven into the architecture. 

Garcia’s over-the-top aesthetic continues upstairs, though guest rooms and suites have a cozier look. He’s designed each room individually, but they’re all outfitted in dark wood and crisp white, with richly hued throw rugs, woven blankets, and hand-painted surfaces — from armoires to tea sets — warming things up. Bathrooms are laid with Italian marble; writing desks are made of heavy mahogany. Standard amenities include king-sized beds with Egyptian cotton sheets, Turkish towels. 

It’s the kind of place where you could hole up all weekend. But then you’d miss the chance to mingle with the Vagabond’s in-house painters and poets when they emerge from their ateliers to sip cocktails in the hotel’s one-of-a-kind salon. Plan your time wisely — there’s also a vast number of attractions within easy walking distance of the hotel’s front door — or just extend another day or two.

content:
Alila, the Southeast Asian boutique-hospitality powerhouse, is expanding to the west, and they’ve alighted on Indian shores — the west-coast state of Goa, to be exact. There will be some of you who need little more encouragement than just the name, and it’s not hard to see why — the place looks pretty much exactly like what you’d expect from Alila in Goa, which is to say, crisp contemporary design, glassy infinity-edge pools, locally-inspired pitched-roof architecture, and a span of flawless sand between lush plantation land and the waters of the Arabian Sea.

The rooms and suites indulge Indian coastal style with a few visual references, but underneath that the concept is very much modern luxury. Though the mode of the day is unplugging, it’s not enforced — 40-inch LCD screens and wireless internet keep you connected. Most, however, come with terraces or balconies as well as deep soaking tubs, for a more low-tech form of recreation.

As for the facilities, you’ll find everything you expect from a boutique luxury resort, including pools, a spa, and separate family-friendly areas to keep the kids contained. This being India, there’s even pitch for playing cricket, the ideal holiday sport — not only is it more social than tennis, but it moves, most of the time, at a vacationer’s pace.

content:
An offshoot of the adjacent Beau-Rivage Palace, a hotel we’ve described in these pages as “one of the few remaining for the modern aristocrat,” the Angleterre isn’t exactly slumming it either. From the outside, it looks like a classic Swiss resort, all manicured gardens and stone façades, set at the edge of Lake Geneva with the snowcapped Alps above, but inside it’s something else entirely, as thoroughly contemporary as the palace next door is classic. 

Not that it lacks for history, nor for atmosphere. Hotel Angleterre counts one Lord Byron as a one-time resident. (Fleeing scandal in England, he arrived in 1816 in a replica of Napoleon’s coach, with a peacock and a monkey among his entourage.) Strolling the gardens or taking a meal on the breezy terrace of the restaurant, watching antique ferries cruise across the lake, it’s easy enough to appreciate the place’s original appeal. It’s just that now, after a day exploring the towns around the edges of the water or plodding through the nearby vineyards, you can retire to a room with a pristine bathroom, a fine glowing screen, wi-fi and all the rest. 

Hotel Angleterre is sufficiently high-functioning, in fact, that it’s a top local choice for business travelers and conference attendees. (One of the converted mansions is dedicated exclusively to private functions.) If you’re in Lausanne on business, it’s a fine option, while guests here for leisure are in good historic company, and perfectly well taken care of — though if you and your animal entourage plan to make an entrance like Byron in a horse-drawn coach, these days they may be more understanding at the old-school place next door.

content: If you’re skeptical of a hotel that calls itself an “urban village,” try to reserve your judgment for just a moment. It’s true that the hoteliers behind the Rosewood Beijing get a bit high-concept at times — what we’d call a concierge, the hotel refers to as “Rosewood curators.” But look past the branding exercises and you’ll find an exceedingly professional, exceptionally well-executed hotel, and one that’s packed with local character. The hotel is designed around two main elements: exposure to China’s rich cultural heritage, and plush apartment-style accommodations. The striking entryway and lobby are filled with paintings inspired by ancient Chinese art forms, from gongbi brush works to shui-mo ink washes, and each of the spacious guest rooms features an original piece of cloisonné metalwork. Not that the pleasures are all quite so high-minded. Each of the spacious residential-style rooms comes with floor-to-ceiling windows looking out over the city skyline, large walk-in closets, and even TV screens built into the bathroom mirrors. At every level, the amenities are plentiful — 600-thread-count linens by Frette, Blu-ray players, Sony Sound Bar speaker systems and bespoke bath products by the Florentine perfumer Lorenzo Villoresi. If the guest rooms don’t already sound restful enough, you can always recharge inside the Sense spa. Deluxe spa suites come with private balconies, separate living areas and access to the hotel’s executive lounge, ideal for afternoon tea or evening cocktails. For everyone else, there’s the yoga room, fitness center and sixth-floor swimming pool — surrounded, of course, by more art, specifically works by leading Chinese sculptors. All this and it’s right in the heart of the business-centric Chaoyang District — meaning that, between meetings, the hotel itself is pretty much your best bet for a contemplative and art-centric cultural experience.

content:
To say that Canyon Ranch Tucson is an all-inclusive spa and wellness resort is a bit like saying the Beatles were a rock band from Liverpool — it’s certainly accurate, but it leaves out both of their central roles in defining their genres, as well as the significance of their continued influence on the form. Founder Mel Zuckerman opened Canyon Ranch Tucson at the tail end of the seventies, seeking to replace the somewhat punitive approach of the health spas of the day with something more positive, more empowering, and more spiritually transformative.

Long story short, it worked, and for decades travelers have made the pilgrimage to this site, a few minutes’ drive outside of Tucson, to chill out, to work out, to dry out, or some combination of the three. While the serious health focus means there’s no alcohol served here, and the cooking is uniformly healthful, mealtimes are a source of pleasure all the same. So are the accommodations, a selection of rooms and suites in a soothing modern style, equipped with luxuries that are substantial but always tasteful. If it were an ordinary hotel, Canyon Ranch would be a very fine one, secluded as it is on 150 acres of spectacular Sonoran desert landscape, with every creature comfort anticipated and effortlessly provided.

But of course it’s no ordinary hotel; this is an experience that demands an active approach from its guests, even if the activity is limited to selecting spa treatments and other forms of relaxation. Canyon Ranch’s advisors reach out ahead of your stay to make a plan that’s consistent with your goals, and to schedule your activities, whether they’re fitness classes, medical assessments, coaching sessions, art lessons, or spiritual wellness experiences. In between your pre-booked activities you’ll find there’s always something on, from a hike you’ll want to join to a class you’ll want to drop in on. 

By nightfall you’ll have had a full day but a thoroughly relaxing one all the same. And, ideally, by the end of your stay you’ll have at least begun down the path of one tranformation or another, whether it’s a renewed dedication to health, a new outlook on spiritual or mental wellness, or a whole new direction for the path of your life. How many hotels can honestly say that?

Please note: Canyon Ranch Tucson requires a minimum stay of two nights.

content:
If you’re familiar with the Swiss Alps, you don’t need to read any further: the Gstaad Palace name tells you more or less all you need to know. Gstaad is one of the most exclusive ski areas in the world, and this landmark hotel is a proper palace, a historic one that recently celebrated its 110th birthday. Let your imagination run wild. Whatever you’re picturing is probably about right. Truffle fondue, charming wood-vaulted ceilings and glittering chandeliers, champagne by the fireside, fondue at La Fromagerie, dressing for dinner at Le Grand. 

Gstaad Palace is, in short, a glamorous winter fantasy come to life. Lit up at night, looming high above the hamlet from its hilltop perch, the turreted structure looks like a castle. The interior is much as it was in the palace’s early days, though fresh renovations, some timed with the hotel’s centennial celebration, have added or improved upon a range of amenities geared to the modern jet-setter, including a sprawling, state-of-the-art spa with hammam and a massive granite wall cut from fifty tons of locally sourced rock. Of course, there are pros and cons to updating. Guest rooms and suites, though perfectly elegant and cozy, have a somewhat blander look than they once did — think beige and pale blue, plaid duvets, botanical prints. Superior rooms and suites offer more classic luxuries, with refined seating areas, beautifully tiled steam baths, and, of course, magnificent views. 

At the end of the day, it’s the old-fashioned grandeur of the Gstaad Palace, the historical mystique, that make it so special. Le Grand Restaurant and La Grande Terrasse have been recently renewed, and are looking as elegant as ever. What makes Gstaad Palace feel doubly rare and special is the fact that it’s only open for select months of the year, through the heart of winter’s ski season and in the blooming height of summer. This feels about right for a place of this pedigree: in past days, as in the present, the most well-heeled travelers don’t travel on the off-season.

How to get there: Gstaad Palace is located approximately 81 km by car from Bern Airport via A6 and Route 11. Alternatively, Geneva International Airport is approximately 156 km away by car via A1, A9, and A12.

content:
According to many New England luxury travelers, this is Cape Cod’s top hotel, and when upscale Bostonians hit out for the coast, as often as not this is where they do it. Chatham, on the quaint little elbow of the Cape, is a classic, unspoiled seaside town, and the Wequassett Resort and Golf Club is the rambling little village resort we always dreamed we’d find there.

A classic 18th-century colonial house makes up the heart of the place, and the cottages cluster around, some with views of the lawn and gardens, others overlooking Pleasant Bay. The accommodations range from cozy little queen rooms in the cottages that range across the 20-acre grounds to a new batch of luxury rooms, with balconies and sweeping views of the waters of the bay. Even the most basic are decidedly high-end, however, with Molton Brown bath products and plush terry robes, and the timeless New England style provides a much-needed break from modernity.

Wequassett’s culinary offerings ensure that you don’t have to venture out on the town if you don’t want to; there’s a restaurant that’s much in demand, a fine casual bar and grill, and a poolside barbecue that might add a dimension to your idea of New England cuisine. Despite its name, Wequassett doesn’t have its own golf club; what it does offer is guest access to the members-only Cape Cod National Golf Club, right next door, as well as close proximity to two public courses. Tennis courts are available on-site, there’s a resident pro to tune up your game, and the nautical setting on Pleasant Bay makes for fine swimming, windsurfing and sailing.

How to get there:

Directions from Hyannis Airport (19 miles):
When leaving the airport, enter the rotary following signs for Route 28 South. Follow Route 28 to your first set of lights and turn left onto Willow Street. Follow Willow street to Route 6 heading East towards Provincetown. Stay on Route 6 to exit 11. Turn left at the end of the ramp; go 25 yards to Pleasant Bay Road (your first left). Proceed to the second stop sign; the entrance to Wequassett will be directly ahead.

content:
Austin, now that it’s booming, is home to a hotel from just about every boutique and luxury chain under the sun. But the Texas-based ZaZa group took its time. Long a familiar name in Dallas and Houston, ZaZa hits the state’s capital city at a moment when it takes more than just a quirky design sense to stand out. Fortunately for everyone involved, Hotel ZaZa Austin is very much up to the task.

Of course, a quirky design sense is very much part of the package; Hotel ZaZa Austin is an eclectic blend of eras and influences, from bohemian to modernist, from retro to contemporary. The one conspicuous absence is any Lone Star kitsch. Rooms are not just stylish but substantial as well, with plentiful lounge and work space and marble bathrooms stocked with Bigelow bath products.

On the ground floor, ZaSpa is open to guests and locals alike, while Perfect Strangers, the lobby-level café, is the spot for breakfast and hand-pulled espresso drinks. Group Therapy, meanwhile, is the hotel’s restaurant, set on the seventh-floor rooftop, right next to the pool deck with its stylish rows of loungers — which, in classic Austin style, features live music a couple of nights a week.

content:
The sequel to the original Tucson, Arizona installment, Canyon Ranch Lenox necessarily differs when it comes to local details. The setting, obviously, is not the Sonoran desert but the Berkshires of western Massachusetts; guests arrive to an opulent 19th-century mansion, formerly a Jesuit seminary. And the clientele, though global, is more likely to hail from New York and Boston than Los Angeles and Phoenix.

Its concept, however, is the same: an all-inclusive spa resort that goes deeper than you might expect, in just about every dimension. The spa itself spans some 100,000 square feet, and is almost comically well-equipped. The health and fitness offerings are legion, and are supplemented by care that ventures into medical territory. And the mental and spiritual wellness offerings are led by people who are not merely kind and thoughtful, but possess advanced degrees in subjects like psychology and theology.

All of this hints at what it is about Canyon Ranch that rewards a little bit of advance planning. There’s rather more to it than finding an available room and popping in for a night or two. This is an extremely high-touch experience, and demands much of its staff, as well as some investment in time and energy from its guests. You’ll choose a pathway, or a theme for your stay, from a health intervention to a lifestyle reset or even a commitment to build resilience or reconnect with joy. And you’ll work with a Canyon Ranch advisor to plan your core activities in advance of your arrival.

And once you’re on site, you’ll be kept as busy as you want to be. Along with your scheduled sessions you’ll find plenty of drop-in classes and activities, from morning yoga to hiking, tennis, tai chi, qi gong, and even 12-step recovery meetings. Some guests prefer a bit more down time, but even a full schedule in this environment is anything but stressful. There’s no alcohol served here, and the cooking is uniformly health-conscious — that said, it’s also delicious, and mealtimes are a highlight of the experience. Any hotel with a wellness focus is capable of nudging its guests into a change of pace, but few take it anywhere this far — Canyon Ranch is proof that you get out what you’re willing to put in.

content:
It may still be the most charmingly low-key of Colorado’s major ski resort towns, but that doesn’t mean Telluride hasn’t gone upscale; it’s just that it’s done it in a charmingly low-key way. Lumière with Inspirato combines boutique-hotel good looks with distinctly residential comforts, and its position in the enclave of Mountain Village affords a measure of seclusion from the town, as well as ski-in/ski-out access to the famous slopes.

It’s a modern construction, and the room footprints are suitably large — even the queen and king rooms come with kitchenettes and luxe oversized bathrooms, and the suites, residences and penthouses very quickly verge on presidential-suite territory. At the high end you’ll have a working fireplace, a Wolf gas range, a Sub-Zero refrigerator, and more lounge space than you’ll know what to do with.

And even when the Lumière is at its most hotel-like, it’s still possessed of a friendly, homey flavor. There’s an old-fashioned concierge desk and Bijou for an après-ski drink or an organic, seasonal bite, but it’s all delivered with an unpretentious light touch. Relaxation, not ostentation, is the name of the game: the terrace’s hot and cold pools and the hotel’s massage and yoga offerings are simply a balm for sore muscles.

How to get there: Located in Mountain Village, Lumiere is just 6.5 miles from Telluride Regional Airport and 70 miles from Montrose Airport.

content:
If, as we contend, Shanghai is going to be the future’s unofficial capital, it’s going to need more extraordinary hotels of every description — not just modern-design boutique hotels but classic grand hotels as well. The Peninsula Shanghai, on that score, certainly qualifies as a rather large step in the right direction; with its soaring, marble-clad Art Deco lobby (and its location on the Bund, a location where classic architecture is the rule) it already feels like it’s been here more or less forever.

In the rooms, as well, it’s clear that this is the sort of luxury hotel that worries about intangibles like atmosphere just as much as it does about thread count or square footage. They’re a microcosm of this hotel’s century-spanning appeal, historical style meeting modern construction and technology (from jetted tubs to iPod docks), resulting in some of Shanghai’s most desirable accommodations.

It’s old-meets-new elsewhere as well, from the Peninsula’s restored 1934 Rolls-Royce Phantom to its spa, where 21st-century treatments are administered in an environment that’s a dead ringer for 1920s Paris. The restaurants, on opening, immediately moved into Shanghai’s top tier, as expected — from top to bottom, this Peninsula perfectly illustrates the concept of the instant classic.

content: Set out to find a luxury hotel on a Greek island and you know more or less what you’re getting into: whitewashed architecture, visual simplicity, endless Aegean views. What sets a hotel like Cosme apart isn’t its direction, but its magnitude. It’s set in the village of Naoussa, on the northern coast of Paros, an island that’s rather more tranquil than some of its neighbors, though hardly less desirable. And in its 40 suites you’ll find a thoughtful, tasteful approach to luxury, and a style that’s memorable and modern while remaining unobtrusive — as always, the setting and the seascapes are the main attraction.\n\nMany of the suites come with plunge pools, and all of them feature custom-designed contemporary furniture by the Spanish designer Jaime Hayon and luxe bathrooms stocked with Korres products — in fact the Elios spa, named for the Greek sun god, is a partnership with Korres, the Greek skincare brand. Meanwhile the public spaces are filled with works by modern Greek artists, and the restaurant, headed by the Greek chef Yiannis Kioroglou, is similarly devoted to the local tradition — and among the offerings are classes in the art of Medite-grecian cooking.

content:
Whether they knew it or not, the Mondrian brand was always destined to turn up in Ibiza, a destination that’s equally dedicated to glamorous nightlife and idyllic beach life. This gleaming terraced structure stands proudly over the bay at Cala Llonga, its exterior an almost impossibly pure shade of white. And inside, the brand’s signature minimalist-chic look softens to off-white and cream, but retains its heavenly, almost unearthly atmosphere.

In the rooms and suites, a warmer, more organic mood predominates; though the overall impression is still unfailingly glam, you’ll find textures that feel hand-crafted, reminiscent of this island’s rustic side. They can get as sunny as you like, and, more importantly, they can also block out the midday Mediterranean sun. The best ones, as you might imagine, are those furnished with views of the beach and the bay.

That beach is just steps away, on the other side of a pair of outdoor oceanfront swimming pools. And the Mondrian comes equipped with several distinct dining and drinking venues, ranging from a beachside bar with a DJ booth to a seafood-focused Mexican restaurant and Sun & Moon, serving light bites and cocktails from noon to midnight.

content:
Its close proximity to Capri, Sorrento, and the Amalfi Coast, as well as a certain slightly edgy reputation, means that Naples, compared to many other major Italian cities, is rather underserved in the boutique-hotel department. That’s not to say there’s nothing worth noting, of course — it just means a hotel like Caruso Place Boutique Wellness & Suites takes on an outsized importance. Fortunately for all involved, it’s a fine example of the luxury boutique genre; housed in a 16th-century palace, with a privileged location across from the Galleria Umberto I, Caruso Place is the kind of plush, stylish, pint-sized hotel at which Italian hoteliers excel.

The cozy Classic and Superior rooms are contemporary in style, with all the modern basics, plus impressive bathrooms equipped with oversized color-therapy showers. Meanwhile the suites are expansive, and a little more lavish in their appointments, some with balconies overlooking the Teatro San Carlo or the Galleria, while the Wellness Suites add jacuzzis, either in the bathroom or, in the case of the Berio suite, in the corner of the bedroom under its distinctive arched ceilings.

As for the wellness offerings, they stop just short of what you’d consider a full-service spa, but they’re more than adequate for a hotel of Caruso’s small size. And while there’s no restaurant per se — just a fairly lavish breakfast, plus appetizers, pastries, and wine tasting later in the day — Naples is not the sort of city where any visitor need worry about going hungry, and Caruso’s staff has all the connections you need.

content: It’s perhaps not surprising in this ever more connected world that the Turkish-based Rixos luxury-hotel group should count the Dalmatian coast of Croatia among its most successful venues. Rixos Premium Dubrovnik stands on a cliffside overlooking the sea, a mile from the walled medieval old town, its rooms and suites cascading down the terraced slope like benches in a Roman theatre. It’s an impressive site, to be sure, and makes for impressive views — against such a backdrop, the hotel itself could get away with shirking some of its responsibilities, and it’s to its great credit that it doesn’t.\n\nThe rooms and suites are highly polished but also tasteful, in soft colors against white backdrops and hardwood floors. The best ones look out to sea from private balconies, but all of them, of course, have access to jaw-dropping views from the hotel’s public spaces, including its sprawling pool deck and its glass-walled Mediterranean restaurant, the aptly named Turquoise. There’s also a substantial spa and fitness center, and ladders leading down to the sea; additional restaurants include Libertas, a seafood restaurant on a terrace, and Uma Teppanyaki, for Japanese fare with a far-ranging view.

content: The SLS Baha Mar resort complex is a hotel envisioning itself as a tropical sanctuary for connoisseurs of the best global luxury has to offer. Comprised of 297 rooms in a gleaming, coral-hued tower whose wavelike roof lends an uncanny lightness, the SLS Baha Mar overlooks not only two swimming pools, resplendent in sunshine, but over 3,000 feet of uninterrupted white-sand beachfront. Rooms are furnished in classic neutrals with highlights of blue and green that nod to the seafront outside, and some come with enviable balconies for taking in the view. Restaurants include Carna, overseen by Italian butcher Dario Cecchini, and the Californian restaurant 25° North which sits beachfront within the Baha Bay Beach Club. There’s no shortage of places to stop, lounge, and sip, either; both Bungalow and Skybar enjoy poolside and beachside atmospheres, while the Bond nightclub promises a night out like nothing back home. \n

content:
The distinctive high-rise tower that contains the Sofitel Mexico City Reforma stretches some 40 floors above the city, granting its occupants spectacular views of the Paseo de la Reforma and the rest of this sprawling city. In typical Sofitel style it’s unabashed about its Parisian influence, though it’s no carbon copy of the City of Light — it’s lovingly tailored to its Mexico City setting, and features roughly equal parts New World vigor and Old World glamour.

In the rooms, the focus is the extraordinary vista from the floor-to-ceiling windows; the décor is modernist-inspired but warm and organic, with lively patterned carpets to raise the energy level. The comforts themselves are high-end, with the French accent extending to the L’Occitane bath products, while automated curtains and Nespresso machines strike a modern note.

L’Occitane is also the partner for the hotel’s spa, which draws much of its inspiration from the city’s pre-Hispanic tradition. And a partnership between Paris and Mexico City is all but guaranteed to bear fruit in the restaurants, which include Balta, the Mediterranean-Mexican wood-fired kitchen, and a stunning French-meets-Mexican rooftop restaurant and bar.

content:
Though we hesitate to wade into any regional rivalries, we’re comfortable declaring that Toronto is Canada’s biggest, busiest, most cosmopolitan city. It’s only fitting, then, that its top-end luxury hotels should be absolutely first-rate. Among the usual suspects when it comes to this sort of thing is Ritz-Carlton, but the Ritz-Carlton Toronto is an unusual one — the design is rather more modern than you’ll find in more typical examples of this venerable luxury brand, while the top-flight service and faultless comforts you expect are all exactly as they ought to be.

Rooms and suites are lavish yet tasteful, in keeping with the brand’s reputation, with impressive views through full-length windows and a mix of traditional and modern luxuries, from marble bathrooms to in-mirror HD televisions. There’s a Clarins spa that’s the equal of any in town, while both TOCA (the fine-dining Italian restaurant) and the DEQ Terrace & Lounge are hot tickets for locals and hotel guests alike.

The location, right at the heart of Toronto’s city center, places its guests scant minutes from the convention center and some of the city’s finest cultural destinations, while the local hockey, basketball, and baseball teams play within easy walking distance as well. This is good news for tourists, of course, but it’s also good business — a hotel like the Ritz-Carlton draws a fair proportion of its clientele from the performance and athletics worlds, which means you never know who you’ll spot in the lobby....

content: Mountain View may be most famous right now as the location for Google’s headquarters, and in fact the Ameswell Hotel is part of a mixed-use development that contains one of Google’s newest offices. And with access to neighbors Apple, Facebook, and the NASA Ames Research Center, the Ameswell caters to an audience with a taste for novelty and innovation. This means boutique-hotel good looks, classic luxury-hotel comforts, and an array of meetings and events space that’s suited for everything from a tech conference to a spectacular outdoor wedding.\n\nRooms feature plentiful sunlight, luxe Sealy mattresses dressed in Rivolta linens, and subtle high-tech infrastructure including ultra-fast wi-fi and medical-grade air filtration. Meanwhile the common spaces are made to be just as comfortable, from the hotel’s library to its pool, its state-of-the-art spa and fitness center, and its lawn, which opens onto the Stevens Creek Trail, a favorite for bikers and hikers. Roger, the flagship indoor/outdoor bar and restaurant, serves seasonal Californian cuisine, while the Flyby Café keeps guests optimally caffeinated, and the Airstream Bar serves drinks and light fare within sight of the pool, the lawn, and the firepits.

content:
Given Houston’s status as America’s fourth-largest city, it’s perhaps a bit surprising that there isn’t a boutique-hotel scene quite on the scale of those in places like New York, Los Angeles, or Chicago. But it’s certainly not for lack of effort on the part of Texas’s small but faithful contingent of boutique hoteliers. Hotel ZaZa Memorial City is the sequel to the decade-old Museum District installment, and brings the brand’s familiar high-end, high-style experience to the west side of Houston.

Where the Museum District edition is ornate and almost Baroque, the Memorial City version is clean-lined and bright, inspired in part by the mid-century modernism of Palm Springs. There’s art everywhere, including David Hockney prints in the corridors, and the suites stop at nothing to establish a memorable visual identity — the Magnificent Seven suites are all wildly different, as are the four Concept Suites.

The idea is luxury-hotel plushness with boutique-hotel personality, and on that score they deliver. Not only are the in-room comforts first-rate, but the ZaSpa offers a full range of treatments, and the Tipping Point Restaurant & Terrace is among the neighborhood’s finest tables. You’re also close by to some of Houston’s best shopping, and if you’re here on business, you might be able to work from home — the ZaZa features some 11,000 square feet of meeting space.

content:
Malabar House is an example of a hotel concept that’s vanishingly rare in South India, even as it thrives in Sri Lanka — the colonial-house luxury boutique hotel. This one is a Dutch-era mansion, located in the historic Fort Cochin district of the Keralan city of Kochi, and it’s been running as a hotel for over ten years now under the watchful eye of a European couple and a dedicated staff of locals.

It’s not hard to imagine how a house like this could have been spoiled by trendy minimalist interiors, in some misguided pursuit of hipness. Instead there’s plenty of classic ambience about the place, the rooms liberally furnished with antiques and artworks, with only the minimally necessary modern intrusions — air conditioning, television, that sort of thing.

There’s really nothing about the Malabar House that’s not endlessly charming, from the courtyard and pool to the Malabar Junction restaurant to the private balconies and roof gardens of the better suites. Just out front is a lovely little park, the beach and the picturesque Chinese fish nets not far beyond, and the enormous antique market, in a place that’s really honestly called Jewtown, is a pleasant walk from the hotel’s front door.

content:
The main focus of the Sofitel Frankfurt Opera is clearly stated in the name; it’s set not just in the Opera District, but right on the Opernplatz itself, just across the road from the newly rebuilt Alte Oper. But this is a fantastic location for business travelers as well — it’s also the central business district, with the historic city center a short walk in the other direction. Local color, then, is a given; this Sofitel, like all its siblings, emphasizes its Frenchness, both in style and in atmosphere.

The rooms are subtly Parisian in aspect, though in typical Sofitel style it’s a tasteful resemblance, nothing the least bit kitschy; jewel tones against rich earth tones, with just a hint of Art Deco. Functionally, these brand-new rooms and suites are state-of-the-art, with Illy espresso machines, Bose sound systems, and Lanvin products in the exquisitely comfortable bathrooms.

A French spa in a German hotel might just be the perfect combination, as glamorous extravagance meets serious wellness. Lili’s, the cocktail bar, serves Le Goûter coffee and French pastries, and does double duty as a performance venue. And Restaurant Schönemann combines German and French flavors alongside a wine list representing the best of both countries.

content:
Walking down the quiet, tree-shaded streets of San Isidro, it’s hard to believe you’re just a quick train ride away from the noisy and traffic-congested center of Buenos Aires. For decades this leafy residential suburb has been synonymous with porteño wealth and exclusivity — it’s the kind of place where handsome polo players hang out at sidewalk cafes and socialites walk their dogs by the river, and San Isidro Plaza Hotel perfectly reflects the quiet refinement of the neighborhood. 

The owners, in a nod to the locals’ predilections, have aimed to create the atmosphere of a private club. So the hotel has none of the old-fashioned glamour or cutting-edge design of the Buenos Aires hotels; in fact, from the outside, it looks like a contemporary apartment building. Inside, the design is minimalist, with high ceilings, glossy hardwood floors, smooth black leather sofas, oversized white ottomans, polished granite countertops and chrome fixtures. Guest rooms, suites and studios all feature flat-screen LCD televisions, free wi-fi, and views — some face the steeple of the nearby cathedral, others have private balconies where guests can take their morning coffee.

There’s a small swimming pool and a fully stocked ‘health club’ to help guests keep up, or make some kind of attempt at keeping up, with the locals’ high standards of beauty and physical fitness. Forgoing that, there’s also a fashionable bistro downstairs serving dressed-up versions of Argentinian classics like steak and chorizo — not to mention the myriad fine dining institutions of San Isidro itself, all within walking distance of the hotel.

content:
A few miles to the south of downtown Denver and the stadium district, in the upscale country club–adjacent enclave of Cherry Creek North, the Clayton Hotel & Members Club aims to thread a very particular needle: to be desirable yet inclusive, chic yet unstuffy, to be a private members’ club without universally drawing from among the already privileged. 

Guests find themselves members of a surprisingly diverse society — one that draws heavily from Denver’s blossoming creative communities — and are set up in impressively stylish and unpretentious luxury digs as well; designers AvroKO have combined mid-century modernist style with subtle visual references to Colorado’s landscape and history. The result is as plush as any downtown luxury hotel, and a good deal more memorable.

Meanwhile the Clayton’s restaurants dramatically depart from the ranch-focused cuisine that’s ubiquitous in Colorado. Both Kinis and Cretans take their inspiration from Greece as well as the greater Mediterranean, while the rooftop restaurant serves lighter fare by the poolside — and Chez Rock, the cocktail bar, is a Moroccan-accented nightspot featuring live DJs and unusual interpretations of classic cocktails. It’s a side of Denver you’ll be glad you went a little bit out of your way to see.

content:
There’s very little of the typical hotel experience about Hotel Valdepalacios, an hour and a half outside Madrid. Take the setting: the villa nestles among fields and orchards, as far as the digital camera’s eye can see. Nicely proportioned nooks, white wash, and soft light abound. But “villa” doesn’t really cover it. “Deluxe country estate” works better. One room might feature a bed festooned with snowy drapery and a window accented by flowery curtains, while another has a decidedly less dainty vibe, thanks to the bold striped fabrics and a private entrance off the courtyard. Some are on the ground floor, while some are in the attic (offering better views of the palm trees, meadows, and distant mountains). In the center, a nod to the area’s long-ago Moorish past, a tiered fountain, gurgling and burbling its message of relaxation to all.    

Despite the secluded, old-world setting, the kitchen skews slightly modern, with updated takes on traditional Catalan specialties. Veggies, fruits, and eggs come from on-site producers. If you’re going out to roam for the day, ask for a picnic to take with. Consider asking too for use of the hotel’s horse and cart. Or for a rowboat to ply the lake. Or a sangria on ice to sip as you sit by the pool. Alas, you’ll probably have to bring your own walking stick and sturdy shoes to roam the hundreds of hectares that constitute the grounds. Luckily you don’t have to bring anything but you to the spa, where treatments range from standard beauty pick-me-ups to hydrotherapy.  


How to get there:
From Madrid, Valdepalacios Hotel Gourmand is a one and a half hour drive, located 9 kms from Exit 148 of the A-5 national main road, on the Oropesa-Puente del Arzobispo road.

content:
For too long luxury travelers to Morocco have confined themselves to a small handful of cities. But less than an hour up the Atlantic coast from Agadir is Taghazout, a fishing village turned holiday destination, and the seaside Fairmont Taghazout Bay, a luxe and stylish village-like resort whose sandy-colored modern structures circle a wandering lagoon-style swimming pool, and whose back side looks straight out into the Atlantic over a vast expanse of beach. 

The rooms, suites, and villas are handsome and thoroughly well-equipped; even the smallest span some 50 square meters, while the largest villa comes with four bedrooms and an infinity pool. The interiors mix quietly stylish modern luxury with local Moroccan elements; the overall impression is remarkably open and sunny, especially in comparison with Morocco’s famously private riad hotels.

It may go without saying that where there’s a Fairmont hotel there’s an expansive spa and wellness complex. Meanwhile, close by, a Kyle Phillips-designed course welcomes golfers, while the hotel’s Surf Club caters to guests in search of waterborne adventures. And the restaurants and bars, for their part, range from Moroccan classics to a steak-and-seafood venue and the impressive Japanese-style Morimoto.

content:
Parklane, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa, Limassol is luxury hospitality on a large scale, and the experience that it delivers is all the more memorable for that fact. It’s set on a lushly gardened parcel of land on the south coast of Cyprus, a few minutes outside of Limassol proper, and it’s likely some guests never venture off the property — this is a fully self-sufficient resort experience, complete with high-end retailers and a Clefs d’Or concierge to help make sense of it all.

Parklane’s 222 rooms, 34 suites, and 18 villas span the range from traditional double rooms all the way to a three-bedroom villa with a private swimming pool. Even the base level is luxurious, with stylish furniture, bedside control panels, and lavish bathrooms.

Multiple pools and an extensive spa and fitness program are among the leisure facilities, as well as tennis courts, a mini-football pitch, and direct beach access. The greatest extravagance, however, might be the kids’ club, set in a castle that’s larger than some boutique hotels, and staffed by child-care professionals. Meanwhile the hotel’s many restaurants include Nammos, an outpost of the famous Mediterranean restaurant, as well as La Petite Maison, a culinary tribute to the French Riviera.

content: The Domes name is well known to fans of Greek luxury hotels, but Domes Aulūs Zante is something ever so slightly different: a full-scale resort that aims to preserve the stylish cool and the easy tranquility of the established Domes hotels. It’s set on what might be the finest beach on the island of Zante, or Zakynthos, on the Ionian side of Greece. And while this island is no stranger to the buzz of youth-market tourism, from within the grounds of Domes Aulūs Zante you’ll hear nothing of it — you might as well be on an entirely private island.\n\nVisually, the style is luxe and subtle, unmistakably Greek but entirely without kitsch; this is the state of the art in high-end resort design, all warm neutrals and touchable textures, tasteful to the core. It’s a family-friendly resort but not a families-only retreat — accommodations range from romantic “cocoons,” “nests,” and “retreats” all the way up to three-bedroom suites. Restaurants include Greek meze, an Italian trattoria, and more; and activities run the gamut from days by the poolside or on the beach to more conservation-minded or culturally oriented day trips, tours, and experiences.

content: At first glance it may seem difficult to reconcile the visual impression made by Weber’s Boutique Hotel with its claim to have been open — and family-owned — since 1969. But it’s clear that this is an establishment that hasn’t been content to rest on its laurels. The restaurant came first, a classic upscale steak house with live lobsters and a live piano player, and it’s still here in something approximating its original form — which feels like a time capsule in comparison to the hotel, which is as modern as they come, and stylish to a degree that’s positively shocking when you consider that this is Ann Arbor, Michigan, a city that, for all its charms, isn’t exactly at the cutting edge of boutique hospitality.\n\nThe exteriors are a contemporary surprise, while the rooms opt for a more classic 20th-century modernist style, combining clean lines, designer furniture, and a restrained color palette. It’s a look that’s appealing enough on its own terms, and also feels like a nod to the futuristic optimism of the local industry — for Ann Arbor, thanks to the prestigious University of Michigan, has emerged as something of a high-tech mecca. And Weber’s one-of-a-kind restaurant isn’t the only dining and drinking venue; the Habitat Bar features live music, and the self-explanatory Coffee Bar serves third-wave brew from local roaster Hyperion.

content:
For a country with so much Caribbean coastline, Colombia is surprisingly short on beachfront hotels, particularly in the luxury resort category. Many visitors to Cartagena de Indias discover in short order that this famously picturesque port city isn’t, in fact, much of a beach destination at all. But the nearby Isla Barú, a longtime day-trip destination that’s home to the new Sofitel Barú Calablanca Beach Resort, offers a tropical paradise within easy reach. 

A scenic 40-minute boat ride away from Cartagena, the hotel is the region’s first LEED-certified property. This stylish modern resort is set on a quiet cove, complete with three restaurants, seven bars, a state-of-the-art spa, four infinity pools, and, of course, a private beach. All rooms and suites are elegant and light-filled, outfitted in natural materials and sophisticated earth tones; a Colombian artist created the original artwork and handmade tapestries, all inspired by native birdlife and seascapes. Even the most basic rooms have balconies with sea views, and higher-level suites have large terraces with Jacuzzis and kitchens with butler service.

A colorful Colombian-style breakfast buffet is served with panoramic water views, and an impressive array of restaurants and bars offer Caribbean and international dishes and drinks with a French twist. Many visitors don’t leave the premises once they arrive, which is understandable, but the resort staff happily arranges sailing classes, mountain biking tours, and other excursions. Otherwise, there’s plenty to do at the hotel, from coffee tastings and spa treatments to film screenings under the stars.

content:
Montreal’s Queen Elizabeth has seen some things; its most famous guest is the one who gave it its name, and John Lennon and Yoko Ono are not far behind. But in its 21st-century form it’s not content to rest on its historical laurels. After a thorough renovation it’s now the decidedly contemporary Fairmont The Queen Elizabeth, and it’s once more right where it belongs, in the top tier of Montreal’s luxury hospitality scene.

Its setting could hardly be more central, convenient to both downtown and Vieux-Montréal, and while it’s got much to offer design-agnostic business travelers, it’s frankly a lot more stylish than it strictly needs to be. Visually, its interiors are a tribute to the era of the hotel’s founding, with the benefit of 60+ years’ perspective, incorporating only the most successful elements of mid-century Modernism circa 1958.

The in-room comforts are decidedly luxe, and so are the Queen Elizabeth’s services, including an expansive wellness program and an upscale bistronomic restaurant. And it’s certainly not every day you come across a luxury hotel with a suite that’s a detailed reproduction of John and Yoko’s famous “bed-in for peace.”

content:
It’s hard to believe that the Francis House, a château-style Napa Valley gem, sat abandoned for half a century. Once a prominent merchant's house and later a hospital — some of Calistoga’s living residents were born here — the place was boarded up and graffiti-covered until the current owners discovered the property and transformed it into an elegant boutique hotel in 2018. All of the building’s interior was unsalvageable, but its original stone walls were beautifully restored making it a stand out feature of the hotel.

Inside and out, the hotel is imbued with a French country style to match the architecture. The carefully landscaped grounds include fragrant herb gardens and citrus trees, a tennis court, and a pretty swimming pool framed by cheerful red umbrellas and chaise longues. Sunlit rooms have period charm, with Chantilly lace curtains, chandeliers, antique writing desks, brass luggage racks, and vintage mirrors. But the modern amenities are notable, too, from heated floors and custom blackout curtains to Dyson hairdryers and heated Toto washlets. The hosts personally prepare breakfast at a communal table, and the stone firepit is a lovely spot to congregate after a day out exploring the surrounding wine country.

content: Silicon Valley may lack a single urban center, but modern, urban-style boutique hotels are an increasingly common sight in every town from Sunnyvale to Redwood City. The Park James takes part of its name from Menlo Park, the next town up from Palo Alto, and its location places it close to Stanford University as well as a number of vital destinations for Silicon Valley business travelers. But before it was a tech and innovation hotbed, this part of California was blessed with quite a bit of natural beauty — and with its plentiful outdoor lounge space the Park James takes advantage of the exceedingly pleasant climate.\n\nThe hotel’s design is full of references to Menlo Park’s history, including its Irish influence and its equestrian heritage. The rooms are contemporary in style, warmed by organic materials like wood and leather, and the luxuries, though subtle, are substantial. The suites, uniquely, feature king beds that fold up into the wall, converting the entire space into a meeting room, in case you’ve got business that isn’t ready for public discussion. But if you’re feeling social, there’s always Oak + Violet, a farm-to-table modern Californian restaurant with a stylish indoor dining room as well as an expansive courtyard patio.

content: Sofitel’s Legend sub-brand is just what it sounds like: a collection of historic hotels with stories to tell and reputations to uphold. In Panama, it’s represented by the Sofitel Legend Casco Viejo Panama City, occupying what was once the Club Unión de Panama, a century-old Spanish Colonial–style edifice in the city’s UNESCO-listed historic waterfront district. In its former life it hosted such luminaries as Albert Einstein and Queen Elizabeth, and in its new incarnation — after an extremely thorough restoration and modernization — it’s once again aiming for the top echelon of visitors to Panama.\n\nImagine a typical city-center Sofitel hotel — a modern high-end luxury hotel with a pronounced French accent — and add several decades’ worth of character and atmosphere, and you’ve got the picture. Thanks to the hotel’s unique position, the majority of its rooms and suites have views out to sea; the relatively humble courtyard- and city-facing rooms, however, are worthwhile as well. There’s a spa in partnership with KOS Paris, as well as a spacious fitness center. And it’s in the restaurants and bars that the combination of Paris and Panama shines the brightest, from proper Parisian pastries at Vera Café to locally inspired brasserie fare at Caleta.

content: This is what luxury looks like in San Francisco in the mid-2020s: a bit minimalist, a bit understated, with plenty of warm tones and organic textures. The Jay, Autograph Collection is just the latest evolution of the 25-story Brutalist tower that stands at Battery & Clay, in the Embarcadero district, and it’s emblematic of the times as well: not quite an independent, but nor is it strictly a chain. The interiors, by AvroKO, owe much to the Japanese-American modernist sculptor Ruth Asawa, and more broadly pay tribute to a century of Californian aesthetics, from Arts & Crafts on through to the present day. The TransAmerica Pyramid is a block away, and Embarcadero Center is reachable via an elevated walkway.

content:
From a single hotel in downtown Manhattan to a family that spans North America, Thompson Hotels is still going strong. Now under the Hyatt umbrella, the brand has brought its distinctive mid-century-influenced style to Texas — and brought a bit of Texas into its style at the same time. Thompson San Antonio stands tall above the River Walk, home to the city’s finest restaurants, bars, cafés, and shops, and its interiors, modernist though they may be, are adapted to the locale, filled with rugged textures in wood, leather, and stone.

Vast windows mean impressive views as well as plentiful sunlight, tamed by the rich, dark colors of the bedrooms. The ordinary king rooms are swanky and spacious, and the suites are positively extravagant, featuring lavish touches like freestanding soaking tubs, fully stocked wet bars, or spa-like bathrooms with jetted tubs.

An impressive fitness center is joined by an outdoor pool with private cabanas and its own lounge and bar. Landrace, the flagship restaurant, is helmed by the award-winning chef Steve McHugh, and serves an upscale, modern interpretation of classic Texan flavors; a second restaurant, the Mediterranean-inspired Moon’s Daughers, looks out over the city from the 20th floor.

content: Compared to many luxury resorts on the island, V Villas Phuket - MGallery Collection is intimately sized. The designers opted for space and exclusivity at the hotel’s remote hilltop location overlooking Ao Yon Bay — instead of squeezing in as many rooms as possible, they built just nineteen villas, many of which feature two stories and three or four bedrooms. Apart from a few that face the hills, the rest have dazzling ocean views, and all come with private infinity pools and personal butler service around the clock. \n\nThe interiors are spacious and elegant, with floor-to-ceiling windows and sliding glass doors opening onto large wooden decks seemingly suspended over the sea. Indoors and out, the decor is minimalist, characterized by natural hues that mirror the surrounding landscapes. Standard amenities include Bose sound systems and marble bathrooms with twin spa baths, and the highest-end presidential villa features a sleek kitchen, living room, dining room, wine cellar, and art gallery. Breakfast is served in the Art Deco-style restaurant, or on request, the hotel’s signature floating breakfast can be arranged at one’s private pool. At sunset, the striking rooftop bar, with its wide open-air deck and DJs spinning tunes, is a picture-perfect spot for reclining on a daybed with a tropical cocktail.

content: Once one of the humbler beach towns in San Diego’s affluent North County, Oceanside is on the upswing, and a string of stylish new hotels have popped up in its lively downtown. Mission Pacific Beach Resort is one of them, occupying an enviable piece of waterfront real estate right in front of the town’s historic wooden pier. Many rooms and suites in the seven-story building face a quintessentially SoCal view — rolling waves, surfers, seagulls — and all guests have access to the resort’s crowning glory, a rooftop pool and bar with palm trees, retro-styled daybeds, and sunset panoramas over the Pacific. \n\nThe interiors are modern and down-to-earth, outfitted in natural materials and colors that mirror the surrounding landscape. Rooms have hardwood floors, linen-upholstered headboards, and built-in bespoke furnishings in pale wood, plus eclectic details like sculptural lamps and original artwork curated by the Oceanside Museum of Art. Bathrooms are spacious with sophisticated lighting systems and oversized walk-in showers. Many rooms have private balconies, and apartment-like suites have a boho-chic air, with cozy sectional sofas facing views of the sea. While it’s hard to top drinks at the rooftop bar, the hotel’s other venues take their shot: coffee and breakfast burritos are served on a sunny ground-level terrace at High/Low, Valle is notably the only MICHELIN-Starred Mexican restaurant in Southern California, and sweet treats are on offer at the Top Gun House, the adorable historic cottage — now part of the hotel’s property — famously featured in the 1986 film.

content: There are just a handful of places to stay in Barr, a quaint village on the Alsace Wine Trail. The 5 Terres Hotel & Spa, part of the MGallery Hotel Collection, is one of them, and it’s everything you’d want of a hotel in such a picturesque setting. It’s right in the center of town, steps away down a cobblestoned street from the town hall and the tourist information office. The half-timbered 16th-century building is a historic landmark — it was once used as a factory and later a brewery — and though traditional from the outside, with its cheerful wooden shutters and window boxes spilling over with bright flowers, the interiors have been smartly redone with a modern edge. \n\nRooms and suites are atmospheric, with exposed wooden beams or steeply angled ceilings, pale oak flooring, original stone and brick details, leather headboards, and velvet accents. The upper-level Signature Suite has a private terrace with views over the vineyards. Downstairs, a stylish gourmet restaurant and a trio of attractive spaces await wine enthusiasts: a lively bar, a restored conservatory, and a pretty plant-lined terrace. A level beneath that, the building’s old sandstone vaults have been converted into an ethereal spa with indoor pools framed by stone archways — arguably the most striking area of the hotel, it’s not to be missed.

content: V Villas Hua Hin demonstrates just how far Hua Hin has come in its evolution from a sleepy fishing village to one of the most fashionable beach towns in Thailand. Located on one of the area’s most pristine stretches of sand, this luxury boutique hotel consists of 23 villa suites, each with a private swimming pool and sundeck. Amenities include stocked wine refrigerators, Bose sound systems, and personalized butler service. The beach beckons, but so do the infinity pool and whirlpools with their view of the sea, as well as the hotel’s spa. Meanwhile the hotel’s restaurant offers cooking classes and wine tastings, and the town’s famous Cicada Weekend Market is a short walk away.

content: Picturesque alpine villages line the road from Bergamo to the ski resorts of the Bergamo Alps. Thanks to its medieval monuments and jazz festival, Clusone is arguably the most notable of them, and Collina Luxury Relais is easily the region’s most extravagant hotel. The owners timed the opening with the winter holidays, making the most of the location en route to the Colere and Monte Pora ski centers. But this design-focused hotel, positioned on a hilltop surrounded by mountain scenery, is a worthwhile destination in all four seasons. \n\nRooms are modern but cozy, with pale wood paneling, sophisticated lighting systems, and private patios with views of the Alps. Larger suites have wood-beamed ceilings and spacious terraces with outdoor Jacuzzis. The hotel’s chalets are particularly stylish, with skylights, knotty pine walls, and inviting open-air seating areas. More striking still is the beautifully illuminated spa and its temperature-controlled indoor-outdoor swimming pool. Breakfast is served al fresco in summer, and in winter with scenic mountain views through huge picture windows; the surrounding landscapes are a playground for outdoor activities throughout the year.

content: The once low-key beach community of Oceanside, California has undergone a transformation in recent years, its refreshed downtown now home to resorts and restaurants to rival its North County neighbors. Hyatt is a driving force behind the glow-up with a few stylish hotels in the neighborhood, including the Seabird Ocean Resort & Spa. The Seabird is modern and elegant, set slightly back from the beach, with sweeping views of the Pacific and the historic Oceanside pier from many of its rooms and common spaces, including the spacious third-floor pool deck.\n\nInside, the aesthetic is modern but casual, with a cheerful white, yellow, and royal blue color palette and lots of floor-to-ceiling glass windows to make the most of the waterfront location. Rooms have a contemporary beachhouse look, with pale gray wood paneling, herringbone carpets, wicker lamps and ottomans, framed photography curated by the Oceanside Museum of Art, and sleek tiled bathrooms with walk-in showers or freestanding tubs. Many rooms overlook the Pacific, and the best suites feature huge private terraces with panoramic views of the sea and sky. Apart from the light-filled spa and the pool, the Seabird features the poolside Shelter Club, beachfront dining and cocktails at Piper and the Shore Room, respectively. Guests are encouraged to check out the rooftop bar at Mission Pacific Beach Resort, the hotel’s sister property next door — ideally at sunset.

content:
Portugal’s southern coast is enough for most hotels, but Domes Lake Algarve, in the spirit of going the extra mile, adds a private lake, just yards from the Vilamoura harbor, to its offerings — which already include access to the beach at Praia de Falesia. This extravagant resort looks, from the lake side, practically like a city unto itself, its terraced wings and villas dotted with balconies facing out to sea.

The Domes hotel brand originated in Greece, and while you won’t find the typical blue-and-white Cycladic color scheme here — the style is authentically Portuguese — there is a certain minimalist confidence to the décor, and a willingness to let the view draw the eye out the window. The rooms (“retreats” in the Domes vernacular) and the suites are luxe enough, and the one- and two-bedroom Residences offer a bit more privacy and self-sufficiency.

Like so many Portuguese seaside resorts, Domes is family-friendly to a remarkable degree; activities for kids are plentiful and well-supervised. For the adults there’s the Soma spa, as well as a fitness program with personal trainers. And a multitude of restaurants and bars serves everything from cold drinks by the poolside to upscale Portugues fare with an Italian accent, in tribute to the region’s Roman settlers.

content: After originally opening in 1919, Ojai’s longest-standing hotel, El Roblar, has been restored to its former glory and reopened as a 50-room boutique bolthole. The sensitive restoration has thankfully retained the property’s Spanish Revival architecture, including the Mission-style entry archway and the lobby’s stone fireplace, and added in design elements that pay homage to the Ojai Valley such as Monterey-style furnishings and locally sourced artworks. Guest rooms are divided across the Main Building, the private bungalows—which come with large garden patios—and the newly built Sycamore House, and nod to the unspoiled surroundings with warm, earthy shades and layers of natural wood.\n\nRestaurant La Cocina and the Condor Bar tap into Ojai’s long-standing links with Mexico and serve a California-Mexican menu complemented by local wines, cocktails, and a strong collection of agave spirits. Outside, gardens filled with palm and dragon trees and Spanish-style fountains surround the pool, which sits against a backdrop of the Los Padres Forest and Topa Topa mountains.

content: Though its Spanish Colonial building aesthetic represents something of a departure for the brand, Park Hyatt Aviara Resort, Golf Club & Spa is every bit as luxurious as its minimalist-chic overseas relations. In fact, inside its doors, the look is ultra-contemporary, a sophisticated and subtle take on California coastal living. Its accommodations are unmistakably high-end, following a thorough 2020 renovation, and at 327 units, the resort offers plenty of choice. Spaces are extremely generous, and the appointments are as fine as can be.\n\nNor are the words “Golf Club & Spa” mere window dressing. For many guests it’ll be the Aviara Golf Club, with its Arnold Palmer–designed course, that is the reason for the visit. It’s joined by a racquet club, for tennis and pickleball enthusiasts, as well as the Miraval Spa, which offers everything from massages and skin care to meditation, acupuncture, personal training, and beyond. Meanwhile, a diverse array of restaurants ensures that guests need never leave the 250-acre property.
