content:
The first Dutch boutique hotels we saw were marvels of the modern minimalism that was in the ascendant in the turn-of-the-millennium Netherlands. Since then, however, we’ve seen a flowering of eclectic styles — but none quite so ornate as that on display in Hotel TwentySeven. This 1916 building on the central Dam Square is home to a private club for the upper crust of Amsterdam society and industry, and, on its upper floors, to a luxury boutique hotel that’s as intensely atmospheric as anything we’ve ever seen.

“Neo-Baroque” hardly begins to capture the sheer opulence and ornamentation of a hotel that’s festooned with Nepalese carpets, Italian curtains, French wallpaper, and no end of sumptuous furnishings and contemporary artworks. But the visual impact is only one of Hotel TwentySeven’s strengths. The bar is one of Amsterdam’s most sought-after (and exclusive) nightspots, and the restaurant, Bougainville, is the proud recipient of a Michelin star.

The concept was to create a luxury hotel where “literally anything is possible,” thanks not only to the encyclopedic array of amenities and comforts but also to the ultra-personalized approach to service. What this means in practical terms is that you’ll have your own butler, who’s capable of sorting out nearly any whim that crosses your mind, as well as a team of personal trainers, shoppers, assistants, tour guides, even child-care providers.

Orlando’s Lake Nona Wave Hotel is known for its technology, and we’re not just talking about its gently curving silhouettes; it’s among the first to feature smart windows, which dim automatically in response to bright sunlight, as well as Toto toilets and, in selected rooms, high-tech beds and sleep-quality apps. Just as important, from our perspective, is the fact that its interiors are, if anything, even more distinctive in their design than the hotel’s memorable exterior. 

The rooms, in particular, are among the most stylish in town, though that doesn’t mean minimalist or severe — modernist, yes, but of the sunny, colorful, somewhat utopian mid-century variety. They’re outfitted with luxe touches like Frette linens and Payot bath products to complement the high-tech gadgetry. And while they start out at a comfortable enough size, the suites quickly grow to 875 square feet or more.

Also substantial are the wellness offerings, from the Chopra Mind-Body Spa to the expansive Lake Nona Performance Club, under whose roof you’ll find a fitness center and swim club as well as a cycling studio, a climbing gym, and even an indoor track. Meanwhile the restaurants include the verdant Haven Kitchen and the upscale pan-American Bacán, featuring influences from the entirety of the Spanish-speaking Western Hemisphere.

A beach resort containing 216 guest rooms, three swimming pools, and twelve restaurants sounds big — until you hear about the competition along the oceanfront. In fact, if you can believe it, the Puente Romano Marbella is one of the smaller and cozier resort options along Spain’s so-called Golden Mile. And not just in terms of numbers: the scale feels a good deal smaller than it is, thanks to the resort’s clever layout, modeled after an Andalusian village, as well as its relatively low-lying three-story architecture.
 
But let’s be realistic: you’re not going to be worrying about precisely how many people are lying around on chaises once you’ve arrived in paradise. And make no mistake, this is paradise, of a sort. All guest rooms, elegantly appointed with marble floors and traditional regional decor, feature private terraces — many with views of the sea. There’s free wi-fi, flat-screen TVs, and iPod docking stations; the top-end Grand Suites feature lavish extras like Persian stone bathrooms and wraparound terraces with Jacuzzis.
 
If you’re staying in one of those, you might not want to venture out — that’s what room service is for. Everyone else can take advantage of the services on offer in Puente Romano’s “village,” including several gorgeous swimming pools, clay tennis courts, a wellness center with Turkish bath, botanical gardens, an oceanfront cocktail bar, and no fewer than seven restaurants.

content: San Francisco was an early adopter of the boutique-hotel trend, but never this far north — as any local could tell you, only the dullest kind of tourist trap would set up shop at Fisherman’s Wharf. But that was before the Kimpton Alton Hotel came on the scene. Named for the rock-and-roll poster artist Alton Kelley, it’s inspired by San Francisco’s countercultural history; in this context, its bohemian-modernist hybrid style and its voluminous collection of vinyl records aren’t just nods to the current hospitality trend, but expressions of the hotel’s unique character.\n\nThe bottom line is that this would be a stylish and memorable hotel in any neighborhood, and if it opens up Fisherman’s Wharf and nearby North Beach to style-conscious travelers then it’s hard to see how anyone fails to benefit. The rooms add turntables to the Kimpton signature yoga mats, and the brand’s customary social hour — accompanied by complimentary drinks in the lobby — will help you settle in. And among the hotel’s many partnerships with Bay Area creative types is Abacá, the restaurant, an inventive modern Filipino restaurant by the accomplished local chef Francis Ang.

content: If your iconic image of a holiday in Puglia is the minimalism of a white masseria nestled in an olive grove, then Paragon 700 might not be for you. But if you like to be surprised and a bit unsettled, with its bold modernity, this irreverent, provocative, and decidedly unconventional hotel will show you a different aspect of this region.\nParagon 700 Boutique Hotel is nothing if not unique. Its rooms and suites are all different, each one an eclectic mix not only of the delicate and the rough-hewn but also of furnishings and objects from all around the world. The house’s old cistern is now a small and striking subterranean spa, while the building’s interior courtyard is an unexpected oasis, featuring Ostuni’s only hotel pool. content:
We’ve seen some masterfully renovated Alpine chalets in our time on this earth, but nothing like Alpaga. Here no fewer than ten chalets, ranging in size from quite substantial to very cozy indeed, have been stitched together into a sort of alpine-design hamlet, which in its entirety comprises one of the most luxurious hotels in the mountain town of Megève. Naturally the result is rather more stylish than your typical Alpine village — the proprietors have a track record with this sort of thing, having established such high-elevation favorites as Le Val Thorens and the Hôtel des 3 Vallées in Courchevel.

The hotel’s 26 bedrooms and 7 suites are divided between four of the larger chalets, and they’re a masterful blend of rustic texture and modern sheen. They’ve got balconies or terraces, and under the knotty-pine surface they’re as well equipped as any urban boutique-hotel room. Seven suites are contained in 2 other chalets, each one rather more like an apartment than a hotel suite, with full kitchens and views of the Val d’Arly. And if you simply must have a chalet all to yourself, they’ve got several of those as well, which sleep up to eight, ten, or twelve guests in similarly lavish comfort.

Two restaurants, La Table de l’Alpaga and the more casual Le Bistrot, see to guests’ gustatory needs, and private chefs are on hand in case you’d prefer to have a private dinner in your own chalet. The hotel's outdoor pool invites guests to enjoy a swim year-round, no matter the season.

And let’s not forget the whole point of Megève: in summer you’ll hike the Vallée Blanche, and in winter you’ll ride the hotel’s shuttle to the town center’s ski lifts.

content:
Baden-Baden is well-known as a spa, resort and convention town, and since 1872 Brenners Park-Hotel & Spa has been its finest hotel. This is a side of Germany that is often overlooked: here, at the edge of the Black Forest, one may indulge in all the finest creature comforts life has to offer, from the French-inflected cuisine to the healing effects of the thermal baths.

Of course the Spa at Brenners Park goes beyond mere baths — practically any treatment imaginable is available here, European, Asian, or otherwise, and all in a refined Black Forest style. This is the best spa in one of Europe's most celebrated spa towns, which is a bit like being the best restaurant in Paris, or the best museum in Florence. And there is no shortage of athletic and other leisure pursuits, whether your tastes run to golf, tennis, riding, or biking, and the Black Forest offers a wealth of opportunities for climbers, hunters, and other outdoor types.

None of this, though, is enough to overshadow the hotel, itself one of the most luxurious in all of Europe. The buliding is located amidst idyllic parkland, alongside the Oos river, and overlooks Lichtentaler Allee, a charming old-fashioned tree-lined road. The architecture and decor are all sumptuous 19th-century luxury, with authentic antique furnishings, and the rooms are opulent and impossibly comfortable, all featuring private terraces and palatial modern bathrooms (marble, inevitably).

The Black Forest is enchanting, and Baden-Baden no less so — it would be easy (with the proper funds) to imagine yourself one of the royals who once made their summer homes here. The city is spectacular, and the casino is world-famous, but connoisseurs of unique hotels may well find Brenners Park-Hotel & Spa to be the main attraction.

How to get there: Brenners Park-Hotel & Spa is approximately a 15-minute drive from Baden Airport (FKB).

content: Belle-Île-en-Mer already boasts quite the list of VIP visitors: Dumas, Baudelaire, and Monet, to name a modest few. Not that anyone is unwelcome — far from it, as this Breton island’s population balloons each summer with tourist traffic — but uncharted territory this certainly is not. Now for the silver lining: the island’s southwestern Côte Sauvage hasn’t lost an iota of its rugged, sharp-cliffed beauty thereby. You can have your castle after all in Castel Clara Thalasso & Spa Hôtel. Commanding sea views are the name of the game; many of Castel Clara’s 63 rooms, split between two slate-roofed Sixties buildings, and all of the public spaces operate accordingly. Just as well, given the beige-on-white interiors, a boundary-respecting exercise in what Brits call “sensibility.” Small touches — model ships, turquoise accents, period lanterns, wainscoting — call the seafaring life to mind, but none so strongly as the actual seascape. Get an ocean-facing balcony room, period. Once you’ve had your fill of looking at the sea, of course, you should get down to experiencing it. They mean the second half of the hotel name quite literally, offering a host of aquatic treatments across the spa’s 28 rooms. There’s also the island’s natural appeal; avail yourself of the hotel’s bikes and you’ll have plenty to explore, including 95 km of coastal paths, gorse-and-grain valleys, and a near-inexhaustible succession of picturesque hamlets. Café Clara does an excellent imitation of a fishmonger’s spread with daily, bountiful seafood buffets for breakfast and lunch. Come dinnertime, Le 180° brings the gastronomic dynamite, gorgeously presented plates best enjoyed with a selection from their encyclopedic cellars on the panoramic terrace (hence the name). Who knows, a setting this dramatic might well inspire you to join the ranks of Impressionist masters. How to get there: Ferries depart year-round from Quiberon ; the trip lasts approximately 45 minutes each way. Several water taxi services are also available from Quiberon, Vannes, Port Navalo, and Locmariaquer.

content:
The Dolomites are home to lodges of all descriptions, from quaint old wooden contraptions to ultra-modern eco-lodges. But there’s nothing else quite like the Gardena Grödnerhof Gourmet & Spa Hotel. Constructed in 1923, it’s about as ornate as these things can be; a 21st-century restoration left its majestic silhouette intact, even as it updated its color palette and its interior finishes.

Its rooms and suites contain plenty of classic Alpine gestures, like exposed timbers and panels of knotty pine. They’re also equipped with modern furniture and up-to-date comforts, as well as balconies with views of the town and the valley. 

The village of Ortisei, in the Val Gardena, is nothing if not picturesque, and offers easy access to the Dolomiti Superski area. In summer, the region offers a wealth of trails for hiking and biking. And travelers in any season benefit from Gardena Grödnerhof’s impressive spa.

As for restaurants, the Grödnerhof comes with two; given the setting, the hearty Restaurant Gardena would be more than adequate, but it’s joined by the MICHELIN-Starred restaurant Anna Stuben.

content: Gross Flotbek, in the western suburbs of Hamburg, is a mere 15 minutes via the S-Bahn from the bustling port city, and yet it feels a world apart. This was Denmark once, if you can believe it — and while the 200-year-old farmhouse complex that’s home to Landhaus Flottbek doesn’t date back quite that far, it’s nevertheless inspired by the traditions of Scandinavian hospitality. Hygge, the restaurant and bar, is the most visible example, named as it is for the untranslatable (but coziness-adjacent) concept that is Denmark’s most recognizable contribution to the world of hotels.\n\nLandhaus Flottbek’s rooms and suites pursue this concept in their own way, or in four different ways — some come in a slightly more delicate cottage style, or a rustic-meets-elegant barn style, while others recall Scandinavian urban modernism or a Hamptons-inspired beach-house vibe. All are luxurious, but well on the right side of ostentatious, and the house’s suburban setting goes a long way toward establishing a tranquil atmosphere. Meanwhile there’s plenty to do between here and the Elbe, and if the S-Bahn isn’t calling your name, you can easily reach Hamburg via a traditional riverborne barge.

content:
The Matterhorn is the focus; this imposing, eerie mountain peak, standing upright above the high Alps, is possibly Switzerland's most recognizable icon, and the high mountain town of Zermatt the Alps' classic resort town. The Grand Hotel Zermatterhof has been here since 1879, and was the favored alpine getaway of the aristocracy, as it is today — though today's visiting aristocrats are as likely to be film stars and rockers as they are royals and statesmen. The view is extraordinary—and most rooms have baclonies from which to enjoy it—but the hotel is extraordinary as well.

If you are expecting some sort of upscale ski chalet, you will be pleasantly surprised; this is called a Grand Hotel for a reason (the Swiss, apparently, don't do hyperbole). Bathrooms are marble and tile with heated towel racks, and the bedrooms are enormous, and so elegantly appointed that if not for the Matterhorn looming outside, one could mistake this for a five-star city hotel.

And don't get us started on the service — where some resort hotels might employ rosy-cheeked ski bums, Zermatterhof goes the traditional grand hotel route, with a polished and professional staff. Winter is, naturally, the high season, but it's well worth the trip, if only for the breathtaking sleigh ride to the hotel.

content:
Kimpton and Palm Springs were made for each other. This venerable American boutique-hotel brand, now under the IHG umbrella, made its reputation on the wager that boutique hotels could be a lot less forbidding and exclusive, but still remain stylish — an attitude that’s perfectly suited to the easy, extraverted hedonism of this Southern California desert town. (And both, it must be said, share a certain predilection for mid-century Modernism.) The Rowan Palm Springs presents both of these hospitality institutions at their best.

At seven stories high, and containing some 153 rooms and suites, the Rowan is sizable by boutique standards, but it’s far from crowded. The rooms are spacious, and light is plentiful, thanks to the floor-to-ceiling windows; there’s a yoga mat in every room, and the elevated views offer an unusual perspective on this low-rise town — as does the rooftop swimming pool.

Spa services are available in-room, and there’s an extensive fitness center as well as a fleet of PUBLIC bikes for exploring the town. The rooftop is home not only to the pool but to a modern Californian restaurant called 4 Saints; there’s also the Mediterranean-inspired Juniper Table and two bars, the indoor Window Bar and the poolside High Bar.

content: No children are allowed at the Wittmore, and the same goes for photos. Both policies make sense once you step inside this sultry and silent boutique hotel, tucked away on a narrow alleyway in Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter. The hotel leans all the way into the neighborhood's dark, romantic vibes, especially on the ground level with its rich wood paneling, red velvet loveseats, cozy fireplace, and French doors opening onto a courtyard patio. The atmosphere lightens up a bit in the rooms and suites: botanical wallpaper, vintage telephones, and floor-to-ceiling windows opening onto the patio's greenery. Up on the rooftop terrace, the atmosphere is downright cheerful, and it’s especially enchanting at sunset.

content:
Even by Dubai’s standards the building that’s home to Atlantis The Royal is a spectacular one, an architectural statement piece set along the beach on the outer crescent of the manmade Palm Island. And what’s inside is no less impressive — this is by any measure one of the most extravagant, luxurious hotels anywhere in the world.

Nor is it small, weighing in at 795 rooms and suites. All of which, by the way, are ultra-luxe, to say the least, beginning with the merely vast 600-square-foot king and queen rooms, which face either the Palm and the mainland or out into the Arabian Sea. Ascend the range and you’ll eventually find yourself in one of the penthouses, which reach their apex in the extravagant Royal Mansion, featuring four bedrooms across two levels plus a private terrace with its own infinity pool.

Additionally, you’ll find no fewer than 17 restaurants, most notably Dinner by Heston Blumenthal, the recipient of a MICHELIN Star. There’s a spectacular spa as well as a 22nd-floor infinity pool. And Atlantis The Royal goes all-out when it comes to live entertainment, drawing A-list DJs and performing artists to its numerous venues.

content:
It pays to get to know Croatia’s Adriatic coast. Among the dividends is Boutique Hotel Alhambra, a carefully restored concern on the southwest shore of the narrow Cres-Lošinj archipelago, hugging the curves of Čikat cove, a pristine and clement-weathered harbor in limestone and dolomite, softened by characteristic stands of pine and palm. You can tell right away that this was once a grand old villa — however thoroughly renovated, its architectural personality still comes through in the Austro-Hungarian façade, picturesque in every detail, from the arched loggias to the elegant quoin corners to the terra-cotta roofing. 

Indoors, public spaces run the gamut of styles. The lounge bar features eccentric parquet flooring and curvilinear seating somewhere between retro-futuristic and mid-century cool, while the main restaurant personalizes the view with gorgeous glass frontage and a spacious terrace, perfect for a leisurely bottle of local wine. The heated indoor saltwater pool is the star of the show at the spa, augmented by a waterfall and a captivating geometric wall treatment, though the saunas and specialty treatments give it a run for its money.

The 36 rooms and 15 suites hit all the right notes, chiefly visual: furnished balconies permit enviable Mediterranean views over intricate, wrought-iron rails, and Dean Skira’s concept lighting maintains an open brightness throughout. Bathrooms include deep soaking tubs, vessel sinks, and natural amenities against a backdrop of checkered stone and mosaic. King beds feature oversize headboards and cream-and-tan linens, accented with Adriatic blue and tawny orange. Alhambra rounds out the experience with wi-fi, satellite TVs, and docking stations, though they won’t be the clincher: that honor goes to the private beach and bar.

How to get there: Boutique Hotel Alhambra is a 20-minute drive from Lošinj Airport. Ferry service is also available to Cres Island from Brestova on the mainland or from Valbiska on Krk Island.

content: L’Auberge Basque is a small inn and restaurant belonging to chef Cédric Béchade, located in Saint-Pée-sur-Nivelle, near the Atlantic Coast in the Basque country, and a perfectly self-contained slice of Basque-accented French country-house life. What sets it apart from many other chef-owned auberge hotels in France and elsewhere is its attention to detail, and its unique personality: this antique inn, more than three centuries old, was expanded with an unapologetically modernist addition, and the resulting building is a lively hybrid of the traditional and the contemporary.\n\nThat goes for the interiors as well, furnished from top to bottom by the Belgian brand Flamant; the look is classic in spirit but with a modern simplicity and an inspiring mix of weathered materials and crisp clean lines. Even the humblest rooms are more than a little bit of luxurious, and some add terraces or balconies as they grow. They’re fine enough that it’d be an impressive hotel even without the restaurant — but of course it’s the French-Basque cooking of the Alain Ducasse–trained Cédric Béchade that makes the whole thing tick.

content: We expect stately, luxurious interior design from Rosewood, and the Rosewood Bangkok certainly doesn’t disappoint. What’s a surprise, however, is the very distinctive angular form of this 30-story skyscraper, inspired by the wai, the traditional Thai greeting. The whole thing is a visual tour de force, inside and out, and the views are extraordinary, but the pleasures of the other senses are never neglected. \n \nThe contemporary rooms and suites are wonderfully comfortable, dressed in soothing neutral shades and flooded with natural light thanks to expansive windows overlooking Bangkok’s skyscrapers. The views continue from the 9th floor indoor-outdoor lap pool and the fully equipped gym, and post-workout there is Sense, A Rosewood Spa for cocooning treatments rooted in Thai tradition, reiki sessions, and blowouts and manicures at the hair and nail salon. The restaurants serve impressive interpretations of Thai, Chinese, and European flavors as well as a diverse selection of whisky, cigars, and vinyl records at the speakeasy bar, Lennon’s.

content: Sister hotel to the equally impressive Clair de la Plume, in the village of Grignan, La Ferme Chapouton lies just on the edge of the village proper — and, while Grignan is technically a mile or so outside of Provence, travelers find themselves in the familiar stone farmhouses surrounded by the lavender fields that are characteristic of the region. It’s a storybook escape, a 1760-vintage farm that’s evolved into a splendid little hotel with 13 exquisite rooms, a plentiful supply of bucolic outdoor space, an award-winning bistro, and a clear view of the picturesque Château de Grignan and Mont Ventoux.\n\nThe rooms are unique, and combine historical architecture with understated contemporary décor; connecting rooms are available for families traveling together. In addition to the farm’s gardens, there’s a swimming pool for a break from the summer warmth. A stroll into the village takes just a minute or two, and restaurants are plentiful, including a pair belonging to sister hotel Le Clair de la Plume. Back at the farm, however, is a fine option: a bistro serving Michelin-rated traditional fare either in a dining room by the fireside or out on a terrace with a view.

content: Bandol, in a region perhaps best known for its wines, is also a splendid seaside destination, less than an hour from Marseille. Here, on a spit of land between the marina and a sheltered beach, is the Hôtel & Spa Île Rousse Thalazur Bandol, a 67-room luxury boutique hotel in a clean-lined contemporary style. Its pleasures are on the subtle side, especially compared with its cousins to the east, on the Riviera; the spa, with its wide array of seawater-focused treatments, is an impressive one, and is complemented by the presence of not one but two private beach clubs.

content:
You’d be forgiven for thinking that Tuscany had an absolute monopoly on Italian rural idylls, but it turns out neighboring Umbria is pretty handy with a countryside escape as well. And it’s hard to think of anything that’s missing from Borgo La Chiaracia Resort & Spa’s version of the idea. You’ve got classic farmhouse-style architecture, bucolic views for miles, an indulgent focus on food and wine, and an equally virtuous focus on wellness and relaxation.

Despite its historical style, Borgo La Chiaracia is brand-new, built from the ground up for its intended purpose as a luxury resort. And with only 26 rooms and suites, it puts its square footage to good use — the accommodations aren’t just state-of-the-art, but are generously sized as well, and all are unique, many incorporating charming throwback details like timbered ceilings.

The Umbrian landscape isn’t just for admiring — the hotel’s restaurant, Radici, aims to put guests in direct contact with the land, via the medium of impeccably locally sourced produce and ingredients (and wine). And the word “spa” isn’t in the hotel’s name by accident — SPA Livinna goes beyond a couple of treatment rooms, adding an indoor and outdoor pool, a steam room, sauna, hydromassage, and multi-sensory showers.

content: The Bavarian town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber is a beautifully preserved medieval gem, but that doesn’t mean its lodgings are necessarily backward-looking in their style. Villa Mittermeier stands right by the Würzburger Gate at the entrance to Rothenburg’s old town, and the building that it occupies is indeed a classic one. But what family owners Ulli and Christian Mittermeier have created here is a boutique hotel that’s right at home in the 21st century.\n\nThe interiors are marked by their contemporary decoration and their modern furniture; the contours of the building may be historical but the high-tech comforts and the vibrant color schemes are not. And as successful as it is as a boutique lodging, the Villa Mittermeier is equally devoted to the culinary arts; the highly regarded restaurant counts a MICHELIN Star among its accolades.

content:
The family-owned Hotel Neiburgs preserves its 1903 façade, but step inside and you'll find a sophisticated blend of past and present. The interiors embrace modern influences—from minimalist color palettes and modernist furnishings to artworks by contemporary Latvian artists, including a member of the Neiburgs family itself.

Guest accommodations strike a careful balance between old and new, combining period details like parquet floors and exposed beams with clean-lined, modern construction. The smallest category is a studio apartment, complete with a kitchenette, and the spaces scale up from there: many suites span two levels, and some can be joined with neighboring studios to form two-bedroom configurations.

Guests have access to a small spa and a serene library furnished with Ligne Roset armchairs. The hotel’s restaurant, Neiburgs, is a well-established name on Riga’s culinary scene—a smart introduction to Latvian cuisine, and thanks to its streetside terrace, also to one of the capital’s most picturesque corners.

content:
Though i-Suite has no official connection to the makers of those various i-Devices with which we’re all familiar, we could be forgiven for thinking that the future, if Rimini’s intently forward-looking experiment in hotel design is any indication, will be brought to us by a certain design-oriented tech company. Rounded edges in a palette of fresh-from-the-factory white and gleaming chrome abound. Plastic is the material of choice here, and though it’s not the last and only word in interior designer Simone Michell’s vocabulary, it seems to inform all the rest. Even the concrete, whether in the bowling-ball-smooth floors or the undulating exterior walls, suggests plasticity. 

It’s no surprise that the future also has a lot of glowing screens in store. All of the rooms include LCD TVs that serve as PCs and entertainment systems, many of them mounted in places you might not expect — in a mirror, in the bathroom, or in the case of the Life suites, fixed to the ceiling above the bed. Then there are the screensaver-worthy views of the Adriatic through large picture windows, often set behind remote-operated curtains that lend additional drama to a gaze out the window. Opt for the “Lover’s” version of the Dolce Vista suite and you can enjoy views of a different sort; the room comes with a cocoon-like Corian bathtub in the center of the room. 

The entire sixth floor of the building is occupied by a spa wrapped in curved windows with yet more sea views. You’ll want to get well buffed for a trip to the LED-lit, indoor-outdoor pool, or for a night out at Rimini’s many bars. Visitors have been partying here for the past 150 years or so, and the i-Suite suggests a future that’s every bit as lively. 

How to get there: i-SUITE is approximately 15 minutes by taxi from Federico Fellini Airport Rimini.

content:
There was a time not so long ago when we wouldn’t have expected a city of Saarbrücken’s size, as appealingly cosmopolitan as it is, to be furnished with a boutique hotel of this caliber. But in the 2020s, you never know where you’re going to find a hotel like Esplanade. It’s a charming 19th-century school building on Max Ophüls Square in the atmospheric Nauwieser district, just to the east of the riverside town center. 

And in its current guise it’s been given a thorough renovation in an upscale, design-conscious contemporary style, updating its Gründerzeit exterior with interiors that call on modernist masters from Harry Bertoia to Le Corbusier. Though the 16 rooms stop short of full-on luxury-hotel opulence, they’re provided with luxe comforts like Nespresso machines and rain showers. 

In fact, this is not only an attractive and quietly luxurious boutique hotel; it’s also the site of a two-Michelin-starred restaurant, also called Esplanade, under the direction of chef Silio del Fabro. The capital of Germany’s smallest state might not see the volume of traffic that passes through Berlin or Munich, but there’s no reason it can’t welcome visitors in equally high style.

content:
The Britannia name dates back to 1870, when British aristocrats used to visit Trondheim, just south of the Arctic Circle, on salmon-fishing expeditions. Today Trondheim is much more than a fishing town — it’s Norway’s third-largest city, a university town in a spectacular setting with a booming restaurant scene. And its most glamorous hotel, the Britannia, now hosts style-minded luxury travelers from all around the world.

Its interiors are a surprise to anyone who thinks Scandinavia is synonymous with modernism. After a thorough renovation, these spaces are contemporary, but the spirit of the ’90s — the 1890s — is alive and well here. The rooms feature proper luxury-hotel comforts, complete with Hästens beds, Carrara marble bathrooms, and Nespresso machines, and the look is equally palatable to traditionalists and design aficionados.

There’s a spa, a well-equipped gym, and an indoor pool, all part of the Britannia Club, where memberships are extended to hotel guests. Among the hotel’s four restaurants is the century-old Speilsalen, which was recently awarded its first Michelin star, as well as a French brasserie, a grill called Jonathan, and a cocktail bar and separate wine bar, with a collection that runs to 2,000 labels.

content:
In contrast to its sister hotels, many of which occupy repurposed historical structures, NH Collection Madrid Eurobuilding is as modern as they come: a high-rise luxury hotel and convention center in the Spanish capital’s northern financial district (and walking distance from the Bernabéu stadium, home of Real Madrid). It’s also a cut above most of its sisters in terms of sheer luxury: there’s a lavish and vaguely futuristic spa with a wealth of water features, as well as a restaurant with no fewer than three Michelin stars, chef David Muñoz’s exceptional DiverXO.

This is a business hotel first and foremost, and the exceedingly professional service reflects that fact. But all of the NH Collection hotels are influenced by contemporary boutique-hotel design, this one perhaps more than most — perhaps it’s the fact that a new build means a blank canvas, but the Eurobuilding’s public spaces are little short of spectacular, filled with unusual design pieces and eye-catching contemporary art. 

The rooms, as ever, are more sedate, but hardly less handsome, their minimalist lines and neutral tones brought to life by focused pops of red or violet. “Mood rooms” include colorful mood lighting, while the VIP suites feel like modern design showrooms — and all levels of accommodation are equipped for flawless luxury-hotel comfort.

content:
Hotel Indigo - Stratford Upon Avon isn’t just located in Shakespeare’s hometown, it’s set right across the street from New Place, the playwright’s final family home. As such it’s positively steeped in Tudor charm; the building incorporates elements that date back to the 15th century, and however contemporary its interiors may be, there’s never a shortage of antique atmosphere.

IHG’s Indigo-branded hotels are allowed a very long corporate leash, after all, and while you could argue there’s a house style, or at least a common approach to color and décor, each one is highly individual. That’s certainly the case here; some of the rooms are quite a lot more contemporary than others, but you won’t find timbers like those in the attic rooms in many other boutique hotels.

Meanwhile the public spaces are free to lay on the throwback vibes a little more heavily. The Woodsman, a farm-to-fork restaurant, is an attractively old-fashioned space in the hotel’s historic wing.

content:
This utterly tranquil clifftop property on Mallorca’s east coast didn’t always involve cocktails by the Jacuzzi. In fact, the main house was originally built as a retreat for an ailing monk who required frequent seawater treatments. After some serious updating a few years back, tje adults-only Can Simoneta offers accommodations that are far from monastic — without sacrificing the peaceful harmony of the hotel’s natural setting.

Two stone buildings, one which offers more dramatic views over the Mediterranean, house eighteen suites and guest rooms. Elegant furnishings, like romantic four-poster beds and delicate cream-colored linens, contribute to the simple and calming atmosphere. The most desirable quarters feature terraces and huge picture windows; all contain contemporary amenities like satellite televisions, internet connections, and sleek, spacious bathrooms that belie the buildings’ modest heritage.

Can Simoneta, though only an hour’s drive from Palma airport, is quite secluded — certainly not the place for vacationers looking for round-the-clock activities and nightlife. This sea haven is better suited for leisure-seekers who like to listen to birds and stroll around flowering gardens, or watch the sunset from the natural pool near the water’s edge. Candlelit dinners for two are regularly arranged on the cliff’s edge at the à la carte restaurant Can Simoneta La Terraza, while Can Simoneta Gastronomic serves a tasting menu that brings together Mediterranean and Mexican flavors. Nearby bays and caves provide easy excursions for those who find enough energy to climb out of one of Can Simoneta’s hammocks.

content:
From the outside, there’s little to suggest that Giardino Mountain, in Champfèr, right next to St. Moritz, might count itself a design hotel. The exterior looks almost edible in that pure classic Engadine way, as though it’s a marzipan miniature. But once you’re through the doors, the fruits of the 2011 renovation are immediately apparent. Proprietors Daniela and Philippe Frutiger, owners of a couple of hotels on the shores of Lake Maggiore, clearly weren’t intimidated by the luxe competition, nor were they overly reverent in approaching the restoration — Giardino Mountain is still an Alpine classic, timbered ceilings and all, it’s just been updated for an audience that’s a bit more visually adventurous.

Rooms range from cozy singles on up to spacious junior suites, all outfitted in a pale wood and cream palette, with accents in saturated fuchsia or lime. They’re identifiably Alpine in appearance, though contemporary through and through — it’s a look that’s immediately familiar to boutique-hotel aficionados, and refreshingly cosmopolitan in style.

Meanwhile two bars and three restaurants, including the two-MICHELIN-Starred Ecco St. Moritz, all but eliminate the need to venture outside the hotel’s walls — and the spa is a perfect restorative for a day spent on the slopes, or a summertime destination unto itself. 

How to get there: Giardino Mountain is approximately 205 km by car from Milan-Malpensa Airport via SS36, SS37, and Route 3. Alternatively, the hotel is approximately 207 km by car from Zürich Airport via A53, A3, A13, and Route 3.

content: Château de Vignée, an 17th-century manor and farmhouse in the Ardennes, is a perfectly lovely place, a red-brick castle whose turrets evoke storybook adventures. Inside, it’s surprisingly contemporary, its rooms and suites presenting a soothingly sedate vision of modern luxury. What elevates it into something extraordinary is the presence of its restaurant, Arden, where chef Marius Bosmans, a veteran of some of Belgium’s finest kitchens, prepares dishes crafted from vegetables grown in the hotel’s own greenhouse. A small spa by the banks of the Lesse provides further avenues for relaxation, and the landscape is ripe for exploration.

content: There’s plenty of scenic shoreline around Lake Constance — known as the Bodensee in German — one of the largest lakes in central Europe. Arguably the loveliest stretch is in the foothills of the northern Alps near the Swiss border, where the medieval city of Konstanz rises up on the waterfront. RIVA occupies one of the stately Art Nouveau villas on the lakeside promenade, and while the boutique hotel blends in with its surroundings, it’s been expanded and fully reimagined inside. The sleek, mostly white interiors, flooded with natural light, are reminiscent of a modern art gallery, while up on the rooftop, an ethereal outdoor pool, heated year-round, has dazzling views over the water.\n\nRooms and suites are minimalist and smartly designed — some with parquet floors, dark wood paneling, and soaking tubs, others lighter and brighter with private balconies facing the lake. All feature sophisticated lighting systems, Nespresso machines, and luxurious bathrooms with heated floors. On the villa’s ground floor, the two-MICHELIN-Star Ophelia specializes in creative French cuisine, and the more casual Lakeside has a convertible glass facade to make the most of the water views. As the sun goes down, glowing lanterns illuminate the open-air terrace and a dreamy outdoor lounge set amid landscaped gardens. In colder months, the fireplace-warmed Riva bar and walk-in wine cellar are especially inviting.

content: Set amid riverside vineyards near the intersection of Germany, France, and Luxembourg, Victor’s Residenz-Hotel Schloss Berg comprises two buildings — one modeled after a Roman villa and the other resembling a Renaissance-era castle. There’s the Three-MICHELIN-Star Victor's Fine Dining by Christian Bau, another restaurant serving Italian cuisine, plus a German-style beer garden, and a spa inspired by ancient Roman baths. There’s a lot going on here, suffice it to say. But the mélange of cultural influences infuses the place with character one wouldn’t typically expect of a hotel that’s part of a chain, in this case, Victor’s, with more than a dozen locations across Germany.\n\nThe eclectic, more-is-more philosophy also applies to rooms and suites. Rooms in the villa feature sumptuous drapery, gilded headboards, richly carpeted floors — some in bold shades like emerald green or coral red — and artwork inspired by Roman antiquities. Those in the castle have a fairy tale aesthetic, with ornate mirrors and jewel-toned canopies over the beds. In both the villa and the castle, top-level suites offer extra space and beautiful views over the vineyards below. After breakfast, served on the terrace in good weather, a seemingly endless array of hiking and biking trails, wineries, and museums are within easy reach.

content:
The Swiss city of St. Gallen is primarily known for the extravagant beauty of its thousand-year-old abbey cathedral, and it’s right alongside the abbey in the center of town that the Einstein St. Gallen makes its home. Next to such a landmark, its charms can’t help but look somewhat subtle, but make no mistake — this is the finest hotel in town.

Rooms and suites are traditional and elegant, clad in marble, cherry wood, silk curtains and down duvets, with parquet floors or lamb’s-wool rugs, and though they’re classic in style they come equipped with all the present-day luxury-hotel necessities. In the Superior category, in the Junior Suites, as well as on the dedicated Ladies’ Floor — a welcome feature that’s not uncommon in this part of the world — you’ll also find docking stations and Nespresso machines.

They also take wellness seriously around here, and the Einstein Fitness Park offers spa treatments, massage, capacious fitness facilities, and a beautiful atrium pool. And for the other kind of restoration, you’ll have two restaurants and a bar at your disposal: the two-Michelin-star Einstein Gourmet, the more casual Bistro St. Gallen, and the elegant, English-style Einstein Bar, wherein you can relax properly at the Davidoff Cigar Lounge.

content: Portofino has some fabulous hotels, but only a few of them are set on the town’s charming central piazza, one of the most photographed spots on the impossibly picturesque Italian Riviera. Splendido Mare is one of them, and it’s a toss-up whether it’s more pleasant inside or out. The boutique hotel is tucked into a row of pastel-colored buildings on the cobblestoned Piazza Martiri dell’Olivetta, with its fragrant citrus trees, open-air cafés, and white sailboats bobbing in the harbor just steps away. Stepping through the front door, you’ll find Splendido Mare colorful and chic: redesigned by Studio Festen in 2021, the décor takes inspiration from the village’s nautical history and the retro glamour of its midcentury heyday. \n\nThe street-level lobby and bar features terracotta flooring, vintage Italian furnishings, and original artworks by Ligurian artists, while rooms and suites have antique pieces, Carrara marble bathrooms, and custom lighting crafted in northern Italy. The simplest rooms, overlooking the piazza, have light-filled bathrooms with walk-in showers, while suites come with private balconies facing the marina. With a private garden terrace and an ultra-spacious bathroom with a tub, the lavish signature suite takes up the building’s entire penthouse level. Breakfast can be served in rooms or on the restaurant’s terrace, and the adjacent bar serves aperitivi at tables on the piazza. In a playful wink to days gone by, Splendido Mare has another amenity that’s hard to come by: its very own gelateria, a fifties-styled ice cream parlor with a wide window for ordering a takeaway cone while standing in the square.

content: That’s a portmanteau of “Swiss” and “Texan”, if you’re wondering, and it’s a gamble that pays off bigger the longer you stay. Hotel Swexan draws on this dual heritage to conjure the effortless charm of continental service standards plus larger-than-life Texan swagger. It’s a lot of hotel in the Harwood district, itself a walkable oasis in Uptown Dallas, and there’s no shortage of must-try activities without even leaving the grounds. Call it cowboy entrepreneur: spacious, no-expense-spared rooms with commanding views, but also a freewheeling sense of humor and up-for-anything energy in the decor. It looks, feels, and acts like the flagship property it is. Head to the roof at some point every night and drink it in.

content: You’re not going to just happen across the 12th-century Slovene village of Spodnja Idrija, but it’s worth going out of your way when you know a hotel like Kendov Dvorec awaits at the end of the road. In its early days — records go back to 1377 — it was a country manor, and though the village has filled in around it, it still feels splendidly secluded, surrounded by gardens, lawns, and apple trees. Today it’s a classic small luxury hotel, with an old-world atmosphere that feels untouched by the passage of centuries, and an elegant restaurant that specializes in Idrija’s local culinary traditions, including trout from the Trebušica river.\n\nThe rooms and suites differ widely, not just in size but in their decoration as well. There’s nothing off-the-rack here, but rather a painstakingly assembled collection of antiques and unique pieces; the Master Suite is a particular highlight, spanning nearly 500 square feet plus an expansive outdoor terrace. And in the warmer months you’ll want to spend plenty of time out of doors — like any proper country-house hotel, Kendov Dvorec’s grounds are perfect for al fresco lounging, and the surrounding village and countryside are nothing if not picturesque.

content: Chef Kris de Roy worked in multiple Michelin-starred kitchens along the way to opening his own establishment, and in 2013 his own Restaurant Hofke van Bazel, tucked away in the picturesque East Flanders village of Bazel, was awarded a Michelin star of its own. As you will have gathered from the context, though, Hofke van Bazel is more than a restaurant — following the European tradition of chef-driven destinations, it’s a luxury boutique hotel as well.\n\nAnd a fine one, we might add. Two suites are contained in the original restaurant building, while three more are housed in the neighboring Relais de Bazel, a newer building that’s a worthy complement to the original structure. The suites in the old building are a touch more traditional, while the new ones display a more modern aspect, but they’re all clearly cut from the same artistic cloth. And they’re all more than a little bit luxurious — especially the loft in the new building, which offers impressive views from its wraparound terrace. Perfect for a culinary pilgrimage to the restaurant of the same name, and ideally located for visitors to Antwerp, which is less than half an hour’s drive away.

content:
It takes something special to stand out amid the futuristic, ultra-luxurious hotels on Dubai’s rapidly expanding skyline. One&Only One Za’abeel features not one but two shiny high-rises, connected by the world’s largest cantilever — and the cantilever is topped by the longest infinity pool in the UAE, dazzling and vertigo-inducing, more than 30 floors up from street level. 

Japanese architects Nikken Sekkei drew up the hotel’s ambitious design, and One&Only, best known for its high-end hotels in places like Greece, Mexico, and the Maldives, infused the interiors with their signature beach resort aesthetic. There’s still a somewhat formal atmosphere in many areas of the hotel — this is Dubai, after all — but One&Only’s various entertainment venues have a distinctly festive vacation vibe. In addition to the show-stopping infinity pool, with its timber-lined pool deck and Japanese-Peruvian bar and restaurant, there’s a quieter Balinese-inspired pool and garden on the fourth level, a sleek three-story spa, and an array of award-winning eateries and glamorous cocktail bars.

With so much on offer, the rooms and suites could feel like an afterthought. But they’re a getaway on their own, spacious and light-filled with floor-to-ceiling windows, minimalist décor, custom bath products, and spa-like bathrooms, many with soaking tubs. All have sweeping city views, and some face Burj Khalifa, the world’s tallest building. One&Only One Za’abeel calls itself the first urban vertical resort, and while competitors in the same category remain to be seen, a hotel this striking may just convince beachgoers to try a vacation in the big city.

content:
The stately building that houses A22 was originally constructed in the 1930s and served as the American embassy. With an ultra-modern addition and a thorough interior redesign, it now bridges the gap between classic and contemporary with ease and panache. The hotel takes its name from its address — Ausekļa iela 22 — blending local character with a cosmopolitan edge.
Its 20 rooms and suites are plush, stylish, and memorable, with rich textures, warm lighting, and carefully curated design details. The Presidential Suite pays tribute to John F. Kennedy, who stayed in these very rooms as a 22-year-old during a visit to Riga — an anecdote that gives the hotel a touch of historical glamour.
The hotel’s refined culinary offering, the restaurant JOHN, still bears his name, as does the exclusive 16-seat JOHN Chef’s Hall. It’s an intimate, elegant setting that perfectly encapsulates the A22 experience — where heritage, design, and gastronomy come together with remarkable style.

content: Seville has plenty of luxury hotels; until recently, they were all on one side of the river, clustered around the cathedral and the Alcázar. Cavalta Boutique Hotel is the first high-end property on the other side, in the Triana quarter, best known as the birthplace of flamenco. This 12-room boutique hotel, occupying a quaint corner building with wrought-iron balconies and cheerful ceramic tilework, stays true to the neighborhood’s bohemian roots. Rooms are simple and modern, with natural wood flooring, exposed brick walls, and colorful details from decorative headboards to emerald-green accent walls. It’s the common spaces that bring Cavalta to the next level, including a lovely rooftop garden, pool, and cocktail bar. The restaurant, Balbuena y Huertas, restaurant serves as a stylish meeting point for locals and travelers alike.

content: The green hill that is Montjuïc, rising up over Barcelona, was famously chosen as the site of the 1929 World’s Fair; the cable-car journey to the top is worthwhile for the museums, botanical gardens, and of course, the views. The InterContinental Barcelona, opened in 2021, offers luxury lodgings for those who’d rather stay up in this elegant district overlooking the Mediterranean. The hotel has plenty to like, from a rooftop pool and open-air bar with glittering views over the city to a restaurant  by Victor Torres, the youngest chef in Spain to earn a MICHELIN Star. The common spaces are pristine and modern, with lots of white marble and eye-catching light fixtures, and rooms and suites adhere to a similar aesthetic. Rounding out the hotel’s offerings are a sleek subterranean spa and a lively lobby-level cocktail bar and café.

content:
Midway between Madrid and Zaragoza, the agricultural region of Castilla-La Mancha has a tradition of grain cultivation that dates back to medieval times. Though many of its flour mills are no longer in use, one was reborn as the boutique hotel El Molino de Alcuneza. 

Most rooms are located inside the restored landmark and feature rustic wooden floors, exposed beams, antique furnishings, and bathrooms lined in hand-painted tile. In a newer building beside the pool, suites are more spacious and modern. All have views over the surrounding wheat fields, and the hotel’s restaurant leans fully into the theme with a menu of seven varieties of homemade bread. Organic wheat, spelt, and rye are the centerpiece of the breakfast spread, too, in the form of irresistible pastries, toast, and cakes paired with locally made cheeses and jams.

content: It’s entirely understandable if Belgrade missed out on the first wave of the boutique-hotel revolution. What’s important now, from the perspective of international travelers, is that there are now hotels in town of Saint Ten’s caliber. The stately old building, in the central district of Vračar, was built in the Twenties by architect Stojan Veljkovic, and over the past century it’s served as a backdrop for more than a few pivotal moments in the city’s political history. It’s since seen a dramatic modern addition, and today its interiors, though thoroughly contemporary, exhibit a certain seriousness, a sense of sober luxury that’s well suited to the history of the place.\n\nWhat this means in concrete terms is large spaces, luxe finishes, glass-walled stone bathrooms with rain showers or soaking tubs, and little details like espresso machines and bedside reading lights. The lobby bar is an all-day lounge that’s equally functional for a business meeting or a romantic cocktail or two, and L’Adresse transforms from a bright and sunny semi-formal dining room by day into an elegant fine-dining restaurant by night. Add a sauna, a massage room, and a “cardio meditation” room and you’ve got yourself a thoroughly modern boutique hotel.

content: Bangkok’s State Tower is best known as the home of Sirocco, the highest open-air restaurant in the world — and while the restaurant is an unmissable experience, waiting for the elevator to the lobby need not be. A few levels down, Tower Club at Lebua is a luxurious hotel-within-a-hotel occupying the 53rd through 59th floors. Every room is an ultra-spacious suite with an elegant living room, a spa-like bathroom with a walk-in shower and soaking tub, and floor-to-ceiling glass doors opening onto private balconies with panoramic views over the city and the Chao Phraya River. Some have multiple bedrooms, including the Hangover Suite, where perks include complimentary cocktails at the 64th-floor Sky Bar, a filming location for the 2009 comedy for which the suite is named. Like Sirocco, it’s part of the Dome at Lebua collection of rooftop restaurants and bars, along with the Two-MICHELIN-Starred Mezzaluna and Two-MICHELIN-Starred Chef’s Table, and Tower Club guests also have exclusive access to a poolside lounge serving gourmet snacks and drinks all day.

content: Burgundy is full of family-run hotels, but there’s something especially warm and welcoming about Maison Doucet. It’s due in part to the fact that this riverfront house was the childhood home of the owner, chef Frédéric Doucet. Like his menus, built around local and seasonal ingredients, the hotel is grounded in its place — and like the village of Charolles, nicknamed Little Venice for its romantic canals and footbridges, Maison Doucet is nothing if not pretty and peaceful.\n\nRooms and suites and bright and character-filled with original wood-beamed celings, cozy king-sized beds, and sleek, smartly outfitted bathrooms, some with freestanding tubs. The décor is mostly white, save for parquet floors and pops of color including patterned headboards and jewel-toned accent walls. In addition to a full spa, the grounds feature an outdoor swimming pool and a six-seater Jacuzzi. The wine country is a key element of the appeal, as is, of course, Mr. Doucet’s gastronomic restaurant.

content: Quiet luxury might have become an overused buzz phrase, but it’s hard to find a better way to describe Van Oys Maastricht Retreat. Sophisticated guest rooms blend natural stone walls and exposed beams with muted earthy shades, and in the higher category rooms, private terraces and balconies look onto the surrounding gardens. The same soothing palette sets the scene in the spa, which eschews the latest trend for high tech treatments and anti-aging in favor of back-to-basics relaxation. But the true heart of the hotel lies in the kitchen, with farm-to-table fare at Maes and elegant fine dining at Create complemented by wine ateliers and cooking classes led by Michelin-experienced chefs for a fuller immersion in the local terroir.

It laid empty for many years before being restored, reborn, and relaunched by the Corinthia Hotel Group in 2024. The sympathetic and detailed renovation work is best exemplified by the stunning Palm Court with its stained-glass skylight, while the 126 bedrooms blend classical elegance with modern facilities and contemporary levels of comfort.

content: Medieval Carcassonne, the birthplace of cassoulet and the Languedoc red wines that pair with it, is a foodie destination, so it stands to reason that several of its best hotels are attached to fine dining venues. So it is at Hôtel Le Parc, a boutique hotel that was created as an elegant and practical addition to the celebrated La Table de Franck Putelat. Come for the creative tasting menus and relax afterward, if you’ve adequately planned ahead, in one of the hotel’s ultra-chic rooms and suites. \n\nThere are just seven of them, and they’re all quiet and refined, outfitted with sophisticated lighting and modern but earthy decor — bearskin rugs, carved wooden chairs, artwork and design objects inspired by nature. Each has a large private terrace facing the surrounding landscape, making the most of the hotel’s leafy location beside Carcassonne’s old ramparts. Bathrooms are spacious and contemporary, with walk-in showers and housemade products, and several suites have private indoor or outdoor Jacuzzis. A lavish breakfast spread featuring local fruits and freshly baked bread can be enjoyed in the restaurant or delivered to one’s terrace.

content: Sometimes a name contains almost everything you need to know about a hotel. Tivoli Kopke Porto Gaia Hotel is a partnership between Portugal’s Tivoli hotel group and the venerable port wine producer Kopke, situated in Vila Nova de Gaia straight across the River Douro from the city of Porto itself. And it’s impressive on all counts, from its  stylish rooms and suites to its supremely restful wellness offerings, its vast contemporary art collection, and its swanky restaurants and bars.\n\nThe bedrooms are set in the winery’s old warehouses, which makes for some unusual floor plans, including a few rooms that trade windows for skylights. By the time you’re in a suite, you’re treated to plenty of space and some remarkable views of Porto across the river. An expansive spa and pool lends the hotel something of a resort atmosphere, and its restaurants, helmed by Chef Nacho Manzano, make it a culinary destination. Meanhwile both Gaia and Porto’s riverfront neighborhoods are easily walkable.

content: Ansitz Steinbock comes by its stone walls honestly. This sturdy structure’s foundations were laid in the 13th century, and while it’s been thoroughly renovated by hotelier Elisabeth Rabensteiner, its historical aspect is the first thing you’ll notice. The setting is the mountain village of Villandro, or Villanders, not far from Bolzano; the cuisine in the eponymous fine dining restaurant is pure South Tyrol, accompanied by Alto Adige wines. \n\nAnd the suites are as handsome as can be; though they retain features like original timbers and eccentric floor plans, they’re furnished with luxurious modern pieces and decorated with a keen, style-conscious eye. As for the destination, it needs little introduction — safe to say if it can be done in the mountains, it can be done within a fairly small radius around Villandro, as the seasons permit.

Though the Thailand-based Anantara brand made its name with a series of East Asian luxury resorts, it’s recently expanded into some European capitals, with equally impressive results. Anantara Palais Hansen Vienna Hotel stands right on the Ringstrasse, and occupies a 19th-century structure designed by Baron Theophil Edvard von Hansen.

Much care was taken to preserve the building’s historical elements, but what’s inside is, functionally, as modern a luxury hotel as any in town. The rooms and suites are generously sized and subtly high-tech beneath their contemporary-classic surfaces; the spa brings state-of-the-art Thai treatments to Central Europe.

Brasserie Sophie handles breakfast, while Theo’s Lounge & Bar serves drinks in the palace’s vast inner courtyard. The culinary highlight, though, is the one-MICHELIN-Star EDVARD, named for the Baron von Hansen himself.

content:
Casa Lavanda began as a family home, built by hand in the village of Ulupelit, less than an hour’s drive from Istanbul. And while it’s evolved over the years, it still feels deeply personal. Now a luxurious 16-room boutique hotel surrounded by forest, it’s stewarded by owners Feryal and Ahmet Şen and their two sons, and exhibits their love for slow living. 

Each room is individually named after a different variety of tree — cedar, cypress, laurel — and styled with handmade furnishings and carefully curated artworks and objets. Each one takes in a view of the hotel’s natural surroundings, and the vistas outside are complemented by the classic, understated style of the interiors.

Also on site are a biodynamic culinary garden, a spa with forest-facing saunas and a swimming pool, as well as a restaurant led by one of the family’s sons, an Italian-trained chef. An inspiring model of a more thoughtful way of life.

content:
There was a time when the Ace Hotels were strictly a Pacific Northwest phenomenon, and eyebrows were raised when they began work on a hotel in New York’s once-neglected NoMad neighborhood. But now the Ace Hotel New York feels like the flagship of this often-imitated hip hotel chain. Not only has it put this stretch of Broadway back on the map, it’s also got the kind of multi-purpose public space — co-working space by day, after-work drinking spot in the evening, and a full-fledged nightlife venue featuring DJs or live music as the hours tick by.

Its other public spaces are no less essential to the Ace’s appeal. The lobby is a versatile space suitable for everything from co-working to cocktails and events, Bistro 29 is a modern French restaurant, and Libera is the spot for late night drinks. And while Stumptown Coffee is no longer quite the rarity it once was, this was the first on the East Coast, and single-handedly raised New York’s coffee game upon arrival.

The Ace’s real innovation may be its rooms. This is a hotel that’s largely intended for people who plan to spend plenty of time out on the town, and for whom top-flight luxury is not a priority. Here attention is paid to the things that matter, from the carefully curated selection of snacks and drinks to occasional extras like turntables and acoustic guitars. There are certainly plusher rooms in town, but these might just be the coolest.

content:
A hotel doesn’t need much more than great rooms, inspiring public spaces, and thoughtful, efficient service. Of course it’s not as easy as it sounds. But when you’ve got the kind of pedigree the Ludlow Hotel has — it’s related to the Bowery, the Marlton and the Maritime, among other New York favorites — you’re beginning with a bit of a head start.

The Ludlow’s lineage is especially apparent in the ways in which it resembles the Bowery: the rooms are open and bright, with sun streaming through large casement windows, and the impeccable vintage styling feels historically rooted yet freshly finished. As a social center the Ludlow is just getting started — Dirty French, a fairly self-explanatory restaurant from the Major Food Group, another well-regarded local outfit, is joined by the lobby lounge, with its promised trellis garden, is sure to make a few nightlife lists.

And the service is an illustration of why we find ourselves loving the mini-chains — a hotel group with a manageable number of properties has some experience at providing a quality product, but with a long way to go before it becomes an ultra-standardized mega-corporation. The result is a hotel with personality in all the right places: the style can be quirky, but it’s best if the service isn’t; it’s great when the nightlife is a bit unusual, but in the room you want everything in the right place.

So we’ve got high hopes, and no reason to think we’ll be disappointed here. The Lower East Side, though no longer quite the wildest place in New York, is a long way from being tamed, and has long been a bit under-serviced in the hospitality department. Here’s to the Ludlow changing all that.

content:
From the outside it’s clear enough that the Bowery Hotel is a relatively recent addition to the neighborhood, but what’s inside is such a faithful homage to classic New York you’d be forgiven for starting to think it’s been here forever. Its eclectic, bohemian look helped usher in a new kind of romance in boutique-hotel style, and the timelessness of its aesthetic means the romance is still fresh long after the glossy minimalism of some of its contemporaries has begun to fade.

The rooms are inspired by an imaginary prewar Manhattan apartment, with furniture and design elements sourced from all over the world, many of them vintage or salvaged. With cast-iron frames on the full-length windows, patterned rugs on the hardwood floors, and beautiful weathered brass fixtures in the marble-and-tile bathrooms, the Bowery’s visual style is a distinctive and memorable one.

Gemma, the Bowery Hotel’s trattoria, is a neighborhood fixture, and for good reason, thanks to its confidently executed modern-classic Italian fare and its warm and convivial atmosphere. And the Bowery’s lobby bar is much more than an ordinary hotel lounge — with its warren of armchairs and sofas and its typically stylish clientele it’s one of downtown Manhattan’s most desirable spaces.

content:
Suffice it to say that the Saint James is anything but typical. In Paris an hôtel particulier, a freestanding house, is unusual enough — something like the Saint James, almost a country-style château, surrounded by a wall and garden, is vanishingly rare. It’s fresh off a thorough renovation by Laura Gonzalez, who has updated its unique interiors for a new decade; return visitors will find it subtler and more sophisticated than before, but no less expressive.

The building’s neoclassical atmosphere is playfully heightened by the new décor, and eclectic, worldly influences add depth to the design: Japanese wallpapers, Chinese antiques, and contemporary fixtures and furnishings by top French talents. Many of the bedrooms also benefit from country-house quantities of space to work with, spreading out quite comfortably, in contrast with the typical Parisian hotel room.

Bellefeuille, the hotel’s restaurant, has earned a MICHELIN Star; also notable is the Guerlain spa, which spans two floors and includes a rare indoor swimming pool. The Library Bar, too, has been updated to match the rest of the hotel’s transformation, and the Saint James Club, an English-style social club, draws its own crowd of creative, cultured Parisians.

content:
New York real estate prices being what they are, you can see why a spacious hotel room can easily run you a month’s rent back home. The flip side of this rule is that an affordable room is often laughably small. The Arlo NoMad, however, goes a long way toward solving the equation — through a combination of clever, compact layouts and the plentiful sunlight afforded by the full-length windows of a brand-new hotel building, its rooms manage to feel livable rather than laughable, in spite of their modest square footage.

In practice this means the bed occupies the majority of the room, with a front-row view straight out those big windows, and a bathroom that’s got space for a glass-enclosed rain shower. In size they range from cozy bunk rooms to relatively expansive king rooms, but they top out there. If you’re the penthouse-suite type, then the Arlo might not be for you — but some rooms do come with a terrace that’s as large as the room itself, for when the weather permits some al fresco lounging.

Anyway a hotel like the Arlo isn’t strictly about maximizing the in-room luxury. Here you’ve got plenty to tempt you out of your sleeping quarters, from the Middle Eastern cuisine at Lamalo to the second-floor cocktail bar, BARlo. Meanwhile a second rooftop bar provides an alternative venue, and a 24-hour bodega serves coffee and snacks around the clock. From here you’re close by to Murray Hill, lower Midtown, the Flatiron, and Koreatown — and the rest of Manhattan is only a subway ride away.

content: It’s the oldest story in real estate: the red-light district, down at heel and thus affordable for the creative artists who make up the avant garde of urban renewal, inevitably becomes the up-and-coming neighborhood where the rest of the city comes out to play. So it is with Paris’s Pigalle. And eventually, inevitably — if we’re lucky — along comes a hotel like Le Pigalle. The proprietor is no rank beginner, having cut his teeth on a couple of Alpine resorts, of all things — though he seems more at home, frankly, in this edgiest of urban districts. And while the eclectic décor has that perfectly measured casual charm that looks as though it just sort of came together, it’s the work of a pair of talented architects, and features contributions from any number of artisans and craftspeople local to Pigalle. Rooms dispense with most of the luxury-hotel trappings and focus on what matters: inviting spaces, whether compact or capacious; iPads and turntables, complete with enough music to get you through the night; and plentiful personality, in the form of artworks, objets, books, and furnishings both modern and vintage. A hotel like this doesn’t just get by on guest rooms, of course. The ground floor features a café, a restaurant and bar (overseen by Camille Fourmont, from Buvette, a wine bar in the 11th), and a kiosk selling a carefully curated selection of books and newspapers. At the weekend the hotel puts on a proper party, complete with DJ, and even on a Sunday night it feels like a nexus of activity. And it bears keeping in mind that Pigalle hasn’t entirely lost touch with its red-light roots — mixed in with the cocktail bars of SoPi are some establishments that lend a decided edge. (It also bears keeping in mind that Le Pigalle Paris is far from the quietest hotel in our Parisian collection; if you’re here in search of perfect silence you’ve come to the wrong place.)

content:
Of all the haunted hotels, the Chateau Marmont has to be the most glamorous. Located on LA’s Sunset Strip, it’s where Clark Gable and Jean Harlow got sizzling while she was on her honeymoon with another man. Howard Hughes got himself a penthouse and a pair of binoculars and spied on the girls by the pool. If you’re going to misbehave, a young William Holden was told, do it at the Marmont. And needless to say, the ghost at the Marmont is inclined to be naughty. One guest claimed it got into her bed.

The building is pure movie set. Constructed along the specifications of the Loire Chateau Amboise, it is a perfect eighteenth-century replica, fluted pillars graced by ivy and untouched by mold, with a swimming pool to boot. The lobby is dramatic, with gothic vaulted ceilings and dark wood. The restaurant is the perfect refuge from the cutthroat LA world outside; it seats about twelve, serves upscale gastro-pub fare from the new version of the Bar Marmont next door, and is always quiet and never rushed.

Hotel rooms are swank, Golden-Era Hollywood at its most cheerful, straight out of a Preston Sturges flick, and every one of them is different in size and style. Pick your favorite, as every guest seems to have their own. There are pool-side cabanas that make you want to don on your movie-star glasses and two-piece white swimsuit; there are frothy Deco palaces à la Carole Lombard, Latin bungalows, and cheerfully frilly Doris Day nooks. Together with embroidered Frette linens, it’s no wonder that so many guests just move in, joining a roster that includes Jim Morrison (who jumped off its roof), F. Scott Fitzgerald (who had a heart attack buying cigarettes across the street), and Robert De Niro.

Greta Garbo loved it because it was the only place where birds would sing on her window, and when the parties got too loud, her elegant Swedish figure could be found stretched out on a sofa in the lobby, softly slumbering far away from the noise. 

The Marmont’s greatest charm, however, has been its privacy. More people than Garbo have come here to be alone. Some guests don't leave their rooms for weeks. It's even easier now, with the introduction of room service that is discreet, and a telephone system that actually works. There are many spots on Sunset to be bad, but the Chateau Marmont has been doing it since 1929 and it’s still going strong. And if, while you’re there, your sweetheart, like Harlow, disappears into the arms of a high-powered someone else, there’s always a most obliging ghost.

How to get there:
Chateau Marmont is a 30-minute drive from Los Angeles International Airport, but the trip can take up to an hour in traffic. Valet parking is available for $65 USD per night.

content:
Among travel writers it’s most famous as the final overnight resting place of Oscar Wilde, but L’Hôtel is perhaps even more notable for having been a boutique hotel before the concept of a boutique hotel had even been invented. This Left Bank cult classic packs as much personality as it’s possible to pack into its 20 rooms — which have been redesigned by no less singular a Parisian designer than Jacques Garcia himself.

In this case, at least, there’s no contradiction between boutique personality and luxe grandeur; by virtue of its scale, L’Hôtel can’t offer the full palace-hotel treatment, but its guests are spared no comfort. Every room is different, and not subtly different, either — though they bear the stylistic signature of the same designer, each one is an experience unto itself.

The subterranean hammam pool is a memorable luxury, and it’s possible to book a massage by the poolside. Meanwhile, the hotel’s social life takes place in Wilde’s Lounge, a nightspot as decadent as its namesake, dedicated to apéritifs, cocktails, and jazz. In Parisian boutique-hotel style, you’ll have to venture outside for a restaurant; given the setting in Saint-Germain-des-Prés, you won’t have far to go.

content:
In Paris we’re always on the lookout for something that shows a little restraint, whether that means understated style, unimposing atmosphere, or reasonably affordable rates. It’s rare to find all three at once, but that’s more or less what the Hôtel Keppler offers: a sensible amount of luxury, a surprising degree of quiet (for a hotel just off the Champs-Élysées), and interiors that manage to avoid excess in either direction, whether antique or avant-garde.

This style demonstrates the difficulty of grading hotel design along a single dimension, from ancient to modern. Here Pierre-Yves Rochon wraps classic elements in modern clean lines, creating interior spaces that are at once eye-catchingly contemporary and full of historical character. At a glance they’re definitively Parisian, but also definitively 21st-century.

Though at thirty-nine rooms it’s intimate enough, the Keppler quietly features a few bigger luxuries — there’s no restaurant, but there is a sauna, a steam room, and a small gym, all of which might come in handy after a long day pounding the Parisian cobblestones. Better suited to a romantic getaway or a shopping expedition than a business trip perhaps, but executives lucky enough to have business in central Paris will likely have few complaints.

content:
Italy isn’t exactly hurting for impressive small hotels, but Torre di Moravola stands out all the same. Frankly, they had us at “thousand-year-old Umbrian hilltop watchtower converted into a seven-room boutique hotel,” and that was before we ever saw inside. For while the exterior may be a thousand years old, the interiors are as modern as they come.

It may have a little something to do with the owners. Christopher Chong is an architect, a former Norman Foster associate, and his wife, Seonaid Mackenzie, is a designer. And what they’ve done is more than a renovation. Within the outer shell of the tower they’ve constructed an entirely new inner structure, with seven strikingly modern suites arranged around a central stair.

This turns out to be a surprisingly green way to build. The old stone walls keep temperatures stable, and the central stair gives rise to convection currents which ventilate as well as any air conditioning system. And the suites, with their stone walls and sunken baths, stay remarkably comfortable, despite their minimalism, while solar panels have made the hotel very nearly electrically self-sufficient.

Most unexpected, perhaps, is the rooftop infinity pool, with obviously wide-ranging views of the tower’s surroundings; there’s also a spa set in the forest with its own views of the valley, equipped with a sauna, a marble hammam, and a jacuzzi on the terrace. Meanwhile the restaurant follows the slow food philosophy, and you’re minutes from the ancient town of Montone, which offers other options, none of them particularly fast. As Italian countryside getaways go, it’s hard to do much better — and as a design pilgrimage it’s practically a religious experience.

Please note: Torre di Moravola is open seasonally from the end of March through mid-November.

content:
Malibu is a destination whose reputation, at least for visitors, rests more on legend than experience. It’s a magical little stretch of coastline, but one whose hotel options have historically been thin. No longer; the Surfrider Malibu is a Fifties icon transformed by its new owners — a Californian architect, an Australian-born free spirit, and an Italian race car driver — into the boutique hotel this town has always deserved, set right on the Pacific Coast Highway, directly across from Surfrider Beach.

The look is pared-down and elegant, a sort of bohemian minimalism, the 20 rooms decorated in light neutrals that are full of organic textures, from the reclaimed teak floorboards to the modern-rustic furnishings created by local designers. Upstairs rooms have private terraces with partial or full views of the Pacific. They’re far from lavish or opulent but they’re luxurious in their details, and life here is anything but difficult — though more than a little bit glamorous, the vibe here is light-hearted and fun.

And while some of our favorite hotels use their public spaces to interact with the local scene, the Surfrider’s roof terrace restaurant and bar is for guests only, in keeping with the intent of the hotel: more a private Malibu beach house than a typical boutique hotel. It’s a refuge, but not an isolated one — the views of the pier, the Pacific, and one of California’s most famous beaches lend it an unmistakable sense of place.

Please note: The Surfrider Malibu is a small property with only 20 rooms. Book early as rooms sell out quick. For a view, book an upstairs room — if storage space is a concern, book a suite. For arrival, be aware that the reception is open from 6:30 AM until 10:30 PM.
