content:
It makes sense that a “Hotel of the People” would go where the people are. The sequel to the hip, youthful Mob Hotel in Paris thus finds itself in Lyon, the second largest urban area in France. The setting is the newly redeveloped Confluence, the waterfront district where the Saône and Rhône rivers come together. Which is a fitting metaphor — the Mob Hotel’s proprietor, hotel impresario Cyril Aouizerate, intends this to be a place where people, travelers and locals alike, similarly come together.

The building’s distinctive contemporary silhouette is a hint that the hotel within is an unusual one, but it’s more than a matter of design. Aouizerate has spent years discovering what makes a hotel an appealing place to be, and this is the result of his study; there’s more to do here than sleep, to say the least. You’ll find yoga classes, live music, pop-up shops, and all manner of one-off events, in addition to the perennial charms of the hotel’s Mediterranean restaurant and its lively lounge and riverfront terrace.

Not to be overlooked are the rooms, which are thriftily decorated but don’t feel bare — raw concrete and blonde wood contribute visual texture, and some strategic pops of color bring the décor to life. They’re by no means enormous, but that’s not the point — for the Mob’s guests, they hit all the right notes.

content: You might imagine you know what to expect from a 19th-century mansion hotel in Bordeaux, but Yndō Hotel’s unusual name might just be a clue that you’re in for a surprise. The exterior of this hotel particulier remains as traditional as ever, oriented as it is around a quiet central courtyard. Once you’ve ventured into the interior of the house, though, you’ll see what we mean — the architecture is still classic, but the interior design is totally contemporary, as is the hotel’s art collection. Everything is carefully sourced by the hoteliers, who hand-picked the designers, the artisans, and of course the artists, and the result is a visual experience where every angle feels meticulously considered. That’s most of what matters in a design hotel, to be honest — the rest is taste, and that’s something Yndō’s proprietors have in spades. Witness the twelve rooms, all different, from the “cosy” rooms with their warm woods and neutral tones, to the “crazy” rooms with their saturated colors and postmodern flourishes, and the suites, which are eclectic, stylish, and luxurious. There’s no formal restaurant, but in a hotel of this size, there doesn’t need to be. Instead the kitchen serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner — or, indeed, anything you’d like, 24 hours a day — in the hotel’s dining room, on the terrace, or in your room or suite. And this being Bordeaux, a glass of extraordinary wine is always at hand....

content:
St. Barth isn’t exactly clamoring for attention — flying just under the radar suits tony Londoners and Parisians fine, thanks — but some opportunities you can’t pass up. Namely when they’re some ways outside of Gustavia; not to knock the capital, but yachts are yachts, and keeping up with the Joneses (Jacqueses?) is one of the easiest roads from unspoiled to spoiled, especially in the tourism world. Anyway, all roads are easy on a Caribbean island. Take one northwest to the Colombier hilltop overlooking Flamands beach and you can’t miss Hotel Gyp Sea Saint Barth. 

Here we have the next in a prestigious line of Sibuet offspring, a colonial stunner exemplifying plantation Francophilia. You don’t have to be a style nomad to appreciate the white-sand beaches, naturally, but it helps in parsing the décor; seashell, yes, coral, yes, but also model ships and cordage and sundry merchant-marinisms in polished wood. The 21 bungalows and villas may sound like sugary cocktails (“Pineapples,” “Jungle Passion”), but on the whole they stick to tasteful variations on the earthy-meets-beachy formula, spicing up canopied four-posters and vintage furnishings with vivid turquoises and saffrons. Freestanding tub, check, private terrace, check. 

If that sounds like a tropical garden, let’s talk about tropical gardens — here it’s palm, banana, mango, cactus, and bougainvillea sheltering the outdoor pool, or it’s Pure Altitude spa’s divine botanical treatments. The slow life continues at the beach club, Gyp Sea, and at the chef’s table, an institution devoted to intoxicating haute-Caribbean flavor profiles with a veritable doctorate in seafood. As if that weren’t enough, the bar builds on the world summoned dreamily from the past: lazy mahogany ceiling fans, fragrant curls of cigar smoke in the fumoir, and a truly world-class fleet of rums.

content:
Soho House has a knack for finding buildings with character, but they’ve outdone themselves with Soho House Paris. This 19th-century apartment building in Pigalle, the former red-light district turned nightlife playground, is distinctive enough on its own terms — but it turns out it was once inhabited by the family of the writer, artist, and filmmaker Jean Cocteau. Today it’s been given the Soho House treatment, which means its style resembles an English country house with an urban Parisian edge, plus a wealth of inspiration from Santo Sospir, Cocteau’s Cap Ferrat villa — and from the Art Deco style that’s more or less synonymous with Parisian luxury.

Rooms range from the Tiny Attic to the Big Boudoir, and while they place a strong emphasis on visual impact, they don’t neglect comfort — you won’t mistake Soho House Paris for one of the city’s grand palace hotels, but it’s full of thoughtful little luxuries and unobtrusive modern conveniences.

As lovely as the rooms are, it’s the common spaces that make up the bulk of Soho House’s appeal. Club members — of which you are one during your stay — have access to an impressively equipped (and staffed) fitness program, as well as a steam room and sauna. A substantial art collection adorns spaces like the Winter Garden, the Petit Salon, and the Pool Terrace, where members and guests dine and drink. And the basement Cabaret Room, a performance and events space, is pure Moulin Rouge fantasy.

content:
Often the grandest and most luxurious hotels lack a little something in the personality department, but that’s not the case with the Anantara Siam Bangkok Hotel. The building that it occupies, right across from the Royal Bangkok Sports Club in the heart of downtown, was formerly a Four Seasons, and before that a Peninsula. But now, as the flagship of the Bangkok-based Anantara group, it’s evolved into its final form: an opulent, colonial-style grand hotel that’s quickly become a favorite among upper-crust locals.

With 354 rooms and suites, its scale is as grand as its atmosphere, though it spreads out rather than up, and feels splendidly secluded despite its urban setting. The rooms are contemporary in style and in color, though they’re full of authentic old-world Thai detail, and in terms of comfort they’re the equal of just about any modern luxury hotel.

You can expect the full complement of services as well, from the Anantara Spa and the lovely outdoor pool to an astonishing eight food-and-beverage venues. These range from the lobby, with its all-day menu and afternoon tea service, to the upscale Japanese Shintaro, the Tony Chi–designed Madison steakhouse, and the venerable Spice Market, one of Bangkok’s most famous high-end Thai restaurants.

content:
The logo for Istanbul’s Lampa Design Hotel is a nod to the owner’s personal collection of antique gas lamps, but it also evokes a familiar fantasy: rub the magic lamp and make your wishes. A perfect location in the central neighborhood of Şişli? Granted. Modern, art-filled guest rooms stocked with amenities? Sure. A cool coffee bar and a Turkish-style breakfast buffet? You got it.

True, these wishes are within the realm of reasonable expectation: this is an urban boutique hotel, not a five-star resort. But it’s surprising how many small hotels fall short of the ideal. Not Lampa Design Hotel. Thanks to thoughtful design and a modest scale — the hotel has just twenty rooms — it’s both stylish and practical, the kind of place where every detail has already been considered.

The aesthetic is modern industrial, heavy on iron and glass, especially on the ground level. It’s here, at Lampa Lab, that you’ll plan your day over breakfast, answer a few e-mails in the adjacent workspace, or have afternoon tea on the small patio, lined with cheerful terrariums. Upstairs, guest rooms and suites have a cozier look, with parquet floors, large picture windows, and original artworks by the late avant-garde painter Fikret Mualla Saygı. Standard rooms are on the small side, but they’re efficiently laid out with bespoke furniture and elegantly illuminated by customized lighting systems. In-room features are plentiful across categories, too, including marble-lined bathrooms with rain showers and products by Co.Bigelow, LCD TVs, free wi-fi, and complimentary coffee, tea, and bottled water.

It’s the little things, isn’t it? And it’s the big things, like the important fact that you’re right in the heart of Istanbul. This popular new option is proof that you don’t need to trade off location for style or substance: at Lampa Design Hotel you get all three wishes.

We love an edgy, bohemian boutique or a glossy style experiment as much as anyone, but there’s something to be said for the pleasures of a classic grand hotel. Especially a classic grand hotel in a beautiful old European capital like Trieste, where the Starhotels Savoia Excelsior Palace stands rather majestically over the waterfront, with half its rooms facing out into the bay.

The facade of the century-old building is as it always was, but the interiors are fresh off a total renovation, the look updated but not quite re-imagined — it’s a very contemporary elegance, but one that’s in keeping with the building’s classic style. Along with the copious hardwood and marble in the guest rooms you’ll find tactile luxuries like feather beds as well as must-have conveniences like LCD televisions and wireless internet.

A fine restaurant and a dramatically styled cocktail bar offer views out to sea from oversized windows. There’s more meeting and events space than you could possibly need, and the central location means most of this compact city is easily accessible. This stunning old city is where Italy meets Eastern Europe, or perhaps vice versa — and for an introduction you could do much worse than the Savoia.

content: The American-born dancer Loïe Fuller was nothing short of a sensation from her first appearance at the Folies Bergère, her swirling silk robes memorably captured in works by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec and Auguste Rodin; Miss Fuller celebrates her legacy and the Art Nouveau movement she personified. Just steps from the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Élysées, it’s a boutique hotel from the Drawing Hotels Collection, a Parisian brand that creates one-of-a-kind hotels in close collaboration with artists, designers, and the NIDO architectural agency. The building’s fanciful stone façade dates back to the late 19th century, but the interiors are the work of five artists who were invited to revitalize its rooms in the spirit of the Belle Époque.\n\nA large-scale installation by Raphaëlle Peria occupies the ground level; dedicated to the theme of changing seasons, it features a beautiful carpet patterned with hand-drawn water lilies and delicate botanical murals that curve around the breakfast room. Upstairs, each floor represents a singular creative vision — romantic, boldly graphic black and white florals on one, dreamy nocturnal nature imagery on another — and no two rooms are alike. But they all have custom-designed wallpaper, flooring, and decor, charmingly tiled Italian-style bathrooms, cozy bathrobes, and Nespresso machines. There’s plenty of old-world character, too, that predates the artists’ interventions: many rooms have antique frosted-glass partitions, wrought-iron balconies, or cozy reading nooks. Downstairs, the glass-ceilinged lounge bar serves Art Nouveau-inspired cocktails, and an art concierge stands by with advice for exploring the city.

content:
Oliverea is just down the road from Big Indian, in the Catskills of New York State; it’s home to only a few hundred people, and doesn’t exactly loom large in the public imagination — but that’ll change now that it’s home to the third Eastwind hotel. Like its siblings, the Eastwind Hotel - Oliverea Valley is inspired by rural Scandinavian (or maybe Baltic) design; two of Eastwind’s three founders are from Germany and Lithuania, respectively.

Unlike the other Eastwinds, this one began as an empty lot; the buildings were purpose-built for hotel use, and the hotel’s 27 rooms are as stylish as anything in rural New York State, combining as they do a rustic unpretentiousness and a minimalist Nordic simplicity. The rooms in the lodge are furnished with vintage mid-century pieces, and the trademark triangular cabins range from tent-sized all the way up to 400-square-foot suites, the latter of which come with en-suite bathrooms.

Dandelion, the restaurant, is the work of Eastwind’s third founder, a veteran of the New York City restaurant scene. The cuisine is not just local and seasonal but conceptually tailored to the Catskills setting, with an emphasis on “hunter-gathering and conscious farming.”

content: Just a couple of miles outside of Avignon’s city center, on the island of Barthelasse, which bisects the Rhône river, there’s a patch of countryside that’s as bucolic as anything in Provence. Here, combining the tranquility of a country bed and breakfast with easy access to one of France’s most picturesque medieval cities, is the Mas de Capelou, a beautiful 17th-century farmhouse that’s been converted into a lovely little hotel, one that retains its historic aesthetics even as it offers a contemporary boutique-hotel experience.\n\nThe old farmhouse’s period architecture remains intact, and has been meticulously preserved and restored, while the decoration of its five rooms reveals the attention of a modern eye — there’s a focused simplicity to the interiors that feels remarkably fresh. The four apartments, by contrast, are more modern in character, without losing touch with their Provençal personality. The visuals, however, are only a small part of the Mas de Capelou’s appeal; the idyllic little swimming pool is a fine place to soak up some sun, and the grounds offer ample opportunity for pastoral relaxation. La Brousse restaurant serves a tapas-style menu which can be enjoyed over a game of pétanque and alongside one of the hotel’s own cocktail creations.

content:
Sometimes a hotel’s appeal is as simple as the sum of its parts. The Sri Lankan coast is an extraordinary place for a holiday, and the luxury-tent safari camps of southern Africa offer an unforgettable immersion in nature. Put the two together and you’ve got Wild Coast Tented Lodge, on the southeast coast of Sri Lanka, sandwiched between a gorgeous beach and the utterly wild Yala National Park, home to elephants, leopards, monkeys, and much more.

Though the idea of a tented camp is a slightly retro one, Wild Coast engaged a group of contemporary architects, whose creations — called “cocoons” and “urchins,” the latter for kids — feel futuristic, or maybe retro-futuristic, right down to the copper basins and bathtubs. You’ll feel like an adventurer, albeit one for whom no comfort is too plush, including a spa and a stunning infinity pool.

The food and beverage program is a particular focus, owing perhaps to the fact that Wild Coast, along with sister hotels Cape Weligama and Ceylon Tea Trails, is owned by the Dilmah tea company. (The tea, needless to say, flows abundantly.) Other facilities include fitness space The Quarry, the open-air Dune Lounge for taking some quiet time and enjoying the sunset, and The Fossil Room for younger travelers to learn about nature and biodiversity through play. The centerpiece of the experience, though, remains the Lodge’s incredible array of curated experiences — rangers accompany guests on game drives and nature walks, a Junior Ranger program adapts the experience for kids, and bike tours, guided visits to ancient jungle monasteries, and Sri Lankan cooking classes ensure that the setting leaves its mark on every guest.

content:
The idea of Bavaria in the Rockies may raise eyebrows, but it’s no gimmick — this remarkably authentic Alpine-style resort is owned by the same Faessler family that opened the original Sonnenalp hotel in Ofterschwang in the years immediately following the First World War. It’s the sort of personality that no contemporary designer could possibly fake: almost more European than its counterparts in the Alps, it’s the perfect antidote to the commercial luxury on offer elsewhere in Vail.

The service is charmingly old-world, as are the interiors: each of the 127 rooms and suites is decorated in classic style, with wooden ceiling beams and even the occasional set of antlers. Each comes with a gas fireplace and an expansive marble bathroom complete with double sinks, heated floors and a deep soaking tub. Views are of Vail Village or Gore Creek.

There are no half measures here: the Sonnenalp boasts no fewer than four restaurants, from Southwestern-style cuisine to a formal European restaurant. Winter is obviously Vail’s strong suit; the lifts are just a short walk through the village from the hotel’s front door, and any other winter sport you can imagine can be arranged. Or take it easy at the Sonnenalp’s spa, offering everything from massage and beauty treatments to aromatherapy and yoga, as well as the distinctive alpine pleasure of an outdoor Jacuzzi.

content:
Many of the Catskills’ old resorts are back, in one form or another, but few of them can claim as long a history as Callicoon Hills. The original house dates back to 1905, and by the ’40s it had established itself as a resort, well in advance of the Catskills boom of the Sixties. It’s always been known for its singularly laid-back, laissez-faire atmosphere, and the slogan “a friendly place for nice people” is as true now as it was then. And while today’s Callicoon Hills retains its delightful throwback atmosphere, it’s right at home in the boutique-hotel era of the 21st century.

It turns out that the slightly homespun charm that allowed the original Callicoon Hills to be overshadowed by a generation of bigger, grander Catskills resorts is exactly what makes it so memorable, and so inimitable, today. Comforts like air conditioning and swanky subway-tile showers have been added to the accommodations, and Conover Club, the restaurant, is no mere camp cafeteria, but a proper restaurant and bar specializing in modern American comfort food. Add a perfectly charming swimming pool and a setting that’s surrounded by all manner of outdoor activities and you’ve got yourself a stone-cold classic of the Catskills camp genre.

content:
It’s not the first image that springs to mind when you think of visiting the Cape, but maybe it should be. The wine country has as much to recommend it as the coast — more, one supposes, if you’re into wine — and hotels like the Cellars-Hohenort are a big reason why. The magnificent Table Mountain serves as a backdrop to this winery-estate manor house, in the Constantia Valley region just east of Cape Town proper.

The old house is a stunner, and it’s been well kept — the rooms are charming but quite modern, rather large, and the views none too shabby either. Two pools keep guests cool while a third belongs to the Madiba Villa, a separate two-story courtyard house with its own service kitchen and its own butler — accommodation options run the range from this luxury villa all the way down to some very smart single rooms.

The Cellars-Hohenort is surrounded by manicured gardens and comes complete with a spa, a beauty salon, even some conference rooms — but like any proper winery-estate hotel, it’s geared just as much toward drinking and dining as anything else. As for dining, the Conservatory offers a garden-forward blend of seasonal plates, traditional classics, and Liz McGrath's own recipes.

How to get there: The Cellars-Hohenort is approximately a 25-minute drive from Cape Town International Airport and 15 minutes from Cape Town City Center.

content: If only these red brick walls could talk. Hotel Palazzetto Rosso, located in the heart of Siena’s medieval center, has been hosting travelers since the Middle Ages. Plenty has changed since the inn’s original heyday, when traders from all over the world came to Tuscany on business. But the building itself was constructed according to 13th-century planning regulations, and the original façade, decorated with traditional wrought-iron ensigns and flares, remains the same. Inside, the hotel has changed with the times. Tuscany is more of a leisure destination than a merchants’ crossroads, and the nine-room Palazzetto Rosso is much more than a place to rest your head between trade deals. It’s a place to linger over cappuccino at cheerful red N7 table that resembles a piece of oversized origami, or to relax in a 3D armchair by Pedrali. Indeed, the decor at Hotel Palazzetto Rossi represents a greatest hits list of contemporary Italian designers. There’s old-world elegance in the architecture, to be sure — high vaulted ceilings, rich frescoes, curving archways — but the slate gray floor tiles are by 14 Ora Italiana, the mod Zippo banquettes and cool white bar by Claudio Dondoli and Marco Pocci, the lighting scheme by Michele De Lucchi and Giancarlo Fassina for Artémide. All told, it’s a satisfying mix of Tuscan tradition and cutting-edge design. Take the bistro tables by Luca Nichette for Casamania: they’re done in black and white, the official colors of Siena. It’s impossible to guess just how many people have climbed up the imposing brick staircase that leads from the lobby to the guest rooms and suites above. No two rooms are alike, but all feature a mix of old and new. Expect painted friezes, wood-beamed ceilings, stone fireplaces and Venetian drapery alongside striking modern design pieces, Smart TVs, and contemporary artwork. Some suites contain unexpected amenities. In Suite 3, for instance, the bathtub is located in a giant glass and concrete cube in the center of the room, while other rooms offer priceless relics from the past, like a sink fitted with an antique fountain. All rooms and suites have views over some sort of interesting Italian scene, whether it be the silhouette of Monte dei Paschi Bank — the oldest extant bank in the world, thank you very much — or a cobblestone street filled with locals standing in line for gelato. Indeed, all of Siena’s historic treasures and pleasures are just outside the Hotel Palazzetto Rosso’s front door. A fair number show up on the breakfast buffet table, too — check out the spread of local charcuterie and cheese — and in the hotel’s charming enoteca, a quiet candlelit venue to enjoy a glass or two at the end of the day.

content:
We may go to São Paulo for a taste of Brazil but when the Paulistanos are in the mood to escape, some head east: to São Sebastião, a coastal enclave some two and a half hours away. It’s not a resort town, per se, nor is it the “humble fishing village” of Brazilian-tourism cliché — it’s a town whose inhabitants, some of them part-timers, privately carry on the business of enjoying the beachfront geography and (nearly) tropical climate. Which makes it ideal for a small and intimate getaway like the Ilha de Toque Toque Eco Hotel.

Its situation just outside of town means it’s on the quiet side, which is entirely the point. The 14 rooms sit on a hillside fifty meters above the sea, with hammocks on their decks, overlooking a charmingly unfinished beach. Quite a contrast with the high-rise hotels of somewhere like Rio — here the activities are more on the sedate side, with guests lounging by the pool, in their room’s hot tub, plunge pool, or sauna, or in the spa (by L’Occitane au Brésil) — or else making their way down to the beach or exploring the jungle on foot or mountain bike. There’s nothing all that glamorous about it, aside from the glamour inherent in disappearing to the Brazilian seashore for a while — which, for many of us, is more than enough.

content:
We’re all for hoteliers recycling the local architecture rather than splashing out for brand-new buildings. Provence has its farmhouses, America its motor inns, and Belgium, lucky Belgium, seems to be covered with abbeys, monasteries, nunneries. Check into a boutique hotel in Brussels called the Dominican and you know exactly what you’re getting into.

Though in this case it’s not exactly all damp stone and sconces. Inside it’s more accurate to say it’s abbey-inspired, brought very much up to date by the Dutch firm FG Stijl, whose name you may recognize from a growing list of high-end boutique commissions across Europe.

The rooms, while not excessive in size, are surely bigger than your average monk’s cell, and they’ve got the comforts that count in all the right places — feather beds, in-room espresso machines, the kind of bathrooms you want to cancel your morning meetings for.

There’s a bit of a spa, a little gym, a pleasant inner courtyard and a rather informal lounge/bar/restaurant, whose full menu is available anywhere you like until 11pm. Perfect for a bit of cloistering, but also close by to the opera house and to some fine shopping, should any more worldly temptations strike.

content:
Vivanta by Taj Coral Reef Maldives, in spite of (or perhaps by virtue of) its unwieldy name, is the sort of place that needs very little by way of explaining. It’s an overwater villa resort on a pocket-sized Maldivian island, and as is so often the case when it comes to this sort of hotel, in this part of the world, a significant portion of our readership will be already packing its bags. But for those who require some elaboration — or for those who need a capsule explanation of the genre — we’ll indulge in a little description.

The Taj group are no new hands when it comes to high-end hospitality. And the Maldives aren’t exactly rookies when it comes to the whole desert-island castaway fantasy. Half of the sixty-odd thatched-roof villas are of the overwater variety, with ladders in place so that it’s only a couple of steps from the bedroom to the shallow lagoon. The beach villas, however, are scarcely less impressive, boasting added indoor and outdoor space to make up for the unspeakable privation of opening straight onto the beach rather than straight into the water. It’s perhaps a matter of personal preference but we can’t imagine anyone’s complaining.

Just be sure you’re ready to disconnect for a bit. Electronic communications are of course effortlessly provided, but don’t expect to stroll into town or shop the local galleries. There aren’t any. Once you’ve completed the sub-one-hour speedboat ride from Malé airport you’re alone with your thoughts, your companion and the sea. Which is, needless to say, more or less entirely the point.

content:
The Oberoi Rajvilas is, quite perfectly, the India of our imagination, with all her beauties distilled and dusted down, plus the conveniences and the luxuries that only a modern mind could dream of. Fortress walls gleam white in the moonlight, surrounding an 18th-century Hindu temple rising out of a lotus-strewn pond. Carved elephants rear at entrances, and fountains glitter lavishly with hand-painted blue tiles. Dancers perform by candlelight, as you dine off of handmade tablecloths. Men stalk the grounds in uniform, shooing the birds away. The beauty is almost unreal—not the ravaged beauty of history, but the unspoiled beauty of dreams. So it’s not surprising to find out that most of The Oberoi Rajvilas is only five years old, though constructed using traditional techniques like camel-pulled mills. It’s also not surprising that the architects took more of their inspiration from paintings than real life. This isn’t authenticity, it’s fantasy, but it definitely feels and looks good.

The ratio of staff to guests here is five to one. Staff scurry out to greet you with a glass of watermelon juice after you emerge from your air-conditioned jeep. At every turn, there is someone—dressed in traditional costume—somberly awaiting your instructions. Warning. If being waited on bugs you, you may want to steer clear; some people find the scope of servility here a little unnerving. The rest of us just lean back by the blue tiled pool and wait for our drinks to be topped up or indulge in an Ayurvedic at the Spa. But for the ultimate in exoticism and pampering stay in a tent inspired by those taken by royalty on hunting chests. Decorated with Victorian beds, steamer trunks and claw foot tubs and roofed in thick silk with rollaway rugs, they also boast air conditioning and hot water. And did we also mention that they come with cooks, servants and dancers?

So if you want to experience India as reality, by all means, get into a rickshaw and take your chances in the heaving mass of the Pink City. But if you want to preserve India as a fantasy then the The Oberoi Rajvilas is the place for you. We promise that it won’t disappoint your imagination.

There’s a certain set of tradition-bound travelers for whom every town, no matter how big, really has only one place to stay — the Copacabana in Rio, the Peninsula in Hong Kong, the Oberoi when visiting the Taj. In Buenos Aires, that hotel has more or less always been the Alvear Palace. It’s the high-society heart of Argentina, a place where bejeweled socialites gather to sip tea, and where a freshly pressed business suit would be perfectly fitting breakfast attire. (The Alvear’s breakfast, as anyone in these circles will tell you, is legendary.) And behind all the surfaces — the gleaming white marble, the Persian rugs, the teardrop chandeliers — there’s an exceedingly comfortable, unfailingly well-run hotel, every bit the match of all the pomp. 

The rooms are so ornate, with their floral-print gold-colored bedding and Louis XVI furniture, they almost feel out of time. There are heaps of fruit and flowers, heftily framed oil paintings on the walls, deep baths with vials of the finest Hermès suds at their sides. Butler service is round-the-clock, and for those who’ve brought a staff of their own, the various royal and presidential suites can more than comfortably accommodate bodyguards, personal advisors or on-the-go entourages. 

Adorned with marble pillars and gold leaf, the lobby is a freeze-frame of hotel luxury circa 1932, and no less the dazzling for its age. There are perhaps fewer exotic furs draped over ladies’ shoulders, but only fractionally fewer, and demoiselles toting bags from Recoleta’s high-end shops remain a regular sight. 

The hotel’s haute French restaurant has long been a major social venue for the nation’s elite. There’s no better place to catch some high-level gossip or score an invitation to the Colón Opera gala, should that be your thing. In short, if you’d like your temporary address to the best in Buenos Aires, the Alvear Palace is it.

A hotel called the Bellevue makes a certain implicit promise. And the Hotel Bellevue Dubrovnik, its glassy façade perched on a cliff above picturesque Miramare Bay, with the spindly arms of the Croatian coast on either side reaching out toward the Adriatic, does not lack for scenery. One can gaze out at it from any of the ninety-one rooms and suites — from the classic sea view room, the superior sea view room, the deluxe sea view room, and in especially panoramic fashion from the suites, all with sea views. It’s less than a kilometer — and a pleasingly walkable one — from the 6th-century old city of Dubrovnik, but given the hotel’s setting and orientation, the water feels closer than the land. 

Behind the glassed-in balconies and the oversized windows are accommodations with about the subtlest, most dialed-back nautical theme you’ll ever encounter. In fact, though the dark woods and canvas-white palette would not be out of place on one of the sailboats blowing about outside, the most nautical element here (vista aside) is probably the enormous bathtub you’ll find in the bedroom of some of the better suites. 

The Bellevue’s size lands in a sweet spot, large enough that you’ll have more amenities than you’re likely to use, but small enough that the hotel doesn’t dominate the natural (or, on the other side, the residential-architectural) surroundings. It feels more like a base than a self-contained fortress. The two restaurants, one with an innovative Mediterranean menu, the other a seafood restaurant divided between a terrace above the beach and a cave cut into the cliff, strike just the right laid-back note. Same goes for the bar, which is also divided in two, this time by an enormous palm-tree cased in glass. Off campus, any number of activities are on offer, from cultural and historic tours to yacht excursions and even, in case you’d like a higher angle on those landscapes and seascapes, sightseeing flights on two-seater planes. 

How to get there:
Hotel Bellevue is about a half a mile (800 meters) from Old Town and approximately 20-40 minutes by car from Dubrovnik Airport (depending on traffic). Taxi service is approximately 45 euros each way.

Until recently none of the Whitsunday Islands’ lodging options offered quite enough luxury to match the jaw-dropping Great Barrier Reef setting. But with the addition of Qualia, on Hamilton Island, the package is now complete. 

Situated at the northern tip of the island, Qualia enjoys its own private peninsula with coast or beach on three sides. The leeward villas provide spacious, south-facing “great room” spaces with a giant adjoining verandah; windward villas improve upon that by adding a plunge pool on the balcony, and a separate bedroom and dining room inside. Also available is a commodious Beach House option for group affairs, complete with two bedrooms, a large private pool and dining space for ten.

Architecturally, Qualia is unobtrusive and unpretentious, just discreet wooden buildings tucked into the jungle foliage. All accommodations are finished with pleasant wood accents and comfy contemporary furnishings in a variety of eye-catching colors — there’s a fortunate lack of beige here. 

Now while it would be easy to spend all one’s time relaxing in any of these aforementioned villas, that’s not the recommended approach. Of course the Great Barrier Reef environs are just screaming to be explored, and Qualia’s attentive staff are happy to get you suited up and on your way. Neighboring Dent Island offers some of the world’s best golf, and there’s always some quality time to be spent even more motionless on the beach or in the first-class spa.

And after a tough day of exploring sea or land, Qualia’s two restaurants can provide a gracious and satiating end to any itinerary. The Long Pavilion is the haute-cuisine option, regularly hosting culinary events and serving inventive, contemporary Australian fare. Down the hill, the Pebble Beach cafe can be found adjacent to the pool and gym, providing a dressed-down but still creative menu and a bar that’s particularly welcome at sunset.

Please note: Qualia does not allow guests under 16 years of age. Qualia has a 2 night minimum stay policy.

How to get there: Qualia is located on the northern tip of Hamilton Island (located in the Whitsunday Islands off the coast of Queensland). There are direct flights from Cairns, Brisbane, Melbourne or Sydney to Hamilton Island Airport.

content: The Soho House brand, as you might suspect, was born in a more central neighborhood. But in the intervening years, Shoreditch has evolved into London’s hippest neighborhood, a center for the arts in particular — making it an obvious choice for another Soho House club and hotel. Redchurch Townhouse benefits from a very fine location, right around the corner from sister club Shoreditch House, which is across the road from Shoreditch High Street station. Its membership, naturally, draws from the local creative industries, which means that as an overnight guest — and temporary club member — you’ll rub elbows with local artists, designers, and entrepreneurs.\n\nYou’ll be welcomed as a member, which means a low-key check-in experience and as little — or as much — attention as you require. The accommodations, in typical Soho House style, are equal parts modernist-chic and bohemian-eclectic, and range from the refreshingly straightforward Tiny rooms up to the Large, which find space for roll-top tubs. The smallest are perhaps best suited for impromptu overnight stays, but they’re more than adequate if what you want is a foot in the door and a table at Cecconi’s, the club’s famous Italian restaurant — a hot ticket, even in Shoreditch, where the competition includes some of the finest restaurants in town.

It shares a street with the similarly named Margutta 54, but that’s not all — Margutta 19 also shares an owner, the luxe and glamorous Rome Luxury Suites. And if you had nothing else to go on, “Rome luxury suites” is a good start towards describing Margutta 19’s appeal. The best hotels in Rome are small, and the Via Margutta, just up the road from the Spanish Steps, in the shadow of the Villa Borghese, is one of the city’s most prestigious streets, known for the artists who once called it home.

Inside this well-preserved palazzo you’ll find high-end contemporary Italian elegance at its finest. There’s one deluxe room, which is lavish but compact, and the rest are suites, spanning well over 400 square feet and equipped with luxuries like king beds dressed in Frette linens, in-room Nespresso machines, and indulgent travertine marble bathrooms with walk-in showers and separate bathtubs.

Not every hotel in this town has a restaurant, but this one does — the fine-dining Assaggia, whose Michelin-starred chef delivers upscale Roman cuisine in a space with a stunning outdoor terrace. Meanwhile, for an evening drink, you’re welcome on the rooftop at Babuino 181, another Rome Luxury Suites hotel just around the corner.

content:
The trouble with the bed and breakfast is that too often it feels like exactly what it is: someone’s house, with the bedrooms simply tidied up a bit. Too rarely do they go the extra length of creating accommodations with personality, to say nothing of the kind of immersive, forget-yourself comfort that keep the world’s luxury hotels in business. Enter Vedetta Relais: not simply a “luxury B&B,” though it’s certainly that, but one that’s devoted, it seems, to the art of the unforgettable.

In terms of the accommodations, you get to choose your pillow: aloe, mallow-scented, goose feather, et cetera. Some suites let you watch the woods from the shower, store your clothes in an 18th-century dresser, or recline on an actual lynx skin procured on an actual safari. All suites have been given the name of a character, then decorated in his or her style: The Unstoppable Explorer, for instance, has battered suitcases still bearing the stickers from travels long concluded. In terms of the morning repast, you get to choose your breakfast time: early, medium, late. Food is seasonal and organic. So far, so tailored and accommodating. And in terms of the location: it’s pretty ideal. Vedetta Relais is situated on a hill, with views of the Maremma countryside stretching to Elba. 

The house has been in the owner’s family for generations, and she’s not shy about sharing its history. But unlike so many farmsteads-turned-hotels, this one offers activities and adventures. During the day, you can swim in the pool, ride on horseback, sail in the Gulf of Follonica, visit the medieval towns that dot southern Tuscany, or try the on-site archery course — and at night, you can stroll olive groves or listen to opera divas invited to sing for the evening.  

Please note: Vedetta Relais requires a minimum stay of two nights from the end of May through June and weekends in September as well as a five-night minimum in July and August.

At first glance, the Grand Hôtel des Thermes is the archetypal French seaside luxury hotel — an impressive Belle Époque edifice fronting a long stretch of beach. But unlike the grand hotels of the Côte d’Azur, this one’s got no oceanfront boulevard, no built-up beach club, nothing but sand and sea. This is the Atlantic coast of Brittany, a classic destination that’s nevertheless avoided the fate of a place like Cannes — which means that the Grand Hôtel des Thermes still feels like a proper escape.

Though its silhouette remains as classic as ever, its interiors have seen substantial updates, bringing them entirely up to date. The look is still historically informed, with references going back to Art Deco and beyond, but this is every inch a modern luxury hotel. You’ll find some extremely cozy rooms — the European tradition of the single room is alive and well — but you’ll find expansive spaces as well. Some face the city, but the best views, naturally, are those that look out over the beach.

As you’d expect, given the name, thermal baths feature prominently in the spa’s offerings. There’s also a saltwater pool and a “parcours aquatonic,” a sort of aquatic maze that applies a succession of jets, currents, and showers as you traverse it. Three restaurants and a piano bar round out the hotel’s offerings with enough variety that you needn’t leave the property; Saint-Malo, however, is irresistible, its walled city just a short walk from your door.

content:
Not every hotel has to stage a doomed, lonely revolution against the prevailing standards of hospitality. Sometimes it’s enough simply to be very, very tasteful — taste being second on the list, behind those revolutionary new ideas, of what’s lacking in the hotel world today. (Even first, actually, if you’re of a more traditional temperament.) And taste is what the Oriental Residence Bangkok has going for it in spades.

It’s also got more than a little bit of comfort; the smallest accommodations are junior suites, and the full-size suites could practically pass as luxury apartments, complete with full kitchens. And for all that, the style is light, simple, spare, contemporary — a far cry from the heavy ostentatiousness of many a Bangkok luxury hotel.

And while it may not be a proper grand palace hotel, it’s got enough in the way of conveniences for most of us. Along with a fitness center and a bit of meeting space, it’s got two French-inspired restaurants, the casual Café Claire and the fine-dining Khao Restaurant. Meanwhile its location in the embassy district means the surrounding neighborhood can easily carry some of the weight — you’re close by to some of Bangkok’s best restaurants and shops.

Perhaps no city in the United States is as famous for its precipitous decline as Detroit — the decline of the American auto industry hit it like a natural disaster, turning whole neighborhoods into post-apocalyptic ghost towns. But where there’s a low, there’s an opportunity to rise up, and today Detroit is also famous for the urban revitalization that’s currently in full swing. It’s a story that’s intimately bound up with the rise of the Detroit-based Shinola, a retailer selling watches, bicycles, and lifestyle products manufactured largely in America. And to this story we can add another tangible improvement that Shinola has made to downtown Detroit: the Shinola Hotel.

For this project the watchmaker brought in plenty of outside expertise, from Gachot Studios and Kraemer Design Group to New York’s NoHo Hospitality Group. The result is a stylish, youth-oriented boutique hotel that plays up its historical heritage, its interiors recalling an idealized version of Detroit’s manufacturing heyday. It’s not just a lodging, but a social space as well, or more precisely several social spaces: its 16,000 square feet of dining, entertainment, and retail space include San Morello, an Italian restaurant, along with a cocktail bar (Evening Bar), a beer hall (The Brakeman), and two fast-casual restaurants, Penny Red's and Mister Dips. Parker's Alley, part of the Shinola Hotel, also features a variety of local shops and makers. This vibrant hub has put its corner of Detroit back on the map in a big way, all in one fell swoop.

content:
On the south side of Bali, at least, the days of exploration are pretty much over. The best you can hope for is a private little slice of paradise — if it’s not going to be wild, it may as well be as lush as possible. Lush is something the Belmond (née Orient Express) hotels and resorts do well, of course, and on that score the Belmond Jimbaran Puri Bali is just what you’d expect: though just a few minutes’ drive from the airport, it’s remarkable for the completeness of the escape it provides.

The style is classic, even conservative, again no great departure from the Belmond form book. The star here isn’t an architect or a designer but the setting itself, and the villas and suites are geared towards tactile pleasures as much as visual ones. The physical comforts are flawless, the pools (if you’ve booked a pool villa) are too, and the cream of the crop are the beachfront villas — the others, it must be said, have a bit more of a jungle/garden vibe than the whole white-sand thing.

And if you don’t have your own pool, you’ll find the resort’s central one is quite up to the task. As for the other amenities, it’s the usual five-star Balinese stuff — a gorgeous spa, a couple of restaurants serving Indonesian and European fare, and the sort of attentive service that reminds you why you bother with luxury hotels in the first place. Thread count is one thing, but you can replicate that at home — in a hotel like this it’s the staff that makes the stay.

The walled town of Saint Paul de Vence is just 15 kilometers from Nice airport, midway between Cannes and Monaco, but seems to belong to a different world, with its narrow streets and its centuries-old fortifications — and its spectacular vistas over the valley and the Mediterranean beyond are shared by the lovely Le Saint-Paul.

The hotel itself is a bit on the cozy side, a result of its heritage as a private residence — evidently sixteenth-century Frenchmen made do with spaces somewhat smaller than today's sprawling executive suites. What they lack in sheer square footage, these rooms make up for in charm and comfort, decorated in printed fabrics and antique furniture, many with balconies opening onto a dramatic valley view.

Le Saint-Paul's restaurant is gaining in reputation, not least for the physical surroundings; one vaulted dining room is decked out with murals and frescoes, another features a fountain, and terrace dining is available for those who wish to savor the open air and the views.

We’re open about our admiration for Europe’s modernist ski lodges — but even so, Lagació Mountain Residence stands out. Too often, when updating the classic Alpine-lodge look, the temptation is to push things too far. When ski hotels start resembling high-altitude nightclubs, it’s easy to forget that warmth — in every sense — is the very essence of a mountain retreat.

Here, the lines are clean yet the textures remain rustic: knotty pine paneling and abstract rugs with a subtle cowhide resemblance ensure the Alpine character is never lost. The result is twenty-four apartments — they prefer the residential term — that feel urbane without ever slipping into urban, thanks also to the Dolomite peaks framed by expansive windows.

The spa, with its focus on recovery as much as relaxation, tends to both muscles and skin. As for dining, the hotel serves breakfast and light snacks during the day, while a partner restaurant provides delivery that doubles as convenient room service — perfect for evenings when you’d rather not cook in your apartment’s kitchen.

Unless you’re an academic, an aerospace engineer, or, you know, French, you probably don’t pay a huge amount of attention to what goes on in Toulouse. The south gets more tourist traffic than the southwest, but that doesn’t mean there’s nothing to see here: a look at the Hôtel Le Grand Balcon reveals a hotel as sophisticated and cosmopolitan as any design-conscious European boutique.

In this it helps to have a designer of Jean-Philippe Nuel’s caliber; the interior architect’s work might be more familiar from Parisian haunts like the Hôtel Thérèse, but he’s in top form here as well, mixing sober modernism with whimsical touches including a cloud motif, a nod to the hotel’s heritage — this used to be the lodging of choice for French air mail pilots. The rooms are sensibly named, from Cosy on up through Classic and Deluxe to the Suite Saint Exupéry, named for the literary aviator who once made his home here.

The location is quite central, just off the Place du Capitole, and the city center is easily walkable. In typical French city-boutique style there’s no restaurant per se, just breakfast in the stylish little lounge bar — after that you’re on your own at the heart of a charming old city.

In the heart of Cagliari, mere minutes by foot from the marina quarter, is a luxury boutique hotel that shows an uncommonly refined side of the Sardinian capital. Artistic director Giorgio Casu has crafted a distinctive style that bridges different eras while incorporating the work of numerous Sardinian artists, designers, and craftspeople; Studio Pilia led the architectural design and renovation of the residence.

Each suite is unique, not only in the decorative choices but in the layouts dictated by this historical structure. You might find antique brickwork alongside modern concrete, or old timbers above new hardwood floors. 

Sardinian cooking, specifically seafood, is an area of special focus, and for good reason — siblings Claudio and Caterina Murgia, for whom Casa Clàt is named, are also the administrators of the Nieddittas mussel farming cooperative. The hotel’s restaurant serves mussels among other Sardinian specialties; the revelry carries over into the hotel’s lounge bar and into its delightfully green courtyard garden.

content: Though it may not be grand in scale, this Budapest hotel is extraordinary in its own way. Hotel Collect can certainly boast a prestigious location — it’s right across the road from the Károlyi-kert, the French-style garden that is the city’s oldest park. And that French influence is visible in the Hotel Collect as well, with both Belle Époque and Art Deco echoes in the rooms, with plenty of black lacquer and gold, combined with a bit of modernist furniture and a penchant for vivid colors and bold textures.\n\nAt just sixteen rooms it’s very much on the small side, and the intimacy suits it well, lending it a residential aspect — even if the rooms are unmistakably cut from luxury-boutique cloth. The courtyard is patterned after a Parisian café, and while the hotel doesn’t have a restaurant of its own, the lobby bar serves coffee, tea, and pastries. And just down the road is the Centrál Café and Restaurant, one of the city’s most famous spots, open from breakfast on through to late night.

content:
Aman has a hotel in Greece — while that’s not quite all we think you need to know, we’ll understand if a few of you are already entering your dates. Anyway, if you’re at all familiar with what the Aman group does, and you’ve ever laid eyes on a photograph of the Aegean coast, then you already know where we're going with this.

Inspired by the (what else?) classical Greek architecture and surrounded by olive groves, Amanzoe is set high over the clear turquoise sea. It’s just a short drive uphill from Porto Heli, but it’s a carefully designed world in itself, featuring a spectacular reflecting pool and a series of expansive terraces, charming walled gardens and a striking cocktail bar, a library, the Aman spa and a yoga pavilion, and just to top it all off, an exquisite poolside fireplace. Though the exterior is inspired by ancient tradition, the interior is sleek and cool, with polished stone and smooth marble, floor-to-ceiling windows that open and close according to the weather, clean lines amid the classic columns. All of this, of course, faces a magnificent Aegean backdrop.

So what we’re talking about — the reason Amanzoe is a can’t-miss — is the natural perfection of the Peloponnese, further enhanced by Aman’s precision and elegance. Guest rooms aren't just rooms, but freestanding pavilions. Each is a grand mini-monument to modern luxury, with high ceilings, marble walls, and pergola-shaded terraces with private swimming pools and unobstructed views of the sea. Even more opulent are the villas, should you require additional privacy, up to nine bedrooms, and a swimming pool lined in sumptuous emerald-hued marble.

Thanks to Amanzoe’s thoughtful layout, you’ll be looking at the water from nearly every vantage point, not least the Beach Cabanas, each with a private pool and terrace garden. It’s enough to make you want to hop on a bicycle and cruise downhill to the resort’s private Beach Club. The staff, anticipating your needs, already knows you’ll want a ride back up.

How to get there: Amanzoe is about a 2½-hour drive from Athens, or a 2-hour ride via hydrofoil from the Athenian port of Piraeus. Helicopter charters are available as well; from Athens Airport (ATH), it’s a 25-minute helicopter flight.

content:
Some of you might remember another Stockholm hotel that went by the Lydmar name, a rowdy, almost painfully hip sort of place, where the focus was very much on the nightlife, and the revelers at times threatened to overwhelm the guests. Well, that was then, and this is now — around the turn of the new millennium that was what boutique hotels were about. Today, more and more, they’re focused on the traditional values of hospitality, and once again the new version of the Lydmar is exemplary.

It’s fair to say that in terms of design, Stockholm tends to be a step ahead. By the time most of us figured out what “Scandinavian design” looked like, the Swedes had already moved on to the next thing. Look around Lydmar and you’ll see very little in the way of stark minimalism. These days Scandinavian designers are mining a rich history — there’s the odd mid-century modern chair or sofa, for example, but plenty more that’s traditional, almost rustic.

At its best the new luxury hotel avoids ostentation whenever possible, and this one is no different — it’s quietly stylish, but more focused on quality materials and on fostering an intimate atmosphere. And though you won’t mistake it for a bar with a boardinghouse attached, the Lydmar does have plenty going on: there’s a smaller, more intimate music venue, as well as a restaurant and lounge that are destined to become local favorites. And you won’t have to look far to find it — the location is stellar, absolutely central, next to the Grand and right up against the Harbor and the old town.

All of the Palisociety hotels share a certain unpretentious, vintage-inspired warmth, and for all their stylishness, tend more toward a cozy residential vibe than an intimidatingly high-fashion one. And this is all the more true of Le Petit Pali at 8th Ave, Carmel-by-the-Sea, a 24-room inn that’s perhaps closer in its scale and its concept to a seaside bed-and-breakfast than an urban boutique hotel.

It occupies a charming and thoroughly Californian Craftsman-style building, which is aesthetically a perfect match for Palisociety’s eclectic interiors. The rooms display a contemporary color sense and a certain sense of visual composure, while in their details they’re full of vintage and antique-style furniture and artwork, as well as up-to-date boutique-hotel comforts and, in some cases, gas fireplaces — more welcome than you might expect, if it’s your first time ont he California coast.

A daily Continental breakfast features pastries from one of the better local bakeries as well as Champagne among the beverage options; in the afternoon, drinks and hors d’oeuvres are available for guests as well. Beyond that, you’re at the mercy of Carmel’s restaurateurs; not a difficult spot for a traveler to be in, to be fair.

content:
The original Soho House members’ club in London was followed up by another in downtown Manhattan; and though the brand’s focus on the creative industries is a natural fit for Los Angeles, Soho Warehouse DTLA is set not in Hollywood but in a 1916-vintage warehouse in the downtown Arts District — which is not just an arts destination, but is also central to the L.A. food scene.

Like the other Soho House locations it’s a club first, and a hotel second, but overnight guests earn the benefits of temporary membership — this means access to the 50-foot rooftop swimming pool, as well as the House’s public spaces, including the Rooftop Terrace and Bar, the House Kitchen, and the Garden, an impressive indoor-outdoor dining and drinking venue. There’s art everywhere, including a massive mural by Shepard Fairey, and the lavishly outfitted gym spans two floors of the building.

The rooms are handsome, to say the least — in typical Soho House style they’re eclectic and warm, crisp and contemporary but full of retro-inspired character. They’re also quietly luxurious, even if the visual panache obscures this fact; there’s no hiding the fact that even the Cosy rooms are generously sized. It’s a long way from central London, but this concept has proved to be an eminently adaptable one.

content:
The Under Canvas hotels bring the concept of luxury camping to some of the most famous outdoor destinations in the United States, and this one might be the most famous destination of them all. Under Canvas Grand Canyon is set just 25 minutes from the South Rim, and there’s much more to do here than just peer down into the canyon — this corner of the Southwest is perfect for hiking, biking, or rafting, and hardy explorers might feel compelled to descend to the bottom of the canyon on a guided mule drive.

In what is by now classic Under Canvas style, the tents are a cut above the ordinary camping experience: think king beds, full en-suite bathrooms, and wood-burning stoves, with meals served beneath the peaked canvas roof of the restaurant tent. Here you’ll find more or less the same comfort as you would in a brick-and-mortar luxury boutique hotel, along with the instant immersion in nature that ordinarily only comes with do-it-yourself tent camping. If there’s a better way to see this most iconic of Southwestern natural attractions, we haven’t heard of it.

Please note: Under Canvas Grand Canyon is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from mid-April until late October.

content:
Hotel Arpoador’s location has always been a strength: right at the end of Ipanema, just around the corner from Copacabana, at the base of the peninsula of the same name, which is home to some of Rio de Janeiro’s finest ocean views. And after a thorough redesign by local firm Bernardes Arquitetura, the hotel is an attraction unto itself, a fine example of a modernist concrete-and-glass structure warmed with organic materials like wood and rope.

The exterior, now subtly clad in timbers, feels more inviting than ever; the interiors are still minimalist, but they’re anything but arid, in a subtle nautical color scheme. Rooms on the beach side of the hotel frame jaw-dropping views, and even the city-side rooms are handsome enough, and all come with thoughtful luxuries like espresso machines and high-end robes and bath products.

Arp, the beach bar and restaurant, feels like something from a far-flung resort, despite its urban location, and is open every day from dawn to dusk. Beyond that, fear not — Rio de Janeiro isn’t exactly known for rolling up the sidewalks early, and the Arpoador’s location means you’re never far from the action.

content:
Halfway between Seville and the coastal city of Cádiz, in the Andalusian countryside, Hacienda de San Rafael occupies a five-acre estate which still serves as a working farm, producing olive oil alongside what’s now a thriving, if still small-scale, hospitality concern. Brothers Anthony and Patrick Reid are also the proprietors of Corral del Rey, in Seville proper, and their talent for human-scale luxury boutique hospitality is just as evident here as it is there.

The rooms start out at a very generous 45 square meters, and flank a central courtyard. Their interiors are an eclectic mix of Andalucian, Indian, and Zimbabwean elements, and they’re exceedingly comfortable, with king beds, private verandas, and splendid marble baths. Meanwhile the Casita Suites and Pool Suites take things up a notch or two. They’re really villas, each with a private pool, and each one a self-contained residential experience — and a luxurious one, at that.

To this the estate adds three swimming pools, nestled in citrus and olive groves, as well as a pair of outdoor bars and a restaurant that features the best of market-fresh Andalusian cooking. Pair it with Corral del Rey for a powerful city-country combination, or just hole up here and live the good life, Andalusian style.

content:
One of a pair of Le Petit Pali hotels in Carmel-by-the-Sea, Le Petit Pali at Ocean Avenue takes the trademark nostalgia-tinged Palihotels style to another level. Even the bigger, more urban Pali properties feel charmingly home-like, but the bed-and-breakfast–inspired Le Petit Pali inns are even more so; this one, at 34 rooms, is pleasantly intimate, and a fine match for the relatively tranquil atmosphere of this classic California coastal town.

The rooms and suites range from relatively cozy queen rooms to more expansive kings and a one-bedroom, 470-square-foot suite. Some come with gas fireplaces, and all of them freely combine vintage- and antique-inspired furniture and artworks with unobtrusively modern boutique-hotel comforts: rain showers, Nespresso machines, Marshall Bluetooth sound systems, and SMEG mini-fridges.

In keeping with Le Petit Pali’s European inspiration, it features a daily Champagne Continental breakfast, with pastries from the local Rise + Roam and marmalade from Marmalade Grove. There’s also a daily social hour — six hours, if we’re counting — serving California wines and other drinks alongside light bites from other local purveyors. And while a full lunch and dinner service are beyond Le Petit Pali’s ambitions, you’re well placed to explore the local culinary scene.

content: It’s the fate of all successful holiday destinations, sooner or later. Now Phuket is certainly nobody’s idea of a hard time, exactly, but it’s not uncommon to be troubled by the nagging suspicion that what began as a place to escape to is slowly becoming a place to escape from. Fortunately it’s possible to do so without leaving the island entirely. Sri Panwa, for example, does an admirable job of setting itself apart from the crowds, first of all literally: it’s atop a hill at the end of a cape, on the somewhat isolated southeast corner of the island.\n\nEleven swanky modernist villas survey the seascape through full-length windows, offering a perspective that’s a bit different from the usual beachfront villa fare. This is more like luxury-apartment living than the whole barefoot resort thing (not that shoes are especially strongly recommended here). Two-bedroom villas are actually in the majority, which means families are well cared for, though it’s every bit as well suited for couples; a private infinity pool that seems to fade directly into the waters of the Andaman Sea will do wonders when it comes to setting a mood. As do the spa, the vibrant modern-Thai restaurant, and the perhaps surprisingly well-populated bar — if this is the future of Phuket then just tell us where to sign.

content:
Sister to the original Il Borro luxury-hotel estate near Arezzo in the spectacular Tuscan countryside, Viesca is about half an hour closer to Florence, and offers a similarly blissful experience: a 16th-century manor house surrounded by villas, cottages, and gardens, and an atmosphere that effortlessly joins classic country-estate living with the comforts of a modern high-end hotel.

The rooms and suites are spacious, contemporary in construction, and antique in atmosphere. For larger parties there’s a family cottage that sleeps up to six, and then the villas are on another level entirely — each comes with its own private pool, and each one is a self-contained residence. The largest one, Villa Viesca, is the old manor house itself, with nine bedrooms and its own garden and chapel.

Guests share a common pool, as well as a pair of well-kept grass tennis courts, and yoga classes and in-room spa treatments are available as well. And the surrounding countryside offers plenty of attractions, from wine tours to horseback rides and mountain-bike excursions. The highlight of the estate, however, might be Il Borro Tuscan Bistro Viesca, which is a restaurant, a bar, and a specialty grocer all in one — and which offers cooking classes to those who wish to take a bit of Tuscan knowledge home.

content:
There are larger and more spectacular castles in France, but Château Cordeillan-Bages makes the most of its relatively intimate size. It’s set in the village of Bages, in the heart of Bordeaux’s Haut-Médoc wine region, on the left bank of the Gironde estuary — just a half-hour down the river from the city of Bordeaux itself, on the same estate that produces Château Lynch-Bages’ wines.

The house itself dates back to the middle of the 19th century, with some elements remaining from a 17th-century structure; its 28 rooms, however, aren’t shy about incorporating contemporary elements in the décor, as well as all the modern comforts you’d expect from a proper luxury boutique hotel.

Its natural setting provides plenty of opportunity for leisure, as does its outdoor pool and its gym and sauna. Food and wine, however, are the twin main attractions. A tour of the winery can be arranged, and a bottle of the local product is never farther than an arm’s length away. Café Lavinal, under the direction of chef Gabriel Gette, serves refined local cuisine, accompanied by the contents of a wine cellar that runs to some 1,800 bottles.

content: One of the most luxurious hotels on the Costa Brava sits on a bluff at the north end of the Bay of Roses, just above Bonifaci Beach. Vistabella has been a jet-set favorite since the Sixties — just don’t expect a dated mid-century vibe. The original hotel was constructed with an eye towards timeless classicism, and its interiors range across a variety of styles, from the frilly-but-focused Mediterranean-style junior suite to the more decidedly minimalist junior suites, with their monochrome décor, mosaic-tile showers, and egg-shaped freestanding bathtubs. (There’s also the Surrealist Suite, an homage to Salvador Dalí, whose house-turned-museum is nearby, in Cadaqués.)\n\nIn spite of Vistabella’s relatively modest size — just 34 rooms and suites — it comes with the services and facilities of a much larger hotel. A generous handful of restaurants see to the needs of hotel guests, locals, and visitors alike, from the self-explanatory La Tapa to the coastal Italian aMare, the Beach Restaurant El Pirata, and the Mediterranean restaurant Els Brancs. There’s also a Nuxe spa, complete with an indoor pool and a sauna, and it’s a short walk from the hotel to the beach.

content:
The advent of apartment-sharing has had an effect on the hotel business, to be sure, but anyone who thought it meant the end of the line for hotels would have to be surprised. Some hotels have suffered, others have raised their game to compete, and some, like Frankfurt’s extraordinary lyf East, have managed to create a synthesis of the best of both worlds. They’re threading the needle by calling it a “guest community,” which means the occupants of its 100 suites and its various social spaces are as likely to be long-term tenants as they are overnight guests.

It’s an impressive piece of architecture by Franken Architekten, with colorful, varied interiors by Studio Aberja, featuring furniture and design pieces by carefully selected suppliers, as well as a vast amount of work by local contemporary artists. And it’s a good thing — you’d go mad spending a week in some hotels, but this one never stops feeling lively and stimulating. The comforts, too, are intended to be long-lasting, from the upscale Fennobed mattresses to the Bang & Olufsen sound systems.

Equally welcoming are the lyf East's many common spaces, from the Parlour, with its library and record collection, to the rooftop terrace, with its view over Frankfurt and the Main basin. Community kitchens allow for self-catering, with a little help from the hotel’s indoor farm, and a bar, a bakery, and an all-day restaurant are on hand when you’d prefer to leave it to someone else.

With Portuguese hospitality still booming, it’s time to look beyond the more obvious destinations along the coast or in the established wine regions. Just outside the town of Fundão, where the plains meet the Gardunha mountain range, is a 17th-century convent, lovingly restored and converted into the Convento do Seixo Boutique Hotel & Spa.

It’s one of those names that rather straightforwardly says most of what you need to know about the place. In the main building, period architecture and modern design combine to create rooms and suites that are visually rich and extremely comfortable, while the outlying villas, a new addition, are contemporary through and through, and feel just as tranquil as the old monks’ cells — but with more expansive views of the surrounding countryside, thanks to their balconies and their full-length windows.

Another addition since the monastic days: a full-service spa, complete with a heated indoor swimming pool, a salt-water flotation pool, a salt cave for halotherapy, and a selection of massages and body treatments. The restaurant and bar, too, are decidedly 21st-century, despite their historical surroundings — here you’ll find a contemporary take on the Portuguese culinary tradition, and a soaring double-height lounge with a menu of creative cocktails.

Despite its relatively modest capacity — just 56 units — The Resort at Kapalua Bay, Maui has all the facilities of a much larger resort, as well as a privileged location that’s flanked by a pair of golf courses, a nature reserve, and a marine reserve with some phenomenal diving and snorkeling. Safe to say you’ll be hard pressed to think of anything that’s missing.

Those 56 units, or Residences, are aptly named, given that they’ve all got full kitchens, laundry machines, and soaking tubs in marble bathrooms. The two-bedrooms actually sleep up to six, thanks to space for extra cribs, while the largest four-bedroom residences can sleep up to ten — all of them outfitted in a contemporary style that suits its island environment without lapsing into tropical kitsch.

Meanwhile the spa spans the usual facials and massages to hair treatments and mani-pedis, plus there’s a gym, hot tub, and outdoor pool. You’re also surrounded by ample opportunities for less structured exercise, from kayaking and snorkeling to hiking trails and golf. There’s a pool bar and beach bar for relaxed day time dining and the main restaurant is an indoor-outdoor space that serves modern Hawaiian cuisine based around fresh seafood and local produce with a fantastic panoramic view.

content:
Tech capital, rock-music mecca, that place where they throw the fish — whatever your mental picture of Seattle looks like, we’re willing to bet the Hotel Sorrento comes as a pleasant surprise. This century-old Italianate charmer stands on First Hill, a short-but-steep walk from Downtown, and it’s a window into an upscale, old-world side of Seattle, and a reminder of a time when it was gold, rather than the internet, that brought waves of new settlers to the Pacific Northwest.

Architecture and atmosphere aside, of course, today’s Sorrento is a thoroughly contemporary experience. This is an independent luxury hotel that’s learned the lessons of the boutique-hotel boom, combining plush comforts with loads of personality. No two rooms are quite alike, though they’re all classic in style, and come with high-end details like 42-inch televisions, goose-down pillows, and marble bathrooms stocked with Le Labo products.

The views from First Hill are impressive, taking in a panorama that includes the waters of Puget Sound and Lake Washington, as well as the peak of Mt. Rainier to the south. From here you’re surrounded by shops, restaurants, cafés, bars, and museums. And Hotel Sorrento gives you a few reasons to stay in: the Dunbar Room combines European bistro and American steakhouse flavors with Pacific Northwest seafood, while the Fireside Room is the lobby-level lounge and bar with a daily five o’clock wine hour.

content:
Stunning sunset views, check. Whitewashed walls and complimentary cocktails, check. What distinguishes Tsitouras Collection from the various other high-end lodgings on Santorini is the hotel’s structure: unlike the sprawling resorts with infinity pools, Tsitouras is comprised of just five freestanding cottages situated on a cliff overlooking the sea. 

Each cottage is attended by a butler staff, and is individually decorated according to one Greek theme or another. The House of Porcelain, for instance, is full of Royal Copenhagen china, while the House of Nureyev contains original sketches of the famous ballet dancer performing in Athens. The interiors are anything but spare, however — Dimitris Tsitouras, the namesake art collector who restored the hotel’s main building in 1985, has filled guest quarters with an impressive array of antique treasures that complement each cottage’s theme. From Beidermeyer chairs to Byzantine icons to Yamaha pianos, the details within these mini-museums stand in sharp contrast to the minimalist style of many contemporary hotels.

Newly added is a swimming pool up on the Maria Callas terrace, supplying guests with another reason to languish in the sun. Lying poolside with a view as stunning as this one is remarkable indeed, but the chance to enjoy the natural beauty of Santorini while sleeping in the presence of a Picasso ceramic piece, as you could in the House of the Sea, is a one-of-a-kind opportunity. Don’t be surprised if you see some of the hotel’s furnishings under glass in the future — Mr. Tsitouras is currently working on a museum to house some of his many artifacts.

Please note: The Tsitouras Collection is open seasonally from early April thru October.

How to get there:
Santorini (Thira) can be easily reached by plane or ferry. Flight time from Athens is approximately 45 minutes. Ferries from Athens' Pireaus port to Thira take approximately 3 hours.

RIMBA by AYANA Bali is a tropical princess with a suitably mellifluous name. Not much unexplored territory remains here in Jimbaran, the South Bali version of Beverly Hills, where impossibly luxurious villas crowd one another for that coveted sunset perch. So they looked inward, capitalizing on over 220 clifftop acres to set aside this portion — just as lofty, just as replete with botanical wonders, and just as spectacular, especially around sunset.

If this was once a fishing village in the traditional model, you won’t be able to tell by the rooms; they’re resolutely forward-looking, and they come by the hundreds, differentiated less by eclectic design decisions than by elevation — the quicker to reach the pools, say, or the better to take in the views. Their clean geometry with recessed lighting stands aside, careful not to try to outdo the sheer natural magnificence, softening the sleekness with an earthy palette of greens and umbers. 

Public spaces, on the other hand, cling a bit more authentically to the past. The mind-boggling variety of dining options to be had in the resort at large include the Kecak dancers and rice paddy at Kampoeng Bali and the 25-meter infinity pool and poolside Mexican plates at Unique. Speaking of which, RIMBA enjoys seven of its own pools, some of them multi-level, as well as a rooftop spa; a shuttle takes you to the beautiful and secluded white-sand Kubu Beach.

Here’s a quick précis for non-Francophiles: Saint-Paul-de-Vence, roughly ten miles west of Nice, is one of the oldest medieval towns on the French Riviera, and a long-time haven for artists, Rolling Stones, and everything in between. Marc Chagall used to live here, as did the likes of Bill Wyman and Roger Moore. Today, art-minded travelers usually come to visit the Fondation Maeght museum. But lovely Saint-Paul is really a destination in its own right, within easy day-trip distance of Cannes and Monaco, and the newly opened La Vague, a quick trip outside of town, is the hot new place to stay if you’re here.

Privately owned for years, the fifty-room property is peaceful and contemporary — and, thanks to thorough renovations, impeccable. This is not the quaint French hotel you book with hopes of recreating medieval romance. La Vague might as well be brand-new, with spotless all-white furnishings, vibrant modern murals, swiveling satellite TVs, a Scandinavian-inspired spa and hammam, and a high-end bistro — having breakfast here, you’ll feel like you’re at a stylish cocktail bar in the city, not a dining table in the French countryside. Side note: if you’re in town on a Sunday between May and September, don’t miss the bistro’s prix-fixe brunch barbecue, held on the terrace and featuring a mouth-watering array of grilled meats, fish and local produce.

Outside, find well-manicured grounds, complete with a tennis court and a large, inviting swimming pool surrounded by crisp white chaise lounges. There’s a fitness center, too, if all the rich food is weighing on you. Otherwise, there's the town itself, where you can get your fill of art and history before returning to La Vague — and all the comforts of the 21st century.

San Sebastián is an underratedly glamorous city, especially in September, during film festival season. It’s this connection that Zinema7 trades on, and the large-format film-star portraits in the guest rooms are only the most conspicuous example — locals will remember that one of the city’s iconic golden-age cinemas once stood on this very site.

From a historic movie house to something of a historic hotel; there’s nothing else in town like this very contemporary hundred-room boutique hotel, alone among San Sebastián’s old-world luxury palaces. The décor is modern, full of mid-century influences, recalling the postwar era when the film business was at its most chic. Rooms, presided over by those unique film-star shrines, are clean-lined, contemporary-luxe, equipped with flat-screens and DVD players in case a cinematic mood strikes.

In festival season it’s understandably a pretty tough ticket, but during the rest of the year San Sebastián can’t quite fill the Zinema7 with nothing but the beautiful people. It’s got a brisk side line in business and conference travel, and for those on the company dime, it’s a real find — stylish, wired and central, it’s of a considerably better class than the usual business hotel.

How to get there: Zinema7 is located in the city center of San Sebastian, within walking distance of the rail and bus stations.  San Sebastian Airport(EAS) is approximately 20 km away, and Bilbao Airport(BIO) is roughly 100 km away.
