content: The Mira Hong Kong overlooks neither the waters of the harbour nor the dense thicket of waterfront skyscrapers, but the urban oasis that is Kowloon Park, a dose of greenery that’s far from typical in this dizzyingly vertical city. And there’s plenty to see inside the Mira as well; this is one of Kowloon’s most stylish hotels, encompassing a range of moods, from the swanky curves of the entry and reception to the mid-century glamour of its accommodations, complete with Arne Jacobsen egg chairs and, in the suites, private terraces with outdoor sound systems.\n\nNor are sight and sound the only senses attended to by the Mira. There are three restaurants in house: Whisk, an innovative Modern European restaurant; Cuisine Cuisine, a second modern Cantonese option; and a third, Yamm, featuring a buffet-style range of Asian and global favorites. A chic lobby café fills in the gaps, and a verdant, palm-fringed open-air lounge occupies the fifth-floor courtyard terrace, and brings in live DJs on weekend nights. Meanwhile the Mira’s spa, with its glassy infinity pool, its color-enhanced aromatherapy showers, and its wide array of massages, treatments, and wellness classes, offers a contrasting note of tranquility.

content:
In Newport, Rhode Island’s historic district, tradition isn’t exactly in short supply. But with the Cliffside Inn, the New England–based Lark Hotels has transformed a beautiful Victorian house into a lovely 16-room boutique hotel. And not just any Newport Victorian — this one happens to have been the home of the painter Beatrice Turner, whose artwork adorns its interiors. 

Every room is different, though all are comparable in style after an extensive 2019 renovation, with eclectic Victorian-meets-contemporary interiors, stylish modern bathrooms, and luxe touches like gas fireplaces and Lather bath products. The rooms in the original house and the carriage house are perhaps a touch more authentic than the newer Cottage Suites, but the latter are notable for their extra space and their extra measure of seclusion.

Breakfast is a lavish affair served in the house’s common spaces, and every evening at five there’s a complimentary wine service and snacks. Bellevue Avenue, a few blocks to the west, is lined with restaurants, and there are many more within walking distance. And if the house isn’t quite perched precariously over the cliffside, it’s not far from it — Newport’s famed Cliff Walk, with its astonishing sea views, lies just at the end of the street.

content: Tuscany gets most of the attention, but the neighboring region of Umbria is just as beautiful, and blissfully low-key in comparison. Set amid vineyards and olive groves, Altarocca Wine Resort is a perfect place to base yourself while exploring the wineries and medieval hilltop villages — or to stay put and do next to nothing. This luxury hotel has it all: two gorgeous outdoor swimming pools and a third pool located inside a modern spa, an excellent restaurant focused on seasonal slow food, a wine cellar open for tastings, and meticulously landscaped grounds laced with footpaths around the estate’s orchards and gardens. \n\nA trio of handsomely restored villas house the guest rooms and suites. Some have vaulting wood-beamed ceilings and canopy beds, others have terra cotta flooring and private balconies facing views of the Duomo of Orvieto; all are classically elegant with rustic-chic accents. Breakfast, served on a terrace with views of the countryside, is a picturesque start to the day, followed by a leisurely poolside bistro lunch with wine pairings. And for dinner, Altarocca turns up the glamour: its Invinum Gourmet restaurant makes culinary art from the finest Umbrian ingredients, including, naturally, olive oil and wine produced on site.

content:
We’ve been fans of the Singaporean hotelier Loh Lik Peng since the beginning. And we’ve also followed with great interest the continuing evolution of the Sydney hospitality scene. So when it comes to the Old Clare Hotel, we’re doubly hooked. Not only because Chippendale, just to the south of the central business district, could do with a stylish boutique hotel as a part of its continuing transformation, but because Peng, who’s made a career out of turning derelict historical properties into buzzing, contemporary boutique hotels, is just the man to do it.

He had help, of course. Sydney architects Tonkin Zulaikha Greer are well known in Australia, and for good reason, as they’ve got a knack for putting existing, often industrial, spaces to new use. And you could do worse, for a canvas to work on, than the Art Deco Clare Hotel, which has been joined together with the Victorian-era Carlton United Breweries headquarters by enclosing the alleyway that ran between the two. The result is roughly one part lovingly preserved historical patina and one part ultra-modern, ultra-tasteful luxury, an impressive achievement and one that puts the Old Clare at the top of a lot of design junkies’ must-try lists.

They won’t be disappointed. Peng’s hotels have a history of delivering on their design promise with substantial comforts and a vibrant social life — here represented by the Clare Bar, with its high-design pub atmosphere, as well as a rooftop bar that features cocktails, light bites, and a perfect al fresco vibe. The Old Clare’ll put Chippendale on the map for future visitors to Sydney, and that’s more than you can expect most boutique hotels to do.

content:
Clearly the attraction here is the proximity to the ruins of the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, hidden away almost eight thousand feet up in Peru’s Andes mountains. There are other places to stay in the general area of Machu Picchu, but there’s only one luxury hotel within the protected sanctuary itself, on a mountain top literally just yards from the walls of the citadel, offering unparalleled access — you’ll watch the sun rise and set over the ruins, and have the opportunity to visit in the afternoons and evenings, after the tour groups have packed up and gone home.

Created in the Seventies as a government-run lodging, today the Sanctuary is a Belmond (formerly Orient Express) hotel; meaning that while the rooms aren’t overly large, they are comfortable and well-appointed, and the service rivals that on offer in many a big-city luxury hotel. One restaurant serves a buffet lunch to all comers, including day-trippers, while another is for the exclusive use of hotel guests, serving slightly more upmarket Peruvian and international fare.

Guided tours of the ruins are available, of course, and can be arranged by the hotel, which recommends two full days to properly take it all in. Nights are cold, and the rainy season runs from November to March — be prepared to dress accordingly.

How to get there:
A 3.5-hour train trip takes passengers from Cusco to Aguas Calientes, and from there it’s a half-hour bus ride up the mountain to the Belmond Sanctuary Lodge. To travel from Cusco to the hotel by foot along the old Inca trail, allow four or five days. There are no taxis from Machu Picchu Town to the Machu Picchu Citadel; the only form of transportation is on public buses.

content:
Even among grand hotels Mount Nelson, A Belmond Hotel, Cape Town stands out. This lush urban sanctuary, affectionately known by locals as “the Nellie,” has been the grande dame of the local hospitality scene since its opening in 1899. It’s set amidst nine acres of manicured gardens, ancient trees, and rolling lawns, and its seven historic wings frame spectacular views of Table Mountain, Lion’s Head, and Devil’s Peak.

And though it retains its period style, Mount Nelson is in spectacular shape for a 125-year-old hotel. The rooms and suites combine classic inspiration with a contemporary decorator’s eye as well as first-rate modern comforts; the Signature Suites are particularly lavish, more akin to private residences than ordinary hotel accommodations.

Guests unwind beside two large heated pools or play tennis on floodlit courts, with instruction by a resident coach; kids enjoy a supervised play center staffed by professional childminders. Meanwhile the Librisa Spa, set within a row of restored Victorian houses, offers a range of treatments along with yoga classes and personal training sessions.

As you’d expect from a hotel of its caliber, Mount Nelson cuts no corners in its culinary offerings. Options range from casual al fresco poolside dining to the intimate Chef’s Table experience; the hotel’s afternoon tea is a local legend, while Sundays are livened by the sound of Jazz Brunch. Just outside the hotel’s gates lies Kloof Street, alive with bars, cafés, and art galleries, and the city’s famous beaches and the Cape’s historic wine estates are within easy reach.

content:
Until recently, the only hotel filling the luxury-in-the-Atacama niche was Germán del Sol’s Explora—understandable since most craggy edge-of-the-world desert moonscapes haven’t got even one upscale adventure hotel. Now, though, there’s competition, and some of the finest comes in the form of Awasi, a slightly more modest but hardly less impressive lodging, in the riverside town of San Pedro de Atacama.

In some ways it’s austere, almost ascetic; rather than a modernist architectural statement, it’s a throwback to the past, comprising just eight adobe cottages furnished not with Scandinavian design classics but with rustic custom-built pieces. This restraint is all the more impressive for the fact that Awasi’s owners are an architect and a decorator, Francisco Rencoret and Paula Domínguez.

This was no busman’s holiday, however; from the results it’s apparent that they consciously steered clear of the territory marked out by their professional work, opting instead for maximum authenticity, meticulously researching local traditions and sticking whenever possible to indigenous materials.

In spite of all this, though, Awasi doesn’t exactly lack for luxury. You get a whole cottage to yourself, after all, with a private open-air courtyard, and decadent modern bathrooms, complete with marble baths, towel warmers, indoor and outdoor showers, and a vast selection of herbal soaps, salts, lotions and unguents. Breakfast, lunch and dinner are catered for, with the menu changing daily.

With comforts like these it’s tempting just to stay in—but the central appeal of Awasi is its natural setting. Your all-inclusive rate covers not just meals and transfers, but excursions as well; a small fleet of 4x4's and drivers are on hand to lead an ever-changing array of loosely structured tours and day trips, from hikes and nature walks to culture and archaeology tours, sporting adventures, even astronomer-led nighttime stargazing outings.

Awasi Atacama has a 3 night minimum stay requirement.

How to get there:
Awasi is approximately a 90 minute drive from Calama Airport.

content:
Normally, book a 16th-century château hotel, and you know what you’re getting into — food and wine, postcard-perfect scenery, and rooms that look a bit like a museum exhibit, drafty and full of creaky antique furniture. The surprise at the Château de Massillan is that while the food, wine and scenery are just as you’d expect, the interiors are chic and contemporary, designed by someone with a 21st-century eye.

This makes sense in light of the fact that the owners are London interior designers, whose spare, graphic style makes the most of the château’s twelve rooms. Nothing is lost in the visual translation — if anything the views of the Côtes-du-Rhône countryside look better from within these modern-luxe bedrooms. These days bathrooms are as important as bedrooms — all but one of the rooms come with bathtubs, and all are spacious, well-lit and well-mirrored.

Dining is understandably a big deal here — breakfast in-room, lunch al fresco in the courtyard by the pool, dinner in the traditional dining room beneath an ornate crystal chandelier, accompanied by an extensive wine list. You’re twenty minutes from Avignon, should you wish to explore, surrounded by world-famous vineyards, historical attractions Roman and French, and miles and miles of great outdoors, suited for hiking, biking, even canoeing.

content: Present-day Turin is perhaps better known for its industrial heritage, but a hotel like Opera 35 reaches a little bit further into the past, bringing modern boutique-hotel hospitality and design to a 19th-century Belle Époque setting. The building, a characteristic example of the era’s residential stock, has been carefully preserved; today its frescoes and stucco share space with contemporary Italian design furniture and modern fixtures and fittings. And the face it presents to the street is only part of Opera 35’s charm — the interior courtyard is an unusually tranquil outdoor space, located as it is within the center of a vibrant modern city.\n\nThe accommodations range from relatively conventional rooms and junior suites to more expansive and unique studio apartments, which add kitchens as well as space for up to four guests, making them a natural choice for extended stays or for travelers with kids. That kitchen will come in handy — like many small hotels in European city centers, Opera 35’s service is limited to breakfast, a light lunch, and aperitifs. Given the location, however, you’re hardly on your own, and the staff will help you choose among what must be a hundred restaurants within walking distance of the hotel.

content: The original Zoku, in Amsterdam, is a clever, compact, efficient little boutique hotel, and a stylish and livable one at the same time. In some ways it seemed so perfectly Dutch as to be possible only in Amsterdam; as the phrase Zoku Vienna reveals, though, this is decidedly not the case. It’s an apartment hotel, but not in the dull, beige, under-decorated way. Instead, its lofts, through some kind of advanced spatial wizardry, pack a whole residence’s worth of comforts into a hotel-room-sized area, including a living room, a kitchen, a dining table, and office space — provided your work is the sort of low-impact, laptop-centered work that’s the norm for today’s young creative class.\n\nIf you need more than that, it should be said that Zoku Vienna is full of meeting and events spaces of various sizes, from proper conference rooms to little co-working booths. And if you just want a change of scenery, its less structured common spaces are even more plentiful, from the rooftop, with its greenhouse, restaurant, bar and terrace, to the lobby’s Kindred Spirits bar and the adjoining Living Room. The restaurant’s tables are communal, naturally, as is the atmosphere all throughout — in fact you may find it difficult to drag yourself outside, though the Prater park is just across the road, and historic central Vienna just beyond.

content: The Luberon town of Cadenet is, by any account, a special place. But it wouldn’t do justice to Auberge La Fenière to speak of it only in terms of location, without discussing the people behind it — specifically the third-generation chef/owner Nadia Sammut, who is, after her mother, the second chef to have overseen La Fenière’s kitchen in its Michelin-starred era. Ms. Sammut regards La Fenière as no mere restaurant or lodging but a Place of Life, pursuing health, environmental stewardship, education, and all manner of human flourishing alongside the practices of cooking and hospitality.\n\nOf course those venerable practices are anything but neglected. As a hotel, La Fenière is a beautiful little gem, a mere six rooms decorated in a minimalist-chic style, packed with organic comforts, most of them overlooking the gardens, the olive groves, and the swimming pool. And as a restaurant, the MICHELIN-Starred Le Goût du Bonheur is an impressive one, not only for its culinary creativity and charming atmosphere but for the fact that it manages to effortlessly avoid gluten and dairy without feeling in any way impoverished; its “vegetal and marine” flavors are accompanied by thoughtfully chosen natural and biodynamic wines.

content:
The original Soho House could only have been established in London, a city with a history of members’-only clubs, and a place where the film, theatre, and art worlds are packed shoulder-to-shoulder; the concept translated fairly easily to downtown Manhattan as well. And here in West Hollywood, with a bit of adaptation, is a slightly sunnier version of the Soho House concept, in the form of the 34-room Holloway House.

Its location places it close to the storied nightlife of the Sunset Strip, but that’s almost secondary; Holloway House, like any Soho House establishment, doesn’t need to be close to the action — it is the action. Its Club restaurant, its Mandolin Mezze rooftop terrace, and its Club-adjacent Bar and Library are among the hottest tickets in town, and they’re for members only — which, if you’re an overnight guest, includes you, for the duration of your stay.

The rooms, of course, are perfectly capable of standing on their own. The Soho House style is roughly equal parts carefully composed contemporary design and eclectic, bohemian personality, and though the comforts are subtle, they’re decidedly high-end — and Soho House’s clientele, drawn largely from the Los Angeles creative industries, appreciates the attention to detail.

content: For half a century, the convivial Bar Américain was a favorite meeting place for Arles residents. After the café fell on hard times, an entrepreneurial duo swept in and brought new life to the building, restoring its interiors and opening their own restaurant and twelve-suite hotel. Maison Volver is everything you’d want of a petite urban hotel in a French city: stylish and slightly bohemian, but not trying too hard. On the street level, a lively restaurant with sidewalk seating and chalkboard menus serves up seasonal produce and local wines at rough-hewn wooden tables. \n\nAn old spiral staircase leads up to guest rooms, which are individually decorated with a mix of antiques and modern Scandinavian decor. Pretty details include terrazzo floors, white linen curtains, Murano lamps, colorful wallpaper, and kimonos in lieu of standard bathrobes. Bathrooms are light-filled and stocked with all-natural products, and most have ceramic-tiled bathtubs. Suites offer spacious living areas with sofas and writing desks. A gourmet homemade breakfast can be delivered to rooms on request or enjoyed alongside locals who swing by for their morning coffee. Arles’ historic center is at your doorstep, and the train station is just a five-minute stroll away.

content: Think of the Costa del Sol and you quite naturally imagine your hotel will be right front and center on the beach. Anantara Villa Padierna Palace Benahavís Marbella Resort, in contrast, lies some ten minutes inland — and, as it turns out, that makes all the difference. Well, that, and a few stylistic differences. Rather than the whitewashed Andalusian style you might expect, Padierna Palace is a dead ringer for a Tuscan villa. Not only that, but there’s more than a whiff of English country-house style in the hyper-luxe interiors. Safe to say it’s one of a kind — and it’s got the star-studded guestbook to prove it.\n\nThe accommodations are plush, and range from quite large rooms to downright enormous suites, and the service is first-rate. A small handful of restaurants and bars serve everything from upscale modern Spanish cuisine to classic cocktails, and the wellness and fitness offerings are particularly encyclopedic, from the Thermae spa to the racquet club and the three 18-hole golf courses. And despite your landlocked location, you’ve got more than one option for a swim — Padierna Palace’s pool is something rather special itself, and you’re a mere shuttle ride away from the Puro Beach Club, on the shores of the Mediterranean.

content:
You get the feeling in the southern Alps that the national borders are somewhat beside the point. The historic spa town of Lana, a few miles to the northwest of Bolzano, is Italian, sure, but this close to Austria it’s a vision of Italy that’s got very little to do with Rome, Venice or Milan. It’s a place where, for one thing, you’ll find Schwarzschmied — a hotel which, judging from the name alone, has strayed far from its Latin roots.

Look closer, though, and you’ll find a distinctly Italian version of the alpine good life. The design may veer towards Nordic simplicity but there’s also a thread of modernist-inspired contemporary Italian luxury design in the sleek, low-slung furnishings and the rich, earthy background colors. The open-plan spaces admit plenty of sunshine, and among the options are family suites which include separate bunk rooms for children.

The main attraction, obviously, in this most scenic corner of the Alps, is the outdoors, which in winter means skiing and in summer means anything from biking to hiking to golf and guided meditation walks. Wellness, naturally, is at the top of the agenda, and Schwarzschmied offers yoga, pilates, massages and spa treatments, and a culinary philosophy to match: in the restaurant, slow food meets minimalist design in an attempt to soothe the soul along with the digestion — with vegan and gluten-free options available as well.

How to get there: Hotel Schwarzschmied is approximately 148 km by car from Innsbruck Airport in Austria via E45, SS38, and SP69.

content:
There are other luxury hotels in St. Moritz, but the Kulm can credibly claim to be the original. It was the first, at any rate, dating back to 1856, and if certain others are perhaps more recognizable, it’s nothing to do with the merits of the place. This is as fine an Alpine five-star gets: have a look at the view from the balcony over the lake and tell us if you don’t agree.

While many a classic grand hotel has undergone a character-sapping renovation, the Kulm remains, aesthetically at least, exactly as it was: from the iconic exterior profiles of the four charmingly mismatched buildings, to the imposing colonnaded lobby with its grand marble staircase, to the bedrooms themselves, with their rich floral-print fabrics and finely carved pine woodworking. Beneath the surface, however, the rooms have kept pace with the times, right down to the wi-fi and the heated towel racks.

Obviously St. Moritz has a lot to recommend it as a ski town, and in winter this place is a paradise. Modern resorts run all four seasons now though, and the Kulm is no different. if it’s not the ski slopes, it’s the lake, the golf courses and the alpine trails — and neither the Kulm’s spa and wellness center nor its handful of upscale restaurants depend on any particular weather.

Please note:  Kulm Hotel St. Moritz is a seasonal hotel, open for winter from the beginning of December until the beginning of April.  In summer, the hotel is open from mid-June until the beginning of September.

The Soho House model — a members’ club oriented towards professionals in the arts and creative fields — was always destined to be a good fit for Amsterdam, not only because its intended audience is plentiful here, but also because its eclectic aesthetic is a perfect match for a city whose styles range from historic canal-house coziness to stark postmodern minimalism.

Set in the monumental 1930s Bungehuis, a beautifully restored Art Deco edifice, Soho House Amsterdam is as fully realized as any of the other Soho House properties: a lively mix of classic architecture, modern design, and contemporary art, in this case by a panoply of Dutch artists. The rooms feel collected rather than designed, and while they shy away from typical luxury-hotel opulence — and this being Amsterdam, they start out a bit compact — they are nothing if not comfortable.

Even more than most luxury boutique hotels, a club like Soho House relies on the quality of its (semi-) public spaces to attract members and guests. Here there’s a typically lavish athletic club and Cowshed spa, as well as events spaces and a 36-seat private cinema. Cecconi’s, the brand’s signature Italian kitchen, makes an appearance as well, and the Club menu is served all throughout the house at any time of day.

content:
The safari experience has changed in many ways since Hemingway’s day. For one thing, you’re here to photograph the wildlife, not bring it home. Perhaps most important, from the perspective of a lover of high-end hospitality, is that safari lodges are only getting more and more luxurious. Esiweni Luxury Safari Lodge is a case in point. Its setting, in the Nambiti private game reserve, is stunning, varied, wild, and chock full of animals. And back at the lodge, the living is easy indeed: it’s a Relais & Châteaux hotel owned by a French couple for whom “savoir vivre” is serious business.

That doesn’t mean their lodge looks like a French chateau. Esiweni combines contemporary construction and design with native materials and craftsmanship. With just five suites, it’s an intimate experience — at capacity, that’s a mere ten guests. Private terraces offer spectacular views, and the heated floors and luxurious bathrooms place physical comfort front and center.

Esiweni’s restaurant, where a South African chef, trained in London, combines Parisian traditions with local flavors, is a particular delight. And of course there’s more to experience than life at the lodge — you’ll want to leave plenty of time for sunrise and sunset excursions in an open-air 4x4 with an experienced ranger.

Time has a way of softening things; so it is with medieval castles converted into romantic getaways, like the lovely Pousada Castelo Óbidos, located just inland from the ocean, a short drive north of Lisbon. There’s quite a colorful history here involving falconry, fierce battles, and child brides. But you don’t need to worry about that when you’re wandering through the gardens or relaxing with a glass of wine on the stone terrace. A stone terrace called Porta da Traição — the Gate of Betrayal.

Suffice it to say that the castle had its moments back in the 13th century, but it’s probably quieter, and altogether more romantic, today. Now managed by the upscale Pestana chain, has just seventeen rooms, spread between the original castle and a newer “cottage” wing. The castle rooms have the thick walls, quaint hand-painted tiles, wooden shutters, and darkly romantic atmosphere you’d expect of an old and tastefully restored fortress. The cottage rooms have a brighter, more modern feel, though the blue and white color palette, and the four-poster beds, still look traditionally Portuguese. All guest rooms are spacious and lit with chandeliers — befitting a place where kings and queens used to sleep — and stocked with high-end amenities, from bed linens to bath products. Superior cottage rooms and cottage suites have balconies or terraces, not to mention fireplaces where you can really get into the spirit of medieval times.

Beyond guest rooms and suites, the castle is a delightful place to walk around. Unlike some historic landmarks converted into hotels, the Castelo Óbidos hasn’t been stripped of its personality and recast with minimalist furnishings and mood music. You’re still bound to bump into a coat of armor here, and the occasional oil painting. The buffet breakfast, featuring an array of Portuguese pastries you won’t find outside these particular borders, feels royal, indeed, and the village of Óbidos, with a range of of down-to-earth wine bars and cafés, is just a short stroll away. Why romanticize the past? The present looks pretty good in this town.

How to get there: Pousada de Obidos Historic Hotel is located approximately 80 km by car from Lisbon Portela Airport via A8.

content:
The appeal of Switzerland’s lakeside hotels is just as it was a century or more ago: a genteel sort of calm and comfort surrounded by some of the world’s most breathtaking landscapes. A shame, then, that so many of the hotels themselves are also just as they were a century or more ago — tranquil almost to the point of sedation, and taking stylistic conservatism to undreamt-of heights of blandness. This, thankfully, is not a problem Giardino Lago has. If you want to see what a classic lakeside escape looks like, updated for the modern boutique-hotel era, look no further.

Lake Maggiore straddles the Italian-Swiss border, and while the town of Minusio, where Giardino Lago is set, lies on the Swiss side, adjacent to Locarno, there’s a pronounced Italian accent to the hospitality here. Rooms are at once contemporary and classic, in that effortless Italian style, and there’s a focus on the finer things in life that one perhaps associates more with the Mediterranean than the Alps.

With fourteen rooms and one suite, it’s an intimate escape, hardly larger than a country house, and as it’s family-owned, it’s not a stretch to think of it in this way. The proprietors obviously have a keen eye for the finer points of architecture and design, and a way with an inviting public space as well — the rooftop lounge and outdoor terrace are where you’ll likely spend the bulk of your time, all the better to take in the panoramic views of the lake and the mountains beyond.

How to get there: Giardino Lago is approximately 113 km by car from Milan-Malpensa Airport via SS336, A36, A9/E35, A2, and A13. Alternatively, the hotel is approximately 211 km by car from Zürich Airport via A4/E41, A2/E35, and A13.

content:
Where else but in New Zealand would you actively seek out a working sheep ranch for a bit of rural high luxury? This is lodge country, where plush interiors and rugged exteriors go hand in glove. And this particular sheep ranch, Rosewood Cape Kidnappers, lies not on some dull green hillside but on the headlands overlooking Hawke’s Bay, on the North Island of New Zealand — a stunning setting in a country that’s not short on stunning settings.

The lodge itself isn’t hard on the eyes either — the building is a peculiarly modern sort of rustic, and the interiors are elegant, understated, clearly built at least as much for comfort as for good looks. They’re all suites, and they all have sweeping panoramic views up and down the coast, plus a full complement of modern and classic conveniences — flatscreens, iPod docks, luxury bathrooms, fireplaces.

In keeping with the subgenre of NZ lodge hospitality, you can expect a very upscale dining experience. The sourcing is local, with produce literally from the backyard when possible, but the dishes are refined — gentlemen, pack a jacket. There’s a small spa as well, and the on-site golf course — designed by visionary golf architect Tom Doak — is one of the finest in the world. These are large-scale luxuries, for such a small place — that’s the key to understanding Cape Kidnappers.

content:
The whole point of New Zealand, from an outsider’s perspective, is the outdoors — there’s city culture there, of course, but what’s worth going on and on about are the natural gifts of the place. So a hotel like Azur plays to all its location’s strengths; it’s urbane and sophisticated, just a few minutes from the center of Queenstown, but mostly it’s just immersed in natural splendor, with views of Lake Wakatipu and the Remarkable mountain range, and easy access to all the activities, from water sports to heli-skiing, that both entail.

It hardly gets more private than this: nine freestanding villas, practically self-contained residences, just the lack of a kitchen keeping them out of luxury-condo territory. Breakfast is served en-suite or in the lodge, and a variety of canapés and baked goods appear at various times of the day — tea time, cocktail hour, et cetera. Spa tubs sprawl under panoramic windows, and those fireplaces see a bit of use during ski season. It’s almost hard to imagine leaving — luckily Azur provides complimentary transfers to Queenstown’s restaurants.

Of course you’ll want to get out at some point. Holing up in your villa pales in comparison to what the South Island setting has to offer — it’s a destination for all seasons, offering literally any outdoor activity imaginable, depending on the time of year.

How to get there:
Azur is approximately a 15 minute drive from Queenstown Airport.

content: A few blocks from its sister on Danforth Street, Blind Tiger Carleton Street carries on in the same style: a six-room guest house in a charming residential neighborhood, decorated with a carefully curated selection of vintage furnishings and local artworks, all within easy walking distance of the best this city has to offer. It’s the work of Lark Hotels, the group responsible for many of New England’s finest boutique hotels — which may be why, in spite of their small size and their private nature, the Blind Tiger houses manage to be such friendly and sociable places.\n\nThe Carleton Street rooms are no less full of character than their Danforth Street counterparts, though they are, in at least one way, rather more low-key — televisions are entirely absent, replaced by luxe touches like Lather bath products and waffle kimono robes. And the house’s services are similarly minimal; breakfast takes the form of a self-serve toast and yogurt bar, augmented by a pantry stocked with coffee, tea, and locally sourced snacks. Because as pleasant as it is to stay here, you’re meant to get out and about; to that end, the concierge is on hand with recommendations tailored to your interests.

content: Not some rough-hewn medieval tower, but an opulent 18th-century palace built by a Piedmontese aristocrat, Castello di Guarene remains true to its original vision even in its modern guise as a luxury boutique hotel — there’s nothing the least bit stark, spare, or minimalist about this particular Italian castle. The historical structure contains twelve rooms and suites of varying size, from the 40-square-meter Classic room to the Luxury Suite, which spans an extraordinary 200. But what they’ve all got in common is a maximally ornate interior style and views of the castle’s extravagant gardens as well as the Piedmontese hills or the distant Alps.\n\nOf course, while the castle’s atmosphere may be antique, its comforts are contemporary; in among the silk and velvet tapestries are contemporary niceties like LED televisions and wireless internet access. The restaurant, with its vaulted ceilings, is another memorable space, and the cuisine is more than worthy of its surroundings — not only are the ingredients and recipes of the surrounding landscape put to fine and inventive use here, but the wine cellar contains an encyclopedic collection of rare vintages from Piedmont and beyond.

content:
Florence is perhaps best known as a cultural destination, a place where you feed your mind by exposure to Europe’s greatest concentration of artistic treasures. But this is a city that’s also not averse to creature comforts, either — after all, all those treasures only ended up here because of Florence’s immense wealth. A hotel like Hotel Number Nine, then, is perfectly placed to cater to the needs of both the body and the mind.

It’s housed in a seventeenth-century palazzo in the city center, two minutes’ walk from the Duomo and close by to everything else in this compact town. Classic stonework provides the historical gravity while modern furniture and bold colors display the ease with which Italians mix old and new. And the rooms, similarly, are classic and contemporary at the same time — it’s palazzo living for the modern era.

And when it’s time to relax the mind and devote a little attention to the body, there’s the Spa Number Nine, with facilities including a jacuzzi, a sauna, and a Turkish bath. Moreover, there's also a capacious and well-equipped fitness center and a phalanx of instructors and personal trainers. Think of it a bit like a fitness- and wellness-oriented luxury resort experience with an urban boutique hotel location, a hotel that’s equally rewarding as a pied-à-terre or a place to shut yourself away from it all.

content:
It’s a common knock against Switzerland to say that the uniformly high quality of life somehow crowds out anything in the way of personality. Now, there are certainly places where this might ring true, but the Hotel Helvetia Zürich is not one of them. This place positively drips with character, all without sacrificing the coziness and comfort that’s quintessentially Swiss.

It starts with the neighborhood: the Helvetia makes its home at the edge of Kreis 4, one of Zurich’s most vibrant districts, and it’s picturesquely perched above the Sihl river, south of where it meets the Limmat. The 19th-century building itself is well preserved, its historical character left largely intact, but its interiors have seen some recent interior-design attention. The result is tasteful, attractive, and effortlessly hip, unmistakably individual — a great homegrown, organic exception in a world of off-the-shelf boutique-hotel concepts.

Thirty-four rooms and two luxury apartments are the sum of the accommodations, which means the Helvetia sticks to a fairly intimate scale. They’re comfortable and contemporary, and the top-floor apartments add kitchenettes and daybeds to the mix. And you’d do well to make time for the hotel’s restaurant — here the dining room is a local attraction unto itself.

content:
There are hotels that bowl you over with their undeniable hotel-ness: the doorman, the bellhop, the smiling concierge and the hustling waiters, pushing room service carts up and down the corridors. And then there are places that are barely hotels at all, little more than a comfortable and exquisitely designed guest house, trading all the pomp for a more personal charm, privacy and intimacy.

Hotel De Witte Lelie, the White Lily, is quite plainly an example of the latter genre. Here three seventeenth-century canal houses have been joined together to create Antwerp’s most luxurious small hotel. You can take the name almost as literally as you like; the expansive public spaces are swathed in plush white rugs, sofas and armchairs, with more than a few lilies to be seen, and the guest rooms are white-on-white and lighter than air, contemporary rather than modernist, as stylish and elegant as any in this fashionable city.

That’s not a typo — Antwerp is not just a port city, and the European center of the diamond trade, but the epicenter of a Belgian fashion explosion as well, and your fellow guests at Hotel De Witte Lelie are just as likely to be stylists or designers as they are traveling businessmen or diamond importers. Let’s just say you may wish to consider dressing for the breakfast buffet.

After that, there’s little to be had in terms of services, but it would be churlish to complain. This is no urban resort, simply a stylish and exquisitely comfortable pied à terre from which to explore the museums, boutiques and restaurants of this charming city.

content:
There’s nothing that catches the eye of a mountain-hotel aficionado quite like an Italian hotel with a German name. It’s the sort of thing that only happens in South Tyrol, the Alpine corner of Italy. About midway between Verona and Innsbruck, Austria, not far from Bolzano, is where you’ll find the Lake Spa Hotel Seeleiten. It’s set by the side of Lake Caldaro, in a spectacular wine-producing valley surrounded on all sides by mountain peaks.

The hotel itself is eye-catching as well, a long lodge-like structure surrounded with a sort of timber exoskeleton. The rooms and suites are attractively modern, retaining a bit of knotty pine for Alpine tradition but generally tending towards a contemporary simplicity and a sophisticated sheen. The single rooms are smallish, but the junior suites are generous, and by the time you’re in a suite (or an apartment) you’ll have more space than you know what to do with.

Wellness is an area of particular focus — there’s a substantial spa with a wide range of treatments, as well as a trio of pools: one indoor, one outdoor, and one a lake-like “water world” with its own sandy beach. Activities include anything you can do on the lake, as well as golf, tennis, hiking, biking, and tours of the region. And those vineyards in the middle distance aren’t just for show — along with the hotel’s Alpine/Mediterranean cuisine you’ll have the opportunity to taste wines from the hotel’s own winery, as well as others from the immediate area.

content: There’s often a sense around Waikīkī that the best time to visit might have been a few decades ago, before the beachfront filled in with towers. White Sands Hotel proudly declares itself to be the “last of the vintage walk-up hotels,” and it’s exactly that: a low-rise, three-story compound oriented around a palm-lined swimming pool and plentiful lounge and garden space. It’s an intentional throwback to the Seventies, when Honolulu still felt like a world apart from the continental U.S., and when laid-back bohemianism had yet to be replaced by sanitized luxury.\n\nNeedless to say, at White Sands you won’t find the same kind of extravagance you’ll find at the local luxury resorts — and you won’t miss it. Here you’ll find romance, atmosphere, and personality — and if you’re old enough to remember the real Seventies aesthetic, rest assured, this is an idealized, updated version. The hotel will hook you up with a boogie board and a beach chair if you’re after some waves, and back at the hotel you’ll be grateful for the restaurant, Heyday, a knowingly nostalgic restaurant by a couple of well-known local restaurateurs.

content:
Adrian Zecha knows hotels. The Aman founder’s vision of small-scale, high-design, no-expense-spared resorts more or less established the luxury boutique hotel as a genre, and under the Azerai banner, he continues to develop his hospitality vision. Legacy Mekong stands on an islet in the Hau river, just outside the Mekong Delta city of Can Tho, accessible only by boat — and that small separation is all it needs to create a complete and transformative escape.

The accommodations range from relatively humble rooms with garden, lake, or river views all the way up to a five-bedroom villa with a private pool. In typical Zecha style, however, all rooms are thoroughly luxurious, their style equal parts classic and contemporary. There’s no essential comfort left out, and on the other hand there’s no needless opulence — nothing to break the spell of a faultless travel experience.

Equally impressive are the Grill, the Café, and the Lounge & Bar, each one combining local traditions and flavors with modern techniques and inspirations. Wellness offerings include a spectacular infinity pool as well as a yoga pavilion, a Pilates studio, a tennis court, and a stylish and thorough spa. And the excursions, naturally, focus on the Mekong delta, including tours of the famous Cai Rang floating market.

content:
If the aesthetic looks familiar, you’re not imagining things: Arrive Palm Springs is a Palisociety venture, an adaptation of the group’s accessibly glamorous look and invitingly sociable atmosphere to a modernist-inspired compound in the Uptown Design District. The architecture is distinctive, and traces its heritage to the local style, but you wouldn’t call it retro — this is no space-age throwback, but pure 21st-century Palm Springs.

The rooms are not just photogenic, they’re exceedingly comfortable, though they stop short of excess; Studio rooms come with king beds, marble-accented bathrooms, and automatic shades, while the Patio rooms add a touch of private outdoor space, complete with a fireplace. Interiors feature some retro-inspired elements, from Victorian-style wallpaper and curvaceous leather armchairs to modernist chairs, desks, and lamps — the look is appealingly eclectic, which lends a certain warmth.

And in a hotel like Arrive, you’re meant to spend as much time in the public spaces as in your room. Fortunately they make it easy, with a vast expanse of poolside lounge space, as well as a café by the Arizona-based Cartel Coffee Lab, an ice cream shop, and an indoor/outdoor restaurant and bar.

content:
In Lecce, the Baroque jewel of the Salentine peninsula, this luxurious little hotel is a tribute to the memory of Antonia Fiermonte, the owners’ grandmother, an artist and extraordinary woman who lived in the first half of the 20th century. The estate on which La Fiermontina Luxury Home stands can trace its roots to the 16th century, and the house itself to the 17th. It’s been substantially rebuilt, however, with the help of the local architect Antonio Annicchiarico; what stands here today is a tribute to the arches and vaults of the classic Pugliese masseria, but a thoroughly modern one.

The family is well-connected in the art world — Antonia was a talented artist and we invite you to discover her history in the Fiermonte Museum — and La Fiermontina’s interiors are full of paintings, photographs, and sculptures, not to mention contemporary Italian design furniture.

Zèphyr, the restaurant, serves fine modern Puglian fare surrounded by the courtyard’s citrus groves. And La Fiermontina never misses a chance to celebrate the local traditions, offering everything from on-site cooking classes to tours of the city of Lecce and the greater Salentine peninsula.

content:
Brussels is a major city, but a compact one, and you don’t have to get very far out of town before urban life gives way to peaceful countryside. Indrani Lodge is less than an hour’s drive from the city center, in the village of Loupoigne, but that’s more than far enough for this restored medieval farm to serve as an escape for all sorts of travelers, from couples on the run for a weekend from Brussels to a full house of guests attending one of Indrani Lodge’s yoga retreats. (Yoga is an everyday specialty here; retreats aside, multiple classes are held daily.)

The medieval farmhouse buildings conceal ultra-modern interiors. Indrani Lodge’s rooms, all unique, combine period architecture with contemporary design and contemporary art, resulting in living quarters that are timelessly stylish — and more than a little bit luxurious. The spaces vary from merely large to downright sprawling, in the case of the 200-square-meter Loft, and if you’re traveling with your family or entourage, the whole house is available all at once.

Meanwhile a wellness center offers massages, as well as a sauna and a heated indoor pool. And the restaurant, Elements, is joined by Petits Elements, both serving dishes crafted from local and seasonal ingredeints, many grown on site.

content: It’s been a while since these bagni were really nuovi — the thermal baths at Bormio, in the far Alpine north of Lombardy, have been an attraction since at least the Roman Empire, and the hotel dates back to 1836. As a destination for foreign visitors it may not be on the same level as your Tuscanys, your Amalfis, your Lake Comos. But if the Grand Hotel Bagni Nuovi is any indication, Bormio is capable of playing in Italian hospitality’s highest league. It starts with some subtle design, as throughout the seventy-four rooms and suites, restraint is the watchword. Historical elements meet contemporary design with that thoroughly Italian effortlessness. Space is plentiful, as it should be, and there’s more than a touch of luxury: many of the white marble-clad bathrooms feature whirlpool baths fed by thermal waters, and the Royal Suite, built for Vittorio Emanuele III, still holds his original pink Candoglia marble bathtub. When it comes to facilities you’re spoilt for choice. In addition to the grand dining room and the café, Bagni Nuovi guests have access to the restaurant at the sister hotel, the Bagni Vecchi. Same goes for the spa — the Bagni Nuovi’s treatment rooms are more than extensive enough, but the Vecchi’s add a bit of variety. A shuttle connects the two, and also links you to the ski lift, giving both hotels’ guests the run of the town. Please note: Minimum night restrictions may apply.

content: Contrary to stereotype, most of Stockholm’s best hotels are grand 19th-century edifices. But in Hotel Six you’ll find the modernist paradise you’ve always expected from the Scandinavian boutique-hotel scene. At Six is part of the redevelopment of Brunkebergstorg Square, whose Sixties Brutalist style has come back around from retro curiosity to contemporary inspiration, and the interiors, by the London-based Universal Design Studio, show the way forward — as does the art collection, which is museum-quality, and rather than recede into the background, takes center stage, beginning with the Jaume Plensa statue that dominates the entry stair.\n\nAt Six’s rooms and suites are no less stylish, in their dark monochrome palette, and they feature some real luxuries, including high-end locally made bedding and bath products. Standard rooms are spacious, with desks and lounge seating, and by the time you’re in a suite you’re in what feels like acres of space. An elegant little drink cabinet replaces the ordinary minibar, and the views, thanks to the building’s elevation, are unusual for Stockholm. The Dining Room is the high-end modern-Scandinavian restaurant, and Blanche & Hierta is a coffee house, a wine bar, and a delicatessen all in one. Meanwhile the Cocktail Bar is the chic nightspot, while Hosoi is a more casual space with an emphasis on DJs and live music.

content:
Regardless of where you’re staying in Berlin, there’s a fair chance you’ll end up at the Amano one evening. That's because the hotel’s hip rooftop bar — laid-back but fashionable, with sweeping skyline views, manned by serious mixologists — is a destination in itself, frequently cited by both locals and travel magazines as one of the city’s top spots for a sundowner. But this isn’t just a bar with a hotel attached; the Amano group’s high standards and innovative design inform all of the hotel’s spaces, not just those that are open to the public.
 
Since opening in 2009, the modern 163-room Amano has attracted mostly business travelers. But that demographic is changing, with the hotel offering hipster-friendly amenities including bicycle rental, “pedestrian navigation systems,” and iPods programmed with walking tours of the neighborhood. The design doesn’t hurt, either — the interiors were done by Esther Bruzkus Architects, the well-established Berlin design group. The look is contemporary, but not cold: think leather banquette seating running the entire length of the far wall, huge picture windows, striking accents in bronze and mirrored glass, glamorous columns seemingly inspired by old-world Berlin, but reimagined with eye-catching industrial materials. 

Guest rooms and apartments, playfully categorized into Standard, M, L and XL, are crisp and cool, with shining parquet floors, done up in bright whites and sophisticated charcoal. Apartments come with stylishly equipped kitchens and extra living space; some have small private balconies. But apart from the XL, which has a lavish, slightly sultry look that makes it stand apart from the rest of the hotel, the guest rooms are more about function than form. Generally speaking, there's no splashy artwork up here, nothing trendy or gimmicky, just clean lines and well-made furnishings, luxurious linens, wi-fi that always works. (You’re in Germany, where everything always works.)
 
If there’s anything missing, it’s a restaurant — though there is a garden breakfast area, as well as the popular Amano Bar and the quieter Amano lobby bar. But thanks to its central location, on a quiet side street in Mitte, you’re just around the corner from a wide range of dining and nightlife venues, including the popular Mani restaurant at the Hotel Mani, also known as the Amano’s little sister.

content:
San Cristóbal de las Casas is nestled in a picturesque valley near Mayan archaeological zones, and its Spanish Colonial heart is bursting with Baroque churches and Neoclassical buildings. Throw in a dash of Moorish influence and, more recently, the Zapatistas, and you’ve got a heady historical brew. Hotel BO distills the cultural elements that have been in flux here for centuries, while at the same time paying tribute to the elements that shape the landscape — water, fire, air and earth.

If that sounds a bit new-age, rest assured that you won’t find a backlit crystal anywhere in the hotel. Quite the opposite, in fact: the grounded, forward-thinking design carves up the public spaces in clean-lined modern style (don’t miss the sleek geometry of the courtyard pool, interrupted by a single tree). The 22 guest rooms steer clear of minimalism, however — they’re vibrant without being riotous, their bright colors tempered by plenty of handsome local wood. Several rooms offer private solariums or terraces, and the panoramic views deliver some of the most vital scenery in Chiapas. 

Between the breezy aesthetics of the open-plan areas and the laid-back warmth of the rooms — woolen throws, for example, round out the décor — it’s easy to forget about design-hotel pretension altogether, and convince yourself that Hotel BO is really just an all-inclusive garden party. And at Lum, the hotel restaurant, chef Ricardo Muñoz Zurita isn’t about to dissuade guests from this idea, as he pairs classic Mexican cuisine with expertly selected wines and tequilas.

How to get there:
Hotel Bo is located 40 minutes by car from Angel Albino Corzo International Airport.

content:
Bringing crisp minimal design out of the city and into the wild, Southern Ocean Lodge is a shining example of very modern and very Australian architecture: clean open spaces, neutral tones and tons of glass wrapped in an environmentally friendly package. Located on Kangaroo Island just off the South Australian coast, Southern Ocean Lodge is unexpectedly hip for such a remote and rugged locale, sporting a cool, unlabored vibe that doesn’t interfere with its beautiful coastal surrounds. 

Comprising 25 sea-facing rooms, the lodge hovers over the mallee scrub, offering wide views of ocean, sky and whatever fauna happens to venture past: expect anything from kangaroos to echidnas to native birds. Inside, paintings by local artists complement pure white walls, with bespoke furniture and Ecosmart fireplaces creating the type of relaxed, uncluttered feeling one vows to recreate at home. 

Tuning out is the main past time at Southern Ocean Lodge (only the Baillie Pavilion has a TV) and guests can choose to do this on their private terrace, in their sunken lounge, or on one of a long list of nature tours. The surrounding national parkland offers so much by way of exploration — sea lion-spotting, kangaroo-meeting and hiking included — that the lodge provides each guest with a custom itinerary. Of course, some may opt to do nothing more demanding than enjoy the property’s gourmet meals and open bar, including a walk-in cellar stocked with locally-produced wines, all included in the tariff. 

Daily sunset drinks in the lodge’s Great Room allow guests to swap travel stories while taking in views of the Southern Ocean. An onsite spa with floor-to-ceiling windows offers a further chance to unwind while watching — and being watched by, presumably — the local wildlife.

How to get there: Kangaroo Island is located only 15 km from the shores of mainland South Australia. QantasLink provides regular 40-minute flights from Adelaide (ADL) to Kangaroo Island–Kingscote (KGC).  Located at Hanson Bay on the island's southwest coast, the lodge is a 50-minute drive from the airport. The lodge operates small group transfers connecting with all scheduled flights. Please contact CustomerService@TabletHotels.com for assistance with airport transfers.

content: Even a place as over-developed and over-traveled as Cozumel can show you its best side, given an impressive enough hotel. Here, that hotel is the Intercontinental Presidente Cozumel, set on a somewhat secluded stretch of beach to the south of the city proper. And though the property is dotted with palm trees and thatched roofs, this is, in essence, a totally modern luxury hotel, with over 200 rooms and suites, four restaurants, and a wealth of leisure and adventure opportunities.\n\nThe accommodations are unashamedly luxe, some enjoying elevated views from the hotel’s tower wing, others at ground level overlooking the pool and gardens or the beach. Every one comes with a patio or balcony, and they’re furnished with typically high-end comforts. There’s a spa whose treatments draw from Maya tradition, as well as a kids’ club with a cultural slant, and the hotel’s dive center can prepare you for a visit to the marine preserve at the island’s southern end. There’s also a putting green and a tennis club, and all manner of excursions can be arranged, from dolphin-watching to archaeological tours.

In the South of France there’s no need to reinvent the hospitality wheel. Le Mas de la Rose is a stone-cold classic of the Provençal farmhouse-hotel genre, a 17th-century example that’s been thoroughly restored without sacrificing any of its historical charm. The setting, at the foot of the Alpilles, is appropriately bucolic, and the estate is as well, with its typical lavender and olive groves.

Each room is subtly different, though all are lovely, in a soothing faded-to-white color palette with textures that beg to be touched. Some rooms add bathtubs and/or terraces, while the suites and the apartment sleep up to four. There’s a beach-style outdoor pool and a Jacuzzi by its side, and leisure offerings include tennis and petanque courts as well as billiards and ping-pong.

As fine a place as Le Mas de la Rose is for lounging around, the surrounding countryside beckons as well, as do Arles and Aix-en-Provence. Just be back in time for dinner — Le Potager du Mas, the hotel’s restaurant, is worth the trip all on its own, thanks to its menu of local, seasonal dishes, all crafted from locally sourced ingredients including fruits and vegetables grown on site.

content:
First things first, to facilitate the conversation with your taxi driver: XVI means “sixteen,” as you’d guess, and is pronounced “dieciséis,” as you might remember from the first week of Spanish. The number is key to the concept behind the Hotel Casas del XVI, a chic colonial-style hotel located in the historic center of Santo Domingo. Sixteen isn’t the address, or the number of rooms: it’s the century that the hotel evokes and celebrates — the birth of what’s now considered the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.

The idea here is to recreate the experience of Spanish nobility who came to the New World in the city’s early days. So it’s old-fashioned glamour to the hilt, plus the modern amenities you wouldn’t dream of doing without. The casas in question are a pair of elegant neighboring villas, gloriously restored and refashioned into a seven-suite hotel. Casa del Arbol has a cozy library, a sleek kitchen and bar, and an outdoor dining area. Casa de los Mapas, meanwhile, faces out onto a charming central courtyard that's straight out of your vacation fantasies: towering palm trees, a swimming pool that glows turquoise at night, candlelit daybeds where one of the hotel’s dedicated butlers will be more than pleased to serve you a mojito, or a Mamajuana if you’re feeling adventurous. 

You can guess at what you’ll find in these guest rooms. Four-poster beds, arching doorways, gorgeously tiled floors: check, check, and check, plus iPhone docks, flat-screen TVs, and bath products by Antica Farmacista. What you might not guess is just how many adorably quirky details you’ll discover at Hotel Casas del XVI. Hotels this high-end often trade off character for bland but tasteful luxury that’s meant to appeal to every possible guest. But Casas del XVI has, in addition to its traditional architecture and colonial antiques, purple walls, modern art, floating bathtubs, light fixtures shaped like pineapples, indigenous crafts, a collection of old maps. It’s a hotel with a big personality, rich with colorful details — and it’s worth mentioning that it’s extremely LGBT-friendly, something that’s by no means a given in this part of the world. The idea is to relax and recharge, much as the fresh-off-the-boat Spanish elite would have done in the 16th century. But don’t be surprised if the place makes you feel more stimulated than you'd planned — more likely to break out your sketchbook than roll over and take a nap.

Set in three acres of manicured garden in Marrakech’s Palmeraïe, Les Deux Tours is nothing if not an escape. Though your proximity to the old city means you’re anything but isolated, you won’t exactly feel the hum of the medina’s busy streets. Instead you’ll exult in the quiet that surrounds the resort, itself comprising half a dozen individual riads, available for rent either room by room or in their entirety.

There are 44 rooms in total, and it’s clear they’re made more with an eye towards atmosphere than fashion. Though not untouched by contemporary design, Les Deux Tours is a classic at heart, drawing its stylistic inspiration from an era when the phrase “boutique hotel” hadn’t yet been invented. The standard rooms are spacious and, when desired, full of light — and the suites are downright majestic, especially those with access to private plunge pools.

Here there’s room for a central dining room, to cap off a day that began with an en-suite breakfast. By day all the charms of Marrakech are accessible, though the grounds and gardens of Les Deux Tours tempt many a guest to stay in. And of course it just wouldn’t be Morocco without the hammam.

These days the political intrigue takes place elsewhere, but once upon a time this Turin was the first capital of the freshly united Kingdom of Italy. Hence its numerous piazzas, each awash with statuary — not to mention the actual palaces, from which (one imagines) Turin Palace Hotel derives its name. It’s appropriate enough, given the building’s century and a half of heritage, nearly all of them as this very hotel. And though it’s been thoroughly modernized inside, the edifice still fits right in with the monumental grandeur of its neighbor, the Porto Nuova train station.

At 126 rooms and a presidential suite, the Palace is thankfully cozier than the station. The gleaming décor mostly toes the business-formal party line, every now and then allowing itself a charmingly framed print or a burst of fresh flowers. Rooms come in muted, delicate pastels, great for diffusing the light and easing travel-weary eyes. Modestly lustrous surfaces predominate, balanced by plush, curvilinear seating and luxe bedding. En-suite bathrooms lend a vintage touch with checkered tiles, classic lever handles, and old-fashioned cross knobs on the faucets. Higher-tier rooms are on the upper floors, naturally, offering private balconies from which guests can survey picturesque terra-cotta roofs in every direction.

Contemporary comforts — free wi-fi, flatscreens, organic bath amenities — hit all the right notes, as does the on-site spa with a hammam and sauna. Les Petites Madeleines, the restaurant, presents contemporary Italian fare with gastronomic aplomb on spotlessly white tableware; avail yourself of the terrace, weather permitting. If you’re still hungry, rest assured that the Turinese love their cafés nearly as much as they love their piazzas. If the Chapel of the Holy Shroud is full, consider waiting out the crowds at the Parco del Valentino, a botanical garden on the banks of the Po.

The city of Siracusa on Sicily’s eastern coast is a place where the style and architecture of the Mediterranean’s great empires, from the Greek to the Roman to the Byzantine, still linger. Cities with this kind of history always seem to have a proliferation of luxury hotels housed within grand old buildings, and Siracusa is no exception. But why not take advantage of the kind of modernism that Italians do best, a sensibility that imbues even the starkest minimalism with a casual sumptuousness? The UNA group are old hands at this urbane decadence, and Una Hotel Siracusa is a perfect example.

The 44 guest rooms don’t really adhere to a rigid formula, so don’t be fooled by the predominantly black-and-white style. Witty mod-era and ‘70s-influenced accents abound, especially within the aptly named Circle Room, with its perfectly round bed, luminescent nightstand, and curvaceous furniture. On the more spacious end, deluxe suites offer private terraces with pebble flooring and wooden lounge chairs, a mellow alternative to the hotel’s trendy rooftop terrace — the Sky Roof cocktail lounge — which is well worth visiting for the panoramic view of the historic city.

Far from an afterthought, the hotel spa offers a variety of cutting-edge wellness treatments in its beauty clinic, along with a hydrotherapy pool cut from natural rock. Una Hotel Siracusa takes freedom-of-relaxation seriously, and — even encourages — newly refreshed guests to dine in their bathrobes. The restaurant is chic, but not painfully so, and it’s almost certainly the only place in Sicily where one can eat sushi among robe-clad vacationers.

content:
Belize’s reputation as paradise on earth is not entirely undeserved — and in paradise, even connecting flights and airport transfers turn out to contain an unexpected element of pleasure. The trip from Belize City to Ambergris Caye involves a commuter flight and then a boat ride, but that flight (over the Barrier Reef) only helps the eye adjust to all the tropical blues, and that speed boat trip along the warm Caribbean water ranks as one of the more romantic, full-sensory hotel arrivals out there. And at the end of the really not so arduous journey, as these things go, you find yourself at Las Terrazas. 

Situated right on the white sandy beach, Las Terrazas is a resort in the proper sense of the word — there’s a huge infinity pool, a fine-dining restaurant, a spa and wellness center, the works. That’s why it’s surprising to realize that there are only 37 guestrooms. “Rooms” isn’t the right word, either — at Las Terrazas, they’re more like luxury apartments, with one to three bedrooms each, all outfitted in casually elegant Belizean-produced furnishings. The two-story oceanfront residence, opening straight onto the beach, is particularly paradise-like, as is the oceanview penthouse suite, complete with private plunge pool. 

But even in the standard residences, there’s plenty of room, and more amenities than you’d ever need for a lazy island vacation — including a fully equipped kitchen, a separate dining room, and two large bathrooms. Put it this way — if you need a little space from your traveling companion, you’re in the right place. At night, if you wished, you could put on your matching fluffy bathrobes (complimentary) and retreat to your two separate flat-screen TVs.

Then again you came to Belize for the sun and sea. Las Terrazas offers a 5-star PADI-certified dive shop and complimentary scuba lessons in the pool. For something tamer, there’s a fleet of kayaks and Hobie Cats ready to be taken into the water; for something even more relaxed, there are lovely white-cushioned chaise lounges waiting on every terrace and stretch of sand.

How to get there: Belize International (BZE) is the closest major airport to Las Terrazas. From Belize International, it’s a 20-minute flight to the San Pedro air strip, followed by a short drive to the local marina and a private 10-minute boat ride to the resort. Transfers cost $199 USD per person, round trip, and must be arranged at least two weeks prior to travel.

There’s no mistaking the Palihotels aesthetic, marked as it is by a distinctive palette of soft colors and an eclectic design sense that’s equally reminiscent of modern boutique hotels and classic European inns. This is true even when the hotel in question is a renovation of a 1958 motel, which is what the Palihotel Hollywood is — now a 76-room boutique hotel right on Sunset Boulevard, complete with a spa, a courtyard swimming pool, and a poolside restaurant and bar.

Rooms vary widely, and go well beyond their motel origins — spacious doubles, queens, kings, and suites, and even a few with balconies. The so-called Night Owl rooms are extra-cozy, with windows that face a corridor rather than outside; even these are equipped with luxe and thoughtful touches like SMEG mini-fridges, Nespresso machines, and Diptyque bath products.

The eye-catching checkerboard pool deck is the daytime social heart of the hotel, as guests recline on poolside loungers and sip margaritas in the shade. The restaurant, Benny’s on the Blvd., serves breakfast and Texas taqueria-inspired fare into the afternoon. And at night Benny’s transitions to cocktail-bar mode; for dinner, guests are turned loose on Hollywood’s star-studded restaurant scene.

content: It may seem odd to follow up three Miami-area boutique hotels with a restoration of the oldest continually operating hotel in Nantucket, but what the Life House hotels share is less a copy-paste stylistic identity and more a conceptual approach — one that prizes authenticity and fidelity to the uniqueness of the setting. This old sea captain’s house became an inn in the 1830s, and while it’s been thoroughly redesigned — and functionally been brought up to 21st-century luxury-boutique standards — it’s full of details that suggest a long and eclectic history. A fine breakfast is the only meal served, unless you count afternoon tea in the gardens, but from this location you’re meant to get out and explore the town, which has no shortage of excellent restaurants among its many charms.

content: Montréal’s hotel scene is unique in North America, largely because of the high concentration of historical atmosphere in Vieux Montréal, the city’s old quarter. But there’s plenty of personality, architectural and otherwise, to be found elsewhere around town. The so-called Golden Square Mile is the historic commercial district, and among its regal old edifices is a stunning neo-Renaissance structure that was originally the home of one the city’s movers and shakers, Lord George Stephen — and it’s for him that the structure, in its new guise as a luxury hotel, is named today: Le Mount Stephen Hotel.\n\nDon’t get too attached to the 1883-vintage façade, however. Though the historical building contains the restaurant and the bar, both of which make the most of their beautifully preserved 19th-century spaces, the guest rooms occupy a modern addition — and we do mean modern. As you check in you’re transported straight to the 21st century, into rooms and suites that are not just contemporary in style but loaded with up-to-date comforts like chromatherapy showers, Toto washlets, and Nespresso machines. The best of them are truly extravagant, adding massive skylights, fireplaces, and bathtubs, while the three-bedroom Royal Suite spans the entirety of the 11th floor.

content:
The Catalonia Berlin Mitte is, if you’ll excuse the analogy, the opposite of a mullet: party in the front, business in the back. Only in Berlin would you find this particular mix, with edgy industrial-chic public spaces, graffiti-strewn corridors (painted by some of Berlin’s best-known street artists), and… rooms that are nothing if not restrained, sedate, valuing practicality above all else.

It’s a bet on the proposition that outrageous design is all well and good when you’re out and about, but comfort demands that it be left at the threshold to your bedroom. We know quite a few design-hotel devotees who secretly agree. In a budget-friendly city hotel, comfort is at a premium, and there’s no sense in subjecting guests to the disorienting estrangement of a total reinvention of the hotel-room experience. What you’ll find instead is a room that’s restful, quietly stylish, contemporary, yet functionally transparent — everything you expect to find is exactly where it should be.

Downstairs is where you go to for a bit of stimulation. The name of the restaurant, Kunstwerk, might overstate its case a bit, but it’s an attractive space, to be sure, and the lobby is a fine example of the vintage-infused style that’s currently the norm in Berlin. And from there you’ve got the city at your feet — the U-Bahn station is right in front of the hotel.

The village of Broc in the central French region of Auvergne is the setting for Origines, an unusual small hotel and a Michelin-starred restaurant by chef Adrien Descouls, an Auvergne native. It occupies a distinctive modern building, made even more so by the contrast with the 14th-century castle whose walls it adjoins. And the view from the dining room and the public spaces is an unusual one, taking in a panorama of the volcanoes that are Auvergne’s most memorable natural feature.

As is typically the case in France’s high-end restaurant-hotels, Origines is small in size — a mere twelve rooms and suites. They’re unapologetically modern in style, decorated in warm neutrals and soothingly minimalist in their décor. Natural materials like raw oak predominate, and some of them make use of the local volcanic stone. They’re full of luxe details, and the top-end suite features a freestanding whirlpool bath by the foot of the bed.

And as you might expect from a chef-driven hospitality experience, Origines features an impressive breakfast — a “peasant”-style spread made up of the very finest local ingredients, served in the dining room or en suite. The restaurant proper, meanwhile, is a destination unto itself, and a tribute to the culinary traditions of Auvergne.

The fourth Kimpton hotel in the greater Miami area is the Kimpton Hotel Palomar South Beach, which stands discreetly along the banks of Collins Canal, in the Sunset Harbour neighborhood on the Biscayne Bay–facing side of the island. In the typical Kimpton manner the Palomar is attractive, but wears its stylishness lightly, and goes out of its way to feel approachable. 

It’s perhaps in the rooms and suites that the Palomar makes the most of its ever-so-slightly out-of-the-way setting; there’s a resort-like aspect to the accommodations, especially the ones that come with balconies or terraces facing the canal. All of them, naturally, come with Kimpton-standard luxuries like Frette linens and Atelier Bloem bath products, and yoga mats are available upon request.

A variety of wellness-oriented activities are available, from massages to kayak rentals to yoga or interval-training classes offered by “wellness partners” in the Sunset Harbour district. And among the Palomar’s common spaces are a rooftop pool and lounge, a beach club at 21st and Collins.

content:
The K Club is possibly Ireland’s most imposing country hotel, and without a doubt its poshest. While some of the castles and manor house hotels can be disarmingly friendly, even over-familiar, this one is all buttoned-up elegance, a throwback (in spirit) to the days when the gentleman’s game had a strict dress code.

The hotel itself is a magnificent Georgian mansion, settled on seven hundred acres of land, along a mile-long span of the famed River Liffey, and even in this most picturesque of countries, it’s hard to imagine a setting more scenic. Rooms are classic in decor, packed with antique furnishings, and walls are lined with rich printed fabrics, the overall effect recalling some of the grand hotels of Paris.

Perhaps that’s no accident — the Barton Restaurant serves French cuisine alongside upscale Irish fare, served in an impossibly formal environment, and while the Palmer Restaurant and the South Bar & Restaurant overlook the two golf courses.

These courses are world-famous, and justifiably so — The K Club is the only place in Europe where you’ll find 36 holes designed by Arnold Palmer, and is accordingly the site of the Irish Open for 2023, 2025, and 2027. Meanwhile, those not addicted to golf may pursue another brand of strenuous idleness in the spa, partaking of a wide range of treatments and therapies.

Horseback riding and clay pigeon shooting round out the suite of gentlemanly outdoor activities, and we hear the Liffey is particularly friendly to fishermen, stocked with trout and salmon. And should the country life prove too slow, Dublin is less than an hour’s drive away.

Unless you can somehow transport yourself to Jay Gatsby’s world of grand estates and garden parties, Newport, Rhode Island is your best bet for evoking jazz-age elegance. The town is famous for its mansions, lovely to drive by and gawk at, but the urban waterfront is the heart of the Newport experience. Forty 1º North is an exceptional new boutique hotel infused with crisp nautical atmosphere and an artistic take on eco-hospitality.

The hotel’s twenty-eight guest rooms, some with expansive cottage-style accommodations (think fully equipped kitchens), take the dusky New England color palette from the hotel’s lobby and public spaces and bathe it in natural light from the working floor-to-ceiling windows. When opened, these windows usher in the waterfront breezes from Newport Harbor, naturally cooling the rooms and practically eliminating the need for air conditioning.  Design that integrates the prevailing winds is no accident: at Forty 1º North, green initiatives abound, from the recycled glass-and-shell concrete walkways to the organic Malin+Goetz bath products. We’re especially fond of the innovative ways in which the hotel combines eco-friendly living with efficient service: check out the iPads in each room for daily newspaper delivery, directory assistance, maps, and menus.

Another pleasant surprise is the hotel’s two restaurants, impressively varied for a smallish boutique. The Grill is all dockside romance, where you can enjoy the raw bar in an atmospheric open-air lounge. Christie’s is a hip, quirky alternative to the high-end seafood joints that dominate the neighborhood, offering Asian tapas in a colorful, mod-inspired setting.

The stately corner building at Vesterbrogade 9/a, located in Vesterbro – one of Copenhagen’s trendiest neighbourhoods – has operated as a hotel for almost a century. Following extensive renovations, it reopened in 2023 with a new name and a refreshed identity, and is now part of the NH brand.
Housed within a beautifully restored 19th-century structure, the hotel effortlessly combines its historic architectural elements with contemporary Scandinavian design. Its interiors are inspired by ‘Joanne’ – an imaginary, well-travelled, open-minded woman whose personality influences every detail of the space. This is reflected in the soft, feminine textures and in meeting rooms dedicated to three real, influential women from Danish culture.
The rooms are bright and airy, with high ceilings and a modern yet down-to-earth decor. Natural materials feature throughout, from wicker lampshades and raffia headboards to linen curtains and light wood furnishings. The atmosphere is distinctly cosy, suited to the Nordic climate, with plush patterned carpets, fluffy down duvets, heated floors, and playful touches such as custom stationery, vintage-style vanity mirrors, and bathrooms clad in retro bronze tiles.
The dining offering is varied, ranging from Joanne’s Italian Restaurant & Bar to the "Danish bodega" Pinden and a charming rooftop bar.
