content:
America’s postwar investment in roadside motels continues to pay dividends. After a thorough reimagining at the hands of New England boutique hoteliers Lark Hotels and Californian designers EDG Design, the Bluebird Spa City Motor Lodge has transformed itself into the sort of stylish, modern lodging that every small town needs at least one of — especially a town like Saratoga Springs, whose population swells on summer weekends as thoroughbred racing fans converge on the oldest track in the country.

That’s not to say Saratoga Springs is otherwise empty; it’s a compelling four-season destination, with an art and music culture that’s remarkable for a town of its size. This is a hip audience, not easily impressed. Fortunately Lark is the real deal, and the Bluebird Spa City Motor Lodge is too. The rooms are carefully considered, with a minimalist, slightly industrial accent, and enough color (and greenery) to keep them feeling warm.

In the atrium at the center of the hotel, beneath the retractable roof, is the hotel’s lounge, whose blue-tiled floor is a clever reminder of the pool that stood on this spot when the Downtowner was a very different kind of hotel. And while there’s no restaurant, this location is as central as it gets, with more cafés, restaurants, and bars than we can name within a three-block radius from your door.

content:
To call this Swiss hotel “Le Mirador” is a bit of an understatement. The word “mirador,” or lookout, is the same term assigned to tourist-crowded platforms on Spanish roadsides, the kind where everyone piles out of the car to take snapshots of a silvery sea or a faraway horizon at sunset. That’s all well and good, but the “mirador” at Le Mirador Resort & Spa is something more — it’s a jaw-dropper of a backdrop, a spectacle of nature that verges on the sublime. 

Switzerland’s like that, of course, especially on the perennially dazzling Lake Geneva. Le Mirador is located on Mont-Pèlerin, overlooking the lake, amid vineyards that UNESCO has specially recognized. Le Mirador is not a large resort, but a rather intimately sized 64-room hotel. Superior and Deluxe rooms, housed in the older and more historic part of the hotel, are spacious, with private balconies overlooking the lake. The look is classic, not contemporary — think gold-flecked tapestries and sumptuous floor-to-ceiling drapery. Junior suites, in the hotel’s newer wing, have more of a modern look, plus natural stone bathrooms and more sizable terraces. Amenities vary — some have full kitchens, others carved-marble baths — but they have one thing in common. Views: that’s what you get at Le Mirador, no matter where you’re sleeping.

Le Mirador is home to a spa by Alpeor, not to mention an indoor swimming pool topped with a glass dome, a fitness center with panoramic views of the lake, and several tennis courts. Restaurant Le Patio is joined by the Mirador Lounge, with its own astonishing view. Raise a glass of Chasselas and toast to your good health, and your good fortune: if you’re staying at this hotel, your life is going pretty well indeed.

How to get there: Le Mirador is located approximately 84 km from Geneva International Airport via A1 and A9. Alternatively, round-trip train tickets are available from Geneva for approximately 112 CHF; the trip takes one hour each way.

content:
There’s more to Greece than Athens, the islands and that long, squiggly coastline. In the country’s northwest, out along the border with Albania, is the rugged and mountainous region of Zagori. It’s a landscape of rocky cliffs, verdant slopes and tiny, ancient villages clinging to the hillsides. And among the many lost-in-time-looking villages, one of the most picturesque of all is Aristi — a smattering of traditional stone homes at the edge of a stunning national park, and home to Aristi Mountain Resort. 

As resorts go, it’s a small one, a modest but attractive collection of stone structures perched high on a hill, with views of a steep mountain valley dropping away below. The look is homey and somewhat rustic throughout, but there are enough soft edges to keep things well out of “roughing it” territory. King-size Duxiana mattresses come standard, the bathrooms are modern, and at the top end of the scale the rooms come with a wood-burning fireplace and a garden, a deck or an outdoor jacuzzi. 

The homeyness extends to the public spaces as well. There’s a cozy lounge for sitting by the fire, a simple but tranquil spa, and a pool overlooking the valley. The restaurant, Salvia, turns out deeply satisfying dishes based on traditional recipes, revolving around the same ingredients they’ve been using for centuries — wild boar brought in by local hunters, mushrooms and greens collected from the mountainside, cheese from a small nearby farm, and a cellar full of good Greek wine. 

Of course a trip to this wilder part of Greece wouldn’t be complete without spending some time outdoors. There’s any number of largely un-touristed mountain towns to drive between, as well as more adventurous activities ranging from rafting to horseback riding to hang gliding. Whether from the water, the ground or the air, the scenery won’t disappoint. 

Please note: Aristi Mountain Resort requires a 2-night minimum stay. 

How to get there:
Aristi Mountain Resort is about a 45-minute drive from Ioannina’s King Pyrros Regional Airport (IOA), or about a 3.5-hour drive from Macedonia’s Thessaloniki International Airport (SKG).

content:
Lake Placid has twice hosted the Winter Olympics and, as any local will tell you, it’s perhaps an even finer summertime destination. So it’s no surprise that Laurel Lake Placid is oriented towards outdoor recreation. Its stylish Scandinavian-meets-Japanese minimalist aesthetic is a welcome departure from the region’s more rustic, more familiar Adirondack lodges.

Northeastern boutique-hotel fans might note the involvement of Lark Hotels, a group that specializes in exactly this blend of local tradition and stylish, up-to-date design. Their touch is evident not only in the visual environment but in the service and the subtly luxe amenities as well. The rooms and suites include some more capacious options for larger parties — with bunk beds added some sleep up to six. 

And The Lounge at Laurel Lake Placid, the hotel’s restaurant and bar, is equally well suited to summer or winter, serving snacks and light bites alongside beer, wine, and cocktails in a space with views of downtown Lake Placid and Mirror Lake. Beyond the hotel’s doors you’ll find not just ski runs but Lake Placid itself, as well as mile after mile of trails and even a museum dedicated to the 1932 and 1980 Winter Games.

content: The Cycladic island of Ios is perhaps a touch less famous than some of its neighbors, but scarcely less spectacular, and the uncommon stylishness of Liostasi Hotel & Suites makes a compelling case. It’s perhaps not as isolated as some island luxury boutique hotels, but the convenience of its location, a short walk from town, is undeniable. And the experience from within Liostasi’s grounds is as sedate as you want to make it — though it overlooks the town and the harbor from its terraced pool deck, its resort-like atmosphere makes staying in an attractive option indeed.\n\nIn the interiors you’ll find a style that marries rough-edged rustic touches with the polished sheen of urban boutique-hotel design, as well as a wealth of unusual contemporary artworks. Every unit has a balcony or a terrace with a view, and a couple of the suites come with plunge pools. And the common spaces are equally appealing, from the main pool to the Elemis spa to Cine Liostasi, the hotel’s open-air cinema, and the poolside Grandma’s Restaurant, an award-winning Greek eatery whose menu is substantially more modern than its name might lead you to believe.

content:
Though this splendid old edifice has recently celebrated its 150th birthday, by local standards La Villa Guy is still practically brand new. Béziers is one of France’s oldest cities, dating back to pre-Roman times, and La Villa Guy is uniquely located in a one-hectare park right in the city center, a designated historic monument with an Andalusian aesthetic and a Moorish-inspired garden. As for the hotel, it’s as unusual as its setting: just six rooms and suites, plus a pair of lounges, a bar, a billiards room and library, a swimming pool, and even a balcony and rotunda with a commanding view of the park.

Its proprietors, Les Collectionneurs, are responsible for a number of distinctive, historic boutique-style hotels, and they’ve made great theater of this one. The rooms and suites all mix contemporary boldness with classic romance in varying proportions; there’s not a square inch of this place that is without visual interest. And the visual isn’t the only sense that’s catered to: there’s a spa that, though small, is as lavish as those you’d find in a much larger luxury hotel. Breakfast is served in one of the lovely lounges; for lunch and dinner you’ll be briefed on the best that Béziers has to offer.

content:
If you’re out to establish the quintessential British country-house hotel, you could do a lot worse for raw material than the 400-acre Surrey estate of the 20th-century newspaper baron and wartime minister Lord Beaverbrook. The house itself is a unique one, a Victorian-era Neoclassical mansion, and in its present incarnation, with interiors by Soho House designer Susie Atkinson, it’s nothing short of spectacular — a modern take on the classic country house hotel, with a personality and a point of view unlike any other.

The balance with any country-house hotel is to project gravitas without heaviness, and to be warm and welcoming without overdoing the irreverence. An impressive smattering of modern art is balanced against an equally impressive collection of antique objects and furnishings from all over the world; and the hotel’s rooms feel up-to-date without losing touch with their history. The original House is joined by the Garden House and the Coach House, as well as the Village, a few minutes’ drive from the main house, where a handful of cottages stand on the site of what was once workforce housing.

This is a first-rate luxury hotel, evident not just in the lavish in-room comforts but in the facilities as well, which range from a spa, indoor pool, and tennis/pickleball/paddle courts to a private cinema, an inventively programmed kids’ club, and various outdoor challenges from the Bear Grylls Survival Academy. Meanwhile no fewer than four restaurants see to guests’ gustatory needs, alongside a pair of cocktail bars for good measure.

content:
Neither on the beach, on the (relatively) busy streets of Palma, or on some isolated hilltop, Hotel Son Sant Jordi presents another version of Mallorcan life. It’s set in the rural town of Pollensa, on the island’s north side, and it’s made from a cluster of picturesque 17th-century townhouses surrounding a quiet garden with a lovely little pool.

Character is the name of the game here, and it shows through in the décor; the rooms are decorated in classic Balearic style, with a touch of contemporary design in the details. The garden-facing rooms are the most tranquil, but the street-view rooms are anything but hectic themselves — Pollensa isn’t exactly New York City. Twins, doubles, and junior suites comprise the bulk of the accommodations, while family suites, sleeping up to four, are provided in a separate building.

Indoor and outdoor lounging space is plentiful, and the restaurant — open three seasons — serves typical Mallorquina cuisine in a dining room that spills out into the gardens. From here you’re close by to mountain peaks, sandy beaches, and sundry other island attractions, including the capital, a mere 60 kilometers away — and never far from a bit of peace and quiet back in Pollensa.

content: Now that Brussels is a metonym for the European bureaucracy, the Belgian capital is in danger of having its fashionable side overlooked. Then again, maybe that’s not such a bad thing, if it means a place like the Zoom Hotel can fly a little bit under the radar. This, in its tidy, buttoned-up sort of way, is among the most stylish hotels we’ve seen lately, a minimalist industrial-chic boutique whose rooms are decorated with cinema lights, smart monochrome tiled bathrooms, and a crowdsourced photography project that fills the hotel with an ever-changing series of artistic views of the Brussels streetscape.\n\nStyle aside, the Zoom has much to recommend it. The rooms are comfortable and efficient, if not exactly designed for maximum luxury. You’re just off the Avenue Louise, home to some of the city’s best shopping, as well as any number of restaurants and nightspots. The Zoom itself, like many European four-star hotels, is missing a restaurant of its own — but for a certain type of Belgophile, the gap is more than adequately filled by the Zoom Beer House, which serves hundreds of local brews alongside a selection of Belgian chocolates.

content:
It wasn’t all that long ago that the Dominican Republic was known chiefly as the place where baseball players come from — as a travel destination it came into its own only recently, and as a high-end one, more recently still. The apex, though, has to be the opening of the Tortuga Bay Villas, at the (itself not at all un-luxurious) Puntacana Resort & Club.

Located within a vast gated residential community, the 13 villas and their 30 suites were designed by none other than Oscar de la Renta, and they’re a fine example of the new minimal-luxe, with just enough of the bells and whistles: home theaters, miniature kitchens, huge and indulgent bathrooms, and views of the Caribbean or at least the golf courses. Some come with Jacuzzis and all come with golf carts, for when you’re too blissed-out to move under your own power.

Privacy and exclusivity are obviously the name of the game, but Tortuga Bay’s special relationship with Puntacana means that if you need more than one pool, one beach, one restaurant, you’re free to roam the larger resort at your leisure — an especially fortuitous arrangement when it comes to leisure activities, as it means Tortuga Bay can offer diversions few other 30-room hotels can manage: from diving and sailing to a kids’ program and a full-service marina.

content:
In South America, there’s no contradiction between high adventure and high luxury. Even so, few hotels are up to the standard of Belmond Las Casitas. The location would be impossible to find fault with — the Colca Valley is one of Peru’s natural wonders, a region high in the Andes that’s home to everything from bucolic farmland to active volcanoes and a canyon that’s grander than the Grand. And the hotel is no slouch either: this estate spans twenty acres, one for each of its casitas, resulting in a small-villa luxury experience that would be difficult to top.

They’re rustic enough so as not to feel gratuitous or out of place. But once inside they lack for nothing in the way of comfort. Modern amenities like wireless internet are accounted for, as are old-fashioned charms like soaking tubs, plunge pools, and under-floor heating. The packages include room, full board, and any of a range of activities, which means Colca Canyon is your playground. Spa treatments are available as well, and might just be necessary after a half-day’s trek on horseback. It’s a destination that’s slightly off the radar, but not for lack of quality — and as long as the hotels continue to be as small and luxe as Belmond Las Casitas, it might just stay that way.

How to get there: Belmond Las Casitas is a hundred miles to the north of Arequipa Airport (AQP).

content: Since the Fifties this splendid, sprawling palace has been at the top of Jaipur’s luxury hotel market. Rambagh Palace began its life as a guest house for Rajasthan’s royals, and the more things change, the more they stay the same — it’s a part of the Taj hotel group now, and is more or less a guest house for the modern version of royalty: the well-heeled high-end travelers who keep the world’s five-star hotels in business.\n\nAs far as the experience goes, it’s more or less what you’d want it to be. Rather than design-hotel surprises, the Rambagh Palace aims for an old-world aristocratic fantasy — and, for the most part, it succeeds quite admirably. Many of the basic rooms have been renovated and are nothing if not comfortable — but if you’re really after the full effect then you’d be well advised to move up to the suites. Not just for the space and the added comforts but for the design as well; this is where you’ll find antique style to match the Palace’s public spaces, plus views of the gardens, and butler service as well, which you don’t need us to tell you is a good thing.

content:
Certain images may spring to mind when you think of Zürich — bankers in suits, expensive chocolate, ice-blue lakes, sharp church steeples. It’s the kind of city where you’d expect to stay in a state-of-the-art business hotel, or at least a prim and proper guesthouse. Townhouse Boutique Hotel Zürich, located on the Bahnhofstrasse in the heart of town, is neither of these. 

It’s a cozy boutique hotel that’s fashioned, as the name suggests, after an English townhouse. It’s refined but not formal, the kind of place where you can browse books. Forget about the city’s buttoned-up reputation: these 23 guest rooms, and three suites, are charming and slightly quirky, lined with vibrant vintage-inspired wallpaper by Designers Guild. The pattern, it should be noted, matches the upholstery on the desk chair. There’s a sense of humor and whimsy to the decor, a suggestion, in the mix of antique pieces and the occasional bouquet of fresh flowers, that character is more important than  perfection.The dimensions are larger than what you’d expect in this downtown location — read, there’s enough room to actually unpack your suitcase — and in-room amenities include large LCD TVs, iPod docks, and a DVD player, complete with a library of movies to borrow.   

The hotel’s onsite eatery, Palette Bar Café, serves Breakfast and even Lunch or Dinner with an oriental touch For variety’s sake, there’s no end of other options in the city. But Townhouse Boutique Hotel Zürich is one of those rare hotels where you actually might feel at home for a few days. Did we mention it’s a block from the main train station? Don’t worry about that early departure time: you can make your own cappuccino before you go.

A setting like this, along the banks of the Haya River, seems like the perfect setting for a traditional ryokan. But the Hotel Indigo Hakone Gora isn’t interested in being a traditional ryokan. Make no mistake — in the abstract, many of the ingredients are in place, from the soothing waters of the spring-fed onsen baths to the perfectly framed forest views. But this is a modern, boutique-influenced hotel through and through, and it’s visible not only in the design, which makes liberal use of modern furniture, graphic art, and non-traditional colors, but in the sheer eclecticism of its international influences.

For example: the rooms are decorated with elements that read as rather ryokan-like, and each one, crucially, comes with its own spring-fed onsen bath. But they’re Western in their layout, with elevated furniture rather than tatami mats, and the artwork, though it depicts local scenes, is unmistakably contemporary.

The hotel’s public baths, too, take a traditional form and give it a modern update, with eye-catching interiors, including a vast screen displaying ever-changing visual art, and a international-style spa treatments. And the restaurant serves not a traditional kaiseki dinner but a menu of international comfort food — sourced, however, from within ten kilometers of the hotel.

content:
Parisian real estate being what it is, there’s almost no way to open a hotel that’s both humanely comfortable and genuinely affordable within the actual city limits. Which is why you’re looking at a hotel in Saint-Ouen. This is the product of Cyril Aouizerate, a hotelier whose populist bona fides are indisputable — he was one of the co-founders of Mama Shelter. So we’re inclined to trust him when he says his new project, Mob Hotel of the People, is worth a few extra minutes on the Métro.

It’s a sensible location for a youth-culture hotel, set as it is within walking distance of the famous Saint-Ouen flea market. And once you’re on the Mob’s grounds you’ll be shocked by the amount of space — not just in the rooms, which are a shade more generously sized than the Parisian norm, but in the hotel’s public spaces as well, including its rooftop terraces and the restaurant’s courtyard garden, which also serves as an outdoor cinema and occasional music venue.

Rooms, meanwhile, are pared-down, unfussy, and stylish, with all the necessary comforts. The Mob’s target audience — the People, if you will — aren’t here for palace-hotel luxury. What matters is that the rooms are a relaxing place to sleep and an attractive place for some small-scale entertaining, to complement the social life of the hotel’s common areas. All this, and you’re just minutes from the rest of Paris by car, bus, or subway.

First, a word about the name. Little Beach House Barcelona is set not in Barcelona proper, but a half-hour away in Garraf, a fishing village turned holiday spot. And with 17 rooms it’s really only little when compared with the urban properties that are the core of the Soho House collection. It’s a restoration of a Fifties hotel which leaves just enough of the original intact for a bit of retro atmosphere. The rest is pure Soho House, which is to say easygoing, bohemian glamour — words that apply just as appropriately to the hotel as to its clientele.

For, like any Soho House property, it’s a members’ club as well as a hotel. Many of its guests, then, are weekenders from Barcelona, drawn from the rolls of the city club’s members. Of course, you’re a member, for the duration of your stay — which means you’ve got the run of the house, from the multitude of cozy lounge spaces to the seasonal semi-outdoor spa. 

The rooms retain their original square footage, which isn’t enormous, by contemporary standards — but they’re uniformly comfortable, not to mention stylish in that signature Soho House manner. And for a lodging of the Little Beach House’s size, it’s impressive that there are not one but three restaurants: the indoor-outdoor Club, the beachside La Caseta, and the fairly self-explanatory Beachroof.

First-time visitors to Santa Monica may occasionally be surprised to find it a bit less laid-back and bohemian than they expect. The Pierside Santa Monica sets out to fix all that. This isn’t just the first luxury boutique hotel to open in Santa Monica in quite some time, but its address on Colorado Avenue at Ocean Avenue makes it the closest one to the iconic Santa Monica pier — a victory for anyone who’s a stickler for truth in hotel names.

What’s inside is a hotel that’s modern and visually surprising, but true to its Southern California inspiration, incorporating a wide range of influences from Arts & Crafts and surf culture to mid-century Modernism and some handsome custom-designed contemporary furniture. The most impressive rooms are perhaps the ones with views of the pier and the Pacific Ocean, though there isn’t a substandard one in the house.

The Board Shop is what it sounds like and more: a place to rent a surfboard, some beach chairs, or even a ukulele or a Nintendo Switch. Meanwhile the Surfing Fox is the Pierside Santa Monica’s coastal Californian restaurant and bar.

content:
Double-check that map before you leave. This Montréal is a long way from the Canadian one; it’s in the southwest of France, not far from Toulouse, in a region called the Malepère, whose gentle hills embody France’s rural beauty as convincingly as anything in Provence. It’s here, at the heart of a medieval village, that you’ll find a small hotel for the apartment-sharing era: Camellas-Lloret Maison d’Hôtes, a beautiful little guest house featuring just four stylish bedrooms, plus one more expansive garden apartment.

The style is an eclectic mix of charming traditional architecture and understated contemporary furnishings, all finished in a soothing neutral palette. It’s no luxury hotel, but nor is it by any means uncomfortable: beds feature handmade mattresses and linen bedding, bathrooms are stocked with Aesop products, and the garden apartment features a private lounge and a kitchenette. And the house’s four rooms share a conservatory with a communal dining table as well as a salon stocked with books to enjoy with a drink in front of the fire.

It’s a delightful place from which not only to sample the best of the region’s food and wine traditions, but to soak up some history as well — nearby is Carcassonne, the medieval citadel, as well as the Bastide St. Louis and, in the surrounding mountains, a number of ruined fortresses.

content:
You’d be forgiven for thinking of Girona as a gateway to Barcelona. That popular misconception was set up the moment the largest budget airline in Europe chose the northern Catalonian city as one of its principal hubs. But you’re mistaken if you think that Girona is just a place to make a connection, to disembark from a plane and board a shuttle bus for the hour-long drive into Gaudi’s waterfront wonderland. Because the ancient city, dense with Gothic architecture, is a great destination in its own right. 

A number of excellent hotels have opened in recent years to accommodate the influx of tourists passing through. Or at least the tourists who’ve done their homework. Hotel Camiral is one of these. It’s a chic resort set just outside of town, on the edge of Spain’s premiere golf course. We probably don’t have to tell you that the landscaping at Hotel Camiral is lovely, nor that there’s a fantastic pool. But we will anyway: the grounds are green and rolling, with views of the Pyrenees off in the distance, and the pool is large, gorgeously lined in aquamarine tile and surrounded by cool white chaises longues.

And what about the guest rooms, you ask? They’re as spacious and quiet and light-filled, and as packed with amenities, as you’d expect of a high-end resort like this one. But they’re also filled with charming details that pay homage to the region’s rich history: oak flooring, hand-painted Spanish tiles, and gilded mirrors add character to the earth-toned design scheme. Standard features include pillow-top mattresses, Egyptian cotton linens, and soaking tubs. Many rooms also have private balconies overlooking the gardens. Suites, of course, come with plenty of extras, from four-poster beds and fireplaces to tech-forward lighting controls and standalone baths stocked by products by Natura Bissé.

A hotel on the periphery of a world-class golf course would be incomplete without a state-of-the-art spa. Hotel Camiral has that, naturally, plus a sunlit fitness center and several elegant dining and drinking venues. Bistro Restaurant, with gourmet Catalan cuisine and open-air seating, is the hotel’s signature restaurant, but you can also have snacks delivered to your poolside daybed. Even if you have no intention of swinging a club, you can have a civilized drink overlooking the greens at the Club House. 

When you’ve had your fill of R&R, head into town for some serious sightseeing and a lively dining scene. The Hotel Camiral bills itself as a five-star stay near Barcelona. That last part is just for the tourists. And that's fine. We’re into the peace and quiet, the lack of hype — we’re happy for Girona to remain a relatively under-the-radar gem.

content:
The grand hotels of Lake Como are renowned, but they’re not the only way to experience this part of Lombardy. Just off the southeastern arm of Como is the smaller Lake Annone, on whose shores you’ll find not a Belle Époque palace but what might be their modern equivalent: Bianca Relais, a Fifties residence given a very flattering contemporary makeover by architect Giuseppe Manzoni.

With plentiful terrace space and floor-to-ceiling windows it makes the most of its view of the peaks across the lake. The rooms and suites — just ten of them — are minimalist-luxe, tending towards monochrome tones, each one livened by bold printed wallpapers and curvaceous modernist furniture. The inward-facing units look onto a tranquil garden, which is pleasant, while the lake-facing ones are considerably more dramatic.

Its natural surroundings offer plenty of opportunity for recreation, from sailing and kayaking to cycling and golf. The main event, however, is dinner: Bianca sul Lago, under the direction of chef Emanuele Petrosino, is the proud recipient of a Michelin star; there’s also a café, Drop, serving a more casual menu by the same chef, accompanied by signature cocktails and views of the lake.

content:
The Lake District of northern Patagonia is where you go to get your dramatic mountain landscapes tempered by some lush green hillsides — it’s no less scenic than what lies further south, but just a little more hospitable. Near Lake Ranco, on the Chilean side, you’ll find Futangue Hotel & Spa, a luxury adventure hotel in the now-classic Patagonian style, combining modern architecture, high-end comfort, and a setting that places it close to the end of the civilized world.

Futangue’s rooms and suites are contemporary in style, but rustic in inspiration, with plenty of bare wood and organic textures like leather and fur. The spaces are generous, as are the comforts — bathrooms feature walk-in rain showers stocked with products made from plants from the neighboring Valdivian rainforest.

The hotel’s spa is an elaborate double-height space with views of the Patagonian panorama from its saunas and its indoor pool, as well as a second, half-Olympic outdoor pool. The restaurant, Mesón del Caulle, is overseen by Karime Harcha, a highly regarded local chef, and sources its ingredients from Lake Ranco and the Valdivian region. Speaking of which — as comfortable as the hotel is, you’re presumably here because you’ll be getting out and about, embarking on activities that range from fly-fishing and horseback riding to kayaking, mountain-biking, trekking, and just about anything else you can do in the rainforest, in the mountains, or on the water.

content:
Italy is practically covered with beaches and villages and wineries that you’d happily go a bit out of your way for. But it’s also got more than its share of attractions so striking, so magnificent, that you’d plan a whole trip around it. Castelsardo is one of these. The medieval village was built on a rocky promontory rising up out of the Mediterranean on the northern coast of Sardinia. It’s majestic to behold at dusk, when all the lights in the town start flickering on, and perhaps even more so at night, when the entire village is aglow, appearing to float on the sea. It’s a place you have to see for yourself, ideally while relaxing on one of the terraces at Bajaloglia Resort. 

With just 24 rooms, Bajaloglia is more of a boutique hotel than a traditional resort. It’s set on a hill across the water from Castelsardo, strategically positioned to offer spectacular views of the region’s star attraction from most of its guest rooms and public spaces. The Classic rooms are just that: classic, done up in a cheerful blue, white, and gold color scheme, with the standard amenities you’d expect and sliding glass doors that lead to a private patio furnished with a table and chairs. Suites offer more space, both indoors and out, and privileged views of the sea and Castelsardo. 

Either way, you’ll want to be beside the hotel’s lovely aquamarine swimming pool at sunset: the breezy terrace is the best place to take in the scenery while sipping a spritz. Wander around the grounds before dinner at the hotel’s Ristorante L’Incantu. Stone-lined pathways carved into the hilltop grounds, fringed with myrtle trees and prickly pear, lead to natural alcoves and white linen-draped gazebos where you can get a minute to yourself. 

Not that there’s ever much of a crowd at Bajaloglia — which is more or less the point. You’re trading off the peace and altitude for proximity to the beach and to the historic sights themselves: you can’t be up high and down low at once, you can’t be right next to the centro storico and also enjoy views of it from afar. But once you’ve had your fill of peace and quiet, Bajaloglia is an ideal jumping-off point to explore this beautiful stretch of the Emerald Coast.

content:
Overlooking Rittenhouse Square in one Philadelphia’s toniest districts, this very modern 33-story high-rise gives away little about the luxurious small hotel that lies within. An elegant and charming classic, the Rittenhouse is one of the city’s most exclusive lodgings, offering not only the largest rooms in Philadelphia—each spanning some 450 to 1,700 square feet—but some of the most lavish as well, decked out in rich mahogany and vibrant fabrics and offering far-ranging views of the Square and the city.

Facilities are big for such a small hotel, from plentiful meeting and events space to the Rittenhouse Spa & Salon, offering massage and beauty treatments, fitness programs, and an indoor pool.

Same goes for the cuisine; the Rittenhouse is home to the French bistro-inspired Lacroix and the Mary Cassatt Tea Room and Garden, serving an authentic British afternoon tea in an ornate living room and an outdoor garden hung with a few of Cassatt’s original works. Upstairs, works by local artists adorn the guest-room walls — talk of Philly as New York’s sixth borough may be exaggerated, but this city has always been big on culture, and is home to a thriving art scene, a scene that has found a champion in the Rittenhouse.

content: RAI is Amsterdam’s exhibition and convention center, and the neighboring Nhow Amsterdam RAI is a forward-looking statement by architect Rem Koolhaas’s OMA. With 650 rooms, it’s the biggest hotel in the Benelux region, but aesthetically it’s as out-there as any little urban boutique. Three small gyms keep guests fit, while a pair of restaurants and bars, one on the ground floor and another on the rooftop, keep them fed and watered.

content:
The Urbanauts hospitality group is mounting something of an insurrection in Vienna — making an end-run around the traditional hoteliers, while at the same time delivering a professional product that amateur apartment-sharers can’t match. Graetzlhotel Meidlinger Markt joins the Belvedere and Karmelitermarkt installments as the third Urbanauts location in Vienna, this one in the Meidling district, about two miles to the southwest of the city center.

The concept is the same: a series of old storefronts retrofitted and rehabilitated as stylish hotel suites, where you’ll enjoy the privacy and independence of an apartment-share as well as the care and quality of professional hospitality. Here you’ll collect your key from a café right on the market, and show yourself to one of nine unique suites, each one retaining some of the character of its original use: a cobbler’s shop, a florist, a confectioner and a record shop among them.

They’re comfortable and well-designed, modern but not flashy, with plenty of cozy soft edges to balance their visual impact. Naturally this Graetzlhotel, like all of them, is light on traditional hotel amenities — there’s no restaurant, to say nothing of a pool, spa, or conference rooms. But that’s not why you’re here. You’ll live like a Viennese local for the duration of your stay, and you’ll do it in Meidling, one of the city’s most charming quarters. It’s a model we’d like to see catch on in more cities — but until then you’ll catch us in Vienna with the Urbanauts.

content:
In Newport, where “summer” is a verb, where tennis is still played on grass, and where the very smell in the air is a sort of privileged New England potpourri of ocean breezes, butter-poached seafood and warm-from-the-dryer white laundry, something as down-to-earth as a tasteful little b&b like the Attwater can seem rather revolutionary. For one, they’ve got a penchant for colorful contemporary furnishings — and a quick look at the photos should make it clear that we don’t mean that in some snarky, euphemistic way. In fact the interior design could easily work in any number of the United States’ more design-conscious cities. At the same time, it’s all threaded with subtle nautical references, tinged with teals and navy blues that just look better this close to the Atlantic. 

And the Atlantic is close indeed. Newport Harbor is just three blocks away, while Bellevue Avenue, the famous local mansion district’s main drag, is less than that. The lovely First Beach is a ten-minute walk at a leisurely pace, and it’s hard to imagine adopting anything but a leisurely pace around here. In short, though the hotel’s style is edgy by local standards, the location is very much in the middle of historic Newport. 

The rooms, at least until you get toward the top of the range, tend to be on the small side, but they’re opened up considerably by big sunny windows and lots of fresh white paint. Designer linens, comfy waffle robes and small details like Keurig coffee machines make it tempting to spend long mornings in the room. But don’t miss breakfast. The sunny café is simple enough in its look, but the baked goods (think cheddar-scallion scones and home-made Oreo-style cookies) put the usual b&b spread to shame. 

Breakfast sets the tone for what promises to be a lot of good eating. This is a town that loves its festivals, especially when they’re dedicated to food. There’s Seafood Fest, Oktoberfest, Newport Blues and BBQ, and, especially to the point, the Newport Wine and Food Fest. In fact there are few places in the American Northeast whose calendars so fully reflect a local dedication to leisure. There’s also the America’s Cup sailing championship, the famous Newport Folk and Jazz Festivals, the Boat Show, and really, the list goes on. It’s always been easy to have a good time here, and now that there’s a b&b that’s as stylish as it is homey, it’s only gotten easier.

content:
Melbourne is already one of the world's most comfortable and enticing cities, and South Yarra is no exception, maintaining a fashionable and cosmopolitan cast outside of the city’s center. The downtown area is easily accessible by train — with a station just minutes from Lyall Hotel and Spa's front door. South Yarra, though, is Melbourne’s preferred district for upscale shopping, has a thriving restaurant and bar scene, and is a compelling destination in its own right. All of this in a peaceful residential setting — so much cosmopolitan excitement usually comes at the price of an agonizing night spent listening to car horns, or haggling with taxi drivers.

The residential neighborhood and apartment house flavor make the Lyall a uniquely comfortable experience. Each floor features a mini art gallery and a lounge complete with fireplace. Suites themselves, from studio plan to two bedroom, are Oriental in flavor, elegantly furnished and attractively designed, complete with kitchens and walk-in closets. The Platinum Suite's Bang & Olufsen entertainment system and outsized dining area may be enough to convince guests that this is indeed a private apartment, and Melbourne their new home.

In other ways, the residential atmosphere gives way to one more reminiscent of a resort hotel. To that end, the Lyall offers spa and fitness facilities, as well as one excellent restaurant — the Bistro Lyall — and a Champagne Bar, serving French champagne by the glass.

At the end of the day, Melbourne is a city much like any other (though perhaps a little bit better),  and there are plenty of hotels, large and small. But there is absolutely no reason to settle for a typical hotel experience, and, frankly, no reason to book a room downtown when the Lyall is just nine minutes away by train. If business requires your attention in the city center, then by all means take care of it, but at the end of the day, retire to South Yarra, and experience Melbourne like a local.

An overwater bungalow resort, properly executed, is nothing short of heavenly. And there’s every reason to trust that IHG will get it right. The InterContinental Bora Bora Resort & Thalasso Spa stands in the shadow of the picturesque Mount Otemanu, providing an extra level of scenic appeal for what is already possibly the most photogenic form of hospitality yet devised. And the visual sense, needless to say, is not the only one that’s in for a feast here.

After all, the whole point of an overwater villa is that you can dangle your feet in the lagoon any time you like. Many of them add plunge pools, for another aquatic option, and lavish spa-like bathrooms are universal. (Turns out you can fit quite a lot of modern luxury beneath a thatched roof. And unlike many resorts of this kind, every single unit stands over the waters of the lagoon, as do the Deep Ocean Spa’s treatment bungalows.

The dive center is on hand to equip you for underwater adventures, and kayaks and stand-up paddle boards are available as well. Meanwhile three restaurants and three bars offer a varied culinary experience, from the French-accented fine dining Le Corail to the al fresco Mediterranean Reef Restaurant.

content: Edgartown, Massachusetts, on the island of Martha’s Vineyard, is among the most historic places in the United States. Once home to the American whaling industry, it’s now one of the leisure capitals of the Northeast, and many old sea captains’ stately homes have been transformed into guest houses and hotels. Faraway Martha’s Vineyard comprises six of them; and while, with nearly two centuries in business under one name or another, it’s one of the oldest hotels in the country, its new owners have updated it for the 21st century, even as they’ve preserved the atmosphere that makes it so unique.\n\nThe rooms and suites differ slightly from unit to unit in size, layout, and finishes, by virtue of their being set in several distinct houses. All, though, share a consistent throwback-maritime style, entirely appropriate to their setting, as well as the comforts and subtle luxuries you expect from a modern boutique hotel. And while there’s no shortage of places to eat and drink around town, Faraway Martha’s Vineyard has one of the best: The Newes from America, an upscale pub that mixes British and American influences and makes excellent use of the freshest local seafood.

content:
There are hotels in North Africa where you’ll get a whitewashed, tourists-only experience, but Jnane Tamsna, in Marrakech’s Palmeraie, is not one of them. This is one of too few Black-owned hotels of any description anywhere, and its owners, the Senegalese-Parisian lawyer-turned-designer Meryanne Loum-Martin and her husband, the American ethnobotanist Gary Martin, have sought to preserve authenticity above all else — the hotel’s Diversity Excursions are a model for respectful cultural tourism.

And the hotel itself is a stunner. It’s spread across five houses, whose décor and furnishings represent a celebration of Moroccan design tradition and African art and craft in general. Its 24 rooms are tastefully luxurious, each one with its own terrace, and each house has its own pool and gardens — the villas can be booked in their entirety, if you’re traveling in numbers.

The cuisine, naturally, is painstakingly local; dinners may be served in the communal dining room or out in the sprawling gardens. And while the excursions, whether by bike, sidecar, or camelback, are the hotel’s pride, there’s plenty to do on site as well, from tennis to cooking classes to calligraphy and even magic lessons for kids.

If you look at the Grand Hôtel du Lac and see a spectacularly well-preserved 1868-vintage example of the classic Swiss lakeside grand hotel, well, you’re mostly right. As a matter of fact, longtime patrons of this Vevey favorite will recognize that it’s in what might be the best shape of its life — which is high praise for Pierre-Yves Rochon, the Parisian designer who presided over its extensive renovation. Today it’s a classic luxury hotel with just enough contemporary visual interest to still feel fresh — and of course the timeless views of Lake Geneva and the French Alps beyond its southern shores are nothing short of awe-inspiring.

It’s a smallish hotel, as these things go, a mere fifty rooms and suites, all of them decorated in a lush classic style with a calmingly contemporary focus to the graphics and palette. Nespresso machines and Guerlain bath products set the tone, and no comfort is spared; Superiors and Junior Suites add balconies, which are arguably essential to the experience.

As is customary in Swiss grand hotels, the Grand Hôtel du Lac features a spa that’s nothing short of extravagant. Meanwhile EMOTIONS by Guy Ravet is the fine-dining restaurant; beyond that is a cocktail bar, a wine-tasting room in the cellar, a seasonal lounge and restaurant overlooking the marina, and Buddha-Bar Beach, a summertime poolside pop-up by the legendary nightlife brand.

content:
Guanajuato is a labyrinth of underground passageways, cobbled alleys, and colonial architecture nestled in one of Mexico’s most picturesque valleys. Functioning as a silver-mining hotbed, a Jesuit college town, and a UNESCO world heritage site, Guanajuato’s diverse historical résumé gives it a lost-in-time feel. Cars are useless when traversing the city’s narrow, winding thoroughfares, and Edelmira Hotel provides a stylish home base from which to launch delightfully meandering, self-guided walking tours.

A glittering ultra-modern hotel would look absurdly out of place among such well-preserved 19th-century architecture, but that’s not to say that proper amenities are scarce. As a traditional inn transformed into a contemporary boutique, the Edelmira’s 27 well-appointed rooms don’t skimp on creature comforts like flatscreens and wi-fi. Stone walls and archways keep the spirit of the original structure alive (not to mention artfully integrated), providing an earthy framework for décor that’s both understated and chic. The color palette favors turquoise, which is more charming than it perhaps sounds, while the king beds are surrounded by plenty of exposed wood and patterned throws.

The living spaces aren’t what you’d call expansive (the building is two centuries old, after all), but public areas — namely the pool, courtyard, restaurant, and day spa — offer lovingly designed mini-escapes, and the view from the terrace is the antidote to any hemmed-in feelings. Take a long look at the soaring architecture, the pastel houses cascading down the mountains, and you’ll understand why Guanajuato native Diego Rivera created such massive paintings — a view like this begs for a mural.

Hotel Edelmira is conveniently located 30 minutes from the Del Bajío International Airport.

content:
Though Bodrum doesn’t yet have quite the same cachet as some of the similarly idyllic stretches of coast in the Mediterranean, Kuum Hotel and Spa is a big step toward changing that. With its striking modern architecture, its positively enormous (and enormously inviting) spa, its several seaside restaurants and its DJ-fueled nightlife, the hotel is anything but modest. A glance at some of the available transport options — yacht, helicopter, private jet — should settle the question entirely. 

And why should it be modest? The hotel makes its home on a particularly spectacular rocky cove, surrounded by the Bodrum peninsula’s already gorgeous landscape of rolling green hills and sparkling yacht-speckled bays. The hotel oozes a casual Aegean glamour, best viewed from the vantage point of the enormous overwater terrace. Fitted with shaded daybeds, a bar and several restaurants, it’s the social nexus of the hotel. And like the aforementioned spa, it’s a draw for guests and non-guests alike. 

The rooms are a quiet contrast to the buzz of the public spaces (though there are farther-flung hotels for anyone looking for a fully restive escape from the nightlife). The entry-level accommodations are pared down in a way that might feel cold in, say, Fairbanks or Helsinki, but with Mediterranean light pouring in and the wash of color from the blue Aegean on the other side of the window, the cool stone floors and spotless white décor are a complement to the warmth of the surroundings. Every room comes with its own terrace or balcony for closer looks at the seascape, and both the balconies and the views only get bigger as you go up the scale. 

Please note: Kuum Hotel & Spa is open seasonally from early May through late October.

How to get there: Kuum Hotel & Spa is approximately a 1 hour drive from Milas-Bodrum Airport.

content:
In a town whose trendier neighborhoods are positively bursting with boutique hotels, there’s truly nothing quite like Recoleta’s Hub Porteño, an eleven-room homage to the signifying power of marble and to the grand old city of Buenos Aires itself. Its proprietors land somewhere between hoteliers, civic boosters and high-end inbound tour operators, their project as much a rose-colored lens on the city as it is a base from which to explore. If you’ll forgive us for getting a little misty-eyed about it, you’re not so much booking a room as you’re booking an experience — a lovely place to stay, yes, but also a staff dedicated to getting you into the top restaurants, or showing you around the coolest estancia out in the countryside, or booking your tickets to the Buenos Aires Philharmonic, if that’s your thing. 

It’s all included in the price of your stay — the meals they book for you, a private vehicle and guide (if you enjoy traveling that way), your seats at the polo match. Just give them a sense of your tastes and interests, and they’ll take care of the rest. As you step off the street (and it’s a street with a certain cachet amongst locals who care about addresses), you enter a sort of portal into Hub’s vision of Buenos Aires — a portal bedecked in white marble, if you can find it beneath all the gleaming layers of polish. Through the old-fashioned wood-paneled bar, past the ultra-modern restaurant with a tree running through it (and a former El Bulli chef manning the burners), and finally up to your room, which puts to shame the slapped-together “design hotels” in other parts of town. 

The spacious rooms are fitted out in modern Argentine style, with wool textiles, animal hides on the hardwood floors, leather headboards over the bed and lots of natural light. The bathrooms, of course, are covered in marble, some of the mirrors gilded in, well, gold. Up on the roof is a sofa-covered terrace. Surrounded by climbing vines and views of the city, with a bar at your disposal, it’s about as far from the street traffic as you could get without leaving the city. And it’s just about as far from the thumping clubs in other parts of town — though if you’re into thumping clubs and other parts of town, the staff at Hub can take you there, too. 

Please note: Children under 12 years of age are not permitted at Hub Porteño.

There are few places in Europe as picturesque as this corner of Bavaria, where the fairy-tale Neuschwanstein Castle stands on a forested mountainside overlooking the waters of the Alpsee and the peaks beyond. The Ameron Neuschwanstein Alpsee Resort & Spa takes some of its stylistic cues from the ornate historicist castle, as it includes three antique hotels among its buildings; to these it adds a pair of contemporary buildings that complement the historical structures without imitating them.

The result, as is typical for the Ameron hotels, is impressive, a tastefully stylish experience that provides some present-day context for the 19th-century wonders that surround it. The rooms and suites in the historical hotel buildings are a handsome mix of period architectural elements and antique and modernist design gestures, while those in the newer buildings are more straightforwardly contemporary. All of them are comfortable above all, and many of the views are extraordinary, facing either Neuschwanstein Castle or its counterpart, Hohenschwangau.

As you’d expect from a luxury hotel in the Bavarian Alps, there’s an extensive spa and wellness program, and opportunities for outdoor recreation abound. Meanwhile, the hotel’s restaurants include Schloss Bräustüberl, the traditional option, complete with a beer garden, as well as Lisl, serving refined farm-to-table Alpine cuisine.

content:
There’s something deceptively understated about the name Rooms Hotel — the connotation being, perhaps, that it’s a practical, utilitarian sort of hotel, nothing more than a place to hang your hat. But both properties in the Rooms Hotels line, one in Kazbegi and the other in Tbilisi, offer quite a bit more than four walls and a roof over one’s head. Rooms Hotel Kazbegi, in fact, is grand and memorable, and the setting, in northern Georgia’s Caucasus Mountains, is downright cinematic. Spot the wooden lodge from far away, dwarfed by the dramatic scenery, and you’ll be glad you made the trip. Rooms, what rooms? You might forget where exactly you unpacked your suitcase when you’re drinking in views of snow-capped peaks from the hotel’s terrace or sipping Georgian wines by the roaring fireplace.

Rooms Hotel Kazbegi operates on that old entrepreneurial concept: if you build it, they will come. (And, conversely, if you don’t build it, they won’t come; how many people do you know who have vacationed in the remote reaches of Georgia lately?) So build it they did, just a few short years ago, with a hip young designer duo at the helm. The architecture draws on the style of a traditional mountain lodge — airy, open spaces, floor-to-ceiling windows, cozy leather sofas — but there’s a modern and sustainably minded twist here, with furnishings by Restoration Hardware and the Belgian label Flamant. Native wood, exposed brick, vintage carpets, clean lines and retro-inspired light fixtures and barstools, books to page through, globes to spin: this isn’t your grandfather’s cottage in the mountains, so to speak. The rustic-chic aesthetic prevails in the restaurant, in the charming and sun-drenched library, and on the large terrace, and there are even wood-planked floors around the indoor swimming pool.

And about those rooms — which rooms? You know, the guest rooms: they’re minimalist and sophisticated, outfitted with a subtler touch than you’ll find in the adorably quirky public spaces downstairs. There’s plenty of wood, of course, and lovely writing desks, and private balconies facing the surrounding forest and mountains. Spare and silent, they feel like mini refuges from the world outside, and from the rest of the lodge itself. They are, well, rooms — places to sleep — before an epic hike in the natural playground that awaits outside, and after a modern Georgian-style feast and drinks by the fire downstairs.

How to get there: Rooms Hotel Kazbegi is located approximately 169 km by car from Tbilisi International Airport via E117.

content:
Some hotels, even some very fine ones, exist mostly for economic reasons — maybe New York’s luxury hotels were full to bursting, or Berlin’s boutique supply was running thin. But the best of them are often motivated by something else entirely. It would be a stretch to claim that northern Poland’s Lake Wulpińskie had a massive pent-up demand for a boutique hotel along the lines of Galery69. Not that we’re complaining — the more gorgeously designed, art-infused boutique hotels there are in the world, the better, as far as we’re concerned. Lake Wulpińskie is the setting Małgorzata and Wojciech Żółtowsky envisioned for their creation, and so if you want to see it, Lake Wulpińskie is where you’ll go.

This one, even more than most, is a labor of love, and Galery69 is as much a showroom for their modernist, locally sourced handiwork as it is a hotel. The proprietors themselves are furniture makers, and everything you see here (or sit on, or lie on) was made by their own hands. The twenty-one rooms are all different, all inventive, never the least bit dull; twelve of them look directly out over the lake via the panoramic terrace, which is a view worth having, if you can get it. And the Masuria region is itself quite full of character — the Żółtowskys are as proud of their surroundings as they are of their hotel, and they’re only too happy to show you the countryside at its best.

How to get there:
Galery69 is located 126 miles (about a 2.5-hour drive) from Warsaw.

content:
For a Glasgow address you could do a whole lot worse than Blythswood Square itself — this gorgeous green space, just to the west of the city center, drips with Georgian charm. So too, for its part, does the Kimpton Blythswood Square, a hundred-room luxury boutique which stands behind one of the four identical listed façades that face onto the square. Needless to say, for a Glasgow address, you could do much, much worse than the Blythswood Square Hotel — every city, as far as we’re concerned, needs one absolutely essential classic-meets-contemporary luxury boutique, and this, for Glasgow, just might be the one.

The renovation must have been an extraordinary one, judging from the pains that have been taken to preserve the building’s original Georgian character alongside its modern improvements and contemporary decoration (including some only-in-Scotland touches, like the very liberal use of Harris tweed upholstery). The contrasts are deftly handled, never awkward, the rich hues of the modern furnishings set off brilliantly against the stately architectural backdrop. Classic rooms make the most of the basics — plush beds dressed in Egyptian cotton, baths clad in Spanish marble — and the better rooms and suites quickly grow to sprawling proportions, as in the extravagant signature suites. You’ll lack for nothing, either in comfort or character — this place, to put it simply, is up there with any of ‘em.

There’s a full-service spa, an inviting (and capacious) bar, and a restaurant occupying the massive old ballroom, as well as a salon whose afternoon tea service, for our money, leaves most conference rooms in the shade — literally, in the case of the 40-seat basement cinema.

content:
Deep-forest eco-lodges have been slower to arrive in Colombia than in other parts of Central and South America, but Cannúa, perched on a mountainside in Antioquia, is the kind of place that’s worth waiting for. Not many hotels can claim access to a hiking trail established by pre-Hispanic indigenous people, nor are they built from bricks crafted on site from the soil of the estate itself.

The lodge’s ten rooms and eight free-standing cabañas are modern in style, though suitably rustic in their materials, and all of them look out through vast windows at a far-ranging view of the Valley of San Nicolas. Basics like wi-fi and private bathrooms are present as a matter of course, and the contrast between the clean-lined, loft-inspired design and the natural panorama outside is nothing short of breathtaking.

It’s not just environmentally sustainable but socially sustainable as well, with authentic connections to the local community; in addition to a modern Colombian restaurant, serving dishes crafted from ingredients grown in the hotel’s own permaculture garden, there’s a spa and a number of excursions, from birding to hiking to coffee and chocolate tasting.

content:
You might think the oldest city in America would be somewhere in the vicinity of Plymouth Rock, but you’d be wrong. St. Augustine was the capital of Spanish Florida long before the Mayflower arrived. And by those standards, the lovingly restored homes that make up The Collector Luxury Inn & Gardens are relative newcomers — it’s not every day in the United States that you can sleep in a structure that dates back to the 1790s.

The nine historic buildings are divided into 30 rooms and suites, in a style that’s perhaps best described as contemporary colonial, where modern luxuries and historical atmosphere go hand in hand. If your only experience of Florida involves Miami or the big resorts, you’re in for quite a surprise. Despite its location in the center of town, The Collector feels like a little village unto itself, and the word “gardens” isn’t in the name just for decoration.

You’re likely to spend a fair bit of time lounging in those gardens, or seated around an outdoor fire pit or by the pool. The Well, the hotel’s bar, operates out of an old garage, and by the time the bartenders are done with you, you’ll be living in a throwback Floridian fantasy that’s straight out of Hemingway.

content:
Located just a block from Rittenhouse Square in Center City, Kimpton’s Hotel Palomar Philadelphia makes its home in the former headquarters of the American Institute of Architects. No surprise — the 1929 Art Deco building is a beauty, and the hotel does well to make art and architecture its theme. Period details and contemporary, eye-catching works by Philadelphia artists abound. Not that it feels like a museum; the place positively glows with warmth — in the lighting, in the soft carpets and neutral-toned furnishings, and neither last nor least in the gorgeous fireplace that forms the centerpiece of the lobby lounge. 

The 230 guest rooms are just as inviting, with Frette linens on the beds and Atelier Bloem amenities, marble vanities and recycled glass tiles in the lavish bathrooms. Children get special gifts on arrival, and if you register a pet (feline and canine friends of all sizes are welcome) then your room will be ready with a bowl and a doggie- or kitty-bed. 

For the rest of us, nightly wine tastings, jogging maps and bike rentals are all free of charge. Business travelers are within easy range of Philadelphia’s largest concentration of office buildings, in Center City. Alternatively, let associates come to you at the hotel’s own 24th and 25th floor meeting rooms, its enormous penthouse ballroom with views of Philadelphia’s skyline on three sides, or in the bar and restaurant, Square 1682.

content:
A luxury spa hotel on the shores of Lake Garda is an easy sell already — and a spectacular location on the Sirmione peninsula, which juts dramatically into the lake’s southern waters, makes Hotel Ocelle Thermae & Spa a particularly memorable one. It’s also a particularly stylish one — while many of its competitors are defiantly old-fashioned, the Ocelle embraces a modernist-inspired style that reinforces the restorative atmosphere promised by its spring-fed pools and its lavish spa.

The views from the peninsula are extraordinary; the lake itself is fringed by mountain peaks, and the peninsula’s coastline is dotted with rocky island-like slabs, known as the Seychelles of Sirmione. The lakefront suites partake in these dramatic vistas, while the standard rooms have balconies overlooking a quiet side street.

Hotel Ocelle’s thermal pools are its spa’s most unique offerings, though they’re joined by a long list of alternatives, from massages and saunas to a Himalayan salt cave and an “emotional shower.” There’s a small sandy beach right beside the infinity pool, and while the hotel itself serves only breakfast, lunch, and light poolside fare, the staff is happy to make arrangements and any of Sirmione’s restaurants — you’re only a few minutes’ walk from the town center.

content:
The Explora hotels tend to begin with locations that are flat-out extraordinary, places like Patagonia or the Atacama Desert. And then they create hospitality experiences that are equal to the setting, featuring inspired design, top-shelf comfort, and world-class service. Even within this tradition, however, Explora Valle Sagrado is something special — the sacred valley in question is the Urubamba Valley, at the end of which, of course, is no less singular a place than the Inca ruin of Machu Picchu.

Explora Valle Sagrado is, in fact, built on an ancient Inca site of its own, a fact which was discovered during construction and led to some improvisation on the part of the architects. The result is, for lack of a better phrase, modernism done right — local materials like adobe and wood are put to beautiful, unfussy use in Explora’s powerfully minimalist spaces. And the comforts, naturally, are anything but austere, from the bedrooms and bathrooms to the lavish Pumacahua Bath House spa and the extraordinary Peruvian and international fare served in the hotel’s restaurant. A hotel like this could make a location in a parking lot seem magical, and a setting like the Sacred Valley could make a Motel 6 feel inspiring — together they’re nothing short of unforgettable.

content:
Cape Town suffers from no shortage of luxury hotels, that’s for sure. But rare is the degree of historical character on display at Ellerman House. It’s almost a century old now, and looks every bit as old as it is — which, in a business that’s increasingly obsessed with youthful looks and modern design, is a sure-fire way to distance yourself from the crowd.

No amount of designer furniture, anyway, could measure up to the sea view from Ellerman House’s hilltop vantage, and faced with the choice between a hip bar with a bouncer and a terrace restaurant with proper, professional service, we know which one we’d pick. Not to say the place looks old, by any means — it’s so well-kept you’ll think you’ve gone back a hundred years.

There are just eleven rooms and two suites, so it feels more like a manor-house getaway than a hotel per se, and despite their historical style they’ll compete with any modern hotel room on pure comfort. And if for some reason you’re of a mind to reject the old-world atmosphere of the place, they’ve got an answer for that as well: a pair of lavish three-bedroom villas, which marry the location, views and service of the Ellerman House with a grown-up modern style that’s straight out of the architecture journals.

content:
Perhaps no destination in the Northeast feels quite so quintessentially New England as the island of Martha’s Vineyard. And on the Vineyard, there’s no place more stately and upright than Edgartown. So it’s no small matter when a 15-room Victorian inn undergoes a makeover, trading its traditional interiors for a bright and lively look that adds mid-century modern and French Caribbean influences to the mix. This irreverent playfulness is something of a trademark for the Massachusetts-based Lark Hotels, and it’s just part of what sets the Christopher apart from the typical Vineyard inn.

The other part is, well, the rest of the experience. Despite its antique good looks, this is a thoroughly contemporary hotel, aimed less at the habitual travelers who’ve been coming to Edgartown for decades and more at a generation that’s accustomed to the upscale boutique-hotel experience (not that they’d be sad to develop a decades-long following of their own).

With 15 rooms it’s by no means large, which makes for personalized service and an easy, convivial atmosphere. The lounge and the back courtyard with its firepit are the hotel’s social spaces, and the location, just off Main Street, is convenient and central — and an impressive and inventive breakfast sends you out into the streets in style.

content: It’s not uncommon to talk about the Caribbean as though it were a single destination, but one of the reasons for its perennial appeal is that it’s a place that offers a near-infinite variety of experiences. At one extreme there’s the all-inclusive beachside mega-resort; at the other extreme there’s a place like Le Jardin Malanga, just outside of Trois Rivières, Guadeloupe. Nestled into the forest ten minutes up the hillside from the beach, it’s blessed with stunning views of the nearby Saintes islands. And it’s far from a mega-resort, or even a resort — it’s just a Twenties-era colonial mansion plus three freestanding cottages, making for an atmosphere that’s as tranquil as can be.\n\nLe Mansion Coloniale contains a suite that sleeps four and a pair of “triple” bedrooms, while the more contemporary cottages each come with a pair of bedrooms plus a children’s room on the upper level. A small open-air restaurant serves French-Caribbean cuisine, and the infinity pool is positioned with a view out to sea. And there’s more to the island than just the hotel and the beach — the tropical forest conceals wildlife, waterfalls, and even La Soufrière, an active volcano.

content:
Thanks to the influx of Austrian, German, and Swiss settlers to Argentinian Patagonia at the turn of the century, the lake region’s architecture tends toward chalet-style lodges and wooden cottages. Certain areas of Bariloche, complete with tourist-friendly German shepherd puppies and decorative gables, feel so campy that you’re almost expecting to hear a yodeler off in the distance. The Aldebaran Hotel, by contrast, is refreshingly modern and understated. While the design stays true to the mountain lodge spirit with traditional wood beams and fireplaces, the hotel isn’t channeling The Sound of Music — the style is classic and uncluttered. 

The ten-room boutique is located on a cliff overlooking the crystal-blue lake of Nahuel Huapi, a solid 20-minute drive from the city of Bariloche. The relatively remote setting, not to mention the designer’s use of natural building materials like smooth gray stone and locally produced timber, lend the Aldebaran a pleasingly down-to-earth atmosphere. Inviting public spaces include the lodge’s main sitting room, featuring intimate white-cushioned nooks and huge picture windows facing the lake, and the hotel spa with its innovative inside/outside swimming pool that makes a paddle under the stars possible regardless of the lake’s temperature. Guest rooms are outfitted with cozy fabrics in neutral tones and brightly colored woven tapestries. Awash with natural light, each room contains a daybed or a plush armchair and a private lakeview terrace or balcony. The amply sized bathrooms, done up in earth-colored tile, are just as appealing.

The hotel’s Sirius restaurant, occupying a seductively lit, stone-inlaid space, prepares organic regional cuisine — think homemade bread, grass-fed beef, and a bottle of Malbec — that encourages guests to dine onsite. The Aldebaran’s location is a trade-off, after all — the city’s attractions aren’t exactly within walking distance, but hikers, rafters, and kayakers will find the hotel’s proximity to unspoiled lakes and mountains an unqualified asset.


How to Get There

Aldebaran Hotel & Spa is approximately a 25 minute drive from Teniente Luis Candelaria International Airport (BRC).

content: There’s a sweet story behind the Pergola, a 15-room boutique hotel a short stroll from the beach in the fishing village of Cascais. In 1925, a local businessman purchased a pair of side-by-side chalets with a French-style garden in the middle, then renovated them and gifted them to his two daughters. They remained in the family until the mid-1980s, when one of the chalets was turned into the town’s very first hotel. \n\nMany of the chalet’s original features remain — cool stone floors, hand-painted tiles, a grand iron staircase — and the historic garden beside it, lovingly tended by one of the daughters for decades, is still one of the property’s finest assets. Meanwhile the guest rooms are both quaint and modern, bright white with a single accent wall or headboard in bold Portuguese patterns. They’re all full of natural light, with high ceilings, decorative crown molding, and parquet floors. Deluxe rooms have spacious vintage-looking bathrooms and private balconies overlooking the gardens, where an exquisitely presented breakfast is served each morning.

content:
The seaside village of Charlestown is one of Cornwall’s most picturesque destinations, and home to Antonia’s Pearls, which comprises a cabin, a loft, and a Georgian townhouse restored by owners and operators Antonia and David in a style that’s chic, unpretentious, and memorably eclectic.

The Marine Villa is the three-bedroom Georgian villa, with its own garden and a view of Charlestown’s harbor. Hidden in a private garden is the Sea Cabin, a two-bedroom escape that’s perfect for a family, and the one-bedroom Sail Loft for couples.

You’re welcome to prepare your own meals — there’s a proper kitchen and dining room in every unit — or have them delivered from Antonia’s kitchen. And of course the village itself has much to offer in the culinary realm, and the nearby coastline and countryside is full of attractions, from a maritime museum to surfing beaches, from the Tate St Ives to the Eden Project and the Lost Gardens of Heligan.

content:
A fixture in both central London and downtown Manhattan, the Soho House members’ clubs have been expanding, both to far-flung global locations and to major cities in the United States. And it’s in a picturesque 1908 industrial building in the neighborhood of Fulton Market that you’ll find Soho House Chicago, an establishment that is, if you’ll forgive what sounds like overstatement, much more than simply a hotel.

What is it, then? Well, it’s an extremely stylish co-working space, as well as a very fine set of restaurants and bars, plus a handful of events spaces that include a plush 30-seat screening room, an 80-foot rooftop pool, and a spa and fitness center that rivals some standalone athletic clubs. All of this is ordinarily available only to members, a clientele drawn largely from Chicago’s creative industries. But it’s also a luxury boutique hotel, of a sort, and as an overnight guest you’ll be entitled to all the benefits of membership for the duration of your stay.

Not that the rooms aren’t impressive on their own; they’re quietly luxurious, and as richly textured and eclectic as any Soho House rooms, and studiously avoid anything obviously post-industrial, much less minimalist. Add access to spaces like the pleasantly divey Fox Bar and the classic Northern Italian Cecconi’s Taverna, on the rooftop, and the case for membership begins to become clear.

content:
The Soho House brand may have gone global, but its heart remains in this West End neighborhood, still haunted by the film and theatre folk who made up the original club’s membership. And Dean Street itself is the very heart of Soho — in fact the flagship Soho House is just four doors down the street from the Dean Street Townhouse.

It’s more a case of synergy than redundancy. The Soho House at 76 Dean Street is full of social spaces, including a private cinema, but no bedrooms. This is where the charming Townhouse fits in. Inside you’ll find a surprising country-house undertone to the atmosphere, both in the common spaces and in the 39 rooms. They range from Tiny to Bigger, all of which understate the matter somewhat; even the smallest are comfortable indeed, especially when supplemented by the Townhouse’s public spaces, and the largest ones find space for luxuries like four-poster beds and freestanding tubs.

Downstairs is a restaurant that’s packed with works by contemporary British artists, and whose tables are packed with Soho House members and other neighborhood locals. Of particular note is the afternoon tea service, a modern alternative to the offerings of some more traditional luxury hotels.

content: Kettner’s is a restaurant first, and not an ordinary restaurant — opened in 1876, it’s served the likes of Winston Churchill, Oscar Wilde, and King Edward VII. And while there’s a gap in its history on the way to its present incarnation, Kettner’s Townhouse is back in action thanks to the steady hand of the Soho House group. Like any Soho House it’s now a members’ club, and features lodgings in addition to its dining room. And when the house isn’t fully booked by permanent members, it’s open to bookings by temporary members — which is to say overnight guests, who earn the benefits of membership for the duration of their stay.\n\nWith so rich a heritage it’s perhaps not a great surprise that Kettner’s features rather more in the way of antique atmosphere and historical detail than the typical Soho House property. The restaurant itself serves Mediterranean-accented modern British fare in partnership with the Clarence Tavern, and it’s accompanied by a Champagne bar and a piano bar. And the rooms, as you’d expect, range from Tiny to Big, and come decorated in a unique but recognizable variation on the eclectic Soho House style.

content:
Montage Big Sky is another hotel where the constituent parts of the name tell more or less the whole story — the Californian purveyor of lavish high-design resort experiences meets the rugged Rocky Mountain wilderness of southwestern Montana. This isn’t Jackson Hole or Aspen; until now, Big Sky hasn’t seen high-end hospitality on Montage’s level. And, likewise, it’s a long way from Laguna Beach; the untamed wilderness is close at hand, as is some of North America’s finest skiing.

With 139 rooms, suites and residences it’s no small addition, and it also comes with an 11,000-square-foot spa, ski-in/ski-out access to the lift system at Big Sky Resort, and access to Spanish Peaks Mountain Club’s Tom Weiskopf–designed 18-hole golf course. There’s also a tubing hill, bike and Nordic trails, and Compass Sports, a recreational outfitter. Meanwhile the rooms and suites are expansive and lavishly furnished, with enough rustic edge to the décor to retain an authentic sense of place.

For all its extravagant high-end comforts, Montage Big Sky’s atmosphere nevertheless remains unpretentious and down-to-earth. Alpenglow, the lobby bar, is a dramatic triple-height space with astounding views through full-length windows, while Backcast is the après-ski venue, and Beartooth Pub & Rec serves hearty fare in a casual, convivial atmosphere. Meanwhile Cortina, the signature restaurant, adds a Northern Italian accent.

content: We love the plucky little independent hotels, of course, but there’s something to be said for a brand name that puts a complete picture in your head. In the case of Kimpton, that’s a smart, stylish, and accessible vision of boutique hospitality, a place that’s inclusive rather than exclusive — and, crucially, that’s not confined to a couple of big cities on the coasts. Take Dallas, for example. Here architects Perkins + Will have transformed a century-old landmark in Deep Ellum into the Pittman Hotel, named for its original designer, the pioneering African-American architect William S. Pittman.\n\nIt’s just what you expect from Kimpton, and we mean that in the best possible way: lively public spaces, inspiring and historically informed design, and just the right measure of luxury without crossing over into excess. The rooms are elegant, and somewhat eclectic, spanning a century of modernism and decorated with original contemporary artworks. The neighborhood is a lively one, full of music venues, restaurants, and art galleries, and the Pittman’s own atmosphere is similarly vibrant, thanks to Elm & Good, a tavern-style restaurant and bar with an open kitchen and a delightful outdoor patio. It’d be a standout anywhere, and elevates the Dallas hotel scene single-handedly.
