content: The Balearic Islands are plentifully endowed with rocky cliffs, pristine beaches, evergreen forests, and rugged mountains, but only a singular occurrence of natural hot springs. They’re located near the southern coast of Mallorca, and Fontsanta Thermal Spa & Wellness is the closest hotel. So close, in fact, that its spa, built around the springs’ mineral-rich thermal waters, is Fontsanta’s main draw and namesake — the name, after all, means “sacred fountain.” But this quietly stylish adults-only retreat has plenty to offer beyond its subterranean springs, like privileged views over the spectacular landscape and a guests-only beach club on Es Trenc, one of the island’s loveliest stretches of shoreline. \n\nA collection of stone buildings houses the restaurant, spa, and two levels of guest rooms, all of which open onto private furnished terraces. The interiors are modern but down-to-earth, with wide wood-plank floors, beamed ceilings, a color scheme of white and beige, and furnishings upholstered in linen. Outside, breakfast is served beneath the trees, and white canopied daybeds surround the hotel’s outdoor pools and Jacuzzis — though you'll need to reserve a time at Fontsana’s gorgeous spa and its thoughtfully designed hydrotherapy circuit for access to the region’s healing waters.

content:
It’s an age-old question whether it’s preferable to stay on the beach or on the hill overlooking it. Francesco Mansi chose the latter when he selected Hotel Miramalfi’s clifftside location in the 1950s; instead of opening his hotel in the pretty seaside village, he opted for a property with postcard-like vistas of Amalfi and the Tyrrhenian Sea. The hotel’s design makes the most of its position — dazzling views are available from its terraces, restaurant, saltwater pool, guest rooms, and even the parking lot.

Hotel Miramalfi is still run by this family, and though the place has been renovated and refreshed several times, the mid-century modern interiors are true to their origins. Rooms are compact, airy, and light-filled with checkered tile floors and a cheerful maritime-inspired palette of white, royal blue, pale pink, emerald green, and turquoise. French doors open onto private balconies overlooking the sea; each has a pair of striped chairs and a small table, ideal for morning coffee or evening aperitifs. Suites have separate seating areas and larger bathrooms with walk-in showers.

A flower-lined staircase leads down to the sea, winding past the pool and several terraces furnished with umbrellas and chaise longues, all conveniently attended by waiters from the pool bar. Meanwhile an elegant terrace bar offers additional outdoor seating and the best views in the house.

content:
On the San Miguel de Allende hospitality scene, low-key and residential is the name of the game. The modest size of its finest hotels means there’s always room for one more exquisite example, and Casa Blanca 7 fits the bill. It’s a 300-year-old house in the city’s Spanish Colonial historic center, and as its name might suggest, it’s got a touch of Moroccan atmosphere, recalling in a subtle way the ultra-private riad hotels of cities like Casablanca and Marrakech.

With just ten suites it can’t help but feel more like a private house than a hotel, and the suites themselves, designed by Fisher Weisman Collection, are impressively detailed and perhaps surprisingly contemporary. The details are luxurious, from the Portuguese cotton linens and goose-down pillows to the bath products, labeled Hecho SMA — meaning “made in San Miguel de Allende.”

The courtyard, more than anything else, is a reminder of the finest small Moroccan hotels. And it’s fitting that chef Mike Garcia, born in Mexico, spent time in France, Spain, and North Africa; to Casa Blanca 7 he brings an appreciation for traditional Mexican flavors as well as influences from both sides of the western Mediterranean.

Mykonos is already as desirable as any destination in the Mediterranean, and the luxe and alarmingly stylish Kalesma only raises the stakes. It’s set on a hilltop on the island’s west side, fifteen minutes from town, and feels like a private refuge — one whose suites and villas pay tribute to classic Cycladic architecture as well as modern interior design, and feature Rick Owens furnishings among their adornments.

There’s nothing smaller here than a one-bedroom suite, complete with a walk-in shower, a separate freestanding bath, another (outdoor) shower, and a private heated infinity pool, as well as an outdoor kitchen. From there the suites and villas only grow larger and more extravagant, culminating in the seven-bedroom Kalesma Leto Villa, practically a hotel within the hotel.

Kalesma Mykonos is also home to a spa in collaboration with Dr. Barbara Sturm; yoga and Pilates sessions are available as well. And there’s a decided focus on the other kind of restoration; the primary restaurant, Pere Ubu Mykonos, is joined by a poolside bar, a tavern-style restaurant called Kuveda, and the Aloni Sunset Lounge.

content:
The smallish Balkan country of Montenegro fights above its weight in the travel world thanks to its spectacular Adriatic coast. Here, near the opening of the Bay of Kotor, is a Venetian-era military hospital that dates back to 1732, meticulously preserved, restored, and expanded into the Lazure Hotel & Marina, a luxury boutique hotel with a perfect seaside location and the kind of classic atmosphere a new build couldn’t hope to match.

That’s not to say Lazure is a throwback experience, though. Inside, you’ll find the historical architecture effortlessly updated with contemporary interior design; alongside weathered sections of stone wall are modern fixtures and furnishings, bright accent colors, and contemporary artworks. They’re both stylish and indulgent, especially the bathrooms, and the suites are impressively large.

One restaurant, the more formal Rosemarine, serves upscale Mediterranean fare in spaces that range from the dining room to the terrace with a view of the marina, while a second, Augusto Brasserie, occupies an interior courtyard. The adjacent marina building is home to Wine O’Clock Gastro Bar, and the Lazure Spa includes an indoor pool and a separate kids’ pool as well as saunas, a jacuzzi and hammam, and a thoroughly equipped fitness center.

This is France, yes, but this corner of Lorraine, mere minutes from the point where the borders with Germany and Luxembourg meet, has a character all its own. And the same can be said of Le Domaine de la Klauss, whose rough-hewn stone walls put one in mind of a medieval fortification, but whose modern-luxe interiors and five-star services make it anything but forbidding.

The hotel’s rooms and suites occupy a variety of spaces, from the original structure to the more contemporary — but still stone-clad — outbuildings. The most humble among them are spacious and exceedingly comfortable, and the suites quickly enter into exceptional territory, culminating in the 80-square-meter suite atop the Domaine’s tower, with its bedside Jacuzzi and its panoramic view of the valley.

Le Domaine’s spa spreads out over 800 square meters, and offers a panoply of treatments in partnership with the Gemology brand. The setting, naturally, affords access to a wealth of outdoor pursuits, including equestrian activities in the company of the Domaine’s Iberian horses. Most central to the experience, however, is the cuisine, from Le Komptoir, the wood-fired bistro, to Le K, the more formal gastronomic option.

content:
Bruges, if you’ll excuse the left-field analogy, is something like the Kyoto of Belgium — it’s where you go to experience the meticulously preserved past in all its glory. You might expect Hotel Sablon, given its status as the oldest hotel in town, to serve this time-machine function. But as venerable as the structure may be, the Sablon’s interiors are shockingly up-to-date — this is a modern boutique hotel, through and through, and the contrast of its interior design with its 16th-century architecture is as striking as any we’ve ever seen.

Contemporary artworks and furniture adorn the Sablon’s stately spaces, from the central staircase to the rooms and suites; every one is different, though all are decked out in rich colors, luxe textures, and high-end comforts. In the classic European style the floor plans vary widely, from the very compact Single all the way up to the Sablon Mansion Suite or the vast Loft, spanning some 84 square meters.

There’s no restaurant per se, but there is a lovely breakfast, and a bar, the Livingroom, serving cocktails and light bites both indoors and in the garden courtyard. Fear not; Bruges suffers from no shortage of delightful options, as well as plenty to see and do.

content:
Southern cities don’t get much more picturesque than Charlottesville, home of the legendarily scenic University of Virginia as well as Thomas Jefferson’s Monticello estate. And  boutique hotels don’t get much more picturesque than the Oakhurst Inn, a beautiful 27-room lodging in an upscale residential neighborhood — and National Historic District — just off the university’s South Lawn.

Safe to say the location is just about as convenient as can be. In many university towns, that would mean a constant din of noise, but the Oakhurst Inn feels tucked-away and sedate. Rooms and suites are divided among a couple of well-preserved historical houses, and they combine classic architecture and contemporary design, including custom furniture, and modern boutique-hotel amenities like Malin + Goetz bath products. 

Categories range from a standard with a queen bed all the way up to a sprawling Penthous Suite up under the eaves of the old house. Rather than a traditional lobby, the Oakhurst Inn features no fewer than four libraries for lounging. And while for dinner you’re at the mercy of greater Charlottesville’s (excellent) food scene, for breakfast, lunch, and weekend brunch there’s the Oakhurst Inn Cafe and Espresso Bar.

content: The first boutique hotel to open in Tbilisi felt like a novelty. The second, perhaps, marked the beginning of a trend. But the third — Stamba Hotel, upscale sister to the successful Rooms Hotel Tbilisi — is evidence of a bona fide movement. The Georgian capital has opened itself up to the world in a big way, and the world, it seems, likes what it sees. This is a buzzing, cosmopolitan city, a revelation to those of us who remember when it was locked up behind the Iron Curtain, and a fashionable playground to a younger generation for whom that story is ancient history.\n\nThere’s more than a slight family resemblance between Rooms and Stamba; the latter occupies a classic Thirties building, once home to a famous publishing house, and the building’s post-industrial patina gives it a visual identity all its own — along with surreal flourishes, like the trees that grow through the five-story central atrium. The rooms go all in on retro style, with leather headboards, brass fixtures, and weathered textures, and while they’re unpretentious, they’re possessed of more than a touch of luxury. Meanwhile the public spaces attract travelers and locals alike — Café Stamba, the restaurant, is a hot ticket, as is the Pink Bar with its enormous crystal chandelier.

content:
The concept of the art hotel is familiar by now: we’ve come a long way since the days when standard hotel room decoration featured generic watercolor seascapes or framed reproductions of iconic artworks. But rarely does a hotel commit to the concept so thoroughly as the new Art Mai Gallery Nimman Hotel in Chiang Mai.

The hotel is eight stories tall, with a modern art gallery on the ground level. And above that, each of the seven floors was designed by a different contemporary Thai artist working within a certain theme or genre. Categories include classics like Pop Art (fourth floor) and Impressionism (seventh floor), as well as Nude Art (on the second floor, if case you fancy taking a stroll down this particular corridor.) It’s not quite as racy as it sounds, but these rooms and suites, seductively outfitted in black and white, are for adults only.

Needless to say, the in-room aesthetic varies widely at Art Mai Gallery Nimman Hotel. On the Abstract Art floor, for example, the exposed brick walls and earth tones evoke the cozy feel of an artist’s studio, while the top-floor Lanna Romantic rooms, with their sophisticated grays and minimalist canopies, look comparatively exotic. The square footage varies widely, too. Most floors have a range of room categories, including an Artist Signature Room — spacious, open-plan suites that are practically miniature art galleries. Standard amenities across categories include flat-screen TVs, spacious work areas, complimentary wi-fi. And, yes, artist’s easels stocked with canvases and paint, should creative inspiration strike.

Elsewhere in the hotel, there’s a sleek infinity pool and terrace with views over the city, and the industrial-chic Jarid Restaurant, specializing in Thai fusion cuisine and cocktails, some of which were inspired by the same modern artists responsible for the interior design. It’s an art-filled enclave, yes, but a practical place to stay, too: the downtown location makes it an ideal jumping-off point to explore the city, preferably on one of the bicycles handily provided by the hotel.

content:
It would be criminal to upset the natural beauty of NZ’s South Island with overbearing design, and this boutique hotel strikes a harmonious balance between the holistic and the hip. Positioned amid some of the world’s most dramatic topography, the Queenstown Park Hotel strives not to compete with its surroundings — how could you even begin to outshine a mountain range dubbed “The Remarkables” — but effortlessly blends into the landscape, both visually and ecologically.  

While timber, glass and stone dominate the property’s somewhat masculine exterior, interiors show a softer side, thanks entirely to the sensitive touch of local designers Comber & Smith. Rooms are light-filled, with unfussy interiors flowing into private outdoor nooks, a terrace or patio attached to every room. 

Views here aren’t optional: you either get one of The Remarkables or one of the mountains directly behind the property. The Tower Suite, located in the property’s stone turret, boasts vistas of both, in case you just can’t decide. This one also features a full kitchen, in contrast with the kitchenettes elsewhere, and  flat-screen TVs, underfloor heating and free wifi are standard throughout. For those wanting to drink in more than just scenery, complimentary canapes and wine are served in the lounge before dinner, with gourmet picnic hampers available to guests who want to take their fine dining into the great outdoors.  

It’s just as much substance as style. The QPH exhibits a progressive attitude towards sustainable hospitality. With only 19 rooms, its impact on carbon levels is by default less guilt-inducing than that of the big hotels, but the QPH takes it further, going local for its produce, using cruelty-free toiletries, recycling waste materials, abstaining from chemical cleaning and using sensor lighting in common areas. All this would probably be enough, yet the QPH has even more to court visitors, namely its warm New Zealand service and a top location just across the park from Queenstown proper. Wakatipu Lake is a five-minute walk away and the gondola that scales the mountain range less than two.

content:
An hour and a half from Bordeaux, deep in the Dordogne countryside, a beautiful 17th-century manor house once belonging to a Catholic order has been lovingly restored by its husband-and-wife owners and opened to travelers under the name of La Chartreuse du Bignac. It’s a house that’s both grand and yet somehow humble, possessed of a certain ramshackle charm even as the experience is elevated into luxury territory. 

The rooms and suites are divided between the main house and a couple of historical outbuildings, and with just 12 units on some 50 acres of land, it’s incapable of feeling crowded. All of the units display some degree of period detail, from timbered ceilings and stone walls to, in the case of the suite made from the old mill, a glass floor looking down into a flowing stream. And as rich as they are with historical charm, they’re also outfitted with high-end comforts, including plush beds and stylish modern bathrooms.

In the old barn you’ll find La Chartreuse’s restaurant, which serves modern dishes crafted from local and seasonal ingredients with a view of the estate and the distant hills.

content:
The first Soho House members’ club in continental Europe is Soho House Berlin, and its proprietors could hardly have wished for a more evocative setting — this Bauhaus structure is both historically significant and aesthetically distinctive. Not that Soho House has treated it with undue reverence; its renovation feels intentionally unfinished, with industrial rough edges that provide a pleasing counterpoint to the retro bohemian-luxe furnishings. And there’s art everywhere, including a Damien Hirst shark in the lobby — a spray-can sketch, not a preserved one — and works by innumerable contemporary Berlin-based artists.

Rooms start out Tiny, which is a slight exaggeration, but only slight; from there they range up to the aptly named Extra Large, which spans 100 square meters and comes with an ornate freestanding bathtub. At all levels they’re handsome in that inimitable Soho House way, and exceedingly comfortable at any size. But in the end you’re here not to shut yourself in your bedroom, but to inhabit Soho House’s members-only spaces.

These include a gym and spa that rival many standalone facilities, as well as a plush screening room that seats 30. Cecconi’s, the brand’s signature Northern Italian restaurant, is present as a matter of course, and members — that includes you, as an overnight guest — can order from the Club menu as well.

content:
Annecy, the “Venice of the Alps,” is supplied with more historic charm and storybook beauty than most cities of its size. A less confident hotelier might lean into the prevailing mood of Alpine coziness, but Hôtel Hébé is free to indulge its elegant side. The result is a high-end boutique hotel that offers some contrast with its setting, while never going so far as to feel out of place.

In the rooms, the knotty hardwood floors are a subtle echo of Alpine lodge style, while the prevailing mood is one of clean-lined, contemporary sophistication — modern furniture, contemporary art, and up-to-date conveniences like Malongo coffee makers and Bang & Olufsen TVs and sound systems. Some feature cozy little terraces facing the street; all are as comfortable to the touch as they are easy on the eyes.

An à la carte breakfast made from locally sourced organic products — Boulangerie Rouge pastries, Alain Michel cheeses — is a promising start to the day, while the bar serves espresso, wine, and a light menu until late at night. And the Hôtel Hébé’s location, in the heart of Annecy’s picturesque city center, places an infinity of restaurants, cafés, bars, and more within easy walking distance.

content: Not many luxury hotels can claim to have been in operation for more than 160 years, and still fewer have remained independent and family-owned for all that time. Beau-Rivage Geneva, however, is exactly that. It’s among the most luxurious hotels in town — set right on the shores of Lake Geneva, overlooking the city’s famous Jet d’Eau — and it didn’t get that way by resting on its 1865-vintage laurels.\n\nThe interiors, by the French designer Pierre-Yves Rochon, are thoroughly renewed, even as the atmosphere of aristocratic elegance remains undisturbed. The suites, named for such luminaries as Charles de Gaulle and Elizabeth Taylor, scale extravagant heights of luxury, while even the more ordinary rooms remain faultless in their comforts. Rivage Café serves artful bistronomic fare complemented with bottles from the hotel's prestigious wine cellar, which can also be enjoyed as part of a dedicated wine tasting. Safe to say the Beau-Rivage continues to earn its place in the pantheon of Geneva’s extraordinarily luxe high-end hotels.

We’ll forgive you, just this once, if you don’t bother reading this description. If you know your luxury hotels, the name Six Senses Fiji says more or less all you need to know. It’s set on a splendid, sunset-facing stretch of beach nearly half a mile long, its sustainably minded and prioritises renewable energy, waste-reduction and conservation programs, and like anything with the Six Senses name on it, it spares absolutely no expense when it comes to luxury.

With just 24 villas it’s not the kind of place where you can go overlooked — and that’s doubly true given the fantastically friendly and personable staff. Every villa comes with a plunge pool, a private deck for lounging or dining, and an open-air bathroom. And they’re all stylish in an understated way, with a modernist simplicity that’s pleasing to the eye but with organic, natural finishes that feel eminently suited to the place.

The Six Senses name is more or less synonymous with the brand’s spa experience, which is typically lavish here — the spa is practically a village unto itself, with offerings ranging from massages and beauty treatments to alternative medicine and holistic interventions.

As you might imagine, given its South Pacific location, the diving isn’t half bad either — here you’ll find everything from scuba and snorkeling to surfing, stand-up paddling, and kayaking, with instruction available in both surfing and diving. And on land you’ve got nature walks, challenging hikes, tennis courts, and villages to visit — safe to say you’re well placed to absorb everything that Malolo Island has to offer.

content:
Tradition is important in France. Particularly in a place like Chamonix, considered one of the oldest ski resorts in the world. Building a brand new hotel here, in other words, is a bit of a gamble: to compete with the glamorous old lodges and chalets in the valley, things have to be just so. At Hotel Héliopic Sweet & Spa, they are. Ideally located just steps from the Aiguille du Midi cable car, it’s a modern hotel with a slightly retro look. Nothing too out there, of course, nothing that breaks too seriously from the Chamonix norm — the main buildings are shaped like chalets, and there’s a spacious bar and library for après-ski drinks. 

But there are other features at the Héliopic, ones that suggest a forward-thinking concept of a ski vacation in Mont Blanc. It’s a tech-friendly hotel, for starters, with large 3D maps in the lobby to help you plan your outdoor adventures, and quick and complimentary wi-fi throughout. And guest rooms, in a departure from the region’s standard aesthetic, are simple and minimalist, with oak parquet floors, gray tweed rugs, and crisp white sheets. All rooms have private balconies with mountain views. And a flat-screen TV, of course. Everything you need, nothing you don’t.

There’s other stuff you don’t quite need at Hotel Héliopic, though, and we’re glad for it. Drop your kids off at the dedicated children’s area — and grab yourself a handful from the serve-yourself candy and popcorn bar while you'e at it, whether or not you have kids — before hitting the subterranean swimming pool or the lavish wood and stone Nuxe Spa. This isn’t your everyday spa experience, it’s worth noting. Nuxe has a Japanese-style whirlpool, an ice grotto, a tea shop, a tepidarium, and a hanging Egg chair by Pierantonio Bonacina. Join the social scene at the bar, or, if you’re too tired after a day of skiing to bother with drinks or reservations at the Héliopic’s elegant restaurant, skip it. You can always stop by Epicerie du Midi, a gourmet grocery kiosk, for high-end takeout and in-room snacks, and perhaps grab a French film from the DVD library, too.

content:
The Alpine experience is all about landscape — limpid mountain lakes, soaring evergreens, and some of the most iconic summits on the planet. Das Kronthaler, a ski-in/ski-out fixture towards the German side of Austria’s western corridor, makes the most of its setting. There’s guided hiking at various levels of difficulty, mountain biking, skiing of all varieties, golf, and tobogganing. Then there’s paragliding, horseback riding, Nordic walking, and a slew of watersports in and around the nearby Achensee in the summer months. And, come winter, there’s plenty of skiing.

In typical Tyrol style, the hotel’s gym and spa facilities are equally encyclopedic, the better to tone and soothe worn bodies. Take your pick of the Finnish sauna, a massive indoor/outdoor pool, an “infrared cabin,” or a standard array of gym machines. Thanks to the panoramic windows, you can still gaze longingly on the mountainscape while you sweat. To their credit, the views are never quite out of sight, as amply evidenced by floods of natural light throughout the public spaces. You’ll be glad for the seating — swank cube armchairs or velvet chaises longues, likely — when you first catch sight of Karwendel and Rofan rearing their majestic peaks in the distance. 

Rooms depart somewhat from the typical Tyrolean formula (think slabs of knotty pine and spruce, antlers, expeditionary tchotchkes, parquet flooring), though never far enough to raise concern, focusing instead on cleansing minimalism with small notes of color in the linens. Clean, polished lines lend buoyancy to square, pine-forward forms, a modern note in keeping with the flatscreens, wi-fi, and other present-day must-haves. Most rooms open on some sort of furnished balcony, though the roof chalets take it to the next level (pun intended) with freestanding tubs and petite garden lounges. 

By this point you’ll have worked up an appetite, no doubt. An on-site kitchen serves nuanced Tyrolean plates paired with a broad assortment of wines, as well as cornucopian breakfast and lunch spreads, and the promise of a perfect champagne or espresso on the roomy rooftop sundeck. Digest — the food, the landscape — at your leisure, and pity the soul for whom any of this becomes mundane.

How to get there: Das Kronthaler is located approximately 128 km by car from Munich International Airport via E45, B318, B307, and B181. Alternatively, the hotel is approximately 58 km by car from Innsbruck Airport via A12, Kasbach, and B181.

content:
Let this be a lesson to anyone who organizes their travel searches by country. When you’re looking for a ski getaway, be sure and throw in a search for Andorra, or else risk missing out on at least one extraordinary small hotel. Hotel Grau Roig is located in the town of the same name, in the Andorran Pyrenées, and while its exterior looks cozy enough — to the untutored eye it’s something like a brown-brick Bavarian lodge — it’s what’s inside that counts.

Namely, rooms and suites that wouldn’t look out of place in just about any urban European design hotel. A far cry from the timber-and-antlers look of the typical ski lodge. With the exception of the strangely old-fashioned standard rooms, the interiors at the Grau Roig are pared-down and contemporary, in palettes of dark brown, with floors (and sometimes paneling) in medium-toned wood. Fixtures are up-to-the-minute, with special attention paid to the bathrooms — essential in a ski hotel — and the look is slightly retro-flavored, though anything but dated.

There’s a spa that’s perhaps better equipped than one expects from a hotel of this size, as well as copious meeting and events space. A pair of restaurants serve a market-based menu of local dishes and traditional Andorran cuisine, and the Theatre of Wine is something unique indeed: a restaurant of just ten covers serving “minimalist mountain cuisine” accompanied by an astonishing array of wines.

In winter the appeal is obviously centered around the ski slopes, but the Pyrenées in summer aren’t exactly a letdown either — whatever the season, a taste for adventure will stand you in good stead here.

content:
Downtown Auckland evolved dramatically in the first decades after the Second World War, and has continued to do so: its central business district is now as modern as any world capital. With one exception. High Street, running in parallel right alongside Queen Street, the city’s main thoroughfare, fell into neglect and disrepute — and, along with it, so did the landmark Hotel DeBrett. But as so often happens in down-at-heel city-center districts, High Street is now prized for its historical character, and has become one of the city’s hippest neighborhoods — as, along with it, the renovated and reimagined Hotel DeBrett has become one of the city’s hippest hotels.

In its new incarnation it reflects High Street’s creative, eclectic character right back at it, thanks to its new owners, John Courtney and Michelle Deery, the latter of whom actually served as the hotel’s interior designer. Her signature is most visible in the wildly patterned, brightly colored carpets, but extends throughout, down to the inspiring contrast of mid-century modern furniture and Art Deco architecture.

And though it may have been named after DeBrett’s Guide to Etiquette, there’s nothing at all stuffy about the hotel’s crowd. Surrounded as it is by galleries, theaters, cafés, and unique shops, from secondhand boutiques to bespoke tailors, it’s naturally a magnet for all kinds of creative types. You’ll find travelers and locals alike in DeBretts Kitchen, which sits in the hotel’s central glass-roofed atrium, as well as in the twin bars: Housebar, the Twenties-inspired cocktail bar, and Cornerbar, something more like an upscale local pub.

content:
Rajasthan is home to some historic hotels, some luxurious hotels, and some unique, lovingly hand-crafted hotels. In The Johri, Jaipur, it’s got all three. This spectacular building once went by the name Lal Haveli, and was the private residence of an eminent family, set right in the heart of the Johri bazaar, which is famous for its jewelry. Today it’s committed to its public-facing role as a hotel rather than a house, a joint venture between restaurateur Abhishek Honawar and jeweler Siddharth Kasliwal, and sister hotel to the pair’s equally exquisite 28 Kothi.

With just five suites it retains the intimacy of a private house, and each suite is named after a gemstone and decorated in the corresponding hue. Heritage architecture and traditional crafts are mixed with a contemporary color sense and a variety of contrasting graphic patterns; the result is anything but minimalist.

There’s a restaurant, also called The Johri, that’s quite a lot bigger than a five-suite hotel needs — it’s a local fixture as well, serving inventive locally sourced Indian fare, all vegetarian. And the Pukhraj Lounge, with its murals depicting Rajasthan’s wilderness, is unforgettable; it’s the venue for afternoon tea and, by night, a cocktail lounge.

A younger generation in Brussels is casting off the chocolate-box preciousness for which the city was formerly known, in favor of a brutalist-inspired industrial-chic aesthetic — of which JAM is quite possibly the perfect example. It’s set in a disused 1970s building that was initially home to an art college, and you’d have to think the old faculty, wherever they are, would approve of the use to which their old workplace has been put.

Like many youth-oriented boutique hotels it’s got dormitory-style shared rooms, as well as large-format private rooms that sleep up to six, in case you’re traveling with a band or other entourage. It’s also got classic doubles and even singles, of course, and in all categories you’ll find a fun mix of utilitarian plywood built-ins and colorful vintage pieces, as well as necessities like flat-screen televisions and coffee makers.

The accommodations are fun and comfortable enough, but a hotel like JAM truly shines in its public spaces. Unique among Brussels boutique hotels is Atsukan, a Japanese-style bathhouse with ten private tubs. On the rooftop there’s a terrace and a plunge pool, as well as a cozy bar with an Italian dinner menu, where locals and hotel guests mix and mingle.

It took some time for the boutique-hotel revolution to reach the ski towns of North America, but it’s safe to say it’s officially arrived. The first mountain resort from Montage’s design-oriented Pendry brand is the Pendry Park City, which is at once the most stylish resort in the Park City area and the most luxurious entry in the Canyons Village resort area. Expect the classic timber-lodge paradigm to start looking uncomfortably dated any day now.

The Pendry has everything a classic lodge would have — ski-in/ski-out access, cozy wintertime comforts, an extensive spa and wellness program — and it does it while looking as modern as any city-center luxury boutique hotel. The rooms are exceedingly comfortable, but clean-lined as well, without a hint of alpine kitsch. Pillow-top mattresses and marble bathrooms with walk-in showers are much appreciated after a day on the slopes (or the trails), and the suites and residences add extras like full kitchens, fireplaces, and terraces.

Restaurants include Kita and a Japanese grill. There’s also the Pool House Bar & Grille, oriented around the swimming pool in summer and the fireside in winter, and there’s Après Pendry, a European-inspired après-ski lounge with an open fireplace and a surplus of deep sofas and armchairs.

Most of the camps from the Montana-based purveyors of tented luxury are set out west, but Tennessee’s only full-scale national park has one of its own. Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains lies just outside of Pigeon Forge, home of Dollywood, and is surrounded by a spectacularly forested mountain range that reaches clear across the North Carolina border — smaller and perhaps more subtle than some of its counterparts in the Rockies, but no less appealing a place for a bit of outdoor immersion. 

As is the case at any Under Canvas resort, you’ll camp in style: king beds, wood-burning stoves, proper en-suite bathrooms, and hotel-quality comforts and furnishings. Tents sleep two to four, and include private decks with lounge chairs and, in the Stargazer tents, a skylight for viewing the constellations overhead. The idea is to combine luxury-boutique hospitality with tent-camping adventure, and, as usual, in the hands of Under Canvas, it works.

Additional inducements include a proper restaurant, plus a fire pit for evening s’mores, as well as live music and beer, wine, and canned cocktails. Meanwhile the resort’s Experience Coordinators are on hand to help you plan your daytime activities in and around Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

Please note: Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from early April until late November.

content: Around the other side of the Gulf of Naples from Capri is the larger island of Ischia, which may not benefit from the same proximity to the Amalfi Coast, but which is nevertheless a stunning destination in its own right, with similar views back to Naples and Vesuvius. San Montano Resort & Spa’s hilltop location makes the most of this situation, with the marina at Lacco Ameno in the foreground and the panorama of the bay in the background. It’s easily reachable by boat, and even easier by helicopter; there’s also a hydrofoil for pedestrians and a ferry for cars, both departing from Naples.\n\nThe style is contemporary-classic, with rooms and suites in a wide variety of orientations, from the courtyard-facing garden rooms to the lavish sea-facing suites. With nearly a hundred rooms and suites its resort designation is well earned, but it’s not so large as to be overwhelming — just big enough to support the comprehensive services that make it a fully self-contained experience, if you want it to be. A handful of restaurants serve everything from modern Italian fine dining to wood-fired Neapolitan pizzas by the pool, and there’s a full-service spa as well as a beach club that’s reachable by shuttle.

content: We often talk as though “traditional” and “modern” are in opposition, but in Switzerland, they’re serious about upholding the values of traditional hospitality, even if some of the aesthetics have changed. Landgasthof Kreuz Kappel, for example, was established 350 years ago, and from the outside, it looks it — though well maintained, it’s a timeless example of traditional Swiss architecture. Inside, however, it’s another story: the rooms in the main house are modern and minimalist in style, while the newest rooms, built in the old barn, use more typically traditional materials and textures, though to no less contemporary effect.\n\nOf course, what matters about Landgasthof Kreuz Kappel is less the architecture and more the ends to which it’s put. A hotel like this isn’t aiming to reinvent the concept of the hotel, it’s simply applying three and a half centuries of expertise. The fruit of all that labor is somewhat intangible, but it consists in large part in getting the details just right: the comfort of the beds, the functioning of the bathrooms, the efficient layout of the bedside lamp and switches. And nowhere is that feeling of rightness more in evidence than in the restaurant — and it had better be, as the hotel’s owner is also the head chef.

From a glance at the place, you’d think there’d been some mistake — surely this lush neoclassical red-brick monument, now home to the Blackburn Inn, couldn’t have begun its life as the Western State Lunatic Asylum. Then again, Virginia isn’t like most places; nor is the town of Staunton, in the Shenandoah Valley, 40 miles to the west of Charlottesville. And while we’ve seen institutions converted into boutique hotels before, few of them began with such lavish raw material as the Blackburn Inn.

That’s not to downplay what the new proprietors have done with the place. The interiors are stylish, not overly devoted to the building’s visual heritage, an eclectic mix of farmhouse style and modernist flair, with a result that’s incredibly warm and anything but institutional. And the benefits of a new build are everywhere in evidence: the bathrooms are large and luxe, and the rooms are wired with contemporary conveniences like USB outlets.

Second Draft, the Blackburn Inn’s New American bistro and bar, serves dishes made from locally sourced ingredients. And from here, you’ve got the charming town of Staunton at your feet, as well as the fourteen breweries of the Shenandoah Beerwerks Trail and all the attractions of Charlottesville, of Western Virginia, and of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

A lot of what’s special about the Northwest happens on the coasts. But not all of it. Startlingly close to Seattle, in the foothills a half-hour east of the city, stands Snoqualmie Falls, a 270-foot clue as to how the Cascade mountain range got its name. And just above the falls — almost perilously close — is one of the Northwest’s most remarkable hotels, the Salish Lodge & Spa. (If you’ve seen Twin Peaks, you’re plenty familiar with the Lodge’s dramatic situation.)

With a backdrop like this, an understated approach to the décor is the only sensible way to go. Interiors are contemporary-rustic, elegant but far from overbearing, full of country charm but lacking any rough edges. Think fireplaces and flat-screens, spa tubs and feather beds, and a typically Northwestern approach to pet care, in which dogs are as well cared for as humans. It’s worth springing for a river view, since all rooms come with balconies, patios or at least window seats — though nobody has to walk far to see the falls.

The Salish Lodge is a natural choice for a destination wedding, and the spa makes it a natural choice for a quick weekend getaway as well. Come winter it’s close to the ski slopes at Snoqualmie Pass, and in summer it’s a fine place to bike, hike or fish. Add a bit of stylish, upscale seasonal dining and it’s hard to think of a reason why you’re not on your way already.

content:
It’s all the way the other side of Ireland from Dublin, but the boutique townhouse hotel No. 1 Pery Square could, in a pinch, serve as a setting for a film of Joyce’s “The Dead.” Originally built in 1830 and restored with great precision, the hotel gets the aesthetic just right, from the ornate marble hearth to the gilt-framed mirrors. It never verges on rococo, but if the common areas feel a bit too vintage for your tastes, fifteen of the twenty guest rooms have been made over in a more modern, clubbier style. 

The period-style rooms are hard to resist, however, with their suitably expansive sash windows overlooking the garden — it’s here that the natural grace and elegance of the style asserts itself. Even in the regional gloom, there’s a light freshness to the rooms that’s enhanced by their spaciousness. The single Townhouse Suite offers an intriguing combination of old and new, with multiple flatscreen televisions, a private bar, and top-floor views of Limerick and surrounding mountains of Clare.   

The hotel stresses its townhouse origins, with the personalized attention of a bed and breakfast that also feels like a neighborhood focal point. The restaurant, the Long Room, is at once upscale and congenial. The bar specializes in bespoke cocktails and herbal infusions, while the drawing room offers classic afternoon tea. The basement is given over to the spa, which is exactly as a boutique spa should be: soothing, candlelit, and lined with exposed brick.

Take a twenty-minute boat ride from Malaysian Borneo’s Kota Kinabalu and you’ll find Gayana Eco Resort fringing a small cape on Gaya Island’s northern coastline. With its thatch-roofed villas and sprawling decks, the Gayana is wholly faithful to the over-water genre, on equal footing with its Fijian and Maldivian counterparts. Throw in room-service-by-raft, a marine research center and a spa that offers 180-dollar caviar facials and the resort’s split personality begins to emerge: soulful-slash-super-luxe, earthy yet indulgent, remote but refined.

Of the forty-four villas on offer, there are four types, each endorsing a different perspective of this rather wild part of the world. Ocean aficionados should go for the Buya bungalows, facing — naturally — the ocean. The most spacious of the selection, these have the widest decks, with front-row access to Gaya’s teeming coral reef and its mild sea breezes — something that won’t go unappreciated this close to the equator.

The Bakau, Pantai and Rimba villas face the mangroves, lagoon and jungle respectively, each with its own merits. The Rimba villas have the most limited water access, but in exchange, guests can enjoy the 24-hour nature channel that is the Borneo wilderness — monkeys, hornbills and jungle soundtrack included.

Villas are all five-star as far as amenities go — LCD televisions, DVDs, oversized showers, bouncy beds and boutique toiletries arranged amid a calming natural palette — no bold color statements here. If it’s neon splashes and surrealist shapes you’re after, you’ll have to head underwater to take part in the resort’s coral replanting scheme, or to Gayana’s research center where a “touch-tank” lets you get within squishing distance of Malaysia’s indigenous sea life. 

Outside the resort, the opportunities for adventure abound, and might just be enough to lure you from the spa or from your bungalow’s mini-jetty. This is Borneo after all; the jungle is mere steps from the infinity pool, and it’s your obligation to go home just a little untamed.

How to get there:

Gayana Eco Resort is less than an hour by car and ferry from Kota Kinabalu airport (BKI).

Those with a keen eye for geography will have noticed that there’s more than one Gallipoli on the Mediterranean — it’s derived from the Greek for “beautiful city,” which is a recurring sentiment in these parts. This one, in Puglia, is set on a small island connected to the mainland by a walkable bridge. And within a 17th-century house in the warren-like town center is Palazzo Presta, a surprisingly colorful and contemporary boutique hotel that’s packed with personality, thanks to its talented designers and the art and objects collected by its globetrotting proprietors.

Each bedroom is different, and we mean different — not just a fresh color scheme but a whole new inspiration, from Morocco to the Americas to the Silk Road and Japan. Underlying the eclectic décor is the historical architecture of the house and its neighbors, as well as modern, if unobtrusive, boutique-hotel comforts.

What makes Palazzo Presta more than a guest house is the inclusion of a restaurant, Lazzaro & Caterina, on the ground floor; it’s joined by a rooftop bar called Laurus, as well as the Libreria del Mare, a speakeasy-style bar hidden away within a functioning library displaying volumes by local publishers.

Soho House’s expansion is notable not only for how well its urban-creative members’-club concept has traveled, but for how effortlessly the brand has developed an equally strong line of far-flung destination clubs — including Soho Roc House, a 44-room escape on the south coast of Mykonos, close enough to the beaches and nightlife to feel convenient but removed enough to offer the privacy a members’ club demands.

Tiny rooms are available for those in search of little more than a swanky crash pad, while the Big and Large+ units expand to suitably resort-like dimensions. Aesthetically, they’re pure Mykonos, though filtered through the boho-chic Soho House sensibility. And while they aren’t ostentatious about it, they’re plenty luxurious, some containing freestanding tubs, others with balconies or verandas facing the Aegean.

The gym and spa are full-featured and well-programmed, and the pool and gardens are perfect for lounging; this stretch of coastline is rocky, but swimmers have access to the Aegean all the same. Meanwhile the restaurant serves a Mediterranean version of the classic Soho House Club menu, while the Pool Bar fills in with drinks and light fare during the day.

If ever there were a destination that was fated to have a Kimpton hotel, it’s Tulum, where the prevailing style has always been one part boutique style and one part accessible, approachable warmth. Unusually, the Kimpton Aluna Tulum is set not on the beach or downtown but in between, in Aldea Zama; the result is convenient enough to both the town and the coast while offering a welcome measure of seclusion. 

The style in the rooms and suites is modern and somewhat minimal, though they’re enlivened by colorful accents and tied to their setting by design elements that pay tribute to authentic local crafts. And they’re equipped with their fair share of high-end modern details, from Frette linens to Atelier Bloem bath products. Book a specialty suite if you could use a private jacuzzi, either on the balcony or the rooftop.

There’s a partnership with a beach club, if sand and surf are what you’re after, while on site you’ll find spa services, yoga, two swimming pools, and, in addition to the pool bar, two fine modern Mexican restaurants: Parallel 20˚, which combines Yucatán flavors with those of other cultures on the same latitude, including Thailand, China, and India; and Bhanu Sky Kitchen, a similarly eclectic Mexican-Asian fusion.

Even as modern minimalist luxury resorts began spreading across Asia, the hotels in Cambodia remained more or less synonymous with French colonial architecture and design. Lately, however, a homegrown, Modernist-influenced contemporary style is emerging, one that’s perfectly exemplified by Siem Reap’s brand-new Treeline Urban Resort.

First of all, don’t fret about the “urban.” While Siem Reap is indeed a busy city, the Siem Reap River isn’t exactly Fifth Avenue, and a low-slung, compound-style hotel like Treeline can easily achieve a tranquil seclusion. (One clue as to how is in the Treeline name itself — few hotels are as verdant as this one, inside and out.)

Indigenous stone and wood are the predominant materials, and while the aesthetic may be minimal, the experience is rich and organic. The furniture is handmade, the hotel is packed with local contemporary art, and the rooms and suites are decorated with warm textures and living plants. Not to say that high technology or high luxury are neglected — rain showers and Bluetooth speakers are standard, as are wi-fi and air conditioning, and the spa and rooftop infinity pool add a healthy dose of relaxation.

Meanwhile three different restaurants showcase three different perspectives on the local flavors, from an impeccable breakfast at Seed to a rooftop bite at Canopy or a street-inspired dinner at Romiet Restaurant — as well as one of the city’s finest cafés in the form of Brown Coffee.

There’s always debate about the effects on the places that host big events like the FIFA World Cup, but there’s no question that Santo André, on Brazil’s Bahian coast, came out of the 2014 installment changed for the better. Campo Bahia was finished just in time for the German men’s national team to move in, and they trained here, relaxed here, and restored themselves here in between matches. And judging by the results — a World Cup win — one imagines that they found it entirely to their satisfaction.

Then again, who wouldn’t? The setting is spectacular, on a beautiful beach next to a charming fishing village, and the resort itself is no slouch either. Fourteen villas contain up to six bedrooms each, but can be subdivided for smaller parties — no need to bring the whole national team. They’re contemporary in style, though full of local character, and they’re outfitted with the full complement of comforts, from flatscreens and air conditioning to wi-fi, if that’s your thing.

Campo Bahia’s restaurants serve upscale contemporary Brazilian fare as well as churrasco, and a detox menu is available if you’re looking to keep it light. A L’Occitane spa is on hand to restore your body, and there is — perhaps unsurprisingly, given the athletic roots of this place — an emphasis on sports and fitness, from yoga and a beachside gym to stand-up paddling, cycling, and professional-quality tennis courts. It’d be a bit much to credit Germany’s win entirely to their stay at Campo Bahia, but it’s not hard to imagine you’ll come back a bit better prepared for life’s little challenges.

content:
What’s the big deal? Nhow Rotterdam is just another architectural marvel — designed by none other than Rem Koolhaas’s OMA, of course — whose ultra-stylish interiors offer jaw-dropping views of Rotterdam’s beautifully restored waterfront, the city skyline, and the swan-shaped Erasmus Bridge. Ho-hum.

Sorry about that — our editor has a rare medical condition that causes him to lapse into jaded hipsterism whenever he feels overwhelmed, as some kind of psychological defense mechanism. The simple fact is that the nhow, as they prefer we spell it, is overwhelming in all the best ways. This is a hotel group whose design bona fides are very much in order, and they’re clearly no slouches when it comes to architecture either. OMA is responsible for the entirety of the De Rotterdam mixed-use development, and for the hotel’s interiors as well — so if there’s a certain unity to the vision, it’s no coincidence.

Dutch modern architecture always feels like the future, and this is no exception. It’s enough to make optimists of all of us. Rooms are a marvel of attractive efficiency, which here is not a euphemism — they start out reasonably spacious and sprawl quite outrageously by the time you get to the Horizon Suite. The bar is buzzing, serving cocktails with a view (and a DJ-provided soundtrack), and the kitchen serves global cuisine in an inspired space. There’s a terrace on the seventh floor overlooking the water, and there’s even a stylish little espresso bar for those moments when your enthusiasm outpaces your energy. In lesser hands such a hotel might risk edging into pretentiousness, but there’s no pretending going on here — this is the real deal.

Its name is a reference to Atlanta’s unofficial nickname, “a city in a forest,” and the Kimpton Sylvan Hotel’s location, in a leafy corner of Buckhead, makes good on the promise. This upscale neighborhood was once strictly luxury-hotel territory; a boutique hotel like the Kimpton Sylvan is a welcome addition, and a sign that the two branches of the hospitality world are closer together than ever before.

The building is an authentic 1950s modernist residential building, one that seems tailor-made for its new role. Its interiors make much of the mid-century atmosphere established by the structure; the spaces are crisp and modernist-inspired, from the lobby with its rounded corners to the rooms with their Danish-style desks. And while there are more lavish hotels in town, the Sylvan’s rooms are much more than comfortable enough.

Among the hotel’s greatest strengths is its food and beverage program. The Betty is a New American restaurant inspired by the supper clubs of old, the Willow Bar is set in the hotel’s lush gardens, and St. Julep is an indoor-outdoor bar on the 9th-floor roof terrace featuring cocktails, craft beers, and live DJs.

In contrast with the gleaming modern skyscraper hotels that surround it, Else Kuala Lumpur makes its home in a much more interesting place: the 1930s Art Deco Lee Rubber Building, right in the heart of Chinatown, in the old city center. Inside, however, you’ll find that, despite its historical bona fides, Else is no Art Deco period piece, but rather a high-end boutique hotel in a soothingly minimalistic modern style.

It’s more urban resort than city business hotel, and its rooms and suites feel suitably warm and organic. Room categories come with names like Mantra and Sanctuary, further evidence of the focus on tranquility. And yet right outside is Kuala Lumpur’s Chinatown, filled not only with markets and food halls but with chic retailers and a community of young creative professionals.

Within the hotel, however, the urban-resort atmosphere prevails. There’s an outdoor pool surrounded by cabanas and sensory deprivation pods, as well as a “boutique gym.” And while there’s no shortage of dining and drinking options in the surrounding neighborhood, Else Kuala Lumpur comes equipped with a few of its own, including the casual-chic Raw Kitchen Hall and a high-end Malaysian restaurant called Yellow Fin Horse.

In spite of the name, a reference to its owners’ German heritage, Casa Munich is as Ibizan as they come — a perfectly idyllic Mediterranean farmhouse hotel, on a hill surrounded on three sides by a nature reserve, a few crucial minutes to the south of Ibiza town. From here the island’s legendary nightlife is accessible, but not inescapable; resort-style relaxation is the order of the day, and on this score Casa Munich proves itself quite capable indeed.

The rooms are handsome and understated, with an eclectic vibe that incorporates elements both rustic and modern, as well as influences from all around the world, from the Balearics to Bali. None are small — many come with living rooms and/or terraces — but the multi-unit apartments are particularly spacious, adding kitchenettes to the mix for an extra bit of self-sufficiency.

With just 31 rooms it’s smallish, but comes equipped with services that belie its size; there’s a spa, a gym, yoga and Pilates sessions, tennis and basketball courts, and even a football pitch, and bikes are available for exploring the salt flats of the nature reserve. There are also three pools, one of them adults-only, and a poolside bistro menu to complement Casa Munich’s substantial breakfast.

Please note: Faraway Sag Harbor is accepting reservations from June 2026 onward.

The original Sag Harbor resort (formerly known as Baron’s Cove) has decades of history under its belt; as early as the middle of the 20th century it was a glamorous if low-key escape for the likes of Paul Newman and Jackson Pollock. Over the years it’s grown steadily more upscale, and in between the 2025 and 2026 seasons it saw a significant renovation and rebranding at the hands of the bohemian-luxe Faraway Hotels brand, which leaves Faraway Sag Harbor a little bit more polished without sacrificing the richness of its decades-spanning character.

Its 67 rooms and suites vary in their settings and layouts; some, like the Lofts, feel quasi-urban, while others sit tucked into quiet gardens. They’re full of visual interest without ever lapsing into seaside kitsch, and the comforts are first-class and up-to-date. And there’s much more to it than just accommodations; this compound-style estate has its own heated saltwater pool as well as a tennis court, and a fleet of bikes for loan helps guests navigate the town and the waterfront in style. One last upgrade is Zagara, the restaurant, which features the flavors of the Amalfi Coast.

content: It would be hard to imagine a more distinguished setting for a hotel in Chihuahua than this, right in the heart of the historic city center, next to the Plaza de Armas and the 18th-century cathedral. And the Central Hotel Boutique makes its home in a distinguished building as well: Casa Trías dates back to 1845, and is the city’s oldest estate-style courtyard house. And today, after more than two decades under its present ownership, it’s attained some distinction as a hotel: this is by a considerable distance the most stylish and most luxurious lodging in town.\n\nEach of the Central’s eleven rooms is named for a different poet, and integrates modern furniture, contemporary decoration, antique architectural details, and prosaic (though welcome) comforts like Nespresso machines and Bose sound systems. El Poeta, the restaurant, pursues the theme even further, its well-worn, atmospheric space providing a backdrop for a sophisticated and creative take on the classic flavors of Chihuahua and the Sierra Tarahumara. And a less elevated version of the same cuisine is in plentiful supply all around you — from here, thanks to the central location, all of the old city’s sights are more or less right at your feet.

content:
Most every high-end hotel in Oia — maybe in all of Santorini — faces toward the volcanic caldera at the center of the island’s crescent arc. But Canaves Epitome means to set itself apart from the crowd, and it does so both literally and figuratively. Literally, with a position about a mile from the center of town, on the western extremity of the island’s north arm; this naturally leads to what sets it figuratively apart, which is its westward view of the island of Thirasia and the open sea beyond.

To put it simply: it works. Once you’re within the hotel’s walls, you’ll feel like you’ve left Santorini for your own private island. The color palette differs from the usual white, adding depth with gray, black, and rough stone exterior walls. And the villas and suites are all remarkably luxurious, starting out at 45 square meters and only growing from there — and including, at the very least, a plunge pool on the terrace.

There’s a pint-sized spa, as well as the option of en-suite treatments, and the main pool, an infinity-edged stunner with a view straight out to sea, is accompanied by the Elements Restaurant, serving a range of sophisticated European fare with an emphasis on the finest Greek produce and ingredients.

content:
Imagine an idyllic Brazilian getaway. Chances are you’re picturing the glamorous nightlife and dramatic landscape of Rio de Janeiro, or the white sandy beaches of the northeast, the resorts of Buzios or Florianópolis — but not São Paulo. Here’s a word to the wise: like New York, São Paulo isn’t only the name of a city, but of an entire state. And it’s a state full of lesser-known vacation havens, particularly along the lush north coastline. It’s here — between the ocean and on the Atlantic rainforest, on the scenic route, one might say, between Brazil’s two largest cities — that hotels like the Nau Royal Hotel Boutique & Spa draw stylish beachgoers looking for a little R&R within easy reach of the continent’s largest metropolis.

With a natural landscape this lovely, the trick is simply to feature it, to enhance it, to make it even more enjoyable — a feat the Nau Royal pulls off with panache. It’s a modern getaway, smartly designed and eco-friendly, which feels particularly appropriate in a tropical climate suited to indoor-outdoor living. Who wants to sit inside an air-conditioned room, after all, when you could be drinking caipirinhas by candlelight on a natural wood deck?

There are only 13 rooms, making the Nau Royal a proper boutique. The Garden room is simple, all white and wood with a hammock swinging on the private balcony facing gardens by landscape designer Marcelo Bellotto — and yes, there’s air conditioning and a flat-screen TV, should you desire it. 

Twice its size is the Al Mare suite, with an oceanfront balcony and a separate living room. And twice the size of that is the top-of-the-line Royal Trussardi, the penthouse suite, a breezy all-white retreat with a super king-sized bed and a bathroom with both a Japanese-style bathtub and a pair of showers.

Keep up with the Joneses and pop by the Royal Spa by L’Occitane before dinner, served, of course, in a spectacular oceanfront setting at the hotel’s Azul Marinho restaurant. Chef Marleide Ribeiro excels at preparing the region’s speciality, freshly caught crab, making the restaurant a popular destination for foodies weekending in the area.

Close to the central business district, in the upscale and fashinable Surry Hills, the Ace Hotel Sydney may be the first for the brand in the Southern Hemisphere, but it’s as confidently executed as any of their hotels. Set in an early 19th-century industrial building, it’s got patina for days; it’s pure Ace, but also pure Australia, thanks to the thoughtful work of its designers — you never forget for a second where you are or who you’re staying with.

The rooms are cut from the same cloth as the Aces in North America, with vintage-inspired wool blankets, subtle retro styling, and a vibe that’s low-frills but plenty warm. A few come with turntables or acoustic guitars, and occasional details like unfinished brick walls add a touch of extra visual depth.

As cozy and stylish as its accommodations may be, the Ace hotels are best known for their public spaces. This one features a versatile lobby restaurant and bar, a place that’s as well suited to daytime co-working as it is to a night out. There’s also Loam, sister to the restaurant in the Ace Downtown Los Angeles, as well as Kiln, the glass-walled rooftop restaurant, and Good Chemistry, a café and bar in a ground-floor space adjacent to the entry.

content: Set ten minutes’ walk from the Royal Palace and a few more from the riverfront, the Pavilion can boast of a rather privileged location — fitting, given its history as a royal residence. It’s built from a compound of four villas, one of which belonged to Queen Kossamak, King Sihanouk’s mother. After a careful restoration, these villas now house a total of 36 rooms and suites in a style that’s more or less equal parts contemporary and classic: the buildings are protected, which influences the floor plans, but the décor is light, clean, and boutique-inspired.\n\nIt’s also more than a little bit luxurious, featuring a pair of swimming pools: the Lush Pool, shaded throughout the day by tall trees, and the Sun Pool, whose defining attribute should be self-explanatory. A pair of poolside lounges serve breakfast followed by drinks and a light menu of Khmer and international dishes. Meanwhile a small spa offers massages and other treatments, and the hotel makes bicycles available for those who wish to explore on two wheels. Given its intensely urban location, it’s a marvel of privacy and tranquility, and when it comes to convenience it’d be hard to surpass.

content:
Some Mykonos hotels are so centrally located that, for better or worse, the party comes to you. Others are outposts on distant, tranquil stretches of coast where there’s little more than sea and sand. The all-suite De.light Boutique Hotel falls somewhere in between, close enough to the center of town that you can pop in for some shopping and dining, but far enough out that you won’t forget  you’re on an arcadian island. To put it another way, you can still go to the party, but you won’t feel like you’ve been stuck in the position of weary host.

The hotel is set above Agios Ioannis, a bay sheltered by the westernmost promontory of Mykonos, with just the sort of views such a location might suggest: plenty of polychrome blue, rocky cliffs rising from the water, hills dotted with whitewashed buildings, occasional sailboats, islands in the distance, and not much else. 

The style of the hotel befits the setting; it’s classic Mykonos white and blue, with an emphasis on the white. Rooms are awash in natural light, and the sunniness is amplified by shining white tile floors, occasional pops of color in the décor, and a fastidious lack of clutter. Each suite has a separate sitting area or living room and a private verandah or balcony. Starting with the Superior suites, those outdoor spaces come with sea views, a significant amenity given the setting. 

Tempting as it may be to do all your cocktail-sipping from the privacy of your terrace, the poolside loungers may be harder to resist. The pool here is a beauty, and with a bar and restaurant at its side, it forms the heart of the hotel. And what better than a gorgeous blue pool overlooking the Aegean to build a classic Mykonos hotel around? 

Please note: De.light Boutique Hotel is open seasonally, May through October.

content:
Das Kranzbach may be located an hour from Munich in the shadow of some of the most imposing peaks of the Bavarian Alps, but it’s not about rowdy tourists shedding their cold-weather gear in the hallways. This is a four-season wellness retreat, and while you can certainly take advantage of the region’s ample winter sports opportunities, the spa at Das Kranzbach offers much more than the average après-ski soak. 

The original manor house was built by a young British aristocrat, who commissioned a decidedly English country retreat; to this day, it’s one of Bavaria’s most distinctive architectural anomalies. The later addition of a sixty-room annex means guests have a choice of two very different experiences. Guest rooms in the main house feature chic mod-inspired furniture and some fairly bold choices in décor — clusters of hanging spherical lamps and color juxtapositions that, in theory, should clash, but somehow don’t. The newer rooms, with a crisp wood-and-glass motif, are a bit more conservative without being any less contemporary; modern Bavarian isn’t so very different in sensibility from modern Scandinavian.

The food is never-ending, with a gourmet breakfast, lunch buffet, tea and cakes at mid-afternoon, and a five-course dinner menu. Of course, the spa is the crown jewel of the hotel, and it’s extensive: five pools, a half-dozen saunas and steam baths, and special treatments for expecting parents. Wellness is a concept that’s taken perhaps more seriously here, and it seems virtually impossible that one should manage to leave Das Kranzbach without feeling the difference.

In the scheme of things New Zealand’s luxury lodges are probably more similar than different — or at least, the difference between the luxury-lodge experience and just about any other kind of hospitality is so vast as to overshadow the individual personalities of the lodges. But if you look closely, there’s plenty of character there, with New Zealand’s endless variety of landscape producing lodges, like the Solitaire Lodge, that are utterly unique.

To get hung up on the décor and the furnishings would be (forgive us) to miss the forest for the chairs. What’s special about Solitaire is most certainly its location, close to the popular North Island resort town of Rotorua, but with a lake all its own: Lake Tarawera, which Solitaire overlooks from a hillside atop a peninsula, surrounded by the lake’s calm waters, with a view of the Tarawera volcano in the distance.

Like just about any New Zealand luxury lodge, Solitaire is an outdoor paradise, with a particular emphasis on the lake — and pretty much anything you can’t find at Tarawera you can find at Rotorua, less than a half hour away. As for the suites themselves, they’re modestly, sedately decorated, but thoroughly luxurious, with incredible views from indulgent, freestanding baths. And the cuisine is of special note in this part of the world, with local seafood and produce as well as herbs from the lodge’s own garden, and both breakfast and dinner included in the rate.

On the banks of the Perfume River, in the old imperial city of Hue, is a restored classic, an Art Deco–style boutique hotel: La Résidence. This was once the Governor’s mansion, a piece of colonial history, looking straight across the river at the imperial citadel. And today its colonial-chic luxury is open to the paying public — you don’t have to be the Governor to soak in its historical atmosphere.

In style it’s equal parts Twenties and Fifties, two decades whose distinctive looks have aged well: with ceiling fans silently spinning, French doors opening onto balconies, and the odd four-poster bed, it’s a colonial fantasy brought up to date. The atmosphere is deeply unhurried, and the service comes courtesy of a first-class multi-lingual staff, recalling, again, the French colonial days.

All in all it’s a bit of a resort feeling, despite the city location. Hue is about history and culture, not big-city nightlife: spa treatments, dips in the salt-water pool, and drinks in the Le Gouverneur bar or on the terrace of the Le Parfum restaurant — these sorts of things are more La Résidence’s speed, and guests who are in for a bit of posh relaxation will find themselves amply rewarded.

content:
Just about any place on earth could be described with some variation on “land of contrasts.” But it’s actually a pretty fair description of Spain, in at least one important way. It’s hard to think of another country that has held on to so much of what’s traditional, while at the same time fervently and unapologetically embracing what’s modern. It’s a tendency on display in Spanish cooking, where you can find innovative molecular gastronomy and a traditional workman’s paella lunch within yards of each other. And it’s on display in hotels like Eurostars Pamplona, where an unapologetic modernist hotel stands on the fringes of the historical city of Pamplona.

If these interiors contain any nod at all to the rural Navarre countryside it’s in the materials, the hardwood floors and the rich grains of the furnishings. But texture aside the rooms and suites are as clean-lined and contemporary as can be. And this isn’t the sort of boutique where the good looks crowd out the creature comforts. King beds are standard throughout, and the technology is state-of-the-art.

The hotel’s estaurant, La Biblioteca, serves some of that “land of contrasts” cuisine we were talking about, and the lounges take lounging a bit more literally than most: rather than bustling bars they’re sedate spaces with views of Pamplona’s countryside. Guests wind down further by the pool, and the prospect of a spa treatment may leave some of us feeling almost dangerously tranquil.

For the Pendry brand an Orange County hotel is something of a homecoming, as its parent company, Montage, was born in nearby Irvine, California. The Pendry Newport Beach fits in between its Los Angeles and San Diego siblings, in a tower that stands over the Fashion Island shopping center. Once you’re inside, though, it’s hard not to feel transported to somewhere rather more far-flung, thanks to the Pendry’s talent for cultivating a resort-like atmosphere.

More than a few of the rooms and suites look out over the harbor, the bay, and the Pacific Ocean beyond; all are decorated in a style that’s equal parts Deco-inspired elegance and laid-back California cool. The rooms are generously sized, but nearly half of the units are suites, and the largest ones spread out to surprising dimensions, adding features like dining rooms and kitchenettes.

The Spa Pendry is a substantial one, as is the associated fitness center — no one has ever accused Southern California of paying insufficient attention to bodily health. Nor are dining and drinking neglected here. SET is a modern take on the classic steakhouse, Bar Pendry pursues excellence in craft cocktails, Tree Shack serves healthy Baja-inspired fare, and the Elwood Club, a private members’ club within the hotel, makes its Viamara restaurant and its Elwood Club Pub available to hotel guests when capacity permits.

content:
When the Lancaster opened its doors the phrase “luxury boutique hotel” hadn’t yet been invented — but that’s more or less what it’s always been. Back in the Emile Wolf days it was the sort of place you’d catch the likes of Grace Kelly or Noël Coward haunting its halls. Today, a century on, it’s once again family-owned, and is once again among the purest exemplars of Parisian luxury hospitality, at a scale that’s more intimate and more residential in atmosphere than the city’s grand old palaces.

Thanks to a renovation by Studio Jean Philippe Nuel the Lancaster looks as fresh as ever, while retaining the antique elements that give it its character, including furniture chosen by its original owners in the 1920s. In spite of a location just off the Champs-Elysées, the Lancaster is quiet, the way a private mansion ought to be; its comforts, meanwhile, are first-rate, from the marble bathrooms to the modern electronics.

The service is impeccable, erring more on the side of quiet discretion than overt solicitousness. Monsieur Lancaster, the restaurant, is joined by CopperBay Lancaster, an outpost of one of the city’s finest cocktail bars. The 8th-floor spa, meanwhile, takes in views of the Eiffel Tower and Sacré-Cœur. Most magical, however, is the Lancaster’s little garden, a rare bit of private outdoor peace in the heart of bustling Paris.

It’s a simple fact that the Garden State could do with a few more French-style country estates. East Brunswick, a half-hour from Princeton and a little over an hour from lower Manhattan, is home to the Château Grande Hotel, which is exactly that: a spectacular re-creation of Belle Époque luxury, set on fifteen acres of parkland that’s lush enough to remind you that New Jersey’s nickname was never meant to be ironic.

You might not be surprised to learn that, as photogenic as it is, the Château does brisk business as a wedding venue; fortunately, you don’t have to be rolling 200 deep to book a room for the night. Unlike some historic castle hotels, there’s nothing smaller than a 300-square-foot king room here. The suites, as befits a wedding venue, are vast, and nothing short of extravagant, featuring full kitchens, dining rooms, and, in two of them, spacious verandas.

The restaurant, Orchard Park, is overseen by the James Beard award–winning chef David Burke, whose crowd-pleasing menu is made for celebrations. The wine cellar contains some 1,500 bottles, and there’s also C’est La Vie, the hotel’s cocktail bar, as well as Le Petit Café, the hotel’s espresso bar and bakery.

Please note: Chateau Grande’s pool is closed for construction.

content:
The most successful boutique hotels make the most of the raw material they’re given — in the case of the Amelia Hotel, in the small upstate city of Hudson, that’s a 19th-century Queen Anne–style house on a quiet residential street a short walk from Warren Street, the town’s main drag. It’s undergone a thorough but very sensitive renovation, and has been updated with modern furniture and quietly chic design pieces, as well as pieces by some big names in modern and contemporary art. The result is an experience that’s luxurious but unpretentiously so — details like Matouk linens, Frette towels, and Nespresso machines are welcome comforts but far from ostentatious.

Breakfast is a relatively simple affair, featuring housemade granola and pastries; a restaurant is beyond the Amelia’s aspirations, but the town center is amply blessed in that department. There is, however, a lovely 35-foot swimming pool, fringed with greenery and blooming flowers, as well as an outdoor fire pit and a deck for al fresco socializing and small events. It’s a fine introduction to the virtues of the Hudson Valley, and seems likely to become a favorite among guests who are charmed by the town and the region.

Smaller hotels like The Amelia Hudson fill up quickly. If you can’t find what you’re looking for, contact us and we can help.

content:
China’s hospitality scene is a dramatic blend of the historical and the ultra-modern — sometimes within the same hotel. A memorable example is the Yangshuo Sugar House Hotel, where the Beijing-based Vector Architects have transformed a disused sugar mill — which just happens to be set in an extraordinarily dramatic riverside landscape — into an inspired piece of contemporary post-industrial architecture and expanding it into a fantastically inventive luxury resort.

Concrete never felt as light as it does in these perforated, screen-like structures, which contrast with the weathered brickwork of the original industrial buildings, while all around, the craggy limestone peaks rise at impossible angles. Meanwhile, inside the accommodations, the look is considerably more soothing, to match the high-end comforts — no mere rooms, these are retreats, lofts, suites, townhouses, and villas, beginning at 55 square meters and quickly spreading into the triple digits.

And while any of the units is a self-contained retreat unto itself, Yangshuo Sugar House’s common offerings are no less essential. The Sugar House restaurant, the 1969 Bar, and the Water Pump private dining room are all beautifully restored spaces where guests mingle over inventive contemporary Chinese fare and upscale cocktails and wines. The hotel’s spa is not just lavish but architecturally memorable as well, made from the sugar factory’s old molasses storage tank. And when it comes to leisure activities, Yangshuo Sugar House goes above and beyond, from cultural experiences to yoga and tai chi and even rock climbing on the surrounding limestone cliffs.

From the name you’d be forgiven for expecting rather more gilt than there actually is. (If this were the Hamptons, and not Newport, Rhode Island, it might be a different story.) But the Massachusetts-based Lark Hotels are known for their playful, unpretentious style. Here the references to the Gilded Age are given some ironic distance, and the trompe l’oeil textures and decadent materials, references to the Baroque and Rococo styles of the day, leave plenty of room for designer Rachel Reider’s colorful signature style.

It’s made from a pair of Victorian houses, and it’s located not on the main drag but in a residential neighborhood a short but meaningful distance away — you’re within a reasonable walk of a fair bit of action, but from within Gilded’s walls, the atmosphere is perfectly tranquil. It helps that there are only 17 rooms — while they’re a touch on the cozy side, owing to the Victorian dimensions of the houses, they’re more than comfortable enough, with high-end linens and Lather bath products. 

And they include iPads loaded with information about Newport, which is a lifesaver come lunch and dinner — after breakfast, an inventive small-plates affair, you’re at the mercy of the city’s restaurants, with Gilded as your obliging guide.
