content:
A gracious welcome and a leisurely pace, balmy temperatures and mountain vistas: it’s a typical Georgian getaway. No, not that Georgia. The other Georgia, as in the small country located at the crossroads of Asia and Europe. Considering its position, it’s no surprise that the country has a long and fascinating history, nor that its capital city, Tbilisi, is called the “Paris of Eurasia.” Well, there are a lot of Parises around lately, but you’ll see the sense of it when you’re sitting at a sidewalk café in Old Town. Tbilisi has worked hard to restore its original charm after the grim Soviet and post-Soviet era; a handful of stylish new hotels have been opening their doors lately to accommodate a new influx of visitors. Rooms Hotel Tbilisi is perhaps the most promising among them. 

Indeed, the sleek eight-story hotel, located inside an old publishing house, embodies many of the qualities that make Tbilisi so appealing — elegant architecture, rich traditions in literature and the fine arts, a bohemian spirit, an emphasis on social life. Georgians, for example, are renowned for their lavish feasts and philosophical toasts. Rooms Hotel Tbilisi’s take: ample lounge space on leather sofas in the cozy fireplace lounge, and the Kitchen, an excellent but unpretentious restaurant that uses sustainably grown food, welcomes plenty of locals.

The design takes its lead from the building’s original function, but the Rooms Hotel Tbilisi is hardly industrial chic: faded Persian rugs and colorful vintage pieces add a lived-in feel that makes you want to hang around for another drink. After you’ve had your fill of traditional Georgian wines at the Bar Room, retire to your guest room, where wide wood-planked floors, velvet throws, handmade wallpaper, old-fashioned writing desks, leather headboards, and glowing chandeliers warm up minimal spaces once characterized by cold steel, iron and glass. No details were spared in the name of creating a warm and sophisticated getaway: you’ll have to discover many of them for yourself. It would be tempting to linger at the hotel, but the museums, fortresses, cobblestoned lanes and outdoor cafés of Tbilisi await outside. Go for a stroll though Old Town and it’s practically guaranteed you’ll have Georgia on your mind — the other Georgia — for a while to come.

content:
It’s not for everyone, but if you value atmosphere and history above all else, the Galle Face Hotel is your place in Colombo. This Colonial-era hotel has been at the heart of the city’s social and cultural life for the better part of two centuries, hosting too many earls and presidents and princes even to begin to list. It’s the kind of hotel that gets name-dropped in a breezy tropical song or two, that shows up on the country’s postage stamps, and that employs the world’s (supposedly) oldest living doorman. (In case you want to say hello, that would be Kottarapattu Chattu “K.C.” Kuttan, at your service since 1942.) Like the Copacabana in Rio or the Mandarin Oriental in Bangkok, this is one of those hotels where, at least if you run in certain circles, there’s an almost uncannily high chance that you’ll bump into someone you know. 

So its credentials as a classic are in place, but after all the history, how has the enthusiasm of its guests not dimmed a bit? For one, the location can’t be beat. It’s right in the heart of the business district, which in Colombo also puts it in the middle of the city’s cultural life — yet its position at the edge of the Indian Ocean gives it something of a resort atmosphere, as well. You can step out the door and be at your meeting in minutes (in the unlikely event your meeting is somewhere other than the hotel), but you can also kick back on a lounger on the terrace, staring out at the ocean, and feel like the city is miles away. A serene modern spa only heightens the seaside-resort effect, as do the seemingly endless dining and drinking venues populated by a clubby mix of visitors and well-heeled locals. 

The rooms are pretty much exactly what you’d expect at a 19th-century British-Colonial hotel. Dark wood features prominently (they must go through buckets of varnish), and an upgrade goes a very long way. The entry-level rooms, frankly, are a bit spartan, but by the time you get to the better suites you’re looking at vast oceanside terraces and plenty of well-appointed indoor space as well. One room even has a four-poster bathtub, with intricately carved woodwork and more than enough tub-side shelf space for a dewy bucket of champagne — something vintage, one expects. 

How to get there: Galle Face Hotel is located 22 miles (about a 30-minute drive) from Colombo’s Bandaranaike International Airport (CMB).

After decades at the very forefront of luxury hospitality, the Aman brand has begun to step out of its comfort zone. First from strictly rural modern-luxe resort enclaves to similarly exquisite urban luxury hotels; lately, with some sensitive yet thorough renovations of historical properties. Aman Rosa Alpina, for example, is an update of a 1930s mountain lodge that was already one of the Dolomites’ best-loved independent hotels. And after a transitional period as an Aman partner hotel, it’s been redesigned and refurbished, and enters the pantheon as a fully fledged Aman resort.

Architect Jean-Michel Gathy is responsible for the fruitful marriage of Alpine lodge styling and tasteful, modernist-inspired Aman-style luxury; the exterior retains a respectful chalet character, while the interiors are transformed. Natural materials like wood and stone keep the rooms and suites connected to the landscape, and the simplicity of the styling keeps them equally connected to Aman’s signature aesthetic.

San Cassiano is a highly desirable destination during ski season, and Aman Rosa Alpina makes for an extraordinary ski holiday. But this corner of the Dolomites is equally spectacular during spring, summer, and fall, offering no end of opportunity for outdoor recreation — if it can be done in the mountains, Aman Rosa Alpina can arrange it. Meanwhile the confluence of Italian cooking and Aman excellence makes for memorable dining, and the Aman Spa applies the brand’s high standards to hands-on relaxation.

content: Long before it was a nightlife destination, much less a hotel hotbed, Williamsburg was Brooklyn’s creative capital — and it’s this aspect of the neighborhood that the Sydell Group aims to honor with Penny Williamsburg, an 118-room boutique hotel at the east end of North 8th Street, just yards from legendary hipster nightspot Union Pool. The concept is the classic North Brooklyn apartment, but done properly: rooms include kitchenettes, hardwood floors, and a carefully curated selection of artworks and art books. And the art is hardly limited to just the accommodations — there’s an in-house art gallery as well.\n\nIn fact, Penny Williamsburg comes with artists, too — a subset of its residents are fine arts graduate students from Bard College. For their benefit (and yours) there’s a touch of the Hudson Valley here in the form of a surplus of greenery, from a garden terrace to the in-room plants. And while the food and beverage offerings are a work in progress, the rooftop terrace is soon to be home to a restaurant and bar, complete with a DJ booth and a stage for live performances. Short of subletting an artist’s loft, it’s as close as you can get to the classic Williamsburg residential experience.

content: Arguably the hippest neighborhood in Denver, RiNo, for River North, is the ever-evolving arts and culture district just to the north of downtown. First came the artists’ lofts and galleries, then the shops and restaurants, and now, finally, boutique hotels like the Catbird. This is as modern as they come in the Mile High City, a hotel that, strange as it sounds, is perhaps most reminiscent of Dutch boutique hospitality, thanks to a pervasive modernist influence and an approach that craftily packs a surplus of useful comforts into studio- and loft-sized spaces.\n\nIt’s geared as much towards long stays as to typical two-night tourist trips, and offers services that feel almost residential: a low-key rooftop terrace bar and lounge, a fitness center with Peloton bikes, and the all-day Catbird Kitchen + Marketplace, which functions as a café, breakfast room, bar, restaurant, and co-working space all rolled into one. And next door is a hidden gem in a rather different style — the circa-1890 Klee House is a four-bedroom residence in weathered red brick whose interiors have been given a stylish postmodern makeover, and which is suited for up to eight guests, complete with a private kitchen.

content:
Bhutan is one of the world’s most unique destinations, and the Six Senses Bhutan is not just a single luxury hotel, but five of them, each one in a different location, with a different landscape and a different aesthetic: Bumthang in the forest, Gangtey for a bird’s-eye-view, Punakha for a pastoral, agricultural atmosphere, Thimphu for hilltop views of the capital, and Paro for an impressive re-creation of the ancient stonework of the nearby monasteries.

What they all have in common is what all of the Six Senses hotels around the world have in common: interiors that are contemporary yet clearly influenced by local traditions; comforts that are first-rate but substantial rather than ostentatious; experiences that make the most of the local landscapes and cultures. Accommodations range from expansive suites within each lodge building to freestanding one, two, and three-bedroom villas — privacy, it’s safe to say, is in plentiful supply.

Each of the five lodges also comes with its own typically elaborate Six Senses spa, whose offerings are similarly tailored to the local culture. And you don’t come all the way to the Himalayas to stay in all day, tempting though it may be; each lodge has access to a different set of outdoor activities and cultural experiences.

Important Information about traveling to Bhutan: The Kingdom of Bhutan requires every foreign national (except Indian nationals) to pay a Daily Government Royalty of $65 USD per person, per day and an FIT (“Free Independent Traveler”) surcharge of $40 per day for single travelers and $30 USD per person, per day otherwise. Additionally, foreign nationals (except Indian nationals) are required to pay a non-refundable visa fee of $40 USD per application (one name per application), and a $10 USD Tourism Development Fund fee. It takes 2–3 weeks to complete the visa formalities.

As you well know, we’re all for innovation around here, but there are some classic forms of hospitality that don’t need reinventing. Among them is the French château experience; it’s hard to imagine the Château de Sully would be improved by replacing its furniture with modern pieces, or by giving its rooms a minimalist contemporary makeover.

The setting, in the Norman countryside between Bayeux and the D-Day landing beaches, is bucolic, the 18th-century château surrounded by immaculately maintained parkland. Its rooms and suites are decorated in a style that’s true to the era, though contemporary comforts like satellite TV and in-room Nespresso machines have not gone overlooked.

There’s a heated adults-only indoor pool attached to the spa complex, which incorporates jacuzzis and a sauna as well as massage and beauty treatments. Of particular note is the Château de Sully’s restaurant, where chef Nicolas Fages has earned a Michelin star for his artful and inventive seasonal cooking; sommelier and maitre d’hôtel Grégory Colleville contributes a list of over 300 wines. And for daytime diversions, bikes are available for hire, and a nearby golf course and equestrian facility are at your disposal.

content:
It’s not the only seventeenth-century Baroque palace in town — in Valletta, Malta, Baroque architecture is a seemingly inexhaustible resource. But the Palais Le Brun is unique all the same. It’s the execution perhaps more than the concept that makes it such a remarkable hotel: once the residence of the leader of the Knights of Malta, it’s now a 39-room boutique hotel that sacrifices little in terms of either comfort or atmosphere in the course of its transformation into a modern lodging.

The palace’s classic architecture is still intact, though the interiors have been restored to the point of looking absolutely new — the marble floors in the bedrooms look as though they could have been laid yesterday — and they come with the modern necessities, like bedside USB outlets and espresso machines. The stone-and-tile bathrooms are the clearest exemplar of the approach: classic in aspect, but with the welcome addition of walk-in rain showers.

Patakka, the hotel’s restaurant, is open all day, shading from a hearty breakfast to upscale Mediterranean fare by dinner, all served in an elegant cellar space. And from within Palais Le Brun you’re at the heart of old Valletta, close not only to many historic sites but to a surprising number of bars, cafés, bakeries, and restaurants.

content:
While Thailand in general and Bangkok in particular are world-renowned travel destinations, the capital city’s hotel scene has largely been dominated by big luxury hotels — some global brands, some homegrown. Volve Hotel Bangkok, then, is an outlier: a boutique hotel of just 28 rooms, where the scale is small, the welcome is personal, and the design is thoughtful, mixing contemporary-luxe elements with unique commissioned artworks and a touch of the whimsy that’s essential for making a hotel look stylish but not too precious.

The name is short for “evolve,” so they’re conscious about changing Bangkok’s boutique-hotel game. The design is inspired by the mid-century architecture and design of the neighborhood, Thong Lor, and the hotel is furnished with period furniture, as well as modern pieces — some made from salvaged elements, like the lobby’s table, built from parts of a staircase from the house that once stood on this spot.

Also refreshingly down-to-earth is the hotel’s café and restaurant, the former serving coffee grown and roasted in Thailand and the latter specializing in a cuisine that’s hyper-local and hyper-specific — a selection of classic Western dishes, as interpreted by Chinese restaurateurs in 20th-century Bangkok. Safe to say it’s not what you probably expect — but nor is it something you’ll soon forget.

content:
Mumbai may surprise you — it's a forward-looking, cosmopolitan, international city, modern where New Delhi is historical; and its hotels reflect this fact. This is, after all, Bollywood, home to India's film and entertainment industries (as well as its financial center), legendary for its nightlife, and known around India as the “Manhattan of the East.”

The Oberoi is one of a very short list of candidates for the top hotel in town; it has played host to many visiting celebrities and heads of state, and of course innumerable stars of the Indian silver screen. There are any number of reasons for its success, but forced to pick one, we would put money on the service — genuflecting butlers and quick, efficient bellmen scramble after your every need, giving every guest some variation on the royal treatment. This is a level of service that may seem excessive, but when one considers the level of sensory overload one is likely to encounter just outside, the appeal of the Oberoi is clear. 

To call Mumbai a crowded, busy city would be to comically understate the point. Reasons for visiting are nearly infinite, from business to shopping to sightseeing and beyond — but no matter what awaits out on the bustling streets, it is comforting to know what kind of quiet, elegant hospitality awaits within the hotel.

content:
The IHG-owned Hotel Indigo brand is a global concern, but it’s probably fair to say that its finest and most fully realized hotels are close to home, in the UK. Hotel Indigo Bath is a fine demonstration of how it’s done: take a type of building that’s characteristic of its setting, in this case a row of honey-colored Georgian townhouses dating to 1740, and transform it into something that’s roughly one part modern luxury-hotel sheen and one part authentic local color.

In the interiors and in the branding and design they’ve gone to great lengths to pay tribute to their Georgian inheritance, often in a stylized way that goes beyond strict period correctness. But at the same time, the rooms and suites display unmistakably anachronistic elements as well, from their focused color palettes and era-spanning decoration to their occasional Modernist-inspired flourishes. They’re equipped with lavish Hypnos beds and Nespresso machines, among other modern conveniences; the subterranean suites display rough-hewn stone walls.

And it’s only with the addition of a restaurant that is rather more than an ordinary hotel kitchen that the package is complete. The Elder is the contemporary British restaurant par excellence, serving “field to fork” cuisine with an emphasis on whole-animal butchery, all in a colorful and intimate setting.

A fresh perspective on the Balearic luxury boutique hotel comes courtesy of the Kimpton Aysla Mallorca, and any question about this California-born chain’s ability to assimilate to life on the European continent are laid immediately to rest. This 79-room hotel, designed by the Palma-based architect Guillermo Reynés, feels as local as can be, not only in its architecture and design but in its atmosphere as well, which is as laid-back and bohemian as can be but without sacrificing any of its stylishness. 

The rooms are spacious, bright, and colorful, and come equipped with all the modern necessities, including wireless sound systems, Chromecast-enabled televisions, and in-room espresso machines, as well as Kimpton signatures like yoga mats made from recycled cork. And the suites add not just extra space but in some cases extravagances like private gardens or outdoor jacuzzis.

Meanwhile, the facilities in common include an outdoor swimming pool and a spa by Codage Paris, also responsible for the in-room bath products. And the Kimpton Aysla’s cuisine is eclectic as well — the fine-dining SABA combines Mediterranean and pan-Asian influences, while Zayt Pool Kitchen & Garden Deli is the more casual Mallorcan option.

They call it the Central Business District, but unlike its counterparts in most other places, it’s one of the city’s liveliest neighborhoods — the business of New Orleans, after all, depends to a great extent on entertainment. It’s the perfect location for a hotel like the Kimpton Hotel Fontenot, a truly stunning reinvention of what was previously a relatively undistinguished chain hotel. The result is among the Kimpton group’s most attractive establishments, and the aesthetic and experience are carefully tailored to New Orleans.

Its rooms, for example, display just the right measure of French influence, alongside the understated modernist-inspired design that is a Kimpton signature. And luxurious little details like the custom-made mattresses and the Atelier Bloem bath products elevate the Fontenot beyond the ordinary boutique-hotel experience.

As do the public spaces. This is a famously hedonistic town, and a hotel won’t get far without a decent restaurant and bar. Thankfully the Peacock Room is up to the task, an eccentric, French-accented fantasy with a 19th-century bar, while the café, Gospel Coffee and Boozy Treats, puts a New Orleans spin on a corner coffee shop, with the option to spike anything on the menu with a shot of your favorite spirit.

The Algarve city of Faro is no stranger to tourism, but at the time of 3HB Faro’s opening, this kind of urban luxury resort was without local precedent. The location is central, right in the pedestrianized heart of this compact city. And while the phrase “urban resort” is often meant loosely, it’s entirely apt here — witness the rooftop pool, lined with loungers, that looks out not over a beach but over the rooftops of Faro’s city center.

In its scale, too, 3HB Faro feels something like a resort. Its rooms and suites number just over a hundred, and come equipped with substantial comforts — some of them feature hydromassage tubs or jacuzzis on private terraces. Meanwhile a focused color palette and an uncluttered approach to decoration results in a handsome and photogenic look.

The spa and wellness center is an extensive one, featuring an indoor pool and a sauna and Turkish bath alongside its gym and treatment rooms. Forno Nero, an Italian restaurant, is joined by the rooftop Hábito, serving classic Algarve and Mediterranean flavors with a far-ranging view. Meanwhile all of the city of Faro is within walking distance, and the beaches are a short drive away.

content: There’s no place quite like the Azores, and at the moment there’s nothing quite like the new wave of high-end, high-design Portuguese luxury boutique hotels. Put the two together and you’ve got Aqua - Pópulo Eco Village. The name is partly a reference to its location, a short walk from Praia do Pópulo, a lovely little beach with a well-known surf break. And “eco village” is more or less self-explanatory — though the hotel’s seven luxe apartments are gathered together in a single modern building, it’s built with sustainability in mind, and overlooks the Atlantic on one side and the island’s mountains on the other.\n\nLocal architects SAL and famed interior designer Nini Andrade Silva are responsible for the hotel’s structure and decoration, which strikes a rare balance between urban sophistication and the organic charm of country life. The apartments are spacious and well-equipped, luxurious but understatedly so, and among the hotel’s attractions are a heated rooftop swimming pool and jacuzzi. Kitchens are provided for self-catering, and while there’s no restaurant on premises, there are several nearby, and more in the Ponte Delgada town center, barely two miles down the road.

The most famous part of Yellowstone National Park is, frankly, a bit over-civilized; away from Old Faithful, though, it gets as wild as you could want. Under Canvas West Yellowstone, set ten minutes from the park’s west entrance, across the Montana state line, is a safari-inspired camp of the variety that’s quickly become synonymous with the Under Canvas name — an experience that’s as luxurious and stylish as any hotel, with all the up-close immediacy of tent camping.

Each of the tented suites comes with hotel-style comforts like full en-suite bathrooms, king beds, West Elm furniture, and wood-burning stoves, and they’re available in combinations that sleep anywhere from two to seven — some feature satellite tents just for the kids. 

An on-site restaurant serves breakfast and dinner, using local and seasonal produce, while the grab-and-go selection keeps guests fueled for the day’s adventures, which include just about anything you can do in the Rocky Mountains. Mornings at Under Canvas begin with a yoga session and/or a fine cup of coffee, and in the evening, guests listen to acoustic live music and gather around fire pits for complimentary s’mores.

Please note: Under Canvas West Yellowstone is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from mid-May through late September.

content:
There’s no question Bali is paradise; it’s only a matter of deciding which part of Bali is your personal heaven. If you don’t need the beach, there’s one contender that rises above the rest. Ubud, in the island’s densely forested interior, is no longer a secret, but it deserves every bit of its fame. And a hotel like Samsara Ubud need not reinvent the wheel in order to inspire; a thoughtfully designed, confidently executed luxury villa resort in an environment like this can’t fail to become a success.

That’s more or less the story here. The 17 villas, designed by local architect Popo Danes, are universally large and luxurious, with plentiful private outdoor space including heated pools and outdoor showers. The construction is modern and the style is classic-contemporary, more elegant than rustic, and soothing to an extraordinary degree.

In that vein, Samsara also features a full-service spa, and an infinity pool that’s nothing short of breathtaking, disappearing, in classic Ubud style, into the lush valley. The restaurant serves Balinese and Indonesian dishes in an environment that looks out into that same wild forest, and the poolside bar keeps it casual with drinks, pizza, and a lighter menu.

The Palisociety hotels may have been born in California, but the brand’s colorful, eclectic, European-influenced style travels remarkably well; while Palihouse Hyde Park Village bears an obvious family resemblance to the other hotels of the same name, it looks perfectly at home on the Gulf Coast of Florida. Hyde Park is an upscale residential district just across the river from downtown Tampa, and Hyde Park Village is an open-air mixed-use development with shops, restaurants, and, thanks to Palisociety, a remarkably stylish boutique hotel.

In its public spaces it mixes vintage patterns and antique furnishings, creating an atmosphere that’s inviting and accessible. Meanwhile the rooms are colorful, handsome, equally warm, and somewhat residential in their concept — some of them feature kitchenettes and sofa beds, while all of them come with Nespresso machines, SMEG mini-fridges, and Diptyque bath products.

The Lobby Bar is the extent of the hotel’s in-house food and beverage offerings, featuring breakfast, coffee, cocktails, and an all-day menu. The rest of Hyde Park Village, however, is home to more than a few worthy options, including On Swann, a contemporary American restaurant that’s widely regarded as one of the finest in town.

content: The Baroque city of Lecce, on the outer reaches of the Salentine Peninsula, is one of the most picturesque places in Puglia, and perhaps all of southern Italy. It’s here, in a city-center palazzo that dates back to 1775, that siblings Antonia and Giacomo-Fouad Filali established a luxury boutique hotel that showcases not just Lecce’s architectural history but the family’s extensive art-world connections as well. La Fiermontina Palazzo Bozzi Corso is named for the Fiermonte branch of the family; one of its ten suites is named for Lady Astor, to whom Enzo Fiermonte was married.\n\nIn brief it’s a luxe little gem that combines historical architecture, modern design, and contemporary art in a manner that is inimitably Italian. The Fernand Léger suite is full of works by the French modernist painter, and the John & Yoko Wellness suite is similarly dedicated to its namesakes. A small but lovely spa extends the wellness program, and yoga classes are held on the building’s rooftop. Breakfast is the extent of the kitchen’s offerings, but the location in the heart of old Lecce means a wealth of options lie within a few minutes’ walk from the hotel’s front door.

The island of Capri has long been synonymous with a certain luxe seclusion, and Pazziella, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Capri does nothing to disabuse travelers of this association. Though it’s located within Capri’s town center, a short walk from the central Piazza Umberto I, it succeeds in establishing an atmosphere of luxe tranquility — and much of it is due to the calming effect of the gardens.

With 25 rooms and suites it’s not the smallest boutique hotel in town, but it’s small enough to remain intimate, and to never feel busy. The accommodations range from reasonably spacious Deluxes, complete with private patios, all the way to La Dolce Vita Suites with private plunge pools and the Sea View Capri Suite, with its panoramic balcony.

There’s a central swimming pool beneath the canopy of a vast magnolia tree, surrounded by idyllic gardens dotted with lounge furniture, as well as the P Garden Lounge Bar. The main culinary event, however, is Campanella for its exceptional Mediterranean cooking.

content: With its fairy-tale silhouette and its stone turret, Burg Schwarzenstein looks for all the world like a medieval castle. It was actually built in 1873 as a summer home for a German noble family and later transformed into a luxurious hotel with English-style gardens and sweeping views over the Rhine Valley. Seven rooms with period details — exposed stone, wooden beams, four-poster beds draped in silk canopies — are located in the main building and its castle tower, though most are housed in the modern Park Residence or the cottage-like Guest House a short stroll away. Castle restaurant serves regional specialities and the elegant Burgrestaurant, with its sunny terrace facing overlooking rows of vines, is the perfect spot for a glass of local Riesling.

content:
Grenada has a long way to go before it’s quite as heavily traveled as some of its Caribbean neighbors, but its charms are immediately familiar; it’s got the mild climate, the relaxed pace, the idyllic vistas and the gentle white-sand beaches for which this part of the world is so well loved. And the “Spice Isle” has at least one high-end, small-scale luxury resort to rival the best of them: Mount Cinnamon, on the perfectly picturesque Grand Anse beach, threatens to establish Grenada as a first-tier jet-set destination. (It doesn’t hurt that it’s outside the hurricane belt, either.)

With just 28 suites and villas, it’s smallish, and feels correspondingly intimate. The loose scatter of terra cotta structures conceals some surprisingly contemporary interiors, a sort of clean-lined take on the Greek island style — there’s not a floral-print bedspread in sight, and a welcome scarcity of wicker and rattan. And the comforts range from the merely high-end to the truly extravagant; Nespresso machines and swanky modern bathrooms are standard, and the villas add full kitchens and outdoor living areas with sweeping views.

In keeping with Mount Cinnamon’s intimate scale, you won’t find mega-resort services — just a beach club that turns out to have more or less everything you’ll need, from a bar and an all-day barbecue to a yoga room and a variety of water sports. And what you can’t find there — namely breakfast and dinner — you’ll find in Savvy’s, Mount Cinnamon’s restaurant.

How to get there:
Direct flights to Grenada are available from Miami, Atlanta, New York, Toronto, and London. Mount Cinnamon is a 15-minute drive from the airport.

content: If you’ve done Marrakech, and Essaouira, and Fes and Tunis, then maybe Hammamet — the southerly alternative to bustling Tunis, an expat French Riviera of sorts — is the next destination for you. And maybe La Badira checks all your boxes and more. It’s riad-like, but updated, respectfully nodding to the arch-and-palm aesthetic with a sleeker contemporary infrastructure. The fabulous Mediterranean light is the point, and it works its magic everywhere you look. Out your suite’s floor-to-ceiling window, for example, lending je ne sais quoi to the white-sand beaches and the brilliant seascape. Room interiors mostly defer to that vision with white minimalism, maintaining a faint air of desert minimalism with copious tile and perforated Islamic filigree in the furnishings and wall art. Limpid and sweetly calm, rooms are oriented as they should be: you wake in a king bed looking directly out past a private terrace on the view you came here for. \n \nSensual as the high-albedo plaster and citrus-perfumed air are, you don’t have to subsist on those alone; a trio of restaurants in smartly appointed spaces make sure of that. Adra’s the headliner, showcasing deliriously vibrant gastronomic acrobatics in the Tunisian idiom, but Kamilah and the beach grill hold their own in the open-kitchen Mediterranean fusion and the outstandingly fresh comfort modes, respectively. A whole host of reasons support the al fresco dining philosophy here: a pair of outdoor infinity pools, the discretely floodlit façade, and commanding views of the bay. We suppose you’ll need to wander indoors at some point to take advantage of Spa Clarins or fireside cocktails in the lobby bar, but the name of this hotel drops a telling hint — it’s Arabic for “full moon.”

content:
The Peruvian Andes may seem at first glance to be more a backpacker’s sort of adventure, but La Casona is an option for those who want to start the Inca Trail in high luxury style. This rehabilitated Spanish colonial manor at the heart of the old town of Cusco has joined the Inkaterra family of environmentally friendly boutique hotels.

Its eleven suites are massive and solidly built; there’s a residential feel to La Casona, from the heavy carved wooden doors to the stone fireplaces and the underfloor heating. It’s a small hotel, with the intimacy that comes along with its size — no passersby clogging the lobby — and if you’ve got the means, and a dozen and a half friends to share it with, you can book the whole place to yourself.

The small size doesn’t preclude a few big-hotel luxuries, though, things like massage and spa treatments, and private guides available for all manner of Andean excursions. It may seem a paradox to look for this kind of luxury at the edge of one of the world’s great outdoor adventures — but as a beginning or an ending, easing the transition, a bit of pampering may be just the thing.

How to get there:
Inkaterra La Casona is located 15 minutes from the Cusco Airport. Transfers can be arranged for US$40 for up to 2 guests.

content: Hours away and seemingly a world apart from Cancún’s busy resort zone, the sleepy town of Espita on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula doesn’t see a lot of tourist traffic. A couple of stylish hotels have popped up here in recent years, however, most notably Casona los Cedros, which is best known for its excellent restaurant. The main building, an old colonial villa framed by tropical foliage, was abandoned for decades before a French architect snapped up the property and transformed it into a modern boutique hotel. \n\nThe original structure now houses the reception and bar, while the new addition, built by local craftspeople using traditional materials like stone and wood, features nine minimalist guest rooms outfitted with concrete walls, decorative tile flooring, wooden furnishings, embroidered textiles, and private patios with indoor-outdoor showers. Understated and calm, they’re set around a central garden with an elevated infinity pool and a breezy covered terrace. Cacti and agaves dot the grounds, hammocks swing between trees, and freshly picked herbs and vegetables from the restaurant’s garden appear on the communal breakfast table.

Brazil’s Fasano hotels are local favorites for their triple threat of high-end luxury, ultra-glamorous aesthetics, and exquisite gastronomy, and while the Fasano Angra Dos Reis, in the lush Costa Verde region, may attract less international attention than its sister hotel in Ipanema, it’s not for lack of any of the aforementioned attributes. 

Like the rest of the family, it’s sleek and state-of-the-art, with a fantastic swimming pool and sweeping sea views fringed with palm trees. Guest rooms are as luxe as you’d expect, with marble bathrooms and private patios — most have sea views, too, and all come with complimentary Havaianas flip-flops to help you get up (or down) to speed with the way the locals live.

The hotel’s eponymous fine-dining restaurant serves a dizzying array of seafood-based creations, while the casual beachside Praia serves lighter fare. Also on the agenda are a French-style patisserie, a spa, and a kids’ club; hikes and boat trips are easily arranged. But no one will fault you if you kick off your complimentary flip-flops and settle into a chaise, coconut water or caipirinha in hand, and do absolutely nothing.

It says a lot about what kind of hotel the Bellevue Palace is that it’s the Swiss government’s official lodging, playing host to visiting dignitaries and heads of state as well as Swiss members of parliament. In fact it’s publicly owned, but privately managed, a sort of best-of-both-worlds approach that seems to have paid off — its facilities and atmosphere are flawless, but the service is anything but complacent.

Of course, aesthetically speaking, you wouldn’t expect the Swiss government to take any great risks. This is an absolutely classic city-center grand hotel, and while it’s been continually kept up to date, a visitor from a century ago would feel right at home. The rooms and suites are extremely well equipped, and range from the relatively cozy Superior rooms all the way up to a Presidential Suite whose name is not aspirational, but perfectly factual.

Meeting facilities, naturally, are plentiful, and the wellness offerings include a Finnish sauna and the Bellevie Gym — spelling absolutely intentional. And the restaurants and bars are in a league with the city’s finest, from Le Lobby with its afternoon tea to the Bellevue Bar for cocktails, from the classic Brasserie Vue to the daringly modern Noumi Bar & Grill.

content:
Melrose, in the upscale northern suburbs of Johannesburg, is already an auspicious setting for a boutique hotel, but the Peech Hotel’s setting, just across the road from a park, affords it an extra measure of tranquility. And tranquility is an attribute that a hotel like the Peech can use. This is no nightclub with rooms — quite the opposite, it’s an upscale residential-style lodging whose genteel atmosphere feels at times something like a country estate.

The original rooms and suites occupy the original house and a separate building in the gardens, and they’re plush, stylish, and more than spacious enough, decorated in an eclectic style that’s equal parts heritage and contemporary. Newly added are the so-called luxury rooms, which are larger, somewhat more modernist-influenced in design, and add large walk-in showers and patios. And soon to open is the Peech Villa, which is essentially a two-bedroom version of the luxury rooms — not bad at all, though there isn’t a substandard room in the house.

Food and wine are of particular concern in Johannesburg, and you’ll find some thought has been put into it here. Peech Bistro offers simple, local, seasonal fare, with an unmistakably high-end presentation — and a selection of South African wines to match.

content: Ibiza, right now, is two different places in one: the up-all-night party mecca, and the semi-secluded, quasi-rural island paradise. NH Collection Ibiza is a hotel that can do a bit of both, as it turns out that even the most dedicated reveller needs a quiet place to sleep, eventually. But it’s perhaps most in tune with the private-retreat type, as its rooms are luxurious, light-filled, and though they’re stylish, thanks to designers Baranowitz + Kronenberg they’re rather subtle and sedate about it. Meanwhile you’re walking distance from both the beach and the nightlife, though if you prefer, you’ve got a good reason to stay in as well: SLVJ, the high-end steakhouse brand based in Amsterdam, has an outpost here as well.

content:
Sri Lanka suffers from no shortage of fine hotels, but thanks to a quirk of architectural history, most of them, stylistically speaking, are variations on the “tropical modernism” of the Geoffrey Bawa school. Cape Weligama, on the island’s south coast, a few miles from Galle, blazes its own trail — and what’s unique about it is that it finds its identity by looking to the past. Here the Thai architect Lek Bunnag took inspiration from Sri Lanka’s long history as an explorers’ waystation, incorporating countless elements from the island’s pre-modernist history in this classic-contemporary resort.

Then again, it’s not just the architecture. Cape Weligama’s setting is extraordinary as well. It’s set on 12 acres of terraced clifftop real estate, a hundred feet above the Indian Ocean, which, as you may well imagine, is not at all bad for the views. The freestanding villas cluster around private pools, while the larger ones are divided into multiple suites, which means they’re perfect for families or larger parties. All of the units are outfitted to five-star standard, and they also share a pair of swimming pools — the kid-friendly Cove and the cliffside, crescent-shaped, adults-only Moon Pool.

Other enticements include a spa, a pair of beaches, and ample opportunity to explore the surrounding waterways by boat or kayak. The Society is set on a clifftop with a spectacular view over the Indian Ocean. And the restaurants serve a variety of upscale fare in a variety of settings, from the panoramic views of The Atlas to the chef’s table atmosphere of Tableau.

How to get there: Cape Weligama is located approximately 175 km by car from Bandaranaike International Airport via Southern Expy/E01. Alternatively, chartered seaplane service is available between Tea Trails and Cape Weligama.

content:
A hotel’s business-oriented amenities aren’t usually worth more than a cursory mention — there’s only so much you can say about a conference rooms or a computer center. But EAST, Beijing puts such a stylish spin on the “work” half of the work/life balance, we’re actually kind of intrigued. Billing itself as a “lifestyle business hotel,” EAST offers a smooth, high-tech experience from check-in to check-out, allowing guests to move seamlessly from lounges to surprisingly chic work spaces.

At 359 rooms, the hotel looms large over Beijing’s Indigo development complex, a sort of pop-up cultural and shopping center designed to give residents of such a sprawling metropolis a downtown space to chill out (and spend money, of course). While that makes it sound like a great big dystopian mall, the rooms at EAST are packed with enough quirky elements — not to mention such humane comforts as spacious rain showers — to make them feel anything but generic. Floor-to-ceiling windows abound, so opt for a corner room if you can — the panoramic views are excellent. 

Upstairs rooms come with extra perks and access to a semi-exclusive business lounge that brings the cocktail hour straight to your desk. When it’s time to clock out (or anytime, for those who never clocked in at all), Feast does international cuisine and for night owls, Xian pulls double-duty as a bar and live jazz club, taking its cues from the gleaming industrial design of the nearby 798 Art Zone. 

How to get there:
EAST Beijing is located 12 miles from Beijing International Airport (PEK). Transfers are available by Mercedes Benz or Audi A6 at a cost of 550 RMB each way. The Beijing Train Station is approximately 10 miles from the hotel.

content:
With the opening of its second Toronto boutique hotel, the Montreal-based Germain Hotels has kicked off a study in contrasts — A Tale of Two Sister Hotels, if you will, each one seamlessly integrated into its particular neighborhood. Where the first Le Germain was an infusion of poetic modernity into the theater district, the newer Maple Leaf Square hotel takes its cues from sportier neighbors (namely the Scotiabank Arena, home of the Maple Leafs and the Raptors). Pairing lithe, athletic design with a Euro-chic sensibility, this hotel feels right at home in the downtown office/condo/shopping district.

Making overtures to out-of-towners here for business or sports (or sports business, for that matter), the exterior is heavy on the steel-and-glass look. But where other hotels are content to let half-hearted minimalism stand in for style, Hotel Le Germain plays with a variety of tactile design elements. Here, polished wood and stone, 100% Egyptian cotton sheets, and a wide array of fabrics and upholsteries vie for your attention. Open loft-style floor plans take full advantage of long windows to bathe the 167 guest rooms in an abundance of natural light, while glass-walled showers provide a cheeky counterpoint to the photos of shirtless athletes that decorate the walls. 

Even if you find yourself trapped in the dullest meeting on earth, Le Germain’s corporate gathering spaces do what they can to make things tolerable. The designers wisely skipped the soulless conference room in favor of a private dining area that carries over the wall-to-wall windows and high ceilings of the welcoming public spaces. The most relaxing of these, the lobby lounge, serves cocktails and tapas to help pre-game for an evening in the stands or out on the town. 

How to get there:
Le Germain Maple Leaf Square is located 28km (20-45 min depending on traffic) from Toronto Airport. Transfers can be arranged for $63, one way.

content:
Lark Hotels operates contemporary-style boutique hotels all over the Northeast, each one carefully tailored to its location — so it’s only sensible that in the upscale enclave of Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, its hotels would take on an almost regal air. The Richard, the youngest of the three Larks in town, stands right on Main Street, but offers an almost aristocratic measure of seclusion. Built in the 19th century as a ship’s captain’s residence, it was later converted into an inn, and under Lark’s care it’s been transformed into a chic and contemporary 16-room boutique hotel.

The key to its distinctive identity is that they’ve let the heritage architecture speak for itself, and resisted the temptation to go all-out nautical in the décor. Instead stylish monochromes and sparingly applied accent colors establish a cosmopolitan atmosphere. Every room is different, as you’d expect from a building of this vintage, but all come with the expected comforts, including modern electronics and bathrooms equipped with walk-in rain showers.

There’s an outdoor courtyard where guests gather by the fire into the evening, as well as a front porch that’s made for leisure. And while breakfast is the only full meal, you’re in no danger of going hungry — walk down Main Street towards the water and you’re immediately in the heart of Edgartown.

content:
Set perched in the rocky headlands above its namesake bay, The Plettenberg’s whitewashed walls house 37 stately rooms and suites that could each play the set to a modern-day Merchant-Ivory film. Though a five-star through and through, it breaks the gilt mold, forgoing decorous opulence in favor of a refined simplicity, the better to frame the hotel’s spectacular views of the mountain-backed sea.  

The two stand-alone suites, the three-bedroom Lookout Villa and the two-bedroom Beach House, bear more modern accents than their main-house counterparts, but in all the rooms, swathed in whites and beach-inspired sandy and blue hues, the traditional styling does little to distract from the views. If the suites are off the table, be sure to book a sea view room and let the property’s most stunning feature — the landscape — take center stage.

The breezy serenity of watching the sea for dolphins and whales may reign supreme onsite, but close at hand is an eco-tourist’s dream. It’s well worth peeling yourself off the poolside loungers to take in the Bay’s endless flora, fauna and marine life at closer range. Ozone bath therapy at the hotel’s Fresh Wellness spa is that much more deserved after a long horseback ride through indigenous forests. And cocktail conversation at the chic bar will be far more compelling when sharing the tale of launching off the world’s highest bungee jump.  

Evidence of the region’s bounty continues to the table; at the signature restaurant Seafood at the Plettenberg, chef Grant Parker features local produce and fresh seafood in his modern global cuisine, and for the ultimate in intimacy, the single table for two in the Wine Cellar steeps you in the terroir with an extensive list of South Africa’s best wines.

How to get there:
The Plettenberg is approximately a 1 1/4 hour drive from George Airport and 15 minutes from Plettenberg Bay Airport.

content:
It’s one of our favorite tunes. Start with a small industrial city that’s on the upswing, find a charming old landmark building, bring in a hotshot design team, then give ‘em the old razzle dazzle: bespoke furnishings, Frette linens, farm-to-table cuisine, craft cocktails. That’s the Kimpton Schofield Hotel in a nutshell. The city is Cleveland, and the historic landmark, in this case, the Schofield, an 14-story office building constructed in the city’s downtown in 1902.

The Kimpton group spent five years and fifty million dollars getting the place into shape. It was time and money well spent; the elegant brick facade may be a throwback to gentler times, but the interior is both cool and classic. The look is modern and pleasantly understated, with pale wood and dark slate, linen sofas, copper accents, potted plants, and cozy throw rugs. Over there, an open fireplace, over here, a geometric reading nook that looks like something you’d pin to your Ultimate Dream Home board on Pinterest.

Guest rooms are simple but thoroughly comfortable, featuring pillow-top beds and bath products by Atelier Bloem. Rooms also come with extra perks like yoga mats, and artwork tied to the place: at the Schofield, that means Victorian era-style light boxes with letters you can move around to spell out your own messages. Fun if you’re into poetry, convenient if you’re too shy to call housekeeping to ask for an extra towel.

It’s a Kimpton, after all, so the extra amenities are par for the course, as is the state-of-the-art fitness center, the hosted wine hour every evening, and the fleet of complimentary custom-designed PUBLIC bikes on loan, should you fancy a spin around town. For dinner or drinks, there’s Betts, offering seasonal menus made with locally sourced ingredients in an airy industrial space. All told, it might be a standard formula for a hit song, but it’s one that never gets old.

content:
You’re forgiven if you don’t know much about Mauritius, save for the fact, of course, that it’s a world-class beach destination. It’s the kind of place with such staggering physical beauty — impossibly soft white sand beaches, crystal-clear water, and so on — that it’s become a magnet for honeymooners and resort developers for whom the island’s cultural history is, shall we say, secondary. They just want to stare at the sunset, and who can blame them? Enter Heritage Le Telfair Golf & Wellness Resort. Yes, it’s a resort, and a thoroughly luxurious one. But as the name suggests, it’s a resort that’s closely tied to the island’s past.

The elegant colonial-style hotel sits right on the sand, occupying the strategic location of an important sugar plantation and estate that dates from 1765. Much of the island’s significant history unfolded here; Heritage Le Telfair, in fact, is named for the 19th-century Irish naturalist who helped develop this agricultural landscape. It’s one of several hotels that Heritage Resorts operates here on the dreamy Domaine de Bel Ombre on the island’s south coast. Carving this massive piece of oceanfront real estate into a series of distinct hotels, as it turns out, was a smart choice: Heritage Le Telfair feels more intimate than you’d expect, especially given the fact that guests have access to a dozen bars and restaurants across the Heritage-owned coast. 

Le Telfair’s main building has old-world charm, but rooms and suites are located in new villas, architecturally inspired by the plantation’s original buildings. High ceilings, parquet floors, a subdued color palette of ivory and chocolate brown, French doors leading onto balconies or terraces, many with sea views — you get the picture. Many rooms and suites have romantic four-poster beds draped with all-natural cotton that billows in the breeze, or quaint reading nooks, or period furniture. Or all three, if you’re staying in one of the more opulent suites. Standard amenities in all categories include large flat-screen TVs, tea and coffee stations, and large marble bathrooms.

The landscape itself is lovely, of course, sea-facing and planted with tropical gardens. Activities are plentiful: the resort is known for its European Tour championship golf course, but equally popular are water sports, yoga, the Seven Colours Millesime Spa, or just lounging by the pool. Borrow a bicycle and explore the island, or just hang around this edge of it — you don’t need to go far, as a wide range of high-end dining and drinking venues are spread throughout the Heritage resort grounds. The most picturesque option just might be French cuisine on the veranda at Le Château de Bel Ombre, Charles Telfair’s one-time mansion. You might not ever be an expert on Mauritius, but these historic spaces give you that satisfying feeling that you’re in an actual place with a specific story — not just a gated luxury complex with amazing views of the sea.

content:
Here’s the surprising thing about the Alvear Art Hotel: in a town whose boutique hoteliers are all too often blind to everything beyond the visual, the Alvear is about as well-rounded a hotel as you’ll find anywhere, in Buenos Aires or otherwise. It’s proof that white walls and stripped-down rooms alone do not a “design hotel” make; function is as crucial as form. It’s a gorgeous hotel, to be sure — its airy, free-flowing public spaces all happy conspiracies of fine art, sunlight and gleaming marble — but it’s also a hotel where the rooms are quiet, the beds are dreamy and the bathrooms are big and bright. And where a concierge in a pressed black suit can point you to a good nearby bar or an up-and-coming restaurant without making you feel like you shouldn’t have to ask. 

The rooms are spacious and sunny, with at least as much attention paid to the tactile — Egyptian cotton sheets, deep marble baths, plush rugs and textured walls — as to the visual. Each also comes with free wi-fi and a work desk — not the sexiest details, but then that’s the point: the fundamentals underlie all the rest. Combine that with a well-equipped business center, an elegant bar that feels made for an after-work drink, and a location a few minutes from the city’s financial center, and, for a place billed as an art hotel, it’s a surprisingly good choice for business travel. 

That we’ve gotten this far without mentioning that the Alvear Art Hotel is an offshoot of what’s often considered the best hotel in town, the nearby Alvear Palace, surely says something about the newcomer’s own merit. It’s by no means a clone of its older sibling (or its rich great aunt, is maybe the better metaphor), as the look and feel is decidedly more contemporary. Still, the Alvear polish shines through.

content:
Maps don’t generally do Mauritius justice. The tiny island in the southwest Indian Ocean is a mere speck next to the continent of Africa, but it’s actually quite enormous, if you’re measuring characteristics like white-sand beaches and panoramic sunsets. And Trou Aux Biches Beachcomber has some of the best of both. It’s not for nothing that it’s known as one of the most romantic hotels in Mauritius. 

Recent renovations have only augmented the property’s village-resort feel. Thatched villas nestle among the palm groves, while carefully crafted gardens grow out of the various pools. A dock culminates in a gazebo, surrounded by softly lapping waves, putting the horizon this close. The Beachcomber group essentially inaugurated high-end tourism on the island, first opening a luxury hotel in 1952. After six decades these folks know a thing or two about making sure your experience in the tropics soothes, satisfies, and sates.   

Some rooms have private pools, some have outdoor showers. The spa too blurs the line between inside and outside, offering a range of treatments, including seaweed-based “algotherapy,” in open-air or air-conditioned cabanas. Some suites come with butlers and beachfront verandas, just as you’d expect, although every accommodation style manifests fine, sensitive service. Then there are the tennis courts and bocce lawns and water sports and on-site shops and six restaurants. But nothing beats being on the beach, which abuts a lagoon (oh yes, it’s blue). Looking at the sky and sea will make you feel as if the whole world had gone wide-angle and infinite. Put your significant other in the picture, and that’s a fantasy made real.

content: San Sebastián is a difficult spot to beat. Set in the Basque region of northern Spain, this seaside destination benefits from golden beaches and true-blue waters, but it’s also a hot spot for haute couture, high culture, and fine dining. Chef Nobu Matsuhisa is well known for his eponymous restaurant empire and for his blossoming hotel empire — here his signature dishes come with stunning water views. As do the Nobu Hotel San Sebastián’s 20 guest rooms, which combine the brand’s signature modern Japanese minimalism with contemporary-luxe comforts, local details and, in many cases, terraces looking out over the bay.

content: Though the brand’s name ties it to a particular West End neighborhood, the Soho House line of members’ clubs, hotels, and restaurants has gone global. And given that the East London neighborhood of Shoreditch has become London’s hippest creative district, a Soho House in E1 is a natural next step. Shoreditch House begins with a fantastically central location, in a converted Thirties warehouse right across the road from Shoreditch High Street station. And while it’s a decidedly urban experience, it offers something that’s vanishingly rare in any corner of London: a rooftop swimming pool.\n\nIt also offers the full complement of other Soho House services, including a Cowshed spa, a fully equipped athletic club, and a couple of in-demand restaurants — the izakaya-style Pen Yen and the members-only Club. On the rooftop adjacent to Pen Yen is the Back Deck, a dining and lounge space that hosts pop-up food and beverage concepts. And while they’re only a part of the package, the bedrooms are no afterthought. Here they range only from Tiny to Small+, but they’re not as compact as they sound; and thanks to their efficient layouts and warm décor, as well as the multitude of comforts offered elsewhere in the club, they’re much more than adequate to the task at hand.

content: The Negev Desert of southern Israel is the setting for Six Senses Shaharut, whose 60 suites and villas are constructed from rough and rustic stone, timber, and plaster, a style that belies the polished comforts and professional hospitality that lie within. As always, there’s an impressive spa and wellness program, and the restaurants serve healthful and refined fare made from local, organic ingredients, drawing from the culinary traditions of the Mediterranean and the Middle East.

content: Classic English country house or contemporary spa escape? Visitors to Mallory Court, in Warwickshire, are faced with a choice, at least when it comes to the placement of their bedroom. The original Luytens-style house, which dates back to 1916, is perhaps the headline attraction, and contains nineteen rooms and suites in a style that is, if not strictly antique, at least in keeping with the early 20th-century architecture. But to the Manor has been added a second structure, the Orchard House, which is home to most of the rest of the accommodations, in a more boutique-influenced modern style — as well as the lavish Elan Spa.\n\nA few more rooms in the contemporary vein occupy the Knight’s Suite, which is not a suite at all but an events space and a popular wedding venue. In any style, the bedrooms are luxurious, and the service is professional but neither excessively formal nor overly familiar. The spa’s seven treatment rooms and its various pools and lounges make for easy relaxation, as do the house’s extensive gardens and grounds. The Warwick is the house’s award-winning fine dining venue, and Sencha is the Asian inspired casual eatery located in Orchard House.

content:
Washington wine is no joke, and if the climate keeps on changing, it’s only going to get better. (How’s that for a silver lining?) A wine-themed Seattle boutique hotel is an idea whose time has definitely come — and a stroll through the Kimpton group’s newly reconditioned Hotel Vintage reveals a hotel that’s on friendly terms indeed with the red stuff. And the white, presumably. You know what we mean.

Wine or no wine, it’s hard not to love what they’ve done with the place. The new look is suitably grown-up, but not overly so — dark colors, rich textures, well-chosen furnishings, and a surprising amount of sunlight streaming in through the full-length windows, which is direct or indirect, depending on the weather, of course. The Kimpton hotels are known for friendly details that feel very West Coast — in-room yoga mats, special amenities for pets, an electric car charging station — and the Vintage is, in that respect, no different.

If wine’s your focus then Italian cuisine is a natural choice; Tulio, by Seattle’s venerable Walter Pisano, serves rustic Italian fare from fresh Pacific Northwest ingredients, a winning combination. Washington wine flows freely here as well, of course. And with a location near the heart of downtown, you’ll find the rest of Seattle’s best is close at hand.

content:
If you’re determined to stay in a fine, funky little boutique hotel, or you’re in the mood to have your mind blown by some outré experiments in interior design, then we regret to inform you that Seoul is not yet ready for you. But if you’re a fan of the classic Asian luxury hotel — if, that is to say, you find yourself re-watching Lost in Translation in order to get a look at the Park Hyatt rather than the female lead — then you’ll be well catered for in the Korean capital. And you’ll likely be drawn to one hotel in particular: the Grand Seoul InterContinental.

When it comes to the crucial blend of international style and local personality, the Grand seems to hit all the right notes. The western-style rooms are classic business luxury, with all the bells and whistles, and the ondol rooms are fitted out in traditional Korean style — radiant underfloor heating, kneeling-height furniture, plus the full complement of modern conveniences.

As for services, in this bracket you’ll lack for nothing. A variety of restaurants cater to a wide range of palates, and the health club is fully equipped, with an indoor pool, a fitness center, even a driving range. And there’s always the option of walking outside the hotel, if you feel that you must — the COEX convention center is practically next door, along with its own associated InterContinental hotel, whose facilities you are free to use.

content:
We’re still scratching our heads as to why Argentina’s northern province of Salta isn’t more famous than it is. With its effortless wine-country elegance, the dramatic snow-capped peaks of the Andes serving as a backdrop, and a low-key capital city that drips with colonial charm, it just seems like it ought to be crawling with visitors. If it’s lacking anything, it’s a hotel on the same level as the best ones in places like Patagonia and Buenos Aires. Fortunately, that’s a problem that the Grace hotel group is more than capable of solving — and as it happens, they’ve done it by more or less splitting the difference between the low-key charms of a rustic Patagonian estancia and the high modern style of a Porteño boutique. 

Though the hotel is small, just twelve rooms, the scale of the surroundings is as grand as could be. Grace Cafayate sits on the spectacular Estancia de Cafayate, a 1,360-acre sporting estate complete with an equestrian center, one of Argentina’s most prestigious championship golf courses, an extensive network of trails for hikers and bikers, and a veritable sea of vineyards. Suffice to say that if you like the outdoors, you won’t lack for things to do. 

And if you prefer to take your experience of the outdoors sitting (or lying) down, you’ll still do just fine here. At the spa, the therapists make use of the grapes and vines growing just outside, and the views of the mountains bring the outdoors in as well. Of course the local agricultural bounty is put to even better use in the restaurant, where authentic Argentinian specialties receive refined contemporary treatments, accompanied by quite the enviable wine list. 

How to get there: Grace Cafayate is about a 2½-hour drive from Salta’s Martín Miguel Güemes International Airport (SLA).

content: Le Petit Pali Brentwood fills a gap in the Los Angeles hotel scene: in short, it’s a great place to stay in one of the city’s most stylish neighborhoods, an area that’s surprisingly short on lodging options. Brentwood is mostly residential, and Le Petit Pali offers a rare chance to live like the locals, including NBA stars and A-list actors. Like others in hotelier Avi Brosh’s California collection, the 25-room boutique hotel is a smart redesign of an old inn — in this case, a historic motor lodge on Sunset Boulevard. With four bungalow-style buildings set around a series of outdoor patios with abundant greenery, stone fountains, and string lights suspended above wooden Adirondack chairs, it’s a fashionable home away from home with space to relax indoors and out. \n\nRooms are retro-chic, but with a decided emphasis on the latter; they feature hardwood floors, vaulted ceilings, white brick walls, and high-end details from Bellino linens and Diptyque bath products to gourmet minibars and Marshall speakers. Cheerful patterns are everywhere — striped wallpaper, a plaid throw blanket, whimsical floral headboards — and most have separate living areas. Several come with private outdoor patios, like the LPP Suite, which also has an adorably vintage-looking, fully equipped kitchen and bar. A complimentary continental breakfast is delivered to rooms each morning, and on sunny mornings, it’s a pleasure to enjoy it al fresco on the shared patio. Brentwood’s famous farmers market is a short stroll away, as are many of its cafés and shops.

content: Most hotels in European capitals are either proudly historic or unabashedly modern. Vincci Selección Unuk GL, just outside Seville’s old town, pulls off the rare feat of being both at once: this boutique hotel comprises two adjoining houses, one proudly traditional and the other unmistakably industrial. Marble staircases and wrought-iron railings evoke the past, but the romantic Andalusian patio has a retractable roof, and guest rooms come with wood-beamed ceilings and parquet floors as well as Nespresso machines and futuristic bathrooms. In a city where it always feels like summertime it’s hard to go wrong with a series of open-air terraces, including one with a saltwater pool, to say nothing of a rooftop with a stylish bar and restaurant, twinkling lights, and 360-degree views over the city.

content: It’s no exaggeration to say the Rajmahal Palace is fit for a king: this luxury hotel is owned by the royal family of Jaipur, and counts among its past guests no less eminent a couple than Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh. While this Rajasthani palace is grand in a traditional way, with high archways and glittering chandeliers, the otherworldly interior design — rich with whimsical details, symmetrical shapes, and bold pops of color — looks as meticulously composed as a Wes Anderson film. It comes by its historical character honestly, of course — that’s the royal family’s own classic Ford Thunderbird out front.\n\nThe hotel’s spacious suites, enlivened with decorative handmade wallpaper and furnished with velvet armchairs and ornate wood-carved beds, are nothing if not full of character. Several feature separate drawing rooms; one has a full-service kitchen and a private patio with a heated plunge pool. Guests lounge by the Art Deco-style pool, wander through manicured gardens, drink in the Polo Lounge or the Bar, and dress for dinner at one of the hotel’s restaurants: the Colonnade, for upscale comfort food, and 51 Shades of Pink, for a more formal presentation of classic Jauipur cuisine.

content:
Though it’s the skyscrapers that get all the attention, there’s more to the Emirate of Dubai than just the downtown towers. Less than an hour outside the city, surrounded by a classic Arabian landscape, is Bab Al Shams, a sprawling, low-slung resort complex, whose weathered sandstone buildings tuck discreetly into the windswept dunes. It belongs to the Rare Finds by Kerzner brand, the same operator as the glossy Atlantis and One&Only resort hotels — but with its humble desert architecture and low-profile construction, Bab Al Shams is a different character entirely.

Fortunately for guests, less glossy doesn’t necessarily mean less plush. The rooms and suites are lavish, to be sure, though remarkably restrained, at least by Dubai’s standards. Views are of the garden courtyard or else out into the desert — the second, naturally, is the more inspiring option, though it comes at a price. Private terraces and patios are universal, and space is plentiful throughout, from the humblest deluxe room up to the two-bedroom private pool villa.

With just over a hundred rooms, Bab Al Shams is smallish, but not quite intimate — and its family-friendliness, an obvious asset for those with kids, makes it a less ideal choice for honeymooners and the like. Still, it’s a relatively tranquil escape, and if it’s silence you’re after, the surrounding desert has it in spades — this is more or less the direct opposite of the typical Dubai city hotel experience.

content: If you had to confine your travels, for the rest of your life, to destinations entirely within Italy’s borders, you could still do pretty well for yourself. From Sicily to the Amalfi to Rome to Cinque Terre, the diversity is astonishing — and the mere existence of South Tyrol and the Dolomites feels downright gratuitous. The impossibly picturesque Val Gardena is where you’ll find Hotel Montchalet, an alpine lodge in flawless modern luxury-boutique style, which, though it contains a mere 16 suites, nevertheless features all the comfort (and many of the services) of a much larger and more extensive resort.\n\nThe wellness center, for instance, includes not just a sauna, a gym, and the usual beauty treatments, but a spectacular indoor pool and a Nu Relax flotation-bed program, for cutting-edge relaxation. There’s also a small but impressive restaurant, a reminder that, even in the Alps, nobody lives the good life quite like the Italians. And while a hotel of Montchalet’s size won’t have its own ski shop, the hotel’s shuttle connects you to the nearby lifts, and the concierges can arrange anything from snowshoe walks to heli-skiing excursions — or you can simply settle down in the hotel’s cinema for a private screening.

content: It’s no grand statement, no hospitality revolution. And with just five rooms it isn’t going to fundamentally alter the Jaipur hotel scene. But what makes a place like 28 Kothi so extraordinary is precisely that — that it seems to exist for no reason other than to bring a little bit of gratuitous beauty into the world. A collaboration between an Indian jeweler, a French architect, a Lebanese interior designer, and a restaurateur who splits his time between New York and Mumbai, it’s nothing if not cosmopolitan. And though its luxuries border on the extravagant, the low cost of lodging in Jaipur means this fantasy can be had for a relative pittance.\n\nRajasthani craftsmanship meets modern design in the rooms, which range from a relatively humble single to a suite that spans an entire floor. The location is quiet, discreetly tucked away in a residential neighborhood, and the atmosphere throughout is more akin to a guest house than a hotel. There’s no restaurant per se, and why should there be, for just ten guests? Instead you’ll dine on made-to-order vegetarian dishes as you lounge in the gardens or on the terraces. Let the rest of Rajasthan bowl you over with riotous activity — this is where you’ll retreat for serene, genteel calm.

content:
In Phoenix, once known primarily for its endless low-rise sprawl, there’s something suddenly happening in the city center. Two new downtown college campuses, a busy light-rail line, and a spate of urban redevelopment have left downtown Phoenix utterly transformed. A hotel like Kimpton Hotel Palomar Phoenix — a stylish modern boutique hotel in a city-center high-rise — simply wouldn’t have been possible even a decade ago, and it’s no exaggeration to say it’ll put this rejuvenated city center on the map for a whole new generation of travelers.

The interior style is surprisingly chic, an authentically Southwestern sort of modernism that conveys a strong sense of place without ever lapsing into desert kitsch. And though the hotel occupies the lower floors of the tower, the views from the rooms are still dramatic and far-ranging. Frette linens and down duvets are a matter of course, and like all Kimpton hotels, the Palomar is thoroughly pet-friendly.

On the third floor there’s an open-air rooftop bar as well as an outdoor pool, and Blue Hound Kitchen & Cocktails, the hotel’s flagship restaurant, is a very worthy downtown option. Of course, it’s hardly the only one — from here, at the heart of downtown, you’re a stone’s throw from any number of nightlife, dining, and entertainment options.

content:
Tel Aviv, and its White City neighborhood in particular, has been a destination for design aficionados for decades. This is a young city in an ancient corner of the world — it wasn’t founded until the early 1900s — and its architecture is correspondingly unique: European modernism viewed through the lens of Israeli culture and climate. So when we say that the White Villa, located in the heart of the White City, is one of the architectural icons of the city, that means something.

Built in 1948, the White Villa was the work of one of Le Corbusier’s disciples, and today it is one of the last remaining single-family villas from the era. It was once a private residence — the family on the upper floor, the servants on the ground floor. The interior received a full-scale renovation in recent years to transform the house into a hotel, and the result is 18 airy guestrooms, each a tasteful study in neutrals that’s contemporary but still true to the original mid-century international style of the residence. We think Le Corbusier would approve — and actually, much of his protegé’s original design remains intact, including the grand foyer, fireplaces, and the street-facing veranda.

You’ll want to spend plenty of time on that veranda or on the rooftop sundeck, which features chaise longues and patio tables to soak up the abundant Tel Aviv sun. Many of the rooms feature private outdoor spaces as well. But if you prefer to do your sunbathing at the beach, the sea is just a short walk from the White Villa — as is Diezengoff Square and the very heart of the city center.

content:
We’re not surveyors by trade; we don’t normally travel with distance measuring wheels or clinometers. But we do feel safe making the following claim about Leela Palace, even without the benefit of precision instruments: this place is ginormous. Then again, New Delhi itself is no little village, so a great rectangle of a hotel fits the scene perfectly.   

It sits like a present, waiting to be unwrapped by those arriving for business or pleasure, minus a bow on top. Within, delights abound. We’ll begin with those of the edible variety, from the Qube, framed in glass, with its mix of local and international dishes, to Megu, a temple devoted to all things Japanese, to the handmade wooden accents and equally crafted biryanis and curries at Jamavar to the first Asian outpost of Le Cirque. 

But a discriminating hotel guest cannot survive on good food alone. Accommodations more than live up to the challenge of the soaring, multistoried lobby, featuring mirror televisions and significant lighting in all the bathrooms, as well as grand beds and far-ranging views. Also worth noting is the sheer size of the rooms and suites. We heard that these are some of the biggest rooms in the city, and we’re in no position to argue. Then again size isn’t everything. Anyone can build big, but only some can provide this generous an admixture of experience and focused attention.

content:
Singapore’s colonial-era grand hotels are gorgeous, yes, but one can’t help but feel that there are enough of them already— including the Fullerton Bay’s sister, the iconic Fullerton. So it’s very much to the Fullerton Bay’s credit that it’s not a straight-down-the-line reproduction. It’s every inch a tribute to the Raffles days — that’s Sir Stamford Raffles, not Raffles® Hotels and Resorts — but it’s a contemporary vision, not a historical reconstruction.

It’s the vision of a certain Andre Fu, a Hong Kong–based designer who’s responsible for more than one Far Eastern Tablet hotel already. And sometimes a well-crafted period piece is just more effective than a trip to the archives. Here the materials are familiar — rosewood and latticework figure prominently — as is the color scheme, neutral with a hint of late-afternoon warmth.

But where a decades-old hotel would have to take pains to emphasize its modern elements, to prove it had kept pace with the times, the Fullerton Bay is free to indulge in as much colonial romance as it can handle. And the building’s ground-up provenance means its lines are a bit more sensible, and its comforts perhaps more effortlessly delivered, than might be the case in an antique building — and the hotel’s bay views, it must be said, are even more extraordinary when viewed through modern floor-to-ceiling windows.

The Fullerton Bay’s three restaurants are impressive enough on the plate, and their visual environments are striking as well. Perhaps the most impressive views are to be had from the rooftop pool deck — from here you’ll survey the Singapore waterfront, a vista that seems to stretch back a century.

content:
High-end sustainability is de rigueur for newer Costa Rican hotels, and Los Altos Resort is no exception. Situated along the Pacific coast on twenty-one acres of rainforest adjacent to the Manuel Antonio National Park, Los Altos is noteworthy for using a relatively small amount of its own property for man-made intrusions. Excepting the hillside perch of the hotel proper, the grounds are untouched rainforest, all the way to the sea. With an expansive spa and ocean-view infinity pool, Los Altos caters to guests who like to venture out, as well as those who’d rather have the peace and serenity brought to them. 

Every suite is an airy, apartment-style living space decorated with tropical accents — palm fronds, rattan — that never feel belabored or kitschy. Big floor-to-ceiling windows open onto wide balconies, providing a panoramic view across the treetops to the ocean. The four-bedroom penthouse suites expand upon the standard accommodations’ more-than-ample offerings, with three levels of interior rooms accessed by private elevator, capped off by a personal jacuzzi terrace. 

It’s impossible not to work up an appetite exploring the hotel’s extensive hiking trails and swimming at the private beach. Karolos, the hotel’s restaurant and bar, continues the indoor/outdoor design motif and offers plenty of local dishes and refreshing cocktails. And if you somehow manage to experience everything the hotel has to offer, its proximity to the national park means that you’re never far from a fresh set of adventures.

Los Altos Resort is about a 2h30min drive from the San Jose International Airport.
