content:
Some Irish hotels lean heavily on the historical atmosphere, but we’re always happy to find one that’s comfortable acknowledging the passage of time. In the city of Cork, the Irish Republic’s southern seaport, there’s plenty of heritage to hold on to, but there’s also a healthy dose of modern luxury hospitality, if that’s the sort of thing you’re in the market for, in the form of The Doyle Collection’s River Lee Hotel.

No extra points for guessing the name of the river whose banks The River Lee Hotel hugs. It’s a slightly incongruous sight, this sleek modern building on the edge of this storied river, but once inside the interaction between the hotel and its setting becomes clear — there’s a coziness about The River Lee Hotel that’s all too often lost in contemporary-style hotels, and if it’s not too obvious to bother pointing out, there’s nothing better than a big modern picture window for a hotel room with a pretty view.

The River Club, the hotel’s bar, terrace, and restaurant attracts locals and guests alike, and there’s plentiful space for all sorts of gatherings and events. There’s also a fully equipped gym, complete with a 20-meter pool, sauna, steam room, and jacuzzi.

content: For the first Kimpton hotel in Canada the brand chose not Toronto’s downtown core but a rather less obvious location just to the north — Bloor Street, a setting that’s still convenient to downtown, but which is just to the west of Yorktown, and even closer to the University of Toronto. It’s a neighborhood that’s both upscale and bohemian, the perfect setting for a hotel to which the same adjectives apply. Here a former Holiday Inn has been transformed into one of the IHG sub-brand’s most unusual hotels: the Kimpton Saint George.\n\nGiven its heritage it’s perhaps no surprise that the Saint George is a substantial hotel: nearly 200 rooms and suites across 14 floors. Each unit, however, feels carefully considered, and with all the warmth and personality of a much smaller boutique operation — and the personable service, always a top Kimpton priority, lends an extra touch of intimacy. Frette linens and Atelier Bloem bath products nudge the rooms and suites ever closer to luxury territory. And the hotel’s single food and beverage outlet is a versatile one: the Fortunate Fox gastropub can handle everything from fish and chips to creative craft cocktails.

content: The growing Habitas hotel brand is a global one, and their first safari lodge, Habitas Namibia, is something of a break from the traditions of the genre — less formal, less structured, and ideally more focused on communal living and human connection than the classic safari-lodge experience. The game reserve it calls home is a work in progress, but its game drives are complemented by other activities that highlight Namibia’s various cultures as well as the land itself — and the wellness program, which includes yoga and meditation alongside typical spa treatments, benefits enormously from the stillness of the landscape.\n\nIts rooms are all actually freestanding structures, set on a hillside, overlooking the vast expanse of the savanna through floor-to-ceiling windows. Each one features its own private deck for a more direct view, and even the bathrooms look out over the landscape. There’s plenty of privacy to be had en suite if you want it — but the Habitas ethos is about bringing people together. To that end there’s a restaurant serving upscale Namibian fare and a selection of South African wines, and group excursions and activities are plentiful — though it’s always an option to book a solo spa treatment or simply lounge by the pool.

content: In the seaside town of Camden, Maine, 16 Bay View is just about as central as it gets. It’s just steps from the harbor, set in a century-old red-brick industrial building whose exterior remains lovingly preserved, even as its interiors have been thoroughly transformed. It’s mostly a functional transformation, dividing its spaces into boutique-style luxury-hotel rooms and suites, all designed and decorated in a style that complements the historic structure — despite details like gas fireplaces and built-in flat-screens, 16 Bay View retains an atmosphere that’s pleasantly reminiscent of its original era.\n\nThere’s some variation in size and layout, but they’re uniformly lavish, with high-end beds and bedding, spa-like bathrooms with heated floors, and a full complement of luxe comforts like Turkish Towel Company linens and Gilchrist & Soames bath products. Despite a location alongside one of Camden’s livelier streets, there’s plenty of privacy to be had, even in the street-facing rooms. And while there’s no shortage of places to eat and drink nearby, 16 Bay View’s own restaurant and bar, the throwback-style Vintage Room, is well worth your time — as is the harborside rooftop bar.

content:
Near the old Roman theater on Fourvière Hill, overlooking the Saône and the Lyon old town, the Villa Maïa may be classical in its inspiration, but it’s thoroughly modern in its execution. Its concrete structure was designed by Jean-Michel Wilmotte, decorated by Jacques Grange, and landscaped by Louis Benech, and the result is truly extraordinary, even among high-end luxury hotels.

Perhaps the clearest ancient Roman influence is found in the spa, whose columns and baths lend an old-world aspect to a very modern wellness experience. The rooms, in contrast, are decidedly contemporary-luxe in their style, with high-tech Japanese toilets and Carrara marble bathrooms. Views take in panoramas of the city’s rooftops, or else look out over Mr. Benech’s tranquil gardens. For a truly exclusive experience, the 100m2 apartment suite offers spacious rooms with an unparalleled view of the city.

The lounge, with its elegant bar of Saint-Just glass and polished nickel, offers a selection of wines from the nearby vineyard of Château de La Chaize, a 17th-century chateau that also makes a charming destination for tours. At dinner time, the hotel recommends the eponymous restaurant of chef Christian Têtedoie, located across the street, which has been recognized with a MICHELIN Star — here, in the capital of French gastronomy, a hotel like Villa Maïa would settle for nothing less.

The UNESCO-protected heart of Quito, Ecuador is spectacular enough that it hasn’t exactly suffered from its historical lack of cutting-edge design hotels. But with the advent of Carlota, it’s clear what we were missing: here a century-old landmark building is brought to life by contemporary architecture and transformed into a thoroughly modern boutique hotel, where classic mansion style and cutting-edge art and design combine to create a uniquely memorable hotel.

It’s named for owner Renato Solines’s grandmother, who moved in in the Sixties; this personal connection might have made it tempting to leave everything as it was, but Solines’s wife, architect Veronica Reed, took liberties with the structure and its style, tempering its lushness with hard-edged industrial gestures and modernist-inspired geometries.

Rooms vary widely, as is typical of heritage properties, from the compact Standard Simple all the way to the expansive suites and the top-of-the-line Loft — all of them combining arresting visuals and boutique comforts. And while a hotel of this small size can’t always be counted on for nightlife, Carlota has both a bistro, serving contemporary locally sourced fare, and a rooftop bar, from which you can survey the unique geography of Quito’s cityscape.

content:
It’s hidden in plain sight: Le Marche, to the east of Tuscany and north of Rome, attracts just a fraction of its neighbors’ tourism traffic. And it’s not for lack of appeal. Among Italians it’s known for having a little bit of everything, from rolling hills to dramatic mountains to idyllic beaches, from vineyards to medieval villages. In the foothills of the Sibillini Mountains, with an elevated view of much of the above, you’ll find Hotel Leone, an eight-room luxury boutique hotel that gathers together an astonishing variety of the things that make Italy special, all under one roof.

This means rooms and suites that are decorated in a luxe yet unpretentious style that’s at once contemporary and historically informed. It means a decided emphasis on the good life, whether that means in-room spa treatments or days spent by the poolside. And naturally it means a dedication, bordering on the fanatical, to matters of food and drink — from drinks or afternoon tea on the terrace to dinner in the courtyard to cocktails in the Art Deco bar or a tasting of the finest local wines. All of this with a view of the Adriatic coast, plus access to all that the region has to offer — it’s no wonder Le Marche’s moment in the sun has arrived.

content:
Tel Aviv is no stranger to contemporary design, nor to the tradition of 20th-century modernism — which is why it’s perhaps surprising that one of its finest new hotels is a renovation of an 1866 Ottoman-style classic in the American Colony district. But that’s the Drisco in a nutshell: named for the brothers who built the original Jerusalem Hotel, it’s a contemporary luxury boutique that’s blessed with a century and a half of historic heritage.

Rooms and suites are lavish, and not afraid of a bit of visual ornament — some feature carved headboards, others ornate tilework. The most unique rooms are those in the Villa Drisco, the wooden structure that adjoins the old Jerusalem Hotel, though that’s not to take anything away from the elegance of the main building’s units. Spaces are generous, thoughtful amenities like Nespresso machines and luxe marble bathrooms are universal, and the largest suites expand to a vast 65 square meters.

The lobby’s Drisco Bar is inspiring, with fans spinning beneath an ornate carved ceiling — it feels like the kind of place the foreign correspondents would have gathered, back when that was a glamorous job. And the award winning restaurant, George & John, pairs inspiration from modern Israeli cuisine with broader Mediterranean influences.

Kowloon’s historic center is ordinarily where you’d go for a trip back in time, for a taste of the traditional markets, architecture, and atmosphere, and for something a bit more dark and mysterious than ultra-modern Hong Kong Island. It’s against this backdrop that a hotel like Hotel Stage provides a sharp and welcome contrast.

The interiors are modern, minimalist, highly polished, decorated in a neutral palette that makes the most of the natural light that streams in through the oversized windows. Look closer, however, and you’ll see that, for all its modernist simplicity, this isn’t an example of a blank international style, oblivious to its setting — Hotel Stage is full of works by local artists and craftspeople.

Kitchen Savvy, the all-day restaurant, specializes in Italian cuisine, served in a sunny open-plan space with a pronounced European accent. Meanwhile Muse, the library and lounge, is a wine bar in a dark and clubby setting, serving European vintages surrounded by Hong Kong arts and crafts. And for a stronger dose of local flavor, you need only venture outside; Hotel Stage’s location in historic Kowloon places it close by to Tin Hau Temple, the Temple Street Night Market, and the Jade Market.

Newsflash: there are a lot of gorgeous resorts on Bali. What’s the particular attraction at Samabe Bali Suites & Villas in Nusa Dua? Two points: the clifftop location and the service. The resort is situated high above the water, meaning astounding views from most of the suites and villas — each of which is attended by a round-the-clock personal butler.
 
Samabe isn’t small, but it’s not especially large either: the resort contains 39 suites, seven penthouse villas and 35 freestanding villas. Then again, you can’t really have many more rooms than that when you’re offering this level of personalized service: a butler whisks away your bags, anticipates your thirst for fresh-squeezed juice, arranges afternoon tea or an early-evening happy hour on your terrace, should you desire, and stays at your beck and call even in the middle of the night. 

Accommodations run the range from the oceanfront Samabe Suite — with a king-sized bed and sprawling indoor-outdoor lounge space, including a huge soaking tub with views of the Indian Ocean and a private terrace with a telescope for stargazing — to the lavish Two-Bedroom Penthouse Pool Villa, with a name that pretty much speaks for itself. The look is crisp and modern, with warm Balinese-inspired design accents: smooth dark wood and bright white linens, candles glowing inside glass lanterns, a poppy-red loveseat, throw pillows covered in patterned textiles made by island artisans. Suites and villas all come stocked with thoughtful extras like sun hats and beach bags — but if unplugging completely in Bali isn’t your thing, there are also large LCD screens with DVD players, iPhone and iPad docks, and in-room wi-fi.
 
You probably won’t be yearning for a lot of extra services after checking into one of these lavish suites. But just in case, the complimentary amenities at Samabe Bali include breakfast in bed, classes in yoga or Balinese cooking, a fresh fruit platter delivered daily to your room, kayaks and windsurfing equipment, and 24-hour room service. Should you feel the urge to venture out of your own personal paradise, gourmet meals with a view are served on the patio, or inside the cool stone and timber interior, at the hotel’s restaurant, Rempah-Rempah (meaning ‘rich spices’ in Indonesian.)

How to get there:
Samabe Bali Suites & Villas is located 30 minutes by car from Ngurah Rai International Airport.

There’s plenty to say about the Hotel Eiger Mürrenitself, but perhaps the most remarkable thing about it is what’s outside the doors: its one-of-a-kind hometown. The Eiger is set in the tiny Bernese mountain village of Mürren, population 450. There isn’t even a road in. To get there, you take a funicular from one of the valleys below, or get off the train at the station across the street. Needless to say, you won’t be smelling a lot of tailpipe exhaust — just fresh Alpine air. As for traffic, the only sort you need to look out for will be gliding by on skis or a board. The ski trails pass right by the hotel. 

The Eiger has been in the same family since it opened, all the way back in 1886. Clearly they must be doing something right, and it all comes down to a focus on the fundamentals. The service is warm, the rooms simple and functional, and all the basic ski resort amenities are there, from a sunny indoor pool and jacuzzi with views of the mountains to a couple pleasant restaurants serving hearty Swiss fare and European classics. (Think warm fondue and steak Bearnaise.) 

This isn’t a place you come looking for avant-garde design theatrics or a Dom-popping après-ski scene — more like floral-print curtains and a cozy, almost homey little bar. And that’s fine. The idea is more to relax and rest up between days on the trails. Book well and, even when you’re indoors, the mountains will feel every bit as present, with their snow-capped peaks on view from bed. 

Please note: Hotel Eiger Mürren closes each year in April and May. 

How to get there:
The hotel is located directly across from the Mürren train station, and a five-minute walk from the center of the village. Alternatively, take the funicular from the town of Lauterbrunnen. The village is not accessible by car.

content:
There was a time in the not too distant past when reaching a tropical jungle paradise took a woeful lot of doing. Today you can have an early breakfast, board a morning flight from a major American city, and arrive in time for a mid-afternoon lunch at a place like Pico Bonito, where that hammock on the private verandah of your cabin is surrounded by four-hundred acres of wilderness on the Caribbean coast. And it’s no slouch of a wilderness; it’s a wilderness sluiced with mountain-fed rivers, punctuated by waterfalls dropping into swimming holes at the bottoms of canyons, and covered in a canopy ornamented with birds and butterflies — the kind of thing mid-winter screen savers are made of. 

None of the natural splendor would do a guest much good if Pico Bonito hadn’t also carved out miles and miles of hiking trails, with the occasional lookout tower for spotting birds and wildlife. There’s an expert staff to guide you through it all, too, whether you’re a serious birder (Audubon called Pico Bonito a place “where dreams come true”) or just want to go on a pleasant walk amidst the flora and fauna. The options for accessing the natural world go on and on — boat trips through a manatee reserve, snorkeling the world’s second-largest barrier reef, whitewater rafting a jungle river, to name just some of the aquatic options. 

The cabins are simple — lots of exposed wood, slatted windows, light filtering in through the canopy — but spacious and appropriate for the surroundings. What’s lacking in brass fittings and marble vanities is more than made up for by coastal breezes and the ever-present sounds of the jungle. Same goes for the restaurant, where the atmosphere is casual, unpretentious, and perfectly suited to the surroundings — tropical gardens below, birdsong all around, fresh seafood and local veggies on the plate. When you’ve got ingredients like this, it doesn’t take much finessing to make the recipe work. 

How to get there:
The Lodge at Pico Bonito is 2.5 hours away, by car, from San Pedro Sula airport. There is also a 30-minute commuter flight to La Ceiba, from San Pedro Sula airport.

content:
Kauri Cliffs is located at the northern edge of New Zealand's North Island, perched on a cliffside overlooking the Pacific and flanked by four thousand acres of rolling hilly farmland. Though it is perhaps best known for its world-class golf course, the resort's strengths are its remoteness and its grand elegance, both of which appeal to golfers and abstainers alike.

The golf course is the creation of owner Julian Robertson, once a successful Wall Street financier, who discovered this property (then a cattle ranch) during his novel-writing sabbatical during the Eighties. He returned after the dot-com Nineties irreparably damaged his flagship hedge fund, and though the Great American Novel may have eluded him, the Great Antipodean Golf Course has become a reality. This is due equally to the natural surroundings and to the efforts of designer David Harman, who has built courses for Arnold Palmer and Jack Nicklaus, and whose light touch on this marvelous course avoids the grand gestures of some gimmicky courses, instead letting the spectacular landscape speak for itself.

If the golf course is Mr. Robertson's child, then the hotel itself is the creation of his wife Josie, from the main lodge building (which would not look out of place in the Hamptons) to the outlying cottages, where the guest suites are found. The cottages line the edge of the golf course and face across it, toward the ocean, with dramatic views from private verandas. These suites are spacious and modern, elegantly appointed, with gas fireplaces and huge luxurious bathrooms. This is the sort of place that has “Security” rooms set aside for bodyguards and drivers — and even these second-class rooms would pass for five-star accommodations.

How to get there:

Kauri Cliffs is approximately a 4 hour drive from Auckland or 1 hour by helicopter. Alternatively the hotel is a 25 minute drive from Kerikeri Airport.

content:
Though it’s perhaps more quiet and more discreet than some of its neighbors, Hôtel La Ponche is a significant fixture on the St. Tropez hotel scene. Its small size — just 21 rooms and suites and three apartments — helps it keep its low profile, but in the middle of the last century it hosted everyone from Sartre and Picasso to Roger Vadim and Brigitte Bardot. 

Today, a thorough renovation by Fabrizio Casiraghi returns it to its former glory, and while it’s no period piece, it is possessed of a low-key glamour that’s by no means common, even in this part of the world. The accommodations are classically chic, with only subtle nods to modernity; the most desirable ones look out to sea, some via spacious terraces.

Massages and spa treatments are available, as are yoga and Pilates sessions against the backdrop of the sea. And the restaurant and bar sustains Hôtel La Ponche’s social life, from breakfast on through to last call, with a cocktail menu inspired by the hotel’s most famous former guests.

The Northeastern hoteliers Lark Hotels are well known across the region for their stylish and smart boutique hotels; among their offerings are a number of small-scale, residential-style guest houses, under the Blind Tiger banner. Blind Tiger Burlington exemplifies the form: a private home dating to the late 19th century, lovingly restored and updated with 14 bedrooms, each one unique, all of them combining period architecture with unique vintage details and original contemporary artworks.

Its location is a convenient one, close to both the University of Vermont campus and the city’s compact lakeside downtown district. The house itself, though, feels pleasantly secluded in a residential neighborhood, surrounded by lawns and gardens; indoor public spaces are plentiful as well, from the verdant solarium with its marble floors and abundant plant life to the barroom and the adjacent living room, where guests gather by the fireplace.

The residential concept means there’s no restaurant; guests help themselves to a light breakfast on site, and for lunch and dinner are directed to any number of fine local establishments. Your hosts know the town inside and out, and each room comes with a letter from a local resident with suggestions for your Burlington itinerary.

Montana’s Glacier National Park is greener than its name migh suggest, at least during summer, and from mid-June until mid-September it’s possible to sleep in upscale safari-camp style at Under Canvas Glacier, a collection of luxury tents outfitted with king beds, full private bathrooms, and wood-burning stoves. The Under Canvas concept has now spread all across America, and it’s a simple one to understand: luxury boutique hotel comforts and style, with a degree of outdoor immersion you can ordinarily only find at a self-serve campsite.

Of course conceiving it is one thing; it’s the execution that matters. And Under Canvas has proved to be quite capable at making this idea a reality. With proper king beds, modern en-suite bathrooms, and wood-burning stoves, the accommodations are not just more luxe but more stylish than typical national-park digs; the restaurant, too, is the sort of thing you’d ordinarily find only in a brick-and-mortar boutique hotel. And thanks to the fire pit and picnic areas, the Under Canvas experience is a social one as well — in a landscape as memorable as this, there’s no reason to settle for a forgettable lodging.

Please note: Under Canvas Glacier is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from mid-June through mid-September.

content: Picture an old limestone quarry sitting abandoned for years on Italy’s Gulf of Trieste, an eyesore on a beautiful stretch of Adriatic coastline near the Slovenian border. Then imagine, in its place, an exclusive seaside community rising up like a waterfront amphitheater, sustainably built, car-free, and centering around a five-star resort. The almost unbelievable transformation is the story behind Tivoli Portopiccolo Sistiana Wellness Resort & Spa. With a private beach club, an expansive spa, six stylish restaurants and bars, and just as many swimming pools — and just 58 rooms — it’s designed to feel like a utopia within a utopia. \n\nThe resort’s aesthetic was inspired by the Italian Modernist architect Gio Ponti. Rooms and suites are sleek and functional, calling to mind the look of an elegant turn-of-the-century ocean liner with a nautical color palette, curving lines, and polished wood furnishings. All feature luxurious marble bathrooms, some with soaking tubs, and many have private balconies overlooking the marina. Suites are especially palatial with details like garden terraces and outdoor Jacuzzis. Beyond the confines of the hotel, the picturesque and perfectly planned streets of Portopiccolo are lined with boutiques and wine bars, though it’s hard to beat the ambiance at Maxi’s, the resort’s all-white, open-air restaurant on the marina.

While Silicon Valley might be taking over this corner of California, tech culture hasn’t infiltrated every single house on the block. Case in point: the Stanford Park Hotel. As the name and the red-brick exterior indicate, it’s a hotel with closer ties to the Ivy League than to Facebook, a place where you’ll find rocking chairs on the front porch and old fashioneds served in crystal glasses, not virtual reality rooms and a burrito bar.

The hotel is, indeed, around the corner from Stanford University — a leisurely stroll or a quick bike ride or a three-minute drive, with complimentary bicycles and free parking at the hotel included — and it’s that collegiate air, that dignified sort of elegance, that informs the hotel’s style and character. 

The guest rooms, in other words, won’t be winning any awards for cutting-edge style. But they’re spacious and comfortable, smartly designed with large picture windows and working wood-burning fireplaces, stocked with down blankets and microfiber robes, flatscreen HDTVs, artisanal bath products by ROAM, a coffeemaker and a complimentary morning delivery of The Wall Street Journal. 

The better to keep you informed before you venture down to the Barista Lounge for espresso, or later, when you belly up to the bar at Menlo Grill Bistro, the Stanford Park’s classy restaurant. Better brush up on the headlines and the content, too. This is the intersection of Stanford and Silicon Valley, after all. You never know who you’ll bump into when you’re wading into the indoor swimming pool or working out in the fitness center, who’s enjoying a steak in one of the bistro’s leather armchairs, who’s sipping a craft cocktail out by the fire pit.

content: There’s more to Zorah Beach Hotel than just the name. Enormous country that it is, Brazil boasts enough beach to last a lifetime; this lesser-known stretch, Guajiru, is over 2,700 kilometers from Rio’s famous shores. Yet Zorah differs even from its laid-back, windsurfer-centric neighbors by virtue of curiously eclectic, wonder-cabinet design: its furniture, fixtures, and copious art objects were all sourced from similarly remote collectors or artisans in Bali, India, and the Middle East. Little Buddhas pop up everywhere, by turns mischievous and serene. Here, nature is almost cartoonishly gorgeous, balancing white-sand dunes with palmy tropicalia and temperate, outrageously blue waters. And the accommodations — 22 in all, split between suites, bungalows, and a villa — leave nothing at all to be desired. Even the humblest comes with a personal jacuzzi, a flatscreen, a Nespresso machine, a balcony, and a king-size bed with Egyptian cotton Trussardi linens and goose-feather pillows. Bathrooms are similarly lavish, featuring solar-heated rain showers with L’Occitane bath amenities. And if that’s somehow not enough, feel free to book a bungalow for the royal treatment: four-poster, private garden, two-seater jacuzzi, maybe even a gregarious toucan to keep you company (*toucan not guaranteed). The Asian character emerges quite strongly in the cuisine, favoring off-menu experiments with local seafood and produce. Then there’s the Beach bar, both pool- and beachside, perhaps the best spot for sunset-gazing and a delectably fresh cocktail. Fans of the bubbly will appreciate the hotel’s affiliation with a little brand called Veuve Clicquot. Maybe save that indulgence for after you’ve sampled the hands-on activities: Zorah retains professionals to guide you through horseback rides, sandboarding, buggy tours, and any variety of surfing (kite, wind, or original flavor). How to get there: Zorah Beach Hotel is located approximately 140 minutes by car from Pinto Martens — Fortaleza International Airport via CE-085.

content:
Pittsburgh consistently ranks high on lists of the most livable cities in the US, a fact that’s, at first glance, of only incidental interest to an in-and-out business traveler or New Yorkers dropping in for a friend’s wedding weekend. But it’s actually something of an endorsement for today’s travelers, who tend to combine business and leisure in every trip: apart from the relatively affordable cost of living, what’s so great about the Steel City, anyway? Go for a couple of days and you’ll get it. Poised at the intersection of three rivers, this once-gray city is now about green design and urban biking, the Mattress Factory art museum, Little Italy, craft beer produced in a recycled church. Today’s Pittsburgh is cool, and city developers know it, paving the way for thousands of new hotel rooms in recent years. The Hotel Monaco is one four new hotels opening around downtown’s Golden Triangle alone.

It’s a Kimpton hotel, so you know the drill. Bold design, friendly service, countless complimentary amenities, and a wink — lots of winks, in fact — to the location itself. Note the penguin-shaped lamps in unexpected places: that’s a shout-out, of course, to the city’s beloved ice hockey team. The Hotel Monaco is located inside a stately Beaux-Arts building that was once the headquarters of a law firm. And despite a nod to the architectural history — note the elegant molding and houndstooth drapery — it’s safe to say the atmosphere is a good deal more playful these days.

Guest rooms are vibrantly outfitted with vintage-inspired kelly green headboards, hand-painted black and white bedside tables, birdcage-shaped chandeliers, Italian Frette linens, classic leather armchairs, glass showers, and custom-made Monaco robes. Corner Spa rooms come with deep soaking tubs; lavish Emperor Suites are fit for a rock’n’roll posse. And thoughtful comforts are plentiful for all guests, including Kimpton’s signature in-room yoga mats and complimentary happy hour, plus cruiser bicycles that invite you to join the locals on their city bike baths.

Elsewhere in the hotel, there’s a state-of-the-art fitness center and a sleek restaurant, the Commoner, named after “the Great Commoner,” William Pitt. In fact, the hotel is practically a set-up for a scavenger hunt of Pittsburgh-related lore and legend. Guest rooms feature framed postcards and vintage memorabilia, and conference rooms after Jonas Salk, Rachael Carson, Roberto Clemente and Scott Fahlman. Who’s that last one, you ask? Oh, just a computer scientist from Carnegie Mellon University, best known as the inventor of the smiley face emoticon.

content: Every urban area has its nearby escapes where city dwellers of means can get away and relax. In the case of Bilbao, it’s Getxo, a seaside village where the industrial bourgeoisie built vacation villas at the turn of the century. One of the most notable was a palace on the cliffs overlooking the Bay of Biscay, an English-style landmark that’s since been transformed into the Palacio Arriluce Hotel. The aristocratic interiors have been carefully restored, the croquet lawn is perfectly manicured, the quaint library is stocked with rare books, and the spa pays homage to the neighborhood’s history as a wellness retreat. But bold updates, including the choice to turn the palace’s old chapel into a cocktail bar, give Palacio Arriluce a modern edge.\n\nMany rooms and suites are located in the original mansion, and feature period details like stained-glass panels, coffered walls, and wood-paneled window seats with sea views. Others in the adjacent pergola building come with private patios and gardens partly shaded by a stone colonnade. Across the board, the look is elegant and refined, with chevron wood flooring, high ceilings, velvet furnishings, and a nautical-inspired blue and white color palette. Breakfast is served, when weather permits, on a stone terrace facing the harbor, and a seasonal pool overlooks the bay. In colder weather, Palacio Arriluce’s cavernous wine cellar is a cozy spot for tasting local wines.

content:
Occupying a privileged spot on one of the prettiest plazas in Marbella’s Casco Antiguo, La Fonda Heritage Hotel is a stunner inside and out. The hotel is housed in a trio of 16th-century buildings that have served various functions over the years — church, school, private mansion — and their original features, from stately columns and stone archways to ceiling frescoes and tiled courtyards, remain rich with character, even while the interiors have been updated in a crisp modern-classic style.

Rooms are organized around a series of Andalusian patios, some of which are open to the sky and furnished with plush sofas and large potted plants. None of the hotel’s 19 rooms and suites are alike, but they all have a similar look: luminous, elegant, and contemporary, with wood-beamed ceilings, minimalist decor, and a near-monochrome color scheme. Bathrooms are particularly sleek with subway tiling, sophisticated lighting, and marble walk-in showers. Details like Dyson hairdryers and Marshall speakers are standard; some rooms feature free-standing soaking tubs, large private terraces with sunbeds, or smaller balconies with views over the city’s quaint rooftops and palm trees.

One of the covered patios, with vaulted, greenhouse-like glass ceilings, is home to the hotel’s atmospheric Mediterranean restaurant, and a breakfast buffet is set up amid cheerful greenery on an adjacent patio. Up on the rooftop — and open only on summer evenings — is a cocktail bar serving Spanish wines by the glass, with panoramic views over the old town and the sea beyond.

content:
We admit we never saw it coming, but Tbilisi, Georgia is now home to some of the most fully realized and authentically unique boutique hotels in the world. The Communal hotels make use of antique townhouses in some of the city’s most desirable old neighborhoods — in the case of Communal Plekhanovi, that’s Chugureti, a hip, creative district a short distance from Marjanishvili Square and Tbilisi State University.

With just 14 rooms it’s still guest-house-sized, and at that scale, a hotel can aim for a communal atmosphere without feeling crowded or chaotic. The style is a postmodern mixture of period architecture, classic fixtures and furnishings, and a very modern graphic color sense; no two rooms are alike, but the hotel presents a unified aesthetic and makes an impression that’s nothing if not memorable.

Speaking of communal experiences, there’s a substantial buffet breakfast that serves as an introduction to Georgian cuisine, and later in the day guests mingle in the bar and on the terrace. For lunch and dinner there’s Weller, the hotel’s restaurant, and while it’s worth making time for, it’s by no means the only one in town — the hotel’s vibrant location invites a bit of urban exploration.

content: Tulum has become something of a scene in recent years, as well known for attracting a crowd of influencers and DJs as for its deserted beaches and its once-pervasive tranquility. Ana y Jose Charming Hotel & Spa, however, helps its guests reclaim a piece of paradise. Located on the edge of the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve, the property is fifteen minutes’ drive from the city’s main hotel zone.\n\nThe rooms are a mix of palapa-style roofs and more conventional villas, many of which have views of the surrounding tropical gardens. Many of the buildings offer views of the tropical gardens surrounding the hotel, and a select few look straight out to sea. Here, it’s easy to escape the crowds: unwind on the hotel’s private beach, go for a swim in the infinity pool, or indulge in a Mayan mud wrap at the spa.

content: Set in Ljubljana’s charming city center, within a pedestrian-only neighborhood that has been settled since ancient Roman times, the Vander Urbani is a boldly designed boutique hotel occupying four adjoining townhouses.\nThe contrast between exterior and interior could hardly be sharper: behind a row of traditional Slovenian façades lies a high-design world of glass, chrome, and concrete. The hotel’s standout feature is its rooftop terrace, where contemporary touches — including an infinity-edge plunge pool and a glass-walled yoga studio — are paired with sweeping views over tiled rooftops, the lively streets below and the castle.\nAt street level, the hotel’s own restaurant is led by a French chef whose cooking shows a clear influence from Slovenia’s culinary traditions and agricultural abundance.

content:
In a region experiencing a hard-won renaissance after decades of hardship, Vigo’s Gran Hotel Nagari is a welcome surprise — a modern hotel with all the frills promised by the five imposing stars above its entrance. The hotel’s setting is likewise emblematic of the changing face of Galicia’s business and financial capital; it’s just a few blocks from Vigo’s busy fishing port on one side and a short walk to the growing business district on the other. There’s no question which of the two inspires the hotel’s style. 

In the entry-level Premium Lofts and slightly larger Demi Loft Suites, plush sheepskin rugs are about the only nod to the old Galicia; the rest is a cosmopolitan mix of inset lighting, gleaming surfaces and pared down, subtly Japanese-style décor. Black and white bathrooms, divided from the bedrooms by large glass walls, are stocked with Bulgari bath products. The Gold and Silver Master Suites are furnished with natural fabrics, luxurious silks and plenty of marble, with color schemes to match their names. 

A two-story spa straddles the line between modern and futuristic. There are a few simple, tranquil treatment rooms for everything from Ayurveda to Indonesian spice therapy, but the crown jewel is the rooftop pool. It takes the form of a circuit — sort of like a smaller, not-so-lazy river — fitted with swan-neck- and volcano-shaped features, bubble beds and a series of propulsive jets. If that’s not your speed, there are a couple heated jacuzzis, and by night the rooftop converts into a bar with excellent views of the city.


How to get there:
Gran Hotel Nagari Boutique & Spa is approximately 15 minutes away from Vigo Aiport.

It’s been a while since the New Sheridan Hotel was actually new — 1895, to be precise, which, in Colorado terms, is something like the late Middle Ages. That, obviously, is the key to its appeal: if you want to see what sets Telluride apart from the Rockies’ bigger, busier resort towns, there’s nowhere better to start than a hotel with a generous helping of historic charm, right smack in the middle of this picturesque little downtown, dominated by the looming peaks in the middle distance.

With 26 rooms and suites the New Sheridan keeps things cozy. The Deluxes come with king beds or two twins, and the suites add a sitting room to the mix. The interior-facing rooms are the most affordable, but the views are worth having — Telluride might be the most photogenic town in the Mountain West. 

The New Sheridan Bar has been a Telluride favorite for just about as long as there’s been a Telluride, and the Chop House goes straight for the Colorado classic dry-aged steaks. And while this town is a natural winter classic, it’s scarcely less inviting in summer, which means the New Sheridan is far more than just a ski lodge.


How to get there:
The New Sheridan Hotel is located in the center of town which is approximately 6 miles from Telluride Regional Airport and 70 miles from Montrose Regional Airport.

content:
Vanyavilas is an adventure resort, yes, and technically its 25 luxurious suites are tents, but you won't be roughing it here; these tents are as regally appointed as many hotels' penthouse suites. The tigers are the stars here — the property is located at the edge of Ranthambhore National Park, founded some forty years ago to protect (and showcase) the animals. The park's founder, Fateh Singh, visits nightly to lecture on the park's ecology and to talk about the day's sightings, and he should know — the tract of land where Vanyavilas sits was once his personal property.

This is, we suppose, camping, though on a scale unlike what we remember from childhood outings. The air-conditioned suites are enormous, 790 square feet beneath a vast canvas roof, and walled-in, resulting in an extraordinary degree of privacy. Teak floors and furniture straight out of British Colonial times round out the look, and the bathrooms are particularly over-the-top — as spacious as most city hotel suites, with a lone claw-foot tub in the center of the space.

The public spaces, including the impressive library bar, are in a central building decorated in the style of a royal hunting lodge. Here it is even more difficult to believe you are at the edge of a national forest, surrounded by frescoes and murals depicting the local wildlife. The food is excellent, served in the restaurant or in the courtyard, and while there is officially no room service, the standard of hospitality here is such that the staff will gladly serve your meal anywhere you desire.

As though all that were not enough, there is a heated outdoor pool and a spa to rival any in India. A tenth-century fort overlooks the grounds, and is a perfect destination for a hike, though most guests' minds will be on the tigers; sightings are frequent, and jeep safaris can be arranged (plan at least 60 days ahead). And do take advantage of Mr Singh's visits — it's a bit like getting to talk fish with Jacques Cousteau.

Please note: The hotel operates seasonally from October through June. 

How to get there: Vanyavilas is located in Sawai Madhopur. Rail lines run from Jaipur to Sawai Madhopur in approximately 2 1/2 hours and from Delhi in 5 hours. Vanyavilas is approximately 3 1/2 hours from Jaipur by car.

A boutique villa experience on an Indonesian island? It has to be Bali, right? Far from it — far, in this case, both figuratively and literally. This is central Java — just the next island over, in the hills outside Yoygakarta, the cradle of Javanese culture. And the setting for Villa Borobudur Resort is far in every sense from Bali’s busy beaches. Here in Java’s inland countryside, flanked by distant volcanoes, is Borobudur itself, the 9th-century Buddhist monument that makes this particular stretch of central Java one of Indonesia’s most culturally significant sites.

If you’re here to see Borobudur itself, you could do much, much worse than these six villas — five of them traditional joglo pavilions containing double bedrooms and private bathrooms, and one, Villa Diponegoro, a more self-contained residential-style villa with its own pool and staff. And if, on the other hand, you’re simply here to get away, you won’t be able to avoid seeing Borobudur — the property’s dramatic vistas include views of the temple. Tours, needless to say, can be arranged, and there’s no shortage of other outdoor activity to go along with it — hiking, rafting or bicycling, say, followed by a spa treatment and a meal or an Indonesian cooking class back at the hotel. The meals, by the way, are included in the rate, full board being Villa Borobudur Resort’s interpretation of the local custom of offering house guests something to eat and drink. Once you’ve gotten used to traditional Javanese hospitality like this, Bali will be the last thing on your mind.

How to get there:
Adisucipto International Airport (JOG - Yogyakarta) is located 45 km from Villa Borobudur Resort. The Adi Sumarmo International Airport (SOC - Solo) is located 90 km away.

content:
If you’re after a sense of escape, it’s probably not a bad idea to choose a hotel without an address — no number, no street name, not even a postal code. All the better if it’s situated on a tiny tropical island in the Indian Ocean, one lined with white sand beaches, practically exploding with palm trees and named for a mountain of a hue so jungly green that it’s hard to imagine it existing outside the tropics. That location, of course, is exactly what you’ve got at the Dinarobin Beachcomber, an all-suite, colonial style resort on Mauritius’s Le Morne peninsula. 

On a lesser tropical island the setting would probably be enough, but this is Mauritius, and the competition among luxury hotels is full-starch stiff. The result: four restaurants, including one where you can wear dress shoes if you like, and another where you can sink your toes into the sand, a sprawling spa amidst gardens and pools at the foot of the mountain, and enough sports (bocce, tennis, sailing, diving…) to occupy several Mauritian Olympic teams. Oh, and along with their nearby sister hotel on the Morne, they’ve got their own eighteen-hole golf course, the aptly named Paradis. Put a little extra power behind your stroke and you might end up wading toward your ball in the turquoise-blue water of the Indian Ocean, on soft white sand, beneath the shade of a stand of palm trees — not exactly the worst punishment for missing the green. 

There’s plenty to do, but the postcard-perfect beaches are ultimately the reason all these outstanding hotels are in Mauritius. At the Dinarobin, you can enjoy it up close under the shade of a straw parasol, or from a not-too-distant distance in your suite. All rooms, starting with the entry-level junior suite, face the water and come with covered balconies or terraces, so you can gaze at the water until it inevitably calls you in. Opt for a beachfront suite for unobstructed views and step-out access to the sand. The senior suites are designed to feel like a private apartment. They include a master bedroom, a large terrace with an overhanging straw roof and rattan furniture, a lounge area and an enormous bathroom that has a tub from which you can watch palm trees sway on the other side of a bay window. It all makes for a rather cushy hideout if you don’t want to be found for a while — yet another good reason to stay in a place without an address. 




How to get there:
Dinarobin Beachcomber Golf Resort & Spa is located 70 km (1h15min) from the Sir Seewoosagar Ramgoolam International Airport. The hotel offers a few transportation options.

content:
When you see the Taj group talking about palace hotels, it’s best to sit up and take notice. It’s taking nothing away from their more contemporary business-oriented hotels to say that over-the-top fantasy hotels like the Taj Falaknuma Palace are where their comparative advantage lies. For one thing, they’ve got impeccable taste in palaces; this one, with its English architecture, French tapestries and Venetian chandeliers, still belongs to what remains of Hyderabad’s royal family, and is among India’s most opulent residences.

It’s divided into just sixty rooms and suites, leaving each one with plenty of square footage. Here the Taj approach pays dividends as well, the company’s somewhat conservative house style tempering the extravagance of the palace’s common spaces, leaving the guest quarters extremely elegant yet eminently livable. The standard rooms are far from poky, but it’s the grand suites that really spread their wings, with their cavernous spaces, their top-shelf luxuries and their panoramic views of the city (these last thanks to the palace’s privileged location, on a hilltop on Hyderabad’s fringes).

However sedate the room interiors may be, in the palace’s public spaces, all bets are off. The dining rooms are nothing short of majestic, as is the Jade Room, the venue for the afternoon tea service. The endless ballrooms lend an air of glamour to any bit of business, and the spa, often somewhat neglected in Indian luxury hotels, is here given the attention it deserves.

content: It’s a conscious rekindling of the romance once contained in the phrase “going up to the ’Varsity.” Established by a quartet of Cambridge graduates, The Varsity Hotel & Spa is a modern building, but through its floor-to-ceiling windows you’re steeped in the old Cambridge — you’re practically on top of Magdalene College, and you’re not much farther from St. John’s, Trinity or Jesus. And while it’s the views that largely make the atmosphere, the hotel does an admirable job of fitting itself to its surroundings, with rooms named for Cambridge (and Oxford) colleges and decorated with portraits of alumni.\n\nNeedless to say, it’s quite a few steps up from typical student digs. The look is contemporary, with a modern English taste in bold accents, patterned wallpapers and antique tubs in modern bathrooms. They’re fully wired as well, with iPod docks and game systems — and you can’t host visiting academics without wi-fi. There’s a spa as well as a pretty remarkable gym in an antique brick-walled space, and the restaurant is of the impressive modern British variety which has finally put an end to the old quips about UK cuisine. All in all it’s a strong package, one that would come top of the class in most any town — that it’s in Cambridge, and this particularly scenic part of Cambridge no less, makes it truly extraordinary.

content:
There’s history, and then there’s history. Fawsley Hall has had its share of famous guests, but its Queen’s Suite is dedicated to none other than Elizabeth I, who last checked out in 1575. The old house has Victorian, Georgian and Tudor wings — all of which were contemporary at the time they were built.

That’s not to say you won’t find plenty that’s modern about the place. While the suites are the original article, as are many of the better rooms, Fawsley Hall contains nearly three dozen contemporary-styled rooms, in the main house, the converted stable block, and the spa building. In the older rooms there’s nothing in the way of décor that couldn’t have been installed in the 19th century or earlier; meanwhile the contemporary rooms mix a sedate, slightly minimalist style with modern facilities and occasional period details.

It’s ever so slightly on the large side for an English country house hotel, but that’s not a disadvantage. Guests are served by a fine restaurant as well as the extensive grounds, a first-class spa, and even a small screening room, with films regularly shown on the weekends. And if it was good enough for Elizabeth I….

content:
Until recently the Anantara resorts were pretty much confined to the lush environs of Thailand, the Maldives and Indonesia; their move into the United Arab Emirates comes as something of a surprise. And we’re not even talking about a hotel on stilts off some island in the Gulf — the Anantara Resort & Spa Qasr Al Sarab is an oasis an hour and a half outside of Abu Dhabi, in the middle of the Liwa Desert, which is part of the Empty Quarter, the biggest stretch of bare sand in the world.

So this one definitely isn’t lush. What it is, however, is plush: the most basic rooms are very big indeed, with oversized soaking tubs and stunning views of the dunes, while the suites and villas, it’s fair to say, remind you rather forcefully that you’re in the Emirates, a place that’s not shy about luxury. Space is absolutely not an issue, and the comforts go above and beyond anything you could rightly expect.

You don’t venture this far out into the desert unless you’re in search of some peace and quiet. The Anantara spa goes a long way towards scratching that particular itch, as does the infinity pool, and these are the sort of rooms and suites you could quite comfortably shut yourself in for days at a time.

content:
This isn’t grey postwar Milan, but sunny seaside Milano Marittima, on the Adriatic Riviera along the east coast of Emilia-Romagna. Here the Design Hotel Waldorf sits just yards from the beach, showing off a different side of Italy, that of the sun-drenched tropical escape. It’s on the outskirts of Cervia, perfectly positioned between the monuments of Ravenna and the oceanside excess of Rimini, sharing the same holiday-friendly weather but with quite a lot less cookie-cutter beach-club development.

The hotel itself certainly lives up to its “design” billing, from the vaguely space-age circular building to the simple modernist lines and curves of its furnishings and interior design. Interiors are a collaboration between a poet and a mosaic artist, which makes for a welcome change from the boutique-minimalist norm. There’s plenty of white space to make the most of the sunshine, and colorful lighting effects keep the rooms and the public spaces from feeling too empty.

Each of the 30 rooms and four suites comes with a balcony, most with sea views; suites add spacious, jacuzzi-equipped terraces with a SPA cabin, and the Diamond Suite comes with a private rooftop pool. Sun, sand, seafood — surely it’s a concept we can all get behind, and it’s no surprise that the Italians can do it just as well as anyone else.

content: In quick succession, the lifestyle brand Miiro unveiled a collection of stylish hotels in Paris, Barcelona, and Gstaad, all based on the concept of connection to place. On the edge of Parc de la Ciutadella in Barcelona’s artsy El Born neighborhood, that means a charming 19th-century building, interiors reimagined by a former design director at Soho House, Spanish wine and cheese by small organic producers, and a stylish rooftop terrace with a bespoke egg sculpture beside the pool. \n\nRooms come with Catalan-style timber flooring, hand-crafted beds, cozy reading corners, rainfall showers with Le Labo products, and pieces by local artists. Many have spacious private terraces with views over the park. A chic library and 24-hour fitness center add to the appeal, and the hotel’s Refresh Room, with its changing rooms and showers — standard across all Miiro properties — is a lifesaver, whether before check-in or after check-out.

content: Romance depends on a little bit of mystery, and at Oh la la! Hotel it starts when you arrive. Rather than stroll into a street-level lobby, you’ll walk through a cocktail bar on Place de la Bastille and push against a bookcase that opens a secret door. From there, it’s up a spiral staircase — there’s no elevator — to the upper levels of this one-time apartment building, now shaped into bright rooms overlooking the square. It’s practically the definition of bohemian-chic, which is just what you’d want from a budget-friendly boutique hotel in a lively section of Paris. \n\nRooms are compact, and the aesthetic is minimalist, with blonde wood floors, white walls, and design accents in royal blue and slate gray. The beds are slightly elevated on platforms, and floor-to-ceiling windows let in plenty of natural light; triple rooms, with two separate sleeping areas, occupy the full width of the hotel’s building. Many have views over the square below, though those facing an interior courtyard are quieter at night. Bathrooms are modern and practical, with walk-in showers and L’Occitane products. Apart from breakfast, happy hour, and a few helpful staff members down at the bar level, there's not much more to Oh la la! than simple, stylish lodgings with easy access to cafés, restaurants, and a metro station where you can hop on a train to pretty much anywhere in the city.

Born in London, refined in New York, and now expanding across the world, the Soho House concept is a modern twist on the classic London members’ club — instead of Victorian gentlemen it caters to men and women from all walks of life, with a particular preference for the glamorous creative industries. In Nashville, of course, that means the music world — not only is Music City full of clubs and live venues, it’s full of musicians and recording professionals as well.

Soho House Nashville makes its home in a Bauhaus-inspired red brick industrial building that must have been the most picturesque sock factory in America; this explains the name of the Sock Room and Terrace, an indoor/outdoor performance space that hosts the lion’s share of the House’s entertainment. This, along with Soho House’s other stylish and vibrant public spaces, is open to members only — the good news, for hotel guests, is that a room key makes you a member for the night.

Those rooms, in typical Soho House style, are no mere afterthought. The style is inimitable, thoroughly contemporary but with plenty of retro influence, and the comforts, though not ostentatious, are quietly on the level of any big-name luxury hotel. Meanwhile those famous public spaces are packed with an incredible collection of contemporary art — not least Club Cecconi’s, the signature Northern Italian restaurant that’s a staple of Soho Houses all around the world.

content: Voco Seoul Gangnam is a fine introduction both to IHG’s fashion-forward luxury boutique hotel brand and to the most famous neighborhood in the South Korean capital. The look is vibrant but still restrained; accents in indigo and gold pop against a backdrop of warm neutrals, while touchable textures banish any thought of minimalism. Given the liveliness of the neighborhood you’ll likely spend many an evening out, but the hotel’s restaurant, Amarillo, acquits itself nicely, serving everything from bao buns to Italian pastas.

content:
Though the Emirates may top the charts when it comes to sheer extravagance, there’s a case to be made for Oman as the Arabian Peninsula’s capital of cool hotels. It’s blessed with extraordinary landscapes, a rich cultural heritage, and a prime coastal location at the edge of the Indian Ocean — and the last of these is the variable that best explains the appeal of the Al Baleed Resort Salalah by Anantara.

Salalah is a surprisingly tropical place, and the Al Baleed sits on a perfectly idyllic strip of palm-dotted sand, between the sea and a freshwater lagoon. The hotel itself is meant to recall an ancient fortress, but it’s a rather welcoming fortress, and its rooms combine locale-specific crafts and decoration with a generous helping of contemporary luxury. The result is impressive indeed but somehow never quite ostentatiuos, even in the sprawling beach villas — though we’ll allow that the three-bedroom Royal Beach Villa might just edge over the top.

In addition to the predictably complete selection of luxury-resort services — a massive Anantara spa, a handful of Asian, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern restaurants, and more beach activities than we’ve got space to list — the Al Baleed’s location offers proximity to some extraordinary landscapes as well as some cultural treasures. There’s an archaeological site practically next door, there’s a mountain range and an endless desert to explore, and seafaring options include diving, kayaking, and dolphin-watching excursions.

content:
The Bay of Kotor’s history is colorful, to say the least, but neither pirates nor the Venetian empire threaten any longer — hence the swelling fleets of superyachts, hence the feverish development on the Tivat waterfront, and hence Regent Porto Montenegro, the hotel portion of a sprawling nautical village/dining/shopping/entertainment compound. The region’s days as a Yugoslav Navy shipyard are long gone; nowadays the pleasure-palace vibe reigns supreme, all part of Canadian tycoon Peter Munk’s vision to erect a “Monaco of the southern Adriatic.”

A tall order, it’s true, but again, the historic heritage carries plenty of weight. Meticulously polished local stone, copious arch-play, and terra-cotta roofing lend a distinctly neoclassical flavor to the edifice, ostensibly to channel the grand Italian palazzos of yore. In the rooms, Tino Zervudachi cranks up the maritime with Venetian striped textiles, hardwood flooring, and a boatload of nautical blue. The deep soaking tubs more than suffice in terms of aquatic relaxation, and the gentle surf will doubtlessly lull you to sleep in tandem from your berth in the luxe king bed. You don’t have to feel as if you’ve even left your yacht, in other words, though you’re beyond help if the balcony view doesn’t do anything for you.

The view is arguably better, however, from the Dining Room, a Mediterranean-Montenegrin fusion spot with intriguing al-fresco possibilities; rouse that appetite beforehand with some bubbles at the Library Bar, then return to ease down afterwards with small plates and an impressive selection of top-shelf reliables. An on-site pâtisserie should have your sweet tooth covered, and any guilt can surely be worked off at the fully equipped fitness center or the extensive spa facilities. Us, we’d opt for more drinks at the outdoor infinity pool.

In a world that’s increasingly full of inventive little boutique hotels, it’s easy to lose sight of the traditional strengths of the classic grand hotel. And while the Abano Grand Hotel might not spend much time on the covers of the contemporary design magazines, it’s something of a beacon for spa-goers from Padua and the Veneto, who flock to the town of Abano Terme in search of some healing waters and some old-fashioned five-star luxury.

The surrounding parkland sets a stately mood, as does the hotel’s fairly majestic wedding-cake facade, and while the exterior is all 20th century, the interiors take on a Baroque aspect, festooned with marble, parquet floors and antique furnishings and chandeliers. It’s a conservative look, to be sure, but for more than a few travelers this style is the essence of upscale hospitality.

And whatever your tastes, there’s no arguing with the Abano’s creature comforts. Restaurants include one fine dining room and one more casual poolside eatery, and a terrace bar is the natural setting for an aperitivo. Pools number no fewer than three, of outdoor, indoor and thermal varieties. And those healing waters are the centerpiece of the Abano’s spa program, where modern treatments meet the classic medicinal approach, and all of Padua lines up to take the cure.

content: The Hôtel de Montesquieu, an elegant boutique hotel just off the Avenue des Champs-Elysées, is a particularly fine expression of the Haussmannian vision. Its design adheres to the Baron’s rules — a symmetrical cut-stone facade, a height of no more than six stories, decorative balconies, and attic apartments on the uppermost level. While the collective objective is uniformity, the hotel’s interiors are one-of-a-kind, balancing traditional charm with a pared-down, almost minimalist sensibility. \n\nSuites have their fair share of antique furnishings, sumptuous brocade drapery, and original French artwork, but they’re modern, too, with pale parquet flooring and bold accent walls in shades of burnt ochre, mustard yellow, and charcoal gray. Some have balconies and sleek four-poster beds, while others have seating areas with mint-green paneling and jewel-toned sofas. The attic-level rooms are cozy, quaint, and sunshine-filled. On the ground floor, a space reserved for a shopping gallery in classic Haussmannian style, the Hôtel de Montesquieu features a series of opulent lounges for breakfast, tea, and cocktails.

The Soho House phenomenon, born in the 1990s at the original Greek Street club, has gone global, and now comes in multiple varieties, including urban-luxe creative-industry hothouses and laid-back beach-house escapes. Soho House Mumbai, as it happens, is a little bit of both; set in the glamorous suburb of Juhu, it’s within easy reach of Mumbai’s artists and other creative professionals, even as it stands just yards from the waters of the Arabian Sea.

Inside you’ll find 38 rooms decorated in a style that marries the country-house vibe that is Soho House’s specialty with an outspoken Indian sensibility. The Small rooms are not really all that small, and the largest ones are large indeed — and all of them come with balconies facing either the city or the sea.

More to the point, the public spaces are fantastically rich with detail, and contain a vast amount of art by contemporary Indian artists. There’s an impressive gym on the second floor, and the restaurants are a large part of Soho House Mumbai’s appeal — not only Cecconi’s, the Northern Italian restaurant that’s open to the public, but also the members-only Club restaurant, which serves Soho House favorites alongside Indian and Mediterranean specialties.

content:
It’s not often thought of as one of the most glamorous professions, but the 19th-century notary who lived at Moerstraat 54 in Bruges had impeccable taste; the old family residence is now a lovely little nine-suite luxury bed and breakfast. The Notary is not just well-preserved but has been in many places improved; the antique atmosphere remains intact, but turning its existing rooms into modern guest suites was no small task.

Each one is entirely different in its theme and décor, incorporating a wide array of stylistic influences. Still, disparate as they are, they feel unified in their aesthetic, which is ornate but sedate, and anything but minimalist — in that way, rather like Bruges itself. And for all the classic ambience, the suites’ comforts are as modern as can be, as befits a contemporary restoration.

All of the suites also benefit from the work of the house’s kitchen. Chef Youssef Zairi prepares an elaborate breakfast that highlights traditional Belgian flavors, and the Sunday afternoon tea service is a highlight (and requires a reservation). Meanwhile, the cocktail bar serves its creations both indoors and outdoors — in summer, in the house’s hidden garden, by the side of its idyllic little pond.

content: Once the neighborhood of Miguel Cervantes and other titans of Spanish letters, Madrid’s Barrio de las Letras is also home of Gran Hotel Inglés, the city’s oldest luxury hotel, welcoming guests since 1886. It’s unassumingly tucked away on the narrow, brick-laid Calle de Echegaray, and in its modern incarnation it styles itself an urban oasis — hence the Sisley spa. The interiors, by New York’s Rockwell Group, pay tribute to the Art Deco era, with brass accents, geometric ornaments, and rich, dark hardwood floors, along with custom textiles, lamps, and furniture. The glamorous lobby bar, with sleek leather stools arranged around a circular marble counter and a dramatically illuminated liquor shelf suspended from the ceiling like an art installation, makes a striking first impression — and in a concession to the steady stream of madrileños passing through for drinks, there’s plenty of space nearby to relax with a gin and tonic on a Chesterfield sofa or a velvet armchair. \n\nRooms are similarly elegant with parquet floors and a 1920s-inspired white, bronze, and silver color scheme. Charming details evoke days gone by: decorative wall panels, tufted headboards, vintage valet stands, champagne flutes, and clawfoot tubs in upgraded rooms. The quietest quarters face the inner courtyard, though there's an undeniable appeal to those with small balconies looking out over the street. One upper-level suite is both palatial and garret-like, with steeply slanted ceilings and a private terrace with a Jacuzzi, and the penthouse suite has a formal dining room and a fully stocked bar. For everyone else, there are the many bars and restaurants of Barrio de las Letras just steps away. The neighborhood is a culinary destination, and the hotel is part of the scene, offering forward-thinking Iberian cuisine at the stylish LobByto.

content:
A former farmhouse in the Champagne countryside, the Domaine de Barive sits surrounded by expansive grounds which combine the untouched nature of a wooded park with more manicured French gardens. With a mere 21 rooms and suites it’s rather on the intimate side as lodgings go — but with this much space there’s rather more to it than just the bedrooms.

For their part, though, the rooms and suites are fine ones, ranging from the cozy Classic rooms up under the eaves to the truly spectacular Royal Suite; all are comfortable, to say the least, and are decorated in a pleasing blend of antique elegance and contemporary cool. The bathrooms, in particular, tend toward the lavish, and are modern as can be.

There’s also room here for a proper spa, complete with a pool, a gym, and a sauna, as well as a balneotherapy bath with space for two. And ranking highly among the Domaine’s attractions is the gastronomic restaurant Les Épicuriens, where apéritifs are served in the lounge or on the terrace, and whose dining room looks out over the estate’s park.

content: There are hotels where the name really does just about say it all. Away Chiang Mai Thapae Resort - A Vegan Retreat leaves you in little doubt as to what to expect. The setting, obviously, is the northern Thai city of Chiang Mai, specifically a quiet lane within the walls of the old town, near the Tha Pae Gate. And Away is one of a growing number of hotels and resorts that are catering to travelers who want more than just a handful of vegetarian menu options — in fact, in strict Thai Buddhist style, neither meat nor alcohol are served here.\n\nAway’s 39 rooms and suites are decorated in a contemporary colonial-influenced style, full of modern comforts, and each one has its own private balcony. Some open directly onto the hotel’s pool, and all feel comfortably insulated from the busy city streets. From here you’re well placed for a tour of the Sunday market, or you can stay in and take a Thai cooking class — no pressure, though, as those who prefer to have their cooking done for them will enjoy a wide range of Thai and Western dishes, made with all-vegan (and, as far as is possible, organic) ingredients.

content:
In the heart of Old Saigon, there’s a wrought-iron footbridge with a charming name — Cầu Mống, or Rainbow Bridge — that was built by Gustav Eiffel in 1882,  just a few years before the French architect designed his his iconic tower for the 1889 Exposition Universelle. Today it’s a historical landmark and a favorite venue for photographers and romantics. It’s also the starting point for your stay at An Lâm Retreats Saigon River. The hotel is located twenty minutes away from here, mind you, but you’ll get there by boat, and that boat departs from Cầu Mống Pier. 

Getting there is half the fun, as they say, and you might agree with the sentiment as the speedboat zips along the tributary and merges onto the Saigon River. But that’s before you’ve actually seen the hotel. A short ride upstream, on a curving, lushly forested stretch of shoreline, you’ll spot the wooden dock of An Lâm Retreats Saigon River. That trip was nice, you might think, but it’s decidedly not half as fun as the experience of staying the night at the destination. The boat, after all, didn’t have a personal butler or a private plunge pool. Or a king-sized four-poster bed with a canopy.

Quiet and elegantly appointed, An Lâm Saigon River has the feel of a private retreat with the amenities of a luxury resort. It’s relatively small, with suites and villas (they call them “sanctuaries”) generously spaced out amid tropical gardens. All are outfitted in natural wood and stone, with private sun decks facing the river or forest, and the occasional modern armchair or table designed by An Lâm. (Lâm is the hotel’s owner, but in another life, he was a furniture maker, and the hotel was his private residence.) Wi-fi access and in-room entertainment systems with film libraries come standard, as does round-the-clock butler service. Pool Suites, as the name says, come with private plunge pools, and on the highest end of the An Lâm spectrum are a pair of villas whose assets are self-explanatory: the Riverfront Pool Villa and the Sunset Villa.

Also riverfront is Tram’s Cookery, an indoor-outdoor restaurant with Vietnamese and international dishes made from local and organic ingredients. It’s a fine place to unwind after a busy day of sightseeing and shopping in the city – the speedboat leaves for Old Saigon three times daily — or to rouse yourself after a busy afternoon of lying on a circular chaise lounge beside the swimming pool.

content:
In recent memory Sri Lanka was a fairly obscure locale for a holiday. But now that seems a very long time ago. Today it’s an absolutely first-class luxury destination, especially the Dutch colonial town of Galle, on the island’s south coast. It’s home to a picturesque fortress, with battlements surrounding the old town, and now it’s home to a Fortress of another kind — this one a luxury resort, whose fortifications today serve only a symbolic purpose.

Many of its local competitors are mom-and-pop affairs, which are great for casual intimacy. The Fortress is bigger, just under fifty rooms, and feels a bit more like a resort, albeit a small one — there’s a full-service spa, for example, complete with yoga pavilion and fitness center, and amenities include round-the-clock room service and a pillow menu. Several dining venues serve everything from Sri Lankan cuisine to wood-fired pizza. 

It’s still got plenty of personality, though, with the rooms outfitted in a striking and vaguely retro modernist style. Here raising the luxury stakes hasn’t compromised the experience at all — who could complain about Bose home theaters and in-room espresso machines, just a few steps away from the beach?

How to get there:
The Fortress is a four hour drive from Bandaranaike International Airport. Contact the hotel for airport transfer requests.

content: OKU Kos is an adults-only hideaway that takes the classic village idiom in a decidedly contemporary direction. The rooms and suites are divided among a number of crisply geometric villas, while in their interiors they’re warmed by earth tones, natural textiles, and a general boho-chic vibe. The best suites come with private pools, and the most extravagant units are the beachfront villas; at all levels, though, the accommodations are luxurious, if quietly so. \n\nWellness, of course, is a particular concern here, on the island where Hippocrates was born; the hotel’s offerings include a spa, a hammam, and a fitness and yoga studio, as well as an indoor swimming pool to complement the main outdoor pool. To Kima, the restaurant, serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner in an inviting indoor-outdoor space.

content:
Hotel Metropolitan stands as a bastion of ultra-modern Italian minimalism in downtown Bologna — a refreshingly sleek, African-tinged design hotel in a city that tends to lay the classical richness on pretty thick. A quick walk from the hotel proper and you’ll find a quiet annex, Met’s Apartments, which transfers the hotel’s attention to detail and impeccably crafted urbanity to fully equipped spaces for guests who value the kind of privacy that only apartment-style living affords.

The ten suites are designed according to the modernist principles that seem to be a particular strength of Italian hotels, taking the expected black-and-white palette and wringing an almost retro-futurist environment out of marble, glass, and tile. There’s something cozy about its simplicity, with a black curtain to cordon off the second bedroom and plenty of little nooks for working, reading, or kicking back to watch the sizable flat-screen TV. Don’t expect a cavernous drawing room lined with Renaissance statues, but the living space is fairly expansive for this sort of thing — there’s certainly enough room to host a small dinner party.  

For those who’d like to take advantage of the Apartments’ conveniences without all the cooking and cleaning, the Metropolitan Hotel’s facilities are easily accessible, from concierge service to dining to a steady rotation of clean linens and towels. Outside, the apartment’s central Bologna location makes for an easy trip to a wealth of cultural and culinary landmarks. And when you get tired of exploring, you’re not just going back to a hotel — pick up a bottle of wine and remind yourself that, at least for a little while, you’ve got an apartment in Bologna.

content: While completing a project near the fishing village of Cefalù in the late 1960s, a Sicilian engineer fell in love with the green hills of the island’s rugged northern shore. He bought a piece of land to build his dream house, and half a century later, it’s still in the family — now in the form of a charming boutique hotel, Le Calette, run by his daughter, her husband and their daughter. The name refers to the wildly beautiful setting overlooking the coastline's craggy coves, and the architecture follows the landscape’s lines, with whitewashed Mediterranean villas curving around the cliffs and winding paths leading down to secluded beaches. \n\nRooms are calm and bright, their minimalist interiors enlivened by artisan-made textiles and locally produced art. Some open onto private gardens with Jacuzzis, and suites feature spacious furnished terraces with dramatic views over the bay. Fragrant citrus trees and cheerful bougainvillea frame the hotel’s pool deck and open-air restaurants, and, from June to September, a complimentary shuttle whisks guests away to Le Calette’s private beach on the seafront of Cefalù.

content: Valencia’s Old Town has some fine historic hotels, but perhaps none as notable as this one, set in a 14th-century Gothic palace that served as the private mansion of the Marquis de Caro. It’s the city’s only historical monument hotel, and Caro Hotel leans into the official designation, proudly showcasing a 12-century Arabic wall in its restaurant and medieval coffered ceilings and Moorish archways in the guest rooms. The otherwise modern and minimalist design, with monochromatic decor and sophisticated lighting, evokes the stage-like atmosphere of a contemporary art gallery — all the better to let the building’s historical elements shine. The chic library and multiple outdoor terraces, one with a plunge pool, add to the appeal, as does Xanglot Restaurant, a striking restaurant where both the design and the cuisine take inspiration from the city’s Roman, Arabic, and Christian roots.

content:
It’s not the first thing you might think of when you hear the words “Jersey Shore,” but this stretch of coastline contains a few moments of tasteful stylishness. The town of Bradley Beach, just to the south of Asbury Park, is home to The James Bradley, an improbably fine piece of boutique hospitality, a chic enclave just a block from Ocean Avenue, the boardwalk, and the beach.

The hotel is a labor of love for an owner who grew up vacationing on the Jersey Shore, and who found this old Victorian house too tempting to ignore. After a very thorough renovation it’s been decorated in a style that’s unlike anything else around, its minimalist, neutral-toned interiors serving as a calm backdrop for an eclectic array of modern design furniture as well as vintage and custom-made pieces, and an art collection that’s remarkably serious. Like many of the finest boutique hotels it’s hard to quantify its appeal, but easy to feel the care with which every detail has been chosen.

The James Bradley serves a thoughtfully chosen continental breakfast on weekdays, and a more substantial cooked breakfast on weekends. Given the location, within walking distance of no end of dining and drinking venues, there’s no need for much more on site; all the better for preserving the hotel’s laid-back, residential vibe.
