content:
A stately Victorian office building dating back to 1890 is the setting for the Kimpton Clocktower Hotel, a fine example of the American-born brand’s affinity for British heritage buildings. It’s an approach that strikes a balance between respectful preservation and playful irreverence — what’s meant to be preserved, like the ornate stone-clad lobby, remains as grand as ever, while the rooms and suites, necessarily updated from their tenure as offices, display a more colorful and borderline whimsical approach.

After all, this is the same Kimpton that’s famous for its complimentary social hours, serving wine and beer to all comers; and the same Kimpton that did so much to democratize the boutique-hotel experience, from something rarefied and exclusive to something accessible and welcoming. The rooms and suites carry on in this just-right vein, combining high Victorian style with contemporary colors and design, and providing high-end comforts without ostentation.

Given the Kimpton Clocktower’s central location there’s plenty of dining and drinking to be had nearby. The hotel’s own offerings, though few in number, are worthy ones: the Winter Garden is just what it sounds like, and is ideal for a cocktail or tea, while the Refuge is, aesthetically, Industrial Age Manchester at its most glamorous.

content: The Berkshires of western Massachusetts are thriving; with ample opportunity for outdoor recreation as well as a surprisingly vibrant cultural scene, all within a manageable drive from Boston and New York, it’s not hard to see the appeal. And with hotels like the Constance on the scene, it’s an easier sell than ever. This Victorian-style tavern first opened its doors in 1825, and in its present incarnation it’s a perfectly balanced blend of historically inspired Victorian charm and contemporary boutique-hotel style.\n\nWhile the rooms and suites may be antique in their atmosphere, they’re modern where you need them to be — specifically, they’ve got wi-fi, Apple TV, and modern en suite bathrooms. Some come with reading nooks, others private porches, and all are decorated with unique local artworks. With just 20 units, it’s modestly sized, and while it’s got a lovely living room for a drink or a cup of coffee, it stops short of a proper restaurant or bar — the location, on the edge of Lenox’s compact town center, places it within walking distance of just about everything in town, and Stockbridge lies just a few miles to the south.

On the island of Bornholm, a Danish territory in the Baltic Sea, you’ll find a low-key and unpretentious little boutique hotel that’s a perfect exemplar of Scandinavian hospitality at its coziest. Allinge Badehotel comprises just 24 rooms in a beautifully renovated 18th-century house, updated with furnishings and decorative elements by contemporary Danish designers — quietly stylish but without sacrificing the timelessness of an authentic old seaside inn. The in-room comforts are first-rate, as is the daily breakfast service; for dinner it’s a short stroll into town, which is amply supplied with high-quality restaurants.

content:
There are few hotels that are more clearly a labor of love than Stratford, Ontario’s seven&nine. That is, if it’s even a hotel. Set a scant minute’s walk from the Avon Theatre, one of the anchors of the annual Shakespeare festival, it was built as a private house, and an extraordinary one at that. Architects Shim/Sutcliffe were inspired by the kind of raw-concrete modernism that recalls figures like Tadao Ando and Alvar Aalto, and the house is decorated with modernist classic furnishings and contemporary artworks to match.

Even as a guest lodging, its primary mission is to allow travelers to experience a uniquely artful house from the inside. It’s a totally self-sufficient two-bedroom house with a full kitchen, supplied with a Nespresso machine, Pelee Island wines, and bath products by Le Labo. The contrast with the 19th-century Gothic architecture for which Stratford is known is a striking one, and the town is a surprisingly pleasant and livable one, even outside of the Shakespeare season. 

Please note: seven&nine can only accommodate Friday and Monday check-ins with a 3-night minimum stay and 4-night minimum stay requirement respectively.

content: It’s fair to say RockyPop isn’t the easiest word to pronounce in a sober and dignified tone — but given that the hotel’s stated aim is to shake up the conventional image of the Alpine ski lodge, we’ll happily grant them license to have a bit of fun with the name. And as you arrive in Les Houches, just outside of Chamonix, it’s clear from a glance at the marquee, proudly emblazoned with the phrase “we will RockyPop you,” that they’re in it all the way — this is the ski-resort version of the accessible, youth-oriented boutique hotels that have been taking the world’s cities by storm.\n\nTo that end, RockyPop features fun, vibrantly colored guest rooms, with a bare minimum of old-fashioned luxury — they’re comfortable enough, to be sure, but for this audience, reading lights, comfortable duvets, and HD televisions with unlimited video-on-demand are all you really need. The restaurant is similarly laid-back and casual, with a bit of a food-truck theme going on, and a communal-dining vibe that livens the mood. And they don’t neglect the basics; the ski shop carries everything you need for rental or sale, whether you’re a snowshoer, a skier, or — let’s be honest, far more likely — a snowboarder.

content:
When you’re floating in the rooftop infinity pool at a state-of-the-art boutique hotel like AMANOR Hotel Chiang Mai, looking out over the neon lights and the stream of motorbikes zipping through busy downtown streets, it makes perfect sense that Chiang Mai means “new city.” Not so fast: “new,” in this case, is relative, referring to the date of its founding in the 13th century. The northern Thai city is known for its rich history, particularly its hundreds of old Buddhist temples. But that fact will probably be far from your mind when you’re inside a hotel as thoroughly modern as this one.

Located in the heart of the city center, amid the cafés, boutiques, art galleries and cocktail bars of happening Nimmanhaemin street, AMANOR Hotel Chiang Mai rises up eight stories but contains just 62 rooms and suites. Or “sanctuaries,” as the hotel calls them — a term that sounds a bit more reasonable once you’ve set food inside one. The look is modern, mixing an Asian-inspired aesthetic — spare, calm interiors, a preference for natural materials — with a sort of sixties-era glamour. In any suite, you’ll find retro pieces like an Arco lamp or an modular sofa, as well as walls that mimic the look of traditional woven screens, potted plants, and patios lined with earthy white stones. Standard amenities include king-sized beds with Egyptian cotton sheets, free wi-fi, all-natural bath products, and iPods pre-loaded with music and hooked up to Bluetooth speakers.

Once you’ve had a good soak in your private hot tub, head up to the rooftop for drinks at the ARISE Rooftop Bar: the view at sunset, when the city lights come on against the darkening silhouette of northern Thailand’s hills, is gorgeous. And if you’ve had enough Thai food for awhile — a situation that’s hard to imagine, but to each his own — there’s Lumi Restaurant, the modern Italian restaurant onsite that’s been earning a bit of buzz on the city’s developing food scene. You might only be passing through the “new city” on your way to more dazzling landscapes, but AMANOR Hotel Chiang Mai is the kind of hotel where you wouldn’t mind sticking around another day or two.

How to get there: AMANOR Hotel Chiang Mai is a 15-minute drive from Chiang Mai International Airport.

content: If a few days in and around Reykjavík aren’t enough to satisfy your Icelandic urges, the next logical step is the around-the-island road trip — in which case the so-called Capital of the North plays a central role. It’s also a fine spot from which to view the Northern Lights, if you’re here in winter. And in Hotel Akureyri it’s got a boutique hotel whose style and atmosphere are anything but provincial.\n\nThe utilitarian exterior gives little hint of what you’ll find within. But once you’re inside, you’re treated to some characteristically Nordic clean lines and blonde wood, warmed by industrial touches and artworks that are a cut above the usual hotel fare. The rooms are attractive and thoughtfully laid out, in a number of configurations, from simple double rooms to family rooms with bunk beds and even suites, complete with full living rooms. And among the hotel’s buildings are a couple of more historical structures containing some more classic-style rooms and a handful of self-contained apartments.

content:
The Castillo Rojo is a landmark you might already recognize if you’ve ever been to Santiago. Not only is it an eye-catcher of a building — stately and vermillion-hued — but it’s located a block away from Pablo Neruda’s one-time urban residence, La Chascona, in the lovely and tourist-popular neighborhood of Bellavista. It’s the kind of building you’d stand in front of and wonder about, looking it up on your guidebook map, probably without a satisfying resolution. But that was up until recently, when the house was turned into the Castillo Rojo Boutique Hotel.

The modern restoration took place almost exactly 90 years after the building, which dates from 1923, was designed as the private home of a wealthy family; the Castillo Rojo later served as an artist’s residence. Much of the original charm remains — picture romantic old fireplaces, rustic woodwork, twenties-era light fixtures, an utter lack of elevators — but the 2013 update brought contemporary comforts to nineteen guest rooms, plus a wine bar and a pair of restaurants. You’ll have to take the stairs up to your temporary abode, which adds to the ambience, provided that you’re not totally debilitated by jet lag. Standard rooms are quaint and petite, with 500 thread-count cotton sheets and custom-made pillow top beds, and old-fashioned details from writing desks and vaulted ceilings to framed drawings, dark wood armoires, and elegant wallpaper. Suites have separate seating areas. All room categories include breakfast. 

Breakfast is served in the Bistró Castillo; later, sit out on Castillo Rojo’s terrace, drinking a glass of locally produced Carménère and watching the world go by in the plaza below. The location really couldn’t be better, Neruda or not: you’re steps from the funicular that travels to the top of nearby Cerro San Cristobál, where you’ll take in sweeping views of the Chilean capital and the spectacular Andean scenery that surrounds it.

content:
Tucked away in a quiet cove off the Atlantic, half an hour west of Bordeaux, the nine-room Villa La Tosca is the sort of place that makes you wish you’d been born elsewhere — and perhaps to better circumstances. It’s like a vision of aristocratic leisure, translated for the 21st century and set in a tiny coastal town in southwestern France. The gardens are well-kept, the views of the sea expansive, and the breezy verandahs plentiful. In short it’s a taste of the good life, a low-key seaside hideaway at just the right distance from the more heavily touristed sections of the wine country. 

As the name implies, the building bears something of an Italian influence. It’s considered one of the finer examples of Arcachon architecture, whose practitioners took the best of Italian villa living and gave it a subtle French twist. Today the interiors are perfectly contemporary, full of light and space, and sprinkled with Asian antiques and objets d’art. 

Coziness rather than extravagance is the order of the day. Most of the rooms are somewhat on the small side, though smart design choices do open them up a bit. Up the scale, however, the accommodations are positively sprawling, with expansive sea and garden views to match. And at every level, handmade TRECA mattresses with fine Egyptian cotton bedding make it easy to get a good night’s sleep. 

As for dining — an important element of any hotel stay in this part of France — the meals are casual affairs. There’s no restaurant per se, but let the staff know in advance that you’d like to eat at the hotel and their private chefs (one of whom has a Michelin star) will gladly go to work for you. The settings are casual — open-air verandahs, a fireside dining room, a sunny spot in the garden — but the food, which utilizes the best local ingredients in a region where that really means something, turns out to be quite accomplished. And needless to say, with Bordeaux just up the road a ways, you won’t be lacking for good wine to pair with it. 

Please note: Villa La Tosca is a small property with only 9 rooms. Book early as rooms sell out quick.

content:
Long the biggest name in Megève hotels, the Hôtel Mont-Blanc has done a bit of sprucing up. Actually it goes deeper than that — the new-look Mont-Blanc joins a family that also includes such success stories as Cour des Loges and Les Fermes de Marie, with a new design by the very same Jocelyne Sibuet.

That doesn’t make it a “designer” hotel, necessarily. Sibuet’s work tends toward the classic, not the flashy, and a grand dame like the Mont-Blanc will always be luxury more than look. Still, it’s rare to see an Alpine resort hotel looking this stylish — in the Fifties it made an appearance in the film Les Liaisons Dangereuses, in the Sixties it was sophisticated enough for Jean Cocteau, and in its new incarnation it’ll continue to be a second home for many a skiing Parisian.

As for the nuts and bolts, it’s got everything you’d expect a slopeside hotel to have. A fitness center and a fairly extensive spa are musts. And there’s perhaps more of an emphasis on dining than in the average ski resort. Three restaurants and a couple of lounges serve everything from breakfast to dinner to caviar to the odd glass of mid-afternoon champagne — also a must, if you think about it.

Please note: Hôtel Mont Blanc is a seasonal hotel and is open December through April.

How to get there:
Just 55 minutes from Geneva International Airport (take the Geneva Chamonix motorway, leaving at the Sallanches exit) and Geneva International Railway Station (with the direct high-speed train services operating between Paris and Geneva) it is also connected by motorway to some of Europe's largest cities, including Milan, Brussels, Amsterdam, and Paris.

content: Though it’s a long way from Prince Edward Island, Pacific Grove, on Monterey Bay, is the sort of 19th-century Californian town Lucy Maud Montgomery would have loved. Green Gables Inn is the flagship location of Four Sisters Inns, a collection of sophisticated boutique hotels. It’s long been an incredibly quaint place to stay, but recent renovations have made it more inviting than ever. Common spaces and guest rooms have been brightened and refreshed, the interiors modern but cozy with rustic wood flooring, linen sofas, earth tones, and dreamy watercolor paintings capturing scenes of the sky and the sea. \n\nMany rooms have original fireplaces, soaking tubs, and built-in window seating, and the gable room, following the lines of the Queen Anne-style architecture, has an idyllic reading nook with water views. Behind the main house, a carriage house offers suites with more space. Never mind a fitness center or a pool: Green Gables Inn, keeping with the theme, provides homey comforts like a gourmet breakfast served in a greenhouse-like bayfront dining room, freshly baked cookies, an afternoon wine hour, and bicycles to borrow anytime.

content:
Kos has been relatively late to embrace the boutique-hotel boom. With Lango Design Hotel & Spa, however, the island is making up for lost time. This 54-room adults-only luxury boutique hotel is as polished as they come, a vision in near-monochrome minimalism, set right across the road from Lambi Beach and a few minutes’ walk from the Kos town center.

At this level you can bet that even the humblest double rooms are lavish indeed — space is plentiful, as are the comforts, which include furnished balconies or terraces and even a writing desk. Meanwhile, at the higher end you’ll find such additional inducements as sea views, outdoor jacuzzis, and plunge pools.

As promised by the name, there’s an extensive spa and wellness complex, as well as a photogenic L-shaped outdoor swimming pool. By its side are loungers for daytime relaxation as well as a poolside bar serving cocktails and light bites. And in the evening the action moves into Koan Cuisine, the hotel’s restaurant, which serves Greek, Italian, and pan-Mediterranean flavors, accompanied by the contents of a capacious wine cellar.

content:
Located within a former railway repair shop in Munich, Motorworld is difficult to classify — it’s got museum exhibits, vehicle and accessory retailers, specialty workshops, and, in the Ameron München Motorworld, an automotive-themed luxury boutique hotel. This last feature is perhaps the most unusual member of the Ameron group, a series of hotels in Germany and Switzerland that bridge the gap between business and leisure hospitality while indulging in some impressive contemporary design.

Naturally, Ameron München Motorworld is full of tributes to automotive culture, and some of the studios allow you to park your own car or motorcycle in a glass-walled garage adjacent to your room. The comforts are up-to-date, and the aesthetics, racing influence aside, are a tasteful collage of modernism’s greatest hits, from Bauhaus on through to the Seventies.

There’s a spa, in case you fancy a treatment while your car is getting one of its own, as well as a vast array of meeting and events spaces scattered throughout the Motorworld complex. Meanwhile, the restaurant, Bacio della Mamma, trades on Munich’s reputation as “the northernmost Italian city,” and pays tribute not just to Rome’s culinary tradition but to its gregariousness as well.

content:
Palisociety’s Arrive hotels are all different, carefully tailored to their settings in some of America’s most unique neighborhoods. But they share plenty as well: all are vibrant and eclectic in their design sense, and all include dining and drinking venues that connect them to the local flavors and traditions. Arrive Memphis begins with a lovely old industrial building on South Main, in the city’s Arts District, close to Beale Street and Downtown Memphis.

To this it adds 62 sunny, spacious, and subtly luxe rooms and suites, whose décor contrasts weathered antique surfaces with colorful Victorian-inspired wallpaper and an eclectic mix of fixtures and furnishings, as well as Hudson Made bath products, Marshall bluetooth speakers, and Apple TVs. They’re comfortable but just short of ostentatious, and stylish without crossing over into pretentiousness.

And Arrive Memphis adds a handful of very worthwhile establishments. Longshot is a fun and casual bar and restaurant serving Southern comfort food alongside some serious shuffleboard matches. The slightly more upscale Bar Hustle specializes in creative cocktails, local beers, and wines by the glass. And in a supporting role are a small-batch coffee roaster called Vice & Virtue as well as Hustle & Dough, a well-loved local bakery and café.

content:
Its name is a mouthful, to be sure, but not a word is wasted: Valcastello Dolomites Chalet & Polo Club is everything it claims to be. Most immediately apparent, obviously, are the jagged peaks of the Dolomites, an unmistakable backdrop. But the chalet business is no exaggeration, either — it’s a rare Alpine hotel indeed whose interiors venture quite so far in the direction of aristocratic opulence.

The chateau itself is of 19th-century vintage, and its interiors reflect that heritage with the utmost fidelity: ornate woodwork, fine fabrics, and period artworks abound. The fact that there are a mere eight suites and apartments contributes to the sense of secluded privacy, and the common spaces — a series of living and dining rooms — are nearly as plentiful as the accommodations.

And while you’d think a polo club might get little use in this mountain climate, you’ve likely failed to consider the possibility of snow polo — at Valcastello they play on grass during the summer months, and snow during from December through March. Just another reminder that Valcastello isn’t your ordinary Dolomites chalet — though it’s worth remembering that if the polo ponies aren’t your thing, you’ve still got all the traditional Alpine diversions right at your feet.

We told you we wouldn’t rest until there’s a properly stylish and inventive boutique hotel in every city in America. And while we’re not yet ready to declare our mission accomplished, the advent of the Tennessean Hotel, in Knoxville, Tennessee, brings us one step closer to our goal. The location, bordering on World’s Fair Park, is central, convenient to both the convention center and the best restaurants and breweries in downtown Knoxville. And the hotel itself offers a first-rate luxury boutique experience: stylish, memorable, and lacking for nothing when it comes to comfort.

Every room and suite boasts at least a king or two queen beds, as well as a 55-inch television and Molton Brown bath products. The Drawing Room restaurant and bar serves the best in locally sourced Southern cooking and Tennessee whiskey. And connected to the Tennessean is Maker Exchange, a community gathering hub and exhibition space dedicated to local crafts and art — and which comes complete with its own Tavern and coffee shop.

You’re by no means limited to what’s on the premises, of course — this is an outgoing, convivial town, with any number of dining and drinking venues within walking distance.And while Knoxville’s got plenty to recommend it within the city limits, outdoor types will thrill to the surrounding natural environment; Eastern Tennessee is home to some of the region’s most extraordinary wilderness.

Hotel des Trois Vallées was the first hotel in the postwar resort of Courchevel, and the look, marrying the exterior of a traditional Alpine inn with a cool modernist interior, epitomized the spirit of the times. The effortless style of the hotel’s early days can still be seen today — much of the original furniture, by designers like Charlotte Perriand, Jean Prouvé, and Pierre Paulin, is back on the floor — and today's Hotel des Trois Vallées feels like a vintage film set.

The open-plan lobby is a charmer with its rustic fireplaces, stone walls, rugged wood paneling, and windows framing postcard-like views of the mountains, plus mod sofas and French versions of the Egg chair, a fifties classic. Guest rooms and suites are slightly more subdued, modern and appropriately cozy with blonde wood beds and fluffy white duvets. Some are cabin-like, others more contemporary, with asymmetrical vaulted ceilings; all have flat-screen TVs, private balconies, and fifties-inspired furnishings. At the top end — quite literally, on the top floor of the hotel — La Suite features a living room with a fireplace, two bedrooms, and a large terrace facing the snowy slopes.

After a day on the slopes you’ll likely decamp to the large Jacuzzi, more like the size of a small swimming pool, in the Hotel des Trois Vallées Spa. The lobby opens onto the bar and restaurant, where a large table d’hôte (that’s “communal table,” for non-Francophones), warmed by the nearby fireplace, welcomes breakfast guests. Come for teatime or après-ski, or grab a bottle of Chasselas and a hunk of locally produced cheese from the Épicerie, the hotel’s tiny but smartly stocked gourmet market, and retire to your room before venturing out for dinner.

content:
At a glance Cartagena could easily be mistaken for another of the many picturesque Colonial cities in Latin America, and indeed its narrow cobblestone streets, its sun-dappled public squares, its church steeples towering over the old walled city are all a deep part of its appeal. But what really sets Cartagena apart is how, despite all postcard-perfect backdrops, it never quite feels like a parody of its former self. There’s an easy self-confidence about the place, a confidence that’s perfectly embodied by the Movich Hotel. Step inside, behind its traditional whitewashed façade, and the hotel is as contemporary as can be, all sleek modern lines and sunny, open spaces.

In the guest rooms, the building’s old bones occasionally show through in the form of an exposed stone wall or (in some cases) a Spanish-style arched terrace overlooking the street, but for every reminder of the past there’s something else bringing us back to the present. The bathrooms are big and bright with natural light; all the proper technologies, from the iPod-dock speakers to LCD screens, are in place; and the layout is uncluttered without feeling unfinished. Warm light, pops of bright color and rich natural materials bring it all together. 

Outside the guest rooms, there’s a low-key social element at play in the public spaces, especially on the rooftop. With its smattering of loungers and parasols by the hot tub and pool, plus a bar to keep you from getting parched while you soak in all that Caribbean sun, it’s a fine place to while away an afternoon — or to take some photos, for that matter, with the rooftops of the old city spread out below and the high rises of the modern downtown just off in the distance. 

A fine and atmospheric seafood restaurant, twenty-four-hour room service and a functional little business center round things out, though given the location in the heart of the old city, you’ll want to get out and explore.

If we all know what a film noir looks like, then we can probably get away with extending the metaphor to hotels as well. Hotel Les Nuits is a Belgian noir hotel in Antwerp’s fashion district — which, though it’s not about to knock Paris off its perch in terms of commercial volume, is a genuine style capital, a fashionable, forward-looking and design-minded town. 

The guest rooms, by a designer based in the neighborhood, are compact but comfortable, open-plan and overlaid with quirky noir-ish fittings like black-lacquered headboards or gleaming black subway tiles in the bathrooms, plus unexpected Asian details to remind us that even a stylized hotel in the fashion district can allude, successfully, to Antwerp’s trading-port roots.

The hotel’s restaurant, Les Jours, offers an evolving brasserie-style menu in the capable hands of chef Filip De Pauw. And in good weather, the restaurant extends to a sunny rooftop terrace decked in light wood. It’s one of several public spaces — along with conference facilities — that come as surprises in such a small hotel. 

Given the location, there’s obviously no shortage of shopping to do. It’s an appropriate base from which to explore Antwerp’s avant-garde design and clothing shops. Yet push just a little beyond the attractive new storefronts and you’ll quickly be reminded that people have been buying and selling luxury goods here (not least diamonds) for centuries. For all the work its youthful designers have done to ornament it, Antwerp still has all its cobblestone streets and old canals and its profusion of spindly church steeples — a look unlikely to go out of style anytime soon.

Hotel Les Nuits is 15 minutes away from Antwerp International Airport.

It seems unlikely that it could really be so, but at the Royal Palm Beachcomber Luxury, the sand somehow looks a little more talcum-white, the turquoise-blue water a touch glassier and, strangest of all, the palm trees a bit denser with perfect shade-making fronds than everywhere else on Mauritius. It’s particularly hard to believe given that Mauritius is practically the Platonic form of a tropical island, the hotels here the things that winter workday fantasies are made of. Yet the Royal Palm’s location on the sheltered northwest coast of the island, and its eighty-two spacious, richly appointed suites, truly are the crème of the already rather rich Mauritian crème. 

Every suite here is sea-facing, and given how spectacular this stretch of sea is, that’s an especially good thing. Even the modestly named junior suite has, on top of the beach views, a walk-in closet, an oversized bathroom with a big tub and separate shower, and a sunny lounge that opens out onto a private terrace. The tropical and palm suites, starting at about 750 square feet, are positively enormous, and they only get bigger from there. By the time you get to the penthouse suite, still a couple notches below the top-tier, you’ve got a skylight-lit bathroom, a terrace with its own dining and sunbathing areas, and wide-angle views over the ocean and gardens. 

The three restaurants run the gamut from acclaimed Mauritian cuisine at the romantic La Goélete terrace-restaurant, to Mediterranean and Asian dishes at the beachside Natureaty, to light healthful meals at the tree-shaded Le Bar Plage. There’s also a tranquil spa that is, appropriately enough for an island paradise, brimming with gurgling water features and shingle-roofed treatment cabins, most of which have big bay windows to let the sunlight in. There’s a sports center with more activities than your gym teacher ever dreamed of — circuit training, pilates, squash, and tennis of both the table and court varieties, to name a few. A private excursion on the hotel’s speedboat is yet another way to get your heart racing. When your only other plans are spa treatments and leisurely meals between hours of wading in that warm water and lounging in the sun, it might not be so bad to raise your blood pressure a bit. 

How to get there:
Royal Palm Beachcomber Luxury is located 75 kilometers (90 minutes) from the Sir Seewoosagar Ramgoolam International Airport. The hotel offers several transportation options.

content: Saint-Rémy-de-Provence is home to a number of châteaux, but only one, Château des Alpilles, that welcomes overnight guests. A picturesque sycamore-lined path leads from the main road to a small complex of historic buildings — a medieval farmhouse, a 19th-century manor house, a chapel, and a stone cottage — set in a park planted with centuries-old cypress trees. Extensive restorations transformed the place into a luxury hotel with 21 uniquely decorated rooms, two upscale restaurants, and an outdoor swimming pool. \n\nRooms in the manor house are especially elegant with high ceilings, working fireplaces, period furnishings, and rich drapery. Those in the old farmhouse are modern and rustic-chic, with exposed wooden beams and spacious floor plans with living rooms separate from bedrooms. Lodgings in the chapel are simple and bright with parquet floors, white walls, and private terraces, and the freestanding cottage, once used as a wash house, offers two levels of living space and a large deck. Old-world grandeur is on glittering display in the ground-level lounge and bar with its crystal chandeliers and Belle Époque–inspired decor. The outdoor spaces are equally lovely: breakfast is served in the courtyard, while lunch and free-flowing rosé are available by the pool in warmer weather.

content: The Guinness Book of World Records officially designated Hotel Puntagrande in El Hierro, Spain as the world’s smallest hotel in 1984. But what’s especially notable about this “hotelito” isn’t its small size, but its spectacular location on a piece of lava rock jutting out into the Atlantic Ocean. The original building, a cultural site protected by the Canary Islands government, dates back to 1830. Inside, the hotel looks something like a small nautical museum, its rough-hewn stone walls lined with antique compasses, maps, and bronze-plated boat registrations. \n\nMaritime memorabilia spills over into the rooms and suites, where bathroom mirrors are framed by driftwood and bedside tables are crafted from porthole glass. Some rooms have private wooden decks or romantic four-poster beds; all have direct ocean views. With the rolling tide just outside, and interiors featuring local wood, lava stone, and a cheerful blue and white color palette, it’s rather like sleeping on a ship. The hotel’s wood-lined lounge bar has cozy, galley-like feel, ideal for warming up after exploring the windswept coastline.

content: Though not as widely celebrated as his famous contemporary Antoni Gaudí, architect Enric Sagnier designed hundreds of Barcelona’s Modernist buildings. Casa Sagnier, completed in 1892, served as his family home and studio for the latter half of his life; lately it’s been reimagined as a stylish boutique hotel that pays subtle homage to the Spanish architect. The location on Rambla de Catalunya in the heart of L’Eixample — the same neighborhood where many of Sagnier’s works are highlighted on sightseeing tours — is just one of its many assets.\n\nChief among them is the building itself. The elegant stone façade, with wrought-iron balconies, makes a striking first impression, its oversized picture windows offering a view into the hotel’s busy street-level café and eatery. Upstairs, rooms and suites are modern and cozy with pale parquet floors, leather and wood furnishings, and spacious bathrooms with walk-in showers and locally produced bath products. A surprising number come with private balconies or interior patios, and the best rooms have large terraces with sun loungers and potted plants. Casa Sagnier also features a cozy fireplace room, a fitness center, a rooftop terrace lounge, and a lively ground-level bar with plush banquette seating and great people-watching.

Ten minutes from Newburyport proper, on the North Shore of Massachusetts, is Plum Island, a barrier island known for its long, golden, sandy beach. And at the south end of Newbury Beach, comfortably removed from the action in Plum Island’s village, is Blue - Inn on the Beach. Like many of New England’s most attractive little hotels, it’s a Lark production, and while the décor is suitably maritime-influenced, it’s perhaps a bit more dramatic than you might expect.

The rooms, suites, and cottages are classic in style, underneath it all, but the interiors display a stark contrast between the white-on-white backgrounds and the vivid pops of ultra-saturated blue. All of this without sacrificing warmth; the materials are still touchable and organic, and the in-room comforts include things like Tivoli bluetooth radios and Keurig coffee makers. 

Many of the units feature direct views onto the beach from their balconies or private decks, as does the hotel’s hot tub. The cottages add both more space and more privacy, and the suites are large indeed — the top-of-the-line Blue Oceanfront Suite spans two floors and more than two thousand square feet. And while there’s no restaurant, daily breakfast baskets are provided, and the town of Newburyport is close at hand.

In this business, it pays to be specific; it seems there’s a White Horse of some description in just about every town, village, and hamlet in England. But only one is remembered as the Victorian-era coaching inn where Charles Dickens went to write part of The Pickwick Papers, and that would be the White Horse in Dorking, Surrey. It’s also the only one that recently sank £4 million into a refurbishment to bring it up to the standard demanded by guests who’ve grown accustomed to the boutique hotels of London and the surrounding countryside.

To that end, they’ve decorated the rooms in a style that’s colorful, eclectic, and luxe, in a homespun sort of way, while duck down duvets and Bramley bath products provide just a touch of extravagance. The same goes for the all-day restaurant, whose menu features unapologetically classic British fare, but with an emphasis on the quality and provenance of the ingredients. Just about everything you’ll taste is local to Surrey, from the bread and the sausage to the produce and chutneys and even the drinks from the bar — local wines(!) feature alongside a selection of ales and lagers from Dorking and Wimbledon.

content:
Privacy’s one thing, 180 acres of unspoiled rainforest is quite another. The slopes and valleys of the Western Ghats, the surface of which has hardly been scratched by tourism and development, offer prime pickings for an eco-conscious, low-impact luxury resort like Taj Madikeri Resort and Spa, Coorg. Self-sufficiency is the name of the game here, a considerable 4,000 feet up, and this Taj outpost delivers on all counts: you’d be hard pressed to exhaust its opportunities for dining, exercising, or even just idling with a satisfied eye on the mist-swaddled hills. 

Massive picture windows frame the scene throughout, keeping the impossibly lush flora and cerulean skies in sight at all times. Each of the 62 rooms and villas enjoys a wide-angle view of the region’s cascading greenery, a fittingly natural balance to traditional architectural elements — lofty pillars, gently sloping roofing, ornate wooden screens, hanging lanterns — and a subtly luxurious earth-tone palette. Upper-tier rooms justify themselves with substantial updates like personal fireplaces and plunge pools, though all of them benefit from spacious, hardwood-floored rooms and stone-clad bathrooms with Forest Essentials amenities.

A serene, partially exposed courtyard imbues the whole affair with a suitably reverential air, matched in kind by a contemplative infinity pool and a 30,000-square-foot spa complex, replete with immersive Ayurvedic treatments and all manner of personal training. Sooner or later, though, you’ll need to satisfy the body’s baser needs at a trio of on-site restaurants. Go full-bore regional at Nellaki or broaden the cuisine with all-day  global plates at Fern Tree, whose attached wooden terrace presents yet another opportunity to ogle the landscape; in between, Dew’s lighter fare and a pick-me-up at the coffee shop (Coorg is famous for its coffee plantations) should do nicely. The landscape isn’t just for looking, either — concierge-guided treks allow you to explore to your heart’s content by foot, pedal, or zipline.

content:
You’ve got to hand it to New Delhi’s urban planners — they’re ambitious, if that’s the word for the “aerocity” metro-hotel-retail complex right at the airport’s doorstep. Conveniently accessible both to the city proper and to Gurgaon, its swelling business-district twin, this development is a temple to growth that reads as if the global recession was just a minor blip. Just one among many planned ultraluxury hotels is the Roseate House New Delhi, whose rooms and suites should give an idea of the scale we’re playing with here. 

Soft ochres and eggshells demonstrate upscale design sensibilities — thus the attention lavished on the four-piece bathrooms, complete with rain shower, oversize tubs, and luxury amenities. Plenty of natural wood graces the flooring and wall treatments, and the complimentary wi-fi and LCD TV give you more than just a wall to stare at. Besides appreciable views of the inner courtyard or the cityscape, higher-tier rooms ratchet up the Jeeves factor considerably with 24-hour personal butlers, lounge access, and of course more space than you know what to do with.

Choose DEL for all-day international plates on a constantly refreshed menu, best enjoyed indoors with live cooking stations in front and a sinuous ceiling installation overhead. Its cousin, KHEER, aims for NYC mixology and largely succeeds, though its sheer size and cleanliness challenge the comparison; in any case, its north Indian classics and streetcart craveables keep the mouth excellently occupied. We could go on about the spa’s incredible variety of therapies or the Japanese delicacies at the rooftop pool café, but you get the picture by now. Part of the fun is in the personal discovery, we understand. That’s why we’re only giving you a quick taste of the extracurriculars. Hot-air balloon rides. Metalworking workshops. You take it from here.

It’s not every day a new high-end ski resort is simply willed into existence. But Montana Lodge & Spa’s proprietors are counting on their ability to do just that. Rather than join the crowd in an established resort town, they’re hoping a stylish luxury boutique hotel is all it will take to attract upscale customers to the hitherto humble ski resort of La Thuile.

The first great hotel in an emerging destination is always more exciting than the one that finally turns the place into a bona fide hotspot, and Montana Lodge & Spa is careful not to go too far too fast. The exterior, though modern, is classic in style, taking care to blend in with the established architecture. But once you’re inside, you’ll see you’ve stumbled on something much more than the average ski lodge.

Modern construction means modern spaces; these rooms are genuinely spacious, which is important — it’s not natural to stow yourself into a cramped space after a day under the Alpine sky. The design leans heavily on rustic, unfinished wood, but alongside plenty of luxe modern Italian furniture the effect is far from unpolished. And the comfort is largely in the details: between the Hästens mattresses and the in-room Lavazza espresso machines, you’ve got little choice but to start the day with a surplus of energy. Add a classic Italian restaurant and a brand-new spa, and you’ve got the beginnings of a proper Alpine resort — minus the luxury trappings of an established resort town.

How to get there: Montana Lodge & Spa is approximately 132 km by car from Geneva International Airport via E25/A40 and SS26 and 157 km by car from Turin Airport via E612/E25/A5 and SS26.

content: There’s more to New Zealand than just those rustic rural lodges. Though it may confound the narrative a bit, New Zealanders can do cosmopolitan style as well. The George is a great example, a 53-room boutique in central Christchurch, but which comes with some bucolic views thanks to its position at the edge of Hagley Park. Restaurant 50 Bistro celebrates local New Zealand produce, and serves special menus such as afternoon tea and pre-theatre dining for catching a show, or the sunset views. There’s also a gym, and to make the most of the verdant setting, e-bikes are available to hire for a spin around the park. If you’re still feeling confined (unlikely in this scenic, modestly sized city) you’re never far from the vast expanses of great outdoors that are a New Zealand trademark.\n\nHow to get there: The George is approximately a 15-20 minute drive from Christchurch International Airport.

content:
Water Garden Sigiriya seems like an evocative, almost poetic name for a hotel, but in fact it’s as sensible as they come — which testifies to the magic of its setting. Sigiriya is a fifth-century fortress built atop a natural column of rock in the island’s inland center, and the hotel’s grounds, crisscrossed with manmade pools, lakes, and streams, is quite literally a water garden. 

It’s laid out so as to perfectly frame the views of the fortress in the middle distance, and its finely focused modernist architecture is in keeping with Sri Lanka’s distinctive local style — it’s the work of Channa Daswatte, one of the country’s most highly regarded architects. The 30 villas are spacious and thoroughly well-equipped; some of them feel like private islands, surrounded by the gardens’ water features, while others come with private plunge pools of their own.

A full-service spa stands on stilts above the waters of one of the estate’s ponds, while on dry land the central restaurant spills out onto a terrace from within a breezy double-height space. There’s an outdoor pool and a substantial fitness center, as well as all manner of outdoor recreation, from croquet to archery — and between the villas’ butlers and the hotel’s capable concierges, the service throughout is first-rate.

content: You don’t have to go very far outside of Boston to find a perfectly idyllic seaside town — Portsmouth, New Hampshire is full of shops, restaurants, cafés, and at least one delightful little boutique hotel. Massachusetts-based Lark Hotels took over this 1881-vintage Victorian house and turned it into The Hotel, whose 32 rooms effortlessly blend the 19th-century charm of the existing structure and a light, contemporary, modernist-inspired style that’s a breath of fresh air in a region where tradition, in hotels and design alike, still reigns supreme.\n\nRooms range from cozy queens to more expansive kings and on up to some downright expansive suites, but at all levels they come with thoughtful touches like USB charging ports and iPads loaded with information about Portsmouth’s various attractions. There are no end of restaurants to explore, but The Hotel will supply a small-plates-style breakfast and occasional bites during the day. Meanwhile the location, on the edge of the historic city center, places you within walking distance of all the best that Portsmouth has to offer, from Market Square to the waterfront and beyond. The Hotel isn’t literally the only hotel in town, but it might be the only one you need.

content:
Mannheim embodies many of Germany’s virtues in one contemporary, thoughtful package. Weird as it sounds, they take pride in squareness here — mostly in reference to an unusually orderly city grid, but also on a more abstract level: think smart, stylish urban planning, a design-conscious city that didn’t leave its own layout to happenstance. SYTE Mannheim fits this context well, an upscale take on a historical building within easy walking distance of the central train station and the city’s highlights. Not particularly revolutionary, and all the better for it.

Tasteful highlights elevate the 39 rooms beyond typical transit-friendly fare; the lofted stucco ceilings and herringbone parquet oak floors bespeak quiet luxury without tryhard histrionics. Bespoke furnishings in plush, dark-toned textiles exude comfort, while the bathrooms’ checkerboard and metro-tile motifs radiate vintage elegance. Think soft jazz, retro carpets, and a whiskey with water to take the edge off. 

Public spaces wholeheartedly embrace a handsome, gentlemanly air, intensifying velvet and leather surfaces with charming equestrian accoutrements. Black-and-white photography recalls the Mannheim of yesteryear, redoubling the omnipresent sense of civic pride and fastidious attention to detail.

content:
Vang Vieng was formerly known for its legions of backpackers — partly a result of just how arduous the journey was, over hours and hours of barely functional roads. The transportation situation, happily, has been sorted out, thanks to a new high-speed rail line as well as a modern highway. And the town’s atmosphere has changed accordingly, the late-night revelry replaced by something more sedate, more comfortable, and altogether more grown up. It’s to this modern vision of Vang Vieng that the Riverside Boutique Resort belongs.

Providing dramatic, sweeping views of the nearby limestone mountains, this 34-room hotel presents itself, quite successfully, as a luxe retreat. The French colonial design, while not exactly unusual in this part of the world, is impeccably done. Guest rooms are generously parceled out among two-story structures, where floor-to-ceiling sliding doors unite balconies with suites defined by king beds and wicker furniture. Each room’s atmosphere is inspired by one of eight different regional ethnic groups, which works as both an admirable design principle and a nod to chic art hotels.

How to get there:
Riverside Boutique Resort is approximately 2.5 hours (160 km by bus or car) from the Wattay International Airport (VTE) in Vientiane. However, the best way to reach Vang Vieng is now the high-speed train that connects Laos to China with stop-overs in Vientiane, Vang Vieng and Luang Prabang.

content:
The island of Gran Canaria offers a head-spinning variety of landscapes, making it possible to hike through verdant groves and rocky ravines in the north and then retreat to the south for fun in the sun. The beaches aren’t exactly a secret, and from the outside, Seaside Palm Beach doesn’t look much different than the mega-resorts of the sixties and seventies that are still kicking, with its concrete horseshoe shape rising above the big lagoon-style pool. But inside, it’s an artistic cut above the by-the-numbers hospitality of its neighbors.

A 2002 redesign promised a major overhaul, and instead of going for chic minimalism, French architect Alberto Pinto took elements from the hotel’s Seventies origins and updated the look by fusing glam accents with modern luxe. While this isn’t exactly understated (you’re not staying in a 328-room resort hotel for that, anyway) it’s more stylish than it sounds, with plenty of bold colors and intriguing art objects. Shag carpets and any remnants of leisure-suit beach culture have been jettisoned. Each guest room comes with a spacious balcony, and the color schemes range from bright lilac-green to soothing beige-brown. Amenities don’t change much from room to room, although larger corner suites offer separate living spaces and multiple balconies.

When it comes to sunrise views, the sand dunes of Maspalomas are one of the wonders of the Canary Islands. They’re just outside Seaside Palm Beach, along with a shoreline packed with bars and restaurants. Of course, we’d just as soon recommend staying close to the hotel grounds, which include an extensive wellness retreat and a massive dinner buffet among its multitude of restaurants.

Along the coastal lowlands and backwaters of India’s south-western state of Kerala lies the vast Vembanad Lake, connected to the Arabian Sea by a network of canals, estuaries and rivers. And at the edge of Lake Vembanad is Kumarakom, a tiny town at the edge of a lagoon, crisscrossed by narrow waterways used for navigation and irrigation.

Here you’ll find the Kumarakom Lake Resort, a collection of low-slung villas with red tile roofs, surrounded by palm trees, clustered around a long and winding 250-meter free-form swimming pool. At the coastal end of the resort, an infinity pool seems to reach out into Lake Vembanad itself, and if you’re not already spoilt for swimming options, the Presidential Suite comes with its own private pool.

All the villas, from the Presidential on down, are traditional in style, presenting the sort of polished rusticity one expects from the finest Indian resorts. Features vary — some have views of the lake, others open directly onto the long pool, still others have private courtyards and most feature open-air bathrooms. All are fully functioning modern hotel rooms, despite their traditional appearance; air conditioning and cable television are standard, and a wi-fi network covers the entire resort.

The restaurants serve authentic Kerala cuisine and lean heavily on fresh, locally caught seafood, as well as duck, a local specialty. Leisure facilities include yoga, spa treatments and massage More traditionally athletic types may go in for a mountain bike ride, or a spin through the fitness center, but the serious stress case would do better checking in for some intensive Ayurvedic therapies.

If you want eighteen acres of gardens in the middle of a city as bustling as Jaipur, it’s going to take a palace. Back in the 18th century it would have helped mightily to be a member of Rajasthan’s royal family, but in the 21st century all it takes is a passing familiarity with the portfolio of the Taj hotel group, and specifically the hundred-room Jai Mahal Palace.

Of course you don’t choose a luxury hotel for its gardens any more than you choose a car for the leather on the steering wheel. Jai Mahal’s gardens add to the atmosphere, to be sure, but it’s the palace itself that’s the star of this show. The look is traditional Rajasthani with a colonial-era accent, fittingly enough, and modern comforts effortlessly inhabit these traditional spaces.

Guests face a wide array of dining options, including the pan-Indian Cinnamon, the Italian Giardino and the all-day Marble Arch. Leisure activities include a gym, a spa and yoga classes, as well as some more locally tailored offerings, from nature walks and sightseeing tours to camel-buggy rides. All this and top-notch business services as well — hotels like the Taj palaces are one of the underrated aspects of doing business in India.

How to get there: Jai Mahal Palace, Jaipur is located downtown, close to the main shopping center and historical monuments.

content:
In some cities a hotel this small could get lost in the shuffle, but it’s key to Spicers Balfour Brisbane’s success that it’s perfectly matched to the scale of the city itself. You’re just around a bend in the Brisbane River from the central business district, and yet tucked quietly away in New Farm, in a stylish little nine-room boutique. The feeling is at once cosmopolitan, close to the heart of the action, and quietly residential, no surprise given the construction — this is an archetypal Queenslander, an elevated, veranda-wrapped format that was used for well over a century in the region’s private homes.

The rooms are crisp and contemporary in design, without lapsing into that faceless international style — you don’t want Brisbane to look just like Berlin or Barcelona, and to that end there’s something decidedly Pacific Rim about the textures and colors, not to mention the occasional Asian antique piece. Subtle high-end comforts abound, from Bose sound systems to fine Italian linens. The complimentary breakfast is highly regarded, as is the tea service, for that matter, and the bar’s view of the Story Bridge certainly sets a mood.

How to get there:
Spicers Balfour Brisbane is approximately a 30-minute drive from Brisbane Airport.

content: On first look, Casa Newton looks like a textbook Tuscan fantasy. And while this countryside estate-turned-boutique hotel has all the trappings — set amid the rolling green landscapes of the Val d’Orcia and enclosed by old stone walls, the property is dotted with olive groves, fragrant herb gardens, and scenic vineyards — it’s a stylish upgrade from the standard agriturismo. \n\nEverything from the crimson-hued country house to the stone-lined pool deck, now shaded by vintage-inspired, bubble gum-pink parasols, has been reimagined with mid-century modern flair. Rooms are hip but down-to-earth with exposed beams, colorful patterned wallpaper, and original artwork by contemporary Italian artists; a pair of suites in restored farm buildings nearby have private garden terraces. A pair of farm-to-table restaurants and an on-site winery add to the appeal, and guests are encouraged to enjoy their late afternoon aperitivi anywhere on the grounds.

content:
There are hundreds of hotels to choose from on the island of Mallorca, but few as sophisticated as Portella. Housed within a petite 17th-century palace in the medieval walled city of Palma — a light-filled space most recently occupied by an art museum — this boutique hotel retains many of the building’s original features, like exposed stone walls, terracotta tiles, and marble staircases with wrought-iron railings. But the interiors are also strikingly simple and stripped back, outfitted in natural hues and organic materials, channeling quiet luxury more than old-world glamour.

The minimalist update comes courtesy of local architects Gras Reynés in collaboration with Festen, the celebrated Parisian design firm. The result is elegant and down-to-earth. Rooms and suites are set around a central courtyard; a maze of arched hallways wind past their doorways, leading up to a rooftop terrace overlooking the cathedral and down to a hammam with a gym and steam bath. The smallest rooms, on the uppermost level, have sloping wood-beamed ceilings, while larger suites come with kitchens; the lone apartment features a spacious terrace with views of the Arab baths.

Most charming of all is the way Portella operates — not as a typical hotel, with a reception desk and a fixed schedule, but as a guest house, where everything from check-in to your breakfast order is handled informally and person-to-person.

content: Television Center, the mid-century BBC headquarters in Shepherd’s Bush, is no longer in service; its thorough redevelopment, however, is good news for the hospitality world, as it includes White City House, an outpost of the ever-growing Soho House brand of members’ clubs, restaurants, and hotels. In keeping with the building’s period, White City House leans heavily into mid-century modernist style; although the interiors have been thoroughly rebuilt, they’re a beautiful match for this distinctive building.\n\nThe 45 rooms and suites occupy what once were broadcast offices, and they display the Soho House brand’s characteristic eye for eclectic detail and low-key luxury. Overnight guests earn the benefits of membership for the duration of their stay — this means access to the fitness center, the brand’s largest in London, as well as the all-day Club restaurant, the pan-Asian restaurant called Nori by Studio Kitchen, and the members-only Club. Meanwhile, on the 9th-floor rooftop, another restaurant serves salads, small plates and wood-fired pizzas with a panoramic view of West London. It’s a long way from Greek Street, but the Soho House experience, no matter the location, seems to be always in demand.

content:
A proper boutique hotel is more than just an ordinary hotel with a bit of extra color applied to the décor — to be worthy of the name it’s essential to have some personality, a point of view, a style you can’t order from a catalog. Bradford House, in Oklahoma’s vibrant Uptown district, is what we’re talking about: 36 bedrooms in a well-preserved 1912 apartment house and a modern addition, decorated in a style that’s not just eclectic, but personal.

Bradford House is a labor of love for its owners, Jason and Sara Kate Little, who work in property development but rarely in such a hands-on fashion. Their inspiration began with the house itself and the story of its original owner, and they furnished it with vintage and antique furniture collected from all over France and Italy.

For guests, the upshot is an unexpected and memorable visual environment, along with subtly luxe comforts like Bellino linens and Apple TVs. Bikes are available for exploring Uptown, and your hosts are fervent ambassadors for the local area. There’s also plenty of social life at Bradford House: there’s an elegant little cocktail bar with a classic bent, and a stylish restaurant serving brunch, dinner, and a charming afternoon tea.

content: Mendoza, Argentina’s celebrated wine region, is the kind of place where you spend most of your time out exploring: wine tasting, vineyard lunches, hiking in the foothills of the Andes. Lares de Chacras is an ideal place to base yourself, offering a great breakfast and a restful atmosphere to return to after a day out. There’s strong coffee and pastries to start, a shaded swimming pool for a late afternoon dip, and a charmingly rustic stone fireplace where a fire crackles after dark. Guest rooms are simple and quiet, with wood-beamed ceilings and indigenous artwork; several feature a private balcony or terrace — and a restaurant specializing in steaks and Patagonian lamb means you won’t have to venture out again at night.

content: Located in the lively village of Guéthary on the Côte Basque, the family-run Hôtel Brikéténia is a classic French Basque getaway. The 17th-century farmhouse retains many of its original details in its new life as a boutique hotel, from cheerfully painted wooden shutters to terracotta tiles, but the interiors have been beautifully refurbished in a relaxed rustic-chic style with whitewashed walls and natural wood and stone details. Guest rooms are simple, quiet, and immaculately maintained, with crisp white linens and abundant natural light — the perfect retreat after walking along the beach or dining on the terrace at the hotel’s Michelin-starred restaurant.

content:
The hotel world would be a boring one indeed if no one bothered to innovate. But the joys of a family-owned boutique hotel that’s rooted in the regional tradition shouldn’t be underestimated, especially when it’s as finely crafted and lovingly maintained as the Hotel Tennerhof in the Austrian Alps. This Tyrolean resort is part upscale ski lodge and part wellness retreat, with just as much to offer in summer as in ski season. 

Since 1929, the Pasquali family has been decorating the thirty-nine guest rooms with heirlooms and antiques that reflect the heritage of the region. Even if you’re normally allergic to the storybook charms and whimsy of ornate wardrobes and headboards painted with pastel scenery, suspend your initial reaction for a closer look — this is priceless handmade stuff, not kitsch. At the higher end, suites tend to be a bit more subdued, with big glass doors opening out onto private terraces. It goes without saying that the Alpine view is magnificent, and skiers will find the quick walk to the Kitzbüheler slopes to be a blessing. 

The hotel’s restaurant specializes in romantic candlelight dinners, which can be enjoyed on the terrace when it’s not covered in snow. The wine cellar is suitably expansive, with plenty of opportunity for regional pairings with the restaurant’s original creations. Make no mistake: this is a sumptuous experience, so if you’re craving a utilitarian ski-bum retreat, you’d be better served elsewhere. To put it another way, if you’re likely to cap off a long day on the slopes with a trip to the sauna and a glass of excellent wine, then this is the hotel for you.

content:
If the owners of your favorite café — or in this case, your favorite wine bar or small-batch distillery — suddenly got into the hotel game, you’d probably sit up and notice. So it is with Alex Hotel, located in the heart of Perth’s buzzing Cultural Centre neighborhood. The team behind it already had a good thing going before opening the doors to this cool 74-room hotel. Several good things, in fact, and Alex Hotel is just the latest in a series.

The building is airy and industrial, encased with glass that lets the sunshine into the lobby espresso bar, perfectly lighting the lavish and eminently Instagram-ready continental breakfast spread. Food and drink, and more importantly, socializing in general, are guiding concepts here — fitting, given that the owners are known first and foremost as purveyors of locally roasted coffee, craft beer, and artisanal spirits. They’d be the first to say that guest rooms (“creative bases,” to borrow their phrase) are not the most important part of the hotel. The look is simple but stylish, the beds made up in Italian linens and blankets by local brand Bemboka, the bathrooms stocked with Sodashi products, also local.

The point of staying at Alex Hotel isn’t to hole up in your room, anyway: it’s all about communal spaces here, from the colorful Mezzanine lounge space with its work stations and shaded outdoor terraces — an ideal place to get some work done or help yourself to a glass of wine from the honesty bar while poking through a small library of books and magazines — to the sultry Shadow Wine Bar & Dining Room. The hands-down highlight is the rooftop terrace, the place to be at sunset. Looking down over the cityscape of repurposed warehouses, you might plan your bicycle route for the next day: you won’t be surprised to know that Alex Hotel offers up a fleet of Lekker bikes for guest use. They’ll even give you a lock and a helmet, and a map, marked up (on request) with the staff’s top picks for shopping, dining, and drinking around town.

The complimentary champagne is perfectly chilled in the Eau Palm Beach’s chandelier-lit lobby, a fittingly elegant welcome to one of the most luxurious hotels on Florida’s Gold Coast. This Mediterranean-style resort, once a Ritz-Carlton, sits on a peaceful private beach lined with bright white sun umbrellas and sun loungers. Designer Jonathan Adler reimagined the interiors with his signature mix of bold colors, whimsical patterns, and glamorous mid-century modern décor.

Spacious, light-filled guest rooms are outfitted in shades of blue, all with floor-to-ceiling glass doors opening onto private balconies, many with striking sea views. Suites feature freestanding soaking tubs and large patios. The state-of-the-art Eau Spa, set amid tropical gardens, is a standout feature, as are two oceanfront pools and a chic terrace café overlooking the Atlantic; Nobu Manalapan is the most recognizable name among the selection of restaurants.

content: Elder sister to the smaller, more contemporary Giardino Lago, Giardino Ascona is where you go for something just a touch more classic on the shores of the Swiss end of Lake Maggiore. Here owners Daniela and Philippe Frutiger combine the elegance of Alpine lakeside hospitality with a laid-back Mediterranean influence, which comes with the territory here in the Ticino, the Italian corner of Switzerland. It’d take an architectural historian to explain how exactly this classic villa differs from its counterparts over the border — suffice it to say that for the rest of us it’s a slice of unadulterated dolce vita. The rooms are renovated in a style that’s a touch more modern than the hotel’s classic exteriors, and there’s a stylish spareness to them, as well as a certain rigor to the color palette, that’s eminently pleasing to the contemporary eye. Comforts, too, are modern, with wi-fi and electronics alongside the low-tech charms of the views from the balconies and terraces. An indoor and an outdoor pool, as well as a spa and fitness center, await leisure-minded guests, and Ascona’s golf club is literally next door — to say nothing of the lake itself, whose shores lie just at the end of the road. And you’ll want to be sure you work up an appetite — Ecco Ascona is the proud recipient of two MICHELIN Stars, and Hide & Seek, alongside the lily pond, is the more modern and casual option. How to get there: Giardino Ascona is approximately 120 km by car from Milan-Malpensa Airport via SS336, A36, A9/E35, A2, and A13. Alternatively, the hotel is approximately 220 km by car from Zürich Airport via A4/E41, A2/E35, and A13.

content:
It might strike you that it takes quite a bit of confidence to name your hotel after the city it calls home. But it turns out the Hotel Montevideo has plenty to be confident about. This 80-room boutique-style luxury hotel aims to be nothing less than the finest hotel in the Uruguayan capital, and there’s no question it lands in the top tier. 

The building, an eye-catching modern one, stands over the upscale partially residential district of Pocitos, barely a quarter-mile from the beach of the same name. And its rooms and suites are not just luxurious — though they’re certainly that — but distinctive in their design as well, full of custom-designed furniture that ranges in inspiration from well-loved antiques to modernist design classics. All of them come with at least one balcony, and the long-stay Residences add kitchenettes and walk-in closets.

There’s a swanky fitness center with high-end equipment as well as a heated outdoor pool with a view of the city skyline; the lack of a spa is probably the only thing separating the Hotel Montevideo from the bigger luxury hotels. Then again no one else has a restaurant and bar quite like Polo Bamba and the Polo Bamba Skybar, both overseen by the well-known local chefs Ale Morales and Florencia Courreges.

The word “spectacular” hardly seems up to the task of describing Habitas AlUla, an extraordinary collection of 96 luxury villas in a box canyon in the Ashar Valley of Saudi Arabia. Some resorts use the word “oasis” figuratively but here it’s entirely apt; its founders met at Burning Man, and this is, in a way, the ultra-luxe version of the desert festival, complete with impressive outdoor artworks and an array of immersive outdoor and/or cultural experiences. 

In the villas themselves you’ll find luxury-hotel comforts and a style that’s one part contemporary and one part traditional. Each one has its own shaded outdoor space for enjoying the early morning and late afternoon hours. There’s a spa offering a variety of regionally informed treatments, as well as yoga classes — the Habitas hotels are more about connection than solitude.

To that end the activities are group-focused, and include hikes, camel rides, ATV tours, and visits to Hegra, an archaeological site, and visits to the historic center of AlUla, a half-hour’s drive to the south. Another social space is the incredibly photogenic swimming pool, and the restaurant, Tama, serves a locally sourced menu of Middle Eastern and international dishes.

content:
They take years to plan, scout and develop, and present so many logistical challenges along the way that simply to finish one, to say nothing of a whole trilogy, is possibly enough achievement for a lifetime. Of course we’re talking about movies, but it’s equally true of hotels — just ask Francis Ford Coppola, who, after innumerable films (and a side line in winemaking), has opened his third Central American eco-lodge, La Lancha, on Lake Peten Itzá, near Tikal, in Guatemala.

It’s the third in a trilogy that already includes Blancaneaux Lodge and the Turtle Inn, in Belize. The La Lancha experience is very much of a piece with its sisters: a lush rainforest setting, an emphasis on low-impact living, and close proximity to some Mayan historic sites, in this case the Unesco site at Tikal.

Where it differs is in the finish. This is a more rough and rustic experience, ten rooms with shared terraces, some with views of the lake. You’re not here for the luxury, but for the setting. The immediate rainforest surroundings would be enough, but La Lancha throws in the spectacular Lake Peten Itzá and the Tikal ruins for good measure — plus a restaurant that mixes authentic Guatemalan cuisine with Italian-style wood-fired pizzas and wines from the Coppola concern.

How to Get There:
La Lancha is approximately a 45 minute drive from Flores International Airport or a 3 hour drive from Blancaneaux Lodge. A 1 hour flight links Flores International with Belize International Airport. Flights and overland transfers as well as tours to Tikal need pre-booking.

With Vietnamese travel ever in the ascendant, it’s time to get familiar with a few more destinations. One of them is Phu Quoc, the so-called Pearl Island of Asia, a Singapore-sized island that’s to the west of mainland Vietnam and just off the coast of Cambodia. It’s home to everything we love about this country, from the spectacular white-sand beaches to the picturesque jungles, as well as some extraordinary luxury resorts — including, of course, the very impressive Salinda Resort Phu Quoc Island.

Weighing in at a little over a hundred suites and villas, Salinda isn’t small, but it’s always sedate, thanks to its sheer spaciousness. At every level the accommodations are generously sized and eye-catchingly stylish, not to mention comfortable — king beds, rain showers, private balconies, the works.

The Q'isense Spa is a Thai import, while the hotel’s restaurant selection includes Italian and Indian options alongside its flagship Vietnamese restaurant. The service, not just at the table but throughout the resort, is held to an impressively high standard. And there’s an extraordinary amount to do beyond the resort’s grounds — there’s Phu Quoc National Park, there’s some astonishingly good diving and snorkeling in the surrounding waters, and the local Night Market is not to be missed.

content: In many cases “hotel and resort” is just a fancy way of saying “hotel,” but Rambutan Hotel & Resort styles itself as two properties in one, side by side in the heart of old Siem Reap, just across the river from the city center. To be perfectly fair, they share everything, including the spa, the swimming pools, and the restaurant and bar. But the two wings of accommodations do have their own distinct identities: the hotel side is made up of Balcony Villa rooms, most of them in a two-story duplex orientation, while the resort wing contains Deluxe Terrace rooms with or without rooftop space.\n\nAnd while the resort side may offer a touch more space, as well as extra comforts like outdoor baths, the difference isn’t exactly night and day. With just 26 units between them, they’re both small, and the property never feels crowded or busy. The location is both convenient and quiet, tucked down a side street but just five minutes’ walk from the Old Market. Meanwhile the restaurant and bar serve western and Khmer classics overlooking one of the two salt-water pools, and a small spa offers restorative treatments after a day of temple tours.

content:
No, they haven't gone and turned the original Taj Mahal into a hotel — but this place is so impressive that it would be easy to forget about its namesake altogether. Conventional wisdom holds that this is the finest hotel in India, the equal of any luxury hotel in New York or Paris, and given Indian architecture's flair for the dramatic, it is no surprise that from the outside, this hotel could pass for at least the ninth or tenth wonder of the world. But that's actually the back of the hotel you are seeing from the harbor — legend has it that the architect drew up the plans from abroad, and didn't visit the site until construction had been completed. Supposedly as his boat approached, he saw that the hotel had been built the wrong way around, and was so frustrated that he threw himself overboard. Whether or not this is true, there are benefits to the odd layout; the “back” of the hotel is all guest rooms, with no grand entrance taking up space, and more rooms thus overlook the harbor — and what may have been intended as a driveway and entrance is instead the swimming pool and courtyard, while the actual entrance is a discreet, out-of-the-way affair. 

Mumbai, formerly Bombay, is a bustling and chaotic city, home to (among others) the film industry, and is, like much of India, a study in contrasts, from the opulence of the Taj Mahal hotel to the noise and pollution of the city streets. The better rooms have magnificent ocean views, while the lesser look down on Mumbai's dilapidated rooftops — still a stunning panorama, if not exactly postcard-worthy. The somewhat newer Tower Wing, though still luxurious, is a bit antiseptic compared to the Heritage Wing, dating back to 1903, where this hotel's history was written, its guestbook comprising a Who's Who of travelers to (and within) India for the last hundred years. 

There are no fewer than five restaurants and three bars, as well as every in-house convenience imaginable — but to stay in would be criminal. Mumbai's nightlife is legendary, and even the most jaded traveler can find something worth seeing in this extraordinary city, whether the vast Victoria gardens or just a game of cricket.

content: It would be a missed opportunity if a Victorian seaside town called Port Fairy were anything less than magical. Fortunately for all involved, it lives up to its promise. A few short years ago it was voted “most livable town in the world,” and its historic style and splendid coastline make it tempting indeed. And Drift House just might be one of the most livable small hotels in the world — it’s not just an architectural marvel, combining a classic Victorian house with an uncompromisingly modernist addition, but it’s owned and operated by a family with a keen sense of what really matters in hospitality.\n\nDon’t miss the “small” part: Drift House has just six suites, each completely different, but all more or less equivalent in comfort, give or take a bathtub here or a fireplace there. They’re stylish but not gimmicky, and they’re substantial enough to feel more like apartments than ordinary hotel suites. And while breakfast is the entirety of the food service, it’s quite a breakfast; for lunch and dinner you’ll be only too happy to ramble around Port Fairy — perhaps on a hotel-provided cruiser bike — in search of a bite.

content:
It may come as a surprise to those of us with only the vaguest, headline-driven notions of life in Colombia’s third-largest city, but in many ways Cali is something of a party town. Hopelessly enthralled with salsa music, teeming with bars and cafés that spill out onto the sidewalks, home to a sophisticated culinary scene and populated by famously beautiful people, it’s a destination that — despite persistent issues with crime — feels poised for some serious rebranding. And if Cali is a city with two very different faces, the Movich Casa del Alférez is firmly on its good side, a stylish modern hotel in the upscale Granada neighborhood. Five minutes from downtown and within walking distance of San Antonio, the city’s historic center, it’s a convenient base for both business and leisure. 

Though they feel at home amidst the neighborhood’s elegant homes and old Colonial buildings, the hotel’s tastefully restrained rooms could stand their own in any of the region’s more crowded hotel markets. They’re airy and bright, with plush king-size beds, deeply grained wood floors and plenty of natural light flooding in through oversized windows. Book well and you’ve got a balcony on the other side of those French doors, perfect for lazing about and watching the street life below. 

Come late afternoon, when the daily breeze rolls in and cools the air (the city is warm year-round), you’ll want to head down to the open-air bar. Lit with torches and candles beneath the building’s stone walls and a stand of palm trees, it’s as relaxing as can be — a fine place to unwind, whether after a long day of meetings or a long night on your feet at the neighborhood’s salsatecas.

content: Midtown Atlanta is as creative and cosmopolitan a city-center neighborhood as you’re likely to find anywhere in the United States; it’s only fitting that it should come equipped with one of the most stylish of the Kimpton hotels, the swanky, art-filled, modernist-inspired Kimpton Shane Hotel. It’s as friendly, as approachable, and as personality-driven as any of the other IHG hotels that share the Kimpton name; it’s remarkable, even in this context, for its particular stylishness and for its connections to the local art, music, and restaurant scenes.\n\nThe Shane’s rooms are decked out in shades of gray, with slate-blue headboards serving as the interior visual focus, and the views of Atlanta the exterior. Frette linens and Atelier Bloem bath products strike a luxe note; the décor feels mid-century-inspired but fresh and up to date. Its public spaces are a touch more visually expressive, and include some one-of-a-kind decorative elements and artworks. And the food and beverage program is first-rate; there’s Hartley Kitchen & Cocktails, the signature American restaurant and bar, as well as Aveline, serving wines, beers, and spirits with access to a second-floor patio.
