content:
The original Jupiter, though it’s still going strong, is in some ways an artifact of another era in this city’s history — one of the country’s first “hip motels,” and home to an excellent indie music venue, it’s nevertheless not quite what the new generation of globetrotting travelers expect to find in today’s Portland. It’s for them that Jupiter NEXT is intended.

It’s an unapologetically contemporary structure, towering over its mid-century counterpart just across the street. Its height affords it unparalleled views of the city, especially in its west-facing rooms, and its modern construction allows for generous floor plans and rooms that are as luxurious as they are stylish.

And we do mean stylish. Though it’s a move upmarket, Jupiter NEXT hasn’t lost touch with its origins. Raw concrete and mid-century modernist–inspired furniture lend the building its boutique-hotel good looks, and the lobby’s central staircase, by local fabricator Sol Creations, seems to float on air.

Where the original Jupiter has the rock-and-roll Doug Fir Lounge, NEXT has Hey Love, which is part café, part cocktail lounge, and serves a menu of “tropical-inspired comfort food” in a retro-styled space that’s open from late morning through to late night.

The bottom line: if the original Jupiter is exactly your jam, you might find NEXT to be a touch on the fancy side — but if you’ve caught yourself wishing for something slightly more luxurious, then this one is right up your street.

content:
For some of us, the idea of a trip to Spain’s Balearic islands implies the sort of hedonistic all-night dance debauch that’s practically synonymous with the word Ibiza. But the Balearics are nothing if not varied, and on Menorca, in the ancient town of Ciutadella, you can get what’s practically the polar opposite experience — Divina Suites, an eight-suite boutique hotel in a 17th-century palazzo, is as tranquil a hotel as you’ll find this side of heaven itself.

It’s also, if we may venture a blasphemous opinion, rather more stylish than Paradise itself is likely to be. There’s a playfulness about the design and décor that breathes contemporary life into the old house, where vibrant colors and contemporary gestures contrast with soothing white and historical architectural details. There’s a residential aspect to the comforts, which include kitchenettes and properly usable living/dining rooms.

Among the keys to its peacefulness is its adults-only policy; breakfast is delivered to your suite every morning in a basket, relieving you of the need to pull yourself together for a public appearance. And Ciutadella is seemingly tailor-made for a quiet stroll — this town is a mosaic of distinct eras and styles, and is as picturesque as can be.

content:
On the West Coast, the 19th century is ancient history, and for a hotel that dates back to 1894, as does the Kimpton Hotel Vintage Portland, the word “vintage” is a bit of an understatement. But while in its previous life this hotel was often guilty of resting a bit too comfortably on its history, today’s Vintage, on the inside at least, is a thoroughly contemporary boutique hotel.

When you’re talking about a Kimpton hotel this means social hour in the wine room every evening, it means your pets stay for free, and it means stylish PUBLIC bikes available for exploring the city. There’s live music on the weekends, there’s a game lounge on the second floor, and the service, as always, is as friendly and familiar as it gets. And the rooms are stylish and comfortable, without being aggressively avant-garde or excessively ostentatious.

The location, in downtown Portland’s commercial center, is perhaps a touch straitlaced — you’ll want to get out to the surrounding neighborhoods for the full Portland experience. When you’re ready to come home the Hotel Vintage’s restaurant, Pazzo Ristorante, will be waiting for you, with a hybrid Northwest-Italian cuisine and a bar that features an encyclopedic selection of local beers and Oregon wines.

content: The medieval town of Naumburg was a big deal in the so-called High Middle Ages, a stop on a major trade route and home to an impressive cathedral which is, perhaps unsurprisingly, one of the town’s greatest attractions today. Against this rich historical backdrop, a little bit of contemporary design goes a long way; this explains the impact of Gasthof Zufriedenheit, a hotel whose 19th-century bones — practically a new build by local standards — were thoroughly renovated in 2016, resulting in something that’s subtly modern and surprisingly stylish, yet still in keeping with Naumburg’s deep roots.\n\nGuest rooms start out large, by guest-house standards — the Garden rooms span 24 square meters, and most come with king beds. Suites encompass a whopping 60 square meters, and their bathrooms include showers as well as freestanding tubs. In place of a lobby bar are the living room and a charming courtyard, either one a cozy spot for a cup of coffee, an aperitif, or, in the afternoon, a selection of teas, cakes, and other sweets. The restaurant serves seasonal fare including ingredients from the hotel’s own garden, and the associated wine bar specializes in bottles from producers in the local Saxony-Anhalt region.

content: Sure, in some ways, Vienna is among the most traditional of cities. But it’s often against a backdrop of entrenched conservatism that the most radical experiments take flight. Like its sister, the Graetzlhotel Belvedere, the Graetzlhotel Karmelitermarkt’s suites are made from disused storefronts, in this case near the Karmelitermarkt, an open-air market just to the northeast of Vienna’s city center. And like its sisters — there’s also the Meidlinger Markt — it’s a relatively low-maintenance, high-independence affair, an effort by the Urbanauts group to allow visitors to live, to the greatest possible extent, like Viennese locals.\n\nIt’s the perfect answer to the apartment-sharing economy, an upgrade in terms of design, service, and professionalism, but without sacrificing the autonomy and privacy of apartment life. You’ll pick up your key using a code from a centralized safe, you’ll show yourself to your suite, and from there you’re on your own to explore the shops, restaurants, and cultural attractions of the city’s old Jewish quarter. From here it’s a quick hop across the river to the center of town, for a more typical tourist experience — and then at the end of the day it’s back to your smart, stylish, and eminently comfortable storefront suite for the night. Maybe not one for the butlers-and-room-service set, but for the rest of us it hits just the right note.

content:
Joining the same Swire family that brought us the Upper House Hong Kong and the Upper House Shanghai, the Upper House Chengdu might feel a bit more of a stretch for Western visitors. But it won’t be for long. Already a manufacturing center for many high-tech industries, it’ll be a more frequent destination in the coming years for global techies of all stripes — and they’ll be happy to find at least one world-class hotel awaiting them upon arrival.

The hotel development comes with impressive architectural credentials. Designed by Make Architects to pay tribute to its historic surroundings, it’s a part of the Chengdu Daci Temple Cultural & Commercial Complex, a sort of combined conservation/modernization project. The immediate upshot, for guests of the Upper House Chengdu, is a drastic contrast of old and new — you’ll enter via a century-old Qing Dynasty courtyard building, before being whisked to your accommodations in one of the ultra-modern tower additions.

And those accommodations are predictably first-rate — spacious, bright, classically luxe and subtly high-tech. A handful of restaurants and bars provide ample opportunity for socializing over a meal or a drink, and the extensive spa offerings and the generous indoor pool provide venues for solo restoration. It’s the new breed of city luxury hotel: as much urban resort as office-away-from-home, combined with service that’s top-notch yet never rigid or excessively rule-governed. Get used to it.

content: With pine forests at its back and the Atlantic unfurling at its feet, Bluebird Ocean Point Inn captures the easygoing soul of a classic Maine summer. Situated along East Boothbay’s craggy shoreline, this former summer colony turned boutique inn channels coastal nostalgia with nautical stripes, weathered wood, and porches made for sea-gazing. Days are filled with barefoot rituals: kayaking calm coves, schooner sails at sunset, and lobster rolls enjoyed from Adirondack chairs with sweeping views of Linekin Bay. Come evening, guests gather around fire pits with s’mores and local brews, embracing the simple joy of life beside the sea.

content: A walkable location in Yountville is a gourmet’s paradise; Lavender, A Four Sisters Inn is just across the street from the French Laundry, and a quick stroll away from various wineries and tasting rooms. The hotel consists of a quartet of smartly renovated 19th-century farmhouses, slightly set apart amid gardens blooming with wild roses and hydrangeas. The idea behind Four Sisters, an upscale hotel collection with properties throughout California, is to bring together the sophistication of a boutique hotel with the warmth of a bed-and-breakfast. In the Napa Valley location, this means elegant interiors with a French country twist, plus homey amenities like freshly baked chocolate chip cookies and an afternoon wine hour.\n\nThe simplest rooms, up a flight of stairs in the main house, have vaulted ceilings and feature a king-sized bed, a seating area with a fireplace, a writing desk, and a simple bathroom with a jetted tub. Thoughtful extras range from plush bathrobes and custom bath products to a small library of books and a mini-fridge to keep the Chardonnay cold. Larger rooms and suites, some accessible through private outdoor entrances, have cozy private patios, some with luxurious outdoor tubs. One of the farmhouses has a wraparound porch where a homemade breakfast is served. Lavender provides complimentary bicycles for exploring the Napa Valley Vine Trail, and the hotel’s brick-lined courtyard, strung with twinkling lights, is the perfect spot to relax by the fire with a glass of wine.

With a name taken from a poem by the Englishman Edward Lear, the Owl and the Pussycat wears its literary inspiration on its sleeve — and if you were to imagine what a modernist Sri Lankan boutique hotel dedicated to a Victorian eccentric might look like, you’d be very much on the right track. It’s set right on the water, with a direct view onto the Indian Ocean, just down the coast from Galle, not far from Unawatuna Beach, one of the island’s finest.

It’s a modestly sized hotel, spread across four small buildings containing just 17 rooms and suites; the better ones face out to sea, but all are stylish, colorful, and comfortable. They vary widely in size as well — the largest two-bedroom suite is four times the size of the humblest standard room.

There’s a cozy swimming pool and a bit of outdoor lounge space overlooking the water; this section of beach isn’t swimmable, but it is picturesque. Public spaces also include a drawing room with a capacious library, and Botanik, the restaurant, serving simple and modern Sri Lankan fare in an air-conditioned dining room or al fresco facing the sea.

content: Overlooking the spectacular mountains and valleys of the island’s interior, Madulkelle Tea & Eco Lodge offers an only-in-Sri-Lanka experience: a tranquil luxury boutique hotel set on a working tea plantation. Safari-style tents form the entry-level accommodations, while higher-end options gain solid walls — but all are open to the breeze and in direct contact with the hotel’s idyllic surroundings. A grand dining room offers dishes concocted with vegetables and herbs from the hotels’s own garden, and an English-style bar keeps conversation going long into the night. Day trips and hikes can be arranged, as well as guided tours of tea-making facilities; meanwhile, couples spa treatments are offered in thatched pavilions with mountain views and the nearby trickle of a running stream.

content:
Travelers craving escape are presented with no end of rural options, from private islands to country farmhouses and mountaintop monasteries — those in search of an urban getaway, though, have to look ever farther to find a city that’s sufficiently off the beaten path. Some stop at Prague, others Marrakech, while others settle for nothing short of Zanzibar. A two-hour ferry trip or a half-hour flight from the already rather remote Dar es Salaam will land you in the Stone Town district, the historic Zanzibar city center, a delirious mix of Islamic, Swahili and Western culture and architecture.

And once in Zanzibar it’s hard to do much better than the small, privately owned Emerson on Hurumzi. The atmosphere here is one of antique splendor, the rooms packed with eclectic traditional furnishings, each quite different in layout and features — some have balconies or verandas, others open-air bathtubs or showers, and the suites are particularly luxurious, decked out in fine fabrics and ornate tiled floors.

The Towertop restaurant is one of the city’s treasures, serving an authentic local cuisine from a stunning rooftop venue, with views of the old town’s rooftops and the Indian Ocean beyond, a sight perhaps best seen at sunset.

Though certainly a departure from the everyday, Emerson on Hurumzi is no cocoon. Even the quietest rooms admit the wild sounds of the Zanzibar night, and the morning calls to prayer. Then again, that’s half the point — if it’s silence you’re after, the world is hardly short on high-rise five-star luxury hotels.

Don’t let the Beach Boys’ 1988 hit, with its list of Caribbean names, mislead you — the only Kokomo that matters is Fiji’s Kokomo Private Island Resort. The island itself is a 140-acre speck of a place, a 45-minute seaplane ride from Fiji’s main island. And the resort itself comprises a mere 21 villas plus five residences, which means that even at capacity it still has the rarefied air of a private island retreat.

Villas range from one to three bedrooms, residences from three to six, and in every configuration they’re as lavish as can be — even the one-bedroom villas come with private infinity pools, outdoor showers, lavish bathrooms, and plentiful indoor and outdoor lounge space. The style is part contemporary, part classic South Pacific, and the craftsmanship throughout is first-rate.

Also first-rate is the service, as is the singing — there’s a gospel choir tradition in the region from which many staff members are drawn. The restaurants practice farm-to-table and “dock-to-dish” sourcing, the spa offers everything from massage to yoga to meditation, and the activities, as you’d expect, include just about anything that can be done by sea: fishing, kayaking, surfing, sailing, and diving some of the most extraordinary coral formations in the world.

How to get there:
From Nadi International Airport, guests will be transferred to Kokomo Private Island Resort by seaplane or helicopter.

Five miles off the coast of Abu Dhabi, out there in the waters of the Gulf, there’s a resort that just might change your perception of what’s possible in Emirates tourism. In spite of its name, Desert Islands Resort is just one island, the Sir Bani Yas nature reserve — and to look at the verdant landscape, it’s clear this desert island is more a paradise lost than some scrappy patch of sand.

It’s quite a departure from the regional norm. Desert Islands is run by Anantara, best known for beach resorts in Thailand and the Maldives; so the Arabian palace atmosphere is tempered by a healthy dose of island-resort mellowness. What is typically Emirati is the scale of the accommodations, all of which are equipped to the highest five-star standard — rooms are nobody’s idea of small, and the suites are downright lavish.

The pool, the spa, the restaurants are impressive, as you’d expect them to be. What’s unexpected is the breadth of the leisure offerings, from such slightly exotic pursuits as snorkeling and tennis to unique attractions like archery, trail hiking and game drives. The nature reserve makes for an experience that’s not entirely unlike a safari outing, and if that’s what you picture when you think of Abu Dhabi — well, in this case, it just so happens you're right.

How to get there:
8-seat Cessna Caravan or 50-seat Dash-8 aircraft fly from Abu Dhabi International Airport direct to Sir Bani Yas Island in a matter of minutes. Dash-8 flights, operated by Abu Dhabi Aviation, leave Abu Dhabi and Sir Bani Yas on Thursdays and Saturdays and take 25 minutes. Cessna flights, operated by Empire Aviation, run every Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday and take 50 minutes. Private Cessna charters are available throughout the week. Luggage restrictions apply.

content:
A number of Sorrento’s historic palazzi now function as hotels, but Palazzo Marziale enjoys a unique distinction: it’s owned and operated by the same aristocratic family that’s resided here for centuries. Right in the heart of town, a stone’s throw from the Cloister of San Francesco, the 15th-century palazzo retains many of its period features, including the graceful pale-pink façade, stone columns and archways, terracotta flooring, and leafy interior courtyard. 

Rooms and suites have an old-fashioned air, with antique wood furniture, artwork in gilded frames, and luxurious bedding flecked with fleur-de-lis motifs. Standard rooms are simpler in style, with parquet floors and views over the street; some have French balconies facing the interior patio. Larger rooms and suites are more ornately decorated with heavy drapery, large mirrors, and seating areas with plush loveseats.

There’s no restaurant at Palazzo Marziale, but a sumptuous breakfast buffet is laid out on fine china each morning in a mural-lined dining area. When weather permits, a morning cappucino or an evening aperitivo is served on the hotel’s terrace.

content: At the foot of Austria’s Wilder Kaiser mountain range is a collection of four villages, all excellent bases for exploring the region’s hiking and skiing areas. The smallest village, Scheffau, is considered the most scenic of the four, and one of its best hotels is Kaiserlodge. It’s only a few years old, and it looks like it — this sustainably built lodge has a traditional Tyrolean style, but it’s modern and airy, with lots of pale stone, blonde wood, and glass — and the design was carefully planned so that guests hardly need to leave the premises. There's a natural swimming pond in summer, a steaming-hot rooftop pool with mountain views in winter, the adults-only Natürlich.Spa, a state-of-the-art kids’ club with its own cinema, and a lively restaurant and bar that serves brunch late and practically never closes.\n\nAccommodations range from standard double rooms to spacious suites with multiple bedrooms and well-equipped kitchens. Of particular novelty are Kaiserlodge’s lake suites, which offer direct access to the water via a private footbridge. All have a contemporary alpine look, with natural wood paneling and furniture, sophisticated lighting systems, and large bathrooms with walk-in showers or tubs; most offer views of the snowcapped mountains that loom over the village. Outdoor adventures await nearby in all four seasons, with hiking trails leading directly from the hotel’s front door and mountain bikes available for rent at reception.

content: After launching their flagship property in Brussels, JAM Hotels expanded to Lisbon, applying the same successful formula — snapping up an old office building and transforming it into a youthful, art-filled boutique hotel — on a commercial block in the riverside neighborhood of Santos. The concept works just as well here, if not better, considering the stark contrast between the building’s past and present. Architect Lionel Jadot led a team of designers and artisans through the years-long overhaul, maintaining the structure's industrial character while incorporating colorful artwork and sustainable local materials like cork, terracotta, and wood. \n\nThe result is vibrant but stripped back, with a lobby that looks like a street art exhibition space, rooms lined in raw concrete, and a rooftop pool lined with hand-painted tiles. Rooms sleep from two to six, with the larger dormitory-style rooms featuring modern sleeping pod-like bunk beds with sliding wooden doors for extra privacy. Reinvention is everywhere: handwoven carpets upcycled as curtains, beds built from burnt eucalyptus, bedding made from surplus fabric. Similarly eclectic is the hotel’s fusion restaurant, overseen by a talented young Angolese chef, and the poolside bar with an open-air performance space where local musicians regularly perform.

content:
The word is probably out by now, but just in case it needs repeating: the Yellowstone name signifies much more than just the site of a punctual geyser. Under Canvas North Yellowstone - Paradise Valley is located on the north side of the Montana-Wyoming border, closer to Bozeman and Big Sky than to Old Faithful. Its immediate setting, Paradise Valley, richly deserves its name. That said, it’s less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park’s north entrance, and inside the park you’ll find mile after mile of spectacular scenery, awe-inspiring wildlife, and all the adventure you can handle.

Like the other Under Canvas resorts it’s a tented camp, this one comprising some fifty units spread across a fifty-acre estate by the side of the Yellowstone River. The tents themselves are luxurious by just about any standard — they come with en suite bathrooms, king beds, plentiful hot water, and wood-burning stoves. The camp’s restaurant serves seasonal and locally sourced fare for breakfast and dinner, with grab-and-go options for lunch. And while nightlife and camping don’t always go hand in hand, Under Canvas has an outdoor bar that serves beer, wine, and cocktails (while the kids busy themselves with s’mores).

Please note: Under Canvas North Yellowstone - Paradise Valley is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from mid-June through late September.

The French Alpine ski destination of Val d’Isère is plenty famous in its own right, but Le K2 Chogori, like its sister hotels in Courchevel, takes its primary inspiration from the Himalayas — both its name and its décor are inspired by Tibet’s language and aesthetics. Its location means the village and the lifts are within easy walking distance, and the views of the slopes are a constant reminder of the reason you’re here.

Le K2 Chogori’s interiors are stylish, but still as warm and welcoming as you’d wish from an Alpine luxury lodge. For all its extravagance, it’s family-owned, operated, and designed, which gives it a personality few corporate luxury hotels can match. The accommodations offer a decidedly high-end experience, from the stone-clad bathrooms to the designer fabrics and upscale bath products. 

The Goji Spa by Nescens offers restoration in between days on the mountain, as does, in a different way, restaurant Bottleneck, which serves grilled dishes and cheese fondues. Meanwhile Le 1954, named for the year of K2’s first successful summit, handles everything from afternoon tea and light daytime fare to apéritifs, cocktails, and occasional live music.

content:
The redevelopment of the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront into the purpose-built Victoria Dockside art and design district is big news for Kowloon, the mainland side of Hong Kong. And it’s big news for us as well, for among its hospitality offerings is K11 Artus, a residential-style luxury boutique hotel with an intense focus on art, architecture, design, and culture in general.

It was designed by celebrated architect André Fu for entrepreneur Adrian Cheng, whose K11 art foundation (and retail operation) has made it its mission to integrate China into the international contemporary art world — a mission that’s met with a great deal of success. And K11 Artus will only advance the cause; it’s exquisitely crafted, with seemingly mundane details like lighting and furniture exhibiting the same care as the priceless artworks on display.

Imagine the extravagance and comfort of Hong Kong’s established luxury hotels combined with the taste and style of the most avant-garde boutique hotel, and you’re essentially there. The accommodations range from studios to three-bedroom suites, all of which come with balconies, many with extraordinary views of Hong Kong Island across the water. And while, as a residential-style hotel, it’s light on traditional hotel services, the line between the hotel and the rest of the Victoria Dockside development is fluid — meaning there’s no end of dining and entertainment options right at your feet.

content:
Many Aman hotels are ground-up productions, where every aspect of the building can be painstakingly controlled. Amantaka, by contrast, occupies an authentic French colonial building in old-town Luang Prabang, a city that’s as much a spiritual center as it is a leisure destination. While the building adds some historical gravity, it doesn’t detract at all from the perfectionistic luxury that is Aman’s stock in trade — and the meditative aspect of the setting is perfect for a proper escape.

The result is without a doubt the finest hotel in town, which is something that tends to happen whenever Aman sets up shop. The 24 suites are soothing, spacious, and visually sparse, with outdoor living areas and in some cases private pools. You’ll lack for nothing in terms of comfort, and the service, as always, is out of this world — many Aman guests simply refuse to stay anywhere else, and there are good reasons for that.

And for all the luxe seclusion, Amantaka goes out of its way to provide opportunities to connect with the locale. Your hosts can arrange temple visits, cultural experiences, craft classes, and cruises on the Mekong River. The hotel’s world-class spa incorporates traditional Lao therapies, and the restaurant turns local produce into classic Laotian dishes, or anything you like — if you’ve got something special in mind there’s no question your hosts can make it happen.

How to get there:
Amantaka is located 10 minutes by car from Luang Prabang International Airport. The airport is serviced by scheduled flights from Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Hanoi, Kuala Lumpur, Siem Reap, Singapore, and Vientiane, Laos’s capital.

content: To call the setting magical is no understatement. Boynton Canyon, part of the Yavapai Tribe’s ancestral land, is one of the famous Sedona vortexes — swirling centers of energy associated with healing. Enchantment Resort delivers on both inspiration and relaxation: a dedicated pool concierge and cheerful waitstaff attend sunbathers reclining on chaises, the striking silhouettes of the surrounding red rock formations are reflected in aquamarine water, and the cozy casitas and hacienda suites, built with adobe and outfitted in modern southwestern décor, feature details like private decks and working fireplaces. The stylish Trail House outfits guests for outdoor adventures, and after hiking or cycling, the resort’s collection of contemporary indoor-outdoor restaurants and bars awaits.

content:
The Hotel Le Morgane is designed to appeal to the skier who likes a bit of fanciness with her freeriding, a little stylish minimalism with his mountaineering. After a full day of frolicking in the Alps, it’s comforting to know you’ve got epicurean meals, all-over spa treatments that stimulate the chakras, and a private terrace overlooking the mountains to come home to.

A recent renovation thoroughly reinvented this wedge-shaped hotel, which chain-hotel connoisseurs will recognize as a one-time Best Western. In addition to behind-the-scenes solar panels and water filtration systems, the décor now reflects a new eco-mindedness; wooden chairs have been carved to resemble polished eggs, and carpets look as textured as the canopy of trees outside. Photographs show wildflowers in extreme close-up. More attention has been paid to the feel and the atmosphere, as the phenomenal views have, thankfully, remained the same. The palette is as cool and soothing as the icy crags of infamous Mont Blanc, visible throughout the hotel. 

Ingredients used at Le Bistrot are locally sourced, so they come directly from the Chamonix Valley, as well as nearby Italy and Switzerland. The chef earned his Michelin star for simple seasonal preparations that put taste over showmanship in a refined but unstuffy atmosphere (c.f., the restaurant’s name). If you’ve had your fill of the outdoors, stay in and take one of his monthly cooking courses.    

How to get there:
Chamonix is 88 kilometers from Geneva-Cointrin Airport (GVA).

content:
A hotel that devotes a significant chunk of its interior to meeting spaces and ballrooms isn’t hiding the fact that it’s catering to business travelers, but if you’ve ever been on a working trip to India and stayed at one of the eight Leelas, you’ll know that this in no way entails that the rest of the place should be charmless or utilitarian. In the case of the Leela Palace in the city of Chennai, just off the Bay of Bengal, the standard Asian mega-chain opulence is tempered by a very welcome clubby vibe.

The interiors evoke hushed mahogany-paneled studies — in other words, don’t expect cutting-edge minimalism or museum-of-modern-art furniture. The guest rooms are spacious, with luxury suites offering panoramic views of the sea. Even the smallest rooms provide more space than the average business traveler probably needs, but this doesn’t take away from the overall efficiency you’d expect from a higher-end hotel near the business district of India’s fourth-largest city. 

It goes without saying that the public spaces are designed to meet every corporate need, from high-tech conferences to old-fashioned handshake deals. And for those accustomed to conducting business over drinks or a power lunch, the stately restaurants strike just the right note. 

How to Get There: The Leela Palace Chennai is located 16 km from the Chennai International Airport.

content:
Just as it bridges the physical gap between Vieux Montréal and the busy financial district, the InterContinental Montreal bridges the stylistic gap between the boutiques of the old town and the luxury hotels of the city center. Of course in its fundamentals, in its size and its comprehensive services, it’s much closer to the latter; but in stylistic matters it’s clear that its redesign took its cues from some of its small-but-chic neighbors.

The result is subtle. With high-rise views and floor-to-ceiling windows, these plush, oversized rooms and suites are anything but edgy. But neither are they bland, by any means — the furnishings are modernist classics, and the palette is rich and full of contrasts. In the end, though, you’re here because the visual charms are only multiplied by the tactile ones, from the lavish bathrooms to the plush robes and L’Occitane bath products (in Club rooms and above).

Osco! — exclamation point and all — is the InterContinental’s Provençal restaurant, which comes complete with a pair of private dining rooms for special events. And Montréal being what it is, the bar would have to be a somewhat decadent affair: Sarah B. is named for Sarah Bernhardt, and the specialty is absinthe, both behind the bar and in the emerald-green décor.

How to get there:
Intercontinental Montreal is 5 km (10 min) from Como, 20 km (20 min) from Montreal International Airport.  Transfers can be arranged for USD38 by taxi and USD50 for a limousine.

content: Chicago is home to a good number of landmark hotels, but not many of them are located on the Riverwalk, a scenic pedestrian promenade that runs along the Chicago River. That’s a distinction only held by a lucky few, including the Royal Sonesta Chicago Downtown. Perched high over the riverbanks, right at the spot where the waterway bends around the Magnificent Mile, the luxury hotel is notable for its views — from many rooms and suites, you can look down on the lively bustle of the waterfront, or straight out at the Art Deco–style Tribune Tower.\n\nWith prime urban real estate like this, you might expect space to be at a premium. But the Royal Sonesta’s rooms are surprisingly spacious, even in the standard category. The look is modern and pared-down, with ample natural light, earth tones, framed black and white photography, and colorful accents like tufted emerald-green headboards and abstract artwork. Cozy seating areas and coffee stations are welcome amenities, especially in rooms with river views, and bathrooms feature white subway tile and flattering in-mirror lighting. There’s no pool or spa, though you might not even notice at a location like this, within walking distance of everything in downtown Chicago.

content: Chow Kit is the name, first and foremost, of a neighborhood in the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur, known for its markets and for its thrillingly unsavory old reputation. These days it’s one of the city’s hippest quarters, and is home to a hotel that shares its name — designed by the Brooklyn firm Post Company, the Chow Kit is arguably the first properly swanky luxury boutique hotel in town. \n\nThe rooms are inspired by the neighborhood’s old gambling dens, with furniture and décor that recall the city’s colonial-era opulence alongside comforts and conveniences that place guests squarely in the 21st century. The restaurant, the open-plan Chow Kit Kitchen & Bar, serves a pan-Malaysian menu and serves as the hotel’s social nexus. And the neighborhood, among its other charms, is a highly desirable foodie destination whose markets host a thriving street-food scene.

content:
Fans of the classic Alpine-lodge experience will have no difficulty satisfying their urges in Bavaria. But those travelers who see no contradiction between modern design and timeless mountain views will be grateful for a place like Villa Sonnenhof Boutique Hotel. It’s a minority opinion, perhaps, but it’s popular enough to keep Villa Sonnenhof’s seven rooms filled with appreciative guests.

In the interiors there’s still plenty of richly textured wood — no hotel that’s in a proper dialogue with its site would go without it. But alongside the parquet floors and rough-hewn headboards you’ll find not hunting-party kitsch but contemporary art and modernist furniture, as well as a sparse, restrained aesthetic that makes the rooms into a refuge, and focuses the eye on the scenery outside. And while all are comfortable, the finest is the junior suite, which features a private sauna and a panoramic balcony. 

A proper Alpine breakfast is served in the dining room or, weather permitting, on the terrace; products are sourced from the finest local bakeries, butchers, and other purveyors. The bar serves a thoughtful selection of wines and beers, and the humidor stocks cigars from Cuba, Nicaragua, and the Dominican Republic.

content:
Burgos may not be one of Spain’s most famous destinations, but you can trust the Spanish-based NH Hoteles to present it in its best possible light. The NH Collection Palacio de Burgos is a former convent, a minor Gothic spectacle some 500 years old, and while it’s set across the river from the historic city center, there’s nothing second-class about this location: a four-minute walk across an ancient footbridge and suddenly you’re at the foot of the 13th-century Cathedral of Saint Mary of Burgos, the final resting place of El Cid.

Old cloisters make fantastic luxury hotels, and this one is no different. In typical style the historical architecture is allowed to shine through where appropriate, especially in the common spaces, while in the rooms and suites the balance tips more in the direction of contemporary luxury-hotel design, with dark hardwood floors, modern furniture, and rain showers in the stone-clad bathrooms. 

The restaurant, Palacio de la Merced, bears the former name of the building, and serves everything from an expansive breakfast to a dinner menu that features upscale Castilian favorites. A lobby bar serves a menu of light bites and a substantial selection of drinks.

content:
Set on the French side of the Basque country — and, stylistically, on the traditional side, as opposed to Frank Gehry’s Bilbao — Hotel Ithurria is a classic small farmhouse hotel, family-owned since the Sixties, and still relevant today because the virtues of small-scale, personal hospitality never really go out of style.

Its rooms retain much of their historical charm, though the owners haven’t been shy about updating them with contemporary color schemes and modern fittings to complement the antique furnishings. The smallest rooms are cozy but still comfortable, while the largest are large indeed, culminating in an apartment that sleeps up to five.

Chef Xavier Isabal is responsible for a large part of Hotel Ithurria’s appeal, overseeing a fine-dining restaurant, a casual bistrot, and the self-explanatory “table in the garden.” Local produce and fresh seafood feature prominently in the menus, and the hotel’s wine cellar is extensive.

The surrounding village of Ainhoa is a picturesque one, with many houses that date back to the middle of the 17th century. And there are plenty of reasons to stay in, not least of which is the swimming pool with its views of the surrounding hillsides.

content: Most Alpine retreats in Europe welcome guests with their traditional cozy chalet style, but the AlpenGold Hotel Davos dares to be different. The hotel’s futuristic oval gold exterior makes a striking impression sitting above Lake Davos, and while the rooms inside aren’t lined in the usual Alpine woods, they’re no less cocooning with soft shades and tactile furnishings. The modern design also means they come with floor-to-ceiling and wraparound windows to really show off the spectacular view. There’s six restaurants and bars, including the Cheese Factory, which serves traditional raclette and fondue in the untraditional setting of a glass tube on the rooftop, the vegetarian restaurant atelier VERT, and there’s the Nuts & Co Lounge Bar for casual dinner and drinks. The spa offering is equally extensive, a 1,200 m2 space in collaboration with the Swiss beauty brand Nescens, and fully kitted out with a heated indoor and outdoor pool, a gym and yoga room, saunas and steam rooms, and a collection of Spa Nescens and Alpine Spa suites if you’re looking for privacy.

content:
Argentina’s answer to the wine regions of Northern California or rural France is the province of Mendoza, and it’s here, some twenty miles south of the city of the same name, that you’ll find the Cavas Wine Lodge. This stunning Spanish Colonial villa is every bit as fine as its Northern Hemisphere cousins — luxurious accommodations, quality food, an encyclopedic selection of the best local wines, and a spa complete with so-hot-right-now vinotherapy treatments — and adds dramatic views of the snow-capped Andes to boot.

Surrounding the main building, scattered throughout the vineyards, are fourteen one-bedroom villas, each with a private terrace and plunge pool. The interiors are true to the Spanish look of the exteriors, but contemporary in style, clean-lined and minimalist, with lavish stone bathrooms, outdoor showers, and all mod cons, including flat-screen televisions and wireless internet.

Back at the main house you’ll find the restaurant, wine cellar, and a living room graced with a majestic fireplace. There’s a full-service spa and an outdoor pool lounge as well, and off-site you’ll have access to tours of working vineyards and excursions into the great Argentine outdoors.

How to Get There: Cavas Wine Lodge is approximately a 40-minute drive from Governor Francisco Gabrielli International Airport (MDZ).

content:
Florianopolis, the capital of the Brazilian state of Santa Catarina, evokes tropical beauty through its mellifluous name alone. Boasting an enviable quality of life and some of the most desirable coastline in Brazil, the city is a natural fit for the kind of intimate experience you’ll find at Quinta das Videiras. This boutique hotel replicates the style of a 19th-century Portuguese residence, right down to the deep pink façade and surrounding grapevines.

With only sixteen rooms, guests can expect personalized, attentive service. The wooden furniture has a rustic look, with comforts such as large closets and four-poster beds banishing any thought of this being a vacation retreat for young people, despite the large number of surfers on Praia Mole. At the top of the apartment chain is the one-bedroom Loft suite with its own living room and a private mini-pool on the rooftop and the new Royal suite, richly dressed in a Portuguese style with period furnishings, silk jacquard curtains, and crystal chandeliers. Couples on a romantic trip should consider the Master suite, where they'll find things like bath salts and candles. Bathrooms are a place where the retro vibe is less than desirable, and here, fortunately, they've gone for 5-star modernity, with two sinks, adjustable showers, Victorian baths and glass doors.

In a nod to local tradition, guests who place an order the night before wake up to an in-room Portuguese breakfast served on blue porcelain. While Quinta das Videiras is miles more sedate than the larger resort hotels, its proximity to the Lagoa da Conceicao — the lagoon in the center of the island — situates it within easy walking distance of the city’s vibrant nightlife.

Travel advisory: Passport and visa requirements differ from country to country. Please check with your local authority before booking.

Please note: Children under 12 years of age not are not permitted.	

How to get there: Hotel Boutique Quinta das Videiras is located about 20 min drive from Florianopolis’s Hercilio Luz International Airport. Transfers can be organized for R$50 each way.

content: Set a few blocks from the beach on a tree-lined block, the charming Hotel Saint-Julien feels like a throwback to another era. This guesthouse-style boutique occupies a traditional 19th-century house with an ivory stucco facade and wooden shutters painted deep red, and many of its original features remain, including pine flooring, marble fireplaces, and antique staircases. There’s a wonderful simplicity to the place — don’t expect a pool, gym, or spa, just a cozy dining room where a sumptuous Basque breakfast spread is laid out each day, and a colorful cocktail bar with open-air seating framed by citrus trees. \n\nRooms are quaint, with high ceilings and large windows that reveal views of the city’s red rooftops or the distant sea. Each is done up in a single color, like sage green, mustard yellow, or pale lavender, and the décor features vintage pieces and beachy details like wicker lamps and distressed wood side tables. The owners are well-connected in Biarritz and are eager to suggest spots to eat, drink, and shop in the neighborhood. And while they don't run a conventional restaurant on-site, Hotel Saint-Julien hosts a rotating calendar of visiting chefs in the summer - something like an artist-in-residence program, but for food - where guests can join locals in one of their favorite pastimes.

content: Wildly beautiful but mostly under the tourist radar, southern Corsica’s rugged coastline is home to some of the most dazzling scenery in the Mediterranean. A steeply angled drive along a narrow mountain road leads from the port village of Propriano to Hôtel Marinca & Spa, set on an elevated perch overlooking the sea. The luxury hotel feels like it’s in the middle of nowhere, which is a large part of the appeal, and with every detail taken care of — including several stylish restaurants and bars, a Clarins spa with a hammam and a Nordic-style ice room, four swimming pools, and a private beach with sunbeds attended by staff —  there’s hardly any reason to leave the premises unless it’s for a pleasure cruise on the hotel’s boat.\n\nAn old Corsican villa houses most rooms and suites, almost all of which have a private terrace or balcony with ocean views. Inside, the look is modern and romantic, with herringbone wood floors, a sophisticated white and ivory color palette, king-sized beds, and light-filled bathrooms lined in Carrara marble. Suites feature extras like freestanding tubs and open-air patios with Jacuzzis; one has a private pool, and the penthouse suite has a sizeable rooftop terrace. The in-house pastry chef prepares an array of delicacies for breakfast, which is served on a sunny deck facing the water. For other meals, there's the one-MICHELIN-Star La Verrière and the more casual La Paillote, a boho-chic beach bar and eatery right on the sand.

content:
County Kildare’s Cliff at Lyons is home to a collection of historic mill buildings — now housing the reception, a restaurant, a bar, and a boutique — as well as a series of wisteria-covered manor houses and stone cottages that contain guest rooms and suites. Picturesque courtyards, gardens, and water features add to the scenic charm, including a lily pond and a stream that runs through the property.

The manor house rooms are elegant and classic with a modern twist: parquet floors, bright white finishes, chrome fixtures, velvet headboards, and bathrooms with oversized rainfall showers. Some have antique wooden furnishings and floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the lily pond. Cottages are cozy and rustic-chic with quaint features like fireplaces, hidden staircases, and four-poster beds. Cozier than the gracefully appointed rooms in the main house, they’re equipped with kitchens and multiple bedrooms.

The hotel’s signature restaurant is located in the stateliest of Cliff at Lyons’ old buildings, with adjacent garden seating for al fresco dining, while the Well in the Garden, a two-story spa with a fireplace-warmed relaxation room, is housed in a rose-clad stone building nearby.

content: The Provençal countryside is dotted with bastides, or 18th-century country houses, and while many are now used as private vacation homes, others have been turned into hotels. Le Galinier is a cross between the two. This picturesque property is sometimes rented out in its entirety, but it’s often possible to book a room for a few nights to live out the fantasy of a leisurely existence in the French countryside. Le Galinier comprises an original farmhouse and several outbuildings set in a pretty park with a swimming pool, a pétanque court, and rose gardens. Despite the old-world air, there’s nothing fussy about the place — the grounds have a charmingly wild, slightly overgrown look that feels just right, and the air is fragrant with lavender and verbena.\n\nRooms and suites follow suit with thick walls, terracotta tile or wood-planked floors, linen sofas, and simple wooden furnishings. Some have exposed stone walls and vaulted wood-beamed ceilings, others have fireplaces and antique writing desks. A loft-style apartment has three bedrooms and a kitchen, as does the freestanding Maison du Chef, which opens onto a private garden. There’s little intervention from the staff, whose discreet presence adds to the feeling of being in a dreamy vacation home instead of a hotel. But breakfast served on a sunny stone terrace, and complimentary bicycles for exploring the area, are the perfect touches.

content: Midway between Deauville and Honfleur on the coast of Normandy, the tiny village of Pennedepie has only a few places to stay, most notably Les Jardins de Coppélia, a 17th-century manor house converted into a luxury hotel overlooking the sea. Little has changed about its stately wood and slate façade, an unconventional mélange of steep gables, decorative archways, and details including a fairy-tale turret and an antique dinner bell over the entryway. But its modern interiors are the result of sweeping renovations, and the surrounding gardens have been updated accordingly, with a large wood-lined swimming pool added on one side and twinkling lights suspended over outdoor café tables on the other. \n\nThere’s an old-world flair to rooms and suites with vaulted white ceilings, exposed beams, and rustic parquet floors, but it’s offset by bold, colorful accents and sleek designer furnishings by Roche Bobois. Each room is unique — some have original fireplaces, and others feature clawfoot tubs. But all have Nespresso machines and digital tablets for booking treatments at the Garancia Spa or Le Capucine, the ground-floor restaurant serving seasonally inspired menus with sea views. Natural wines, cocktails made with local herbs, and ciders produced at nearby Manoir d’Apreval are served at the tiki bar by the pool and at the stylish Le P’tit YARD, modeled after the original Le YARD wine bar in Paris. The beach is minutes away, as are the region’s historic port towns.

content:
The Fasano hotels and restaurants are a big deal in Brazil; no less significant a figure than singer-songwriter Caetano Veloso performed at the opening of this one, the eighth Fasano-branded luxury hotel in Brazil. Fasano Salvador occupies a building of some gravity as well, a 1930s Art Deco landmark that was once the headquarters of the city’s daily newspaper, and which stands on Castro Alves Square, in the UNESCO-listed historic city center, with an elevated view back towards the Bay of All Saints.

Inside, the entry and lobby continue in a beautifully restored Art Deco vein, while, as you get into more private spaces like the spa, restaurant, and rooms and suites, a sleeker, more modern aspect emerges, courtesy of Fasano’s favorite architect, Isay Weinfeld. In typical Fasano style, even the most basic rooms are large and luxurious, with warm, organic materials and indulgent, spa-like bathrooms.

The rooftop pool deck has an impressive view of the bay, and is joined by a well-equipped spa and fitness center. And you’ll want to make time for the restaurant, also called Fasano Salvador, where upscale Italian classics are served alongside Bahian specialties and fine wines from the New and Old Worlds alike.

content:
In 1785, King Louis XVI bought a gift for his wife, Marie-Antoinette: a mansion built on the ruins of a 13th-century castle on Île de Ré, an island off the west coast of France. Today, that mansion is La Baronnie Hôtel & Spa, a boutique hotel with all the elegance of days gone by — grand staircases, period woodwork, velvet sofas, an old stone fireplace, decorative toile drapery, cobblestoned courtyards perfumed with lavender and jasmine — plus a sun-drenched Cinq Mondes spa and a cozy cocktail bar. 

Guest rooms are simple and elegant, with wood-beamed ceilings and antique furnishings. Though all share a unified aesthetic, each one is different, and not just in the finer details — they range from relatively conventional historical bedrooms to the Tour des Amis, a tower room in the original structure, and the Indian Lodge, a free-standing cabin constructed from salvaged 18th-century timber.

The gardens offer plentiful space for lounging, and make a fine venue for an evening cocktail; a heated outdoor pool is available from May through October. There’s a generous daily breakfast, served family-style on the sunny terrace, and while there’s no restaurant, the bar serves light bites, and the hotel is perfectly located for exploring the charming island capital of Saint-Martin-de-Ré on foot.

content:
Though not as famous as nearby Chamonix, the French Alpine town of La Clusaz is a true classic — it was an established village long before the ski boom, and when the first lift was installed in the Fifties, it was ready. Today it’s an all-seasons resort town with more character than the more recently built ones, and in the St-Alban, it’s got a boutique hotel to match — one that pays tribute to Alpine-lodge tradition but ultimately presents its own characteristic point of view.

Ski lodges aren’t known for their heady, intellectual atmosphere, but the St-Alban’s bar is chock full of books. It’s designed to resemble an English club, but one with a modernist, Art Deco–influenced style, and it’s absolutely unique in a world full of après-ski cliché. Meanwhile the rooms are one part Alpine tradition — mostly in the form of blond wood and wool blankets — and one part boutique-hotel minimalism, a stylish combination, and one that sacrifices nothing in the way of comfort.

A Nuxe spa elevates the St-Alban into luxury territory, and there’s a ski shop with a capacious selection of ski and snowboard gear. There’s no restaurant per se, just a generous breakfast, room service, and a menu of bar bites — the location, close to the La Clusaz village center, places you within walking distance of many worthy options.

content:
Don’t let the name (which simply refers to the address, Fabianinkatu 6) put you off — Helsinki’s Hotel F6 is family-owned, family-operated, and as friendly as they come. Despite its central location — just across from Esplanadi Park and only steps away from the popular Kauppatori Market — the atmosphere remains relaxed and casual, thanks in part to the inner courtyard lounge, which, weather permitting, offers a delightfully whimsical escape.

The rooms are stylish, spare but not stark, with luxe Unikulma beds and modern bathrooms. Standard and Superior rooms are spacious and comfortable, and the Deluxe category spreads out over 40 square meters and adds an in-room espresso machine and a generous living area with a sofa and desk. And all of it is a picture-perfect example of contemporary Nordic style, with that familiar blond wood and modernist-inspired furniture.

A cocktail and wine bar named for Runar the family dog — named in turn for the architect Runar Finnilä — and a breakfast service featuring herbs grown in the hotel’s greenhouse garden round out the services. While there’s no restaurant, you’re hardly in a food desert here in central Helsinki — and a delivery service will connect you with local restaurants if you prefer to stay in.

content:
As even the interior of Bali increasingly fills with hotels and resorts of every possible description, travelers are turning to Java for their Indonesian forest fix. And central Java’s got attractions of its own, like the 9th-century Buddhist temple at Borobodur. This is the temple that looms in the background of Plataran Borobodur Resort & Spa, an all-villa hotel in the island’s central Menoreh Hills.

The villas themselves are based on traditional Indonesian construction, though they take more than a few cues from the contemporary luxury-villa idiom as well. Spaces are generous, furnishings are luxe, and every one comes with either a plunge pool or a proper swimming pool, as well as an outdoor terrace and a bathroom with both rain shower and bathtub. Safe to say there isn’t a subpar room in the house.

It just about goes without saying that a hotel like Plataran Borobodur comes with a first-rate spa, as well as a pool, a gym, and a yoga pavilion. Patio Venue is the restaurant with views of the Borobodur temple, while the open-air Stupa serves Indonesian fare under the night sky, and the Kastil is an indoor European-style dining room with its own butler service.

content:
The Taj group, though perhaps best known for a string of faultlessly competent business hotels, has a healthy sideline in time travel — the kind of meticulously preserved historical properties that make you feel as though you’ve stepped right into another century. Take the Taj Malabar Resort & Spa, Cochin, on Willingdon Island in Cochin Harbor, as an example: aside from a relatively utilitarian Tower Wing (of which more later), this place stays pretty true to its 1935-vintage, Victorian-style roots.

As with any hotel with a modern wing, you’ve got a choice to make. Here it’s between authenticity and views, to put it bluntly; the original rooms, though renovated, feel positively steeped in history, but the tower suites are fine reproductions, and some add the further inducement of a sunset view over Cochin’s waterways. Much depends on whether you’re a stickler for history — an added benefit is that, from within the tower, you can’t actually see the tower.

What all the accommodations have in common is a full complement of modern amenities; the Taj group are no strangers to five-star hospitality. Four restaurants easily keep everyone fed, and the spa and Ayurvedic center look after guests’ less tangible needs.

content: On a far-flung stretch of Mexico’s coastline where the rugged Sierra Madre mountains meet the Pacific, a pair of creative entrepreneurs founded the Modern Utopian Society of Adventurers, a design-focused hospitality project. The ambitious plans for MUSA include a real estate development with a collection of exclusive residences, but one of the first elements completed was the beachfront Hotelito at MUSA. This thirteen-room boutique hotel sets the tone for the developing community with its tropical modernist aesthetic, sustainable features, and an emphasis on indoor-outdoor living. \n\nMUSA co-founder Andrés Saavedra handled the architecture and interior design. Rooms are airy and minimalist with polished concrete floors, handmade terrazzo tiles, and wood furnishings crafted by local artisans. Each has a private terrace with a plunge pool and an open-air rainfall shower, luxurious amenities from Smeg mini-fridges to bespoke bath products, and original artwork by Mexican artists. A few have jungle views, but most overlook the ocean, like the striking penthouse suite with its terrace facing the sunset. Other highlights include a beach club with an infinity pool and cocktail bar, an open-air gym, a naturally purified freshwater lake suitable for swimming, an on-site surf school, and a restaurant showcasing produce from the property’s organic farm.

content: On the island of Mallorca, Pleta de Mar, Luxury Hotel by Nature is about as far away as you can get from the capital city of Palma. And pretty much everything else — this boutique hotel is surrounded by nothing but green fields and the sea. The owners have thought of everything, from freshly squeezed juices served beside a trio of pools to local wines served beneath the shade of olive trees. A Mediterranean-inspired spa and restaurant Sa Pleta by Marc Fosh, where dishes are prepared over an open fire, round out Pleta de Mar’s refined offerings.\n\nLight-filled rooms and suites, designed to blend into the surrounding landscape, are calm and minimalist with wood-beamed ceilings and pale parquet flooring. They’re furnished with organic materials, including crisp cotton and natural linen, and feature tech-forward amenities like Bang & Olufsen sound systems. Bathrooms are large and spa-like with freestanding soaking tubs, and the best suites have private terraces with outdoor showers and sea views. Silent and stylish, within walking distance of the nearest village but pleasantly removed from civilization, this is one of the island’s most appealing adults-only escapes.

content:
Grand Hotel Belvedere’s name suggests a classic grand hotel from over a century ago, and that’s what it was before it was acquired — and thoroughly renewed — by France’s Beaumier hospitality group. No mere restoration, their reimagining of the Belvedere leaves it as modern as any luxury hotel in Switzerland. But thanks to the sensitivity of its designers, the modern Belvedere is warm and welcoming, rather than edgy and overdramatic.

Plentiful bare wood serves to maintain a connection with the hotel’s Alpine heritage, and while the rooms and suites verge on minimalism, they’re full of visual interest, and contain comforts that are anything but spartan. (The views, too, are as inspiring as the Belvedere name suggests.) The one avant-garde note is struck by the spa, with its concrete surfaces and acute angles — but if there’s anything a spa is supposed to be, it’s a departure from the everyday.

The hotel’s dining and drinking venues include Brasserie Belvedere, a modern Alpine brasserie, and Sonnenbad Lounge & Terrace, which serves grilled dishes and wood-fired pizzas against the backdrop of a spectacular mountain view. Add to this all the charms of a car-free Alpine town, surrounded by world-class winter and summer recreation, and you’ve got a modern classic in the making.

content:
An 18th-century shipowner’s mansion in the old port of La Rochelle is the setting for La Villa Grand Voile, a Relaix & Châteaux hotel with some impressive culinary connections. Here chef Christopher Coutanceau and sommelier Nicolas Brossard have crafted a small and extraordinarily stylish escape, a hotel whose eleven rooms and suites combine Art Deco and maritime influences with a keen contemporary eye and a full complement of subtle modern luxuries.

Strictly as a lodging it’s an impressively unique experience, and displays the sort of attention to detail that’s characteristic of the finest small-scale boutique hotels. The service is personal but still professional, and the atmosphere is warm but as private as you need it to be. It would stand on its own quite confidently without its restaurants; fortunately, it doesn’t have to.

Walk a few blocks toward the water and you’ll find yourself at the Plage de la Concurrence, the site of the Restaurant Christopher Coutanceau, a three-MICHELIN-Star restaurant. And right next door is the more casual La Yole de Chris, a marine-themed bistro; both restaurants, naturally, feature the wine selections and cocktail creations of maître de maison Nicolas Brossard.

content:
Located just about over four hours from Tokyo via the Shinkansen bullet train, Appi Kogen is one of Japan’s largest ski resorts — and in the ANA InterContinental Appi Kogen Resort, it’s got a first-class luxury hotel. It’s an unusually small one — just 38 rooms and suites — but each unit offers the highest standard of service that IHG’s hotels can muster, the Club InterContinental classification.

Visually, they’ve pulled out all the stops; there’s art everywhere, as well as a 400-year-old Japanese beech tree inside the hotel’s club lounge. The rooms and suites look out through vast windows at the ski slopes and the surrounding forest, and the bathrooms, especially, invite contemplation of nature.

So too does the onsen on the hotel’s top floor, whose cypress baths face the surrounding treetops. In addition to the Japanese-style hot spring baths, you’ll find an international-style spa, and the skiing and snowboarding is some of Japan’s finest. At this small size, one restaurant and one bar are quite enough, and they’re stunning: Shiratsuyu serves farm-to-table Japanese/French cuisine in an exquisitely crafted dining room, while Mocco, on the top floor, specializes in Japanese whisky.

content: Any hotel on this site would be a special one; not only is this quite probably Sydney’s most prominent location, affording an elevated view over the Royal Botanic Garden, the Opera House, and the Harbour Bridge. The InterContinental Sydney offers more than that, though. For one thing, its historic wing, home to many of its finest public spaces, is the 1851 Treasury Building, a true-blue Sydney landmark; for another, the modern tower that is the Treasury’s counterpart contains 509 rooms and suites that are just about as luxurious as anything in town.\n\nThe rooms and suites all feature window seats; the views of the skyline are impressive, and those of the harbour even more so. The décor is contemporary but not quite minimalist; the soothing colors and faint Modernist echoes set a tranquil tone. And the details are subtly luxurious as well, from the locally sourced minibar items to the Byredo bath products. Meanwhile the restaurants and bars might be the InterContinental’s most impressive spaces, from the Treasury and the Conservatory, both on the ground floor, to Aster, the rooftop restaurant and cocktail bar, looking out over the harborside panorama from 32 floors above the ground.

content:
The upscale Detroit suburb of Birmingham is perhaps not the first place you’d look to find a place like the Daxton Hotel, a dramatic and art-filled luxury boutique hotel of the type that, not all that long ago, would have struggled to find an audience outside of New York or Los Angeles. The look is bold in black marble and dark wood, setting an authentically elegant tone. And what pulls it back from excessive seriousness is its art collection, which includes some playful and colorful paintings and sculptures prominently displayed in the lobby and other public spaces.

In contrast, the rooms let a bit of light in, and display echoes of multiple eras of architectural history, from Victorian ornament to Art Deco and Modernist gestures and beyond. They’re provided with a generous amount of lounge space, and the bathrooms are particularly stylish in white tile and richly figured black stone.

The hotel’s restaurant, Madam, is frankly more attractive than it needs to be, featuring large-scale artworks, dramatic lighting, and an unusual triangle-chamber ceiling detail. A geodesic dome envelops the bar, and at the table you’ll find a menu drawing its culinary inspiration from a diverse array of global cuisines.

content: There’s something to be said, of course, for innovation, for surprise, for hotels that succeed in unlikely places or unusual genres. But an overwater villa hotel in the Maldives is none of these things. A hotel like the Hideaway Beach Resort and Spa doesn’t need a revolutionary concept — it needs only to deliver on the promise of Maldivian waterside luxury. In the case of Hideaway Beach that means large and lavish villas, some on or near the beach, others suspended over the water, with glass-floored living rooms and water’s-edge plunge pools. In all categories the spaces are generous, elegant, and contemporary, full of luxe details like Nespresso machines, Molton Brown bath products, and less tangible luxuries like butler service, to cater for your every whim. And as impressive as the accommodations are, this place is more than the sum of its villas. There’s the usual spread of restaurants, with options ranging from fresh seafood to wood-fired pizza to a casual poolside café, and activities like yoga, tennis, and an expansive spa. But the star of the show, given the location, is the Indian Ocean itself — from snorkeling and diving to deep-sea fishing or journeys by wooden dhoni or “semi-submarine,” if you can do it by sea, you can do it here.

content: If you still think of Salt Lake City, Utah as a second-rate provincial town — well, maybe it’s better that way, because you’ll have all the more opportunity to be pleasantly surprised by the current state of the place. No one is going to mistake it for Los Angeles or Chicago any time soon, but it’s a more modern, open, and tolerant city than most people give it credit for. And the fact that it’s got a hotel like the Kimpton Hotel Monaco Salt Lake City is proof that there’s plenty for a well-traveled, cosmopolitan guest to love about Utah’s biggest city.\n\nIt’s got Victorian bones, like many of SLC’s downtown buildings, but inside, the Monaco is no nostalgia act — the style pays homage to the early 20th century but the look is contemporary boutique design through and through. The comforts are thoroughly up to date as well, and the little Kimpton extras, like the pet-friendly policy and the evening social hour, underscore the friendly aspect of Salt Lake. Bambara, the restaurant, makes good use of what was once a bank lobby, and the Vault is among the city’s finest cocktail bars. Yes, cocktail bars, even in Utah. You might be surprised.

content:
You might expect a place called Surfers Paradise to be an unspoiled refuge full of endless-summer vibes and world-renowned surfing — and you’d be right about the surfing, anyway. A district of Queensland’s Gold Coast, Surfers Paradise is a bustling tourist destination that offers the nightlife of a coastal city along with some of the world’s best waves. As such, it plays host to an eclectic contingent of revelers, families and beach bums. QT Gold Coast manages to court everyone with a cosmopolitan sensibility that’s both fresh and unpretentious.

The public spaces defy preconceived notions about beachfront hotels — there’s a welcome lack of nautical kitsch, just plenty of bold colors and curvy modern furniture. Bars and lounges pull off the neat trick of seeming cavernous without feeling like repurposed warehouses. The guest rooms take it down a notch, splashing white walls and crisp white linens with sunny hues in the form of orange chairs and crimson throw pillows. And there’s still plenty of room for the view from the floor-to-ceiling windows to take center stage — the hotel overlooks both the mountainous hinterland and the ocean.

Even if you’ve just popped into town for a bit of shopping along nearby Cavill Avenue, you can’t miss the beach. QT Gold Coast makes it easy enough — just step outside, walk for a minute or two, and you’ve got sand beneath your feet. Hungry and indecisive? That’s actually a good thing, because the hotel caters to pretty much any craving with its vendor-packed Bazaar. Taking its cues from outdoor markets, this international sampler is a tasty summation of the QT’s inclusive attitude.

content: Before Saint-Tropez’s glamorous midcentury heyday, it was a quiet fishing village. The charmingly down-to-earth La Ferme d’Augustin, set in an old stone farmhouse in the wooded hills above Plage de Tahiti, is a reminder of these simpler days and timeless pleasures. This boutique hotel is named after the house’s onetime owner, who invited passersby to dine at his table, and food and wine have remained a focus since his daughter took over in the late seventies. \n\nOlive oil and wine are produced onsite, and fruits from the farm’s garden and orchards are beautifully presented each morning at the leisurely open-air breakfast. Rooms are airy and quaint with terracotta tile floors, Provençal antiques, and paintings by local artists; some have skylights or balconies with sea views, and suites come with lovely private gardens. Fresh flowers enliven the hotel’s cozy fireplace lounge, citrus trees frame the pretty outdoor pool, and the beach is just a short stroll away.

content:
The town of Troyes remained mercifully intact during World War II, preserving an abundance of half-timbered buildings dating back to the 16th and 17th centuries. They’re a bunch of Johnny-come-latelys compared to La Maison de Rhodes. The foundation of this eleven-room hotel in the heart of the historical district can be traced back to the 12th century when it housed the Knights Templar. Fully restored in 1998, the hotel acknowledges its history by incorporating original flagstones and Burgundy stone floors along with a pitch-perfect recreation of the half-timbered edifice.

Even taking into account an infusion of modern conveniences, La Maison de Rhodes feels sturdy, ageless, and a little bit mystical. The interior is no storybook fantasy, just meticulously restored, spacious, and full of exposed beams that echo the exterior design. It’s actually pretty understated for a hotel in the Champagne region of France, many of which are just as virtuosic in their restoration, but aren’t content to stop at the limits of taste. Here, the designers are confident enough to let the imposing stone hearths and minimal, well-placed wooden furniture speak for itself. Bathrooms enhance the uncluttered feel while unifying the design; generously sized bathtubs and big tiled showers are installed beneath slanted ceilings, with the occasional bit of stained glass providing accompaniment.

Outside, the courtyard serves as a summer breakfast spot, while the hotel’s La Commanderie restaurant serves local dishes paired with regional wine. Make no mistake, this is gourmet dining — “local dishes” in northern France being what they are — and the cuisine is a perfect match for the elegant surroundings. 

How to get there:
La Maison de Rhodes is located approximately 90 minutes (by car) from Charles de Gaulle (CDG) Airport in Paris. If coming by train, the hotel is a short 15-minute walk from the Troyes railway station. Please contact CustomerService@TabletHotels.com for questions or assistance with airport transfers.

content:
The idea of a zoo hotel — not located near a zoo, but actually on the grounds of one — is something of a novelty. It’s particularly noteworthy when the zoo in question is considered one of the best in the world. The Wildlife Retreat at Taronga is located inside Taronga Zoo Sydney, and when front desk staff mention that it’s possible to wake up to a kangaroo hopping by or a koala clinging to a tree outside your window, they’re not exaggerating — and every stay comes with a two-day admission and a guided afternoon tour of the sanctuary. 

Rivaling the wildlife views are the postcard-like panoramas of the city skyline. This modern eco-lodge looks across the water at the Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge, a scene that’s showcased to dazzling effect in the hotel’s airy central lounge and revealed through many rooms’ floor-to-ceiling windows. 

The hotel, which is owned and operated by the Taronga Conservation Society Australia, consists of five interconnected low-rise structures, sustainably built and designed to blend into the landscape. Inside, the look is safari-chic, with clean lines, natural hues, and materials including timber, recycled metal, and blonde sandstone. Some rooms have direct views of the zoo’s Sanctuary, a native animal habitat created only for guests’ enjoyment, while the largest suites, positioned amid the treetops, feature luxurious spa bathrooms with freestanding tubs.

content:
Right on Capri’s main square, La Piazzetta, there’s a cheerful, pale-yellow palazzo that was once the atelier of the German symbolist painter Karl Wilhelm Diefenbach. Today, it’s home to the Palazzo M Capri, an eight-suite boutique hotel. While the interiors have been thoroughly refurbished, it’s easy to see why the artist produced so many dreamy landscapes capturing his immediate surroundings — the hotel’s entrance is next to Capri’s famous clock tower, and the rear side overlooks the deep blue Gulf of Naples, a spectacle that would move anybody to take up painting.

All of the hotel’s suites have water views, and every single one has a private furnished balcony or terrace from which to properly contemplate them. The interiors are bright and airy, laid-back but elegant, with delicately arching walls and natural light pouring in through large windows. The color scheme is primarily white with accents in coastal-inspired hues like ivory, sand, and turquoise. Each Suite features an espresso machine, with select Suites also offering a convenient kitchenette. Three Suites include private hot tubs — among them, the Bell Tower Suite, which boasts not only sweeping sea views but also a charming outlook over the iconic square and its namesake bell tower.

A continental breakfast is served directly to suites, and it’s worth wandering down to the Bar Palazzo for aperitivi later in the day. Palazzo M does without certain other luxury-hotel amenities, like a pool or spa, but there’s really no need when all of Capri is waiting just outside.

While deeply rooted in history, Verno House is far more than a mere retro reconstruction. It masterfully blends historic inspiration with a fresh, contemporary perspective, creating a space that is both elegant and effortlessly modern.

Every detail of Verno House exudes personality and charm. The interiors strike a perfect balance between refined sophistication and inviting warmth. Rich textures, warm hues, and carefully curated furnishings come together to create an atmosphere that is both timeless and stylish.

The rooms are impressively spacious—far larger than typical city accommodations—and are thoughtfully designed to provide an exceptional level of comfort. High-end modern amenities blend seamlessly with nostalgic touches, such as vintage telephones, adding character and charm.

Guests can also unwind in the hotel’s intimate spa, which features a jacuzzi, steam room, and sauna, providing a tranquil retreat from the city’s energy.

Flava, the hotel’s all-day dining venue, presents an exquisite menu that transitions seamlessly from breakfast to brunch, and into a refined dinner experience.

content:
In Udaipur the Taj brand is most famous for the one-of-a-kind Taj Lake Palace, a glorious, opulent, ancient apparition that seems to float on the waters of Lake Pichola. There’s no sense trying to beat a classic like this at its own game — so the brand-new Taj Aravali Resort & Spa doesn’t even try. This is the other end of the stylistic spectrum: clean-lined, ultra-modern, high-tech, and surrounded not by water but by forested hillsides and the mountains of the Aravali Ranges.

It’s set on some 27 acres of land, all for just 92 units of accommodations: not just traditional rooms, suites, and cottages, but also luxury tents: some with merely panoramic views through floor-to-ceiling windows, and others in a “glass cube” orientation, for 360-degree vistas. What all of them share, of course, is tasteful interior design — perhaps more contemporary than most Taj hotels — combined with top-shelf comforts.

They also all share access to the Jiva spa, as well as a generous handful of restaurants. Javitri, the signature restaurant, is an all-vegetarian affair, while Ridgeview, the grill house, and Tiri, with its all-day pan-global menu, round out the selection. Meanwhile you’re close enough to Udaipur to be in town within minutes — and remote enough to enjoy a bit of rugged mountain adventure during your leisure time.

content:
Of all the various types of historical buildings to be converted into hotels, there might be none better suited than the monastery. To turn a monk’s cell into a hotel room is no great leap, and for all the privacy of the accommodations, a monastery, like a hotel, is also a place for communal living. Hotel Monastère Maastricht is a particularly memorable example: not just any old monastery but a 14th-century one, restored in a way that’s sensitive to its history but not excessively reverent.

In fact there’s a pronounced Parisian accent — at least a visual one — about the Monastère. The 52 rooms and suites actually vary considerably in size and layout, from Small Doubles all the way up to Suites, Family rooms, Triples, and Quadruples. In all of them period architecture meets contemporary colors and design, and the comforts are thoroughly modern.

And while the Parisian accent is just an accent elsewhere in the hotel, in Café Louis it’s the dominant language. This is a French restaurant, full stop, though the ingredients are sourced from Maastricht and the surrounding areas. And this cosmopolitan outlook extends to other areas of hospitality as well: like all of the Vondel hotels, the Monastère affirms that it’s a “straight-friendly” hotel, a bit of irony that underlines just how tolerant the Netherlands, at their best, can be.
