content:
Airport hotels have come a long way, to say the least. Well, a few of them have, anyway — while there are still plenty that deal in nothing but bare-bones convenience, there’s a new breed that aims to give you more than just a place to wait for your flight. Among them is Naumi, the Singapore-based boutique-hotel group, who’ve set up a hotel whose name sums up most of what we’ve written so far: Naumi Hotel Auckland Airport.

Auckland, after all, may not be the world’s most vibrant metropolis, but if you’re passing through here, you’re on some sort of adventure. The Naumi is banking on there being enough colorful characters in transit through New Zealand to fill a hotel that’s more than a little bit colorful itself — there’s art everywhere, and the furniture and accessories come from a who’s who of well-known international designers.

The rooms are swanky, and for all their stylishness, perhaps surprisingly sedate — whether you’re just arriving in New Zealand or about to leave, odds are you could use a restful sleep. Between the blackout curtains, rain showers, and espresso makers, you’re more or less guaranteed to leave in better shape than when you arrived.

content:
For those not well versed in the geography of the Arabian Peninsula: Ras Al Khaimah is the northernmost of the United Arab Emirates, and its capital city, Ras Al Khaimah City, is the capital of the UAE. It’s an hour’s drive from the Dubai airport to RAK City, and occupying the entirety of an island just off the coast of the city is the InterContinental Ras Al Khaimah Mina Al Arab Resort and Spa, a 351-room luxury resort whose atmosphere of luxe seclusion belies its convenient quasi-urban setting.

To that end, the views of the Gulf are highlighted, both in the public spaces and in the sea-facing accommodations. The best of the rooms, suites, and villas are set right on the beach, but even those that open onto the gardens are lavish and elegant, in a style that’s roughly two parts modern minimalism to one part classic traditionalism. Space is plentiful at all levels, and the villas add extra luxuries like private plunge pools or soaking tubs on the terraces.

The facilities in common are no less impressive, from the spa and fitness studio to the sprawling lagoon-like pool. There’s a kids’ club and a separate teens’ club, and a handful of restaurants range from the Turkish-inspired Levant & Nar to the American-style NoHo Bar & Grill.

Ameron Swiss Mountain Davos Resort is exactly what it sounds like: a mountain resort from the Köln-based purveyors of high-design luxury boutique hotels, set in one of Switzerland’s most famous Alpine resort towns. In fact, while Davos may be best known for the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting, it’s an extremely impressive winter-sports destination, and Ameron’s guests are more likely to be here for leisure than for business (though it can certainly handle both).

The rooms come with impressive mountain views, and while they’re decorated with plenty of nods to traditional Alpine style — pine paneling, faux fur, red upholstery — they’re predominantly contemporary in design. They’re modern in their comforts, too, with the full complement of high-tech amenities as well as lavish bathrooms and mountain-facing balconies.

An extensive spa and wellness program is present in a hotel like this one as a matter of course, in this case the palatial 4 Elements Spa & Fitness, complete with an indoor pool and a selection of saunas, showers, and baths. Meanwhile Bacio della Mamma is a remarkably authentic Italian restaurant, Cervolino the fondue venue, and Cantinetta the hip and low-key Alpine-style lounge and bar.

content:
The Third Ward, tucked in between the river and Lake Michigan, is downtown Milwaukee’s coolest neighborhood; it’s full of galleries, shops, cafés, and rehabilitated industrial spaces, not to mention the Milwaukee Public Market. It’s also home to the Kimpton Journeyman Hotel — a newly built boutique hotel whose red-brick facade and rough reclaimed-wood lobby flooring suit the neighborhood to a tee. 

And the Kimpton group’s signature flourishes do too — from daily happy hours to pet-friendly policies to luxury that’s accessible and never ostentatious, theirs is a brand of hospitality that finds itself perfectly at home in the Upper Midwest.

Actually, the oversized soaking tubs in the King Spa rooms are a touch ostentatious, but in the best possible way. Otherwise they’re subtly stylish, full of rich touchable textures, and packed with comforts like Frette linens and Atelier Bloem bath products.

Tre Rivali is the Journeyman’s restaurant, a sprawling, all-day, Mediterranean-inspired Modern American eatery with a wood-fired grill and oven. It’s something of a neighborhood meeting place already, and so, despite the name, is the Outsider, an indoor-outdoor rooftop bar and restaurant whose glass walls and fire pits keep it running more or less year-round.

content:
Twelve hundred years ago the biggest thing going in Hornbach, Germany was the local monastery, and we think it’s fair to say that the same holds true today. But for the first time in a very long while, there’s a new local attraction, in the unexpected form of a deeply characterful modern boutique hotel, the Lösch für Freunde. The concept is familiar — a hotel that’s meant to feel like the home of a particularly hospitable friend, with plenty of social spaces extending the experience beyond the guest rooms. Here, it’s all executed with a disarming sincerity, from the moment your host Olivier welcomes you in. 

The whole operation revolves around the open kitchen, with a pair of long wooden tables where guests gather twice a day for meals. Particularly at dinner, the food is surprisingly sophisticated, with a four-course menu based on whatever looked best at the market that day. The atmosphere, however, is as casual and convivial as can be. You can literally step into the kitchen to borrow a pot or a pan at any hour of the day, though it’s hard to imagine producing anything better than what you’ll get if you just sit back with a glass of wine and watch the staff do their work. 

In addition to the dining area, several public nooks scattered about the house create spaces for relaxing and interacting with fellow guests. There’s a warm, spacious wine lounge with a wood-burning fireplace, a tranquil garden lined with  flowers and hedges, a sunny rooftop terrace with a small spa and even a cigar room with the feel of a private library. Not to put too fine a point on it, but that’s an awful lot of places to hang out for a hotel with just fifteen rooms — the idea being that you’ll make yourself at home, and not just in your own room. 

Still, it’s perfectly possible to find a little privacy. The guest rooms are not only quiet and comfortable, but also bursting with personality. Each has a theme. One is a sort of audiophile’s playground, with a high-end sound system and some cool leather listening chairs. Another, with a set of antlers hanging above the bed and walls covered in rustic wood paneling, feels fit for a woodsman with a quirky sense of decorative style. It goes on and on like this, from the “grandma room” to the garden suite, each as inspired as the last. 

As tiny as the town of Hornbach is, the area around the hotel offers a surprising number of diversions. This is the German wine country, with one vineyard after another laid out across the rolling hills, and the wines themselves are as impressive as the scenery. There are hiking and biking trails, and quaint little towns to explore as well, but the best option is to simply ask Olivier for a recommendation. Soon enough you’ll have a picnic basket full to bursting with local delicacies, and some good, inspired ideas on where to take it.

content:
Resolve a little linguistic ambiguity and suddenly it’s perfectly clear what Stage 47 is all about: not the 47th stage of some process, but rather a design-conscious modern boutique hotel dedicated to the theatre arts, whose address at Graf-Adolf-Strasse 47 places it in the very same building as Düsseldorf’s Savoy Theatre and its Atelier Kino cinema. For obvious reasons, then, it’s a favorite with the theatrical set, and not incidentally a big hit among serious shoppers as well, as the Königsallee, one of Europe’s best-known upscale retail districts, lies just a few blocks away.

The rooms take several strides away from the blankness of hotel minimalism, livening their clean lines with almost baroque patterns and textures. Each is dedicated to a different German actor or actress, whose black-and-white portrait comes close to dominating the room. And while the superior and deluxe rooms are just large enough, the suites very quickly spread out into residential sizes.

All in all Stage 47 is stylish but not domineering, luxe but not extravagant, and accessible in its understated hipness. Perfect for a working actor or a cultural enthusiast of any stripe, and a hotel that does the city of Düsseldorf the best kind of justice.

content: Located on Seville’s main square, just a few blocks from the world’s largest Gothic cathedral, Hotel Mercer Plaza Sevilla has one of the most enviable addresses in town. Plaza San Francisco is something of an architectural showcase, but the hotel’s entrance is elegant and discreet, tucked away behind a row of citrus trees in a pair of 1920s-era buildings that were once family residences. Many of their charming original details remain — high archways, decorative tilework, wrought-iron railings, a central Andalusian patio — and the interiors have been redone in a minimalist style that allows the historic features to shine. \n\nRooms and suites are quiet, high-ceilinged, and light-filled, done up in a sophisticated palette of slate gray, sage green, and indigo. Some have Japanese-inspired wood paneling and mosaic flooring, while others have curving French doors or exposed brick walls. Instead of squeezing in the maximum number of rooms, the owners opted for fewer and better: Hotel Mercer Plaza Sevilla’s suites are large and luxurious, with some set over two levels, and all with palatial modern bathrooms and freestanding tubs. The hotel also has more dining venues than you'd expect at a relatively small hotel — the highlight is the rooftop bar with sunset views over the city’s famous spires.

content: Though it may not be quite as high up as the mountain from which it borrows its name, Le K2 Djola is set in Courchevel 1850, the topmost village of the Courchevel resort network, and is indeed surrounded by some astonishing peaks — as well as the seemingly limitless pistes of the Trois Vallées ski area. Then again, so are plenty of other hotels, and high-end ones at that, including the slightly larger and more lavish Le K2 Palace — “djola” is in fact Tibetan for “little brother.” What sets the K2 hotels apart from the norm is their personality — heavily influenced, as the name might suggest, by the crafts and culture of Tibet.\n\nAt the same time, Le K2 Djola has a bit of an urban vibe as well, a stylish boutique-hotel sheen that is still somewhat rare in mountain hotels. Together with its Himalayan character, this sophisticated stylishness leaves an impression you won’t soon forget. With just 24 rooms, it’s rather on the intimate side for an Alpine ski hotel, and each one is impressively comfortable, as those chilly mountain nights demand. And like its elder sibling, Le K2 Djola places a premium on gastronomy, evident in the impressive breakfast spread and in the elaborate afternoon tea service, featuring beautiful work by pastry chef Sébastien Vauxion.

content: Known for its wineries, orchards, and hiking trails, Borgloon receives plenty of day trippers from Brussels and Maastricht. There are just a few lodgings in town, including the elegant Villa Copis, a hotel that singlehandedly makes a longer stay worthwhile. This stately Flemish-style mansion, built in 1929, was the home of a prominent fruit-growing family for three generations before it was converted into a boutique hotel. Many of its fine original features remain inside and out. Decorative woodwork, crystal chandeliers, hand-painted murals, and marble-framed fireplaces — no longer in use, but charming nonetheless — grace the ground-level common spaces, with large windows looking out to the surrounding gardens with their quiet paths and picturesque gazebo.\n\nRooms are more modern with pale parquet flooring and a sleek white and gray color palette, though they also feature quaint period details like antique writing desks and ornamental lamps. Those on the uppermost level have exposed brick walls painted white, vaulting wood-beamed ceilings, high arched windows, and freestanding tubs. A lovely breakfast buffet showcases regional products from cheese and charcuterie to homemade jams and pastries. It’s served late on weekends, a concession to the leisurely way of life in the Belgian countryside, and the village and surrounding landscapes await exploration on foot or bicycle.

content:
Some destinations are about hard work and self-discovery, but Santorini is all about indulgence, luxury, and finding the optimal spot to catch a breathtaking Mediterreanean sunset. Often called the “supermodel” of the Greek islands, it’s known for the kind of stunning natural beauty that an average hotel would struggle to do justice to — luckily, the upscale Canaves Sunday is anything but an average hotel.

Situated on the cliffs of Oia — one of Santorini’s most picturesque locations — the boutique’s eight suites offer their own take on island decadence. Some offer a more secluded, dreamy experience by featuring a private infinity pool or hot tub, while others, like the gorgeous ten-bedroom villa, provide the space (and the incredible backdrop) to enjoy Santorini with friends and family. All suites feature beautiful handmade furniture, lush courtyards and the minimal, cotton-white interiors that are typical of the Greek islands, as well as balconies so visitors can enjoy the sunsets and near-panoramic views of the Aegean Sea and its cerulean waters in the caldera below.

There’s more to Sunday Suites than just the suites themselves. Guests can book a trip on “Alexandros,” a 69-foot private yacht, staffed with an experienced captain, a stewardess-chef, and a sailor. For a more intimate trip, consider the “Iguana” speedboat, with room for four passengers, or one of four private catamarans. And those who prefer to stay closer to home can lounge at the infinity pool, meditate at the hotel’s yoga facility, or visit the Canaves Oia Boutique, which offers elegant shopping and a personal assistant at hand.

content: Resotel Salamanca (catchphrase: “racing dreams”) is a singular case. We’ll spoil it now, it’s so unguessable: a technicolor, motorsports-themed, 11-room boutique over a gas station on the outskirts of Salamanca. See? Swallow that and you’ll only be impressed, as the service and attention to detail here are nothing short of incredible. There’s a joke in here somewhere, something about nobody expecting the Spanish… Seriously, though, leave yourself some room to be surprised — and to laugh. Juan Carlos, the manager and designer, took over the humble station from his parents, transforming it piecemeal into this speed-demon dream over the years. His su-casa approach informs the neon-heavy, orange-and-blue color scheme, peppering the rooms with all sorts of whimsical discoveries. Sure, there are flatscreens, Nespresso machines, docking stations, and complimentary wi-fi, but there’s also colored toilet paper, rubber duckies, and light-up globes. The design philosophy is one part cartoon, one part efficiency apartment, and one part bionic fantasy, especially in the future-sleek lighting fixtures. Tons of natural light, as well, bouncing off the reflective sheen — quite fitting for the light-hearted kindred spirit. All in all, the ideal pit stop to cleanse the palate between baroque-core visits to European World Heritage sites. There’s a rooftop terrace with garden views, a complimentary breakfast spread, and (down the road a spell) Carlos’s other venture, a pizza restaurant and bar by the tautological name of Pizza Pizza. The kitsch rises to a fever pitch here, a horror vacui assemblage of neon, memorabilia, Speed Racer tchotchkes, and vintage photography. Fill your stomach and your gas tank!

content:
The knock against some big luxury hotels is that they isolate you too much from their setting. But in places like Cancún, whose entire raison d’être is tourism, a little seclusion is often just what you want — and to wall yourself inside the Intercontinental Presidente Cancún is to surround yourself with extravagant comforts in a setting where everything is oriented towards a spectacular white-sand beach.

Its 300 rooms and suites make very few stylistic concessions to tropical themes aside from their nature-inspired color palette, opting instead for a clean-lined and contemporary look that’s not far off from what you’d find in an urban luxury hotel. They’re provided with all the typical high-end comforts, including extravagant spa-like bathrooms, and many have views of the ocean or the lagoon. 

Its restaurants include the self-explanatory El Caribeño, the Le Cap beach club, and, for light fare, Café Urbano. They’re joined by a couple of bars, an IKAL spa, and a capacious fitness center, as well as a wide array of water-sports offerings — and excursions range from cenote or reef tours to Maya archaeological sites or a round of golf at one of the region’s many courses.

content: An Italian couple built the beach getaway of their dreams on a gorgeous stretch of coastline near the fishing village of Watamu, Kenya. Today, it’s the Charming Lonno Lodge, an eight-suite boutique hotel personally presided over by the owners. Set amid beautiful gardens are a saltwater swimming pool and a thatched-roof bar and restaurant. You’re splendidly isolated, but the staff is eager to help plan your excursions into the nearby marine national park and forest reserve.\n

content:
Nestled in the shadow of Mont Blanc, Chamonix offers some of the best skiing in the French Alps, and its particular tourist economy has created the demand for two kinds of lodgings: the bare-bones variety, for ski bums traveling on the cheap, and throwback, chalet-inspired luxury hotels for families and skiers with a bit more money to burn. Neither of these quite sums up Les Aiglons, a thoroughly modern Alpine luxury hotel that’s been carving out its own niche since its extensive 2008 renovation.

Optimized insulation, on-the-spot natural gas and a pioneering dry wood-chip pool-heating system are a few of the more ecologically glamorous results of the makeover, and they work in harmony with the hotel’s surroundings to give the whole place a carbon footprint of roughly zero. This natural integration of the mountainous terrain extends to the full-service garden spa and outdoor courtyard pool — is there anything more refreshing than the sight of steam wisping across the top of a heated pool in winter?

The interior design by Gilles Leborgne does its best to move the conversation forward from its mountain-chalet starting point, contributing the kind of uncluttered rooms and bold red walls more commonly found in urban boutiques.  All the rooms are fully wired, but the real selling point has to be the breathtaking view of Mont Blanc itself — a view which also provides the scenic backdrop for Les Aiglons’ restaurant, where chef David Cochereau changes his menu monthly to reflect the freshness of the local produce.  

How to get there:
Chamonix is 88 kilometers from Geneva-Cointrin Airport (GVA).

content:
Who knew the old R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company headquarters in Winston-Salem, North Carolina was the original inspiration for the Empire State Building? A hotelier could hardly ask for a more architecturally distinguished starting point than this 1929 Art Deco skyscraper right at the heart of Winston-Salem’s newly resurgent downtown district. Kimpton, true to form, adapts their accessible, light-hearted boutique-hotel style to its surroundings, and the result, in the Kimpton Cardinal Hotel, is a delightful throwback to a mid-century era that’s frankly more fantasy than reality.

Not that there’s anything wrong with that. The best hotel stays are almost pure fantasy anyway, and the Cardinal, though shot through with subtle and not-so-subtle references to North Carolina’s visual history, is almost impossibly urbane; though the atmosphere is certainly casual, you may find yourself reaching for the dressier end of your wardrobe when it’s time for dinner at the Katharine, the Cardinal’s restaurant and bar.

And when it’s a Kimpton hotel, some things go nearly without saying. The daily five-o’clock wine social is an institution, as is the chain’s legendarily liberal pet policy, and the service is friendly and familiar yet professional at the same time. It’s no wonder acquiring a Kimpton hotel is something of a rite of passage for an American city, and by that measure Winston-Salem has officially arrived.

content:
This one is a piece of architectural history, as much as it is a lodging. If you’ve followed the Sri Lankan tourism scene you’re familiar with the legacy of Geoffrey Bawa, the master architect known for his marriage of international modernism and Sri Lankan vernacular styles, as many of the island’s most remarkable hotels were designed by Bawa or his protégés. This one, the Last House, is Geoffrey Bawa’s legacy in a more concrete sense — as the name implies, this was the master architect’s final commission.

It’s a fitting monument. Six rooms house guests in remarkably homey style, and the wraparound verandas supply a wealth of public, yet sheltered, outdoor space. You’ll use it, too — the rooms are private, but the atmosphere at the Last House is a convivial one, right down to the market-fresh meals prepared by a talented local chef. It’s much more akin to a country-house getaway than an ordinary hotel stay.

Or maybe it’s more accurate to say “beach house.” The water’s edge is close enough that you’ll hear the surf from your bed, and many rooms have direct sea views. The beach is unspoiled in the best possible way — the nearest town, Tangalle, is five miles away, and it’s not exactly a big tourist center. All in all, a worthy tribute, if you ask us.

content:
Its glass-tower setting notwithstanding, Kimpton Tryon Park is as warm, welcoming, and unpretentiously stylish as any of the other Kimpton hotels. It’s set in the heart of Charlotte, North Carolina, close by to big draws like the convention center and BofA Stadium, as a part of a mixed-use development that’s bringing new life to the city’s Uptown district.

Once you’re through the doors you’re immersed in a world of vibrant color, from the large-scale artworks backing the reception desk to the metallic and jewel tones of the lobby lounge. The rooms are a bit more muted, in gray, white, and indigo, but no less visually interesting, thanks to their varied graphic patterns and material textures. And the other senses are far from neglected; of note are the Frette linens on the pillowtop mattresses and the Atelier Bloem products in the marble-clad bathrooms.

Public spaces include Angeline’s, a modern American restaurant featuring Southern ingredients and Italian-inspired flavors, as well as Merchant & Trade, the rooftop bar, which combines an upscale clientele and an elevated cocktail menu with an indoor-outdoor garden-like atmosphere and impressive views of Uptown and the surrounding city.

content:
We know Taj primarily for its urban luxury hotels and for its coastal beach resorts, but of course it was only a matter of time before the venerable Indian hospitality brand established itself in the Himalayan state of Himachal Pradesh as well. Just over an hour outside of Shimla, set on five acres of forested hillside, is Taj Theog, a lodge-style luxury resort with commanding views of the surrounding valleys and the peaks beyond.

The rooms and suites are beautifully understated, a tribute, perhaps, to the utilitarian values of mountain life — simple modernist furniture, richly figured wood, and accents in classic red are the extent of the ornamentation. The comforts, naturally, are first-rate, and all the more so for the recent vintage of their construction. And while the courtyard-view rooms are attractive enough, it’s worth ensuring you’ve got a valley view — it’s the rare hotel in which you can have breakfast on your balcony with a view of the Himalayas.

As always, a Jiva spa and a handful of very fine restaurants may be taken as a matter of course. Where this Taj departs most dramatically from the others is, perhaps unsurprisingly, in the character of its surroundings — here the excursions make extensive use of the mountain setting, and include day hikes or multi-day treks for a variety of fitness and experience levels.

content:
Reading might not have as many stylish, functionally modern luxury boutique hotels as the capital, but it’s got the Roseate, which is all of the above, and a listed landmark building as well, right on the edge of Forbury Gardens, in the town center.

Heritage hotels often have poky little rooms, but the Roseate was more thoroughly renovated than most, and its floor plan is entirely modern — the superior rooms are by no means small, and the suites are downright expansive. All have plentiful historical character, along with all the comforts of a modern hotel, including underfloor heating and walk-in showers.

A private cinema seats up to 30 — not every luxury hotel can say that — while the Reading Room is among the top local restaurants, and is accompanied by a lounge featuring an elaborate afternoon tea service. It’s an attractive hotel, a comfortable hotel, and if it’d be a contender in the capital, in Berkshire it’s a champion.

content:
With the rise of the boutique hotel, more than a few English country houses responded by jazzing up their décor and their offerings. But not Hambleton Hall. This Victorian house is as classic as they come, and it’s been owned and operated by the same family for decades — there are options elsewhere for irreverent, modern country-house hotels, but this is the genre in its original form.

Hambleton stands on the peninsula that cuts across Rutland Water, which makes for an unusual setting; Hambleton Hall’s grounds extend all the way to the water’s edge. The house itself contains just 17 bedrooms, which helps ensure that its atmosphere remains residential and its service personal. And though its style is traditional, it’s no museum — the proprietors have kept its decoration fresh, and given each room its own visual identity.

Of particular note is the Dining Room at Hambleton Hall, which counts among its distinctions one of the UK’s longest-held MICHELIN Stars. Other diversions include country-house classics like croquet and tennis, as well as bikes for hire, and there’s much to see in the towns and countryside of Rutland.

content:
Many of Santorini’s best hotels are located in traditional yposkafa, or cave houses built directly into the rocks of the caldera. Geography and historic preservation codes limit their size, which is particularly noticeable at Limestone Santorini, an intimate five-suite hotel in a beautifully restored cave house that dates back to 1925. The name refers to its traditional building materials, which include the island’s rich volcanic soil; great care has been taken both inside and out to harness the laid-back charm and rejuvenating powers of one of Greece’s most famous destinations. 

Limestone is located in lower Fira, known for its quiet atmosphere, magnificent viewpoints, and easy access to town. All five suites feature dazzling vistas of the Aegean Sea, and most are angled toward the sunset, the evening spectacle visible from whitewashed private terraces with hot tubs. Inside, they’re calm and minimalist, outfitted in modern Cycladic design — rustic but elegant, with curving lines, stone walls, and a refreshingly all-white palette. High-end beds and built-in bench seating come standard, as do convenient amenities like espresso machines, regional snacks and drinks, beach towels, bathrobes, and all-natural products in the suites’ cavernous, romantically illuminated bathrooms. 

With the exception of one room, which sleeps four and has an indoor hot tub and a separate living and dining area, all of the suites feature ample indoor and outdoor space and are very much intended for romantic getaways. An abundant Greek-style breakfast is delivered daily to each suite — best enjoyed on one’s terrace — and while there’s not a dedicated in-house restaurant, lively Fira’s many restaurants, cafés, and shops are just minutes away on foot.

content:
The building that houses the InterContinental Warsaw is a landmark, but not — yet — for its historical significance. Rather, this jauntily cantilevered tower is remarkable for the way it towers over its mid-rise surroundings, and offers views from its upper floors that no other hotel in Poland — and few hotels in the world, frankly — can match. And inside, as you might expect, is a hotel that ranks, at least by some measures, among the finest in town.

If you’re familiar with the brand you know the InterContinental is not in direct competition with the avant-garde design experiments of its boutique-hotel counterparts. This is where you go to find straightforward luxury hospitality, and the InterContinental Warszawa’s 418 rooms and suites, despite their subtly contemporary gloss, are nothing if not traditionally luxurious: handsome, spacious, plush, conveniently laid out and thoroughly well-equipped.

The spa and wellness center occupy the 43rd and 44th floors, which makes for astonishing views from the indoor pool. And in a hotel like this you can count on an elevated culinary experience — figuratively, in the case of the fine-dining Platter by Karol Okrasa, and literally in the case of the somewhat more casual and versatile DownTown Restaurant, with its views of the Palace of Culture and Science.

content: The hotel is currently closed due to major renovation works Ursulino Valletta is a classic townhouse that retains its historic façade but whose interiors have been transformed into something unmistakably modern. The house’s vertical layout means the rooms adopt unusual layouts to adapt to the existing space, and while some spread out over two floors, they’re not inconvenient, but rather full of character. The graphic palette, meanwhile, provides some uniformity, with black and white predominant, livened by accents in golden yellow, while the house is decorated with an extensive collection of works by local artists. While it’s rather more than a standard B&B, bed and breakfast is indeed the plan here — for lunch and dinner you’ll be at the mercy of Valletta’s well-stocked streets. What it does offer, though, Ursulino Valletta does well indeed: both breakfast and a sunset aperitivo are served on the hotel’s lovely roof terrace, with expansive views over the harbor and the city’s rooftops.

content: In Telluride, Colorado has something unique: a ski town that’s gone upscale, but without losing its air of wild charm. The Inn at Lost Creek sits not on Colorado Avenue, the old town’s picturesque main drag, but in Mountain Village, halfway up the mountain. Here there’s space for a 40,000-square-foot boutique-style ski lodge that offers immediate access to both of the best things about Telluride: you’re at the top of the gondola that connects you to town, and right at the foot of the lift that heads to the top of the mountain.\n\nWith 32 rooms, suites, and condos it’s small in scale, but its services and comforts are big — the hotel’s ski valets will wrangle your gear, leaving you free to refresh yourself in your room’s jetted bathtub (or the hotel’s rooftop hot tub) and warm yourself in front of your fireplace before a drink in the spectacular Great Room or dinner at the hotel’s swanky Siam’s Talay Grille. You’ve got access to the spa at the nearby Peaks Resort, as well as the Telluride Golf Club, and if you’re looking for recommendations or reservations — in Mountain Village or downtown Telluride — the Inn’s concierges are happy to oblige.

content:
The Uruguayan beach resort of Punta del Este was a hot destination a decade ago. It’s also hot now, and will, in all likelihood, still be hot a decade from now. But that’s not to say the place hasn’t changed. Sure, Punta is still the summertime playground of Argentinian restaurateurs, supermodels, nightclub moguls, international yachters and regular old rich kids — but that sort of scene has moved away from Punta del Este proper and into equally lovely outlying areas like José Ignacio. This shift has left the peninsula itself — a stunning stretch of land bordered on one side by the Brava (Río de la Plata, or River Plate) and on the other by the Mansa (Atlantic Ocean) — blessedly mellow. And Atlántico Boutique Hotel is just the sort of place that properly bridges the gap between the two spheres. It’s clearly a stylish place, but not a pretentious one. You can relax here.

Just a block away from Punta’s historic lighthouse, this 43-room boutique has a pared-down, minimal look: hardwood floors, crisp white linens and down pillows, a single flower in a glass vase, big windows facing the water. Some rooms have private terraces; suites allow extra time for lazing about, as they come with kitchenettes where you can make your own coffee in the morning. And in case one huge flat-screen TV isn’t quite up for the task, the suites provide two — one in the living area, one in the bedroom.

Public spaces don’t disappoint either. There’s a pretty swimming pool and garden where you can lounge on a shaded daybed when the beach gets too hot — as you’re only a few blocks away from both the ocean and the river, it’s easy to come and go throughout the day. And if even the laid-back nightlife on the peninsula feels like a bit too much effort for you, you can return to the pool bar and have a cold one under the stars.

How to get there:
The hotel is located 30 minutes from Punta del Este’s Capitán Corbeta CA Curbelo Airport (PDP). Transfers can be arranged for up to 3 people at a one-way cost of $50 per car.

content: Midway between Manzanillo and Acapulco, on a secluded stretch of coastline backed by the Sierra Madre mountains, the tiny village of Troncones has long been a haven for surfers. A handful of remarkably stylish hotels have popped up along the beach, among them Lo Sereno Casa de Playa. This design-forward boutique hotel is made up of just ten rooms, all of them calm and modern, with polished concrete floors and minimalist glass-encased bathrooms. Mexican tradition is built in: rooms feature furnishings made from local materials, handcrafted art from Guadalajara, and sliding wooden doors — employing an ancient cross-ventilation technique — that open onto private terraces. Shaded by palm trees, an open-air bar and restaurant overlook an infinity pool and the Pacific Ocean beyond.

And while some boutique hotels sacrifice comfort in pursuit of visual appeal, that’s not the case here — Capitolo Riviera is, if not a grand hotel, certainly at the luxurious end of the boutique category.\n\nFrom the striking façade to the cocktail lounge to the private balconies in the rooms, every space blends exterior with interior, intermingling lush greenery with geometric concrete ensembles, and is furnished with a splendid array of modern and contemporary Italian design pieces. A pool and spa offer daytime rest and recreation, while the restaurant and bar pay contemporary tribute to the local ingredients and traditions.

It seems the third time’s the charm — Anna & Bel sees this institution (and the neighboring buildings) turned into a stylish and modern boutique hotel. Add an interior courtyard, complete with a heated pool, as well as a Mediterranean restaurant called Bastia, and this is arguably the neighborhood’s first proper, full-featured boutique hotel.

content:
The central Portuguese city of Ílhavo is said to have been settled by the ancient Greeks; of more recent significance is the connection with Vista Alegre, a porcelain maker with 200 years of local history. Montebelo Vista Alegre Ílhavo Hotel is a partnership between the ongoing Vista Alegre concern and the Montebelo Hotels & Resorts group, and is a part of Vista Alegre’s local campus, along with the old factory, which is now a museum memorializing Vista Alegre’s history.

In fact the company founders’ palace now comprises one wing of the hotel, joined by the neighboring Master Painter’s palace and the Bairro Vista Alegre, which once provided workforce housing. In total, the Montebelo Vista Alegre Ílhavo Hotel is a proper luxury hotel, complete with a full-service spa. And its accommodations range widely, from the relatively humble singles and doubles in the Master Painter’s Palace to the rooms and suites in the Founders’ Palace’s new wing and the stylish, modern rooms, suites, studios, and apartments in the Bairro.

They’re all served by the spa and the swimming pool, as well as the Vista Alegre Restaurant, which serves three meals a day focused on the culinary traditions of Portugal’s Central Region.

content:
The version of Greek life that’s on offer in a great many of the country’s hotels is a slightly fantastic one, intended for holiday-specific consumption. But Thessaloniki’s Teight Hotel strives for something different. This is a hotel that aims to capture a version of city life that would be recognizable to a local, and where you won’t know for sure if your neighbor is an overseas traveler or a Thessaloniki resident checking in for a special occasion.

It starts with the neighborhood, which is known for its creativity and its counterculture associations. Any form of touristic kitsch is absent by design. And inside the Teight you’ll find a visual style that’s sleek and chic, locally flavored but thoroughly cosmopolitan. The rooms and suites come with niceties like Nespresso machines and walk-in showers, as well as fine art photographs by local artists.

Also intended as a neighborhood nexus is Moldee, the hotel’s all-day restaurant, which handles everything from a classic Greek breakfast to a casual but stylish dinner drawing broadly from the Mediterranean culinary traditions. There’s plenty more in the neighborhood, of course — and Nikis Avenue and its waterfront promenade is barely a block away.

content:
New York boutique hotels expand to Miami Beach all the time, so why shouldn’t the Philadelphia-based purveyor of boutique-hip serviced apartments set up a Florida branch in downtown Tampa? The immediate location is Tampa’s redeveloped Water Street district, and the building, by Morris Adjmi Architects, is a new build, but one that pays homage to the industrial heritage of the neighborhood; the upper floors are private residences, and the lower ones belong to ROOST Tampa.

Those wide warehouse-style windows contribute to the apartments’ loft-like aspect, and of course admit plenty of South Florida sunlight. The style is modern and minimalist, with just the occasional pop of tropical color; the apartments themselves come in studio, one-bedroom, and two-bedroom configurations. Space is relatively plentiful throughout, and all of the units find space for a full kitchen and laundry machines, and are warmed by vintage rugs and living plants.

A restaurant is beyond the ambition of this apartment-living concept, but between your kitchen and ROOST’s grocery delivery service, you won’t go hungry. There’s a full-featured fitness center as well, including a swimming pool and a jacuzzi; outdoor social space includes a lawn and garden with a number of shared or private barbecues.

content:
Sure, the luxury tented camp at Under Canvas Mount Rushmore has views across the valley to the iconic monument from which it takes its name, a one-of-a-kind sight if ever there were one. But the real star here is the landscape of the Black Hills of South Dakota and the nearby Custer State Park — though less dramatic than some of the nation’s parks, it’s no less wild or beautiful.

You’ll stay in a luxe platform tent, safari-style, with a king bed, an en-suite bathroom, a wood-burning stove, and (crucially) no wi-fi. The Under Canvas experience is meant to combine the luxury of a resort stay and the back-to-nature immersion of tent camping, and it’s hard to argue with the results.

Embers, the resort’s restaurant, is the venue for breakfast and dinner, and grab-and-go lunches are available to fuel you up for outings that include hiking, biking, horseback rides, or a buffalo safari, for a close-up look at the Plains’ most famous animals from the safety of an open-topped Jeep. And in the evening, back at camp, guests gather around the fires for nightly s’mores as well as beer, wine, and cocktails.

Please note: Under Canvas Mount Rushmore is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from early May until late September.

content:
It wasn’t so long ago that hotels like this were mainly a phenomenon of a select few major world capitals. (You know, places like Dublin.) But now news of the boutique-hotel revolution has reached southwestern Ireland, and in fine style, too. On a hill high above Cork’s city center is the Montenotte Hotel, an 18th-century estate transformed into a very 21st-century luxury boutique hotel.

In the Montenotte’s case this means a contemporary design update that’s playful and eclectic but still respectful of its setting. Bold colors and graphic elements liven the stately old house, and there’s a light, whimsical edge to the furnishings, which marry classic silhouettes with vivid contemporary prints. And to the original house’s bedrooms have lately been added a new slate of modern cabins, containing the River Suites and the Woodland Suites, the former with views of the River Lee and Cork’s rooftops, the latter immersed in the lush greenery of the Montenotte estate.

The Montenotte’s gardens are a particular highlight, as is the Panorama Bistro & Terrace — both take great advantage of the hotel’s elevated perspective. There’s a health club as well, with a 20-meter pool, a gym, and a sauna, steam room, and a jacuzzi, and treatments are available in the Bellevue Spa. And, in what’s quickly becoming a luxury-boutique must-have, the Montenotte comes with its very own cinema, a well-appointed screening room that’s available for hire in addition to its regular programming.

content:
Family-owned for decades, the Lake Lodge was one of the first accredited hotels in Colombo. But it’s no nostalgia act. Though it’s still in the family, the newest generation has reinvented it as Nyne Hotels Lake Lodge, a budget-friendly boutique hotel in a style that’s at the same time totally contemporary and authentically Sri Lankan.

Where’s the lake? It’s not some secluded retreat up in the hills, but Beira Lake, right in the city, not far from the U.S. Embassy, the Prime Minister’s residence, and Galle Face Beach. But here on the lakeside, the Lake Lodge’s setting feels secluded indeed — hard to believe you’re barely a mile from the city center.

The villas, naturally, play to this feeling of a private hideaway. Twelve double rooms come with king beds, rain showers, and air conditioning, and the garden suite adds a private terrace. And the hotel’s all-day restaurant serves Sri Lankan specialties as well as international fare, served on the terrace overlooking the lake. It’s a city hotel and a country getaway all in one — just the sort of stuff a memorable stay is made of.

content:
It might not be exactly the end of the world, but compared to the manic bustle of central Mumbai, the swanky seaside suburb of Bandra feels quite comfortably distant. It’s also, not entirely coincidentally, a convenient location for travelers with business in the districts of Bandra-Kurla, Andheri or Worli, and it’s this conjunction — plus, as a bonus, close proximity to not one but two airports — that makes it an ideal location for the Taj Lands End.

Unlike its elder in-town sibling, the Taj Palace, the Taj Land’s End leans towards the modern end of things architectural, a blocky 18-story structure housing somewhere just shy of 500 rooms. Those rooms are, in typical Taj style, just about as luxe as it gets, if, like the building itself, perhaps a bit less traditional, a bit more contemporary, than their crosstown counterparts.

When it comes to the facilities, we won’t waste your time with a list of all the things a contemporary luxury hotel must have — suffice it to say that they’re all here. The bottom line here is that when it comes to classic grand-hotel hospitality, the Taj Lands End is a viable alternative — if the location doesn’t settle it for you, maybe the hilltop sea views or the oddball modernist building will.

content: Located in Poznań in west-central Poland, Blow Up Hall puts a contemporary and artistic spin on one of the city’s 19th century industrial monuments. In fact, the hotel could be considered part boutique address, part-art gallery thanks to its ever-rotating collection of abstract and often bespoke installations and sculptures, created by a group of local Polish artists. Attention to design has also been paid to the guest rooms, each uniquely styled with neutral shades, tactile materials and sculptural light fittings to bring a softness and modernity to the post-industrial interiors. Restaurant arte blends seasonal Polish ingredients, classic French techniques and Scandinavian influences, while b.bar doubles up as an artisanal roastery and café by day and a cocktail bar by night. The minimalist wellness area sets the scene for tranquility and completes the offering with a steam room, sauna, and treatments by Valmont.

content:
Saint-Rémy-de-Provence has more than a few charming places to stay, but Le Vallon de Valrugues & Spa, housed in a Greco-Roman-style manor in a forested park just outside the village, might be the most luxurious. No one’s reinventing the wheel here — with its formal restaurant, elegant guest rooms, and afternoon tea service, the hotel is the epitome of Provençal refinement — but there’s something to be said for sticking with the classic approach. 

Rooms are simple and sophisticated with king-sized beds made up in fine monogrammed linens, wooden writing desks, and modern bathrooms with tubs and plush robes. Many open onto private terraces, and suites have outdoor Jacuzzis or plunge pools.

Le Vallon de Valrugues is a good base for exploring the surrounding Alpilles Regional Natural Park, but there’s plenty to do without leaving the property: the grounds feature pétanque courts and a beautiful outdoor swimming pool that’s heated from April to October, while a luminous indoor pool, part of the spa, stays open year-round. In addition to the main restaurant, the hotel’s bistro serves lunch and dinner overlooking the gardens, and the stylish open-all-day bar hosts live music twice a week. It’s a short stroll into town or an even quicker ride on the hotel’s complimentary shuttle.

content: There’s a certain variety of black pine — the hardy pinus nigra, a tree that can live for more than 500 years — that only grows in the highest elevations of the Andorran Pyrenees. Many of the region’s hotels and homes display furniture built from its golden-hued wood, but the Blackpine Hotel has the unusual distinction of being crafted almost entirely out of it. Its pine-lined rooms and suites are sleek and sculptural, as if they’ve been carved out of solid blocks of wood, then gently sanded down to reveal supple surfaces along walls, ceilings, and floors.\n\nJust off Escaldes-Engordany’s main plaza, this LEED-certified boutique hotel is a surprisingly modern find in a destination better known for outdoor adventures than cutting-edge design. After skiing or hiking in the nearby mountains, the Blackpine and its immaculate rooms make for a peaceful refuge. Rooms have everything you need, and nothing you don’t. Japanese-inspired, they come with luxurious low-slung beds, warm lighting, and elegant bathrooms with suspended copper lamps and sliding wood and glass panels. For added relaxation, there’s a stylish spa with a Finnish sauna and a water circuit.

content: A decade after opening the exclusive, bohemian-chic Scorpios Mykonos — one of the world’s most famous beach clubs — the Scorpios lifestyle brand expanded to include a second location on Turkey’s Bodrum Peninsula. The sleek Scorpios Bodrum has plenty in common with its predecessor: a spectacular location, in this case on a clifftop partly surrounded by the turquoise waters of the Aegean Sea, modern Mediterranean design, a focus on wellness, and a lively cultural calendar highlighting international DJs and local musicians. But at the Bodrum location, you don’t have to leave when the party’s over. \n\nTwelve bungalows, built of stone and arranged in a circle, are slightly set apart from the rest of the beach club. They’re minimalist with character-filled details like low-lying built-in sofas and handwoven Turkish rugs. All have king-sized beds, large private terraces with ocean-facing infinity pools, and luxurious indoor-outdoor bathrooms, many with open-air tubs. Breakfast is served directly to each bungalow, but by midday, it’s hard to resist wandering down to the beach club to people-watch on a chaise longue, which inevitably leads to sharing mezze and sparkling wines in the airy restaurant with sweeping views over the sea. Other highlights include the Ritual Space, with its yoga decks and spa treatments rooted in ancient practices, and the sunset ritual, Scorpios’ signature nightly event with dancing under the stars.

content:
Wilder than a hotel or motel, but easier (and more comfortable) than setting up your own campsite: that’s the concept of the safari-inspired Under Canvas luxury camps — and judging by the speed with which they’ve spread across America’s national parks, it’s an idea whose time has come. Under Canvas Bryce Canyon is set just a few minutes’ drive from the spectacular Utah national park for which it’s named; from the camp you’ll have views of Mount Dutton and Adams Head and the region’s famous red rocks, and you’re within easy driving distance of many of Utah’s wildest places.

There’s no TV and no wi-fi — a blessing — but the comforts, otherwise, are substantial; en suite bathrooms are universal, as are wood-burning stoves, king beds, and plentiful indoor and outdoor lounge space. The lobby tent contains a remarkably complete restaurant which serves breakfast and dinner from seasonal, locally sourced ingredients, and grab-and-go lunches are available for fueling your excursions. And there’s plenty of social life for those who want it: a fire pit is the venue for evening s’mores, and there’s live acoustic music as well as beer, wine, and canned cocktails.

Please note: Under Canvas Bryce Canyon is a seasonal hotel, and is open annually from mid-May through late September.

content:
With an address right on Barcelona’s most famous promenade, a block from Plaça de Catalunya, Yurbban Ramblas Boutique Hotel is steps away from the Font de Canaletas. Drink from the waters of the famous fountain, as the legend goes, and you’re destined to return to the Catalan capital. It’s an idea that aligns perfectly with the Yurbban brand — at Yurbban Ramblas, as at its sister hotels nearby, guests are invited to live like locals. 

Very stylish, plugged-in locals: the hotel’s design and art collection were all created by Barcelona natives, pa amb tomàquet (fresh bread with tomatoes, olive oil, and garlic) is a staple on the breakfast table, a sleek co-working space provides a quiet spot to catch up on emails, and you can help yourself to drinks anytime from the honesty bar. 

Rooms are fashionably furnished, yet compact and practical, in keeping with the theme. They’re minimalist in style, with parquet flooring, white coffered walls and ceilings, black wood furniture, and jewel-toned accents. All have large windows letting in natural light, and while many face an interior courtyard, some look out over Las Ramblas. The “tiny” room is mostly just for sleeping and showering, but suites and family rooms offer plentiful space. Their petite wrought-iron balconies are just for show, but Yurbban Ramblas more than makes up for it with its inviting rooftop terrace with lounge furniture, hammocks, potted plants, and sun umbrellas, not to mention inspiring views over the neighborhood’s iconic architecture.

content:
Shanghai is in the top tier of world cities when it comes to first-rate luxury hotels; it’s difficult to go wrong. The Regent Shanghai Pudong, however, manages to set itself apart. Its most photogenic feature is probably the elevated view of the city’s skyline from its position within the Lujiazui business district. But it’s the complete package that makes this hotel worthy of note — this is, quite simply, a very fine high-end business-oriented luxury hotel, located in a place where standards are, no pun intended, absolutely sky-high.

The Regent Shanghai Pudong’s rooms and suites are Art Deco in their inspiration, a stylistic sweet spot between tradition and modernity. Full-length windows are universal and make for dramatic vistas, and while the aesthetic contains retro elements, the comforts and conveniences are state-of-the-art.

Same goes for the spa and wellness center, set on the hotel’s top floor, affording astonishing views from its indoor pool. Nor are the restaurants and bars anything less than impressive; offerings include Italian at Camelia and Japanese at Mi Teppanyaki, as well as a frankly extravagant Cantonese restaurant, Shàng-Xí, spread across five private dining rooms.

content: Tallinn is home to one of Europe’s most captivating medieval city centers. It’s here, in a picturesque 13th-century townhouse, that you’ll find the Schlössle Hotel, one of the city’s most elegant luxury boutique hotels.\nThe building beautifully preserves its medieval limestone architecture, and despite later alterations, it retains a distinctive Gothic-Baroque character.\nBoth the public areas and guest accommodations are steeped in historical charm; features like rough-hewn stone walls and timbered ceilings give the spaces a unique and timeless character. Complementing the hotel’s summer garden and cigar lounge is the Stenhus Restaurant, which offers a sophisticated twist on classic Estonian flavors in an intimate and atmospheric setting.

content: We don’t often find ourselves moved to praise the United States Army in its capacity as a property developer, but the Presidio, the strategic parcel of land overlooking the Golden Gate, would be a very different place if it hadn’t been set aside for military use a little over a century and a half ago. Now owned and operated by the National Park Service, it’s something totally unique: a bit of near-wild coastline within the San Francisco city limits. And what was once a utilitarian red-brick Army barracks is now the Lodge at the Presidio, a beautiful contemporary boutique-style hotel with unmatched views of the city skyline, the wooded hillside, or the Golden Gate Bridge itself.\n\nThe rooms are comfortable, subtly stylish, decorated with historical photos and other locally inspired artworks. A buffet breakfast and a daily wine-and-cheese happy hour are the extent of the culinary offerings, but you’re not short on options — the Lodge shares this corner of the Presidio with a couple of fine restaurants, and if you’re willing to venture off base you’re in what might be America’s culinary capital. If you’re in San Francisco to do business downtown, it’s fair to say the Lodge is a bit of a journey — but for the rest of us, an urban park with a view of one of California’s iconic landmarks might be difficult to pass up.

content:
In the grand scheme of things, these are still relatively early days for tourism throughout Sri Lanka. But while the cultural triangle in the country’s interior and the beaches of the southwest feel pleasantly under-developed, it’s the east coast that truly retains the excitement of a genuine discovery. It’s a long way from pretty much everywhere, but once you’ve arrived, Passkikudah is pure tropical fantasy — all swaying palms, placid waters and long, powdery beaches. The real surprise, however, is arriving at one of the frontiers of international beach-going and finding a place like Uga Bay: not some sand-swept little mom-and-pop operation, but a thoroughly modern hotel. 

The rooms fan out in a semi-circular sliver facing the beach and the bay beyond, which is another way of saying that no matter which room you book, it comes with a view. There are only two floors; top-floor rooms have private balconies, and bottom-floor rooms have terraces with direct access to the beach. If the choice between the two is just too daunting, there are villas that come with both, plus plunge pools and private bars and dedicated 24-hour butler service. In every case, the interiors are well-appointed, with king beds, spacious bathrooms, and all the usual docks and glowing screens. 

There’s a tranquil little spa built into a hill, a fine bar and restaurant, and an expansive pool that looks like it spills right into the bay, but nothing’s more enticing than that long expanse of sand. And if a secluded, picture-perfect tropical beach eventually starts to bore, there are any number of watery activities on offer, from kayaking to wind surfing to diving amidst a WWII-era shipwreck. 

How to get there:
Uga Bay is located 175 miles from Bandaranaike International Airport (BIA).

content: Córdoba’s old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a few of its historic buildings now function as hotels. But there’s only one “monument hotel” officially designated by the government: La Ermita Suites. The charming boutique hotel is tucked away behind the cheerful façade of an 18th-century chapel. Today, it’s stitched together with the adjacent white stucco buildings, including the house next door, once the dwelling of the hermit who cared for the church — the hotel’s namesake — and now an airy café.\n\nRooms and suites, with their pale wood flooring and crisp white walls, are light-filled and rich with character. One is built around the exposed foundation of an ancient well, a duplex-style room features original stone walls from 1700, and another has a private balcony overlooking the courtyard’s massive red and white caliphate arch, a reminder of the city’s Arab, Roman, and Jewish history. A lone terrace suite has a terrace with a plunge pool and views of the Mosque-Cathedral. In an unusual twist, the breakfast buffet is laid out on the chapel’s altar.

content:
It’s clear from a glance at its decidedly modern architecture — from its glass-fronted restaurant to its lodges, with their rakish silhouettes and primary-colored elements — that Le Domaine de la Résidence is no ordinary country-house hotel. Though it’s set just minutes from the center of Metz, it’s an experience that immerses its guests in nature — its fourteen lodges line the lakeside and dot the forest, providing an instant escape from city life.

Not, however, from modernity. The lakeside lodges carry their primary-color theme into the interiors as well, and add graphic elements as well as modern furniture. Meanwhile the interiors of the Scandinavian-style “Wikkel” lodges stick mostly to unfinished birch, but the details, again, are more modern than rustic, and they’re enlivened by some bold choices in accent colors.

A greenhouse-style structure contains an indoor swimming pool as well as a whirlpool, a sauna, a hammam, and a sensory shower. And the bistro-style restaurant, Vol128, is also blessed with impressive views of the property thanks to its wraparound glass walls; here chef Germain Samoun makes use of fresh seasonal ingredients. The bar, too, is impressive, and adjoins a capacious display-style wine cellar.

content:
Not to be smug about it, but we’ve been saying for years that Shanghai was going to be the business capital of the future. And now that the future is here, that prediction is looking pretty good. Glorious modern luxury hotels are even sprouting up in the traditional environs of the old French Concession; this one, Twelve at Hengshan, was designed by the Italian architect Mario Botta, who brought with him the terra cotta bricks that make up the hotel’s sleek geometric façade.

Just because it’s largely a business hotel doesn’t mean it’s short on character — quite the opposite, in fact. Not only is the architecture almost excessively distinguished, but hidden away from the street view is an elliptical central courtyard, which is an unexpected bit of green in a city that’s better known for other shades.

Meanwhile in the rooms you’ll find things looking a bit more familiar. Which is not a bad thing. The look is Art Deco, Chinese-style, which is also not a bad thing. Nor are the massive windows with their views of the city or the quiet courtyard — they actually open to let the air in, which is either a treat or a slight hazard, depending on the day — or the large and lavish bathrooms and the generous living spaces. Add to that a couple of restaurants and bars serving both international and Cantonese fare, and one of the better hotel spas in Shanghai, and you’ve got yourself an impressive luxury hotel. We told you to watch this space.

content: Anantara Hotels & Resorts went all out for their first property in France. The brand acquired one of the most iconic buildings in Nice — a Belle Époque landmark just off the Promenade des Anglais, one of the first luxury hotels in town when it opened in 1848 — and gave it a five-star glow-up. Local architect Jean-Paul Gomis and London-based David Collins Studio handled renovations, reimagining the interiors with a minimalist sensibility and an earthy color palette. The glamorous rooftop bar, with its curved leather banquettes and views over the sea, is a highlight. Rooms are sophisticated with coffered walls, elegant writing desks, and sleek bathrooms stocked with products made in the south of France; suites have lovely terraces overlooking the water. The hotel’s private beach club, with its striped parasols and chaises longues, is straight out of a French Riviera fantasy.

content:
The historic village of Kapsaliana, built around an old olive mill and surrounded by Crete’s largest olive grove, was all but abandoned in the 1950s. Years later, a local architect discovered the place and transformed it into what it is today: an uncommonly restful and unusually memorable luxury resort by the name of Kapsaliana Village Hotel. 

Period charm is everywhere; the village’s 18th-century buildings feature original stone archways and wood-beamed ceilings. The rooms and suites retain these historical elements while updating the spaces for high-end modern travelers. There’s a lovely swimming pool framed by flowers, as well as a lemon tree-shaded cocktail bar on a beautiful stone terrace.

Meanwhile Elaia, the hotel’s fine dining restaurant, serves artful farm-to-table fare prepared in an open-air kitchen. Round out the experience with a tasting of local wines, a stroll through the orchard, and a visit to the on-site olive oil museum.

content: Comporta is rightfully celebrated for its wild natural beauty: the town sits on a stretch of the Alentejo coast where rice paddies and pine forests border white-sand beaches. The area’s best hotels, like the newly opened Independente Comporta, were specifically designed to complement its unusual landscapes. The hotel is set back from the sea in the quiet countryside, and its design was inspired by the layout of a traditional Portuguese village, with whitewashed villas outfitted by local artisans. To further encourage a communal atmosphere — a skill perfected by the owners, a team of brothers, at their urban hotels in Lisbon and Porto — Independente Comporta has a large saltwater swimming pool and bar, retro-inspired fire pits for after-dark gatherings, and a pair of lively restaurants that attract a stylish local crowd.\n\nRooms are simple and silent, featuring hand-crafted ceramics, colorful textiles, and woven rugs made in the region. All feature private terraces with daybeds and views of the gardens or the pool. Light-filled villas offer more space and extras like private pools and fireplaces. The breakfast spread has an Alentejan twist, and an open-air pizzeria serves snacks and cocktails poolside. The hotel’s signature restaurant, Maroto, is worth planning an evening around, even with plenty of other good dining options nearby.

content: From its location in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains to its world-renowned medieval architecture, Granada is a city celebrated for its beauty and history. And, while the Seda Club Hotel has an ideal location in the heart of the historical center just steps from the Cathedral, there’s nothing old-fashioned about it. The 21 rooms and suites share a contemporary, slightly Art Deco feel with jewel-toned accents and herringbone wood floors, while the bathrooms are especially sparkly, with tiled walls and floors winking at the nearby Alhambra. The Seda Club restaurant frames views of the Plaza de la Trinidad, and the cocktail bar is a swanky spot, but it’s the oasis-like rooftop that calls to guests at the end of a long day’s touring.

content:
The Austrians aren’t about to throw out centuries of Alpine-lodge expertise just because the world’s gone nuts for high-design boutique hotels. Much better simply to subtly modernize the typical old lodges — in the case of Q! Hotel Maria Theresia, right in the heart of the village of Kitzbühel, this means injecting a bit of dramatic, dark-toned contemporary cool, while retaining just enough classic Alpine kitsch to keep the place from losing touch with its personality.

It’s the sister hotel to the Q! Resort Health & Spa, and it’s very much the boutique sister to the Resort’s, well, resort — here the nightlife is emphasized at the expense of the whole wellness vibe, and if the crowd skews just a touch younger it’s no great surprise. The rooms are a bit closer to their original state than the lobby is, more dolled-up lodge than design-temple boutique; they’re charming, and not unstylish either.

The location, too, is perhaps better for nightlife than the Health & Spa, right in the middle of the village as it is. And needless to say you’re ideally placed to ski either Kitzbühler Horn or Hahnenkamm, as the mood strikes you; the latter is a World Cup site, featuring some extremely famous terrain.

content:
Suffice it to say that the Trident rather exceeds what one expects from Gurgaon — especially given this Delhi satellite city’s all-business reputation. You might expect some complicated value-engineering, but this place is anything but utilitarian, from the palatial dimensions of the common areas to the Escher-like composition of walkways and reflection pools to the exhaustive list of luxury-standard facilities.

On an aesthetic level, however, it’s probably the Trident’s simple geometry that packs the most punch. Its design is a triumph of symmetry and order: deck chairs evenly spaced by the pool, trees planted uniformly under arched windows and gardens so meticulously manicured not a single blade of grass seems out of place.

Thankfully it’s not the type of brutal modern architecture that overwhelms. The Trident’s Zen-like approach to opulence reflects the type of no-nonsense attitude that perfectly befits its primary function — that of a business hotel. All the views encourage a serene mental state. Pool-view rooms are the pick of the crop, with immense windows that open up to the reflection ponds. The Trident’s serene seven-acre plot is the perfect retreat for executives looking for a calm place to bed down after a day in one of the world’s more hectic cities.

content:
The fast-growing business capital of Gurgaon, just outside of New Delhi, is a natural choice for the Oberoi group, the home-grown chain whose luxury hotels are in the top tier of India’s hospitality business. Unlike some of the others, the Oberoi Gurgaon occupies a newly-built structure, rather than a classic palace — but there’s more than a little bit of palace atmosphere about it, with its rainforest-like landscaping and its “moat” of pools that circle the hotel, lit up at night with thousands of candles.

A new build means a modern floor plan, which in turn means large rooms, and if the décor feels a touch conservative, the physical comforts certainly impress — bench showers are a small detail but they contribute an air of decadence, and the butler service doesn’t hurt on that score either.

Nor does the 24-hour spa, for that matter. The restaurant adds Japanese and Chinese cuisine to the expected Indian offerings, and serves the lot of it in a stately dining room or outside on teakwood decks over the moat-like reflecting pool. It’s a modern-day palace for the modern-day aristocracy that is India’s burgeoning business class, for whom Gurgaon, with its privatized services and hands-off government, is something of a bizarro-world Versailles for the 21st century.

How to get there: The hotel is located in the heart of Gurgaon, National Capital Region – New Delhi, within easy distance from the International and Domestic airports. The hotel is 25 kilometers from New Delhi city centre and is well connected by road and metro rail.

content:
Airstreams in Arabia is the concept for Caravan AlUla, the Habitas hotel group’s first property in the Middle East, located in a desert canyon twenty minutes’ drive to the north of the ancient city whose name it shares. This is as clear a case of old-meets-new as you’re likely to find in the hospitality world: 22 trailers in Airstream’s distinctive polished aluminum finish, each one opening onto a shaded private patio, set amid date palms and rock walls in what must be one of the world’s most photogenic mobile home parks.

This is luxurious living by trailer standards, of course — the units are air conditioned, and come with kitchenettes as well as private bathrooms, as well as sound systems and unique, locally inspired interior design. They’re highly functional, and as mobile units, they’re temporary — which perfectly suits the Habitas ethos of low-impact hospitality.

And as fun as the accommodations may be, you’ll be tempted out by a variety of diversions, from mingling with other guests at this highly social campground to touring ancient sites, attending talks and performances in the communal gathering tent, and dining at one of Caravan AlUla’s food trucks.

content: If you’re going to Val Thorens, you might as well go to Val Thorens — Le Val Thorens, the hotel, that is, longtime stalwart of Europe’s highest ski resort. Reopened after extensive renovations in 2013, the establishment lays rightful claim to timeless alpine chalet hospitality and unrivaled slope access. With over 600 kilometers of pristine pistes and a commanding panorama from the summit of Les Trois Vallées, Le Val Thorens signifies the thrill of winter sports at least as much as the restful appeal of a hot drink by a roaring fire. Valéry Grégo, the mogul behind this and several sister French Alp destinations, leveraged Gilles Leborgne’s interior design prowess to differentiate the property — and it shows. Prudently, they retained the grand central atrium from an earlier incarnation, tying the space together with a darker palette , clean lines, and an earth-toned smattering of contemporary chairs and sofas (that’s Contemporary in the mid-century, art-historical sense). Taupe and gray dominate exterior surfaces, while consistent use of brushed spruce smartly sidesteps blonde wood overkill indoors. Of course, it’s impossible to fully escape lodge-y accoutrements: beamed ceilings, log fireplaces, stump tables, furs, and so forth. A marked dedication to showcasing local and international art helps offset that tendency, though it does sacrifice a bit of the touchability that’s a ski-lodge hallmark. Which isn’t necessarily a bad thing, as you’ll more than likely be in intimate contact with the landscape instead. In addition to traditional ski-up access, on-site ski shop, and lift passes, the resort pulls out all the stops when it comes to activities: all types of skiing, snowboarding, tobogganing, snowshoeing, snowmobiling, ziplining, and heli-skiing (!). You can even arrange to have equipment waiting for you ahead of time. The rooms, in contrast, offer a staid counterpoint for the slope-weary. They’re plush, low-lit havens outfitted with modern amenities like flatscreens, Bluetooth speakers, and free WiFi. Still, Le Val Thorens does well to orient all perspectives with respect to the mountains’ transfixing vista; there’s real drama in throwing these curtains wide. Après-ski, recuperate in the renovated spa with a heated indoor pool, Turkish baths, and spruce sauna. Restaurants The Fondue and The Val Thorens occupy opposite ends of the gustatory spectrum — the former takes a rustic, filling approach to local specialties, while the latter emphasizes French haute cuisine with an outdoor terrace foregrounding sinuous furniture against a craggy backdrop. And don’t miss the Bar Val Thorens — you can’t, as it’s inside a massive, polished concrete cube — where burnt-pine beams preside over more mainline Scandinavian sensibilities: arresting pops of crimson, gunmetal walls, and design-object armchairs.

content:
A proper medieval castle on the shores of Lough Corrib, expanded by the Guinness family during the 19th century, Ashford Castle is one of a kind. And the task of turning it into a luxury hotel was one its current proprietors didn’t take lightly: in its new incarnation the castle’s historical atmosphere remains front and center even while its comforts have been adapted to the needs of modern luxury travelers. 

Every room’s decoration is different, though they’re uniformly lavish, and furnished with unobtrusive modern amenities. Suites and staterooms expand in size and ambition; the most luxurious are the ones named for Ted Kennedy and Ronald Reagan, as well as the Boathouse, a self-contained residence right on the lakeside.

As is typical of castle hotels, Ashford Castle’s attractions go far beyond the accommodations; a partial list will have to suffice. Restaurants range from the diner-style Stanley’s to the formal George V Dining Room; tea is served in the Connaught Room, and drinks in the Prince of Wales Bar. The Spa at Ashford Castle is a perennial award-winner, and on-site activities range from tennis, shooting, and golf to horseback riding and multiple forms of boating, as well as the oldest falconry school in Ireland.

content: Córdoba had its historical heyday back in the 8th century, when hundreds of mosques and civic buildings were constructed following the Moorish conquest. In comparison with the city’s much older landmarks, Palacio Colomera, built in 1928, is practically brand new — but this elegant palace on Plaza de las Tendillas, rising up four stories and flanked by a pair of decorative towers, is a stunner nonetheless. The property was snapped up by H10 Hotels in 2016 and transformed into a boutique hotel with streamlined, Scandinavian-inspired interiors and a rooftop terrace facing the city’s famous Mosque-Cathedral.\n\nThe street-level lobby opens onto a café and the palace’s original Andalusian patio. The simplest rooms overlook the patio and its gardens, while larger suites have private furnished terraces with views over the UNESCO-honored historic center. The décor is elegant and minimalist, with pale wood floors, a neutral color palette, and charcoal gray-tiled bathrooms with walk-in showers and Japanese appliances. Sunny duplex suites offer plenty of extra space, featuring living rooms on both floors. A breakfast buffet is laid out each day in a room with high coffered ceilings and original Spanish artworks, but the hotel’s undisputed highlight is the gorgeous rooftop bar, serving tapas and festive cocktails every evening as the sun goes down.

content: Chef Mathias Dandine made his name at La Magdeleine, a restaurant-hotel set in an 18th-century bastide in Gémenos. It was only a matter of time before he fell in love with another historic Provençal property — this time, a country manor in the village of Cabriès, just outside Aix-en-Provence. After an architectural overhaul, the place was reborn as La Bastide Bourrelly, a boutique hotel with luxury lodgings, beautifully landscaped grounds with centuries-old sycamore trees, and of course, its own one-MICHELIN-Star restaurant.\n\nRooms and suites are modern and elegant, with bright white interiors, fine wood details, botanical patterns, retro-inspired decor, and spacious marble bathrooms with walk-in showers. Some have private patios overlooking the gardens, and suites come with large, light-filled living rooms. A gourmet breakfast featuring local cheeses, freshly baked pastries, and organic fruit juices is served each morning in the restaurant’s dining room or on its sunny terrace, and a pretty outdoor pool is open to guests in warmer weather. Since the old bastide is located right in the center of town, various attractions are easily reachable on foot, including a historic château, a bookshop, and hiking trails.

content: Once a quiet fishing village untouched by tourism, Palomino has lately developed into a popular vacation spot. The setting, right at the point where the snowcapped Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta mountains and the Río Palomino meet the Caribbean Sea, is a natural wonderland for surfing and river tubing. Many hotels have popped up to accommodate the influx of visitors, but Naio Hotel & Villas, with its modern design and gorgeously landscaped grounds, is one of the only luxury options. \n\nSituated on the water’s edge, amid a dense thicket of palms and tropical foliage, Naio is spacious and peaceful, with palapa-shaded chaises longues on the sand. A collection of thatched-roof villas and suites are set around a lagoon-like pool lined in stone and turquoise tile, and long decks with shaded daybeds stretch out beside it with direct views of the Caribbean. Villas have sizeable private pools in the same style, with sliding glass doors opening into airy living rooms with sectional sofas, fully equipped kitchens, and multiple bedrooms. The décor is rustic-chic and minimalist, though suites are on the simpler side, with high vaulting ceilings, hardwood flooring, and recessed lighting. The hotel’s restaurant and bar are a touch upscale, in contrast with many backpacker-friendly venues in the village, and the region’s many outdoor attractions — the reason everyone’s here — are easily accessible.

content: Located in the rolling hills of Chianti, Villa Le Barone is a living piece of Tuscan history. Home to the Della Robbia family since the 16th century, this former manor retains the warmth of a private estate, with antique furnishings, hand-painted frescoes, and heirlooms scattered throughout its inviting rooms. The gardens, filled with roses and centuries-old chestnut trees, frame an infinity saltwater pool, tennis courts, and quiet terraces with sweeping vineyard views. With farm-fresh Tuscan cuisine, renowned Chianti wines, and a setting halfway between Florence and Siena, it is an escape for those who cherish authenticity, beauty, and the art of slow living.
