content: What began as a simple guesthouse for hikers, opened in 1981 in South Tyrol is now this: a modern alpine lodge with luxurious rooms, a notable fine art collection, and the largest hammam of any hotel in Italy. Garberhof has come a long way in recent years, but despite significant renovations and additions to the original property, this family-run hotel still offers warmth and coziness: the owner personally oversees Garberhof’s in-house production of artisanal gin, and he’s often hanging out in the hotel’s stylish mountain-facing lounge bar, enjoying drinks with guests.\n\nThe interior design is elegant and minimalist, with clean lines, parquet floors, copper fixtures, and huge picture windows that let in abundant sunshine and make the most of the spectacular mountain scenery. Even the simplest room has a private balcony with views, a separate living area, and a spacious bathroom with a walk-in shower and a tub. Larger suites come with large terraces and freestanding soaking tubs. Just as appealing is the hotel's cedar-lined, sun-drenched spa and wellness area with indoor and outdoor pools.

content:
With twelve locations scattered across some of the country’s most spectacular landscapes, Under Canvas hotels bring together the best parts of camping — peace, privacy, immersion in nature — with the comforts of modern high-end hospitality. Under Canvas Yosemite, the brand’s first offering in California, is the epitome of luxury camping, set on 85 forested acres near the park’s west entrance.

Like its sister properties, the Yosemite outpost features a collection of elegant white safari-style tents outfitted with king-sized beds, upscale modern furnishings, private decks, and en-suite bathrooms with hot showers and organic bath products. Some suites are large enough for families, while the romantic Stargazer tent sleeps just two and features a window above the bed for stargazing. 

The airy lobby tent offers café-style dining with outdoor seating where guests can grab a bite before hitting the trail or linger over coffee under the shade of black oak trees. A shuttle into the national park is within easy walking distance, and a nightly campfire with complimentary s'mores awaits every evening — an amenity that experienced campers, accustomed to the responsibility of building the fire and remembering to pack the marshmallows, will especially appreciate.

content:
The Naumi hotel group is based in Singapore, but that doesn’t stop the colorful creations of hotelier Gaurang Jhunjhnuwala from fitting perfectly into the New Zealand hospitality scene. Naumi Wellington, in fact, leans on the local design firm Material Creative to create an experience that’s not just memorable but, ideally, transformative — its richly detailed spaces are as bold as they come, and the riot of floral prints at reception is immediate proof you’re in for something much more opinionated than standard-issue greige boutique-hotel minimalism.

Its rooms and suites are a touch more sedate, but only a touch — there’s seemingly no end to the variations of colors, textures, and prints. And as visually dazzling as they are, they reward the attention of the other senses as well; double-glazed windows keep them quiet, and the furnishings, bedding, and linens are nothing short of luxurious.

The setting, on Cuba Street in the Wellington city center, is nearly as vibrant as the hotel itself, offering access to a wealth of nightlife and dining options. Then again there’s plenty on offer within the hotel’s walls — from a quiet drink in the Parlour or the Atrium to high tea and inventive pan-Asian fare at Lola Rouge, followed by late-night drinks in the adjoining Grand Bar.

content:
Sister hotel to the Communal Hotel Plekhanovi, Communal Hotel Sololaki is near-identical in concept: a townhouse with plenty of historical character, restored and transformed into a richly eclectic boutique hotel. The difference is in the details that make each house unique, and this one begins with its setting — the picturesque mountainside Tbilisi neighborhood of Sololaki was a 19th-century cultural center, and is today home to a wealth of restaurants, bars, and live music venues.

Communal Hotel Sololaki’s accommodations are divided into three sensibly named categories: Cozy, Large, and Suites. All three are cut from the same stylish cloth, combining saturated jewel tones and a varied collection of 20th-century furniture and design objects, from Art Nouveau on through to mid-century Modernism. The feel may be retro but they’re functionally quite up to date — each room comes with an iPad that’s yours for the duration of your stay.

A generous Georgian breakfast is served around a communal table, though if you’re in a private mood, you’re welcome to receive it via room service. And while there’s no bar on premises, there’s no shortage in Sololaki in general — and on your way out you’re welcome to avail yourself of an incongruous taste of Florence via the hotel’s Negroni trolley.

content: A taste of France in the Midwest? No, it’s not a questionable new theme park attraction: La Crosse, Wisconsin was actually settled by French fur traders. It was French people who named this small city on the Mississippi River, and referred to the region’s high ridges as coulées, a term that’s still used today (sans acute accent). La Crosse comes by its French heritage honestly, so it’s no wonder that the cool new hotel in town is called the Charmant Hotel — that’s “charming hotel,” in case you took Spanish in high school. The hotel is new, but the building itself has been here for generations; it’s a landmark that first opened as a downtown candy factory in 1898. “Charmant,” in fact, was the name of the brand’s premium line of chocolates. Now, after extensive renovation efforts, it’s opened its doors again as a stylish 67-room boutique hotel. On first glance, the place has enough old-fashioned charm that you might assume that the owners left a lot of the original details undisturbed. There you’d be mistaken — at least in a sense. Those are the original maple wood floors, it’s true, but the planks had to be taken up, and then soundproof and fireproof materials installed, before the wood flooring was laid back in place. Many of the factory’s original wood beams and exposed brick remain, though, adding an old-world charm to guest rooms and suites. They’re all uniquely decorated in the spirit of gentler days gone by: leather headboards, framed antique photographs, chrome reading lamps, miniature bouquets of flowers. They’re also all cleverly outfitted with high-end beds and rainfall showers, tech-friendly amenities from 48-inch flat-screen TVs to Bluetooth sound systems, and minibars stocked with locally made gourmet products — you may know they’ve got a bit of a thing for cheese around here. Some of the best rooms have private balconies with views over the river. Downstairs at the Charmant, a small range of dining and drinking venues tempt you to stay on the premises, especially on a wintry night. There’s the signature restaurant, serving simple French-inspired cuisine, the Parlour coffee and wine bar, and a cozy lobby lounge. In warmer weather, the hotel’s crowning glory awaits on the rooftop. Wood-fired pizzas and craft cocktails are served on the terrace, with striking views over the Mississippi. Of course, a building with this kind of history wouldn’t be complete without a dedicated “Sweets Bar” specializing in chocolates and pastries. Word is there will also be something edible waiting on your pillow when you retire to your room. Fais de beaux rêves. How to get there: The Charmant Hotel is a 15-minute drive from La Crosse Regional Airport via Copeland Avenue. Alternatively, the hotel is a 2.5-hour drive from Minneapolis—St. Paul International Airport via US-52 and I-90.

content:
It’s not easy to stand out among the countless hotels and mountain inns scattered throughout the French Alps. But Le Fitz Roy is something of an icon. It’s located in the heart of the highest ski resort in all of Europe, Val Thorens; the chalet has served as a meeting place for skiers, climbers and associated hangers-on since its inception. Recently renovated, it’s still grand, but crisp and contemporary, with a see-and-be-seen restaurant, a sunny terrace facing over the slopes, an onsite ski shop and a swimming pool carved into the mountainside.

The updated Le Fitz Roy looks like exactly what it is: a modern take on the Alpine inn. The lobby is minimalist but with a sense of humor; the original stone and wood fixtures have been preserved, and there’s a crackling central fireplace, sleek slate-gray sofas, and antique wooden skis mounted on the wall. Standard guest rooms and suites are done up in a earth-toned color palette, offering slope views, flat-screen TVs, and complimentary wi-fi. Duplex suites are more atmospheric, with wood-beamed ceilings, cowhide chairs and private balconies. The spacious La Suite, a chic duplex with a fireplace and panoramic mountain views, is the modern ski getaway of your dreams (if your dreams are anything like ours).

Downstairs, the square-shaped swimming pool — properly heated, of course, in winter — beckons weary skiers for a leisurely dip, or you can relax indoors at the sauna and Turkish bath. The bustling open-plan lobby opens onto a large south-facing terrace, ideal for a lunch of fresh local smoked trout club sandwiches, or après-ski drinks when the weather's fine, and the library and bar, a perfectly cozy spot to pull up a bar stool when the snow's coming down. Adjacent to the bar is Beca's low-lit, wood-paneled restaurant, considered one of the best in Val Thorens.

content:
Ulagalla Resort inhabits a largely unspoiled 58-acre estate outside the city of Anuradhapura, capital of Sri Lanka’s North Central Province and home to some well-preserved and seriously ancient Buddhist shrines. To ensure that the land remains a suitable home for the peacocks and monkeys that roam freely through its fields and forests, Ulagalla keeps its footprint minimal, generating half its energy from an on-site solar farm and providing bicycles so guests can traverse the expansive grounds without leaving too much of a mark. In short, it’s an eco-resort that doesn’t takes the “eco” part lightly.

The twenty chalets work with the landscape to offer privacy without cutting guests off from the natural world. Decks with secluded plunge pools are standard, and the interior design wouldn’t seem out of place in an urban penthouse, jettisoning any Buddhist kitsch in favor of chic bathrooms, unobtrusive furniture, and a sense that the exposed wood and high ceilings are all in service of a spare, modernist aesthetic. It feels a bit like contemporary apartment-style living, except on safari rather than in the city.

The sunken spa provides a counterpoint to the sleek living spaces, offering traditional therapies in a literally cavernous underground chamber. Moving a few centuries forward in time, the Liya Wela restaurant is part of the estate’s colonial mansion, which also houses the bar and reception area. The city isn’t far, of course, but once you’ve availed yourself of the famous shrines, there are plenty of adventures to be had without leaving the grounds — simply ask the staff, and your horseback-riding or kayaking wish will be granted.

content: It’s hard to imagine a hotel more steeped in Basque culture and history than Hotel Nafarrola Gastronomy & Wine. Occupying an old stone farmhouse outside the village of Bermeo, this eight-suite property is set amid the region’s famous green hills and sheep pastures. The hotel is owned and operated by a pair of brothers who work with local farmers, artisans, and winemakers to stock everything from the all-natural soaps in the bathrooms to the one-of-a-kind ceramics on the breakfast table and the selection of Txakoli in the wine cellar.\n\nThe interiors have been updated with sustainability and simplicity in mind. Rooms and suites feature charmingly rustic original details — exposed stone walls, sloping wood-beamed ceilings — and a minimalist sensibility. Standard rooms are spacious and character-filled with clean lines, bright whites, pale wood Scandinavian-inspired furniture, and standalone soaking tubs. Larger rooms come with private terraces, wood-burning stoves, and Jacuzzis, and suites have skylights for stargazing. Hotel Nafarrola’s farm-to-table restaurant is a fine choice for dining between hikes, bicycle excursions, and touring the Basque wine country.

content: Despite the relative youthfulness of everyone involved, outdoor travel and boutique hospitality took a fairly long time getting acquainted. That’s changing now, though, with the advent of lodgings like the El Capitan Hotel. Though it’s named for Yosemite’s most famous rock face, it’s set not within the national park, but in Merced, some 80 miles away. This is both the last proper city on the way to Yosemite and a significant Central Valley settlement in its own right — which explains why the El Capitan Hotel is dedicated to outdoor adventure and urban culture in roughly equal measure.\n\nThe rooms and suites are visually distinctive — the look is contemporary but retro-inspired, and contains numerous references to Merced’s (and California’s) history. And the comforts are substantial while remaining well on the right side of opulence. The whole of Merced’s charming little downtown district is within a few minutes’ walk, on days when the mountains aren’t calling. And right here inside the hotel you’ll find Rainbird, an all-day restaurant serving dishes crafted from the bounty of the Central Valley; also present is the Mainzer Theatre, a cinema and performance venue with its own restaurant and bar.

content:
The Andalusian city of Córdoba certainly doesn’t lack for romance, but even in this setting, Hotel Boutique Patio del Posadero stands out. One imagines they’ve included the word “hotel” with some reluctance, as this intimate six-room adults-only escape feels more like a private guest house — an impression that’s only reinforced by the enthusiastic presence of Lisa and José, your Italian-Spanish hosts.

Then again not many guest houses can claim to feature interior design as memorable as what you’ll see in the Patio del Posadero’s six rooms. Here original elements of this 15th-century house’s architecture are joined by contemporary elements, Moroccan-inspired gestures, and flourishes that are unmistakably modern. The house’s courtyard is a tranquil oasis, and on the rooftop terrace you’ll find a pocket-sized plunge pool.

When it comes to services, of course, a six-room boutique hotel only goes so far. Yoga sessions and massages can be arranged, and your hosts are quick with recommendations for places to go and things to see. This includes restaurants, naturally — beyond an abundant breakfast, heavy on house-made and locally sourced items, you’re off to wander the winding streets of Córdoba’s historic center.

content:
The 18th-century building that houses the Fort Road Hotel is charming enough, but it’s this hotel’s ties with the Margate arts-and-culture scene that make it what it is. Right across the road from the beach and from the Turner Contemporary gallery, this 14-room boutique hotel is owned by art-world insiders, and their taste in lodging is impeccable. 

The building’s renovation was an extremely thorough one, and the façade is more or less all that remains of the original structure. This left the designers some freedom with the interiors, and the result is stylish and warm, appropriate to the context but not overly bound by tradition. Every detail seems carefully chosen, and every object is impeccably sourced; subtle as it is, it makes a powerful impression.

An impressive collection of contemporary art adds depth to the experience; of particular note are works by Margate local Tracey Emin. Nor are the culinary arts neglected — the hotel’s 35-seat restaurant serves Mediterranean-accented seasonal British fare.

content:
Minutes from Perpignan and the Spanish border is the coastal enclave of Saint-Cyprien; behind its long stretch of beach, on an island in the middle of the lagoon of the same name, is — as you might have guessed if your French is in decent shape — the Hôtel Île de la Lagune. It’s a lovely little villa-style resort, a mere 30 rooms and suites, and styles itself “a large holiday home” — a slight exaggeration, perhaps, but clear evidence it’s got no mega-resort ambitions.

At this scale you get seclusion, genuine tranquility, and some quirky personality. The bulk of the rooms are set in the main building, and are decorated in a modernist-inspired Mediterranean maritime style; six more occupy the Newport Pavilion, and take the Hamptons and coastal New England as their model.

There’s heated outdoor pool on the rooftop, as well as a thalassotherapy spa, and excursions by bike or by sea, including day trips to the beach, can be arranged by the hotel. And on site you’ll find a pair of restaurants: the hyper-local fine-dining restaurant L’Almandin and, by the poolside, a surprisingly authentic Italian eatery called L’Aquarama.

content: Hamburg’s historic Speicherstadt warehouse district is a picturesque and central setting that’s oddly underserved by hotels — in fact the only lodging within the bounds of this UNESCO World Heritage Site is the Ameron Hamburg Hotel Speicherstadt. The building itself is a listed landmark, and inside it’s a collage of 20th-century styles, from Art Deco to mid-century modernism; the rooms, in particular, are warm and soberly handsome in hardwoods, leather, and saturated Sixties colors.\n\nIt’s an eclectic mix for so historic a setting, and feels loose in a way you might not expect from Hamburg. The smallest rooms are cozy indeed, though they spread out dramatically as you ascend the range — and from the high floors the views of the canal and the city are impressive. There’s a wellness center that includes a gym, sauna, and sanarium, and the lobby features a stylish bar. The restaurant, oddly, is set on the other side of the canal, connected via an elevated walkway; the menu is Italian, in another welcome surprise. Speicherstadt’s renewal is part of the HafenCity redevelopment — so the Ameron is joined by plenty of restaurants and cultural sites, including the stunning Elbphilharmonie concert hall.

content:
That’s the rive droite of Laos’s Nam Khan, not the Seine — but the Apsara Rive Droite is hardly less French than it would have been if it were in Paris. Sister hotel to the original Apsara, in Luang Prabang proper, it’s a contemporary homage to the colonial era, a nine-room luxury resort that makes the most of the added degree of seclusion it earns from its right-bank setting.

It’s ever so slightly more high-end than its sister hotel, with generously sized rooms and even a lovely little swimming pool, something you won’t find on the other side of the river. There’s a restaurant and bar that’s more than up to the task of serving as the hotel’s social nexus, and delivering a tasty Lao bite and a cocktail in the process.

There’s a little ferryboat to shuttle guests across the river and back, placing you within walking distance of the temples, and you can borrow a bike if you’d like to venture even farther afield. Dinner at the original Apsara is a fine change of pace. And if you haven’t done your homework on excursions and tours, leave it to the staff — they’re well-trained, knowledgeable, and eager to please.

content:
French alpine hospitality generally sticks to the familiar — acres of knotty blonde wood, a roaring fire paired with a full-bodied red, retro millwork, the odd taxidermy specimen. It can feel as if there isn’t much that hasn’t already been said quite well. But the landscapes around here, not to mention the people, have their own style to spare, so the grand imported gesture would fall flat; and there’s a balance to be struck between kitsch-free vintage poise and smooth, contemporary minimalism. Also, presumably, you’re here to wear yourself out on the slopes, a pastime which calls for much coziness. Hotel Le Kaïla knows what to do.

To be sure, traditional touches in the rooms keep the décor grounded in its own idiom: muted chocolate and ivory tones benignly yield top billing to natural-wood accents, both polished and reclaimed. Sore legs and tipsy heads alike will love the comforting textures — expansive carpets, plush throws — as well as the jacuzzis and steam chambers in the bathrooms. All views are worth parting the curtains for, though a few extra floors wouldn’t hurt in terms of panorama.

L’Eskale ski shop boasts private slope access, plus a fine selection of brand-name accessories. From there, loosen up in the indoor pool, which somehow manages to feel like both an anthracite cave and a liquid sitting room, complete with a bank of bay windows. This being France, and part of the world’s largest interlinked ski system to boot, we’re hardly surprised (and nonetheless grateful) to taste the gastronomic prowess and formidable wine list at l’Ekrin. Après-ski options, too, hit all the right notes: quality cigars and cognac in the smoking lounge, live jazz and fireside bites in the bar.

content:
All of the Taj palace hotels are impressive in their various ways. But the Nadesar Palace, a mansion of a mere ten rooms in the holy city of Varanasi, is so luxurious you might find yourself wondering if there’s been some sort of mistake as to your identity. This was, after all, the Maharaja’s residence, and it’s hard to imagine that the experience could have been much more regal then than it is under the present management.

Needless to say, there’s not a bad room in the house. A very recent renovation leaves them functionally as modern as can be, while the atmosphere pays loving homage to the palace’s history, with classic claw-foot tubs, refurbished antique furnishings and artworks from the Maharaja’s collection. There’s a small spa, a delightful little pool, and three fine meals a day served in the palace’s opulent common spaces.

It’s not often that unique character and top-end luxury coexist under the same roof, and it does come at a price. This one is a favorite for its singular atmosphere — this sort of utterly sequestered privacy is rare coin in the bustling city of Varanasi, and the contrast creates an experience that’s not likely ever to be forgotten.

content:
Back at the turn of the twentieth century, when Burma was still a part of British-run India, the Strand was the finest hotel in town. Built by the brothers responsible for Singapore’s Raffles, the Strand was an elegant colonial palace hotel, a favorite of the British contingent and a symbol of Rangoon’s now long-faded wealth.

Today, after decades of decrepitude followed by a Herculean refurbishment, the Strand is back, the hotel bar providing the natural gathering place for the city’s entrepreneurial class, such as it is, and the guest rooms serving as a security blanket of Western luxury for foreign travelers on expeditions to what may be one of the last vestiges of a pre-industrial Southeast Asia. It’s a vision in ivory white and polished hardwoods, a stark contrast to the backdrop of the city of Yangon, and something of a time machine, offering an uncanny window into the city's colonial past.

content: Mid-century modern style is hardly a novelty in Palm Springs, but the aesthetic is particularly well executed at the Royal Sun. Located on the edge of the city’s downtown, this boutique hotel is a longtime fixture on the local scene, and many of its best features date back to its sixties-era origins. The sharply angled canopy over the entrance calls to mind a classic roadside motel, as does the boxy stone facade with its outdoor corridors and bold tangerine-hued details. More eye-catching still are the interiors, notably the sleek bar and restaurant with checkered floors, curved booths, and retro barstools.\n\nRooms are every bit as smart-looking, with minimalist pale-wood furnishings and decorative accents, including fanciful vintage lamps and colorful headboards that resemble the dreamy ombré of a desert sunset. All feature Revival linens and Le Labo bath products, and while most have a conventional layout, a single suite offers a separate living room with a velvet sofa. Royal Sun’s centerpiece is the oasis-like pool, framed by cacti and facing views of the desert landscape. With rows of fringed red and white umbrellas, towering palm trees, and a cool stucco pool house converted into an open-air bar, it’s pitch-perfect Palm Springs.

content:
There are some Colorado mountain towns that could reasonably be accused of being a bit tame, a bit overdeveloped, but not Crested Butte; it’s just remote enough to deter casual visitors, and the opportunities for outdoor adventure here are truly vast — the ski resort of the same name is just the beginning. In a place like this you can’t always count on a stylish and luxurious little boutique hotel, but in Vaquera House, that’s exactly what you’ll find.

Its ten rooms and suites are sophisticated in their style, but in a way that still feels suitably rustic — this is the Mountain West without clichés or kitsch, an authenticity-based approach that’s perfectly suited to Crested Butte. Heated bedroom and bathroom floors are not just luxurious but practical, given the region’s extreme winter temperatures, as are the heated towel racks; Malin + Goetz bath products, Italian linens, and Spanish tile lend an added measure of refinement.

As for the shared facilities, they’re a bit more extensive than Vaquera House’s residential atmosphere might lead you to expect. There’s plenty of lounge space, including both indoor and outdoor fireplaces, and there’s a hot tub on the roof deck with an impressive mountain view. The house serves breakfast and evening cocktails, and for everything else the staff is on hand with a wealth of local knowledge.

content:
Likely Kolkata’s toniest hotel, the Taj Bengal is something of a throwback to the age of hotel architecture that’s so focused on achieving a dramatic interior atrium that the exterior begins to break a few laws of proportion. To its credit, the gardening staff ameliorates the hotel’s girth with a blanket of vines hanging from the balconies, which help the whole assemblage to merge fairly seamlessly in with its surroundings, the posh, verdant Alipore district. Now containing the Victoria Memorial, the zoo, racetrack and botanical gardens, Alipore has historically been where out-of-towners want to base themselves, particularly back in the days when nearby Belvedere House served as Palace for the Viceroy of India. Now the Belvedere houses India’s National Library and the surrounding district arguably serves as the cultural heart of Kolkata. 

The Taj Bengal takes these ideas of culture, grandeur and retreat and runs with them, predictably accommodating an ongoing parade of heads of state, and packing itself with Bengali artworks.

The opulent Taj houses no fewer than eight restaurants, with cuisines from all continents represented. Solidly eschewing trendiness, standard rooms are subtly decked out with traditional Indian décor while larger suites are a bit more contemporary. Also in proper form, plentiful conference facilities, corporate-friendly suites and board rooms ensure that the Taj Bengal functions as a first class choice for international business. But while the hotel’s all-under-one-roof version of luxury is indeed impressive, the city outside the compound will likely beckon; for this, the Taj will serve as an informative threshold for what lies beyond the garden wall, the obscenely colorful, acutely rough-edged and economically emergent Kolkata that supports the reputation as the Cultural Capitol of India. From this external vantage point, the Taj Bengal with its sturdy exterior and leafy skin is for the world traveler a perfect post to return to and recharge.

How to get there: From Kolkata International Airport, 11 km - approximately 18 mins.

content: For all its charms it’s fair to say that California’s capital city of Sacramento isn’t quite on the level of a San Francisco or a Los Angeles when it comes to forward-thinking boutique hospitality. But a place like the Kimpton Sawyer Hotel is evidence that things are headed in the right direction. It’s a part of the Downtown Commons development, a mixed-use mini-district that aims to revitalize the city center — and a glance at this ultra-modern 11-story hotel tower will reveal that this is a whole new Sacramento.\n\nAs stylish as the Sawyer is, however, in typical Kimpton style it remains accessible, never intimidating — its futuristic aspects are made familiar with the addition of some 20th-century modernist design and even a touch of classic California Arts & Crafts. The atmosphere, too, is always welcoming, from the pet-friendly policy and the signature Kimpton social hour to the laid-back idyll that is the garden-like terrace pool. Also poolside is Revival, the bar and lounge that serves as the hotel’s social hub; Echo & Rig, the restaurant, is both a steakhouse and a full-service butcher, paying tribute to Sacramento’s rich agricultural heritage.

content:
The resort towns on the northern German island of Rügen present quite a different image of the European beach holiday. Ibiza this is not; it’s a much mellower scene, and a somewhat less crowded one as well. A simple, clean-lined modern hotel like the AM Meer & Spa, set on the beachside pedestrian promenade in the town of Binz, feels just the right speed. It’s neither ostentatious nor austere — just an attractive, well-run sixty-room hotel and spa, all oriented toward the sea. 

Except for the handful of single rooms, all the accommodations come with a private deck, the better for taking in the sunlight and sea air. Inside, the emphasis remains on the views. There are glass doors and picture windows practically everywhere you look, most of them facing Prorer Wiek Bay or the wooded hills. A maritime theme runs through it all, but it’s applied lightly — oak flooring patterned to suggest drift-wood, coral-shaped lamps, the occasional porthole window. 

Just out the door is a pristine private beach, and at the end of the day there’s a stylish little bar and restaurant to retire to. And if it’s not all sufficiently relaxing already, an extensive spa is more than up to the task of busting any stubborn, residual stress.

content:
There’s no question that the place itself is special. Located in Barichara, an impossibly picturesque Colombian village that feels frozen in time, Casa Yahri is a gorgeous colonial villa set amid lush greenery and tropical flowers, its sun-drenched terraces overlooking the vast Chicamocha Canyon. But what’s truly exceptional about Casa Yahri is the extent to which every detail is considered, every need anticipated. Whether functioning as a four-suite boutique hotel or privately rented, the house is fully staffed and the experience is all-inclusive, from home-cooked meals served at the time of guests’ choosing to guided adventures into the wilderness. 

If only travel could always be this easy. Especially in a place as remote as this — Casa Yahri is several hours by car from the nearest airport — one expects to be glued to the guidebook or struggling to book excursions using a weak wi-fi signal. But the hotel’s bilingual staff takes care of literally everything, with a dedicated team of concierges and guides to plan everything from cooking classes and coffee plantation visits to whitewater rafting and hiking in the canyon. It frees up travelers to kick back and relax by the bougainvillea-framed outdoor pool or on their private palm-shaded patios. 

The suites are all individually decorated; those in the original 1800s house have knotty wood-beamed ceilings, whitewashed stucco walls, ceramic tile floors, king-sized beds with high-end linens, and furnished outdoor space. The largest suite has a spacious terrace with its own plunge pool. The other two are simpler but just as charming, with colorful textiles and artisan-made objects, and open onto a shared terrace. Casa Yahri’s resident chefs prepare delicious Colombian cuisine at any time of day; the homemade arepas served piping-hot at breakfast can't be missed. A seemingly endless range of cultural and outdoor activities awaits, and the absence of tourists in this far-flung region is a rare luxury.

The Kimpton family of boutique hotels, now a global phenomenon, is certainly not neglecting the United States; among the most stylish lodgings in the Fort Worth city center is the Kimpton Harper Hotel, a landmark 1921 skyscraper whose interiors have been transformed into a thoroughly cosmopolitan and painstakingly localized design-oriented boutique hotel. 

The rooms are swanky, and the views over the downtown district are extraordinary; like any Kimpton the Harper is a friendly, vivacious sort of place. Like any Kimpton it features a daily social hour where guests gather over a glass of wine, and in typical Kimpton style the Harper is extremely pet-friendly, and works in partnership with a local dog-walking agency. And the in-room comforts are legion, from Frette linens and Atelier Bloem bath products to smart TVs and Bluetooth speakers.

You might not expect classic pasta dishes from Fort Worth, but that’s what you’ll find at Il Modo, the hotel’s contemporary Italian restaurant — book a cooking class to learn recipes and techniques straight from the chef. And there are few hotel bars in town as sophisticated as Refinery 714, the 24th-floor lounge with a commanding view of the city.

Set on a spectacular beach on the Andaman side of the Thai mainland, Devasom Khao Lak Beach Resort & Villas is an ultra-luxe seaside resort in the contemporary-classic mold — the style is full of references to local tradition, and though it’s a new build, its architecture includes salvaged elements that are in some cases hundreds of years old. Rooms, suites, and villas come with some luxurious amenities; suites have either a Jacuzzi or plunge pool out on the private balcony, while villas come with their own infinity pool and access straight onto the sands. 

The spa, naturally, is serious business, with gym workouts and sessions of Muy Thai boxing, yoga, and Tibetan singing bowl meditation complemented by time in the steam room and a range of beauty treatments, including traditional Thai massages. Restaurant Takola Thai, which has been awarded a Bib Gourmand distinction by The MICHELIN Guide, offers an upscale take on the authentic local cuisine, and Devasom Beach Grill serves up grilled seafood and meats and wood fired pizza in a relaxed beachside setting.

content:
Orange, California was originally called Richland, and this boutique hotel borrows both its name and its stylistic inspiration from the town’s past. The Richland occupies a beautifully restored residence in Old Towne, including an original two-story wooden house, a freestanding cottage, a stylish bar and lounge, and a newly built event space, all set amid olive trees. The interiors are California cool with a vintage twist — bespoke wallpaper flecked with citrus fruit patterns, exposed beams, dark wood paneling, craftsman furniture. 

Most of the Richland’s rooms are located in the main house. Each is uniquely decorated in shades like sage green, deep turquoise, burnt orange, and mustard. The attic suite is particularly charming, with its high vaulted ceilings and a double-sized walk-in shower, while the cheerful cottage has its own kitchen and a bright living room done up in royal blue and canary yellow. 

Apart from its rooms, the hotel functions like a members-only club, hosting frequent community happenings, from yoga retreats and pop-up events to weddings and parties.

content:
Before opening its doors to travelers in 2019, the Namkhan operated solely as an organic farm. The first accommodations available were glamping-style tents, and though the owners went on to add more conventional suites and villas, a down-to-earth ethic prevails at this elegant ecolodge on the outskirts of Luang Prabang. Sustainable practices and community engagement are key here — as is farm-to-table cuisine, a natural fit given the agricultural setting — but the hotel doesn’t skimp on luxury, either.

Positioned on the banks of the Khan River and planted with lush tropical gardens, the Namkhan has an infinity pool with a thatched-roof pool bar, a peaceful open-air spa, and a riverfront yoga pavilion and gym. Accommodations vary widely, starting with the original tents and including the newer, swankier Namkhan Tents, with private wooden decks facing the water. Meanwhile, in bungalow-style structures closer to the farm, rooms and suites adhere to traditional Lao architecture, featuring wide wood-planed floors and furnished with handmade teak beds and writing desks. And the most upscale options are the modern villas built on the river’s edge; encased in glass, they’re filled with natural light and come with outdoor tubs and fully equipped kitchens. 

There’s no need to cook, however, given the presence of the Namkhan’s restaurant. The airy dining space overlooks the farm and gardens, and it’s common to see staff flitting in and out at mealtimes to pick handfuls of fresh herbs. Cooking classes and coffee workshops are on offer, as are a range of cultural and outdoor activities from kayaking and boat cruises to bamboo weaving and Qi Gong sessions, while a shuttle service runs multiple times daily between the hotel and Luang Prabang.

content: It’s not every night you get to sleep in a real-life castle, or one with the fairytale setting of Grad Otočec. The former castle turned boutique hotel sits hidden away on islet in the middle of the Krka River, making it Slovenia’s only “water castle”, and one of its most unusual stays. The centuries old stone walls and turrets have been restored to their original Renaissance and Gothic glory and now house 16 guest room that feel contemporary but still classic with warm shades of wood and brown. The restaurant serves a seasonal menu of regional flavors and European classics, such as Piran sea bass carpaccio and steak with Dijon mustard and dishes are based around local produce from nearby farms, and even the hotel’s own organic garden. In addition to the main dining room there’s also the cozy Hunting Room for drinks by the fire and in summer months, an outdoor terrace. There’s no spa but there is an 18-hole golf course, and wine tastings take place in the memorable setting of one of the castle’s towers.

If the rest of the Northern California wine country is better suited to lavish European-inspired resorts, the Russian River is perfect for something like the AutoCamp concept. Here, in a grove of towering redwoods near the Sonoma County town of Guerneville, you’ll find rows of custom-fitted Airstream trailers housing stylish guest suites, a modern clubhouse, and a crackling bonfire under the stars.

Most of the rooms are Airstream suites with mid-century modern interiors, picture windows, kitchenettes, flat-screen TVs, and bathrooms with walk-in showers; each has a private outdoor area with a fire pit and dining space. The high-end versions include outdoor wood-fired hot tubs, discreetly tucked into the woodsy setting for privacy. More conventional cabins and canvas tents are also available, all decorated in a similar style and featuring contemporary amenities. 

Grilling supplies, charcuterie, and wine, of course, are available at the hotel’s general store, and complimentary homemade granola is served each morning. There’s plenty to explore in the region, but it’s easy to be lazy here, too — AutoCamp Russian River works with local wineries and breweries to host open-air tastings on-site, organizes kayaking excursions, and arranges for live music around the main firepit at night.

content:
Philadelphia’s ROOST hotels have been, until now, a local curiosity, taking the typically boring genre of extended-stay hotels and applying a high-design sensibility and a boutique-hotel philosophy. ROOST Cleveland sets up shop on three floors of the May Company Building, a 1915 department store that’s now a residential development. And for a taste of Cleveland apartment life, you could certainly do a lot worse than this — these clean-lined, loft-style apartments are as attractive as any hotel rooms in town.

And, as the word “apartment” implies, rather more self-sufficient. The studios come with full kitchens and washers and dryers, while the one- and two-bedroom apartments add generously sized living rooms; all feature custom furniture, living plants, and unique artworks, along with boutique-hotel comforts like Sonos speakers and Sferra linens.

What there isn’t — and it’s no surprise given the apartment-hotel concept — is a hotel bar or a restaurant like you’d find in a more typical boutique hotel. Fortunately, you’re right in the heart of the city center, where dining and nightlife options are not scarce. And ROOST’s concierges are happy to point you in the right direction, and even loan you a bike to speed you on your way.

content:
That there are boutique hotels in Omaha in the first place is a vindication of Kimpton’s approach; a place like the Kimpton Cottonwood would do big enough business in New York or Los Angeles, and in Nebraska it’s downright revelatory. Like all of the brand’s hotels, its visual sophistication doesn’t translate into snobbery or elitism — the Kimpton hotels go out of their way to be welcoming and accessible to all. 

This one, in a Twenties landmark building in the city’s historic Blackstone district, adds a contemporary gloss to the throwback architecture, and in its rooms and suites it marries modernist-inspired boutique-hotel minimalism with echoes of the Gilded Age and works by Nebraskan artists. Atelier Bloem bath products and Frette linens establish the Cottonwood’s luxury-boutique bona fides, and the Kimpton signature social hour gathers guests to connect over an early-evening glass of wine.

Meanwhile the Cottonwood’s restaurant, bar, and, in summer, the pool club are among the most desirable spaces in town. The Committee Chophouse is an elegant modern interpretation of the classic mid-century steakhouse, and the swanky, emerald-hued Cottonwood Bar leans into the glamour of the 1920s.

content: Leipzig isn’t most travelers’ first thought when asked to think of a German city. But it is, by some measures, Germany’s most livable city — which makes the prospect of a charming serviced apartment, in a location that’s equally convenient to the city center and some idyllic green space, a tempting proposition indeed. That’s what you’re in for at Cora Apartments: just three sedate, stylish apartments in a 19th-century Wilhelminian villa, outfitted with everything you’d want as a permanent resident of Leipzig, from a full kitchen and a luxurious balcony to details like a Nespresso machine and free wi-fi.\n\nHere you’ve got the service and personalized attention of a boutique hotel as well as the character and personality of a private apartment. Leipzig is a compact city, which places you within easy reach both of the nightlife and cultural attractions of the town center and the bucolic paradise that is the Leipziger Auenwald, a riverside forest park within the city limits. Perhaps it’s not going to singlehandedly revolutionize the city’s hotel scene, but at its size it doesn’t have to. This sort of place works just fine as a secret kept between a few like-minded friends.

content:
At this rate, it’s only a matter of time before China has as many extraordinary hotels as the whole rest of the world put together. The Lalu Qingdao is the first mainland venture from the Taiwanese group responsible for the phenomenal Sun Moon Lake hotel, and it’s rather more than just a toe in the water — this place, designed by Kerry Hill, the architect responsible for so many of Asia’s best high-end hotels, verges on the monumental, and the location, just across the bay from the city of Qingdao, is positively otherworldly.

This is the sort of hotel where an Ocean View Suite is the absolute bottom of the range of accommodations — from there you will, if you’ve got the means, work your way right past the Presidential Suite to the Sea Villa or the Cliff Villa, each one possibly better suited to a Bond villain than to a mere mortal traveler.

Six restaurants serve a range of cuisines, five from all across Asia and one representing France. China is mad for wine at the moment, and you’ll find bottles stacked all the way to the double-height ceiling. And not only is there a world-class full-service spa, but one that incorporates a Japanese-style onsen hot spring. It’s a high-concept, high-design, high-luxury resort to match any we’ve seen in the world — and if you don’t regularly find yourself headed out Qingdao way, perhaps it’s time to change that.

How to get there: The Lalu Qingdao is approximately 50 km by car from Qingdao Liuting International Airport via S61, S329, and S399.

A luxury hotel in Boston could hardly ask for a more auspicious location than this one, next to bustling Kenmore Square, looking straight across the road at Fenway Park, a short walk from Boston University and nearly as close to Back Bay. content:
The InterContinental Sorrento Mornington Peninsula is a thoroughly modern luxury hotel, but it’s also a piece of history — the hotel’s Heritage Wing is housed in a limestone structure that dates back to 1875. Safe to say Sorrento, an hour and a half from Melbourne, has been a holiday destination for some time — with Port Phillip on one side and the open ocean on the other, the Mornington Peninsula is a pleasant seaside spot, and it just happens to be a wine-producing region as well.

In its current incarnation the InterContinental comprises three wings, and while the stone architecture of the Heritage wing is inimitable, there’s a fair bit of stylistic consistency between it and the modern Main Wing and Riley Lane — all throughout the hotel, contemporary design is tempered with throwback European influence, the aim being a sort of timeless, cosmopolitan glamour.

It’s hard to argue with the results. The Aurora Spa & Bathhouse offers an extensive array of wellness programming, and the Pool Deck is a highlight as well. Meanwhile several restaurants and bars keep things interesting, from Barlow, the Twenties-style cocktail bar, to Audrey’s by Scott Pickett, the flagship restaurant set in the limestone Heritage building.

content:
For Kimpton’s first hotel in mainland China, the brand has chosen an unusual location: not Shanghai proper, but Suzhou, an hour and change to the west. And rather than import the chain’s Californian look and approach wholesale, the Kimpton Suzhou Bamboo Grove meticulously tailors its experience to its setting. The result is a dynamic fusion of local architecture and planning, embodied here as a series of low buildings surrounded by gardens and canals, with ultra-swanky modern hospitality design. 

The 178 rooms and suites are perhaps more luxurious than the Kimpton norm, without sacrificing any of the tastefulness or playfulness that characterize the brand’s visual identity. And Kimpton’s legendarily friendly service is a good match for the extravagant welcome expected of Chinese hospitality, while the brand’s signature pet-friendliness means this warmth is extended beyond the human realm.


There’s a well-equipped gym and wellness program, complete with Pilates equipment and a heated indoor swimming pool. And the restaurants and bars are among the hotel’s most impressive elements; The Grove interprets traditional Suzhou and Huaiyang flavors through a modern lens, Kappo is classic omakase in a thoroughly stylish space, and Bar 168, surrounded on three sides by water, is an unforgettable venue for a drink.

content: Quite probably the oldest hotel in Chennai — and certainly its oldest luxury hotel — the Taj Connemara, needless to say, has seen some history. Over the course of a century and a half it’s played host to the upper echelons of local society, and it’s only fitting that today it flies the flag of India’s venerable Taj Hotels. For all its history, though, what was once the Imperial Hotel has also seen some changes: its continual evolutions included work by the Sri Lankan modernist master architect Geoffrey Bawa, and its current incarnation dates back only to 2018, following a two-year renovation.\n\nIt’s a top-tier business hotel, with all of the services and amenities that implies — but without the bland décor that haunts too many of its competitors. Here the look is beautifully authentic, even ornate, retaining just enough of its regal past to cast a distinguished light on its contemporary luxury style. For less industrious pursuits, the Jiva Spa is on hand to offer relaxation, and the dining and drinking options include the traditional Raintree, the Anglo-Indian Verandah, and the posh-as-can-be Lady Connemara Bar & Lounge. And just as ever, when you’re here you’re surrounded by a who’s-who of Chennai’s leading lights.

content: A stone’s throw from the Cathédrale Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul de Troyes, one of the finest Gothic cathedrals in France, a local family decided to renovate their home, along with the collection of 15th-century buildings next door. Decades later, the result is a pair of luxurious boutique hotels; Le Champ des Oiseaux is the smaller of the two. The elegant timber-framed facade remains, as do many quaint original details — native stone, ornate tilework, wood beams, even antique furniture — though most of it has been carefully restored by master craftsmen, and much of it artfully rearranged. \n\nOld-world charm is plentiful throughout the hotel: romantic brick archways frame the all-day bar, a rustic fireplace warms the dining room, and rooms are set around a quiet courtyard framed by climbing ivy, a space where breakfast is served in warmer months. The simplest rooms are cozy and light-filled with stone flooring, exposed beams, French-made linens, and vintage-styled bathrooms with tubs. Upper-level suites are especially striking with their steeply vaulted ceilings and dormer windows overlooking the courtyard. Also on offer are afternoon tea service, a seasonal outdoor pool, a bicycle rental kiosk, and a small spa ideal for unwinding after a day out exploring the medieval city’s museums or the surrounding Champagne region.

content: The stately late 19th-century buildings at Rosa-Luxemburg-Strasse 11-13 were originally used to house German officers, and they’ve served various functions since, notably as a military hospital during World War I and later as a Cold War–era KGB surveillance station. Today, this restored landmark is home to the stylish Lux Eleven Berlin-Mitte.\n\nRooms blend old-world character and modern design. All feature open floor plans with sleek workspaces, exposed stone details, custom lighting, and double-glazed windows with floor-to-ceiling blackout curtains. Some face views of Alexanderplatz and the nearby TV Tower. Larger suites have courtyard-facing balconies, while the penthouse suite has two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a cozy living room with an emerald-green velvet sectional sofa, and a private terrace. All rooms have kitchenettes with full-sized refrigerators, and while the concept is more “serviced apartments” than high-touch hotel, Lux Eleven does feature a restaurant and bar, Luzii, as well as the more casual Luzii Café & Deli.

content: With a prime location between the turquoise sea and Key West’s lively Old Town, Southernmost Beach Resort, named for its location at the southernmost point of the continental United States, has been a staple on the island’s hotel scene since it opened in the 1950s. But a recent style overhaul, plus the acquisition of a pair of restored Victorian houses next door — welcome additions to the hotel’s small collection of adults-only guesthouses — has breathed new life into the place. The refreshed look mixes midcentury modern with breezy tropical decor: traditional wood flooring with woven throw rugs, large windows facing the water or gardens with palm trees, and an oceanic color palette of bright white, cobalt blue, aquamarine, and coral.\n\nFamily-friendly rooms in the main buildings are simple but sophisticated, while the guesthouses, each run by its own innkeeper, offer more old-world character. Each is unique — some have charming pastel-hued bathrooms and vintage-inspired patterned wallpaper, others have romantic four-poster beds and private furnished patios overlooking the beach — but all operate in a bed-and-breakfast style, with a lavish spread laid out in the dining room each morning. All of the resort’s rooms have access to three beautiful outdoor pools, a spa and fitness center, a private beach, and a range of dining venues, including the poolside Pineapple Bar and the popular oceanfront Southernmost Beach Café. The restaurants, bars, shops, and art galleries of Duval Street are just a short stroll away.

content: If Soho House’s global expansion aims to remain true to its original purpose — that of gathering like-minded creative people in an inclusive but private community — then it was only a matter of time before Tel Aviv became part of the plan. Soho House Tel Aviv, Jaffa is, for now at least, the only Soho House with a turreted tower as part of its construction, thanks to the unique 19th-century building it calls home. And while it’s a decidedly urban experience, its location, barely a quarter-mile from the old port, lends it a seaside atmosphere reminiscent of the brand’s line of beach houses.\n\nThe rooms are beautifully tailored to their setting, combining Soho House’s eclectic, bohemian aesthetic with materials, references, and colors appropriate to this ancient city, as well as a bit of well-earned Bauhaus influence. Some are quite small, others more spacious, and all are comfortable and even subtly luxurious. There’s art everywhere, most of it by well-known local artists, especially in the public spaces, which are the reason for the club’s existence — here Tel Aviv’s creative professionals mix over meals and drinks in the Pantry and the Courtyard Gardens.

content:
Among the Whitsunday Islands of the Great Barrier Reef is Hayman Island, a private island that’s been a luxe escape for well-heeled Australians since at least 1950, when the original Royal Hayman Hotel opened on this spectacular site. Through decades of expansions and improvements it’s slowly evolved into what it is today: the InterContinental Hayman Island Resort.

Its distinctive terraced wings still wrap around a vast lagoon-style pool, separated by mere yards from the beach and the picturesque south-facing bay. The accommodations range from rooms and suites to villas and residences, and the sky is more or less the limit — the four Residences stand on a hillside overlooking the bay and the resort, while even the humblest Lagoon Room is a lavish little retreat unto itself, complete with a marble-clad bathroom and a separate dressing room.

As any private island resort should, the InterContinental Hayman Island features no end of facilities, from a thoroughly well-equipped dive center to a capacious spa and athletic club, as well as a wealth of excursions by sea and land. Meanwhile the restaurants provide plenty of variety as well, from the versatile Pacific to the Vietnamese Bam Bam and Amici, an Italian eatery with a wood-fired oven.

content:
Never one to shy away from the spotlight, the InterContinental brand has chosen, for its location in Fiji, a prominent position on the spectacular white sand beaches of Natadola Bay, just under an hour from Viti Levu’s Nadi International Airport. The InterContinental Fiji Golf Resort & Spa occupies some 35 acres of verdant waterfront land, and rather than a single central structure, its rooms and suites are arranged village-like in clusters of low buildings, none of them taller than the palm trees that surround them.

The accommodations themselves start out at a princely 678 square feet, with generous balcony lounge space, complete with oversized soaking tubs — open to the air, but screened in for privacy. From there they just get bigger and grander, culminating in the Beachfront View Suites, whose patios lie just yards from the South Pacific.

You can rest assured that the words “golf” and “spa” are in the name for a good reason, and the resort’s dive center is a remarkably full-featured one as well. A handful of restaurants and bars are on hand to provide some culinary variety, from the fine-dining Navo to the casual Sanasana and the laid-back Toba Bar & Grill.

content: The southern Taiwanese port city of Kaohsiung may not quite be on Taipei’s level as an international destination, but a hotel like the InterContinental Kaohsiung means visitors can expect world-class luxury hospitality. It’s part of the Asia New Bay Area waterfront redevelopment, and is surrounded not only by corporate headquarters but by significant cultural destinations as well, including the Kaohsiung Exhibition Center and a Music Center containing several concert halls; your neighbors at the InterContinental might be visiting executives, but they might just as easily be concert pianists or K-pop singers.\n\nLike its neighbors the InterContinental is built with sustainability in mind, from its construction methods to its energy consumption and its food waste programs. But none of this prevents its guests from living in the manner to which they’re accustomed — the hotel’s 253 rooms and suites are spacious, light-filled, and plush, and come with luxe details like high-tech Japanese washlets and Byredo bath products, as well as impressive views thanks to the hotel’s status as the tallest residential structure in Taiwan. Add a substantial fitness center and a dramatic indoor swimming pool — plus a handful of Chinese, Japanese, and international restaurants — and you’ve got yourself a perfectly self-sufficient luxury-hotel experience.

content:
In East Cambridge, Massachusetts, by the side of the Charles River, the Kimpton Marlowe Hotel plays on both its riverside setting and its proximity to such engines of innovation as MIT and Harvard — and its address, on a boulevard named for Edwin H. Land, the inventor of the Polaroid camera. The look is playfully sober, if that’s not a contradiction in terms — a sort of soft sci-fi look, one part industrial, one part minimalist, and one part warmly organic, with saturated greens and blues drawn from nature against a monochrom backdrop of white and gray.

The rooms are as likely to be occupied by tech-industry travelers or MIT parents as by history-minded Boston tourists, and they’re suitably swanky, with a plushness to match their sleekness, and luxe details like Atelier Bloem bath products and Tivoli bedside radios. The best views look out over the river towards Boston’s skyline.

Meanwhile the Marlowe is the new home of Cambridge’s well-loved Bambara Kitchen + Bar, an eclectic and globally inspired New American restaurant and bar. And the Lobby Bar is no afterthought; decked out in bold colors and graphic prints, it’s something of an escape unto itself.

content: Échirolles, on the south side of the French Alpine city of Grenoble, offers something unusual: a semi-urban environment just a few minutes from the ski slopes. There are purpose-built ski resorts that aren’t as close to their mountains as Échirolles is to the Isère resorts. And in the midst of it all, an unforgettable hotel. PoMo Hotel & Restaurant is named, one presumes, for the style of its architecture and interior design, a post-modern mélange of contemporary colors, bold graphics and typography, and handsome modernist-inspired architecture and furnishings.\n\nThe rooms are versatile, as befits a hotel that’s roughly equal parts business and leisure destination. They’re stylish enough to feel fun and yet practical enough to serve as a home office for a few days or more. And the restaurant and bar are worth getting to know as well, both occupying a sunlit space that opens out onto a terrace, season permitting. The restaurant handles everything from breakfast and brunch on through to dinner in a modern bistro style, with live entertainment on the weekends. Part urban boutique, part mountain resort, with a bit of something for everyone — what could be more pomo than that?

content: Red-light districts, like Paris’s Pigalle or Amsterdam’s De Wallen, have traditionally occupied prime real estate in European cities. The same is true in Seville, where a one-time row of brothels is now home to Vincci Molviedro, a series of connected buildings on a tree-shaded plaza. The location isn’t just central, it’s fantastically central for exploring the city, and the history is fascinating. Sections of the city’s original Islamic walls are visible in the lobby, and the previously run-down interiors have been thoroughly restored and decorated with traditional Andalusian textiles and hand-painted ceramic tile. Rooms are elegant and simply furnished; many have private balconies or patios. The rooftop terrace features open-air lounge space and a small pool, a particularly refreshing luxury in one of the hottest cities on the continent.

content:
It’s named for a flower — a striking pink lily that doubles as a clue to Lys Martagon’s enviable location. The martagon lily blooms in summertime on the green hillsides of the French Alps, and it’s particularly emblematic of the high-altitude Tarentaise Valley and the village of Courchevel 1850. It’s here, beside the Bellecôte ski slopes, that an elegant old family chalet was turned into a luxurious ski-in, ski-out lodge featuring an opulent spa and a notable art collection.

With just seven suites and a maximum capacity of twenty, Lys Martagon has an intimate air. The interiors are refined but fanciful, mixing elements of Art Deco and Art Nouveau. The common spaces are almost museum-like, with colorful mosaics and stained glass panels, oil paintings in gilded frames, and design objects on display. Rooms and suites are art-filled, too, lined in pale wood and stone but otherwise eschewing traditional alpine charm for a whimsical, more-is-more aesthetic — metallic wall murals, boldly patterned drapery, velvet sofas, sculptural chandeliers. Bathrooms are especially over-the-top, with Sonos sound systems and vibrant pink marble that matches the hotel’s namesake lily; some suites have two full bathrooms. Several rooms have private terraces with fireplaces. 

The spa, with its dreamy blue-tiled pool and indoor and outdoor Jacuzzis, is a highlight, as is Lys Martagon’s restaurant, facing panoramic views of the mountains. A resident pastry chef crafts exquisite cakes on the premises, and a Prohibition-style bar is a cozy spot for aprés-ski drinks.

content: After opening their first hotel in the Maldives, the region’s first art-immersive resort, the luxury lifestyle brand JOALI chose an island in nearby Raa Atoll for the sequel. Like its sister resort, JOALI BEING has a theme — in this case, Wellbeing — and wholeheartedly commits to it. The wellbeing space specializes in healing therapies, the villas are stocked with meditative musical instruments, and the team’s culinary experts curate the restaurants’ earth-to-table menus.\n\nThe architecture was conceived to help guests connect with the natural landscape, and from pretty much every vantage point within the resort, it’s hard to turn one’s gaze away from the aquamarine sea. Over-water and beachfront villas are equally lavish and remarkably spacious; the interiors are grand but modern, with a turquoise, rose, and pale gray palette, romantic canopy-draped beds, and dreamy indoor-outdoor living spaces with private infinity pools and direct views of the Indian Ocean. The bathrooms are palatial, with freestanding tubs, and some villas have outdoor tubs as well. Jadugars await at all hours to attend to any need, even if it’s just a friendly reminder to wake from an afternoon nap to attend the daily sunset ritual on the sand.

content:
The Austrian mountaineering village of Lunz am See has the rare distinction of being the coldest place in central Europe. It’s a locale that requires exceptionally cozy lodgings, especially in winter — and Refugium Lunz, a stylish but understated boutique hotel right on the church square, fits the bill. As the name suggests, the hotel is a refuge from the elements, but also an escape from life’s hectic pace, its calm interiors inviting guests to rest, read, and revel in leisurely breakfasts.

Refugium Lunz occupies an old house that dates back five centuries. The owners, a pair of Vienna-based architects who happened to be walking past on a winter night in 2019, fell in love with the place, and the rest is history. Many of the house’s original features remain, including exposed stone walls, vaulted archways, wood-beamed ceilings, and large fireplaces. But the owners’ professional savoir faire shows through everywhere, the building’s historical charm infused with a modern, minimalist touch and an emphasis on fine craftsmanship — so much so that the hotel won a German Design Award in 2024. 

Rooms and suites are simple but luxurious, with pale wood flooring, crisp white bedding, and large mirrors reflecting ample natural light. All are unique: one has a private sauna, one has a yoga deck, and another has a private balcony overlooking the river. Just as inviting are the common spaces, from the heated outdoor pool and garden to the warmly lit Salonküche, the open-all-day kitchen where guests are welcome to sip a glass of wine while waiting for freshly baked bread to emerge from the oven. Bicycles and hiking equipment are provided, as is a great selection of books; depending on the season, it’s a wonderful place to explore or do nothing at all.

content: Château St Pierre de Serjac was occupied by its original owner’s family through 2011, and the family’s former bedrooms have been updated and turned into eight spacious hotel rooms. Charming older details remain, including marble fireplaces, hand-painted wallpaper, gilded mirrors, crystal chandeliers, and arched wooden doorways. All have a mix of antique furnishings and contemporary decor, king-sized beds, and Nespresso machines; higher-end rooms have freestanding vintage tubs. \n\nThe main pool area, facing the château’s stately facade and rolling greenery, is striking, as is the Mediterranean-style spa. The property’s gardens are the source of fresh ingredients for breakfast, lunch, and dinner in the hotel's upscale dining room. But the experience that can’t be missed here is at the winery itself: on offer are yoga classes and picnics in the vineyard, wine and chocolate workshops, and cycling tours that take participants on some of the nearby routes used in the Tour de France.

content:
All of The Stay’s properties, in Istanbul and beyond, share a common ethos — modern art, high-end design, and environmental awareness are key components — but the Nisantasi location, designed by the Autoban studio and the noted architect Mahmut Anlar, is the most fashion-forward of the bunch. Its address might be the first giveaway: The Stay Boulevard Nisantasi is tucked between upscale shops, cafés, and restaurants in one of the city’s hippest neighborhoods, and the atmosphere extends onto the ground-level gallery, where the hotel has its own patisserie and sustainable clothing store. One flight up, via a staircase illuminated by a digital art installation, an art gallery and cultural space host exhibitions and acoustic concerts. 

The hotel’s rooms and suites are silent and sophisticated, filled with natural light (except for the Atrium rooms, which face the inner courtyard) and decorated in earth tones. All feature custom-made furniture and marble bathrooms with tubs and walk-in showers. The most standard options have Nespresso machines, while larger suites have equipped kitchenettes, separate living rooms, and spacious terraces with potted greenery and cozy wicker lounge chairs. 

The best views are on the rooftop, where modern Italian cuisine is served al fresco overlooking the city and the Bosphorus. Other highlights include the traditional Turkish hammam and indoor pool in the hotel’s spa, which is adjacent to the fitness center.

content: There’s no faulting its name on factual grounds; the Pratap Mahal, Ajmer is indeed located alongside a road called the Pushkar Bypass. But it’s a rather more scenic road than the name suggests, cutting through the Aravalli hills on the fringes of the Rajasthani city of Ajmer. And this resort, the work of India’s venerable Taj hotel group, is something special indeed, a purpose-built oasis that recalls Rajasthan’s ancient architecture, a lavish luxury resort whose rooms and suites are surrounded by courtyards, gardens, and breathtaking views of the surrounding landscape.\n\nThough it’s chock full of traditional gestures like arches and domes, the Pratap Mahal, Ajmer is a new build, which means the comforts are state-of-the-art. Even the standard rooms here feel palatial, not just in size but in style as well, thanks in part to the full-size sit-out balconies. The suites quickly grow to enormous proportions, and, while they remain tasteful, they border on opulence. And no less royal is the treatment you’ll get at the spa, which bases its therapies on yogic principles. You can eat light, healthy fare to match at Aravali, the hotel’s restaurant, or you can opt for home-style regional cuisine instead.

content: For all of south India’s urban and coastal attractions, the mountainous north has an exhilarating appeal all its own — and in the practiced hands of the Taj group, you can be sure of lofty hospitality standards to match. Vivanta Dal View takes full advantage of its environs, an embarrassment of snow-crowned riches comprising the Zabarwan and Gulmarg ranges in the blue distance and the titular lake in the foreground. Crucially, the lake separates you from the milling crowds of Srinagar proper; this hilltop enclave promotes silence and privacy when you need them most, preserving the option of a quick jaunt to the city on your terms. The image of Dal Lake is central, as the name suggests, so ask for a room with an unobstructed view (and a private balcony) for that mystical sunrise and sunset magic. Indoors, the décor embraces the region’s heritage, espousing a comfy glow via copper accents, plush patterned textiles, and evocatively filigreed walnut paneling. The sizable rooms accommodate Kashmiri carpets and oversize bathrooms with ease, not to mention king beds with decorative jamawar motifs on the headboards. Clean lines and contemporary amenities balance the affect, but not so much as to overshadow the sense of timeless domestic comfort. A tea lounge and patisserie sustain the serenity just off the lobby with padded low-slung seating and area rugs; we recommend kehwa, a local herbal tea with saffron and almond notes. More substantial global fare can be had at Latitude, especially on the terrace, or nosh on hip Szechuan plates in Jade Dragon’s sumptuous, gold-and-rose dining room. If those don’t satisfy your thirst for a view, we have a feeling the outdoor infinity pool is just the ticket.

content:
It’s a weird place, the Main Street Hotel, and given how well they’ve orchestrated all the weirdness, we’ll count that as a good thing. Each of the six rooms is a bit like a toy-chest, stocked with the sorts of curios that will make you want to do a lot of poking around, opening up all the drawers to see what’s inside, turning things over in your hands. And there’s a lot of faux fur; let’s get that out of the way. But if you can get past that initial feeling of what-the-fuzz-is-going-on, the anything-but-mainstream Main Street hotel is in fact a very fun place to stay. 

Fun, it turns out, is something Ypres is rather good at — no small thing for a town with a sobering place in WWI history. The last Belgian territory to stay under Allied control, it was virtually leveled in battle. In the intervening years it’s been rebuilt in its former medieval style, and today most visitors come to learn about the town’s history, visiting historic sites and the many memorials. We’ll let you draw your own conclusions about human resiliency; suffice to say, a visit is a moving experience. 

Life, as they say, goes on, and life in this charming Belgian town, history aside, is quite pleasant. At the Main Street Hotel, the day begins with a breakfast that puts to shame the usual uninspired spread. (Inspiration is not something this hotel lacks.) It’s got all the usual cereals and pastries and juices, plus dishes like “eggy crumpets with chili peppers” for those tired of the hotel-breakfast standards. There’s a quirky little bar that looks a bit like the West Flanders version of a drawing room designed by Jack White, a pleasant terrace-garden, and an eminently walkable town just beyond. 


How to get there:
Main Street Hotel is located 1.7 km from Ieper's train Station.

content:
In case it’s not immediately apparent from the checked blue and green glass of this hotel’s facade, Vivanta is Taj’s modern, more youth-oriented sub-brand. This one, the Vivanta Bengaluru, Whitefield, plays the role to a tee — Bangalore is India’s high-technology capital, and it’s no stretch to imagine that the city’s young, tech-savvy workforce prefers geometric forms to stately old palaces.

At 199 rooms and suites one blanches at calling the Whitefield a boutique, but in terms of style and approach there’s no better word for it. The décor is sunny and sparse, and all the rooms provide plenty of room to maneuver, and traditional Taj luxuries meet the new high-tech must-haves: rooms come with yoga kits, a pillow menu and high-end toiletries, as well as IP telephones, 32-inch home theatre systems and extremely fast internet.

Rooms are, of course, only half the story in a hotel like this. Vivanta Bengaluru, Whitefield is extremely well supplied when it comes to public spaces, with a spa and fitness center, a popular lounge, and four different restaurants. What the more traditional Taj luxury hotels are to the old city centers, the Vivanta Bengaluru is to the sprawl of Bangalore — equal parts lodging and gathering place, it’s where the city meets the outside world.

content: Most lodgings along the Col du Tourmalet are simple guesthouses. But the 2023 opening of Hotel La Voie Lactée signals a change. Located in the village of La Mongie, this luxury boutique hotel is directly across from the ski lift and the cable car to the Pic du Midi observatory, offering staggering views of the mountains from the airy ground-level lounge, restaurant, bar, and all of its guest rooms. The owners worked with architect Romain Thevenot to transform the five-story structure, formerly a family-run hotel, into a modern getaway that pays stylistic homage to the building’s past.\n\nLa Voie Lactée means “the Milky Way,” and rooms are named after astronomical features —  galaxy, constellation, the Big Dipper — a reference to the spectacularly starry skies overhead at night, thanks to light pollution restrictions in the area. All rooms have oversized windows letting in abundant natural light, and many have private balconies overlooking the ski slopes. The interiors have a cozy mountain lodge look with a vintage twist: pale wood paneling, midnight blue accent walls, ceramic pendant lamps, retro armchairs, and charmingly tiled bathrooms with large round mirrors. Downstairs, the wellness area has an organic spa, a sauna, and a pair of open-air Nordic-style baths, while breakfast, afternoon tea, and après-ski drinks are served by a fireplace facing the mountains.

The historic building has been meticulously restored with a distinctive design inspired by local history and nature. Vibrant social areas and bold design elements create a refined yet playful atmosphere, solidifying the Kimpton BEM as a standout destination in Budapest. Additional amenities include a small spa with a wet area and a compact yet well-equipped gym.

content: Before Beyoncé shot a music video on the main square, before its colorful cottages and candlelit restaurants became jetsetters’ hotspots, the sleepy beach town of Trancoso was a place to get away from it all. These days, you’ll have to go a bit further afield to get away from the crowd — a few miles down the coast, for instance, to Fasano Trancoso, tucked between tropical forest and the blue sea on a quiet stretch of Itapororoca Beach. The generously sized property features a collection of starkly white, geometric bungalows designed by Isay Weinfeld, the Brazilian architect who co-designed the original Fasano Hotel in São Paulo. \n\nWeinfeld’s minimalist aesthetic works well in a wildly different setting: rooms are sleek, mostly white and beige, with striking wood-paneled ceilings and ultra-spacious marble bathrooms with walk-in showers partly exposed to sunny private gardens. But his style is adapted to suit the setting, too — old wooden oars are mounted on the walls, and outside, hand-woven hammocks flutter in the breeze on the bungalows’ thatched-roof terraces. Some also have rooftop decks with ocean views. Amenities abound, as there’s plenty of space, including two large swimming pools, a beach tennis court, a fitness center, and a spa. While the main restaurant may be more notable, the more casual beachfront eatery and bar, with wooden tables set up on the sand beneath the shade of an almond tree, is more memorable.

content:
The founders of the natural skincare brand Fresh were trailblazers in the “clean beauty” business. Their latest venture, a bohemian-chic boutique hotel in downtown Hudson, is a few hours away from their flagship shop in New York City, but the two have plenty in common: period charm, attention to detail, and, of course, first-rate bath products — the Maker features its own gender-inclusive fragrance. 

A trio of historic buildings is divided into eleven rooms, each one individually designed and outfitted with a mix of Art Deco and mid-century modern décor, and lit by unique vintage pieces from the owners’ collection. Those in the main Georgian mansion-style building have living areas with fireplaces, while Parisian-inspired loft rooms feature dormer windows and French doors leading onto private terraces. 

The artwork, you might notice, is of a rather higher caliber than typical hotel fare; the Maker’s proprietors are serious collectors. Other highlights include a sunny all-day café, an old carriage house converted into a sultry cocktail lounge, a glass conservatory turned into a greenery-filled French restaurant, a cozy library open exclusively to guests, and, perhaps most unexpected of all, an outdoor swimming pool.
