content:
The French Basque Country village of Sare, amid the peaks of the Pyrénées barely a mile from the Spanish border, is the setting for the Hôtel Arraya, a 17th-century structure that formerly served as a waystation for travelers on pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, and has been a family-owned hotel since the middle of the 20th century. While it’s seen some technical upgrades in the intervening years, the spirit and aesthetic of the place would look familiar enough to guests from any era; the exterior is pure Basque Country charm and the interiors follow along in a similarly warm and cozy style.

Many of the rooms feature their original ceiling beams and other antique features, while those of more recent vintage nevertheless remain true to the hotel’s historical inspiration. Modern technological interventions are welcome, and subtle — an elevator is handy, for instance, as are modern bathrooms. The restaurant serves everything from a hearty breakfast to modern Basque-inspired lunch and a beautifully presented gastronomic dinner, all in a lovely dining room or out on the terrace, beneath the shade of the hotel’s old plane trees. Among Sare’s claims to fame: the Musée du Gâteau Basque, whose namesake cake is available at the Arraya.

content:
Any question about whether the word “paradise” is warranted should be put to rest by a look at the Jiuzhaigou Valley; the mountainous backdrop for the InterContinental Resort Jiuzhai Paradise is nothing short of spectacular. This ultra-modern steel-and-glass structure is immersed in dense forest, and is set just a few minutes’ drive from the Jiuzhaigou Nature Reserve, which is, somehow, even more wild and picturesque.

Weighing in at 979 rooms and suites this is certainly no boutique operation. And though it may seem improbable, given the size, it’s laid out in a way that lends its accommodations an uncommon amount of privacy. The residential wings fan out from a central dome that contains what’s practically a private city; the rooms and suites themselves are luxurious but not ostentatious.

It’s in the services and amenities that the InterContinental Resort Jiuzhai Paradise truly sets itself apart. Under a glass roof are twelve terraced pools that together form the Tianyu Spa. And in the mall-like central structure are no fewer than six restaurants, serving everything from traditional Sichuan and Tibetan cuisines to upscale Western offerings. And while the resort itself is remarkably self-sufficient, to stay here without venturing into the surrounding landscapes would be the height of folly.

content: The Sydney neighborhood of Double Bay is set not in the city center but in the upscale eastern suburbs. It’s not the first place you’d look for a hotel like the InterContinental — that’d be by the side of the harbour, with a view of the opera house — but it just might be the second. The InterContinental Sydney Double Bay is less a business hotel and more an urban resort, best positioned for taking advantage of the shopping, dining, and nightlife of this stylish suburb — and it is set within walking distance of a couple of fine beaches.\n\nInside it’s pure throwback elegance, full of richly figured marble and Belle Époque echoes. The rooms and suites are generously sized, and many have balconies with views of either Double Bay village or the bay itself. There’s a rooftop swimming pool as well, and Sydney being Sydney there’s an extensive fitness program with a multitude of class offerings. Nor are guests entirely left to depend upon Double Bay’s substantial restaurant scene — the InterContinental Sydney Double Bay has no dedicated restaurant, but its bar and rooftop serve food alongside their drinks, and the hotel’s kitchen will serve you wherever you choose to dine.

content:
The Lower Saxon town of Celle, in the countryside outside of Hanover, is known for its picturesque timber-framed old town, and for its Renaissance and Baroque-style castle. And just outside that town center, a short walk from the castle’s park, is another picturesque edifice: the 1680 Baroque palace that is now home to the Althoff Hotel Fürstenhof Celle.

Its rooms are divided between the original house and a more modern addition, and the style differs correspondingly, though not as dramatically as one might imagine — the contemporary rooms have an air of historical sobriety about them, and the palace’s rooms and suites have been kept quite up to date, both in their style and in their equipment. All of them feel like light and tranquil country-house lodgings rather than heavily historical castle rooms.

The hotel’s spa includes an indoor pool, a sauna, and a gym, and the bar and restaurant are particularly inviting. The former, the Foyer Bar, feels like a casual, cozy living room, and opens onto the terrace, while the latter, the Taverna & Trattoria Palio, is a remarkably authentic Italian experience — by no means a common thing in this part of northern Germany.

content:
Mumbai is by no means underrepresented in the Taj portfolio, but it’s by no means an underpopulated city, either, so there’s always room for another. Sandwiched between two airports, the 279-room Taj Santacruz Mumbai adds convenience to the traditional Taj opulence that the global business set has come to expect. 

The façade sets a stately tone, blending Art Deco curves and curlicues with stonework of imperial proportions. Further in you’ll find signifiers of high luxury in the lobby: daring chandeliers glittering overhead from a lofty ceiling, mirror-polished surfaces in every direction, and discreetly professional staffers bustling in the middle distance, keeping the whole apparatus oiled. Upstairs, rooms adhere fairly rigidly to a subtly elegant design scheme, elevating amber and goldenrod base notes with traditional Indian decorative accents and timeless touches like etched glass and mother-of-pearl furniture finishes. High-speed wi-fi, LED flatscreens, and substantial desk space should satisfy even the most exacting businessperson, while deep soaking tubs and plush king beds ensure satisfaction on a more basic level. 

Tiqri is the destination restaurant, complete with a six-story, color-changing atrium mural and a heady menu of authentic Mumbai cuisine. A pair of aptly named dining outlets round out the food offerings: Rivea riffs on Mediterranean Riviera classics, while China INC. serves beautifully plated Chinese and Szechuan specialties. Work off the weight and the stress at Taj trademark Jiva Spa or in the jacuzzi-equipped fitness center — and there’s also a Maserati showroom, for some fairly extreme retail therapy.

content: Mere minutes outside of the Forest of Bowland, in the picturesque Ribble Valley, Northcote is a country-house hotel with a reputation for culinary excellence. And though it’s far from the only hotel in England to merit such a description, it’s been at it for longer than most of them: the restaurant was awarded its first MICHELIN Star in 1996. And while the table is still the primary draw, the rest of the experience is anything but an afterthought. Each of the 26 rooms and suites is different, though all are uniformly luxurious, and perhaps surprisingly contemporary in their style and comforts. The hotel’s cooking school is among its most popular recreational offerings.

content:
Don’t let the Surry Hills location put you off for a second — while you’re on the southern edge of the city center proper, a longish walk from the waterfront tourist attractions and the districts where the boutique hotels generally cluster, you couldn’t ask for a better neighborhood. Here you’ve got one foot in the established city center and one foot in an emerging, creative, largely residential district. Not literally; that’d be awkward. And there’s nothing awkward about the ADGE Boutique Apartment Hotel.

In fact the name pretty well sums it up. Rather than a fully serviced hotel, bellhops and all, it’s the sort of place that trusts you to find a meal, do some shopping, entertain yourself out of doors — though of course the concierge is happy to help. And this isn’t your typical apartment swap, either — these apartments are sleek, stylish, and exceedingly well-appointed, with full kitchens, in-house laundry, and open-plan living and dining rooms.

Simply put, it’s a phenomenal location for anyone who’s not in Sydney simply to climb the Harbour Bridge and snap a photo of the Opera House. Scratch a little deeper and you’ll find much of the city’s best dining, shopping and nightlife is quietly tucked into Surry Hills — and the city center proper, should you develop a hankering, is still quite close at hand.

content: Many travelers passing through medieval Alcobaça, a popular stop on trips between Lisbon and Porto, stay in hotels located inside old chalets or restored monasteries. The hilltop Vale d’Azenha Hotel & Residences offers a contemporary alternative. In a rural area just minutes from the historic center, this luxury hotel’s eye-catching architecture is unmistakably modern, its sharp angles and geometric shapes reflected in the large aquamarine-tiled swimming pool.\n\nVale d’Azenha comprises a small collection of rooms, suites, and freestanding villas, all with floor-to-ceiling windows and private terraces overlooking the surrounding landscapes. The décor is simple and sophisticated, with wood-paneled walls and floors and cozy furnishings in neutral colors. Some suites and villas feature scarlet red accents, but mostly the earth-toned decor blends in with the scenery outside. The infinity-edge pool is cleverly positioned amid the treetops, and the hotel’s restaurant, with it's balcony seating overlooking the valley, makes the most of Vale d’Azenha’s peaceful setting.

content: Law and order are woven into the fabric of picturesque Litchfield, Connecticut: the town was home to the country's first law school, and its old county courthouse was recently turned into a stylish hotel. It’s the work of the Provincetown-based Salt Hotels, and like its sister properties across New England, the Abner Hotel is small-scale and design-focused. The landmark building contains just twenty guest rooms and a handful of common spaces that lean into the theme — the one-time courtroom, with its high ceilings, elegant wood paneling, and marble countertops, is now a restaurant, and the seasonal rooftop bar, offering views over the town’s scenic surroundings, is called Verdict. \n\nThe former judge’s quarters and second-story offices have been shaped into rooms and suites rich with vintage character. Each is uniquely decorated, but all feature mustard-yellow walls, dark wood accents, cozy plaid blankets, petite seating nooks, and bathrooms with white subway tiles and walk-in showers. Standard amenities include Tivoli Bluetooth speakers, cotton robes by Tensira, sustainably made bath products, and minibars with local treats. A complimentary breakfast is served in the Courtroom, which morphs into a lively tavern later in the day, a memorable spot for sipping Prohibition-era cocktails by the old jury box and witness stand.

content:
The Hotel Indigo brand is a far-ranging and diverse collection overseen by IHG, which is by any measure a giant of corporate hospitality. But hotels like the Hotel Indigo Cardiff are evidence that corporate ownership doesn’t necessarily imply corporate style. This hotel, after all, could hardly be more painstakingly tailored to its location — from its prominent setting on Cardiff’s city-center Queen Street to the surfeit of local color incorporated into its interior design.

This includes local textiles, pop-culture artifacts, and artworks with Welsh themes, both historical and contemporary, referring to the city’s industrial heritage and its musical contributions — not just in the public spaces but in the rooms and suites as well. The accommodations themselves are squarely in the luxury-boutique tradition, with plenty of visual character as well as plenty of comfort — including “spa-inspired” showers stocked with locally made Mydafai bath products.

And up on the top floor, opening onto a rooftop terrace, is the Hotel Indigo Cardiff’s most impressive offering: Lefel 6, an eatery offering Welsh-inspired menus.

content:
Shenzhen might be best known overseas as a hotbed of tech, commerce, and manufacturing, but as this hotel’s seaside location makes clear, you don’t have to travel very far from the population centers to get to a frankly idyllic stretch of coastline, nestled into verdant mountains and presided over by the curvaceous modern structure that is the InterContinental Shenzhen Dameisha Resort.

Inside are no fewer than 432 rooms and suites; this is no small operation, though in a luxury hotel of this caliber it’s quite easy to forget all about the other 431. The most impressive units look straight out to sea, though those with a garden view are not too shabby either; many come with balconies, and they start out spacious and only get larger from there.

No less extensive are the InterContinental Shenzhen Dameisha Resort’s facilities; among its leisure offerings are five swimming pools, both indoor and outdoor, as well as a vast surplus of meeting and events space. And its six restaurants ensure a varied stay even for guests who never leave the property, ranging from a handful of Chinese options to Mediterranean fare at the Azure, inspired by the south of France.

content: Tucked away in the mountain village of Castione della Presolana in Northeastern Lombardy, the Hotel Milano Alpen Resort & Spa presents a chic Italian spin on the Alpine chalet. Outside, white masonry and dark timber form a more modernist type of lodge, reflected tenfold in the accommodations inside. The Milano promises that every last detail was designed with the guest’s well-being in mind, and in the rooms, this means clean design, soft hues and, when possible, expansive views at the foot of the Presolana mountain. When you’re not exploring the mountain roads on a handful of pre-planned routes, a spa offers a host of wellness treatments, and a cellar awaits with a large selection of wines.

content:
Boutique-hotel style may have taken a little while to make its way to the slopes of the world’s ski resorts, but there’s no question it’s officially arrived. And thanks to the redesign of the Araucaria Hotel & Spa, in the French Alpine town of La Plagne, we can add another example of the trend. Here, at the very foot of the vast Paradiski ski area, is an 84-room hotel whose redesign, by the architect Leslie Gauthier, leaves it head and shoulders above the tradition-bound, visually conservative ski-hotel norm.

It’s also proof that you can have contemporary boutique-hotel good looks without sacrificing family-friendliness. In classic European style, Araucaria's got single rooms, but it’s also got connecting rooms and family-sized rooms that sleep up to five. And at any size, they’re stylishly outfitted in crisp navy blue and gray, with soft textures that provide the requisite Alpine warmth even as they studiously avoid any form of ski-hotel kitsch.

The Spa Nuxe is an impressive one, with a variety of temperature treatments and pools as well as classic massage and beauty treatments. There’s a buffet breakfast in the morning and a rather more elaborate dinner service in the evening, as well as a chic bar that often features DJs or live music. And of course just outside are the slopes of La Plagne and the larger Paradiski combined resort, which means everything you’d need for a day on the trails is immediately to hand.

content:
If Belfast hasn’t been as popular a destination as, say, Dublin, it’s hardly without reason. But as we find in the emerging capitals of Eastern Europe (not to otherwise compare Northern Ireland with Eastern Europe, but bear with us), the effect can be a charming and slightly retro sensibility. The Merchant is, in many ways, exactly the sort of small, intimate, high-end boutique hotel that’s so common in England and Ireland; what they’ve left out is the hard-striving air of slightly ironic hipness that’s so universal elsewhere.

Here, instead of wry modern furniture (trust us, furniture can be wry, and too often is) you’ll find classic interiors, the sort of thing that can only be described as “opulent.” It suits the building, a listed landmark, and it works for guests as well; despite the antique ambience, everything’s sparkling new, and such modern additions as flat-screen televisions will no doubt be accepted with grace. The exceedingly formal Great Room and the much more casual pub-style Cloth Ear make up the dining options, and Berts Jazz Bar is one of three more bars besides. Your location in this compact town is absolutely central, but it may prove difficult to drag yourself out.

content:
There was a time not all that long ago when fans of contemporary hotels, if they were in the market for a ski holiday, had to set aside their preferences and make peace with the typical Alpine lodge. That’s hardly the case anymore — the Ormelune, in Val d’Isère, is as fine an example as you’ll find anywhere of the new-breed fun and funky boutique ski hotel.

The Ormelune should know. It was, until very recently, a member of the old guard. At some point, though, they caught the renovation bug, and the result is far indeed from Alpine kitsch. Rooms are simple, fun, with some slightly rustic touches and an eclectic, almost bohemian style that feels somehow more like the work of a collector or a curator than a traditional designer. Bathrooms, too often merely utilitarian, are stylish here, in rough-looking varnished concrete, with bathtubs in all but the smallest room category.

In the end it’s simply more fun than the Alpine norm. Why on earth skiing should be such a serious affair is a question that’s never been properly answered. The basics are all covered — on-site bar, restaurant and massage are necessities in a slopeside lodging — and you won’t miss the rest.

content: It’s hard to say what’s more notable about the Inn of the Five Graces — the one-of-a-kind setting in a series of restored adobe houses in Santa Fe’s Barrio de Analco, considered the oldest neighborhood in the United States, or the museum-worthy art collection the designer owners acquired over a lifetime of world travels. Rooms feature rustic exposed beams, artisan-crafted textiles, wood-burning fireplaces, and bathrooms lined in colorful mosaic, while suites, arranged around a cluster of quiet courtyards, are lavishly appointed with hand-carved wooden furnishings and soaking tubs framed by inlaid onyx, lapis, and jade. The spa takes inspiration from ancient Silk Road rituals, and a hidden passageway off the main patio leads to the Pink Adobe and the Dragon Room, a revitalized local dining institution and bar where Georgia O’Keeffe was once a regular.

content: A pair of painstakingly restored 16th-century palaces, once the homes of aristocratic Florentine families, have reopened as the luxurious Tivoli Palazzo Gaddi. The location around the corner from the Basilica of Santa Maria Novella is excellent, but there’s no doubt that the hotel’s star attraction is the dazzling panorama of another church, the Duomo, from its rooftop bar. Several suites and rooms enjoy the same view, and their period charm has been well-preserved, though the Renaissance-era atmosphere is more on display in the ground-level salons and ballroom, with their frescoed ceilings and original artworks. Breakfast is served in a secret garden-styled courtyard, and the elegant lobby bar, with its wood paneling and antique fireplace, looks straight out of a gentler past.

content: Many of Puglia’s grand old palazzi have been converted into hotels, a trend that’s especially noticeable in Lecce. Among the best is Palazzo Maresgallo Suites & Spa, an art- and design-focused boutique hotel housed in a 16th-century palace near the Baroque cathedral. A Parisian architect-art collector couple fell in love with the place — with its elegant stone archways, quiet courtyard, and walled gardens, it’s not hard to see why — and personally oversaw its restoration. The finishing touch was the curation of the hotel’s first-rate art collection, including hand-painted frescoes, antique marble sculptures, and murals by the Italian painter Roberto Ruspoli. Highlights include a secret garden with a plunge pool and a rooftop terrace with views over the Roman amphitheater and the Duomo’s bell tower.

content: The minds behind this modern addition to Carmel’s boutique lodging scene already ran one of the best hotels in town: the Japanese-inspired Tradewinds Inn, first opened in 1959 and prominently featured in Architectural Digest after the owner’s daughter, Susan Stilwell, led a style overhaul in the early 2000s. Its sister property a block away, the Stilwell Hotel, takes her name, and offers a similar brand of laid-back California chic. But while the original hotel has an eclectic vintage feel, the Stilwell is modern and minimalist, its interiors outfitted in neutral tones and sophisticated but down-to-earth decor. \n\nRooms and suites are spacious and silent, with views of the sea, the mountains, or the Monterey pines and cypresses that frame the building. All feature hardwood floors and a range of natural materials — wood, linen, cotton, raffia — as well as writing desks, plush robes, Nespresso machines, and marble bathrooms with walk-in showers. Some have balconies, tubs, or fireplaces, and a few overlook a striking open-air courtyard. It’s a lovely spot for breakfast by a row of modern fountains or, after dark, a glass of wine by the glow of the fire. Charcuterie boards and wood-fired pizzas are on offer at the hotel's café, and Carmel’s many shops, galleries, restaurants, and bars are just a short stroll away.

content: Set in an 18th-century palazzo in Bologna’s historic center, the Grand Hotel Majestic già Baglioni is the grand dame of the city's hotel scene. It’s the oldest in town, with a storied past on proud display — remains of an ancient Roman road are visible in the cellar, intricately painted frescoes depicting European history adorn the restaurant’s curved ceilings, and an elegant red-carpeted staircase connects four levels lined in white marble. It’s a landmark that symbolizes old-world grandeur: apart from the updates you’d expect at any luxury hotel, no one’s experimenting with tradition here.\n\nRooms have an aristocratic air, with rich brocade drapery, Murano glass chandeliers, Venetian-style furnishings, antique pieces, and spacious bathrooms with separate showers and tubs. A lavish breakfast buffet is laid out each morning in the winter garden, with seating on the adjacent terrace in warm weather, and the main restaurant features dishes inspired by the cuisines of Emilia and Naples in a refined setting. A smart-looking café and a series of leafy patios are ideal for aperitivi with a stylish local crowd.

Some have private patios with lemon trees and tables for two. Meanwhile a Spanish-style breakfast buffet is served downstairs, and local wines and tapas are on offer in the stylish all-day bar and café.

content: Queenstown, New Zealand’s small size, its mountainous lakeside setting, and its focus on outdoor adventure inspire many hoteliers to pursue a rustic Alpine-lodge aesthetic. But that’s not Naumi’s style. This design-forward boutique-hotel brand is known for its vibrant, maximalist glamour, and that’s as true here as it is in Wellington or Singapore. The Dairy Hotel Queenstown, A Naumi Chapter incorporates a century-old structure that was once home to Queenstown’s first general store — or “dairy,” in New Zealand English. And while its interiors do contain a fair amount of European-inspired Alpine-chic style — antique skis as decoration, and bold plaid carpeting — so too do they contain Naumi’s signature riot of colorful patterns and textures.\n\nThe result is an idealized version of 1920s glamour, and ultimately a very modern high-end boutique hotel. With just 13 rooms and suites it’s suitably intimate, and appropriately scaled for historic central Queenstown. Its modest size means a proper restaurant is beyond its ambitions, but there’s a complimentary daily happy hour in the lounge, while a den provides a quieter space for relaxation; there’s also an espresso station and sweets bar for keeping your energy up, and it’s worth remembering to book a slot in the outdoor Jacuzzi, with its views over Queenstown’s rooftops.

content:
With its brownstone facade and industrial-chic interiors, Rosa Malacca looks more New York than Kuala Lumpur. Somehow, the aesthetic doesn’t seem entirely out of place, given that the city itself, Melaka — once a major international trading center, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site — has long been a cultural melting pot. Why not a boutique hotel reminiscent of a Brooklyn loft, built with clay bricks and recycled wood, with the beams and ductwork exposed? 

Rosa Malacca has all the requisite trimmings, from polished cement floors and concrete floors to the monochromatic color scheme and an open-air courtyard strung with twinkling lights. Guest rooms and suites are larger than the local standard, with bespoke furnishings, a monochrome palette, bold wall murals, and bathrooms lined with subway tile. Higher-end suites come with modern four-poster beds and extra lounge space. 

Downstairs on the ground level, an all-day café features a sleek coffee bar and a rotating menu of comfort food inspired by various international cuisines — and it’s a quick drive to Jonker Walk and its famous night market, not to mention Melaka’s many palaces, churches, and historic monuments.

content:
Right next to Le Botanique, the botanical gardens turned cultural center in the heart of Brussels, this wildly colorful boutique hotel (with cousins in Berlin, London, Milan, and more) adds a little more variety to a city with a long history of unusual boutique hotels. Nhow Brussels Bloom is a capable enough business hotel, especially if you’re in a creative field, but more to the point it’s aimed at anyone with an appreciation for visual stimulation, and especially fans of contemporary art.

The guest rooms feel somewhat gallery-like, given their monochrome backgrounds, sparse decoration, and prominent artworks. And the bathrooms, styled like photographic darkrooms — and spattered with day-glo paint — take some getting used to. Many of them have impressive elevated views of the city, and the suites include a two-level Loft and a capacious, art-filled Gallery.

Meanwhile, down in the cheerfully colorful lobby, there are multiple overlapping social spaces. The breakfast restaurant is augmented by the “waffle van,” which is just what it sounds like; the main restaurant serves a menu inspired by the city’s local street food scene; and amid all this color you’ll also find a surprisingly sober-looking cocktail bar.

content:
The city of Durham is known perhaps above all for its picturesque historical attractions: the university, the castle, and the spectacular Norman-era Romanesque cathedral. In this environment, a rakishly modernist luxury boutique hotel might be accused of a certain insensitivity to its surroundings. Fortunately the Hotel Indigo Durham, though a luxury boutique hotel it is, commits no such faux pas: it’s set not in a decommissioned red-brick Victorian-era university building that goes by the impossibly charming name of Old Shire Hall.

The rooms and suites are unmistakably modern in their design sense, but are full of historical references, whether in the décor, the artwork, the textiles, or even the architecture — some of them preserve the quirks of the hall’s original floor plan. And something like a freestanding copper bathtub can be historical and contemporary at the same time, especially when it’s displayed against the backdrop of a vast modern bathroom.

Tempting enough, but it’s the restaurant that might just seal the deal. Hotel Indigo Durham features not just an ordinary hotel restaurant, but the Marco Pierre White Steahouse & Bar, serving upscale English and French fare in a stunning dining room under the rotunda of the old Durham Council senate chamber.

content:
The concept of the Maldivian overwater resort is a firmly established one; it’s hard to imagine a case where experimenting with the form results in any kind of improvement. Instead, it’s a genre that’s all about detail and implementation — areas where quite often the big chains are the ones with the relevant expertise. All of which is to say: the InterContinental Maldives Maamunagau Resort is a fine example of the type, and an eminently worthy option for connoisseurs of the overwater life.

Of course, not every unit, and certainly not every common space, is on stilts above the lagoon. But on this narrow sliver of an island, just about everything is within a few steps of the beach. Whether you’re on land or on stilts your villa comes with everything you’ll need, up to and including a plunge pool; the style is contemporary but thoughtfully tailored to the Maldivian setting.

Water sports obviously form the largest proportion of the leisure offerings; the reef and the lagoon are heaven for snorkeling, kayaking, and diving, and there’s a very fine swimming pool — and the kids’ club and adults-only Retreat have pools of their own. A spa and fitness center are among the on-land offerings, and the restaurants range from local seafood to Japanese and Mediterranean options.

content:
The Indian Ocean idyll of Mauritius is blessed with more than a few perfect stretches of coastline, and one of them, on the island’s northwest coast, is occupied by the InterContinental Mauritius Resort Balaclava Fort. It’s set on a substantial parcel of land overlooking Balaclava Bay, and spreads across several low-rise buildings, so that all of its 210 rooms and suites face the sea — some more directly than others, of course.

The immediate views from the units’ private patios or balconies are of the gardens, the pools, or the Indian Ocean; inside you’ll find all the comforts expected of a luxury resort of this caliber, plus a style that’s both sophisticated and warm, with plenty of color and local Mauritian character. The standard deluxe rooms are perfectly well suited for most purposes; the family rooms add extra bedrooms for kids, and the honeymoon rooms add jetted tubs on their private terraces.

Of course most of the appeal of a place like this is based on what goes on outside of the accommodations. Here the activities include everything from spa days and scuba diving to golf, tennis, and, for kids, the Planet Trekkers kids’ club; restaurants cover Mediterranean, contemporary Indian, and Asian fusion cuisines.

content:
We eagerly await the day when India’s big-city hoteliers embrace fun, funky, freaky little boutique hotels. Until then, however, we’ll continue to praise them for what they do best — big, extravagant, highly polished luxury hotels. The latter, it should be said, is a natural fit for Gurgaon, New Delhi’s business-focused satellite city. And it’s the latter tendency, of course, which finds exemplary expression in the form of Vivanta by Taj.

Yes, the same Taj that’s responsible for so many extraordinary palace hotels, all over India and beyond. This strikingly modern tower isn’t about to be mistaken for a Mughal monument, but as a contemporary luxury hotel, it certainly doesn’t shy away from monumental effects — the soaring atrium, the sprawling presidential suite, the plunging pool, the expansive, interconnected restaurants.

Inside the rooms the look is contemporary, bright and sunny, modestly restrained in palette. The Jiva spa, on the other hand, aims for otherworldly effect, and does not fall short. In a town whose business-hotel market is as competitive as can be, the Vivanta plays comfortably in the big league, and manages to look stylish doing it, something that cannot truthfully be said of all of the competition.

content:
Some hotels have a hard time making a definitive case for themselves, but not the Goring — this Belgravia hotel can claim, with ample justification, to be second only to Buckingham Palace for absolutely classic London luxury. Officially the last hotel built during Edward’s reign, and the first in the world to feature en-suite bathrooms, it’s now in its second century in operation, and while it goes without saying that much else has been added in the interim, the Goring’s atmosphere is as Edwardian as it ever was.

A fair proportion of the sixty-nine rooms and suites look out over the hotel’s quiet internal garden, though the rest, overlooking Victoria Square or Beeston Place, are hardly troubled by city traffic. Space forbids an exhaustive list of room amenities, and anyway, the point of a hotel like the Goring is that anything that’s somehow left out can be counted on to make an appearance within moments, on a silver platter.

Speaking of which, the Dining Room is a particular strength; its decoration and its kitchen were extensively updated in 2024, and it retains its MICHELIN Star. The cocktail bar, too, is a Belgravia institution, and the afternoon tea is a similarly hot ticket. There are newer hotels, obviously, as well as bigger ones, but none quite like this.

content: Rows of vines extend as far as the eye can see from Magari Estates Hotel, a sophisticated countryside escape near Verona. While wine-growing traditions have deep roots in the Veneto, the thick stone walls of this boutique hotel, originally a hunting lodge built in the 16th century, are even older than the surrounding vineyards. Rooms are quiet and elegant with wood-beamed or exposed brick ceilings, king-sized beds, antique furniture, and marble bathrooms. Some have freestanding tubs or terraces with views. A glance through the windows is all the motivation one needs to step outside for the quick stroll to Fasoli Gino Winery. For the less energetic, there’s also the ancient cellar onsite, an atmospheric venue for tasting the organic wines produced next door, as well as a great restaurant, spa, and seasonal outdoor pool.

content: There’s no beating The Lanesborough’s location: here at Hyde Park Corner you’re sandwiched between the park and Buckingham Palace, and close by to Harrod’s as well. It’s a classic both inside and out — a Regency mansion now divided into 93 rooms and suites in a 19th-century style, each one visually unique but all outfitted with subtly high-tech comforts. All rooms are attended by round-the-clock butler service as well, which is true of no other London hotel. Meanwhile the public spaces are, if anything, even more impressive, from the extravagant Lanesborough Club & Spa to a selection of restaurants and bars, led by the elegantly domed Lanesborough Grill. Keep an eye out for the hotel cat, Lilibet, a Siberian named for the late Queen.

content: The restaurant at Hotel Erbprinz is something of an institution in the area, after first receiving a MICHELIN Star in 1967, but the hotel attached to it is worth a visit in its own right. Just across the street from Ettlingen Castle in Germany’s Black Forest, this elegant 18th-century building first served as a stagecoach station; more than two centuries later, hotelier Bernhard Zepf turned it into a five-star hotel. The place still has an air of old-world glamour, with several open-to-the-public venues — a cozy wine bar, a cigar lounge, and Café Erbprinz, overseen by pastry chef Jasmina Knebel, wife of the restaurant’s chef, Ralph Knebel — adding to the convivial, special-occasion atmosphere. \n\nGuest rooms are refined and mostly classic in style, with dark wood flooring, richly colored carpets, and delicate linen curtains framing floor-to-ceiling windows. Newly renovated rooms are more modern, with speckled marble bathrooms, striped rugs, and wall-sized botanical murals, and suites have a vintage twist, with midcentury modern furnishings and antique details. The hotel’s crowning glory is the Sky Suite, featuring a soaking tub with views of the forest and a private terrace with an outdoor sauna. Downstairs, the hotel’s beautiful spa has an ethereal indoor pool, a snow room, and Japanese-style relaxation rooms with built-in wooden daybeds, perfect for unwinding after sightseeing — or a multi-course meal with wine pairings.

content:
The seaside town of Arcachon is one of the gems of coastal New Aquitaine; the town overlooks the picturesque protected bay of the same name, and is a popular escape for travelers from Bordeaux and beyond. Just off its compact town center is the Victoria Boutique Hotel, behind whose unassuming façade lies a colorful and characterful 24-room hotel that combines laid-back seaside charm with crisp contemporary design.

Inside the rooms you’ll find custom-made furniture and a lively color palette that sets warm accents against marine blue, along with photographic prints depicting the region’s natural beauty. Some have private terraces, others freestanding tubs; even the most basic deluxe rooms are more than comfortable enough, and come with modern details like Nespresso machines and Chromecast televisions.

From here the beach and boardwalk are just steps away, and the rooftop — the venue for breakfast and for evening cocktails — offers a tempting view of the town and the bay. In typical French boutique-hotel style there’s no on-site restaurant; instead you’re encouraged to explore the town, though not without recommendations from the Victoria’s concierge, who can set you up with a picnic basket, a bike tour, a boat rental, and more….

content:
Right in the heart of southern Taiwan’s Kaohsiung City is the Hotel Indigo Kaohsiung Central Park, a boutique-style hotel operating under the umbrella of the hospitality megacorporation IHG. Like all of the Indigo hotels, it’s full of playful design gestures, some retro and some modern, and is aimed at a boutique-hotel audience, offering details like a pet-friendly policy and a pillow menu.

Underneath it all, of course, it’s a thoroughly professional operation — not quite a luxury hotel on the order of IHG’s Six Senses or InterContinental brands, but more akin to the family’s Kimpton line of lifestyle hotels. The graphic approach is in evidence in the bedrooms, which are decorated with murals depicting antique-style shop signs — a visual reference to the location, which is not only adjacent to the park but located in a corner of Kaohsiung that’s known for commerce, including a couple of bustling night markets.

And while this central location means there’s no end of restaurants and bars within easy walking distance, the Hotel Indigo offers two to get you started: Wok on the Park serves Taiwanese cuisine supplemented by other Asian and European dishes, while Craft, the café, offers everything from coffee to cocktails.

The InterContinental brand encompasses an enormous variety of hotels, from urban skyscrapers to seaside classics to this, a high-end contemporary interpretation of a classic Queensland estate. The InterContinental Sanctuary Cove Resort is a part of the greater Sanctuary Cove development, a country club, shopping center, and residential neighborhood on Hope Island, roughly a third of the way from Gold Coast to Brisbane. This is where seemingly all of Australia goes on holiday, and the appeal of a place like the InterContinental is the way it feels, despite its substantial scale, like something of a private enclave.

The resort’s 251 rooms and suites are quietly contemporary in style, combining a tropical vibe with subtle elements of Art Deco and Modernism. Some have views of the gardens or golf course, others the lagoon or marina.

Guests benefit from access to two golf courses, including the only Arnold Palmer course in Australia, and swimmers will appreciate its one-acre lagoon pool, which comes complete with a white sand beach, calm waters, and none of the deadly sea life for which Queensland is so well known. Also present are a spa, a tennis club, a lap pool, and a marina, and no fewer than four restaurants.

content: One underrated aspect of global hospitality brands is the way they occasionally crop up in places where boutique hoteliers fear to tread. The Bulgarian capital is working on its homegrown design-hotel scene, but in the meantime, the InterContinental Sofia will be the clear choice of many an international traveler. The location is as central as can be, right on Narodno Sabranie Square, across from Alexandar Nevski Cathedral. And behind its understated modern façade, the InterContinental is the very picture of the modern high-end luxury hotel.\n\nThis means interior design that is tasteful enough to appeal to the old guard, but stylish enough to show a real awareness of the importance of a strong visual identity. The rooms and suites are decked out in soothing neutrals and carefully selected gem tones; the best ones have views of the city’s rooftops, the cathedral, and the mountains in the distance — and all are outfitted to the latest luxury-hotel standard. A state-of-the-art spa is present as a matter of course, as are a couple of upscale restaurants — Ador is a dazzlingly opulent space while Floret is a touch more private.

content:
The reborn Regent brand is aimed squarely at the high end of the luxury-hotel market, and their selection encompasses both rural resorts and urban business hotels — and the Regent Chongqing is a member of the latter category. Of course, at this end of the hospitality world, the distinction is more about location than about concept; while the busy port city of Chongqing is a more likely destination for business travel than for rest and relaxation, a stay at the Regent Chongqing will be as restorative as you allow it to be. 

Just downstairs is the Jiangbeizui Central Business District, but from within the Regent’s rooms and suites it’s a distant concern. Many units have views over the Jialing River, and all admit plentiful sunlight through floor-to-ceiling windows. Sizes range from spacious to sprawling, and the comforts, both high-tech and low, are uniformly top-quality.

Meanwhile the Regent’s spa features four treatment rooms, a well-equipped gym, and a 25-meter indoor pool. Restaurants and bars include Chongqing hotpot as well as Cantonese and Japanese options; the most inspiring space might be the River Terrace, an open-air cocktail bar with a panoramic view.

content: A few miles south of New Delhi and just west of its namesake 10th-century reservoir, Taj Surajkund Resort & Spa, Delhi NCR has quickly established itself as a welcome alternative to the expanding finance-tech nexus that lies just over the horizon. It’s far enough from the city to have earned its country-resort pedigree, an advantage its proprietors intend to preserve; by the same token, Taj Surajkund Resort & Spa's relatively youthful brand freshens up what might otherwise have lapsed into some pretty sedate territory. The edifice deliberately recalls the quintessentially Indian baori, an embellished stepwell structure built to capitalize on seasonal water cycles. A baori’s secondary purpose — as a social “cool” spot offering leisurely relief from the midday sun — matters more in this context, abstractly captured by the Taj’s tiered, leafy façade, especially when a cheery glow sets in come sundown. Luxe-chic rooms promote breezy relaxation with a clean, open layout, buoyantly blending warm tones with modest splashes of primary color. Blonde parquet flooring comes insulated to ensure quiet, uninterrupted sleep, while private balconies allow you to properly appreciate the morning sun over a steaming mug of your choice — and in the distance, the verdant Aravalli Hills that make this a desirable retreat in the first place. Staff are glad to guide you there on a series of excursions: 14th-century fort tours, Islamic architecture exploration, and terra-cotta craft sessions barely scratch the surface. If blown glass is your thing, an on-site “art lounge” should scratch the itch. There’s also a gratifying array of dining options; Oasis forms a solid foundation with all-day global plates, though you won’t want to miss Paranda’s Punjabi specialties and Haryana comfort plates. Signature cocktails can be had against a handful of aesthetically perfect backdrops — on the roof, in a glass-lined lounge, in appreciation of the landscaped courtyard, or, who are we kidding, in the outdoor infinity pool. And in case you rekindle an appetite for more cosmopolitan distractions, the bright lights and big city are just up the road.

content: The Italian luxury hotel group ROMEO went big for its launch in the Eternal City, a boutique hotel located in a 16th-century palazzo next to the Piazza del Popolo. Alain Ducasse is onboard, overseeing not only ROMEO Roma's signature restaurant but an à la carte breakfast exclusively for guests, and behind the design is the late, great Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid. Her bold, futuristic aesthetic is unmistakable throughout the hotel — note the chiaroscuro effect in the striking black and Carrara marble lobby, and the sculptural curves of walnut and ebony wood paneling in guest rooms — a satisfying counterpoint to more traditional elements, like restored frescoes and statuary, on display throughout the building. The Sisley Paris spa has an indoor-outdoor pool with a transparent floor revealing the archaeological site beneath it, and the rooftop The rooftop Champagne Bar in partnership with Krug offers sweeping views over the city’s rooftops.

content:
The Santa Barbara wine country may not be as well-established as its northern counterparts, but that just means the possibilities are greater. Here, in between the twin towns of Santa Ynez and Solvang, hotelier Kimberly Walker has transformed a disused 22-room motor lodge into the Hotel Ynez, returning a mid-century gem to something that matches — or even surpasses — its former sheen.

The most consequential change — would-be motel renovators, take note — was to replace the parking spaces outside each room with proper patios and landscaping, which now opens onto a central garden beneath a vast oak tree. The rooms themselves bear almost no trace of the motel era, with their whitewashed wooden ceilings and their quietly luxurious furnishings and bedding. At very least, they come with hammocks; some add private yards with fire pits and/or hot tubs, while others have indoor fireplaces or even full kitchens.

A lovely Fifties-vintage swimming pool has been restored to its former glory, and a wealth of indoor and outdoor lounge areas complement the private spaces. Hotel Ynez serves coffee and tea in the mornings, but does without a restaurant or bar — there’s a small market supplying wine and light bites, but for anything more you’ll want to get out and explore, either by car or on one of the hotel’s Linus bicycles.

content: Not far from Cortona, the hilltop village immortalized in Under the Tuscan Sun, Borgo 69 is an idyllic escape in the Italian countryside. All the behind-the-scenes work has already been done — in this case, by a former set designer and his Roman-born partner — to achieve the perfect balance of refinement and rusticity. Set amid the estate’s sprawling olive grove, the hotel’s twelve sustainably built villa suites surround an aquamarine infinity pool. Each has one, two, or three bedrooms, a state-of-the-art kitchen, and a private patio overlooking terraced gardens and the rolling green hills beyond.\n\nThe villas’ interiors are light-filled and cozy, with open floor plans, wood-beamed ceilings, original artwork hanging on white walls, and fireplaces lined in exposed brick. The décor is thoughtfully chosen yet understated, from linen armchairs and wooden dining tables to raffia rugs and cushioned wicker sofas, and each bedroom has an en-suite bathroom. Borgo 69’s stylish but casual atmosphere continues at the restaurant, Emporio di Ines, named after the co-owner’s mother. Lunch and local wines are served in the leafy courtyard, Venetian-style small plates are crafted using produce from the kitchen garden, and the bar menu sticks to the classics, mixing up traditional aperitivi like negronis and spritzes. The medieval village of Pozzo della Chiana is only a short walk away, and the staff will gladly arrange nearby activities, from winery visits to hot-air balloon rides.

content: Spread across a rocky peninsula on Brittany coastline, Domaine de Rochevilaine feels more like a tiny Breton hamlet than a hotel. Set on the site of what was once a historic abbey, the hotel has acquired an unusual mix of buildings over the years, including two centuries-old stone manor houses, a fisherman’s cottage, and a granite castle. The gastronomic restaurant serves up a seafood-driven menu and in the spa, treatments include marine-based salt scrubs and seaweed wraps.

With orchard paths, a vegetable garden and salt air drifting in from the coast, Casa Mãe offers a slower version of southern Portugal.

content: Hotels in the Dodecanese don’t get much more historic than the century-old Albergo Gelsomino, designed and built in 1927 by Italian architect Rodolfo Petracco as a guesthouse for Italian officials. It stands right on the beach, a minute’s walk from the port and the old town, and its unique silhouette cuts a memorable figure along the seaside boulevard.\n\nInside, it’s been updated in a striking, seductive style that blends modern comforts with Art Deco inspiration. With a mere eight rooms, it’s exclusive by nature, though welcoming in its atmosphere. The views of the Aegean from the rooms and suites are alluring, to say the least, and they’re complemented by a closer view from a sunbed at the hotel’s posh beach club.

content:
Koh Phangan is famous for its full moon festival, but on the opposite side of the island, far from the beach parties, the coastline is quiet and pristine. It’s an idyllic setting for one of the region’s most luxurious resorts. Accessible by private speedboat from nearby Koh Samui, Anantara Rasananda Koh Phangan Villas is located on Thong Nai Pan Noi, a secluded white-sand beach that’s considered one of the best in Thailand. Rows of chaise longues shaded by cheerful red umbrellas face a dazzling expanse of calm aquamarine water, and just behind a border of coconut palms, the resort’s thatched-roof two-story buildings are tucked into lush jungle vegetation.

Suites and villas all have private gardens or terraces with plunge pools, and while the best rooms are ocean-facing — a few even have direct beach access and private lounge space on the sand — they’re all spacious, lavishly appointed, and designed for indoor-outdoor living. The look is elegant but down-to-earth, with native wood paneling, vaulted ceilings, and deep red accent walls. Home theaters, Nespresso machines, and extra-large bathrooms with walk-in showers come standard, and freestanding villas feature extras like open-air terrazzo tubs and complimentary minibars. 

A focal point of the property is the central infinity pool with a swim-up bar and sea views, Thai massages and Ayurvedic treatments are available in the Anantara Spa’s outdoor treatment areas. The resort’s all-day bistro overlooks the pool area, and Yukinoya, a stylish Japanese restaurant, specializes  in Teppanyaki menus. Beachfront yoga classes and film screenings are on offer, and staff happily arrange boating and snorkeling excursions in the surrounding nature reserve.

content: Ayutthaya was the capital of Siam for more than four centuries, and although Sala Ayutthaya is a feat of modern design, it’s strategically positioned to showcase the city’s rich past. The boutique hotel is located on the banks of the Chao Phraya River, directly across the water from a temple built in 1353, its elegant Khmer-style tower on grand display from the restaurant’s open-air terrace, rooftop bar, and riverfront suites. The Bangkok-based design studio Onion considered the historical context, discreetly tucking away the pool — and by extension, the swimsuit-clad guests lounging on the white marble pool deck — in a quiet courtyard framed by a labyrinth of whitewashed and exposed brick walls. Some of the hotel’s strikingly minimalist rooms feature private pools or decks, and all have freestanding soaking tubs.

content:
This island’s gorgeous beaches and rich cultural history form the backdrop for Argini Syros, a 19th-century private residence that’s been transformed into a magnificent 11-room luxury boutique hotel.

It’s set in the historic center of Ermoupoli — the city of Hermes — and, though restored and renovated, retains its neoclassical architectural style. What’s inside is suitably ornate as well, though with complementary modern gestures — sleek design furniture and modern marble bathrooms share space with frescoed ceilings.

In spite of its small size, Argini Syros offers some impressive luxuries, most notably its spa, with its indoor pool and hammam. The restaurant, Elexis, opens onto the central courtyard, while the rooftop bar offers views of the hillside city and the sea.

content:
Whereas the typical InterContinental is best described as “tasteful,” this one is downright unusual — and we mean that in the best way. The InterContinental Perth City Centre inherited its modernist structure, with its distinctive square windows, from an earlier hotel, but it’s leaned into its role as one of Perth’s most memorable lodgings, filling its spaces with unique gestures like patterned carpets that echo the architecture, and a truly remarkable collection of contemporary Western Australian art.

The rooms and suites maintain the monochrome-plus-gold color palette established in the public spaces, and are warmed by an unusual depth of detail and texture. Lavish marble bathrooms with rain showers are the norm; suites add separate bathtubs in addition to their dedicated living space. And the views of the various landmarks of Perth’s central business district are nothing if not impressive.

Meanwhile the hotel’s restaurants combine Western Australian flavors and ingredients with Spanish recipes and inspiration; Heno & Rey is the tapas bar whose seating spills over into an outdoor area at the corner of King and Hay, while Ascua is the slightly more upscale option featuring dry-aged meats and seafood prepared on a wood-fired grill.

content: Trading off Scandinavian practicality for French countryside charm is Villa Provence, a boutique hotel built around a cobblestoned courtyard in one of Aarhus’s most desirable neighborhoods. The Francophile owners transformed the traditional Danish townhouse into a Provençal-inspired retreat, outfitted with romantic chandeliers, retro film posters, and one-of-a-kind antiques unearthed in the south of France. Each room is a quaint pied-à-terre with hardwood floors and eclectic decor; all have writing desks, and many have sloping walls, four-poster beds, or clawfoot tubs. The organic breakfast spread is a highlight, and guests can help themselves anytime from the adorably vintage bar cart, and carry drinks out to the hydrangea-framed patio.

content:
The next Balearic island down from the famous Ibiza is the smaller-scale, lower-key Formentera — which, now, has a rather surprisingly luxe hotel, the Five Flowers Hotel & Spa Formentera. It’s inspired by the Sixties, and specifically, in the hotel’s words, the “hippie lifestyle” — which makes some sense, as the era that birthed the Balearic travel boom. But don’t expect yurts and ramshackle, bohemian decoration. Five Flowers is five-star luxury, for one thing, and aesthetically seems to borrow as much from swinging, modernist London as from the Woodstock variety of hippiedom.

The hotel is oriented around the central pool deck, surrounded by lounge chairs and shaded daybeds, all in a soothing white-on-white. More colorful are the interiors, from the lobby with its gold-and-pomegranate upholstery and graphic daisy motif to the rooms with their own accents in ultra-saturated pink and yellow. “Whimsical” just about covers the in-room atmosphere, with two-dimensional clouds floating above the beds and a curvaceous space-age quality to the fixtures and furnishings.

A second pool hides away on the rooftop, and the spa and fitness offerings are first-rate. There’s a fine-dining restaurant named Janis, after Janis Joplin, and a second, more casual one called Imagine, and a cocktail bar on the roof with a panoramic view of the island and the sea.

content: \tThose whose work takes them to India likely know the Taj hotel empire well — with an outpost in every major city they’re a mainstay of the high-end business-hotel market, where efficiency meets luxury, and traditional Indian style meets contemporary international design. And those with business in Chennai know the Taj Coromandel — the city is one of India’s industrial centers, and the Taj, one imagines, is where quite a lot of business changes hands.\n\nIt’s saddled with a slightly disappointing building, but the interiors, on the heels of a major renovation, are very much up to the current Taj standard: a contemporary take of the classic luxe-colonial look, crisp and smart but well short of anything you’d call design-y. Rooms start large enough and scale on up to absolutely massive — but you don’t have to book the presidential suite to get the basics, including wireless internet, plush bed and bath, and a very workable desk. And as is the custom in a hotel of the Taj Coromandel’s stature, an array of services are designed to keep visiting executives (and you) fit and fed, from the pool and 24-hour gym to the restaurants, one Indian and the other Italian.

content: There’s a rich history behind Castle Leslie Estate, set on a thousand countryside acres in County Monaghan: the Leslie family, descended from Attila the Hun, has lived on the property since 1665, and it’s home to the oldest plumbed bath in Ireland. Old-world charm is built into its wood-paneled sitting rooms with gilded oil portraits, buttery soft Chesterfield sofas, and crackling fireplaces. Rooms are split across two properties, The Castle and The Lodge, and are just as atmospheric. In The Castle, 21 guest rooms are uniquely decorated with a mix of decoratively carved four-poster beds, rich fabrics, and heirloom antiques, and none have screens or minibars, the not-so-subtle implication being, of course, that refreshments and entertainment are best enjoyed in the Blue Room with views of Glaslough Lake or perhaps in the Drawing Room in front of the De La Robbia fireplace. The 50 rooms in The Lodge sport a more contemporary look but with their period-inspired furnishings and roll top bathtubs, are still in very much in keeping with the building’s historic features. This is also where a lot of the action happens in the main Snaffles Restaurant and Conor’s Bar & Lounge, but guests can also enjoy some downtime with a massage or facial in the organic Victorian Treatment Rooms, and there’s always solitude to be found in the castle’s lovely gardens and quiet library.

content: At first glance, it is a sleek newcomer in Baixa’s central square. Look closer, and Convent Square reveals itself as something far older: an 800-year-old cloister turned contemporary retreat. Original tombstones, 17th-century tiles, and Indo-Portuguese textiles gently preserve its history, while the hushed courtyard, once used by Dominican nuns, remains its soul. Each afternoon, a tea ritual retraces Portugal’s spice trade legacy. Upstairs, the rooms are modern in feel, but anchored by the building’s centuries-old bones. Step outside, and you're in the city. Stay in, and you're somewhere else entirely.

content: On the road that leads from Geneva to Mont Blanc, Hotel Restaurant Baud is a scenic stop, and a practical one. The sophisticated restaurant is an ideal spot for a leisurely lunch or dinner, and the gardens invite you to step onto the wide, grassy lawn with a glass of wine and while away the afternoon on the banks of the Menoge River. It’s not the kind of place where you’d want to be in a rush, so you might as well stay overnight and enjoy a perfectly prepared café au lait and alpine landscapes the next morning. \n\nThe hotel, like the restaurant, is contemporary and quietly luxurious. Standard rooms are stylish and cozy — fluffy duvets, goose-down pillows, plush armchairs, modern bathrooms with oversized showers. Larger suites have living areas with sofas, writing desks, soaking tubs, and views of the gardens. Jewel-toned accents and bold patterns prevail throughout, and a few suites are thematic, like the dreamy blue-hued Picasso suite and the dramatic Vermeer suite.

content:
Several of New Zealand’s finest boutique hotels are the work of the Singapore-based Naumi Hotels concern, and among them is Queenstown’s stylish Central Hotel. Here the Wanaka-based creative agency Undercurrent was charged with adapting Naumi’s ultra-vibrant maximalism to the South Island setting, and the result is a thoroughly local spin on the brand’s characteristic fantasy.

There’s something almost Parisian about the saturated secondary colors that set the tone, and the visual interest is wall-to-wall, thanks to the eclectic collection of furnishings and artworks. The rooms and suites are nothing if not photogenic, but their appeal runs deeper than that, as their thoughtful comforts venture into luxury-boutique territory.

That’s true of the common spaces as well, which include a sauna and a lovely little courtyard garden. The Central Bar showcases New Zealand wines, while the Lounge hosts its own cocktail hour in addition to self-serve espresso and sweets. And while there’s no in-house restaurant, the Naumi hotels pride themselves on their connections with their neighborhoods, and the Central Private is no different — the staff is amply supplied with recommendations for restaurants and much, much more.

content: An oasis in the desert on the northern fringes of the Saudi capital, the InterContinental Durrat Al Riyadh Resort & Spa is like nothing else in town. The InterContinental Hotels Group seems capable of operating in a wide variety of styles, and this one, perhaps unsurprisingly given the location, is among the most traditional hotels on their roster. It’s laid out like a village around a winding lagoon, and its buildings mostly spread horizontally, topping out at six stories. The concept is compound luxury living — Durrat Al Riyadh is a fully self-contained, self-sufficient experience, less than an hour from the city center but properly secluded on the outskirts.\n\nThe accommodations are lavish, as expected, and visually they’re a touch more playful than the public spaces, mixing modern elements with tributes to tradition in a style that’s never anything less than thoroughly palatable. Leisure facilities include an outdoor pool, tennis courts, and an 18-hole mini-golf course, as well as a circus-style kids’ club. The spa and health club offer a dizzying array of holistic treatments, as well as a steam room, sauna, and jacuzzi. Meanwhile the restaurants range from the lobby café and the poolside bar to the Café Lagoon hookah lounge and Les Palmiers, an Arabian bistro.

content:
The Hotel Indigo brand appears in a lot of places, but it’s perhaps most notable for the way it brings the high-design style that used to be exclusively found in major capitals to cities where boutique hotels were a little bit later to arrive. Hotel Indigo Dundee is a fine example: a renovation of a charming 1822 industrial building that, having made itself over with modernist furniture and contemporary art, now feels as fashionable as anything in Edinburgh, or London, or New York.

Rooms are visually sparse but enlivened by Pop-inspired pops of color and clever nods to local culture, and are furnished with subtle luxuries like Nespresso machines and lush local textiles. Plenty of original architectural detail remains, including some original brick ceilings, while in terms of function the spaces are as modern as can be, down to the subtly integrated electronics and the luxe tile-and-slate bathrooms.

Meanwhile the Indigo’s setting, a short walk from Dundee’s compact city center, lends a touch of tranquility without taking away from convenience. Daisy Tasker, the hotel’s restaurant, is a Scottish bistro, serving modern interpretations of local favorites alongside eclectic international influences, all in a stylish space that’s roughly one part minimalist and one part cozy.

content: The super-highrise buildings that tower over Chongqing’s busy Yuzhong district are both architecturally striking and meaningfully positioned at the confluence of two rivers, once the site of the city’s old imperial gate. InterContinental Chongqing Raffles City occupies a unique space within the ultramodern complex: while rooms and suites are housed within one of the vertical towers, the hotel’s lobby and dining venues are located in the Crystal, a “horizontal skyscraper" elevated 75 stories above the street. \n\nChecking in at reception on the world’s highest sky bridge is an experience, though the views from guest rooms are almost as inspiring — or vertigo-inducing, depending on your perspective. The interiors are sleek and contemporary, outfitted in shades of white, ivory, and beige, with floor-to-ceiling windows letting in abundant natural light. Bathrooms have marble fixtures, recessed lighting, walk-in showers, and freestanding soaking tubs. Standard features include Tivoli sound systems and Dyson hairdryers, while suites also have spacious living areas with modular sofas, walk-in closets, and views of the Yangtze. A large fitness center with a mosaic-tiled indoor pool occupies the 43rd floor, but the InterContinental’s main attraction is its series of high-end restaurants and bars stretched out along the dramatically curved and glass-walled Crystal building, all with startling views over the megacity below.

content:
The InterContinental hotels and resorts are a versatile bunch, setting up shop in city centers and resort destinations alike. In China, in particular, they lay claim to some truly spectacular locales — like this one, on a peninsula stretching out into the waters of Qiandao Lake, which is indeed dotted with over a thousand forested islands. This is the descriptively named InterContinental One Thousand Island Lake Resort, set right at the water’s edge, looking out over the lake at the distant mountain peaks.

Its 264 rooms and suites are styled in a manner that’s both modern and traditional, but always subtle, the better to draw the eye to the windows; some units face into the forest, others straight out to the lake, but all benefit from the tranquility of their natural surroundings. They range a bit in size and plan but they’re universally spacious, with spa-like bathrooms containing rain showers and separate bathtubs. 

Better than spa-like bathrooms is an actual spa, in this case a lavish one with nine treatment rooms and an indoor and outdoor pool. There’s a very well-equipped kids’ club as well, in case your children aren’t quite satisfied with blissful contemplation of nature. And the hotel’s multiple restaurants include Chinese, Japanese, and European options.

content: Among the most scenic locales in the Dolomites is Val Gardena, and one of the valley’s finest lodgings is the Alpenroyal Grand Hotel Gourmet & Spa. Built in the fifties, it nevertheless exhibits a traditional Alpine style in its architecture, while its interiors have been brought up to date — still classic, but exhibiting a touch of modern furniture and up-to-date comforts. Many of the rooms and suites feature impressive views of the surrounding peaks, and like any hotel of its caliber Alpenroyal is a four-season destination. Nor are “gourmet” and “spa” included in the name by accident; the former is a nod to the hotel’s four restaurants, from fine dining to fondue, and the latter refers to the expansive, thoroughly modern and mostly subterranean spa and wellness complex.

content: Hidden away on 163 acres of emerald parkland with the River Maine flowing through it, Galgorm Spa & Golf Resort delivers serene relaxation, be it via its 72-par course or its extensive spa and wellness offerings. Rooms are homey, yet contemporary, outfitted with Rolf Benz furniture and plaid accents. The Thermal Village Spa is the first of its kind in Ireland, featuring several saunas and a milder sanarium, as well as riverside soaking tubs, and a snow cabin, for an invigorating Finnish-style plunge. The Castle Championship Course at the Galgorm Castle is the home of the Northern Ireland Open, and is just the most convenient option, with several links courses accessible nearby. In addition to afternoon tea, the dining venues range from a formal restaurant in a riverside conservatory to a more casual Italian option and a bar and grill.

content: In a lovely park planted with centuries-old trees, Château de Noirieux is a luxury hotel on the banks of the River Loir. The estate comprises several beautifully restored historic buildings, including a stone castle and a 15th-century manor house, now home to a collection of elegant ivory-hued rooms and suites, as well as a chapel and an orangerie. There’s splendid attention to detail inside and out, from a rare Érard piano and custom room fragrances to a lavish breakfast served on the sunny veranda, and outdoor pool add to the appeal.

content: Anantara decided against starting from scratch for its first property in Ireland, opting instead to snap up a Dublin landmark — the waterfront Marker Hotel on Grand Canal Square — and transform it into an ultra-modern luxury hotel. The Portuguese architect Aires Mateus took inspiration from the island’s rugged coastal landscape in his original designs for the geometric building, which resembles a rock formation eroding over time, and the interiors are striking and somewhat cave-like, with striking cantilevers and angular shapes framing the city’s largest hotel lobby. Rooms are sleek and contemporary, with floor-to-ceiling windows, moody charcoal-hued walls, and marble bathrooms with soaking tubs. The Anantara Spa features an enclosed infinity pool — well suited to Dublin’s climate — but the hotel’s crowning glory is the rooftop bar: with a clever indoor-outdoor layout and views of the Irish Sea, it’s a hit in all seasons.

content: A short drive inland, in the village of Beauvoir, Ermitage Mont-Saint-Michel is a luxurious small hotel within easy reach of one of France’s most famous landmarks. Its seven rooms, housed in a stately 19th-century stone villa surrounded by peaceful greenery, are usually booked up well in advance, and it’s easy to see why. Elegant but understated, with old-world details like clawfoot tubs and decorative wooden headboards, the interiors exude French country charm; most rooms have private balconies. Services and common spaces, from an attentive concierge to a lavish breakfast spread, match the high standards you’d expect at a place its owners proudly call the smallest five-star hotel in Europe.

content: A short drive or ferry ride down the coast from Dubrovnik in the village of Cavtat, Hotel Supetar occupies a century-old villa right on the waterfront promenade. Though fully restored, this boutique hotel oozes old-world charm, with its open-air decks shaded by white sun umbrellas, a cozy wine bar serving locally produced varietals, and fragrant citrus trees framing the swimming pool. \n\nIndividually designed rooms feature a mix of modern and vintage: some have elegant patterned wallpaper and white marble bathrooms with bronze fixtures, while attic rooms have sloped ceilings, romantic writing desks, and bay windows overlooking the village. No cars are allowed in the historic center, but the hotel arranges buggy rides to nearby attractions, and the boat to the big city stops at the dock across the street.

content: It all started in Shoreditch, East London in 2006 and now this cool hotel brand has spread far and wide. This Brussels outpost opened in 2023 and houses 198 bedrooms boasting a subtle ’70s groove but with better technology. In the rooms, materials like velvet contrast with concrete structural elements, and the pleasingly retro colors are a far cry from the minimalism of the previous generation of boutique hotels.\n\nThe brutalist building, which is next to the Botanical Garden, was once the European HQ of IBM but now it’s a veritable fun palace, with an atmosphere where all-day co-working shades effortlessly into revelry. Highlights include a modern Peruvian restaurant and a fabulous rooftop bar serving Mexican flavors with far-ranging views over the gardens and the rooftops of the city.

content: With its pristine pine forests and gorgeous beaches, Turkey’s Datça Peninsula feels like a secret island mostly undiscovered by international visitors. By far the most luxurious (and most remote) of the region’s few hotels is D Maris Bay. Set back from the main road on a protected nature reserve, this exclusive resort is framed by volcanic mountains and overlooks a turquoise expanse of water where the Aegean and Mediterranean converge. \n\nWith two pools, a sprawling spa, more than a dozen upscale restaurants and bars, and five white-sand beaches, including one with a glamorous French Riviera-style beach club and another set up for snorkeling, it’s the sort of hotel where the rooms could feel like an afterthought. But with their cool modern interiors, Turkish artwork, and nature views, they’re perfectly designed for a break from the sun.

content: The InterContinental Doha Beach & Spa is, like many of IHG’s delightfully straightforwardly named properties, exactly what it sounds like: a wellness-focused luxury resort by one of the biggest names in the business, within sight of the skyscrapers of the Qatari capital but surrounded by palms and beaches rather than buildings and boulevards. The vast swimming pool, surrounded by loungers and lawns, is dwarfed by the private beach, which is slightly more than a mile long — and within this perimeter is a self-contained luxury experience that, for all its seclusion, may as well occupy its own private island.\n\nWith some 375 rooms and suites it’s a large-scale operation, but a thoroughly relaxing one — with this much space, and so long a menu of facilities, it’ll never feel crowded. The spa is enormous, as is the athletic club with its tennis and squash courts. Even the smallest room covers more than 400 square feet, and the largest ones are large indeed. Meanwhile the resort’s restaurants and bars number over a dozen, and span a vast range of concepts, from Peruvian and Greek restaurants to a French brasserie, a Parisian-inspired nightclub, and the surprisingly specific Belgian Café.

content: A proper mid-century hospitality icon, the InterContinental Jordan has been a mainstay on Amman’s luxury-hotel scene since it opened in the Sixties. And while the spirit of ’62 is very much back in style, at least in the world of design, this is not a hotel that’s content to rest on its laurels. What you’ll find within its walls is not a restoration or a re-creation of a Sixties luxury hotel, but a thoroughly modern one whose style pays tribute to classic Modernism as well as the long, long history of Arab architecture and design.\n\nIts rooms and suites are luxurious, as you might expect, and eminently tasteful — this is not a hotel that’s given to excess for its own sake. That said, it also suffers from no shortage of luxuries; the spa, the health club, the pool terrace, and the Club lounge are all as lavish as they come. And among the InterContinental Jordan’s greatest strengths is its wide-ranging selection of restaurants, from the award-winning Lebanese restaurant Bourj Al Hamam to upscale Indian at Indu, the Soba Sushi Bar, and some surprising Mexican fare courtesy of Cinco de Mayo.

content:
The InterContinental Hotels Group is one of the biggest names in luxury hospitality, and encompasses everything from typically lavish city-center luxury hotels to one-of-a-kind resorts in relatively far-flung locales. The InterContinental Kunming is, strangely enough, a bit of both — it’s set within the limits of the city of Kunming itself, but rather than some city-center skyscraper, it finds itself in the quasi-rural lakeside district known as the Dianchi National Holiday Resort.

Its 536 rooms and suites enjoy views of the gardens, greenery, and waterways; their interiors, perhaps incongruously, are as contemporary as they come, decorated in a minimalist style that would look equally at home atop a 35-story hotel tower. Most of them are equipped with private balconies, and all of them are outfitted with the top-tier comforts that you can expect from any InterContinental hotel.

The spa and wellness center is a vast one, perfectly in proportion with this expansive resort. And the hotel’s dining and drinking venues range from international cuisine at the Butterfly Bar to Cantonese and Yunnan flavors at the Shang Tao Chinese Restaurant and a selection of Chinese, Japanese, and Mediterranean flavors at the Market.

content:
The InterContinental brand encompasses everything from lavish mountain resorts to equally lavish skyscraper-bound city hotels and, in the process, demonstrates that the two extremes have much in common. The InterContinental Quanzhou is closer to the latter category, standing over the waterfront in the port city for which it’s named. But its setting, within the mixed-use Tahoe Plaza retail and entertainment development, lends it something of a resort aspect; there’s even an amusement park on site.

Fortunately the carnival atmosphere does not extend inside the InterContinental’s doors. This is as stately and sedate a luxury hotel as anything in the brand’s portfolio; the style is contemporary, but far from avant-garde. The in-room comforts are high-end, from 49-inch LCD televisions and rain showers to, in some units, deep soaking tubs with views over the Jinjiang River.

Meeting and events facilities are legion, and further inducements include a spa, a fitness center, and an impressive indoor swimming pool. And among the InterContinental’s restaurants and bars are Commune, a versatile open-kitchen restaurant concept, and Cai Feng Lou, serving a high-end interpretation of local Quanzhou favorites as well as Fujian and Guangdong dishes.

content: In some cities the local InterContinental hotel is as conventional as it is luxurious, wowing guests with sheer large-scale hospitality excellence rather than anything you’d describe as an element of surprise. The InterContinental Tianjin Yujiapu Hotel and Residences, however, manages a bit of both; as a piece of architecture, it’s plainly operating on another level from just about every luxury hotel on the planet, including most of its brandmates, while underneath it all is the sort of ultra-plush, highly professional hospitality experience you expect from a top-tier business hotel, InterContinental or otherwise, in China or anywhere else.\n\nYujiapu is Tianjin’s famous financial district, and right next door to the InterContinental is the high-speed rail link to Beijing. Its rooms and suites, plainly, are aimed at business travelers, though these days, at this end of the market, that implies resort-level comforts. The meeting and events facilities, naturally, are truly vast, while the fitness center and the indoor pool are impressive indeed. And among the InterContinental Tianjin Yujiapu Hotel’s strengths is its wide-ranging food and beverage program, including the upscale Cai Feng Lou Chinese Restaurant, the multifaceted Commune All Day Dining Restaurant, and three bars, including a Sky Lounge.
