content:
After turning a pair of antique townhouses in Tbilisi into boutique hotels, the creative minds behind Communal Hotels set their sights on Georgia’s wine capital. Communal Hotel Telavi is somewhat different from its big-city predecessors, as it’s housed in a historic villa with a rooftop sunroom and a courtyard swimming pool — but it’s still in an urban area with easy access to nearby cafés, shops, and restaurants, not to mention the vineyards just outside town. Like its counterparts in Tbilisi, Communal Hotel Telavi is a tribute to Georgian culture, with the owners preserving the best parts of the original structure — in this case, Moorish archways, sunbaked tiles, and decorative balconies — and infusing the space with a modern sensibility.

As the name indicates, Communal Hotel Telavi isn’t a place to hide out in one’s room: the philosophy is all about common spaces and social experiences, from the shared breakfast table to the lively poolside bar. An all-day eatery serves local dishes and natural wines on the ground level, adjacent to the pool area, while a greenhouse-like living room on the highest level, furnished with plush sofas and potted plants, is a quieter spot to gather or relax. 

In a hotel of this style, rooms and suites could feel like an afterthought, but they’re as thoughtfully appointed as the rest of the property. Colorful and eclectic, they feature bold emerald-green or midnight-blue accent walls, richly patterned fabrics, handwoven rugs, original artwork, and vintage details from writing desks to velvet daybeds. The simplest rooms overlook the courtyard, while larger suites have extras like clawfoot tubs and balconies with city views; all are cozy hideaways to unwind between socializing and wine tasting.

content: The interior highland enclave of Ubud is home to some of Bali’s most extraordinary resorts, but none quite like Capella Ubud, whose tented villas bring guests as close to nature as they can get without sleeping outside. It’s not quite camping, as they feature all the comforts of a permanent structure, including indoor and outdoor bathrooms and private pools — and the hotel’s design, by Bill Bensley, is anything but utilitarian.\n\nTents are styled not in drab safari-style khaki but in rich, dark colors, and decorated with Balinese crafts. Each one comes with its own plunge pool, as well as an up-close view of the surrounding forest. The local culture is highlighted here, with performances and educational experiences given as much attention as simple creature comforts. And in some areas, the two threads are woven together: the Auriga spa is inspired by the moon cycle and Balinese wellness traditions, and the restaurants serve a Indonesian cuisine and an Asian-inspired tasting menu.

content: The Rocky Mountain luxury ranch experience doesn’t get much more luxurious than this. The all-inclusive Brush Creek Ranch stands on some 30,000 acres in south-central Wyoming, an easy enough drive from Denver and a much easier one from the nearby Saratoga Jet Center. The range of experiences on offer is a broad one, from tending the ranch’s goats to indulging in a spa treatment or even skiing the ranch’s private slopes. A variety of rooms, suites, and cabins see the homestead’s original buildings transformed into luxury lodgings. And the cuisine is a suitable mix of the high-end and the rugged, making use of ranch-grown ingredients served alongside Brush Creek Distillery spirits.

content: Of Courchevel's six villages, the highest, Courchevel 1850, is also the most exclusive. And of the village’s luxurious ski-in, ski-out lodges, La Sivolière is one of the most highly regarded. The hotel’s comparatively secluded piste-side location, tucked into the forest just outside the center of town, is just one of its assets. The elegant chalet exemplifies traditional Savoyard style; it’s built of stone and timber inside and out, with slanted ceilings, large bay windows, and open fireplaces. \n\nRooms are cozy yet lavishly appointed, featuring ample wood paneling, velvet armchairs or sofas, Diptyque candles, and sleek marble bathrooms. Larger suites and apartments have extras like fireplaces and kitchens. La Sivolière’s alpine charm continues in the restaurant and bar; its huge picture windows, framed by fir trees, face direct views of the snowy mountain. An après-ski alternative awaits at the hotel’s luminous spa and indoor pool. After breakfast and a quick stop to suit up in the hotel’s ski room, complete with heated sofas and knowledgeable local guides, it’s just a push away to the Dou du Midi slope and wintry adventures in Les Trois Vallées.

content:
Naumi Hotels made a splash by opening one of its whimsical, high-design properties in New Zealand's capital city — it was such a hit, in fact, that the Singapore-based brand opened a second hotel right next door. Naumi Studio Wellington is the original and the larger of the two, housed in a stately landmark building on hip Cuba Street. 

The elegant Edwardian-era facade offers a first impression that's somewhat misleading, partly because it’s painted white, a shade scarcely seen inside the hotel. The interiors are colorful and dreamy: the dramatically lit lobby is dominated by a playful mural and a larger-than-life, Alice in Wonderland-like flower sculpture by Angus Muir, the stylish street-level restaurant is lined from floor to ceiling in sultry red, and high tea and cocktails are served in a fanciful emerald-green parlor inspired by the look and feel of a Parisian conservatory. 

More is more upstairs, too, where local artists and designers are behind the vibrant decor, from eye-catching floral wallpaper and boldly patterned carpet to modern art installations and jewel-toned furnishings. Standard rooms are cozy and compact, with striking hand-painted headboards and handy modern comforts, while larger suites offer living areas with plush sectional sofas and cocktail bars with vintage glassware. Just outside, the neighborhood’s lively cafés, bars, shops, and galleries await, and Naumi Studio feels like an authentic part of the city’s creative scene.

content: Situated at the foot of the Pieniny Mountains, midway between Kraków and the Slovakian border, Szczawnica is one of the oldest spa resorts in Poland — though one of its best hotels is relatively new. Szczawnica Park Resort & Spa’s decorative facade mirrors the Alpine-inspired architecture of the guesthouses and villas around town, and like other hotels in the area, it’s built around naturally occurring mineral springs. But unlike its quaint wooden counterparts dating back to the 19th century, Szczawnica Park is modern and sprawling in scope, occupying a large streamside complex with three stylish hotel buildings, a state-of-the-art spa and wellness center, multiple swimming pools, and a range of slow food-focused dining venues.\n\nRooms are outfitted with rustic-chic decor — hardwood floors, a sophisticated charcoal-and-white palette, plaid throw blankets, and moodily lit murals depicting nature scenes. Some have sleek kitchenettes or two-story layouts. Most rooms are housed in the main building, Hotel Szczawnica Park, while larger suites suited to families, including some with outdoor hot tubs, are located in the nearby Szczawnica Park Residence. Spacious apartment-style suites are in a third building, Willa Park, each with a private balcony facing the mountains. A generous Polish breakfast buffet is served in the hotel’s elegant dining room each morning, and outdoor adventures like skiing, hiking, and rafting await in the surrounding landscape.

content:
It's a bumpy journey down a dirt road — albeit a scenic one framed by cacao and pineapple trees — to the gates of Hacienda Bambusa. Located on a working farm with views of the Andes, this boutique hotel is housed within a traditional two-story villa that’s been beautifully restored and updated to host travelers passing through Colombia’s central coffee-growing region. It’s the only hotel around for miles, and it feels like a place to settle in for a few days, relaxing barefoot by the pool with a cup of café con leche. 

Eight suites open onto the hacienda’s wraparound balconies, which are strung with woven hammocks and lined with bamboo armchairs. Inside, they’re elegant but slightly rustic, with thick clay walls, king-sized beds with crisp white linens, and bathrooms with colorful ceramic tile and copper fixtures. Old-fashioned wooden shutters keep the glaring sun out during the hottest part of the day, then open to reveal views of the property’s carefully tended gardens with lush flowers and fruit trees. 

There’s plenty to do on the grounds of the farm, from hiking, bird watching, and mountain biking to coffee and cacao tastings. A refreshing dip in the deep blue-tiled pool is the perfect follow-up to any outdoor adventure. Both breakfast and dinner are served in picturesque outdoor settings when the weather cooperates — a lavish buffet in the morning and a gourmet barbecue-style meal served on white linen to end the day. Both are welcome features for those who venture off the property during the day for coffee tours, market visits, and hot-air balloon rides in the area.

content:
Lily Country Club, a half-hour outside of Oslo, takes the traditionally golf-focused idea of the country club and expands it in as many directions as the concept will allow — resulting in a remarkably diverse rural escape. Yes, there’s golf, courtesy of the neighboring Miklagard Golf Club. But the dining and drinking venues, for example, go far beyond typical clubhouse fare, and include a French- and Italian-influenced brasserie as well as a modern cocktail bar.

The accommodations, too, are anything but secondary to the golfing experience. Here you’ll find nearly 500 rooms and suites, decorated in a handsome and warm contemporary style — luxurious, but typically Norwegian in their avoidance of anything flashy or ostentatious.

There’s a spa and wellness center that’s very much the equal of the club’s golf facilities. And Lily Country Club also offers access to a number of outdoor explorations that go far beyond the fairways and manicured greens, from self-directed hikes to guided alpaca treks across the Norwegian landscape.

content: There are several fine places to stay in the city’s historic center, though none as striking as Atrio Cáceres. The petite 15th-century Palacio Paredes Saavedra was thoughtfully restored by acclaimed Spanish architects Tuñón y Albornoz, and the result is dazzling: the building’s original vaulted ceilings and arching doorways remain, but the stone walls are overlaid with pale wood, and the floors with polished concrete, giving the interiors an ethereal glow. The beautifully illuminated central courtyard evokes the city’s old-world charm, while upstairs, the hotel’s suites are cool and minimalist. There’s a small pool, a wellness center, and a gym, and most importantly there’s a restaurant of considerable distinction: the three-MICHELIN-Star Atrio.

content: There was a time when it wasn’t so easy to find a properly stylish boutique hotel in the American heartland; and if Omaha, Nebraska isn’t in the heart of the heartland, then we don’t know what is. Fortunately, times have changed, and cities like this one can now offer lodgings on the level of the Hotel Indigo - Omaha Downtown. It’s something of an homage to what might be the most glamorous era of Omaha’s history — Prohibition, when the saloons and speakeasies were forced underground, and happenings spread by word of mouth.\n\nIt’s no surprise, then, that the Indigo’s interiors lean rather more heavily on Twenties decadence than on the sort of Old West kitsch that tempts some other hoteliers. Meanwhile the building’s hardwood floors, exposed brick walls, and unfinished ceilings lend the rooms and suites an urban-loft aspect; they’re full of subtle retro detailing as well as all the comforts a 21st-century boutique-hotel guest demands. And that attention to detail doesn’t end at the threshold to the guest room; the hotel’s bar, Anna’s Place, is a speakeasy-style craft-cocktail bar with an inventive modern menu.

content: Fortitude Valley may sound like the name of a cowboy film or a remote western outpost; in fact it’s a hip and vibrant suburb of Brisbane, full of upscale shops and restaurants, and home to Hotel X Brisbane Fortitude Valley, an unmistakably modern concrete-and-glass structure that towers over its mid-rise surroundings. Aesthetically, it’s got all the panache of a one-off boutique hotel whose rakish style is its calling card. As it happens, it’s a member of IHG’s Vignette Collection, the edgier, more design-oriented arm of the InterContinental Hotels Group empire.\n\nThe rooms and suites are a heady cocktail of off-kilter angles, eye-catching artworks, and vivid violet and indigo accents. Some of them come with balconies or terraces, and the expansive Hotel X Suite is a proper penthouse, complete with a double-size bathtub. The immediate neighborhood has plenty to recommend it, including live music and Brisbane’s Chinatown; the city center is just a few minutes away. Not that you need to go out — Bisou Bisou, the French bistro, is open all day, and Iris, the rooftop bar and restaurant, serves drinks and Spanish-inspired bites with a panoramic city view.

content:
Some global chains might feel intimidated at the prospect of opening an Alpine-style resort in Korea’s Taebaek Mountains, but not this one. The Intercontinental Alpensia Pyeongchang Resort shows the influence of classic European mountain lodges, as well as plenty of Korean heritage in its art and design. But underneath it all it’s the same large-scale, ultra-luxe, eminently palatable, highly professional hospitality that is the InterContinental brand’s stock-in-trade.

Many of the 238 rooms and suites have views of Alpensia Lake, while others look out at Mount Balwang and the surrounding range. Some rooms feature a bit of Alpine style in the form of pine wood and red upholstery, but for the most part this is the InterContinental look at its most cosmopolitan — close the shades and you could be in Seoul or Shanghai.

Summertime visitors will be happy to note the presence of several world-class golf courses, as well as a water park, an alpine coaster, and a vast expanse of terrain for hiking. And in winter the opportunities for skiing are legion, and there’s even a luge track nearby. Flavours, the restaurant, keeps guests restored with a diverse menu of Korean and international recipes.

content: Lijiang, high in the mountains of China’s Yunnan Province, is a thriving modern city, if a smallish one by Chinese standards. But it’s best known not for its novel features but for the Old Town of Lijiang, an incredibly well-preserved 13th-century district that’s been recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It’s here, amid the ancient Naxi architecture of the Old Town, that you’ll find the InterContinental Lijiang Ancient Town Resort, which is exactly what it sounds like: a substantial modern luxury resort that does its level best to blend in with its richly historical surroundings.\n\nThe hotel’s 267 rooms and suites are inspired by the Old Town setting, but are a contemporary tribute, rather than a strict period reconstruction. That is to say, its luxuries are as modern as those you’ll find in any InterContinental, even as the experience is one of a kind. The spa and fitness center are as lavish as the word “resort” suggests, complete with an indoor pool. And the hotel’s restaurants and lounges are led by the flagship 7 Colors Chinese Restaurant, serving Yunnan and Sichuan dishes in a vast and atmospheric dining room.

content: Santorini’s cave houses have been around for centuries, but it wasn’t until the 1980s that enterprising islanders began turning them into hotels. The Chaidemenos family was one of the first to get in the game: starting with a small property in the village of Oia, they transformed the rustic interiors of two caves, previously used as storage spaces for wine, into luxurious all-white hotel rooms overlooking the Aegean Sea. The Canaves Collection has expanded significantly since then, but Canaves Ena, formerly known as the Canaves Oia Boutique Hotel, is the original — and for some, the best. \n\nThe recently renovated hotel has four levels built into the volcanic cliffs, with traditional Cycladic architecture and minimalist interiors that don't distract from dazzling views over the caldera. Rooms have curving white walls, cool tile floors, and natural wood accents, plus modern bathrooms and private verandas with outdoor lounging and dining space. Amenities include plush bathrobes, custom bath products, Nespresso machines, and complimentary Greek wine on arrival. Suites have tubs instead of standard walk-in showers, and some have plunge pools or Jacuzzis; the river pool suite, as the name says, has a private pool that flows like a short river onto the terrace. For everyone else, Canaves Ena’s dreamy aquamarine-hued infinity pool, with a row of partially submerged chaise longues facing a panoramic seascape, is a highlight; strategically positioned for memorable sunset views is Adami, the hotel’s stylish restaurant.

content: Quaint villages dot the hilly landscapes of the Appenzellerland, a region so deeply rooted in Swiss tradition that yodeling festivals and cattle shows are commonplace. Stylish hotels are relatively few and far between, which makes Appenzeller Huus Löwen especially notable. This boutique hotel, though it’s housed in a timber-and-stone building that dates back to the 11th century, features a modern sensibility both inside and out: solar panels cover the steeply angled roof, and rooms, light-filled and lined in pale knotty wood, have a sleek quasi-Scandinavian look. Whimsical flower murals enliven the breakfast area downstairs, while the rooftop terrace, with a hot tub and wood-burning stove that can be booked for private use, overlooks views of green pastures and snow-capped mountains.

content: Hundreds of historic lodges and roadside motels line Route 66, and some have been revamped for modern travelers, like ARRIVE Albuquerque. Housed in the former Downtowner Motor Inn, which opened in 1965 on Central Avenue — the section of the iconic highway that cuts through the city’s downtown — it’s now a smart-looking boutique hotel courtesy of the California-based Palisociety collection. The vintage facade hasn’t changed much, save for the addition of a large mural by local artist Nani Chacon. But inside, the hotel is bright and modern, featuring a mix of playful midcentury-inspired decor, vibrant textiles, and shapes and colors that mirror the region’s Southwestern landscapes. \n\nRooms have cheerful checkered-tile floors, floral-patterned headboards, fine Italian linens, custom-built furniture, and retro-styled bathrooms stocked with Grown Alchemist products, as well as thoughtful amenities like curated minibars and Victrola Bluetooth speakers. Spacious suites come with separate living rooms furnished with modular sofas, wooden counters with stools, and workstations. Downstairs, off the lobby with its domed ceiling and quarry floors, the DWTNR Cocktail Bar & Lounge specializes in comfort food and cocktails, a contemporary twist on classic Americana, including drinks served poolside at ARRIVE’s stylish swim club.

content: Forte dei Marmi, now a glamorous seaside resort, has an interesting connection to Italian art history. This Tuscan town, close to the Apuan Alps and their marble quarries, was an important trading hub for the region’s famous white Carrara marble — the very same used for Michelangelo’s David, among many other treasures. It makes sense that the Magic Collection Retreats, a hospitality brand inspired by art, should set up shop here. The Magic Forte dei Marmi is a modern villa that doubles as a showcase for contemporary Italian artists, featuring site-specific installations, original artworks, and one-of-a-kind design pieces inside and out. \n\nThe hotel has just a handful of suites, and each is unique. The minimalist décor is gallery-like — with white flooring, white walls, sophisticated lighting systems, and large windows letting in abundant sunshine — creating an ideal backdrop for the colorful art collection. One has a bathroom whimsically tiled in a yellow floral pattern, another has an art installation built from paperback books, and a third has a large private terrace with deck furniture covered in vibrant textiles. There’s a creative twist, too, to the hotel’s stylish cinema, open-air spa and fitness center, and quirky, mosaic-lined swimming pool. The Magic Forte dei Marmi is just a block from the beach, but complimentary bicycles make it easy to explore town.

content: With nearly a hundred naturally occurring mineral springs, the mountain town of Velingrad, Bulgaria is considered the spa capital of the Balkans. Even its simplest guesthouses offer wellness treatments, and its best hotels lean fully into the theme with vast mineral pools and state-of-the-art spas. Among these is Kashmir Wellness & Spa Hotel, a sophisticated retreat tucked into a centuries-old pine forest on the edge of town. The spa complex, like the hotel itself, is modern, light-filled, and built of native wood and glass, offering an impressive array of indoor and outdoor pools, Jacuzzis, salt rooms, and saunas, many of which face views of the woods and the Rhodope Mountains beyond.\n\nRooms and suites are rustic-chic, with wood-paneled walls and ceilings, exposed stone details, customizable lighting systems, tufted leather headboards, gray and white plaid accents, and whimsical contemporary art. The stylish cabin aesthetic works especially well in the larger suites, with two levels connected by a floating wooden staircase, but every room has a balcony with forest views. Elsewhere at the hotel are an open-air poolside bar and a stylish whiskey club, and the alpine-styled Pashmina restaurant has an expansive terrace with views over a small lake.

content: Rotenburg is one of those blink-and-you’ll-miss-it German villages dotting the countryside between Bremen and Hamburg, especially if traveling via the Autobahn. content:
Despite what its name might suggest, the InterContinental Hangzhou Liangzhu is not quite a luxury hotel designed in tribute to the prehistoric Liangzhu culture that flourished here during the Neolithic era. Rather, it’s a top-flight business hotel from IHG that’s set in suburban Hangzhou, ten minutes’ drive from the David Chipperfield Architects–designed Liangzhu Museum, on the UNESCO-listed site of Liangzhu Ancient City. 

The hotel’s designers, Hirsch Bedner Associates, did in fact draw some of their aesthetic inspiration from the Liangzhu culture, with details in jade, stone, and bronze to complement the sleek contemporary spaces; for the uninitiated, the result is another powerfully luxurious InterContinental hotel with a look that’s nothing if not memorable. Rooms begin at a very generous 45 square meters, and the comforts, as you expect from this brand, are state-of-the-art.

Leisure facilities include an indoor and an outdoor swimming pool, and there’s plentiful meeting space for travelers who require it. The Liangzhu cultural attractions are immediately to hand, while downtown Hangzhou is a manageable drive. And the hotel’s restaurants include the all-day Commune, mixing Western and Hangzhou flavors, and Sakana, an intimate Japanese option.

content:
Bozeman, Montana’s status as the gateway to Yellowstone National Park means that tourism has long been a major factor in the city’s development; an addition like the Kimpton Armory Hotel Bozeman is a sign that it’s entered a newly upscale era. The landmark that is the 1940s-era armory building once used by the Montana Army National Guard has been augmented by a substantial contemporary addition; the result is the city’s first luxury boutique hotel.

And an impressive one it is. Inside, the look is sophisticated and modern with rugged details — hand-stitched leather and wood, a rooftop fire pit, a basement whiskey bar — that are in keeping with the building’s origins and the destination itself, a hub for outdoor adventure. Rooms are elegant but down-to-earth, featuring custom beds with Frette linens, warm lighting, large workspaces, cozy throws and pillows in plaid flannel, and minibars stocked with local treats. Bathrooms are as sleek as you’d expect at a Kimpton hotel, as are other amenities the brand is known for: an evening happy hour, a 24-hour fitness center, and complimentary bicycles. 

Other highlights include the outdoor pool on the terrace, conveniently heated year-round, loaner snowshoes and sleds, and the rooftop bar with views of the Rocky Mountains — there’s even a pop-up winter chalet where you can warm up with a glass of wine while protected from the elements.

content: In a valley between the Dolomites and the Riesenferners, where the conceptual border between Italian and Austrian cultures is fluid, Hotel Quelle Nature Spa Resort presents a characteristically Alpine version of the good life. What began as a humble country inn is now a proper luxury resort, its Alpine-modern structures containing some 69 rooms and suites, alongside an expansive spa and wellness center. There are eight indoor and outdoor pools, including a rooftop infinity pool, 12 saunas, a wellness garden, a fitness and activity program, and treatments that range from the merely relaxing to the borderline medical. The style is contemporary verging on boutique-hotel cool, but never losing sight of its connection with the mountain-lodge life. And the cuisine is suitably hearty for a hotel whose guests spend their days experiencing the great outdoors; flavors range from South Tyrol to the Mediterranean.

content: Around here we prize memorable hotel experiences above all else. Sometimes that means surprises, stylistic innovations, or audacious experiments. And other times, that means traditional hospitality practiced at the highest level — nothing revolutionary, just excellence. The latter category is what earns the Taj hotels their reputation, and the 2017-vintage Taj Swarna is a prime example. Here in the Punjabi city of Amritsar, any daring architectural statement has no less than the monumental Golden Temple to contend with. So the Taj opts for a certain stately warmth, and a contemporary look that pays tribute to India’s traditions even as it keeps one foot firmly in the present.\n\nThe rooms and suites look out through floor-to-ceiling windows, and while the style is certainly pleasing to the eye, there are inducements for the other senses as well, from Ploh bathrobes to Forest Essentials bath products. Three restaurants cover a wide variety of cuisines, from comfortable international fare to traditional Amritsar cooking to the Chinese Room, with both Sichuan and Cantonese options. The Jiva spa, meanwhile, continues the theme of indulgence, featuring everything from traditional beauty treatments to five-hour Ayurveda-informed therapies. Taj Swarna may not revolutionize your idea of what a hotel can do, but it’s a fine reminder of how easy life in a hotel can be.

content: After a smart refresh, the oldest family-run hotel in Salzburg is also one of the city’s most fashionable. Hotel zum Hirschen dates back to the early 1500s, and while its pitched roof and elegant living rooms are very much a product of their time, it’s the work of contemporary designers and artists that makes the place stand out today. There’s local talent behind the newly minimalist interiors, bespoke lighting systems, and modern art collection, and the Vienna-based landscape architect Karin Standler designed the stylish central garden, where guests linger over breakfast on sunny days. Rooms are cozy and simply outfitted with king-sized beds, garden views, and walk-in rainshowers with locally produced bath amenities; a collection of larger apartments, lined in pale wood, have a distinctly Scandinavian feel. Austrian wines, coffee, and cake are served all afternoon at the lively Hirschen Bar, and bicycles are available for exploring the city.

content: Housed in a century-old Art Nouveau–style landmark next to Porvoo Old Town’s gate, RUNO Hotel Porvoo occupies a prominent space that’s long been associated with Finnish literary tradition: RUNO means “poem,” Finland’s national poet J. L. Runeberg stayed on the premises in the hotel's prior iteration, and the façade features mythical symbols from Kalevala, the Finnish national epic. Countless other details pay homage to the building’s history, from restored tile fireplaces to renovated antique windows and tables built out of 300-year-old pine floorboards. But after a style overhaul by Studio Joanna Laajisto, RUNO’s interior is also a showcase for modern Nordic design. \n\nThe ground floor is airy and open with a cozy bar, one-of-a-kind artworks by youthful Finnish artists, American Shaker-inspired furnishings, and large sofas to sink into. Up an old wooden staircase are quiet rooms outfitted in earthy hues; all have pale parquet flooring, hand-painted wall panels, glowing pendant lights, and custom furniture and fixtures created by Laajisto. Bathrooms are spacious and spa-like with a mix of unexpected details including bespoke bathrobes, high-end hairdryers, and rustic towel racks crafted out of salvaged farm equipment. Upstairs, the fireplace-warmed Attic Sauna offers a contemporary twist on a traditional Scandinavian spa, while downstairs, the RUNO Kitchen and Bar serves updated Finnish classics made with local ingredients.

content:
First, a little orientation: Lifou is one of the outer islands of New Caledonia, a French territory a few hundred miles off the east coast of Australia. And on the south side of the island, on a picture-perfect white-sand beach, is the InterContinental Lifou Wadra Bay Resort, a high-end seaside escape from a brand that knows a thing or two about delivering a consistent luxury experience to any corner of the globe.

It’s smallish, for an InterContinental, at just 50 rooms; Lifou Island isn’t yet the sort of place that can handle much more. This leaves plenty of attention to be paid to each one of its rooms, bungalows, and villas, and it shows. The rooms are a perfectly measured blend of luxury-hotel swank and tropical canopy-bed fantasy, while the villas add private outdoor hot tubs and direct beach access.

The spa benefits from the combination of French and Melanesian traditions, and so do the restaurants, the high-end Ömöm and the more casual poolside Sewen. Kayaks, paddleboards, and snorkeling equipment are available on site, and if you’re a scuba diver you’ll want to set aside time to explore Lifou’s lagoon up close.

content: While the menu at Don Alfonso 1890’s starred restaurant may be more or less what you expect, given its setting just inland from the Amalfi Coast, it’s safe to say the interior design probably isn’t. This renovated 19th-century house, in Sant’Agata sue Due Golfi on the Sorrentine peninsula, has traditional elements, but the fanciful color scheme — rose, magenta, and bubble-gum pink, with accents in canary yellow, lime green and cherry red — feels straight out of Alice in Wonderland. Outside, a wide covered porch twinkles with tiny lights after dark; relax with drinks after a cooking class or a tour of the wine cellar and cheese aging room, located in a pre-Roman tunnel.\n

content:
As more travelers to the Yucatán Peninsula venture off the well-worn path between Cancún and Tulum, the hotel scene continues to level up in destinations like the capital city of Mérida. Take Adoro Hotel Boutique, a stylish adults-only hotel inside a restored colonial mansion a short stroll from the main plaza. 

It’s at once grounded in its place — each suite is named after a traditional Yucatecan song and features decorative pasta-tiled floors and handcrafted furnishings — and oriented to design-conscious guests, its sophisticated common spaces swathed in ivory, silver, and butter yellow in homage to Mérida’s nickname, “the white city.” 

Some rooms have romantic four-poster beds and ornate chandeliers, others private gardens with plunge pools. Highlights include a restaurant serving elevated regional dishes, a pretty courtyard pool, and near the entrance, an imposing poplar tree whose roots are fed by an underground cenote.

content: Not far from the Adriatic coast, near the border of Marche and Abruzzo, Relais Villa Corallo is an elegant getaway in a relatively undiscovered section of central Italy. The stately stone mansion was built as a private residence in the mid-19th century, and much of its old-world character remains. The interiors feature original parquet flooring and ornate fireplaces, grand staircases and glittering chandeliers, while the surrounding park, shaded by oak and cypress trees, is laced with paths to explore on foot or bicycle. Suites are all unique, with details like four-poster beds, designer wallpaper, and light-filled marble bathrooms with freestanding tubs. The estate’s organic farm sources most of the ingredients for the hotel’s refined Retrovilla Bistrot — even the olive oil is pressed on site, using olives from the trees by the pool.

content:
It’s a rather prosaic name for such an unusual hotel, but it gets to the point — Athens, Georgia is still a small city, and the downtown and the university district are indeed one and the same. Hotel Indigo Athens Downtown - University Area is remarkable even from a distance, thanks to its barnlike silhouette, whose agricultural associations are tempered by its very modern gray-and-red color scheme.

The interiors, too, marry “modern farmstead” architecture with contemporary urban style; the rooms feel a touch studious, in a nod to the neighboring university, but they’re much more stylish and luxurious than any student digs, with particular attention paid to the spa-like bathrooms. And there are some subtle local touches, if you know where to look — the in-room artwork, for example, is full of references to the legendary Athens music scene.

It’s in the Madison Bar & Bistro that the country-meets-city approach pays the clearest dividends. This farm-to-table restaurant and bar showcases not only the produce of local farmers and purveyors, but serves it on farm tables crafted by local artisans; all of it is accompanied by cocktails, wines, and a selection of local microbrews.

content:
In locations where other prestige luxury brands fear to tread, you’ll often find an InterContinental all by itself at the top of the hospitality market. That’s the case in Bandung, Indonesia’s second city, two hours’ drive to the south and east from Jakarta. Though home to millions, it’s got nothing else quite like the InterContinental Bandung Dago Pakar.

Like many of InterContinental’s properties it’s one part business hotel and one part luxury resort — set on the mountainous northern fringe of the city, it’s surrounded by lush greenery, and offers far-ranging views. In typical InterContinental style the rooms are large and lavish, though visually restrained — the décor is muted, almost minimalist, though full of details that pay tribute to classic Indonesian styles.

There’s a resort-style infinity pool, as well as the Zen Spa, and plenty of events space — this is a popular wedding destination, on top of everything else. Damai Restaurant, the hotel’s Indonesian kitchen, serving everything from breakfast on through to dinner; it’s joined by Tian Jing Lou, the upscale Chinese restaurant, overlooking the Mountain View golf course and the Bandung skyline from its perch atop the hotel.

content:
Hotels like the Hotel Indigo Tulsa Downtown are evidence that, by now, the boutique-hotel revolution is over, having long since been decided in favor of the insurgents. These days even Oklahoma’s second-largest metropolis can boast of a lodging with luxury-boutique swank and high-design good looks. The location, on Santa Fe Square in the vibrant city-center Blue Dome district, could hardly be more auspicious; here you’re surrounded by Tulsa’s finest restaurants, and a short walk from either the Arts District or the historic commercial center.

In the rooms you’ll find what might be a surprisingly urban loft-style look, featuring raw concrete ceilings, hardwood flooring, modernist-inspired furniture, and murals and photographs depicting scenes from Tulsa’s oil-rich history. This is no skyscraper, but neither is the Blue Dome a particularly high-rise district — which means the views of the city’s rooftops are memorable ones.

With the entertainment district just outside, the Indigo doesn’t need to offer all things to all people — one versatile bar and restaurant is all that’s required, and the Prospect Local Bar and Kitchen is up to the task, serving breakfast, lunch, dinner, room service, and drinks.

content:
We’ve long said that the future of luxury hospitality is already on display in China, if for no other reason than the fact that even the 26th-largest city is in need of truly world-class luxury hotels like the InterContinental Hefei. This 405-room tower benefits from an unusually pastoral view thanks to its location alongside Swan Lake, which also places it within walking distance of the Hefei Grand Theater opera house.

Its rooms and suites are elegant in a way that leans more classic than contemporary, right down to the richly figured marble in the lavish, spa-like bathrooms. The views are far-ranging, especially those in the rooms that face the lake, and while the atmosphere may strive for timelessness, the in-room technology is entirely up to date.

Also state-of-the-art are the Spa InterContinental and the associated fitness center and indoor pool; outside is a private garden that enjoys the same verdant tranquility you’ll find across the road at Swan Lake. And the restaurants and bars, naturally, go all out, from the Cantonese and Sichuan Cai Feng Lou to the all-day international Commune and Tsingtao 1903, which serves Western-style barbecue along with Qingdao beers.

content: When it comes to overnight lodgings in Versailles, you can’t get any closer to the Château than Les Lumières: this luxury boutique hotel is literally its neighbor, located just steps from its front gate. Housed in a pair of meticulously restored historic pavilions, Les Lumières is not just a wildly convenient place to stay while enjoying a leisurely visit to King Louis XIV’s royal residence — it’s practically a museum unto itself. The theme is the Age of Enlightenment, and at check-in, guests receive a key enclosed in a small book that tells a story of the famous philosopher, explorer, or writer their room is named after, from Descartes to Voltaire.\n\nThe style in the common areas channels the classic elegance of the Grand Siècle with heavy crystal chandeliers, oversized mirrors, and an opulent Belle Époque staircase. But rooms and suites, high-ceilinged and spacious, have more of a modern edge: some feature bold patterned wallpaper and others have coffered walls in crisp sage green, but all have colorful accents, from mustard-yellow or cherry-red duvets to velvet ottomans in turquoise or navy blue. Some offer direct views of the Château, as does one of the hotel’s highlights, the gorgeous Galerie des Lumières, with its blush-pink banquettes and high arched windows. Sparkling wines are the stars in the gilded Bar des Philosophes.

content: Positioned right next to the Parsenn funicular, which provides direct access to the ski slopes and hiking trails of the Swiss Alps, the Seehof Davos is one of the oldest hotels in town. Opened as a family-run guesthouse in 1869, the hotel was expanded a few times before it was snapped up by the German-based Precise Hotels & Resorts group and reborn as the luxurious Precise Tale Seehof Davos. Restorations preserved many of the building’s loveliest features — classic alpine architecture, a cozy fireplace-warmed bar, a breakfast room with mountain views — and additions include a state-of-the-art spa and an elegant bistro specializing in fondue.\n\nThe rooms and suites were thoroughly renovated, and though their amenities are modern, the look remains traditional. Most are lined in fragrant Swiss stone pine, with blonde wood floors and paneling, crisp white beds with plaid details, and framed landscape photography. Suites evoke the feel of a mountain chalet with decorative wood ceilings, wool rugs, spacious living rooms, and bathrooms with deep soaking tubs and recessed lighting. A few offer private balconies with mountain views. A trio of dining venues includes the Restaurant Chesa Davos, with outdoor seating on a picturesque terrace in summer or in a cavernous, chandelier-illuminated dining room in winter. Various other restaurants and bars are within blocks, and access to seven ski areas is just a cable car ride away.

Tennis courts and an outdoor swimming pool add to the appeal, as does L’Inattendu, a one-MICHELIN-Star restaurant, and a chic garden bistro with sea views.

content: There’s more to see on the Wild Atlantic Way than anyone can fit into a single road trip, and an overwhelming number of charming family-run inns to stay at along the way. Teach de Broc, in the southwest, stands out for its location — this boutique guesthouse is set amid scenic sand dunes beside the entrance to the famous Ballybunion Golf Club in County Kerry, a five-minute stroll from the beach — and for its elevated style and service. \n\nRooms are simple but elegant, with polished wood furnishings, earth-toned decor, fresh floral arrangements, and modern bathrooms with walk-in showers. All have views over the rolling green landscapes of the golf course, and breakfast starts early to accommodate guests with early tee times. The hotel has plenty of amenities for golfers, including a dedicated locker room and storage area, though Teach de Broc is equally convenient for outings to nearby caves, cliff walks, and beaches. As the sun goes down, the hotel’s stylish bistro and wine bar is a lively gathering spot, offering gourmet takes on Irish classics.

content:
Though the cultivation of wine in Wales goes back as far as Roman times, there wasn’t much of an industry here for most of the intervening millennia — a few short years ago the mention of Welsh wines would have been met in many places with puzzlement. But the local craft has advanced quickly enough to produce not only some notable exports but arguably the first hotel of its kind in the UK: the surprising and picturesque Llanerch Vineyard Hotel.

The estate and its vineyards are surrounded by ten acres of woodland that lend the experience a feeling of seclusion, even though the location is actually quite a convenient one, mere minutes from Cardiff. And the in-room experience is as tranquil as can be, thanks not only to the pastoral views but to the warm, modernist-inspired interiors and the quietly luxurious comforts.

Of course the accommodations are only part of the appeal of a vineyard hotel. Tastings and tours make up a large part of the programming, and a woodland walk is a fine way to work up an appetite for a meal in Llanerch’s bistro-style restaurant, whose locally sourced dishes are a celebration of the bounty of the Welsh countryside.

content:
The InterContinental brand makes good on its name by installing similarly world-class luxury hotels on six out of seven continents, and in Luanda, the capital of Angola, they’re the first of the world’s global luxury brands to arrive on the scene. The prestigious Miramar district is, among other things, the city’s embassy district, and in fact the InterContinental is practically right next door to the American embassy.

Inside the hotel you’ll find 377 rooms and suites that are crisp and contemporary, each one featuring its own palette of a single saturated color against dazzling white. The beds are plush, the desks are functional, and the bathrooms are spa-like in their extravagance. And the views — this 24-story structure towers virtually alone over Miramar, and from the upper floors you can see for miles in every direction.

It’s got more meeting and events space than any hotel in town, as well as an outdoor swimming pool with an expansive deck, served by the Peri Peri Grill & Bar; the other food and beverage venues take a fittingly intercontinental approach, from Portuguese and Angolan fare at Curadoria to French classics at Le Petit Choux and Spanish tapas at La Boqueria.

content: Petit Soleil styles itself as a “boutique bed and beverage,” on the hunch, presumably, that the Californian and French wines, the local beers and ciders, and the classic cocktails are a bigger draw than the (admittedly impressive) breakfast. San Luis Obispo is, after all, at the heart of California’s other wine country, the southern counterpart to Napa and Sonoma. This viticultural connection also explains the pervasive Frenchness of Petit Soleil, whose rooms could almost pass for Parisian, if not for their alarming spaciousness. In addition to the daily breakfast service there’s a complimentary apéritif hour, and when weather permits — and it almost always does — the revelry spills out onto Petit Soleil’s charming patios.

content: Considering it’s part of a chain with dozens of hotels across Spain, Vincci Selección Posada del Patio, in Málaga’s old town, is surprisingly full of character. As the name suggests, this luxury hotel occupies a historic posada, but the site itself is much older — glass panels in the lobby reveal ruins of the ancient city walls, including Roman-built stone sections that date back to the fifth century. \n\nThese days, the interiors are modern but fanciful, with art installations resembling flamenco fans framing the reception, abundant greenery around every corner, and vibrant murals cascading across the walls. Rooms are similarly contemporary and colorful, with parquet floors and bold, tropical-inspired art. Some have balconies and separate living rooms, including newly refurbished suites, located on an exclusive floor with its own terrace. For everyone else, there’s the rooftop with a plunge pool and views over the city skyline.

content:
Bangladesh may not yet be a boutique-hotel hotbed, but it is a place where you can find luxury hospitality practiced at the highest level, thanks to hotels like the InterContinental Dhaka. The city-center location is nothing if not convenient, and while at 226 rooms and suites it’s no small operation, neither is it a skyscraping behemoth — there’s room here for individualized service and a bit of the personal touch.

In its aesthetic it’s essentially a cosmopolitan, international-style business hotel, but with plenty of Bangladeshi influence, from the patterned screens inherited from Islamic architecture to a color palette that’s decidedly local. The rooms are tastefully swanky, with marble bathrooms and modernist office chairs, and the comforts are state-of-the-art.

And despite its city-center location, the InterContinental Dhaka has plenty to offer to leisure-oriented guests. Along with all the expected business and events functionality you can expect to find the HARNN Heritage Spa, an outdoor pool lined with cabana seating, and several restaurants: from the versatile and eclectic Elements and Café Social to the Amber Room grill, the Opus Lounge & Bar, and the Aqua Deck, serving lighter fare by the poolside.

content: On a rising stretch of Cebu’s south coast, NUSTAR Resort & Casino is part city hotel, part island escape, and part integrated pleasure palace, with far-ranging views, lively interiors, and plenty of space to properly unwind. And NUSTAR Hotel is one of two lodging options within the resort — it’s the younger, hipper counterpart to the formal five-star Fili hotel.\n\nThat’s not to say it’s lacking in comforts, by any means. NUSTAR Hotel’s rooms and suites are oversized, with deep soaking tubs and floor-to-ceiling windows that look out over sea or skyline. And while the atmosphere is design-hotel hip, it’s also relaxed and unhurried — though the energy picks up in the tasting room, lounge, and pool villas. The casino’s attractions speak for themselves, as does the integrated shopping mall; NUSTAR Hotel features the highly entertaining Good Luck Hot Pot and the modern pan-Chinese Mott 32 to go along with Fili’s half-dozen restaurants.

content: Founded by monks in the 13th century, Megève was a quiet alpine hamlet for hundreds of years. The village’s transformation into a world-class ski resort began in 1901 with the opening of its first lodge, the Grand Hôtel Soleil d’Or, a historic landmark that still maintains a local standard for elegance and luxury. Old-world charm is abundant in its cozy, bright rooms with parquet floors, exposed wood beams, cheerful patterned wallpaper, and bathtubs with mountain views, and especially in top-floor rooms tucked beneath the building’s sloped eaves. \n\nMeanwhile, downstairs, the in-house pastry chef prepares gourmet hot chocolate and sweet treats near a roaring fireplace, and the dark wood-paneled La Fromagerie serves up raclette and fondue by candlelight. The liveliest après-ski scene is up on the rooftop, where the enclosed lounge’s wraparound windows reveal panoramas of the surrounding mountains and snow-covered rooftops.

content:
You certainly can’t accuse the InterContinental group of failing to live up to their name. In fact it’s increasingly the case that the first proper luxury hotel in an emerging travel destination will be found under the IHG banner. That’s true, at least, of the InterContinental Tashkent, a 216-room luxury hotel situated within the Trilliant Business Park complex, a mixed-use commercial, convention, and retail development just off the city’s central Amir Temur Square.

Most of the InterContinental’s 17 floors are given over to its rooms and suites, which spread out to princely sizes and freely combine minimalist-adjacent modern design with ornaments inspired by the local traditions. The height of the Trilliant development means most of them have impressively unobstructed views of the city, as well as plentiful daylight.

Spanning two floors is the E’quilibrium Wellness Club, comprising a spa, a fitness center, and an indoor pool. The InterContinental is the first Leed Gold–certified building in all of Uzbekistan, a substantial environmental achievement. And on the top floor, with the finest city views, is Ember, a grill-focused restaurant, as well as the punningly named Embar terrace bar.

content:
Kimpton’s global era continues with their first hotel in Bali, set right in the thick of the action: Nusa Dua, on the east side of the island’s southern protuberance. There are plenty of upscale resorts in the area, but the Kimpton Naranta Bali manages to differentiate itself by occupying a sort of Goldilocks zone, offering a mix of boutique-chic style and tasteful luxury that is, for many a visitor to this corner of Bali, exactly the right blend.

This is an all-villa resort, and the accommodations are uniformly spacious, before even taking into account their outdoor lounge space and, in many cases, their private plunge pools. And while most of the charm of a Balinese villa is low-tech, they do come with some welcome modern interventions, like espresso machines and Marshall bluetooth speakers.

As for the location: it’s near the beach, but not on the beach, and adjacent to the Bali National Golf Club, though it does have its own beach club, a short ride away, where drinks and light bites are available. For a more full-featured restaurant or bar, it’s back to the hotel, where the options include a pool bar, a casual café, and Aki & Jack’s, serving Japanese cuisine with a side of barbecue.

The name can be read as a reference not only to the Orient but to the immediate geographic situation; EAST Hong Kong is set in Taikoo Shing, just around the bend from Wan Chai and Causeway Bay, a setting that’s still urban and convenient, if not absolutely central. In fact EAST is the more business-oriented of Swire Hotels’ sub-brands, which makes EAST Hong Kong a cousin to the ultra-luxe Upper House. 

And while it’s a more affordable, attainable experience, it’s plenty luxurious, and far more memorable than most business-oriented luxury hotels. The vibe here is high-design contemporary boutique chic, with modern furniture and eye-catching photo murals in the rooms, plus espresso machines and some impressive views, especially from the bay-facing side. 

While there’s plenty to do in the surrounding neighborhood, the hotel’s own offerings are worthy ones, from Sugar, the rooftop bar and terrace, to FEAST (Food by EAST), a casual all-day eatery that features Asian and European flavors.

content:
A pope, a king, Mark Twain, and Elizabeth Taylor are just a few of the distinguished guests who’ve passed through the halls of Hotel D’Inghilterra. This elegant 19th-century palazzo, set on a quiet pedestrian-only street around the corner from the Spanish Steps, is home to one of Rome’s legendary old hotels. The landmark reopened in 2024 after year-long renovations, its old-world grandeur only enhanced by its design-forward makeover. 

The opulent interiors are freshly outfitted with bespoke wallpaper, Murano glass chandeliers, supple velvet loveseats, and decorative mosaics by Roman artisans. Rooms and suites are glamorous, lined in oak and marble, with antique furnishings draped in rich Italian fabrics; some have private balconies, mirrored bar cabinets, and ceramic lamps handcrafted in a Florentine atelier. And among the additions is a SPA Suite, an intimate space, clad in travertine and tucked away beneath vaulted ceilings.

Meanwhile the ground-level Café Romano, with its cozy wood-paneled bar and chocolate-brown tufted leather banquette seating, is a perfectly stylish spot for dinner or an aperitivo. The highlight, however, might be Terrazza Romana, the hotel’s rooftop cocktail bar, with its unique view over the Eternal City.

After a day in the mountains, guests can unwind at Altitude Wellness Spa or soak in Ella’s Baths, where fresh air and Alpine views offer the purest kind of therapy.

content: The resort town of La Grande-Motte isn’t your garden-variety Mediterranean getaway: conceived in the 1960s as an eco-friendly modernist seaside utopia, it’s a product of ambitious urban planning. While Hôtel La Plage is not as eye-catching — or as eyebrow-raising — as its pyramid-shaped neighbors, this luxury resort was designed in the same bold spirit. Low-lying and geometric, it sits right on the beach, with floor-to-ceiling glass revealing sweeping ocean views from most rooms. The look is minimalist but down-to-earth, with natural hues, clean lines, and lots of native wood, and all have private balconies or terraces. The private beach club, with rows of elegant white umbrellas shading cushioned deck chairs and an open-air cocktail bar, is a major perk in summer, though the shoreline is lovely for strolling throughout the year.

It is run by a French couple with a long-standing love for Malta, and each room is themed around a different aspect of the island, from maritime history to Maltese spirituality, using sculpture, color, and subtle design cues. Central sights are all within easy reach, either by ferry or a walk across the harbor. Everything feels easy here, including coming back.

content: Most of the Vincci hotels are in Spain, but one of the best is in Portugal, prominently positioned beside the Don Luís I Bridge that connects the cities of Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia. Vincci Ponte de Ferro is on the latter side, housed in a trio of old warehouses originally used to store wines produced in the region. But the restored interiors don’t look like any storage space you’ve ever seen — they’re sleek and industrial, with exposed granite walls, double-high ceilings, and huge wrought iron-framed windows. \n\nStyle-wise, the hotel’s knockout features are the cool lobby bar and a rooftop terrace with striking views of the landmark bridge next door. But the rooms and suites are great-looking, too, with pale parquet floors, bold accent walls, and modern bathrooms lined in colorful tile. A wine bar pouring local reds is a nice touch that pays homage to the site’s history.

content: It’s not the most famous Massachusetts beach town, but Dennisport, on the Nantucket Sound side of Cape Cod, is a picture-perfect seaside escape, sandy beaches and all. Set a minute or two inland, tucked in among residential neighbors, is Bluebird Dennisport, another modern classic from the Lark Hotels family.\n\nThe rooms feel like something from a swanky and styled-up mid-century motel, while the two-bedroom cottages come with full kitchens and fire pits. The outdoor swimming pool is a summertime must, while the adjoining greenhouse-style indoor pool extends the season. And as convivial as the on-site atmosphere may be, and as charming as Dennisport is, the whole of the Cape is within relatively easy reach.

content:
California’s wine country has plenty of luxury lodging, but precious little along the lines of the Cottages at Little Saint. Healdsburg’s Little Saint is itself unique, a restaurant, café, bar and events venue that hosts astonishingly high-quality touring acts in its intimate performance space. Against that backdrop, the Cottages are easy enough to understand: four small houses transformed by the designer Ken Fulk into spaces that are both comfortable and creatively inspiring.

The smallest weighs in at 345 square feet, and is a cozy escape for two — or it can connect with its next-door neighbor to form a three-bedroom getaway. That the two of them, Court and Spark, are collectively named for Joni Mitchell’s 1974 release, says something about the Cottages’ aesthetic. (The others are Gimme Shelter and Déjà Vu.)

And if the cottages themselves are quiet and relatively low-maintenance, that’s because the rest of Little Saint fills in with ample amenities and plenty of sociability. It’s not out of the question that a guest might stay on site for the duration of their stay — but with all of downtown Healdsburg within walking distance, it’s by no means a necessity.

content:
There’s much more to the Yucatán than the Caribbean resort towns. In the inland countryside near Mérida, surrounded by the jungle landscapes of the Cenotes Rings State Reserve, is Galopina, a five-room escape whose architectural distinction and residential atmosphere make it quite unlike anything else in the region.

Five suites, to be precise — each one comes with a private terrace and a view of the surrounding greenery. The style is modern but warm, its visual spareness emphasizing rich textures in concrete and wood. Meals are served in the house’s dining room or on the terrace, and are crafted from local ingredients, including the produce of the hotel’s own garden.

And while quiet seclusion is Galopina’s stock in trade, there’s plenty to do in the region: the countryside is dotted with cenotes and archaeological sites, the towns of Izamal and Valladolid are close by, and the city of Mérida is less than an hour away.

content:
It’s tempting to suspect that if you’ve seen one luxury safari camp, you’ve seen them all. But then a place like Xigera Safari Lodge comes along and underlines the importance of taste, personality, and point of view. It’s owned and operated by a family with generations of safari-lodge experience and a personal connection with Botswana, and it shows in the lodge itself, which is full of the work of local artists, designers, and craftspeople.

The setting is the spectacular Moremi Game Reserve, which offers not just motorized game drives but aquatic expeditions as well. Private guides are available for maximum flexibility, and the 12 luxe tented suites are each served by a private butler. And as for the accommodations themselves, they’re as lavish as a tent can be while still remaining, technically, a tent.

Something similar applies to the rest of Xigera’s services, from the spa with its yoga pavilion to the culinary program, which, needless to say, goes far beyond camp fare; expect chef-cooked meals, South African wines, and impeccable environmental measures to boot.

content: Andros is one of the less famous Cycladic islands, and one of the least developed — neither of which is a drawback for fans of small-scale boutique hospitality. In fact its relative wildness and seclusion is a great strength of Onar Andros, a cluster of 18 low-profile, well-camouflaged villas and houses set between a quiet beach and a protected wetland.\n\nThe interiors are soothingly minimal in the classic Cycladic manner, dressed in a neutral palette that ranges from white to straw. Spaces are generous, both indoor and out, and the atmosphere is as tranquil as can be. The only choice to make is whether to be closer to the beach or higher up the hillside. Meanwhile guests gather around a communal table for informal meals crafted by Onar’s chefs from fresh local ingredients.

content: The village of San Pancrazio, in the picturesque Valdambra Valley, is a fine illustration of what it is that makes Tuscany such a compelling destination. It’s here, within the walls of a 17th-century noble residence, that you’ll find Palazzo Tiglio, a family-run boutique hotel with as much classic Tuscan character per square inch as any hotel under the sun.\n\nWith just seven rooms it’s a boutique hotel in the classic sense; at this scale a residential atmosphere is effortlessly sustained. The rooms themselves are as classic as they come, offering a window into what the Tuscan aristocratic life must have looked like. Meanwhile an outdoor pool, surrounded by gardens and olive trees, offers daytime relaxation, while the dining room and restaurant terrace bring hotel guests and San Pancrazio locals together at the table.

content:
There are certainly places in Poland that are less picturesque than the shores of Lake Rożnowski; similarly, there are hotels that are a good deal less luxurious than Heron Live Hotel. This is the contemporary grand hotel par excellence: a silhouette that might have been familiar a century ago, but executed in a modern architectural style marked by confidently minimalist interiors.

Its rooms and suites display a luxe modernist influence, and feature views of the forest canopy or the waters of the lake; some top-floor units stand under the mansard roof and look out through sloped panoramic windows, while the high-end suites open onto terraces for even more immediate views.

On the lower levels facing the lakefront is an expansive spa and wellness center, complete with an outdoor jacuzzi and an astonishing glass-walled infinity pool. The marina is the gateway to a variety of boating experiences, and the mountainous surroundings offer ample opportunity to skiers, bikers, and hikers. Meanwhile three restaurants range from the summertime Marina to the wintertime Sienna 104 and the year-round flagship, Botanika.

content: In the hospitality world, cave hotels and Cappadocia are synonymous — nowhere else can you find such a density of cave-dwelling lodgings. Like the best of them, Cappadocia Cave Suites isn’t entirely underground, but a hybrid of natural limestone caves and stunning stone-walled structures, offering not just subterranean accommodations but elevated views over this famous landscape as well.\n\nDespite its name, Cappadocia Cave Suites does feature some standard rooms alongside its large and varied selection of suites. Options include a balcony view, a private pool, or the multi-room Family Suite. The décor, naturally, leans toward the traditional. Meanwhile Nana Cappadocia, the restaurant, serves contemporary Turkish fare alongside local wines. Don’t miss the chance to see this unique landscape via hot air balloon — private tours may be arranged with the help of the hotel’s concierge.

content: Built in the 1960s and adapted in 2022, this 13-suite hideaway in the South Tyrolean hills takes a maximum of 26 guests at a time, a deliberate ceiling that shapes everything about the experience. content: Zlatibor, in western Serbia, is home to more than a few hotels and resorts, but none so decidedly modern in style as Bor Hotel by Karisma. This futuristic structure rises above the treetops in a setting where one might expect a more traditional mountain lodge. Nor is what’s inside any less adventurous, as contemporary artworks fill the modern interior spaces.\n\nJudicious use of pine wood and other natural materials anchors this contemporary design in mountain tradition, and the comforts are the equal of any Alpine lodge. This is a four-season mountain destination, with as much to offer hikers and cyclists as skiers. The spa and wellness center are always in season, as are the restaurants, which range in their inspiration from Italy to East Asia.

content: Country house hotels don’t get much more classic than Weston Manor Hotel, a beautifully preserved 15th-century house in the Oxfordshire village of Weston-on-the-Green, a reasonably athletic stone’s throw from both Oxford and the Cotswolds. Set on 12 acres of gardens, it contains enough Tudor and Georgian details to keep an architectural historian busy for days, along with an unpretentious atmosphere that makes it rather more welcoming than its imposing silhouette might suggest.\n\nRooms and suites are divided between the original house and its former stables; all are handsomely styled, in keeping with the house’s public spaces, while the comforts are appealingly modern (and include underfloor heating). A bar and terrace serve more casual all-day fare, while the Lavender Restaurant plays the role of manor-house dining room with aplomb.

content: It’s hard to tell from Europa Palace’s youthful good looks that this icon of the Italian Riviera has been welcoming guests since 1874. The hotel’s minimalist style is thoroughly on point with each room’s sober neutral palette complemented by clean lines, pared back furnishings and tactile materials. The subdued design also allows the views to take centerstage, either over Sanremo’s attractive Art Nouveau casino, promenade, or the Mediterranean. The natural stone decor of the spa creates a soothing setting for what can be a full afternoon of relaxation, hopping between saunas, hammam, hot tub and pool, capped off with a facial or massage. Rêve Bistrot is open for aperitivo hour and dinner and puts a contemporary riff on Ligurian cuisine — ask about a wine tasting with the sommelier to dive deeper into the local wines — while the 6th floor rooftop terrace serves weekend brunch in winter and opens up fully in summer to serve sunset drinks and seafood dinners with a view of the coastline and Mediterranean Sea.
name: Europa Palace Sanremo
policy: The historic hotel of Sanremo has been completely renovated to welcome its guests in an elegant and contemporary atmosphere. Europa Palace is a destination within a destination for those dreaming of an Italian getaway filled with relaxation and privacy, ideal for both a romantic escape and a longer stay exploring the beauty of the region.As one of the top three grand hotels in Sanremo, Europa Palace offers a stunning view of the Ligurian Sea and the promenade, with the prestigious Sanremo Casino just behind it. The hotel is located in the heart of the Flower City, close to the city center and shopping streets.Hotel Europa Palace is easily accessible by car, just 5 km from the Sanremo exit. The train station is only a 5-minute taxi ride away from the hotel.

content: Just to the east of Rome’s historic center, between the Roma Termini rail station and the historic neighborhood of Rione Monti, Hotel Viminale stands discreetly behind a 19th-century façade. History, architectural and otherwise, is all around — which frees the Viminale to pursue a clean-lined, modernist-inspired aesthetic, a look that makes a case for Rome as a style capital on a level with Milan.\n\nIn the rooms, neutral tones and handsome parquet floors strike a sober note that’s contrasted with colorful contemporary artworks and modern furnishings. In typical Roman boutique-hotel style they’re compact, but plenty comfortable. The common spaces, too, are suited to the hotel’s small scale, with a breakfast room joined by a garden and a terrace. For lunch and dinner, you’ll dine out — not a difficult proposition in this eminently walkable corner of Rome.

content:
At first sight Natiia Relais doesn’t look like a typical wine resort. Firstly, the façade has the appearance of a medieval castle, a fashionable 19th century update to the 18th century noble property.  And secondly, whilst most wine resorts sit surrounded by vineyards and countryside, Natiia Relais can be found just by the shores of Lake Garda, meaning there are some stunning lake views from its contemporary guest rooms. 

It does still have the vineyards, however, ten hectares in total, enough space to invest in its own kitchen garden to supply restaurant Osteria, which also hosts Italian cooking classes. Naturally various wine tastings are also available, plus picnics in the vineyards accompanied by a bottle from the resort. But the hotel is about wellness as much as wine, with a large indoor and outdoor pool, a sauna, hammam and whirlpool, plus a menu of relaxing massages.

content: Martigny stands quite literally at a crossroads: this Swiss city is connected via old Roman roads to both France and Italy, whose borders lie mere miles away. Today it’s more a cultural than a commercial destination, as well as something of a gateway to the Alps; and in Hôtel Borsari, Martigny has a hotel that pays tribute to its history via the medium of the modern design hotel.\n\nIt’s part of a city-center mixed-use development called Quartier LôDzè, which comprises a coffee bar, a wine and charcuterie bar, a restaurant called Le Cercle Kitchen, and Les Bains Publics, a modern (and extremely stylish) Roman bath complex. For its part, the hotel is a stunner as well, a heady mix of modern Swiss and German design from names like Dieter Rams alongside influences from the ancient Roman and Greek worlds. The resulting hotel is retro-tinged, but ultimately fresh, and feels intentionally low-tech in comparison with the typical modern luxury hotel.

content: Spain’s Meliá hotels have gone global in a big way, and their overseas outposts are quite often among their most luxurious. That’s certainly the case in Vietnam, where Meliá Vinpearl Phu Quoc occupies a prime parcel of beachfront on the Gulf of Thailand. Here more than 500 villas form a substantial neighborhood — or even a small town — surrounding a central lagoon. And its situation within the larger Vinpearl complex of resorts means it’s got access to activities and amenities even beyond its own substantial offerings.\n\nNot that much is left out here. The villas are thoroughly luxurious, ranging from one to four bedrooms, all of them with private pools and all of them decorated in a handsome contemporary-colonial style. At this scale facilities like a spa, a yoga center, and a well-equipped kids’ program are present as a matter of course, and activity offerings include just about anything that a person can do on or near the sea. Meanwhile the restaurants range from Vietnamese to Italian offerings, and many more lie further south along the length of the greater Vinpearl resort area.

content: Kingston, Ontario’s Smith Hotel is an unusual one on both the large and the small scale — the former because it’s made not from a historical residence but from a 19th-century church, and the latter because its units are less like typical hotel rooms and more like loft apartments, split across two levels and full of contrast between modern design and antique ecclesiastical architecture.\n\nThe lofts occupy the lower levels, with the main floor of the church now functioning as a co-working space. Each one features an open-plan living room, a small but fully equipped kitchen and dining area, and plenty of mid-century modernist-inspired style. Services like a spa or a restaurant are beyond the ambitions of this residential-style hotel, but with downtown Kingston close by the Smith’s offerings are more than enough.

content:
Once a fortified residence home to one of Italy’s noblest families, and still owned by its descendants today, Baglio Oneto celebrates the region’s long tradition of Marsala wine making, although staying here isn’t limited to just oenophiles. The hotel’s picturesque spot on the coast of western Sicily, surrounded by 35,000 square meters of vineyards, ancient olive trees, and various flora and fauna, suits anyone looking to slow down and switch off. As do the facilities, which include a saltwater infinity pool with a view across the Stagnone Nature Reserve and Egadi Islands.  

The 47 rooms sport rich green shades that nod to the olive trees outside and come decorated with traditional Sicilian touches such as colourful ceramics and hand-crafted wrought iron. The views are quite something, especially from the balconies and terraces which sit right above the vineyards and countryside. Sicilian, Italian and Mediterranean dishes crafted with organic local produce and the hotel’s own herbs are served each evening, either in the wooden beamed restaurant or al fresco in the historic stone walled courtyard or on the terrace. By day a number of experiences can be organized on property, including cooking classes, yoga sessions, massages and of course, wine tastings, but there’s plenty to explore around the resort too, from horse riding and kite surfing to day trips to Marsala.

content: It would be a shame to go all the way to Zanzibar to find minimalist, international-style architecture. Fortunately that’s the last thing on Xanadu Luxury Villas & Retreat’s mind. These nine villas are inspired by the rich tapestry of Arab and African influences that made Zanzibar what it is, and the result is a style and an atmosphere that’s unique — and uniquely memorable.\n\nXanadu also excels in the realm of pure comfort. Its villas are mere steps from the beach but are tucked into the forest for privacy; each one comes with a private pool and is served by a personal butler. Villas come in one- and two-bedroom varieties, and they’re almost compound-like in their self-sufficiency. Only the spa, the beach, and the island’s natural and cultural charms are capable of tempting guests out beyond their villas’ walls — that, and Ganda, the restaurant, where a team of 8 local and international chefs serve a diverse and elevated cuisine.

content: There can’t be many hotels of any description much further north than VALO Ice Cube Villas, and certainly none more stylish. Here, in Finnish Lapland, 150 miles north of the Arctic Circle, stand four modern, cube-shaped villas, each one framing an impressive view of the landscape through panoramic windows. The interior style is Nordic modern-luxe, warmed by textures of wood, stone, and fur.\n\nThey’re warm in a literal sense as well; jacuzzis, saunas, and indoor and outdoor fireplaces see to that. Thus it’s as fine a setting for viewing winter landscapes (and the Northern Lighs) as it is for summertime stargazing. Outside, winter guests ski Europe’s northernmost resort, or set out on snowmobile or dogsled safaris; summer is for hiking, biking, fishing, and experiencing the indigenous Sàmi culture.

content:
It’s hard to beat the location of Epona, which sits surrounded by many of the sights that make Sens worth a stop along the Burgundy wine route. The attractive neo-renaissance town hall is right opposite the hotel, and Sens Cathedral, the Museé de Sens and the lovely Jardin de l’Orangerie are only a couple of minutes’ walk away. This also means the hotel offers some enviable views, particularly from its contemporary styled suites, which overlook the town hall, cathedral, or the city's rooftops. 

Facilities include a playroom, an unusual but welcome addition for a hotel of this size, a fitness room, and in-room treatments on request in lieu of a spa. Restaurant La Table d’Epona highlights local Burgundy produce and cuisine, complimented of course by a collection of Burgundy wines, and the hotel bar serves drinks and light snacks from lunch until late. The outdoor terrace is a pleasant spot for dining al fresco in summer, but the rooftop bar is the real highlight for drinks with a view of Sens Cathedral.

content: Hotel Indigo Sydney Potts Point spreads 105 rooms across in Kings Cross, where the Coca-Cola sign still glows above the street. The neighborhood's neon-lit past was once packed with theatres, all-night bars, and bohemians. Now it makes room for Japanese-French restaurants, independent galleries, and boutique retail, though the edge hasn't disappeared completely. Rooms play with art deco motifs, wall-to-wall windows framing Rushcutters Bay or the city skyline, plus curated collections of books and vinyl. Luc-San by Luke Mangan does French-Japanese fusion one floor down. The X covers Australian breakfast and strong coffee. Performance venues and the museum strip are within walking distance.

content: InterContinental Sydney Coogee Beach repurposed the former Crowne Plaza into 198 rooms that face either the ocean or the residential streets behind it. The design follows a coastal rhythm: curved joinery, pale timber, sun-bleached whites, and wall-to-wall glass. The 22 suites add outdoor baths and separate living areas with unobstructed water views. Rick Stein made his Sydney debut here, cooking simply prepared seafood in the style that established his reputation across England and two Australian coastal outposts. Sunrise yoga happens on the sand, private pickleball courts are bookable by the hour, and the property includes an infinity pool and rooftop bar overlooking the beach.

content: Set up on a cliffside above its own private bay, InterContinental Danang Sun Peninsula Resort sits surrounded by lush mountainous rainforest and sweeping sea views. The mix of rooms, suites and private penthouses and villas take design cues from traditional Vietnamese architecture and come with guaranteed bay views, including from the huge marble bathtubs and larges terraces that overlook the gardens and sea. Penthouses and villas also come with luxurious extras such as private infinity pools, rooftop terraces, and their own saunas, steam rooms and Jacuzzis. There are four restaurants and two bars, including the One-MICHELIN-Star La Maison 1888, and of course in a setting this idyllic, there’s a comprehensive spa with a yoga pavilion, tai chi and meditation sessions, and treatments rooted in sound healing and traditional Vietnamese and Thai rituals.
