content:
The Inn at Mattei’s Tavern has been a fixture in the Santa Ynez Valley wine-country town of Los Olivos since as far back as the 1880s. Safe to say, though, that in its original form it was a shade or two less luxurious than it is now, under the direction of Auberge Collection. It comes by its retro vibe honestly, in other words, but alongside its historic charms you’ll find all the trappings of a modern Californian luxury resort.

Its accommodations range from beautifully restored 19th-century cottages to rooms and suites in a handful of new buildings, designed to complement the original style — so there’s less to distinguish the old from the new than you might expect. All of them are exceedingly comfortable, even luxurious, though in a down-to-earth, unpretentious way.

And there’s much more going on here than just a fine collection of bedrooms. The Lavender Barn contains a remarkably full-featured spa and wellness center, while the Tavern itself is now an upscale Californian restaurant supplied by the farms and ranches of the Central Coast. Local wine is abundant, as you’d expect, and wine tours, whether guided or self-directed, feature prominently on most guests’ agendas.

content: L'Isle-sur-la-Sorgue's Sunday antique market draws dealers from across Europe, and L'Isle de Leos - MGallery puts you steps from the action. The building hugs the Sorgue River; some rooms have French doors that open straight onto the water, the current audible underneath. Interiors lean into jewel tones: burnt orange velvet, deep green accents, brass lighting that feels more 1970s than Provençal cliché. La Roue restaurant operates under a glass roof, serving seasonal cooking that changes with what is available at the market. Le Nego Chin, the bar, gets crowded on weekends attracting locals who come for the wine list. The pool is in a courtyard garden, surrounded by plane trees.

content: This château near Nantes commits fully to a round-the-world decorating scheme. Rooms channel different destinations: Venice gets Murano glass and carnival masks, St. Petersburg brings Russian tapestries and marble, and the Maharaja apartment piles on carved wood and jewel tones for six guests. Gardens follow the same logic: Mexican courtyards transition into Balinese sculptures, then Moroccan tilework. La Table de Marquis serves French brasserie fare, Le Bar Zélélé mixes cocktails indoors, and the Salon Nomade operates poolside under canvas in summer. The underground spa runs treatments, and the concierge arranges Muscadet tastings in nearby Clisson. Extravagant, borderline excessive, committed to the bit.

content: Tucked into a quiet corner of North Egremont, Prospect is more than just a retreat, it is a reawakening. The lake does most of the talking, catching the light at all hours, while a chorus of rustling maples and wind chimes fills the gaps. This is a place shaped by intention, from the hand-built Scandinavian-style cabins and restored wetlands to the Cliff House’s suspended porch and knockout views of the Taconic Range. Come for the lake. Stay for the reminder that you don't need much to feel full.

content: With a name like “King’s Garden” you might expect a regal vibe from Hotel Kungsträdgården, and that’s what you’ll get. This stately 18th-century building wears its Gustavian style proudly, and while in its current incarnation it’s a thoroughly modern luxury boutique hotel, it’s as far as it gets from minimalism — a 2010 renovation updated its classic opulence with a contemporary color sense and the full complement of modern comforts.\n\nThe rooms and suites range widely in size, in classic European grand-hotel style, and if there’s a touch of a French accent about the aesthetic, it’s matched by the cuisine in Brasserie Makalös, which serves Parisian fare in a soaring courtyard space, while the adjacent Crystal Bar stands beneath what must be Stockholm’s largest chandelier. Meanwhile, the Royal Opera is steps from the hotel’s front door, with the Royal Palace and the Nobel museum not much farther.

content: Not so very long ago, a high-design Thai luxury resort might have gone in for a minimalist look, with a white-on-white palette and blank, uniform textures. Devasom Hua Hin, however, opts for something much more historically informed. Its architecture is unmistakably an homage to Thai tradition, and its interiors feature not only soft seaside colors but a tasteful degree of ornamentation as well, resulting in a warmth that’s rare among newly built luxury resorts.\n\nAccommodations range from rooms to suites to villas; they start out spacious enough and only grow from there. With only 24 units, however, it easily maintains an intimate atmosphere, and the village-like layout lends itself to privacy. On-site attractions include an infinity pool and a fine beach, and the cuisine is a particular point of pride.

content: Though it’s most definitively an urban boutique hotel, SILQ Hotel Bangkok feels a little bit like a resort. Its dedicated “wellness floor” features a Japanese onsen, a sauna and a CrossFit gym, and opens onto an indoor-outdoor saltwater swimming pool. Its style, meanwhile, is one part modern and one part classic, and touchable textures are a point of pride, as the hotel’s name might suggest.\n\nRooms range from a variety of spacious studios to multi-bedroom suites and the palatial penthouse, which features a private terrace and its own plunge pool with a view of the city skyline. To all of this SILQ Hotel Bangkok adds a versatile restaurant whose cuisines range from Thai to Indian to Italian, as well as a whiskey and cigar bar and a poolside lounge — and downstairs, the streets of Phrom Phong offer an endless array of dining, drinking, and shopping options.

Don’t let the rustic outward appearance of Braccialieri give you the wrong idea. Whilst it exemplifies slow living, or “eco glamping,” if you choose one of the six tented villas in the olive grove, the clue is in the name “luxury resort” — Braccialieri is the modern-luxe version of Sicilian country living, with high-end furniture and décor by well-known Italian designers alongside authentic old-world details.

The three suites in the main house are a step up from their tented counterparts when it comes to space, but in truth there’s nothing less than luxe about the eco-villas. Anywhere you stay, you’re treated to the same convivial atmosphere. By day, guests gather around the unique red-and-white checkerboard pool, and in the evenings dinner is served at Dodici Zappe, housed in the old mill, which combines modern culinary artistry with unpretentious Sicilian tradition.

content:
Gonten, Switzerland’s Appenzeller Huus family comprises three hotels side by side: the three-star Huus Bären, the four-star Huus Löwen, and this one, the five-star contemporary-luxe Huus Quell. Newly constructed, it resembles its historical siblings in its silhouette, but its details are unmistakably modern — just as, inside, it contains gestures towards traditional Alpine design, but updated for the 21st century.

Its 30 rooms and suites are similarly a perfect balance of Alpine coziness and luxury-boutique stylishness, and they’re as comfortable as they are visually appealing. They’re restorative enough on their own, but they’re joined by what might be the region’s most extravagant spa and wellness center, which ranges over 2,200 square meters and contains nine pools, eight saunas and stream grottos, and even a high-tech biohacking lab.

And in the areas of dining and drinking, Huus Quell benefits from access to all three of the Appenzeller Huus hotels; options range from the very traditional Löwenstobe to the architectural spectacle that is the gourmet Quell restaurant.

content: The Grand Hotel Residencia enjoys a prime location on the coast of Gran Canaria, sitting under leafy palms just a few minutes’ walk away from the sandy beach of Maspalomas. Attractive rooms come in sky blue shades with a mix of prints and textiles, dark wood four poster beds, and the highlight, balconies surrounded by lush greenery. The restaurant serves a Mediterranean-inspired menu with a particular focus on local ingredients; the fruit and vegetables for instance come from a nearby finca on the island. There’s also a pool bar for tapas, and in the evening, a piano bar for live music and aperitifs. The slow living, seaside experience is enhanced with some spa time, or for a more serious approach to wellbeing, the hotel can even organize physiotherapy. Golfers will also find five of the island’s seven courses close by the hotel, and plenty of other sports take place at sister address Seaside Palm Beach, which sits just next door, including tennis, yoga, and Tai Chi.

content: Built as a private residence in 1880, the hotel once known as Chateau Belvedere was, by the middle of the 20th century, the most glamorous lodging in town. Today, as the Hotel Belvedere, it’s no less impressive — just a touch more low-key. After a thorough restoration, its decades-spanning historical charms are on full display, complemented by a touch of era-appropriate contemporary design; the result is a first-rate luxury boutique hotel on a modest, local scale.\n\nHotel Belvedere’s 19 rooms and suites are all unique, following the buildings’ historical floor plans; all are a thoughtful mix of contemporary and classic, and the comforts are uniformly high-end, though anything but ostentatious. Bathhouse at the Belvedere is a modern spa in an atmospheric space that recalls a classic European bathhouse; meanwhile the Lounge serves a menu of small plates alongside its wines, beers, and cocktails.

content: More than a few European boutique hotels are made from what were once private aristocratic residences; what sets Palazzo Arone apart is that it’s still tended to by its original owners, the Baroni di Valentino — a fact that likely accounts in large part for the extremely fine condition of this 16th-century palazzo, set in the heart of historic Palermo.\n\nThe sense of continuity with the house’s past is everywhere in evidence; historical flourishes are plentiful, and the ornate interiors are punctuated by carefully judged contemporary interventions, including modern design furniture and up-to-date boutique-hotel comforts. And while even the humblest Classic room feels luxurious, Palazzo Arone’s suites are among the most impressive in town. And while there’s no typical hotel-style restaurant or bar, guests are by no means on their own — a sunset aperitif is often accompanied by live music, and a chef is on hand for dinner, market tours, and cooking classes.

content:
Small is beautiful in Puglia: Tre Bacili is a classic 18th and 19th-century Salentine mansion that’s living a second life as a beautifully refined six-room luxury boutique hotel, one which counts among its charms a lovely little outdoor pool and an adults-only policy that contributes to the property’s air of discreet tranquility and romance.

The house’s architecture has been lovingly restored, and in archetypal Italian style its historical elements are counterposed against modern furnishings and other contemporary design gestures. The comforts, too, are up to date, if unobtrusively so; the result is an experience that combines the best of old and new.

Tre Bacili’s bistro offers breakfast and cooking classes, and if you book in advance for a group of four or more, also lunch and dinner. Meanwhile the village of Spongano is nothing if not picturesque. When it comes time to explore, Lecce is close by, and any number of coastal towns and beaches are even closer; the hotel’s own serviced beach club stands a few minutes’ drive away.

content:
The Reverie Saigon proudly calls itself the most spectacularly extravagant hotel in Vietnam, and if anything they’re not giving themselves quite enough credit. A more opulent hotel anywhere would be big news; in Ho Chi Minh City it stands alone, an exemplar of ultra-luxury set atop the 40-story Saigon Times Square skyscraper.

Its style tends toward the traditional, though with the ornament turned up to 11, and with a modern sensibility showing through in its unusually colorful décor. The views of the city and the river from the hotel’s rooms and suites are difficult to match — for the most part, this remains a low-rise city. And while even the humblest king rooms are spacious and luxurious, the apex accommodations are the two-level signature suites, one designed by Provasi and the other by Poltrona Frau.

As for facilities, nothing is left out: wellness offerings include a spa and an outdoor pool, while among the culinary attractions is a One-MICHELIN-Star Cantonese restaurant called Long Trieu.

content:
To get straight to the point: with Anantara Mina Ras Al Khaimah Resort, overwater villas have arrived in the Emirates. This is far from Anantara’s first UAE establishment, but RAK’s geography makes it unique; its stilted structures look across a tidal lagoon at a wetland nature reserve, rich with coastal wildlife.

There are plenty of dry-land accommodations as well, which overlook the property’s gardens and beach. But it’s fair to say it’s the villas that make headlines: not just the overwater villas but the Peninsula villas as well, whose pool decks extend out over the coastline and take in panoramic sea views. The comforts throughout, naturally, are first-rate, and the spaces are generous at all levels.

Water sports feature prominently in this Anantara’s offerings, as does the expansive Anantara Spa. A multitude of restaurants range from Southeast Asian to South American fare and just about everything in between.

content: The Var village of Cotignac is a certified member of “Les Plus Beaux Villages,” and for a slice of Provençal life, you could certainly do much worse. It’s here, on two and a half acres of parkland, that you’ll find Lou Calen, a small hotel that was briefly famous in the Seventies as a haven for rock stars and the like — a boutique hotel before its time. Now it’s back, and perhaps more glorious than ever, again welcoming the sort of guests who’d rather disappear into the Var hills than walk along the promenade at Cannes.\n\nToday’s Lou Calen is luxurious, and as private as ever. Its 36 rooms and suites are divided between the main house and a hamlet-like set of outbuildings. All are architecturally distinct, and decorated in a style that combines Provençal tradition with modern and contemporary art and design. Meanwhile the Jardin Secret restaurant is joined by a more casual bistro as well as an on-site pastis-bar.

content: One of North Yorkshire’s classic country houses, Crathorne Hall was built at the dawn of the 20th century, and during its time as a private house it counted among its guests such eminences as the Queen Mother, King (then Prince) Charles and two members of Monty Python. It’s now well into its second career as a country-house hotel, and as a member of Hand Picked Hotels, it’s among the finest in the region — and retains, to an impressive degree, its historical character.\n\nFunctionally, of course, it’s thoroughly up to date; the rooms and suites come with high-tech comforts as well as low-tech luxuries like Hypnos mattresses and views over the Leven Valley. And outside of the bedrooms, you’ll find the country-house life perfectly represented: the Edwardian Room and the Nancy Tennant Bar serve tea, drinks, and much else, and the Leven Restaurant is a contemporary classic in a richly historic dining room.

Hotels like Cheshire’s Rookery Hall are a reminder that even in the boutique-hotel era there’s plenty to love about the classic forms of hospitality. This Georgian-era house stands on nearly 40 acres of land, close enough to Manchester and Liverpool for convenience’s sake, but secluded enough for a proper country getaway.

The original house, naturally, remains as elegant as ever; the rooms (and one suite) are divided between the main house and a tasteful late-20th-century addition. The latter are a touch more contemporary in style, but only a touch, and there’s no sense of second-class about them.

Among the most welcome contemporary interventions is the spa, which transforms the old stables into a striking modern space featuring an indoor pool under a glass roof. Meanwhile, for dinner, it’s back to classic elegance; the Restaurant at Rookery Hall is handsome in dark wood, and is complemented by the Drawing Room & Bar and the casual Spa Café.

content:
Sorrento’s coastline is home to some of Italy’s most iconic hotels, but there is something luxuriously low-key about Relais Villa Savarese. Housed in a 19th-century former private residence, this intimate boutique hotel sits hidden away in a lush, leafy garden seemingly far from the summer crowds, and yet it’s just a ten-minute walk from Sorrento’s town center and a few minutes from the nearest beach. There are just ten light-flooded rooms, each attractively dressed in soft pastel shades, parquet flooring and antiques, and the higher category rooms come with balconies overlooking the pleasant garden.
 
Outside, a large swimming pool is shaded by palms and citrus trees, and is intended as much for lounging, perhaps with a book borrowed from the library, as it is any actual swimming. And while there’s no restaurant, the hotel serves snacks all day, and guests won’t be short of dining options with Sorrento being such a short stroll away.

content: Housed in a restored 15th century property, Académie Hôtel Lyon is full of the same historic charm as the cobbled streets that surround it. Situated in Vieux Lyon, Lyon’s UNESCO-protected old town, the hotel still retains many of its centuries-old design elements, including its listed courtyard, arched stone doorways, and a sculpted coat of arms. Given the age of the building, rooms are understandably on the smaller side, but feel cozy rather than cramped, with parquet flooring, wood panelling, and the original French beamed ceilings. There’s no restaurant — although you can stop by for a drink at the cocktail bar linked to the hotel — but you won’t be short of options in Vieux Lyon, which is one of the city’s gastronomic hotspots.

content: Any photographer knows that sometimes, for the best views of your subject, you have to take a few steps away. The Lost Garden - Porto Emotions Lodge stands just outside of Porto, across the Douro River, on the Vila Nova de Gaia side. Thus it’s a modest walk or a very short drive from Porto’s picturesque center, and yet it offers a pastoral atmosphere, set amid verdant gardens and woodlands.\n\nIts design style is appropriately nature-focused, but stylish all the same; the rooms feel resort-like, rather than urban, and the minimalist-rustic style is supremely soothing. The nature-forward approach extends to the details; much of the furniture is locally handmade, and the hotel produces its own soaps and aromatherapy scents. A repurposed grocery store now serves as the hotel’s breakfast venue and café, and the Lost Bar opens onto a terrace with a view of the river and of Porto.

content: The unreasonable beauty of Val Gardena would elevate even an average hotel to must-stay status. Thankfully, the hoteliers of the Italian Dolomites are rarely content to be average. Almhotel Col Raiser is a South Tyrolean classic, a traditional Alpine hotel that’s been continually refreshed but never departed from its classic look — if you love knotty pine, you’ll be in heaven here.\n\nEven the cozy “Romantic” rooms feel more spacious than they are, thanks to the spectacular mountain views. The junior suites and suites, meanwhile, border on lavish, and benefit from walk-out balconies for even more immersion in the Alpine setting. Wellness facilities include a sauna and an outdoor hot tub facing the peaks, while Rita’s Kitchen serves abundant South Tyrolean fare with equal attention to nutrition and flavor.

content:
Visitors from outside the UK may not be aware that the New Forest got its name almost a thousand years ago, and is thus one of England’s best-preserved natural places. Rhinefield House is nowhere near as old — this Tudor-Gothic hybrid was constructed in the late 19th century — but its dramatic architecture and its idyllic setting combine to make it a tempting escape.

With the exception of a handful of historical rooms and suites, the hotel’s bedrooms are set in a newer addition, and it’s to their credit that they don’t reproduce the main house’s style. Instead they opt for a contemporary look with a country house influence; meanwhile, their newer construction makes for more modern comforts.

Dining options are suitably multifarious, from the fine-dining Armada Restaurant to more casual options. A spa and an outdoor pool provide opportunity for relaxation, while the setting encourages outdoor recreation, whether on the house’s expansive grounds or along the trails of the greater New Forest.

content: It’s an auspicious coincidence for English-speaking travelers that Stayeva 11’s address sounds like it was always intended for a hotel. This 15th-century house stands just within Dubrovnik’s fortified city wall, right next to St. John’s Fort, which overlooks the harbor. It’s been a family-owned guest house since 2014, but only in 2020 was it upgraded to its present form: a stylish three-room mini-boutique that combines energy-saving green measures with luxurious comforts like underfloor heating and kitchenettes with SMEG appliances.\n\nAt this size it’s a perfectly reasonable candidate for a whole-house rental, but even in its room-by-room configuration it feels more like a residence than a hotel. It helps that the family owners are also your hosts; and while there’s no space for a restaurant or breakfast service, they’re happy to guide you to all the best of Old Town Dubrovnik.

content: Everything about Hotel Villa Fanny is surprising, from the name to the setting, right in the heart of central Cagliari, an urban location that doesn’t stop the villa’s grounds from spreading out over a thousand square meters of gardens. It’s set within easy walking distance of the medieval city center and the marina, and yet it maintains an atmosphere more akin to country-house calm, a welcome contrast indeed.\n\nThe villa itself has been beautifully preserved and attractively updated; as is typical in Italian boutique hotels, historical architecture and contemporary design go happily hand in hand. Rooms vary, as they often do in antique houses, from cozy double bedrooms to expansive suites, including one that stretches out across two levels. A heated jacuzzi adds to the garden’s appeal; the hotel’s kitchen serves breakfast and a light lunch, while the bar offers light bites in addition to cocktails and wine.

content: As the name suggests, Nammos Hotel Mykonos is a sister of sorts to Psarou Beach’s well-loved Nammos Beach Club, an overnight addition in a chic boutique style that enables club and restaurant guests to recover in between bouts of revelry without ever leaving Nammos World. Though the accommodations are restful, the social life here is lively, especially down at the beach. Nammos Restaurant is part of the beach club, which means the atmosphere is always festive. And for a bit of proper peace and quiet there’s always the Nammos Spa, offering wellness and beauty treatments as well as a stylish Dior x Technogym fitness center.

content: Here in Huddersfield a manor house hotel is an uncommon sight; Manor House Lindley, however, is the real deal, an authentic Georgian house rescued by an ambitious designer-turned-hotelier and transformed into one of West Yorkshire’s most unique hotels. With just 11 bedrooms it’s not extraordinarily large, and thanks to its situation it’s a semi-urban refuge rather than a country-style getaway.\n\nAll the same, it’s as private as a manor house should be, and its interiors mix classic correctness with an eclectic modern influence to create a space that’s anything but ordinary. Its public spaces attract not just overnight guests but locals as well, who gather for dinner, for afternoon tea, or for a drink in one of three in-house bars.

content: The spectacular west coast of Scotland is arguably the main attraction here, though Knockinaam Lodge Hotel is entirely worthy of its unique setting. This 19th-century house stands just steps from a private cove on the Irish Sea, and feels perhaps even more remote than it is — guests are here not to be seen but to properly get away.\n\nThey’re aided in that endeavor by the lodge’s modest size; it contains a mere 10 rooms and suites, including one named for its most famous occupant, Sir Winston Churchill. And though the interiors have been subtly updated over the years, he’d recognize the style — the look is contemporary-classic, with an emphasis on classic. A fine restaurant serves a four-course lunch and a seven-course dinner, all crafted from local ingredients, including herbs from the hotel’s own gardens.

content: Sitting in the heart of the Cedofeita neighborhood, One Shot Palácio Cedofeita is housed in a sensitively restored 1831 mansion which used to welcome some of Porto’s most esteemed merchants and art patrons. Rooms are bright and contemporary with all white walls, candy striped beds and pops of blue velvet furnishings, and yet somehow, they blend seamlessly with ornate original elements such as carved wood ceilings, traditional Portuguese blue and white tiling and stained-glass windows. The restaurant is also the most opulent example of the hotel’s original architecture, its gilded gold moldings and columns making a spectacular setting for dinner. Other facilities include a gym, sauna, and an outdoor pool and large private terrace for evening drinks.

content: Anantara Sir Bani Yas Island Al Sahel Villa Resort has all the attractions of a relaxing resort hotel, whilst also offering a safari experience on the private island of Sir Bani Yas. The hotel’s 30 villas are set across the savannah in the style of a traditional fishing village and come with complete privacy, except perhaps from a few wandering gazelles. There are daily game drives to see more of the wildlife, as well as plenty of other outdoor activities including archery, watersports, and horse riding. There’s plenty of activities to keep children entertained, including a family-friendly nature drive and a kid’s club, and adults-only time can be found in the spa, where signature treatments are rooted in Arabic beauty traditions. Other facilities include an outdoor pool, gym, and four restaurants including the South African-inspired Savannah Grill and Mediterranean cuisine at Olio.

content: In the hills above Alaró, Finca Banyols carries the weight of centuries as a former olive oil mill, its stone walls and timber beams now restored into a refined rural retreat. Treatments in the spa draw on ingredients harvested from the land, including olive oil and honey, a fitting tribute to its origins. With gardens, pools, and private trails, the Finca offers a stay where Mallorca’s history is inseparable from its setting.

content: Italy’s farmhouse hotels come in a multitude of shapes and sizes, differing region by region; if you want to see how Basilicata differs from Tuscany or Umbria, compare Torre Fiore Hotel Masseria with its more typical northern cousins. This whitewashed structure is uniquely ornamented, and is surrounded, village-like, by the hotel’s 13 rooms and suites. Its hilltop perch offers a view of the not-so-distant Ionian Sea, and its small size ensures that the hospitality feels personal.\n\nIt’s a family affair — the owner was born in Pisticci, the nearest town, and returned from abroad to open Torre Fiore. Its rooms, in classic Italian boutique-hotel style, freely mix antique and modern elements, and while the style is consistent, each one is unique. Meanwhile the restaurant is open to hotel guests and to the public, and is thus suitably serious about the cuisine of Basilicata; cooking classes are available for guests who wish to re-create the experience at home.

content: There’s no law that says a boutique adaptation of a 1950s motor lodge has to go in for mid-century modernist nostalgia. The motel that’s now Farmhouse Paso Robles was designed in a country-cottage style, which is an excellent match for what draws most of the region’s 21st-century visitors: the region’s booming trade in wine production.\n\nThe renovation accentuated the rustic-chic style of the original Farmhouse, and the resulting hotel feels more like an agricultural village than a roadside motel, its cottages connected by paths that wind across sculpted gardens. There’s a touch of Moroccan and Italian influence in the interiors, and the atmosphere is as tranquil as can be, even with downtown Paso Robles just a few blocks away — a fleet of Linus bikes is available for getting out and about. Curated minibars bring local products into the rooms, and there’s more to discover in the Farm Shop.

content: It should be clear from the name alone that Silk n’ Cotton differs from the typical Athenian hotel. It turns out the concept is simple enough: this family-owned and -operated apartment-style boutique hotel is an extension of the ground-floor fabric store with which it shares its 1920s Art Deco edifice. That’s the extent of the common spaces, so for a restaurant or café you’ll hit the streets; the location, however, is just about as central as can be, and places all the best of Athens right at your feet.

content: Located in the tiny town of Crawfordsburn, the 17th century Old Inn has everything you would want from a cozy countryside stay: rustic beams, roaring fires, hearty cuisine, and a cocooning spa. Victorian-inspired guest rooms blend a mix of rich textiles, dark wood furnishings, standalone copper tubs, and in the Cottage, a four-poster bed, and all come with rolling countryside views. Head to the restaurant for comforting pub classics and French-inspired dishes, and traditional afternoon tea, and Bar 1614 for a fireside nightcap. Seven North, the hotel’s restaurant, serves Mediterranean fare in the building’s central courtyard and an adjacent dining room.

content:
Sitting on the edge of the medieval hilltop village of Sancerre, perched just above its famous vineyards, Les Hauts de Sancerre is a rural retreat underpinned by understated elegance. The eight rooms and suites feature a refined contemporary palette of bright white walls and light wood furnishings and come with views across the village and vineyards.

Restaurant La Table d’Arnaud follows the rhythm of the seasons and shows off the surrounding terroir through a creative gastronomic menu, naturally complemented by a collection of Sancerre wines. 

Guests can immerse themselves further in the region’s winemaking savoir faire through tours and tastings with local winemakers, explore the estate on foot or by bike, or cocoon themselves with nature-inspired treatments in the spa.
name: Les Hauts de Sancerre

content:
Sitting just above the town of Villanders at an altitude of 1,200 meters, Felder Alpin Lodge is an exclusive-use retreat surrounded by some incredible Dolomites views. The centuries-old mountain farmhouse has been authentically restored by three passionate local owners, who have retained the traditional Alpine style whilst adding in thoughtful contemporary touches such as Italian designer lamps and furnishings picked up from travels to Bali and Morocco. 

Guests can take over the “Black Kitchen” to show off their own culinary skills with fresh ingredients brought in by local farmers, or sit back, relax and let the lodge’s private chef take you on a gastronomic tour through the region, or further afield. Other lodge facilities include the original stube lounge, a ski room, a Finnish sauna, haybeds for yoga classes, and an underground wine cellar, as well as four hectares of meadow for taking in the panoramic mountain views. Felder’s experiences also immerse guests in South Tyrol, whether through traditions such as hay bathing and butter churning, embarking on a guided glacier tour, local wine tasting, or even building an igloo.

content:
There are just three rooms at Maison Jullian, a boutique hotel in Béziers. They’re named after the wife and daughters of Martien Jullian, a local vineyard owner who built the late 19th-century villa — a folie, or petite urban château — as his family home on the edge of the oldest canal in Europe. 

Quaint and rich with historic character after restorations by the new owners, the interiors are filled with romantic details: wisteria wallpaper by Laura Ashley, a wardrobe crafted out of an antique travel trunk, a mother-of-pearl chandelier, a cast-iron clawfoot tub. Two rooms incorporate the castle’s turrets, one repurposed into a reading room and the other into a boudoir, and all have views over the Canal du Midi. 

While there’s no doubt the upstairs suites are dreamy, equally intriguing are the owner’s original Moorish-style billiards room, with its stained glass windows and high domed ceiling, now a restaurant specializing in slow food, and the English gardens, with their antique greenhouse and natural swimming pool.

content: Many luxury hotels in Marrakech’s medina are housed in traditional riads, but Riad Nyla Wellness & Spa has the unusual distinction of occupying two. They’re located side by side, connected by a secret passage on the rooftop — which is also where you’ll find a gorgeous greenery-framed terrace with a decorative fireplace and an ethereal swimming pool lined in white stone. \n\nThe rest of the hotel, dreamt up by Italian architect Mattia Siviero and interior designer Corinne Dressler, is just as visually striking. Rooms are minimalist by local standards, outfitted in earth tones like ivory and terracotta, with polished mosaic flooring, arched doorways, and glowing pendant lights. Some overlook the central patio, which doubles as a venue for a welcome cup of mint tea or a lavish Moroccan breakfast. Completing the range of highly photogenic interiors is a subterranean spa with a modern hammam and turquoise-tiled pool.
name: Riad Nyla Wellness & Spa

content:
Though it is in fact a house in the country, Brimstone is not at all a typical country-house hotel. Here the style of hospitality owes more to luxury boutique hotels and to owner-operated guest houses than it does to the classic country mansions of aristocratic origin. It’s set in the Lake District, among some of England’s wildest landscapes, on the 35-acre Langdale Estate.

Here, rather than butlers or footmen, you’re attended by “hosts,” who can facilitate anything from a fresh towel to a climbing expedition — outdoor wear is provided via the Epicentre Bootroom. Guests also enjoy complimentary access to the Brimstone Spa’s elaborate Thermal Experience, as well as drinks and snacks in the Reading Room. 

The rooms and suites are spacious, and are as plush as the surrounding peaks are rugged; all come with balconies and at least one proper bathtub (the Duet Suite comes with a pair). Meanwhile Stove, the proprietors’ restaurant, is a short walk from the hotel, and just beyond that is Wainwrights’ Inn, the even less formal pub option.

content: On the historic streets of Olhão, a small Algarve city just to the east of Faro, a 19th-century house has been restored to its circa-1870 splendor and opened to the public as a boutique hotel called Casa Amor. And while its historical aspect is part of its charm, it’s more than simply a restoration project; Casa Amor’s owners (and designers) have Parisian roots, and a cosmopolitan sensibility is evident throughout.\n\nA mere ten rooms, decorated in a mix of antique furnishings and eclectic artworks, occupy the upper floors. What turns Casa Amor from a chic guest house into a proper boutique hotel are details like the little rooftop pool, the café with its French pastries, and the restaurant, where guests mingle with Olhão locals over local, seasonal dishes.

content: Behind the seemingly straightforward name of Guest House Raleigh is a boutique hotel that rewards a closer look. This handsome 19th-century Folk Victorian–style house now stands on Bloodworth Street, walkably close to all of downtown Raleigh. But it was moved here in its entirety from a historic residential neighborhood that was threatened with demolition. Now it’s part historical restoration, part contemporary boutique hotel, effortlessly weaving together the two stylistic threads.\n\nThe rooms and suites are touched by modern minimalism, but with antique accents and plenty of charm, especially in the 535-square-foot Historic Suite. Contemporary comforts abound, from in-room Keurig coffee makers and Malin + Goetz bath products to Brooklinen bedding and Coyuchi towels. A light breakfast is served en suite, and while there’s no in-house restaurant, Guest House Raleigh’s location is convenient to no end of options.

content: In terms of atmosphere, a quiet lane on the fringes of the Napa Valley town of St. Helena is a long way from Los Angeles, where the Palihotels brand was born. But the quirky European-accented charm of Le Petit Pali St. Helena is a perfect fit for the California wine country — and this setting affords the Petit Pali concept some space to expand to a more resort-like experience.\n\nRooms and suites look out over the surrounding vineyards, as do the freestanding cottages, which come with fireplaces and private patios. This is still an upscale bed-and-breakfast at heart, offering a champagne continental breakfast in the morning and light bites and sweet treats throughout the day. But if there’s one rural setting where a hotel can comfortably go without a restaurant, it’s Napa Valley, which is stuffed to the gills with high-end culinary attractions.

content: If Catalonia’s boutique-size farmhouse hotels aren’t as famous as their counterparts in Provence or Tuscany it’s not because Hotel Mas del Sol isn’t pulling its weight. This lovely little escape lies just over an hour’s drive up the Costa Brava from Barcelona, and then a bit inland — enough to offer day-trip access to the coast while remaining blissfully untroubled by tourism.\n\nThe heart of the place is a 14th-century stone farmhouse, and a handsome one at that. But the style here is far from medieval. A contemporary design sensibility brightens the rooms and suites with graphic wallpapers and modern furniture; most of the rooms and suites are housed in newer buildings, though a handful are set in the original house, and their up-to-date comforts happily coexist with the weathered stone walls. Breakfast is served outdoors, weather permitting, and with advance notice the Bistro del Sol can prepare dinner for guests as well.

Not to say its suites, with their unique blend of antique charm and contemporary stylishness, couldn’t perfectly well stand on their own. But it’s only when you consider them together with the fine-dining L’Orangerie restaurant and Il Giardino, the more casual pizzeria, that the picture comes entirely into focus. They call the Imperial Suite “the queen of the Relais,” and it’s certainly the most ornate; the others, however, aren’t far behind — even the smallest junior suite spans some 45 square meters. In the vault you’ll find a wellness area and an indoor therapeutic pool, complemented by the outdoor swimming pool, with its view of the gardens and grounds.

content: The no shortage of beautifull riads in Morocco, but it’s not often you get to stay in a 19th-century palace. Riad Mayfez’s owner leaned into the palace’s eclectic mix of architectural styles, where Arabic-Moorish elements sit alongside an Art Deco villa, and added her own mash up of influences into the mix to show off her love of two places, Morocco and London’s Mayfair. A black marble swimming pool sits at the center of the riad and is complemented by an extensive wellbeing offering including a Jacuzzi, facials and massages, and a marble and mosaic lined hammam. Other on-property facilities include a library, kid’s rooms, and cooking classes in the kitchen, or ask the team about organizing tours of Fez and beyond.
name: Riad Mayfez Suites & Spa
policy: Mayfez is not a conventional hotel.Our former Vizier’s residence, listed as a historical monument, emphasizes on intimacy and exclusivity, with only 6 suites and 1 deluxe room, set on 16000 Sq. Ft. of lands in the heart of the medina of Fez.Branded the most romantic boutique hotel in Africa and the Middle East by the World Luxury Hotel Awards, Riad Mayfez blends East and West, thus creating a style that speaks the language of romance, blending differences into an eclectic unity.Mayfez has two hearts, one that breathes in the garden, reflected in the quiet pulse of the black heated marble pool, and another that soars with the winds upon the panoramic terrace, beating to the infinite horizons of FezDeeply rooted in a slow travel concept, Mayfez is an invitation to feel and contemplate.Challenging the tourism landscape in Fez, we leverage our rich history and prime location to encourage you to do less, but better.We have broken free from the usual hospitality codes to bring freedom and personalisation to the art of welcoming. No reception, no set schedule, no set restaurant, but several dining areas, each offering a different atmosphere, named l’Odalisque for their versatility and the culinary pleasures they are hiding.Our concept combines Moroccan heritage with contemporary elegance to deliver an experience of refined authenticity and a bit of nostalgia. We orchestrate your stay according to seasons and desires, turning activities into well-being rituals, tours into authentic moments of emotion. Celebrating sustainability, community support and flavours, we weave the delights of the table and the Spa rituals into a single concept where body and spirit are equally nourished, and well-being becomes a true art of living. Sourced locally, the finest ingredients come to life in our chef’s hands, transformed into fragrant pastillas and tagines simmered to perfection, adorned with herbs and edible flowers from our garden.My’Spa is rooted in Morocco’s ancestral beauty rituals, embraces organic treasures, certified to the highest international standards and cruelty-free. Wrapped in the soothing fragrances of rose, orange blossom, and sun-warmed herbs, every ritual becomes a journey both timeless and ethically mindful.Riad Mayfez is located a 6 minute-walk down into the medina and offer a service of both escort and porter.Regarding reservations: Riad Mayfez Suites & Spa requests and shares additional information with its guests to ensure the best possible stay. It is therefore recommended that you contact Mayfez directly to finalize your personalised experience.

content:
Capella Taipei styles itself a “modern mansion,” and it’s not hard to see their point — the line between top-tier luxury hotel and luxe private residence is not always sharply focused. It helps that the designer is André Fu, the man responsible for a good share of the world’s swankiest hotels. Here the interiors are dazzling yet understated, and feel like spaces you could easily spend more than a few nights in.

The hotel occupies the upper floors of a high-rise in the tree-lined Songshan district, its 86 rooms offering panoramic views of Taipei and the surrounding hills. The six terrace suites are rare for the city: each comes with a private deck, a lap pool, and a skyline-facing jacuzzi.

And while there’s much in this food-obsessed city to tempt guests out for the night, Capella Taipei holds their interest with no fewer than five restaurants, ranging from Cantonese to omakase.

content: The picturesque Italian Riviera town of Santa Margherita Ligure has grand seaside hotels, but sometimes some smaller-scale hospitality is what’s called for. Villa Gelsomino is only moments removed from the beach and the town center, on a hillside overlooking the harbor. But that small measure of seclusion makes all the difference.\n\nIt helps that this 19th-century villa contains a mere six bedrooms, and that its interiors remain decorated in their original aristocratic style. In some ways it’s more guest house than hotel — at this scale you can’t expect a spa or a multitude of bars. Dinner is available, with 24 hours’ notice, however, and it’s an all-Ligurian affair, accompanied by wines from the villa’s selection. For a private and discreet Italian Riviera experience it’s tough to beat.

content:
Lilløy Lindenberg is, in a literal sense, a private island hotel, but it’s at once less extravagant and more memorable than the phrase might imply. This is no luxury resort, but a wild, rocky island in the North Sea, home to little more than a beautifully restored farmhouse and a boat launch — the latter a crucial part of the experience, as the final ten-minute stretch of your journey will take place by sea.

It’s the project of a pair of Bergen-based designers, and by all evidence, their taste is impeccable. The house’s four rooms are decorated in what they call an “antique Scandinavian folk style,” paired with judicious modern interventions as well as hand-made local crafts. Each room is as different as can be; one sits snugly under the peaked roof of the main house’s attic, while another, a free-standing unit right at the water’s edge, looks out at the waves through floor-to-ceiling windows.

Needless to say, everything you could possibly need is provided, from plant-based chef-made meals to groceries for self-catering — there’s no popping down to the shops from here. Everything is locally sourced, much of it foraged, and all of it selected with care.
name: LILLØY LINDENBERG

content: Debaines Hotel Santiago might sit in the heart of city’s historic downtown, but everything about it says modern urban bolthole. Minimalist rooms sport white walls and clean lines but still feel warm and inviting with their oak flooring, rich orange and mustard hues, and dark wood furnishings. Restaurants include the relaxed all day dining Gran Café and the lunchtime only Copper Room, which serves a mix of local and European dishes alongside an exclusively Chilean wine list. The excellent location means many of the city sights are within easy walking distance including the Opera House Teatro Municipal, the main square Plaza de Armas, and the Museo Bellas Artes.

content: Set among sun-bleached vineyards in Sicily’s remote southeast, Wine Relais Feudi del Pisciotto is an 18th-century estate turned boutique wine hotel with a deep connection to its landscape, and a cellar to match. The setting is wonderfully isolated, save for the agricultural town of Niscemi ten minutes away. Rooms are spread across former farm buildings, some with original features like stone troughs or panoramic terraces, while others occupy the recently restored aristocratic residence. There’s a generous pool, a small spa, and pine-shaded paths that open onto wide views of the surrounding hills.

content: Adler Spa Resort Sicilia is set on a protected stretch of coastline within the Torre Salsa nature reserve, where Mediterranean views and eco-conscious design go hand in hand. Built with local clay, volcanic stone, and cedar wood, the resort sits low on the land, designed to follow the contours of its setting. Suites are minimalist and low-slung, each with a private terrace facing the sea or gardens. The spa is expansive, with panoramic saunas, thalasso pools, and sea-view treatment rooms. Days here can be as active or unhurried as you like, with coastal hikes, fitness classes, and delicious Sicilian cooking drawn from the estate itself.

content: Mexico City’s Pasaje Parián is a shopping mall, yes, but that means something different in Roma Norte than it would in King of Prussia or Sherman Oaks; imagine a smaller, Porfirian-era New World equivalent to Milan’s Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II and you’re on much firmer ground. Not only is it an authentic local landmark, but upstairs from its retailers and restaurants you’ll find Hotel Parián, the first hotel in Mexico by the Lark Hospitality brand.\n\nIts rooms are stylish, modern, and minimalist, though they’re warmed by surfaces in natural wood and vibrant accents in deep green. Soundproof windows and blackout shutters isolate the bedrooms from the busy surroundings, and the custom furnishings, built-in storage, and modern bathrooms are both efficient and comfortable. Some rooms face the inner atrium, others the streets outside. And thanks to the wealth of offerings just downstairs, the hotel itself can afford to go without much in the way of public space; the hotel’s terrace serves as a dining room where guests can order from Pasaje Parián’s restaurants.

content: In a way, Le Hameau de Saparale hasn’t changed that much since it was built back in 1845 as a self-sufficient hamlet, home to 25 families who cultivated olive oil and wine from the surrounding lands. It even had its own post office and police station. It’s now home to hotel guests rather than local vignerons, but it still retains all of its 19th century rustic charm, and its acres of vines, olive and orange trees for unspoiled views that end with the Cagna mountains.\n\nThe 16 guest rooms, all located in the main building have been tastefully decorated in classic neutral shades that complement the original stone walls, wood flooring and exposed beams. Some come with terraces and balconies that overlook the vineyards, but for more privacy, check into one of the three former sheepfolds, now turned into independent villas with their own heated pools, hammams and Jacuzzis. In the restaurant, daily changing dishes highlight the local produce of the Ortolo valley and the hotel’s own vegetable garden, and come paired with wines from the well-stocked cellar, including bottles produced by the Hameau de Saparale winery. Wellness takes place in nature, with the pool, spa treatments, and yoga classes all designed to be enjoyed outside.
name: Le Hameau de Saparale

content: Set high up in the Dolomites, the adults-only Alpine Boutique Villa Gabriela is a year-round mountain retreat where you can do as much, or as little, as you like. Ten cozy rooms are dressed in a contemporary Alpine style with wood paneling and soft textiles, and some with added extras such as balconies for summer, and Finnish saunas for warming up in winter. As the view changes outside from thick snow to vibrant green—the hotel sits in the heart of Alpe di Siusi, the largest high alpine pasture in Europe—so do the activities, from skiing and romantic horse drawn sleigh rides to cycling, climbing and even golfing. After a day out on the slopes, there’s a restaurant and well-stocked wine cellar to come back to, and a spa with a sauna, steam room, and an outdoor Jacuzzi with a view of the Sciliar mountains.

content: Lima isn’t always mentioned in the same breath as Berlin and Amsterdam, but it’s here that the Nhow brand chose to establish its first hotel in the Americas. The location in Miraflores is a fine one, prominent and central, and the building is a distinctive modern one, its translucent surface lit softly from within. Inside, any thought of minimalism is quickly banished; the colors are riotous, the Inca-inspired artworks and design motifs are bold, and the spaces are richly varied. This Technicolor sensibility is something of a Nhow trademark, and it’s well suited to this lively, intensely localized boutique hotel.\n\nEven the entry-level rooms are generously sized and comfortably appointed with the full array of boutique-hotel must-haves; the suites quickly expand to opulent proportions, and the penthouse comes with a hot tub and a sauna, alongside what might be the best view in town. The hotel’s liveliness extends, naturally, to its public spaces, from a restaurant specializing in the flavors of the Amazon to the 13th-floor pool bar, which transitions from a sedate daytime gathering space to a vibrant club-like setting by night.

content: Sitting surrounded by nothing but sea and mountain views, the adults-only Hotel César Lanzarote is all about slowing down and switching off. Guest rooms take their cues from nature with layers of tactile materials in shades of blue and green, and plenty of leafy potted plants to bring the outside in. All rooms come with a mountain or sea view, and some come with a patio. There’s a restaurant and bar but really the facilities here are all about getting outdoors, either lounging around the infinity pool, enjoying the gardens and terrace, or dining al fresco in the picnic area. You can even cook up your own BBQ. The wellness offering includes yoga classes, a gym and soothing spa treatments, or get your fitness fix out in nature by hiking, biking, horseback riding, and golfing.

content: LuganoDante takes the second half of its name from the poet Dante Alighieri and its inspiration from the Divina Commedia, with nods to the famed work dotted throughout the property. It’s both an attractive, playful boutique hotel and a thoroughly capable business hotel; the interior “green area” is an Edenic little escape. It’s also got a luxurious air about it, not least in the accommodations, which are thoughtfully furnished and crisply stylish in shades of blue that nod to the nearby Lake Lugano. And in Flamel Restaurant & Mixology Bar you’ll find the hotel’s social heart, and cocktails that pay our homage to French alchemist Nicolas Flameland a menu whose flavors combine Italian and Mediterranean influences.

content: You don’t have to love a dram to check into the Dowans Hotel, but if you do, you’re in the right place. Sitting in the heart of Speyside, Scotland’s picturesque whisky county, Dowans is neighbors with more than 50 whisky distilleries, some of which are in walking distance from the hotel. Although you might not even need to leave try them; the hotel’s bar The Still stocks around 750 whisky references with something to suit beginners, and some rare bottles to excite the seasoned connoisseurs. Gastronomes can enjoy another taste of the Scottish terroir in Restaurant 57, which sources much of its meat and fish from within a 30-minute drive away. There's also traditional British afternoon tea served daily, the Mbar for cozy nightcaps by the fire, and a summer terrace with views of the rolling Scottish countryside.

content: As you travel to the south along Boracay’s White Beach, the numbers go up and the atmosphere grows steadily less tranquil. The Lind Boracay stands on one of Station 1’s prime beachfront spots, with direct access to the sand and wide-open views of the water. Rooms are large by local standards, all with balconies and a design that mixes soft curves, graphic details, and just enough color to lift the neutrals. \n\nDetails like Malin + Goetz bath product and sculptural lighting nod to its lifestyle-hotel roots, while the service remains distinctly Filipino: warm, attentive, and unpretentious. Numerous pools dot the property, and the rooftop infinity pool is a particular gem. The Spa Wellness pursues its self-explanatory mission with gusto, and restaurants range from local fare to Thai and Mediterranean options.

content:
Sitting on the banks of the Golden Horn, Aliée Istanbul originally began life as the Aynalıkavak Pavilion before later becoming one of the city’s most important shipyards. The centuries-old property has undergone a dramatic transformation to be reborn as a hotel, but the years of history can still be felt in Aliée’s bones, namely the original stone walls and arched windows that have been left exposed in the guest rooms, and the 600-year-old hammam that is currently being restored to soon reopen as the private Heritage Villa. 

The muted color palette of the rooms and suites shows off some rather lavish furnishings, including handwoven silk Turkish rugs, bespoke bas-relief headboards, and carved dual marble sinks, as well as the sweeping views across Istanbul and the Golden Horn. The design gets ramped up a notch in the public spaces, the Little House restaurant is an actual house built inside the lobby and guests will find pink Murano chandeliers in The Pink Bar. And that’s just two of the hotel’s many F&B options. The rest of the facilities are equally impressive; there’s an Olympic sized lap pool at Aliée Swim Club, and The Well + Spa at Aliée is a vast three-level wellness area with its own swimming pool, a marble Turkish hammam, various saunas, and a mix of high tech and traditional wellness treatments.

content: A 1907 building in Pioneer Square, the city’s oldest and most historic neighborhood, is the setting for Populus Seattle, the second “carbon-positive” hotel in the United States. (The first was Populus Denver.) This means not just conservation measures like adaptive-reuse construction and a pedestrian-friendly location, but active measures like planting a tree for every hotel stay.\n\nOf course, carbon math isn’t all that matters. Populus Seattle also benefits from rooms and suites that are modern with a warm retro edge, and comforts that are substantial, if not opulent. Salt Harvest, the restaurant, serves upscale Pacific Northwest fare, while Firn, the open-air rooftop bar, shows off the redeveloped waterfront. Meanwhile a ground-floor café represents Seattle’s coffee culture, and more than a few local attractions are close at hand, from Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park to Pike Place Market and the whole of downtown.

content:
An enchanting seaside villa, built in 1919 by the Cornish Trewhella family, now hosts this stunning property, a true embodiment of Sicilian-style Dolce Vita. In the common areas — lobby, bar, and restaurant — shades of green and blue set the mood, while the walls come alive with vibrant works by local artist Alessandro Florio, inspired by the colors of traditional Sicilian carts.
Glimpses of the sea peek through the windows, best enjoyed from the panoramic pool or the exclusive beach club reserved for guests. Its terrace restaurant provides the perfect setting for unforgettable sunset aperitifs. For an even more exclusive experience, guests can dine “les pieds dans l’eau” with the Brizza dining experience — advance booking recommended.
The rooms are bright and welcoming, reflecting the relaxed, sun-kissed spirit of the location. And when you’re ready for a change of pace, a shuttle will take you to the lively heart of Taormina, at the sister property, the Grand Hotel Timeo — also reachable via the nearby funicular.

content: Stockholm is known as one of the capitals of Scandinavian design, so it’s no surprise that Stockholm Stadshotell oozes effortless cool. It took a whole roster of creatives to sensitively revive the hotel’s historic home, a late 19th century Stockholm landmark which originally paid homage to King Oscar I. It’s now a celebration of craftmanship, with minimalist rooms stylishly outfitted by the city’s top designers, from the bespoke burl wood headboards right down to the retro radios. The two restaurants, one housed in the building’s former chapel, shine a light on local ingredients and Nordic flavors with daily changing dishes that come summer, can be enjoyed al fresco in the courtyard. And to suit the Swedish temperatures all year round, there’s also a traditional Scandinavian sauna and cold plunge.

content:
It would be difficult to dream up a more picture-perfect castle-hotel experience. Ballynahinch Castle Hotel & Estate stands on 700 acres of riverside woodland in wild Connemara, offering its guests the quintessential Irish countryside experience alongside the kind of traditionally minded hospitality that’s quickly becoming a lost art.

The rooms are handsome, spacious, and up to date in their equipment, though gloriously traditional in their interior-design style. They’re divided between the 17th-century house and a newer addition, as well as a five-bedroom lodge and a six-bedroom cottage, both in an attractive contemporary-classic style.

In classic country-house style the public spaces are as inviting as the accommodations, from drawing rooms and lounges to the terrace, the café, the Fisherman’s Pub and Ranji Room, and the fine-dining Owenmore Restaurant. Meanwhile, outside the castle’s doors, activities include everything from picnics and walks to fly fishing, boating, cycling, and hiking in the mountains of Connemara.

content: To say that Marlfield House is rather understated by country-house hotel standards is not a criticism; there are grander castles in Ireland, but few places that strike such a pleasant balance between traditional luxury and modern conviviality. This 19th-century Regency-style house is certainly a splendid one, don’t get us wrong; the estate, too, has much to offer, including woodland, gardens, and a lovely ornamental lake.\n\nIn the main house are 18 bedrooms, each one antique in style and subtly modern in its comforts. The Lodge, meanwhile, is a two-bedroom cottage with a touch more privacy. And the Pond Suites are modern, sustainably constructed open-plan free-standing villas surrounded by woodland, whose interiors split the difference between country-house elegance and boutique-hotel chic. To all this Marlfield House adds a pair of restaurants, the formal Conservatory Restaurant and the more casual Duck Terrace Restaurant, Café  & Bar.

content: As outdoor-oriented travel continues to grow in popularity, places like Moab, Utah are more in demand than ever, at all levels of the market — from tented camps to luxury developments. Lionsback Resort is the latter. A hotel, complete with food and beverage service and other centralized amenities, is in the works, but the first phase of Lionsback’s development is here: a collection of residential-style casitas, designed in a modern style and outfitted with high-end comforts.\n\nThey come in two- and three-bedroom varieties, and all feature decks and patios complete with hot tubs. Fire pits and grills are available, and each one comes with a full indoor kitchen. The design is sustainable, and the lighting is Dark Sky compliant — this town is famous for, among other things, some of the best stargazing in the country. It’s also famous for its trails, a few of which are within walking distance; meanwhile, the town of Moab itself is two miles away, and the entrances to Arches and Canyonlands National Parks are not much farther.

content: Overlooking the port, and a short walk from both the beach and the center of Banyuls-sur-Mer, Villa Camille Hotel & Spa could hardly be blessed with a finer location, at the heart of one of the Côte Vermeille’s most picturesque towns. This 1888 villa is easy on the eyes as well, and that’s before you’ve even passed through its doors; what you’ll find inside is a graceful contemporary update that turns this historical structure into something timeless.\n\nThe interiors are minimalist but in a warm and organic way, and the comforts, while substantial, are unobtrusive. Much of the furniture is modernist; a nod, perhaps, to the Danish heritage of the villa’s original architect. Meanwhile the Spa NUXE features a sauna, an ice cave, and a swimming pool alongside its treatment rooms.

content: Though in technical terms it’s a bed and breakfast rather than a hotel, the experience on offer at Maison à Deux Mains is far more luxurious than what the phrase ordinarily connotes. This 18th-century residence stands at the heart of the Grand Cru town of Aÿ-Champagne, just outside of Èpernay, and was once owned by the local grower Henri Goutorbe.\n\nIn its current incarnation it retains much of its historical charm, updated with a healthy dose of contemporary glamour. The five bedrooms are on a level with those found in many a modern luxury hotel; some can be combined to form two-bedroom suites. A locally sourced breakfast is provided, and on nights when the local restaurants are closed, a five-course dinner can be arranged; champagne, naturally, is in plentiful supply.

content:
If you’ve never thought to wonder whether you’d rather sleep in a lakeside château or in a floating lodge out in the water, you’ve never been to Brindos, Lac & Château. It’s a pleasure to consider such a question, and you’ll be forced to do so when venturing to this one-of-a-kind luxury hotel in the Basque country, just inland from Biarritz. 

The estate is built around an opulent 1930s-era mansion with glamorous rooms featuring canopied beds and views over the gardens or the water. Electric boats ferry guests from the shore to a series of ten floating lodges, each with a private terrace furnished for outdoor dining or lounging. 

Facilities include the hotel’s striking spa, an outdoor pool, an elegant chocolaterie, a chic cocktail bar illuminated by modern chandeliers, and an outdoor bar set up on the pontoon with cheerful white umbrellas and picturesque lake views.

content: Birmingham, Alabama’s Painted Lady is named not for its colorful exterior — this historic 19th-century structure, handsome as it is, is finished in sandstone brick — but for the colorful life of one of the building’s former tenants, the madam-turned-cholera-nurse Louise C. content: A two-story mid-century motel alongside the Coast Highway is an auspicious beginning, in the hands of the right hotelier; Avi Brosh’s Palisociety has ample expertise with this sort of thing, and under their direction this property’s potential has now been fully realized. Le Petit Pali Laguna Beach is packed with character, both inside and out, blending coastal California cool with a healthy dose of Northeastern prep style and a pronounced European accent.\n\nIt’s less over-the-top lavish than some of its near neighbors, but that’s by design; it’s hipper than they’ll ever be, and at a small fraction of the price. None of which is to say there’s anything less than swanky about these 41 rooms and suites, with their Diptyque bath products and their Grind espresso machines. Equally important, of course, is the social life; the day begins with a champagne continental breakfast, and drinks are served by the poolside.

content: There are nine car-free villages in Switzerland, including Wengen, a picturesque hamlet on a sunny mountain terrace in the Bernese Oberland. A few minutes’ stroll from the train station and the ski lift is Braunbär Hotel & Spa. This stately wooden chalet dates back to the late 19th century, though it was thoroughly updated inside for its reopening in 2025. \n\nRooms have a retro Scandinavian look with framed vintage travel posters, globe-shaped wall sconces, and built-in benches and bookshelves made of pale wood. Many open onto private balconies with scenic views, and family rooms feature stylish bunk beds tucked away behind crimson drapery. Of the hotel’s dining venues, a restored cable car has been turned into a cozy fondue cabin for two, while the terrace with an open-air fireplace is great for après-ski. The spa’s gorgeous glass-encased pool features panoramic views of the snow-covered Alps.

content: Housed in a decorative red and white building in the design district of Santos, Hermitage Castelo Casa Chafariz is classically Portuguese in style. Despite careful renovations and luxurious upgrades inside, its five serviced apartments have an old-world air, their original dimensions and layouts intentionally preserved. The interiors blend elements of Scandinavian minimalism — white walls, sleek marble-lined kitchens, sophisticated lighting systems — with period details like quaint wooden shutters and exposed beams. \n\nEach apartment comes with elegant living and dining spaces, and some have multiple bedrooms. Still, the location in one of Lisbon’s hippest neighborhoods may be the hotel’s greatest asset. Casa Chafariz takes its name from the adjacent Chafariz da Esperança, an 18th-century fountain that’s considered a Portuguese national monument, and the surrounding neighborhood, filled with cafés, galleries, and boutiques, is delightfully walkable and picturesque.

content: There are plenty of hotels in Saint-Germain-des-Prés, but their style has always leaned towards classic rather than cool. That is, until a new wave of boutique design hotels moved in, a trend bolstered by the opening of Hôtel Dame des Arts. Designer Raphael Navot transformed the 1950s former theater with richly layered interiors, think cream-hued bedrooms warmed up with a tactile mix of wood, porcelain, and bamboo and accessorized with an eclectic mix of artworks. Select rooms come with balconies overlooking the iconic Paris rooftops; some with a glimpse of the Eiffel Tower. Downstairs, restaurant Pimpan serves a contemporary take on French cuisine and in the Saint Germain spirit, there’s live music three nights a week. Come summer head to the secret garden courtyard or rooftop bar for a hard-to-find 360-degree city view.

content: With a historic winery, a tasting room, a wine museum, an excellent restaurant, and an elegant boutique hotel, Quinta Nova de Nossa Senhora do Carmo is a place to park the rental car and stay put for a few days. It’s one of the oldest wine estates in the Douro Valley — which is itself one of the world’s earliest known wine regions — and the proprietors perfected the place over time. \n\nThe hotel occupies an 18th-century manor house overlooking terraced vineyards and the Douro River beyond. Outfitted in calming pastels and Portuguese antiques, rooms are peaceful and light-filled, and many have private terraces opening onto fragrant gardens. A traditional farm-to-table breakfast is served around a large wooden table in the winery house each morning, and the grounds feature a pretty pool, a small chapel, and quiet lounge spaces indoors and out, plus a trio of trailheads that invite scenic strolls in the surrounding hills.

content: Downtown Boulder already had plenty going for it: a stunning location at the foot of the Rockies, with a charming and thoroughly walkable commercial and entertainment district just blocks from the campus of Colorado’s flagship public university. The addition of St Julien Hotel & Spa, just off the west end of pedestrianized Pearl Street, takes it over the top, adding a thoroughly luxurious 201-room hotel to this small city’s considerable charms.\n\nThe style is contemporary-meets-classic, the interiors striking a balance between luxury-hotel elegance and Mountain West ruggedness; in the most desirable rooms the eye is drawn outside to the Flatirons, the rock formations that are Boulder’s most distinctive geological feature. The spa, meanwhile, is a substantial one, spanning some 10,000 square feet, complete with a 50-foot indoor pool. And Jill’s, the hotel’s upscale restaurant, is a versatile one, with a touch of a French accent.

content: Hotel Victoria has looked out over Stavanger’s harbor since 1900, a turreted landmark with roots as deep as the city’s modern history. Once home to the city’s first cinema, and host to royals from Norway to Siam, it has long been part of the city’s cultural fabric. Inside, the 107 rooms are individually styled with antique accents, custom furnishings, and tall windows that frame the blue waters or city streets below. Some rooms still retain original chandeliers and timber floors. Nestled right along the waterfront, with boutiques, cafés, and the old town just a few steps away, it is a classic, refreshed for today’s travelers.

content: Imagine you had a pair of stylish friends who bought and restored an old Victorian house on the Isle of Wight, stocked the kitchen with great wine and produce from the local farmer’s market, then invited you to stay for the weekend. That’s what it’s like to check in at the Terrace Rooms and Wine, a boutique guesthouse set just above Ventnor’s historic esplanade. It has just six rooms, each with a handcrafted Hypnos bed and views over the water. One has a fireplace and a charming built-in window seat, another has a clawfoot tub positioned in front of large bay windows. Everyone’s invited to a four-course breakfast and evening wine tastings led by the owner, who also cooks up a communal feast on Friday nights using only products sourced on the island. The onsite wine shop is also a great spot to pick up a bottle for a picnic or a boat ride up the coast.

Tucked into the historic Garden City district, and set, as its name promises, right on the banks of the river, its interiors draw on both Egyptian influences and European grandeur — courtesy of designer Pierre-Yves Rochon — with a stately two-story atrium at its core.

This landmark was expanded and updated over the years — the mill was dismantled and the building transformed into a half-timbered manor house in the early 1900s — but the place still oozes period charm, with Baccarat crystal chandeliers illuminating the oak-paneled dining room, champagne served on riverfront terraces, and wooden boats floating idly by. Rooms are elegant and quaint, some with sloping ceilings and alcove balconies, others with reading nooks and Jacuzzis, and all furnished with antiques. The outdoor pool and gardens are scenic spots to relax and sip apéritifs after rowing over to the hotel’s private island.

content:
The idea of a hotel that’s both luxurious and low-key is a rare thing, and something to celebrate. Here, on a hilltop above Lake Orta, is just such a place, a project conceived by a pair of architect brothers who have transformed a bit of disused farmland and an old stone watchtower into La Darbia, a thoroughly unique boutique hotel — one that’s luxe, but not ostentatious.

They take pride in the fact that not a single tree was removed to make way for the hotel. Still, each one of La Darbia’s 20 apartments manages to have a view of the lake. The style is modern-rustic in a thoughtful and original way, and the construction is of residential quality — a local master carpeneter was engaged for custom pieces.

Each unit comes with its own kitchenette, and a zero-kilometer breakfast is delivered via room service daily. You’ll want to come out and join the rest of the guests for dinner, though, as La Darbia’s restaurant, with its terrace overlooking Lake Orta, is among the hotel’s great strengths.

content:
For the daily contrast of modern urban living and millennia-old historical sites, not many places can compete with Rome. Hotel dei Barbieri, though tucked away down a quiet side street, is among the best-located Roman boutique hotels — not only is it close to the Pantheon and the Campo de’ Fiori, but it’s mere yards from the Largo di Torre Argentina, the site of some recently unearthed ruins, including the spot where Caesar is believed to have met his end.

Of course you’re also surrounded by restaurants, wine bars, gourmet food shops, boutiques, and all the other accoutrements of city-center living. As for the hotel itself, it’s a stunning update of a 17th-century building, and its interiors mix lovingly preserved period architecture with cutting-edge contemporary design — another signature of modern Italian luxury-boutique hospitality.

The hotel’s own restaurant, bar, and café are worthy additions to the neighborhood, serving exquisite local fare in an intimate and dramatic space. And while it’s more than a mere pied-à-terre, you’ll likely be spending quite a bit of time on your feet in the surrounding city — Trastevere, just across the river to the south, is home to more than its fair share of fine restaurants, and to the southeast lie the Forum and the Colosseum.

content:
While New York’s got no shortage of very fine luxury hotels, what it hasn’t got is a surplus of hotels that are both stylish and affordable. The Freehand hotels are aimed at travelers with exceptional taste, not necessarily unlimited budgets — and in the Freehand New York they’ve succeeded where many an attempt has failed, thwarted by the daunting arithmetic of the Manhattan real-estate market.

The designers, Roman and Williams, are no strangers to the New York boutique-hotel scene. Here their eclectic, retro-inspired style turns what was once a humble residential hotel into something much livelier and more livable, with simple wooden furniture and unique artworks by Bard College students. While hostels, in the shared-bedroom sense, don’t exist in New York, the Freehand is the next best thing, adding three- and four-bed bunk rooms to the typical kings, queens, and suites.

Studio is the name of the Freehand’s all-day café and restaurant, a spot that’s equally well-suited for a working lunch or the beginnings of a night out — a night that probably includes a drink at the George Washington Bar, a cocktail bar that’s classic but unfussy. Comodo, meanwhile, is a pan-Latin restaurant from the team behind Brooklyn’s Colonia Verde, serving Mexican, Colombian, Peruvian, and Brazilian flavors interpreted from a New York point of view.

content:
You’d be hard pressed to find a more exemplary hospitality success story than casa9 in Mexico City. Originally built in the early 20th century as a decadent private residence for a wealthy family, the home slowly fell into disrepair and became lost in the vast expanse of the city. Decrepit and overgrown with local fauna, the house was left neglected for decades before a new family eventually purchased the structure, and they were quick to give it a second chance at life along with a top-to-bottom makeover. Now — years later and world away from where it was — it exists as one of the most exquisite bed and breakfasts in Mexico City.

With just four rooms, everything about casa9 is intimate. Architects Rafael Rivera and Javier Claveri (of trailblazing architectural firm Habitación 116) are known for their playful and experimental designs, and that’s something that’s on full display here. Wood paneling that recalls mid-century modernism, floor-to-ceiling window walls, and elegant, minimal furnishings that would make the Eameses blush — that’s the look in a nutshell.

The location, too, can’t be overlooked. It’s well situated in La Condesa, which is designated as a “Barrio Mágico Turístico” along with neighboring Roma. Together, these two neighborhoods are considered the center of the creative communities in the city, as well as two of the most architecturally significant neighborhoods in all of Mexico City — not hard to see why it’d be a desirable spot for the sort of person who’d call casa9 home.
