content:
Please note: Amangani will be closed from April 7 2025 - Summer 2025 for renovations.

The legendary Amangani is not just Jackson Hole’s most exclusive resort, but its most impressive as well. This was the first outpost of the Singapore-based Aman chain in the Americas — and should Wyoming seem an odd choice for a brand mostly known for Bali-style luxury spas, one look at the hotel itself will convince you of its absolute rightness.

Amangani’s location is extraordinary: set at seven thousand feet above sea level, it’s carved into the hillside at Gros Ventre Butte, overlooking the meadowed valley of Jackson Hole with a view of Teton Pass and the Snake River Range in the distance. It’s an imposing structure, hewn from rough Oklahoma sandstone with accents of glass and Pacific redwood — a sort of Eastern minimalist take on a rustic Western theme, and unlike anything in Wyoming if not all of the Rockies.

There’s an understated glamour to the interiors, which tread a middle path between luxury-hotel opulence and international boutique minimalism — constant is the insistence on fine craftsmanship and materials, and the distinct Asian influence is pervasive yet never kitschy.

It’s hard to imagine suites more comfortable or luxurious than these. Each includes a fireplace, king-sized platform bed, and a private balcony with a commanding view of the valley below. Bathrooms are impossibly spacious, with slate walls, redwood floors, separate showers, and deep soaking tubs with mountain views.

The Grill serves breakfast, lunch and dinner in a 65-seat redwood-paneled dining room. The cuisine is Western with organic leanings, serving steaks and seafood with regional produce. A zinc-top bar and a lounge with vast two-story windows overlooking the Tetons offer venues for drinks and socializing.

And no Aman resort would be complete without a world-class spa. This one, perhaps unsurprisingly, emphasizes physical fitness over decadent pampering, though the latter is certainly available. Outside a hundred-foot swimming pool and whirlpool take in views of Wyoming’s snow-capped peaks — possibly the perfect image to convey the contrast that makes Amangani so unusual.

How to get there: Amangani is located about 20 minutes from Jackson Hole Airport.

content:
We always liked Liz Lambert’s style, beginning with her first ventures, Austin’s stylish and urbane Hotel San Jose and the luxe, bohemian Saint Cecilia. El Cosmico, however, has left the traditional hotel world behind, trading in rooms and suites for trailers, yurts, tents and tepees, a sort of post-hippie hospitality commune on the outskirts of Marfa, itself something of an oasis of creativity in the vast expanse of west Texas.

Architects Lake/Flato and Jack Sanders of Design Build Adventure are responsible for the design, such as it is, and while landscape designers rarely get top billing in hotel projects, this place would be dirt if not for the work of Mark Word and Billy Spencer. But the most immediately noticeable design elements are the vintage Fifties trailers — which, at El Cosmico, are essentially the luxury suites.

Clearly this experience is going to have to involve an expansion of one’s comfort zone. Only one of the trailers, the Imperial Mansion, has an indoor shower, making it the closest equivalent of a presidential suite — the others move their facilities outdoors. Further on down the range are the yurts and tepees, with facilities shared in the central bath house. And for a nominal fee you can pitch a tent on site, making the El Cosmico experience available to pretty much anyone with the wherewithal to get there.

That experience includes not just a supremely mellow communal atmosphere and close access to Marfa, but a few other things besides — wood-fired Dutch hot tubs, for one, and a shared outdoor kitchen and barbecue area. The long-term vision for the place involves music festivals and all manner of countercultural happenings — and of course there’s nothing stopping you from pulling up, pitching a tent, and making your own entertainment.

The Barcelona-based Mercer chain is known for hotels that thrive on the contrast between historical architecture and modern interiors, and the Hotel EME Catedral Mercer is perhaps the purest example of this tendency. Not only do its sleek, minimalist spaces stand behind a 16th-century façade, but the hotel directly faces Seville’s cathedral and La Giralda, its Moorish bell tower.

From the rooftop pool the view of the cathedral is perhaps at its most extraordinary, though some of the suites have terraces in positions that are scarcely less advantageous. For the most part, however, the hotel is oriented inward, toward a central courtyard, in the classic Andalusian manner, providing a soothing shelter from the light and heat of the day. And the rooms themselves, modern though they are, borrow arabesque patterns for their interior ornamentation.

To these considerable charms the EME Catedral Mercer adds what might be a surprising amount of social life. The rooftop terrace at night becomes a venue for music and cocktails with a view of the city, and is joined by the Corner, the hotel’s lobby bar. Meanwhile Mi Arma serves the distinctive local cuisine with a view of La Giralda, and Al Lado is the Italian option with the open kitchen.

Out-of-town guests could be forgiven for believing that Miami Beach and Miami are one and the same. But if you never set foot on the mainland, you’ll miss out on Little Havana, one of Miami’s most unique neighborhoods. And that means missing out on Life House Little Havana, the first hotel from a hospitality startup (!) that aims to deliver a luxury-boutique experience at a price that its competitors can’t match.

Here they’ve given an existing hotel a contemporary-classic makeover, resulting in rooms that look a bit more like Hemingway’s Miami — dark wood and colonial atmosphere — than they do the fashion hotels of South Beach. Rooms come in king and queen sizes, as well as suites, including one with four capsule-style bunks, ideal for a traveling band or a group that doesn’t need much privacy.

As for public spaces, the garden courtyard is a splendid place for a drink, to say nothing of the rooftop bar and restaurant. And while staying in feels cozy enough, you’re encouraged to get out and experience Little Havana, the heart of Cuban culture in the United States; Life House’s staff are on hand with recommendations. The Life House ethos is one of travel as a transformative experience, which is a philosophy we’re more than a little bit partial to ourselves.

content:
Walk into a good boutique hotel in Milan and you’ll understand something about the city itself. This is Italy’s financial center, the capital of industry, presiding over one of the largest economies in the EU. It stands to reason that the best hotels in town are a far cry from the romantic waterfront palaces of Venice or the quirky pied-à-terres of Rome. The Milanese ideal is smart and sleek, stylish yet eminently suited for business, and always quietly but forcefully impressive. Senato Hotel Milan is an excellent example — but not in the dark, heavy, masculine manner that’s become something of a Milanese luxury-hotel trademark. 

It’s located in a historic building, though one that’s practically new by Italian standards: a Neoclassical urban mansion, dating from the early 1900s, once a wealthy family’s private residence. But there’s little nostalgia here for days gone by. Apart from the facade, and structural details from high arching windows to a wrought-iron railing snaking up the rear staircase, there’s little to remind you of the building’s past. Lined with smooth marble, the place is modern and elegant — minimalist with extravagant accents, from the lobby’s glowing lamps, handcrafted in the shape of a ginkgo tree, to its unusual wood furnishings and brass tables, each unique and custom-designed by the Italian architect Alessandro Bianchi. He was the mind behind the entire project, in fact, his visions brought to life by a meticulous team of Italian craftsmen.

Upstairs, the 43 guest rooms are spare and silent. The sophistication is in the details, from the Carrara marble bathrooms to the handcrafted brass lamps. In classic Milanese style, the floors are laid with herringbone oak, but the decor is almost entirely white; state-of-the-art soundproofing blocks the noise of the city outside. The result is a space so calm and pristine that you almost feel guilty unpacking your suitcase and disturbing the balance. Some of the better rooms have small private terraces, while spacious Junior Suites have larger garden terraces with views over the Duomo and the city skyline. 

You’ll sleep surprisingly well here: appropriate, as you, like everybody else, probably have plenty on your Milan agenda. Stop by the Senato Hotel’s buffet breakfast for a pick-me-up caffé — if you’re truly doing as the Milanese do, it’s sure to be one of many.

As hotel concepts go, it’s not a difficult one to get your head around: simple, sunny, clean-lined, colorful design, with a city-center location, personable service, at a nightly rate that doesn’t require a phone consultation with a financial planner. In a perfect world it wouldn’t be hard to find, but in this world a hotel like Hotel One Shot Prado 23, in Madrid, is something rather special.

Spanish hotel chains, lately, excel at this sort of thing, and if this one is any indication, One Shot won’t be a one-shot for long. (In fact there’s a second already in the works, but never let facts spoil a good joke.) With wood floors, white walls, selectively applied bursts of vivid color, and an inspired selection of modernist chairs and ultra-contemporary fixtures, this is a look that just about anybody can wear well — and no longer is it the exclusive province of the so-called “luxury boutique.”

It bears mentioning that the concept is fairly hands-off; besides a tea-and-coffee setup on each floor, there's no food or drink program to speak of, and you'll likely have to handle your luggage yourself. That said, it’s perfectly placed for doing the arts-and-culture circuit of Madrid, and as a pied-à-terre it offers just enough comfort to be getting on with — this isn’t a hotel for holing up, it’s a home base, and an exceedingly sharp-looking one at that. To take full advantage, rent an electric bike and ask for a custom contemporary-art itinerary.

content: The east side of Paris is hipper than ever, thanks in part to a vibrant youth culture that stands in stark contrast to the much-mythologized tourist sites closer to the center. Ten years ago it would have been strange to stay in a hotel that’s closer to Belleville and Père Lachaise cemetery than to the Louvre or Notre-Dame. But that’s exactly where the hôtel de la Nouvelle République is — five minutes from the Place de la République, from which it takes part of its name — and with its retro-inspired, earth-toned contemporary interiors, it presents a fresh, comfortable, and attainable perspective on modern Parisian hospitality.\n\nAnother benefit of its location in the 11th is that the Hôtel de la Nouvelle République offers exceptional value for money. And while you certainly wouldn’t compare it to the city’s five-star palace hotels, it’s not at all spartan — not only are the tactile comforts well-chosen, but you’ll find details like triple-glazed windows, reading lights, and tablets loaded with thousands of magazine titles. Breakfast is served in the hotel’s café, and you’re welcome to help yourself to coffee and tea throughout the day.

When the first One Shot hotel opened, we had a feeling that, despite the name, there’d be more. After all, who can resist a stylish, youthful update to Madrid’s stately, formal atmosphere? Hotel One Shot Fortuny 07 is located in Almagro, an upscale neighborhood that’s home to embassies, art galleries, expensive homes, and high-end shops and restaurants. Which is to say, a hotel could get away with being a whole lot more conservative than this one.

Instead you’ll find these elegant spaces, with their hardwood floors and Art Deco flourishes, livened up with curvaceous modern furniture, adventurous contemporary artworks, and accents in eye-popping Klein blue. Single rooms start out at a cozy 15 square meters, but come with comfy beds, work desks, and rainfall showers. And as you move up into Executive and Premium rooms, on your way up to the One Shot Suite, you’ll add plenty of interior space, and, in the suite, a bathtub and a private terrace.

The public spaces, it must be said, are still something of a work in progress. A fine breakfast and a serviceable fitness room are well-established, as is an art gallery showing a series of photography exhibitions. Coming soon is Olivia te Cuida, an outpost of a well-loved local restaurant; in the meantime the staff is happy to recommend the best bites in Almagro.

We love a hotel that reinvents its genre, but the classic Lake Como luxury-hotel experience is one that doesn’t exactly cry out for revision. Here in Moltrasio, a sleepy town on the western shore a short drive from the town of Como, you’ll find the Grand Hotel Imperiale Resort & Spa, a 1922 Art Nouveau gem that’s more than up to the task of delivering the archetypal Como holiday: an atmosphere of elegance, a spectacular setting, and comforts that are nothing if not restorative.

The spa complex itself is modern both in its treatments and in its architecture and design, but it doesn’t detract from the atmosphere a bit — the rooms and suites, meanwhile, remain true to the hotel’s century-old style, both in the main hotel and in the stunning semi-private Villa Imperiale.

A dramatic lakeside swimming pool is among the Imperiale’s greatest strengths, as are its two restaurants: the more casual Ulivo serves guests in the hotel’s garden, while the more formal Imperialino is set right at the lakeside, and serves simple but unmistakably high-end Italian fare with the sort of view that’s precisely why you came to Lake Como in the first place.

In a restored Art Deco building in the newly christened Faena District of Miami Beach, the eclectic and accessible Hotel Trouvail establishes itself in what’s probably the most laid-back place on the East Coast, and thus the most natural home for the stylishly relaxed vibe you’ll find on display here.

Where many of Miami Beach’s boutique hotels are forbiddingly formal in their style, the Trouvail is stylish in a more approachable way. The rooms and studios have a residential feel, and many come with kitchenettes for a bit of self-catering. They’re low-key but quite attractive, and though they avoid all the clichés of Miami Beach hospitality design, they certainly don’t feel out of place. 

Nor does Greenbrier Swim & Social, except insofar as a multi-purpose dining space with a pool, a lounge, a patio and an all-day menu of American-meets-Mediterranean fare and creative cocktails is less common than it should be in South Beach. And while the hotel is set a block and a half back from the beach, its Beach Butlers can arrange transportation to some of the best spots, along with beach chairs, umbrellas, towels, and even a packed lunch. Some travelers may well prefer the fashion-show velvet-rope atmosphere of some other Miami boutique hotels, but for many of us the casual-chic Hotel Trouvail is likely to become a favorite.

content:
A stone path leads past the green grass, hedgerows, and delphiniums to a honey-colored fifteenth-century manor house. The damp air is sweet with the scent of hydrangea. In the lobby, chintz cushions soften the flagstone floors, fireplaces, and wood beamed ceilings. It couldn't be more English, except for the fact that Le Manoir aux Quat'Saisons, A Belmond Hotel is the brainchild of a Frenchman, the celebrated chef Raymond Blanc.

And this Frenchman has made sure to make Le Manoir more playful than your typical English country home. Throughout there are touches designed to tweak the notorious stiff upper lip. No matter what time of day, a bottle of Champagne awaits. And the baths are naughtily large, with candles ready for lighting. In one room, twin baths lie side by side underneath a canopy — and Le Manoir is the first house in the country to sport bathrooms that open onto bedrooms, ensuring that your pleasure is seamless.

But just as Le Manoir is un-English in its surroundings, it is equally un-French in its food. The self-taught chef Raymond Blanc scorns the trappings usually affiliated with haute cuisine. “The protocol of the table kills the joy,” he explains. The vast grounds outside include the two acre kitchen garden, where he grows his own vegetables and herbs. And though the dishes are divine — deep sea scallops and macaroni in black truffle cream, with the Burgundy and Sancerre flowing like nectar — and the prices admittedly steep, everywhere in the dining room is the buzz of lively conversation and the relaxed expressions of people having an unpretentious good time.

There's no gym or pool at Le Manoir; for those in dire need of exercise, there's croquet, and the hotel also hosts one of the most respected cooking schools in the country, for anyone interested in duplicating their meals at home. Otherwise wander around the grounds safe in the knowledge that like in most ancient country homes, there was once a poltergeist in residence, but superstitiously-bent Blanc has had it exorcised.

How to get there: Le Manoir aux Quat'Saisons, A Belmond Hotel is about a 50-minute drive from Heathrow Airport or an hour from London proper. Alternatively, guests can take a 45-minute train ride from Marylebone to Haddenham and Thame station (10 minutes from the hotel) or a 1-hour train ride from Paddington station to Oxford station, which is 25 minutes from the hotel.

content:
Sure, it’s a Metro ride away from the sights of central Madrid, the Royal Palace, the opera house, the museums; but for the sort of travelers who’ll stay here, the Hotel Puerta America is a sight unto itself. It’s practically a museum of modern architecture and design, from John Pawson’s lobby and Christian Liaigre’s restaurant up through floors by Zaha Hadid, Norman Foster, Marc Newson and Ron Arad, to name just a few.

And of course what makes the Hotel Puerta America better than any design museum is the fact that you get to live, at least temporarily, inside the exhibits. Zaha Hadid’s rooms, for example, are molded from black, white or orange plastic, and their flowing forms recall anything from ice caves to sci-fi film sets — anything, that is, except the traditional square hotel room.

The same goes for the higher floors; though some of the architects and designers are ever so slightly more traditional, all the work is completely fresh, and these rooms look like no hotel interiors you’ve ever seen. And while the demands of form require some adjustments in function there’s really very little for even the most pampered luxury traveler to miss — business facilities are plentiful, the top-floor “attic” contains a fitness center and a rooftop bar with an inspiring view, and the hotel’s ground-floor bar and restaurant are stunning and successful spaces.

content: It may sound like some kind of all-inclusive Caribbean resort, but Pillows Luxury Boutique Hotel Anna Van Den Vondel Amsterdam is located just to the southwest of Amsterdam’s city center, far from any beach, in a row of beautifully restored 19th-century buildings. All the same, it’s not exactly the grittiest version of urban living. With the verdant Vondelpark just steps away, and with views of its own private garden — not to mention rooms and suites that are piled high with luxe comforts — it’s more than deserving of its exceedingly soothing name.\n\nIn fact there’s something almost cloudlike about Pillows’ rooms and suites, with their velvety textures and subdued soft colors. Period architectural details like French balconies or overhead beams combine with a clean-lined, contemporary visual style. The look is sleek but the textures are enveloping, and what the bedrooms may lack in pure square footage — this is still Amsterdam, after all — they more than make up for in coziness. And it’s not just the private spaces that trade in gentle comfort; the Living is what they call the restaurant and lounge, with its large central fireplace, and it’s open around the clock, a boon to those of us who find irresistible the temptation to oversleep.

Proof that the boom in Portuguese boutique hospitality isn’t confined to the mainland. Sul Villas & Spa is set on a cliff high above the southern shore of São Miguel Island, in the Azores, overlooking waters that owner Rodrigo Herédia knows well — he was a pro surfer before embarking on a career as a hotelier. Sul Villas, though, is less a surf shack and more a high-design boutique-style resort, one where you’ll likely spend more time in infinity pools and soaking tubs than paddling out to catch the next set.

With just twelve suites it’s a decidedly small-scale operation, though there’s naturally nothing small about the comforts. Kitchenettes and private terraces are universal; some of the larger suites add jacuzzis or private plunge pools. And along with the clean-lined contemporary design, modern conveniences like air conditioning, wi-fi, and Bluetooth sound systems are available as a matter of course.

Beyond breakfast and some light poolside fare you’re on your own, but the restaurants of the village of Santa Cruz and the town of Lagoa — both within walking distance — are more than capable of filling the gap. For the most part, this is a low-key, low-maintenance escape, though the staff can arrange all manner of activities, from nature walks on up to diving, surfing, and swimming with dolphins.

Sharing a bit of hotel DNA with New York’s Dream hotels, and fresh off a total renovation at the hands of the Rockwell Group, the Time New York stands, as you might suspect, a few blocks from Times Square. It’s also given, as you might suspect, to certain flights of surrealism, as are the Dream hotels — but where the old Time was all bold primary colors, the new Time is soothing pastels and soft watercolors, against relatively sedate monochrome backgrounds.

After all, the last thing you need in a Midtown hotel room, a few stories above some of the busiest streets in America, is a neon light show. These rooms are far from dull, though — they’re quietly stylish, tightly composed, and eminently comfortable, making the most of their relatively economical spaces. (Less economical and more extravagant are the expansive Deluxe Suites and the sprawling Penthouse, naturally.) Add up-to-date in-room technology and a couple of frills — Frette linens and Margiela bathrobes — and you’re in business.

The hotel’s own fitness center opens any day now, and until then you’re a guest at Equinox, down the street. Also newly opened are Serafina, the all-day restaurant with a Northern Italian menu, and LeGrande Lounge, just off the lobby. And with midtown Manhattan at your feet, you don’t need to limit yourself to dining in — you’re in probably the best-served square mile of North America, from a dining and drinking perspective.

content:
Travelers in search of a bit of that old-fashioned Spanish castle magic are unlikely to be disappointed by Castell d’Empordà, a very thorough reconstruction of a long-abandoned medieval castle in the mountains just outside of Girona. What does come as some surprise is how much red meat there is for fans of contemporary architecture. For while the medieval construction provides the skeleton of the place — as well as the greater portion of the character of the main building’s rooms — the owners haven’t been shy about introducing modern elements, from the furnishings in the castle’s bedrooms to the stunning parasol-like design of the restaurant’s rust-colored roof.

The Castle and Tower rooms, located in the original building, are the most atmospheric of the lot, their medieval stone walls accented with well-chosen furnishings, both modern and antique. Meanwhile the Garden rooms and suites offer more space as well as a more contemporary aspect, in a subtle modern structure next to the old castle. The shared spaces continue this marriage of old and new, from the lounges to the restaurant to the wine-cellar bar or the rooftop terrace — there’s not a single space in the Castell that’s anything less than dramatic.

And while we don’t wish to traffic too heavily in cultural stereotypes, we can’t imagine anyone will be terribly shocked to learn that the Castell d’Emporda’s owners — and, perhaps more to the point, its architects — are Dutch. Sometimes it takes an outsider’s perspective to make the most of the local traditions; whatever the case, there’s no denying that the contrast between the ancient structure and the contemporary interventions is an inspiring one.

Please note: Castell d’Emporda closes seasonally from mid-November to April. 

How to get there:
Castell d'Emporda is located 50.7 km from Girona Airport and 138 km from Barcelona Airport.

content: Those for whom the Dream Midtown is a recurring one may find themselves feeling a bit of whatever the opposite of déja vu is — a feeling that, despite the evidence, they haven’t been here before. Chalk that up to a substantial renovation, which has left one of Broadway’s most accessibly stylish boutique hotels looking more fetching than ever. Here it’s possible to hide in plain sight, more or less midway between Times Square and Columbus Circle. The rooms are compact, but not cramped, with plenty of space for a comfortable allergen-free bed and a bathroom with fixtures in Carrara marble, not to mention wi-fi and 40-inch televisions. With a sunny palette and accents in chartreuse and aubergine they’re rooms you’re happy to come home to, and they’re certainly conducive to a decent night’s sleep (along with requisite dreaming). At least as much energy has been put into the Dream’s new public spaces, from Serafina, the Fellini-inspired restaurant, to The Rickey, a throwback-themed cocktail bar by mixologist Jimmy Swet. The crowning achievement, however, has to be PHD Terrace, twin sister of Dream Downtown’s PHD Rooftop Lounge — here, rain or shine, you’ll take in far-ranging views of Midtown Manhattan while also taking in music by a rotating roster of DJs and drinks by a team of expert bartenders.

content:
There’s pedigree and then there’s pedigree. This hotel is housed in a palace owned by a princess, and it’s named after one of its most famous guests, Napoleon III, who lived here in 1830. None of which would matter all that much if Residenza Napoleone III weren’t still a deeply pleasurable place to stay, as unapologetically opulent, one has to imagine, as the day the emperor checked in. That the hotel is located right off Via Condotti, an easy walk from Rome’s best high-end shopping and many of its major sights, is almost beside the point; Residenza Napoleone III is a destination unto itself, and staying there a singular experience (as it ought to be, given its singular price point). 

Actually, there are two experiences on offer — that of living like an emperor, in the Napoleon suite, and that of staying in the quirky guest apartment of a latter-day royal family, in the Garden suite. Either way, to get there you pass through a pair of massive wooden doors, walk through an arcade lined with Doric columns, and climb a staircase stacked with antique marble busts. Needless to say there are attendants to take care of the luggage. If you’re staying in the Napoleon suite, you’ll be surrounded by enormous oil paintings, 16th-century tapestries and hand-stenciled walls, your bed covered in Italian linens and velvet pillows and surrounded by silk drapes. The marble bathroom is stocked with Bulgari toiletries. Breakfast is served en-suite with proper silver. As for the plasma screens, the plumbing, the air conditioning, the Bose sound system — yes, it all works just fine, because while the fantasy is fun, no one really wants to live exactly like a 19th-century emperor. 

In the Roof Garden suite, the opulence is slightly less extravagant, the fittings relatively contemporary. A quirky layout — spiral stairs to reach the entrance, stairs down to the little nook of a bedroom, stairs even farther down to the tiny bathroom — acts as a reminder that this is indeed a converted old palace, not a purpose-built hotel. It’s a slight compromise compared to the every-comfort-accounted-for Napoleon suite, but that’s a very high bar. The payoff for these (trifling) inconveniences comes in the form of a spectacular, multi-level terrace, bursting with herbs in terra-cotta pots and overlooking the roofs of the Eternal City. There’s any number of vantage points for admiring the city’s landmarks. It’s possible to get closer, at street level, but that’s awfully far away.

content:
We’ve long sung the praises of American mid-century motels as raw material for modern boutique hotels, but the Phoenix Hotel has been at it for longer than we’ve been online. San Francisco’s original rock-and-roll hotel was a counterculture haunt in the ’80s and ’90s, and thanks to a courtyard with space to park a tour bus — and a neighborhood that was, shall we say, tolerant of a bit of revelry — it was the lodging of choice for rock stars from David Bowie to Nirvana. 

And just when it was beginning to feel like it had lost touch with its roots, it’s been taken over by Bunkhouse, the Texas-based hotel group headed up by Liz Lambert, whose Austin hotels are perennial favorites. It’s an inspired combination, one that effortlessly improves the Phoenix’s style and atmosphere without sacrificing its rock-and-roll spirit. 

It’s no luxury hotel, but it’s perfectly comfortable, and it’s every bit the musician’s favorite it once was — there’s no telling who you’ll find sitting by the pool, or occupying a booth at Chambers eat + drink, the hotel’s restaurant and bar. Here in the Tenderloin you’re close to most of San Francisco’s downtown neighborhoods, and close to no fewer than three legendary concert venues: a half-mile from the Fillmore, a few blocks from the Warfield, and right around the corner from the best of them, the Great American Music Hall.

content:
Yes, this is Tuscany, but not the Tuscany of vineyards and olive groves — this is the Maremma, the province’s seaside region, which presents to travelers an altogether different face. The Sense Experience Resort is set amid pine trees by the beach, just outside the village of Follonica. And while its weathered stone construction is a reminder of Tuscany’s deep history, what lies inside is a luxurious, health-conscious eco-resort that’s as modern as they come.

It’s modern not just in design — though the carefully controlled color palette and the organic-inspired graphic geometries certainly are that — but in concept as well, combining personal wellness and ecological health in a way that verges on the devotional. The accommodations are luxurious, lacking nothing in terms of comfort, but the atmosphere is more restorative than decadent.

And rather than loll about some Renaissance villa, waiting for the next pour of wine, you’re encouraged to get out and about, whether to the hotel’s pool, the beach, a yoga class, or for a bike ride, a round of golf, or a bit of sailing or diving. Don’t worry — they’ll be pouring wine when you return, accompanied by fresh and healthy fare from the Sense’s modern Tuscan restaurant.

content: Just to the north of the souk in the Sidi Ben Slimane district is Riad 144, and you’ll have the quintessential “am I lost?” Marrakech medina experience as you wind your way down a rabbit’s warren of alleys on your way to the house’s heavy front door. But once you’re through, you’ll find you’re in for something a bit more dramatic than the ordinary riad hotel. Not that the ordinary riad hotel is a hard time, by any means — but Riad 144 turns the intensity up to 11 and throws away the knob.\n\nAll the better to maximize the contrast between a difficult, often overwhelming city and the oasis of calm that every riad aspires to be. Here four suites, two “mini-suites,” and two bedrooms — some of which can be combined, for more advanced permutations — come decorated in distinct individual styles, some dark and moody, others bright and sunny. And while it’s notable for its intensity, it is, underneath it all, absolutely traditional, down to the tadelakt and moucharabieh. As is the hospitality — here you’ll engage in time-honored riad pursuits like lounging in the courtyard, watching the sunset from the rooftop, decompressing in the hammam, and enjoying housemade traditional Moroccan cuisine for breakfast, lunch and dinner.

content: An ethos of “pure love” — plus a clothing-optional beach, and, crucially, no kids. This, in a nutshell, is the appeal of Azulik, a wellness-oriented retreat on the Caribbean coast of Tulum, a town that is itself somewhere in the space between the unspoiled idyll of an undiscovered escape and the buzzing excitement of one of the region’s hippest destinations. Azulik, like Tulum, is a bit of both; but its tranquil atmosphere and its unusual architecture, ecologically sensitive approach, and low-tech comforts tip the balance more towards serenity than revelry.\n\nTo that end the villas are without televisions and without electric light. (Don’t fret, there’s a plug for charging your devices.) What they do have is Mayan mosaic bathtubs, decks with daybeds, and views of the surrounding jungle and/or the waters of the Caribbean. Three restaurants span an impressive range, from avant-garde Mayan cuisine to traditional Mexican fare and — taking advantage of the seaside location — sushi. And it wouldn’t be a wellness resort without an impressive spa, based on ancient Mayan rituals but offering treatments that are perfectly familiar to international spagoers. Tulum may not be the end of the world anymore, but Azulik is as calming as it gets.

content:
Viewed from the right angle, Tel Aviv looks as sophisticated as any of Europe’s style capitals. One such angle is framed by the rooftop lounge of the Brown TLV Urban Hotel, which frames the skyline’s nighttime panorama. Or from more or less anywhere inside the Brown, come to think of it — from the Seventies-inspired décor of the Living Room to the sleeker, more contemporary look of the Brown’s 30 swanky bedrooms.

They’re billed as “intimate” and “urban-sized,” which, yes, is a polite way of saying they’re a little on the small side. They won’t feel cramped, though; with big plush beds, work stations, walk-in showers and plenty of closet space, there’s not much more you’d ask for. The smallest are aimed at the solo traveler, while those at the higher end of the range add sitting areas or small balconies.

A single spa suite caters to guests in need of a little pampering, a chic little meeting space offers the city’s best-looking boardroom, and they’re working on opening a restaurant — until then you’re in the capable hands of a couple of neighboring cafés. There’s nothing particularly revolutionary about it, except for the location — it’s high time Tel Aviv, with its famously glamorous nightlife, got the boutique hotel it so richly deserves.

content: Paris’s 15th arrondissement is underrepresented on the boutique-hotel map of Paris, but Hôtel Clarisse will change that. In fact a little bit of physical distance from the ordinary tourist haunts means a little bit of a thematic departure from the archetypal Parisian experience — and a location in a less expensive corner of town makes for truly affordable nightly rates. The design leans heavily on industrial and salvaged materials, and the public spaces are more British in aspect than typically Parisian. One thing that is absolutely typically Parisian — Clarisse’s rooms are cozy, though their uncluttered design means they don’t feel cramped, and the triple and quadruple rooms quite comfortably sleep three and four, respectively. This is meant to be a pied-à-terre, not a second home, and the time you do spend in the rooms will be easy on the eyes; a recent renovation leaves them looking stylish and utterly modern, in a color scheme of navy and white with mosaic-tiled bathrooms. As for the location, it’s in an unexpectedly green setting, adjacent to the Parc Georges-Brassens and the Porte de Versailles Exhibition Centre — while a metro stop of the same name connects you to the rest of the city within minutes.

content:
Safe to say there’s nothing else quite like it in New York City. Governors Island, of course, isn’t exactly typical of New York neighborhoods — set between Brooklyn and the Statue of Liberty, a short water-taxi ride from Pier 25 in Manhattan, it’s a city park that enjoys unparalleled views and an inimitable atmosphere, one that’s impressively pastoral given that you could swim to Brooklyn from here (in principle; don’t try it).

Collective Governors Island offers the sort of grown-up summer-camp experience you’d ordinarily drive to the Catskills to find, accompanied by live entertainment and cocktails on the Sunset Terrace. Tents feature air conditioning, en suite bathrooms, Frette robes, and high-end bath products, and the top-end Outlook Shelter is a cabin-like structure with an indoor soaking tub facing the Statue of Liberty.

Activities include mindfulness, meditation, and yoga sessions, as well as food and beverage classes ranging from wine tasting to lobster poaching and oyster shucking. Meanwhile, each morning, a buffet breakfast is served in the main tent — and dinner options range from a la carte seafood to a five-course tasting menu. And it’s not the only game in town — Governors Island has a few restaurants of its own, including a very fine oyster bar.

Smaller hotels like Collective Governors Island fill up quickly. If you can’t find what you’re looking for, contact us and we can help.

content: When it opened, a little over a half-century ago, the Kahala immediately turned heads, as much for its opulence as for its audacious location, in an upscale neighborhood around the sedate far side of Diamond Head from busy Waikiki Beach. It didn’t take long for this revolutionary to become the establishment, however, and the Kahala quickly became the place to stay in Honolulu, playing host to entertainers, heads of state, and every American president since Lyndon Johnson. And while it’s kept itself quite up to date in the ways that matter, the Kahala still exudes a certain mid-century charm, an attribute that’s a decided advantage in this era of rough-edged, funky boutique hotels. There’s a time and a place for those, of course, but a hotel like the Kahala is for when you want a touch of that old-fashioned, discreet, white-glove treatment. (White gloves purely metaphorical; this being Honolulu, even the top hotel in town keeps it casual.) It’s also where you go when you want Honolulu minus the crowds. The Kahala’s beach is blissfully quiet, the service is friendly and personal, and four high-end restaurants treat you to some of the island’s best cooking. And the activities are beyond compare; scuba, surfing, and stand-up paddle lessons are a matter of course, but how many hotels have a family of dolphins living in a lagoon, attended by trainers and marine biologists?

content:
Rome’s got enough monuments already, to say the least, which is why, in this city, even the best high-end hotels are more likely to be smaller-scale, lower-profile boutique-style properties. That’s certainly the concept behind the Hotel NH Collection Roma Fori Imperiali. It’d be foolish to try to compete on sheer grandeur with its surroundings — it looks directly out over the Altare della Patria, and stands at the top of the Via dei Fori Imperiali, with the Colosseum at the other end and the ruins of the Roman Forum along both sides.

42 rooms and suites isn’t quite bed-and-breakfast territory, but neither is it terribly large, and there’s a touch of upscale residential atmosphere, which is something Rome excels at. The style is contemporary, and a touch minimalistic, but thanks to mural-sized wallpaper illustrations depicting historic Roman villas, there’s a strong current of imperial opulence as well.

The views from many of the rooms are extraordinary, but the best ones are to be found on the rooftop, at the Secret View cocktail bar. The only question is: rooftop cocktail at sunset, before dinner at the Restaurant Oro Bistrot by Natale Giunta, or after? Perhaps the safest choice is to do both....

content: The Dakhla Lagoon, on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, is notable as a destination for windsurfing and other water sports. It’s also the site of Caravan by Habitas Dakhla, a sort of seafaring counterpart to the brand’s luxury camp in the Agafay Desert outside of Marrakech. Caravan Dakhla is nothing if not immersive; Habitas aims not only to preserve the natural environment, but to bring guests in close contact with the local culture, and the local culture is present here in every aspect of the experience, from the interior design to the artistic and educational programming.\n\nIts accommodations freely mix classic riad style with modern loft touches like floor-to-ceiling windows with views of the lagoon. All throughout, they’re stylish but also painstakingly localized, and they feel warm and handmade even as they incorporate modern high-tech comforts. A partnership with the kitesurfing brand Naish means it’s possible even for a novice rider to get out on the water; some still prefer to lounge by the pool or take an art or cooking class. Levante, the restaurant, brings everyone together under one roof with a menu that marries Moroccan cooking with Latin American influences.

content:
Somewhere between a mini-resort and a boutique hotel, Belmond La Résidence d’Angkor is just about as close as you can get to the heart of Siem Reap — which, in turn, is the closest city to what is for many Cambodia’s main attraction, the temples at Angkor. The hotel stands right at the river’s edge, and a short walk from the bustling city market.

What’s more important, though, is what’s within its walls. With just fifty-five rooms, it’s not terribly large, and feels even more private from within the bedrooms — they’re generously sized, with ample bathrooms behind sliding doors, and private balconies that look out over the lush central courtyard and the pool. It’s a modern building in classic Khmer style, and the interiors walk that same line between contemporary and traditional — clean lines, white walls, but with hardwood floors and traditional wooden furnishings.

One thing that makes the Belmond a mini-resort rather than a maxi- is the absence of a dedicated spa complex; massages and spa treatments are available in-room, however. A restaurant, a lounge and a pool bar are perhaps more options than you’d expect — turn inward and make it a self-contained resort experience if you wish, or get out and sample the street life, the street food, and the unmissable Angkor Wat.

content:
Though the national borders are of secondary importance when it comes to the Alps — nature doesn’t much care whether it’s in Italy, or Austria, or Switzerland — you know you’re in Italian territory when you encounter a hotel with a name like “SILENA, your soulful hotel.” It’s nothing if not memorable, and in that way it’s entirely fitting for a hotel as unique as this one.

Its form is a thorough refutation of the idea that contemporary architecture is in any way cold or inhuman. The design, by the Bolzano-based architecture firm noa*, combines bold ornaments, like the mashrabiya-style screens that adorn the façade and select interior spaces, with an austere, modernist-inspired minimalism, all rendered in simple materials like concrete and Alpine-appropriate wood.

To this transformative architecture you can add the restorative effects of a Southeast Asian–inspired wellness program, where the spa is properly feng shui’d and the typically Alpine leisure pursuits are joined by yoga, Qi-Gong, and guided meditation, and a Literature Lounge and Tea Library coexist harmoniously with a more traditional restaurant, where painstakingly sourced local ingredients are lovingly prepared in the Slow Food style. The proprietors, Simon and Magdalena — hence the name — are a personal trainer and a literary type, respectively; no surprise, then, that their hotel caters to both body and mind.

A relatively remote corner of the eastern end of Crete is where you’ll find White River Cottages, a collection of stone houses in a valley called Aspros Potamos, whose direct translation gives the hotel its name. It’s a refreshingly tranquil and pastoral experience, with access to some impressively wild countryside and with an atmosphere that’s a fine mix of rough-edged rustic charm and contemporary boutique-hotel polish. 

The cottages themselves vary widely in size, from studios to three- and four-bedroom layouts. All are charmingly traditional in their construction, but are up to date where it counts: air conditioning, wi-fi, sleek modern bathrooms. Each one comes with a shaded outdoor space, perfect for a quiet meal — and each one also comes with a fully equipped kitchen.

Given the cottages’ self-sufficiency, it’s perhaps no surprise that the hotel’s services are low-key, and the common spaces minimal, amounting to a (substantial) swimming pool and some outdoor lounge space. The village of Makrigialos is within easy walking distance and is where you’ll find yourself at dinnertime, while the island’s beaches and gorges are tempting destinations for a day trip with White River Cottages as your base.

content:
History is relative in Mexico City, where Spanish churches and palaces stand on sites once occupied by Aztec temples and pyramids. Such is the case at Casa9 Zocalo, a new boutique hotel located in one of the oldest houses in Mexico City, which itself stands on the grounds of an older ceremonial temple. Needless to say, Casa9 has deep historical roots, and the property has once more undergone a transformation, as a team of architects, blacksmiths, stonemasons, and carpenters has restored the house’s colonial grandeur. 

The result is striking. Passing through the entryway — handily located downtown, as the name indicates, across the street from the zócalo or central square — is like stepping back in time. The central patio is framed by soaring stone archways and romantic greenery, while wide open-air staircases lead to the upper level with just three rooms and suites. Each is a quiet retreat from the busy streets outside, with large shuttered windows or French doors opening over the courtyard. They’re outfitted from top to bottom in polished wood, from the beamed ceilings to the hand-carved furniture to the gleaming parquet floors. Two are set up like standard hotel rooms with one or two queen beds, but the spacious La Restauradora suite feels more like a stylish apartment with a large living room and a huge bathroom with a built-in marble tub.

Two levels of stately terraces, ideal for sinking into a rocking chair after an afternoon of sightseeing, offer plenty of lounge space — so much space, in fact, it feels a bit like renting a private house. The owners specialize in this concept: they run another B&B-style hotel of the same name in Condesa. For lovers of history and architecture, however, the zócalo-adjacent location can’t be beat.

content:
The Habitas hotels pride themselves on connection, in a couple of different dimensions — first and foremost, a connection with nature, which Habitas San Miguel achieves by virtue of its immersion in the countryside a mere ten minutes from the center of San Miguel de Allende. And the resort’s accommodations are built for just that purpose: each one is a freestanding casita that opens onto a view of the countryside right at the foot of the bed. 

The pod-like casitas mix contemporary elements like floor-to-ceiling windows and modern furniture with traditional crafts and décor, and they’ve all got outdoor decks for lounging. They offer privacy and seclusion when you need it, but the Habitas ethos is also one of fostering human connection, and to that end there’s a wealth of cultural programming and a number of group-oriented outdoor excursions.

Sound baths, yoga classes, and music lessons are offered on site, as well as horseback and mountain bike rides; the nearby city of San Miguel de Allende is close enough for a guided visit to an artist’s studio. There’s also a spa, for some solitary restoration — and the hotel’s restaurant, Communidad, is the center of Habitas San Miguel’s social life.

content: We’re the first to admit that it’s not the most dignified word in the English language, but there’s no other expression better suited than “glamping” to describing the experience on offer at the Collective resorts. Set in the eponymous hills an hour outside of Austin, Texas, Collective Hill Country is both wild and plush; its tents, built on elevated platforms, feature king beds dressed in 1,500-thread linens, en-suite bathrooms, and wood-burning stoves. The Family Suite adds a satellite tent with a pair of single beds for the kids, and you’ll have a proper desk as well as wi-fi in case you’re WFH (working from the hills).\n\nActivities range from Collective’s own fusion of yoga and pilates to horseback tours, hikes, e-bike rides, and the Axe & Arrow Club. There’s no spa, quite, but the option of an in-room massage may prove to be a tempting one. The meals, too, are suitably impressive, with the Three Peaks Lodge restaurant handling everything from the made-to-order breakfast to an unusually refined five-course tasting menu for dinner — executive chef Laura Collins has high-end restaurant experience, and it shows.

content:
The riad hotel is a tradition that was perfected a long, long time ago, and what separates a great one from an average one is not a difference in concept, but in execution — which, for the most part, comes down to its proprietors’ taste. A glance at the photos will show that Riad Camilia is as tasteful as they come, and a quick look around the house reveals that it’s packed with comforts that belie its small size.

Two rooms and four suites is just about as small as riads get, and each one is entirely distinct in décor, though they’re all roughly equal parts Parisian- and Moroccan-inspired. A good riad feels like a private residence, and Riad Camilia certainly is that — there’s plenty of privacy, and many of the units can be combined for families or larger parties.

It’s set in a residential neighborhood within the medina, which means it’s within walking distance of most central destinations. Facilities include not just the usual courtyard nooks but a couple of plunge pools, a rooftop terrace, and a hammam as well. And like the best of them, Riad Camilia excels when it comes to a lavish and festive dinner service, featuring traditional Moroccan flavors tailored to guests’ personal tastes.

content: It’s hard to describe what the Graduate hotels are up to without making them sound kitschy, but in hospitality, concept is only part of the package — the delight is often in the details, and in the execution, and it’s there that the Graduates distinguish themselves. This one, a block from the University of California’s Berkeley campus, has plenty of fun with its concept, though; the fictional archaeologist Indiana Jones was a professor as well, and the Graduate Berkeley imagines what he might have done with a 144-room 1928-vintage hotel on Durant Avenue, a block off of Telegraph.\n\nThat explains the lobby’s vast collection of National Geographic magazines, and the eclectic décor more generally — it looks collected rather than designed, and neither modernism nor minimalism makes much of an appearance. The rooms are unfussy but not spartan, and they’re far more comfortable than student digs. And the public spaces are where the Graduate really shines; this is a convivial place, with a lively lobby scene and a restaurant, Henry’s, that updates classic pub fare for Berkeley, which is, thanks to Alice Waters, the spiritual home of farm-to-table cooking. (Coming soon: an outpost from Tartine, the much-loved San Francisco bakery.)

In terms of pure distance, midcoast Maine isn’t all that far from Portland, or even Boston and New York. But it’s only now, with the advent of Rockland’s 250 Main Hotel, that contemporary boutique-style hospitality has arrived in the region. And given the local creative traditions — Rockland has long been something of an artists’ colony, and a shipbuilding town before that — it’s certainly not out of place. Its exterior is relatively modest, in keeping with the rest of the town’s visual style. 

Inside, though, it’s full of art, it’s full of stylish modern furniture, and it’s marked by an industrial interior-design style that’s totally contemporary even as, in details like the lobby’s weathered ceiling slats, it pays tribute to Maine’s midcoast heritage. The rooms are proof that clean and modern can still be warm and cozy, and the uncluttered spaces are warmed by rich textures, vibrant color accents, and unique artworks. And they’re not precious about these spaces — 250 Main is pet-friendly.

Breakfast is served at the hotel, and for lunch and dinner you’ve got no shortage of local options — Rockland punches well above its weight in this department. Beyond that there’s the Farnsworth Art Museum, which counts among its collection a wealth of paintings by the Wyeth family. And if the outdoors are more your speed, you’re right on the doorstep of the Maine Coastal Islands National Wildlife Refuge.

content: If ever there were a name that leaves no doubt as to what kind of experience a hotel is meant to evoke, it’s got to be Summercamp. The town of Oak Bluffs, on the island of Martha’s Vineyard, has a rich history as a Methodist camp destination, centering around Summercamp’s neighborhood of Wesleyan Grove. But the name’s not only a reference to the building’s history — Summercamp, in its current incarnation as a Lark hotel, is a fun and stylish hotel that aims to bring to life a modern-day, grown-up version of all of our summer-camp fantasies.\n\nTo that end, it’s perhaps the most playfully of the hotels Rachel Reider has designed for Lark, full of bright colors, graphic patterns, and mid-century design. And while you wouldn’t mistake it for a cabin in the woods it’s got just enough rustic texture to earn the Summercamp name. The rooms, at every level, are rather more luxurious than camp rooms, and the suites are downright lavish. And, just like at camp, the bulk of the action takes place outside of your sleeping quarters: in the lobby, the lounge, the game room, or the hotel’s veranda. Snacks are available in the camp canteen, and with a location in the heart of Oak Bluffs, you’re surrounded by restaurants, not to mention the beaches, the waterfront, and ample opportunity for outdoor recreation of every kind.

content: Istanbul, maybe more than anywhere else, is a city marked by the vivid contrast between the old and the new. And any hotel worth its salt in this famous crossroads of a city — spanning not just the ancient and the modern but Europe and Asia as well — will embody this contrast to a noticeable degree. That’s certainly the story with the Manna Boutique Hotel. By local standards it may lean slightly toward the modern side, housed as it is in a contemporary building in the business district of Gayrettepe. But its design is not just stylish but is clearly rooted in local tradition, with enough Ottoman accent to lend it an unmistakable sense of place.\n\nIt’s not just the neighborhood’s first design-oriented boutique hotel, but a luxurious one as well. The public spaces mix contemporary design and historical details, while the rooms are stylish and minimalistic but with plush comforts and enough ornament, including richly figured stone and touches of organic texture, to feel warm and welcoming. There’s a wellness center that includes massage, a Turkish bath, and a gym, and there’s plentiful meeting space, which is savvy, given the clientele. And there’s the restaurant, MannaManje, which serves Turkish and international cuisine in a lively café setting.

content:
The typical Tulum boutique hotel is set right on the beach, and it’s not hard to see the appeal of that approach. But for a stay that’s more centered on nightlife than on communing with nature, Tulum’s town center offers an increasing number of options — none, perhaps, quite so moody and atmospheric as Aroma Tulum, a hotel whose décor might not look out of place in New York, were there not a slightly suspicious number of tropical plants on display.

The exteriors? Black, as are the walls and ceilings of the suites, and even the chaises longues that line the rooftop garden. Aroma leaves thatched-roof kitsch to the eco-resorts down by the beach — which is, incidentally, a mere fifteen minutes away. Here, however, what you’ll find are polished concrete floors, modernist furniture, and a look that’s more geared to the hours after sunset.

Beyond breakfast, there’s no restaurant, but the hotel’s urban setting means there are any number within a few minutes’ walk. The bar is a stylish space that spills out into the garden outside, and it’s not out of the question that there’ll be live music or a DJ on any given night.

Just across the Main from its sister hotel, Lindenberg Rückertstraße, Libertine Lindenberg signals with its name a slightly more freewheeling approach to the communal-hotel idiom. That’s due in part to its setting in Frankfurt’s cobblestoned Alt-Sachsenhausen district — AKA the “apple cider district” due to its classic taverns and museums, though a younger and more avant crowd has taken up residence as of late. The Libertine fits right in, that is, every inch of its arty, cozy personality a quiet rebuke to Frankfurt’s buttoned-up, businesslike image.

The individually designed suites span seven floors, trending more towards warm, sun-drenched texture than excess. Custom, handmade fittings, furnishings, and knick-knacks are the rule: oversize wall hangings and eccentric lamps liven up the skylit pastels, balanced underfoot by woven carpets and plenty of polished hardwood. If you want to get zany, press a button to listen in on recording sessions at the in-house studio — or book a private session of your own.

Food is huge here, thankfully, and quite readily available; besides the upstairs kitchen with personal nooks for each guest, there’s a living-room café (lean back to take in Dennis Rudolph’s entrancing ceiling fresco) and a 24-hour in-house grocery called Lekker. Stock up there on produce from Libertine’s own biodynamic farm, piquant spices, and a whole range of themed home accessories because why not. If you’re feeling a bit rusty with kitchenware, drop in on a Wednesday cooking course, or skip straight to cocktails at the make-it-yourself bar and let the chef handle the heavy lifting. That’s how it is here — you dictate the pace and they’ll deliver. Anything from white-glove service to hands-off DIY goes at Libertine.

content: It hardly seems like Wheatleigh can be real — a 19th-century Italianate mansion in the Berkshires of Western Massachusetts, set on a 22-acre estate surrounded by parkland designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, complete with a small but high-end French restaurant and a mere 19 rooms and suites. It’s ideal for some rural seclusion, if that’s what you’re after, but this corner of the Northeast is full of culture as well; the town of Lenox is steeped in literary history, and you’re just a few minutes’ walk from the Tanglewood estate, the summertime home of the Boston Symphony Orchestra.\n\nWhile Wheatleigh has been updated for a contemporary luxury-hotel audience, the architectural character of the house remains very much intact. The interiors show the attention of a modern decorator’s eye, but the style is still pure Gilded Age elegance, and high-tech interventions like Roku televisions and Bose sound systems remain unobtrusive. The Portico restaurant is the more formal option, with just eight tables and a phenomenal menu by Jeffrey Thompson, and the Lounge serves more casual fare. Though it wears its English and Italian inspirations on its sleeve, Wheatleigh is an American original through and through.

content:
To say Aman Summer Palace is an example of the Aman group gone urban would be perhaps a bit misleading. This one is technically in a city, which is a departure from the usual Aman setting—whether on the beach in Bali or by the side of a mountain in Wyoming, one thing they all are is secluded. But while Beijing is one of the world’s biggest, most riotous cities, and only getting bigger, the experience the Summer Palace offers is hardly what you’d call an urban one.

It’s right next door to the Summer Palace proper, and occupies its own private compound, a collection of hundred-year-old guest houses surrounded by tranquil ponds and verdant gardens. It would have been an unforgivable crime against architecture to have spoiled this site with tacky luxury villas; all the same, the occasional well-integrated modern touch is more than welcome. The electronic gadgetry, easy to miss in a suite full of bamboo blinds and ornate hand-carved screens, is state-of-the-art, and the bathrooms are low-tech but very modern, with massive soaking tubs and separate showers.

The prevailing feeling on the grounds of the Aman Summer Palace is one of quiet; unlike the busy tourist site next door, it’s closed to the public, and you’re far more likely to encounter one of some 300 staffers than a fellow guest. There’s a massive hospitality infrastructure beneath the Summer Palace’s surface — both figuratively and literally, with the pools, spa, and fitness center (including Pilates studio and squash court) all located underground. If the trademark away-from-it-all Aman experience is what you’re after, it’s entirely possible here—the Summer Palace is perfectly self-sufficient. But the Beijing location means there’s a lot more available in the way of diversions. Wall tours, Palace and temple walks, even shopping excursions; the combination of Aman seclusion with big-city Beijing bustle is a uniquely formidable one.

content:
The first upscale boutique hotel in Sri Lanka’s interior brings new meaning to the phrase "instant classic." Though it opened in 2005, Kandy House has roots two centuries old — from 1804 on it was home to one of Sri Lanka’s ruling families — and the stylish, newly renovated interiors stop a bit short of trendy minimalism, instead mixing modern fixtures and materials with traditional architecture and an impressive array of antique furniture.

All of the eight rooms (and one suite) are contained in the old manor house, so the experience is a remarkably authentic one — there’s no television, so you’re forced to engage with your environment a bit, throw open those windows or even step out on the veranda and survey the grounds of the estate and the jungle beyond. Authentic doesn’t mean uncomfortable, though, as even in the two rooms that don’t have air conditioning, the ceiling fans and the gentle hill country breeze keep things cool, and the four-poster beds and claw-foot tubs are classic low-tech luxury.

In fact there’s little to do here that wouldn’t have been possible to 19th-century guests as well — the courtyard and the veranda are still the house’s main attractions, though the pool is presumably of newer vintage. Food is upscale traditional Sri Lankan, with produce selected daily from the market in Kandy proper. And for a look into Sri Lanka’s pre-colonial past, you can't do better than the city of Kandy and its surrounding region — this part of the interior was the last holdout against colonization, and cultural monuments abound, including the Temple of the Tooth Relic of Buddha (which is, if you’re wondering, pretty much exactly what it sounds like).

Please note: The Kandy House only accepts children over the age of 12.

Amsterdam, when it comes to hotels, is so often a tale of two cities; one is the futuristic wonderland of modern Dutch architecture and design, and the other a storybook vision of antique canal-house charm. Hotel JL No. 76 is a little bit of both: comprising a pair of 18th-century townhouses, the 76 is nonetheless decorated in a contemporary style, and while it’s not nearly as whimsical as some of the city’s more overtly design-oriented boutiques, nor is it nearly as staid as some of its more traditional neighbors.

Sometimes splitting the difference leaves you neither here nor there, but in this case the result is a hotel that gets the balance just right. The architecture is more or less intact, lending a bit of individuality to the historical spaces, and the décor is full of contemporary color, from modern furnishings to custom-designed wallpapers by Dutch artist Barbara Broekman. Standard and Executive rooms differ mainly in space — king/twin beds and rain showers are universal — but the Family room adds a pair of bunk beds, an upgrade for kids over the usual cot or sleeper sofa.

A restaurant and honesty bar serves breakfast, lunch, dinner and drinks in a cozy ground-floor environment, and the hotel’s location, just off the Museumplein, means plenty of alternatives are available. Fans of extremes will find hotels in Amsterdam that are perhaps more focused on design, on history, or on white-glove luxury — but when a bit of versatility is called for, the answer just might be JL No. 76.

content:
When it comes to boutique hotels in Paris, there’s love, and then there’s big love. Love, in this case, is the original Hotel Amour, located in the Pigalle quarter — Grand Amour, in the 10th arrondissement, is the second incarnation. The sister hotels have almost everything in common. Both are passion projects by a creative powerhouse, graffiti artist turned nightlife entrepreneur André Saraiva, and his team of hotshot designers. Both hotels have bars and restaurants that are magnets for stylish Parisians. And neither is located in one of Paris’s more refined neighborhoods. That’s no mistake: the vibe here is edgy and seductive, not prim and proper.

Guest rooms are divided into three categories: small, medium, and large. Small really means small — this is Paris — and even the large room has steeply vaulted ceilings and a freestanding bathtub just steps from the bed. Of course, the Grand Amour is loosely based on the Japanese concept of the “love hotel,” so that was a conscious choice, not a necessity.

Unlike at the original Amour, with its erotic artwork and black-painted hallways, the Grand Amour has more of a vintage sensibility and a contemporary sense of humor. The walls are lined with fully stocked bookshelves, the walls are painted in jewel tones; there’s an old-fashioned clock radio on the bed stand, and minimalist graffiti scrawled across the shower tiles, and the occasional framed Helmut Newton photograph, to set the tone.

What’s not here is a flat-screen TV or even a telephone. The assumption, it seems, is that you came here to get away from work, to disconnect and to indulge. So take a hint. Downstairs, the happening bistro and rear courtyard garden are fabulous places to feast on a late breakfast or relax with an aperitif. The Grand Amour has a bit of buzz around it, so it’s hard to beat the people-watching opportunities. And why else are you in Paris, if not to drink wine and watch stylish French people in their natural habitat?

content:
Among Mexican beach resorts, modern design isn’t exactly an everyday sight. But hotelier Rafael Sainz Skewes set out to challenge the thatched-roof stereotype. There’s no reason sun, sand and surf can’t comfortably coexist with clean-lined, modern concrete architecture. Here, in the seaside village of Troncones, a half hour up the coast from Zihuatanejo — a place so idyllic you’d be perfectly happy with another thatched-roof palapa — is the distinctly modernist, totally unforgettable Hotel Lo Sereno Casa de Playa.

Minimalist though it may be, it doesn’t sacrifice warmth. With just ten rooms, it feels intimate, and the surfaces, modern as they are, are left unfinished, so they feel human and handmade. The rooms are simple but complete, never ostentatious but more than comfortable enough, with private terraces and spa-like bathrooms. And a little bar and restaurant with a terrace serve as the hotel’s social hub.

It’s all delightfully low-key, and that goes for the town as well. Troncones is known to locals and surfers, but it’s far from becoming a resort. For now, thanks to Lo Sereno, it’s just a pretty little village on a beautiful Pacific Coast beach — and one with just the lightest little touch of modern, cosmopolitan design.

The resort cannot accommodate children under the age of 15.

content:
More cowboy than urban, frankly; the first thing that strikes you about Urban Cowboy Catskills is that the rustic vibe, rather than being replaced with hard-edged minimalism or Scandinavian modernism, has been left intact, or even heightened. Sure, it’s a contemporary, carefully curated, and very self-aware sort of rustic, but it’s all the more likeable for it; why go to the trouble of leaving the city if the city just follows you around?

There are exceptions. A walk-in rain shower or a Japanese cedar bathtub take liberties with the style, but it’s worth it in the name of comfort. Urban Cowboy’s 28 rooms and suites are divided across five separate buildings, and they range in size from the generous cabin-style rooms in Walden to the vast six-bedroom suite that occupies the second floor of the Lodge. They’re all cozy, and not in the way that actually means “small” — with Pendleton blankets and décor that leans heavily on wood and leather, they feel warm and thoroughly welcoming.

Same goes for the staff, especially in the Public House restaurant and bar, which specializes in wood-fired, vegetable-focused cooking. There’s a Iglu sauna in a trailer, an import from Estonia — the only one in the United States — and while group activities are plentiful, you’re also free to ramble unsupervised across Urban Cowboy’s 68 acres. Just don’t be surprised if what you remember best is cocktail hours, campfires, and communal living.

Smaller hotels like Urban Cowboy Catskills fill up quickly. If you can’t find what you’re looking for, contact us and we can help.

content:
Once the grand homestead of Sienese and French noble families, the Castel Porrona Relais is now a hotel. And with its lavish interiors, Moroccan-style hammam, a majestic outdoor swimming pool, and “wine therapy” baths, the place is still fit for a king. You can rent the original castle, complete with five suites, private butler and chef — but even a relatively humble room or suite is an experience fit for a king.

Royal history aside, updating a 900-year-old dwelling to today’s five-star standard is no small task. But the team behind Castel Porrona Relais has done a first-rate job of preserving the finest elements of the property. They’ve kept the original architecture, and many of the loveliest details within it — smooth stone and red brick, terra-cotta tiles, exposed wooden beams — and the verdant landscape that surrounds it, from old olive groves and vineyards to cheerful sunflower fields.

They’ve also done a nice job of improving on the meager comforts of the medieval era. The 25 guest rooms and apartments feature modern amenities like flat-screen TVs, free wi-fi, and coffee machines. But the look is old-world, with romantic four-poster beds, dark wallpaper, gilded mirrors, intricate tapestries and original artwork. Suites have spacious seating areas and views of the rolling hills.

Elsewhere in and around the castle, guests have access to a range of civilized living rooms and the Agua SPA with its adjacent outdoor pool, gloriously illuminated at night. You can soak in wine for the health benefits, then sip some afterward at Il Chiostro, the hotel’s restaurant. The chef specializes in high-end interpretations of traditional Tuscan cuisine: dine under the stars or choose a table in the regal dining room. Just save some room for the next day: this region, within easy distance of Siena and Montalcino, is a perfect place to join a winery or olive oil tour, an outing that the concierge will happily arrange. Go ahead, act like royalty for a day — if you can’t do it here, then where?

The word “Kurhaus,” taken literally, means “cure house,” and that’s what the Kurhaus Cademario has always been, from its founding in 1914 as a care home or sanatorium to its current incarnation as a high-end spa retreat. Likewise, the shores of Switzerland’s Lake Lugano have always been a destination for travelers in search of a cure, whether a literal one or just a spell of rest and relaxation. 

Kurhaus Cademario sits in a particularly auspicious position, on a sunny south-facing mountainside overlooking the lake and the panorama of the mountains beyond. Its 82 rooms and suites range from a generous 22 square meters to a palatial 45, and all are decorated in a contemporary style that pays tribute to the past while never looking dated — and all are equipped with up-to-date comforts and views of either the lake or the gardens.

In any Swiss Alpine luxury hotel, you can expect an extraordinarily lavish and well-equipped spa, and Kurhaus Cademario’s DOT.Spa is certainly that. And you can also expect a culinary approach that’s not just healthful and refined but abundant — from the pool bar to the Agra Bar to La Cucina, you’re certainly never at risk of going without food or drink.

content:
Boutique hotels in Buenos Aires: it’s hard not to feel as though if you’ve seen one, you’ve seen them all. The city is saturated with stylish small hotels, but a few distinguish themselves from the pack. CasaSur, for instance, started out as one hotel — the CasaSur Art Hotel in Recoleta — and grew into a small collection, including CasaSur Bellini and this one, CasaSur Palermo.

Like its longer-established sister hotels, CasaSur Palermo has a clean, modern design sensibility and a gourmet restaurant that’s a destination in itself. As the name indicates, it’s located in Palermo — Palermo Hollywood, to be precise, so named for the film and TV studios located here, a hip neighborhood lined with street murals, coffee shops, galleries and cozy cocktail bars. The hotel is located in the middle of the action, containing 54 rooms and seven suites, all laid with hardwood floors and outfitted with minimalist decor and geometric wallpaper. Standard amenities include private balconies, Nespresso coffee-makers, 42-inch LED TVs, and iPod docks.

Up on the rooftop, there’s a lovely terrace with views over the neighborhood, and a bar open in warmer weather.  Also at the hotel is a small spa, and the chic Sacro restaurant, serving plant-based cuisine with a focus on wellness. On the ground level, there’s a solarium with a small swimming pool — nothing over-the-top, but a good place for a dip after a street art tour or a cycle through the neighborhood. The pool is like the hotel itself. It’s a fashionable place, to be sure, but CasaSur Palermo isn’t a hotel that’s trying hard to make a statement. There’s an understated sophistication, a practical bent, to this and the other CasaSur hotels — there’s everything you need, and not a lot you don’t.

When a Berlin hotel takes a French name, it’s a sign that something a little bit out of the ordinary is happening within its walls. Provocateur, in the western district of Charlottenburg, just off the Kurfürstendamm, aims to import the exotic glamour of 1920s Paris to present-day Berlin, nearly a century later. It’s something of a sequel to Roomers in Frankfurt, but this is no chain hotel; Provocateur is truly one-of-a-kind.

From the outside this meticulously restored early modern Art Nouveau building is quintessential West Berlin. But once you’re over the threshold, you’re immersed in a vibrant, textured burlesque fantasy. The rooms are romantic as can be, full of opulent details and touchable surfaces. And the appeal is more than just visual; beneath this throwback dressing is a thoroughly luxe and contemporary hotel room, from the tiny Petite on up to the sprawling De Luxe.

It doesn’t end there. The restaurant, Golden Phoenix, is a vision in retro Chinoiserie, and it appropriately serves a French-Chinese hybrid cuisine by celebrated local chef Duc Ngo. And the bar is the gateway to an impossibly decadent evening, with the burlesque vibe turned up to ten and an extremely knowledegeable staff of bartenders supplying the refreshments.

Midcoast Maine, the stretch of the Atlantic coast that lies just beyond Portland, is splendid enough on its own terms, a place where some of America’s wildest landscapes and seascapes meet the highly civilized traditions of New England hospitality. A stay there can be improved, however, with just a touch of boutique-hotel influence, which is what you’ll find at the Inn at Ocean’s Edge. Here, on the shores of Penobscot Bay, betwen the picturesque towns of Camden and Belfast, is a hotel that combines old-world elegance and modern hospitality in roughly equal measure, to great effect.

18 of the rooms occupy the main inn building, with 12 more in a separate hilltop structure, and a couple of studio suites in the poolhouse. None are in any way second-class — the main inn is closer to the action, the hilltop rooms are a touch more private, and the poolhouse’s main attraction hardly needs naming. In all categories they’ve got king beds, gas fireplaces, and Gilchrist & Soames bath products.

Two massage rooms, a hot tub, and a sauna make up the Inn’s spa services, and the infinity pool is a fine place to while away the afternoon. And from here you’re close by to Lincolnville Beach, Owls Head State Park, and, an hour and a half away, the well-loved Acadia National Park.

Even by the lofty standards of Tuscan landscapes, the Maremma coast is something special, as those signature rolling hills slowly give way to Tyrrhenian seascapes. And while an Italian villa-style hotel is always worth a look, an ocean view can only be an improvement. That, in a nutshell, is the appeal of Villa Talamo: a picture-perfect Tuscan villa, with all the extraordinary food and wine that that implies — plus the sea. 

With just eight rooms, each one of them unique, it’s just about as intimate as they come. And its interiors deliver what might be the purest dose of classic Tuscan style we’ve ever seen — you’ll be hard pressed to find much evidence of the 20th century in the décor, to say nothing of the 21st. 

The estate is full of gardens, courtyards, outdoor lounges, and little nooks for relaxing, with or without a glass of wine. Speaking of which, while you’ll inevitably be eating and drinking your way across the Maremma by day, you’ll want to return in time for a sunset aperitif — and with a bit of notice, Villa Talamo’s chef can prepare a meal made from the hotel’s own garden produce and market-fresh ingredients.
