content:
First, a disclaimer: the Shoreline Hotel Waikiki is not, strictly speaking, located on the shoreline, but a few minutes’ stroll from the beach. What you get in return for that quick stroll is a hotel with an indie vibe and a relatively small scale. This is Waikiki, home of massive resorts, chain restaurants and discount clothing shops. By local standards, a hotel with 125 rooms is practically a bed-and-breakfast; intimate, stylish, and eco-conscious, the Shoreline excels at trading bloat for island beauty.

You don’t need a 24-hour fitness center with complimentary personal trainers? You don’t need a kids’ club, or seven onsite restaurants, or a staff member to spray mineral water over your body as you lie by the pool? Perfect: the Shoreline is just the ticket, and you save on the resort fees that the rest of Honolulu’s hotels pile on. Guest rooms are simple and bright, outfitted in white and natural wood, mixing modern decor and retro-inspired details like Wegner wingback chairs. Amenities include flat-screen LCD TVs and free wi-fi; bathrooms have marble countertops and oversized showers.

There’s a small swimming pool on the rooftop, and a singular dining and drinking venue, the rustic-chic Heavenly Island Lifestyle café, on the ground level. It’s open all day, so you can drop in for coffee or drinks on your way to and from the beach. And the beach, of course, is why you’re really here. The Shoreline Hotel Honolulu, it goes without saying, doesn’t have its own private beach club. But they’re more than happy to lend you a towel and point you in the right direction.

You don’t have to travel too far up Maine’s Atlantic coast to get some of that classic New England seaside atmosphere. Twenty minutes short of Portland, in the town of Scarborough’s charming little waterfront district, stands the Higgins Beach Inn, a Colonial Revival classic built in 1897 — set just a block from Higgins Beach itself, a splendid little sandy beach that’s one of Southern Maine’s best-loved vacation spots.

Some New England hotels could be accused of sticking a little too closely to tradition, but the Higgins Beach Inn takes some liberties — the seaside style in the guest rooms is turned up to 10, with vibrant colors, vintage postcard-inspired illustrations, and a bit of retro patina. The details, however, are modern boutique to a tee, from the bedside reading lamps to the Gilchrist & Soames bath products. The smallest rooms are cozy indeed, while the suites spread out with enclosed porches, sofa beds, and full-size bathtubs.

Meanwhile the inn’s restaurant, Shade, is no small part of the hotel’s appeal, serving oysters on the half-shell, a range of fresh seafood, and other classic New England beach fare on a covered porch, accompanied by cocktails, craft beer, and wine on draft.

If the coastal towns down by the New Hampshire border are where you get your introductory-level Maine experience, then the more remote midcoast is the intermediate material — Camden, nestled between the mountains and the Atlantic, is well worth the extra distance. It’s here that Whitehall is entering into what is, in a way, its third life; the mansion, built in 1834, was turned into a hotel in 1901, and now, after a 2015 renovation, it’s a vibrant tribute both to 19th-century New England and to mid-century modernism in its particular Northeast flavor.

The rooms and suites vary widely in size and in plan, from a relatively humble double room to a pair of 500-square-foot suites. They’re unified by their contemporary-classic visual style, their focused color palettes, and their well-chosen touches of luxury. Whitehall’s location, right on High Street, places you within walking distance of the center of Camden, and also within walking distance of Mount Battie and its hiking trails. It’s a splendid escape, a fine advertisement for the charms of midcoast Maine, and a town that’s got a bit of culture as well — it was in this very house that the poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, something of a local legend, first began her career.

Please note: Whitehall is open seasonally from early May thru October.

content:
San Francisco is a booming tech capital, a perennial tourist destination, and regularly fills up with convention-goers — all of which combine to make it one of the busiest hotel markets in the country. You’d think, then, that this city would be chock full of hotels like the Marker: fun, funky, colorful, comfortable, and set within walking distance of most of what’s worth seeing in downtown San Francisco.

We’ll focus on the positive, which is that the Marker does in fact exist, and it’s all of these things. It’s set on Geary Street, just two blocks from Union Square, and not much farther from the Financial District and the convention center. And while from the outside it’s an attractive enough, if relatively unassuming, Victorian-style building, what’s inside is pure fantasy, like a particularly colorful dream of Belle Époque Paris assembled with the keen eye of a contemporary designer.

The rooms are just as colorful, as well as comfortable, and even if they stop short of luxury-hotel territory they’ve got high-end linens, up-to-date electronics, and luxe modern bathrooms. And while this part of the city is particularly well served with excellent restaurants, you’ll want to make time for Tratto, the hotel’s Italian trattoria, serving rustic Italian fare alongside creative modern cocktails.

content:
For the most part, you don’t go to Cartagena, Colombia — a city established by the Spanish nearly five centuries ago, with thousands of years of native history before that — to see minimalist architecture and futuristic design. Rather, you come to the historic center of this stunning old city to luxuriate in the atmosphere of the colonial era, an atmosphere that’s in plentiful supply at the Hotel Casa La Factoría by Faranda Boutique.

The location could hardly be more picturesque, a short walk from the Plaza de Santo Domingo, surrounded the colorful houses and ancient churches of the old town. And once you’re through the hotel’s gates, you’re treated to a tranquil and luxurious experience — the hotel contains just 28 rooms, which means its lobby bar, its rooftop terrace, and its indoor pool are blissfully uncrowded.

Rooms combine historical architecture with contemporary design and modern comforts, and the hotel’s restaurant, Candelaria Cocina Nikkei, is a bit of a curveball — its Japanese-Peruvian is perhaps not the first thing you’d expect from Cartagena. It’s well worth a visit, though — and for more typical fare, your old-town location places you within walking distance of a wide variety of classic Colombian restaurants.

content: The Maidstone has been an East Hampton fixture since the middle of the 19th century, and displays a depth of character that’s impossible to build new. And under the ownership of LDV Hospitality, responsible for the popular Scarpetta restaurant brand, it’s a low-key but high-style escape, a boutique hotel that mixes the retro atmosphere of an antique inn with a tasteful touch of Mediterranean-accented contemporary design and some thoughtfully chosen high-end comforts.\n\nThe result is fun and fresh while remaining grounded in history. Each of the 19 rooms, suites and cottages is different, as is typical of a 150-year-old property. All of them come furnished with Frette linens and Santa Maria Novella bath products, as well as everything you’ll need for a day at the beach, including a pass. And of course the accommodations, under LDV’s direction, are only half the story: the restaurant, LDV at the Maidstone, is fundamentally Italian, but is tailored to its East End location, with Long Island oysters and other local seafood featured prominently on the menu.

content: When beige refers to the color of ordinary hotel carpets and upholstery, it’s a symbol of what Tablet is here to save you from: namely bland, boring, corporate chain hotels. But when beige refers to the organic sailcloth with which eight luxe, colonial-style tented guest rooms are covered, it’s anything but dull. Here, in Siem Reap, virtually in the shadow of Angkor Thom, is something truly unique. The Beige sits by the riverside, to the north of the temples, and feels like a proper rural escape. Yet you’ll be in Angkor Wat, or in the modern city center, in a flash.\n\nIt would be an extraordinary enough place to pitch a tent of your own, but this is luxury camping, make no mistake: the tents are villa-sized, air-conditioned, with private terraces and luxurious indoor-outdoor baths. What’s more, they’re staffed by assistants who are on hand for everything from rolling up tent panels to drawing baths to arranging excursions and tours. There’s a spa tent as well as a yoga platform, and a library, an infinity pool, and a communal fireplace for lounging. And it’s all accompanied by organic Khmer cuisine made largely from ingredients produced by the Beige’s own farm.

content:
Not yet a boutique-hotel hotbed, the port town of Cowes, on the north coast of the Isle of Wight, can certainly support at least one stylish lodging. The Georgian townhouse that’s now home to Foresters Hall has long been a local fixture — it’s named for its original use as a meeting place for the Ancient Order of Foresters — but its most recent chapter began in 2022, when Sarah Curran and Peter Sussman, a couple of film-industry professionals, sought to parlay their years of experience as travelers into their first hospitality venture.

Its accommodations are divided between the main house, the adjacent Lodge, and the poolside Garden Suites. They’re all different, as is typical of historical houses, though they’re united by the decorative eye of their proprietors, who have outfitted Foresters Hall with period-correct Georgian decorative elements as well as contemporary pieces and artworks collected during the couple’s pre-Foresters life. That saltwater swimming pool is a welcome surprise; no less welcome is the cocktail bar, which opens onto the poolside terrace.

Please note: Foresters Hall is a seasonal hotel, currently closed for the 2025-2026 autumn-winter season.

content: For a cosmopolitan city that sees so many international visitors, Santiago has a surprising shortage of worthwhile boutique hotels. Especially in comparison with — dare we touch on the age-old rivalry? — its sister city on the other side of the Andes, Buenos Aires. Then again, restoring beautiful old townhouses isn’t rocket science. Two can play this game, even if one has been a bit slow out of the blocks. Casa Bueras Boutique Hotel, located in the bohemian neighborhood of Lastarria — arguably the most desirable place to stay in the city — is located inside a well-preserved antique building that dates from 1927. Some of that old-fashioned charm shows through to the present day: note the chandeliers, high ceilings, tiled flooring, marble fixtures, and a rear stone staircase that tumbles into a verdant courtyard garden with a swimming pool. But they’re not recreating the roaring twenties here, exactly. Modern artworks, sleek modular sofas, and boldly painted walls add a contemporary edge to the house. The same is true in guest rooms and suites, where bathrooms are done up in cool slate gray and amenities include large picture windows, pillow-top mattresses, blackout curtains, and iPod docks. Junior suites, featuring private balconies, are a big step up from standard rooms, which are on the small side. The rear patio, charmingly candlelit at night and facing the petite swimming pool, is the hands-down loveliest place to be at Casa Bueras Boutique Hotel. Here, the Deli Lounge restaurant serves an international menu. Skip the sandwiches, if you’re feeling adventurous, and go for something authentic to Chile — camarones al pil pil (fresh shrimp sauteed with garlic, white wine, cilantro and chili pepper) with a glass of Sauvignon Blanc made in the nearby wine country. Make it a whole bottle; there’s hardly a sweeter place to enjoy it in Santiago. When you’re finished, venture into the side streets of Lastarria, lined with art galleries, cocktail bars, and boutiques. content:
As Tuscan cities go Florence and Siena get a lot of attention, and deservedly so. The walled city of Lucca, however, is no slouch when it comes to picturesque Renaissance architecture, nor to phenomenal food and wine. And thanks to hotels like Palazzo Dipinto, it’s got lodgings that hold their own against just about any other Italian town you’d care to name.

And as is so often the case in Italian boutique hotels, they’ve opted for an understated, almost minimalist contemporary style — there’s no sense in attempting to outshine the palazzo’s historical charm, let alone the grandeur of the city outside. Here antique timbered ceilings and other period-correct architectural details happily coexist with neutral-toned modern Italian design furniture and the full complement of boutique-hotel conveniences — rain showers, upscale bath products, the works.

The lobby and the winter garden are both comfortable and attractive multi-purpose social spaces, while the breakfast room doubles as a bar. Beyond that, you’re at the mercy of Lucca’s restaurateurs and barkeeps. Fortunately, it’s a city that’s very much up to the task, and if you go home hungry, you’ll have some explaining to do — not least to the Palazzo Dipinto’s staff, who are quick to assist with a recommendation or a reservation.

content: The oldest continuously operating hotel in Tel Aviv — and something of a local icon, thanks to its distinctive dome — also happens to be one of its best. Hotel Nordoy was built in 1925, an early work by architect Yehuda Magidovitch, and it pre-dates the Art Deco style that’s often associated with the city. As you’d expect, there’s almost a century of Tel Aviv history on display in the Nordoy’s interiors. But where some hotels with this kind of heritage would be too precious to do anything more than dust off the furniture, Hotel Nordoy has evolved as the decades have passed.\n\nThat’s why you’ll find contemporary art and up-to-date fixtures and electronics alongside an eclectic collection of furnishings, from antique pieces to early modernist classics. The rooms start out spacious enough, and as you ascend the hierarchy you find yourself in spaces that are unusually large, especially for a historical hotel. Many have balconies, and all have parquet floors and plush modern beds. Meanwhile, under that famous dome is the treatment room of a small spa, and alongside it is a rooftop lounge with views of the city below; the hotel’s own neighborhood includes among its charms the Nachalat Binyamin market.

content: Please note: We are not taking reservations for this hotel at the current time. Gstaad, that glittery tiara of the Swiss Alps, isn’t much for novelty. Of note, however, is the restoration of a grand old European hotel — Gstaad’s first luxury hotel, to be precise, a 1910 edifice with snow-blanketed sophistication to spare. More than a century later, that heritage still draws today’s Ernest Hemingways and Elizabeth Taylors to Park Gstaad — it’s just that now they cavort in contemporary interiors by Federica Palacios. Cozy gemütlichkeit radiates from the chandeliers and arched windows, a gleaming beacon as night falls early. Incredibly, the original lift was restored to full functionality, a true turn-of-the-century engineering marvel. And the rooms are textbook subtle luxury: never outsize or gauche, tranquil without lapsing into sedateness. Views of the forest or mountains predominate, understandably, while a definite bias for natural wood and charcoal tones sustains a timeless, chalet-style warmth. A handful of drinking and dining options make for difficult decisions come mealtime, especially the live-fire Patagonian plates at Chubut and the hyper-seasonal Mediterranean concoctions, plus a robust sushi selection, in the elegant restaurant. There’s also an honest-to-goodness wooden chalet, Waldhuus, planted in the garden; it’s the genuine item, complete with fondue, checkered tablecloths, and crown-glass windows. The spa and fitness complex is extensive, to say the least; there’s even a golf simulator somewhere in there. Just because you’re over 1,000 meters in elevation, of course, doesn’t mean you’re stuck inside. The slopes of Bergbahnen are a quick walk away — if you don’t get sidetracked by the luxury shopping outlets in the village’s main thoroughfare, that is — and concierges are happy to give interested parties the skinny on activities: in winter, from ice-kart racing to dogsledding, and in summer, rafting, climbing, and biking.

content:
Rome has plenty of great hotels. This one, though, is something else entirely. The Rooms of Rome has higher aspirations — architect Jean Nouvel has created 24 unique apartments within the Palazzo Rhinoceros, an immersive, interdisciplinary “art environment” conceived by the Fondazione Alda Fendi-Esperimenti. It’s more than an art gallery, and more than an art hotel: when it opened it featured Michelangelo’s “Crouching Boy” as its centerpiece, thanks to an ongoing affiliation with the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.

The fact that the apartments manage to be worthy of the artworks is testament to Jean Nouvel’s talents. Old and new often collide in Italian hotels, but rarely to such extremes. The exterior of this landmark 17th-century palazzo was hardly restored at all, and in the interiors, crumbling plaster, battered tilework, and unfinished concrete were left bare in places, to heighten the contrast with the hyper-modern furnishings and the steel panels concealing appliances and wardrobes. Meanwhile trompe l’oeil murals show illusory windows and hallways — the effect throughout is unpredictable, to say the least.

Also unpredictable: the cuisine isn’t strictly Italian, but has pronounced Russian overtones thanks to Caviar Kaspia Roma, an outpost of a well-loved Parisian restaurant. And it’s hardly your only option — from the Palazzo’s location at the foot of the Palatine Hill, you’re close to the old city center, and you’re straight across the river from Trastevere, one of the city’s most food-focused neighborhoods.

content:
It’s a testament to the strength of the Nobu brand — and that of Santorini, for that matter — that you know exactly what to expect from this hotel. Nobu Santorini, the first of its name in Greece, stands on a cliffside in Imerovigli, with an enviable view of the island’s famed caldera. And while the hotel itself owes as much to the familiar Cycladic style of whitewashed stone houses as it does to Nobu’s signature architectural minimalism, it’s as stylish as anything on the island, and as distinguished as any of Nobu’s other global outposts.

The accommodations are all suites and villas — not a standard room in the house. They’ve all got king beds and private terraces with views, and many of them come with private plunge pools as well. Spa treatments are available en suite, and there’s a decent gym, as well as easy access to the hiking trail that connects Oia and Thira. And, as you might imagine, there’s a restaurant whose reputation precedes it: Nobu Santorini serves the brand’s signature Peruvian-inflected Japanese fare, with additional influences from the Greek and Mediterranean traditions — all in an open-air setting that highlights the views you came here to see.

Please note: Collective Vail is a seasonal property and open from June thru September.
 
It’s close, but not too close, to the famously upscale resort town of Vail proper — Collective Vail is set on a thousand acres of ranchland a few miles to the west, offering access to the town’s attractions when you want it, and perfect seclusion when you don’t. (It’s worth mentioning right at the outset that it’s open from May to October — you wouldn’t want to sleep in a tent during the snowy months.)

Its ten luxury tents feature plush linens, en-suite bathrooms with rain showers, and wood-burning stoves (plus electricity), offering a rare combination of proper high-end comforts and close contact with nature. Three Peaks Lodge serves a “farm-to-ranch” breakfast, and dinner options range from a self-grilled “BBQ experience” to a five-course tasting menu. 

Activities include anything you can do in the Rockies outside of the snowy season: horseback rides, mountain biking, fly-fishing, and much more. If you’re looking for an indoor restaurant meal or other signs of civilization, the busy resort town of Vail is about half an hour away, and Beaver Creek roughly half that — from the campsite, however, you’ll feel as secluded as can be.

content:
Athens has some impressive hotels, but the St. George Lycabettus stands above them all — at least literally it does, from its rather spectacular vantage point halfway up Lycabettus Hill, with a view straight across at the Acropolis (and over most of the rest of the city besides). This kind of real estate is obviously highly desirable — the neighborhood is the ritzy enclave of Kolonaki, where most of the city’s best museums and boutiques are located.

So the crowd here is upscale to match, and the hotel, naturally, is suitably luxurious as well. Styles vary in theme from floor to floor, but all 154 rooms and suites are unapologetically posh, with hardwood floors, rich fabrics, and the kind of clean lines that make the most of their allotted space. Many, especially corner suites, are almost worth it for the views alone — all that boutique-hotel stuff is just a welcome bonus.

In a location like this one a rooftop pool is pretty obviously an asset, and the rooftop restaurant’s views are none too shabby either. Service, happily, is very much up to the standards set by the building and the neighborhood, and while the ground-floor lounge does a bustling business, the St. George never forgets that it’s a luxury hotel first, and a nightclub only third or maybe fourth.

Walk down any street in Bangkok, and it’s the colors that get you: the colorful signs and awnings, the red and blue taxis, a seemingly omnipresent shade of teal popping out at you everywhere you look. The modern interiors at the Siam@Siam Design Hotel, in the heart of downtown Bangkok, are as colorful as the city itself — but whittled down to bold splashes of red, orange, and gold to contrast more sedate neutrals. Design-wise, there’s a lot going on, from the lobby to the rooftop, but it fits the frenetic vibe of the city. 

This hotel just feels the way Bangkok should. (But if you’re looking for something a little more muted, check out the heritage rooms — still modern in execution, they’re styled as an homage to traditional Thai design.) There are a wide range of room options to suit just about every type of traveler, from business executives to honeymooners to travel buddies. Upgrade to the grand biz class rooms, and you’ll not only guarantee yourself a spectacular perch over Bangkok, but you’ll also gain access to the executive lounge on the 22nd floor, which includes business facilities, breakfast and snacks, and high tea and happy hour each day.

While we’re on the subject of food: you have a number of options when you stay at Siam@Siam, including a wine bar, an all-day international restaurant, and a French restaurant and bar. But once the sun goes down and the humidity dulls a bit, head straight to the rooftop restaurant with its 360-degree panorama of the bright lights and skyscrapers of downtown Bangkok — you’d be hard pressed to find dinner with a better view anywhere in this city (although the outdoor infinity pool about halfway up the building comes close). But if you prefer to see Bangkok from ground level, this is a good home base: You’re just a couple blocks from the national stadium and many of the city’s best restaurants and shopping malls.

content:
If you’re in San José, you’re likely on your way somewhere else. But that doesn’t mean you have to settle for a generic chain hotel near the airport. Welcome to Hotel Presidente. Located in the heart of San José’s historic downtown, within a few blocks of the key cultural attractions in the Costa Rican capital, it’s conveniently located for a bit of sightseeing and exploring. And it’s not just practical, but subtly hip. It’s the sort of place with exposed brick walls and parquet floors in the lobby, and a garden with lounge space on the rooftop; it’s the kind of hotel that lends complimentary bicycles to guests.

An industrial chic aesthetic prevails downstairs — think deconstructed book cases, cool lighting fixtures, Chesterfield sofas, the occasional antique, even a vintage neon sign. Upstairs, Hotel Presidente’s 91 rooms and suites have a more understated look. The standard city-view double room is simple and pristine, almost minimalist, with a pair of white beds, pale tile floors and dark wood panels, a single piece of modern art hanging on the wall, and in the bathroom, lighting that doesn’t make you feel terrible about yourself after a long flight (or a week exploring the jungle.) Bump up a level to one of the superior rooms, reportedly the largest in downtown San José, or a suite with a separate seating area.

There’s free wi-fi and a fitness center, and best of all, included in the nightly rate – a throwback to gentler times? — is a great breakfast buffet. Treat yourself and go back for seconds. Wherever you’re headed, whether cycling around old San José or venturing onward to the beaches and volcanoes of tropical paradise, you'll be glad for the extra sustenance.

Just a few paces from the line separating the French Quarter from the Marigny, where Frenchmen Street meets Esplanade Avenue, is a small hotel that turns the Gallic inspiration up to ten. The Frenchmen Hotel is a set of three cottages, now painted a matching robin’s-egg blue, divided into just 27 rooms which together comprise an impressively intimate and beautifully atmospheric boutique hotel.

The interiors are unified in their color scheme and their aesthetic, but each room is different, owing to the details of these historical structures. In size they range from relatively modest to downright palatial; the finest ones have loft bedrooms or balconies at the front of the building looking over Frenchmen Street. The comforts are substantial, but the vibe is more boutique than luxury — that’ll suit guests just fine, as you don’t come to the Marigny to get away from it all.

Instead you come for the energy, the street life, and, above all, the nightlife. Live music is a necessity here, and the Frenchmen’s bar, Midnight Revival, doubles as a jazz venue. There’s a second bar on the rooftop, serving craft cocktails in the open air. And while there’s no restaurant in-house, the neighborhood has that angle more than covered.

Seattle’s not just a college town, but the University of Washington dominates the northeast side of town; and while new high-rises are sprouting all through the University District, the building that now houses the Graduate Seattle has stood on this spot since the 1930s. Today it’s a sort of postmodern revival of its Art Deco origins, and a member of a hotel group that’s quickly come to be synonymous with the unusual intersection of boutique hotels and American universities.

Like its sisters this Graduate is subtly tailored to its location, but you’ll find the echoes of the Thirties are the strongest element, followed by some subtle purple (for the university’s colors) and plaid (for the prevailing fashions of Seattle’s Nineties pop-culture heyday). The rooms are comfortable but stop short of ostentatious luxury — this is still the U District, after all, and the city’s booming high-tech centers are each a lake away.

What this Graduate goes without is a restaurant or a bar — it makes do with a lobby lounge, and lets the busy University District fill in the gaps. And it shouldn’t go unremarked upon that while the campus is close, just across the street is the Neptune Theatre, a very fine music venue in a city that’s got some competition.

Something of a stylistic outlier for Lago di Garda, the Aqualux Hotel Spa Suite & Terme is no crumbling castle or Renaissance villa but a gleaming modern glass-and-steel eco-hotel, surrounded by pools and stuffed with fitness facilities of every description. The location, in the town of Bardolino, along the shores of Lake Garda, is half an hour from Verona, and places you less than a kilometer from the lakeside beach. But Aqualux is no beach hotel, but a self-contained resort — its buildings ring a central courtyard, and its balconies overlook a multitude of gardens, patios and pools.

Rooms are clean-lined and modern, the Comfort rooms looking out over the town, the Aqua rooms facing inward. They’re spacious enough, but it’s the suites that truly spread out, reaching 45 square meters in the case of the Family suites. And while the accommodations are more than comfortable enough, they’re only half the story — Aqualux’s main selling point is its extensive spa, with three saunas, a Turkish bath, four “beauty cabins,” and a separate women-only section. Meanwhile multiple pools — indoor, outdoor, saltwater, kids-only — see to your hydrotherapy needs. Top it off with two restaurants and one lounge and you’ve got a remarkably complete resort experience.

Aqualux Hotel Spa Suite & Terme is located 23 km from Verona Villafranca Airport.

content: Athens, Georgia is a unique place — named, of course, for the birthplace of Western culture, it’s not just home to one of the biggest public universities in the South, but it’s also something of a counterculture capital, with the best music scene this side of Nashville and a bohemian streak a mile wide. Hotel Abacus does its level best to do justice to the local tradition, which in UGA’s case means satisfying diehard Bulldogs fans on game day as well as rock-and-roll types in town for a pilgrimage to the 40 Watt.\n\nDespite its boutique-hotel good looks, the atmosphere at Hotel Abacus is plenty down-to-earth — the Foundry restaurant is pure retro Americana, and Iron Works Coffee is a charming grab-and-go café. Meanwhile the rooms and suites marry mid-century modernist style with 21st-century boutique-hotel comforts. And you don’t have to travel far to get a taste of the current Athens music scene: the Foundry restaurant opens onto a small theatre that features a wide array of local and national acts.

content: It might not sound relaxing to travel halfway around the world to stay on a farm, but agriturismo is among the most charming ways to experience authentic, rustic Italy. You won’t even get your hands dirty here: the Masseria Agnello, tucked just off the Realmonte coast on the island of Sicily, is an ex-farm, no longer a working producer. But despite a major renovation to turn it into the modern luxury hotel it is today, it maintains the property’s agricultural and historical roots everywhere you look. Take the 10 guestrooms, for instance. They’re found in the stables and peasant workers’ quarters, but with fully modern touches introduced during the renovation process: en suite bathrooms, air conditioning, and a curated mix of modern and antique decor. The style is simple but elegant. The stone facade of the exterior sneaks indoors too, and it serves as the perfect design complement to the exposed wooden beams and chandeliers. And the views are part of the package, too: each room looks out onto the garden and the ubiquitous olive groves — and, farther afield, onto the sea. If you want to get more in depth with your surroundings during your stay, the staff here is happy to arrange activities that help you connect with the land and with this part of Sicily. Learn about local agriculture, take a Sicilian cooking lesson with the hotel chef, take a day trip to the local Greek temple ruins — a UNESCO World Heritage Site, they’re among the world’s best preserved — or scale (or admire from a distance) the famous Scala dei Turchi, a postcard-perfect white cliff next to the beach.

The first of the Private Mansions hotels was the dark and moody Mayer Manor — so for a sequel they went in a brighter, sunnier, more heavenly direction. Newly added is the Secret Chapel, an option a short walk away for guests who find the original Manor to be altogether too conventional a lodging. This one is more or less exactly what it sounds like: a chapel used in secret by Catholics during the 18th century, now upgraded with a kitchen, a claw-foot tub, and a bed where the altar used to be.

It’s worth being totally clear about the fact that the Secret Chapel is scarcely more than a bedroom, a bathroom, and a kitchenette — if the original Mayer Manor is too low-touch for you, then the Secret Chapel will be too. A traditional hotel it most certainly isn’t —  but for an atmospheric, unique, and totally unforgettable stay, there’s not much that can top it, in Amsterdam or anywhere else.

content: The first wave of boutique hotels in Mexico City was concentrated in the upscale residential districts, but Mumedi takes contemporary design straight to the Zócalo, the city’s vast, bustling central square. It’s a museum first, exhibiting everything from graphic and industrial design to photography, illustration, even architecture. It’s got a design shop stocked with local work, as well as an inventive modern restaurant that combines traditional Mexican cooking with international influences as well as the concept of “food design.” \n\nAnd even in its role as a hotel, it’s something of a “living showroom,” with the wares of its various suppliers and craftspeople on display. But to hotel guests, Mumedi is first and foremost an unforgettably stylish place to stay. Its six suites aren’t just full of artworks, they are themselves artworks, each one spacious and full of not just visual interest, thanks to the delightful contrast of historical architecture and contemporary design, but tactile comfort as well. This is a remarkably quiet place to hide away from the crowds of the city center, and it goes without saying that it’s perfectly placed for exploring Mexico City’s sights — even as its museum is itself one of the area’s most compelling attractions.

With a name like that, and a location on Main Street right across from the University of Virginia, it’s no great mystery what Graduate Charlottesville is trying to accomplish. This is a hotel that’s squarely aimed at the young — or, as the cliché goes, the young at heart: nostalgic alumni, visiting academics, or anyone else who’s got a fondness for a stylized, idealized version of college life.

What’s perhaps most remarkable about Graduate is its restraint. Nothing would be easier than to take the college-days theme far into kitsch territory, but the combination of tweedy patterned fabrics, retro-inspired furnishings, and vintage artworks stops just short of too much, and the result is both stylish and fun. You won’t mistake these rooms for six-star hyper-luxury, but that’s beside the point — they’re more than comfortable enough, and certainly far beyond the way any of us actually lived during our university days.

The rooms are only part of the package. As you’d expect, the social life plays an outsized role — Trophy Room, the rooftop restaurant and bar, serves locally grown, farm-fresh dishes and creative cocktails with an extraordinary view, while downstairs Poindexter Coffee keeps the caffeine flowing, along with wine, beer, cocktails, and light bites.

Located in San José del Cabo, the quieter, more upscale cousin of Mexico’s west-coast party capital, Viceroy Los Cabos is remarkable for its architectural distinction: it’s a dramatic statement by Miguel Ángel Aragonés, a Mexican architect celebrated for his boldly unconventional designs. This is one of the most aggresively stylish of the Viceroy hotels: sleek and otherworldly, all clean lines, cantilevers, deep shadows and stark white cubes — “floating boxes,” to borrow the architect’s apt phrase — mirrored in still blue reflecting pools.

Viewed from above, the hotel is an archipelago of modern design. Delicately illuminated pathways lead across the water, winding between the hotel’s various buildings and spaces, from oceanfront pool to art gallery to cocktail bar to spa. The sushi restaurant, Nido, is one of the more innovative indoor-outdoor spaces we’ve seen around these parts. “Nido” is Spanish for “nest,” and that’s exactly what the restaurant’s airy interior is like — if you can picture an elegant nest balanced on sea water in front of the beach. And meanwhile Nube, the rooftop bar, is the perfect place for a sundowner (and then a few more).

But back to those floating boxes for a moment. They contain nearly 200 guest rooms: each is a modern retreat, pristine and white, with streamlined décor by the Italian brand Poliform and floor-to-ceiling windows letting in abundant sunshine and views of the sea. As is typical for Viceroy, you’ll find a perfect balance of style and substance — these interiors are photogenic, but equally pleasing to the touch, and contain thoughtful luxuries like Nespresso machines and Polk Audio sound systems.

Activities, naturally, lean toward the life aquatic, though there’s also a cinema with daily screenings and a separate kids’ club with its own pool. Swim, dive, parasail, or just settle into a chaise by the pool or down at the hotel’s private beach club. The big, touristy Cabo is just down the coast, but from here you’d never know it.

content: It would have been hard to imagine a generation ago, but this stretch of Friedrichstrasse, just a few blocks north of Checkpoint Charlie, is again the commercial and cultural center of the unified Berlin. And with Berlin booming, there’s need for something that would have been doubly unthinkable: luxury suites intended for extended-stay executive travelers. This is where the Mandala Suites come in — the higher-end, all-suite sequel to the Mandala Hotel in Potsdamer Platz. Naturally, you don’t have to be a visiting CEO to make the most of these expansive, light-filled suites. They start out at 68 square meters and eventually spread all the way to 100, and in contrast with the affectless minimalism that’s often meant to signify high luxury, these suites are decorated in a warm, crafty style, prizing coziness over ostentation. For dinner or lunch you’ll be dining out — there’s no shortage of restaurants nearby, most of them suitable for transacting a bit of high-stakes business — but breakfast is served high above Berlin, with views of the city’s unique skyline. The top floor is also where you’ll find the sauna, as well as a gym with similarly far-ranging views.

Think of Dutch hotels and chances are you’re imagining either an Amsterdam canal house or some cutting-edge piece of contemporary design, but the Netherlands, of course, contains multitudes. Set on the old hunting grounds of the Dukes of Brabant is one of the country’s finest golf courses, and alongside the course is one of the country’s finest hotels, the stately yet stylish Duke Club.

Its 20 suites are a new addition, designed by Famke van Eerd-Hinrichs with an eye towards satisfying the expectations of the traditional-minded golfing audience along with those of contemporary-minded travelers with boutique-hotel experience. Rich, ultra-saturated colors and vibrant patterned textiles and wallpapers provide plenty of visual interest, and the comforts are first-rate, with subtly integrated high-tech elements as well as old-fashioned luxuries like heaping king beds and spa-like bathrooms — and, in proper country-house style, butler service is included as well.

The Duke Club is a private members’ club as well as a hotel, with a gym and spa and plenty of meeting space, and there’s a highly regarded fine-dining restaurant as well as a brasserie and a terrace for an al fresco meal.

It took a surprisingly long time for the two trends of outdoor adventure travel and youthful boutique hospitality to come together, but the LOGE hotels are an example of exactly this kind of overlap. LOGE Mt. Shasta is positioned to take advantage of one of Northern California’s finest all-season outdoor destinations — it’s a five-minute bike ride from town, a few minutes’ drive from Lake Siskiyou, and a few more minutes in the other direction from the ski slopes and trailheads of Mt. Shasta itself.

Accommodation options include covered campsites, hostel-style bunk rooms, and — most importantly, for Tablet’s purposes — hotel rooms, ranging in size from “standard double” to “single king” to “whole crew.” The look is hip but not fussy, the comforts minimalist but not lacking, and the whole thing is dog-friendly and generally low-maintenance — nobody minds if you forget to leave your boots outside.

There’s a gear demo and rental center for checking out snow equipment or cruiser bikes, and while you’ll likely spend your days rambling around Mt. Shasta, the evenings are set up for communal fun, with a game room, fire pits, outdoor grills, a full kitchen, and even weekend movie nights and live music.

Travelers to Playa del Carmen have plenty of choices already, but something new, luxe, and stylish is always welcome. Marquee Playa Hotel offers its own perspective on the Riviera Maya scene, drawing inspiration from, of all things, the golden age of Hollywood glamour — monochrome portraits and film stills adorn the walls, and while the interior-design style is mostly minimalist, you just might catch a glimpse of Art Deco here and there.

Marquee Playa’s location places it right in the thick of the action, two blocks from the beach in the bustling town center. But its small size — just 20 rooms — lends it an air of privacy, and from its rooftop pool and bar you’ll overlook the city and the sea from a pleasant distance. Rain showers, blackout curtains, and plush mattresses set a tone of luxury in the rooms, and at the high end you might find a private terrace and a soaking tub.

The rooftop bar is the entirety of Marquee Playa’s food and beverage program, but it’s more than sufficient — it’s an attractive space with an expansive view and an all-day menu of fresh, locally sourced Mexican fare, as well as a well-chosen list of cocktails, beers, and wines.

content:
The idea of Provence doesn’t generally need much in the way of a sales pitch. The South of France’s most famous region is known globally for its gastronomy, its access to the Mediterranean, and its role in the film industry, and it needs little introduction. But if the sheer scale of French Riviera tourism causes you to shudder, allow us to introduce you to the quieter, (relatively) undiscovered side of this region. Mas des Herbes Blanches Hôtel & Spa thinks of itself as the region’s best-kept secret. 

It looks onto the picturesque villages of the Luberon region — accessible to Provençal cities like Avignon, Aix, and Marseilles, certainly, but still a world away from the tourist throngs. Drive up the hillside this hotel occupies, take in its stone facade, smell the rosemary and lavender that the region is known for, and you’ll realize you’ve stumbled into the heart of Provence. The hotel itself looks like it’s been operating under the Provençal sun for generations (in the best possible way). In reality, it’s been welcoming guests for about four decades and received a full-scale renovation in 2016 — so the modern touches you’d expect from a contemporary luxury hotel are decidedly in place. Today there are 33 guest rooms and 15 suites, all bathed in exceptional natural light. Tasteful neutrals drive the decor, with striking red accents, all of which ensure the sun has center stage. The proprietors clearly want their guests to get the most out of the hotel’s location in the countryside. Upgrade to a pool suite for a private outdoor pool and terrace. But even a classic room includes an outdoor balcony with excellent views. 

“Bathed in light” seems to be the running theme here, and it’s one of the major selling points of the luxurious Sothys spa on the premises. The same goes for the hotel restaurant — and if a sunny, welcoming dining room or in-house bistro aren't enough for you, take your meals out on the terrace overlooking the Luberon countryside. Local food, like Luberon rack of lamb, is your best bet: Mas des Herbes Blanches Hôtel & Spa makes sure a guest doesn’t have to leave the hotel to experience why chefs from Julia Child to Daniel Boulud have drawn culinary inspiration from this part of France.

content:
Thessaloniki has its fair share of luxury hotels, but Imaret, located in a fascinating historic monument in Kavala’s old town, is in a category all its own. Built in 1813 along the city’s Byzantine walls, this Ottoman-era complex — notable for its grand domes, marble columns, and elegant archways opening onto enclosed gardens — once housed a Muslim educational and cultural center with an elementary school, a college, prayer halls, and a soup kitchen. After careful restorations, the building was transformed into a luxury hotel, the old schoolrooms shaped into stylish suites, a central courtyard turned into an open-air patio with an ethereal swimming pool. 

Thanks to the building’s historically protected status, staying at Imaret is something like sleeping in a museum. Rooms and suites are rich with character: curving lines, chestnut floors, handmade oriental rugs, intricately tiled surfaces, and glowing ornamental lanterns at every turn. Some have exposed brick walls and garden views, others have copper sinks and sumptuous brocade sofas. Suites have living and dining spaces ideal for sipping tea and reading. 

A low-lit, traditional hammam offers body treatments inspired by ancient practices, and a sophisticated breakfast is served on Haviland-Limoges porcelain in a glass-walled greenhouse. In summer, dine al fresco in the orange tree garden, and don’t miss late-night drinks in Imaret’s moody, opulent bar, seemingly a world away from the buzz of Greece’s second-largest city, yet deeply grounded in its past.

content:
Safe to say when this hotel opened its doors three centuries ago, this stretch of road between Delft and The Hague was a substantially less urban environment. And while this lovely antique building is now surrounded by modern buildings containing various high-tech concerns, to arrive at Savarin itself feels like something of a trip back in time.

That’s before you enter. Inside, this beautiful heritage building has been thoroughly renovated — not only brought up to modern five-star luxury-hotel standards, but decorated in a modern, minimalist style, with design furniture and saturated splashes of color set off against a few well-preserved historical details. And as luxurious as Savarin is, it contains only 35 rooms and suites, which preserves an air of uncommon tranquility.

It’s helped in this endeavor by the Cityspa Savarin, which includes an indoor pool, a hot tub, and various saunas and steam baths in addition to treatment and massage rooms. Adjacent to the spa is the Petit Café, for a light and healthful meal to accompany the spa’s restoration. More substantial is the Bistro L’Éntrée, a Parisian-style bistro; the crown jewel, however, is Restaurant Savarin, the hotel’s lavish fine-dining restaurant.

content: At this point in boutique-hotel history, there’s a limit to how thrilling another New York or London hotel can be. Not so in Kansas City, Missouri, where a new boutique hotel is big news indeed. The Fontaine takes its stylistic cues from Renaissance Venice, which would be enough, on its own, to set it apart from the ordinary business hotels with which it shares its hometown. But there’s more to its appeal than just its visual identity — the atmosphere, from top to bottom, is one of urbane sophistication, but it’s light-hearted enough to still feel approachable here in this down-to-earth Midwestern city.\n\nWith 132 rooms and suites it’s a comfortable size, with accommodations that span the range from comfortable Traditional and Deluxe rooms to extravagant suites, including a Presidential Suite that’s worthy of the name. At all levels you’ll have luxe touches like Carrera marble vanities and walk-in rainshowers, as well as Egyptian cotton linens and goose-down pillows. Parker, the rooftop restaurant, has impressive views of the surrounding city, and the bar is an upscale cocktail venue with a terrace by the poolside. And the Solarium Lounge serves breakfast in a soaring, sunny space, the perfect place to start the day.

content:
In a region with such a long and rich history as Sicily — the Greeks settled on the island in the 8th century B.C.E. — a hundred-year-old villa is practically brand new. It’s true that the hilltop Villa Mon Repos is not one of the older buildings around. But it’s certainly one of its more glamorous. Marlene Dietrich was a guest even before the the Art Nouveau-style structure was turned into Taormina’s first casino in the early sixties, and it went on to attract the likes of Cary Grant and Gregory Peck along with stars of the Italian cinema.

That crowd has moved on, and Villa Mon Repos is back to its decidedly quieter original function. ‘Mon Repos’ is French for ‘my place of rest,’ a name that lends itself more to relaxing over a leisurely breakfast than doubling down at the blackjack table. It’s a tranquil boutique hotel these days, elegant but beach-casual, with drop-dead gorgeous views of the sea from nearly every room. The original villa contains four suites, but the property extends well beyond the landmark building, with fourteen free-standing “luxury residences” scattered around the surrounding park. The trade-off is what you’d expect: there’s more historic charm to the suites, with their French windows and moulded ceilings and doorways, but more room to stretch out in the spacious residences.

What all of the guest quarters share are first-rate amenities, from the fine linens to the all-natural bath products, from flat-screen TVs to complimentary wi-fi. All suites and residences feature bay views; most, though not all, have private terraces. You could have breakfast there, or in Tout Va, the hotel’s restaurant, located in the original villa, or by either infinity pool; there are two, one next to the main house and another tucked away in the park, between residences.

There’s plenty to see and do within walking distance, but Villa Mon Repos, as the name suggests, is also a blissful place to do nothing. The villa’s lower terrace was reportedly Dietrich’s favorite vantage point to admire the views of Isola Bella and the deep blue Bay of Sirens, and lemons were, quite famously, her favorite cocktail garnish. That’s a fruit that happens to grow plentifully on the island: you do the math.

content:
Picture a beach paradise in Southeast Asia: white sandy beaches, clear water, tropical foliage. Chances are you’re picturing Vietnam or Thailand. But Otres Beach, a seaside enclave on the western coast of Cambodia, is consistently named one of the best in this region of the world. The fact that the secret’s not totally out is part of what keeps the water pristine and the hotels relatively uncrowded.

It’s a colorful fifteen-minute tuk-tuk ride from the coastal town of Sihanoukville to this stretch of paradise, and to Tamu, a sleek boutique hotel right on the sand. There are just fifteen rooms, situated around a swimming pool and facing the sea, each with a private balcony. Some have small gardens; others have Balinese-style outdoor showers. Inside, the look is minimalist — polished cement floors, wide white beds, low sofas and cushions that invite a lazy afternoon lounge. And that’s exactly what you’ll be doing here. You’ll lounge by the sea, under a tree, and by the pool, even by the breakfast table — coffee, lunch, and cocktails are all served on daybeds on the beach.

Once you’ve properly rested and worked on that base tan, more active pursuits await. There’s yoga on the beach with Tamu’s in-house instructor, snorkeling and kayaking, mangrove tours and fishing trips. The hotel will gladly make the arrangements for an unforgettable picnic on a virgin island nearby. Tamu’s restaurant, naturally, sources ingredients from local markets and farms. So there’s plenty of exotic fruit to go around, whether packed in the picnic basket or blended into your sunset cocktail. Cambodia: let’s keep it quiet for now.

content:
As unique as the Alps are, there’s something particularly special about the Dolomites, the Alpine range that extends into the Italian region of South Tyrol. It’s here, on the Ritten ridge, not far from Bolzano, that you’ll find Hotel Weihrerhof, a hotel that takes both the Alpine enthusiasm for wellness and the Italian appreciation for the good life to their logical extremes, in a perfectly peaceful retreat on the shores of an idyllic mountain lake.

The Weihrerhof is small, just 23 rooms, which contributes to the intimate atmosphere and the sense of calm. And of course the SeaSpa doesn’t hurt — though this is the Italian side of the border it’s reminiscent of the intensive, hyper-indulgent spa culture of the German-speaking world. Meanwhile the cuisine is pure South Tyrol: it’s painstakingly local, with herbs grown in the hotel’s own garden, and a flexible approach can cater to any dietary need.

And of course the accommodations themselves complete the package. The look is contemporary, though not without nods to Alpine tradition — knotty pine wood and crimson fabrics abound. And while the emphasis is on relaxation rather than adrenaline, activities encompass the full range of what’s possible in the mountains, from hiking trails to mountaineering and more.

content: San Francisco’s hotel situation has always been a high-pressure one. These, collectively, are the busiest hotels in the country, and they try hard to distinguish themselves from the crowd. So it’s refreshing that Mystic Hotel manages to be so relaxed. This is a hotel owned by a celebrity chef, after all — Charlie Palmer of Aureole and Dry Creek Kitchen fame — but it doesn’t go in for big branding gestures. Instead it’s a sensitive renovation of a 1906 building, leaving as much of the original architectural personality in place as possible, and the vibe, when all is said and done, is more akin to a classic prewar San Francisco apartment than a typical boutique hotel.\n\nIn true SF style the rooms are definitely on the cozy side — if you’re craving space you’ll want the suites — but they’re long on character, and what they lack in flash they make up for in authenticity. The same can be said of Burritt Room + Tavern, the hotel’s restaurant, which is stylish in a dignified sort of way and serves craft cocktails and a menu of local, seasonal American fare, to the tune of live jazz six nights a week. As for location, it’s hard to imagine something more central than Mystic’s position, two blocks up Stockton from Union Square. From the financial district and the theatre district to Chinatown and the best of San Francisco’s shopping, there’s not much that isn’t walkably close. For feeling like a local, it’d be hard to beat.

content:
Don’t worry, there will be more hotels. The Last Hotel’s name comes from the lasts used by shoemakers to form their shoes, a reference motivated by the original use of this beautifully renovated century-old building in the the historic Garment District that makes up a part of the Downtown West neighborhood of St. Louis. In its present form, however, the Last is a high-end boutique-style hotel, one that mixes local character and professional luxury in roughly equal measure. 

Rooms are decorated in a vibrant industrial-chic style, with echoes of Bauhaus and Art Deco, and come with typically upscale comforts, from bedside Bluetooth alarm clocks to handsome tiled bathrooms with walk-in showers. The suites make space for proper work desks as well as a generous sitting area by the window.

Meanwhile the public spaces include the ground-floor Last Kitchen, an Italian-inspired steakhouse that also goes by the name Ultima Cucina, as well as the Pantry, for coffee and grab-and-go breakfast and snacks. The most unique space, however, just might be the poolside Rooftop Bar & Lounge — maybe not so noteworthy in a place like Miami, but a rare pleasure in St. Louis.

content: In an age when many luxury hotels offer a mind-boggling range of services and amenities, it’s refreshing to encounter one with a less-is-more approach. Max Brown 7th District is a boutique hotel with clearly stated priorities: ultra-comfortable beds, excellent coffee, great music, and a killer location in Vienna’s stylish and central Neubau neighborhood. Nail the basics, they suggest, and no one will miss overpriced minibars or round-the-clock room service. \n\nThe straightforward approach extends to the rooms, which are named for their sizes, ranging from small to extra large. All are furnished in cheerful primary colors with whimsical local artwork and vintage-inspired details, like rotary phones and Crosley record players with curated selections of vinyls. There’s an appealing breakfast buffet, movie nights hosted in the hotel’s theater, and a Mediterranean restaurant on the ground floor. But as the proprietors know, these offerings are all secondary to one of the hotel’s top attributes: its address, within easy walking distance of Vienna’s museums, cafés, and art galleries.

content: For nearly a century, one of San Sebastián’s larges plots of land was occupied by a riverside tobacco factory. When the industry was privatized, the factory closed, and the Basque government snapped up the property with the plans to open a cultural center. Today, this landmark building has been cleverly redesigned — a prism-like glass roof now encloses the large interior courtyard, lending the structure a striking new silhouette. Today this old tobacco factory is the Tabakalera International Center for Contemporary Culture — and the One Shot Tabakalera House boutique hotel. \n\nBefitting its unique location, the hotel’s aesthetic blends industrial cool with art gallery–style elegance: lots of glass and concrete, large windows, high ceilings, exposed pipes, futuristic light fixtures, and an abstract sculpture creeping up the white walls behind reception. Rooms are minimalist, with blonde wood paneling, built-in furniture, leather accents, and pops of turquoise and ruby red. Larger rooms come with modern four-poster beds and free-standing tubs; duplex rooms have upper-level living rooms with plush sofas and writing desks. Rotating art exhibitions enliven the hotel’s common spaces — even the breakfast area has a street art theme — and the city’s famous Old Town is just a short stroll away.

content:
It may fly somewhat under the radar in Rio de Janeiro, full as it is of towering luxury hotels, but the family-owned Ipanema Inn has much to offer guests who prefer a hotel with a lower profile and a smaller scale. As the name might imply, it’s set just one street back from Ipanema Beach, that paradise on earth — and with such an attraction in the neighborhood, many guests don’t need twenty-four-hour entertainment from their hotel.

So the Ipanema Inn is relatively low-key — but that doesn’t mean sleepy. Its design, by the local architect Bel Lobo, is a conscious tribute to Brazilian modernism, complete with chairs by the master Sergio Rodrigues and other mid-century design pieces. Standard rooms start out smallish, though perfectly comfortable, and by the time you’re in the Duplex Suite you’re edging into luxury-hotel territory.

“Brazilian modernism” is also an apt description of the Ipanema Inn’s restaurant, Quitéria, which makes inventive use of classic flavors in a lovely space whose walls are liberally hung with contemporary art. Meanwhile, not only are you steps from the beach, but you’re surrounded by urban life, from cafés, restaurants, and bars to all manner of cultural attractions.

content:
Wallonia gets short shrift when it comes to tourism, which is a shame given the wealth of attractions in Belgium’s southern region. Take Naxhelet, for example: snug on a verdant plateau between the Mehaigne and Meuse valley, this stately renovated farmhouse offers a healthful quiet that’s a million (metaphorical) miles from Antwerp or Brussels. They wouldn’t have it any other way — Walloons, in true Belgian style, take an enormous amount of pride in the hyper-local way of life.

The main event here is the Naxhelet Golf Club. Martin Hawtree saw to the course architecture, meticulously planning 30 holes with an eye to the the character and view of the landscape. No modern golf course would be complete without a clubhouse, of course, which serves light meals and libations both indoors and out-. For a meal with legs, drift over to La Cuisine, ably honoring the farmhouse’s heritage with seasonal, produce-driven plates — many grown in the on-site gardens. 

The hotel’s interiors make excellent use of natural wood in the parquet flooring and beams overhead, retaining the weathered, time-softened vibe that might otherwise have disappeared beneath the renovation’s updates. 33 rooms and a couple spacious suites don’t skimp on the contemporary amenities, though: expect Smart TVs, complimentary wi-fi, Nespresso machines, and elegant marble bathrooms with Italian showers. In case that isn’t enough to relax you fully, there’s also an extensive array of wellness options — indoor pool, sauna, hammam, hot-spring baths, to name a few — and a terrace in every room. Some combination of the above will do the trick, we promise.

How to get there: Naxhelet Golf Club is located approximately 84 km by car from Brussels Airport via E411 and E42.

content:
A little over three hours from Portland, the city of Bend, Oregon is one of America’s great outdoor destinations, a mecca for mountain bikers, trail runners, climbers, river rats, and snow-sports enthusiasts, thanks to its position at the foot of Mt. Bachelor. It’s a natural fit for the Northwest’s homegrown adventure-hotel mini-chain: LOGE Bend strikes a balance between youthful, boutique-hotel inspired aesthetics, low-frills, utilitarian comfort, and warm, welcoming sociability.

It’s set on the southwestern edge of town, on the road to Mt. Bachelor, which means it’s a quick drive to the ski resort and an even quicker bike ride into town — and the trail network crosses the property, so you can hike or bike from your front door. The rooms are pet-friendly, and though they’re stylish, they’re unfussy, and come in a range of sizes to suit families and groups.

The hotel’s rental shop is stocked with cross-country skis and snowshoes, and there’s a fleet of Raleigh City Cruiser bikes that are free for guests’ use. There’s also an outdoor lounge with lawn furniture, hammocks, and grills, and the Entrada Cafe serves coffee, kombucha, and a short list of beers and wines, along with breakfast and all-day light bites.

content:
You may not know Andrée Putman by name, but chances are you’re familiar with her work. You’ve seen her modernist aesthetic on the silver screen, and on the pages of Vogue, and inside the lobby of Morgans boutique hotel in New York. The late Parisian designer worked on film sets and hotel interiors ad campaigns for the likes of Louis Vuitton and Veuve Clicquot, to name a few highlights from her impressive resumé. But The Putman, a boutique hotel in Hong Kong, remains one of the few places where her creative vision was fully realized. 

The hotel is located in the city’s busy Central District. Behind the Art Deco-style facade, there are 28 suites furnished with Putman’s custom décor, including her Crescent Moon sofa, and illuminated by her signature lighting system. (Did we mention she also designed furniture, crystal, carpets, and flatware?) The look is elegant and understated, with floor-to-ceiling windows — many rooms overlook the harbor — earth tones, and in the bathroom, hand-laid Italian tiles by Bisazza. Amenities include bed linens by Frette, standalone bathtubs by Villeroy & Boch, and rain showers by Dornbracht, and bath products by MALIN + GOETZ.

Each suite also comes with a state-of-the-art kitchen that’s cleverly hidden behind an electronic screen. At the press of a button, the screen opens, revealing a Nespresso machine and Zwilling cookware — touch the button again and it closes, concealing from view those unwashed crystal wine glasses from last night.

That’s the thing: Andrée Putman didn’t design every last thing at The Putman. But she did choose everything, and her approach was both stylish and practical. The Putman is a boutique hotel if you need it to be, and if you’re in town for longer, consider it a smart apartment building — one that conveniently includes a fitness center and housekeeping, but none of the traditional hotel services, like a lobby or concierge — that serves as a home away from home.

content: Now this is the Switzerland that design fans want to see. The Hamlet isn’t quite a village, but a townhouse in Old Town Geneva, divided into 18 serviced apartments. It’s an appealing enough proposition, but what makes it truly unusual is its design. Owners Tara and Christoph first enlisted creative family members to reimagine the 18th-century space, and in partnership with Vitra, they’ve turned the Hamlet’s interiors into what’s practically a modernist design exhibition, furnished with pieces by the likes of Jean Prouvé, Jasper Morrison, and Charles and Ray Eames. They’re also equipped with high-end details like Bang & Olufsen sound systems and Aesop bath products. All this could begin to feel overly staged, but these spaces are residential, highly functional, and profoundly calming — just as modernist living was always intended to be. Anyone who’s inspired to take a bit of this atmosphere home with them will be pleased to note that the ground floor is home to its own Vitra furniture and accessories shop. But they’ll spare you the hard sell — this place is about living well at the heart of Geneva, and you’re perfectly placed to get out and enjoy the best of this charming, walkable neighborhood.

content:
For reasons which we don’t need to dwell on here, Warsaw has some distance to cover before it matches certain other European capitals as a destination. But things are going in the right direction, and the potential is limitless. And it’s never a bad sign when a city’s boutique hotels look like Autor Rooms. Small but mighty at just four rooms, this converted townhouse — a collective effort by some of the city’s most relentlessly inventive designers, architects, and general-purpose creative types — clearly demonstrates the wisdom of investing in hometown pride. 

As the name might suggest, they take as much pride in their interiors as a novelist might in a manuscript, weaving unique features like bay window nooks and private balconies into a unified statement in clean minimalism. Eccentric lighting fixtures and curvilinear furniture lend a mod-futuristic vibe to the building’s original stucco, parquet flooring, and transom windows. Framed local artwork grounds the experience in this city in particular, but they’re by no means humorless; vintage radios and sleek in-room shower cubicles make sure of that, the former Bluetooth-equipped and the latter featuring Tołpa products. 

The common space holds it all together, supplementing a living/dining room with a spacious terrace and full kitchen. Take breakfast — homemade pastries, eggs, and excellent coffee — here to the accompaniment of a Poland-centric vinyl collection, blueprinting your day with helpful suggestions from the folks who know Warsaw best. Tour a gallery, stroll the Vistula, snag a couple paperbacks, and before you know it, you’re a Warsaw regular already.

content:
While we wouldn’t want to accuse designers in general of taking insufficient care with their work, we will say that a hotel designer who’s willing to live with their work every day has got some serious skin in the game. The Woodhouse Lodge isn’t just a Sixties-vintage A-frame lodge transformed into a contemporary boutique hotel, it’s also the home of hotelier and interior designer Megan Pflug, who moved from Brooklyn to Greenville with her artist husband to open it.

And where some designers might have gone all in on the spirit of ’62, Pflug studiously avoided Sixties furniture and design, letting the lodge’s mid-century architecture contrast with warm, organic-feeling Shaker-inspired interiors. The result is eclectic but still focused, and is a memorable look that’s anything but off-the-shelf. The ten rooms are all subtly different, each with its own pattern on its leather headboard, and all come with thoughtful little luxuries like Luft mattresses, Brooklinen bedding, and bath products by the local Village Common. 

For all its comfort and style, however, the Woodhouse Lodge is still the sort of low-key lodging that rewards self-sufficient travelers. Public spaces include a lovely lounge with an open kitchen, as well as four acres of tree-lined lawns. A planned expansion will bring a more thorough food-and-beverage program — for now, there are snacks for sale in the kitchen, and a breakfast served on weekend mornings.

Mere feet from the city’s central train hub — all puns entirely intended — stands STAYTION Mannheim, the hotel where “music meets industry.” The experience within largely holds true to that motto, repurposing all sorts of pipes and careworn wood and caged bulbs towards a designer’s ode to the textures and patinas of modernity. Colorful and contemporary in equal measure, STAYTION roughs up Mannheim’s smooth edges just enough for the modern boutique flavor to take hold.

The 43 rooms, distributed across 6 themed floors — mostly musical — keep that textural energy going with hardwood flooring, subway tiling in the bathrooms, and vibrantly toned accent walls. Well-chosen curios — snare-drum nightstands, old-fashioned radiators — add custom character, while the building’s angles allow for unusual exposures, a definite plus in terms of light and views. Snag a pre-loaded iPod from reception on your way in to set the desired mood; doubtless it will resonate with the headboard murals and wall quotes.

content: Washington’s coast is a little wilder and less developed than California’s, but it’s spectacular in its own right — and, perhaps surprisingly, it’s something of a surf destination as well. The city of Westport, on the south side of Grays Harbor, is two and a half hours from Seattle, but for surfers and other water-sports aficionados, it’s well worth the drive. What it lacked was a hotel with a bit of style, until founders Johannes Ariens and Cale Genenbacher raised some funds to turn a disused mid-century motel into LOGE Westport, a colorful and cleverly outfitted boutique-style adventure hotel.\n\nAs hip as it is, it’s far from frilly, with a touch of Seventies to the décor and bare-bones comforts for self-sufficient travelers. Instead of a restaurant there’s the Sands Cafe, serving third-wave coffee and expertly brewed espresso alongside a short but powerful selection of breakfasts and snacks. There’s plentiful outdoor space for socializing, as well as a covered outdoor kitchen with a community grill, and the gear shop (a partnership with the Seattle-based outdoor retailer Evo) offers everything you need for a surf outing at Westport State Beach.

Nicaragua’s Costa Esmeralda is more than worthy of its precious-gem nickname. This stretch of Pacific coastline is home to dramatic jungle landscapes and an impressive amount of surfing, and now that the highway’s finally been paved, it’s open for business. Don’t worry, it’s early days, and the prospect of some soulless mega-resort is a long way off; for now, the apex of the tourist trade on the Emerald Coast is something more along the lines of stylish boutique hotels like Meson Nadi.

Meson Nadi’s setting, a few minutes down the coast from the surfers’ mecca of Popoyo, is extraordinary, just across the road from the beach, on a beautiful bay where the sunsets are predictably outrageous. With just six suites, the atmosphere is unusually intimate, and the style is memorable, a mix of indigenous craft and Bauhaus modernism. Little things like air conditioning and wi-fi go a long way here, and the comforts are first-rate.

A pool, yoga lessons, a spa and a small restaurant make Meson Nadi an appealing enough place to pass the day — though you’re within striking distance of no fewer than twenty surf breaks, and volcano hikes and motorcycle tours are on the menu as well, if you’re up for something a bit more active. Just be sure you’re back in time for sunset.

Robey Hall is the third Habita hotel north of the border, after New York’s Hotel Americano and Chicago’s original Robey. And it’s another effortlessly hip boutique hotel in the Grupo Habita mold, one that similarly extends itself to a wider audience than the typical luxury boutique. Located in Wicker Park, one of the city’s hippest neighborhoods, this renovated early-1900s warehouse goes long on rough-edged historical patina and accessible, inclusive charm.

It’s got plenty of traditional double rooms, and even some singles as well, but Robey Hall is perhaps most notable for its bigger rooms, some of which sleep four on a pair of queen beds or a queen and a twin-size bunk bed. They’re perfect for larger parties, traveling bands, or just for spreading out a bit.

H!Bar, the lobby lounge, is a flexible space serving beer, cocktails, and Metric coffee, with occasional live music and other events. And for a more substantial meal, check out the modern American fare at the nearby Cafe Robey, attached to the neighboring sister hotel. Remember, though, that you’re in Chicago, one of the best dining cities in America — and that you can check out one of the hotel’s tokyobike bicycles for help in getting around on your own.

Most travelers to Montevideo are on their way somewhere else, to the classic Uruguayan resort of Punta del Este, maybe, or the trendy beach enclaves around José Ignacio. But the historic port city is worth a visit on its own. Across the wide expanse of the Rio de la Plata from Buenos Aires, it’s the other birthplace of tango, a quiet bastion of elegant architecture with a clamoring seafood market and an appealing seafront promenade. A few good hotels have popped up around town, giving you an extra reason to make a night of it in the southernmost capital in the Americas. Own Montevideo is one of these. 

After a handful of successful ventures across the water in Argentina, the Own group brings their particular brand — in this case, contemporary style, a relatively small scale, practical amenities and customizable services with some luxuries thrown in — to Uruguay. Located in the upscale coastal neighborhood of Las Carretas, the hotel has 44 rooms across five categories. They’re all larger than you’d expect, outfitted in blonde wood and earth tones. Amenities include 42-inch LCD TVs, minibars stocked with Uruguayan wines, and iPod docks. Several rooms and suites have small private terraces. Perhaps more notable, though, is the fact that you can have breakfast delivered to your room, free of charge, if you’d rather not get dressed to dine in the restaurant. As the name implies, a guiding concept at Own Montevideo is that you can choose your own adventure.

content:
In the Occitan village of Collias, a short distance from Uzès, stands an edifice whose foundations were laid a thousand years ago. Today’s Château Collias is less ancient than it sounds — its medieval core has been augmented by Renaissance expansions, an 18th-century façade, and a 19th-century renovation in an Italianate style. And now, of course, what you’ll find inside is a thoroughly modern, thoroughly 21st-century luxury hotel experience.

For that you can thank the owners, Christophe Tailleur and Philippe Huber, both experienced hospitality professionals; here they’ve kept in place all the history and all the atmosphere of the Château’s thousand years of history, while providing its eight bedrooms with all the modern must-haves, including Nespresso machines and high-end local bath products.

The estate’s expansive park offers plenty of opportunity for immersion in nature, whether by the poolside or contemplating a view of the UNESCO-listed Gorges du Gardon Natural Reserve. Farther afield, you’ll find sights like the Roman-era Pont du Gard, as well as the picturesque town of Uzès and the cities of Nimes and Avignon. Leave time for the artfully prepared local cuisine of the Château’s restaurant.

content: Leavenworth, Washington is, on one level, an architectural curiosity, consciously redesigned in the 1960s to resemble a sort of idealized Bavarian village. Quite independent of its Alpine-kitsch aesthetics, however, it’s become one of the Northwest’s mountain-sports meccas, home to no end of adventure-sports enthusiasts, its population swelling in the summers and winters as its streets fill with skiers, snowboarders, climbers, cyclists, and more. LOGE Leavenworth Downtown is Leavenworth in a nutshell: on the outside a detailed replica of a Bavarian inn, but on the inside a boutique-style adventure hotel for a new generation of explorers. \n\nThis means handsome blond wood and modernist-inspired furnishings alongside a pet-friendly policy and a fleet of Raleigh cruiser bikes. The comforts are smart and sustainable, never fussy, and the atmosphere is casual and down-to-earth, despite the interiors’ boutique-hotel looks. There’s a bar and café, serving beer, cocktails, breakfast, sandwiches, and light bites, all in keeping with Leavenworth’s surprisingly vibrant social life — where there’s a Bavarian influence you can generally assume there’s plenty of beer. That said, both sociability and tranquility are live options here; LOGE Leavenworth Downtown’s location is a quick walk from both the town’s busy main drag and a verdant riverside park.
