content:
The “Versailles Château” in the hotel’s name is a reference to the neighborhood, not to the famous palace itself — Le Louis Versailles Château Hotel-MGallery is set just ten minutes’ walk from the Palace of Versailles itself, and offers a taste of palatial grandeur on a slightly smaller and more intimate scale. (The last bit of the name signifies that this is part of Accor’s MGallery collection, which combines unique hotel properties with polished, professional service.)

Le Louis is a 19th-century hotel, as its façade makes perfectly clear, but its interiors have been updated to keep pace with the times. The lobby bar, beneath an arched glass atrium and a modernist chandelier fit for a Sun King, is a contemporary space in tones of emerald and gold, a theme that carries on, though more subtly, into the rooms and suites, many of which feature parquet floors and trompe l’oeil ceilings.

There’s just one restaurant, the perhaps surprisingly contemporary Alcôve, serving modern French cuisine in a colorful, elegant setting. This and the lobby bar are the only food and beverage venues, but thanks to the hotel’s smallish size — and its central location — they’re more than equal to the task.

content:
New Zealand’s natural beauty is so phenomenal, they can get away with some truly understated place names. Imagine the most spectacular place the name “Bay of Islands” could possibly describe, and you still won’t be prepared for the real thing. It’s notable mostly for its unique geography, but this region is also home to a world-class hotel, namely Eagles Nest.

This hotel is a legend around New Zealand, but it’s not as well known overseas, perhaps a function of its small size; comprising just four villas, with an absolute maximum capacity of 22 people at a time, there’s a limit to the number of evangelists this place can produce.

Those who do manage to secure a reservation here are bound to go home raving about the place. The four villas are luxurious homes, designed in an utterly modern style, with brushed-metal appliances in the full kitchens and glass-walled showers in exhibitionist boutique hotel style. Villas sleep as many as eight and as few as two, in the honeymooners’ favorite called First Light Temple (that’s the one with the glass shower, as you may suspect). The larger villas have their own infinity pools and private Jacuzzis, and all come with such necessities as LCD televisions and gas fireplaces.

There’s an infinite variety of dining options, all centering around the essential question of how much you wish to make use of your personal chef — though self-catering is an option, and there are a number of restaurants nearby.

And there’s an embarrassment of choices for activities as well, from sailing and deep-sea fishing to spa treatments, swimming, or old-fashioned idleness. The one thing there’s not: shared public spaces. Each villa is rather like a self-contained mini-hotel, making it one of the most intimate escapes available anywhere.

How to get there:
Eagles Nest is approximately a 45 minute trip from Kerikeri Airport. Guests can drive the entire way besides a 5 minute trip using the Opua car FERRY to get to the Russell peninsula. There are ferries every 10 minutes and prices vary according to your vehicle's size.

content:
As Irish castles go, Mount Falcon is a relatively recent addition, dating back to the late nineteenth century. This means it’s not wedded to any specific historical details, though, which can arguably be a strength. Imagine adding a range of detached self-catering lodges to a thousand-year-old castle, and the word “sacrilege” comes to mind. In Mount Falcon’s case it’s just a sensible expansion, and a new twist on the tradition of Irish country hospitality.

The old house’s four original rooms and the two deluxe suites are classic in style and lack for no reasonable luxury — for decades Mount Falcon’s guests, a discerning bunch, found them more than satisfactory to requirements. The expansion adds twenty-six superior rooms, which are stylistically quite continuous with those in the old house, and though newer, no less comfortable or attractive.

On top of that, a number of one-, two- and three-bedroom lodges expand the offering beyond the traditional hotel paradigm. What they lose in old-castle romance they gain in privacy, residential atmosphere, and practical details (read: fireplaces).

Of course the accommodations are only half the story. Once you’ve said everything there is to be said about the rooms, you still haven’t touched the grounds, the golf, the fishing, or the spa and it’s heated indoor pool — to say nothing of the kitchen, whose modern interpretations of traditional local ingredients show Irish cooking in its best possible light.


How to get there:
Mount Falcon is approximately a 30-minute drive from Ireland West Airport Knock (NOC), 3 hours from Dublin, and 1½ hours from Galway.

content:
The Westin Chosun was established in 1914 as, simply, the Chosun Hotel, named for the dynasty that had ruled Korea for five centuries. It was a smallish but grand affair, a four-story European-style hotel with a Louis XVII living room and elevators from New York. This was the new center of Korean tourism, its first Western-style hotel, and introduced such Western cultural novelties as ice cream and dance parties.

It has been a long nine decades since then, and Seoul is now as modern and cosmopolitan as any other world capital — and though the Westin Chosun's name and silhouette have changed, its position has not. This is the city's top business hotel, located deep in the heart of the traditional downtown area on the north side of the Han river, within walking distance of almost all possible business destinations, from banks and government offices to historic landmarks and shopping districts.

Guest rooms are the city's largest, and though recently renovated, they have retained their idiosyncratic character — somewhere between all-out Far East set design and buttoned-up European elegance, they are a million miles from the beige standard one expects from a business hotel chain. And the rest of the facilities are no less impressive; the business center and conference rooms are stat-of-the-art, and guests have access to the City Athletic Club. There are no fewer than eight restaurants, including not only Japanese, Italian and French options but the ever-popular O'Kim's Irish Pub & Sports Bar as well.

content:
India is home to some grand old historic palace hotels, even in Mumbai—but this most modern of cities is booming, and a number of spectacular and utterly modern business hotels have landed in the suburbs, nearer the airport, rather than in crowded and historic South Mumbai.

It’s here, near the Bandra-Kurla business district, that you’ll find the sprawling Grand Hyatt Mumbai. Frankly, this isn’t the most postcard-perfect place for travelers intent on seeing the sights of the old city to set up shop—it is, however, ideal for business travelers, or anyone looking for a completely self-sufficient hotel experience. It’s possible to stay at the Grand Hyatt for days without ever leaving the grounds, dining in the hotel’s four restaurants, treating yourself to spa treatments in the health club, even shopping in the on-site mall. More than a hotel, it’s billed as a “lifestyle complex,” and includes 149 serviced apartments in addition to its nearly six hundred traditional guest rooms.

Accommodations are strikingly modern and spare, without any trace of touristy Indian kitsch, yet with enough personality to avoid the “where am I again?” feeling occasioned upon waking in many more anonymous business hotels. Rooms are open-plan, decorated in light woods and earth tones, and feature ingeniously designed bathrooms, placed behind floor-to-ceiling sliding partitions, with separate baths and showers.

Twenty-five-inch plasma TVs are standard, along with every technological amenity you could expect. Ground-floor Grand Club rooms feature private patios, a charming and welcome touch, and the suites are so massive you’ll wonder if you’ve been shown to one of the apartments by mistake. Perfect for the busy executive traveler, or anyone who wants a completely over-the-top luxury hotel experience—just do remember to come home again, or at least to venture out for a walk every so often.

content:
Le Relais de Franc Mayne is housed in a 16th-century château. Not the sprawling estate style that’s so common in the Bordeaux countryside, but the other kind —  a down-to-earth wine château, the sort of place where one of the main attractions is a series of old stone quarries where Cabernet Franc ages in oak barrels. Which isn’t to say that anyone is roughing it at this impeccably restored nine-room hotel: sophisticated lighting, decadent silks in bold hues, plasma televisions, a plush billiards room, and vintage wine tastings are just a few of the features putting a contemporary spin on this country-chic property.

Though the unadorned stone exterior is simple, the interior is anything but. The proprietors, perhaps unable to choose between diverse design schemes, selected a different stylistic theme for each individually decorated guest quarter: canary yellow walls in the Pop Art room, zebra prints in the African Lodge room, carved wood in the Indian Fusion room, and so on (suffice it to say, the British Landscape room is not the most exotic of the bunch.) High thread-count linens, DVD players, and wireless internet access come standard, and all rooms afford views over the vineyards surrounding the hotel.

The antique dining room, an intimate venue featuring ornate candelabras and bunches of pink roses, is decidedly more traditional for a French country estate. The cuisine, however fresh and well-prepared, takes a backseat to the red wine produced on the premises — visit the quarries before strolling through the vineyards and then into the medieval town of Saint-Emilion.

content: Staying overnight at Taniya, located in the historic castle town of Takayama, is akin to sleeping at Fallingwater or another architectural landmark. Positioned beside the Kusakabe Family Residence, an old merchant’s house designated an Important Cultural Property, this century-old inn is an extension of its notable neighbor, both showcasing ancient Japanese techniques carried out by local craftsmen. The residence functions like a museum, while Taniya is a traditional two-story wooden townhouse with clay walls, earthen floors, decorative shoji screens, finely made tatami mats, and a cypress bath overlooking a quiet courtyard. Since the property is rented out in its entirety, guests have exclusive access to the house’s peaceful tea room, an elegant wood-lined kitchen, and a stylish reading room with sculptural furniture made by a local artisan.

content: Palermo’s lovely Palazzo Natoli bears the name of the 18th-century marquis for whom it was built, as well as that of the famous novelist who came later in the family line. History, it goes without saying, seeps from every corner of this magnificent house, and indeed from the whole of the neighborhood, close to the cathedral, along the Via Vittorio Emanuele. In its present incarnation, however, it’s a surprisingly contemporary and satisfyingly luxurious boutique hotel, its interiors designed in that inimitably Italian contemporary-meets-classic manner.\n\nNine of the twelve rooms are set in the palace proper, with three more in the neighboring building, including the Family room and the Garden apartment. In all cases they’re handsomely decorated and equipped with all the modern necessities. Beyond breakfast the hotel’s café serves snacks, aperitivi, and wine; the hotel’s concierge, meanwhile, will happily handle restaurant bookings. Cooking classes, golf, and even sailing tours can be arranged as well.

content: The highly esteemed Fufu brand operates high-end, modern ryokan-style inns across Japan; Fufu Karuizawa Yokou No Kaze is set in eastern Nagano Prefecture, with a view of the volcanic Mount Asama. The local hot springs feature calcium–sodium sulfate–tinged water, and the inn’s restaurant serves a uniquely Japanese variation on French cooking, making thoughtful use of seasonal local ingredients.

content: Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui is, as Thai island escapes go, perhaps as good as it gets without owning an island outright. content: The highest hotel in France takes the ski-in, ski-out concept to a new level. Le Refuge de Solaise isn’t just positioned near the slopes: it’s located inside an old cable car station sitting high above Val d’Isère in the French Alps. Only accessible by gondola, the wooden chalet is now a boutique hotel with accommodation options ranging from luxurious suites to dormitory-style bunk beds. Amenities vary widely — higher-end rooms have fireplaces, freestanding tubs, and glorious views over the valley — but the rustic-chic aesthetic is consistent throughout, with massive windows letting in abundant natural light by day and industrial lamps casting a warm glow over knotty wood-paneled walls at night. A pair of restaurants offer traditional French dishes and wood-fired pizzas before a dazzling snow-capped backdrop, and the cozy bar doubles as a breakfast venue. The hotel’s sleek spa, complete with a heated indoor pool, is a great place to decompress after a day out in the mountains.

content:
When it comes to modern high-end luxury hotels, there’s no place in the world that comes even close to being on China’s level. Not only are extravagant new towers going up in the booming secondary cities, but Beijing’s hotel scene continues to scale new heights as well. A member of the same Urban Resort Concepts group that brought us the extraordinary PuLi in Shanghai, the PuXuan Hotel and Spa is a monumental addition to the capital city’s hospitality scene.

The building, by the Beijing office of the German architect Ole Scheeren, is a sober and dignified one, though it’s contemporary to its core — an imposing silhouette for the business hotel of the future. Inside the lobby and the public spaces it’s rather warmer, full of rich details and natural colors, as well as examples of various Chinese art and craft traditions. And the rooms and suites naturally take things in a softer direction — the visuals, still crisp, are complemented by plush textures and next-level luxuries.

Many rooms overlook the Forbidden City, a short distance away — you’re fifteen minutes’ walk from Tiananmen Square, and close to the Wangfujing shopping district. Here at PuXuan, however, there’s plenty to tempt you to stay in, from the two restaurants, the ONE-MICHELIN-Starred Fu Chun Ju and Rive Gauche, also featured in The MICHELIN Guide, to the Guerlain Spa at The PuXuan Hotel and Spa and the inner sanctum that is the Tea Room, which offers a tranquil moment and an introduction to Chinese tea culture.

content: Parma, Bologna, Prosecco: a list of Italian destinations can sound, rather deliciously, like a glorious spread of antipasti and aperitivi. Diehard cheese enthusiasts will be pleased to learn that the Asiago Plateau is a real place — and a strikingly beautiful one at that — northwest of Venice in the province of Vicenza. And it gets better: there’s an excellent hotel up here in the mountains. Meltar Boutique Hotel is located inside a restored old farmhouse in the middle of, well, nowhere, making it a perfectly tranquil getaway from the tourist crush of the Veneto. Technically, the hotel sits on a golf course. But other than a few manicured greens, there’s nothing but fields and woods and cross-country skiing trails as far as the eye can see. The hotel itself has just nineteen rooms. They’re surprisingly modern, if not exactly cutting-edge: each comes with an LCD TV and free wi-fi, but the building’s bones are old, and the architecture largely original to the 19th-century farmhouse. The look is cozy and rustic-chic: vaulted wood ceilings, parquet floors, romantic patterned wallpaper in a sophisticated palette of white, charcoal, taupe and ice-blue. Each offers unobstructed views of the surrounding landscape and mountains. Meltar Boutique Hotel is about getting away from it all — and, to be fair, it’s also about the nothing-is-too-much-trouble staff, and the Turkish bath and spa. There’s a yoga center, if that’s your thing, and endless opportunities for skiing, in the winter, or enjoying that favorite Italian pastime, the passeggiata — a leisurely walk — anytime of year. Or you could stay close to the hotel and enjoy some cheese, or take a cooking class with Meltar’s chef: on request, you’ll tour local wineries and visit producers of wine and cheese to shop for your ingredients. If you have any appetite left after indulging in hand-rolled pasta and tiramisù, relax by the hotel’s elegant fireplace with a glass of Barbera. This is what Italians call il dolce far niente: the pleasure of doing nothing. How to get there: Meltar Boutique Hotel is approximately 133 km by car from Venice Marco Polo Airport via A57, A4/E70, A31, and SP349.

content:
In buttoned-up, no-nonsense Frankfurt, a sculptural steel-and-glass tower of a business hotel is enough to stand out — though not too much. It helps that the JW Marriott Hotel Frankfurt also happens to be one of the city’s largest hotels, though in Germany’s financial capital, that sort of superlative is far less important than the fact that it’s about as functional, comfortable and well-run a business hotel as you’ll find, in Frankfurt or anywhere else. 

The rooms are spacious, with all the screens and gadgets you could hope for plus tasteful flourishes like original art by the German painter Hartwig Ebersbach. Ride the elevator high enough and you’ll find some enormous skyline-view suites, complete with living rooms and fireplaces, and in the Presidential Suite, an en-suite sauna — but you hardly need to upgrade to find yourself in a very comfortable room. 

If there’s one area where the hoteliers let fly a bit, it is, appropriately, in the business facilities. There’s a venue for any sort of meeting you might need to have, on just about any scale, right up to a grand ball beneath a ceiling embedded with over a hundred-thousand crystals. Perhaps more critically, all the technology you’d need is also at hand, and the restaurants and bars are perfectly suited to striking — or celebrating — a deal.

content:
More high-functioning than high-concept, Silicon Valley’s centrally located Domain Hotel makes no bones about the clientele it’s courting. Put it this way: they offer a free weekday shuttle service to the Googleplex, Apple, or any other office within a ten-mile radius. Square that radius, multiply it by pi, and you’ve got an area that covers a pretty substantial chunk of the tech industry. 

As suburban business hotels go, the Domain is a bold one — a modern, colorfully lit lobby, thematic rooms with aqua-blue or forest-green walls. There’s free high-speed wired and wireless internet throughout, plenty of conference and business space, in-room work desks with ergonomic chairs and ample room to stretch out, and a 24-hour business center that, diplomatically, supports both Mac and PC platforms. Complimentary underground parking is a thoughtful touch, too, especially in this sunny, car-happy part of the state. 

When the work day is done, there’s a heated pool, hot tub and fitness studio on premise (as well as a full-scale gym, free for Domain guests, across the street). Or if you want to unwind by partying like <del>Ken Kesey</del> Sean Parker, Stanford is just a short drive away. For a more safe-for-work evening, the hotel’s cutely named restaurant and bar, Bytes, should do just fine. 

Getting there:
Domain Hotel is an easy 15-minute drive from San Jose Mineta International Airport, 40 minutes from SFO, and about an hour from downtown San Francisco. The hotel offers a shuttle service from the San Jose airport, subject to a fee.

content:
In the city of Dijon, just across from the 14th-century Gothic Saint-Bénigne Cathedral, is a rather more modern building: a 1960s Brutalist office building that’s now home to the colorful and irreverent Mama Shelter Dijon. This is a brand with a reputation for playfulness, and it’s richly deserved — the décor is full of light-hearted references to Dijon and the Burgundy region, and the hotel has gone so far as to collaborate with local makers Edmond Fallot on a house brand of Dijon mustard.

To turn an insurance office into something so warm and inviting is no mean feat; architect Benjamin El Doghaïli and the rest of the Mama Shelter team are in top form here, lending visual interest to seemingly every square foot of the space. Long gone is the stark minimalism with which Mama Shelter was once associated, replaced by a charmingly madcap maximalism. 

And while it’s no luxury hotel, neither is it a spartan affair — the rooms are as comfortable as they are efficient, and the public spaces are thoroughly welcoming, from the garden patio to the multi-purpose restaurant, terrace, and bar, serving everything from breakfast and brunch to late-night dinner, wines, and cocktails.

content:
The Latrobe Building, a 1912 apartment tower in Baltimore’s Mount Vernon neighborhood, is now the venue for the unusually named Ulysses, a high-concept, high-design boutique hotel by the hospitality brand ASH NYC. It’s inspired in part by the era of the building’s construction, and, in subtler ways, in part by the contemporaneous novel by James Joyce whose name it shares — as well as the aesthetic sense of the Baltimore-born filmmaker John Waters.

It’s a heady mix for any boutique hotel, especially one in stylistically conservative Baltimore. The result, however, is nothing if not memorable, and while it’s thoroughly unusual it never crosses over into theme-hotel kitsch. Its interior design is eclectic, with pieces sourced from as far afield as India. And while you wouldn’t accuse the rooms of minimalism, they are design-forward in their own slightly baroque way.

Ash Bar is the name of the restaurant, open from breakfast through dinner and beyond, serving classic mid-Atlantic fare accompanied by a substantial menu of drinks. And it’s Bloom’s that’s the more bar-like bar, open from five o’clock until midnight, pouring creative cocktails in a decadent, mirror-strewn space.

content:
It’s a long story, but Pullman is now an Accor brand, with a worldwide selection of hotels that are both business-oriented and boutique-inspired. The Pullman Lima Miraflores is named for its location — the upscale seaside residential and commercial district of Miraflores, on the city’s south side — and it’s a fine ambassador for its brand, combining eye-catching, locally inspired contemporary design with forward-looking sustainability measures and efficient, personable luxury-hotel service.

The hotel’s distinctive checkerboard façade is a bold addition to the neighborhood, while the green roof is evidence of a commitment to minimizing its environmental impact. With 237 rooms and suites it’s a substantial hotel, and even the humblest rooms spans a generous 30 square meters; at all levels they’re decorated with contemporary furniture and lively, vaguely Bauhaus geometric murals above the headboards.

Six meeting rooms help establish the Pullman’s executive bona fides, but of more interest are the leisure facilities, which include a swimming pool on the rooftop terrace, with a view of the seaside and the city skyline. The hotel’s restaurant is a versatile, open-plan space, as well suited to a proper sit-down dinner as to a working laptop lunch; in addition to the restaurant’s bar, there’s a second one on the terrace, which presumably does brisk business around sunset.

content:
Sister hotel to the stately and luxurious Bergen Børs, the 249-room Zander K Hotel is rather more youth-oriented — modernist, minimalist, and with a more utilitarian approach to its comforts. This isn’t meant as a criticism, though; while its luxe sister is decidedly high-end, Zander K’s got everything a design-focused boutique hotel needs, and nothing a low-maintenance modern traveler would find excessive.

Bergen is Norway’s famously rainy second city, and Zander K’s artwork acknowledges the weather, with cartoonish depictions of storm clouds and umbrellas. The design, by the Swedish firm Claesson Koivisto Rune, is crisp and utilitarian, the rooms making liberal use of blond wood and a whole monochrome rainbow of gray tones.

The public spaces are considerably less sparse; the lobby is a classic multi-use all-day space, serving everything from breakfast and espresso to cocktails and organic beers and wines, and features a menu of locally sourced dishes for lunch and dinner. It’s a fine place to work, to socialize, or simply to lounge — and right outside the hotel is the central rail station and, a few blocks beyond, the heart of what might be Norway’s most scenic, livable, and unique cities.

content: The name has changed many times since the Steigenberger Wiltcher’s, the grand dame of Brussels’ Avenue Louise, first opened its doors in 1913. But its old-world grandeur remains, the marble and brass polished to perfection in the chandelier-lit lobby. After extensive renovations in recent years, this landmark luxury hotel is even more refined than before, its hundreds of guest rooms modernized and outfitted with handy features like deep soaking tubs and Nespresso machines. Suites are palatial, with extras like kitchens, private meeting rooms, and butler service. Guests have access, for an extra fee, to a sleek spa with an infinity pool. But the hotel’s true highlights are its elegant restaurants and bars, including the open-air La Terrasse, a cozy library lounge, and the see-and-be-seen Loui Bar. Thanks to the location in the center of the city’s upscale shopping district, you’re likely to take your afternoon tea alongside stylish locals as well as fellow guests.

content:
Just as Tel Aviv itself sits at the perfect intersection of the ancient past and the modern present, so too does a hotel like the Lighthouse. It takes its name from the building it calls home, the Migdalor — Hebrew for “lighthouse” — an office tower in central Tel Aviv that was built in 1972 but neglected for years, until architect Nestor Sandbank and Brown Hotels breathed new life into the building and helped revive the surrounding area.

The hotel occupies significant parts of the old structure, turning once-derelict offices into exquisite gathering spaces — the lobby, for one, occupies the former offices of a travel company, and the fifth-floor hotel restaurant was previously a nightclub. The rooms are a visual feast, blending mid-century modern aesthetic with hipster amenities like vintage-style Marshall Bluetooth speakers and Molton Brown toiletries. Nearly all of the 100 suites feature at least partial views of the Tel Aviv skyline, and some even come with outdoor Jacuzzis on spacious private terraces. 

There’s a restaurant on the fifth floor, serving farm-to-table Israeli fare next to its own expansive green terrace. To take in even more of the sights, two sundeck terraces offer sunbeds, an outdoor hot tub, and more gorgeous views of the city, as does the Haiku Skybar, the open-air rooftop bar with a 360-degree panorama of the whole of Tel Aviv and the Mediterranean.

content:
While hoteliers in New York and Los Angeles strain mightily against sky-high real-estate prices, smaller regional cities like Chattanooga, Tennessee are flourishing like never before. This highly livable town has long been popular among outdoor types, and lately it’s been redeveloping its downtown district as well — and now, in the form of the Dwell Hotel, it’s got its first proper boutique hotel.

It’s a renovation of the century-old Stone Fort Inn, and its new owner, first-time hotelier Seija Ojanpera, has outfitted it with vintage furniture and modern artworks, and redecorated it in a bold and colorful mid-century modernist style. Every room is different, and each one’s style is fully realized. Some have balconies, and every one comes with a rain shower and a separate soaking tub, while the suites, in addition to spreading out a bit, add fireplaces.

The bar, Matilda Midnight, goes all in on the mid-century vibe, featuring craft cocktails and inventive small bites, a refreshing departure from the New South comfort food that’s all the rage (mostly outside of the South) at the moment. It’s nothing if not sociable — that famous Southern hospitality is no myth.

content:
In some towns the Four Seasons is among the most conservative luxury hotels in town. But in Mumbai, and in India in general, it would take some doing to out-classic some of the grand old palace hotels. Here the new Four Seasons is all contemporary: from the gleaming glass facade of the Four Seasons Tower to the brand-new fleet of twenty Series 7 BMWs.

Here it should be noted that contemporary isn’t the same as avant-garde. The stone-clad lobby is impressive, almost monumental, but in subdued, natural colors. Upstairs the guest rooms avoid both colonial clichés and Taj Mahal kitsch, but they’re definitely not cutting-edge — the interiors take a back seat to the views, especially if your room faces the Arabian Sea, and the focus is on the creature comforts: marble baths with separate soaking tubs, oversized LCD televisions, all the usual five-star trappings.

The location, in the southern Worli district, means many business travelers will find it ideally placed. But it’s not all about work. The spa covers two whole floors of the building, and if you can’t find relaxation there, or in the Four Seasons’ daily yoga sessions, then we don’t know what to do with you. 

How to get there: Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport is 20 km (12 miles) and approximately one hour by car from the hotel, while Santa Cruz Domestic Airport is 15 km (9 miles) and approximately 45 minutes by car from the hotel.

content:
It’s only a century and a half old, but this town goes out of its way to show its age. Fans of modern architecture and towers in green glass will feel more at home in mainland Vancouver — Victoria, on Vancouver Island, is something of a throwback to the era with which it shares its name, the sort of place that puts the British back in British Columbia. And a block from the scenic Inner Harbour is the Magnolia Hotel & Spa, a lodging that, for all its newness, is equally at home in the 21st century and the 19th — which means that, for this timeless town, it’s perfectly contemporary.

And in spite of a slight tinge of grand-hotel formality, the Magnolia is a modern boutique through and through. With sixty-four rooms it’s kept to a personable scale, and the service is pure West Coast charm. The décor is classic, never breaking the spell that’s cast by the views of the historic downtown, and the bathrooms stick with tradition as well — deep soaking tubs are a highlight. In fact indulgence, in one form or another, is what the Magnolia is all about: the Spa Magnolia cements the hotel’s status as a getaway destination, and The Courtney Room, just off the lobby, would have suited the Victorian Victoria just as it does the modern one.

content:
Despite being known as a manufacturing base and financial hub, Córdoba has the youthful heart of a college town. Three historic universities line the city’s Jesuit Block, a gorgeous display of Latin American baroque architecture. Minutes away is a century-old townhouse that served as a drugstore, residence, and school before an extensive renovation transformed it into the Azur Real Hotel Boutique.

The lobby is a nod to the building’s evolution, with exposed brick and a stone fireplace presiding over an inviting modern daybed, hinting at the friendly hospitality within. 16 uncluttered guest rooms feature pared back neutral shades and furnishings, complemented by dark wood paneling and sleek lighting. Some rooms come with balconies, but the Azur Suite gets top billing with its own private Jacuzzi and outdoor patio.

The townhouse might be intimate, but the services are impressive, from the remarkable subterranean spa and the rooftop terrace with its plunge pool and open-air restaurant, to Casa de Mate, an apothecary showcasing the history and tradition of yerba mate and local Córdoba plants.

How to get there:
Azur Real Hotel Boutique is located 10.8 km (25min) from Ambrosio LV Taravella International Airport. Transfers can be organized in a private sedan or van for US$30 per car for up to three guests, one way.

content: The tiny, mile-wide Kouri Island, informally known as Love Island for its heart-shaped rock formations, lies just two short bridge crossings from the main island of Okinawa. This little speck of paradise is fringed by sandy beaches, and though it’s solely a leisure destination, it’s not a busy one. This means plenty of tranquility is on offer at One Suite The Grand, a 21-room luxury boutique resort in a contemporary-classic style. content: Claude Monet was so entranced by the interplay of light and shadow around the alabaster cliffs at Étretat, a village on France’s northern coast, that he tried to capture it in twenty different paintings. If you’re staying at Les Tilleuls Étretat, a luxury hotel that’s just a short walk away, you’ll have the chance to view the dramatic scenery at sunrise, sunset, and anytime in between. The 18th-century mansion exudes old-world elegance, surrounded with leafy gardens and featuring a handful of quiet suites with original oil paintings, antique oak furniture, parquet floors, toile prints, and spacious walk-in showers. Some have clawfoot tubs and several open directly onto a sunny terrace; the largest suite has a living room furnished with Chesterfield sofas. There’s a small cinema for watching French films while sipping wine from the hotel’s 900-bottle cellar. Or ask the include a bottle in a gourmet picnic basket, packed for day trips on request.

content: Set high in the French Alps above the ski resort of Megève, Flocons de Sel is an elegant getaway with sweeping views of the valley below. It’s particularly enchanting in winter, when snow covers the landscape and open fireplaces crackle inside the boutique hotel’s wooden chalets. Guest rooms and suites are light-filled and minimalist, lined with pale wood and stone; eclectic details add alpine character, from animal hide rugs and patterned wool throws to a side table made out of a tree stump. All have bathtubs and private terraces facing the surrounding mountains, and some have wood-burning stoves. A pair of freestanding chalets offer extra privacy, with two levels of living and sleeping space. The hotel offers free shuttle service to the nearby ski lift, and afterward, access to a rustic-chic spa with a beautifully illuminated indoor pool. Chef Emmanuel Renaut presides over the extraordinary restaurant.\n

content:
The bulk of the Venetian tourist trade centers on Venice proper, but the Lido, the barrier island that shields Venice from the Adriatic Sea, is a destination unto itself; it’s home to the film festival, for one, as well as some elegant grand hotels, including the renovated Ausonia Hungaria. The famous Liberty-style façade, dating back to 1907, is still in place, but what’s inside is now an entirely contemporary luxury hotel, complete with modernist-inspired furnishings and décor and all the essential 21st-century comforts.

Its century-old floor plan results in a wide variety of rooms, from the aptly named Cozy Room — still spacious enough for a king bed — to the expansive Amazing Suite. The art pays tribute to the era when Venice was at the height of its powers, while the interior design recalls mid-century modernism at its most utopian.

There’s a spa with an outdoor pool as well as a Thai massage center, plus a private beach, and the island offers golf and horseback riding among its outdoor diversions. A handful of restaurants and bars include The Mode, for upscale modern Italian fare, and 28.5, the rooftop restaurant and lounge with an impressive view of the Lido, the lagoon, and Venice in the distance.

The hotel’s restaurant serves Pacific Northwest cuisine from local ingredients, and the location places you close to much of the best of this corner of Portland, including Tom McCall Waterfront Park, Pioneer Courthouse Square, and what might be the greatest book shop in North America, Powell’s City of Books.

content: Silicon Valley as a concept might be the virtual capital city of the future, but Palo Alto as it actually exists can feel a touch anti-climactic, and its hotels are often disappointingly ordinary. But one hotel in Palo Alto feels suitably grand, at least once you’re through its doors: the El Prado’s vaguely postmodern NorCal Mediterranean-villa façade conceals a very contemporary luxury boutique hotel, whose interiors — especially in the guest rooms, which are remarkably stylish — recall some of Europe’s better high-end small hotels.\n\nGiven that it’s more or less the only hotel of its kind in town, it attracts a rather eclectic clientele, including tech-industry executives with a taste for a bit of grandeur and guests of Stanford University. And it’s quite capable of catering to all their needs, with capacious business facilities and a walkable location that’s convenient to the local shops and restaurants. It may not be a window into the future, exactly, but it makes a compelling case for the present.

content: The original 21c Museum Hotel in Louisville, Kentucky was ample proof of the notion that a well-executed boutique hotel with a contemporary art focus could thrive in, if not quite the unlikeliest of American towns, then not exactly the likeliest, either. And the new 21c Museum Hotel Bentonville goes one further: its namesake town of Bentonville, Arkansas, is no precious artist’s colony, but the heartland home of the Wal-Mart retail mega-chain. Then again, maybe Bentonville’s not such a curveball. Say what you will about Wal-Mart as a cultural signifier, but the Walton family itself is the force behind the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, a first-class museum, and an architecturally distinguished one at that — not to mention one that’s open to the public, free of charge. It doesn’t take much more than that to kickstart a thriving art scene, and if the 21c is evidence of anything, it’s evidence of that. It’s also a very fine hotel, on its own merits. The 104 rooms, designed by architect Deborah Berke, are clean-lined, crisp and contemporary, yet never sacrifice comfort or coziness — they’re more or less everything you’d want from the letter C. The Hive is the restaurant and bar, serving fresh and local American country cuisine in a communal setting, and the cocktail bar is proof that Louisville isn’t the only place to go looking for bourbon and rye. And with twelve thousand square feet of exhibition space, also open to the public, the 21c happens to be a first-class contemporary art museum in its own right.

content:
Most of the time, it’s enough for an airport hotel just to be comfortable and convenient, and on those two counts the Hyatt Regency Incheon certainly comes through. Just a three-minute shuttle ride from Incheon International Airport, it feels like an oasis — a calm and quiet place to recharge after the rigors of air travel. What really sets it apart from the typical airport hotel, however, is that it’s also a well-equipped, highly functional business hotel. That’s obviously a good thing if you’ve got business in Incheon, but it also means that a long layover in Seoul doesn’t have to leave you scrambling to catch up when you get to your final destination. 

Even if you don’t have any work to do, it’s an excellent place to rest up between flights. The rooms are spacious and well-appointed, with king-size beds covered in goose-down duvets. Elegant granite baths and all the proper technology, from iPod docks to LED screens, make it easy to hole up in the room and fight off the jetlag in style. And when you’re eyelids get heavy from too much time in front of the monitor, there’s a cloud-like bed tempting you to take a nap — as for productivity, just tell yourself that getting over jetlag a little sooner will pay dividends later on. 

There’s also a surprising array of distractions outside the rooms. The hotel’s aptly named Restaurant 8 is essentially eight restaurants in one, with separate sections dedicated to various cuisines. It’s a bit like an airport food hall, only more relaxed, and far more attractively designed. A garden-side pool further enhances the oasis effect, and offers a welcome dose of sun and greenery after spending a while in airports and planes. And if you really want to work off any residual travel stress, the on-site karaoke bar ought to do the trick.

content: The Fife Arms is located not in Fife but in Braemar, deep in the Scottish highlands. And while its name is a remnant of its past as a Victorian-era coaching inn, inside it’s much more than a trip back in time. It’s the passion project of the Swiss gallerists Manuela and Iwan Wirth, and is correspondingly filled with extremely impressive artworks. The rooms and suites vary in size but are quite uniformly luxurious and ornately decorated — only in the spa will you find anything approaching minimalism. Multiple dining and drinking venues include the dazzling Clunie Dining Room and the impressively well-supplied Bertie’s Whisky Bar.

content:
The local hotel scene is a diverse one; the Arts District on the north side of downtown Nashville, Tennessee is where you’ll find the city’s most refined boutique hotels, and the Fairlane Hotel is a fine example. A former bank building, it dates back to the Seventies, a decade that informs its interior design; while reminiscent of the mid-century modern style that’s the default for hip-meets-serious hotels, it features the warmer tones and unusual color accents of the decade of its construction.

Its rooms and suites benefit from plentiful sunlight, vintage-inspired décor, and “peek-a-boo” showers, a sign that the Fairlane is intended at least as much for pleasure as for business. That said, there’s plentiful meeting and events space, as well as a thoughtfully equipped fitness center.

Ellington’s, the restaurant, is the Fairlane’s social hub, serving a menu of retro-themed dishes and cocktails in a stylish indoor-outdoor space. It’s joined by the Champagne-centric Bouquet Bar as well as Cheese Gal, for a cheese board and a glass of wine, and for breakfast and lunch there’s the self-explanatory Bagelshop. And just outside, there’s much, much more — the bustle of Broadway lies just a few streets to the south.

For food and drink, you’re on your own, but despite the Moss Hotel’s pastoral vibe, you’re surrounded by restaurants, bars, and all the best of Hobart city life.

content:
Less than three hours’ drive from Shanghai is the mountain resort of Dong Qian Lake — call it Lake Tahoe to Shanghai’s San Francisco, or Lake Placid to Shanghai’s New York. Then again, it doesn’t really compare to those places, in one important respect: neither Lake Tahoe nor Lake Placid has anything like the Park Hyatt Ningbo Resort and Spa. In a few short years, this hotel has amassed a reputation as one of the best of the thirty-odd Park Hyatts; and this, need we remind you, is a group whose bad days are better than many hotel chains’ most successful efforts.

It was the first Park Hyatt in China, but there’s nothing tentative about it. It’s arranged like a village along the shore of the lake, a sprawling cluster of pavilions and villas, erected in a classically influenced contemporary Chinese style. The Standard rooms — the Park Hyatt, thankfully, hasn’t succumbed to the room-category inflation that makes every room “superior” at the very least — are large and lavish for most purposes, though if you can swing a View or a Deluxe you won’t go wrong. Meanwhile the suites are downright extravagant, with seemingly acres of space, and the villas are the stuff of hospitality fantasies.

The fixtures and furnishings are predictably first-rate, and the service, an area where mainland China still lags ever so slightly behind the rest of the Asian luxury market, is quite up to the usual Park Hyatt standard — which, as you’ll know, is a high standard indeed. Also highly rated: the restaurants, one of which specializes in local seafood and regional flavors, and the spa, which draws heavily on traditional Chinese medicine.

content: The streets of heaven, we’ve heard, are paved in gold — but in Split, we can confirm that they’re lined with white marble. They’re a throwback to the city’s glamorous heyday: around 300AD, to be exact, when the Roman emperor Diocletian chose this seaside settlement as the ideal place to build his retirement palace. Thanks to the Roman ruins and the idyllic location on the Adriatic coast, Split remains one of Croatia’s most popular destinations — the kind of place where you’d like to stay close to the historic center, but not right in the middle of the tourist action. Someplace like the Hotel Luxe, a quick five-minute walk from the palace. The Luxe is a contemporary boutique hotel, but the aesthetic is far from minimalist. With shiny metallic design accents, deep purple satin, sculptural white chaises longues and ceilings studded with tiny lights resembling stars in the night sky, the look is more extravagant than understated. The bold design is especially noteworthy considering the simple building the hotel is located inside — an old waterfront factory. The converted spaces aren’t lofty and atmospheric, as you might expect: guest rooms are on the boxy side, but smartly designed with painted wood furnishings, striped rugs, spacious bathrooms, flat-screen TVs. All but the most basic rooms feature views of the water; Superior rooms have private sea-view balconies. Apart from the location around the corner from the port, and the hotel’s fresh, brand-new feel — something of a rarity in a city as old as Split — the Hotel Luxe’s notable attributes include the small wellness center, an ample buffet breakfast, and a Cigar Lounge with great people-watching opportunities over the street below. And after returning from sightseeing, it’s a relaxed spot to sip rakija, the local version of grappa.

content:
Austria’s second city is a youthful town, a university town, and thus perfect for a hotel like the Daniel. After all these years finally smart modern design is available at budget rates: there’s nothing at the Daniel over 100 euros, and in fact the most basic rooms start at €69, a price that in most towns guarantees a fairly sad experience.

Here for that price you get a central location, moments from the train station and the Kunsthaus and a short walk from the old town, and you get a clever if stripped-down modern hotel, outfitted in a cheerfully utopian style by Berlin’s Studio Aisslinger. Rooms won’t quite bowl you over with luxury, but again they’re far more than adequate, air conditioned, with satellite TV, internet access and charming little balconies, half of them painted in Easter-egg colors.

A breakfast buffet and a 24-hour espresso and tapas bar keep guests fueled up, and most anything else you’d need is a short walk away. What’s more, anything that’s not within walking distance is surely within range of the Daniel’s fleet of rental Vespas — this is a service we’d like to see a few more budget hotels take on. In fact we’d have no complaints if there were more hotels like the Daniel. But now we’re just daydreaming.

How to get there: 
Hotel Daniel Graz is located just steps from Graz’s central train station. The hotel is about a 2-hour drive from Vienna International Airport (VIE), and about a 3-hour drive from Salzburg.

content:
About the only thing L’Hotel du Lac has in common with a traditional ryokan is its country setting — in this case, on the shores of Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture. The rest is pure of-the-moment luxury, and we don’t mean flatscreens juxtaposed with tatami floors and futons. This is wall-to-wall modern design, a precise aesthetic stripped to its essentials without feeling too spare. It can be a bit jarring to step out of the postcard-ready surroundings and into the airy, glass-walled lobby, but once you’ve arrived in your guest room, it all comes together.

The concept of “serenity” is one of those hotel intangibles that’s difficult to describe, and just as difficult to fake. Guests simply know it when they experience it, and the rooms at L’Hotel du Lac are serene without even trying. There’s no trick — just modern hospitality done very well, right down to the spacing between the sofas and tables. Private audio-visual rooms (read: home theaters) are a welcome touch, and if you’re in the mood for something a bit rustic, free-standing villa suites offer more in the way of country living, with lofted hideaways and sloped ceilings.

While it’s not a resort, per se, the facilities certainly aren’t skimpy. The tennis court, pool, and outdoor baths serve to relieve any vacation atrophy, and there’s a well-stocked library for rainy days. Cuisine at SOWER, the hotel restaurant, is enhanced by local produce. And the after-dinner hangout is a chic lounge outfitted with hundreds of varieties of shochu.

How to get there:
Chubu Centrair International Airport is approximately 2.5 hours by car (90 miles/150 kilometers). Nagahara Station (JR LINE) is 10 minutes by car to the hotel.

content:
Luang Prabang is one of those destinations where you hardly need an extraordinary hotel to have an extraordinary experience — which makes the fact that there are several of them feel almost gratuitous. Not that we’re complaining. In the case of Sofitel Luang Prabang it means a rare conjunction of historical architecture and modern design, and a chance to inhabit an ancient place in an atmosphere of the utmost contemporary luxury.

The architect, Duangrit Bunnag, is responsible for some very fine modernist beach hotels in Thailand, and here he’s wedded a handful of original French Colonial structures (including the old governor’s mansion) to a number of new buildings, heavily influenced in turn by traditional Lao architecture. The result is a strangely timeless blend, especially in the guest suites, which feel not just sequestered in space but somehow lost in time as well.

Only some of them come with private pools, but all are indulgent in their own way, with private gardens and spa-like bathrooms. Of course there’s a proper spa as well, for when “spa-like” isn’t quite enough, and a main pool for a more serious approach to swimming. Add a fine restaurant and lounge, as well as a cooking school, and the culinary angle is more than covered — especially when you add the restaurants at 3 Nagas, the sister hotel, just a few minutes down the road.

How to get there: Sofitel Luang Prabang is conveniently located just 5 minutes from the central area of town and a 15-minute drive from the Luang Prabang Airport.

content:
Edinburgh stands out as one of the UK’s most cosmopolitan cities — and certainly the most international in Scotland. In this context, a stylish boutique hotel like The Rutland, where designer prints and modernist furnishings replace tartan and antiques, feels perfectly at home.

That said, it’s not purely a continental-style design boutique: with its bars and restaurants, there’s more than a touch of pub spirit about The Rutland. The rooms — each individually designed — are no afterthought, decorated in calming neutrals with vibrant graphic accents. Two offer castle views, a striking counterpoint to the contemporary interiors, and three are junior suites with a clear emphasis on comfort. In addition, The Rutland features 13 serviced one- or two-bedroom apartments.

When it comes to dining, the hotel presents a lively and varied culinary scene. The Huxley delivers relaxed, all-day dining from breakfast through dinner, while Kyloe is renowned for serving some of the best steak in the city. Meanwhile, Heads & Tales pairs Asian-inspired fusion plates with an inventive cocktail and gin offering.

content:
Some of the “boutique hotels” in America’s provincial capitals feel like baby steps, watered-down versions of what went over big in New York a decade ago, perhaps underestimating the sophistication of their audiences’ tastes. The Chambers Hotel, by contrast, plays in the big leagues, and sets a high standard indeed for whatever is to follow in the Twin Cities.

In fact, looking at the big picture (a sorry pun, as you’ll see) the Chambers might actually be ahead of its coastal cousins. This is no mere design hotel, no 1990s-style boutique; the next thing is the “art hotel,” where the art collection, not the interior design, is the focus. And the Chambers’ collection leaves most New York hotels (most hotels anywhere, really) in the dust: Minnesota is probably the last place one could reasonably expect to see one of Damien Hirst’s formaldehyde-preserved carcasses, but here you’ll find his Judas Iscariot (a rather grim-looking decayed cow’s head) along with works by any number of other artists, Young and British or otherwise.

All of this is not to say that design has been somehow overlooked at the Chambers. The rooms feel like movie-set versions of New York loft-style hotel rooms; the same idea, with high ceilings and oversized windows, but much bigger — Minnesota certainly has the edge in terms of buildable space. No comfort is spared, from pillow-top mattresses and feather beds to flat-screen televisions, in the bedrooms and in the glass-tiled bathrooms. And just outside is the best of what the city has to offer, including the Art Institute, the theater district, and some of the best shopping this side of Chicago.

content:
Few hotel brands are quite as successful at combining an instantly recognizable house style with careful tailoring to its locations. Mama Shelter Toulouse is full of subtle references to the architecture of this rose-colored Renaissance city; it’s more full, of course, of street art and youth-culture references, as well as some knowing nods to Toulouse’s thriving rugby fandom.

The facade of an old cinema conceals some 120 rooms, which range in no-nonsense style from size Small on up to XXL. The in-room comforts at all sizes are low-key where it doesn’t much matter, and luxurious where it does, specifically in the beds; movies are free, and the bath products in the oversized rain showers are organic.

There’s a 20-seat CineMama cinema in the basement, a tribute to the building’s original use, and there’s plentiful public space besides — the main restaurant, decorated with greenery, is an Argentine grill with an Occitan accent, while the bar features table football, DJ sets, live music, and festive cocktails. The finest space, however, just might be the rooftop, serving wine and tapas under striped umbrellas with a far-ranging view of the Ville Rose.

content:
Most UNESCO World Heritage sites aren’t exactly hotbeds for stylish, avant-garde hotel options; certainly this holds true for Lijiang, China. Fortunately there are plenty of other reasons to visit this ancient and historic settlement in northern Yunnan province. Three hundred and fifty-four of those reasons come in the form of the city’s famous bridges. (Presumably if a place is going to be called the City of Bridges, someone’s got to count them.) Above all, however, one comes for the stunning natural surroundings; this is one of the most wildly beautiful corners of a country with quite a few wildly beautiful places, and the fact that there’s as fine a hotel as the Pullman is really just icing on the cake. No, it’s not the most achingly hip hotel out there, but then again hipness, in a location like this one, is simply beside the point.

That location, by the way, is technically outside of town — not that you’re going to mind once you see the surrounding scenery. Visible from the hotel grounds are the snowcapped peaks of the Yùlóngxuě Shān mountain range — including the wonderfully named Jade Dragon Snow Mountain — and it’s an easy trip to the region’s most spectacular sights. 

From outside, the resort’s look is that of a traditional local village, with the pleasing angles of the pagodas reflected in a tranquil central pond. But from inside, the Pullman is minimalist, even stark, with huge panes of spotless glass, expanses of immaculate white, and thoroughly contemporary amenities. Guest rooms are pristine, if a bit spartan at the entry level; the more lavish villas come with extras like underfloor heating, private courtyards and outdoor soaking tubs facing the mountains.

The Mandara spa specializes in treatments inspired by the region; think pu-erh tea body scrubs and acupressure facials. The resort’s ZUN Chinese restaurant does gourmet regional cuisine and the sleek XI Western restaurant offers al fresco seating, but the most interesting dining experience on site is Open Kitchen by Pullman, where you can watch dexterous local chefs prepare your food before you dine.

content:
Here’s a hotel that knows how to make an entrance. The Park Hyatt Beijing follows the format of its cousins in Shanghai and Tokyo, occupying roughly the top half of a 66-story skyscraper. Nice view if you can get it, right? The stroke of genius is that the lobby is on the 63rd floor, so everyone shares in the panorama — from up here you can actually see the curvature of Beijing.

And if it’s rumored to be a tad less polished than the Tokyo and Shanghai installments, it’s simply a function of the location. What Beijing may lack in refinement and sophistication — and it’s catching up quickly, mind you — it more than makes up for in sheer exuberance. This Park Hyatt, for its part, is every bit up to the standard implied by the name — it’s just that some of its charms (the view, the glass-enclosed arch of the pool deck) are bolder than usual.

No less elegant, though. The rooms are everything you expect them to be — more, if you factor in the vertigo-inducing views — and the hotel is run, as is the custom, with pinpoint efficiency. The Park Hyatts, at least in East Asia, are practically at the point where all you need to hear is the name, and for a high-end chain hotel, that’s the whole point of the exercise.

content:
Sometimes a hotel isn’t just a hotel, it’s a modern architectural landmark. Here’s what you need to know about the Mineral Lodge, located at an altitude of 1200 meters in the Rhône-Alpes region of the French Alps. The project was conceived by celebrated architect and philosopher Christian Girard, one of the founders of the École Nationale Supérieure d’Architecture Paris Malaquais, and constructed on the ruins of an old chalet-style farmhouse perched high in the mountainous landscape. The result is a sustainably built and tech-forward stone and rock structure with spectacular views over cliffs and valleys — and a pretty inspired piece of design.

Some liberties have naturally been taken with the concept of a traditional chalet: there are rules for how these can be built, you see, that vary according to the hamlet. This is a modern, minimal chalet with airy open spaces, smooth wood, soaring ceilings, huge skylights, sharp angular staircases, gigantic glass panes, and a concrete roof.

Five silent, perfectly sleek guestrooms feature all the stone and wood details you’d expect, plus large flat-screen TVs, luxurious walk-in showers and linens you’ll want to take home with you. Some rooms have private terraces; otherwise, the lodge’s panoramic terrace and chic glass-encased living area are the best places to gape at the gorgeous scenery and contemplate the day’s hike or ski run. (When you’re through contemplating and ready to get moving, the ski slopes and trails of Les Arcs Paradise are just outside.) And if all this talk of modern design and minerals strikes you as a bit cold? Architecture aside, the lodge still has the guest in mind — the floors are all heated from underneath.

content:
Perched as it is on the edge of Lake Wakatipu and surrounded by the Remarkable mountains, Queenstown is the ideal focal point from which to experience New Zealand’s diversity of landscapes. As a haven for ruddy outdoorsy types and backpackers cruising through on the cheap, the city isn’t lacking in vibrant nightlife, and avoiding the all-night party scene in favor of laid-back sophistication used to mean finding a hotel or villa outside of town. But a few recent additions have established toeholds of luxury in the heart of the city, one elegant example being the Sofitel Queenstown Hotel & Spa.

As always, the Sofitel name carries with it a certain refinement, a Parisian put-togetherness. With 82 guest rooms, two restaurants, a lounge, and a spa, the hotel is large enough to accommodate a wide range of travelers, from grown-up ski bums to honeymooners to hikers. Most of the rooms offer private balconies, and all are equipped with the modern conveniences of wi-fi, pillow menus, and espresso machines. There’s nothing radical or avant-garde about the design, but everything from the king beds to the rain-shower bathrooms is just right.

The Nue Lounge, a champagne and martini bar that also features a selection of local wines, ensures that the hotel cultivates its own brand of nightlife for guests and discerning Queenstown residents. The Vie restaurant best embodies the hotel’s attitude of urban sophistication tinged with rustic living, as it overlooks a landscaped garden complete with a waterfall. And it's not for nothing that they mention the spa in their hotel’s official name; with treatments and interventions that span the distance from the beauty salons of Paris to the Maori mud baths of Rotorua, it's a spa that’s worth setting aside some time for.

content: The German-born architect João Federico Ludovice, responsible for many of Lisbon’s glittering 18th-century palaces and churches, didn’t skimp on luxury for his own private residence, either, designing an opulent five-story mansion that occupies an entire city block in Bairro Alto. As the name suggests, the Palácio Ludovice Wine Experience Hotel pays homage to its original owner and to the building’s later use as a headquarters for the Port Wine Institute. \n\nThe result is bright and airy, with a smart mix of old — carefully preserved frescoes, exposed stone archways, blue-and-white tilework — and new, including a vertical garden in the courtyard atrium and custom wool carpets inspired by the vineyards of the Douro Valley. Rooms and suites are light-filled and elegant with Art Deco details, bespoke furnishings, and spacious bathrooms stocked with Caudalie products. Downstairs, the stylish Federico restaurant is framed by lush plants and art installations inspired by the architect’s passion for goldsmithing.

content: Lieser Castle presides over a stretch of the lush, winding Moselle river in southwest Germany. The hotel is perfectly positioned to explore nearby gems (Trier and Luxembourg are both within an hour’s drive) or the region’s famous white wine vineyards.

content:
If there’s one overriding regional trend in luxury hospitality at the moment, it’s the rise of China’s regional cities as a high-end hotel market. Simply put, as impressive as the luxury hotels of Shanghai and Hong Kong may be, the rest of the country is catching up, if not progressing to another level entirely. Take, as an example, the Four Seasons Hotel Hangzhou at West Lake.

West Lake itself is more than just a body of water. It’s a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it’s something like Hangzhou’s version of Central Park, if Central Park were hundreds of years old, and dotted with ancient temples. The Four Seasons blends effortlessly into this environment, with its 17 acres of gardens and waterways and its low-slung traditional pavilions.

With just 78 rooms, this is on the small side for Four Seasons, and while they’re stylistically somewhat conservative, they’re tailored to the location, with plentiful nods to traditional Chinese design. They’re also extravagantly comfortable, from the deluxe rooms all the way up to the suites and the three-story, three-bedroom villas, each one a lavish residence unto itself.

And the facilities, however carefully hidden among the pavilions and the pagodas, are the equal of any urban Four Seasons. The restaurants serve upscale Chinese and Western fare, and the hotel offers an extraordinary 11 private dining rooms, each one with a terrace overlooking the gardens.

content:
While Cincinnati sits on the north bank of the Ohio River, cross over to the south and you’re in Covington, Kentucky. And a few blocks from the river, in a building that started its life as a department store — and Kentucky’s first skyscraper, back when skyscrapers were a comparatively modest thing — is Hotel Covington, a 114-room boutique hotel that’s by some distance the most stylish place to stay on this side of the river.

Inside the rooms, the look is contemporary, but with more than a passing nod to the glamour of the early 20th century. The renovation of this old building was total, which means the floor plans give you generous 21st-century dimensions. And the amenities are right up to date, including Bluetooth sound systems and mini-fridges stocked with a thoughtful selection of local products.

Coppin’s Restaurant and Bar is the most atmospheric of the hotel’s spaces, with rough brickwork and industrial architecture providing the backdrop to a menu of hyper-local American fare — this is more or less the exact spot where North meets South, and it’s apparent at the table. And for something more casual, there’s a walk-up window for late-night take-out, as well as an artisan coffee bar in the lobby. Don’t be surprised if you find yourself developing a strong preference for the Kentucky side of the river.

content:
We’ve seen a single factory building converted into a boutique hotel before, or some quaint old warehouse. The Factory Hotel, though, rather outdoes itself. It occupies not just one industrial building, but a whole factory complex, north of the Münster city center. And the building at its center, the old Germania brewery building, is history in charming red brick, something straight out of the Industrial Revolution, and very much more attractive that the average factory.

That’s the outside. Inside the hotel it’s another world. Suffice it to say that there’s very little in here that’s anywhere near as historically oriented as the exterior of the old brewery building. Here, in a separate building, you’ll find a more modern version of industrial chic, with rough raw concrete walls set against rich wood floors and modernist furnishings.

So the accommodations are stylish, and more than a little comfortable. Equally impressive, however, is the extent of the Factory’s other services, scattered throughout the Germania compound. The fitness center rivals any private health club, with its pool, gym, spa and roof terrace. Three restaurants cover the major cuisines of western Europe, and two clubs respectively focus on live performance and DJ nights. And with no fewer than nine distinct meeting spaces (served by no fewer than three catering kitchens) it’s the sort of place where you might just be able to get your employer to foot the bill.

content:
The exclusive Uruguayan resort of Punta del Este caters to the cream of Brazilian and Argentinian high society, most of whom come to stay in ostentatious seaside palaces or big-money casino hotels. French-style farmhouse hotels, on the other hand, are quite understandably few and far between, and when it comes to country house hotels crafted from converted Tudor-style water towers, well, there’s really only one: the Hotel L’Auberge.

Located in the rather prosaically named Barrio Parque de Golf, the Auberge offers a measure of tranquility and quiet, the closest thing you’ll find to pastoral farm life amidst the hotels and yacht clubs of the Punta del Este. As for the hotel itself, it’s a charming mix of French and English influences: the original building and the first few rooms decidedly in an English manor style, the newer ones decked out in the soft pastels of Provence. Whatever the style, all forty rooms are luxurious, some with jacuzzis, others with fireplaces, and all with modern amenities like high-speed internet access. The tower rooms are necessarily the smallest, but compensate with plenty of personality, while the suites positively sprawl. The hotel’s restaurant is an excellent one, and the afternoon tea service is a Punta del Este institution — golfers would do well to schedule early tee times, so as not to miss tea time.

How to get there: Hotel L'Auberge is located 80 miles east of Carrasco General Cesáreo L. Berisso International Airport.

content:
Maybe it’s mostly Kraftwerk we’re thinking of, but it’s hard not to see Dusseldorf as something of a futuristic city. And if the future of big-brand luxury hotels looks anything like the Hyatt Regency Dusseldorf, then it’s going to be a fine future indeed. It’s a striking waterfront structure, a perfect complement to the contemporary architecture that lines the city’s Media Harbour, and it’s a good deal more alive, visually speaking, than your typical luxury hotel.

Don’t get us wrong — there are crazier boutique hotels out there, to be sure, hotels that can blow your mind with a single well-placed interior-design gesture. But there are an awful lot of very lukewarm luxury hotels as well, places that seem to have been designed by accounting spreadsheets rather than human beings. This particular Hyatt Regency combines the best of both approaches: enough inspiration to make guests feel that all-important spark of individuality, plus the hard-won consistency and flawless professionalism that the big chains practice so well.

The amenities, however, are perfectly predictable, and this is one area where predictability is not a bad thing. The rooms are perfectly comfortable and well organized for business travel, and the bathrooms are borderline indulgent, with walk-in rain showers and separate bathtubs. The restaurant and bar do a fair bit of local business, achieving the aim of mixing the hotel guests with the general public. And this being Germany, you can count on some highly developed wellness facilities: here the Rive spa is accompanied by a modern Technogym fitness center which looks out over Media Harbour.

content:
Small chance you’ll have any trouble remembering which side of the border you’re on. Your room at Cameron House on Loch Lomond is positively drenched in tartan, in seemingly infinite variations, and with the halls lined with beyond-life-sized portraits of bearded, kilted men, a proud gallery of skulduggery — their word, not ours. You’re immersed in an atmosphere that’s unapologetically, thoroughly Scottish, and it’s the blend of decadence and defiance that makes Cameron House — a bit like Scotland itself — so appealing.

In fact the setting is easily half the appeal. They’re hardly exaggerating when they say the Cameron House is on Loch Lomond — arrival by water can be arranged via the hotel’s cruiser. Just about everything you can see from your window is part of the Trossachs National Park, full of mountains, lakes, forests, paths, and horizons that look like they were painted on by J. M. W. Turner. The hotel sits amidst this beauty, lord of all it surveys.

Golf, naturally, is a part of the proceedings. During the day you can play the nine-hole Wee Demon, deserving of the name by every account, or the 18-hole Carrick. Twice named the country’s best, the Cameron House’s spa offers classes as well as treatments, including those that work the so-called high road (head massages) and the low road (foot massages). By night, you can sip one of the 250 single malts on offer and retire to your plush room, complete with walk-in shower and fluffed-daily duvet.

content:
Not quite a hotel, not really a bed and breakfast, Bloomestate is the sort of small, individually-owned lodging that defies categorization. At the edge of the old Dutch colonial town of Swellendam, in South Africa’s Western Cape, it’s more likely a stop on a longer tour of the country — but anyone who makes the effort will be amply rewarded by the mellow atmosphere and the well-composed modernist décor.

At just seven rooms Bloomestate is small by any definition; the way they’re spread about the grounds, though, means it’s more than just a guest house. Color schemes vary, but all are bright, from tangerine to lime, and all are furnished with modernist classics, with Barcelona chairs at the foot of every bed. And the comforts, while more residential in style than out-and-out luxurious, cover all the necessities, including DVD players and iPod-docking stereos.

There’s no restaurant proper, just a fairly extensive breakfast served in a communal dining room. However you’ll quickly find that the restaurants are among the greatest charms of this scenic old Cape Dutch town, including at least one that’s actually within walking distance from the hotel. It’s not a full-service resort by any means, with service at your beck and call — but after a day exploring the town or the surrounding country it’s a fine place to unwind.

How to get there:
BloomEstate is approximately a 2 hour drive from Cape Town, Cape Town International Airport and George.

content: In the world of aristocratic-style luxury hospitality there are roughly two schools of thought. One preserves the original structure, be it a château or a townhouse or a country manor, and attempts to restore it to the condition in which its original inhabitants would have enjoyed it. But a second, more modern approach, is to take whatever liberties are required in order to reach today’s equivalent of the same level of luxury. Shakespeare in modern dress is no less powerful a theatrical experience; and a hotel like L’Aigle Noir Fontainebleau MGallery is anything but diminished by the contemporary flourishes that update its 16th-century Neoclassicist architecture.\n\nIn its current incarnation L’Aigle Noir is a visual feast, its 46 rooms and 10 suites decorated in anything from deep jewel tones to vibrant repeating patterns to bold graphic murals, and sometimes all three. In terms of comfort they’re pure modern luxury, with all the 21st-century details in place. And they’re supported by services that are thoroughly high-quality, if not quite palace-hotel lavish, including plenty of meeting and events space as well as everyday necessities like Le Montijo, the cocktail bar, and a restaurant by A L’Epicerie Pastatime.

content: Most of the hotels belonging to Marriott’s Aloft sub-brand are, for all their contemporary-design accoutrements, somewhat pod-like affairs — identical rooms with identical layouts, often in locations that are chosen more for convenience than character. But the Aloft Philadelphia Downtown is a different story. It’s located, first of all, not in a purpose-built matrix of repeating corridors alongside some lonely airport road, but in the 1925-vintage Liberty Title Building, a North Broad Street landmark, right in the city center, that’s full of vintage Classical Revival architectural personality.\n\nThe lobby’s soaring 27-foot ceilings and massive triple-height windows date back to the days when bank lobbies were grand; today it’s home to the reception as well as a lounge and bar, and some large-scale contemporary art. Upstairs, the rooms bear traces of their former lives as well — the building’s historical layout means there’s some variation in floor plan from room to room, the original windows are still intact, and they’re all decorated with artwork bearing the seal of Liberty Title & Trust. It’s a low-frills experience, to be sure — beyond the bar and a 24-hour snack bar, you’re at the mercy of the neighborhood, which, to be fair, offers plentiful options — but it’s a considerable step up from the ordinary bare-bones business hotel.

content: You’d be hard pressed to find a hotel that serves up a richer helping of Luang Prabang’s Old Quarter appeal than this trio of UNESCO World Heritage buildings, situated at the epicenter of Lao culture. Formerly the late-nineteenth-century royal residence, the 3 Nagas have traveled quite the winding path over their century and change of existence: from mansion to ice-cream factory to their current incarnation as a stylish and contemporary boutique hotel. Recently restored under architect Pascal Trahan’s watchful eye, these buildings boast a wealth of period-appropriate details, including torchis plasterwork and traditional clay-tile roofing. Inside, the trappings lend a palpably regal air — dark, exotic woods lend luster to the surfacing, while lofty ceilings accommodate luxurious, king-size four-posters. Traditional weavings and private terraces keep you in direct contact with the land, a resonant theme around these parts: when a riverside courtyard, an elephant park, and unreal cataracts wait just outside, you’d be a fool to opt for a cocoon instead. Put another way, they don’t bother with flat-screens here, instead offering complimentary bikes to visit local Buddhist shrines, nightly craft markets, and the famed tak bat almsgiving ceremony, featuring hundreds and hundreds of saffron-clad monks. You won’t miss the TV, we promise. The style is necessarily a bit less stark and sleek — a bit more classic, but certainly no less chic — than the global boutique mean, but that’s no great loss given the mood and the extras. The staff have perfected that discreet, there-but-not approach that’s the trademark of high-end Far East hospitality. They’re happy to chauffeur guests in swanky vintage cars, and while this venerable property doesn’t include onsite spa or gym facilities, guests are entitled to use those at the nearby Hotel de la Paix. And after all this, 3 Nagas is probably just as well known for its dining as for its rooms, which says something about the quality of the cuisine. Les 3 Nagas centers on upscale, organic Lao specialties in a cascade of earthy local ingredients. Finish with a Lao Lao Sling or rice wine moonshine at bar Mango 3; you’ll want to opt for al fresco seating beneath the (what else) mango trees if at all possible. But don’t linger too long, there’s exploring to do. How to Get There: 3 Nagas Hotel is approximately a 15-minute drive from Luang Prabang International Airport (LPQ).
