content:
What, you weren’t expecting opulent old-world Hollywood glamour among the recycled wood cottages and artisanal coffee shops of Portland? You’re not alone — and we hope you packed something other than hiking boots. At the Hotel deLuxe, indeed, less isn’t more: more is more. This 100-year-old hotel is a rare symbol of over-the-top grandeur in a city known for its pared-down style and earthy simplicity. Just step into the lobby — the deLuxe retains the art deco mirrors, twinkling chandeliers made of Czech glass, and gold-leaf ceilings of yesteryear. 

Upstairs, the 130 guest rooms are almost as romantic, with rich floor-to-ceiling drapery and vintage glass light fixtures befitting the boudoir of a forties-era starlet. That’s the idea, in fact, to make the guest feel like a movie star. Each room features a “Make It So” button, a pillow menu, and an honor bar with a short list of recommended food and wine pairings; the hallways are lined with old film stills. At the top of the line, the Marlene Dietrich Suite is as whimsically extravagant as you’d expect, with an eight-foot circular bed and panoramic city views.
 
An elegant breakfast is served to guests seated at velvet banquettes at Gracie’s, the deLuxe’s restaurant. Elsewhere in the hotel, the gilded architecture is preserved, even if some of the rooms’ original functions have changed to accommodate a modern clientele. The Crystal Room, once containing an orchestra pit and grand piano, now serves as a screening room for the deLuxe’s pop-up cinema series. The Driftwood Room cocktail bar, on the other hand, has hardly changed since its heyday: with dramatic beamed ceilings and a dark, curving bar, the seductive 1950s-style lounge is a fixture on Portland’s craft cocktail circuit. And you know, in this town, of course, they’re not kidding around when they talk about craft cocktails — get in the spirit of the glamorous environs and sample from the Manhattan menu, or try a fizzy champagne concoction, the house special.

content:
When people talk about Dutch design they’re generally thinking small — quirky furniture, innovative products, whimsical graphics and installations. But in hospitality what’s more relevant is the large-scale Dutch design philosophy: the efficiency, the economy, the canny cleverness that allows this most densely populated of countries to tackle its geographic challenges and live together harmoniously. CitizenM is, in that sense, Dutch hospitality design distilled to its purest essence — and the CitizenM Hotel Rotterdam shows what this enterprising chain can do with the home advantage.

The setting is the Oude Haven, the newly redeveloped old harbour, a bustling nexus of urban activity — perfect for an efficiency-minded, youth-oriented “affordable luxury” hotel. What exactly does that mean? In Hollywood the saying “put the money on the screen” is a reminder to avoid blowing the budget on items the audience won’t notice. Here a similar edict is at work: by placing Frette linens on the wall-to-wall king beds, they put the money where you’ll feel it the most.

And then they cut out the rest. It’s largely a self-service operation, from kiosk-based check-in to the vending-ticket food concept, where café meets cafeteria meets public library. This is the co-working space of the future, essentially, just with better drinks and desserts. There’s an art focus as well that’s quite welcome, as a bit of high culture in the lobby library goes a long way toward beating the dot-com blues. It’s not for everyone — some of us still want our shoes polished, our baths drawn for us — but if there were a CitizenM in every major city, the world would indeed be a better place.

content:
It’s hard to even remember the dark ages before the invention of vinotherapy, when wine and spa treatments had to be enjoyed separately. These days, though, they’re best taken together. And these days, most everywhere there’s a wine industry, there’s an ultra-modern haute-luxury spa hotel — like the Loisium, in the village of Langenlois, in the Kamptal Valley wine country of Lower Austria.

It’s a trend that’s given birth to some cutting-edge architecture, and the Loisium is no exception. The building, by the American architect Steven Holl, is nothing if not distinctive — the cubic hotel and spa buildings, with their slightly crumpled aluminum skins, tower over the surrounding vineyards.

Interiors are modern as well, if a little less imposing — the open-plan rooms and suites come in unexpected geometries, and look decades younger and more stylish than the spa-hotel norm. The Vineyard restaurant serves a pared-down modern cuisine, rooted in the agriculture of Lower Austria, and plates are paired with the very wines that are the reason for this place’s existence.

The thousand-square-meter Aveda Wine Spa is arguably the main attraction, complete with fitness center twenty-meter heated outdoor pool. Or if it’s simply the vino you’re after, and not the vinotherapy, go for a cellar tour: the 900-year-old cellars lie just beneath this 21st-century hotel.

content:
Seen from the Red Sea at night, the Kempinski Hotel in Aqaba rises up like a retro monument to 1970s-style modernism. Furthering the effect, a rotating array of neon lights up the concrete, semi-concave shape. Jordan isn’t Nevada, of course, and still less is Aqaba Vegas, but you’ll be forgiven if you see something of a resemblance.

In daylight you’ll see that the sea abuts a beach, which in turn abuts an infinity pool ringed with chaise longues. As the country’s only port, Aqaba works hard, but it’s also becoming the diving, fishing, and all-around seaside resort center for the area. With an eye toward the water it’s easy enough to ignore the tourists, and the Kempinski does its best impression of a secluded oasis. That sea view is easy enough to come by here, whether from your room’s bathtub or balcony or from a table at AM/PM, the enormously fashionable fine-dining restaurant.

Sociable souls will spend time at the hotel’s three bars, including the swim-up one and another that holds a nightly dance party. Aqaba is situated such that you can experience the desert during the day, with hikes in Wadi Rum or tours of Petra, and sleep to the sound of cresting waves at night.

content:
There are times when you want something a little more decadent than the ascetic charms of the ryokan. The Japanese countryside is home to some astonishing luxury hotels as well, the Windsor Hotel Toya among them. This Hokkaido hotel, with its mountaintop view of Lake Toya, hosted 2008’s G8 summit, a testament to the Windsor’s creature comforts as well as its business facilities; let’s be honest, if it’s suitable for heads of state, then you’re unlikely to find yourself wishing for more.

Western rooms come in two styles: the “casual” style is calculated not to offend, while the “premier” style is contemporary, with more than a little bit of minimalist influence, resulting in a look that’s several degrees sharper than the soporific luxury-hotel standard. You can probably guess which one we prefer. And for the traditionalists, a number of tatami-style rooms and suites are available as well.

Spaces are generous throughout, from the superior rooms on up to the sprawling G8 and Presidential suites, and the comforts are what you’d expect from a recently renovated high-end hotel. The facilities are similarly first-rate — the Windsor comes equipped with pool, spa and fitness center, and restaurants and lounges are well-conceived eateries.

But it’s the location that puts the Windsor over the edge from merely quite nice to something more like sublime. Hokkaido isn’t generally short of natural charms in the first place, but Lake Toya is something to behold; this volcanic lake is nearly circular in shape, with a peaked island situated photogenically at its center, and the Windsor takes this all in from a height of two thousand feet. Not a view you’ll soon forget.

content: The Niseko ski region on Hokkaido deserves more than passing mention. The resorts here boast world-class powder, sophisticated architecture rooted in ancient tradition, and vistas to rival Switzerland’s. Muwa Niseko adheres to the idiom beautifully, a private, tranquil ski-in/ski-out resort with rooms stacked atop one another like whimsical building blocks. Inside, the look is alpine-chic, for the most part — think blonde wood, abstracted headboards, and geometric light fixtures. Full kitchens and in-room laundry imply you could extend your stay quite easily. As if that wasn’t enough, there are also a pair of genuine onsen; the infinity version outdoes itself with captivating views of Mt. Yotei.

content:
Poland’s second city, Kraków, is impossibly old and impossibly picturesque — so much so that it would arguably be a mistake for a luxury hotel to attempt to compete in the arena of historical splendor. Much more sensible for a hotel like the Mercure Kraków Fabryczna City to opt for a more contemporary, Modernist-influenced style, and leave the ancient opulence to the rest of the city.

That’s not to say the Mercure is without historical interest. The Fabryczna (or Factory) City development is a mixed-use complex built from the brick-clad century-old structures that once comprised the state-owned vodka distillery, and the hotel makes much of the post-industrial textures of its warehouse-style buildings. The rooms and suites themselves venture into Art Deco and Bauhaus territory and beyond, meanwhile, with delicate herringbone floors, mid-century graphic elements, and classic modernist furnishings.

The hotel’s position within the Factory City means it has easy access to no fewer than six restaurants, including two in-house, as well as its own pool and wellness center. And though the development is largely self-sufficient, you’re not isolated; the old city center is a scant two miles to the west.

content:
Just across the street from the Yale School of Art, a block and a half from the university’s Old Campus itself, is Graduate New Haven, the Bulldogs franchise of the rapidly blossoming Graduate hotel group. The concept is simple: college towns need convenient, stylish, and relatively affordable lodgings, and the common purpose of most visitors provides a ready-made identity for the hotel. 

Here that naturally means plenty of Yale Blue in the décor, and a slightly ironic upper-class flavor to the rooms and suites themselves. At its heart, though, the Graduate New Haven is the furthest thing from formal — loaner bikes help guests get around the campus and its immediate surroundings, while a pet-friendly policy makes it the obvious choice for dog owners. 

An outpost of the brand’s proudly bookish Poindexter café is present, and the Old Heidelberg bar, a local fixture from long before the Graduate took over, has been renovated and reimagined as a restaurant and bar serving an upscale take on the classic pub experience. Best of all, it’s quite a bit easier to get into the Graduate New Haven than it is to get accepted to Yale itself — graduation week aside, that is….

content:
The idea behind the Graduate hotels is a simple enough one: boutique hotels in university towns that are fun enough to remind you of your college days but fine enough to attract visitors who’ve become accustomed to a bit more luxury than typical student digs. Each one is tailored to its location, but avoids obvious references like the school colors or mascot — the Graduate Richmond, next door to Virginia Commonwealth University, pays specific tribute to Richmond by honoring the pathbreaking tennis star Arthur Ashe.

The style throughout is an eclectic blend of preppy Americana and mid-century modernism, and the rooms particularly recall the optimism of the glory days of American higher education. Of course in those days nobody had Malin + Goetz bath products, to say nothing of free wi-fi, and these rooms, with their king and queen beds, are palatial by student standards.

So far, so good — but these hotels are about more than sleeping accommodations. Brookfield, the lobby café and bar, makes much of its tennis-club vibes, while Byrd House, the rooftop bar named for city founder William Byrd, is the Graduate Richmond’s headline attraction, serving beers and cocktails alongside a Southern-inspired menu of locally sourced fare.

content:
Built hundreds of years ago by the Portuguese and Dutch, the fortified city of Galle marries European architectural tastes with the humid climate and colorful culture of southern Sri Lanka. The Lighthouse Hotel, too, is characterized by contrast: an imposing brick exterior gives way to airy terraces where breezes sweep in from the Indian Ocean, simple woven hammocks swing on a porch near an ornate bronze spiral staircase, coconut pudding and champagne granita are served on tables covered with white linen. The late great Geoffrey Bawa, Sri Lanka’s most famous architect, had a flair for detail that’s evident throughout the Lighthouse, one of his final projects.

And the joy is in the details, after all, for travelers who’ve journeyed all the way to the remote southern tip of Sri Lanka. The spa offers first-class facials and massages, of course, but besides nature walks and rainforest excursions or jaunts to Galle Fort, there’s not much to do here except float in one of the huge blue pools, doze in a hammock, or watch the waves crashing up against boulders on the rocky shoreline — which is entirely the point. High-ceilinged guest rooms are simply and fashionably furnished with wooden frame beds and pristine white sheets. Pricier “theme suites” are more elegant, but all guest quarters feature private balconies overlooking an aquamarine sea. The spicy, innovative dishes at the Cinnamon Room restaurant sustain guests through the leisurely hours; lamb burgers with chili are served by the pool for those who can’t wait until dinner.

content: Around the west side of Darling Harbour, in the newly bustling district of Pyrmont, is something that’s a little bit rare, at least in this city: a freestanding, purpose-built, single-use luxury hotel, with an enviable location that makes for spectacular harbor views — and an independent one at that. The Darling isn’t part of one of the big high-end hotel chains that are arguably at their best on the Pacific Rim, but it’s certainly learned some lessons from them, chiefly about balance. The Darling is stylish but not eccentric, classic but not conservative, luxe but not ostentatious, and it backs up its atmosphere of glamour with tangible comforts to match.\n\nIn fact, were you so inclined, the Darling is the kind of hotel you don’t actually have to venture outside of. Within the Star Sydney or Star Integrated Resort, of which the Darling is a part, five restaurants span the range from an Australian grill to classic Milanese to Japanese, Chinese, and an outpost of David Chang’s Momofuku. Nightlife options include a Vegas-style club, a classic cocktail bar, a sports bar, and a live music venue. And the Star casino is an offering that other Sydney hotels aren’t able to match. But you’re not likely to be the shut-in type, and with all of Sydney’s splendors at your feet, you’ll be glad for the location, just off of Darling Harbour and within walking distance of the central business district, the Rocks, and the rest of the inner-city suburbs.

content:
Saint Barthélemy has always been an exception in the Caribbean, an exclusive and upscale Gallic outpost surrounded by what in a pessimistic mood can seem like island after island full of tacky overdevelopment and overcrowded beaches. Frankly it’s hard not to think slightly elitist thoughts here — and few hotels really embody what’s unique about St. Barths quite like the Fouquet's Saint-Barth.

The hotel stands high on a hillside above the harbor town of Gustavia, and is one of the island’s classic grand dames, if that’s even the right phrase for a tiny 21-suite hotel, however celebrated and luxurious. The interiors are a blend of contemporary luxury and old-world charm — the French influence is evident, and results in a look that’s a good deal more refined than what we’re used to seeing even in the Caribbean’s better hotels.

The key to the appeal, however, isn’t the style, but the sheer luxury of the place: private plunge pools, multi-jet showers, kitchenettes, and of course the jaw-dropping views. There’s the extensive spa, the sort of thing you’d usually associate with a much larger hotel, as well as a fine French restaurant — it may be at the dinner table that St. Barths in general (and the Fouquet's Saint-Barth in particular) really puts the rest of the Caribbean to shame.

What stands out is the fact that the building also houses an ancient temple, a decorative 1200-year-old structure that rises up in the hotel’s glass atrium like a special exhibit at a museum. It’s not just for show: a monk leads daily services every morning, just one of several traditional features at this otherwise contemporary hotel. Miso soup and tofu are served for breakfast, drawing classes are offered every evening, and the rooftop has an open-air bath, plus adjacent indoor baths and saunas divided for men and women. Rooms are minimalist, with smooth wood paneling, crisp white linens, and low sofas built in beside windows overlooking the city.
name: Candeo Hotels Osaka Shinsaibashi

content: The Singapore EDITION marks the brand's first foray into Southeast Asia, and even in a corner of the world that's particularly known for ultra-luxurious hotels — not to mention the neighbors on swanky Orchard Road, including the Four Seasons on one side and the St. Regis Singapore on the other — it lives up to the hype. The lobby makes a striking impression with its curving white marble walls, tropical plants, and a grand domed ceiling adorned with glimmering gold leaf. Beyond the light-filled conservatory is a spacious courtyard draped with live greenery that's visible from the rooftop pool nine stories up. \n\nMost rooms and suites overlook the central garden, with foliage forming a lush backdrop for the spare, silent interiors. The decor is mostly white and beige, with oak flooring, cream-colored rugs, and floor-to-ceiling windows with bedside-controlled blackout curtains. In-room amenities are as high-end as you'd expect — Frette linens, La Bottega robes, Le Labo products — and the marble bathrooms are especially lavish with freestanding tubs and custom lighting. Breakfast is served on a leafy terrace overlooking the courtyard garden, and up on the roof, a tree-framed poolside bar serves Singaporean cocktails and street food-inspired small plates.

content:
Saint Gervais les Bains is a ski town, but not only a ski town — though it stands at the foot of Mont Blanc, and offers access to a vast network of ski runs, it’s got a permanent year-round population, and was established as a spa town long before the advent of ski tourism as a mass phenomenon. All of which is by way of explaining the fact that this Alpine village manages to sustain a hotel of the caliber of Le Saint Gervais Hôtel & Spa Handwritten Collection — a stylish, contemporary luxury boutique hotel that wouldn’t look out of place in any of France’s major cities, occupying a lovely Art Nouveau heritage building from the early 20th century.

The rooms and suites are divided between the original structure and a contemporary addition; all combine retro atmosphere with modern interiors and comforts. There’s a spa equipped with an indoor pool, jacuzzi, sauna, and four treatment rooms, and a small outdoor pool offers views of the village and the mountains. Meanwhile Avanti, serves authentic Mediterranean cuisine with homemade pizzas, and is complemented by the elegant Marie Paradis Bar.

Though Le Saint Gervais is no ordinary ski hotel, it does offer ski-hotel services, including passes and storage, and the Mont Blanc Tramway is close at hand — every room reservation includes a tramway ticket. And in summer, the village offers access to no end of Alpine recreation, from hiking and biking to rafting, paragliding, and more.

content:
Most Graduate hotels are devoted to a single campus; the Graduate Providence is a local landmark within walking distance of five major universities, including Brown University, Providence College, and the Rhode Island School of Design. Built in 1922 and occupying the site of the former Providence Biltmore, it’s got no shortage of charm, while embodying the spirit of this quaint collegiate town, and its location offers easy access to the whole of downtown Providence.

The hotel’s 294 rooms and suites are spacious, and many offer enough space for multiple guests. Strong pops of color mix with playful patterns, and boutique-hotel details like Malin + Goetz bath products lend a luxe aspect. This is one of the more refined Graduate looks, owing perhaps to the close presence of its Ivy League neighbor — though it’s far more vibrant than the ultra-traditional luxury hotel that preceded it. 

There’s a spa, unusual in Graduate hotels, as well as plentiful meeting and events space. Guests can grab everything from breakfast to a post-dinner drink at the bookishly themed Poindexter Coffee, and Graduate Providence features the first Reiners restaurant and bar, a sports-themed experience that’s a worthy alternative to the downtown district’s many fine dining and drinking options.

content:
In a luxury hospitality industry crowded with often indiscernible brands, Sofitel’s claim to distinction is its Frenchness — not just in its ownership, but in its style as well. And while the Sofitel Kuala Lumpur Damansara, in the upscale Damansara Heights district of Malaysia’s capital, pays generous tribute to its immediate surroundings (as any decent luxury hotel should), this is Kuala Lumpur with a noticeable French accent.

Its green glass towers rise high above its verdant surroundings, a few minutes’ walk from downtown Damansara and its MRT station. Inside it’s clear you’ve entered a modern, style-conscious luxury hotel; soaring spaces are decorated in figured stone and bold, bright colors, setting a tone that’s as vibrant as it is elegant.

The rooms and suites carry on in a similar, if more restful key; here the bright colors and playful graphic elements serve as accents on a backdrop of soothing neutrals. The Parisian influence arrives in the form of subtle nods to Art Deco design, as well as ornately figured mirror frames and dark, lavish marble bathrooms.

A handful of restaurants and bars include the pan-Asian Kwee Zeen, the Cantonese/Imperial Chinese fine-dining restaurant Wan Chun Ting, and Nizza, a Mediterranean restaurant whose menu and décor recall the Côte d’Azur.

content: It’s an understatement to call Boutique-Hotel Blaue Burg’s location spectacular. Perched more than 4,000 feet above the fairy-tale landscapes of Bavaria, it’s set amid the peaks of the Allgäu Alps, right next to the oldest castle ruins in Germany. A fine dining venue has brought more traffic to the steep mountain pass in recent years, and since staying the night makes more sense than driving back down the mountainside in the dark, the property has expanded to include a stylish family-run boutique hotel. \n\nIt’s quiet luxury all the way inside Blaue Burg’s elegant suites. Most are mountain chalet–chic, with oak flooring, knotty pine walls or exposed wood beams, and light-filled bathrooms with soaking tubs, although one is done up in Moroccan style, with arching doorways and a clay shower. Many have private balconies or terraces, and all offer dazzling views over the valley below. Plush robes and slippers, Nespresso machines, and an extensive pillow menu add extra coziness, and the hotel’s spa, with multiple fireplace nooks, a Finnish sauna, and a wooden deck facing the Alps, is just as inviting.

content:
The neighborhoods around airports are in particularly dire need of a bit of personality, and that’s something the Citadines Connect Sydney Airport has in plentiful supply.

The style, sensibly, looks just a little bit backwards, to the days when jet travel was novel, exciting, and even glamorous — the exterior is clearly contemporary, but the interiors go mid-century modernist mad, with bold colors, busy patterns, and clean-lined modern furniture. It’s meant to deliver the opposite of the soporific effect of a typical beige-carpeted business hotel, and while there’s no mistaking the setting, adjacent to the airport, for Kings Cross, it’s fair to say the result is something memorable.

Rooms range from Economy all the way up to First Class — though they start out substantially more comfortable than an economy-class airline cabin — and feature 55-inch televisions, rain showers, and blackout curtains at every level. Meanwhile a rooftop cinema and a delightful cocktail bar are the envy of many a boutique hotel, to say nothing of virtually 100% of airport hotels. May they all look like this someday.

content:
Downtown Denver’s cultural district has come a long way in a few short years, thanks in no small part to Daniel Liebeskind’s extravagant addition to the Denver Art Museum. And if you see echoes of Liebeskind’s jagged diagonals in the facade of the ART, it’s no coincidence. This 165-room boutique hotel weaves together a number of disparate design threads, and manages to integrate itself seamlessly into a neighborhood that’s already full of architecturally eclectic monuments.

As you enter you’ll pass beneath a massive LED light installation by Leo Villareal, and you’ll never again be out of sight of at least one piece of contemporary artwork. This includes the guest rooms, whose neutral tones and sparse décor impart a gallery vibe. But the comforts tell a different story; touches like Illy espresso machines and Gilchrist & Soames bath products are about more than just visual appeal.

FIRE, the restaurant, serves New American cuisine with a local emphasis, and is no less drenched in artworks; it’s full of sculptures and installations, and has commanding views of downtown Denver. And from here you’re close to the Golden Triangle Creative District as well as the new arts district along Santa Fe and the perennial nightlife center of LoDo — and the Denver Art Museum is practically right next door.

content:
Pressed for a theory as to why the Philippines don’t quite get their due as a holiday destination for Westerners, the only explanation we can offer is that it’s a really long flight from both North America and Europe. More and more long-haul travelers are making the pilgrimage, however, and the local hotel scene is undergoing something of a quiet renaissance — and the Crimson Resort & Spa, on the island of Mactan, right next to Cebu, is a prime example.

Quiet because it would be impossible to argue that Crimson’s design, however handsome, is one for the history books. It’s a conservative look, one that’s clearly meant to appeal to the broadest possible audience, and to place the visual focus squarely on the extraordinary environment that is Mactan Island itself. But it’s clear that they’ve learned the lessons of the last few decades of high-end boutique-influenced Pacific Rim villa resorts.

Here 40 villas offer that exceedingly private brand of luxury — think plunge pools, four-poster beds, jaw-dropping ocean views — while another 250 guest rooms offer a more accessible version of the experience, sacrificing a bit of space and privacy but not skimping at all on comforts or conveniences.

A three-tiered infinity pool cascades across the central courtyard, and the private beach is only a few steps away. The promised spa is an expansive one, with no fewer than 14 therapy rooms, and the charmingly named Crimzone is where you park the kids for the duration of your massage. Add two restaurants, a beach club bar and grill, and even a sports bar (!), and your entertainment is sorted. All this just twenty minutes from Mactan airport.

content: Enough with the coastal condescension. Why on earth shouldn’t Indianapolis have a high-end luxury boutique hotel with a museum-quality art collection? Ever since the 21c opened in Louisville, Kentucky, it’s been our express wish that every American city of feasible size should follow suit. And Indianapolis has done so, in the form of the Alexander. This one happens to be a very credible partnership with the Indianapolis Museum of Art, and features some original commissions alongside collection pieces. And for patrons of the hospitality arts, the hotel side of things more than holds up its end. The rooms are visually stylish, sedate, and full of modern furnishings and contemporary comforts, with plenty of attention paid to the other senses: surfaces in wood and leather, plush down duvets, extra-large California king beds, and bath products by Gilchrist & Soames. Market Table is the Alexander’s free-flowing, open-kitchen restaurant, serving breakfast and lunch made with the best of Indiana’s local produce. Meanwhile Plat 99 is the craft cocktail lounge, augmenting its substantial drinks menu with charcuterie, cheeses and other tapas-style dishes. On the whole it’s a thoroughly cosmopolitan experience. content:
One of the items on our global wish list is that every major city in America should have a hotel like this one. In a landscape dominated by cost-cutting chain hotels, there’s an advantage to be had by showing a little bit of personality, something that the Moonrise Hotel, in St. Louis, Missouri, has got in spades.

For a good start, it’s located in what’s probably the best neighborhood in town, the Loop. This is St. Louis’s nightlife and dining district, and it’s a much better spot for a mid-rise rooftop bar like the Moonrise’s than the city’s oversized downtown. Inside you’ll find it’s got a bit of a theme, and charmingly that theme is space. It lends itself to a bit of curvaceous mid-century modernism, and at the Moonrise, modernist design is fun again, rather than painfully fashionable. Suites pay homage to the city’s famous residents, and the rooms come with all the necessities, from plasma TVs to stylish modern bathrooms.

Fun is probably what separates the Moonrise, and other Midwestern boutique hotels, from their cousins on the coasts. Here you can’t help feeling that the style is meant to be inclusive, not exclusive, curiosity-provoking rather than alienating, right down to the little revolving replica moon atop the hotel’s roof.

content:
From the same Ennismore/Accor partnership responsible for brands like Hoxton, Delano, and Mondrian comes Hyde, an upscale boutique-hotel concern with a laid-back, bohemian vibe. And where better to stretch your laid-back, bohemian legs than Ibiza? Hyde Ibiza stands proud above the sands of the idyllic Cala Llonga Bay, and offers its guests a generous helping of seaside restoration, along with a side of the vibrant nightlife for which this island is so well known. 

With 401 rooms and suites it’s a substantial hotel, but the in-room experience is more soothing than stimulating — organic materials and warm neutral tones strike a note of tranquility, and the style skillfully blends the modern boutique-hotel lines and rustic Balearic textures. Private balconies don’t hurt, either, especially ones with views of the mountains and the bay.

A beach club and three swimming pools (with occasional DJ sets) see to guests’ leisure needs; guided hikes, taking advantage of the mountainous surroundings, are a more active option. And no one goes hungry, either — Hyde Ibiza’s restaurants include Cuyo, a Mexican kitchen, along with a modern Japanese restaurant and a handful of casual venues by the poolside or down at the beach.

There are certainly bigger and grander hotels in Kyoto than Higashiyama Shikikaboku, but you won’t find many places that are quite so transcendently tranquil. It’s set close to where the city gives way to the mountains, where green spaces are interleaved with urban ones, in a district with strict controls on new construction. And with just eight rooms — and an adults-only accommodation policy — it’s just about as private as can be.

The building and its interiors showcase hundreds of years of fine Japanese design and craftsmanship, from the minimalist, Brutalist-inspired architecture to repurposed karakami tiles by the 16th-century printer Karacho. The hotel’s owner happens to be an interior designer, and the rooms, each one unique, interpret traditional Japanese hospitality design through an unmistakably contemporary lens.

Artworks are everywhere, in the rooms and in the public spaces, including the hotel’s artfully composed little tea salon. There’s an open-air bath available for guest use, and the rooftop is a gem. In the morning you can count on a breakfast by the Italian-trained chef Ryo Sakatsuji, making use of the produce of a couple of local farms. And from here, a wealth of unusual attractions are within easy reach, from the Heian Shrine to the Nanzenji Temple and much, much more.

content:
The next island over from Tahiti proper is Moorea, and it’s here, on the island’s longest white-sand beach, that you’ll find Sofitel Kira Ora Moorea. This shallow lagoon is the perfect setting for a couple of rows of classic overwater bungalows, while a few more stand on solid ground just beyond the beach, as does the resort’s most extravagant lodging, the two-bedroom Luxury Villa.

It doesn’t get much more spectacular than this, between the lush green mountains and the crystal-clear waters of the lagoon. The bungalows come with everything you’d find in a dry-land luxury suite, from air conditioning and wi-fi to lavish oversized bathrooms with rain showers. And the overwater accommodations add glass floor panels, for a view downwards into the lagoon.

Le Jardin Spa & Beauty is as extravagant as you’d expect, and the Sofitel brand’s French heritage is evident in the attention given to the cuisine: Pure, the restaurant, combines French and Polynesian flavors and techniques, and the wine list goes long on French vintages. The view, naturally, is an extraordinary one, and dinner is accompanied by live entertainment drawing from the local Tahitian culture.

Located in Athens, NY, a historic community on the Hudson River just two hours from New York City (and right across the river from the city of Hudson), the Stewart House feels both elegant and accessible, historic but never stuffy. Meanwhile there’s an Art Deco bar, a farm-to-table tavern, and a waterfront grill (open seasonally Thursday through Sunday), and the hotel places you right on the riverside, at one end of Athens’s walkable main street.

content: Not only is Salar de Uyuni the world’s largest salt flat, but when, as occasionally happens, it’s flooded with calm, shallow water, it creates the world’s largest mirror, 129 kilometers across. It’s so large satellites use it to recalibrate themselves — and for those closer to earth, the boutique Hotel Luna Salada offers a similar (though metaphorical) reset. Constructed almost entirely of salt blocks, Luna Salada features rooms outfitted in bright Andean colors — without televisions, preferring the unfamiliar to take center stage. Both tours of the Salar and of the vast night sky are offered, as well as an immersive steam room with panoramic view. While the village of Uyuni is a half-hour away, the area’s best restaurant is Tanupa, right here at the hotel.

Set on 15 acres of riverside parkland in the Dee Valley, at the edge of the vast and wild Snowdonia National Park, Palé Hall is nothing if not secluded — a situation that only heightens the effect of its high Victorian opulence. Over the course of its colorful history it’s played host to guests no less eminent than Winston Churchill and Queen Victoria herself. And in its current incarnation as a luxury hotel it’s among the finest in Great Britain.

The rooms and suites in the original house retain their classic style, while the Garden Suites, in the estate’s renovated coach house, take on a more contemporary aspect. All of them are plush as can be, and mix modern comforts with classic touches; the Victoria Room still contains the house’s original bathtub.

Palé Hall’s smallish size allows for an unusually high standard of service, though the atmosphere is not an excessively formal one by any means. Leisure pursuits range from garden walks to mountain climbing and everything in between; lunch, tea, and dinner are served in the Henry Robertson Dining Room.

content: Just beyond the outermost southwestern fringes of London, near the Surrey town of Guildford, is a hotel that’s roughly one part travel history and one part contemporary luxury boutique. The Queen Anne–style estate known as Barnett Hill was built in 1905 by the grandson of the pioneering travel agent Thomas Cook, whose widow later sold the house to the British Red Cross for institutional use. Fortunately for us, however, it was recently acquired by Alexander Hotels, who undertook a dramatic renovation aimed both at restoring the estate’s former glory and in bringing it up to the standards of Alexander’s other London-adjacent luxury hotels.\n\nIn practical terms this means the exteriors are all-original, while the interiors have been reimagined to varying degrees; while the Oak Hall Restaurant still retains most of its Edwardian stateliness, the rooms and suites feature generous splashes of color and a contemporary edge to the furnishings. Rain showers are standard, while some of the suites add egg-shaped modernist tubs. Afternoon tea is served either in one of the lounges or on the garden terrace, and its Sunday lunch service is a classic British roast served in the wood-paneled Oak Room. If you absolutely need a day spa, then you’ll find fault here, but for something a little more low-key than a full-on country house luxury hotel, this just might be your Goldilocks.

content:
At the accessible end of the Lake District, a mile or two above Windermere, the grandest of the lakes, there’s a family-owned country house hotel which, over the last two decades, has quietly, painstakingly made a reputation for itself. Despite a welcome modern influence in the design — and in the architecture of its graceful expansions — Gilpin Hotel & Lake House is a classic.

As its name suggests, it’s in a sense two hotels in one. The Gilpin Hotel is the original house, surrounded by modern lodges clad in natural wood and stone, while the more intimate six-bedroom Lake House is set on its own 100-acre estate, about a mile away. They’re linked by an on-demand shuttle service, and while the Lake House is supplied with its own treatment room, hot tubs, and saunas, Lake House guests are welcome at the Gilpin Hotel for dinner and for anything else that strikes their fancy.

And while some country house hotels go too far in the direction of playful modernity or historical correctness, Gilpin Hotel & Lake House is a measured blend of the two. Even the classic rooms in the old house have evolved with the times — they’re contemporary Georgian, not period-reenactment Georgian. And the modern rooms and suites in the newer buildings are just plain contemporary, their clean lines and cutting-edge gadgetry lending themselves to a feel that’s much more urbane than you might expect from the Lake District.

The expansive and thoughtful public rooms are meant to be lived in rather than rented out, and the spa is fully equipped. And the restaurants are impressive as well — the fine-dining SOURCE at Gilpin Hotel is joined by the more casual Asian-accented Gilpin Spice.

content:
Not enough gets said about the Aegean side of Turkey, north of about Bodrum, but everything you love about coastal Greece applies in equal measure to Alaçatı. In fact, this picturesque seaside town was varyingly Greek and Ottoman at different points in its history. These days it’s a pretty cosmopolitan place, and it’s only fitting that one of its finest hotels should be brought to you by a family of immigrants from Greece — who thankfully expanded their color palette beyond white and Aegean blue when it came time to decorate the Viento Hotel Alaçatı.

Essentially, it’s a townhouse hotel, one that’s positively dripping with charm, designed in a contemporary style but one that makes liberal use of the historical bones of the house and a well-curated selection of antique furnishings. And here “charming” and “comfortable” aren’t competing interests that must be balanced, but mutually reinforcing objectives.

The kitchen serves farm-fresh fare, which is certainly no bad thing, and your hosts are only too happy to teach you everything they know about this attractively historic town — which, if you’re the windblown type, happens to be a bit of a hotspot for windsurfing, kitesurfing and all manner of water sports.

Please note: Viento Hotel Alaçatı cannot accommodate children under the age of ten.

content:
It’s all in the name at The Edgewater. Perched on the south shore of Lake Mendota, the hotel affords guests some of Madison’s best views, period — and this is a city that’s not short on natural beauty. And the hotel buildings themselves, newly renovated, are easy on the eye as well, possessed of a certain Upper-Midwest charm all their own, sturdy and un-frivolous in the American Craftsman tradition, with the occasional Art Deco indulgence.

The hotel’s 202 rooms feature completely remodeled interiors and fittings, especially in the spa-stye bathrooms, which include Kohler fixtures, oversize tubs with rain showers, and in-mirror TVs. Most rooms take full advantage of the unobstructed lake vista with panoramic floor-to-ceiling windows and/or private terraces. Relax and unwind on pillow-top mattresses with Egyptian cotton sheets — HDTV and an in-room wet bar certainly help, here. For extra points, mosey down to the full-service spa and fitness center for a session with a personal trainer, massage or mani/pedi.

Alimentary offerings comprise three restaurants and a café called, The Market, all overseen by Executive Chef Matt Chingo. His New American, regionally sourced specialties grace the tables of signature Statehouse restaurant, as well as the more casual Boathouse and Icehouse, highlights of the waterfront and the central plaza, respectively. And, of course, thoroughly local and justly famous craft brews remain the order of the day in these hardier climes, though Martinez's custom cocktails put up a brave fight. You won’t lack for handy tipples, either, as Wisconsinites take pride in the fact that the state consistently ranks among the nation’s highest in alcohol consumption per capita. While you’re at it, sample the wares and take in one of the plaza’s many events: concerts, conventions and a converted skating rink in winter. Rumor has it there’s even a dinner cruise in the works….

content:
Airport hotels, all else equal, are rarely anyone’s first choice. But airline schedules being what they are, they’re an occasional inevitability. They’re awful, of course, almost without exception. But it’s the exceptions which just might restore your faith in the whole enterprise of hospitality. There’s really no great need for citizenM Paris Charles de Gaulle to be as impressive as this, and we love a hotel that goes further than it strictly has to.

What does this mean? The simple fact of its eye-catching modern design means the citizenM leaves other airport hotels far behind. The additional fact that these arresting rooms also make great functional use of their somewhat limited space is a perennial citizenM selling point. And of course the informal, self-service concept of the 24-hour reception, lounge and canteen suits layover guests to a tee — air travel rarely defers to scheduled mealtimes, and late-night arrivals could generally do without the whole reception-desk song and dance.

All you’re really left wishing is that it were closer to Paris itself. There’s no popping out for a stroll to the corner bakery, that’s for sure. But if that’s your concern, then for all its charms this citizenM isn’t aimed at you. Put this one on your list for the next time you’ve got an overnight layover.

content:
A new addition to the burgeoning subgenre of over-the-top Persian Gulf megahotels is Shangri-La’s Barr Al Jissah Resort & Spa, a sprawling (and sparkling new) tripartite hotel complex overlooking the bay of Al Jissah, in Oman’s capital city of Muscat.

The family-friendly Al Waha and the middle-of-the-road Al Bandar are fine enough hotels — luxury hotels, even — but we’re really here to talk about Al Husn. This one, “the castle,” bills itself as a six-star, which is a tricky definition to pin down, but essentially means something on the order of if you’re not comfortable here then the problem is you, not the hotel.

What are on average the biggest hotel rooms in Oman have views of the deep blue waters of the Gulf of Oman, some with more dramatic views over the bay and the adjoining coastline. The look is a sort of contemporary-Arabian palace style, equal parts clean lines and finely carved latticed woodwork, the kind of modern-luxury look that’s more about textures and materials than finishes and frills. Rooms and suites here come with butler service, which may go some way to earning that sixth star, and Al Husn’s guests have access not just to their own private restaurant, bar, and even beach, but to the rest of the resort’s facilities as well — everything from pools, restaurants and bars to the Chi spa, the dive center, and the marina.

How to get there:
The resort is approximately 45 minutes by road from Seeb International Airport. Taxis are readily available at the airport and cost approximately $30-50 USD. Agree to the fare before leaving the airport, as meters are not commonly used in Oman.

content: For those who dream of an escape to the Tuscan countryside, it’s hard to imagine a more idyllic getaway than Villa Svetoni Wine Resort, just a few minutes’ drive from the hilltop town of Montepulciano. The hotel is located inside an 18th-century villa surrounded by olive groves and picturesque vineyards — the source of the delicate Sangiovese-style reds the Svetoni family has been producing here since 1865. Rooms are charmingly rustic, with high ceilings, exposed wood beams, hardwood floors, and handwoven rugs. All have writing desks, framed vintage photos of the winery, and windows opening to views of the bucolic landscapes outside, plus modern stone-lined bathrooms with walk-in showers.

content: The word “pulse” here refers not just to the rhythm of São Paulo, that most urban of Brazilian cities, but also to the steady biorhythm of bodily wellbeing. Pulso Hotel Faria Lima whisks you away from the chaos below to a cloistered vision of ultramodernity courtesy of luminary architect Arthur Casas. The way it’s laid out, you could flit from spa to meal to conference call to bed (and back again) without ever losing sight of his sophisticated, upcycled aesthetic. Grab a room with a terrace to play up the contrast between the hotel and the city. It’s like falling asleep in an abstract treehouse in the middle of a modern art museum.

content: A lush and private garden surrounds A Cheda, a self-described “lodge de charme” just a short drive away from Bonifacio. The boutique hotel’s rural stone house is home to a collection of cozy cottage-style guest rooms which blend traditional Corsican limestone, exposed stone and wooden beams with Mediterranean-inspired shades of blue and sunshine yellow. Family-friendly suites sleep up to four, and some rooms come with saunas and private terraces. The rather lovely outdoor pool enjoys a verdant setting surrounded by the garden’s leafy foliage and tall palms and makes a pleasant spot for laidback summer lunches. By night the hotel serves al fresco aperitifs of local Corsican wines and the gastronomic restaurant L’A Cheda is also rooted in the local terroir; herbs and vegetables are even picked fresh from the hotel’s own vegetable garden. A poolside wellness center completes the offering, with a Jacuzzi, Finnish sauna, and a range of treatments including reflexology, Reiki sessions, and Swedish massages.

content:
The idea of a Bavarian mountain lodge might feel a bit old-fashioned, but it really shouldn’t. With winter sports — and adventure travel in general — more popular than ever, it’s a type of hospitality that’s correspondingly more relevant than ever. The fact that this part of the world’s been at it longer than most means their expertise is worth trusting. And hotels like Staudacherhof, in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, prove that the form is open to stylistic evolution and even innovation.

It opened as a bed and breakfast some 100 years ago, and Staudacherhof is still in the family. Were Franz-Josef Staudacher here to see it now, however, he’d marvel at how things have changed. The rooms and suites take three distinct styles: some delicately traditional, others modern-rustic in bare knotted wood, and still others decidedly modernist in style, though made from materials that the family patriarch knew well. And all of them are spacious and more than comfortable — in these mountains it’s a hardy kind of luxury, but it’s luxury all the same.

In that vein, there’s a pronounced emphasis on wellness, from spa and beauty treatments to Ayurveda to all manner of active sports, including hiking, biking, and (obviously) skiing. And, in classic Bavarian-lodge style, you’ll be in no danger of going underfed — the restaurant serves everything from schnitzel to health-conscious, Eastern-influenced “Bayurvedic” cuisine.

content:
Hong Kong might be the home of the highest concentration of extraordinary luxury hotels, but if you’re looking for the absolute state of the art, look a hundred or so miles away, up the Pearl River in Guangzhou. This is, by most accounts, the heart of the booming Chinese economy, and we can certainly attest to the boom that’s taking place in the city’s hospitality scene. To wit, the brand-new Mandarin Oriental, Guangzhou, which opens an even half-century after the original Mandarin Oriental set up shop in Hong Kong. It could be a coincidence, but either way, it’s something of a symbol.

This is the picture of the perfectly modern luxury hotel: a skyscraper in a huge Chinese city, with some 263 sprawling, richly finished, highly luxurious rooms and suites. The design, by Tony Chi, is a touch conservative, but that’s to be expected given the audience — it just means the visual pleasures are subtle ones, derived from balanced lines and expertly selected materials. The views don’t hurt either, and the bathrooms, the current frontier of the luxury-hotel arms race, have to be seen to be believed.

The Oriental Club, as usual, gets you another level of service and comfort, though we admit it’s hard to imagine being disappointed in the standard Mandarin experience. There’s a generous handful of restaurants and lounges, including a flagship restaurant specializing in Cantonese cuisine, as well as an outdoor pool, a practical infinity of meetings and event space, and a spa to rival any hotel spa anywhere. Add to that the fact that this very same skyscraper is also home to the Taikoo Hui high-end mall complex, complete with its own encyclopedic list of restaurants, and it’s no exaggeration at all to say you could easily spend a week here without venturing out of doors.

How to get there:
The Mandarin Oriental is located 22 miles from the nearest airport, Guangzhou Baiyun International (CAN). The hotel can provide a limousine transfer for an additional charge.

content: Traditionally, bathing is somewhat of a ritual in Japan (to put it rather mildly), and to go to an onsen ryokan — a ryokan with natural hot-spring baths — is to get a quick in-depth lesson on this aspect of the culture. So it should be expected that at Oncri, in the southern prefecture of Shiga, the bathing facilities are just as much an attraction as the recently renovated guest rooms and the pair of locavore restaurants. The water of the Furuyu hot spring is known for being a bit tepid, at about 100°F — a point that serious onsen-goers count in its favor, as the mild waters allow for longer, more indulgent soaks. There’s the standard indoor bath, a walking bath (for wading), and six kinds of outdoor baths, including the fragrant hinoki cypress tub and the waterfall-like streaming bath. Somewhere among all the options you’re sure to discover a soaking style that suits your particular fancy. The guest rooms are furnished in either traditional or modern styles (tatami mats and low seating or sofas and beds, respectively), and all come with a view of the verdant mountains. If you prefer a bit more interior personality, there are also the Atelier rooms, which feature winning pieces from an art competition hosted by the ryokan. After some relaxing soaks and some good seasonal meals at Oncri’s Italian and Japanese restaurants, you might come away with a new perspective on the idea of a spa retreat. Either way, you’ll surely have had one of the more high-pleasure lessons available in traditional Japanese culture.

content:
The Malmaison Newcastle arrives just in time to take part in this once-drab city's renaissance. Where once the town belonged to coal miners and ship builders, today it's a more cosmopolitan city, home to the new Baltic museum, built from a converted grain silo, and the Gateshead Millennium Bridge, an arched footbridge across the river Tyne that swings upward into the sky to let large ships pass beneath.

Rather like the Baltic, the Malmaison is housed in a repurposed industrial building — in this case a grand old warehouse alongside the Tyne. The hotel is a design statement as well, easily the most stylish in Newcastle, with such Continental flourishes as a French-speaking elevator and a Parisian-style brasserie. Guest rooms are chic yet exceedingly comfortable, with massive plush beds and extensive CD libraries, and the hotel comes complete with a fitness center and spa.

Still, the Malmaison is no uptight “luxury” hotel. All the comforts are provided, and the look is smart, but the feeling is more laid-back and informal than in more traditional hotels. It's the perfect place to get your first taste of the new Newcastle — many rooms have views of the Tyne, and all the architectural sights are within easy reach, with the shopping district close at hand.

content:
SUJÁN Sher Bagh is the original SUJÁN tented camp, built back in 2000 by a family of wildlife filmmakers who, while not luxury hoteliers, have managed to combine modern comforts with a deep respect for the natural surroundings.  Set on the edge of Ranthambhore National Park, also known as India’s most celebrated Tiger Reserve, and a natural habitat for the Royal Bengal Tiger, Sher Bagh’s nine Tented Jungle Suites sport an old-world safari style with handcrafted rosewood furniture, brass bathtubs and stone showers, and private verandas for taking in the views of nature. The semicircular layout of the camp means your neighbors are easy to ignore, but if you are looking for more privacy then the more secluded, and romantic, Royal Sher Suite comes with its own heated plunge pool, an outdoor fireplace and an open-air tree shower and bathtub. Top billing, however, is given to the Imperial Raj Bagh Suite thanks to its two bedrooms, private swimming pool and large deck.

There’s an outdoor fireplace for swapping safari stories around the campfire under the starlit sky, as well as a library lounge and the Jungle Bar where cocktails are mixed to secret recipes. Dinner is served in the dining tent using produce from Sher Bagh’s own organic gardens, farm and dairy. Days are often spent out on game drives, as well as tigers there are leopards, sloths and some 300 species of birds to spot, but there are many other experiences on offer such as cooking classes, guided excursions to local NGOs or Ranthambhore Fort, an 8th-century UNESCO World Heritage Site, or simply enjoy some relaxation time by the heated outdoor pool or in the SUJÁN Spa.

Please note: Sher Bagh operates seasonally. The property is open from early October to mid-May.

How to get there: The nearest airport to Sher Bagh is in Jaipur, 170 kilometers away. There is an airfield in Sawai Madhopur, 14 kilometers from Sher Bagh and a helipad, 4 kilometers from the camp. The nearest rail center is Sawai Madhopur Junction, located 12 kilometers away. There are several trains each day from Delhi, Mumbai, Jaipur, Jodhpur, and other cities. It takes either 3.5 hours or 5.5 hours (depending on the train you choose) from Delhi, overnight from Mumbai, 3 hours from Jaipur, and 7 hours from Jodhpur.

content:
With every decade that goes by China opens itself further to the West. By now Hong Kong feels like it’s right next door, and Beijing and Shanghai are quickly losing their air of exoticism. Even Xi’an, the eastern end of the Silk Road, is finding itself more and more accessible to foreign travelers; surely it’s a sign of the times that the top hotel in town is the Sofitel on Renmin Square, an utterly modern luxury hotel from the French-owned international chain.

Outside it’s a fairly typical commercial building, about as Chinese as any Sofitel anywhere — which is to say, not a lot at all. Inside, though, there’s a generous helping of local color, from the rich colored fabrics in the rooms (it wasn’t called the Silk Road for nothing) to the rows of vases in the restaurant, a visual allusion perhaps to the Terra Cotta Soldiers in Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum, less than an hour to the east.

Services include the usual array of five-star offerings, as well as some rather unique ones — restaurants include the usual Cantonese and Mediterranean offerings as well as a Muslim restaurant, serving halal cuisine as a tribute to the region’s Islamic history (yes, really).

Please note: At Sofitel on Renmin Square, there is a 10% service charge that is not included in the room rates.

Travel advisory: Passport and visa requirements differ from country to country. Please check with your local authority before booking.

content:
We’d be willing to bet that when you imagine five-star luxury hotel in the heart of Luxembourg City, the chances of your coming up with something that looks like the Sofitel Luxembourg Le Grand Ducal are slim indeed. Though Luxembourg is not exactly well known as a hotbed of modern interior architecture, this is the kind of hotel that goes a long way towards changing the public’s perception of a place.

This is a chain that knows what they’re doing, taking the most agreeable elements of corporate hospitality—the consistency, the service—and marrying them with a visual sensibility that’s always at very least slightly ahead of the curve. Here at the Grand Ducal they’ve gone several steps further into the future. Rooms are anything but conservative: colors are vivid, furniture rakishly modern, yet the comforts, underneath it all, are the equal of any city-center luxury hotel.

And the public spaces are no less distinctive. The Grand Ducal trades dainty salon style for a striking, graphic look, especially in the bar, L’Observatoire, where the décor competes with the panoramic views, and in the top-floor restaurant, Mu, with its modernist furniture and its artfully composed French dishes.

content: A rare find that blooms in a rugged, pristine alpine valley — the comparison to the flower is an apt one. Three generations in and going strong, Das Edelweiss Salzburg Mountain Resort is a testament to the Hetteger family’s past mastery. They’ve of course perfected the ski-in, ski-out idiom (including their own ski depot, replete with the latest and greatest), and the après scene is arguably just as opulent. There isn’t a room in the place without a postcard view, and even the most modest of them doesn’t skimp on natural wood and floor-to-ceiling windows for the full effect. For best results, grab a front-row seat to a snowcap sunset in their infinity pool.

content: Big name brands might have moved to Bermuda in recent years, but Cambridge Beaches is one of the island’s original hotels, which has been welcoming guests to Bermuda’s sandy shores since 1923. It still retains all of its charm today, with cute pastel-hued cottages and suites spread across the private peninsula and offering exclusive access to four beaches and two coves, as well as Atlantic Ocean views. The infinity pool overlooks Mangrove Bay, or there’s an indoor pool in the spa, which focuses on classic massages courtesy of French brand Caudalie. Evenings are just as relaxing in the three laidback al fresco restaurants, all with bay views, and can be kicked off, or rounded off, with tropical cocktails at The Sunken Harbour bar.

content:
The same Bunkhouse brand responsible for about half of the finest hotels in Texas has expanded beyond the confines of the Lone Star State. Hotel Genevieve, in Louisville’s lively East Market neighborhood, adapts the mini-chain’s signature variety of unpretentious boutique charm to this uniquely French-influenced riverside city. It’s a new build, but one designed to fit in among downtown Louisville’s finest examples of French-inspired architecture.

Hotel Genevieve’s rooms and suites are colorful, and more than a little bit Parisian in style; the colors, in particular, are rich and saturated, and their curvaceous furnishings feel like an Art Deco homage. And Bunkhouse has always had an eye for details; present in every room are luxe touches like Sferra linens, Kassatex towels, and Ortigia bath products.

Like any great boutique hotel, Hotel Genevieve is more than just the sum of its rooms. Restaurants include the versatile Bar Genevieve. Lucky Penny, the swanky semi-secret cocktail bar, is one of the hotel’s finest spaces, and the Mini Marché is an expertly curated convenience store, while a new restaurant will be opening this fall.

content: England’s old coaching inns are perfect material for regional boutique hotels, and the Hare and Hounds, in the Berkshire market town of Newbury, is a fine example. This 17th-century Georgian inn has historical character to spare, but it wears it lightly, updating the experience for well-traveled and sophisticated visitors. The 30 rooms are spread between the original coach house and a handful of outbuildings; all are charming and full of personality. These days a British pub can aspire to greatness at the table, and the Hare and Hounds’ menu ranges from a classic English breakfast to elevated seasonal fare for dinner.

They’ve got high ceilings, full kitchens, and private balconies complete with gas grills overlooking the quiet neighbors at Andersonville’s St. Boniface Cemetery. Upstairs, a rooftop deck offers an opportunity for some low-key socializing, as do the Club Room and the Library — the latter can be booked for afternoon tea, provided by Vanille, a local patisserie. And while the neighborhood’s charms are a key piece of the Guesthouse’s appeal, the Loop is accessible via a Red Line stop, a fifteen-minute walk away.

The Hotel Vermont isn’t without some traditional regional charms, however, such as the outdoor wood-fired kitchen and bar, featuring pizzas and lobster rolls alike. Nor is it meant to be a one-stop destination for travelers; several of Burlington’s premier bars, restaurants, and gastropubs are just down the street, and its lakeside location puts the city’s attractions within easy reach. \n

content: The “Centric” in Hyatt Centric Montevideo refers partly to its location — the hotel is outside the historic center, but metaphorically at the heart of the action, in the stylish and desirable neighborhood of Pocitos — and partly to the mega-chain’s new sub-brand. The Uruguayan iteration is the latest in a line of boutique-style hotels aimed at a more youthful crowd, with bolder modern design and tech-friendly rooms. Montevideo, if you’re not aware, is the other birthplace of tango, a quieter counterpart to brash Buenos Aires, located across the border in Argentina. The two cities are well-connected by frequent ferries across the Rio de la Plata, a river so wide it looks like the ocean. And the Hyatt Centric Montevideo sits on a prime piece of real estate right on its shore. From many of the guest rooms, all you see is water; outside the front doors, you’re steps away from La Rambla, the wide waterfront promenade that runs for miles along the coastline. So while you can certainly use the hotel’s spotless fitness center or go for a swim in the small but beautifully tiled indoor pool, you’ll almost certainly feel the urge to walk, run, or cycle with the steady stream of locals passing in front of the entrance. Guest rooms and suites are what you’d expect of a brand-new Hyatt – spacious and sleek, with ample work space, flat-screen TVs, large bathrooms, free wi-fi – with the occasional piece of interest, like a red wall, a gilded mirror, or a quirky light installation. Familiar comforts with a contemporary edge, that’s what the Hyatt Centric Montevideo has to offer. And they do it well. Some rooms have kitchenettes; otherwise, there’s Plantado restaurant, with its open kitchen and a striking olive tree rising up through the center of the dining room, a grab-and-go deli, and a lobby bar where you can sample up-and-coming Uruguayan wines. It’s a plush place to return to after a day of tango and chivito — that’s the national sandwich, piled high with slices of grilled steak — or sand and sun, as the case may be.

content:
Hotel Lilla Roberts spans more than a century of Helsinki history — from its origins as a power station designed by Selim A. Lindqvist, later expanded by modernist architect Gunnar Taucher, to its present incarnation refitted by Jaakko Puro. The result is a stylish and contemporary hotel in the now‑familiar boutique style, one indelibly marked by Helsinki’s distinctive visual character. The interiors, blending Art Deco elegance with modern comfort, feature dark tones, geometric motifs, and golden accents, creating an intimate yet glamorous atmosphere. 
Rooms range from standard to suites, many boasting beautiful rounded windows that highlight the building’s unique architecture.
The spacious lobby offers inviting lounge areas and ample space to gather by the fire with a drink in hand. Here you’ll find Bar Lilla, seamlessly connected to Krog Roba — a well‑regarded bistro serving a refined introduction to the pan‑Nordic cuisine that continues to captivate the culinary world.

content: To look at the photos you’d think the balance in question was mostly a matter of some sort of pinewood deficiency. But the Arosea Life Balance Hotel, in Val d’Ultimo, in the South Tyrol region of the Italian Alps, is about more than just pared-down décor. Here the natural building materials and calming modernist design are mere backdrop — the unending series of health, wellness and relaxation offerings, in the spa and otherwise, take center stage. (Among them is the opportunity to bathe in freshly sheared sheep’s wool, which we are assured is not a translation error but a real activity.) And to these, of course, are added the various summertime and wintertime attractions of the Alps, which scarcely require enumeration.\n\nAll that pine in the rooms and suites was apparently chosen for its therapeutic effects, and whether or not it aids in respiration, there’s certainly something calming about it. Same goes for the wide open spaces, the walk-in closets, and expansive bathrooms — and if you’ve scored a suite with an outdoor sauna, then you don’t need us telling you what’s relaxing and what isn’t. Cap it all off with some health-conscious Italian cooking — best of both worlds, that — and a bit of oxygen-enriched water — can’t hurt — and you’re well on your way to restoring the balance.

content:
Formerly something of a no man’s land, the northeast corner of downtown Seattle has recently sprouted a collection of shiny modern towers. Olive 8, crowned by a frosty blue glass halo, stands just slightly above the others, and provides a neat and tidy home for Hyatt’s new business-boutique hotel, where mod-luxe meets Northwest chill, with a focus on healthfulness. The location, on Olive Street at 8th Avenue, makes for a central home-base for visitors, about halfway between Pike Place Market and the vibrant Capitol Hill.

While many of Seattle’s hotels hold tight to the city’s (relatively short) history, Hyatt at Olive 8 is gleamingly modern and entirely unsentimental. The lobby and public spaces exude an International Style tautness that leans more toward elegant than cozy. Rooms are pleasantly spare and buttoned-up, but never cold, while the bathrooms, similarly modern, benefit from warm stone shower surrounds. Dark wood accents and thick throw blankets keep your senses situated in the Pacific Northwest. 

Among the hotel’s attractions is its green roof, a gesture towards sustainability that’s perfectly at home in this earth-loving region. While the native grass seedling may offer less immediate pleasure than the sunny mosaic-tiled indoor pool, it’s nice to know the building itself is working to keep the environment healthy. Meanwhile, keeping you healthy is the on-site Elaia Spa, with a list of organic body treatments, delivered in warmly modern spaces. Urban, Olive 8’s in-house restaurant, concentrates on farm-to-table cuisine, rendering its name somewhat ironic. While rustic fare in such a crisply modern downtown setting might seem conceptually misaligned, the contrast it creates is quintessentially Seattle.

Please be advised that our pool and hot tub will be closed for unexpected and necessary maintenance and repairs starting June 20th and until further notice. The locker rooms, steam room, and sauna will still be available.

content:
The Troisgros family achieved culinary fame generations ago in the Loire city of Roanne, before undertaking high-profile projects in Paris and even Tokyo. But it’s in Ouches, mere minutes outside of Roanne, that Marie-Pierre, Michel, César and Marion established what’s simply known as Troisgros, a masterful small hotel to go along with the enormously successful restaurant.

As in all the finest projects of this type, it’s difficult to say which is more impressive. Safe to say the lodging is anything but an afterthought; here an antique farmhouse and estate was transformed by architect Patrick Bouchin into an inspired and inspiring contemporary hotel, one that remains connected to the past but is firmly rooted in the present.

Its 15 rooms, suites and apartments are luxurious, but understatedly so, and are as confidently stylish as any city-center design hotel. The look is neither too rustic nor too avant-garde, but perfectly judged as a subtle supporting act to the stunning glass-walled Le Bois sans Feuilles, the Troisgros family’s Three-MICHELIN-Star restaurant.

content:
Sister to the Terence Conran–designed Fitzwilliam in Dublin, this Belfast outpost, it’s no shock, is very much in the same vein — a classic yet not exactly show-stopping city-center building whose stately exterior conceals a surprisingly sexy luxury boutique hotel. There’s scarcely a more central location in town than this one, right next to the Grand Opera House, and from here it’s hard to see Belfast as anything less than a proper cosmopolitan capital.

Rooms are dark and masculine, yet set off with accents in bright yellows and greens — a wise choice for adding a bit of lightness, given the gloomy tendencies of the local climate. The sophistication goes deeper than just the visuals; the bedrooms come with high-tech entertainment systems and the bathrooms, with their separate tubs and high-flow rain showers, are nothing short of indulgent.

The restaurant is a slightly less imposing version of the Dublin outpost’s eatery, and it strikes a note of simple urbanity, using the best ingredients from across Northern Ireland. All in all it’s the sort of place that’s more than suitable for a business traveler, and absolutely ideal for anyone accustomed to traveling with one eye on luxury and one eye on style.

content:
A few more hotels like this one and Jakarta just might shed its “only on business” reputation. Kosenda Hotel is the kind of fresh, inventive, authentic boutique hotel that just about any city in the world would love to call its own. Like most of the best boutique hotels, this one is the product of a very involved founder — Ruben Kosenda is a local entrepreneur, an experienced traveler, and a man who knows originality when he sees it. 

Here he’s assembled a local and international dream team that seemingly couldn’t help but result in an extraordinary hotel, incorporating influences that range from traditional Indonesian Betawi houses to the classics of modernist Danish furniture. The common denominator, seemingly, is natural wood — rarely does a hotel so contemporary present itself with such organic warmth.

Rooms come in three categories, Petita, Comforta, and Spatia — no extra points for guessing which one’s the largest. Even the Petita, however, are quite comfortable, with thick pillow-topped mattresses, goose down duvets and pillows, 32-inch televisions, iPod docking stereos, and stylish, efficient bathrooms. Comforta rooms spread a bit, adding walk-in rain showers, and Spatias come with kitchenettes, living rooms, and the whole junior-suite treatment.

And like all the best boutique hotels, it’s an authentically inviting meeting place, its social spaces packed with locals and travelers alike, from the buzzing lobby café (complete with La Marzocco espresso machine) to the Waha Kitchen restaurant to the romantic rooftop garden lounge. Jakarta’s still a long way to go just to see a boutique hotel, but this one might just be the push you need — and if you’re regularly called to the Indonesian capital on business, the Kosenda just might become your new routine favorite.

content:
China is vast, and contains multitudes. Lijiang, for example, the home of this particular Banyan Tree resort, is a UNESCO World Heritage site, an ancient town surrounded by endless rice fields with a spectacular view of Jade Dragon Snow Mountain (which needs little additional description) and just generally about as scenic as a place can be.

As for the resort itself, it more than lives up to the promise of its location — its 55 villas are in the no-holds-barred luxury vein, scattered amidst tranquil gardens and pools. Within them you’ll find just the necessities — sprawling bedrooms, palatial bathrooms, and yet more pools: jet pools, plunge pools, or even full-fledged swimming pools. And should anyone need to unwind a bit after all that plunging and pooling, there’s a spa to end all spas, and a dizzying array of treks and tours for the restless, conducted on foot, bike or horseback, through the rugged Yunnan countryside.

Travel advisory: Passport and visa requirements differ from country to country. Please check with your local authority before booking.

How to get there: To get to Banyan Tree Lijiang travel to Kunming International Airport. From there it is a 40 minute domestic flight to Lijiang Airport. Alternatively, you can take a flight to Shanghai International Airport, followed by a four and a half hour domestic flight to Lijiang Airport. Lijiang Airport is approx. a 40 minute drive from Banyan Tree Lijiang.

content:
While the spires and bridges of Prague might be the unofficial mascots of the Czech Republic, there’s a lot more to the country than its capital. The Central Bohemian countryside may not evoke the same absinthe-soaked visions, but places like the St. George Forest — home to several coveted species of wild mushrooms — have a magic all their own. Situated at the edge of that forest, about an hour northeast of Prague, Chateau Mcely is the modern five-star incarnation of a 17th-century hunting lodge.

Of course, European nobility in the Baroque period weren’t about to retreat to the countryside in anything less than princely accommodations, so the “lodge” is decidedly palatial. A stroll through the carefully manicured gardens surrounding the main house gives you a pretty good indication of what’s to come: a tribute to rural opulence that’s both detailed and dreamy — a fairy tale with attentive service. The 23 high-ceilinged rooms go heavy on the old-world charm, with chandeliers sparkling above wrought iron beds, and writing desks that hearken back to the days when Rilke came to visit. 

If the hotel had simply stopped at the guest rooms, it would still be worth a visit. But the meticulous renovation extends to the facilities as well, and a high level of outside-the-box thinking for this sort of classically beautiful building. The library, for example, houses 18th-century scientific instruments, and the basement Alchemist Club melds high-tech wine preservation, a well-stocked humidor, and a vintage 1950s jukebox. For deep relaxation, the on-site Mcely Bouquet Spa offers purely natural cosmetics, which are hand-blended in the chateau's laboratory. 

Not bad for a 300-year-old hunting lodge near Jabkenická obora, where the world-famous Czech composer Bedřich Smetana composed and lived.

How to get there:
Chateau Mcely is located 70 km from Václav Havel Airport in Prague. The closest railway station is Nymburk (approximately 16 km from the hotel).

content: Perched high over the Aegean on a remote stretch of the island’s southern coastline, Noma Milos is a sophisticated and sustainably built boutique hotel with sweeping water views. content: The Emory is, perhaps surprisingly, the first all-suite hotel in London; between that and the fact that it counts Claridge’s, the Connaught, and the Berkeley as its siblings, you can expect a thoroughly high-end experience. The building, by Richard Rodgers, is a modern marvel, and the interiors are the work of a dream team of hospitality designers. Add a very fine location in Belgravia and an atmosphere of confident, sober luxury — as well as an outpost of New York's ABC Kitchens restaurant, a rooftop bar with a view, and a private health club that might just be the most lavish in London — and you’ve got a recipe for success.

content: The mountainside city of Nikko is a classic Japanese holiday destination; here, by the side of the Kinugawa river, is Kinugawa Keisui, a ten-room luxury hotel in the modern-ryokan idiom. Hot spring baths are a part of the experience as a matter of course, both in-room and in the hotel’s communal onsen complex. Each room has a semi-open sunroom as well as a balcony with a view of the surrounding greenery; inside, the look is clean-lined and contemporary but also warm and organic. In the hotel's ambitious concept restaurant, you can enjoy wood-fired cuisine that transcends genres.

content: Niseko, on Japan’s northern island of Hokkaido, is an adventure-sports mecca, and more specifically something of a winter wonderland. It’s here, in the long shadow of the volcanic Mount Yōtei, that you’ll find Sansui Niseko, an ultra-stylish, ultra-modern luxury boutique hotel that also happens to offer ski-in/ski-out access as well as a lavish onsen bath complex and a spa. Many of the units feature conventional bathtubs with views of the countryside, and the penthouse has not one but two private onsen baths. Make time for Sushi Shin by Miyakawa, an outpost of the Michelin-starred Miyakawa in Sapporo.\n
