content:
If you went by what the travel press says you’d think Marrakech and Morocco were different names for the same place. But there are other cities in Morocco — one of them, Rabat, even happens to be the capital. It’s less a pure holiday spot than Marrakech or Essaouira, of course, but its seaside location is charming enough, and like any capital, it’s got a need for some decent hotels: quite a bit more than decent, in fact, judging by the Sofitel Rabat Jardin des Roses.

Sofitel can typically be counted on to raise the stakes wherever they go; their Parisian-influenced style is sexier than the typical luxury hotel, and they’ll match up to many a boutique in the looks department. This one is suitably North African–influenced as well, with mashrabiya-style wooden screens and ornately carved headboards. Underneath it all, however, it’s an utterly contemporary luxury hotel, with all the bells and whistles that entails.

Plus a few extras. A pool is probably to be expected, but an Andalusian garden, an orange grove, and a driving range are a bit above and beyond. As for the location, it’s anything but standard business-district fare — here you’re in the heart of the historic city, near both the Royal Palace and the Mausoleum.

content: The Berchtesgaden Alps have welcomed travelers of all sorts, from mountaineers, sanatorium residents, eco-tourists, and sports junkies to the Romantics of yesteryear. Rising from the ashes of an old-school luxury hotel, Kulturhof Stanggass instead fixes its gaze firmly on the future. Don’t worry, you’ll still get a knockout panorama of the Watzmann massif every morning — but you’ll also swap anecdotes over long tables and live music in the beer garden. There’s also the One-MICHELIN-Starred restaurant Solo Du. Take a bracing morning plunge in the natural pool, or finally dig into Thomas Mann in the stillness of your blonde-wood balcony. Clean, simple, healthy, eternal: let these be your bywords as you drink in nature’s magnum opus.
name: Kulturhof Stanggass

content:
High in the Holywood hills, five miles outside of town, you’ll find what may be Belfast’s grandest old hotel. The 19th-century Culloden Estate and Spa cuts an impressive silhouette, surrounded by twelve acres of wooded parklands and gardens overlooking the waters of Belfast Lough. Once a bishops’ residence, then a private home, today it’s the sort of place that hosts pop stars and heads of state on their way through town.

Behind this imposing Gothic exterior lies a lush interior; no drafty castle, the Culloden is stuffed with antiques and artworks, stained glass and Louis XV chandeliers. Guest rooms are decked out in rich fabrics and antique furnishings, with marble bathrooms, separate showers and tubs, and views of the gardens or the Lough. Suites come with king beds, stereo systems and superior views.

Dining options include the informal Cultra Inn and Vespers, serving locally inspired dishes. Golfers are in heaven, surrounded by a number of fine courses including the Royal Belfast, and the athletically minded can make use of the hotel’s pool and fitness center. Sailing the Lough is a popular pastime as well, and the grounds and gardens make for excellent walking. Perhaps best of all, the shops, restaurants and nightlife of Belfast’s city center are just minutes away.

content:
Don’t let the tricky spelling of La Co(o)rniche deter you. Just know it reads as non-standard for French people, too, and move on to the more important details of this rather spectacular hotel, located in the Pilat-Plage region, at the foot of the highest sand dune in Europe. If you haven’t heard of Pilat-Plage, you’re not alone, or you just don’t have any aristocratic French ancestors. Quiet and otherworldly, this is an off-the-beaten-path destination where the sea meets towering dunes and thick pine forest; it was the playground of princes, dukes, even Napoleon III. La Corniche was a Basque-style hunting lodge built in the 1930s, thoroughly updated by none other than Phillipe Starck in 2010 — which is when it became La Co(o)rniche.
 
The dark wood-lined lobby, with its oil paintings and period furniture, remains mostly true to the original. But the artful Starck touch is unmistakeable almost everywhere else, from fanciful glass sculptures and collage-studded ocher walls to a Murano lamp, designed by the French artist Aristide Najean, casting an ethereal glow over the hotel’s romantic old staircase. Guest rooms are located in the main house or in freestanding wooden cabins connected by a series of sandy paths. The former all feature private terraces with sweeping views of the bay or the ocean, while the latter, with gables trimmed with old-fashioned gingerbread on the outside but bright white and whimsical inside, featuring quirky art pieces and asymmetrical mirrors at every turn, add a welcome modern twist to the cozy cabin concept. Cabins by Philippe Starck, if you will.
 
The Carita beauty salon occupies its own cottage amid these cabins. On the edge of the property, Card restaurant does French-style seafood on a waterfront terrace lined with elegant white umbrellas. The adjacent bar, run by a friendly local, is pleasantly unpretentious. It has indoor and outdoor space, and good specials on oysters — a must in a region known in France for its oyster farms.

content: A lodge doesn’t get much deeper into the heart of the Peruvian Amazon than Inkaterra Hacienda Concepción. Accessible only by a scenic canoe ride from the nearby town of Puerto Maldonado — a 25-minute flight from Cusco — Hacienda Concepción puts you right in the thick of it, with all the excursions that entails, all led by skilled local guides. Five rooms occupy the main lodge, and another 25 cabanas offer a touch more privacy. While high-end luxuries are absent, the experience is comfortable, and totally immersive. It’s as eco-friendly and sustainable as can be, and the dining room serves dishes prepared with organic and local farm products.

content: In a bucolic landscape filled with farmhouses, Villa Flor stands out both in architecture and character. This Art Nouveau-style villa, in the Swiss village of S-chanf and overlooking the Engadin Valley, was built at the turn of the century, not long before the nearby wilderness area became the country’s first national park. It remained a family residence until 2009 when the building was renovated and turned into a chic guesthouse. The owner is a former gallerist, and it shows — the villa’s original features, from the old spiral staircase to hand-painted frescoes, have been carefully restored, the charming interiors have been enhanced by family heirlooms and antiques discovered at local flea markets, and rotating exhibits feature the work of Swiss and international artists.\n\nVilla Flor has seven uniquely decorated suites. All feature pine flooring and original wood paneling — or in the case of the upper-level rooms, original vaulted wood beams. A few have a Scottish feel, with tartan patterns and mountain views, while others are lighter and loft-like, with artisan-made wallpaper and Nordic-inspired furnishings. All include a gourmet homemade breakfast served in the elegant dining room, and afternoon tea or cocktails are served in the hotel’s cozy living room and library.

content: Surrounded by coral reefs and 24 white-sand beaches, Lizard Island sits 240 kilometres from the Queensland coast, closer to the continental shelf than the mainland. Villas and suites are tucked into the landscape with bleached timbers, soft linens, and open-plan layouts that pull the outside in. There are no locks, no schedules, and no need to keep track of time. Between morning dives and afternoons on empty beaches, the pace slows over seafood lunches. You’re off-grid here, but never far from a mojito or a perfect sunset.

India’s southwestern state of Kerala is, perhaps unsurprisingly, something of a paradise when it comes to beach holidays. And Kovalam, near the state’s southern edge, has quickly transformed itself from the archetypal fishing village into one of India’s most exceptional destinations. It’s here, set on a lush green hillside just a few minutes’ walk inland from Samudra Beach, that you’ll find Taj Green Cove Resort & Spa, a perfect example of the sort of quietly stylish, highly competent luxury hospitality which is the Taj group’s specialty.

Its setting is near enough to the beach for convenience’s sake, but just removed enough for an added measure of privacy — it’s closer to the edge of a tranquil lagoon, and is surrounded on three sides by dense forest. The resort itself combines traditional Keralan architecture with a pronounced Balinese influence, and its cottages and villas lack for nothing when it comes to comfort.

Like any Taj resort worth its salt, this one comes with a Jiva spa, capable of restoring even the most world-weary traveler. And a more urgent form of restoration is available at the three restaurants: Curries, the upscale Indian option, Bait, specializing in ultra-fresh seafood, and Jasmine Bay, the versatile all-day eatery.

content: Sicily isn’t just famous for its gorgeous coastline, but for culture as well. Duomo Suites & Spa, located in the heart of the island’s second-largest city, is a window into the island’s more cerebral side. This part of town is, simply put, a Baroque wonderland for architecture fans, a charming labyrinth of cobbled passageways that open onto picture-perfect piazzas and palaces. Duomo Suites & Spa is located inside one of these, a four-story structure that dates to the 18th century. But inside, the look isn’t ornate or overly decorative, it’s spare and minimalist, with a cool color palette and geometric design details. Pop art murals and poetic text, all paying homage to Italian cinema, enliven the white walls. The landscapes and cultural identity of Sicily, of course, have served as both setting and inspiration for a range of classic films. Indeed, many of the hotel’s suites and rooms are named after specific movies, from from The Godfather to Il Postino and Cinema Paradiso. Standard rooms at Duomo Suites & Spa are simple and comfortable, but larger rooms and suites feature balconies, separate lounge space furnished with sofas or director’s chairs, and extravagant design details from intricate tiled floors to round beds made up with circular red velvet duvets. Upstairs, the hotel’s rooftop terrace is an impossibly lovely spot for late afternoon drinks with views over the cathedral of Santa Ágata, patron saint of Catania. When the sun slips lower in the sky, casting the skyline into stark silhouette, it’s time to head down for dinner. Pasta alla norma, Sicily’s indulgent pasta dish, made with sun-ripened tomatoes, fried aubergine, and fresh basil, was invented in Catania, but the region is also renowned for its fabulous seafood. Beaches, architecture, gourmet cuisine? Welcome to paradiso. Booking Details: Duomo Suites & Spa requires additional information from guests to ensure the best stay possible. As such, reservations can only be confirmed through our customer service team. Contact us for assistance. Rates begin at 200 EUR per night.

Most Ritz-Carltons look, from the lobby if not from the street, like something out of Revolutionary France; in 21st-century Beijing that would just be perverse. Here, in a modern glass skyscraper on Beijing’s very sensibly named Financial Street, is a new breed of Ritz-Carlton, one that departs in two ways: not only is it strikingly contemporary, ever so slightly on the minimalist side, but it’s also very identifiably Chinese.

Nowhere, though, do the visuals threaten to overwhelm the pure old-school luxury of the place. In the rooms the contemporary furnishings are more notable for their comfort than for their looks, and no expense has been spared in making these rooms the absolute state of the luxury art: everything’s totally wired and electronically controlled, and televisions include 37-inch LCD screens in the main room, 15-inch in the lavish marble bathrooms.

The main restaurant is upscale Chinese, showcasing the cuisines of seven different regions; secondary restaurants include a Northern Italian option and a “flexitarian” vegetables-and-seafood choice. The spa is as impressive as you’d expect it to be, and the fitness center is up to the highest standard — and here, as anywhere, the Ritz-Carlton is perhaps best known as a destination for a fine afternoon tea.

How to get there: From Beijing Capital International Airport , 35 km - approximately 40 mins.

content:
The appeal of staying in a chain hotel, any chain, is a certain consistency, an ability to know what one can expect in advance. If you are visiting a place like Milan, New York, or Tokyo, you may prefer to be surprised by the seemingly endless variety of hotels; you may welcome the unexpected, and relish the satisfaction of seeing how different hotels find unique solutions to the same basic hospitality puzzle — how to make their guests happy.

But in a city where one's lodging options are constrained, a city with no market for independent, adventurous boutique hotels, the consistency of a chain hotel is a welcome guarantee. And few hotel chains manage to turn consistency into an advantage quite as well as Ritz-Carlton.

Thus the Ritz-Carlton St. Louis draws strengths from the brand's basic template, yet without that “where am I again?” feeling so common to bland corporate chains. Here the familiar drawing-room atmosphere of the wood-paneled old-world lobby is a welcome immersion into a world of luxury seemingly foreign to the upscale suburb this hotel calls home.

Thus it's almost like a vacation within a vacation — inside this hotel, you are no longer in St. Louis, but in some sort of Democratic Republic of Ritz-Carlton, a place where all bathrooms are marble and the Cigar Bar is the obvious nightlife choice. And this particular outpost has its own distinct personality — dinner is served not just inthe traditional fine dining restaurant but in the Wine Room as well, with the food chosen to complement the wines, rather than the other way round — and this must take some choosing, as this hotel boasts the most extensive wine list of any Ritz-Carlton anywhere.

You’ll hear the word “suburb” bandied about, but don’t get the wrong idea: in Johannesburg, a suburb is simply a neighborhood. So 54 on Bath, though advertising its location in the suburb of Rosebank, is actually located in the most central part of the city, on Bath Avenue (no points for guessing the number). And it’s a favorite among South African travelers for good reason. It’s a member of Tsogo Sun, Africa’s leading hotel chain, and therefore offers a range of familiar amenities: free wi-fi, spacious guest rooms, tasteful décor, tech-forward facilities for business travelers. 

Design-wise, 54 on Bath doesn’t stray far from the brand’s standard: guest rooms and suites are large and elegantly outfitted with huge windows, fluffy feather-top beds, roomy work desks, and sleek bathrooms, all in a sophisticated palette of black and white, charcoal, teal and chocolate brown. Welcome details include big flat-screen TVs, minibars, Illy coffee machines, and black-out curtains.

Comfortable as these accommodations are, the hotel’s public spaces are where 54 on Bath has something more original to offer. There’s a modern fitness center, and a classy lobby with a white baby grand piano. But the hotel’s crowning glory is its gorgeous outdoor swimming pool — long, narrow, and beautifully illuminated at night — on the fourth floor. It’s bordered on one side by an inviting grassy lawn, and adjacent to the champagne bar and Level Four restaurant, it’s a prime spot for afternoon tea or sunset cocktails.

An 18th-century ancestral house converted to an intimate boutique hotel, the AC Ciudad de Tudela boasts a brand of elegance can certainly be called contemporary — with the caveat that most hotels would seem positively futuristic surrounded by the Gothic architecture of Tudela’s gorgeous palaces and cathedrals. While the European boutique experience largely depends upon this sort of melding of old-world ambience with modern amenities, the AC Ciudad’s attention to detail and lack of pretense make it worthy of consideration, whether you’re in northern Spain to tour the wineries or to check out that obscure annual tradition, something to do with some running bulls.

The hotel’s ample and well-tended public spaces — courtyard garden, meeting rooms and lobby — are suffused here and there with a blue glow that lends an urban-nightlife sheen to the cozy sitting-room atmosphere. The forty-one guest rooms are a world away from the opulence of a trendy Madrid luxury hotel; instead, they offer a more provincial take on modernist comfort, in a palette of oranges and lemony creams. This no-frills sophistication gives way to delightfully sleek bathrooms, where vanity lights flank the mirror above an all-glass sink.  

The hotel restaurant, Alcazaba, is a workhorse that prepares breakfast, lunch and dinner, in addition to providing 24-hour room service. Abundant fresh produce provides the basis for a few innovative variations on the traditional regional cuisine. And, of course, legendary local wines offer tasty complements. For scenery-hunters, the above-mentioned Gothic architecture finds its apex in the 12th-century Cathedral de Tudela, a quick walk from the hotel.  

How to get there:
The hotel is located 58 miles from Pamplona Airport (PNA).

content:
From a Western perspective the Mandarin Oriental hotels are largely an urban phenomenon — in most of the world’s major cities, among the top three or four luxury hotels is invariably a towering modern Mandarin. For their first hotel in the People’s Republic of China, however, the Mandarin group has gone off-script. Sanya, you may have gathered, is a town on the coast of Hainan island, and this particular Mandarin Oriental makes the most of its setting, with a low-slung villa-resort profile — albeit one that’s both finished and serviced in typically impeccable Mandarin style.

The location really is rather stunning, occupying some thirty acres of lush beachfront land. Hainan’s extreme southerliness offers some clues as to the nature of the landscape, as you’re much closer to Vietnam than somewhere like Macau. The accommodations are woven into the landscape amid the palms — the rooms and suites in low buildings with balconies, the villas and pavilions in freestanding stone buildings along the beach or perched on the hillside.

Interiors are somewhat rustic in aspect, a fitting departure from the Mandarin group’s typically urban style, but they’re as crisp and clean as any, and outfitted with everything you’d expect from a brand-new luxury hotel. The leisure offerings, as well, are expanded, to suit Sanya’s purpose as a tropical island getaway; the Spa Village is a large and secluded complex, where it’s easy (and pleasant) to get lost amid wooden pavilions and endless pools. It’s not your typical MO, but it’s none the worse for that fact — at this very moment any number of Pacific Rim executives are no doubt arranging a bit of business on Hainan.

content:
Signs abound that New Zealand has confidently shed its once-provincial self-image. Among them is the Sofitel Auckland Viaduct Harbour, a sleek and contemporary luxury hotel that’s, in terms of style, nothing if not cosmopolitan. With a location right on the downtown marina the Sofitel can’t help but become something of an emblem of Auckland’s hospitality scene. The end result is unlikely to leave anyone feeling let down.

It’s a modern and fairly low-slung glass building, with two wings that extend out over the water. The combination makes for some inspiring views through those full-length windows, especially from the front corners. Inside the rooms the look is crisp and modern, looking local without overplaying its Asian-inspired hand. And while it sounds like a footling detail, in today’s overly climate-controlled world we’re suckers for a sliding glass door that opens out to a proper balcony.

This is not a difficult life. The in-room comforts are legion, and the ubiquitous soaking tubs are not bad either. The spa and wellness center are modern and more than suitable given the hotel’s modest size. A couple of stylish restaurants and lounges come close to completing the package — add one high-end flagship restaurant and this place would be absolutely self-contained. Then again perhaps that’s the point — one seam left un-sewn, as an entry point into the city.

It’s not the last word in boutique style, or in gilded luxury-hotel opulence, but if discreet comfort is the last word in hospitality, then The Last Word is aptly named. A high-end ten-room guesthouse in Franschhoek village, in the South African winelands, isn’t exactly a hard sell in the first place, but when those rooms (and suites) are as tranquil and elegant as these, a bit of boastfulness in the name is more than justified.

The big double rooms have oversized stone-clad bathrooms, as well as private patios and gardens; they’re anything but cramped. The classic suite is almost fifty per cent bigger, and the two pool suites come with their own private pools, which means they’re pretty well self-contained. The Last Word can be played either way — it can be an exceedingly private escape if you want it to be, but it’s also perfectly sized for a bit of classic country-house social life.

One central pool serves the rooms that don’t have their own, and it’s the daytime hub of the place, at least in summer. There are plenty of reasons to step out, though — the Franschhoek valley is naturally blessed, and it’s a paradise for foodies and wine lovers. It’s a good life.

Unless you’re a wine connoisseur familiar with Chardonnay varietals, the Margaret River region of southwestern Australia may be something of a mystery to you. Here’s a quick update: slightly inland from the Indian Ocean, the vineyard-surrounded town is located about three hours’ drive from Perth. The recently renovated Cape Lodge is one of a few grand estates in the area. Boasting an award-winning restaurant, its own lake and vineyard, as well as easy proximity to beaches, a cave-filled national park, and, of course, all the viticultural attractions a wine lover could desire, the Lodge is a peaceful retreat far from, well, pretty much everything.

The ten newly constructed “super luxury” suites are roomy, sparely furnished spaces, some featuring jacuzzi baths. Despite the finer amenities (wireless internet, high-quality linens, CD players) of the suites, some find the lodge’s original rooms are cozier and warmer. And then on the other hand there’s the ultra-plush Vineyard Residence, a three-acre property fit for a family — that is, if your family likes gazebos and marble bathrooms, high vaulted ceilings and elegant hardwood, not to mention a separate guest house and a helicopter handing pad. 

It’s probably no surprise that the Cape Lodge’s wine cellar is top-notch — the culinary dimension is central to the Cape experience, centered around a lakeside restaurant, serving fresh local seafood and the finest Western Australian produce. Touring is an option, with the choice between the hotel’s Bentley and Rolls; or just hide away, and make use of that gazebo.

content: If ever there was a hotel that efficiently adapted to time and circumstance, it's the Hotel Glacier in Grindelwald. The original hotel opened near the foot of an alpine glacier in 1864, back in the days when huge blocks of ice were harvested and transported by horse and carriage to Interlaken. Over the past century, the glacier has retreated dramatically — only its uppermost portion remains, and it’s a good distance away in the mountaintops — and the hotel has evolved accordingly, with a modified layout that makes the most of the setting while staying true to the property's history.\n\nThe owners approached the most recent renovations with sustainability and style in mind. The chalet maintains its original shape, but its scope has been extended to include a spa, a wine cellar, and a set of new rooms. The once-rustic decor is now modern and eclectic, with mountain motifs appearing throughout the hotel, from the colorful mosaic mural in the restaurant to the patterns on bedspreads and headboards. Rooms have parquet floors, deep charcoal-gray accent walls, COCO-MAT beds, Marshall speakers, Nespresso machines, and Apple TVs. Many have balconies, and the best rooms have private wooden decks with outdoor hot tubs and sweeping views of the Alps. For everyone else, there’s a common terrace for lunch or drinks overlooking the scenery, and when winter weather takes over, a cozy fireplace lounge awaits inside.

content: Though set within the city limits, Aleenta Retreat Chiang Mai achieves a rural-resort atmosphere thanks to its verdant setting at the foot of Doi Suthep Mountain, as well as the privacy afforded by its compound-like layout. The experience combines the luxurious comforts and devoted service of a Thai luxury resort and the personality and depth of detail of a thoughtfully designed boutique hotel. \n\nRooms are contemporary in style, and all come with a balcony, while the residences and villas have more luxurious amenities such as separate living rooms and private plunge pools. The spa, occupying its own pavilion by the poolside, is key to the Aleenta’s appeal, and personalized programs that incorporate meditation, Tibetan sound therapy, yoga classes, massage treatments and more make the hotel something of a wellbeing retreat, if that’s what you’re looking for. There’s also health-conscious dining at the farm-to-table Garden restaurant, and the swanky open-air 1892 Bar specializes in ultra-fresh local flavors.
name: Aleenta Retreat Chiang Mai

content: The great novelist and playwright Jules Verne was born in Nantes, France. In the historic city center, a boutique hotel pays homage to his oeuvre with a collection of avant-garde apartment-style suites inspired by his books. The original architecture, featuring high-ceilinged, loft-like spaces with exposed stone walls and wide-planked wood floors, lends itself well to the imaginative interior design. The Voyage in a Balloon suite has a suspended bed accessible by a wrought-iron ladder, the Extraordinary Voyage room is partly constructed out of wooden shipping containers, and the From the Earth to the Moon suite has a sleek bathroom resembling the cabin of a spaceship. Across the board, the aesthetic is quirky but modern, the rooms stocked with luxurious amenities and furnished with a mix of industrial-chic decor and vintage curiosities. Many have views of the Loire River — indeed, one suite sits right on the water, housed inside a 1930s-era riverboat that’s docked nearby at Quai Henri Barbusse.

content: Despite the name, the Nest Hotel Incheon, on Yeongjongdo Island near Seoul, isn’t small and cozy: this ultra-modern luxury hotel has hundreds of suites, a theater, a spa, and a large infinity pool, not to mention additional pools for spa treatments and a kids’ club. The nest imagery comes from the hotel’s symmetrical design; its levels stack one on top of the other to allow 360-degree views of pine forests and the Yellow Sea. Minimalist guest rooms feature floor-to-ceiling windows, slightly tilted to let in maximum sunlight throughout the day, and private balconies with pocket gardens. There’s a white marble-lined restaurant, plus an industrial-chic library and coffee bar. Everything you need, in other words, to stay in the nest until catching your flight out from Seoul’s airport, a ten-minute drive away.

It would be surprising if the Hotel Du Vin Brighton didn’t drip with personality, given the setting — not only are its 49 unique bedrooms divided among several renovated structures, but the structures themselves are unusual, some in a mock-Tudor style, others Gothic revival. No chance of a dull and dreary double-loaded corridor here.

The seaside is perhaps more than a literal stone’s throw away, but not by much. And the rooms, though outfitted with the necessary luxuries, are unpretentious, as they should be — even the top-of-the-line suite, with its twin freestanding tubs right smack in the middle of the bedroom, feels sweetly haphazard, more authentically curated, somehow, than the crop of modern design hotels. A more highly polished approach would run counter to the ramshackle charm that’s among Brighton’s strengths. The onsite Bistro du Vin serves French-inspired dishes.

content:
If you haven’t been paying attention to Scottsdale you might be surprised to find its demographics have shifted a bit. What was once a haven for upscale golf resorts and Southwestern art galleries is now a nightlife and entertainment mecca, with a new breed of hotels to match — including the W Scottsdale, an outpost of the Starwood-owned boutique-style luxury chain.

It’s the full W treatment from top to bottom, including the slightly precious room categories (Wonderful and Fabulous instead of Standard and Superior, for example) and the bar, which is no cozy little lounge — it’s a poolside debauch called Sunset Beach, and comes complete with daybeds, “lounging pods,” and TV-equipped private cabanas, as well as a guest list and a tightly controlled door. Welcome to the new Scottsdale.

Business travelers will find the W well equipped, but they’ll need to bring their patience — the bathrooms are a bit too intimate for traveling with someone you don’t know extremely well, and the poolside scene doesn’t exactly knock off early. It’s perhaps at its best when you’ve come for leisure, and you can make the most of the Bliss spa, the excellent gym, and the stylish, upscale Sushi Roku restaurant.


How to get there:
W Scottsdale is approximately a 20-minute drive from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX).

content: Once upon a time, this hotel in Newark, California was a pretty humble place, back when what’s now Silicon Valley was mostly considered cow country. Set on the east side of the bay, it’s ten minutes from Palo Alto, Mountainview and Silicon Valley proper. It’s not a place for rambling around on foot, but it is equidistant to the three Bay Area airports, and a convenient choice for travelers with business in the South Bay. \n\nWhile the exterior lacks the drama of some of the flashier hotels in San Francisco, the interiors feel fresh and perfectly contemporary. Naturally there’s an abundance of well-equipped meeting space, as well as a spa, heated outdoor pool and 24-hour gym. And despite the South Bay location, the airy, open-plan rooms look surprisingly urbane — though with comfortable work stations and plenty of room to spread out, they’re appropriately functional, too.

content:
It says something about the state of the business world, and the world in general, that something like the Sofitel Guangzhou Sunrich is no longer the least bit surprising. Not that it’s unremarkable in any way: this gleaming twin-towered colossus of a hotel is said by many visitors to count among a small handful of the world’s finest (and most extravagant) hotels. But where else but Guangzhou would you expect to find such a place?

And while too much consistency often breeds boredom — see most corporate hotel chains for an illustration — the Sofitel group’s stylistic consistency feels more like a family resemblance than a carbon copy. The only given is that it’s going to mix Parisian grandeur with the most elevated possible version of the local interiors style, and that’s certainly true here. Rooms are almost excessively well-appointed, and the suites are positively palatial, all furnished with photos of Parisian cityscapes to match the real-life Guangzhou views at the windows.

As for the facilities and services, this Sofitel comes with the standard suite: swanky restaurants, L’Occitane spa, high-tech gym, and copious events space. As well it should. Given the current vogue in China for all things European, it’s hard not to envision the Sofitel Guangzhou Sunrich remaining at the top of this town’s heap for quite some time.

content:
It’s not exactly what comes to mind when you think of Malaysia. The Cameron Highlands is a cool, mild region, almost a mile above sea level, a few hours north and inland from Kuala Lumpur. Here, in a place named for a British explorer (and known for its tea) it’s perhaps no surprise to find a hotel like the Cameron Highlands Resort, a contemporary colonial-style hotel, packed with civilized attractions like stone fireplaces, a reading room (complete with wireless internet access), and, of course, a daily high tea.

The 56 rooms and suites are handsomely furnished, with timber floors, beamed ceilings, four-poster beds, and linens in neutral tones of cream and beige. Many of the guest quarters contain private balconies overlooking the adjacent golf course; the spacious Jim Thompson and Cameron suites have French doors leading out to particularly panoramic terrace views. Too old-fashioned for your taste? Flat-screen televisions and in-room coffee makers cater to guests who’ve had their fill of tea and books.

There’s no pool — it’s cooler up here than you think, so it’s not a glaring omission. There is, however, a Spa Village, which offers a variety of unique treatments using the area’s natural resources of tea and strawberries. Guests can choose from a number of onsite dining options, including the region’s only Japanese cuisine. Visitors to Malaysia may not have been expecting high tea and sushi — somehow the Cameron Highlands Resort makes it work.

Getting there:

Cameron Highlands Resort is approximately 3 1/2 hours from Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Private transfers are available for approximately US$200 one way.

content: Perched on a cliff overlooking the East China Sea, its rectangular white façade standing out in stark relief against the blue sky, Emil Nakijin is an ultra-modern boutique hotel with just five suites. They’re lined up in a row facing the ocean, each with oversized stainless steel sliding glass doors opening onto private terraces with open-air baths and infinity pools. The linear layout is a hallmark of the Hiroshima-based design firm Shinichi Ogawa & Associates, and the bright interiors are nearly identical — minimalist and all-white — with nothing to distract from the spectacular surrounding landscape. There’s no restaurant, spa, or conventional hotel services, but suites are well-outfitted for doing absolutely nothing, which is exactly the point of this sleek and silent escape.

content:
Malmaison’s expansion continues apace, with this, its tenth installment, and its first ever new build, a big deal for a chain whose specialty has been renovations, some in unlikely neighborhoods. This one’s a big deal, impeccably located in the booming waterfront district at Princes Dock, and opening just as the city of Liverpool is undergoing a bit of a renovation of its own.

Once inside this sparkling new building, though, you’ll find the familiar Malmaison style very much intact, all rich woods and deep, masculine colors, from the soaring lobby lounge all the way on up to the sumptuous black-and-violet bedrooms. In them you’ll find all the boutique trappings, from entertainment centers to custom-branded robes to ultra-high-end bath products in the gleaming black-and-white bathrooms.

Again, in classic Malmaison style, you can expect a well-equipped gym, a rather good brasserie, and a hotel bar that’s something of a focal point for local celebrities, media types, and assorted well-heeled hipsterati. Best of all, though they must have raised the money for the building from somewhere, they didn’t get it by adding on to the room rates — actually they did it by selling luxury apartments upstairs, if you’re wondering, and the result is that the prices are well in keeping with those of the rest of the budget-luxe Malmaison empire.

content:
There's something of a revolution afoot in the UK — we all know London as the world's most competitive (and expensive) hotel market, the central front in the battle of chic high-design boutiques against stuffy, old-fashioned hotels. But there are interesting things going on all across the country, as the UK, more than any other country, is turning run-down industrial areas (and in some cases, entire cities) into hip retail and commercial destinations.

All of the Malmaison hotels fit this bill — they are inevitably retrofitted into existing buildings, whether warehouses, factories, or, in this case, a former bus and train depot. The décor is, of course, richer and earthier than most boutiques, in typical Malmaison style — wrought iron staircases and chocolate and taupe checkered carpets set the tone. And the cuisine is, unsurprisingly, French, served in a basement brasserie with a vaulted ceiling.

This town has softened quite a bit in its new incarnation, and the characters you encounter on those Leeds side-streets are likely to be shoppers or revelers, depending upon the hour. Victoria Quarter and Harvey Nichols are close at hand, in case you have money to burn, and there are any number of bars and restaurants nearby, to add a little variety once you have eaten at the Malmaison brasserie. Possibly the most stylish game in town.

content:
There’s a lot more to Greece than the islands and the capital. For a seaside experience that’s a bit of a departure from the Cyclades circuit, there’s Parga, on the mainland’s northwest coast, and the little emerald in Parga’s crown: Salvator Hotel Villas & Spa.

It’s set on a hillside above the town, about a mile from the beach, surrounded by greenery which is reflected in the interior color scheme — just when maritime Greece had just about become synonymous with blank white and Aegean blue, here’s a new modern Greek idiom, all natural wood and vibrant olive green.

The eclectic, slightly bohemian look is a welcome change for this part of the world, but underneath it all is a classic boutique hotel. Comforts are legion, terraces or balconies universal, bathtubs nearly so, and the two-bedroom villas add kitchens, fireplaces and private pools.

Everyone else shares the main pool on a terrace cut into the hillside, which is the daytime heart of the hotel. The spa is on hand for more intensive relaxation, and the hotel’s restaurant and cafe see to guests’ immediate needs. Beyond that there’s Parga town, reachable via an almost negligible car ride, and it’s from Parga’s beaches that you’ll get up close and personal with the Ionian Sea.

Please note: Salvator Hotel requires a three-night minimum and is open seasonally, May through October.	

How to get there:
Preveza and Ioannina Airport are both approximately one hour by car to Salvator Hotel Villas & Spa.  The Port of Igoumenitsa is approximately 40 minutes by car to the hotel.

content:
Fairmont Le Montreux Palace is the city’s biggest and grandest hotel, with a sprawling Belle Epoque facade that dominates the lakeside, itself almost enough to keep Montreux architecturally anchored in the 19th century. Inside it’s more of the same, enough meticulously preserved opulence to stun the most jaded jet-setter, making pretenders out of the majority of so-called “grand” hotels.

There may be a certain homeliness lost to all this determined splendor, but there’s something to be said for a return to the days when a hotel felt like a hotel, rather than an overgrown bed and breakfast. As in any grand hotel, there’s a certain caste system to the guest rooms, the cheapest rooms being a touch crowded, the better ones more spacious, and the best overlooking the lake rather than the mountains. Some rooms open through French doors onto small private balconies.

Beneath all the old-world elegance, Fairmont Le Montreux Palace is a fully modern business hotel, with all the trappings: wireless LAN in all rooms, extensive meeting facilities, and a distinctly un-Swiss Amrita spa, offering the latest treatments and a well-equipped fitness center. There are several restaurants and bars to choose from, including the Montreux Jazz Café and Funky Claude’s Bar, named for the founder of the famous Montreux Jazz Festival.

content:
The Mondrian Hong Kong is new, but the building isn’t. This triangular 40-story high-rise, formerly the home of the Panorama Hotel, has been a fixture on the city skyline for years. And while the interiors have been thoroughly reimagined, the architectural structure remains, complete with quirky curving walls and sharply angled hallways. 

The building’s unconventional shape turned out to be an ideal match for the art-forward Mondrian brand and its first hotel in China. On the upper levels, wraparound corner windows — following the slanting lines of the original structure — reveal dazzling views over the city and Victoria Harbor, and downstairs, moody gallery spaces exhibit glittering mosaics and larger-than-life underwater photography. The eclectic art collection is impressive, but the hotel itself feels like a large-scale, Hong Kong–themed art installation, from the dramatic glass-walled lobby to the whimsical wallpaper-lined corridors and the sultry cocktail bar. 

The design pays homage to the city’s history and coastal character; expect nautical-inspired red and white striped rugs, sand-colored terrazzo flooring, local art, and wooden sewing boxes stocked with snacks, a nod to Hong Kong’s reputation as one of the world’s tailoring capitals. The theme continues at the flagship bar on the 38th floor, where creative cocktails incorporate ingredients like tea and sesame, and at the rooftop cultural space and concert venue, hosting a lineup of Hong Kong–based musicians and performing artists.

content:
Carcassonne is the largest walled citadel in Europe, and the Hôtel de la Cité sits behind the ancient fortifications, with the Romanesque Château Comtal and the Gothic Basilica of Saint-Nazaire as its neighbors. Though the citadel’s ramparts date back to the 13th century, and the original Roman village some seven hundred years before that, the Hotel de la Cité is not quite one hundred years old. In its current incarnation as a member of the MGallery Collection, however, it looks like something straight out of the 15th century, the rooms packed with antique furniture and ornate woodwork, and stained-glass windows adding color to the sunlight.

Some rooms open onto balconies or terraces overlooking the ramparts of the citadel, while others look out windows onto the narrow cobblestone streets — only conveniences like air contitioning, satellite television and spacious modern bathrooms break the illusion of time travel.

The Michelin-starred Barbacane restaurant is, for many, almost worth the trip in itself; you haven’t had cassoulet until you’ve had it here, and the chef is available for lessons, in case you’d like to attempt your own. A more casual brasserie and summertime terrace restaurant round out the gastronomic options, and guests sip cocktails to the tune of gentle piano accompaniment in the library bar. The only downside is that, sooner or later, you have to return to the twenty-first century, at least until you can spare the time to visit again.

Please note: The hotel is located within the fortress structure with restricted vehicle access.

How to get there: Hôtel de la Cité is approximately a one-hour drive from Toulouse Blagnac International Airport. You can reach the hotel by train from Toulouse in a little over an hour as well.

content: First off, we don’t expect you to keep it strictly confidential — a secret this good is worth sharing with at least a few trusted friends. The town of Chambéry, in the Savoy Alps, is itself something of a well-kept secret, at least overseas, but it’s a stunner: charming pedestrian streets, plenty of history, and a location that places it at the foot of the mountains. And in the heart of its fortified town center, very nearly hidden behind an unassuming door, is the secret we’re here to tell you about: the Petit Hôtel Confidentiel. \n \nIts 15th-century exterior does little to prepare you for the very contemporary boutique hotel inside. Interiors range from the truly monochrome “Infinite Black” rooms to the lighter schemes of the Club and Deluxe rooms — throughout, the atmosphere is more Provençal than urban. The small spa is accompanied by a gym, pool, sauna, and hammam, and the restaurant is only open for breakfast every day as well as lunch and dinner Tuesday through Saturday. Weighing in at a mere fifteen rooms and suites, it’s as intimate as they come — and its hands-on family owners ensure there’s always a personal touch.

content:
This is Alpine chalet living done right. That is, with consummate respect for privacy and a slew of opportunities to engage directly with what is arguably Nature’s grand finale. At an altitude over 3,400 feet and comprising just four chalets, HochLeger will have you convinced that you’re homesteading on a fresh frontier — you’ll forgive the luxury trappings for straining the illusion, we hope. Or just ditch the illusion and revel in the sky-high infinity pool, we don’t judge.

The ambience behind the three chalet types — Hunter’s, Sports, and Romantic — pretty much explains itself, though all partake in an extravagant display of natural wood; floors, walls, ceilings, and furniture make a gorgeous and sustainable statement in matured pine, larch, and fir. All three two-story buildings feature private terraces and al fresco or freestanding tubs with Natural Beauties amenities, arresting mountain views, and (nice touch) champagne tables. Color schemes vary between sensual and autumnal, accented in turn by the inevitable trophy antlers and an open dolomite fireplace. Balancing the old-world elements is a flatscreen, a Dolby surround sound system with docking station, and the all-important complimentary wi-fi.

The real home run comes with the full-scale kitchens, complete with handpicked, antique farmhouse cabinets and stone countertops that function as altars to abundance. Stocked sideboards boast regional, seasonal ingredients from the area’s own farmers and artisans: rustic breads, fortifying local milk and butter, forest jams, wild honey, and savory cuts of meat. What’s more, a delivery service stops by daily, first with breakfast rolls and Italian espresso, later with fresh strudel and coffee — or book the on-site chef to whip up an entree from his rotating menu.

content:
The starting point of the Silk Road, Xi’an is one of the oldest cities in China — which, of course, is really saying something. But until fairly recent developments brought an influx of industry and business to the city, the imperial capital didn’t see many international visitors. Now with the Economist naming Xi’an one of China’s thirteen emerging megalopolises, the game’s officially on. It’s no wonder the French-owned luxury hotel chain Sofitel has opened multiple locations here, most recently the Sofitel Legend Peoples Grand Hotel Xi’an.

Lest you get the wrong idea, picturing a megalith of a hotel to fit the scale of the megalopolis, let’s be clear: the Sofitel Legend only has 71 rooms, and history to boot. Located right in the heart of the city, on Renmin Square, the building originally opened its doors in 1953 as a state guesthouse. Today, it’s still an imposing structure surrounded by perfectly landscaped gardens, but the interiors have been thoroughly refurbished to business traveler standards. The design, though elegant, is a bit of a mix: there are elements of French and Russian architecture, high molded ceilings, Art Deco details and Chinese artworks. Guest rooms and suites are noticeably spacious, and more romantic than you might expect. All come with Sofitel’s signature king-sized bed, made up with 600 thread-count sheets and goose down duvets, pillow menus, silk bathrobes and sleek bathrooms stocked with Hermes products. Suites are extravagant in both size and style, with dining rooms and kitchenettes. But even the most standard room comes with 24-hour butler service, an especially useful amenity when you’re (inevitably) jet-lagged.

In line with the hotel’s cultural eclecticism, the restaurant — Dolce Vita, which doubles as the breakfast venue — is Italian, not Chinese. Perhaps the most atmospheric space in the hotel is the 1953 Lobby Lounge, a throwback to the building’s original look, serving afternoon tea and cocktails. The more opulent Louis XIII Bar stocks rare cognacs, perfect if you’re entertaining — or better yet, being entertained by someone with an expense account.

content:
Think of Mexico and many of us think of the over-developed mega-resorts — which makes a place like Las Mañanitas such a welcome surprise, and such a well-kept secret. In fact it’s the restaurant, believe it or not, that gets most of the attention; but these 29 rooms are something special as well, a break from the tropical kitsch we’ve come to expect, a surprisingly elegant place.

Cuernavaca, of course, is quite literally about as far as you can get from the seaside tourist traps; this historic town lies well inland, around an hour from Mexico City, and while the sand and surf are nowhere to be found, it’s a city of culture, with a number of archaeological sites and beautiful old haciendas, as well as a location conveniently close to the ancient village of Tepoztlán and the wide open spaces of its surrounding national park.

Fitting, then, that Las Mañanitas specializes in the quiet life
 — its twenty-one rooms and suites surround gorgeous central gardens, each room with its own private terrace or patio. Flamingos stand around a Japanese pond, or amidst sculpture gardens, as guests lounge by the swimming pool. The décor may not be everyone’s cup of tea, with its slightly formal and colonial look, but what the rooms may lack in visual impact the make up for in charm and comfort.

The restaurant is justifiably famous, serving Continental cuisine alongside Mexican specialties, all on the terraces overlooking the gardens. It’s something of an open secret that the big resorts are a bit weak in this area; one more reason to gloat as you breathe in the crisp mile-high air.

How to get there: Las Mananitas is approximately a 1½-hour drive from Mexico City–Benito Juárez International Airport.

content:
If the Four Seasons Hotel Macao, Cotai Strip looks a bit like something straight out of Monte Carlo, the resemblance is not entirely accidental — the Cotai Strip is Macau’s answer to Monte Carlo, or perhaps Las Vegas. From the exterior this Four Seasons is perhaps more Vegas than French Riviera, but once inside the lobby, under the rotunda, you’ll certainly be struck by the heavily European Casino Royale atmosphere of it all.

In fact you’ll want to look slightly further west for its inspiration. This Four Seasons is designed in a Portuguese-Chinese hybrid style, an expression of Macau’s unique history. The 360 rooms and suites, spread over 19 floors, are perhaps a little bit more Asian in aspect, the décor rich in golden tones. Underneath, however, the rooms are as modern as they come, with the current standard 42-inch plasma screens and another LCD screen over the bathtub. We wouldn’t expect anything else but classic looks and state-of-the-art comforts from the Four Seasons.

If there’s a departure from the Four Seasons template it’s in the scale. No fewer than five pools serve the guests here, as well as three restaurants (two of them Cantonese and Portuguese, naturally) and two bars. There’s a full-service spa as well, and the services are so comprehensive it’s easy to imagine never setting foot off the grounds. Unlikely, though — it’s a rare guest who will resist the call of the Cotai Strip’s casinos, starting with the connected Plaza Casino.

content:
High-design boutique hotels are not exactly new, but there’s still a little thrill in coming across one in an unexpected place, like the Hanseatic port city of Bremen. Here, quite literally on the banks of the Weser, is the Hotel ÜberFluss, an exercise in historical contrast: it’s a modern building grafted onto an old merchant’s residence, which is in turn built atop the ruins of the old city wall.

That’s the exterior — the interior is one hundred per cent contemporary, the sort of chic and cheeky stylishness that’s big business in Hamburg, in Berlin, in Amsterdam (and it’s the work of a Dutch design firm, incidentally). The color scheme is heavily monochrome in places, earthy in neutral in others, and decorated with classic modernist furnishings and oversized black-and-white photo prints. Creature comforts aren’t forgotten either; the bathrooms, particularly, border on decadence, many of them open to the bedroom.

The same can be said for the spa, which swaps the usual tired Zen clichés for a darker, more dramatic, underground sort of vibe. The restaurant, FreudenHaus, serves a contemporary take on regional North German fare, and the associated lounge is the hotel’s point of interface with the local nightlife scene.

Please note:
The pool and sauna will be closed for maintenance from October 26–30.

content:
The coastal provincialists may approach it with skepticism, but the Hyatt Centric Downtown Minneapolis is grand indeed, just like its underrated upper-midwest hometown. The décor is old-fashioned in the best sense of the word, not dusty or dated, but full of sumptuous, classic materials — marble bathrooms, rich leather sofas and chairs, deeply varnished dark hardwood furniture — that never go out of style. They also do some things that, regretfully, have gone out of style, like nightly turndown service and even complimentary shoe shines. In short, there’s not a lot of corner-cutting in evidence. 

For business and leisure alike, the location could hardly be better. The hotel is set right in the heart of downtown, in America’s second-densest theater district. That puts it just blocks from the Walker Art Center (one of the top modern art museums in the U.S.), equally close to the offices of the city’s (and some of the world’s) largest businesses, and an easy hop from the convention center. It’s also connected to Minneapolis’s skyway system, a seven-mile network of enclosed elevated walkways connecting various parts of downtown — no small thing during the frosty northern winter. 

If braving even the skyway sounds a bit too much, there’s plenty to explore at the hotel itself. You could get your exercise by merely touring the athletic club. It spans some 58,000 square feet and contains, beyond the standard modern workout machines, the likes of a boxing studio, a track, racquetball and squash and handball courts, and an indoor lap pool. The hotel also holds a fine restaurant and bar, plus all the business facilities you could need, but even if you’re here on business, it would be a shame not to get out and explore Minneapolis. It’s a worthy city, with a hotel to match.

content: Otahuna Lodge is New Zealand’s grandest historic homestead, a turreted Queen Anne estate set among daffodil-dotted gardens just outside Christchurch. Built in 1895 for a prominent Canterbury statesman, it is now a private lodge layered with carved kauri, stained glass, and roaring fireplaces. No two suites are alike, each reflecting the house's original bones, from inglenooks to wide verandas. Days here centre on orchard walks, seasonal menus, and quiet, fireside moments. The luxury is low-key, the atmosphere personal, and the connection to its heritage unmistakable.

content:
By now you’re probably prepared to see a W cropping up just about anywhere, but Doha? How, quite frankly, is the high-design luxury chain’s whole nightlife-centric, anything-goes approach supposed to work in buttoned-up Qatar? The answer: pretty well indeed. For foreigners the W Doha provides a fine introduction to a city that’s working hard to become a world capital — and for locals the W offers a much-needed excuse to kick up the old heels, metaphorically at least.

The style may tempt you to call it a boutique, but with 445 rooms this is definitely the big time. That’s an asset actually, when you consider the W’s big and bold approach — 445 rooms means up to 800-some guests roaming about the place, only adding to the general air of chic sophistication.

Everyone comes together in the bar, itself something of a rarity in this country, even now. And upstairs, whether you’re a sheik or a financier or simply a nomad on a budget, there’s a room for you — they start, in typically understated W style, at “Spectacular,” before passing up through “Extreme WOW” and into the realm of the residences, with all the comfort and service of a W room and the added benefit that it’s yours alone.

content:
A country as big as India is going to contain plenty of variety; here in the Western Ghat mountains, among the hill country’s coffee and spice plantations, there’s a rural idyll that’s as yet untroubled by large-scale tourism. This is where you’ll find Evolve Back Coorg, on 300 acres of working plantation land, a 49-room resort whose rustic charm and remote location set it apart, figuratively as well as literally, from India’s more ordinary luxury hotels.

Evolve Back Coorg’s accommodations are split between the single-room cottages and the suite-like villas, many of the latter featuring private pools. The look is traditional through and through, and the comforts, while certainly luxe enough, refuse to engage in the high-tech arms race — gadgetry is entirely beside the point here. Instead you’ll be encouraged to disconnect a bit, and the sedate atmosphere and the stunning surroundings go a long way towards helping you in that direction.

An ayurvedic spa doesn’t hurt either, and the family-friendly pool area offers a different kind of relaxation for parents, in the form of fully supervised activities for children. The plantation is big enough for a decent nature walk, and it’s a bird-watcher’s paradise; off-site activities include plantation tours, river rides and visits to a nearby elephant camp.

How to get there: Evolve Back Coorg is located in Siddapura, Coorg. The nearest airports are Mysore (MYQ) - 110 Kms, Bangalore (BLR) - 275 Kms, and Mangalore (IXE) - 195 Kms.

content:
Modern-design luxury boutiques are nothing new in Istanbul, but with the advent of the Key Hotel, the western Anatolian coastal city of Izmir is getting in on the act as well. The Key’s cubic structure dominates its slice of the waterfront, and the wraparound terrace on the top floor is visible from a distance; but it’s not until you’re inside that the Key really begins to take off.

And if the building itself didn’t convince you, a look at the interior finishes ought to be proof that the Key’s proprietors weren’t interested in cutting any corners. This place is as appealing to the touch as it is to the eyes, possessed of a stately modernist luxury of the sort that’s familiar from Italy’s best urban boutiques, all crisp edges, neutral tones and luxe materials.

The rooms are elegant and comfortable, with rain showers, soft cotton-satin linens, and the full complement of modern electronics. But it’s the three suites that really shine, all of them on the top level surrounded by that wraparound terrace. The lobby bar does double duty as a quiet little library, and the flagship restaurant serves upscale Aegean fare with views over the Gulf of Izmir. All in all the Key is a gem, hidden in plain sight — if you’ve got business in Izmir, lucky you, and if not, a hotel like this one just might make it worth a trip.

content: Rooftop pools are a relatively common feature at luxury hotels, and plenty of Japanese inns have onsen baths. But Candeo Hotels Osaka The Tower merges the two concepts, setting a new standard in Japan and abroad: its 31st-floor Sky Spa earned the Guinness World Record for the highest open-air infinity-edge public bath in existence. With panoramic views over Osaka, it’s the hotel’s main selling point, but there’s plenty more to like here: the riverfront location beside Dojima Park, a generous Japanese breakfast served in the airy 17th-floor restaurant, a state-of-the-art fitness center, and modern rooms with floor-to-ceiling windows, built-in sofas overlooking the city skyline, and sleek wood-paneled bathrooms with spacious walk-in showers.

This 17th-century palace is right on the Via del Corso, a location that couldn't be more convenient for sightseeing and shopping; inside, the interiors evoke the grandeur of the era, the original marble staircase, rich wood paneling, and coffered ceilings all carefully refurbished. The rooms are just as elegant, with modern four-poster beds, original artworks, colorful stripes and patterns, and fresh floral arrangements. Some suites have private terraces.

content:
Like all its siblings, the Graduate Columbia, S.C. blends collegiate nostalgia with local color, in this case the historic Southern charm of downtown Columbia, South Carolina. The colors are bright, and the patterns are bold — this is a town (and a region) in which the concept of minimalism holds very little attraction.

All of the Graduate hotels are convenient to the schools they serve, but this one is set on the campus itself, and it’s not just rather more luxurious than the typical campus hotel but remarkably unpretentious as well — it’s a pet-friendly hotel and bike rentals are complimentary, while boutique-hotel touches like Malin + Goetz bath products lend the style of a big-city operation. 

The hotel’s restaurant, the Trophy Room, gives some indication of the centrality of collegiate athletics to Columbia’s student life; for obvious reasons the Graduate is in high demand on Gamecocks football home-game weekends, and guests appreciate the hotel’s close proximity to Williams-Brice stadium, which is just two and a half miles away.

content:
Leuven is a land of superlatives. It boasts the oldest Catholic university in the world, which also happens to be the largest university in the country. Then there’s the longest bar in Europe, which is within staggering distance of the smallest bar in Belgium. Martin’s Klooster is a bit harder to quantify—but by our metrics it’s the top hotel in town.

Leuven is inherently a pretty mellow place, and the Klooster is nothing if not relaxed. Individually decorated but generally sharing the same calming brown-and-beige palate, the bedrooms tend to whisper rather than shout. There are 40 rooms in all, including two fashioned from the original sixteenth-century towers. Some even feature fireplaces, latticed windows, and stained glass, which echo the building’s past lives as a convent and private residence for a member of the royal court. Common spaces are cozy, full of cushiony chairs and conversation nooks.   

An interior courtyard heightens the sense of peacefulness, as does the car-free cobbled street that borders the Klooster’s exterior. Most of Leuven’s noteworthy sites are within walking distance, from the lively Old Market to the extremely ornate City Hall. And for those who simply can’t get enough, tours of the Stella Artois brewery, in operation since 1366, and the tiny, artisanal, and much, much younger Domus brewery are available as well.

content:
As close as it is to London — globally speaking at least — Birmingham’s hotel scene could scarcely be more different. Simply put, with neither the immense demand nor the astronomical real estate costs, England’s second city feels less pressure to innovate. However, there’s a lot more to hotels than novelty, and nowhere is that more true than at the high end, a space the Hyatt Regency Birmingham occupies with confidence. Though design trends come and go, and the concept of the boutique hotel is a relatively new invention, the basic notion of luxury is something much more timeless.

If you’ve been in a luxury hotel in the last couple of decades you will recognize the basic shape of the Hyatt Regency. As we said, that’s no criticism, and it certainly shouldn’t imply that the place looks dated — in fact the look is quite a bit more fresh and crisp than the average business hotel.

The rooms are spacious and look out across the city from full-length windows, and the details are all correct: plasma televisions, high-speed wireless, and the little things, like plush robes and soft slippers. There’s a full-service spa, complete with 24-hour gym and swimming pool, and the city-center, canal-side location means tea in the lobby after a day at the shops is a snap.

content:
They call Hainan Island the Hawaii of China, but as of this moment it may have surpassed Hawaii in at least one important respect: Hawaii suffers from an abject shortage of Park Hyatts. It’s located in a spanking-new resort community along the scenic inlet of Sunny Bay, only a couple of miles over from the longer-established Yalong Bay. So it’s safe to say you’ll have all the conveniences of home, and then some — though, Park Hyatts being what they are, you’ll be able to make it as private an experience as you like.

Most of the two hundred units face directly out to the South China Sea, and all of them, standard rooms included, are spacious, handsomely contemporary and exceedingly well-equipped. The freestanding villas, of course, are where you go for the full-on Bond-villain treatment, complete with private pools and butler service. But at any level you’ll find you’re in for one of the most lavish beach-resort experiences you’ve ever seen.

Much of the above, frankly, follows logically just from the mere mention of the Park Hyatt name. Though the collection has grown quite a bit in recent years, there are few other brands that are quite as consistent at meeting the expectations they’ve created. Five pools, eight restaurants and bars, and (naturally) a spa — though it’s not finished quite yet — and still the whole thing feels calm and serene, a far cry from the circus atmosphere at some resorts of similar size.

content:
Graz deserves to step out from behind Vienna into a spotlight of its own. Besides the humbling variety of architectural styles in its extraordinarily well-preserved Old Town, it’s rich in history: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was born here, Kepler taught and studied here, and the Ottomans and Napoleon’s army both swept through. In the center of it all looms Schloßberg, a verdant hill crowned with the remains of a 16th-century fortress. And at the foot of that hill, nestled on the east bank of the Mur and nearly as old, waits Schlossberghotel — Das Kunsthotel, more than a match for its heady surroundings.

It began its life as a hotel in the Sixties, gradually acquiring adjacent buildings and modernizing facilities over the decades; think of it as ancient mastery’s bemused retort to the contemporary boutique sensibility. Joyful, grounded eclecticism rules the roost here, most palpable in the vast range of original artwork displayed on just about every vertical surface they could hang a frame on. In fact, the hotel sponsors an “Artists in Action” program to foster ongoing works in progress right on the premises.

Balance is key: each of the 49 rooms and four suites is a study in space versus substance, tempering ornate period fixtures and antique furnishings with stretches of parquet flooring, sizable windows, and vibrant textiles. And there’s also an octet of futuristic apartments with all the idiosyncratic lines and floor-to-ceiling windows you could ask for.

The lobby bar and lounge keeps things convivial with amusingly mixed-period seating, carpets, and mirrors, equally suitable for a mug of coffee or a snifter of cognac. Take breakfast in the winter garden, or better yet, on the rooftop terrace, weather permitting; between the cataracts of ivy, shady reading nooks, whimsical stone paths, and sunbath, we’re sure something will blend perfectly with the captivating views over the city’s rust-hued roofs.

content:
If you’ve heard of the French town of Morzine, you might also know who George Hincapie is, or what a flamme rouge signifies. Thanks to the steep Col de Joux-Plane incline nearby, Morzine, located in the Rhône-Alpes region, has hosted several Tour de France stage finishes. Not to worry if the two-wheeled life isn’t your cup of tea: this mountainscape is a magnet for hikers, skiers and snowboarders, too, and a family-run chalet like Hotel La Bergerie is the kind of place you’ll want to stay.

Maybe it’s the satisfyingly Alpine façade, the angular wooden roof, or the snow-capped peaks behind it. In winter, the central fireplace and cozy bar fit for après-ski; in summer, the swimming pool and terrace designed for unwinding after an afternoon climb. If you have little ones in tow, there are charming French amenities for them, too — a table d’hôte where children dine separately from their parents, and family-style suites with kitchenettes where you can make your own coffee and sandwiches for hiking and skiing excursions.

Guest rooms are comfortable and spacious, with views of the surrounding landscape, but they’re true to the place — this isn’t Paris, after all — decked out in blond wood and traditional printed fabrics with a few tech-forward amenities like flat-screen TVs and wi-fi access. Winning style points isn’t the goal: you’ve come here to get away, to enjoy the mountains, to see a small slice of Alpine culture. La Bergerie is located in the center of the village, so guests can walk everywhere there is to go. There aren’t too many places to go, and that’s part of the charm.

Please note: La Bergerie is open from January to April. The minimum stay is 7 nights, and arrivals must take place on Saturdays. 

How to get there: The hotel is located 54 miles from Geneva (GVA) airport.

Geographically, it’s only an hour from the airport; figuratively, though, Villa 32 is just about as far as you can get from the clamorous urban cityscape of downtown Taipei. While the vast majority of the city’s high-end business and leisure travelers take in the sights from the top of a city-center high-rise hotel, a fortunate few (just five rooms’ worth) soak in the luxurious solitude of this stunning modernist retreat.

Soak, literally. While Villa 32’s architecture and interiors are remarkable enough, its ace in the hole is its access to the Beitou hot springs — each of the five guest rooms is served by its own geothermic bath, and the semi-public springs are worth it for their foggy mountain views.

As for the rooms themselves, they’re faultless in style, from the spartan simplicity of the oversized Japanese suites, complete with tatami mats, to the familiar luxury of the stylish Western rooms. Back when this was a private home (what a house it must have been) its cellar held one of Taiwan’s best wine collections; today the cellar’s for sharing, its bottles accompanying a selection of Tuscan dishes, served in the dining room or out in the leafy quiet of the hotel courtyard.

Villa 32 is limited to guests 16 years and older.

content: By its very name, Not a Hotel Fukuoka suggests a follow-up question: then what is it? That’s the point — it’s essentially a dynamic sequence of short-term residences, just eight in total, but also a series of vertical gardens and multi-use lifestyle hubs. If that sounds like word soup, it’s because the architects built it to transcend the divide between organic greenery and bold materials thinking. The “rooms” are enormous, each equipped with oversize windows, statement furnishings, and lighting that’s somehow both functional and experimental. The names are just evocative thought starters: Sound, Bar, Atelier, Retreat. The idea is to embrace the liminal lifestyle and see where it takes you.

content: You might find yourself taking some of the décor home after a stay at Almayer Art & Heritage. All are accessorized with bespoke furnishings and of course, contemporary artworks. Corte restaurant serves a menu rooted in the terroir of the Dalmatian coast, complemented by local Croatian wines and Mediterranean inspired cocktails in the bar.

content: Though Rome does have a few full-sized palace-style luxury hotels, the city’s most characteristic form of hospitality might be its small-scale, residential-style luxury boutique hotels. The Place 217 is prominently located on the Via Cola di Rienzo, a few minutes’ walk from the Piazza San Pietro and the Vatican. It’s tucked away, however, on the sixth floor of a 1930s residential building; it’s easy enough to miss from street level, which only adds to the air of seclusion that’s essential to this type of urban escape.\n\nIt’s got just a handful of rooms and suites, and they’re all comfortably sized, especially for so central a neighborhood. The style, as is customary in Rome, shows respect for the building’s original architecture even as it features contemporary furniture and décor. There’s a junior suite equipped with a whirlpool tub and a sauna, and the top-floor suite has a view of the dome of St. Peter’s Basilica. There’s no restaurant, but the Prati district suffers no shortage, and nor do the surrounding neighborhoods — cross the Tiber and you’re right in the most heavily traveled part of the city.

content: Is it a classic colonial-style Raffles, or a sleek contemporary skyscraper hotel? Perhaps a bit of both. Raffles Jakarta certainly cuts a modern figure from the exterior view, set as it is in a gleaming glass tower in the Indonesian capital’s tony Golden Triangle. Step through its doors, however, and you’re treated to a classic polished-stone lobby, its soaring spaces decorated with oversized artworks by the 20th-century painter Hendra Gunawan. And it’s in the rooms that the synthesis is completed: though they’re unmistakably modern in their comforts, their equipment, and above all their high-rise city views, their style is timeless, with echoes of every era for the past century or more.\n\nThe Raffles spa experience is among the most thorough in the world, and here it’s joined by a fitness center, an expansive outdoor pool deck, and even a tennis facility. In addition to the pool bar and the lobby patisserie there’s a Writers Bar, a worthy re-creation of the Raffles Singapore original, as well as the Arts Café, an upscale restaurant serving a wide variety of European and Asian dishes. And while it’s a self-contained luxury hotel experience, it’s by no means an island — it’s connected to Lotte Shopping Avenue, a mixed-use shopping, dining, and entertainment complex, as well as Ciputra Artpreneur, a major theatre and gallery space.

content:
Just about every college town in America could use something like this: a modern boutique-style hotel, preferably campus-adjacent, with enough personality to be memorable while also appealing to all sorts of guests, from college-age travelers to parents, alumni, and visiting academics. For the University of North Carolina, that hotel is Graduate Chapel Hill, set on Franklin Street a short walk from campus. 

In typical Graduate style it’s tailored to the setting, and in the case of UNC that means a healthy dose of Tar Heels basketball, including plentiful tributes to alum Michael Jordan — the most extravagant of which is a detailed reproduction of his on-campus dorm room, circa 1983.

Hotel guests, thankfully, can expect something a little more spacious and stylish than a dorm room. Carolina blue is much in evidence, and the headboards, playfully, are styled to resemble basketball backboards. But with their sunny décor and vintage furnishings, they’re several steps up from student digs, and some even come with balconies.

Social life is just as important, and at Graduate Chapel Hill there’s the Trophy Room restaurant and bar, serving pub fare and Southern classics in an indoor-outdoor space. Borrow a bike for a self-guided spin, or hit this compact town on foot.

content:
Just off Market Square in downtown Knoxville, Tennessee is the kind of boutique hotel we’ve long maintained every city in the world could use at least one of. The Oliver Hotel makes its home in a handsome 1876-vintage building, and while it’s historically informed, it’s as contemporary as they come, with 28 rooms that mix period architectural details with a focused, contemporary color palette and a well-chosen collection of mid-century modern furnishings.

The atmosphere is elegant enough, but at the same time playful, never taking itself all that seriously. Double Queen rooms are perfect for friends traveling together, while the Kings get romantic, and the suites begin to stretch out to 600 square feet or more.

In a hotel like this the social spaces are at least as important as the rooms, and the Oliver has those covered: Oliver Royale is the upscale new American restaurant, serving dishes crafted from local ingredients alongside a drink menu that’s particularly deep in the area of whiskeys and bourbons. Peter Kern Library is the dedicated cocktail bar, with a speakeasy vibe and a menu of drinks named for literary figures. And Tupelo Honey Cafe is the most casual of the three, a modern Southern comfort-food establishment that’s open from brunch on into the night.

content:
European ski resorts already lead the way in combining world-class winter sports with top-shelf luxury, but even in the context of the French Alps, Airelles Val d’Isère stands out. It’s a proper ski-in ski-out resort hotel, but at the same time it’s unusually refined, its architecture and décor combining classic Alpine-lodge warmth with a generous measure of Renaissance-era character — and the service, as in other Airelles hotels, is unusually devoted.

With just 41 units, it’s not overly large; accommodations range from the substantial Premier and Deluxe rooms through various suites on up to the five apartments, each with its own butler in addition to spectacular top-floor views and a degree of spaciousness that’s almost excessive, especially by ski-resort standards.

There’s a Guerlain spa complete with a 20-meter pool, and a very substantial ski program — Val d’Isere is not just an attractive mountain town but a serious winter-sports destination. You’ll also find among its restaurants La Grande Ourse, the latest incarnation of a longtime Savoyard classic, as well as Loulou, an Alpine version of the well-loved Parisian Italian-French restaurant of the same name.

content:
Just outside one of Germany’s best-preserved medieval towns, the castle-like Meiser Spa Resort looks like a historic landmark in the Bavarian countryside. But unlike the stone towers and colorful gabled houses inside Dinkelsbühl’s city walls, this building has only been around for a few decades, its timber-framed facade and ornamental turrets a nod to the region’s rich architectural past. Its interiors feature traditional alpine elements, too, like exposed beams and stone fireplaces, but with a pared-down modern edge. 

This is one of the largest resorts in southern Germany — mostly thanks to the hotel’s vast and continually expanding, state-of-the-art spa with indoor and outdoor pools — and it feels like it. Rooms are spacious and silent, and while some are contemporary in style, others take inspiration from a country house aesthetic with deep red carpeting, knotty pine walls, and plush sofas upholstered in plaid. All come with spa-quality bath towels and robes, and many have private balconies with nature views. Suites feature extras like free-standing tubs and cozy living rooms. 

The sprawling wood-paneled restaurant serves an early breakfast, late-night cocktails, and everything in between, and a greenery-dotted open-air terrace, overlooking the pool area, is particularly inviting in warmer months.
