content: Right on the corner of Parker’s Piece and just a ten-minute walk from Cambridge University sits another of the city's historical landmarks, its oldest hotel, the University Arms, which has been hosting guests and serving locals since as far back as 1834. Edwardian influences can be seen in the printed headboards, bespoke armchairs and writing desks, whilst bookshelves stacked with books from Heywood Hill of Mayfair, and a Book Butler service to handpick a more personalised selection of tomes, is of course a nod to Cambridge’s literary reputation. Views are equally attractive, whether overlooking the inner courtyard, historic Regent Street, or Parker’s Piece. Restaurant and bar Parker’s Tavern have been going for as long as the hotel and now serve a mix of British classics and international favourites, and there’s a regular programme of events, including Friday night Jazz sessions and free Saturday morning city tours.

content:
The Hoshinoya hotel group is nothing if not diverse, encompassing a skyscraper in Tokyo, a riverside resort outside of Kyoto, and a ryokan-style hotel in the Nagano mountains. What they have in common is a devotion to both contemporary luxury and Japanese hospitality tradition. Hoshinoya Taketomi Island adapts the concept to a beachfront resort on a small Okinawan island — a resort that’s styled after a traditional village, red tiled roofs and all, in order to comply with the island’s strict adherence to heritage architecture.

Thankfully, no such code pertains to the hotel’s interiors. Hoshinoya’s designers always keep the local traditions in mind, but here, as elsewhere, they’ve applied a contemporary hand. Each pavilion is a self-contained unit, some with tatami-style furniture and others Western, and all of them with vast windows open to the air, as well as deep, restful soaking tubs.

The presence of a spa may be taken for granted, and here it’s joined by an outdoor pool and a beautiful white-sand beach. The island itself is remarkably undisturbed — you’ll arrive by boat, and you’ll get around on carts drawn by water buffalo. And, like the other Hoshinoya hotels, this one features an extraordinary restaurant, helmed by chef Tatsuo Nakasu, whose “Nouvelle Ryukyu” cuisine projects Okinawan tradition through a French prism.

content: If you’re not from the Midwest, you may not know much about Iowa City, aside from a reasonably sure bet that it’s a city located somewhere in the state of Iowa. What’s most significant about Iowa City, arguably, is that it’s the home of the University of Iowa — and if you’re a literary type, what’s most significant about the university is the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, the most famous creative-writing program in the country. All of which is to say: don’t be surprised when you check in to the Graduate Iowa City and find yourself surrounded by yard after yard of packed bookshelves.\n\nIt’s a literary town, and the hotel’s Poindexter Coffee is a fine place to read or write. But it’s also a fine place to fuel up for Hawkeyes football game day — the Graduate is no library. The restaurant Wilder serves favorites from some well-known restaurants, from Umami Burger to Sam’s Crispy Chicken, Krispy Rice, and beyond. And the rooms are one part historical kitsch, one part contemporary boutique-hotel style, with all the comfort you need, including Malin + Goetz bath products and the usual high-tech gadgetry. It’s a significant step up from the lodging options previously on offer in Iowa City — which is the Graduate group’s mission in a nutshell.

content:
At this late date, most American cities of any appreciable size have at least one high-style, high-design boutique hotel. But not many of them begin with raw material of the Durham Hotel’s caliber. The mid-century modern Home Savings Bank building is something straight out of the Mad Men era, and Commune Design — whose work you know from some of the Ace hotels, among others — didn’t shy away from the inspiration.

The Durham Hotel is more than just an eye-popping color scheme. (Though it certainly is that.) It’s also an homage to local arts and crafts, from records by indie mega-label Merge to the Cone Mills denim in the staffers’ uniforms to the one-of-a-kind Raleigh Denim quilt on your bed. Unsurprisingly, you’ll find the same philosophy at work in the restaurants’ menus, where James Beard award winner Andrea Reusing draws on a long list of North Carolina producers and presents a solid case for the region’s culinary heritage.

All this is much more than just good branding. For first-time visitors, a night or two in a hotel is more or less the only chance for a new city to make an impression — and it’s hard to imagine coming away from the Durham feeling anything other than impressed.

content: The British Empire is long gone, but not without a trace. Zimbabwe’s Victoria Falls Hotel, an Edwardian-style grand hotel dating back to 1904, is the country’s oldest and most opulent hotel by a considerable distance, and is one of Africa’s most famous hotels. And while this probably isn’t the venue for a debate about the legacy of colonialism, the world would certainly be poorer in at least one respect without the Victoria Falls. As you may have gathered from the name, there’s a certain natural wonder quite close at hand — the mile-wide wall of water, with its hundred-meter drop, is locally known as “the smoke that thunders,” and it’s no ordinary waterfall.\n\nSo it’s only fitting that the Victoria Falls is no ordinary hotel. Its 161 rooms and suites are still thoroughly Edwardian in style, having been updated with modern technology but thankfully without any update to the aesthetics. Standard rooms are more than comfortable enough, suites begin to border on the lavish, and the Royal and Presidential suites are worthy of the name. And as a classic old-style grand hotel, the Victoria Falls comes with all the fixings, including thre restaurants, two bars, a pool, a spa, a hair salon, and all manner of meeting and conference rooms. To put it simply, there’s no place on earth quite like Victoria Falls itself — and they just don’t make hotels like the Victoria Falls Hotel anymore.

content:
For a long time the picturesque Southeastern town of Sandwich was longer on quirky charm than it was on proper luxury — and the same was true of the Bell Hotel. But out of charm and luxury, the second is the one that’s easier to add via renovation. And now that it’s got a healthy measure of each, the Bell can rightfully count itself in a class with the best of England’s outlying small-town inns.

The renovation was in many ways something more like a restoration, undoing a few of the building’s more questionable improvements — uncovering, for example, a magnificent parquet floor. But in the rooms it’s unquestionably a step forward, leaving the interiors stylish, sumptuous, up to date, and not a bit less charming than they were before. The tones are mellow and the luxuries are understated, with modest televisions and digital radios being the extent of the electronic intrusions.

In the restaurant you’ll find the kind of upscale-rustic farm-to-table cooking of the sort for which the best British inns are rightfully famous. The town is scenic, and the beach is a very short drive away, as are the golf courses at Prince’s and Royal St. George’s. All that and not a word about the Earl.

content:
Sometimes it really is all about location. In the case of the Sofitel Florianopolis it makes all the difference. What would ordinarily be simply a stylish, well-crafted luxury hotel, the sort of thing Sofitel can turn out without breaking a sweat, is elevated, by virtue of its situation, into something quite extraordinary. For Florianopolis is like no other town: here, just off the bridge to Santa Catarina, you’re in the heart of the city, but also steps from some world-class surfing, and perched over a panorama that takes in the island, the mountains and the waters of the bay.

The building is distinctive from a distance, a sleek modern glass tower in the front row of the city’s residential high-rises. And it’s distinctive within as well, its décor graphic and modern, with more than a tinge of Art Deco, as is the Sofitel house style. The rooms are residential in concept, with comfortable work spaces, luxurious bathrooms and plentiful natural light. A full-service spa sees to your corporeal needs, and the restaurant and bar import a note of worldly Parisian elegance, a welcome contrast with the laid-back ambience of Florianopolis. It’s as suited to business travel as any Sofitel anywhere, though the surroundings are enough to test anyone’s focus.

content:
It can be argued that New Zealand’s hospitality world is a victim of its own success in one important sense — thanks to the popularity of the rugged country lodges, the more cosmopolitan urban hotels end up neglected. Of course the urban hoteliers are working to put things right, and with hotels like the Ohtel, in the capital city of Wellington, they’re making great strides.

This is a high-design boutique hotel in the most sophisticated international style, right down to the meticulously curated collection of mid-century modernist furnishings and the racy (and yet quite luxurious) glass-walled bathrooms, complete with two-person soaking tubs. The style is modern but there’s an obvious emphasis on traditional craftsmanship and well-chosen materials. High-quality beds, baths and furnishings strive for honest old-fashioned comfort, while the latest technologies keep you connected, and aim for an infinitely customizable experience.

With just ten rooms the Ohtel comes at a very manageable size, and it’s owner-operated, which, combined with that natural New Zealand friendliness, means there’s none of the attitude that usually accompanies a hotel that’s so stylish. An excellent start for Wellington, and a reminder that there’s more to life than just the lodges.

content: To truly appreciate the spectacular location of Quinta São José do Barrilário, positioned high in the green hills of the Douro Valley, framed by terraced vineyards that slope down to the Douro River below, you’d have to see it from the air. Luckily, you can get quite close from this luxury hotel’s rooftop infinity pool. The building has a slightly curving shape, following the lines of the landscape, and its rooms feature floor-to-ceiling windows to make the most of the natural surroundings. Their interiors, modern and wood-lined, take inspiration from the region’s winemaking traditions — custom-made beds look like they’ve been crafted out of giant wine barrels. The restaurant serves wines made at the adjacent vineyard, and locally cultivated grapes are incorporated into treatments at the hotel’s spa.

content: In a place as ridiculously picturesque as Ile de Ré, it’s difficult to choose whether to stay on the beach or in the village. Hotel Les Bois Flottais offers a happy medium, located midway between the island’s golden beaches and Le Bois-Plage-en-Ré, with its charming outdoor cafés and lively open-air markets. White stucco and terracotta cottages encircle a pair of outdoor swimming pools, housing guest rooms with vaulted wood ceilings and rustic-chic beach decor in natural hues of ivory, beige, and sky blue. Each is unique; some have wicker armchairs and bathtubs, others have lofted sleeping areas and private patios. A leisurely breakfast is served on the terrace, and later in the day, an onsite bistro specializes in locally sourced products like lobster and oysters. Borrow a bicycle and explore the nearby coastline, then come back to the boutique hotel for a glass of wine — made on the island, of course — by the pool at sunset.\n

content: When Berliners need a break from the big city, they escape to the Spreewald, a fairytale forest dotted with quiet meadows and crisscrossed with canals. It’s possible to make it a day trip, but it’s more relaxing to stay over at a boutique hotel like Strandhaus Spreewald. This sustainably built hotel is set on a lush green landscape on the bank of the Spree River, and its design makes the most of it: an open-air beer garden and riverfront lawn offer ample outdoor lounge space, and many guest rooms have balconies or terraces with water views. Interiors are calming, with oak parquet floors, spa-like walk-in showers, and crisp white linens. Rent a paddleboat or a bicycle at reception to explore the Spreewald’s famous waterways and the charming town of Lübben.

If you want to do some exploring of your own there’s bikes available for hire, or the team are full of Arezzo recommendations.

content: Lyonnais have gladly made the short trip to Charbonnières-les-Bains for generations — ever since the town’s priest discovered its iron-rich mineral springs in the late 18th century, prompting the construction of a spa resort. The old thermal baths are gone now, but the area’s most luxurious hotel still offers many of the same features that have traditionally drawn visitors from the big city: lush landscapes, peace and quiet, and relaxation by the water. Le Pavillon, part of the upscale Partouche Hotels collection, is set on a wooded estate beside the Domaine de Lacroix-Laval with its 16th-century château and English-style gardens. Giant trees frame the property, with greenery visible through every window, including from inside the gorgeous spa with its large indoor pool, Jacuzzi, and hammam. \n\nRooms and suites are decorated in shades of ivory and slate gray with colorful pops of deep turquoise and scarlet red. The look is understated and elegant, mixing Art Deco details, like geometric rugs and sleek canopy beds, with dark wood furnishings and bold black and white botanical wallpaper. Bathrooms have tubs and separate rainforest showers, and all rooms have private balconies or terraces overlooking the surrounding forest. The breakfast buffet is served in a light-filled dining room with massive wraparound windows revealing panoramic views of the woods, and a fireplace warms the cozy Le Bar du Pavillon. Across the street, the hotel’s restaurant, Le Grandioz, is located inside the Pasino Grand, considered one of France’s most beautiful casinos.

content:
Wherever there’s an American college town with a less-than-stellar hotel scene, there’s a Graduate hotel, either in the works or open for business. In Annapolis, Maryland, home of the United States Naval Academy and St. John’s College, that’s exactly the case — this fast-growing, niche-focused hotelier has taken over what was previously an attractive but undistinguished national chain hotel and transformed it into something distinctive, colorful, and impeccably tailored to its setting: the Graduate Annapolis.

In typical Graduate style its design, especially its color scheme, is dictated by its location: in this case the official blue and gold of the Naval Academy, and beyond that a pervasive maritime theme that pays homage to the famous Chesapeake Bay. The rooms, obviously, are both more playful and more luxurious than Navy cadet digs — Malin + Goetz bath products, for example, are not yet government-issue.

Here you’ll also be treated to breakfast sandwiches and espresso or cold brew at Poindexter Coffee, as well as Trophy Room, serving creative cocktails and “coastal eats” — which, in Maryland, tends to involve some of the tastiest crab around. And this is the heart of the Arts District, which means there’s more than Navy football and naval warfare on offer in the surrounding neighborhood....

content:
Where there’s a classic American college town, there’s a Graduate hotel. A captive audience and a typically collegiate tolerance for less-than-luxurious living conditions means most university-adjacent hotels are nothing to write home about, but these ones are different. Ann Arbor is home to the University of Michigan, and the Graduate Ann Arbor is barely two blocks’ walk from the campus, in a mid-century tower that gives little indication of what sort of hotel is inside.

The answer: a stylized, idealized version of the nostalgic, eclectic digs we might have liked to have lived in during our own student years. Thanks to the building’s elevation, the rooms have some impressively far-ranging views, and what’s inside isn’t exactly hard on the eyes, either: think mid-century modernist retro, with color schemes that incorporate the classic Wolverines colors, maize and blue, as well as warm textures of tweed and natural wood.

Poindexter Coffee sets an appropriately studious tone, while the Allen Rumsey Cocktail Lounge is both a retro-themed bar and a supperclub-style restaurant, specializing in hearty American fare served in deep, cozy booths. If the college life had looked like this, there’s a very real chance we never would have bothered to graduate....

content:
On the whole, the Nordic capitals are rather less a hotbed of clean-lined modernist design than you might imagine — here Art Nouveau is the visual language of luxury, and coziness, not coolness, is the prevailing hospitality trend. But in Scandic Paasi, the Finnish capital of Helsinki has a hotel that’s unapologetically modern in style, a riot of color hidden away behind a relatively nondescript facade, tucked in between historic buildings in the Siltasaari district, near Hakaniemi Market Square.

The lobby is a full-spectrum color experience, and while the guest rooms focus on one or two colors at a time, they’re scarcely less vibrant, with bold patterns and hyper-saturated fabrics. There’s a touch of throwback elegance to the architecture, but the furnishings — and the overall design sensibility — are decidedly modern. Some come with kitchenettes, and some, in true only-in-Finland style, come with private saunas.

And while the restaurant is breakfast-only, the bar is open throughout the day and well into the night, and the hotel’s immediate surroundings are plentifully supplied with places to eat and drink. All told, it’s one of a handful of unusually memorable hotels in the huge Scandic collection, and a welcome addition to the Helsinki scene.

content:
Though they’ve wisely dropped the tongue-twister from the official name — go on, try saying “bistro Bristol” — the Hotel du Vin Bristol is very much in the family business, bringing wine, design, and fine French-inflected bistro fare together under a single roof. Or a row of roofs, properly speaking — the Hotel du Vin makes its home in the wonderfully named Sugar House, itself a landmark row of 18th-century warehouses in the heart of town, a few blocks from Bristol’s renovated docklands.

The forty rooms and suites are classic urban-industrial retrofits, from loft-style double rooms to suites that are actual lofts in the split-level sense — some have sitting areas upstairs, others bathrooms with one or even two roll-top bathtubs (showers, throughout the hotel, are of the high-flow walk-in variety). The emphasis placed on the bathroom is one example of the transformational experience the Hotels du Vin aim for, but a minor one.

Of course the major example is what’s downstairs. The lounge, the billiards room and the popular bar set a social tone. You don’t call your hotel the Hotel du Vin unless you’re serious about wine, which this establishment certainly is. And it’s no less serious about its Bistro, a favorite even for Bristol, a town where high-quality dining experiences are in plentiful supply — it's open for lunch and dinner seven days a week.

content:
If you’re of one of the generations that grew up reading The Wind in the Willows then you already know Fowey Hall — you just know it as Toad Hall. The real thing has some distinct advantages over the fictional version, however, beginning with the fact that this one, existing as it does in the physical world, has a roof that will actually keep the rain off your head.

Of course there’s plenty more than that. This house, in the village of Fowey, on the southern coast of Cornwall, is a quintessentially contemporary manor-house hotel. There’s very little reinvention going on here — not much in the way of funky modern furnishings or outré décor. Nor is it modernist or avant-garde in any way. It’s more a case of incremental improvement; there’s a full-service spa, and modern electronics in the rooms, but the Victorians would have had these things too, if only they could.

It’s in the area of family-friendliness that Fowey Hall especially shines. There’s plenty of entertainment for kids, as well as supervision. And as a result the atmosphere is neither stultifyingly stuffy nor tragically hip — it’s as casual as a manor-house hotel can be, which is no small distinction in this day and age.

content: Chengdu’s nickname, “city of abundance,” initially referred to the wealth of temples, monasteries, and dynasties’ worth of architectural talking points; may as well throw business hotels under that moniker, too. With this 29-story behemoth — opened 110 years to the day after the New York original — the St. Regis flag takes its place among the Sichuan capital’s jostling business-district hotels. As expected, it hits all the keynotes: an easy walk from Mao-dominated Tianfu Square in one direction, just as close to Chunxi Road in the other, and centrally located within China’s answer to Silicon Valley. Those who know St. Regis will know what to expect: like any well-trodden formula, the rooms and public spaces radiate a just-so comfort that’s there because it works. DiLeonardo Design brings an Art Deco veneer to the public spaces — there’s something of a chandelier theme — an effort all the more welcome for staying out of the way of handier modern fixtures in the rooms proper. Which is to say, crisp linen paired with gleaming surfaces and an inoffensive color scheme is just fine, but you’ll derive considerably more pleasure out of the iPad controls, docking station, free wi-fi, integrated surround sound, and Nespresso machine. Floor-to-ceiling views don’t hurt, either, and you really can’t go wrong with an oversize marble bathroom; Remède toiletries and a separate rainforest shower make it even more worthwhile. For an immersive, cleansing follow-up, head to neon-bedecked Iridium Spa to enjoy two pools, steam rooms, on-site personal training, and Thalgo spa amenities. In fact, “staying out of the way while empowering guests” could be the (admittedly clunky) motto of the St. Regis staff, known as they are for unobtrusive, 24-hour butler service. All those little touches — flowers on request, suit pressing, daily delivery of coffee with newspaper — do much to grease the wheels, preserving the sense of quietly efficient routine that often goes overlooked in edgier enterprises. It’ll put you in the mood for at least one of the hotel’s six restaurant and lounge options, surely. Vantage XXVII is the requisite rooftop bar with nightly entertainment, right next door to Yun Fu, offering lavish and private dining for the discerning suit.

content:
To be fair, Thailand’s shape — long, skinny and dotted with islands — does give it a reasonably high beach-to-inland ratio. But that’s no excuse. By far the greatest bulk of the country’s land mass is in the mountainous north. And while the simple pleasures of the beach certainly do beckon, there’s magic in them there hills, and a hotel like Katiliya Mountain Resort & Spa, in the scenic northern province of Chiang Rai, makes for quite a forceful reminder.

Katiliya’s hilltop location means sprawling panoramic views of the surrounding forested hillsides, and the all-suite construction means the interior spaces do some sprawling of their own. In style they’re residential, contemporary enough but with endless expanses of indigenous wood, and the bathrooms meet the current luxury standard, with twin basins and separate baths and showers. All come with oversized king beds and private balconies offering impressive views.

The Spa On The Lake is pretty much exactly what it sounds like, and it’s a tough proposition to turn down — the treatment rooms’ private terraces and the spa’s outdoor Jacuzzi look out over the surrounding mountainscape. So, too, does the Terrace restaurant. In fact the views are just about inescapable, and many a guest has left Katiliya converted to Thailand’s inland pleasures.

How to get there:
Katiliya Mountain Resort and Spa is located in Chiang Rai, the northern-most province of Thailand. The resort is a 30-40 minute drive from the Chiang Rai International Airport.

content:
Though you’d never know it from the mass media, there’s a lot more to New Zealand than luxury lodges, adventure sports and Lord of the Rings tours. Queenstown, for example, may be known for its alpine setting, a mecca for skiers and snowboarders, but it’s a cosmopolitan city as well, as amply demonstrated by the urbane Spire hotel.

Here there’s no trace of ski-lodge anti-chic, but rather a dramatic palette of reds, greys and black, and modern designer furnishings by the likes of Eames and Philippe Starck. The ten oversized rooms come with private balconies, deep tubs, heated floors and gas fireplaces, and a pillow menu — yes, it’s that kind of place. Thankfully, it’s also got that kind of service; the youthful staff apparently hasn’t gotten the memo that boutique service is supposed to be sullen and sniffy.

All this does come at a price, but the Spire is the only way to do Queenstown in such high style. It’s not just for upmarket ski bums either; Lake Wakatipu is a popular summertime destination, and the Spire even comes with meeting facilities to cater to those lucky enough to be sent here on business. And with a restaurant by chef Rex Morgan (not to be confused with the American comic-strip doctor of the same name) the Spire is a focal point for Queenstown’s nightlife as well.

How to get there:
The Spire Hotel is approximately a 15 minute drive from Queenstown International Airport.

content: There’s only one museum in the world dedicated to the work of the American artist Keith Haring; surprisingly, it’s not in New York, but in the foothills of the Yatsugatake Mountains, a two-hour drive from Tokyo. The acclaimed Japanese architect Atsushi Kitagawara designed the Nakamura Keith Haring Collection and the adjacent Hotel Keyforest Hokuto, both part of a larger art-themed resort. This boutique hotel is visually striking, its modernist silhouette and sharp angles standing out in contrast with the surrounding forest. Each of its six rooms is named for a natural element — air, water, sunlight, and so on — and features minimalist décor in refined but down-to-earth materials like native wood and stone. All have private balconies overlooking the woods, the rooftop terrace offers panoramic mountain views, and the resort’s open-air baths, fed by local hot springs, invite soaks under the stars.

content: On the edge of the city park in downtown Kanazawa, Korinkyo used to be an art gallery — and with its industrial-chic look and its high-arched windows letting in abundant natural light, it still looks the part, even though it’s been transformed into a minimalist boutique hotel with a focus on Japanese art and design. Rooms are bright and airy with a pale white, beige, and gray color palette, exposed beams, curving walls, vintage pieces, and ivory-tiled bathrooms with walk-in showers and freestanding tubs; many details, from teacups to bathrobes, were created by local artisans. Interiors are perfumed with delicate fragrances from the hotel’s on-site distillery. Up on the rooftop, a pair of open-air cypress baths are a wonderful spot for a relaxing soak with views over the treetops.

content:
Istanbul is rather famously too large and sprawling to have a single city center, but it’s hard to imagine a much more prominent location than the one enjoyed by Sofitel Istanbul Taksim. It’s set mere meters from the square of the same name, alongside the pedestrianized İstiklal Avenue, and counts as its neighbors not just high-rise structures but ancient churches and Ottoman mansions as well. The building takes the form of a modern addition behind and above a historical façade, and once you’re inside, you’re presented with an unmistakably contemporary hotel experience.

The rooms and suites are designed in a rich and colorful style that incorporates both Turkish and French influences; they’re full of thoughtful and functional comforts like work desks, espresso machines, and chic marble-clad bathrooms stocked with Atelier bath products. They’re decorated with paintings by the Turkish artist Devrim Erbil, and from their windows they offer elevated views of the Bosphorus and Istanbul’s rooftops.

Meanwhile the spa is another fruitful French-Turkish hybrid, containing a Turkish hammam as well as treatments featuring Lanvin products, and an eye-catching mosaic-tile indoor pool. The Oven Brasserie & Terrace is the hotel’s versatile restaurant.

content: With its picturesque canals and elegant waterfront palaces, Aveiro is sometimes called the Venice of Portugal. This seaside town got its first five-star hotel when one of those palaces was reborn as the MS Collection Aveiro - Palacete Valdemouro. The 18th-century landmark still has its original Moorish details, coffered ceilings, glittering chandeliers, and neoclassical facade, but the interiors have been smartly updated with polished parquet floors, luxe floor-to-ceiling drapery, and a mix of modern and Art Deco elements. Each room is named after a character from the works of Eça de Queiroz, the Portuguese novelist and diplomat who once lived here, and a literary theme prevails: there’s a cozy reading room, writing quills fashioned into art, and a large mural of the author by the courtyard swimming pool and café.

content:
In Brazil, the Fasano brand is a symbol of cutting-edge glamour, and their hotel in mountainous Minas Gerais, in the heart of one of the country’s largest cities, lives up to the reputation. Hotel Fasano Belo Horizonte is a luxury hotel renowned for its high-end restaurant and bar and its sleek, spacious guest rooms, with their gleaming hardwood floors and crisp white Egyptian cotton linens. 

The look, in warm natural tones of cream, wood, and copper, is something of a Fasano signature, and is emblematic of a specifically Brazilian vision of luxury. Even the humblest Superior rooms span nearly 300 square feet, and their marble bathrooms are furnished with high-pressure showers and Havaianas flip-flops; suites quickly grow to vast proportions.

Gero Belo Horizonte is the first outpost of the Fasano family’s high-end Gero restaurants to be found in a hotel setting, while Baretto, the plush cocktail bar featuring live music by local talent, brings in a steady stream of stylish Brazilians. content: Generations of European nobility wintered in Pau, at the foot of the Pyrenees. Today, the resort town is still renowned in France for its fresh mountain air, and Hôtel Parc Beaumont Pau Centre was strategically built to make the most of it. And thanks to a location in the historic center, Pau’s attractions are easy to explore, including the castle-turned-museum where King Henry IV was born.

content: Many of the Loire Valley’s elegant châteaux were constructed with limestone extracted from the region’s famous troglodyte caves. Some of those caves were historically used as private dwellings or wine cellars, and a particularly large one, located on the banks of the Loire River in Rochecorbon, was home to a monastery. It’s since been transformed into Hotel Les Hautes Roches, the first luxury hotel of its kind in France, with pretty landscaped gardens framing an outdoor pool on the riverfront and low-lit, atmospheric passageways leading through the renovated cave inside. \n\nThe monks’ former cells, built right into the rocky cliffs, were smartly converted into stylish guest rooms. Though they’re short on natural light, the design is modern, with eye-catching murals, creative lighting, and atmospheric stone-lined bathrooms with tubs. Some have minimalist Scandinavian-inspired décor, while others feature bold botanical patterns and scarlet-red carpeting, and many offer views of the river. A pair of more traditional rooms, unconnected to the cave, are located in the hotel’s adjoining building. The 18th-century manor house doubles as a dining venue, housing the hotel’s formal restaurant and a more casual bistro, both with scenic terrace seating across from the water.

content:
Just under two hours down the Willamette Valley from Portland is Eugene, Oregon, a small city that is, in its capacity as the home of the University of Oregon, one of the hippest college towns in the western United States. And with the advent of the Graduate Eugene, its hotel scene has grown measurably hipper — this one-time Hilton in the city’s downtown district, a few blocks from the campus proper, is now decked out in Ducks green, and its reception desk is a display case featuring dozens of historic Nike running shoes.

The now-famous shoe brand was born here in what’s called TrackTown USA, and it turns out Graduate founder Ben Weprin is a bit of a collector. Upstairs, the rooms go heavy on Pacific Northwest atmosphere, with plenty of wood grain and saturated green. And the university’s duck mascot is everywhere, as are stills from Animal House, the John Belushi college comedy that was shot here in Eugene.

And it wouldn’t be a Graduate without some inviting social spaces. Poindexter, the café, serves hot breakfast sandwiches, smoothies, pressed juices, and of course strong Northwest-style coffee, while the Trophy Room, the lobby-level restaurant and bar, is a tribute to the university’s storied athletic history.

content:
Tranquil it isn’t. Right on Canal Street, the spine of Manchester’s Gay Village — now a very inclusive, very mixed nightlife district — is the Velvet Bar and Restaurant, a longtime fixture on Manchester’s party scene. The latest addition to the Velvet family is the Velvet Hotel, occupying the floors above the restaurant and bar; if it’s not exactly the perfect recipe for sleeping the sleep of the just, it is absolutely ideal as a place to retire at the end (or, really, in the middle) of the night’s activities.

There are a lot of ways a nightclub hotel could go very stylistically wrong, but the Velvet falls prey to none of them. The look is bohemian, industrial, Edwardian, and yes, more than a little bit velvety, all at the same time. If it’s not quite seven-stars-in-Dubai luxurious it’s certainly more than comfortable enough, with luxe robes and slippers and a full complement of electronic gadgets.

Anyway it’s not about basking in solitary opulence so much as it is about stylishly shacking up, with a measure of fantasy thrown in as seasoning. This is usually the part where we enumerate the hotel’s dining and drinking options, but in this case they’re more or less self-evident. Suffice it to say that in this part of town you’ll be hard pressed to think of Manchester as England’s second city.

Out of their three tented camps in camps in Rajasthan, the founders of SUJÁN say that SUJÁN Jawai is their most ambitious conservation tourism project yet, a place where guests are immersed in the region’s wildlife and culture while only lightly touching the natural surroundings. Just ten tented suites are set against the backdrop of the Aravalli Mountain range and come luxuriously kitted out with all modern comforts and surprisingly contemporary interiors, plus large open verandas to take in the sweeping views. The Felidae Suite is ideal for groups of four, with two tents connected by a plinth and verandah, while Honeymooners tend to opt for the Royal Panthera Suite, which sits apart from the camp with its own heated pool, lounge and dining tent. For larger groups of friends and family there is Eden at Jawai, a private encampment accessible via its own entrance and comprising three double bedrooms, a pool, boma, and a lounge and dining area for more intimate evenings. 

Shared facilities include the SUJÁN Spa, the dining tent, bar, a campfire, and a heated pool. The twice daily safari drives are the main attraction here, led by expert guides who are ready to spot roaming antelopes, boar, and over 245 species of birds, although with this being leopard country, the sometimes-elusive cats are quite naturally the primary focus. Other experiences include biking, hiking, and horseback rides, as well as walks with the Rabari tribe and visits to nearby religious temples, shrines and villages to learn more about the region’s culture and SUJÁN Jawai’s conservation work in the local communities.

Boutique hotels have been slow to arrive in Belgrade, for world-historical reasons that don’t need to be dwelled on. It’s only now that there’s much of an alternative to the traditional business-hotel chains, but Townhouse 27 is doing its level best to drag the hospitality scene in the Serbian capital into the twenty-first century.

Its design-hotel aspirations are kept subtly in check, with expressive elements limited to quirky textures and inventive lighting. Belgrade might not be ready for a total design revolution. This is a business hotel as much as it is a design hotel, and there are traditional sensibilities to consider. And aside from the views of the city, which are no small thing, works by Belgrade-born artist Gabriel Glid add to the rooms’ visual interest.

Downstairs, there’s a shady little garden — perfect for a mid-morning pick-me-up or a dessert break — and more substantial fare at the all-day, Serbian-centric restaurant and bar. Shorter excursions of every cultural persuasion are available within city limits, of course, including the enormous, gorgeous, clifftop Kalemegdan park just a few blocks north. Get a little lost, why don’t you.

content:
Venezuela doesn’t see a lot of tourists these days. But in a big city — even one as reputedly dangerous as Caracas — the entrepreneurial spirit never really dies. Subscribing, perhaps, to the optimistic “if you build it, they will come” philosophy is the chic Cayena Caracas. Its clever design anticipates any traveler concerns about safety: the hotel is located in the exclusive neighborhood of La Castellana, set back from the street, tucked away behind heavy doors. Stepping inside is like arriving at a private villa surrounded by gorgeously landscaped gardens and terraces.

Guest rooms are plush and quiet, furnished with modern four-poster beds and spacious bathrooms with marble fixtures and rain showers. The look is classic and sophisticated, the subdued color palette of white, beige, and black warmed up by the high-tech lighting system. Standard amenities include Illy coffee machines, iPod docks, goose down comforters, 42-inch flat-screen TVs, bath products by Acqua di Parma, 24-hour room service, and free wi-fi. Higher-end rooms and suites have private patios with daybeds and views of the mountains.

Cerro El Ávila, the towering centerpiece of the Cordillera de la Costa, and the natural boundary between the city and the Caribbean Sea, is particularly lovely to behold from Cayena Caracas’ rooftop terrace and swimming pool. If you’d rather run on a loop than swim laps, there’s a small fitness center downstairs.

Also on the ground level: La Sibillia, the hotel’s buttoned-up Italian restaurant, serving perfectly al dente pastas in a white linen setting. And then there’s an inviting trio of “social living rooms.” One has a fireplace, all have smartly stocked bookshelves and elegant lounge space. It’s a perfect place to browse through the books on Venezuelan architecture and geography, and perhaps plan an onward journey to the mountains or the coast.

If Tokyo, Hong Kong and Singapore were the rehearsal halls where the big hotel chains put in the long years perfecting their craft, Shanghai, Beijing and the rest of mainland China are where the performance is finally taking place. There’s a sense of exuberance on display in hotels like the Sofitel Beijing Central, and it’s contagious — a place like this can’t help but get you a bit excited about the great Chinese economic experiment.

Here the hotel’s vibrant colors make their way from the bedrooms to the building’s exterior, as the entire façade becomes a pixelated video screen, capable of displaying the W logo in a wide variety of colorways. This doesn’t mean the interiors have gone all sober, though. The rooms come equipped with the usual extravagances, both visual and tactile, from high-gloss Hollywood-style lighting to the W signature bed and the standard Bliss bath products.

It’s aimed perhaps more at the culture industry than anyone else, thanks to a location that’s close to the Beijing Concert Hall, the National Centre for Performing Arts, and any number of galleries and museums. But business travelers won’t feel left out — there are veritable acres of meeting space, as well as a gym, spa and heated indoor pool. You know the drill: it’s a proper luxury hotel, but one for an audience that’s slightly younger — or younger at heart — than Beijing’s typical high-end traveler.

content:
Admittedly, Sofitel is not the first luxury hotel brand that comes to mind when we think of India. But just as Taj suggests a certain sort of opulence even in, say, Cape Town, a Sofitel in Mumbai promises a gleaming, contemporary French style that works nearly anywhere. The cool, stylistically coherent interiors of a place where everything seems quadruply polished — the copper-and-glass staircase, the metallic bar stools, the white and black marble in the bathrooms, and even, it almost seems, the luminescent throw pillows on the beds — work especially well in a city of Mumbai’s dizzying scale.

For as stimulating as it is, it’s the kind of megalopolis that compels an experienced traveler to be extra sure to find a comfortable, well-managed hotel that can act, to use a cliché that here is truly apt, as an oasis. This oasis takes the form of a contemporary Art Nouveau building with a glassy, clean-lined exterior. Inside, all the rooms have dark wood floors, oversized tubs with separate showers, Sofitel’s famously cushy beds and toiletries by L’Occitane. All the comforts of Mumbai’s grand old hotels are here, but at this brand-new Sofitel they’re packaged with relative restraint, a virtue in short supply amongst the competition. 

Perhaps we shouldn’t be surprised that such a French hotel is making a home in Mumbai. While the growth of India’s economic muscle is anything but a modest spurt, the development of cosmopolitan Mumbai appears downright steroidal. That “BKC” in the name of the hotel stands for Bandra Kurla Complex, the hotel’s home and the center of Mumbai’s financial district. It’s surrounded by the offices of several multinational corporations and it’s a short hop from the Indian stock exchange. The location is excellent if you’re doing business here, and the recently built Bandra-Worli bridge connects Bandra with the city center when it’s time for some leisure in the city — and by leisure we mean mind-boggling sensory overload, the sort of leisure that puts you in need of a good night’s sleep. 

How to get there: The hotel is also served by 2 train stations at Bandra and Kurla and has easy road access from the Western Express Highway.

The advent of air travel is enough to make one indulge in a bit of nostalgic worry for the resorts along the Baltic Sea, places which must necessarily have seen some decline in attendance now that it’s half a day’s flight from Munich to the Maldives. The island of Rügen, however, is still going strong, positioned just off the coast of northeastern Germany, and while some of the appeal is historical, it’s by no means purely a retro trip, as evidenced by the swanky, subtly modern Cerês am Meer.

You might expect sunny colors at these northerly latitudes, but the Cerês am Meer’s charcoal-and-white bedrooms pop in their own way when struck by the low Baltic sun. The clean contemporary style stands in contrast to the surroundings: the hotel stands in the center of Binz, Rügen’s classic resort town. And it’s anything but a case of some brash newcomer, setting out to upset the luxury status quo — the Cerês’s modernity feels cool and controlled, and the king beds and expansive Baltic-facing balconies (not to mention the spa, the fine-dining restaurant and the rooftop lounge) drive home the point that this is simply the new face of the luxury hotel.

How to get there:

The Sofitel chain is one we’ve generally got a lot of time for; they do many of the things we want from a chain (service, professionalism, above all consistency) and very few of the things we don’t (bland décor, dull atmosphere, that deflating feeling when consistency turns into sameness). And in sleepy, serious Luxembourg City, the Sofitel stands out.

Here, right across the street from the European Court of Justice, you could be forgiven for expecting something a little more safe — say what you will about international lawyers, but they’re not necessarily the most raucous crowd. So full marks for style to the Sofitel Luxembourg Europe, whose interiors, conservative by Sofitel standards, are nevertheless a cut above the sort of beige-on-beige business hotel you might expect to find in its place.

As such it’s pretty much the top hotel in Luxembourg’s Kirchberg plateau, and all manner of international business gets done in its restaurants, from Italian cuisine at Radici to the locally-themed De Feierwon. If it’s lacking anything, it’s in the pampering department; no pool, no spa, no fitness center — this is no urban resort, but a business hotel through and through.

content:
Though in recent years it’s often overlooked in favor of bolder, brasher Miami, Palm Beach is, to many minds, the more desirable South Florida destination. There’s a classic, old-world atmosphere here that the trend-chasers of South Beach just can’t match. And this is the feeling that the Brazilian Court Hotel & Beach Club distills to its essence.

The construction dates back to the Twenties, and inside it’s refreshingly free of rattan and other tropical kitsch. A renovation has left these interiors looking sharper than ever; they retain their dark mahogany woodwork and their accents in leather and brass, while added visual interest is provided in the form of black-and-white prints by the portrait photographer Terry O’Neill. Eighty studio rooms and suites wrap around quiet central courtyards, and all come with top-notch appointments and amenities, including jetted tubs in the marble bathrooms and wine fridges in addition to the expected minibars.

This is grown-up luxury at its most romantic. What you lose in beach-front convenience (don’t worry, it’s only two blocks away) you gain in tranquil seclusion. Some travelers may prefer the fashion-show atmosphere and velvet-rope nightclubs of Miami Beach — a distinctly different sort of traveler, however, prefers the quiet elegance of Daniel Boulud’s Café Boulud, and the refined charm of the Brazilian Court Hotel.

The 21c Museum Hotels, true to their name, are known for bringing museum-quality contemporary art collections and world-class luxury boutique hospitality to cities where neither one can be taken for granted — not places like New York or Los Angeles but Louisville, Kentucky or Bentonville, Arkansas. For their tenth installment they’ve chosen St. Louis, Missouri, and turned a century-old Renaissance Revival–style YMCA building into a 173-room hotel and museum.

In the rooms and suites you’ll find 21c’s signature modernist style, a look that’s stylish enough for design fans but straightforward enough for traditional luxury-hotel guests. Every unit, naturall, comes with its own piece of original art, and all feature upscale details like 50-inch televisions and Malin+Goetz bath products.

They’re among the finest lodgings in town, but 21c doesn’t stop there. Woven throughout the building is 14,000 square feet of exhibition space, and the building’s former life as a YMCA means it already had space for a full-scale athletic club, including an indoor pool and even a running track. The restaurant, Idol Wolf, is inspired by the Spanish tapas tradition, and the Good Press café serves coffee by local St. Louis roasters.

The more relaxed second restaurant Le ROC still showcases Conte's style and the region’s seasonal ingredients, but it really is worth pushing the boat out with a night at the two-MICHELIN-Star headliner La Table de Yoann Conte.

content:
When Val Thorens, in the French Alps, calls itself “the roof of Europe,” it’s a reference to the fact that it’s the highest-elevation ski resort on the continent. But it’s not just the altitude that makes it special — it’s part of Les Trois Vallées, which means access to what might be the most abundant wealth of ski slopes in the world. Hotel Pashmina Le Refuge sounds like just the sort of place you’d like to wrap yourself up in at the end of a day on the valleys’ mountainsides, and upon further inspection, it turns out it’s aptly named indeed.

Anyone who’s spent much time in traditional Alpine lodges knows there’s such a thing as too much coziness. Here at Pashmina it’s tempered with quite a bit of visual interest, a modernist reinvention of the lodge style for a new generation of guests. The rooms range from cozy doubles with balconies all the way up to the three-bedroom Apartment-Chalet, and everything in between, with plentiful creature comforts and a lively, contemporary look.

Add a L’Occitane spa and two restaurants — one of them the proud owner of a Michelin star — and you’re in proper luxury-hotel territory. And with a ski shop and the never-ending list of outdoor activities, it’s a very fine base camp for a bit of Alpine adventure.

content:
If you’re a cynic you could worry a bit about the quite possibly over-the-top results of a global luxury-hotel brand taking on a project in a Persian Gulf boom town. But The Ritz-Carlton Bahrain, in the capital city of Manama, while not exactly shattering all the stereotypes, goes just enough against the grain to make it very much worth taking note of.

For one thing it’s a renovation of an already-existing resort, and it’s more of a sprawling villa complex than the colonnaded palace you might be thinking of. The interiors have had a thorough renovation by Pierre-Yves Rochon, whose style is characteristically opulent while remaining very much within the bounds of good taste. 

And the accommodations are up to The Ritz-Carlton’s usual high standard — everything, from the city-view standard rooms to the top-end sea-view suites and the 19 haute-luxury villas, comes equipped with the state of the art in creature comforts and technological wizardry. There are no fewer than 17 restaurants, 18 if you count the afternoon tea service in the lobby — what may be surprising is that they, along with the Burlington Club whiskey-and-cigar bar, are among Manama’s most in-demand destinations.

content:
If you’re in Cairo to do the major tourist destinations then Heliopolis might not be the obvious choice — but if you’re here to see the city at its most contemporary and stylish then it’s hard to do much better than the Gabriel. For while it may be a fairly classic boutique hotel, elegant but with a slight modern edge to its interiors, luxe with a generous helping of stylish nightlife, this is a town where classic boutique hotels are far from a common sight.

Rooms start out quite generously sized, and they’re stocked with all the necessities, from 46-inch LCD televisions and iPod stereo systems to Bulgari bath products. Needless to say, Egyptian cotton linens are included as a matter of local pride. And the suites are proper suites, not just bedrooms with dividers — here they add living rooms, bars, walk-in closets and guest bathrooms.

By day the Gabriel’s social nexus is the swimming pool, and it’s not much different by night, when the poolside Roof Bar turns into a fully fledged nightclub. The Salt restaurant and bar offer forward-thinking Mediterranean-Asian cuisine in a Starck-like environment of chandeliers and mirrors. And while the Pyramids are not exactly in your front yard, you’re quite close indeed to Sun City, the site of some of Cairo’s best shopping and dining.

How to get there:
The Gabriel is located just 3 miles from Cairo International Airport (CAI).

content:
Another Malmaison hotel means another charming, storied old building, its exterior lovingly restored and its interior thoroughly renovated, resulting in a stylish and deeply comfortable boutique hotel. Put that way it sounds like a bit of a formula, but people only complain about formulas when they’re bad ones — in this case, why tamper with success?

The building in question is an old Great Western railway hotel, built by none other than Isambard Kingdom Brunel. It fell on some pretty hard times (read: fire) but that’s what property developers are for — if it had remained a successful rail hotel then Malmaison could never have snapped it up and installed their trademark dark, clubby and masculine look throughout.

Where there’s a railway hotel there’s naturally a rail station — in this case just across the road — which makes the Malmaison Reading more likely for quick-break Londoners (it’s less than an hour away) than for style-hungry jet-setters just in from Milan or Tokyo on some kind of sexy business trip. That said, the swanky brasserie and bar don’t discriminate — locally sourced cuisine and top-shelf cocktails taste about as fine to your aunt and uncle from Swindon as they do to international men and women of mystery.

content:
Every parent thinks his or her child is above average — and, numerically speaking, some of them are bound to be right. Same goes for luxury hotels: every big business chain thinks its hotels strike just the right balance of style and comfort, of privacy and sociability, of traditional elegance and contemporary cool. The thing about the Mandarin Oriental group is that, quite often, they do.

The rooms, in typical Mandarin style, start out pretty close to the limit of clean contemporary luxe, and the suites edge ever closer. The best views overlook the enormous roundabout that circles Jakarta’s triumphantly kitschy Welcome Monument, but any angle on this endless city is an impressive one. It’s worth springing for Club Level service and a deep soaking tub, though by no means is life in the Superior Rooms difficult.

This kind of hotel isn’t just a refuge, it’s an interface with the local culture. Public spaces range from Cantonese and French restaurants to a cake shop and a poolside café. And if you’ve got any doubts about Jakarta as a destination, they’re misplaced. Every city claims to be vibrant and energetic, but Jakarta’s vast size, fast pace and eclectic mix of cultures make it the sort of place you just might need a proper luxury hotel to recover from.

content:
The group might be best known for its splendid high-rise luxury hotels, but the Park Hyatt Jeddah, on the city’s coastal South Corniche, takes a different tack. This Park Hyatt is strictly a low-rise affair, with perhaps a more leisurely bent than some of its cousins. Given the location, it’s not out of the question that you’re here on, shall we say, higher business, as Mecca is less than an hour’s drive away.

To give it its full name, it’s technically the Park Hyatt Jeddah Marina, Club & Spa, and it earns every word; it’s tucked between the coastal boulevard and the water, with yachts docking along its piers, and during the day there’s something of a private-club atmosphere as hotel guests mingle with locals visiting the day spa or the Park Hyatt’s restaurants. The atmosphere is elegant yet relaxed, and the style, though sophisticated, is also quite thoroughly localized, the architecture and design tailored to suit Jeddah’s particular visual language.

The rooms and suites are spacious, with open-plan bathrooms and, in most cases, views of the Red Sea, and all are decorated in a clean and elegant contemporary style. For business travelers it’s certainly more than suitable, a short enough drive from Jeddah’s central business district. But one gets the impression this Park Hyatt aims to be something more like an urban resort; not one but two spas serve hotel guests, one for men and one for women.

How to get there:
Park Hyatt Jeddah is located in Jeddah's Al Hamra (business) district, just minutes away from the central business district. The hotel is 35 minutes (by car) from King Abdulaziz International Airport.

content: Just 30 miles north of Tahiti, The Brando occupies the atoll of Tetiaroa, once reserved for Tahitian royalty. Marlon Brando came across it while filming “Mutiny on the Bounty” and later obtained the lease in exchange for cash, and a homemade apple pie. Today, it is a carbon-neutral hideaway with 35 villas set between palms and reef, cooled by sea breeze and lined with polished stone. Breakfasts come with honey harvested on a nearby motu, and check-in starts with a cocktail by the lagoon. Everything here is dialed back, intentional, and extraordinary.

content: The whitewashed Hotel Fariones, the first hotel on the Canarian island of Lanzarote, was built in the Sixties on the best piece of real estate its owners could find. This prime spot on a scenic cove, richly planted with tropical gardens and overlooking the sea, has only become more valuable as the resort town of Puerto del Carmen has grown up around it. After extensive renovations, the hotel reopened in 2020 to some fanfare, the interiors reimagined by a local designer, starting with the airy white lobby with bold Spanish artwork and huge glass windows looking out to the palm tree-framed infinity pool and the ocean beyond. Rooms and suites are beautifully appointed with elegant parquet floors, stylish tile-lined balconies with sea views, and spacious, spa-like marble bathrooms with walk-in showers. There's a sprawling fitness center with tennis courts and swimming pools, plus an array of fine restaurants, terrace cafés, and a pool bar open to the public; guests in upper-level rooms also have access to the exclusive rooftop pool and bar.

content:
When it comes to hotels, we’re all for novelty, and in these pages you’ll find hundreds of listings to prove it. But there’s also something to be said for consistency. You’re talking about the fulfillment of basic needs, after all, things like food and sleep — not areas where we always feel like taking huge risks. And ultimately, consistency is what the big luxury chains are built on. Take the Four Seasons Jakarta, for example.

There are hotels in town that are more modern in style, and hotels that are more classical as well. The Four Seasons walks a middle path, with a colonial look and all the business-class trappings. There are times when you want to be soothed, rather than challenged, by a hotel, and these plush rooms, complete with marble baths, deep soaking tubs and private balconies overlooking the city, are nothing if not soothing.

Facilities, as you might expect, are pretty much comprehensive; there’s a fitness center open around the clock, and the spa is worth the trip in itself. Restaurants include a steakhouse and an upscale Cantonese option, and the business facilities are top-notch as well — it’s certainly more than adequate for leisure guests but this city-center Four Seasons is squarely aimed at the high-end business traveler.

content:
Here’s proof that the Mama Shelter hotels, even in the era of their Accor-backed expansion, still have adventure on their mind. When you imagine a hotel group taking the path of least resistance, Belgrade, the Serbian capital, doesn’t leap immediately to mind. But the way this town is going, it’s absolutely ripe for a stylish, budget-conscious, youth-oriented boutique hotel — and that, naturally, is the role that Mama Shelter Belgrade was born to play.

The design is by Philippe Starck protégé Jalil Amor, who worked on the original Mama Shelter in Paris all those years ago. This is no reproduction, however — the visual approach is as riotous and whimsical as ever, but the details are tailored to the setting, where Austria-Hungary meets the Balkans. And while the rooms do incorporate some bold design gestures, they’re simpler and more sedate than the public spaces, creating a transition in mood that’s almost luxurious, in its own intangible way.

The location, on Knez Mihailova, a pedestrianized street that anchors a shopping and entertainment district, could hardly be more central. But Mama Shelter is, as usual, something of an entertainment district unto itself. The Mama Belgrade restaurant serves wood-fired pizzas as well as Serbian classics and international dishes, and the open-air rooftop bar is an extremely hot ticket — be prepared to book in advance.

content:
For some travelers, full immersion, rather than haughty seclusion, is the only way to experience a new place, and Senegal’s Tama Lodge provides just that — without sacrificing the comforts of a luxury hotel. The lodge, which sits on the very edge of the continent, blends the colors and charms of the beachfront with authentic Senegalese construction and décor; local materials and artwork abound in the guest cabins, which from the outside evoke the shape and character of traditional masks. The rooms themselves aren’t overly luxe, but the Touareg camel leather carpets, bed frames hewn from tree trunks, and Kuba fabric curtains lend them an unmistakable sense of place. You won’t forget it at the restaurant, either, where the menu is updated daily to account for the latest hauls of fresh fish, local meats, and exotic fruits.

content:
A century-old hotel in the heart of the Styrian capital of Graz sounds like a recipe for an old-fashioned stay, but even though Das Weitzer has been in the family for generations, it’s kept pace with the times. This section of town has transformed into a creative district — the “friendly alien” art museum is a short walk away — and as you pass through the doors of this elegant old grand hotel, you may be surprised at the contemporary interiors and the youthful atmosphere.

The rooms retain their century-old architecture, but the design spans the whole century, mixing parquet floors and ornate mirror frames with modern furniture and a minimalist, graphic sensibility. Visually sparse, they’re nevertheless full of tactile comfort, and some of them have very fine views of the old town and the Schloßberg, the mountain at the center of the city.

Der Steirer, the restaurant, presents a modern interpretation of the region’s classic cuisine, while the Kaffee Weitzer showcases the Austrian talent for cafés — it’s much more than a coffee bar. More unusual, though not at all unwelcome, is Blumeninsel, a full-service florist, keeping the hotel constantly supplied with fresh blooms.

content: Much of the buzz about Detroit is focused on its inner-city renewal, but that’s far from the only story in town. There’s plenty worth knowing about in the outlying suburbs as well — and this includes the lovely town of Birmingham, Michigan, home of the Townsend Hotel. The building dates back only to the 1980s, but in hotels, as in so many other areas of life, it’s what’s inside that counts. In the case of the Townsend what’s inside is an absolutely classic luxury hotel, one that you’d swear had existed in its present form for half a century or more.\n\nThis means swanky guest rooms with marble bathrooms and all the high-end fixings, public spaces that are straight out of a prewar English country house, and an award-winning fine-dining restaurant, the Rugby Grille. It also means an afternoon tea service that wouldn’t look out of place in Downton Abbey, and a classic cocktail bar. Walking distance from downtown Detroit attractions you’re most certainly not — but you are close by to many of greater Detroit’s sporting, cultural and commercial attractions, which, needless to say, is even better.

content:
It’s easy for a Western traveler to underestimate the significance of Macau, but for Asian hospitality chains, it’s equally as important as Hong Kong, much in the same way American hotel groups are sure to be in top form in Las Vegas. No surprise, then, to see the attention lavished upon the Mandarin Oriental Macau by its proprietors; this hotel is a brand-new replacement for a hotel that was scarcely two decades old, and even by Mandarin’s high standards, it’s an impressive one.

What it isn’t is particularly understated. This is a casino town, and you don’t win extra points for subtlety. What matters in a place like Macau is luxury, which the Mandarin has in spades. The look might be a touch flashier than the group’s typical style, but it’s one that’s well suited to its high-rolling clientele, as are the massive soaking tubs and the far-ranging city and sea views through the floor-to-ceiling windows. All of this matters, of course, but as is so often the case, it’s in the area of service that the Mandarin truly excels itself. 

Outside the rooms, the facilities are equally comprehensive, from the state-of-the-art spa and fitness complex to the generous selection of restaurants and lounges. The casinos are easily accessible from the location in the waterfront Nape development, including the MGM, accessible via a walkway.

How to get there: Macau can be easily reached by ferry from Hong Kong.  Approximate travel time 1 hour. Macau International Airport is located on Taipa Island, approximately 20 minutes by ferry from Macau.

content:
Jakarta is an exotic place, to be sure, and many of its hotels are heavy on showmanship. But Jakarta is also the capital of Indonesia, a vast nation, and an important player in the global economy. As such, it needs a few no-nonsense business hotels, of which the Grand Hyatt is king. 

Fears of a bland and homogeneous hotel experience prove baseless, however; the Grand Hyatt is up to the standards of the best business hotels in any major city. The look is perhaps a bit less modern than that of the latest business hotels, incorporating traditional Indonesian materials and craftmanship. But this is no museum — every modern amenity is accounted for, from the electronic controls that run the 428 rooms and suites to the 24-hour business center and extensive conference facilities. The fitness/leisure center is beyond comprehensive, with an outdoor lagoon swimming pool that has to be seen to be believed, and several outdoor tennis courts - all right in the middle of one of the largest cities in the world. 

We recommend a drink on the terrace at sunset to the sound of the call to prayer from nearby mosques. Those of you being called will have better things to do, but others will also be touched by the multitude of voices calling it the end of a long and hot day. In fact everything one could wish for is on-site, or close at hand; the location is central, adjacent to the Plaza Indonesia (prime shopping territory) and close to a number of government offices and cultural institutions. Soekarno Hatta International Airport is 40 minutes away by car.

content:
Somehow Gravetye Manor is only an hour from the city, and, incredibly, just 12 miles from Gatwick airport; but it feels a good deal more remote than that, with an air of pastoral calm worlds away from the rush of today's cosmopolitan London. It is as though chain hotels had never existed and white walls were unheard of — it's all oak paneling and country charm here.

This is a place that seems remote not just in terms of distance, but in terms of history as well. The manor dates back to 1598 and everything about it suggests a continuation of the Elizabethan way of life — starting from the meticulously preserved décor (and in the new addition, a convincing replica of the original style).

This is a small hotel, just 17 rooms, and achieves what all the best country house hotels are shooting for: the illusion that customers are house guests of a wealthy country relation. Service is efficient and always proper but never stuffy.

And it's a good thing, as you will likely be seeing quite a bit of the hotel staff, and your fellow travelers. Gravetye Manor is a retreat, an escape; as such, there is not much in the way of entertainment. If you feel the need to flirt at the hotel bar, London has dozens of more suitable hotels — but if you would prefer an afternoon spent walking through some of England's most sumptuous gardens (courtesy of the leading landscape gardener William Robinson, one of the mansion's former owners) then this is the hotel for you.

How to get there:
Gravetye Manor is approximately a 1 hour drive from London and only 20 minutes from London Gatwick Airport.

content: Prosperous trading in port towns along the Baltic coast led to the construction of lavish estates in the countryside, including an 18th-century palace outside Gdynia. Today, it’s home to Hotel Quadrille, one of the only Relais & Châteaux properties in Poland. Though the interiors have been reimagined with an Alice in Wonderland theme — black and white checkerboard floors, whimsical patterned wallpaper, fanciful light installations, overstuffed velvet armchairs — it’s a sophisticated, adults-only escape. \n\nThe Quadrille’s rooms are named after and inspired by great writers: the Lewis Carroll room, with its avant-garde design and opulent open-plan bathroom, edges into Tim Burton territory, while the wood-beamed Emily Brontë suite and the attic-like Jane Austen room are quaint and cozy. The White Rabbit Restaurant serves twelve-course tasting menus in the style of a colorful tea party, and larger-than-life outdoor sculptures in the surrounding park evoke the second chapter of Carroll’s absurdist masterpiece.

content: A few blocks from the 12th-century Gothic cathedral in medieval Saint-Brieuc, Edgar Hôtel & Spa occupies one of the city’s newer architectural landmarks. This stately mansion was commissioned by a wealthy shipbuilder in 1840, later serving as a convent and then a police station before it was transformed into a boutique hotel. \n\nPeriod charm is plentiful in its grand ground-level spaces with original wood flooring and in attic-like suites with sloping ceilings beneath the building’s mansard roof, though the interiors are decidedly more modern than quaint. Rooms feature boldly patterned wallpaper and spacious bathrooms with walk-in showers, and many have floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the courtyard garden. Adding to the appeal are the glass-roofed restaurant and a small spa with a hammam and tea shop.

content:
The Waldorf Astoria Helsinki brings together four historic buildings dating from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, uniting them into one of the Finnish capital’s most impressive luxury boutique hotels. content: Saint-Palais-sur-Mer, on Charente-Maritime’s Atlantic coast, is a lovely little seaside town marked by colorful examples of Basque-style architecture — one of which is the 1920s villa that’s now home to the Hôtel Hemen, a luxury boutique hotel whose chic interiors and high-end comforts belie its low-key atmosphere. content:
The North Shore Chicago suburb of Evanston is home to Northwestern University, and with the renovation and restoration of the 1927-vintage Homestead Hotel, it’s now also home to an outpost of the hotel brand that has quickly become synonymous with American college towns: the Graduate Evanston.

In typical Graduate style it’s packed with local references — not just headboards in Northwestern purple, but details from Evanston’s and Chicago’s history. The rest of the rooms, by comparison, are more restrained, though they’ve got plenty of Twenties style, as well as modern comforts like Malin + Goetz bath products.

Another common thread among all Graduate hotels: The Homestead Room, a restaurant and bar that’s similarly tailored to the campus it calls home, especially the achievements of its various athletic programs — make a plan well ahead of time for Wildcats football weekends. Meanwhile, the university district’s main drag, with all its restaurants, shops, and cafés, is just to the west, while the shores of Lake Michigan lie just a block or two to the east.

content:
Melrose Arch is the name of one of Johannesburg’s newly hip districts, a planned and gated community right smack in the middle of the city — an oddity, perhaps, to those of us used to a less orderly sort of gentrification, but actually rather sensible, given the degree of disorder in Johannesburg’s recent history.

The hotel of the same name is rather like the neighborhood — the Melrose Arch is a design-heavy hotel in the tradition of New York’s or London’s marquee boutiques, and like the gated district it calls home, what it lacks in spontaneity and surprise it makes up for with a certain sparkling efficiency.

The familiar monochrome palette is livened by a few dashes of color, like the foyer floor that changes color, cycling through the spectrum beneath your feet, and the glossy minimalism of the place is broken up by the occasional baroque flourish. Rooms are stylish and comfortable, each with a flat-screen television built into a paneled-wood wall, and a deep standalone tub visible from the bed, but for a not entirely opaque curtain.

In fact any modern hotel’s bathroom layout says a lot about its clientele, and as a rule if the bath or shower is semi-exposed, then you’re not dealing with a straight business crowd. Guests here are more likely hanging out in the hotel’s bar and restaurant (or those of the surrounding Melrose Arch district) than making use of the 24-hour business center and the conference facilities.

content: This stylish new boutique hotel pays homage to days gone by with its reference to Mumbai’s old name. Located in a colonial building in the heart of the historic center, Abode Bombay mixes a cosmopolitan design sensibility — think custom-built wood furniture and a monochrome palette —  with warm nostalgia for the past. The teak floorboards were sourced from demolished buildings, and the intricate floor tiles were traditionally hand-laid; the silk pillow cushions were crafted out of old saris, and the Art Deco antiques were sourced from local markets. Guest rooms are simple and comfortable, with modern decor; some share baths. There’s a photogenic library, a small spa room, and a breakfast featuring masala chai and a selection of Indian delicacies, with many of Mumbai’s highlights just a few minutes’ walk away.

content: There’s something inherently relaxing about the term “all-inclusive,” especially as you take a peek at the fine print. At Curtain Bluff, a 72-suite oceanfront luxury hotel located on a sandy peninsula in Antigua, what’s included is a room with ocean views, fresh seafood feasts served al fresco at a pair of restaurants, twice-daily snorkeling trips to a nearby reef, yoga classes, kayaks, windsurfing equipment, a kids’ club, a lavish afternoon tea followed by happy hour, live entertainment, even room service and minibar items. And two beaches separated by a bluff: one, on the bay, is ideal for sunbathing, while the other, on the ocean side, is better for surfing. Curtain Bluff is elegant and low-key, thanks, in part, to its size: it opened in the 1960s with just 22 rooms, and the hotel retains much of that intimate charm and attention to service today.

content:
We’ve long been cheerleaders for the boutique-hotel world’s expansion beyond the big coastal capitals and into the smaller cities of the American heartland. As it happens, quite a few of these cities are college towns, and the Graduate hotel group is on the case. It doesn’t get much more “heartland” than Lincoln, Nebraska, frankly — and the Graduate Lincoln is the hotel we always hoped we’d someday see in the Cornhusker State.

Of course, we couldn’t have predicted that it would look quite like this. The Graduate hotels are all painstakingly tailored to their locations, and the Graduate Lincoln is no different — behind the facade of what was once a Holiday Inn is a  hotel that’s positively stuffed with minutely detailed Nebraskan arcana. It’s also stuffed with contemporary boutique comforts like Malin + Goetz bath products. We won’t spoil all the surprises for you, though we will reveal that some rooms come with vintage arcade games.

And then there’s heartland food culture. Graduate Lincoln’s restaurant and bar, Single Barrel, serves classic comfort-food dishes as well as tiki-themed cocktails and a well-selected list of beers. Get there early on game-day Saturdays as you’ll be joined by a throng of pre-gaming Huskers fans.

content:
Foreign visitors are well aware of Machu Picchu and Lake Titicaca, and for good reason. But the Paracas District, along Peru’s central coast, has awe-inspiring historical relics and a unique, lovely landscape — minus the masses. Hotel Paracas takes full advantage of its location: a peninsular desert surrounded by the Pacific Ocean. The two outdoor pools, with their bright white day beds and lounge chairs, look out on just this geography. 

Plenty of the bungalows, villas, and chalets do too. Next door is the 900,000-acre Reserva Nacional de Paracas, sometimes called the Peruvian Galápagos. Nearby are the Ballestas Islands, easily seen from the hotel’s private yacht, and the Nazca Lines, easily seen from the hotel’s private airplane. 

Location matters in other ways. Geometric designs on floors and walls echo those found on the petroglyphs and weavings created by the area’s pre-Incan cultures. More recently, locally crafted textiles and furniture have been used to decorate the accommodations, which also feature marble bathrooms and 400-thread sheets. 

Naturally, the bar offers several takes on the country’s most famous beverage, the Pisco sour (Pisco is a Peruvian brandy), and the two restaurants serve many preparations of freshly caught fish, such as ceviche and tiraditos. And with Starwood now running the show, service, including treatments at the huge spa, promises to be as exacting as expected.      

How to get there:

Hotel Paracas is ten kilometers from Pisco airport (PIO). Complimentary shuttle service is available.

content:
From the outside it’s not immediately clear what caliber of hotel this is, especially in a city with as much distinctive architecture as Leipzig has. But give it a chance. Behind that ’70s exterior is a very modern, very sleek luxury hotel — though the Westin isn’t located in the old town, this is still the Leipzig of Wagner, Bach or Mendelssohn, not the industrial Leipzig of the GDR days.

Materials are uniformly rich, and after a recent renovation, the design is crisp and minimal, and the colors are toned down — it’s a very adult look, a serious and dignified take on the contemporary design hotel from one of the bigger names in traditional business hotels. And underneath it, it’s a classic five-star, with all that entails: flat-panel televisions, wi-fi everywhere, those famous Westin beds, and a full-service spa and 24-hour gym at your disposal.

The location, just off the main rail station, could hardly be more central, and opera tourists will find all their destinations, from the opera house to Mendelssohn’s old digs, are within walking distance. As are any number of restaurants — though with the Westin’s own Yamato sushi bar and Falco fine dining restaurant, you’re not exactly desperate in that department.
