content: If you’re a real luxury-hotel freak, then simply the name Waldorf Astoria Beijing probably conveys just about all you need to know. While a cursory glance at the building’s exterior reveals that this, at least in terms of visual design, is not your grandfather’s Waldorf Astoria, the experience that’s on offer would likely be familiar to your dear old hypothetical granddad — design that’s elegant and eminently palatable, comforts that are beyond first-class, and service to rival any luxury hotel anywhere. The building, by the Chicago/Beijing-based Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill, feels perfectly judged — equal parts modern international luxury hotel and ancient Chinese courtyard palace, a public monument and a private hideaway in equal measure. And the interiors, by the master luxury-hotel designers Yabu Pushelberg, combine ascendant-China grandeur (black lacquer and overtones in red and gold) with timeless Western luxury-brand restraint. As for service, the place is practically crawling with concierges; the staff-to-guest ratio is nearly one to one, but can be counted on to feel like ten to one. A near-embarrassment of high-end facilities and amenities may be taken as a matter of course: three restaurants, full-service spa, massive heated pool, and plentiful meeting and events space. Still to come is a second phase of development, wherein the main tower’s rooms and suites will be joined by a series of detached, low-lying hutong villas, a reference to China’s traditional low-rise courtyard construction.

content:
If you’re familiar with Banyan Tree’s success at bringing the private-villa concept to some of Asia’s most desirable coastal real estate, their foray into Macau may at first seem a bit odd. After all, the densely populated region’s status as something like the Vegas of the East — with all the attendant glitz that nickname suggests — doesn’t exactly scream “eco-resort.” But Banyan Tree has proven quite adept at making its style work in disparate places, and here the hotel slots itself comfortably into the Galaxy Macau casino, carving out a generous 246 suites that take the experience into the sky.

Just because the setting is an urban resort doesn’t mean that the rooms skimp on space — each suite boasts a private indoor plunge pool, situated to offer views of the gambling mecca that sprawls along the peninsula. High ceilings and partitions foster a sense of openness, while the rigorous geometry of right angled-furniture and massive mirrors are softened by Chinese art objects and hanging lamps. Crisp professionalism is to be expected in a hotel of this magnitude, but it never overshadows the sense that an incredibly relaxing soak or massage is just around the corner — or in the living room of your Spa Suite. 

Guests looking to combine the Banyan Tree ethos with the opulence of Macau can opt for a pool villa — an exquisite penthouse with jaw-dropping outdoor space, complete with a private garden and the requisite pool. These suites feature in-room dining and butler service, but if you’re inclined to venture out, there’s always the signature Saffron restaurant for Thai and Belon for fresh seafood.

content:
Because you haven’t always got time to nip off to the Lake District, or Scotland, or Spain, it’s good to know you’ve got options just outside the M25. The Crown, in Amersham, is probably best known for its cameo in Four Weddings and a Funeral, but a combination of convenience, fine hospitality and thoughtful cuisine has kept it relevant even as the early-period Hugh Grant films have become film history.

As it’s no longer necessary to bed down for the night just a few minutes into a cross-country journey, the Crown has reinvented itself as a destination. This is the picture of the modern coaching inn, playing host to weekenders, stolen romantic moments and, not uncommonly, a bit of last-minute trade involving the after-dinner crowd.

That doesn’t mean the lodgings are an afterthought, of course. Owners Tej and Sarina Dhillon brought in designer Ilse Crawford for a bit of collaboration, and the result is a perfectly judged mix of coaching-inn tradition and low-key, unpretentious contemporary style — the one exception being number 12, known both for its Four Weddings role and for its 16th-century décor.

content: Hong Kong’s vibrant energy is intoxicating but everyone wants a little downtime, and for that, The Hari is perfect. The hotel’s location in Causeway Bay and Wan Chan means it’s close to the action, but inside, it’s restful refinement at its best. The 210 rooms, including three suites, are polished sanctuaries, courtesy of the sharp eye of interior designer Tara Bernerd. Wood paneling, linen wallcoverings, and stylish furnishings create warm and inviting spaces, while windows frame views of the iconic skyline just outside. content:
Proving there’s more to Australia’s Sunshine State than its beaches, Spicers Peak Lodge gives travelers an excuse to head inland. A world away from the bars and bright lights of Queensland’s Gold Coast, this property is a sophisticated and modern ranch retreat, set amid rolling hills and eucalyptus. 

The Lodge is nothing if not private — the only neighbors are the property’s own Brangus cattle, and access to the Lodge is best had via helicopter. Most guests, however, arrive much less conspicuously by 4WD pick-up service — not a bad idea if you’d rather sit back and enjoy the scenery than attempt to rally drive up the dirt road to the top of the mountain range. 

Featuring all natural hues, cathedral ceilings, walls of glass and a healthy smattering of open fireplaces, the interiors of Spicers Peak Lodge bring the beauty of the surrounding wilderness indoors. Constellations can be viewed from bathtubs and sunsets enjoyed from the warmth of the communal living area where guests gather for cocktails and gourmet canapés every evening. 

Spicers Peak is perhaps as well known for the restaurant as for the lodge. Gourmets are ideally catered for, with multi-course degustation dinners prepared every night by the onsite chef, plus the best of Australian and international wines in the cellar. Daytime activities for the somewhat energized include swimming, billiards and tennis, while the sprawling national parkland beyond the property provides endless opportunity for nature walks and picnics. 

With only ten suites in total, service here is exceptionally attentive. Gifts materialize in rooms while guests are out, private picnics are orchestrated at whim and requests are happily and discretely carried out, the relatively a small number of staff lending a warm and personal touch to hospitality. 

Suites at the Lodge are comfortably luxurious. Most have their own fireplace, Spa Suites, not surprisingly, have spa baths, and technologies include DVD players, CD player and, for those who don’t want to completely escape, free broadband internet.

content: When you’re staying in the center of the world’s largest ski area, hanging around the hotel is hardly a priority. But it’s hard to resist doing just that if you’re a guest at Le CouCou. Just a quick slide away from the lifts of Méribel, this ski-in, ski-out luxury hotel is housed in a ten-story wooden chalet with a wide terrace overlooking the slopes, indoor and outdoor pools separated by glass, three restaurants, and a Tata Harper spa. Interiors are sophisticated but warm, flooded with natural light and furnished with a mix of antique pieces and custom-made modern decor. \n\nEclectic details include retro-inspired murals and a collection of vintage cuckoo clocks, though guest rooms have more of a classic ski lodge aesthetic, featuring wood paneling and cozy, colorfully patterned carpets. A generous breakfast buffet with fresh pastries and locally produced charcuterie is ideal for fueling up before a day out exploring Les 3 Vallées. After a day on the slopes there’s a choice of hearty fondue or raclette at Le Fumoir, gourmet dishes of oysters, blue lobster, and Sologne caviar at the bistronomic Biancaneve, or cuts of the world’s rarest meats at Beefbar. Guests can also enjoy aprés-ski drinks at The Bar des Pistes, or on the deck with panoramic views over the landscape.

content:
Like the Taj Mahal, The Blue Mansion was inspired by a love story. Cheong Fatt Tze, a wealthy Chinese businessman, built this opulent mansion, located in historic George Town on the Malaysian island of Penang, for one of his wives. Today it’s a luxury hotel that doubles as a museum and occasional film set — you saw it in “Crazy Rich Asians.” 

Tinged with virbant indigo, the mansion is majestic inside and out, featuring a series of strikingly picturesque courtyards and fanciful details from Chinese carved screens and colorful mosaic murals to large Gothic windows fitted with Art Nouveau-style stained glass. Guest suites, designed according to the principles of feng shui, are palatial and peaceful. Some have clawfoot tubs and elegant living rooms, others have deep Jacuzzis and gilded beds; all are beautifully appointed and filled with priceless art and antiques. 

The hotel restaurant offers gourmet tasting menus, while the sultry bar offers gorgeously presented cocktails and live music sets highlighting the guzheng, a traditional Chinese stringed instrument, after dark.

content:
The Shangri-La hotel group may have found its worthiest namesake in this Lhasa venture. Lucky them — around these parts, the Himalayan landscape does the heavy lifting, and any halfway-decent hotel could draw tourist traffic with judiciously placed windows. Lucky for us, this hotel goes far beyond halfway. It’s largely predicated on the business-class luxury chain model, sure, but a beating Tibetan heart persists behind it all, especially in the design philosophy and the cuisine.

First things first: acclimatization is an absolute must at 12,000 feet. Tempting as it is to go straight for the cocktails, you’d do better to visit the on-site health clinic or the 24-hour oxygen lounge beforehand (not just a gimmick — trust us, it helps). Once your head’s on straight, you can twist it right back off at Shambala, the hotel’s tapas-and-cocktails bar with a garden terrace, or Lodgers Lounge, the gorgeously chandeliered and high-ceilinged tea bar with truly stupefying views of the mountains. For heartier fare, Shang Palace melds Cantonese and Sichuan cuisine in an intimate setting, while Altitude maintains an all-day international buffet with live cooking stations.

Shangri-La’s 262 rooms and 17 suites make ample use of rich Tibetan visual details, balancing earthy golds and ochres with vivid striping and intricately patterned textiles. Captivating filigrees smarten up lighting fixtures and foot chests, while the ivory-hued walls and dark woods lend a peaceful, meditative quality that ties it all together. Downstairs, a fully equipped gym, swimming pool, and spa await should you need to mix some action into all that stillness. Opt for the Horizon Club for dedicated concierge service, a private lounge, and complimentary breakfast and evening cocktails.

Beyond the Shangri-La’s doors, Lhasa is rich with rewarding finds for your inner explorer. The Potala and Norbulingka palace complexes, respectively the former winter and summer residences of the Dalai Lama, are both within walking distance. Two of Tibet’s holy lakes are within a day’s journey, not to mention the abundance of monasteries with more than 13 centuries of priceless historical artifacts. Roof of the world, heart of the Himalayas, land of the gods — whatever you call this mountain paradise, you’re sure to satisfy your loftiest ambitions here.

content:
A sleepy alpine valley as the setting for a modern design hotel — you must be in northern Italy. The sleek black-clad acute triangle that is Nerocubo stands in the midst of a natural landscape that has inspired awe since the Stone Age. Ostensibly geared for business travelers who desire access to a modern, full-service hotel en route to more urban destinations, the Nerocubo is also sited for easy access to the nearby Lake Garda and the Dolomite mountains, so the work-play balance needn’t be neglected. Excellent skiing and trekking opportunities abound, with visits to the thermal baths to round off the R&R.
 
Inside the hotel, the matte black seamlessly winds its way through the minimalist décor, anchoring the palette of white, wood and muted jewel tones. The rooms are functionally diverse, including a wellness suite with its very own neon-lit sauna, a business suite with adjoining living/conference room, and an oversized deluxe family suite that features a freestanding entertainment center. And it’s worth noting ahead of time that if you book a room with a view — such as the Sky or Panorama suites, with their full-length windows — you’ll awaken to a stunning view of the surrounding Dolomites.
 
Fitness suites are outfitted with weights, benches, and cardiovascular machines, wellness suites offers massage and a sauna directly in-room, and business suites provide space for en suite conferencing and meetings. For those who are interested solely in play, the full-service wellness center houses a turkish bath, sauna, solarium, and pool, with an “ice waterfall” that probably sounds more appealing after a spell in the sauna. There’s a lending library, ample business and conference facilities, and the restaurant and lounge stay open late with an extensive menu and a typically Italian wine list.  

How to get there:
Nerocubo is approximately 45 minutes’ drive from Verona’s Valerio Catullo airport (VRN) and 55 minutes’ drive from Bolzano (BZO).

Despite its industrial past, it’s plentifully supplied with light — rooms get plenty of sun, and the split-level suites look out through double-height windows. And while this is a country town, the Hotel du Vin feels a bit more like a city club, with three private dining rooms to add to its French bistro. Meanwhile the wine selection is serious and deep, as it ought to be in a place called the Hotel du Vin.

content: Thanda Safari Lodge stands apart, not for how much it offers, but for how thoughtfully it does. Thanda means “love” in Zulu, and this privately owned reserve delivers exactly that: a deep love for land, culture, wildlife and its guests. Opened by Zulu royalty and spanning 14,000 hectares in northern Zululand, Thanda Safari is proudly conservationist and unapologetically rooted in local tradition. Backed by genuine ties to the local Zulu community, this private reserve offers access to the Big Five. Suites are expansive, circular, and designed for privacy, each with its own plunge pool and boma. It is a safari experience that doesn't try to impress, it simply gets it right.

content: A few blocks from Piazza di Santa Maria Novella, an aristocratic Florentine family built a grand villa; avid supporters of the arts, they spared no expense commissioning local artists to create one-of-a-kind hand-painted ceiling frescoes, murals, and stuccoes throughout the building. Years later, the 19th-century mansion was reborn as the luxurious boutique hotel Dimora Palanca. The Tuscan architect Stefano Bibiani led the careful restoration effort, preserving the villa’s best features — the art, of course, but also its stately columns, original parquet flooring, and marble staircases — while interior designer Paolo Dovichi infused the interiors with modern décor by Italian brands like Maxalto and Flos. Rooms and suites are sleek and elegant, many featuring quaint balconies overlooking the jasmine-scented courtyard garden, and an array of art-filled common spaces include a drawing room, a chess lounge, and a cozy lounge bar.

A complimentary shuttle service connects guests to the heart of Florence in just 15 minutes.

It’s a classic love story—with a twist. Owner Dieter Morszeck fell in love, not with another person, but with Portugal’s stunning Alentejo winemaking region. He bought more than 200 acres and set to work redesigning the estate with an eye on sustainability and a dream of sharing this beautiful place with discerning travelers. Mission accomplished.

At first glance, these accommodations - defined by a minimalist sensibility - could easily be in a cosmopolitan destination but one glance out the window at the rows and rows of grapes is immediately grounding. This is a place to unwind by the pool soaking up the surroundings or walking or biking through the gardens and vineyards. Three restaurants put the focus on epicurean pursuits with plenty of wine tasting, naturally.

content: There are just a handful of places to stay in the New Bund, also known as the Qiantan International Business Zone. It’s one of Shanghai’s newest neighborhoods, and hotels in the area tend to match its modern sophistication, including the design-focused Artyzen NEW BUND 31 Shanghai. Rooms and suites are calm and minimalist with extra-high ceilings, huge windows, pale wood floors, and accent walls in shades inspired by traditional Chinese gardens: rose pink, grass green, and cerulean blue. The sleek wooden furniture is custom-made, and local artists are behind the black-and-white ink artwork on display. Slate gray bathrooms have vaulted ceilings, deep soaking tubs, and separate rainfall showers. The hotel’s restaurant, Shanghai Modern, offers seating on an open-air terrace, and the adjacent lounge serves afternoon tea in a canopied secret garden.

content: The Trigano family, first famous for the Club Med resorts, took a decidedly youthful turn when they launched the Mama Shelter line of urban boutique hotels. And though the Mama Shelter flag flies over cities as distant as London, Belgrade, and even Los Angeles, the soul of the brand remains in France. Mama Shelter Rennes, in fact, plays an outsize role in its hometown’s boutique hospitality scene; while Mama Shelter has competition in places like Paris and Marseille, there’s nothing else quite like it anywhere in the country’s northwest.\n\nMama Shelter Rennes occupies a landmark building at the heart of the medieval city center; while all of the exterior and much of the interior has been carefully preserved, the atmosphere inside is as rambunctiously postmodern as any of the brand’s hotels. The vibe throughout is communal and convivial, from the restaurant, bar, terrace, and rooftop to the three (!) karaoke rooms. A spa, an indoor pool, and a smallish but well-equipped gym are on hand for a spot of self-care. And the rooms, as is the Mama Shelter custom, are efficient in their layouts, playful in their décor, and perfectly equipped for an audience whose tastes lean toward the boutique side of the boutique/luxury divide.

content: Asheville, North Carolina is a Southern city with a counterculture streak — and, not incidentally, a surplus of decommissioned industrial buildings in lovely red brick. content:
The word “guesthouse” slightly understates the scale, but it captures the concept: Kinn Guesthouse looks and feels like a perfectly modern design-forward boutique hotel, but with a slightly low-key, all-suite residential vibe. This means a self-guided check-in with no traditional front desk, and a set of fully stocked kitchens for guest use.

The suites, for their part, are as stylish as any big-city boutique hotel, and benefit from plenty of extra space as well as substantial comforts — the bedrooms are furnished with attractive, usable pieces, including luxe Omaha mattresses and bedding by Brooklinen, and the bathrooms are positively indulgent. The look is the sort of urban-loft aesthetic at which this storied industrial city excels, made even more modern by the inclusion of some adventurous color choices and eye-catching contemporary art.

Guests with an appetite for self-catering are welcome to use one of Kinn Guesthouse’s fully stocked communal kitchens; for full service, there’s the Wolf on Broadway, a restaurant and bar by the local restaurateurs Wolfgang Schaefer and Whitney McAllister. Beyond that, downtown Milwaukee is blessed with seemingly no end of worthwhile restaurants and bars, not to mention shops and other attractions — though the service concept may be low-profile, your hosts are full of recommendations.

The first foray into India for the Singapore-based Raffles Hotels & Resorts is a suitably monumental hotel — Raffles Udaipur is set on a 21-acre private island in the middle of Udai Sagar Lake, and guests arrive at the lakeshore launch for an unforgettable arrival by boat. The gardens and grounds are spectacular, and the entry hall, with its soaring columns and marble floors, is nothing short of regal — as is the service, which is as devoted as you might expect from the conjunction of Raffles and a Rajasthani palace.

Meanwhile the hotel’s 101 rooms and suites are scarcely less extravagant; there’s nothing the least bit minimalist about any of them, and lake views, happily, can be found all up and down the range. Some come with private gardens, still others with private pools, and the suites are practically self-contained residences. At every level they’re 

The common facilities include a very extensive spa and wellness program as well as a multitude of meeting and events spaces, suitable for anything from a conference to a wedding. A handful of restaurants serve everything from upscale Rajasthani flavors to coffee and pastries at the Raffles Patisserie; the hotel’s highly polished nightspots include the swanky English-style Writers Bar.

(It’s also downtown-adjacent, in the other direction.) This slightly less campus-centered location doesn’t cramp the Graduate Columbus’s style, though — the rooms, for example, are every bit as Buckeyes-focused as you’d expect from an installment of the Graduate brand.

The hotel is full of references to Ohio and Columbus history, including and beyond OSU — perhaps an enlargement of a coin commemorating track star Jesse Owens, or an embroidered portrait of native son John Glenn, depicted in full astronaut regalia. Scarlet and gray, the OSU school colors, feature prominently in the décor, but the look transcends school-spirit kitsch, edging into eclectic, contemporary boutique-hotel territory.

As in many Graduates, there’s a Trophy Room café, serving breakfast and coffee in a self-consciously scholastic environment. And while some Graduates feature elaborate campus-themed restaurants and bars, the Graduate Columbus leaves the provision of food and beverages largely to the neighborhood — there’s a Shake Shack in the building, and any number of other worthy restaurants and bars in the greater Short North area.

content: Minutes away from the seaside resort of Touquet-Paris-Plage, Le Pré Rainette looks like an old-fashioned country manor with a red-tiled roof and whitewashed walls. But the building is actually a new construction modeled after the region’s traditional farmhouses. The owners hunted for antique treasures to furnish the place accordingly: among their finds are big wooden tables, romantic old fireplaces, and vintage tiles. The main house has a few guest rooms, one featuring a freestanding tub with views of the surrounding forest, the other a two-room suite that’s perfect for families. A separate cottage offers a kitchen and a cozy living room. On the beautifully landscaped grounds that surround both houses, there’s a heated swimming pool, rose gardens, and a pond populated by frogs that inspired the hotel’s name. The owners lend bicycles for exploring nearby trails or pedaling to the coast.\n

content:
If Queensland’s Gold Coast is Australia’s version of Southern California, then Coolangatta is its Venice, or maybe its Laguna Beach — it’s the exceedingly unpretentious, chilled-out side of the Gold Coast suburbs. Which means that a hotel like The Pink Hotel is guaranteed to stand out. It’s as relaxed as you could want it to be, perfectly in tune with its setting, but there’s an urban edge to the design that feels unusual here. 

With occasionally risqué graphic murals, stylish modern furniture, exposed timber ceilings, polished concrete floors, and unique neon artworks in every room, the accommodations are almost precisely the opposite of what you’d expect from a low-key beach town — there’s nary a vintage surfboard or Polynesian motif to be found. The hotel’s four suites add a fold-out couch in the lounge and a record player, and all rooms come with Bluetooth speakers and Smeg mini-fridges.

And the public spaces are no less unexpected. A hotel isn’t ordinarily where you’d look to find a hip little hair salon and tattoo shop, but there you are. The rooftop lounge with its Astroturf and open cabanas is delightfully unpretentious, while the Janitors Closet piano bar and the Sugar Cube function/karaoke room are intensely atmospheric. And Eddie’s Grub House completes the package: it’s a burger bar featuring live music, an encyclopedic selection of whiskies, and probably the most vibrant crowd in town.

The name is ever so slightly ambiguous, but a glance at the décor will probably be enough to reveal that this is neither Ohio nor Oxfordshire but Oxford, Mississippi, home of Ole Miss, the University of Mississippi; also home to all things seersucker, sweet tea, and genteel Old South charm. It’s set in the heart of the city, about a mile from campus, and is as well suited to nightlife as it is to the life of the mind.

When it comes to paying tribute to the locale, Graduate hotels always go all the way — but what makes them great is the way they stop just short of theme-hotel kitsch overload. If you’re dead set against mixing patterns, then the gingham, tartan, and polka-dot motif in the guest rooms might cross a line, but for most of us it’s good preppy fun, and it’s accompanied by an up-to-date understanding of what makes a boutique hotel room function properly.

Cabin 82, the hotel’s café, is a detailed homage to the local county fair, as well as a damn fine place for a chicken biscuit. And the Coop, up on the fourth-floor terrace, is an unexpected rooftop restaurant and bar, featuring memorable views of The Square and live blues acts several nights a week.

content:
A lot of big business hotels claim to occupy a “privileged” position, or offer a “unique” or even a “commanding” view. In the case of the Four Seasons Riyadh, though, it’s a tough proposition to argue with. It’s a part of the Kingdom Tower, an award-winning, vaguely bottle-opener-shaped 99-story skyscraper. And though the hotel only goes about halfway up, the view is still certifiably commanding — the Kingdom Tower doesn’t just dominate the skyline, it is the skyline.

Luxury hotels in the Arab world are a conservative lot, no matter how opulent — the Toronto-based Four Seasons group is a perfect fit. Colors are muted and everything’s impeccably tasteful, clothing the lavish rooms and suites in a rather unassuming look. It would be hard to compete with the view, anyway.

It’s a business traveler’s paradise, with all the boxes checked: 24-hour business center, internet everywhere, and long hours in the pool, spa and gym. There are a handful of dining options on-site if you’re pressed for time, and the neighborhood offers many more, plus some of the best shopping Riyadh has to offer. Don’t miss the top-floor skybridge, for the near-infinite views.


How to get there:
All major international and domestic airlines serve King Khaled International Airport, which is about 30 minutes from the hotel. This airport is served by Emirates, Cathay Pacific, British Airways, Air France, Lufthansa and Saudia, which provides commuter service from Jeddah and Dammam daily.

content:
There’s more to India than riotous city scenes and stately old palace hotels. Two hours south of New Delhi, and less than an hour south of the tech-heavy satellite city of Gurgaon, there’s a luxury resort that’s quite unlike what we’ve come to expect from five-star Indian hospitality. This is the Westin Sohna, a thirty-five-acre estate that’s as tranquil as Delhi itself is chaotic, home to a hotel that’s as understatedly modern as the Taj Mahal is unashamedly traditional.

With just ninety-seven rooms, suites and villas, the Westin is intimate — especially in light of its corporate lineage. The result is not just a quieter, more sedate experience, but also that when it comes to services and amenities — and sheer space across its thirty-five acres of gardens and grounds — there’s more to go around.

The rooms are sleek and modern yet still identifiably local in character, and they’re outfitted with all the luxe necessities, from LCD televisions and rain showers to the Westin-signature Heavenly Bed. Also Heavenly is the spa, all sixteen thousand square feet of it, and it’s a veritable United Nations of massages and treatments, from Thai and Balinese to Chinese and Ayurvedic. The end product is a resort that’s tailor-made for some serious unplugging, and is used as such by Delhi residents and business travelers alike — the proximity to Gurgaon, with its high concentration of multi-national corporate headquarters, means this place sees more than its share of (extremely relaxed) business junkets.

How to get there:

The Westin Sohna Resort & Spa is located less than 40 miles from New Delhi’s Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) and is 45 minutes from Gurgaon.

content:
Just the phrase “airport hotel” is enough to summon a certain gloom, a utilitarian look, a dull business-park location and a philosophy that places economy above aesthetics. The Aviator Hotel, however, is a different animal. The concept was dreamt up by the Scottish hotelier Ken McCulloch, the man responsible for such formidable lodgings as One Devonshire Gardens, and it’s an ambitious one: by turning its back on the traditional conception of the airport hotel, and embracing everything that’s cool, romantic and dazzling about aviation, it’s done nothing less than re-invent the genre.

Then again Farnborough Airfield is not exactly your typical airport. Here in this corner of Hampshire you’ll see more Gulfstreams than Airbuses, more CEOs than package-holiday tourists, owing both to the fact that it’s home to a fair few corporate headquarters, and also close enough to West London for private-jet access. This explains why the Aviator isn’t called The Economy Class, for one thing, and why it’s more like a private club than an ordinary business hotel.

The corridors radiate off a central lobby like blades on a propeller, and the rooms are luxe, masculine in color, clubby in paneled wood, with comforts that are on the level of any luxury hotel. Upscale dining in the Brasserie and fine cocktails in the Sky Bar complete the experience — this is the rare place where a drink in the bar of an airport hotel sounds positively enticing.

content: Locals and design enthusiasts alike sat up and paid attention when the Belgian artist Laurence Leenaert, founder of the Marrakech-based lifestyle brand LRNCE, announced the opening of a five-room, adults-only guesthouse in an old mansion near the Bahia Palace. Rosemary is a jewel of a riad hotel with every detail curated by Leenaert and her Moroccan partner, including vintage pieces uncovered on her travels around the world, and many carried out by a team of local artisans, from bespoke homewares and hand-carved furnishings to stained glass windows and custom terrazzo floors. Each room is uniquely outfitted with decor from the LRNCE line; some have private balconies, and others offer views over the courtyard patio with its giant jacaranda tree. A traditional breakfast is served on the rooftop terrace, and the hotel’s charming hammam opens on request.

content:
Though it’s located within the city limits of the Sichuan capital — and, incidentally, not terribly close to any ocean — the Ocean Spring Resort Chengdu - MGallery feels nothing like an urban hotel. It’s a solid twenty miles from the center of this sprawling city, and it’s set on a sliver of parkland, adjacent to the Tianfu International Finance Center, which happens to be home to a natural hot spring.

Combined with its closed-in, compound-like construction, this situation creates a rural-resort vibe at Ocean Spring — one that its rooms and villas, with their garden views and (in the latter case) indoor-outdoor lounge space, only serve to heighten. The villas come with their own hot spring pools, while all guests share access to the 3,500-square-meter hot spring bath and spa complex, as well as extensive facilities for fitness, for meetings, and for chess(!).

L’Orange, the all-day restaurant, displays some French influence, and showcases the produce of Jintang, the agricultural region just to the east of the city. Meanwhile the Spring Bar keeps guests mingling over an astonishing variety of teas, as well as wines, cocktails, and a light all-day menu.

content:
We all know the Park Hyatt hotels tend to be something special, even by luxury-hotel standards. And we’re equally aware that Qatar has a taste for a certain extravagance in construction. Still, by any standard, the Park Hyatt Doha is surprising — from the outside, it’s monumental enough to be a museum, while on the inside it’s as well-composed, quietly lavish, and eminently livable as any Park Hyatt anywhere.

Even the humblest of its 187 rooms spans some 40 square meters and includes blackout curtains, a 55-inch television, a Nespresso machine, and a marble bathroom with both a rain shower and a separate soaking tub. Safe to say there’s nothing to find fault with, and plenty to love, including the décor’s subtle interplay of traditional craft and modern design.

Also on hand is a vast spa, fitness, and pool complex, as well as a wealth of business facilities. It’s also got no fewer than three restaurants, including the upscale Japanese Sora as well as Opus, an open-kitchen concept helmed by a team made up of Qatari celebrity chef Shams Al Qassabi and the Michelin-starred Jean-François Rouquette.

And beyond the Park Hyatt’s doors, the immediate setting, Msheireb Downtown Doha, is a planned redevelopment of the city’s historic Mushayrib district; upon completion, the Park Hyatt will be surrounded by museums and cultural attractions as well as a panoply of business and commercial destinations.

content: For most hoteliers, college towns are a missed opportunity, or maybe just easy money — a captive audience and a few guaranteed periods of sky-high demand mean that most of them don’t try all that hard. But if you didn’t sleep through your economics classes, you might have learned that an irrational market presents an opportunity. It’s a lesson that the minds behind Graduate Hotels certainly learned, and the Graduate Bloomington, just off the west end of the Univiersity of Indiana campus, goes all out to make the grade. Like the other Graduates in college towns across America, it’s full of personality, and painstakingly tailored to the particularities of its setting. Here that means paying plentiful tribute to the university’s basketball tradition — Larry Bird is the most famous Hoosier, but far from the only one — and décor that celebrates Indiana’s agricultural history even as it updates it for the boutique-hotel era. The lobby contains vintage bleachers from courtside, and there are graphic nods to Indiana grad Will Shortz, the man who’s become synonymous with the New York Times crossword. And any day now they’ll draw open the curtain on Poindexter Coffee, serving breakfast sandwiches and pastries alongside the expected strong brew. (Not that kind of brew — local laws prohibit alcohol sales in this particular corner of downtown.)

content:
If there’s one thing India does well it’s massive, lavish, and extremely well-equipped business hotels — unfortunately for the more design-sensitive among us, they tend to be extremely conservative in style. Not so, however, the ITC Sonar, on the outskirts of town near the Science City. This is a sleek, modern and surprisingly green hotel, billing itself as a “business resort” — and set on sixteen acres of land, with golf, tennis and jogging facilities, it’s more than just a slogan.

The Singapore-based Kerry Hill Architects laid out this wide-open resort along lily-padded waterways, bringing a bit of riverside romance to what could otherwise have looked a bit like an office park. Rooms are spread about the grounds, the more basic ones occupying the tower, the more lavish ones in low-slung secondary buildings, with views out over the lush surroundings. All rooms, tower or otherwise, are standard high-end luxury, crisp and contemporary but not overwhelmingly high-design.

From the pool, spa and fitness center to the modest handful of restaurants and bars, you’ll find the ITC Sonar to be a pretty self-sufficient hotel. If there’s a down side, it’s in the fact that it’s a taxi ride from the city center — but that’s the trade you make for such country charms as the lily ponds and the pitch & putt golf course.



How to get there:
From Netaji Subhas Chandra Airport, 14.64 km - approximately 17 mins.

content: Located in the heart of Burgundy, the medieval town of Beaune is a bastion of wine-country tradition. Not the first place you’d expect to find a contemporary boutique hotel, let alone one with colorful interiors by a California-based designer and a Vietnamese restaurant conceived by the late James Beard Award–winning chef Charles Phan. Mirabel Hotel & Restaurant Group partnered with a local fifth-generation winemaking family to create Maison 1896, easily the most luxurious hotel to open in the area for years. The glamorous Beaux-Arts-style corner building is historic, and plenty of in-room details are quintessentially French — gilded mirrors, elegant writing desks, original oak beams, quaint dormer windows — but the handmade custom beds, heated limestone floors, and smart-looking blue-tiled cocktail bar feel refreshingly modern.

content: Tucked away in an opulent mansion in Nîmes’ UNESCO-protected historic center, just a few blocks from the famous Roman amphitheater, Margaret Hotel Chouleur may well be the most romantic boutique hotel in town. It’s hard to say which space is the loveliest — the striking ground-level Rouge restaurant, with its high-arching scarlet walls and towering bar, the elegant library with its jewel-toned sofas and vintage cocktail carts, or the grand spiral staircase leading up to the sophisticated rooms and suites, with their hardwood floors, leather furnishings, and boldly tiled bathrooms. But the distinction probably belongs to the hotel’s open-air courtyard: bordered on three sides by the building’s decorative walls and strung with twinkling lights, it’s a wildly picturesque spot for a morning dip in the plunge pool or a sunset apéritif.

content: Steps from La Rochelle’s historic market and a short stroll from the port, Maison des Ambassadeurs is the only high-end hotel in town, though it feels more like the elegant home of an aristocratic French family. For many years, that’s exactly what it was: the upscale abode of the diplomat Albert Bodard, a native of the city who always returned to his favorite residence between stints in Mexico, Iran, Afghanistan, and China. He reportedly loved receiving guests in the elegant salons of this 18th-century house, and the social atmosphere lives on in its lively ground-level bar, where afternoon tea and apéritifs are served all day by a grand stone fireplace and tables spill out onto a pair of sunny poolside courtyards in warmer weather. In homage to Bodard’s heyday, the look is mid-century modern — rooms have parquet floors, leather headboards, vintage lamps, and antique writing desks  — with a color palette inspired by the nearby ocean and salt flats, where guests are welcome to venture on the hotel’s e-bikes.

content: Naturalis is best known, at least in Italy, as an organic beauty and skincare line, whose ingredients are cultivated on an 18th-century farm in Puglia — which is also home to the brand’s elegant countryside retreat, Naturalis Bio Resort & Spa. A larger saltwater pool, lined in pale stone and bordered by canopied daybeds, is a highlight.

content: Clever, functional design and affordable luxury are the hallmarks of TRIBE, the Australian-born hotel brand. Lyon is an arts and culture capital, and its bohemian neighborhood of Croix-Rousse, known for its silk-weaving tradition and lively street art scene, was the perfect place to open a hotel that doubles as a creative hub and social space. Indeed, TRIBE Lyon Croix Rousse’s primary selling points are its common spaces: a light-filled all-day eatery and bar, a coffee shop that runs in collaboration with a local roaster, a 24-hour lounge with co-working areas, and an open-air patio for reading or relaxing.\n\nThe rooms are, in a sense, secondary — but they’re smart in their simplicity. Each comes with a TRIBE signature bed, a coffee and tea station, and a compact, vintage-styled bathroom with a rain shower. The look is minimalist but cheerful, with rose pink and emerald green accent walls, retro reading lamps, and sixties-inspired modular furniture. In addition to the lively common areas, TRIBE Lyon Croix Rousse offers a small fitness center and grab-and-go gourmet snacks prepared by the hotel’s chef. Both are available around the clock; the invitation is implicit to come and go as you please.

content: Los Cabos has earned a well-deserved reputation as one of Mexico’s hottest destinations. Known as a playground for honeymooners and hipsters, it’s often fallen short for those with kids in tow. Not at Solaz, where family-friendly service and amenities are top notch. Add in a sandy beach, surprisingly rare in these parts, and you have a winning combination. Of course, just because you can bring the kids doesn’t mean this resort forsakes style. The 145 rooms and suites are the epitome of coastal chic, showcasing sea views while sporting eye-catching Mexican huanacaxtle wood details. Even if you didn’t book one of the rooms with a private plunge pool, you’ll have plenty of space to stretch out at one of four Olympic-size infinity pools or on the sandy beach. From a fitness center and spa, kids’ and teens’ clubs, and a collection of restaurants running the gamut from casual to upscale, Solaz offers the full resort experience.

content: It’s a bit of a journey to get to Dunes Lodge, a luxury hotel perched on a remote desert plateau in southern Namibia — but the effort pays off every night, as you fall asleep under the stars. Guest rooms aren’t rooms, exactly: more like tents with wooden frames and canvas blinds that roll up and down, as open or as closed to the surrounding landscape as you like. Each has a bathroom and a deck, but there’s no air conditioning or electricity. There’s more technology around the main lodge — there’s a wi-fi signal if you’re desperate to Instagram a snapshot from your sunrise balloon ride — and inside are lounge spaces, a library, and an excellent restaurant specializing in organic African cuisine paired with Namibian wines. After a morning safari, take a dip in the beautiful swimming pool, located on an elevated wooden deck that seems to rise up out of the desert landscape like a glimmering mirage.\n\nBooking Details: Wolwedans Dunes Lodge requires additional information from guests to ensure the best stay possible. content:
A trip to Chilean Patagonia certainly qualifies as getting away from it all — especially a luxury jungle lodge with just a dozen suites, on a private nature reserve that’s most easily accessible by helicopter or boat. Huilo Huilo Nawelpi Lodge is a jumping-off point to explore the glacial lakes, volcanoes, and hot springs of the southern Andes, but the hotel is a destination in itself. Treehouse-like bungalows, connected by a network of forest catwalks, feature rustic-chic wood-beamed interiors, parquet floors, fireplaces, soaking tubs, and private terraces. There’s a heated outdoor pool, an elegant spa, and a gourmet restaurant and bar, all with views of the surrounding woods. Look out for wildlife: Nawelpi means “Spirit of the Puma” in the region’s indigenous language.

content:
The old-fashioned charm of Quito survives, in part, because the Ecuadorean capital remains somewhat off the tourist radar. Le Parc Hotel is a pioneer on the scene. Quito’s first proper boutique hotel, rising twelve stories and containing 30 executive suites, is a model of sleek urban design and European-style comfort.

Take just one peek into the ultra-contemporary lobby and you’ll feel like you’re not in Ecuador anymore, for better or worse: gothic chandeliers, asymmetrical chaises in white leather and zebra prints, conceptual art pieces, a minimalist (and horizontal) gas fireplace, red shag rugs on glossy hardwood floors, and a cocktail bar so slick it looks like it belongs on the cover of a men’s fashion magazine. Glass, stone, earth tones and stark shades of black, white, and silver continue throughout the suites. Each of the individually decorated guest rooms comes with floor-to-ceiling windows, flatscreen TVs, L’Occitane amenities, and free wifi; some feature futuristic in-room soaking tubs with views over the city.

The dramatically trendy black-and-white interior may seem a little cold during the continental breakfast, but the atmosphere works well later in the day when guests sample South American fusion cuisine at Blu, the hotel’s restaurant, and congregate for cocktails in the cool lobby bar or on the rooftop terrace. A small gym and spa round out the Euro-style boutique offerings at the stylish Le Parc, located around the corner from the Quito’s financial district and the national soccer stadium.

content: Half a world away from its Beaux Arts forebear, on a white stretch of beach where Yalong Bay National Resort’s verdant mangroves meet the South China Sea, this St. Regis property satisfies the typical East Asian resort hallmarks: isolation, opulence, and the kind of fawning, maximalist service that many C-suite travelers have come to expect. It’s the type of immersive, cloistered retreat where you needn’t leave the premises for any reason whatsoever. Here on Hainan Island, the southern tip of China’s southernmost province, is a sanctuary purpose-built for the business elite. Case in point: St. Regis Sanya makes a point of offering the region’s only sail-in and sail-out services for luxury yachters, no doubt a major privilege given the world-class marina just next door. Come to think of it, just about every aspect of the stay centers around waterfront appeal — a full suite of water sports, massages on the beach, speedboat and jet-ski excursions, private pools surrounded by manicured tropical flora, and of course a bevy of al fresco dining options. The rooms take full advantage of the visual smorgasbord, pairing floor-to-ceiling views of the bay and/or jungle-clad hills with furnished private balconies. Wisely, they’ve opted to emphasize glass and polished marble to retain an airy, light-drenched feel in the interiors. Everything comes in smooth, calculated curves offset by plenty of negative space. It’s resolutely unchallenging and well-suited to a daily siesta. Of course, textbook luxury abounds; look just about anywhere and you’ll find chenille furniture, sumptuous area rugs, mahogany highlights, and oodles of track lighting. Bathrooms in particular go all-out with in-mirror TVs, double vanities, deep-soak tubs, rainforest showers, and Remède bath products. A tasteful blend of technology and aristocracy rounds out the experience: each room boasts flatscreens, an iPod dock, and a built-in sound system, but you’ll also encounter a butler service window, complimentary shoeshines, and in-room flower arrangements. Really, it would be hard not to lapse into a soothed, frictionless haze after just a few hours here. Everything from the persimmon-and-eggshell palette to the high, coffered ceilings to the gardened courtyard with attached spa facilities bespeaks a breezy, island M.O. Take in the champagne-sabering ritual and live jazz at the Drawing Room, go for a poolside cocktail (hell, go for three), stroll through the banyan groves, and don’t feel bad about unadulterated indulgence. You can afford to be this carefree.

content:
The world needs more hotels like the Dormero in Hannover: simple, shiny, clean, with a name that’s fun to say and a regular dance party off the lobby. Like its siblings elsewhere in Germany, the Dormero Hotel in Hannover offers no-nonsense modernity. No pampering, but no pretension either. Soundproofed rooms come with two huge screens, one for TV and one for the Internet, perfect for multitasking. Cute red touches offset the white-and-gray décor and prevent the monochrome from being monotone. 

In addition to the aforementioned party, the bar has the beers you’d expect given the locale. It also has cocktails you might not expect, including one called “sweet & sour meets balls,” which we’re hoping tastes better in German. Screens flash kooky close-ups and forlorn landscapes; occasionally go-go dancers do their thing on tables or the bar to live music. The mellower restaurant skews Italian (a big breakfast is included). There’s also a small spa on site, with workout facilities. Finally, we should mention the free mini-bar, luxe touch in a sensibly priced hotel. As you might expect, the property is popular with business travelers.   

Steps from the hotel’s entrance is a tram stop, so you’re always fairly close to wherever you need to be. Maschsee, the lovely lake in the center of town, is an easy walk. You can take a boat ride or just take in the scenery.

content:
Could a hotel possibly be more emblematic of its place? Just three miles from the new international airport, on the border between Delhi and economically booming Gurgaon, the 322-room Leela is as ambitious, as modern, as opulent and as highly functional a business hotel as you’d expect given its location — that is, if your expectations have kept pace with Gurgaon’s steroidal growth. 

Guest rooms, by the prolific interior design firm Hirsch Bedner, are spacious and contemporary. Each one includes a large work station and thoughtful details like Bose iPod docks and laptop-sized safes with built-in chargers. All accommodations other than the Executive suite, which has views of the business district, overlook the Rajokri Nature Reserve, an unexpected expanse of quiet green in sharp contrast to the frenzy of the city. It’s a reminder that, not terribly long ago, this was a sleepy town on the way-outskirts of Delhi. 

Those hundreds of lavish guest rooms, views and all, are really only the beginning. There’s also a 20,000-square-foot spa, an enormous fitness room with glass walls overlooking the nature reserve, a heated outdoor pool, and enough ballrooms and board rooms and conference facilities to host a lifetime’s worth of meetings. The dining and drinking options are just as impressive. The flagship restaurant has no fewer than seven separate exhibition kitchens, another restaurant is home to a sous-chef who was formerly a Master Chef judge, and for complete gustatory overload, another still offers four guests each night a thirty-six-course Italian dinner. Then there’s Rubicon Bar, presently home to one of the world’s nine remaining bottles of fifty-year-aged Glenfiddich. Let’s hope you can expense it.

content:
As a place so strongly defined by its historic past, a place visitors come to stroll the cobblestone streets, escape the frenzied pace of Buenos Aires and admire the beautifully preserved colonial architecture, Colonia can be forgiven for being a bit predictable. That, after all, is its appeal; the town has looked and felt about the same for the past 250 years. So it comes as a surprise that instead of an old-fashioned colonial-style hotel in the Barrio Histórico, we have the Costa Colonia, a decidedly modern hotel that trades views of old stone homes for sunsets over the Rio Plata. It’s the sort of mid-size apartment-style hotel you’d sooner expect to find in Palermo Soho. There’s a minimum of fussiness, instead an abundance of sunlight pouring in through floor-to-ceiling windows, modern blonde wood furniture, crisp white linens and airy curtains. 

Even the smallest of the rooms, the 450-square-foot Loft, includes a kitchenette and a balcony, so if you don’t want to make the pleasant half-hour walk into the center of town, you could stay in to cook a light meal and enjoy it in open-air privacy. Better yet, upgrade to one of the river view rooms for, you guessed it, excellent views of the Rio Plata. By boat, it’s only forty-five minutes across that river to Buenos Aires, but when you can spend all day soaking up Colonia’s old-world charm without giving up the comforts of 21st-century accommodations, you might not be eager to leave. 


How to get there:
Costa Colonia is a 5-minute drive from the Port of Colonia or about 3 hours and 30 minutes from Montevideo Carrasco International Airport. Transfers from the Port of Colonia can be organized for $10 per car.

content: Bhutan is famous for its rugged mountain landscapes and its Gross National Happiness philosophy, and both come together at Gangtey Lodge, a 12-room luxury adventure hotel in the picturesque Phobjika Valley. It’s aimed, the owners say, at grown-up backpackers who’ve graduated to the luxury market, and it strikes a fine balance between monastic seclusion and plush comfort.\n\nJust up the hill is the Gangtey Monastery, for a look at the real monastic life; here, by contrast, you’ll have an en-suite fireplace, as well as underfloor heating and a roll-top tub with a panoramic mountain view. You’ll also have informal gourmet meals and treatments courtesy of the lodge’s spa. And among the excursions on offer are all manner of outdoor experiences, as well as such cultural offerings as guided meditation sessions with the monks.

content: Queen Victoria of England stayed at the historic Hotel Goldene Rose in 1891, but you wouldn’t guess it from a look at the sleek, understated Queen Vicky Suite. The room where she once slept, like the rest of the hotel, has since seen a thorough modernization. The project, which involved stitching together the old hotel with its adjacent buildings, was an ambitious one, especially considering its location in Dinkelsbühl, one of Germany’s most picturesque medieval towns, where tradition and history are especially revered. Designers NOA carried it off with style, keeping many of the property’s best original features — the quaint half-timbered facade, a romantic staircase, antique mirrors — while breathing new life into a landmark.\n\nRooms have an open layout, with original dark wood beams, pale parquet flooring, and a subdued color palette of white and gray. Some suites are bi-level, with a lofted sleeping area framed by vaulted trusses and a living area with a hanging swing-style sofa. Each features a large, intricate tapestry, a nod to the town’s medieval past, but the bathrooms are almost futuristic. Plenty of interesting old-world details await discovery throughout the hotel, from the fireplace-warmed bar, Vicky, to an antique ballroom that’s now used as a modern cinema. But perhaps the best of all is the attic-level infinity pool, with views of the cathedral through the original gables of the hotel’s roof.

content: The Mediterranean coast of Morocco, to the east of the Strait of Gibraltar, is relatively under-traveled, compared to Atlantic destinations like Casablanca and Essaouira. But it’s not without appeal. One of the attractions, in the town of M’Diq, about twenty miles to the east of Tangier, is the Sofitel Tamuda Bay Beach & Spa. As you’d expect from a Sofitel in Morocco, it’s got more than a little bit of a French accent. It’s to the local firm GM Architects, though, that the buildings owe their very pronounced modern Moroccan style.\n\nThe interiors inherit the royal-and-white color scheme and the mixture of neo-Moorish and modern European design languages, and add colorful murals to the mix, in the process elevating them above ordinary boutique-luxe minimalism. Between the multiple swimming pools, the lavish Sofitel spa, the idyllic Mediterranean beach, and the well-equipped fitness center, guests’ needs for physical relaxation are quite well satisfied, while the food and beverage options include a swanky cocktail bar and Le Marche des Saveurs, which presents a succession of Moroccan, French, Italian, and Asian flavors in a dining room that’s almost as colorful as its cuisine.

content:
Perhaps the purest example of an American college town, Storrs, Connecticut was literally put on the map by the establishment of the school that would eventually become the University of Connecticut. It should come as no surprise, then, to see the Graduate Storrs decked out in Huskies navy, white, and gray — nor, indeed, to find it not near but right on campus, on Bolton Road, amid dormitory complexes and academic buildings.

In typical Graduate style, the interiors are adorned with visual references to the school and the state of Connecticut, from classic New England plaids to references to the university’s first-rate basketball program — if you arrive in athletic shoes, you’ll hear the telltale squeak of the lobby’s basketball-court flooring. Rooms come packed with plenty more Huskies imagery, as well as wallpaper depicting various Connecticut-specific collegiate scenes, plus small boutique-hotel comforts like Malin + Goetz bath products. 

And in a Graduate hotel, the social life is as important as the accommodations; there’s a Poindexter café, for breakfast and coffee in a self-consciously studious environment, as well as the Trophy Room, a restaurant and bar that does double duty as a shrine to UCONN basketball

content: If you know the Graduate hotels, you won’t be surprised to find the lobby of the Graduate East Lansing decked out in Spartans emerald green, with a portrait of Michigan State alum Magic Johnson — made from shoelaces — hanging above the reception desk. The hotel, set just across Grand River Road from the Michigan State University campus, has something of a captive audience, and it knows it well; not a single opportunity to refer to the university’s history is missed, right down to the initials woven into the patterned carpets and the basketball-themed wallpaper hanging in the bathrooms.\n\nIn the rooms, the décor ventures out to rural Michigan, with plaid blankets and artwork depicting nature scenes; the walls are papered in regulation Pantone 567 green, and the headboards are what you might call a Spartan tartan. Meanwhile, the closer you get to the rooftop Graduate Rock Bar — named for its centerpiece, a replica of The Rock, a campus monument — the more you’re surrounded by artifacts from MSU’s sporting history, especially its championship basketball squads. And Poindexter, on the ground floor, is something all Graduate hotels have in common: a café with a self-consciously bookish vibe, perfect for co-working or even some actual studying.

content: Some Alpine chalet hotels stick with determination to the traditional style of a century or more ago; others throw out everything except the mountain views and the peaked roof and upend your expectations with avant-garde design. Alpina, in the Haute-Savoie town of Les Gets, charts a middle path. The mountain-lodge silhouette remains intact, as do the familiar tropes of French Alpine hospitality design: pine paneling, red upholstery, and a pervasive atmosphere of rustic coziness. But all of it has been updated for boutique-savvy 21st-century travelers — this is a hotel with history, but not a historical re-creation.\n\nA location at the heart of the village, and close to the ski lifts, is a large part of Alpina’s appeal. Its rooms range from cozy-but-comfortable singles all the way up to quadruple rooms, plus expansive suites and flexible options for interconnecting accommodations. The relaxation area features an indoor pool, a jacuzzi, a sauna, and a steam shower, and there’s a playroom suited for multiple ages featuring everything from wooden toys to arcade games. Meanwhile the restaurant, Oxalis, serves refined local classics, while the Fireside lounge is ideal for après-ski (or après-hike).

content:
We said we wouldn’t rest until there was a proper independent boutique hotel in every city in America. And while we’re not there just yet, the addition of Beloit, Wisconsin is definitely the right kind of progress. Hotel Goodwin may take its inspiration — and its name — from a 19th-century Beloit landmark, but in its current incarnation it’s every bit a 21st-century boutique hotel.

In the rooms there’s no shortage of space, and each one is outfitted with a 65-inch television, a turntable with a small record collection, and a Keurig coffee maker. The bathrooms are lavish, stone-clad, stocked with Gilchrist & Soames bath products, and feature walk-in showers or, in some rooms, a three-sided glass shower that extends into the bedroom.

And despite its small size — a mere 34 rooms — Hotel Goodwin comes with a wealth of dining and drinking options. Velvet Buffalo, the wine bar, also serves stone-fired pizza and a Sunday brunch, while Truk’t specializes in street-style tacos, accompanied by over a hundred tequilas and whiskeys. Lucy’s #7 is the burger bar, Merrill & Houston’s is a classic steakhouse, and Blue Collar Coffee is exactly what it sounds like. The ace in the hole, however, might be the Rooftop, a bar and events space with an open-air view of the rooftops of downtown Beloit.

content: The city of Lille, at the northern tip of France, has a Flemish-inspired old town filled with brick townhouses and quaint cobblestoned streets. But one of its finest luxury hotels, located nearby in the business district, represents a stylistic departure from traditional Flemish and French architecture. A futuristic triangular glass structure houses the Hôtel Barrière de Lille, complete with a two-story casino and a range of high-end restaurants and bars. It’s evident from outside that guest rooms and suites are flooded with light through floor-to-ceiling windows; inside, they’re spacious and sleek, outfitted in blonde wood paneling, rich jewel tones, cheerful polka dot carpets, and large mirrors that reflect views over the city and the treetops in the neighboring park. Also present are a state-of-the-art spa and a buffet breakfast served on a terrace that’s heated year-round. There’s always a party going on in one of the hotel’s ground-level venues, but when you’ve played your last hand, guest rooms are perfectly soundproofed.\n

content:
There are cities and then there are Special Economic Zones. We’ll spare you most of the backstory; suffice it to say that Shenzhen’s exponential growth has meant that it’s very quickly become the sort of place where the great luxury-hotel groups of the world are falling over one another for the opportunity to practice the art of hospitality on one of the world’s most prestigious stages. This, in short, is how you end up with a hotel like the Langham Shenzhen, where a century and a half of English hospitality heritage meets one of the great cities of the twenty-first century.

It’s apparent at a glance that the Langham is confident in its traditional approach. But for some subtle electronic wizardry, these rooms could have been put together at more or less any time in the last hundred years. The smallest of them is a capacious 40 square meters — that’s 430 square feet — while the ordinary suites are twice that or more, and the Presidential Suite and Chairman’s Suite expand into further multiples.

A handful of restaurants serve everything from upscale Cantonese fare to a note-perfect British high tea complete with Wedgwood china. And the spa, fitness center, and twin swimming pools are all suitably grand as well. In terms of quality the Langham Shenzhen is up there in the top tier — and if you lean towards the classics, then your decision is already made.

content:
Imagine the Saudi Arabian equivalent of the Waldorf-Astoria and you’re well on your way to understanding what sort of place is the Qasr Al Sharq. In fact there’s a good reason for the comparison — it just so happens it’s part of the Waldorf-Astoria collection. Of course this being Jeddah, rather than New York, you’ll find certain concessions made to the locality; the style, obviously, is more suited to the gateway to Mecca than the gateway to the Upper East Side.

In terms of scale as well it’s a bit different from its distant Manhattan cousin. While the typical seven-star hotel (if there is such a thing) spreads hundreds of rooms over dozens of floors, the Qasr Al Sharq holds just forty-six very lavish suites, some of them quite beyond what’s normally considered presidential — rather strengthening the case for its boast that it’s more palace than hotel. We could go on and on enumerating the amenities and the extravagances, but suffice it to say the Qasr Al Sharq has a legitimate claim at being one of the most luxurious hotels in the world.

As for Jeddah, it’s not just a business destination, or a waystation on a pilgrimage. The Saudi second city is a popular holiday destination, with a seaside setting that offers some relief from the furnace-like heat of Riyadh and other inland capitals. As such the Qasr Al Sharq offers some serious leisure opportunities, including a women-only spa, a rare thing indeed in this part of the world. It’s probably not a value proposition, and it’s certainly not for the budget-minded, but for pure richness of experience it’s in a high class indeed.

content:
In a townscape ruled by geometry, the Park Hyatt Canberra has landed smack in the middle between the London Circuit hexagon and State Circle. The building itself is a radial plan that hints at some intended posh governmental design vestige from Canberra’s early days. And unlike the slick Diamant Hotel across the river, the Park Hyatt takes the high road with a restrained design palate more appropriate for dignitaries than DJs. Why might this be a good thing? Well, the Park Hyatt doesn’t just do “restrained” with a bucket of beige paint and a pillow mint, it actually manages to capture the subtle sovereign stateliness of the Capital itself. Canberra is not exactly a picture of pomp, but it has a comforting air of democracy that reappears in the courtyards and crown moldings of the Park Hyatt.  

All of the expected qualities of the Park Hyatt brand are in full force here — you’ll find impeccable service and impeccably buttoned-up accommodations at all levels. Arrivals take place under a porte-cochere worthy of a high-security presidential visit. Once across the threshold the lobby and public spaces are airy and lightly formal, and lastly guest rooms are bright with classic contemporary furnishings, sort of how you’d imagine an Officer’s Club scene from a novel might play out. Bathrooms get a slightly more risky with extreme use of black and white marble; perhaps those are for a different chapter.

In proper Commonwealth fashion, tea is served promptly at 2:30 in the Lounge, regardless of one’s distance from the Crown (16,984 km, in case you’re wondering). Dinner can be more of-the-hour at Axis restaurant, overlooking the lake and serving up modern Australian fare. The Clubhouse contains a gym, pool and spa and can help wind down the day. And once retired to one’s quarters, of course, all state business can wait for tomorrow.

content: Getting away from it all to connect with nature is the whole point of traveling to the remote Akan-Mashu National Park in Eastern Hokkaido, and there’s hardly a better place to do it than one of Wakkanpuri Resorts’ luxurious waterfront villas. Both are positioned on the edge of Lake Kussharo, the largest crater lake in Japan. Though they differ in style — RERA (meaning “wind”) is thrillingly exposed to the elements, with waves splashing against its huge picture windows, while the two-story FURE (meaning “red”) is larger and calmer — both have minimalist living rooms warmed by wood-burning fireplaces, indoor baths fed by hot spring water, and multiple bedrooms. A short path leads to the lakeside restaurant, where the hotel’s chefs serve traditional Japanese cuisine with views of the water.
name: WAKKANUPURI RESORTS

The higher of the two, Schloss Schauenstein, is an ivy-clad masterwork that looks right at home amid the rugged alpine crags and winding valleys. A handful of rooms lend some levity to all that stonework with contemporary, colorful accents and upscale comforts.

content:
Fairmont La Marina Rabat Salé is part of a luxe marina complex on the banks of the Bouregreg River, slightly removed from Rabat’s old medina. It’s no riad hotel but a sizable modern retreat, equipped with a rooftop swimming pool, two fitness centers, and several high-end restaurants. The sleek, spacious interiors are what one would expect from a Fairmont hotel, but there’s a distinct Moorish aesthetic in the mix: the elegant ground-level spaces, though mostly monochromatic in color, are enlivened with artisan-made glass lanterns, geometric tiled flooring, decorative ironwork, and keyhole archways. 

Guest rooms and suites are more contemporary, light-filled and decorated in crisp black and white. Patterned rugs and wall panels, gold-framed mirrors, and abstract artwork depicting Moroccan landscapes add visual interest. Many have balconies with water views, and suites feature furnished outdoor terraces. All have luxurious bathrooms with products by La Bottega.

The hotel is home to one of the best spas in the city — another perk of staying in a newly built hotel — as well as a Moroccan restaurant and a French brasserie. The atrium-like lobby bar, with its white marble and lush greenery, is a treat, but the real highlight is the rooftop, which offers panoramic sunset views and stays open late into the night.

content: Less than two miles from the Austrian border in Germany’s Allgäuer Mountains is a luxury hotel with a name as unique as its setting: HUBERTUS Mountain Refugio Allgäu, a 66-room ski-to-door lodge designed for mountain comfort. content: Shanghai’s Xuhui district is notable for its 19th-century shikumen laneways, narrow roads lined with traditional brick townhouses. They’re a rarity in the high-rise era, but some have been preserved for their architectural heritage, and a few of them find new life as villas in the luxurious Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li. The three-story villas’ extravagant interiors incorporate Parisian influences, courtesy of designer Jaya Ibrahim, as well as the full complement of modern comforts, from Bose sound systems to Diptyque bath products. \n\nAn elaborately equipped spa is an integral part of the experience; this one offers a range of treatments influenced by traditional Chinese medicine. No less essential is the restaurant, Le Comptoir de Pierre Gagnaire, the first outing in mainland China for the famed French chef. Nor is that the extent of the French influence — La Boulangerie is a classic Parisian-style bakery, and Le Bar maintains a European accent as well.

content:
It’s certainly not every day that a design-oriented boutique hotel opens in Chișinău, the capital of Moldova. BERD'S Hotel is no half-measure, but is a fully realized luxury boutique hotel, from its monumental modern exterior to its stylish minimalist rooms, an inspired blend of cosmopolitan contemporary design and traditional Moldovan art and culture.

Visually it’s all down to the Italian architect Luca Scacchetti, whose work underlines the close historical connections between Italy and Moldova. In the rooms this means Tibetan-style Moldovan hand-woven carpets alongside luxe design furniture by Poltrona Frau and lighting by Flos, both contemporary Italian concerns. Signature rooms and suites add freestanding bathtubs, and the Prestige Suite features its own jacuzzi as well as design elements by Antonio Citterio, the Milanese master of luxury home design.

A full-service spa offers everything from massage to the Institut Кérastase, for a thorough beautification. And Arome Locale, the restaurant, takes its cues from Berd’s  design concept, in a moody, elegant space, complete with a capacious wine collection and an expansive cocktail bar.

content:
Chengdu, the capital of China’s Sichuan province, is perhaps less familiar to foreign visitors than places like Beijing or Shanghai. But in an increasingly global world, first-class business hotels like the Shangri-La are needed everywhere, not least in the high-tech industrial center of southwestern China.

The hotel is something of a one-stop shop for business travelers. It’s attached to the 30-story Shangri-La Office Tower, which stands on the banks of the Jinjiang River in central Chengdu. And there’s room, seemingly, for everyone — with just shy of 600 rooms, the Shangri-La is up there with some of the biggest luxury hotels in Asia.

In terms of comfort and design this hotel is the state of the luxury-hotel art — visually it’s a blend of traditional elegance and contemporary chic, and the rooms are as well-equipped as any, with plentiful working space and oversized spa-style bathrooms.

Of course there’s also an actual spa, called Chi, plus a fully-equipped health club. Two restaurants and a lobby lounge cater to business lunches and leisure guests alike, and Mooney’s, the eerily detailed Irish pub, offers the rare opportunity for a pint of the dark stuff on a terrace in Chengdu.

content:
If you’re well-versed in top-flight modern business hotels and you know your Indian cities, the Park Hyatt Hyderabad’s name alone tells you pretty much everything you need to know. It’s an impeccably polished high-end business hotel to suit its tech-driven, business oriented hometown, every bit the equal of the other Park Hyatts of the world — which, needless to say, is a rather high bar in terms of luxury and service. 

The Hyderabad outpost is set in the upscale Banjara Hills area, ten minutes from the Central Business District and the tech hub — a distance that’s just about right when the work day is done and it’s time to sprawl out a bit, away from the crowds. And there is plenty of space in which to sprawl out. Even the most basic rooms are quite large, with king beds, oversized work desks and big, modern bathrooms. The materials are rich, as well, comprising hand-laid walnut parquet floors, feather bedding, high-end robes; the list goes on. 

Outside the guest rooms, the services are best described as comprehensive. Everything from a spa and a sauna to salon and shoeshine service is on offer. This is the kind of hotel that still keeps a doctor on call. There’s also an entire team dedicated to meetings and events, plus plenty of banquet halls and meeting rooms, with all the infrastructure of a top business hotel in a tech-oriented city. 

Last but by no means least is a strong collection of dining and drinking options — an elegant Northern Italian restaurant and wine bar, a Southeast Asian restaurant oriented around an immaculate open kitchen, a dining room where guests can choose from an eclectic menu of classic European cuisine and authentic Indian comfort food, and even a casual lounge for pastries and champagne — pastries and champagne being the sorts of things one takes casually, without need for occasion, at a Park Hyatt.

content:
Canberra, though roughly midway between Sydney and Melbourne, sees but a fraction of the tourist traffic — it’s a purpose-built inland capital, like Madrid without the history or Brasilia without the concrete. But in Peppers Gallery Hotel, Canberra has got itself a high-end boutique hotel that wouldn’t look out of place in either of the neighboring seaside cities.

It’s rare that a city’s first contemporary-style boutique hotel comes off quite so well as this one. The ’20s-vintage building underwent a thorough renovation at the hands of some of Australia’s top architects, and the result is stylish and chock full of personality — especially in the bedrooms, which are minimalist at eye level and more detailed below and above, with modernist furnishings and ornate patterned ceilings.

What it may lack in downtown grit Peppers Gallery more than makes up for with a thoughtful and convenient package of services and amenities. The lakeside hotel is a part of the New Acton development, which includes a number of restaurants, bars and a smattering of retail shops, in addition to the hotel’s own lounge, wine parlor and dining room. It’s a win for everyone; there’s a small fitness room right next door, as well as a standalone day spa, and the hotel’s guests enjoy complimentary access to the Fitness First health club, ten minutes’ walk through the park.

How to get there: Diamant Hotel Canberra is located 15 minutes away from Canberra International Airport (CBR). For guests arriving to the hotel by car, parking is available, but should be pre-booked.

content:
It’s clear from a glance at the main building — where a traditional Swiss lakeside hotel building stands attached at the hip to a minimalist, modern structure — that Seerose Resort & Spa is something unusual. Here the rooms come in distinct styles, and while you might imagine that means a choice between classic and contemporary, it’s not quite so simple.

The “Classic” rooms, in fact, are decorated in a contemporary style that Seerose calls “natural chic” — it’s warm and organic, subtle and understated, and in the lake-facing rooms this serves to draw the eye outward. Meanwhile the “Elements” rooms are even more modern, and decorated with graphical nature motifs. And in what used to be the boathouses you’ll find the “Cocon” rooms, decorated in warm wood and textured concrete, with up-close views of the surface of the lake.

They inherit their name from the hotel’s Cocon Thai Spa, a remarkably authentic experience that’ll have you straining to remember you’re still in Switzerland. Meanwhile two of the three restaurants are Thai-accented as well, from the fine-dining Swiss-Thai fusion of Cocon to the more casual Samui-Thai; Swiss-French cuisine is represented by the Restaurant Seerose.

content: On the road that leads from Bayeux to the beach in Normandy, there's an elegant English-style estate with a colorful history. Once a hub for producing hemp to make fishing ropes, the property was later occupied by German officers during World War II. Today, Château La Chenevière is a luxury hotel that embraces the past — the name means “hemp fields,” and the original rooms and walled gardens have been carefully preserved — while offering a range of clever updates. The old glass-roofed conservatory was transformed into a modern bistro with a vegetable-driven menu and garden seating by the pool, and the stables now house sleek guest quarters.\n\nLight-filled rooms and suites exude period charm and a casual but put-together French country aesthetic, with elegant woodwork, exposed beams, paisley wallpaper, floral patterns, and furnishings in leather or velvet. Marble bathrooms are stocked with Diptyque products, and some have freestanding soaking tubs. A few come with private patios, and all have views over the surrounding park with its century-old trees. A stroll around the wooded grounds, with its rose gardens and tennis courts, is a welcome diversion after indulging in the breakfast buffet — the lavish spread features local goat cheeses, fresh-baked pastries, artisanal jams, and honey produced at the beehives outside.
