content: In terms of its location, Yunohama is one of Yamagata Prefecture’s loveliest hot spring towns: its picturesque coast is lined with hotels and inns overlooking the Sea of Japan, and its sandy shores face the largest swimming beach in the region. The newly renovated Kameya Hotel makes the most of all of it. Every room has a direct water view and a private onsen, or bath, though they vary in style — some are traditionally Japanese with tatami mats and smooth wood paneling, but one has a curving copper ceiling inspired by a nearby shrine, and another, a dream-like suite five stories above the ocean, is outfitted only in white and glass. Guests also have access to the hotel’s larger stone and cypress baths, one of which has ocean views, as well as the only natural spring-fed drinking fountain in town.

content: A ski resort near Nagano may sound like an unlikely spot for a hotel dedicated to a Danish modernist architect, but there’s a longstanding relationship between the two. The furniture company Onecollection produces Finn Juhl’s designs in Japanese workshops, and its cofounders seized a chance opportunity to snap up an old ski lodge in Hakuba and reimagine it in his name. The result is a sleek six-room boutique hotel, House of Finn Juhl, with a striking blend of Japanese and Scandinavian elements. Suites are named after Juhl’s signature pieces — the Chieftain Chair, the Poet Sofa, and so on — and though each is unique, all are minimalist and cozy with futuristic lighting systems, organic bath products, and soft damask linens by Georg Jensen. An elegant bar and lounge face views of the Japanese Alps.

content: Among the notable recent additions to Maebashi is the art-focused Shiroiya Hotel, housed in a 1970s-era concrete building redesigned by the architect Sou Fujimoto. The project is the brainchild of another noted creative — local Hitoshi Tanaka, founder of the Japanese eyewear brand JINS — who conceived of the place as a “living room for the city” to be enjoyed by guests and residents alike. The main tower’s facade features a mural by American artist Lawrence Weiner, while Leandro Erlich’s striking “Lighting Pipes” installation is exhibited in the four-story atrium. The newly built green tower, a whimsical structure inspired by the topography of the nearby mountains, is an artwork in itself.

content: It’s a rare golf resort, even in Scotland, that displays the sort of old-world elegance you’ll find at Mar Hall Golf & Spa Resort, a spectacular 19th-century Neo-Gothic house (and 240-acre estate) on the banks of the Clyde, just a few minutes’ drive from Glasgow. Accommodations range from Classic rooms to Grand Suites, which feel more like a private residence with separate lounge areas, grand pianos and pool tables, or book the Spa Garden Suites for your own outdoor space. \n\nDining options take you from day to night and include afternoon tea at The Gallery (or perhaps a drink at its marble-topped champagne bar), local Scottish cuisine at The Dining Room, and signature cocktails at The Sláinte Bar. As the name suggests there’s both golfing and spa time on offer thanks to the 18-hole Earl of Mar championship course and a complete wellness area with pool, sauna, steam room, and treatments. Or choose from one of one of the many traditional Scottish activities that the hotel can organize, including falconry, axe-throwing, clay pigeon shooting, and private whiskey tours.

content:
Expect neither a hidebound period re-creation nor a fashion-chasing lifestyle boutique from the George in Rye. This 400-plus-year-old coaching inn by the East Sussex seaside has been cleaned up and classed up just enough to suit the modern taste, while neither throwing the historical baby out with the newly renovated bathwater, nor needlessly altering the antique character of the place in pursuit of some idea of design-magazine sophistication.

Just a classic small inn is what it is, a modern classic: such timeless comforts as fine linens, plush heaping beds, and deep antique-style bathtubs. Bedrooms retain period touches, like half-timbered ceilings, and the overall floor plan is charmingly ad hoc, with a maze of narrow stairs and walkways rather than the highly rational double-loaded corridor of the typical modern hotel.

Food is an essential part of the package as well. The George Grill serves up the sort of fresh and seasonal fare that’s de rigueur these days: local seafood, regional meats and produce, and even wines from the South of England, a proud gesture with France a long stone’s throw away.

content:
Two blocks from Dickinson Street and few minutes’ walk from the University of Arkansas campus, Graduate Fayetteville offers a boutique-hotel experience steeped in Ozark charm. Like the other Graduate hotels, which offer stylish, upscale accommodations in college towns across the country, Graduate Fayetteville caters to diehard Razorback fans as well as visiting academics and parents. 

It’s a rare high-rise Graduate, with expansive views of the town and its surroundings. Rooms are playfully decorated in bright colors and distinct patterns, and come standard with free wi-fi and Malin + Goetz amenities. Reclaimed wood floors and vintage-sourced furniture in the rooms and common spaces lend the hotel a distinct local character and a touch of a rustic vibe. And for a properly luxe experience, there’s the Washington Suite, complete with a sleeper sofa and its own wet bar.

Work up a sweat in the hotel’s fully equipped gym, or go for a swim in the indoor-outdoor pool, which is open year-round. The Trophy Room, the hotel’s restaurant, offers everything from breakfast to post-dinner drinks, all served in a playfully stylish double-height space that’s (thankfully) a long way upmarket from the sorts of places actual college students do the bulk of their dining and drinking.

content:
Nobody is about to mistake Bansko, Bulgaria for St. Moritz. But it’s certainly not without its charms. You can actually afford to ski here, for one thing; and if you’re having an increasingly difficult time telling one Alpine resort from another, you’ll find Bansko has an almost comical abundance of character. And the affordability extends to the hotels as well — here’s a top-end luxury hotel, the Kempinski Hotel Grand Arena, which is located literally right at the bottom of the gondola, charging a nightly rate that might not even get you through the door of the worst hotel in Gstaad.

One look at the Grand Arena’s distinctive exterior and you can tell you’re not in the Alps anymore. The rooms may be a bit on the mild side, but you don’t come to a ski resort to admire the furniture. There’s plenty of character out in the streets as well — this has only been a ski resort for a little more than a decade, so the old town is perhaps quainter than most. Of course, if you’re used to Courchevel or Park City or Whistler, you’ll find the slopes themselves a bit quaint; but that’s sort of the point. Bulgaria is still lovably bizarre, the Grand Arena rolls out the red carpet for cheap, and the ratio of experience to cost is at an all-time high.

content:
Nicknamed Slovenia’s Tuscany, Brda is where the Mediterranean meets the Alps — an idea that sounds almost too good to be true, and one that sounds even better when you realize it’s also a wine region. Set in the rolling hills, framed by terraced gardens, olive groves, and 200-year-old vineyards, the elegant Peterc Vineyard Estate is a luxurious adults-only hotel attended by its owners, a local husband-and-wife duo with a penchant for art, outdoor living, and great food and wine. 

There are just a handful of rooms, all with parquet floors, large windows, French-inspired decor, original artwork, and spacious bathrooms with Italian ceramic tile and walk-in showers or tubs. A few have private terraces, and most face views of the vineyards and the sea. But what’s especially impressive is the hotel’s array of spaces and services designed for guests’ pleasure, including a swimming pool and sun deck, cherry orchards to wander through, and an open-air fire pit for relaxing over a glass of wine. 

A lavish breakfast buffet is served until noon, afternoon tea service starts not long after, and private picnics in the vineyards, complete with quilts and pillows, can be arranged on short notice. The house specialty is a a crisp Rebula that’s great any time of day — an as aperitif, paired with seafood at lunch or dinner, or for sipping under the stars — and the estate’s bike manager happily arranges cycling tours with tastings in the surrounding wine country.

Note: Peterc Vineyard Estate has a 3-night minimum stay requirement.

content: The Wellness & Sporthotel Jagdhof sums up the Bavarian good life in its name alone. Just south of the Bavarian Forest national park, where the German, Czech, and Austrian borders converge, it’s a classic holiday resort with a dizzying array of options to exert oneself and recover afterwards. No judgment for just relaxing, of course — posting up on a lounger with a spritzer and a good book is par for the course around here. But if you’re feeling inclined then there’s all manner of fitness, wellness and beauty facilities to take advantage of — in fact there might be no other wellbeing area quite like this in Germany. There are huge indoor and outdoor pools, a natural bathing lake, tons of fitness classes, saunas and a steam room, a female-only spa space, and beauty treatments that range from traditional massages to the latest cosmetic treatments — and the list goes on. Rooms up the cozy factor with warm earth tones, natural wood, and plush textiles, balanced by floral accents and balconies to invite a little nature in.

content: Expectations are low for a hotel near a busy international airport. The look blends sleek South Korean elements with old-world European grandeur; bejeweled chandeliers sparkle in the hotel’s common spaces, done up in sultry black, red, and gold, while suites are monochromatic with lavish marble bathrooms. The more-is-more aesthetic continues across the lavishly decorated bistro and cocktail bar, a striking spa, and the outdoor swimming pool with partially submerged chaises and two tiers of open-air lounge space. Art Paradiso has a notable art collection, but more importantly, it’s steps away from Paradise City’s innovative indoor-outdoor art installations and architectural exhibits, plus a theme park, upscale shopping and dining, and more.

content:
Founded by King Frederick II in 1763, Königliche Porzellan-Manufaktur (KPM) is a porcelain manufacturing factory with a royal pedigree. Each piece is a work of art — it’s common for 25 artisans to work on a single coffee cup before it's stamped with KPM’s signature orb and scepter — and the brand brought the same level of precision to bear when the time came to design its first luxury hotel. KPM Hotel & Residences is located on the factory grounds, occupying a privileged position on the edge of Berlin’s leafy Tiergarten park, but the architecture has little in common with the property’s stately original buildings. The work of Axthelm Rolvien, a prize-winning German architecture firm, the hotel is striking and sculptural, featuring a slate-gray steel facade and a cubist silhouette. 

The sleek, monochromatic interiors follow a similar aesthetic, but elegant art objects in white porcelain, made at the adjacent factory, pay subtle tribute to the site’s history. Rooms and suites are minimalist with wide-planked wooden flooring, cutting-edge lighting systems, bespoke furnishings, and ultra-modern stone bathrooms. Downstairs, an elegant breakfast is served on KPM china, the on-site restaurant serves Asian-inspired cuisine, and a stylish communal pantry and kitchen offers complimentary Nespresso and cold drinks around the clock. Take a coffee up to the rooftop; there’s no bar, but the open-air terrace is a lovely place to relax.

The location is a bit removed from Berlin’s beating heart, but a fleet of bicycles and e-bikes is available for a casual pedal through the park, while the hotel’s electric Porsches are ready to whisk guests away to museums or dinner reservations. If time permits, a tour of the porcelain factory, with an optional hands-on workshop, is a fascinating way to spend an afternoon.

content: The central Pennsylvanian town of State College is, sensibly enough, the home of Penn State University, and Graduate State College is the local branch of the Graduate hotel group, whose boutique hotels reliably take their inspiration from the campuses they serve, and present to guests an idealized version of the collegiate life. In this case, they took the old-fashioned Atherton Hotel, set two blocks from Penn State’s expansive campus, and transformed it into a contemporary boutique hotel — one that’s dressed in Nittany Lions livery and filled to the brim with subtle and not-so-subtle references to the university’s history and identity. \n\nRooms are decked out in the school’s familiar blue and white, and furnished with comforts that are a cut above the ordinary campus-adjacent hotel. They’re playful but not quite gimmicky — and the same can be said of the hotel’s bookish Trophy Room, as well as the Trophy Room restaurant, which really comes to life during football season (and on the weekend of the annual THON fundraiser). Stylish enough for students, traditional enough for parents, and comfortable (and dignified) enough for visiting professors — that’s the Graduate brand in a nutshell.

content: China is increasingly where you go to see the most impressive modern luxury hotels, and that’s certainly true of this one — Capella Tufu Bay is a collaboration between architects Jean-Michel Gathy and Bill Bensley, both hospitality design all-stars. The public spaces are monumental, especially the circular lobby with its ornamental pool, and the rooms and villas are suitably residential — at their substantial size you wouldn’t call them “cozy,” but they’re warm and plush even as they verge on opulence.\n\nNor is design the only thing Capella Tufu Bay has going for it. Capella’s hotels and resorts are famous for their personal service, and for the cultural authenticity of their experiences and excursions. A first-rate spa, too, is present as a matter of course; this one includes a hammam and a snow cabin among its offerings. And a wealth of restaurants and bars see to guests’ needs, from a chic and casual poolside bar to Lan Ting, an elevated Chinese dining experience.

content: Take your pick at Le Presbytère, a one-of-a-kind boutique hotel in the village of Saigneville in northern France. You can sleep in a single bed in the former quarters of a priest, or you can spend the night in a vibrantly painted wooden trailer — what the owners refer to as a roulotte gitane, or gypsy caravan — parked in the garden. The hotel is built around a restored presbytery, though most accommodations are housed in a modern annex where cozy, simply outfitted guest rooms have whitewashed walls, vaulted ceilings, and pale wood furnishings. The gypsy caravans, of course, are another thing entirely: lined with wood paneling and cheerfully decorated with colorful textiles and artwork, each is large enough for a double bed and a private bathroom. One has a small kitchen, ideal for preparing a charcuterie board and opening a bottle of wine to enjoy beneath the shade of a Japanese cherry tree.

content: As the name may suggest, Macalister Mansion is an opulent reminder of Malaysia’s British colonial period, named for a Scottish governor who presided over Penang back when it was called Prince of Wales Island. Today this boutique hotel in historic George Town offers old-world grandeur, from the mosaic-lined swimming pool with a swim-up bar to an art collection with a range of pieces specifically commissioned for the space. There are just eight suites, outfitted in sleek blonde wood, glass panels, and crisp white linens. They’re all unique, with varying features, from modern four-poster beds to a private balcony overlooking the pool; all feature Nespresso machines and Bang & Olufsen sound systems. A pair of sophisticated restaurants, a wine bar, and a cigar lounge await after a day out exploring the UNESCO-honored historic center, a short drive away.

content: South Korea’s coastline is deeply indented with countless smaller peninsulas jutting into the sea, and the Ananti Namhae, a luxury hotel with a golf course, is located on two of these fabulously scenic natural landforms, one part of the property connected to the other by a scenic footbridge. This family-friendly resort offers the standard comforts, like the requisite outdoor pool, and plenty of traditional Korean features as well, including a modern version of a jjimjilbang, a spa with aromatic indoor and outdoor pools. A central clubhouse contains a stylish bookstore and café, a design shop, a sleek kids’ club, and a modern eatery serving Mediterranean cuisine, while bright and well-appointed guest rooms, with floor-to-ceiling windows and marble bathrooms, are spread out across the grounds. Free-standing villas come with their own gardens and plunge pools, plus unobstructed views of the water. \n

content: Sitting right on the edge of Lake Lucerne, the Hotel Schweizerhof Luzern is rather impressively still run by the fifth generation of the Hauser family, who originally opened the hotel back in 1845. Nightcaps can be enjoyed in the Schweizerhof bar, although it’s also a popular spot with locals for an after-work drink. The fifth-floor spa rounds out the offering with its fitness room, sauna, massage treatments, and sweeping lake views.

content:
If swaying palm trees and a tropical island setting don’t exactly jive with your idea of China, consider this: the People’s Republic has a competitive national beach volleyball team, and they have to train somewhere. That somewhere just happens to be Sanya, a coastal city on southern Hainan island, and Hotel Pullman Oceanview Sanya Bay, it just so happens, is the sort of hotel that justifies the flight.
 
With 469 guestrooms, two swimming pools, a spa, a water park, tennis courts, a pair of restaurants and a private beach, the Pullman is more of a resort than a hotel. But given this range of offerings, and the massive building’s glowing resort-style facade, the place has a few surprises in store. Interiors are airy — even fully open-air in some cases — with towering beamed ceilings and magnificent views over the water, as in the striking dark wood-paneled lobby and lobby lounge, where you might be tempted to linger with a cocktail while staring out at the sunset. 

Guestrooms range from the standard, with amenities including a rain shower and a private balcony, to larger suites and apartments with ample living space and deep soaking tubs on private patios overlooking the ocean. At the top of the line, villas come with their own private pools. All rooms the contemporary comforts you’d expect from a business hotel; the Pullman simply has a little more style and character.
 
The most attractive spaces on the property are the gorgeous Red Sun Bar on the 17th floor, open to the sky and the ocean, and the resort’s private beach, well-equipped with complimentary umbrellas, cabanas and chaise lounges. Other highlights include wines by the glass at Vinoteca wine bar, dim-sum at The One Chinese Restaurant, and watching the chef prepare your dinner at Open Kitchen. After dinner, feel the sand between your toes at the breezy thatched-roof Beach Bar — you’ll have to remind yourself you’re still in China.

content: Just a two-hour drive from Sydney, the lush green hills of the Southern Highlands are a refreshing alternative to the beach scene. Standing out amid the region’s many traditional inns is the stylish Osborn House. It’s been functioning as a guesthouse since 1892, but it’s become new again — a fresh, whimsical retreat with a nostalgic air — under the direction of Linda Boronkay, former Design Director at London’s Soho House. Twelve of the hotel’s 22 rooms are located in the beautifully restored main house, where an English country aesthetic prevails; the other rooms are down a path in rustic-chic bungalows with fireplaces and outdoor bathtubs. The common areas are picture-perfect, from the cozy living rooms and colorful indoor-outdoor restaurant to pretty gardens and striped cabanas by the pool, and the waterfalls and hiking trails of Morton National Park are a stone’s throw away.
name: Osborn House

content: Innit Lombok takes its design inspiration from traditional Lombok Lumbung homes, but its minimalist cubic villas make a thoroughly modern style statement. Imagined by a team of Indonesian architects, each property sits stilted up off the ground, hovering above a living area placed directly on the sand to blur the boundaries between indoors and out. Sustainable natural materials such as wood, stone and concrete have been sourced locally from the region and further blend the villas into the surrounding landscape, while inside an open plan design and sea-facing beds continue to connect guests with nature.\n\nThere’s laidback dining at restaurant Anakampung with communal dinners and an outdoor barbeque pit right on the beach for grilling freshly caught seafood by the waves. In fact, it’s hard to resist Innit’s 300m stretch of private white sand at any time of day, or lazing around the 35-meter-long infinity pool, but if you are feeling more active then kayaking, surfing, paddleboarding, visits to Lombok lobster farm and fishing expeditions to catch your own dinner are some of the experiences on offer.
name: Innit Lombok

content:
Like all the other Graduate hotels, the Graduate Cincinnati is roughly one part tried-and-true boutique-hotel formula and one part local color. Here, on the campus itself, the hotel takes its inspiration not just from the University of Cincinnati but from the whole city’s history, paying tribute to its setting with visual references to Bearcats athletics and Reds baseball, the products of the old Kenner toy factory, and Cincinnati natives Bootsy Collins and Roy Rogers.

It’s remarkably colorful, even by Graduate standards, a welcome contrast to the drab décor of the typical college-campus lodging. And while the rooms may not be enormous, they’re more than comfortable enough, they’re full of visual interest, and they’re pet-friendly, for a small fee.

Poindexter, the hotel’s ground-floor café, is a fixture across all Graduate hotels, serving breakfast and coffee in an ironically nerdy-hip setting. Specific to Cincinnati, though, is Fiona’s, named for the local zoo’s beloved hippopotamus; it’s an all-day bar and restaurant decked out in Mondrian-style geometric shapes and primary colors, serving as everything from dinner venue to cocktail bar to lively daytime co-working space.

content:
Compared to some French cities, Grenoble’s charms are on the subtle side; its mountainside location provides some topographical interest, and it’s a major center for education, science, and technology. Similarly, the Park Hôtel Grenoble, unassuming as it is, reveals hidden strengths: a city-center location adjoining the verdant Parc Paul Mistral offers the appeal of an urban luxury hotel with a touch of country charm, and its interiors are more colorful and more contemporary than you’d be led to believe by its relatively humble façade.

The rooms are decked out in stately monochrome, livened by color-block accents in crimson or turquoise (but not both); the comforts include such niceties as Clarins bath products and Nespresso machines. The suites, naturally, are much more expansive, with lounges large enough for a business meeting as well as an unusual amount of artwork.

A breakfast buffet, a bar and lounge, and a room service menu are the extent of the food and beverage program; in the center of Grenoble you’re presented with a wealth of restaurant options within a minute’s walk. There’s also a substantial fitness and wellness center, and a shuttle connects the hotel with the local resorts during ski season.

content: Less well known than Japanese terms like wabi-sabi and ikigai is the concept of teioku ichinyo — “the oneness of garden and building” — which informs the design of a visually striking boutique hotel in the historic heart of Kyoto. Its focal point is a trio of quiet courtyards planted with willow and maple trees. Sunlight and greenery are gracefully showcased inside the glass-walled, two-story lobby lounge and minimalist rooms outfitted in the colorways of traditional kimono textiles. The sleek terrace restaurant and sake bar are popular with locals, but the ethereal subterranean bath is exclusive for guests, and a by-reservation-only private bath lounge, on the main level off of one of the courtyards, blurs the lines between indoors and out.
name: Mitsui Garden Hotel Kyoto Sanjo Premier

content: Even by Kyoto’s lofty standards, Hotel Utano Kyoto Besho is something special. The setting is Ukyō-ku, where the mountains meet the northwest corner of the city — a place known for its tranquility and its natural beauty, and for centuries an escape from urban life. The house itself dates back to the early 20th century, and is a historic example of its era’s hybrid Japanese-Western style, complete with a lush Japanese garden.\n\nInside you’ll find a wealth of traditional Japanese construction styles and methods, as well as ten bedrooms — some in the shoin-style main house or the sukiya-style annex, others in the Spanish-inspired wing. Each room comes with its own hot spring–fed onsen bath, open to the garden breeze. And in a handsome, classically styled dining room, lit softly by washi paper, guests are served breakfast and a gourmet dinner featuring Awaji Island seafood.
name: Hotel Utano Kyoto Bessho

content: Georgia’s capital city has a good range of independently run boutique hotels, but the most luxurious lodgings are generally part of international chains, as is the case with Swissôtel Tbilisi. Breakfast is served in the Swiss-styled café, and all of Tbilisi’s main attractions are just a stroll away.

content: From the location to the design to the award-winning restaurant, there’s nothing ordinary about Retiro Costiña. It’s set deep in the Galician countryside, and comprises seven pill-shaped villas scattered around a central lodge that serves as this small resort’s gathering space. Stark white and oblong, the villas remind ever so slightly of spaceships, while their minimalist interiors radiate serenity. This isn’t the sort of resort that comes with cascading pools or tennis courts; instead, nature serves as the inspiration for activity and renewal. It’s all anchored by chef Manuel Garcia’s restaurant, which is a destination unto itself; guests migrate from the kitchen and the wine cellar to the dining room and lounge throughout the course of a meal.

content: For Westerners, Rabat feels a bit like a wonderful secret. Less well known than Casablanca or Marrakech but equally mesmerizing, this imperial capital city is a place of architectural treasures and wonders waiting to be discovered. In the midst of this magical place, the Four Seasons straddles both ancient and modern worlds. Set at the edge of the Atlantic Ocean, this 12-acre resort was once the summer residence of Morocco’s Sultan Moulay Slimane. Six restored historical buildings entice, while five brand-new ones effortlessly blend old and new. Similarly, the rooms and suites blend the romance of Moorish design with modern comforts. Of course, it doesn’t end with exquisite design; it’s a Four Seasons, after all, so expect nothing short of anticipatory service along with fine dining and first-class amenities.

content: The legendary fashion designer Karl Lagerfeld never made it to Macau to see his namesake hotel in person, but he designed its interiors from top to bottom, and his presence is everywhere. It’s an unapologetically glamorous experience, and its rooms are marked by what might be a surprising deference to classic Chinese interior design — filtered, of course, through the Lagerfeld sensibility. The spa and health club are suitably lavish, and the restaurant, Mesa by José Avillez, makes the most of Macau’s Portuguese connection. Meanwhile the Book Lounge is inspired by Mr. Lagerfeld’s own home library and features four thousand books hand-selected by the designer himself.

content: Rather like California, Australia is finding its retired motels to be fertile raw material for renovations. Kyah, in the Blue Mountains of New South Wales, takes Palm Springs as its aesthetic inspiration, turning a Seventies motel into a very modern — but still Seventies-inspired — 46-room boutique hotel. This boutique hotel has a rustic-chic beach-house atmosphere, with wide wood-planked floors and a laid-back honor bar where you can pour your own coffee or beer. content: There’s a Switzerland for all seasons at Chalet RoyAlp Hotel & Spa. The hotel offers experiences and activities for every type of weather, from hiking and golfing in summer to skiing and sledging in winter, but the Swiss chalet-style accommodation works all year round. Wood-lined rooms and traditional checked Alpine textiles cocoon guests after hitting the slopes, whilst the floor-to-ceiling window flood rooms with summer sunlight. Of course, spa time is always appreciated, particularly here where the wellness offering includes a pool, sauna, hammam, jacuzzi and more, plus treatments from the likes of cult French beauty brand Biologique Recherche. There’s two restaurants to choose from, plus a cigar lounge and a pop up summer terrace, but gastronomes might enjoy the chance to sit at the Chef’s Table right in the heart of the action.

content: Croatia has never been more popular with travelers than it is now — though most of its visitors flock to Dubrovnik and Split, leaving some of the country’s most scenic destinations comparatively off the radar. Take the medieval port city of Šibenik, perched on the edge of a beautiful bay on the Dalmatian Coast, home to a cathedral and a fortress that are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Heritage Hotel Life Palace is one of just a handful of hotels in the area. And it’s everything you’d want from a boutique hotel in the car-free Old Town: housed in a restored 15th-century palace on a cobblestone square, it’s full of historic character, and with seventeen rooms and suites, it’s neither too big nor too small. \n\nEach room is different, but all feature elegant period details — stone doors, exposed brick walls, wood-beamed ceilings — and Renaissance-inspired decor, from original hand-painted murals and gilded mirrors to brocade drapery and Baroque writing desks. Nearly all have bathtubs, and the best have French doors opening onto private balconies. The ground-level café spills out onto the square with outdoor tables ideal for breakfast or a glass of wine. There’s no formal restaurant on site, but it’s a pleasure to wander through the labyrinth of side streets on the way to dinner, or down to the waterfront at sunset.

content: Take a glamorous Art Nouveau–style mansion near the beach. content: Thanks to its location near Mount Ishizuchi, one of Japan’s highest mountain peaks, Saijo is known as the country’s spring-water capital. An eco-friendly initiative out of the University of Tokyo prompted the construction of a series of water-themed architectural projects, including the Itomachi Hotel. It’s Japan’s first zero-energy hotel, with two airy levels connected by open-air walkways and topped by a large, angular roof. Rooms are stark and minimalist, with blonde wood flooring, pale green tilework, simple writing desks, and luxurious beds on elevated platforms. Some have living areas with sleek modular furniture and private terraces; all have access to an ultra-modern coworking space and kitchen, a stylish café, and riverside gardens with futuristic water features.

content: Fairmont went big for its first hotel in South Korea: the Fairmont Ambassador Seoul, part of the Parc.1 complex on Yeouido Island, occupies one of the tallest skyscrapers in the country. Rooms and suites, outfitted in sophisticated neutral hues and featuring spacious marble bathrooms, serve as similarly impressive lookout points, with retro leather armchairs thoughtfully positioned by the oversized windows.

content: Just outside Sarzeau, near the wooded coastline of Brittany’s Rhuys Peninsula, is an elegant 16th-century manor house that used to be an orphanage and agricultural school. content: Though they’re nobody’s idea of a cutting-edge boutique outfit, Fairmont has earned its following by offering a consistently high-end luxury experience that’s both tastefully rendered and classic in its aesthetics. And a hotel like the Fairmont Jakarta is proof that this is no less true in a financial-district skyscraper than in a grand old Canadian railway hotel. The location in Senayan, next to the stock exchange and close by to the convention center, is as central as it gets, and the hotel, naturally, is equally well equipped for business and leisure travelers.\n\nThe Fairmont’s 488 rooms and suites are a reminder of the power of understated elegance — no matter how busy the street life (and central Jakarta is busy indeed), you can’t help but be calmed by fifty (or more) square meters of hardwood and marble. The suites are more than twice as large, and at all levels you’re treated to top-flight comforts as well as elevated views of the capital. Add the Willow Stream Spa and a couple of restaurants, including the upscale Indonesian kitchen 1945, and you’ve got all the makings of a properly luxe urban escape.

content: You’ve heard of boutique hotels housed in old breweries, and in monasteries, hotels in lighthouses, even hotels in caves. But a hotel inside an old telecommunications office? What, pray tell, is the charm in that? Well, plenty, it turns out, if you’re talking about the new Hermitage Menteng - Jakarta. Once known as ‘Telefoongebouw’ — it was built by the Dutch in 1923 — this Art Deco landmark is charming and elegant, brimming with vintage charm but thoroughly updated with five-star amenities. Including touch-tone phones, much as you might have hoped for an antique rotary. You might guess at the building’s original function when approaching: it’s located in the heart of the well-heeled neighborhood of Menteng (which is, incidentally, the same neighborhood where Barack Obama spent his childhood and attended elementary school). The hotel’s stately exterior is striking from outside, and inside the luminous lobby, the look is palatial, with high coffered ceilings, polished white Carrera marble floors, rich drapery, glass partitions and sumptuous chandeliers. Upstairs, guest rooms and suites at the Hermitage don’t have quite the same antique character. But they’re lovely nonetheless: sleek and quiet, they come with espresso machines, pillow-top mattresses, and 40-inch LED TVs. Suites feature extra perks from Hermès bath products to Bose docking stations and private balconies or terraces, depending on the category. On the atmospheric ground level, L’Avenue, the hotel’s main restaurant, serves French dishes prepared with traditional Indonesian ingredients. Nearby, on a central patio outfitted with white wicker furniture and umbrellas, the more casual Courtyard Café does small plates and cocktails. At night, the Wine & Cigar Room, with its dark wood paneling and leather sofas, is a cozy spot for drinks — do as the Dutch colonialists would have done and order a jenever. But the real standout for cocktails is yet another of the hotel’s venues: the panoramic La Vue rooftop bar, adjacent to the Hermitage’s infinity pool. The bar offers views over the city as the sun goes down, and a casual aesthetic characterized by whitewashed wood and sea glass — don’t let the Dutch thing fool you, you’re still on the coast of Java.

content: High above Kraków, in the wooded folds of Wolski Forest, Zinar Castle has quietly watched over the city for nearly a century. Originally built during World War II for the German commandant, then known as Schloss Wartenberg, the limestone villa has been reimagined in 2024 as a refined five-star property. Its 34 rooms combine contemporary workmanship with pieces by celebrated Polish artists, while the two-level U Ziyad restaurant unfolds across arched arcades and open-air terraces. With forest trails on its doorstep and the Old Town just minutes away, Zinar Castle offers a rare pairing: total escape with Kraków still in view.

content: There are great places to stay in Portugal’s Serra da Estrela Natural Park, but few are as visually striking or as rooted in regional culture as Casa das Penhas Douradas. content: Toulouse was officially named a UNESCO Creative City of Music in 2023, and Hotel Les Capitouls Toulouse Centre - Handwritten Collection embraces the theme. But instead of opera and classical music, two art forms which with the city has long been associated, this boutique hotel takes inspiration from more contemporary music, specifically that of 1980s Manchester. Posters from Joy Division and New Order concerts hang near reception, and vintage cassettes form the basis of art installations. The cavernous, coolly lit lobby, with its exposed brick walls, high archways, glass roof, and welcoming cocktail bar, feels more like a live music venue or a recording studio than a hotel.\n\nRooms are compact and stylish, with distressed wood-plank flooring, midcentury modern decor, and dramatic murals with bright, delicate flowers highlighted in sharp chiaroscuro against a dark backdrop. Bathrooms have a rock-and-roll edge, too, with asymmetrical mirrors and vintage-style floral wallpaper. There’s no restaurant, but with a central location like this, in the heart of historic Toulouse, you’re unlikely to miss it — and the chic Wilson Bar, which stays open late, is a good spot for a nightcap.

content: The magnificent setting of the Fairmont Le Manoir Richelieu, perched high on the Pointe-au-Pic bluffs overlooking the St. Lawrence River, is no coincidence. The location was specifically chosen by a Canadian shipping company that hoped to attract travelers aboard its new passenger vessels from Quèbec City in the late Victorian era. Resembling a grand ivy-clad French château, the luxury hotel is just as striking to behold today, not to mention easier to access. With hundreds of rooms and suites, indoor and outdoor pools, a state-of-the-art spa, an array of upscale dining venues, and easy access to outdoor activities from golf to winter sports, it’s an easy retreat that feels both modern and timeless.\n\nThe hotel’s historic rooms got the Fairmont treatment during major renovations in the late nineties. They’re elegant and classic with sophisticated dark wood furnishings, patterned carpeting, and large bathrooms with Le Labo toiletries. Many have tubs and river views, and the regal La Charlevoix Suite features a baby grand piano, a romantic fireplace, and a lavish marble bathroom with a Jacuzzi. But some of the hotel’s most sweeping views are for all to enjoy: breakfast, lunch, and dinner are served with a dazzling backdrop of water and sky at the Bellerive Restaurant, and the nearby Bar Le Zéphyr, with terrace seating facing the river, is a lovely spot for cocktails at sunset.

content:
In the Brothers Grimm folktale “The Town Musicians of Bremen,” the four elderly animal protagonists never make it to the smallish city — they end up waylaid by an empty house instead. Barring any such fairy-tale mishaps, you’ll be satisfied with what you find here. Like its quietly stylish siblings worldwide, the Hotel Bremen appeals to both business and pleasure travelers, with clean, contemporary design, a convenient location, and highly professional service. 

It might not challenge your notions of cutting-edge décor. You might not see a supermodel flanked by stylists or be able to rub elbows with royalty. Bremen’s charms are more modest than that, from the first-rate Gothic architecture to the annual Freimarktor, one of Germany’s oldest festivals. Businesspeople will like the built-in desk with ergonomic chair and speedy room service, while those traveling with little ones will appreciate the on-site playroom and special kids’ rooms, decorated with cartoon characters and connected to the parents’ rooms. All rooms either overlook a peaceful atrium or occasionally spirited street.

The hotel is an easy walk to Bremen’s Town Hall, home to the world’s largest wine cellar and some of its oldest wines. Tours of the brewery that makes Beck’s and St. Pauli’s Girl are also available; the Bremen Brewers Guild, founded in the late fifteenth century, is the oldest in the country, and the renovated waterfront or the Wallenlagen park (keep an eye out for the windmill) are good choices for pre-pint perambulations.

content:
Take Cologne, a city that prides itself on its cultural heritage and its modern art scene, and New York, a city that famously offers a head-spinning range of galleries. Now compress the spirit of these two cities into one design hotel, and you’ve got a sense of the inspiration behind The New Yorker. Situated, like any self-respecting up-and-coming gallery, in an industrial part of town slightly (though still walkably) removed from the city center, this hotel offers far more than the average art-centric boutique. Sure, the guest rooms are sleek and stylish, but the hotel was designed to host cutting-edge events, and its bar and public spaces are just as vital to the overall atmosphere.

Despite practically oozing creativity, the New Yorker doesn’t thumb its nose at commerce — on the contrary, it welcomes business guests with a refreshing fervor, providing fully customizable meeting spaces in the form of a library and a quirky, colorful lounge. These spaces are a world away from the stodgy conference rooms of most business-oriented hotels. And the guest rooms are chic without relying too much on stark graphic contrasts; with plush red rugs and elegant wooden furniture, the minimalism never feels less than vibrant. 

Besides the breakfast buffet, snacks and drinks are available in the lounge and, weather permitting, out in the garden — if you’re lucky, someone will be barbecuing out there. In the loft space, a full kitchen complements the exclusive hang-out suite, complete with winter garden; the perfect place for an intimate get-together or retreat.

content:
The Hoshinoya hotels — part ryokan, part luxury hotel — are all similar in their basic concept. But while the monumental Hoshinoya Tokyo stands in a skyscraper in the heart of the capital, Hoshinoya Kyoto could hardly be more different. It’s small, a mere 25 rooms, distributed among a collection of low-profile buildings. And despite its name, it’s set not in Kyoto proper, but a 15-minute ride up the river in a traditional wooden boat.

The architecture is unmistakably Japanese but also unmistakably modern, and the interiors are a delightful update on ryokan convention, dressed in modern colors and subtle graphic patterns. The rooms are as comfortable as can be, though far from opulent, passing over high-tech diversions like televisions in favor of tranquil views through vast windows and — perhaps the most memorable feature — beautiful cypress soaking tubs.

Spa treatments are available in-room, and a wide variety of traditional Japanese cultural experiences are on offer as well, from ikebana lessons to Zen meditation. Among the most venerable traditions in ryokan life, of course, is the local cuisine — Kyoto’s culinary heritage is a rich one, and here chef Ichiro Kubota applies techniques and knowledge from all around the world to a menu drawn from hyper-local, hyper-seasonal ingredients.

Generations of well-to-do European families have retreated to the elegant lodge in the Austrian Alps and, more recently, a wave of namedrop-worthy celebrities in pursuit of fresh air and mountain scenery. This chalet-style hotel has its own ski school, a heated saltwater pool that’s the largest in any hotel in Europe, a gorgeous sauna complex, and a slew of restaurants serving Tyrolean specialties crafted with ingredients from Stanglwirt’s on-site farm. Rooms and suites feature traditional Swiss stone pine floors, walls, and ceilings, cozy details in wool and linen, and private balconies, many facing the peaks of the Wilder Kaiser.

content: In its early 20th-century heyday, the Grand Hotel in Mürren hosted skiers from all over Europe, earning the nickname “Switzerland’s first palace.” Almost 150 years after first opening its doors, and just in time for ski season, the landmark is reborn as the Hotel Mürren Palace. Many of the building’s original assets remain — the dazzling setting on a high-altitude plateau, panoramic terraces facing snow-capped peaks, crackling fireplaces warming up a lively après-ski scene — and a new building has been added. The old ballroom has been turned into an elegant breakfast area, and rooms have been smartly updated with parquet floors, midcentury modern décor, and stylish bathrooms, many with tubs. Suites and maisonettes have extra living space and perks like Jacuzzis or kitchenettes; every room has a private balcony overlooking the mountains and the Lauterbrunnen Valley below.

content: Well off the beaten path in the scenic Parc Naturel Régional des Volcans, Instants d’Absolu Ecolodge & Spa is a stylish retreat in the middle of nowhere. This restored farmhouse is the only hotel — indeed, the only building of any kind, save for a bird observatory across the water — on the wooded shores of the deep blue Lac du Pêcher. There are no screens or phones here, just quiet, sun-filled suites, a lakefront restaurant, a state-of-the-art spa, and refreshing views of natural landscapes all around. Covered in snow in winter, these landscapes are a playground for hiking and horseback riding the rest of the year. \n\nThough the main house is fairly large, Instants d’Absolu is intimately sized, with just a dozen rooms. Each is uniquely decorated, but they all have some features in common: hardwood floors, an earthy color palette, writing desks, linen drapery, antique pieces, and rustic-chic details like alpaca throw pillows and bedside tables made of tree trunks. All guests get timed-entry access to the spa with its open-air Japanese-style bath, and a large terrace facing the lake is perfect for reading or bird-watching. A short walk along the water, past the greenhouses where the kitchen staff grows vegetables and herbs, leads to a wooden chalet housing a restaurant with a grill and inviting open-air tables.

content: There are certain features you can expect at any Raffles hotel; among them are personal butlers, a world-class spa, and a glamorous bar serving riffs on the Singapore Sling, a nod to the brand’s flagship location and the signature cocktail invented there. Raffles Bali is no exception — here, butlers double as private buggy drivers, the spa specializes in energy healing, and the house cocktail is the arak-based Bali Sling. This Indonesian expression of the Raffles template works beautifully, in no small part because of the resort’s stunning location on the Bukit Peninsula overlooking Jimbaran Bay — but also due to the thought and care that’s clearly gone into the hotel’s elegant design.\n\nSpread out on a grassy expanse that slopes downward to the sea is a collection of villas with private pools, tropical gardens, and water views. The aesthetic is modern Balinese — high vaulted ceilings, dark wood floors, teak furniture, batik fabrics — and each has a lavishly appointed bathroom with indoor and outdoor showers and a soaking tub. The three- and four-bedroom villas are incredibly roomy, and a single hilltop villa offers supreme sunset views. Nearby, at the property’s highest point, is the Writers Bar; below, a beachfront infinity pool and an open-air restaurant.

content:
Lombok is known for its lavish resorts, and Pullman Lombok Merujani Mandalika Beach Resort, Accor’s first five-star hotel on the island, keeps up with the neighbors. It’s located on the quiet beach of Kuta Mandalika, set slightly back from the water’s edge on beautifully landscaped grounds with swaying palm trees. Winding paths lead through tropical gardens past a huge swimming pool and resort buildings modeled after the traditional shelters of the native Sasak people. 

Everything is oriented to maximize the resort’s greatest asset: its position overlooking the Indian Ocean. Many rooms, suites, and villas have sea views. Like the architecture, their design takes inspiration from the island’s indigenous culture and natural landscapes — the elegant wall panels mimic native wood carvings, and colorful murals channel the island's vibrant wildflowers. All rooms have bespoke Pullman beds, locally made bath products, Bose sound systems, modern workspaces, stocked minibars, and palatial bathrooms with soaking tubs and walk-in rain showers. Higher-end suites and villas have sea-facing terraces or private gardens, some with plunge pools.

The Pullman Lombok’s spa, fitness center, and restaurants are all first-rate, and the indoor-outdoor lobby bar is a breezy spot for coffee or cocktails with a view. The decoratively tiled swim-up bar, with two rows of stools elevated just above the pool’s surface, is another highlight, as is the street food cart that rolls around the resort, offering gourmet versions of Indonesian and international snacks and drinks.
name: Pullman Lombok Merujani Mandalika Beach Resort

content:
The Fairmont hotels, aesthetically speaking, are a fairly conservative lot, but they’ve got an eye for classic elegance — from the regal European inspiration of the Canadian railway hotels to the Southeast Asian contemporary-luxe style of the Fairmont Sanya Haitang Bay. The setting, on the south coast of China’s well-traveled Hainan Island, is idyllic, and the views are picturesque, taking in Wuzhizhou Island and the limitless seascape beyond.

With 523 rooms and suites it’s practically a village unto itself, complete with a kilometer-long salt-water canal winding its way through the property — a dragon boat ferries guests from check-in to their accommodations. The rooms and suites themselves are typically luxe, with plenty of space to spread out in and an interior-design style that makes generous use of the wood and stone construction that’s native to the region.

Meanwhile, the restaurants include an all-day Southeast Asian café, a Spanish-style grill, and Yuen Court, which combines Cantonese and Hainanese flavors. Along with the spa are no fewer than three swimming pools — one of which features a poolside lounge, and the outdoor deck at the Ocean Lounge is just about as pleasant as it gets.

content: Apart from being Albert Einstein’s birthplace, Ulm is best known as the home of the world’s highest cathedral steeple. Downriver along the Danube is the city’s largest park, home to a singular hotel that sits prettily on the edge of a natural lake. Though the setting is bucolic for an urban hotel, LAGO hotel&restaurant am See is hardly rustic. Its modernist architecture, with its clean lines and bright, open spaces, was influenced by the Ulm School of Design — a progressive institution shuttered in 1968 — whose students were directly involved in the plans for the fifth floor. \n\nRooms are minimalist, bathed in natural light, and outfitted with hardwood flooring and down-to-earth colors meant to blend in with the natural landscape. All feature floor-to-ceiling windows, and many have water views, as does the spa on the uppermost level. Breakfast is served on an open-air deck when weather permits, and the one-MICHELIN-star Seestern, housed in a Nordic-style boathouse right on the water’s edge, is a noteworthy asset.

content: The Okinawan city of Ishigaki is home to countless conventional hotels, but Seven x Seven Ishigaki is anything but conventional. The concept is “luxury self-hospitality,” meaning a combination of low-touch, low-profile service with high-end comforts — combining the freedom of a good apartment share with the ease of a proper luxury hotel.\n\nHere the design, too, is unconventional, a modern and minimalist look that’s nevertheless welcoming and identifiably local. The standard rooms are comfortable enough, while the deluxes and the suites quickly grow to large proportions; the latter come with extras like private pools or saunas. Nor is the cuisine what you’d expect: not traditional Okinawan fare but a “Latin Italian” hybrid that combines Italian, Spanish, and Mexican flavors.

content: Nicknamed the Moroccan Riviera, Tamuda Bay is home to several world-class resorts, including an exclusive retreat by the Royal Mansour Collection. Like its sister hotels in Marrakech and Casablanca, Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay is architecturally grand and ultra-luxurious. Moroccan artisans were brought in to decorate the sleek seaside palace with intricate zellige tile, marble mosaics, and traditional woodwork, thousands of seashells adorn the walls of the striking lobby, and hand-crafted wooden chaise longues line the pool and private beach. Spacious suites feature custom four-poster beds, airy living rooms with sculptural sofas, and large private terraces overlooking the gardens or the sea. Opulent beachfront villas have their own pools and dedicated butlers. The hotel’s ethereal spa is a destination in itself, as are its high-end dining venues overseen by noted Spanish, Italian, and French chefs.

content: Hall might not be as well known as Tyrol’s capital of Innsbruck, but it once played a major role as one of Austria's major trading sites, where salt was such big business that the town was even named after the Celtic word for it. It’s hard not to feel the history here, rooms still retain their mix of Gothic beamed ceilings, Baroque moldings, and centuries old stone walls, but the protected building has been sensitively updated with contemporary shades of grey and bespoke furnishings, including some crafted from the building’s old wooden slats. In the mornings owners Ursula and Marek serve up a seasonal and regional breakfast, including their own homemade products, in the lovely Baroque hall, which still sports its original wooden floor and decorative 18th century stucco ceiling.

content:
Wordplay aside, it can actually be difficult to snag a reservation at No Vacancy, an eclectic boutique hotel occupying a prime second-floor space in Kansas City’s lively Crossroads neighborhood. There are just eight rooms, plus a charming interior courtyard and a stylish lounge, and the place is sometimes entirely booked out for weddings or events. 

No Vacancy is not a conventional hotel. There’s no front desk, and rooms are more like studio apartments. No two are alike, but they’re all infused with ample natural light and a cozy, bohemian-chic sensibility: exposed brick walls, wood-beamed ceilings, large windows framed by breezy white drapery, and potted plants. They feature a mix of mid-century modern pieces and quirkier furnishings, like bamboo barstools, a metallic gold disco ball over the bed, or a woven wicker chair suspended from the ceiling. Three have kitchenettes; one a freestanding clawfoot tub, and another a romantic four-poster bed and a vintage wet bar. 

At the end of the main hallway, the colorful communal lounge, with its plush banquette seating, opens onto the inviting courtyard patio. Both offer plenty of space to work, socialize, or relax over coffee or drinks.

content: Sitting in the Northumberland countryside just an hour outside Newcastle, The Tempus is a surprisingly new addition to the historic Charlton Hall Estate. Whilst the estate dates back to the 19th century, as does its wedding venue property Charlton Hall, The Tempus has been built from scratch using original stone, slate and timber from the domain’s old farm buildings, meaning it still has the air of a charming country house, albeit a modern version of one. Inside the 52 eclectic bedrooms also feel contemporary with a mish mash of stripes, florals, and leopard print paired with beamed ceilings and stone fireplaces. The Orangery is the hotel’s signature restaurant, serving classic British dishes, Sunday roasts and afternoon tea, or there’s the Tipi, which is as the name suggests a large outdoor tipi, for wood-fired pizzas in summer and winter-themed pop-ups.

content:
A 19th-century Victorian mansion in a park outside of Manchester could be a recipe for a dreary time, but not only is this no ordinary park — Bruntwood, in Cheadle, is a vibrant public space, full of woodlands, ponds, and a sporting complex that includes a BMX track — but Oddfellows is no ordinary Victorian mansion. On the architectural level it’s a faithful restoration of a Gothic Revival structure, but its interiors mix period details with elegant modern design and plenty of quirky, light-hearted visual fun.

The rooms, in keeping with the theme, preserve Victorian detail but introduce playful touches and modern luxuries, and they vary widely in size, plan, and individual style, from the Park rooms, with king beds, spa-like bathrooms, and Nespresso machines, to the Tower Suite, which is just what it sounds like, spread over two floors.

The hotel’s spa, in an outlying building, is called Pigsty, and includes a mud room among its therapies. Meanwhile the Galloping Major restaurant serves modern British cuisine and the Stud Room bar pours inventive variations on classic cocktails. It’s the modern country house hotel for a generation that cares more about comfort than correct etiquette.

content: China has long been home to some of the most impressive conventional luxury hotels in the world — but it’s also home to some unusual ones, like the village-style Xitan Hotel Beijing. Despite its name, it’s located not in the city proper but in the mountains to the west, a spectacular setting for a hotel that aims to restore its guests to a closer relationship with nature.\n\nThe guest quarters are arranged around courtyards in the traditional style, while the interiors, though historically inspired, take a more contemporary turn. Space is plentiful, the atmosphere is tranquil, and the comforts are first-rate; despite its unusual presentation Xitan is, at its heart, a thoroughly modern luxury resort. To its accommodations it adds the Qin Spa, with a particular focus on hydrotherapy, as well as a restaurant, The House of Rong, which is part of China’s well-known Xin Rong Ji culinary concern.

content: There’s no doubt this is the Chinese Century for luxury-hotel enthusiasts; Banyan Tree, for example, counts among its offerings nearly as many properties in China as in the rest of the world combined. Banyan Tree Chongqing Beibei stakes its territory in the mountainous northern outskirts of the city of Chongqing, and in so doing exposes a global audience to the region’s rugged beauty — and its natural hot springs.\n\nThe resort’s accommodations are built in a style inspired by the local traditional architecture, and they’re residential both in atmosphere and in scale — the smallest Retreat spans some 80 square meters. The interiors are handsome, and historically inspired, though they’re equipped with all the requisite modern luxury-hotel comforts. These are augmented, outside the rooms, by offerings like the Banyan Tree spa, with its spring-fed baths; meanwhile three restaurants serve a variety of Sichuan, Cantonese, and international cuisines.

content: From the outside, BULL looks like your typical Cotswolds coaching inn: all golden stone and historic charm. Inside, it is anything but. Owned by Matthew Freud, it’s a curious, quietly subversive stay filled with Banksys, Dalís and Damien Hirsts, seven wildly varied dining and drinking spots, and bedrooms stocked with mezcal negronis and midnight snacks from a pantry called The Trough. Lighting is pitch-perfect, the service smart but unstuffy, and the wine cellar is hidden behind a French prison door and home to Idris Elba’s poker table. At BULL, every corner comes with a plot twist.

content: Seven x Seven Itoshima offers a different take on the seaside resorts of southwestern Japan: the brand’s concept combines “self hospitality” with luxury, on the theory that today’s travelers prefer low-profile, low-touch service even as they enjoy top-shelf facilities and comforts. The setting, right on one of Itoshima’s finest beaches, is idyllic, and gives each of the hotel’s 47 rooms and suites a view out to sea.\n\nThe design is as modern as the concept, while the comforts mix high-tech and low; it’s still hard to beat a bathtub that’s open to the sea breeze. Yoga classes and e-bikes are available to guests, as are stand-up paddle boards and lessons. All in all, an inspired and unconventional vision of the traditional seaside holiday.

content: The ultra-luxe Patina hotel group chose, for its first foray into Japan, not Tokyo or Kyoto but Osaka: specifically, a parcel of land that looks directly out over Osaka Castle and the surrounding park. This glass-fronted structure is draped in greenery, and what’s inside is a hotel that’s state-of-the-art both in its comforts and in its warm-toned quiet-luxury aesthetic.\n\nIt’s also identifiably Japanese, thanks to the subtle and sensitive work of its architects, who took their inspiration from centuries of local craft. Beneath this sober surface the rooms and suites are nothing short of lavish; the spaces are generous, the comforts are first-class, and the views are like nothing else in town. A high-tech spa and wellness center adds to the appeal; multiple Japanese restaurants are joined by Iñaki, a Basque restaurant with a 19th-floor view of the castle.

content: One of Canada’s original grand railway hotels, The Fort Garry Hotel still holds its place as a Winnipeg icon. Built in 1913 and now a National Historic Site, its château-style silhouette opens into marble floors, chandeliers, and wide corridors that once hosted the likes of Louis Armstrong and King George VI. The Palm Room remains its heart, with a domed ceiling, live jazz, and a menu shaped by Manitoba’s seasons. For a stay with presence and history, there’s nowhere else quite like it.

content:
Deep in the heart of Central Java, nestled between jungle-clad volcanoes, Hotel Le Temple Borobudur is a mere 700 meters from its namesake, the 9th-century Borobodur Temple. The accommodations, all freestanding villas, start with gorgeous teak wood and floor-to-ceiling windows; those on the higher end extend the luxury with private plunge pools. The hotel honors the local heritage with a full roster of activities, including traditional handcrafts and ceremonies, plus luxury-hotel staples like spa treatments. And no one visits without getting up close to the UNESCO-listed temple itself; guided tours of Borobodur and other nearby attractions are readily available.

content:
Located on Gediminas Avenue — often referred to as the "Champs-Élysées of Vilnius" — this historic building dates back to 1917 and began operating as a hotel in 1939. In the late 1950s, it was redesigned and reconstructed by architect brothers Algimantas and Vytautas Nasvyčiai, officially reopening as the Neringa Hotel in 1960. Alongside its legendary restaurant, the hotel quickly became a key cultural hub in Vilnius and a national symbol of modernist architecture.
Following a three-year renovation, the hotel reopened in 2021. While modern engineering solutions were implemented, the building’s historical character was carefully preserved — including its original façade, artistic features, and core design concept.
The interior design draws inspiration from the Lithuanian seaside, featuring a warm color palette and locally sourced materials, arts, and crafts. The flooring in the rooms mimics sandy beaches, while the beds have sun-shaped headboards. Custom-made Lithuanian textiles are used throughout, with patterns replicating the original 1960s restaurant tapestries.
In addition to the namesake restaurant, the hotel features several bar options: one in the lobby, a rooftop bar with panoramic city views, and an underground bar. The rooftop also houses a small, pleasantly bright fitness room.

content: The Hoshinoya name is highly regarded around Japan because of the brand’s reputation for impeccably crafted, exceedingly relaxing ryokan-style luxury hotels. With Hoshinoya Tokyo, the question is whether this approach can survive the transplant from the forests of rural Japan to a skyscraper alongside Tokyo Station. Feel free to read on for details, but if you’re pressed for time, the answer is yes. Where there’s a ryokan, there’s an onsen, a spring-fed bath — and even here, in central Tokyo, there’s a hot spring, one whose waters emerge from nearly a mile underground. The hotel’s ground-floor entry bears a convincing resemblance to a Zen garden, and by the time you’re inside, it’s clear that this is a hotel unlike any other: a ryokan in both form and function, but one that’s contemporary in style and imposing in scale, as befits its unusual location. Each floor of the hotel functions as a self-contained unit, with an ochanoma — a living room stocked with refreshments — for every six rooms. As for the rooms themselves, they’re among the city’s most luxurious, and their style, a seamless blend of contemporary design and ryokan tradition, is absolutely unique. Equally luxe is chef Noriyuki Hamada’s basement restaurant, with its hyper-local fine-dining menu, and the 17th-floor spa, which combines onsen tradition with modern treatments. Most luxurious of all, however, is something that’s harder to quantify — this might be the quietest, most peaceful place outside of the Imperial Palace.

content: Among the attributes that make Kyoto unique are its machiya townhouses, traditionally built with a shop on the ground floor and living quarters upstairs. This one, historically known as Onyado Niwa, has been thoroughly restored and re-imagined by the Tokyo-based architects Studio Aluc. Two wings were united under a single roof, and the whole of the inn was transformed into a modern machiya inn, now known as Nazuna Kyoto Higashi Honganji.\n\nThe seven rooms are all different, and all combine historically minded woodwork and atmosphere with contemporary design interventions; each one features a handsome cedar bath. The common spaces, too, are richly varied and detailed, and are full of gestures paying tribute to traditional carpentry. Breakfast is served daily, and a shabu-shabu dinner can be arranged with some advance notice.

content: Niseko’s world-class powder snow might make it one of Japan’s top ski resorts, but it’s not limited to winter travels. On the contrary, it’s a destination that can be enjoyed in all seasons, which the Nikko Style Niseko HANAZONO fully celebrates with its sensorial design concept. In the lobby, a large LED light installation and DJ booth play colors and sounds according to the time of year and day, whilst in the contemporary rooms, large picture windows offer a view of the changing seasons. The restaurant and bar serve up a mix of international dishes and drinks, but local Hokkaido ingredients and Japanese sweets are at the forefront: you’ll find the trendy shaved ice dessert “conayuqi” on the menu. The hotel’s traditional Japanese onsen can also be appreciated all year round.

content: High in the Togakushi mountains, Awai offers two distinct stays: a minimalist former public hall for two, and a traditional thatched-roof home shaped by generations of local craftsmanship. The thatching process is part of a broader philosophy, drawn from “yui,” the mutual-aid systems that once sustained rural Japan. Guests are invited to slow down in a setting shaped by nature, history, and intention. Days unfold between forest walks, nearby shrines, and shared meals made with local ingredients. You come for the setting, and stay for how easy it all feels.
name: Awai Togakushi

content: On Cathedral Island in Wrocław’s oldest quarter, The Bridge MGallery occupies a rare position: between history and what comes next. The building draws from its Gothic surroundings without imitation: all stone, steel and glass, balanced by warm light and sculptural detail. Wax candles float above beds; portraits of Wrocław’s past residents, created with the National Museum, hang in every room. A rooftop terrace overlooks the Oder, while a waterfall wall in the foyer echoes the river below. A solid stay in one of the city’s most historic spots.

content: If there’s one designer that suits Dubai’s glitz and glamour, it’s the vibrant sun-soaked Versace. But at Palazzo Versace the design house becomes more than just a brand — it’s an opulent Italian lifestyle. A grand neoclassical façade hides haute-couture interiors with rooms dressed in Versace’s bespoke furnishings and pastel-hued silks. The nine restaurants and bars have also been given the golden Versace touch, whether it’s through the Italian menus or the jungle-print wallpapers and grand Roman columns. Outdoor terraces are a nod to the courtyards of traditional palazzos and offer views of the Dubai Creek. Three outdoor pools are set amongst the lush, landscaped gardens, or guests can retreat to the low-lit marble and mosaic spa for a traditional hammam experience.

content: Opened in 1892 by a prominent Wrocław banker, Hotel Monopol became the city’s most distinguished stay, hosting names like Marlene Dietrich and Pablo Picasso, who famously left behind a sketched dove on a restaurant napkin. Restored in 2009, it still wears its history well: sandstone façades, curved ceilings, and expanses of black and sable marble. Rooms are dramatic and tailored, with exposed brick, dark woods, and high ceilings framing views of St. Dorothy’s church. It may have hosted legends, and it’s known for its exceptional hospitality even today.

content: There are views at every turn from The Ritz-Carlton, Perth. Standing tall amongst the glossy urban redevelopment of Elizabeth Quay, the hotel offers prime views across the skyline and the Swan River below, as well as a handy location for getting to some of the city’s main sights either on foot or by river cruise. In the sleek suites and studios — there are no mere rooms here — beds and baths come with a view from the floor-to-ceiling windows. Post-swim the spa offers the full works for a complete day of R&R.

address: Bab Samhan, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Diriyah
content: The development of the historic city of Diriyah, known as the birthplace of Saudi Arabia, is a cornerstone of the country’s wide-ranging initiatives to attract more international visitors. Setting a high standard for the many new hotels set to open in the area is Bab Samhan, part of Marriott’s Luxury Collection. Its low-lying brick buildings, magically illuminated at night, mirror regional architecture, as do the hotel’s labyrinthine passageways leading to open-air courtyards planted with fig and olive trees. Rooms and suites feature traditional Najdi design, hand-dyed linens, ornamental lanterns, and hand-crafted tea sets. Several sleek Middle Eastern restaurants and a serene blue-tiled indoor pool add to the appeal, and the UNESCO World Heritage Site of At-Turaif is a short stroll away.

content: Tucked away in the Topatopa Mountains between Los Angeles and Santa Barbara, bohemian Ojai — famous for its mystical sunsets, scenic hiking trails, lively art galleries, and spiritual retreats — is the Sedona of southern California. The perfect place, in other words, for a hotel made up of a collection of refurbished Airstream trailers and a tiny house. Arranged in a semi-circle around a lush botanical garden, each has a private outdoor space framed by greenery, and a few come with hammocks strung up between palm trees.\n\nEach of Caravan Outpost’s lodgings is unique — some Airstreams feature original vintage fittings, while others are newer. Inside, they’re compact and cleverly outfitted with a queen bed and a double foldout, both made up in high-end linens, as well as modern kitchenettes and bathrooms with showers. The singular cabin is similar in size, but with two levels of space, the lofted sleeping area tucked away beneath quaint wood-beamed ceilings. There’s no bar or restaurant on site, but the central garden is an oasis ideal for coffee, picnics, or drinks under the stars, and the hotel provides  bikes for pedaling around town.

content: In a village where most hotels are housed in traditional wooden chalets, Nosalowy Park Hotel & Spa stands out for its large scale and its unconventional architecture. It occupies the former Villa Marilor, an elegant Austrian-style mansion set in a wooded park near Zakopane’s railway station — since its construction in 1905, this stately brick building was the first sight travelers would see when arriving in the Polish mountain resort. Today, it’s one of the most luxurious hotels in town, its interiors thoroughly renovated and reimagined with a mix of modern elegance and whimsical Art Deco. Rooms are sleek and beautifully illuminated, with French windows and marble bathrooms with stained glass panels. Many have private balconies, and suites on the upper floors feature panoramic views of the Tatra Mountains. The light-filled indoor pool and spa are a highlight, and the striking Restaurant Marilor is the best place to take in the villa’s old-world grandeur.

content: The notion of a “land of contrasts” might be the most tattered cliché in the travel writer’s vocabulary, but the extremes on display in Japan are remarkable. From the sensory overload of Tokyo to the utter tranquility of the countryside around Karuizawa is just over an hour by train, but the two places feel like entirely different worlds. Hoshinoya Karuizawa’s environment is as pastoral as can be; it’s set on a hot spring, by the side of a small lake, surrounded by forests that double as a sanctuary for wild birds — and it’s no stretch to think of the resort itself as a sanctuary for travelers.\n\nHoshinoya Karuizawa’s concept is ryokan-like, complete with onsen baths and traditional kaiseiki dining. But its scale is rather larger: its villas contain dozens of rooms, and the spa goes beyond the typical hot-spring baths. The accommodations are contemporary in style, though they retain plenty of traditional Japanese character, and they’re impressively luxurious, some with floors heated geothermally, others with terraces looking out over the forest. Exterior views abound, from the rooms to the spa to the restaurant — it would be hard for a luxury hotel to get much closer to nature, and that’s the appeal of Hoshinoya Karuizawa in a nutshell.

content: Long before the term “eco-lodge” existed, the Varty family built Londolozi on a bend of the Sand River in Sabi Sand. Established in 1926, it became the original blueprint for luxury safari camps - wild, soulful, sustainable and purposefully ahead of its time. Its five lodges feel more like a village: thatched roofs, dolerite stone, soft linen, and stories passed down through generations. Game drives follow leopard tracks through the grass, and evenings return to open-air dinners. Few places in Africa feel this deeply lived in, or this deeply loved.

content:
Most of the Maldives’ luxury resorts occupy an entire private island — Waldorf Astoria Maldives Ithaafushi takes the concept one step further, taking up not one but three interconnected islands in the South Malé Atoll, including an exclusive island, Ithaafushi, that can be rented out in its entirety. 

Every suite is a villa with its own infinity pool, and many are set overwater. All feature custom king-sized beds, lavishly appointed bathrooms with double vanities and standalone soaking tubs, and sliding glass doors opening onto wooden decks with daybeds and hammocks. 

In addition to 11 restaurants, a series of oceanfront pools, and a beach club with a water sports activity center, the resort is home to the largest spa in the country. Built on stilts over the shoreline, its treatment rooms are furnished with glass flooring so you can enjoy water views even while face-down on the massage table.

content: Hirado Island, in southwestern Japan’s Nagasaki Prefecture, is a spectacular maritime escape, and Kikka Hirado is one of the most memorable ways to experience it. This is a thoroughly modern hotel that shows there’s more to Japanese hospitality than the ryokan tradition; with its five ultra-modern rooms and suites, its sauna and wellness area, and its local and seasonal restaurant, it’s a remarkably full-featured hotel in spite of its extremely small size.\n\nThis size, of course, reinforces both its sense of seclusion and the personal touch of its service. Meanwhile the rooms, with their vast sea-facing windows, bring guests in direct contact with nature. The restaurant, too, looks out over the water through full-length windows, and the wellness area’s deck invites further contemplation. From here the island’s unique cultural sites are close at hand, as is the city of Hirado.

content: Improving wellbeing through nature is at the heart of Greenity Iwata. Sitting on a hilltop overlooking the coastal city of Iwata, the hotel’s large volumes and high ceilings connect guests with the surrounding forest and tea plantations, whilst outside, the vast garden is filled with around 700 types of trees, plants and herbs. \n\nThe rooms’ calming neutral shades are also punctuated with highlights of green, from both the furnishings and the views of leafy treetops. Three restaurants serve up a mix of French and Japanese cuisine and prioritize seasonal organic produce from both land and sea. The full spa offering completes the wellness experience with a yoga room, beauty salon, Finnish sauna, and, of course, time in Japan’s famed open-air hot springs.

content: Tendō might not be a well-known destination outside of Japan, but for the domestic market, the city is one of the country’s major hot spring resorts. Choose from classic Japanese design in one of the seven outdoor cottages known as hanare, patterned after the structures traditionally used for tea ceremonies, or a room with slightly more contemporary styling in the main house. content: Once a 17th-century Franciscan monastery, Herbal Hotel is one of Wrocław’s oldest buildings with its vaulted ceilings, ancient well and cloistered corridors which exhibit centuries of history. Over time, it became home to Elizabethan sisters, a wartime ecumenical circle, a pharmacy garden, and even student housing. Today, it holds 66 elegant rooms, each shaped by the building’s original structure, some with soaring ceilings and garden views. Carefully restored, never overdone, Herbal honors its past without getting stuck in it. For guests who value architecture with a story, and still want crisp sheets, it’s a rare find.
name: Herbal Hotel

content: Occupying a thoughtfully restored 19th-century building in Old Tbilisi, Sandali Metekhi is everything an urban boutique hotel should be. It’s perfectly located on the edge of the Mtkvari River in one of the oldest neighborhoods in town, an ideal base for exploring the city. Sealing the deal are a traditional Georgian breakfast and a rooftop terrace with expansive views over the city and the hills beyond.
