content:
A short drive from Tbilisi, Bioli Wellness Resort feels hidden away in the Kojori hills — not only because it’s surrounded by native forest, but also because of its biophilic architecture. The main building is topped by a sloping grass-covered roof, and rooms are housed in sustainably built, energy-efficient bungalows designed for indoor-outdoor living. 

The simplest lodgings at this luxury retreat are anything but: rising up on stilts amid tall trees, one-room cottages are airy and modern with king-sized beds, floor-to-ceiling windows, rustic-chic wood-paneled bathrooms, and private rooftop terraces. Striking wood and glass chalets, featuring two levels of space, have sunny living rooms, lake views and decks with Jacuzzis. 

Everything from stress management packages and detox treatments to massages and facials is available at Bioli, though you’re just as likely to soak up the resort’s calming effects while strolling in the woods or sipping organic wine by the lounge’s fireplace.

content: About two hours from Nagoya, the relatively remote Takayama City is prized for its mountain location as well as its picturesque traditional buildings. Behind one of the town center’s well-preserved façades — that of a classic two-story machiya townhouse — is Machiyado Ichiryu, an urban ryokan that takes some welcome liberties with the genre.\n\nA city-center ryokan isn’t unheard of, but more unusual is one which, like Machiyado Ichiryu, goes quite so modern in its furnishings — although the look is more subtle and sober than flashy. And where there’s a ryokan, there’s a restaurant serving dishes meticulously crafted from seasonal local ingredients.

content: Moritosha is a different kind of art hotel; not one dedicated to an expensive collection of rare artworks, but one dedicated to Mingei, the folk craft movement known as “the art of the people.” The building was once a training facility built by one of the movement’s woodworkers, and today is a museum, a café, and a shop, as well as a unique small hotel.\n\nThe rooms are simple, almost ascetic in their equipment; comfortable, but minimalist rather than luxurious. content: Hotel H15 Francuski has been part of Kraków’s cultural fabric since 1912, the city’s first purpose-built hotel, and once its most modern. Opposite the Czartoryski Museum and steps from the Barbican, it is a landmark of Kraków’s past, and still one of its most distinctive stays.

The 15-story property is Green Key certified, with geothermal heating, floor-to-ceiling windows that maximize natural light, and thoughtful systems to reduce energy and water use. Rooms are bright and minimal, with bold color blocking and local artwork. Downstairs, the lounge draws pre-game crowds and post-show regulars. Service is upbeat, the vibe relaxed, and the location unbeatable. For travelers who value sustainability, good design, and genuinely warm hospitality, Alt keeps things simple, and gets them right.

content: Sitting by the banks of the Goulburn River, The Mitchelton Hotel Nagambie makes a striking sight amongst the sprawling vineyards of the Mitchelton Winery Estate. Australian design duo Hecker Guthrie imagined the hotel’s graphic blocky structure as a modern ode to nature, with rooms dressed in elegant shades of grey, tactile materials and timber accents to create a harmonious link with the natural surroundings, which can be enjoyed from balconies overlooking the river or vineywards. The Muse Restaurant offers a self-described “paddock-to-plate” menu that celebrates local Goulburn Valley produce, and guests can even go out and catch their own dinner in the next-door river. The spa offers a complete wellness experience with gym, outdoor infinity pool, and natural plant-based treatments. Book a massage al fresco for more panoramic views.

content: Surrounded by 17 acres of Kent woodland, The Beacon sits above what was once known as Happy Valley, a hillside of spring-fed lakes and pleasure gardens that drew visitors in the 18th century. Built in the 1890s, the house later sheltered Basque refugees and Jewish children during the war before becoming a disco, a pub, and eventually a family home. Its seven bedrooms are richly detailed, with velvet curtains, turret bathtubs, and views that stretch across the Kent hills. The setting is peaceful, the welcome sincere, and the view worth pausing for.

content: There’s an elephant called Jabulani who roams the grounds at Jabulani Safari, but he’s not named after the place: the luxury lodge, located on a Big Five private game reserve in the Greater Kruger Area, is named after him. The project started with the rescue of its namesake elephant calf and the establishment of the country’s first dedicated elephant orphanage, later expanding to create one of South Africa’s top safari lodges. \n\nJabulani Safari is still a wildlife refuge first and foremost, much to the delight of guests who rise early for guided game drives and gather for sunset drinks with a view of the resident elephant herd silhouetted against the sky. No expense was spared in outfitting the hotel’s lavish suites — standard features include king-sized beds draped in gauzy canopies, freestanding stone baths, traditional fireplaces, and wooden decks with private plunge pools — and its villas are even grander. Gourmet dinners are served by starlight or in the elegant dining room of the main lodge.

content:
Of the 115 islands that form the Seychelles archipelago, only a few are off-limits to the general public, including Denis Private Island. The 375-acre coral islet doubles as a wildlife reserve with its own air strip, century-old lighthouse, and of course, an exclusive luxury retreat. The hotel has just 23 cottages and villas, all outfitted in colonial style with wood flooring and furnishings made at a nearby carpentry workshop. 

They’re generously spread out along the island’s northern coast, so each has its own semi-private beach with lounge chairs as well as a wide furnished veranda and a garden courtyard with an open-air shower. Inside, each cottage features a living room, writing desk, and a spacious bathroom with a tub, and top-of-the-line villas have plunge pools and massage pavilions for on-demand spa services. Fishing and snorkeling outings are easily arranged, and the island’s resident giant tortoises are just a short bicycle ride away.

content:
It’s enough to make you wonder why anyone stays anywhere else. Hapuku Lodge, near Kaikoura on the eastern coast of New Zealand’s South Island, is that most rare of lodges: splendidly located, stunningly designed, small, personable, and yet still quite affordable. It seems there must be a catch somewhere, but if there is, we can’t seem to find it.

Hapuku is owned by a family of architects and builders, and it shows: the Olive House Apartment and the Lodge rooms are simple and contemporary, and the tree houses (yes, they’re literally tree houses, ten meters off the ground) are as modern as can be, clad in copper shingles and unfinished-looking local woods.

In these inspiring surroundings many of us would be content with a sleeping bag for a bed and a garden hose for a shower. Of course we don’t have to be. Like any New Zealand lodge worth its salt, Hapuku is exceptionally comfortable; beds are custom-made, bathrooms border on the decadent, and rooms are supplied with all the technological gadgetry the contemporary luxury traveler is accustomed to. The food, as is the Kiwi custom these days, is simple, organic, and locally sourced, and served communally — though private dining is available if you’re shy.

Don’t get us wrong, if you’re staying in any one of New Zealand’s countless luxury lodges, you’re doing something right. But given a choice between taking out a second mortgage to sip tea in some Edwardian sitting room and actually saving money at Hapuku — and did we mention the treehouse’s indoor-outdoor shower? — we know which one we’d choose.

How to get there:
Hapuku Lodge is approximately a 2 1/2 hour drive from Christchurch International Airport or from the Interislander Ferry in Picton. It is a 3 1/2 hour drive from Nelson.

content:
A modern take on the classic Alpine hotel, the lakeside Neusacherhof is a strong argument for the continued relevance of the form: full-length windows frame views of the Weissensee, and knotted pine serves as a soothing backdrop for modern design furniture in the hotel’s handsomely minimalist rooms and suites.

In a hotel like this the accommodations are only part of the story. The bathhouse and spa offer a range of therapies, from yoga and massage to a Finnish sauna and the “Wunderkammer,” a salt-brine steam room. A private beach is the gateway to a wide variety of water sports, and of course anything that can be done in the mountains can be done with Neusacherhof as home base.

A typically Alpine sensibility undergirds the food and beverage offerings as well; the cuisine is typically hearty, and widely varied, from the inn’s unpretentious kitchen to the Italian fare on offer in the boathouse and Rouge Noir, the one-MICHELIN-Star fine dining establishment.

content: Opened in 1891 as the only first-class hotel on St Helier's seafront, the Grand Jersey has accumulated more history than most. During the German occupation of the Channel Islands from 1940 to 1945, the hotel was commandeered as military offices and quarters, its furniture burned for fuel, leaving it unable to reopen immediately after liberation. It has since welcomed the Queen Mother, and Queen Elizabeth II chose it in 2005 to host the lunch marking the 60th anniversary of the island's liberation. The 108 rooms, many looking directly over St Aubin's Bay toward Elizabeth Castle, range from teal and olive-toned deluxe rooms to full suites with separate living areas.

content: A plantation house on the edge of one of Africa's oldest rainforests, surrounded by working tea fields still harvested by the local Gisakura cooperative. content:
When you think of Newcastle your first thought is almost certainly not of elegant country house hotels. But Seaham Hall & Serenity Spa, in a coastal village just minutes outside the city, is nothing if not elegant — this was the site of one of Byron’s weddings, after all. But the mere existence of the house isn’t the end of the surprises. Wait till you see what they’ve done with the place.

The massiveness of the renovation was balanced, apparently, by its sensitivity — though there’s a decidedly fresh sparkle about the public spaces, the style is still very much in keeping with the house’s heritage. The rooms are, if anything, a little bit more contemporary, and below the surface they’re as modern as they come, with the lighting and entertainment systems controlled by central bedside panels — but equally impressive are lower-tech charms, like working fireplaces and the occasional sea view.

In a manor house hotel a fine dining restaurant is a given, and an underground walkway leads to the remarkably well-equipped Serenity Spa and its attached fitness center. Meanwhile, a few minutes one way is Newcastle, and a few minutes the other way is Durham — and when it comes to the natural setting, this stretch of North Sea coastline borders on the sublime, as does the Lake District to the west.
name: Seaham Hall Hotel

content: Lamai is Koh Samui's more laid-back alternative to Chaweng, and Rocky's has been part of its coastline long enough to feel like it belongs there. Rooms are warm and individually styled: soft neutrals, earthy tones and tactile fabrics, with the newer lofty ocean-facing categories adding generous balconies and pool access. content: Cinephiles or old-school spa-town connoisseurs might know Mariánské Lázně better as Marienbad, but by any name it’s been one of Czechia’s most famous destinations since its thermal waters were discovered in the 19th century. What now stands as Swissôtel Mariánské Lázně was previously a handful of disparate historical structures, combined via contemporary annexes and additions to form a unified whole: a 21st-century luxury hotel with authentic Art Deco roots.\n\nModern design and contemporary art fill the interior spaces, from the colorful public areas to the more subdued rooms and suites. The comforts are luxe, but not ostentatious, and the style is chic but well short of avant-garde. Relaxation, after all, is the mission here, from the Swiss-style Pürovel Spa & Sport to the versatile restaurants and bars.

content: Shenzhen's Bao'an District occupies the western edge of the Pearl River Delta, looking out over Qianhai Bay toward Hong Kong. The St. Regis arrived here in February 2025, bringing its second address in the city: 289 rooms across 51 floors where dark oak parquet, Carrara marble bathrooms and intricate marquetry woodwork give the interiors a weight and craftsmanship that the building's glass exterior doesn't hint at. Emerald-hued sofas and sweeping bay views define the living areas. Yan Ting does seasonal Cantonese; the Drawing Room on the 35th floor, framed around Caroline Astor lore, serves afternoon tea, and the rooftop terrace bar is where the city comes into focus.
name: The St.Regis Shenzhen Bao'an

content: Tanjong Pagar is having a moment: heritage shophouses, celebrated restaurants and some of the city's best hawker centers all in the immediate vicinity, with a train station sitting directly underneath the building. The hotel takes its aesthetic from Art Deco and Prohibition-era America, all russet tones, rose gold accents and mirrors; more 1920s cocktail bar than corporate stopover. Rooms are sharp and well thought-out: a wardrobe designed to evoke a traveler's trunk, a nine-pillow menu, high thread-count cotton sheets and a minibar stocked exclusively with local Singapore brands. A robot butler fields additional requests, and the adjoining Virgin Active gym is complimentary.\n\n

content: Chiang Rai sits at the northern tip of Thailand, historically the first capital of the Lanna Kingdom and still one of the country's most culturally distinct regions. Pa Sak Tong is about as private as hospitality gets: a single teak villa above a lotus pond, seven acres of gardens, rice fields and orchards, and a full staff that answers only to you. One group at a time, no other guests. The kitchen team works from the estate's own organic garden, with imported European and Australian provisions filling the gaps. Total privacy, in a part of Thailand that still has something to say.

Seneng Kitchen, named after the farming couple who tend those rice fields, serves an Indonesian-led menu alongside a broader international range, with that landscape as the constant backdrop. Wana Jiwa Spa is built as a villa on the Campuhan riverbank, open to outside guests as well as those staying at the resort.

Family-owned from the start, it has built the kind of loyal following that only comes from staff who actually remember their guests. The kitchen draws from the Aegean, relaxed at lunch on the sand, more sophisticated come evening, with cocktails built on house-made syrups and whatever the local market offers that week.

content: A 14th-century Carthusian monastery on the outskirts of Siena, Certosa di Maggiano has had an interesting life. Today, the rooms run maximalist: patterned wallpaper, bold tiling, mismatched prints, against the original frescoes and vaulted ceilings. The pool terrace is pink and archway-framed, the Magnolia Bar gathers guests around a fire pit under a centuries-old tree, and Siena's Palio is on the doorstep.

content: The Renon Railway built this hotel in 1908 as the upper terminus for its mountain line. The first architectural proposal was dismissed as too urban for the setting, and the Swiss Alpine Art Nouveau version that replaced it has barely changed since. At 1,200 metres above Bolzano, with the cable car still running guests up from the valley, it remains exactly what it was designed to be. Rooms have plank floors and mountain-facing balconies, the Liberty Spa has indoor and outdoor pools, and the 1908 restaurant keeps the founding year in its name.

content: The name Aarunya comes from the Sanskrit for the first rays of the sun, and the Knuckles mountain range, UNESCO-listed and ever-present, is what greets guests at that hour. A former tea and spice plantation, the nine-acre hillside estate now holds eight villas worked into the terrain without a single tree felled, using local materials and craftspeople at every stage. The Sky Tented Villa, under a safari-style canopy, has its own pool and an open-air bathroom framing the valley. Aarogya Spa covers Ayurvedic and Balinese treatments; the Aahaara fine-dining experience ends with a garden-to-table feast at a communal table, to live Sri Lankan music.

content: A 1927 heritage building on Montevideo's main pedestrian street, restored in 2016 and turned into ten suites that mix period details with an irreverent hand. Carrara marble staircases, stained-glass windows and original pine floors share space with contemporary art, mismatched vintage furniture and pieces made in-house. content: Founded by Sarah and Jacob Dusek, the couple behind Under Canvas, the largest glamping company in the US, Few and Far Luvhondo opened in January 2025 as their first safari lodge. The six clifftop suites in the Soutpansberg Mountains are built from heat-treated eucalyptus and stretched canvas, each with a wraparound deck, plunge pool, and unobstructed views over the Vhembe Biosphere Reserve. Beyond game drives, there's leopard tracking, rhino hikes, and Solfari: the world's first solar-powered aerial safari, a cable car gliding silently above 25 miles of reserve. The spa operates beside one of South Africa's largest baobabs, estimated at 3,000 years old.

content: Uluwatu is Bali's clifftop south, and Jumeirah's all-villa property up here is deliberately far from the island's busier corners. All 123 villas take their cues from Hindu-Javanese architecture: duck egg shutters, double-height beamed ceilings, mahogany furniture and deep freestanding bathtubs. A triple-tiered infinity pool descends toward the beach below. Akasa is the clifftop restaurant, with sweeping ocean views and a kitchen that matches the ambition of the setting; Segaran below it is more relaxed, with a Friday terrace that transforms into a street food market of local Balinese specialties. The spa is home to Bali's first authentic Royal hammam, a tradition traced to 14th-century Ottoman bathhouse culture.

Ocean-facing rooms look straight out over one of Biarritz's most central and sheltered beaches. Inside, original Chengal wood floors, embossed wallpaper and colonial wooden-framed windows survive intact, and the rooms are surprisingly generous for a heritage building, freestanding tub and free minibar in each one. Alvin Leung's restaurant anchors the food offering. Check-in and check-out are replaced by a rolling 24-hour stay from arrival.

The open-air Joglo restaurant moves from Indonesian staples to Mediterranean plates without missing a beat; the bar runs on local fruits, herbs and spices. Solar-powered and biodiverse, the sustainability commitments here go well beyond the usual Bali gestures.

content: Just eight kilometers from Verona's center, above the Squaranto Valley on a plateau at 173 meters, Tenuta Delo has been in the same family since 1894. The estate traces its name to the Greek word for bright, a reference that makes sense the moment you see the extraordinary luminosity of the landscape: vineyards, centuries-old olive groves, and woodland falling away on all sides. At the heart of it stands a ninth-century tower, once a lookout against northern invaders. The eight rooms and suites have antique terracotta floors, exposed beam ceilings, and 19th-century furniture; owner Antonia Mozzanega, a literature teacher by training, has filled the living spaces with books, paintings, and rugs accumulated over generations.

Rooms, suites and thatched pool villas face the terraces directly, with canopied beds, locally crafted headboards and private pools that mirror the mountain skyline. content: The Bisalpur family has lived on this estate for centuries. In 2019, the two brothers, Veer Vinod and Paramvir Singh, opened their 1930s Indo-European villa as a four-room guesthouse. content: Built in 1460 for a lawyer to the French king, Château de Saulon has passed through the hands of Burgundian aristocracy, survived the Revolution, and changed hands many times before Thierry Goux bought it in 2018 and brought in design firm Rinck for a thorough restoration. content: Though it’s been open since the 1980s, the Four Seasons Hotel Austin is arguably more relevant than it’s ever been. Austin is, after all, the state capital — but it’s also the tech capital of Texas, and these days the Four Seasons is as likely to host investors and entrepreneurs as it is government officials. And it certainly doesn’t hurt that, like so many of the brand’s hotels, this Four Seasons has seen an update that leaves it looking more stylish than most luxury hotels of its stature.\n\nIts rooms and suites are handsome, combining mid-century modern cool with Texan touches like leather furniture and subtly Western-themed artworks. The setting, alongside Lady Bird Lake, makes for a surprisingly tranquil, resort-like atmosphere — even though Austin’s many live music venues lie just a few blocks in the other direction. And while that means there’s no end of bars and restaurants within easy reach, the hotel offers plenty of reasons to stay in, including a Latin-influenced restaurant, a second-floor terrace bar, and one of the finest spas in town.

content:
The French luxury-hotel brand Sofitel and the picturesque Francophone city of Montreal are a match made in heaven. The Sofitel Montreal Golden Mile stands tall above the city’s modern downtown district, and after a thorough 2025 renovation it’s one of the most stylish luxury hotels in town.

There’s more than a little bit of mid-century modern inspiration, as well as plenty of color and visual texture. Rooms come with plenty of space, including usable desks, and the suites quickly get extravagant: marble baths, soaking tubs, separate sitting areas. Floor-to-ceiling windows are universal, and offer views of the city and/or Mount Royal.

The Golden Mile location is a convenient one for business as well as leisure travelers, though there’s plenty to do without even venturing outside; Renoir, the restaurant, is a French-Quebeçois hybrid, and Nini Salon à Cocktails is the stylish venue for drinks.
name: Sofitel Montreal Golden Mile

content:
To call Ullrhaus a ski hotel would be a bit of an understatement — it’s named for Ullr, the Norse god of snow, and it’s set in St. Anton am Arlberg, the Tyrolean village that is arguably the birthplace of Alpine skiing and offers access to Austria’s largest interconnected ski area. In such a setting an ordinary Alpine lodge might be enough, but Ullrhaus is far from ordinary.

This strikingly contemporary hotel takes its cues from modern luxury boutique hospitality, and aesthetically it feels like an Alpine-Nordic hybrid, with an emphasis on warm, simple textures and a sparseness that reads to some as quasi-Japanese. Its rooms range from spacious and well-equipped doubles to two-bedroom family suites; the Grand Suite comes with a private sauna.

Meanwhile the spa features multiple saunas of its own, as well as a 17-meter indoor pool. Ullrhaus’s restaurant makes explicit the marriage of Alpine, Nordic, and Japanese influences, and on Thursdays through Saturdays during the winter season there’s a nine-course tasting menu that’s far above and beyond typical après-ski fare, to say the very least. And of course we’d be remiss if we didn’t mention that St. Anton am Arlberg is very nearly as attractive in summer as it is in winter, with no end of opportunity for hikers, bikers, and climbers.

content:
Beverly Wilshire, A Four Seasons Hotel is a bona fide hospitality icon. This grand old Renaissance Revival–style edifice has presided over the end of Rodeo Drive since 1928, and is familiar not only to luxury shoppers but to cinemagoers as well, having appeared in Pretty Woman and countless other Hollywood films. Enter, though, and you’ll be anything but intimidated; the standard of service here is such that every guest immediately assumes VIP status.

And though it’s proud of its history, the Beverly Wilshire is anything but stuck in the past. A 2022 renovation leaves the rooms and suites looking refined indeed: soothing but too richly detailed to be minimalist, quietly luxurious but not so quiet as to be forgettable, and contemporary yet suffused with Old Hollywood atmosphere.

The Spa at Beverly Wilshire is among the most highly regarded in town, and the hotel’s pool, with its Italian-villa atmosphere, is justifiably famous as well. Among the restaurants is CUT by Wolfgang Puck, a local institution since 2006; the location, meanwhile, places all the best of Beverly Hills right at your feet.
name: Beverly Wilshire, Beverly Hills (A Four Seasons Hotel)

content: The Waldorf Astoria’s revival is nothing short of cinematic. After a seven-year restoration by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, this Park Avenue landmark re-emerges with its Art Deco soul fully restored: murals uncovered, silver corridors gleaming, and the Grand Ballroom ready to reclaim its place in the city’s story. Inside, designers Pierre-Yves Rochon and Jean-Louis Deniot created calm, residential-style suites that contrast beautifully with the drama of the public spaces. With Michael Anthony's Lex Yard brasserie and the vast new Guerlain Spa, the Waldorf emerges not as a memory, but as proof that true icons never fade—they simply return, more certain of themselves than ever.

content:
Twenty minutes from Perugia, in the impossibly verdant hills of Umbria, is the secluded Murlo Estate, family-owned for centuries and sprawling over thousands of acres. What was once primarily an agricultural concern is now a first-rate luxury resort, the result of a dedicated effort by Alessio and Carlotta Carabba Tettamanti to restore and adapt a wide variety of historical structures, from farmhouses and a water mill to a 14th-century parish church.

Today it’s a model of high-end slow living, a quiet-luxe experience that’s more closely tied to the land and its history than the typical country luxury hotel. The accommodations range from large and lavish Deluxe rooms to freestanding villas of various sizes with their own gardens, private infinity pools, and outdoor Jacuzzis.

Lavish as they are, the accommodations aren’t the whole story. Il Caldaro, the estate’s restaurant, is a serious farm-to-table affair housed within a restored medieval farmhouse, sourcing ingredients from its own farm and from fine local purveyors. They’ll also send a meal to your villa, if you’d rather dine in, or even a chef for a private culinary experience. Cooking classes, wine tastings, even truffle-hunting expeditions further augment the offerings, and the surrounding region offers no end of attractions: culinary, cultural, and historical.

content: The word “village” understates matters somewhat — Premier Village Phu Quoc Resort occupies the whole of a peninsula at the south end of Phu Quoc, surrounded by the crystal blue waters of the Gulf of Thailand. Many of its 215 villas line the east and west sides of the peninsula, each with its own idyllic beach; others climb the ridges and hillsides for extra seclusion and elevated views.\n\nIn fact, were the arrival not so easy, you could easily forget this isn’t a private island. The facilities are so complete that there’s no need to leave the property. Every villa comes with its own swimming pool, and the resort’s main pool winds, lagoon-like, between the peninsula’s two beaches. The elaborate Plumeria spa offers everything from massages and treatments to yoga and fitness classes, and a dedicated kids’ club keeps younger guests entertained. Restaurants and bars range from a deli and grocery to the upscale Market restaurant, from a beachside juice bar and poolside cocktail bar to the seafood-focused Corallo.

content: Siri Sala began with a glimpse from a longtail boat six years ago: three tilting wooden structures where the Chao Phraya branches into Bangkok Noi canal. Thai-Filipino couple Kirati Thepsoparn and Irma Go tracked down the property, discovering it had been inhabited by the same family since King Rama VI's reign. Five years of restoration transformed the trio of traditional ruean into a whitewashed villa with five bedrooms, a jazz bar with crystal chandeliers built from the oldest structure's salvaged timber, and interiors using inherited relics: earthenware jars as scoop showers, vintage cabinets as bookshelves. The White Lotus cast stayed here during filming. Monks still pass each morning collecting alms.

content: Majestic Hotel & Spa has been on Passeig de Gràcia since 1918, still run by the founding family. The neoclassical façade announces itself, but the real surprise is the 1,000-piece modern art collection inside, works by Antoni Tàpies, Josep Guinovart, and Anish Kapoor that would hold their own in any museum. Recent renovations refreshed the rooms and suites with muted whites and contemporary touches while preserving the building's original character. The rooftop pool and La Dolce Vitae bar deliver sunset views. Below, El Bar del Majestic hosts live piano music most evenings. A shoe shiner still makes afternoon rounds, a tradition maintained for over twenty years.

Bratislava’s LOFT Hotel & Wilson Palace is essentially two hotels in one: the former a modern structure with industrial-inspired interiors, the latter a 19th-century palace in an eclectic Baroque and Rococo style. They are connected via a common entrance and share staff and services, but the experiences are remarkably distinct.

LOFT, for its part, comprises some 110 rooms and suites and backs onto the park that contains the Presidential Gardens and the Government Office of the Slovak Republic. Wilson Palace’s 10 elegant rooms, on the other hand, face Štefánikova Street, something of Bratislava’s Champs-Élysées.

Both share a restaurant and bar, the straightforwardly named Fabrika The Beer Pub, and the city center and the Danube are just a short walk to the south.

content: Located in the heart of Bratislava's historic center, Arcadia Boutique Hotel has a long history of its own, 800 years long give or take, thanks to the hotel being housed in a protected 12th century building. Guests spend days sailing, bird-watching, or lingering on the private beach before dinner at the waterfront restaurant. Elegant but unpretentious, it is New England tradition at its most enduring.

The result is four cottage-style suites furnished with botanical tones and heirlooms from the Visconti collection, while wide porches and fireplaces turn the outdoors into living space. Dining, guided by a biodynamic garden, shapes every stay: from picnic-style lunches to refined dinners, the experience is inseparable from the land that sustains it.

content: Unzen's Azumaen draws on layers of history few Japanese resorts can match. The mountain was sacred to Shingon Buddhists from 701, then became a cosmopolitan summer escape during the Meiji era: Europeans and Shanghai expats gathered here for dance parties and rounds on Japan's first public golf course, opened 1913. The 27-room ryokan maintains gender-separated spa facilities across multiple floors, with meals served privately in rooms or dedicated dining spaces. Beyond the property lie Christian martyrdom sites and trails through the country's inaugural quasi-national park, declared in 1911, where volcanic vents still steam through ancient rock.

content: This 1934 hotel became Japan's first government-approved accommodation for international visitors. American baseball legends including Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig stayed here during their 1934 exhibition tour, occupying specific rooms still referenced today. The building stands on a hill overlooking Mikawa Bay, its white walls topped with green copper Japanese-style roofing meant to evoke castle architecture. Art Deco elements are preserved with the lobby's chandeliers and elevator details. Views extend toward Takeshima Island across the water. Rokkakudo, a hexagonal annex from 1936, and a 1916 wooden structure in sukiya-shoin style remain on the grounds as conserved cultural properties.
name: Gamagori Classic Hotel

content: Like its sister hotel Casa do Conto, Tipografia do Conto puts a contemporary riff on a historic Porto property. Once an industrial space for activities such as typography and graphic arts, the building has now entered a new chapter as a ten key hotel, but still retains its original details such as the stone façade. Facilities include a garden, central courtyard, outdoor pool, and bar Hífen, which also hosts a rotating program of exhibitions, concerts and cultural events.

content: Sitting just a 15-minute drive away from Porto, the Pestana Douro Riverside feels like a seaside resort hotel while still offering easy access to city life. Housed inside a former 19th century factory, the hotel bears little resemblance to its industrial past, although each floor is dedicated to a fragrant flower such as lavender, rose and lily as an homage to the scented soaps and candles that were once made here. Bright white rooms are livened up with floral artworks and pops of yellow and blue, and all come with a balcony, and most with a view of the Douro River that runs right outside. The previously urban setting offers plenty of space for a good selection of multi-generational facilities, including one restaurant and two bars, an indoor heated pool and a rooftop infinity pool, a gym, and if you’re travelling with family, a Kids Club and a games room for all ages.

content: Porto has no shortage of cool design hotels, but not all of them boast a central Ribeira location like Exmo Hotel by Olivia. The historic neighborhood is easily the city’s most charming thanks to its medieval maze of traditional pastel-hued houses, and it’s also one of the most convenient for sightseeing, with major sights such as the Sé de Porto, the Torre dos Clérigos, the Church of São Francisco, and Livraria Lello all within a 15-minute walk away from the hotel. In contrast to the historic surroundings, rooms feel ultra contemporary with textured gray walls, neutral hues, and minimalist Scandi-style furnishings, and all come with views of the city or the Douro River, which is an easy three-minute stroll away. In true boutique hotel-style there isn’t much in the way of facilities, just a library lounge and bar for Portuguese wine and tapas, but with Ribeira on your doorstop, and some of Porto’s most exciting restaurants nearby, you won’t be short of drinking and dining options.

content: Housed in a collection of industrial buildings that sit just by the Douro River, The Rebello Hotel lived many lives before becoming one of Porto’s boldest design hotels, including stints as a cookware factory and a wine warehouse. The 19th-century facades and stone structures have been retained to pay homage to the hotel’s rich history, while the newly created suites, studios and rooms feature contemporary interiors take their design cues from the key elements that surround the hotel – water, wine, wood and industry. The subterranean spa has been inspired by Roman baths, and the stylish pool sits surrounded by curved archways and a tranquil lounge area.  There’s also a gym and a treatment menu of massages and facials. Drinking and dining options include Pot&Pan restaurant for a mix of Portuguese and international dishes and pizzeria M’arrecreo, although arguably the highlight might be Bello Rooftop, which has a stunning view across the Douro River.

content: Perhaps the most charming hotel in Porto, the Pestana Porto A Brasileira is housed in what was once the Cafetaria Portuense A Brasileira, which was the first café in Porto to serve coffee in a cup when it opened back in 1903. It still serves coffee in its new role as the hotel’s all-day dining cafe, now called Historical Café, A Brasileira, which thankfully has retained its early 20th century splendor including ornate columns, decorative moldings and arched windows. Elsewhere the hotel has had a more modern makeover, although the shades of burnt orange, burgundy and brushed gold that feature in the contemporary rooms nod to the historic rich wood and gilded décor in the cafeteria downstairs. There’s also a restaurant, A Brasileira, which serves a modern twist on Portuguese cuisine. Other facilities include a gym, and the hotel can also organize cultural experiences such as guided city tours, river cruises, and visits to nearby wineries.

content: There are country retreats, and there’s The Lodge at Primland. Not only is the hotel surrounded by verdant woodland and Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains, but it also sits on its own 12,000-acre estate to fully immerse guests in nature. Most of the rooms are housed in the main lodge, which offers easy access to the majority of the facilities, but for more privacy there’s the option of the chalet-style Pinnacle suites, the cozy Fairway cottages, or the chance to live out childhood dreams by spending the night in the Tree Houses, which sit high up in the treetops with views across the woodland and the Dan River Gorge. \n\nThe three restaurants are rooted in the local terroir and Primland’s farm-to-table ethos and cater for different moods and occasions, from relaxed Southern classics at Stables Saloon to more gastronomic dishes at Leatherhead. The spa is another highlight, with a large pool that opens onto an outdoor terrace, and treatments courtesy of cult French brand Biologique Recherche. But wellness here isn’t just about pampering, it’s also about getting outdoors to enjoy the various hiking trails, kayaking, al fresco yoga classes, or a few rounds on the 18-hole golf course.

content:
The family-owned Relais Balcone di Giulietta takes its name from the famed balcony on Juliet’s House, a museum in Verona’s old town dedicated to Shakespeare’s star-crossed lovers. The house and its balcony didn’t actually belong to Juliet of course, but that hasn’t stopped it become one of Verona’s main attractions, with the hotel also well situated for visiting other major sights such as the Arena, Piazza Bra and Torre dei Lamberti. During the day, you’re surrounded by the lively bustle of visitors, while in the evening guests can unwind and take in the peaceful, evocative charm of this uniquely atmospheric place.
In the rooms a contemporary style has been smoothly blended with original exposed beams and 17th century frescoes, and some rooms come with added extras such as Jacuzzis, chromo-therapy showers, and balconies, some with a view onto Juliet’s. 
There is no bar or restaurant, but you’re in the heart of the city, where options abound.

content: A Benedictine convent founded in the 11th century, Castel Badia spent two hundred years in ruin before its recent restoration. The original abbesses ruled with unusual autonomy for their time, one even defied the bishopric in the 15th century. Today, twenty-eight rooms occupy the reconstructed fortress, each different in layout and tone, balancing exposed stonework with contemporary furnishings. Seventeen gardens surround the property, including one devoted to medicinal herbs. Fragments of the old chapel and crypt remain open to explore. Five minutes from Plan de Corones, the castle overlooks San Lorenzo di Sebato and the valley below.

content: On the island of Austevoll, Bekkjarvik Gjestgiveri has welcomed travelers since the 17th century, when King Christian IV decreed guesthouses be built along Norway’s coast. The hotel’s interiors and artistic direction are by Philippe Starck, which means even aside from the setting it’s a memorable experience. content: The Clements has been part of Cambridge life since 1866, when Archibald Clements opened the town’s first hotel on Duke Street. Its latest restoration lets those details shine once more. Downstairs, the Gallery Restaurant and a speakeasy bar set the tone for convivial evenings, often beginning with the hotel’s own gin, distilled from an 1860s recipe and poured with history in every glass.

content: SCHLOSS Roxburghe might sit surrounded by its own championship golf course, but there’s plenty to do here beyond just improving your swing. The hotel takes a something for everyone approach with a mix of classic countryside sports such as clay pigeon shooting and fishing offered alongside yoga sessions, traditional croquet on the lawn, and family-friendly wildlife tracking. As a complement to SCHLOSS’s packed program of outdoor pursuits, the spa is based around nature being its own form of wellbeing with activities such as archery and estate walks combined with sessions of meditation. There’s also an outdoor heated infinity pool, a plunge pool, two saunas, a hot tub, fitness room and treatments courtesy of ESPA for a complete wellness experience. \n\nGuest rooms and suites are a mix of styles depending on whether they’re housed in the Historic Manor or the contemporary Estate House, but all come with golf course or parkland views, and some with open fires and private balconies. By night signature restaurant Sunlaws and the bistronomic Charlie’s both celebrate the Scottish terroir, and more than 250 whiskies line the walls of Bar 1745, which hosts tasting sessions for guests who want to delve further into the collection.

A fine-dining restaurant celebrates seasonal produce from the region. History, design, and wilderness meet in this quietly glamorous corner of Triglav National Park.

content: Hotel 1928 occupies the former Grand Karem Shrine Temple, a 1928 Moorish Revival landmark reimagined with Art Deco flair and Southern warmth. Original details remain: painted beams, arched windows, hardwood floors, layered now with plush lounges, patterned textiles, and the sparkle of chandeliers in the grand ballroom. The 33 rooms are intimate yet stylish, while public spaces include a café, two restaurants, a library, and tucked-away sitting rooms. Ten minutes from the Silos, the hotel is both a tribute to Waco’s past and a gathering place for its present.

content: While foreign travelers continue to flock to Phuket and Koh Samui, they’re also catching on to a destination Thai vacationers have long known. Hua Hin is no undiscovered hot spot, but a fully established resort city, and many of its best stays are unabashedly large in scale. Among them is the InterContinental Hua Hin Resort, a beachside resort in an East-meets-West style whose size, at 159 rooms and suites, makes it very nearly a boutique hotel, by local standards.\n\nOf course InterContinental is no boutique operation. This is highly professional luxury hospitality, with the seamless ease that’s the hallmark of the best high-end resorts. The style is attractive in a maximally palatable way, another InterContinental specialty. The beach is perhaps the most obvious leisure venue, but the hotel backs it up with a substantial spa and wellness center, in addition to a lovely central pool lined with loungers and daybeds. And a multitude of restaurants serve everything from high-end contemporary Thai cuisine to pizzas by the poolside.

content: In a sheltered bay along the Turkish Riviera, Ahãma offers a slower rhythm of living shaped by nature and stillness. Its rooms and cabanas take inspiration from Japanese wabi-sabi, with sun-washed textures, earthy materials, and an open connection to the landscape. Days unfold gently: sunrise yoga, forest bathing in a pine-shaded pool, or sound therapy sessions near the water. Highlights include the adults-only Êge Umi for Japanese coastal fare and Ay for bold, fire-kissed Aegean dishes. There are no TVs here, but panoramic views of the Göcek Islands more than fill the frame. Ahãma, meaning “beloved” in ancient Lycian, lives up to its name.

content: Le Chambard doesn’t play at being local. It is local. Run by Patricia and Olivier Nasti, the hotel blends Alsatian heritage with refined hospitality, from its timbered walls to its table settings. Rooms vary in layout and mood, but all share a sense of warmth: earthy tones, artisan touches, and windows that catch the changing light over the Vosges or the village below. At the heart of it all is a culinary duo: the rustic warmth of the Winstub and the precision of Olivier Nasti’s Michelin-starred dining room. Kaysersberg may be postcard-pretty, but Le Chambard turns it into something cinematic.

content: Villa René Lalique feels less like a hotel and more like stepping into the private world of its namesake. With just six suites, each referencing the textures and forms of Lalique’s glasswork, the experience is equal parts retreat and revelation. The interiors are curated: family photographs, sculptural lighting, and even a crystal-encased speaker designed with Jean-Michel Jarre. Outside, the woods and hills of Alsace stretch out in all directions; inside, a team devoted to detail keeps everything humming in harmony. This is more than a stay. It is an invitation into a house of art.

content: Warehouse Terrada began as an art storage concern, and is now not just a major exhibitor but has turned the canal-side district of Tennozu into a thriving Tokyo arts district. Nor are they content to stop there — Petals Tokyo is the group’s first foray into hospitality, and it is, to say the very least, no ordinary hotel. Here four houseboats in dramatically divergent styles comprise what might be Tokyo’s most unique lodging. Inside, they’re still distinctive, though more luxurious and more sedate than their exteriors might lead you to believe. Naturally there’s not much space for an on-site restaurant, but Tennozu’s offerings are plentiful.

content: Kohanyu takes the word “natural” as its inspiration, and explores multiple dimensions of this deceptively rich concept. Luxurious, sparsely decorated rooms look out over artfully framed views of the surrounding greenery, and the cuisine is made from freshly harvested local ingredients. It’s a memorable modern twist on the timeless ryokan experience.

content: Otis Harbor Springs offers a serene escape in the heart of Northern Michigan. Located just outside the charming town of Harbor Springs, the property sits near the scenic Tunnel of Trees route. Once inside, the historic inn reveals a welcoming atmosphere with plenty of spaces to relax, from the vintage-inspired Fireplace Lounge to the peaceful courtyard with a pool and bocce court. content:
The owners of the highly regarded Gostilna AS in Ljubljana are behind this mountain retreat, a striking modernist structure set on the hillside above the Julian Alpine village of Gozd Martuljek. Chalet Sofija offers just five suites, each named after one of the owners’ grandchildren. They range from the lavish Suite Izabela, with its panoramic views and 60 square meters of space, to the extraordinary Presidential Suite Izak, whose expansive outdoor terrace nearly doubles its already generous footprint.

Luxurious as the accommodations are, they’re only part of the experience. As you’d expect from restaurateurs of this caliber, Chalet Sofija places equal emphasis on its gourmet restaurant, where the chef-owner personally commands the open kitchen in a dining room framed by distant mountain peaks. An on-site spa adds another layer of indulgence, while the surrounding mountains beckon year-round, offering endless opportunities for skiing, cycling, hiking, and more.

Rates include half board accommodation.

content: In a city full of stars, Los Angeles Fairmont Century Plaza has managed to stand out as one of them since 1966. American presidents and British royalty all passed through the hotel’s doors during its glitzy heyday, plus a rollcall of industry icons when it played host to the Emmys and Grammys. After a Fairmont takeover, and refurbishment, it’s now looking fresh faced once again, with classic contemporary rooms that highlight sunset views of LA with floor-to-ceiling windows and balconies. The F&B offering comprises The Bar at Century Plaza and French brasserie Lumière, which opens onto an attractive garden patio. However, the standout here is the spa, which offers an intriguing mix of classic massages, red light therapy, mindfulness sessions, and power naps on an anti-gravity bed, plus a rooftop pool for a spectacular City of Angels view.

It is a working farm at heart, but one that lets you slow down and experience Douro without filters.

content: It’s an unusual name, but it makes its point: what’s gone missing at Missing Hotel is not the hotel itself, but you, for the duration of your stay. This 11-unit escape is set near the town of Marble Falls, just beyond the outskirts of Austin — close enough for an easy weekend trip, but far enough to feel properly secluded. Call it glamping, if you must, or forest bathing, or just a Hill Country getaway, but the bottom line is the same: a collection of geodesic domes and villas built on platforms amid the treetops, each one with a plunge pool or a hot tub for maximum relaxation. The style is a quirky mix of modern and bohemian, and is nothing if not memorable — and the same goes for the whole experience, which is perfectly comfortable yet delighfully off-the-grid.

content: After pioneering luxury slow travel since 1883, Orient Express is now encouraging travelers to stop and stay awhile in the Eternal City with the opening of its first ever hotel, La Minerva. The storied property first began life as a 17th century aristocratic mansion before being transformed into one of Rome’s grand hotels in 1811, when it pulled in a creative crowd such as Herman Melville, Stendhal, and George Sand. It has now been restored to its former glory by designer Hugo Toro, who has smoothly blended original elements such as marble statues and ornate Murano chandeliers with a more contemporary Art Deco style. Guests can enjoy evening drinks at La Minerva Bar under the building’s historic skylight, or head to the rooftop restaurant and bar for Mediterranean cuisine and cocktails with a view of the nearby Pantheon and the Roman skyline.\nThe experience is further enhanced by Orient Express – La Dolce Vita, a luxury train offering 2-3 day journeys across Italy, featuring refined interiors created by Dimore Studio.

content:
There’s getting away from it all, and then there’s Eriro. This former cottage and inn turned mountain retreat sits at an elevation of 1,550 meters (about 5,085 feet) at the foot of the Zugspitze Mountain, and higher than any other hotel in the area. So high in fact, that’s it’s accessible only by cable car during ski season, and snowcat out of season. Now owned by three local couples, all childhood friends who wanted to respect the region’s heritage, Eriro has been sensitively transformed to introduce guests to a slower way of living and foster a connection with nature.

Corridors lined in natural clay and bobbled wool lead to nine private suites, which put a contemporary spin on traditional Alpine design. Unfinished spruce wood walls are complemented by a soothing neutral palette and layers of tactile materials, while the pared back wooden furnishings have all been crafted bespoke, from the hand carved doors and milking-stool-inspired chairs to the more unusual log baths in seven of the nine suites, which have been dried out and carved from a single piece of wood. There are no televisions, instead guests are invited to play one of the traditional board games or vinyl records that are provided in each suite, or simply admire the spectacular view from the floor-to-ceiling windows. 

Over the course of each stay Eriro’s all-inclusive concept takes guests on a gastronomic journey across the mountainside through locally sourced fresh produce, meat, and cheese, and the fermentations and jams concocted by the team to preserve the flavors of the previous season. Experiences are also rooted in the region, from pottery classes, mountain hiking, and even yodeling, but for a quieter moment Eriro’s spa beckons with its Finnish and herbal saunas, an onsen pool, meditation pool, and bespoke massage treatments based around traditional mountain herbs.
name: Eriro

content:
Transforming the former headquarters of the Dutch aviation company KLM into a hotel for modern travelers feels like a fitting homage to the airline’s founder Albert Plesman. To respect the history and architectural heritage of the landmark 1930s building, many of the original design elements have been retained, including the austere brick and concrete façade, the revolving entrance door, and inside, the KLM reception desks. Also look up to spot the original ceilings near the elevators, which nod to the shape of an aircraft engine.

The 103 guest rooms and 19 short stay, serviced apartments have been given a retro feel with warm shades of brown, burnt orange and a mish mash of abstract patterns. The finishing touch is artworks picked out from the hotel’s 500-strong collection, which includes pieces borrowed from The Hague’s sculpture museum Beelden aan Zee. Another homage to Plesman is the Albert Bar & Lounge for morning coffee, evening drinks and light bites, and Restaurant Suus, named after his wife, which serves European classics from breakfast through to dinner.
name: De Plesman Hotel The Hague

content: Other New Yorkers have indulged country-house fantasies in the Hudson Valley, but none as intricately detailed and meticulously plotted as this. The Six Bells Countryside Inn is the work of entrepreneur Audrey Gelman, known first for a line of women-only co-working spaces and later for the Six Bells home goods shop in Brookyln’s Cobble Hill. There’s a whole fictional backstory and cast of characters involved in the Inn’s creation, but for guests, what matters most is that its eleven rooms (and its inviting public spaces) are as quietly luxurious as they are filled with visual interest.\n\nThis means, among other things, high-end Ostermoor mattresses on canopy or box beds, and painstakingly sourced antique and retro furnishings. The design is historically minded, but not true to any one period or place — unless you count Barrow Green, the fictional English village that inspired the whole Six Bells aesthetic. The Feathers, meanwhile, is the restaurant and tavern, a partnership with Molly Levine, a highly regarded Hudson Valley restaurateur.
name: Six Bells Countryside Inn

content:
Few places in the world can claim to combine a lush rainforest setting with top-flight luxury quite like Costa Rica’s Papagayo Peninsula, and its case is only made stronger by the addition of Nekajui, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve. Here, on a clifftop overlooking the Pacific, stands an understated but substantial central lodge orbited by a constellation of rooms, suites, and villas — some of which are reached via a wooden suspension bridge that hangs across a ravine.

The Reserve sub-brand is Ritz-Carlton’s top-end product, and it shows. Here you’ll find multiple pools for distinct poolside atmospheres, a spa and wellness complex that covers some 27,000 square feet, and a beach club that’s connected to the resort via a funicular that descends the steep hillside. The standard of service is extremely high, and the in-room comforts are first-rate — this is as true in the Treetop Tents, with their canvas construction, as it is in the rooms, suites, and villas. 

To all this is added a generous and varied selection of restaurants, as well as offsite activities that range from a racquet club and a 72-hole Arnold Palmer–designed course to surfing, sailing, and a wide array of excursions by land and sea. It’s tempting to call this the definitive word on the Papagayo experience.
name: Nekajui, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve

Small gardens look out over the baroque skyline, and breakfast is served at a long wooden table carved into the hillside. It is a distinctly Sicilian stay in one of the island’s most visually striking towns.

content: Les Bains Gardians offers a side of France few travelers ever see. content: For almost thirty years the Villa Pétrusse sat empty, its salons shuttered and gardens overgrown. Built in 1880 by textile merchant Henri-Eugène de Kerkhove, with architecture by Pierre Kemp and landscaping by Édouard André, it was once considered a “miniature château.” Its recent restoration has given the villa new life without erasing its past: worn stone staircases, hidden passages, and preserved details now stand alongside 22 rooms, suites, and a penthouse. Overlooking the Pétrusse River and Adolphe Bridge, the hotel captures both the romance of its history and the vitality of its new chapter.

content: On the northern slopes of Mount Etna, Palazzo Previtera stands as a deeply rooted expression of Sicilian culture, history, and intellectual life. This restored baroque residence hosts several bedrooms, two cottages, and a collection of spaces devoted to art, research, and education. Ceilings and interiors have been meticulously conserved, not redone, preserving the original 17th-century craftsmanship. Beyond its architectural beauty, the Palazzo functions as a hub for cultural dialogue, hosting artists, curators, and researchers who contribute to its ongoing evolution. A stay here invites immersion, not just rest.

content: Overlooking the iconic Nubble Lighthouse, ViewPoint Hotel makes the most of its dramatic coastal perch. This updated 1990s motor lodge has been reimagined by longtime locals Joe Lipton and Michelle Friar into a year-round boutique stay with just 18 rooms and suites. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame the Atlantic, while private patios and smart, coastal-modern interiors bring the outdoors in. There is a pool, hot tub, sauna, and beach access, plus bikes, yoga classes, and a shuttle to sister spot Stones Throw. It is relaxed, design-conscious, and exactly where you'd want to be for a Maine escape.

content: High above the island’s southern coast, Ishigaki Hills is home to two modern villas designed for slow days and shared company. Each comes with a heated infinity pool, garden loungers, and wide-open views of the Pacific. Inside, you will find open-plan living areas, thoughtful details like a electric piano and lofted bedrooms, and plenty of space for families or friends to spread out. There is room to cook, rest, and reconnect, whether over dinner or stargazing on the deck. It is a place to pause, breathe, and take in the slowness of island life.

content: Staufeneck Castle has been a hilltop landmark in the Swabian Alps for the better part of a millennium. Extensive renovations helped transform the medieval fortress into the Burghotel Staufeneck, a luxury hotel with sweeping views over the green valley below. Rooms are elegant and luminous with native wood and stone details, and suites feature charmingly sloped ceilings and spacious bathrooms with soaking tubs. Some overlook the castle courtyard, and others face the heated outdoor infinity pool, part of the hotel’s stylish wellness center, which also includes Roman-style baths, an ice grotto, and a log-cabin sauna. Other highlights include a one-MICHELIN-Star restaurant and hiking trails that start at the front door; in winter, staff lead guided nighttime hikes, illuminated by torchlight and followed by a traditional mulled-wine reception.
name: Burghotel Staufeneck

content: Sitara Himalaya, a stylish and luxurious ten-room lodge high in the mountains of northern India, is quite obviously anything but an ordinary hotel. It’s here that Good Earth founder Anita Lal has created a hospitality experience that combines the finest aspects of a private home and a luxury resort, a place that’s motivated not by profit-and-loss statements but by the Vedic concept of oneness with the cosmos.\n\nIndian, Tibetan, and English influences are on display in the interiors, and as stunning as they are, the real star of the show is the setting, a valley fringed by spectacular mountain peaks. An Ayurvedic spa and a Himalayan kitchen provide two avenues to restoration, and the surroundings offer no end of opportunities for exploration.

content: Compared to the many hotels occupying historic buildings in Old Tbilisi, the Mercure Tbilisi Old Town is practically brand new. There are perks to its modern profile — try finding an up-to-date fitness center at any of the traditional Georgian townhouses in the neighborhood — especially considering the perfectly central location just a few minutes’ walk from Metekhi Cathedral, and some of the city’s best thermal bathhouses. Rooms are bright and contemporary, with polished parquet floors, jewel-toned accents, and large windows facing tall trees. The hotel's crowning glory is undoubtedly the spacious rooftop terrace, an ideal spot to sample locally produced wines after a day out sightseeing.

content: Lake Tisza might be second to Lake Balaton in terms of size and popularity, but that’s exactly why it’s worth a visit. The man-made reservoir offers similar sights and experiences but without quite the same number of crowds, from spotting the rare bird species that live here to cycling along the 70-kilometre bike path that follows the edge of the lake. Natur Lodge Tiszafüred respects these natural surroundings with just two quiet wood cabins, each with its own outdoor sauna and jacuzzi as a pleasant way to immerse you in the outdoors. And so you can switch off, quite literally, each cabin comes with a selection of board games and an acoustic guitar, although don’t worry, there’s WiFi and Netflix too.

Expect high-ceilinged rooms with bespoke details, a rooftop bar overlooking the Black Forest, and a spa designed for real downtime. content: Szeged, Hungary may be best known for a university with roots that go back centuries, but it’s a city with a modern side as well. Witness Noir Hotel, a 17-unit apartment-style hotel in the historic center of town. It’s set a mere two blocks from the 19th-century city hall, but inside it’s as modern and as urban as they come, its loft-style apartments featuring raw concrete ceilings, efficient modular storage, and contemporary colors and furnishings. Services are necessarily minimal, given the apartment-hotel concept, but each unit comes with a kitchenette, and the city’s restaurants are close at hand.

content: Two hours’ drive from Budapest, in the lakeside resort town of Balatonfüred, the Hotel Petit Bois offers a thoroughly luxurious experience. The adults-only policy certainly doesn’t hurt, but more important is its atmosphere of Belle Époque elegance, tempered with judicious contemporary flourishes and modern, even high-tech comforts. Many rooms overlook the park that lends the hotel its name, while others have views of the lake. The rooftop bar and restaurant is a particular highlight, opening as it does onto a terrace with a pool; the spa, too, is noteworthy, an elaborate escape in a characteristically Hungarian manner.

content: Near the banks of Lake Schluchsee and surrounded by thick Black Forest trees, Boutique Hotel Mühle is a 17th-century grain mill that has been carefully reimagined as a soulful little retreat. The stream that once powered the mill still runs beside the terrace, and signs of its history show up in the timber beams and tiled stoves. The owners are hands-on and present, and it shows, from the wood-fired sauna to the small, well-run restaurant, where local ingredients take on subtle French and Japanese influences. It is an easygoing place with real character, perfect for slow days and early nights.

content: H11 Rooms is a smart addition to Esztergom, one of the oldest towns in Hungary. Just six rooms are split across two buildings to offer both space and privacy, with each attractively decorated in warm shades of wood and mustard and a mix of textures and patterned wallpapers. Half of the rooms come with a terrace, and one with a fully equipped kitchen, making it ideal for longer stays. Some rooms also offer attractive views of St. Anne's Church. content: Not so long ago, the Baroque and medieval city of Eger, Hungary would have been the last place you’d look for a boutique hotel of any description — much less one as elegant as the 1552 Boutique Hotel. Tours of this picturesque city and the surrounding wine country are available; a short distance away on foot, within the old castle walls, is the associated gastronomic restaurant, 1552 Étterem.

content: You almost feel transported back to the Golden Age of Travel when you step inside Asher Adams. Housed inside what was formerly Salt Lake City’s train depot, the hotel is continuing the building’s legacy as a hub for travelers, but this time is encouraging them to stay a while before rushing off to catch the next train. Many of the building’s original design elements have been restored, from stained glass windows to terrazzo flooring, and whilst guest room don’t quite hark back to the building’s 1909 beginnings, the mid-century décor does give them a suitably nostalgic look. The restaurant and two bars have an all-American feel, with modern American classics at restaurant Rouser and a whiskey-based cocktail menu at bar No. 119. But the standout spot is The Bar at Asher Adams, where you can sip classic cocktails under the gilded gold arched ceiling of the depot’s Grand Hall.
name: Asher Adams, Autograph Collection

With the Nabataean tombs just minutes away, and silence as the loudest luxury, this is AlUla at its most elemental and rare.

Thatched-roof villas come with private gardens and pools, while open-air buggies shuttle guests past lakes, dunes, and roaming wildlife: zebras, giraffes, even golden tigers. content:
Set in the city’s Business Gate district, home to multiple high-profile corporate headquarters, the Fairmont Riyadh is unmistakably built with business in mind. But here, the line between business-friendly luxury and resort-style relaxation begins to blur. 

The art deco lobby makes an impression with black-and-gold geometry, dramatic chandeliers, and seven domes that pay tribute to classical Islamic architecture. Meanwhile the rooms are handsomely understated, in sober dark colors with focused accents; the in-room comforts are predictably high-end, including Le Labo bath products. The entry-level rooms are already spacious, but the suites are where things expand to palatial proportions.

A lavish spa is present as a matter of course, as are a pair of restaurants: a Gatsby-inspired steakhouse called House of Grill and a southern Italian eatery by the name of Che Figata.

content: Unlike Petra and Wadi Rum, which bring in a steady stream of international visitors, the coastal city of Aqaba has mostly been a weekend escape for Jordanians. But that’s quickly changing, as more travelers discover the region’s beautiful and easily accessible beaches, and world-class hotels like Al Manara have popped up to meet the demand. Set on the edge of the Red Sea, it’s the Luxury Collection’s debut in Jordan, but it doesn’t look like any other Marriott you’ve seen. \n\nIts modern architecture pays homage to the ancient port nearby, with stylistic influences drawn from Mediterranean and Levantine cultures, though key elements — native stone walls, decorative tile floors, high vaulted ceilings — are rooted in local tradition. Rooms have a regal air: dark wood furnishings inlaid with brass and mother-of-pearl, bespoke beds topped with Frette linens and richly patterned textiles, marble bathrooms with tubs, floor-to-ceiling windows, and private balconies facing the sea or the mountains. Ivory archways shade the indoor-outdoor bar beside the gorgeous waterfront infinity pool, and a private lagoonside beach club is just steps away.

content: Jordan’s desert landscapes inspired the aesthetic of the Fairmont Amman, whose earth-toned interiors are grand in scale and filled with natural light. But the hotel’s designers, a team from Wimberly Allison Tong & Goo, also took a cue from the region’s art and architecture, outfitting the airy spaces with locally sourced limestone, striking geometric patterns, and original artworks by Jordanian artists. \n\nRooms are elegant and spacious, with bespoke beds, floor-to-ceiling windows, and marble bathrooms stocked with Le Labo products; with fireplaces and kitchens, the suites are rather more like luxury apartments. An outdoor pool offers spectacular views over Amman’s mosques and minarets, as does the rooftop bar, while the spa, the largest in the city, features a one-of-a-kind Dead Sea plunge pool. The hotel’s sleek dining venues, including a Lebanese restaurant topped with a gorgeous stained-glass dome and an opulent tea lounge, are standouts in the upscale Abdoun district.

content: Jordan’s only port city has a lot going for it, perhaps its beautiful coastline first and foremost. Aqaba sits on a peaceful gulf of the same name, an inlet of the Red Sea, with miles of beaches facing an expanse of crystal-clear water and offshore coral reefs. The Westin Saraya Aqaba Resort & Spa sits right near the shore, backing up against the Saraya Lagoon on the other side. It’s quite a location, and the hotel’s design makes the most of it with several waterfront pools and open-air dining spaces. \n\nRooms have great views, too: each has a private balcony overlooking the mountains or the lagoon. The look is fresh and modern, with earth tones and deep blue accents mirroring the landscapes outside, and suites are particularly grand with wood-paneled living rooms and high arching windows. The spa, fitness center, and kids club are all standard for the Westin brand, but the private beach club, with its umbrellas and chaise longues lined up on the white-sand shore of the lagoon, is one-of-a-kind.

content: There’s something pleasantly down–to-earth about Bratus Hotel in downtown Aqaba. Unlike many of the coastal city’s luxury hotels, the majority of which are affiliated with international chains and located in a designated hotel zone, this boutique hotel is part of an independent Jordanian hospitality group that’s focused on sustainability. There’s a vintage look to their wrought-iron balconies and intricately tiled bathrooms, and some face the mountains or the Red Sea in the distance. Rounding out the hotel’s simple offerings are a café, restaurant, and a small spa, and the beach is just a short stroll away.

content:
Thanks to its location between the Caucasus Mountains and the Black Sea, Tbilisi was an important stop on the Silk Road. Only a couple of its many caravanserai — overnight lodgings for trade caravans — remain today, including one that houses the Tbilisi History Museum. The other, a regal red-brick building with a decorative Moorish facade in the heart of the old city, is home to Qarvasla Hotel. 

The restored interiors are industrial-chic, the central courtyard transformed into a sleek lobby lounge with dramatically illuminated greenery, elegant keyhole archways, and opulent light installations suspended from the high ceilings. Moody monochromatic corridors lead to modern rooms with slate-gray carpeting and leather headboards; some have freestanding tubs and private wraparound balconies. 

Live music sets the scene every night at the hotel’s sophisticated restaurant, where a blend of Georgian and European influences pays homage to the building’s position on the historic trade route.
name: Qarvasla Hotel

content: Imitation is a form of flattery in the Valle de Guadalupe, where many luxury hotels and wineries are Mediterranean in style, with ideal grape-growing conditions — sunny days and cool nights — to match. One example is El Cielo Resort, with Tuscan-inspired villas set amid picturesque vineyards and olive groves. Yet there’s plenty of Mexican character to the interiors outfitted in native wood and stone, not to mention inside its excellent restaurant specializing in Baja-Yucatán fusion cuisine. \n\nGround-level suites have king-sized beds, fully equipped kitchens, spacious bathrooms with Jacuzzis, and sliding glass doors that open onto private patios with firepits, while those on upper levels feature high vaulted ceilings and elevated views over the surrounding scenery. Most feature wine cellars or fridges to store a few bottles after a day out exploring wine country, and the hotel’s fleet of bicycles and golf carts makes it easy to join on-site tastings and tours.

content: The small Scottish town of Rothes is at the heart of whisky country, and despite its unassuming name, the Station Hotel is by a considerable distance the finest lodging in town. Its proprietors’ first career was in the whisky business — no fewer than 500 varieties line the bar’s shelves — but they’re naturals at hospitality as well, as evidenced by the sheer quality of this handsome 15-room hotel.\n\nRooms and suites are an understated blend of contemporary and classic, and are quietly, confidently luxurious, down to the Hypnos beds and spa-like bathrooms; they span the range from a plush single room to five lavish suites named for famous distillers. And in spite of the hotel’s small size, it features not just the Spirit Safe whisky bar, but two restaurants as well: the fine-dining Pagodas and the more casual Toot’s Café Bar and Bistro.

content: Once a Saadian residence, Riad Antara now hosts just seven suites behind a carved wooden door near the Bahia Palace. Owners Anne and Laurent bring a sense of warmth that runs through every corner, from the gifted babouche slippers to the rooftop breakfasts. content: Once an important stop on the Silk Road, the medieval Rajasthani city of Bikaner is sometimes referred to as a jewel in the desert. Several of its palaces have been converted into hotels, like the opulent home of the last Maharaja, who died without a male heir in 2003, effectively ending the city’s royal lineage. His sumptuous Art Deco-style residence was converted into Narendra Bhawan, a one-of-a-kind, over-the-top luxury hotel that’s an unmistakable reminder of Bikaner’s glittering heyday. \n\nThe eclectic interiors reflect the prince’s penchant for world travel, with Portuguese tiles, English antiques, rich velvet upholstery, and locally crafted terrazzo floors, and while rooms are uniquely decorated, they’re all lavishly appointed with king-sized beds and rare art objects. Many have soaking tubs and spacious living rooms with vintage bar carts. The palace’s elegant ground-level parlors have been transformed into a glamorous bar, an upscale restaurant, and a pastry shop, while up on the rooftop, an infinity pool overlooks the city’s old quarter.

content:
A naturalist-guided cruise is still the most conventional way to explore the Galápagos, but Pikaia Lodge makes a strong case for considering a land-based adventure. Considered the archipelago’s first luxury hotel, it’s located on the edge of a volcanic caldera on the island of Santa Cruz — a dramatically beautiful setting, to say the least — with an ultra-modern design that stands out from its rugged surroundings. 

Rooms and suites are sleek and minimalist with floor-to-ceiling windows facing panoramic views of the mountains and the vast Pacific. All are lavishly appointed with supple bamboo wood flooring, spacious Peruvian travertine marble-lined bathrooms with soaking tubs, and private terraces or gardens. 

Other highlights include a large infinity-edge pool, a Japanese-inspired wellness center, and an elegant all-day restaurant. South American wines are served by glowing firepits after dark, and the lodge has a private fleet of boats for excursions around the island.

content:
Whether you know it as Karlovy Vary or Carlsbad, chances are you’ve heard of this most famous of Czech spa towns — for hundreds of years it played host to everyone who was anyone, from Peter the Great to Karl Marx. Now it’s in the ascendancy again, and the top lodging in town is among the most storied in Europe, the 300-year-old Grandhotel Pupp.

They come from all over Eastern Europe and beyond, mostly for the legendary mineral waters, but they stay for the Pupp, an absolute palace of a hotel, made from the old mold. To be frank it’s not going to bowl you over with high-tech amenities, nor with interior design — this place gets by on pure atmosphere. Modern health spas have taken on a distinctly medical ambience, but not so the almost baroque Pupp. Likewise the modern luxury hotel has become a clinical operation — this place, by contrast, drips with character and idiosyncrasy.

Here you’ll experience treatments rarely found anywhere else, as well as chandelier-festooned dining rooms and clubby, wood-paneled dining rooms. If you’re here for your nerves, take in the view of the city from the hilltop behind the Pupp; otherwise an evening in the Pupp’s casino, one of Eastern Europe’s classics, may be indicated.

content: In an undisturbed corner of Al-Ula Old Town, Dar Tantora occupies a maze of centuries-old mud-brick houses which have been sensitively restored with reed-covered ceilings, antique-inspired lighting, and at the entrance, a hard-carved door that preserves the privacy of the village. The 30 tranquil guest rooms sit surrounded by the gentle rustle of date palms and combine a respect for the past with modern comforts; there’s a record player and a collection of vinyl to set your own mood, and although the hotel is powered by electricity, the gentle flicker of candlelight from the traditional lanterns feels more atmospheric. A quiet rooftop pool, meditation and yoga area and in-room massages offer a deeper moment of relaxation, and restaurant Joontos focuses on local ingredients for its Middle Eastern and Spanish flavors. It does not feel like stepping back in time, it feels like time never left.\n\nPlease note: Our property is designed without modern air conditioning. Our authentic thick mud-brick walls and natural ventilation keep interiors cool and fresh from October to May. Shaded terraces enhance airflow and provide comfortable outdoor spaces.

content: At the intersection of Calea Victoriei and Elisabeta Boulevard, this 19th-century landmark returns to form under Corinthia. Originally opened in 1873, it was the first hotel in Bucharest to install electric lights and an elevator, and later became a center for royal receptions and art exhibitions. Today, just 30 suites occupy the building, each with high ceilings, bespoke furnishings, and views onto the city. Original features of marble staircases, carved columns, and statuary remain, carefully restored. Boulevard 73, the ballroom restaurant, continues the sense of occasion. And once again, the building is doing what it was built to do.
name: Corinthia Grand Hotel du Boulevard Bucharest

content: The first Park Hyatt in the world opened on Chicago’s Magnificent Mile in 1980 — and several decades and multiple rounds of renovations later, it’s still a standout in the brand’s wide-ranging collection. For everyone else, there’s the NoMI Garden cocktail bar on the rooftop terrace overlooking Michigan Avenue.

content: East Lothian’s Golf Coast isn’t short on scenery, but Aberlady might just be its prettiest village, and The Leddie its warmest welcome. Set in a 17th-century inn, it has been renovated with a light touch using mossy greens, delicate wool throws, and the occasional wink of tartan. Upstairs, rooms are calm and comfortable; downstairs, the restaurant and bar fill with locals and golfers over plates of comfort food and pints of house-brewed lager. It’s stylish, deeply Scottish, and just steps from some of the country’s best links.
