content: Set amid the islands of Unzen-Amakusa National Park is L’isola THE BIRD, a small wellness-oriented resort whose unusual name is part of an unusual approach to Japanese seaside hospitality. Here the architecture is unapologetically modern, from the lodge with its recessed balconies to the staggered row of freestanding cottages with their sawtooth pitched roofs.\n\nWhat’s inside, however, is a perfectly timeless seaside escape, however novel its style. Modernist furniture and warm, richly textured materials lend the rooms and cottages plenty of visual appeal, and all of them are oriented to look out over the volcanic Mount Unzen and the Ariake Sea, while the birds that inspired the hotel’s name crisscross the skies overhead. A sauna complex is complemented by an outdoor Jacuzzi and an infinity pool, while the restaurant serves dishes crafed from Amakusa and Kumamoto ingredients.
name: L'isola THE BIRD

content: The Nasu Highlands’ hot springs and hiking trails have attracted Japanese travelers for centuries. Thanks to high-speed bullet trains, the region is now an easy weekend getaway from the capital, with ultra-modern spa hotels like Nasu-Onsen Shinshun no Kago Hewitt Resort maintaining the high standards to which Tokyoites are accustomed. \n\nWith a minimalist design and soaring glass windows, this ryokan-style resort blends into the surrounding forest. Each room is a sleek sanctuary with high ceilings, cedar paneling, bespoke Ploh bedding, a writing desk, and a private onsen that’s partly open to the elements; a few also feature private saunas. Stylish communal spaces include a fireplace-warmed living room and a library with a collection of art books and Karuizawa whiskies, all with peaceful views of the surrounding woods.

content: Maybe these things go on hundred-year cycles; whatever the reason, it’s safe to say Art Deco is enjoying its moment in the sun. Hotel Ivy, A Luxury Collection Hotel, Minneapolis takes, as its starting point, the Ivy Tower, a ziggurat-style landmark reminiscent of some of New York’s early skyscrapers. And while this tower is dwarfed by its modern additions, the style of the Hotel Ivy’s interiors takes on its influence, its ultra-cool clean lines livened by pronounced Deco flourishes. Underneath it all, this is a thoroughly luxurious modern hotel, the lodging of choice for visiting sports teams and many other honored guests. And it’s no dull business hotel: the Ivy’s spa makes it something of a leisure destination, and its restaurant and bar are eminently worthy of their setting.

content: Many travelers visit Yen Tu Mountain, a sacred site that’s considered the birthplace of Vietnamese Buddhism, on a day trip from Hanoi or Ha Long Bay. But spending the night at Legacy Yen Tu - MGallery, a luxury resort located at the base of the mountain, is an unforgettable experience. The hotel offers privileged access to the remote region’s main attraction — a cable car trip and hike lead to Yen Tu’s famous pagodas and Golden Buddha statue, and staying close by means beating the crowds — and the resort, built to resemble a traditional palace and monastery, is a destination in itself.\n\nLegacy Yen Tu opened in 2018, and while the buildings are new, the architecture was inspired by ancient Vietnamese design. Its temple-like silhouette is complemented by interiors rich with color and art — handcrafted ceramic floor tiles, vibrant textiles, intricately woven tapestries — and quiet stone-lined hallways lead to rooms and suites that are just as decorative with dark wood paneling, copper lamps, artisan-made furnishings, and spa-inspired bathrooms. There are no TVs around, adding to the resort’s peaceful atmosphere, but rooms have large windows facing the surrounding forest, and many have private balconies. Gourmet local delicacies and international dishes are featured on the breakfast buffet, and the lavish cocktail bar, though not based on historic precedent, is a particular highlight.

content: A handful of design-forward boutique hotels have popped up in Sopot, a historic seaside resort known for its Art Nouveau and Art Deco architecture. Among them is Hotel Testa, just across the street from the beach, with a minimalist facade that stands out in crisp contrast from its surroundings. The rooms are sleek and light-filled with floor-to-ceiling windows, a moody charcoal gray and deep blue color palette, natural wood detailing, and white marble bathrooms with walk-in showers. Suites have living rooms, kitchenettes, and spare bedrooms with built-in bunk beds. Breakfast is served in the airy ground-level restaurant, with tables spilling onto an outdoor deck when the sun shines. There’s also a small but smart-looking spa, outdoor lounge space on the manicured lawn, and easy access to the seafront promenade and bicycle path that lead into the center of town.

content:
Possibly the grandest urban hotel in all of southern Italy, the Grand Hotel et Des Palmes is certainly Palermo’s most classically elegant lodging. It’s been a part of the city’s history since it opened in the middle of the 19th century, and as the 21st advances, it’s in the finest form of its career, thanks to the preservation of its most iconic elements as well as judicious updates to its rooms, suites, and public spaces.

The accommodations are looking particularly sober, in shades of gray and brown, with antique-style furniture and historical architecture livened by an occasional modern contrast, like the freestanding bathtub in the bedroom of the Suite Terrace. The spaces are generous enough, and the bathrooms, supplied with Acqua di Parma products, are dramatic, in high-contrast black and white stone.

Its city-center location makes it an obvious meeting place for locals and travelers alike, who gather in its three restaurants: there’s the NeoBistrot, a restaurant and “mixology bar” set in an ornate hall of mirrors; Le Palmette, which serves exquisite gourmet fare beneath crystal chandeliers; and Ouvèrture, which opens onto the fifth-floor terrace with a commanding view of Palermo.

content:
Architecturally-minded visitors to Barcelona can’t help but have high expectations these days — it seems every building is either an ultra-modern masterpiece or a centuries-old treasure. These expectations are more than satisfied by Hotel CRAM, a bit of both worlds: a tour de force of modern interior architecture behind an elegant 19th-century facade.

Here modern design doesn’t mean monochrome, either. The obligatory white walls and polished light hardwood floors are livened with splashes of color, from blood red and rust orange to subdued gun-metal grey. The bedrooms are on that highly desirable line between funky and futuristic — they’re sleek, to be sure, but eminently habitable, with plentiful natural sunlight, sprawling platform beds and all the modern must-haves, including 32-inch LCD televisions and wireless internet access throughout.

An outdoor swimming pool offers a break from the heat and the crowds of central Barcelona, while the cocktail bar Mareva is the perfect transition into this city’s legendary nightlife. When it comes time to head out, the life of the city is close at hand; the hotel is four blocks from the Passeig de Gracia and six from the Plaça Cataluña and the Ramblas. 

Most fortuitous, though, is the fact that the hotel just happens to be the new home of the Michelin-starred Angle Barcelona restaurant, where chef Jordi Cruz serves innovative takes on traditional dishes.

content:
Be honest: if we told you there was an Armani Hotel, and that it wasn’t in Milan, your next guess would absolutely have to be Dubai, wouldn’t it? Not just anywhere in Dubai either, but in the towering Burj Khalifa, currently the world’s tallest building, the pride of the city. To say it’s the natural choice for a global fashion brand to set its monument to extravagant luxury would merely be pointing out the obvious. This is the one place where the world lets its consumerist id run wild.

So it’s also no surprise that, as a hotel, the Armani is pretty impressive. The project was overseen by Giorgio himself, who seems to have taken an exacting approach. Not only is every line in broadly the right place, but even the smallest of details in construction and finish are expertly crafted — this is couture quality, not mass-market.

For this you pay couture prices, of course, but it feels earned. The accommodations are expansive and impossibly well-appointed, decked out in Armani’s signature palette of dark greys and neutrals. The views may not be quite as extraordinary as they could be — most of the rooms are on the tower’s eight lower floors, which means you can still actually see the ground, while the Signature Suites and the Armani Suite occupy the rather more rarefied 38th and 39th floors.

And of course it’s quite a lot more than just a bunch of bedrooms. No fewer than nine restaurants and lounges serve townsfolk and travelers in equal measure, many of them drawing on Armani’s Milanese heritage for inspiration. The spa is top-flight, as are the meeting facilities if you’re unlucky enough to need them. And there’s an in-house Armani boutique as well, though the retail therapy need not end there — the Burj Khalifa is part of the massive Downtown Dubai development, which includes the enormous Dubai Mall, as well as an aquarium and an ice rink, included, presumably, just because they can.

content:
The original Mandarin Oriental on Hong Kong island just about cornered the market on over-the-top classic luxury. No surprise, then, that the Landmark, over in Central, is a little bit different. It’s a contemporary masterpiece in a town where tastes run conservative — the interiors by Adam Tihany and Peter Remedios are very near the cutting edge of modern luxury.

Floors in black wood are probably the most immediately striking feature in the guest rooms, but hardly the only notable one — on average, these are purported to be the largest hotel rooms in Hong Kong, and while we don’t have the statistical knowledge to assess that claim, we can say that at 450 square feet, even the smallest rooms at the Landmark are more than spacious enough. The clean lines and muted colors seem to further enlarge the space, and there’s plenty of room for every technological diversion you can imagine, including (finally!) iPod connections for the sound system.

A hundred-odd rooms is smallish for a Mandarin, and necessitates just one restaurant and one bar, the baroque European-inflected Amber and the wildly popular MO Bar — both patronized heavily by Hong Kong locals as well as hotel guests. The spa, by contrast, seems nearly excessive, spanning two floors and offering a byzantine array of treatments. The Central location is right in the thick of it all — think Wall Street and Midtown rolled into one. Shoppers, particularly, have cause to rejoice: guests at the Hyde Park Mandarin in London have to walk all the way across the road to get to Harvey Nichols, while here at the Landmark it’s right next door.

content:
Any doubts about whether Barcelona really is one of the world’s capitals of cool are quickly settled by a look at the boutique hotel scene. And in a city full of funky, well-designed small boutiques, the Hotel Market fits in perfectly.

It’s a hotel-restaurant, to be exact, the sort of place where the food comes first, with the bedrooms in a supporting role. But the lodgings are anything but perfunctory — while the restaurant is a fixture in the neighborhood surrounding the Sant Antoni market, the hotel pulls its weight as well, with fifty-eight rooms decorated in smart monochrome hues and rich hardwoods.

The neighborhood is the Eixample, the extension just outside Barcelona’s old city walls, and this particular corner of it is hip and rapidly improving. Here you’re largely free of the typical tourist traffic, but by no means isolated — the Plaza Catalunya and Las Ramblas are not far off. The restaurant draws more than its share of locals, and the San Antoni market itself is often buzzing. Best of all, perhaps, is the price; even accounting for the fact that it lacks many of the more indulgent services you’ll find in higher-end luxury boutiques, the Market Hotel is an excellent value.

content:
The climate, the seaside, the food, the famously late-partying populace — Barcelona’s got quite a lot going for it, even aside from its hotels. By local standards, Ofelias Hotel is a hotel whose charms are quite subtle — but that says perhaps more about the the quality of the competition than it does about Ofelias itself.

Let’s step back and view the big picture. It’s located in the quite central Eixample district, just off the Parc de Joan Miró, literally steps from the Las Arenas commercial center and a short walk from the old city. At 44 rooms, it’s in the sweet spot size-wise, large enough to offer some proper hotel services while small enough to remain manageably intimate. And the design is impeccable in its restraint — this place is elegant above all else, and while it’s far from the boldest and brightest of Barcelona’s boutique hotels, there’s much to be said for maintaining one’s composure.

Presumably that’s part of the key to why Ofelias manages to draw stylish business travelers in more or less the same proportion as design-hungry leisure guests. Here, as well, convenience is key — while there’s no in-house restaurant (beyond breakfast, that is), you’re close enough to a practical infinity of very fine options to make the distinction rather an academic one.

Please note: Hôtel La Perouse is currently closed for renovations and will reopen in mid-April 2023.

After all these years, there are still a few surprises left on the Côte d’Azur — the famous grand hotels carry on as they always have, but there’s the thrill of occasionally discovering a place like La Pérouse. Cut into a cliffside overlooking the Baie des Anges, this one-time prison is now one of Nice’s most remarkable hotels, offering easy access to the beach and the old town, as well as stunning views of the sea from most of its sixty-three rooms and suites.

Mediterranean style is the rule in the guest rooms, outfitted with antique furnishings and soft country colors, each with a balcony or terrace to take maximum advantage of the views. The location and the atmosphere are charming enough, but the view is the thing — even the hotel’s own brochure issues a strongly worded recommendation in favor of choosing a sea view room.

At the bottom of the cliff sits the hotel pool, surrounded by a shaded garden surrounded by lemon trees, and in the fair-weather months the hotel’s restaurant serves dinner on the terrace by candlelight. You’re seconds from the beach, if that’s the sort of diversion that appeals, and from this prime location on the Promenade des Anglais it’s a short walk into Nice’s historic district if you’re up for a bit of a wander. Proof positive there’s more to the Côte d’Azur than just the old favorites.

content:
Los Angeles has its fair share of fun, youth-oriented boutique hotels, but leave it to Mama Shelter to make many of them look like funeral parlors by comparison. This French import took seven years to turn up on American shores, and they’ve made an entrance that’s worth the wait.

Like the original Mama Shelter it’s bright and vibrant, with only the extras that matter: namely in-room iMacs, free wi-fi, and a surplus of inviting public space. The restaurant unpretentiously combines French and American influences, naturally enough, the bar projects a bit of a game-room vibe, and the coffee shop is buzzing from breakfast on through to early evening.

Also like the original Mama Shelter, it’s refreshingly easy on the budget, and it had better be, because it’s aimed at an authentically eclectic crowd: not the moneyed elite so much as the creative class, who tend to have more taste than liquid cash. This is the new, largely bling-free Hollywood, a destination for a generation of artists fleeing New York’s extortionate rents. The central Hollywood location ensures it’s a bit of a melting pot — relevant local landmarks include Amoeba Music, one of the world’s last great record stores, and that temple to the projectionist’s art, the Arclight, which is among the last places you can count on a properly reverent cinema experience.

content:
Sir Savigny may be an aristocrat, but he’s an aristocrat of the urban sophisticate variety. The Savignyplatz itself is a green idyll sprouting from the Kantstrasse, a block from the Kurfürstendamm, the famous shopping boulevard, and Sir Savigny lies just around the corner. This district, Charlottenburg, was the hip heart of West Berlin before reunification, and while there are edgier boroughs to the east, there’s nothing quite like this comfortably upscale mix of classic elegance and contemporary design.

The same can be said for Sir Savigny, a late nineteenth-century hotel refurbished in a smart contemporary style. In spite of their name, the Business Rooms are stylish, and look out onto the Kantstrasse, providing a bit of activity to get you out of bed in the morning. By contrast the Superiors open onto the courtyard, with balconies that are made for a leisurely bit of espresso-sipping. And the Executive Rooms are the best of all worlds, more than twice the size of the standards, enough to feel like a proper Charlottenburg studio apartment.

And while 44 rooms isn’t terribly small, the hotel maintains an air of understatement, more pied à terre than gathering place. It’s a prime location for such a thing, to be sure, given the dining and nightlife around Charlottenburg — and the Savigny’s bar keeps guests watered and fed, with drinks, tapas and sandwiches into the night.

content:
Downtown Los Angeles is, slowly but surely, reclaiming its status as the center of this expansive city. Its location, significantly to the east of Hollywood, places the Hotel Figueroa practically a world away from the beaches of Santa Monica and the west side. Downtown is all about city culture — this is a walkable world, close to The Broad, MOCA, Hauser & Wirth, and many independent art galleries, as well as Staples Center, Microsoft Theater, L.A. Live and the Convention Center.

The hotel originally opened in 1926 as the first hotel funded and founded by women, and was later in life a Moroccan-themed events space. After a massive renovation, it’s back to its original Twenties Spanish Colonial glory. The rooms are equal parts Twenties throwback and contemporary luxury boutique style, all of them decorated with original works by local artists, most of them women, in keeping with the hotel’s female-dominated art collection, which includes a mural by Bella Gomez.

Another part of downtown culture, of course, is food — here James Beard–nominated chef Casey Lane presides over a pair of restaurants, Breva and Veranda, which apply a Californian mindset to Mediterranean cuisine. Meanwhile Dushan Zaric pours inventive cocktails and well-selected spirits and beers at Bar Figueroa, Bar Alta, and Rick’s, out by the unique coffin-shaped swimming pool. This is a side of Los Angeles that you’d do well to get acquainted with, if you aren’t already.

content: It’s not like the Riviera Maya needed another resort, strictly speaking. But the Grand Hyatt Playa del Carmen brings something fresh to this somewhat overdeveloped stretch of coastline. Traditionally, travelers to “Playa,” that buzzing beach enclave down the coast from Cancún, have had to choose between one of two options. There are the boutique hotels in town, and the sprawling all-inclusive resorts lining the beaches north and south of it. The Grand Hyatt represents the best of both worlds, offering both a central location in town as well as many of the amenities and perks of a resort. Not to mention that the resort has some serious design creed. Mexican architect Javier Sordo Madaleno — the mind behind the strikingly geometric San Josemaría Escrivá church in Mexico City — partnered with New York’s Rockwell Group, lately in the news for opening The New York EDITION. Their combined efforts in Mexico have produced a chic hotel that would be considered interesting enough anywhere, and that’s downright cutting-edge for a place like Playa del Carmen. The building itself is massive, Mayan-inspired but modern, and built relatively low to the ground amid a native mangrove forest. There are waterfalls and infinity pools; the lobby feels like a cool cave. An open-air promenade, El Paseo, seamlessly connects the hotel’s entrance to the beach; lined with several Hyatt-operated bars, eateries, and street food-style stands, it feels like a natural extension of Playa’s lively Quinta Avenida. The spa, perhaps the Grand Hyatt’s true standout feature, is modeled after the look and feel of a cenote — the region’s magical limestone sinkholes, filled with turquoise water, considered sacred by the ancient Mayans. Guest rooms and suites run the range from comfortable to extravagant. All are outfitted in natural wood and a beachy color palette of blue and white, and feature floor-to-ceiling windows, private balconies with chaise seating, spacious bathrooms with walk-in rain showers, and Hyatt’s signature beds with 300-thread-count linens. On the higher end of the Grand Hyatt’s offerings are “Swim-Up” rooms, which, delightfully, are just what they sound like, with private terraces providing direct access to a swimming pool, and, of course, a line of suites with ocean views and plunge pools. It’s a great new place to stay. At the end of the day, though Playa del Carmen is a social destination — not the sort of place where you’ll be tempted to hole up in your hotel room all day. Not when there are freshly grilled fish tacos and mezcal margaritas awaiting downstairs, and beyond, the beautiful people sunning themselves on white daybeds at Mamita’s Beach Club.

content:
Boston is justifiably proud of its colonial heritage, and in terms of architecture and design (if not politics) its conservative streak runs deep. There’s plenty of room for some contemporary style — and while we’re not eager to see a spate of anonymous international-style design hotels, Nine Zero is a big step in the right direction.

It’s a new build, not a retrofit, and its 19-story brick-and-glass facade is quietly contemporary, not at all outlandish, doing its best to fit in with its classic surroundings just off the Common. Inside it’s another story, a smart and modern environment, heaping with personality — bold patterns, rich modern materials and clever lighting effects are masterfully handled, with every detail in its place.

There’s more to a hotel than style, of course, and even the most strikingly modern hotel deals, at bottom, in comfort. Here again Nine Zero succeeds, offering king beds with massive headboards and ten varieties of pillow, and futuristic, efficient bathrooms stocked with Mario Russo amenities. 27” televisions and generous work desks with ergonomic leather chairs are standard, and every room is heavily windowed, maximizing natural light and affording extraordinary views.

content:
As long-haul jet travel grows ever less attractive, we’re rediscovering places like Normandy; an hour and change from Paris, easy enough to reach from London, it’s a place that never lost its appeal, or its dramatic natural beauty. Just inland from Honfleur, by the mouth of the Seine, Le Domaine d’Ablon offers a high-end, boutique-sized Norman country escape — an estate whose original buildings have been divided into suites or converted into self-contained cottages.

Two suites occupy a converted barn, another a 17th-century dovecote, distinctively rounded; a sel-contained 14th-century cottage comes with its own terrace and garden, as well as a full kitchen. It feels rather more like a luxe little village than an ordinary luxury hotel, which can only be a good thing.

However, it’s anything but a self-service experience. The hotel’s staff is capable of arranging anything from a horseback ride on the beach to a visit to the cliffs at Etretat; restaurant reservations are secured as a matter of course. Save some evenings for dining in, though — chef Jérôme Billochon turns the local produce, including what’s grown on the estate, into long-lasting culinary memories.

North Brooklyn has grown up fast. In scarcely more than a decade it’s gone from peripheral artists’ colony to a sort of honorary Manhattan neighborhood. And no longer are we spending our evenings in Williamsburg and hopping on the L for the trip back to the hotel. Despite what its name might imply, the Williamsburg Hotel isn’t the first — but it’s a worthy addition to the neighborhood, an eight-story statement in brick, glass, and weathered steel, making the case for the east side of the river stronger than ever.

Much of the buzz centers on the nightlife, specifically the Water Tower, a glass-enclosed bar with spectacular views of the Manhattan skyline, and the Rooftop/Pool, which includes its own bar and café. Meanwhile Seven Seeds, the hotel’s Eastern Mediterranean restaurant, occupies an intimate but dramatic space off the lobby, where it serves breakfast, lunch, dinner, as well as High Tea and brunch on the weekends.

No less appealing, of course, are the guest rooms themselves, light-filled double-height spaces with furniture custom-designed by the building’s architects, Michaelis Boyd Studio. With a hint of retro modernism combined with some prewar New York textures, they’re nothing if not stylish, and with the extra space afforded by their Brooklyn location — not to mention their prime perspective on the Manhattan skyline — they don’t lack for luxury either. For hoteliers, Williamsburg is a boom town — this is your chance to get in on the ground floor (or the eighth, if you prefer).

Take a sprawling organic farm with a tropical twist, the rolling hills thick with mango and lemon trees. Then add a serious French chef specializing in sustainable cuisine, a tray of colorful Caribbean-style cocktails, and a championship golf course designed by Ian Woosnam. Then place the whole thing on the island of St. Kitts in the Caribbean. It’s a real place, and it’s called Belle Mont Farm.

This former sugar plantation’s cottages and villas were designed by Bill Bensley, an architect celebrated for his work on high-end resorts in Asia. Each is outfitted with a crisp modern sensibility and a certain romantic edge that conjures up the elegance of the West Indies’ colonial era: think polished wood, white shutters, freestanding tubs, and bespoke bath products. As if sweeping views of the sea and forest from your wraparound veranda weren’t enough, there’s a daybed, a plunge pool, and a high-tech home-cinema setup that has to be seen to be believed.

And those are just the standard “guesthouses.” Villas and Farmhouses are even more luxurious, with extras like full kitchens, infinity pools, and wine fridges stocked by the hotel’s sommelier according to your preferences. But you get the picture. Belle Mont Farm is a dream of a place. As an added benefit, it’s eco-friendly and sustainable. True, it isn’t right on the beach, but inland; it’s not a standalone hotel, but one component of a larger development that’s still underway. But you’re unlikely to care about any of that when you’re dining in one of the farm-to-table dining venues, swinging a racket or a club or pedaling on a bike amid bright flowers and lush foliage, or lying face-down on a massage table at the Mango Walk spa.

content: If we’re honest, we don’t come to Dublin for a spell of undisturbed, crypt-like peace and quiet. And it’d be a bit disappointing fo find a boutique hotel that’s too quiet. Fortunately for everyone involved, this is not a problem the Dean has. Though it’s tucked in a row of Georgian terrace houses, it’s anything but sleepy — not only does the location place the best of this rollicking city more or less right at your feet, but the hotel itself is clearly up for a good time as well. It’s clear from the lively décor and the youthful atmosphere in the rooms, which range from very minimal “mod pods” and crowd-friendly “punk bunks” on up to the swankier “superoom” and “hi-fi” categories, and even a pair of truly capacious suites. All of them come with turntables and a selection of classic vinyl, and while they do their best, we can’t in good conscience recommend the Dean for light sleepers or sensitive types — it’s not for nothing that you’ll be issued a pair of earplugs at check-in. The rest of us, however, will find the Dean a perfect encapsulation of what’s fun about central Dublin. It’s not rare that there’s a live band or a DJ in-house, and the rooftop bar and restaurant provides some surprising views of the city along with the expected social life. Get in while you’re still young, or at least young at heart.

There’s no question the multi-talented Pharrell Williams is an expert on good times — as is the Miami-based restaurateur and nightclub owner David Grutman. And there’s no mistaking the mission of their Goodtime Hotel. It’s set one block back from the Collins Avenue strip, in the heart of South Beach, the setting for some of the finest nightlife in the world — and it’s not here merely to observe the scene, but to become one of its pillars.

The danger in this approach is that the Goodtime could become one of those hotels that requires earplugs and a legal waiver for anyone who actually wants to sleep. Fortunately, this is a hotel that knows when it’s time to party and when it’s time to recover. The rooms and suites are colorful and vibrant but they’re also cozy and cocoon-like, and the unflappably friendly service exhibits none of the velvet-rope attitude you might expect from a nightclub hotel.

There’s a pool deck and a beach club, as well as a spa, yoga sessions, and an inventive and well-equipped indoor-outdoor gym. And the social scene revolves around Strawberry Moon, the rooftop space that serves as a Mediterranrean restaurant, a bar, and a swim club — you can expect top-tier talent to occupy its DJ booth (as well as its private cabanas).

There’s a modern Japanese restaurant by Danny Elmaleh, and the neighborhood offers a few gems of its own.

content:
Most hotels located within sight of the California coast have a beautiful view — that’s just elementary geography. But few can boast the kind of turf the Heritage House Resort occupies. This hotel can believably call itself the jewel of the coast without causing you to roll your eyes — among other reasons, you’ll be careful not to take your eyes off of the view. Rare indeed is the hotel with oceanfront property in Mendocino, but Heritage House Resort occupies fully 37 acres of unspoiled cliffside on the coast. 

They’ve welcomed guests here for more than 100 years, and the hotel received a full renovation in recent years. The historic architectural bones, like wooden rafters, remain in place, but the 48 renovated rooms incorporate clean, modern touches. The truth is that you won’t want to spend your time indoors during the day — so you’ll be pleased to know that each room comes with a large private patio for maximum fresh air intake, and many rooms feature an ocean view. The nights can be chilly in this neck of the woods, though, so there’s a gas or wood-buring fireplace in your room for a cozy evening. 

The charming Victorian village of Mendocino is nearby, as is Redwood State Park. But you don’t even have to leave the resort to get the most of the great California outdoors. There are acres of oceanfront trails, gardens, and forest paths open to the guests. Back at the hotel, there’s a stellar farm-to-fork restaurant that also features local wines. As a gateway to the northern California coast, you’d be hard pressed to find better.

content:
Safe to say it’s like nothing else in Florence. Glance Hotel makes its home not in some Renassance villa but in a Fifties building by the modernist architect Italo Gamberini, one that’s been thoroughly updated by contemporary architects AMDB Studio and decked out exclusively with pieces by Lema, one of Italy’s leading manufacturers of design furniture.

The location, in San Lorenzo, is nothing if not convenient, and the modernist simplicity of the décor creates a sharp contrast with the ornateness of the city outside. The rooms are extraordinarily calming, verging on the minimalist but without lapsing all the way into blankness — and luxe little touches like espresso machines and relatively lavish bathrooms give Glance an extra edge in comfort over an ordinary design-focused boutique hotel.

And while it’s something of a stylistic outlier, Glance isn’t divorced from its context. Large-scale photographic reproductions of the city’s most famous artworks decorate the public spaces, and a rooftop pool deck takes advantage of the building’s height to offer a view of the Basilica and the rooftops. And while the hotel’s breakfast service is more than adequate, there’s no restaurant beyond that — this city being what it is, of course, you’ll hardly mind being forced to find something suitable in the streets outside your door.

content: Around here we’re certainly not averse to novelty; in these pages you’ll find countless daring experiments in hospitality. But innovation isn’t the only virtue — the Tuscan farmhouse bed and breakfast, surrounded by vineyards and olive groves, is an archetype that would be difficult to improve upon. Locanda dell’ Artista, just outside of San Gimignano, is as classic as they come, just four rooms and three suites on an 18th-century farm surrounded by 40 acres of gently rolling Tuscan hills. The interiors effortlessly blend period architecture, modern artworks, and furnishings old and new. The result is somehow both casual and correct, in that inimitably Italian style, and the atmosphere is tranquil to an extreme degree — and here the “no children under 14” policy makes a noticeable contribution. Of course Tuscany isn’t all about the inspiring views and the pastoral calm. If you’re here to eat and drink — and you certainly are — you’re unlikely to be disappointed. The restaurant, under chef Adriano Antonelli, makes the most of the bounty of the estate: Locanda dell’ Artista’s farm cold-presses its own olive oil, much of the produce you’ll taste is grown in the kitchen garden, and the wine cellar is packed with an all-star list of Italian wines. It’s a familiar formula, perhaps, but there’s not much to be said for change when the status quo is just about flawless.

The Thompson group made a big splash when it entered the Playa del Carmen hotel scene, importing their particular brand of stylish luxury to a town that badly needed it. The first phase focused on their Quinta Avenida location, a couple of blocks inland from the beach, with its glamorous pool lounge and its quasi-urban style. But for a more barefoot, bohemian vibe, the Thompson Beach House is the place to be.

Like any Thompson hotel the look is heavily influenced by mid-century modernism, and the comforts are luxurious but not ostentatious. You’ll have at least a partial ocean view no matter where you are, as well as a private terrace, and the junior suites and suites add large soaking tubs to the already impressive bathrooms. More than pure square footage or thread count, it’s the sense of thoughtfulness that makes the accommodations so pleasing — the sense that every decision, no matter how small, has been carefully considered, right down to the snacks in the minibar.

C-Grill, the beachfront restaurant, serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner, as well as tequilas, mezcals, cocktails, and craft beers. The location, obviously, offers all the expected aquatic attractions, including a variety of water sports and yoga on the beach. And the Thompson Playa del Carmen on Quinta Avenida is two blocks away, where you’ll have access a gorgeous pool and its accompanying poolside restaurant and bar.

content:
The Graduate hotels tend to play an outsized role in the hospitality scenes of the college towns they call home, but this one stretches the traditional definition of “college town” just a bit. Even many New Yorkers are still unaware that Roosevelt Island is home to the Cornell Tech campus, a satellite of the Ithaca-based Ivy League university. Graduate Roosevelt Island is the island’s only hotel, and in typical Graduate style it’s dedicated to the campus that it serves. 

This being New York, of course, the Graduate is a touch more forward-looking and urban in style than, say, the Iowa City iteration, with architecture and design by the Oslo-based firm Snøhetta. The rooms come with views of the Manhattan skyline, and are bright and colorful — none more so than the Loft Suite, full of childlike charm (and inspired by the Tom Hanks movie “Big.”)

The all-day restaurant, Anything At All, is as versatile as it sounds, and the Poindexter Coffee Cart keeps guests suitably stimulated. And on the 18th-floor rooftop, the Panorama Room bar and terrace offers an astonishing 360-degree view of New York from an angle most New Yorkers have never experienced.

content:
You know you’ve hit the big time when Galileo Galilei is your children’s science tutor. Only the fabulously wealthy and influential Medici family could pull it off — they also commissioned Florence’s Pitti Palace and produced three popes, a duke, and a couple of queens. They didn’t go halfway when it came to leisure, either, a fact that’s on fine display at the Fonteverde Resort in San Casciano dei Bagni — this used to be just one of their many lavish vacation villas.

Though there’s nothing at all modern about the resort’s architecture or interiors, Fonteverde has been technologically updated to accommodate business travelers who fancy a dip in thermal waters between meetings. Today, the property’s 66 guest rooms and 14 suites are divided between the original villa and a newer building. The stately interiors blend elements of Italian Renaissance architecture with a traditional Tuscan style. Public spaces feature antique wooden furniture and rich red velvet, while private guest quarters are furnished more lightly with earth tones and white linens. Roomy marble bathrooms are stocked with spa products, high-speed internet access is available in each room, and individual balconies and terraces offer pastoral views of the hills or the valley (the latter is especially spectacular at dusk.) 

One of the Fonteverde’s main draws, of course, is the region’s restorative thermal spring water — a series of therapeutic pools and the full-service spa offer plenty of opportunities to bathe in it, and dozens of natural springs are within a stone’s throw of the resort, and meanwhile an infinity pool with a countryside view suits those who deign to swim in chlorinated water.

content:
It’s certainly not the first time an overseas arrival has come to New York and made it big. But there’s something so classic, so polished about the Marmara Park Avenue that, name aside, you might not guess it’s the latest venture of a Turkish hotel chain.

With a small collection of five-star hotels, plus an opulent sultan’s mansion-turned-event space on the Bosphorus, Marmara is a symbol of sophistication in Turkey. Meanwhile, back in New York, you won’t find any Ottoman carvings or Oriental carpets — there’s only one real indication of the Marmara Park Avenue’s Turkish roots: a sleek Turkish hammam and a subterranean mosaic-lined swimming pool.

Upstairs, it’s Park Avenue elegance all the way. The 21-story building, which dates back to 1927, once housed the offices of design and architecture firms. With high ceilings, open spaces, and a dramatic Beaux Arts-style entryway built of bronze and steel, the Marmara Park Avenue feels airy and modern, yet charmingly antique, all at once. The Marmara group tapped New York artist-designer Joe Ginsberg to work on the interiors, and his playfully decorative aesthetic and penchant for luxurious materials shapes the hotel’s atmosphere — think limestone walls in the lobby, poured concrete floors patterned with brass inlay, black and gold Mylar wall coverings, a massive abacus made of bird-shaped sculptures by the bar, velvet, silk, and leather everywhere you turn.

There are 128 guest rooms and suites, including a trio of lavish penthouses. Amenities are what you’d expect for a hotel of this caliber: hardwood floors, marble bathrooms, bespoke furniture, complimentary iPads. Dozens of rooms and suites feature private terraces, too. As in the lobby and wine bar, it’s Ginsberg’s taste that defines the look: his photos of the Hamptons hang on the walls, and the custom-made wallpaper is based on photographs he took of the Third Avenue Bridge. Incidentally, the landmark bridge, connecting Manhattan to the Bronx, was constructed in 1898 with funding by the current owners of the Marmara group. Maybe that’s what it takes to build something great in New York: native design sensibility mixed with a bit of global perspective.

Please note:
For stays through August, the Marmara Park Avenue is suspending daily housekeeping due to coronavirus concerns — rooms will be thoroughly cleaned before and after your stay.

content:
These days no respectable fashion empire would be caught dead without a hotel to call its own. Some are exercises in brand-building, while others are a bit more discreet; a guest at the Hotel Monaco and Grand Canal could hardly be blamed for missing the Benetton connection, dazzled instead by the hotel’s contrasts, between seventeenth-century grandeur and chic modern styling.

Public spaces are sleek and dazzling, while upstairs is a slightly different story: guest rooms are not exactly modern, much less minimalist, but more a sort of up-to-date classic style, still a welcome break from the stuffiness of Venice’s more conservative palace hotels, where historical authenticity is valued above all else. Here you’ll find your share of antiques and classic ornamentation in a conscious homage to the old style, along with the sort of clean lines prized by contemporary decorators.

Hotel Monaco’s location is perhaps its strongest suit: it’s situated, as advertised, at the mouth of the Grand Canal, though relatively few rooms actually face the water. St. Mark’s Square is just a block away, and many of the major tourist attractions are close at hand, as are any number of shops, cafés and restaurants.

The hotel’s own Grand Canal restaurant is an elegant Venetian classic, its outdoor terrace seating providing unparalleled views of the Church of Santa Maria della Salute across the canal. And of particular note to Bellini connoisseurs and Hemingway fetishists is the original Harry’s Bar, just steps from the hotel.

content: The Ace Hotel New York, when it first opened, felt like an exercise in minimalism, bringing a vintage/salvage aesthetic and a slightly spartan approach to comforts to a hotel scene that was still obsessed with gloss and glamour. But for their second act, Atelier Ace, the hotel group’s in-house creative agency, has set out to show us what real minimalism looks like. They make it explicit, citing Finnish saunas and Japanese bento boxes as inspirations, which are visible in the interior design — and also John Cage’s silent(ish) composition 4′33″ , whose influence is perhaps more conceptual. That said, Sister City is quiet, despite the fact that, with entrances on Bowery and Freeman Alley, it could hardly be more auspiciously located. The rooms start out small — bento boxes indeed — but are plenty comfortable, in their austere way. Bigger rooms feature a quartet of bunk beds, perfect for a traveling band, and at the high end you can score a king bed or a terrace with a view of the city. Given the location, Sister City is under no illusion that it needs to offer a totally self-contained experience — the Lower East Side is well known for its nightlife and its restaurant scene. The hotel’s offerings, however, are more than worthy of the neighborhood, from Floret, the garden-patio restaurant by award-winning chef Joe Ogrodnek, to Last Light, an 11th-floor bar with indoor and outdoor seating. “Less, but Better” is Sister City’s motto, and it’s one we imagine will resonate with more than a few guests.

The combination of the Nobu restaurant group’s newly minted hospitality brand and Miami Beach’s already glamorous hotel scene would seem to be a natural one. And in fact the Nobu Hotel Miami Beach slots effortlessly into a row of luxury resorts along Collins Avenue — and in fact slots quite literally into the larger Eden Roc Resort. Nobu is a hotel within a hotel, and it’s a world of upscale glamour unto itself, with just over 200 rooms and suites designed by David Rockwell.

In the rooms the look is beach house meets Japanese ornament, and it’s a soothing style that’s well suited to the destination, and a nice break from the mid-century modernism that’s on display elsewhere around town. Nobu may be new at the luxury-hotel game, but they’re a quick study — they’ve got their own signature bed dressed in Fili d’Oro linens, as well as Nespresso machines and spa-like bathrooms, complete with Japanese-style teak benches in the showers.

Naturally, there’s a full-service Nobu spa, as well as a fitness center and no fewer than three pools between the two hotels, plus complimentary beach chairs, cabana rentals, and facilities for water sports equipment rentals.

There’s nothing wrong with those classic New Orleans houses with their second-floor galleries, but there’s life beyond the French Quarter. Mid-City isn’t far away, but the vibe at the Drifter is like nothing else you’ve seen in this town. It’s a renovated mid-century motel, for one thing, the sort of low-slung two-story modernist building we’ve seen rehabilitated to great effect in towns like Austin, Texas. And while youth-oriented boutique hotels are not unheard of in New Orleans, the Drifter goes one further: with its rotating selection of food trucks, its well-chosen craft beers, its third-wave coffee, and its charmingly hedonistic courtyard pool, it’s tailor-made for young travelers with more taste than money.

The rooms, which marry minimalistic plaster walls and well-chosen modernist furnishings, are a case in point — there’s not much in the way of traditional luxury, but sturdy, comfortable beds and bedside Tivoli radios go a long way. The centerpiece, however, is the courtyard, which has been converted from the traditionally charmless parking lot into a poolside lounge that’s just the opposite. With its lush landscaping and its no-frills outdoor furniture it’s the heart of the Drifter, and the crowd from the adjoining café and lounge effortlessly spills outside. Safe to say New Orleans’s reputation as one of America’s most sociable cities is in good hands here.

content: It simply shouldn’t be possible for some of the world’s most storied nightlife to exist just a couple of blocks from a genuinely quiet neighborhood, but West Hollywood is proof that it can happen — and the Montrose West Hollywood, tucked into a residential street three blocks south of the Sunset Strip, makes the most of this contrast. It’s an all-suite, residential-style hotel, and while its recent interior-design makeover leaves it looking stylish, it’s not a 24/7 nightspot like some boutique hotels. (And with bars and nightclubs like Rage and the Viper Room a few blocks away, it certainly doesn’t need to be.)\n\nInstead its suites are made for rest and relaxation, and perhaps a bit of private entertaining. 55-inch televisions, Keurig coffee makers, fireplaces, and fully stocked minibars are standard, and some suites add kitchenettes and/or balconies. A multi-use lounge slowly evolves over the course of the day from a relaxed co-working space to a livelier social scene thanks to the Vino & Vinyl Hour. And while the Montrose does have a restaurant, Tone, crucially it’s for guests of the hotel only — as is the rooftop cafe, for a drink or a light bite by the pool with a 360° view of West Hollywood and Beverly Hills.

content: In 1969, the Spanish journalist Joan de Sagarra coined the term gauche divine to describe the generation of young artists, writers, actors, and creatives who opposed Franco’s dictatorship. The entire first floor of Sixties Ramblas is dedicated to their legacy. This boutique hotel, as the name suggests, celebrates the sixties in Barcelona. Modern with a stylish vintage twist, the place is like a museum, with pop art, murals, and photos capturing iconic symbols from paella and bullfighting to flamenco dancing and the advent of the bikini. Guest rooms are sleek and compact, with hardwood floors and retro-inspired tile showers; some have balconies or terraces. There’s a billiards room and a bike rental stand, as well as a good-looking cocktail bar and restaurant — and thanks to the hotel’s central location, just blocks from La Rambla and the waterfront, countless other options are just outside the door. \n

We’ll spare you a complete explanation of the Hyatt family tree — what matters here is that Hyatt Centric is the hospitality giant’s sub-brand that’s most focused on a design-sensitive but luxury-agnostic youth market. The appeal: a comfortable but relatively low-frills hotel in a convenient location that looks like it was designed by someone who’s seen colors other than beige and brown. It shouldn’t be as difficult as it apparently is, but the good news is that Hyatt Centric Times Square has cracked the code.

The style is familiar to anyone with boutique-hotel experience, and unlike some New York boutiques it’s exceedingly accessible and approachable — you’ll never feel underdressed or unhip here. The rooms, perhaps surprisingly, are generously sized, and the décor keeps things light and breezy. Some of the views are impressively far-ranging, and even the entry-level rooms come with thoughtful conveniences like Keurig coffee makers and JBL wireless speakers.

The location might not be in the hippest corner of town, but you know what you’re getting into with Times Square: for tourists and first-timers it’s impossible to top, and the transit links are plentiful. The restaurant, T45, and the rooftop Bar 54 are a significant step up from the chain restaurants that surround Times Square — though if you’ve got a particular craving, the hotel works with the Grubhub delivery service to bring you whatever your appetite desires.

content:
Who doesn’t love a good makeover story? It wouldn’t be quite fair to cast the old Henry Howard House Inn in the role of ugly duckling, but the transformation of this Greek Revival mansion, at the hands of a pair of New York hotel developers, was a dramatic one. Now, the historic building gets its star turn, reopening its doors as the Henry Howard Hotel, an 18-room boutique that’s every bit as graceful as you’d wish from a long weekend stay in the Big Easy.

Henry Howard, the man, was the Irish-born architect behind the mansion, and half of New Orleans, in fact, particularly here in the Garden District. And as you can tell from a block away, Howard was no minimalist: he was known for his dramatic Roman arches and grand Corinthian columns. So it’s no surprise that Henry Howard Hotel works better as a high-end boutique hotel than it did in its more budget-friendly incarnation. Inside, the mansion practically drips with twinkling chandeliers and original oil paintings in heavy gilded frames; elegant crown moulding shapes the spacious rooms, the wood floors are so carefully polished you can see your own reflection in them. But the old-world charm is set off by a smart urban aesthetic: boldly patterned wallpaper, monochromatic drapery, musical instruments mounted, like sculptures, on the walls.

Guest rooms and suites, too, mix modern and traditional. Some furnishings are custom-made, but many are antiques — you’ll find a tongue-in-cheek painting by a New Orleans artist above a delicate writing desk, and a hand-painted dresser or an old-fashioned armoire beside the geometric canopy bed. It’s a historic mansion, so room sizes and layouts vary, but standard features include free wi-fi, gourmet snacks, and gorgeously revamped bathrooms with all-natural products by Beekman 1802. Many rooms have separate seating areas, ideal for sipping iced tea on a hot afternoon. Book the Penthouse Suite or the Royal King Gallery, with its private balcony, and you’ll be tempted to stay in all day — but at the very least, come cocktail hour, you’ll have to make your way down to The Parlor.

content:
Once upon a time the stylish modern hotels were smallish and independently owned, while the massive towers tended very much towards the beige and bland side of things.  It’s no longer quite so simple. The Eurostars Madrid Tower is no mom-and-pop operation — it’s part of a fairly extensive chain, and occupies 30 high floors of a skyscraper in the business district of northern Madrid. But to look inside is to be immediately convinced of its style bona fides; there are tiny little boutiques out there that wish they could look half this good.

Of course with just shy of five hundred rooms you can forget about that intimate boutique feeling. But they’re not shy about their skyscraper status — witness the photos of famous towers, installed in every room. And you won’t typically find such far-ranging views, such ultra-modern amenities, or even such high-quality construction (right down to the insulation) in hotels more modest than this one.

The up side of something so massive is that it can support extensive conference facilities, a full-service spa, and a well-equipped health club. This being modern Spain, the gastronomy is taken quite seriously, as is the football — not only are many of the capital’s business destinations close at hand, but so is the Bernabéu, home to the storied Real Madrid.

content:
Safe to say the Croatian coastline is no longer much of a secret — there’s nothing quite as crowded as Cannes, but places like Split and Hvar are first-call Mediterranean destinations. Less well known, at least outside of Croatia’s borders, is Ika, a resort town on the so-called Opatija Riviera, on the inner curve of the Kvarner Gulf — a town that’s home, as you may well have guessed, to the Ikador Luxury Boutique Hotel & Spa.

For all the talk about resorts, you’ll be delighted to learn of Ikador’s small size: just nine rooms and seven suites, all of them spacious, colorful, and charmingly Art Deco–inspired. The comforts are first-rate, from the in-room espresso machines to the Hermès bath products, and, in many suites, terraces that look out over the Adriatic.

Despite its small size, Ikador has more than enough to offer for a complete stay, from the rather extravagant Ikalia Spa to the fine-dining Nobilia restaurant and the poolside Riva Lounge. And while the town of Ika is on the pleasantly sleepy side, you’re just a few minutes down the coast from Opatija proper, which is chock full of more than enough restaurants, bars, and other diversions to earn its “riviera” tag.

content:
There’s an argument to be made that this is San Francisco’s most central hotel, located as it is at 4th and Market, between the retail center of Union Square and the tech district of SoMa, and a short distance to Chinatown and the Financial District. Here, what was formerly the Hotel Palomar has been given a thorough style upgrade and along with it a new name: Hotel Zelos San Francisco. 

Still intact is the classic 1907 façade of the Pacific Building — but the interiors have been brought subtly up to date. A hotel right at the city’s crossroads has to appeal to tourists and traditional business travelers as well as hipsters and tech-industry innovators, so there are limits to its eccentricity in terms of design. Here some well-chosen design accents — pops of color, modernist furnishings — add some visual interest to the rooms’ calm, residential coziness. (For contrast, glance out the window at busy Market Street and see what a difference a few floors’ height can make.)

There must be a hundred places to eat with a direct line of sight to the Zelos, but it’s got its own, the impressive Dirty Habit, which is both a craft cocktail bar and a proper restaurant, complete with indoor-outdoor seating and a New American menu. It’s far more than adequate for fueling your excursions, whether to the upscale shopping on the other side of Market or the newly reopened SFMOMA.

Only in Singapore could there be a place like Sentosa Island, a government-established tropical paradise, just fifteen minutes from the financial district. At worst it could be (and in times past has been) a sort of Disneyland version of the Southeast Asia island getaway. These days, though, it’s looking pretty smart, thanks in no small part to the Sofitel Singapore Sentosa Resort & Spa.

You’d never know you were in Singapore. It’s a luxury resort, villas and low buildings scattered across 27 acres of tropical greenery opposite the Sentosa Golf Course (home of the Singapore Open). Clean-lined, contemporary rooms and suites look out into courtyards and water-gardens — they’re not over-large but are plenty stylish, paneled in wood and supplied with all the necessities (massive plasma screen, torrential showers, the works).

The Sofitel Singapore Sentosa Resort & Spa, for all its charms, isn’t small; the up side of this is an encyclopedic list of luxe-resort services, and plenty of activity — there’s privacy to be had, if you’re thinking of a quiet couples’ escape, as well as a great vast pool deck, the sort of place you can turn the kids loose for an afternoon.

content:
Named for its location on Little India’s Serangoon Road, Serangoon House Singapore is as pure an Indian colonial fantasy as you’re likely to find outside of the subcontinent itself. The lobby is dazzlingly opulent, decked out in custom-made antique-style furniture and bold, brash colors; the 90 rooms and suites are a touch more modern, but absolutely no less lavish in style.

Highlights include gilded canopy beds and De Gournay wallpapers depicting scenes from Colonial India, as well as bathrooms in vibrant rose, jade, or emerald-hued marble. There’s a rotary phone by the bedside to complete the time-travel illusion, but fear not — beneath the surface, Serangoon House’s comforts and conveniences are as modern as they come. Those canopy beds have a trick up their sleeve, in fact; bring out a ladder and the upper tier conceals a top bunk, which means every room can sleep up to six.

And the food and beverage program takes a different direction from the one that the décor might suggest. GupShup is an artful, high-end experience, but it’s inspired by chaat, or street food, from all across India, curated by chef Surjan Singh, better known as Chef Jolly.

content: Until now, most of the hotel action in Tulum has taken place along the beach, but Casa Pueblo makes its home downtown — hence the “pueblo.” You’re still just two miles from the surf, but you’ve traded thatched roofs for textured concrete, and the quiet of the jungle for a (relatively) bustling urban scene. What you gain is a uniquely Yucatán spin on the kind of minimalistic visual style that’s familiar from boutique hotels the world over, plus an atmosphere that is, while still casual, considerably less rustic than what you’ll find down by the beach.\n\nThe size is modest: just 16 rooms ringing an atrium planted with local trees. There’s a small salt-water swimming pool as well as an open-kitchen restaurant, both of which stay active enough to feel lively but intimate enough to feel like a refuge from the city outside. And that goes double for the rooms: with mattresses by Mexican prestige brand Luuna as well as high-end Parachute Home linens they’re nothing if not restful, and the visual design, by Derek Klein, Mike Moser, and Jaime Aramburu, only accentuates that sense of calm. It’s still Tulum — meaning there’s plenty of exploring to do by day, and trouble to get up to by night — it’s just a more stylish version than we’ve seen to date.

content:
Imagine Bangkok traffic and you’re probably picturing tuk-tuks and motorbikes zipping down congested roads, not wooden boats sailing at a quick clip along the river. But the city is laced with a network of canals that played an important role in trade and commerce during the 18th and 19th centuries. Many of these waterways have been filled in, but a good number remain. Stay at a hotel like Riva Surya, situated right on the banks of the Chao Phraya River — something like the Grand Canal of Bangkok — and you’ll have easy access to the watery labyrinth that earned Bangkok the nickname “Venice of the East.”

The hotel’s design takes proper advantage of its waterfront position, featuring several terraces and an inviting wooden deck with a swimming pool. Guest rooms and suites all have river views, too, and beautifully tiled balconies. Inside, the look is sleek and the amenities thoroughly contemporary — dark wood and crisp white, 400-thread count sheets, spacious bathrooms, flat-screen TVs, iPod docks — with a few romantic details, like potted flowers and rocking chairs, to warm things up.

There are two restaurants at Riva Surya. There’s Babble & Rum, an indoor-outdoor café inspired by the experience of visiting a traditional Thai marketplace, and the Garden, better suited to al fresco cocktails and small plates. Alternatively, stake out a chaise lounge by the pool and order a frozen drink, watching the boats go by. These waterways, of course, aren’t just for tourists: thousands of locals commute to work each day on public motorboats. But you’ll want to slow down and enjoy the view: a river cruise past the city’s teak houses and majestic temples, ideally ending up at one of its famous floating markets, isn’t an experience you’ll want to miss.

content:
It’s perhaps less famous than it ought to be — when it opened in 1965, the Four Columns Inn, in Newfane, Vermont, was arguably the first farm-to-table restaurant in the United States. The economist John Kenneth Galbraith was a regular, and luminaries like Sting and Mick Jagger passed through the inn’s guest rooms. But all good things come to an end; Four Columns was sold, and sold again, and eventually closed.

Naturally, that wasn’t the end of the story, or you wouldn’t be here reading this. The Four Columns Inn is back in business, and after a thorough renovation, it’s returned to its roots. The guest rooms are looking fresh and contemporary, but without sacrificing any of the rustic coziness that made their name in the first place. And while the Inn is far from ostentatious, there are subtle luxuries throughout, from the Bulgari bath products in the bathrooms to the French linens on the pillow-top beds.

Newly added is a cozy little spa, hidden away in a small house on the property. And back in fighting form is the restaurant, now called Artisan Restaurant, Tavern & Garden, a return to the original Four Columns farm-to-table philosophy.

content:
The UK’s Apex hotel group is carving out a niche for itself as a purveyor of what you could call sub-extravagant luxury. Certainly in London, and to a lesser extent in Edinburgh, there’s a great rush to cater to the stratospherically wealthy, devising ludicrously exclusive amenities and comically lavish accommodations, leaving mere mortals with fewer options all the time. Unto the breach goes Apex, whose Apex Waterloo Place, near Edinburgh’s Waverley station, is a fine illustration of the brand’s finely tuned posh-o-meter.

As a hotel it dates back to the nineteenth century, and its historic facade gives little hint of the vibrant colors and rich textures inside. A 2009 renovation has seen to it that the style is perfectly in keeping with contemporary British hotel modernism, brighter and more clean-lined than you might expect from so stately a Georgian establishment. The rooms are all quite up to date in functional terms as well, with 42-inch televisions and plentiful work space, and the bathrooms are suitably well-equipped, right down to the rubber duck, a trademark Apex gesture. City Doubles are efficient and not at all cramped, and by the time you get into the Deluxes, to say nothing of the suites, you’re in proper luxury-hotel territory, star ratings be damned.

Paphos, on the south-west coast of Cyprus, is enjoying a hospitality renaissance, with a surfeit of glamorous resort hotels. The Annabelle features a stately, classic style. The property offers two swimming pools, four restaurants, and four bars, including the Byz Bar, which serves as the hotel’s main evening social venue.

The rooms and suites offer the most crucial of amenities—space—in plentiful supply, along with all modern conveniences. Most of the rooms have stunning Mediterranean views, and many come with private pools or Jacuzzis on their sea-facing terraces. 

Local activities are legion but an abridged selection would include a trip to the Andromeda Spa, a game of tennis, and a scuba or waterski lesson. Those who prefer culture to sport will find plenty to do in Paphos, with a bustling town market and a UNESCO World Heritage archaeological site.

content:
If there’s any reason at all to regard Playa del Carmen as something less than heaven on earth, it’s the scale of the local tourism trade. But a good boutique hotel can help you recapture some of that undiscovered-paradise feeling. Small scale is what Hotel Morgana’s got going for it, after all: this family-owned hotel is human-sized, and each of its twenty rooms has its own design and its own personality. 

Themes range from the very personal “Frida,” named for the painter Frida Kahlo, to “Maiz,” which takes an agricultural inspiration. What they have in common is colorful tilework against a backdrop of soft neutrals, and some unpretentious contemporary furniture to complement the spare, modernist design sense. All come with basics like air conditioning and Nespresso machines; some feature balconies, others private Jacuzzis, and the suites are particularly spacious, with sofa beds for larger parties.

5th Avenue is just steps away, and that’s where a location in a holiday hotspot pays dividends. There’s plenty to do, from dining to drinking to water sports and archaeological tours — and a cozy, stylish little boutique hotel to return to at the end of the day.

content: Geography pedants will note that this is actually Stock Island, the next one over from Key West, separated by perhaps a hundred feet of water from its more famous neighbor. But Key Next-West has plenty of its own to recommend it, including the fact that it’s got space for a brand-new purpose-built resort like Oceans Edge. Here every room has views over the marina out to sea, as well as no fewer than six swimming pools — this isn’t just the largest resort in Greater Key West, but features the largest rooms as well. If you want ramshackle bohemian town life, head west, but for a contemporary luxury experience, you can stop right here.\n\nThe humblest room comes with a king bed and a balcony, and things only spread out from there, all the way up to two-bedroom suites. Beyond the pools and the marina — fancy a fishing charter? — there are kayaks and stand-up-paddleboards to be had, as well as snorkeling and scuba diving and guided cruises and tours. And while six pools to one restaurant is an unusual ratio, rest assured that the Yellowfin Bar and Grill is up to the task, with its capacious indoor-outdoor seating and service that runs from breakfast straight through dinner and beyond.

content:
Rich as it is in history, Bodrum in the 21st century largely consists of yacht-friendly, scrubbed-clean, self-contained resorts, taking their cues from the white-on-white-sand aesthetic defining the Mediterranean idiom. Analogous, in a way, to their Greek cousins — lofted views over rocky beaches, profoundly blue waters, olive groves, acres of white plaster — but also, as is the case with Susona Bodrum, card-carrying disciples of the contemporary, full-service resort model.

The Susona Bodrum design recipe comprises one part beachy minimalism, one part earth-tone foundation, and about six parts oceanic vista. The 76 rooms, suites, and villas do a fine job of getting out of their own way, arraying swaths of blonde wood and swoopy, curvilinear furnishings so as best to welcome floods of light and knockout Aegean panoramas. Everything invites tranquility — plush platform king beds, adjustable mood lighting, customizable MyBar, entertainment wall, and that infallible proof of vacation mode, tubs with a view. Grab an upper-tier room for a private pool and/or a private balcony, ideal for an unhurried morning espresso.

Standalone units sprawl in a blocky, thoroughly contemporary arc along the beachfront, punctuated here and there with modest docks from which to pursue a huge variety of watersports. Easier, perhaps, to post up with a poolside cocktail or enlist a personal trainer at Tone Gym to work up a sweat with correct posture. The whole idea is to seamlessly transition from heavenly indolence to the active life to idle conversation over wine and hyper-fresh meals. There’s a restaurant and beach club to take care of the latter, plus a café for lighter fare and a pick-me-up. If that doesn’t suffice, Bodrum proper certainly will, just 20 minutes south; sightsee a bit, then give yourself over to a night on the town in its spirited taverns.

Please note: The resort is open seasonally and accepts reservations from May 18 to October 15 annually.

content: Italy is most famous for the depth of its history, of course, and Florence, in particular, wouldn’t be a tenth of the attraction that it is without the art and architecture of the Renaissance. But among people who care about design, Italy is also famous for its high-end contemporary furniture, and for interiors that are elegant in a way that looks forward rather than back. It’s this contemporary Italy that you’ll find within the walls of Domux Home Repubblica. But don’t worry, the other, ancient Italy is just outside — in fact, your apartment comes with a view of no less distinguished an architectural monument than Brunelleschi’s Duomo itself.\n\nMany hotels style themselves as apartments these days, but Domux Home Repubblica’s four units have a more legitimate claim than most. At fifty square meters they offer plenty of space, and two of them have private terraces with views of the city, while the other two make do with balconies. One even comes with an indoor plunge pool, which is not exactly the norm in Florence. Inside your apartment you’ll lack for nothing in terms of luxury — and while, outside your room, such ordinary hotel services as a restaurant or a lobby are conspicuously lacking, you’re in the heart of a vibrant and busy city, one that rewards a bit of self-sufficiency.

content:
Turkey’s got history, to put it mildly, but they’re not afraid of a little modernity either — they’ve taken to boutique hotels with zeal, turning out some of the world’s most stylish and surprising hotels. It’s high time some of the more design-centric names moved into Istanbul, and with the advent of the W Istanbul, it seems they have.

Though there are exceptions, Istanbul isn’t a high-rise town, so the W is a bit of a departure for the ordinarily high-flying chain. Instead of a tower it’s a row of converted townhouses, its 142 rooms tucked discreetly away behind their 19th-century facades. The real fireworks are hidden inside, from the baroque décor and dramatic lighting at the reception to the heavy boudoir romance of the guest rooms. Suites verge on excess, some with chandelier-lit living rooms, others with honeymoon-suite circular beds, but even the standard — sorry, Wonderful — rooms come with cleverly disguised 32-inch LCD televisions and king-size beds with 350-thread linens.

The location, in Besiktas, isn’t quite picturebook Istanbul, but what it is is fashionable and upscale — the shopping here is phenomenal, and you won’t mind being a taxi ride from the historical sites. In-house is a Spice Market as well as a couple of other excellent restaurants, as well as a full-service spa and fitness center — you won’t want to shut yourself in, not with vibrant Istanbul just outside, but if you had to, you could, and comfortably.

Long before Waikiki Beach became the buzzing metropolis that it is, a fantastic pink stucco Moorish-style palace was erected on these famous shores. Now entering its tenth decade, the Royal Hawaiian Hotel offers a taste of a bygone era in Honolulu’s history, a trip back in time to the days when a trip to Hawaii was the last word in far-flung tropical adventure.

It’s fresh off a renovation that’s brought the guest rooms up to date while leaving public spaces as elegant as they were in the Twenties, which means that while the atmosphere is still transformative, the comforts are as familiar as can be. The rooms in the Mailani Tower are necessarily a bit more on the contemporary side, while those in the Historic Building dive a little deeper into the hotel’s stylistic heritage — and no matter which style you prefer, they’re five-star through and through.

Same goes for the rest of the Royal Hawaiian’s facilities. The Abhasa Spa’s treatment cabins are scattered throughout a lush garden, the pool is fringed with private cabanas, and the restaurants range from top-shelf fine dining to a bakery serving Hawaiian twists on traditional pastries. And you’ve got all the attractions of the Pacific Ocean at your feet as well, from stand-up paddling and surfing lessons to sailing excursions and submarine tours.

content:
Though it’s long had a reputation as one of America’s most tradition-bound cities, a look at the Boston hotel scene reveals a town that’s not afraid of a bit of experimentation. Just over the bridge from downtown, in the newly revitalized Seaport, is another example: the stylish, modern, fully wired Envoy Hotel. It’s a member of Marriott’s Autograph Collection, but what you’ll find inside its doors is proof that there are some corporate hotels that can hang in there with the independents — this is their luxury boutique sub-brand, for one thing, and one thing it’s not short on is personality.

Nor is it short on the sort of professionalism that’s the strength of the big chains. The rooms are attractive, contemporary, and a bit whimsical, with TV stands made from old bike frames and furnishings that split the difference between modernist classics and contemporary experiments — and they make the most of their full-length windows and their views of the harbor.

Para Maria, the ground-floor restaurant, offers Latin-inspired cuisine, while Rooftop at The Envoy, located on the top floor, serves specialty cocktails and features transparent "igloos" and fleece blankets, creating a rooftop bar experience that can be enjoyed year-round in Boston.

content: In the last couple of decades Colombia has done a great deal to shed its difficult reputation, and tourism is booming once again — with perhaps no destination seeing more of a benefit than the colonial city of Cartagena. The improvements, at least as far as Tablet is concerned, come not in the form of large-scale development and an influx of mass tourism, but in a new openness to the kind of well-heeled international audience that can support something a bit more individual: an intimate, elegantly styled colonial mansion, transformed into the luxe seven-room Casa de Alba Boutique Hotel.\n\n“Colonial” isn’t just a stylistic descriptor — this house dates back to 1560, and was one of the city’s first stone structures. The renovation that transformed it into the boutique hotel you see today was more recent — just in 2015 — but the restoration was a sensitive one, preserving the building’s historical character while updating it with modern furniture and amenities. The location, in the heart of Cartagena’s historic walled city, is as central as can be, convenient for sightseeing and revelry alike. And meanwhile, the house’s tranquil central courtyard, with its plunge pool, is the kind of low-tech comfort that its 16th-century inhabitants might equally have appreciated.

Apartment-sharing was supposed to kill hotels. But in the end the most creative hoteliers learned lessons from the apartment-sharing trend, and supplemented them with what they do best: professional hospitality. It’s led to a resurgence of urban bed and breakfasts, hotels with residential charm and character to spare, along with boutique-hotel style and service. Hotels like Mexico City’s Chaya Bed & Breakfast Boutique.

The location could hardly be more central — it’s in the heart of downtown Mexico City, facing the Alameda Central park. But for all the activity outside, Chaya could hardly be more tranquil. It occupies the upper floors of a renovated building, with two restaurants, a mezcal bar, an ice cream shop and a café on the ground floor. And once you’re upstairs you’ll find the rooms and suites are surprisingly stylish, in an industrial style with plenty of raw concrete that’s offset against warm wood textures and plush king beds.

Breakfast is served daily — it’s right there in the name, after all — and includes made-to-order Mexican classics alongside continental options. It’s certainly not an old-fashioned bed and breakfast, but nor is it an ordinary hotel. This may not be the last you see of the Bed & Breakfast Boutique concept.

It’s enough to make the rest of Edingurgh’s hotels feel a bit buttoned-up by comparison. Though it’s hidden away inside a listed Georgian townhouse, you’ll know Tigerlily instantly — it’s the one Georgian townhouse with a line out the door, composed of revelers waiting to get in to Lulu, the nightlcub down in the basement.

The basement bit, as it turns out, is key. Anyone who’s ever tried to get a good night’s sleep in one of the world’s lesser disco boutiques will be instantly wary. But that queue’s not for you — checking in you’ll be whisked to reception, and then through the teeming lobby lounge and upstairs, to find a room that’s as restful as the crowd downstairs is restive, decked out in oversized sofas and overstuffed duvets.

The look isn’t entirely sedate — bright splashes of color feel playfully Swinging Sixties — but it’s pretty far from the empty flash of many design boutiques. And of course all the luxuries are accounted for, including spacious, almost decadent bathrooms and all sorts of techno-goodies from plasma TVs to PSPs. Tigerlily’s restaurant occupies a stylish space, and is actually quite a good one. Drinks, however, are the main attraction, whether in the lobby lounge or downstairs at Lulu — hotel guests skip the line and walk straight in.
