To say that Maryland’s Eastern Shore is a regional destination, rather than a global one, isn’t to take anything away from it — in the age of cheap jet travel it’s easy to be seduced by tropical islands and Alpine chalets. Sometimes all you want is a weekend trip within easy reach of Washington, D.C., and thanks to the Wylder Hotel Tilghman Island, this long-established destination has received an infusion of contemporary boutique-hotel style.

This 1898-vintage boarding house has been thoroughly updated, its rooms and suites redesigned in a contemporary-classic style. Maritime colors and materials — wood and brass, sisal and rattan — reinforce the connection to the Chesapeake Bay seafaring life, while the comforts are pure modern luxury: Egyptian cotton linens, in-room spa services, and tablet-based concierge service.

And you’ll find the Wylder has much to recommend it outside of the accommodations, including a saltwater pool and a private marina, as well as partnerships with local fishing charter captains, in case you’ve arrived without your own vessel. Recreation options include kayaks, stand-up paddling, bocce, lawn darts, and bike rides. And no Eastern Shore escape would be complete without Maryland blue crab. The Wylder features a pair of restaurants, Tickler’s Crab Shack & Restaurant and Bar Mumbo, by chef Sean Wheaton, a longtime José Andrés associate.

With a name like Pillows it’s clear you’re not exactly in for a rough ride, but there’s reason to suspect that even among the rest of its family, Pillows Charme Hotel Château De Raay Limburg is remarkable for its plushness. In contrast with its urban cousins, this one occupies a 13th-century castle on the outskirts of the North Limburg village of Baarlo, surrounded by tranquil gardens, totally insulated from the outside world.

Inside are rooms that make instant sense of the Pillows name, their beds heaping with Egyptian cotton linens, their surfaces touchable, their décor soothingly minimal beneath charming beamed ceilings. The atmosphere is timeless, thanks to the contrast of the historical building and the contemporary interiors, though the comforts are entirely modern.

De Tuin van de Barones is the flagship fine-dining restaurant, making the most of local ingredients, many of them grown right here on the estate. And every Pillows hotel features The Living, a more casual multi-purpose lounge space with an all-day menu and an extensive wine list. Fuel up, hop on a bike and explore the forests and nature reserves of these memorable Limburg landscapes, and be back in time for dinner.

Many Sicilian hotels lean into a rustic, unpolished aesthetic, but not Asmundo di Gisira — this Catanian boutique hotel is as cosmopolitan as they come. This 18th-century palazzo in the historic city center, once a bona fide aristocratic residence, has been updated with a dash of modern design and a generous helping of eye-catching contemporary art, the work of an all-star team of architects and artists.

The art isn’t confined to the lobby, either. One of the Art Rooms prominently features a lifelike crocodile as well as a foot-shaped chair by Gaetano Pesce, while others mix classical references with contemporary murals and modernist furniture. And while they’re all different, they share a lively mix of ornate historical architecture, cool contemporary design, and luxury-boutique comforts.

Beyond breakfast, there’s no restaurant, but Asmundo di Gisira places you right at the edge of Catania’s Pescheria market, and close by to a profusion of restaurants. Hotel staff is happy to help with recommendations, not only for meals but for all manner of sights around town — given the character of the hotel, you won’t be surprised to hear that they’re particularly plugged-in when it comes to the local art scene.

From the outside, this classic Georgian building, just north of Princes Street Gardens, couldn’t be more obviously Edinburgh. Once inside the rooms, though, it’s easy to get lost; each of Le Monde’s 18 suites is named for one of the world’s great cities, from New York and Dublin to Cairo, Havana, St. Petersburg — and they’re decorated to match, in a style that fairly accurately conjures the atmosphere of each chosen town.

Even discounting the cities gimmick, the rooms are striking; that they go all the way towards their chosen themes does quite a bit to set them apart from the slightly tedious minimalism of today’s average boutique hotel room. Cairo or otherwise, all the suites come with lush Egyptian cotton sheets, as well as big, decadent bathrooms and plasma-screen televisions.

The world cities theme doesn’t stop there, either. Four restaurants/bars is quite a lot for a hotel of this small size, but it’s just that kind of place — hotel guests and the George Street crowd alike dine and drink in Paris, Vienna, Milan, and the late-night basement bar, Shanghai. And lest one forget, Edinburgh is always an option — many of the city’s best bars and restaurants are within walking distance of Le Monde.

content:
It’s not the newest big-time luxury hotel in Kuala Lumpur, but the Shangri-La is not the sort of hotel that rests on novelty for its appeal. Everything that was impressive about this five-star downtown tower when it opened in the mid-Eighties is still impressive today (minor aesthetic and technological adjustments notwithstanding, it’s not like it’s a time capsule or something). The Asia-Pacific mega-luxury formula is still a successful one, even in the (forgive us) post-boutique era.

So. 662 rooms, at least a hundred of which are suites, but all of which, at any size, are comfortable, elegant, spacious enough, and provided with well-elevated city views. The style walks a line which never wavers into corporate blandness or bludgeoning kitschiness — it feels like Kuala Lumpur without also feeling like a presentation from the local Chamber of Commerce. And the key to this sort of hotel is not just the facility, but the service as well — most anything you want is already at your fingertips, but in the rare event it’s not, there’s an army of staffers on hand to make matters right.

Pool, spa, fitness center, restaurants — all the must-haves are present. And they’re far from your only choice. In the time since the Shangri-La opened, its very central location has somehow become even more central — you’ll probably recognize the Petronas Towers, for instance.

Please note: We are not taking reservations for this hotel at the current time.

It’s one thing to pull off “affordable luxury” in mid-market cities like Rotterdam and Glasgow, as the citizenM group has already done with aplomb, but to build a hotel like this in Times Square is pretty much unheard of. An exceedingly comfortable, visually stylish, reasonably priced hotel just isn’t supposed to exist here, where the real-estate costs are astronomical and the usual standards of “hospitality” stretch the limits of the term. The fact that citizenM has also made room for some seriously inviting public spaces, from the soaring Vitra-furnished lobby lounge to the rooftop Cloud Bar — well, it’s just about got us reaching into the bag of forbidden New York clichés for a good, emphatic “fuhgettaboutit.” 

The key to making it work is citizenM’s extraordinary efficiency. There’s no ordinary reception desk, just a self-serve kiosk for quick, contact-free check-in. And while the rooms are small, the fact is that Manhattan hotel rooms, at this price anyway, are almost always small, and they rarely look this good, or work this well. Beneath your wall-to-wall window is an extra-large king-size bed wrapped in ultra-soft, high-thread-count Italian linens and topped with fluffy down pillows. There’s a high-tech MoodPad (and a downloadable phone app) for controlling everything from the ambient lighting to the free movies to the digital art on the wall. And off to the side is a shower pod that looks like it’s going to beam you up to the nearest hospitable planet, but in fact just houses a wonderfully high-pressure rain shower and some bespoke bath products by the “nose” behind the scents at Comme des Garçons. We could go on and on, but the point is that though the rooms are quite small, they’re very well appointed. And it bears mentioning that these spaces are made to be easily cleaned — if cleanliness really is next to godliness, then in one way, at least, this is heaven. 

Not that this hotel is just a big box of little bedrooms. The hoteliers behind citizenM like to point out that, when you’re at home, you mostly use your bedroom for sleeping, spending the majority of your daytime hours in the living room and kitchen. With that in mind, they’ve designed the hotel to draw you out of the bedroom. The trick is to create an atmosphere that’s pleasantly social, but with enough comfortable nooks that it never feels like more of a scene than you want it to be. Even the high-design lobby has been infused with a certain informality and warmth, and they’ve given the twenty-four-hour canteen the feel of an open kitchen — the idea being that you can wander in and out of throughout the day and night, just as you would at home. The same make-yourself-comfortable vibe extends to the open-office-style mezzanine, to the garden-like terraces and yoga decks, and to the pair of attractive bars. And speaking of distractions, there’s also the small matter of those bright lights calling to you just outside the door.

content: Washington D.C.’s Phoenix Park Hotel isn’t overly impressed with its location at the heart of American history. It’s named for a park in Dublin, and is, in fact, owned by an Irish concern. There’s plenty of Americana to go around in the neighborhood — you’re a few blocks from the Capitol, and more or less right next to Union Station — but once you’re inside Phoenix Park it’s all warm Irish hospitality, thanks in no small part to the Dubliner, which is more or less everything you’d imagine if you were to close your eyes and wish for an Irish pub and restaurant.\n\nFortunately, an authentically Irish hotel doesn’t have to hammer the point home by drenching the guest rooms in four-leaf-clover kitsch. The dominant color here is a deep indigo, against monochrome silver and white. The look is elegant, contemporary, but still classic — stylish enough to appeal to the fashion-minded, yet eminently comfortable for D.C.’s more stylistically conservative elements as well. Though lobbyists and the like will opt for more extravagant (and duller) luxury digs, the rest of us will appreciate some authentic personality, especially this close to downtown, the National Mall, and Capitol Hill.

content:
Berlin may very well be the hipster capital of Germany, and possibly all of Europe. But there’s still business that needs to be done. Still, there’s no reason why the business hotels shouldn’t have a bit of fun. What makes the Park Plaza Wallstreet unique is that its particular idea of fun is in exaggerating, rather than obscuring, its big-business leanings — it’d be impossible to walk across the dollar-print carpets, for example, without picking up on the Wall Street theme.

If everything ’80s is cool again, then it’s Gordon Gekko’s time as well — and he’d feel quite at home in the crisp minimalism of the Park Plaza, livened as it is by occasional flashes of very brash materialist kitsch, including business-motivational aphorisms stenciled in several languages above the bed heads.

It’s got all the basics covered, from the fitness center and sauna to the stylish bar and restaurant. This isn’t the place to actually live the five-star luxe life that the décor plays at — for that you’d be better off in one of Berlin’s extremely unironic five-star luxury hotels — but for a witty, well-designed take on the contemporary business hotel, the Wallstreet is your place.

content:
On the stretch of Caribbean coastline between Cancún and Tulum — that geographically blessed region referred to as the Riviera Maya — there’s hardly a square foot of real estate that doesn’t belong to a resort. And when you’re hurtling south along Highway 307, passing by their gated entrances, it’s hard to tell the difference between them. Of course, all resorts are not created equal. Take Zoëtry Paraiso de la Bonita. When you stack it up against its competitors, it’s a resort that’s got three things going for it: the suites, the amenities, and location, location, location.

There are just ninety suites: small, if not downright intimate, for a resort in the area, meaning you won’t be battling for a spot by the pool’s edge. And unlike many resorts, where you’ll choose between rooms with sea views and those that face “gardens” or the dreaded “courtyard,” all suites at Zoëtry are oceanfront. Better yet, they all have private terraces with chaise lounges or hammocks, and many offer direct beach access. The most modest option is a one-bedroom that clocks in at a spacious 1,130 square feet; features include a living room with original artwork and a marble bathroom with a sunken tub. At the higher end, suites have multiple bedrooms with king-sized beds, outdoor showers, and private plunge pools. 

Most resorts on the Riviera Maya are all-inclusive. At Zoëtry, the concept has been rebranded as “Endless Privileges” — and the privileges are generous indeed, ranging from complimentary minibars, refreshed twice daily, to a sunset Catamaran sail, gourmet menus (including organic options) at a range of dining venues, and maid service three times daily. If luxury is in the details, Zoëtry Paraiso de la Bonita has their bases covered: the bath products are by Bulgari, a bottle of sparkling wine and fresh fruit is delivered daily to each suite, and in-suite dining is available around the clock. You read that right: you can order tacos and margaritas at 3am, if the mood strikes — it’s included. Also included: private shuttles to and from the Cancun airport, which is just a forty-minute drive away. Zoëtry is on the northernmost edge of the Riviera Maya, making it easy to access. You can pop in and out of this resort with minimal effort, but you’ll feel like you’re far from the Cancun hotel zone on these quiet white sands — best of both worlds.

content: For a city with such a glamorous reputation, Rio de Janeiro comes up surprisingly short when it comes to high-end hotels. Sure, there are the classic beachfront landmarks — the historic Belmond Copacabana Palace and the sultry Fasano — and a few perfectly lovely boutique hotels tucked into the hills of Santa Teresa. But it’s hardly enough to keep up with the ever-growing numbers of discerning travelers descending on the cidade maravilhosa. Luckily, the Hyatt brand is getting into the game, adding hundreds of new hotel rooms into the mix. 436 rooms and suites, to be exact: the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro is grand indeed. You can’t really open a new hotel of this size on the prime beachfront real estate of Ipanema or Leblon or Copacabana, so the hotel is located on Barra da Tijuca, a beach that’s a bit further away from the center of the action. But there are are a few perks to the relatively suburban location. The hotel is located between the Atlantic Ocean and the Marapendi lagoon. Every guest room and suite on the property has a private balcony, and the majority offer some sort of water view. The rooms themselves are what you’d expect at a brand-new Grand Hyatt: spacious and light-filled, with floor-to-ceiling windows, modern decor, the brand’s signature Hyatt Grand bed, and bathrooms with deep soaking tubs and separate rain showers. In-room amenities cater to business travelers, from large flat-screen TVs and Nespresso machines to complimentary wi-fi. Unless you’re staying in one of the oceanfront suites, in which case you’ll likely want to linger on your furnished patio overlooking the beach, the real allure of the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro is in its open-air spaces. The hotel sits right on the sand, with direct access to a private beach area – a great place to claim a chaise lounge under an oversized umbrella and relax with an agua de coco. There’s also a large outdoor swimming pool, a 24-hour fitness center with yoga rooms, and a spa, plus three sleek restaurants designed by the Brazilian architect Arthur Casas. One’s Italian, another specializes in sushi, but if you’ve come all the way to Rio, you’ll probably opt for the third. Opening up to the swimming pool and gardens, Cantô Gastrô e Lounge is filled with Brazilian art, hosts live Bossa Nova music in the evenings, and turns out a killer caipirinha, Brazil’s irresistible national cocktail — it's a perfect place to get your bearings before you head out on the town to mingle with nightilfe-loving Cariocas in their natural habitat.

content:
There are those among us for whom the mere fact of a Tokyo boutique hotel designed from top to bottom by the master architect Kengo Kuma is enough to motivate a click on the big orange “book now” button. For the rest of us — or to pass the time before departure — some more detail might be in order. ONE@Tokyo’s location, in Oshiage, near the foot of the enormous Tokyo Skytree broadcast tower, places it well to the east of the city center. But for so singular an experience, a few extra minutes on the train is a small price to pay. Kuma designed everything, down to the uniforms worn by the staff, and the result is a hotel that’s like nothing else.

The building is unmistakable, a ten-story concrete structure whose ground floor is sheathed in loose crisscrossing timbers. And if you know Kengo Kuma’s work, you won’t be surprised to find that wood and concrete dominate the interiors as well. There’s an unapologetic inelegance to the raw materials — plywood, salvaged timbers — but the composition is artful and the feeling is perversely warm. The Studio rooms are compact and hyper-efficient, Loft rooms rather more relaxed, and the Atelier and Library suites venture into luxury territory. Meanwhile the lobby café, with its absurdly long communal table, functions as an all-day restaurant and bar, and the rooftop terrace serves as a secondary lounge space, a “sky forest” with unique views of the Skytree tower and the city lights.

content: Unless you have a private plane, the village of Barra Grande, located on Brazil’s Maraú Peninsula, isn’t exactly easy to get to. And Butterfly House Bahia is another ten miles outside that village. Luckily, there’s a handsome reward for the rather lengthy journey by some combination of Jeep, bus, speedboat and truck. It’s a jungle paradise: miles of white sandy beaches fringed with tall palm trees, clear blue water dotted with colorful coral reef, and a gorgeous (and environmentally conscious) hotel that’s designed to help you make the most of it. Butterfly House calls itself a resort, but that name could give you the wrong idea. It’s more like an upscale version of the Brazilian pousada, or guesthouse, sustainably built with salvaged demolition wood and recycled materials. There are just eleven guest rooms. Three of those are suites, located within the main building — the Butterfly House — and simply outfitted with natural wood furnishings, crisp white fabrics, canopied beds, and private balconies overlooking gardens blooming with bright flowers. The other “rooms” are actually free-standing bungalows. Amenities vary: some have private outdoor showers, others have large front porches. All have charmingly tiled bathrooms and furniture imported from Morocco and France, no small feat if you remember the unpaved road you traveled down to arrive here. Highlights at Butterfly House include a small swimming pool and the continental breakfast of your dreams: picture every tropical fruit you know, and several you don’t, lined up beside an array of freshly baked Brazilian pastries. Wander down to the beach bar (it’s five o’clock somewhere, right? Or at least noon somewhere?) and order a caipirinha, the citrusy national cocktail, to sip on the private beach. There’ll be no line to wait in, and on crowds to contend with: just calm water and pristine sand as far as you can see. The peninsula is a natural playground for snorkelers, surfers, and hikers, all activities that the staff at Butterfly House can gladly arrange. They’ll also give you a lift to nearby Taipú de Fora, the beach that Brazilians voted one of the most beautiful in the country. Which is really saying something: as you’ll note by looking at a map, there’s a lot of coastline in this country, and fortunately, you’ve found yourself on one of the loveliest (and hardest-to-reach) sections of it.

content:
Retro motels refitted into contemporary boutique hotels are one of our favorite genres in America, and we can’t say we’re disappointed to see them cropping up in Australia as well. Cabarita Beach, just outside of Gold Coast on the border between Queensland and New South Wales, is a legendary surf spot, and Halcyon House opens right onto a private section of it — if you want a taste of Australian beach life at its most stylish, this is the place to get it.

The design transformation was extraordinarily thorough; Brisbane-based designer Anna Spiro’s work approaches Wes Anderson levels of perfectionistic detail, and the elegance of Halcyon House’s interiors is more reminiscent of an upscale beach house — no two of its rooms and suites are the same — than an old drive-up motor inn. It’s luxurious, to be sure, but this being near-tropical Australia, it’s an exceedingly casual sort of luxury, and intensely relaxing to boot.

Halcyon House’s heated saltwater pool is a delight, as is the Halcyon Spa, but the most impressive element might just be Paper Daisy, the restaurant — book in advance to ensure a spot at one of the region’s most in-demand tables.

When it first opened, in 1875, San Francisco’s Palace Hotel was the largest in the world. When the rebuilt Palace re-opened after the fire in 1909 it was the city’s most opulent. And when it opened yet again in 2015, after a massive renovation, it was a triumphant return to form for San Francisco’s longest-running luxury hotel. The newly updated rooms are once again worthy of the Palace’s grand Garden Court, whose lavish afternoon tea has always been a local fixture.

The location, adjacent to the Financial District, is ideal for an old-world luxury hotel, and the new rooms, by the Los Angeles–based Italian designer Beatrice Girelli, create a harmonious marriage of century-old architectural details and soothing modern luxury. The colors palette is subtle yet rich, and neither the high-tech amenities nor the retro-inspired contemporary design manage to break the genteel spell. (And if they’ve changed the floor plan at all, it doesn’t show in the square footage — these rooms are positively sprawling, by San Francisco standards.)

And by anyone’s standards the glass-roofed Garden Court is something special — it’s an opulent, ornate space, but it somehow doesn’t feel out of touch with contemporary tech-casual San Francisco. It may, however, inspire you to dress for dinner; whether that means haute couture or just your finest hooded sweatshirt is a matter for personal interpretation.

There’s a standard aesthetic among Greek luxury hotels. As you may know, it involves a lot of white and a lot of marble, stately columns, heavy drapery, perhaps some statuary. NJV Athens Plaza, located around the corner from the Acropolis at an enviable address on Syntagma Square, falls right into line. It won’t seduce you with cutting-edge style or old-world glamour. This isn’t a hotel that’s reinventing the wheel. The NJV Athens Plaza, sturdy and classic, has been welcoming travelers for more than three decades. They follow a formula that works, and the hotel remains an extremely comfortable and convenient place to stay.

So what’s that formula? The unbeatable location, for starters, steps away from both historic monuments and the chic neighborhood of Kolonaki. Then there’s the guest rooms and suites, slightly larger than you’d expect, with floor-to-ceiling windows — some facing out over the square and the Acropolis — simple but elegant monochrome décor, airy marble bathrooms with tubs, and free wi-fi. All rooms and suites are soundproofed, a feature you’ll appreciate in such a busy part of the city.

There are countless cafés and restaurants nearby. But when your legs are too tired to carry you any further — sightseeing in Athens is a rather athletic endeavor — the NJV Athens Plaza has its own offerings. Grab a coffee at the Plaza Cafe, or have an early dinner at the Parliament with views over the lively pedestrian street below. Regardless of where the day takes you, the wood-paneled Explorer’s Lounge, with its green leather armchairs and crystal sconces, is a cozy spot for a nightcap.

Chicago’s Hotel Felix takes its name’s Latin meaning seriously. This hotel is all about happiness, which is a worthy goal if we’ve ever heard one. It helps if you’re into green hospitality — Hotel Felix has Silver LEED certification, the first in the city, thanks to measures encompassing everything from southern-exposure sunshine to high-tech energy reducing heating and lighting, and even its artworks are made from recycled and reclaimed materials. And it helps if your idea of a boutique hotel is something unpretentious, a little understated, with the occasional nod to Chicago’s long history of modernist architecture and design.

Felix occupies a classic brick building whose structure was essentially preserved in the renovation — another green measure, as it saved quite a lot of building material from the landfill. Inside it’s contemporary as can be, however, with luxe comforts and the latest electronics. Amenities include a fitness center, a lobby lounge and a business center, as well as the use of the spa next door at the Godfrey Chicago. For lunch, dinner, or drinks, there’s Troquet, an indoor-outdoor French bistro with a moody bar and lounge of its own. Meanwhile, in the morning, there’s Big Shoulders Coffee Shop — and from there you’re ready to hit the streets of River North, the Felix’s downtown neighborhood.

content: Not far from the shores of Lake Garda is a hotel that is, uncommonly for this region known for its ornate palaces, something a bit more pastoral: a Tuscan-style farmhouse. Boutique Hotel Villa dei Campi feels free to experiment with the form, freely mixing vibrant colors and whimsical decorative elements with its classic architecture and antique furniture. It’s a sustainable experience, built and operated in an environmentally friendly way, and to its ten charming rooms it adds an indoor wellness area with hydrotherapy and Turkish baths, an outdoor lake-style “bio” swimming pool, and a breakfast room under a vaulted brick ceiling.

content:
In some ways, the Eben House is among the most traditional lodgings in Provincetown — it’s housed in one of the oldest remaining Federal-style houses in town, an old sea captain’s house that dates back all the way to 1776. But its proprietors, David Bowd and Kevin O’Shea, are modern boutique hoteliers at heart, and like their nearby Salt House Inn, the Eben House is practically the very definition of the contemporary boutique bed and breakfast.

Rooms and suites are divided between the main house, an adjoining Victorian, and an old carriage house; all are an eclectic blend of period architecture, contemporary décor, and modern boutique-hotel comforts. They vary in size and layout, but all of them partake in Eben House’s inimitable atmosphere, and share access to facilities like the saltwater swimming pool and the sun terrace.

There’s an excellent breakfast, and drinks are available throughout the day; beyond that, in true b&b style, you’re at the mercy of Provincetown’s restaurants, which is not at all a difficult place to be — you’re just a block away from the varied and colorful Commercial Street scene, in the very heart of this bustling town.

content:
New on the hospitality scene in the Netherlands is Pillows, a luxury boutique hotel chain that, as its name implies, tends to focus on the softer, more soothing side of Dutch design. For their first hotel in Belgium they’ve renovated a grand neoclassical building on the south side of the city center, transforming it into a stately and sedate 43-room hotel: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Place Rouppe Brussels.

The guest rooms are clean and contemporary in style but emphasize senses other than the visual, with high-end linens, espresso machines, walk-in showers and wireless sound systems. They’re double-glazed for light sleepers and there’s a pillow menu available on request, naturally — as you’d expect from a hotel called Pillows, they’ve gone all in on ensuring a pleasant night’s rest.

The Living Resto & Winebar is the name of Pillows’ all-day restaurant and bar, a stylish but casual space that functions as the hotel’s social center. And the Salons are a pair of meeting rooms that do double duty as private dining rooms, in case you’re planning a function. It’s plush hospitality on perhaps a smaller scale than we’re used to in the de facto European capital, and if you know our tastes, you’ll know that’s a good thing indeed.

content:
The original Gurney’s, in the Long Island beach town of Montauk, was a masterful reinvention of an 80-year-old seaside hotel, and it’s been a major fixture on the Hamptons scene since its rebirth a few short years ago. It’s hard to imagine topping it, but you’ll never know if you don’t try. Gurney’s Newport Resort & Marina, in the celebrated Rhode Island vacation town, does its level best to re-create the magic on Narragansett Bay.

It’s no tentative half-measure sort of place — Gurney’s Newport, with over 200 rooms, is almost twice the size of the original, situated on ten acres of waterfront land. Its raw material, an ordinary chain hotel, may have been a little less rich in history than the Montauk Gurney’s was, but what’s replaced it has character to spare. The rooms and suites are visually restrained, but unapologetically luxurious, all of them with views of the water.

Impressive as they are, the real story here is the social life. Scarpetta, the Italian restaurant, is the main attraction at night, with the Regent Lounge in a supporting role; in the morning, Corso Coffee is an essential stop, and the Pineapple Club serves casual fare by the pool. Other inducements include the Seawater Spa, multiple wedding venues, and of course the marina, in case you’re of a mind to arrive by sea rather than land.

content:
Hua Hin is a classic Thai beach resort, a quiet seaside village that took on a glamorous new reputation after the royal family built their summer house here in the 1920s. But if you’re picturing a blissful desert-island paradise, think again. Hua Hin is on the mainland, positioned on the edge of the Gulf of Thailand in the southern province of Prachuap Khiri Khan. Convenient, as you don’t have to board an extra plane to get there. But this is no get-away-from-it-all escape. These days, it’s a proper city, with everything — fine dining and a bustling night market within easy proximity, for instance — that entails.

Check into Putahracsa Hua Hin, however, and you’ll certainly feel like you’re living in a stylish tropical fantasy. The hotel is relatively small, as resorts go, with just 67 rooms and suites. Each is a sleek refuge, the design modeled after the look of sixties-era motel architecture. Translation: standard rooms are housed in a two-story building that surrounds the pool. Equal opportunity access to the main attraction, in other words, though the pool, in this case, isn’t just a place to cool off, it’s an infinity pool surrounded by daybeds where you might be tempted to lounge all afternoon with a book and a cold drink or two.

In keeping with the motel theme, guest rooms are laid out in the conventional rectangular shape. All have outdoor terraces with cushioned lounge chairs or day beds, and many overlook the central pool. Interiors are minimalist, outfitted almost entirely in white and earth tones. Bathrooms all have soaking tubs or rain showers. Other standard amenities range from satellite TV and free wi-fi to in-room Nespresso machines. Splash out on a private villa and you’ll get a good deal more than that at Putahracsa Hua Hin, including a private butler and your own plunge pool — though you’d be sacrificing, alas, your chance to stay in the hip Thai version of a traditional motel room.

There’s a day spa and a fantastic oceanfront bar, so there’s plenty of reason to hide out at the resort. Should you wish to venture into town, the hotel’s very own tuk-tuk is ready to take you anywhere you want to go, including the small but famous night market — bring your appetite, and your camera.

content:
Like it or not, Zanzibar now registers on most tourists’ radar; increased traffic over the years has mostly shifted the genre from “adventure junkies and immersionists only” to “government-sponsored Indian Ocean hotspot.” Get outside Stone Town though, and the mythic character re-emerges, particularly at the extreme northern tip, and even more particularly on the northeast shore of the village of Nungwi. On this gentle stretch of coastline, widely considered among the finest beaches in the world, sits Essque Zalu Zanzibar.

Luxurious seclusion is the order of the day. Not that there’s much to tune out — if anything, the pinch-me turquoise waters and lush flora will keep you mesmerized. The suites and villas are arrayed on either side of the central complex and infinity pool to ensure privacy, and the open layouts mean you won’t feel sequestered in your colonial-style king bed. All come with sumptuously appointed bathrooms and LCD TVs; for the truly royal treatment, book an even larger villa and take advantage of a private plunge pool.

The Jetty is situated, understandably, at the end of an elevated wooden walkway. Here’s where you’ll be doing most of your lolling and socializing, depending on the mood; with handcrafted cocktails, live music, hookah, and al fresco Arabian cuisine, it’s not exactly easy to leave behind. Market Kitchen offers more manageable, rustic plates with a heavy focus on organic produce, while Baobab Bar’s resident mixologist prepares daily cocktail specials under its namesake tree.

Personal concierges come standard-issue with most beach resorts, but here it’s honed to an art form: Navigators, they’re called, nodding to the island’s history as a trade hub, and they’re indispensable. They’ll easily handle anything from an in-depth AFRICOLOGY treatment regime at the spa to the purchasing process for on-site artworks that catch your eye, let alone excursions — volcano tours, guided safaris, reef dives — around the rest of the island. The best part? They’re right at your fingertips when you need them, and invisible when you don’t.

How to get there: Essque Zalu Zanzibar is just over an hour's drive from Zanzibar International Airport via Malawi Road.

Chicago is often viewed as a businesslike city, first and foremost, known — perhaps unfairly — more for its downtown architecture than its downtown culture. But the Allegro Royal Sonesta Hotel Chicago is equally suited to business and pleasure; located in the heart of the city’s theatre district (and actually connected to the Cadillac Palace Theater), it’s a natural choice if you’re in town for a show.

Even if you’re not, the Allegro puts on a bit of a show of its own. The look of the rooms and suites pays homage to Art Deco, a throwback to the optimistic era when Chicago’s skyscrapers were first sprouting. They’re luxurious without being ostentatious, and come with generous touches like Atelier Bloem bath products and 43-inch flat screens.

Legato Lounge is the hotel’s restaurant and bar, serving all-day dining and evening drinks. And thanks to the central location, you’re within easy reach of any number of other eateries and nightspots — not to mention the shopping along State Street.

content:
As Caribbean destinations go, Anguilla is relatively quiet. That’s especially true of the East End, also known as Shoal Bay East, where Zemi Beach House Resort & Spa opened in 2016 as the area’s first luxury resort. And what a kick-off it was: here’s hoping it’s a sign of things to come — but not too soon. As the name suggests, Zemi is a beach house-style boutique resort. It’s rather intimate in size, and embodies a certain kind of casual seaside elegance that you’d more likely find at a stylish friend’s vacation home than at a conventional resort.

The property isn’t huge, just six oceanfront acres fringed with palm trees and tropical foliage. A striking infinity pool, flanked with chaises longues angled towards the ocean, is strategically placed to create the illusion that the turquoise waters of the sea and the pool are one. You’ll enjoy the same uninterrupted view of the ocean from your guest room or suite, all featuring private terraces with outdoor furniture. The decor is just what you’d want in a place as naturally beautiful as this: simple but sophisticated, with blonde wood furnishings, crisp white linens, dark wood shutters, smooth tile floors, and plush chairs and sofas upholstered with organic fabrics. Standard amenities include minibars stocked with local treats, bath products by Malin + Goetz, and free wi-fi.

You’d bet that the seafood’s good here, and you’d be correct: freshly caught fish is the basis for Zemi Beach House’s seasonal menus. After dinner, head to the Rhum Room to sample small-batch rums and consider the next day’s activities. Excellent snorkeling and hiking excursions are easily arranged through the hotel, ideally followed up by a deep tissue massage at Zemi’s Thai-style spa. Or you could just go for a stroll down a white sand beach that’s still blissfully unpopulated. We’re happy there’s now a good hotel on this quiet side of the island. But maybe one is enough for now.

content:
The name sounds like an undergraduate English elective, but Elements of Byron has nothing to do with Romantic poetry. Unless, of course, you’re thinking metaphorically — there’s plenty of poetry and romance to the spectacular setting of this beachfront resort in Byron Bay, a coastal town in New South Wales. With just over a hundred private villas, Elements of Byron Resort & Spa is a modern take on the resort concept. There’s the requisite spa, of course, and a range of dining venues, the massive infinity pool, the indoor-outdoor cocktail bar. But the architecture is sleek and contemporary, low-impact and single-story, the curving lines inspired by organic forms — the striking central pavilion is modeled after the look of a windswept sand dune. 

Indeed, there’s an eco-minded bent to the place, and a laid-back, flip-flop–friendly vibe that’s quintessentially Australian. Everywhere you look, there’s another stylish place to relax: hanging chaises suspended over a shallow pool, cozy sofas around the fire pit, a beach chair positioned in front of the calm tidal pools of Belongil Beach. The guest villas are divided into four categories: Dunal, Rainforest, Eucalypt and Wetlands. Needless to say, their design was inspired by nature, and while amenities vary, they’re all drenched with natural light and smartly outfitted with timber floors, stone fixtures, and leather detailing. Standard features include private terraces, king-sized beds, Nespresso machines, in-room iPads, and blackout curtains, should you wish to skip the spectacular sunrise. Some face the beach, others a lake. But they all feel delightfully private, tucked away into the forest.

The main restaurant at Elements of Byron, Graze, offers sweeping views of the turquoise pool from nearly every seat. Get even closer to the water with drinks and small plates at the aptly named Barefoot Kiosk, or wander over to Drift Bar for coffee or cocktails — or down to the beach, or into town. There’s a cool anything-goes atmosphere here: exactly the way a resort in paradise should be.

Inside it’s rather more traditional, its rooms designed with a certain retro elegance; functionally, of course, they’re as modern as can be. Water sports and outdoor activities are plentiful, and the restaurant, Le Palme, opens onto a large terrace with a far-ranging view.

content: Though you wouldn’t necessarily know it from the city’s public image, there’s another side of Portland, one that’s got little to do with hipster culture or gratuitous bird-themed artwork. Like any growing American city, it’s got its luxurious side as well, and the Dossier Hotel isn’t afraid to embrace it. But it doesn’t turn its back on what makes Portland Portland. This is a redesign of a formerly undistinguished chain hotel, and the new proprietors, the Oregon-based Provenance Hotels, have gone out of their way to feature local products and amenities, connecting the hotel with the city in a genuine way.\n\nThe location certainly helps. Here at the north end of Downtown you’re a few blocks from Powell’s City of Books, and you’re within easy reach of a wealth of excellent cafés, bars, and restaurants. Not that the Dossier is hurting in that department — Opal, the hotel’s bar, serves not just inventive cocktails, local beers, and Willamette Valley wines, but an all-day menu of creative bites as well. It’s a luxury boutique experience, to be sure, in a city that’s perhaps better known for something a little less polished; but that doesn’t mean it’s an unwelcome addition to the landscape.

Twenty or so years ago it was just about defensible to say that Melbourne was Australia’s creative capital. But in the intervening years it’s as though Sydney has been hell-bent on revenge. The design scene, like all of its creative industries, is world-class, so much so that top-flight design firms are apparently now sharing projects. The Collectionist Hotel is the work not of a mere one or two design firms but four, each one responsible for about ten of its 39 rooms — and every one of them, even those from the same designer, is different from all of the others, with unique artworks, colors, textures, and design inspirations.

You’ll choose your own room from what’s available in the category you booked when you check in — no need to spend too much time poring over the photos. Though they may differ aesthetically, they’re all similarly equipped, and comfortable indeed. The location, convenient to Sydney University and the hip neighborhoods of Newtown and Glebe, could hardly be more on-trend — which is handy, given that the hotel’s own services stop short of offering a proper restaurant. You’ll have your own kitchen, though, as well as a Nespresso machine, and the Collectionist’s happy hour is the perfect jump-start for a night on the town.

content:
The small city of Noto is one of Sicily’s most picturesque settlements, full of 18th-century Sicilian Baroque buildings, the whole cityscape seemingly sepia-toned thanks to the distinctive yellow hue of the local limestone and the brilliant Mediterranean sun. And Gagliardi Boutique Hotel places you right at the heart of it all, with a rooftop terrace that affords you a panoramic view of a number of local landmarks.

Of course, one (spectacular) terrace does not an extraordinary hotel make. Gagliardi is impressive on the inside as well, with interiors that effortlessly mix baroque ornament with rustic crafts and modern comforts, and artworks by contemporary artists. It’s a relatively sedate experience — Noto is a sleepy town, and you’re here to escape, for the most part — and Gagliardi’s atmosphere is perfectly suited to that end.

Thanks to the terrace bar, the rooftop is the ideal venue for a sunset cocktail, but between breakfast and your sundowner, you’re on your own. Thankfully the location means you’re close by to just about every restaurant in this compact city — and the same goes for all of Noto’s attractions, from the famous town hall to the near infinity of churches and the ruins of the medieval city.

The Padre Hotel was never a forgettable place, to be fair — but it’s only now, after a period of closure and a thorough reinvention, that this 1928 beauty has become the sort of hotel that even the most jaded world traveler could love.

The Padre’s style is playfully retro, with a certain mid-century swank, and there’s more than a little bit of luxury about it — the standard rooms come with California king beds, down duvets and 40-inch flat screens. The suites quickly cross over into total extravagance, with the pinnacle being the Oil Baron Suite, which spans over 800 square feet.

A hotel like the Padre wouldn’t be complete without a few dining and nighlife options: a relatively formal steakhouse restaurant, a second more casual bar and grill, a speakeasy, a roof deck lounge, and a café. Fair to say it’s a huge leap forward for Bakersfield’s hospitality scene.

content:
It’s been called the Gore-Tex Vortex, the People’s Republic of Boulder, and rather aptly, “Twenty-five square miles surrounded by reality.” It’s true that this Colorado town, at the foot of the Rockies, is something of an alternate reality. But it’s one you’ll be glad to inhabit, so long as you have the right outdoor gear, a decent caffeine tolerance, and reservations at a hotel like Basecamp Boulder.

Like a great fair-trade coffee shop — or, come to think of it, a great hiking boot — it’s a hotel that’s aesthetically pleasing and also practical, stylish even as it delivers the goods. And, at least in this case, the goods are pretty straightforward. You want a central location with easy access to the outdoors. Basecamp Boulder has it: the hotel is located downtown, just off Boulder Creek trail, within walking distance of the University of Colorado and Naropa Institute campuses and the popular Pearl Street pedestrian mall. In Boulder, you’ll also want a room that’s spacious and comfortable, a place to rest after all the hiking and biking you're bound to do. Basecamp Boulder has that. And they’re hip, too, done up in a look you might call outdoorsy retro: crisp white and canvas, whimsical hand-drawn maps, vintage clock radios, light fixtures modeled after old-fashioned camping lanterns.

Now that we have the basics covered, let’s go over your wish list. Fancy a rock-climbing adventure at dawn? No problem, you can make your own coffee and breakfast in your in-room kitchenette. Need to get some work done? That 32-inch flat panel LCD TV doubles as a computer monitor. Didn’t want to squeeze your Dahon folding bike into the overhead compartment? The Basecamp Boulder will be happy to lend you a bicycle.

There’s also a fitness center — which may seem like overkill but gets plenty of use in America’s fittest town — as well as a spa and hot tub for unwinding after the day’s adventures, and laundry facilities so you can keep those technical garments fresh. There’s no restaurant, just a coffee bar in the lobby — but with a location like this, you’re likely to be out and about all day anyway, and out again for dinner: just think of the hotel as, well, your base camp.

content: The concept behind Okko, a small chain of four-star hotels with a dozen locations across France, is both style-conscious and practical: the check-in process is virtual, guest rooms are good-looking and functional, and lots of little things, from on-demand movies to happy hour snacks, are complimentary. Okko Hotels Nantes Château, in the center of Nantes, follows the format. The look is sleek and Scandinavian, with guest rooms featuring custom Coco-Mat beds with Italian linen sheets, nice workspaces, luxurious bathrooms with organic cotton towels, and Nespresso machines. Tea, coffee, and fruit are on offer 24 hours a day at the Club, a venue that also hosts an Italian-inspired aperitivo, complete with a gourmet spread of antipasti and wine on the house, every evening. Needless to say, access to the wellness center’s gym and sauna is free, too, and the train station is conveniently located a short walk away.

content:
The proprietors of the stately old McCausland Hotel already did the hard work of converting these two 1850 warehouses in the heart of Belfast into a top-class luxury hotel, leaving it to Jestico + Whiles to work a little bit of design magic, making this place fit to wear the Malmaison name.

At just 64 rooms, it’s the smallest and most intimate of the chain, and it’s possibly the most stylish, blending a number of historical references into a surprisingly modern cocktail. No shocking pink blobs or space-age titanium here—more like dark and elegant vampire chic meets Titanic-era nautical opulence. It may sound odd on paper, but to the eye, the bar’s black velvet furnishings, porthole windows and black wood panels make quite an impression, especially if you’re used to the prevailing whites and creams of London’s boutiques.

It’s more than just the color scheme—the staple Malmaison brasserie is warmly lit by hundreds of candles, and tables are delightfully private, behind solid black partitions. Forget seeing and being seen; you’ll want to bring someone whose company you not only tolerate, but enjoy, as you’ll be seeing quite a lot of them.

Rooms are decadently comfortable, if not quite as striking as the public spaces—but to be honest, we care more for soft and inviting king beds and sensibly luxurious bathrooms than any sort of in-room design statements. Colors are rich, red and brown leather, with more of that black wood paneling, and all the necessities are accounted for, from flat-screen TVs with DVD players to oversized rain showers.

Fine for business, with a small fitness center and wi-fi access throughout; and fine for pleasure as well, especially the Samson and Goliath suites, spacious, with exposed beams and complimentary champagne. The Samson suite even comes with a billiard table, and, presumably, the soundproofing to match.

content:
Rumors of a sort of urban renaissance in Pittsburgh have been circulating for some time. With the advent of the Ace Hotel Pittsburgh, however, it’s probably time to consider them confirmed. The local creative and artistic types don’t just patronize the Ace hotels, they take part in creating them. And in this monumental, century-old former YMCA building in the city’s East Liberty district, they’ve found a potent symbol of the one-time greatness to which Pittsburgh has lately returned.

The ornate architecture certainly provides some visual interest. Against that backdrop, the Ace’s rooms are simple, spare, bright and sunny — they feel comfortably lived-in and yet somehow crisply brand-new at the same time. Small rooms are more than large enough, medium rooms spread quite comfortably, and the suites are spacious indeed (and find room for turntables and Martin acoustic guitars). Safe to say it all feels cozier and more handmade than the typical Steel City clichés would have it.

Equally vital to the Ace equation is an inspired selection of public spaces. The lobby with its café is an inviting option for officeless nomads and all manner of socializing. And Whitfield is the Ace’s anchor, a neighborhood tavern by Brent Young of Brooklyn’s Meat Hook, serving a menu that’s locally inspired and locally sourced — not only are the executive chef and pastry chef natives, but the meat is from a single ranch in nearby Bedford, and is butchered in-house. Meanwhile the old gymnasium is now a multi-use events space with a capacity of four hundred guests, while the ballroom, fittingly, holds about two hundred in a slightly more formal setting.

content:
Raffles may be best known for the 19th-century urban grandeur of its original Singaporean flagship hotel, but the Raffles Maldives Meradhoo is proof that the group can confidently operate in a wide variety of luxury-hotel styles. This resort pays tribute to its heritage with a touch of colonial atmosphere, but it’s a contemporary island resort through and through — from the beachfront villas and residences on the tiny speck of an island that is Meradhoo to the overwater units anchored to the floor of the lagoon a quarter-mile boat ride away.

In a sense it’s two resorts in one, so different are the experiences — overwater villas and residences have terraces with steps that lead directly into the Indian Ocean, while the beach villas and residences are nestled into the trees just a few steps from a sandy beach. The most desirable ones, of both types, are the sunset-facing units, though it’s a scant difference given the elegance and sheer physical luxury on display in every category.

This place is naturally a diver’s paradise, thanks to the easily accessible reefs. And even if you stay on dry land, it’s a paradise of a different sort, thanks to the elaborate spa and wellness center, the multiple restaurants and bars, and the famously attentive Raffles service. Different top-end brands, and different Maldives luxury resorts, have their partisans, but it’s safe to say that the Raffles Maldives Meradhoo belongs squarely in the league’s upper division.

content:
If there were any doubt about the intended effect of a Maldivian overwater villa resort, LUX* North Male Atoll makes it perfectly clear. Here, every single unit, whether on the beach or over the lagoon, is essentially a penthouse suite: a self-contained villa, retreat, or residence designed not in a thatched-roof traditional style but in a modernist style that’s reminiscent of Miami Beach, complete with a rooftop lounge for sunning and dining and a pink-rimmed infinity pool. 

The interiors, too, recall modern luxury hotels rather than humble traditional residences; the contrast of the bright and sunny, almost urban décor and the jaw-dropping views of the turquoise waters of the lagoon is a memorable one. They spare no comforts, from high-tech entertainment and lighting systems to well-stocked minibars and custom-made bath products.

There’s a similarly no-holds-barred approach to the facilities, from the spa with its five overwater treatment villas to the multiple bars and restaurants, the café and ice cream shop, and the round-the-clock en-suite dining service. The dive center is vast and well-equipped, and the other seafaring activities include just about anything you can think of, from canoeing and stand-up paddling to fishing, dolphin-watching excursions, and “turtle quests.” And children are well looked after here; for just about every adult activity, there’s a counterpart for kids.

The citizenM hotels are known for combining vibrant, art-filled common spaces with futuristic, pod-like rooms, low-frills and largely self-serve conveniences, and prices that justify the unusual approach. New York’s Bowery, once down on its luck, is now full of high-end boutique hotels, but in the citizenM New York Bowery it’s also got something a little bit more attainable and scarcely less stylish.

Check-in is contactless and effortless, achieved via a simple touchscreen in place of the usual reception desk. The pod-like rooms are made for ease of use and for extreme cleanliness; they’re dominated by extra-large wall-to-wall king beds, with a little space carved out for an efficient and very modern bathroom. Once you’re out of bed, there’s not much space to lounge, so downstairs you go, to the surprisingly cozy Living Room, a multi-purpose all-day work/social space. Alongside that is canteenM, a self-serve grab-and-go restaurant and bar. The top floor features cloudM, a rooftop bar, and the lobby’s coffeeM is exactly what you imagine it to be.

The Lower East Side’s nightlife is legendary, and the hotel’s location, just a block to the south of the contemporary New Museum, makes it an ideal spot from which to absorb a healthy dose of Downtown culture — as well as a wealth of retail, from mass-market to luxury, if that’s your bag. There’s also one bona fide cultural attraction inside the hotel: a graffiti installation knowns as the Museum of Street Art.

content:
There’s more to Vienna than the centuries-old splendor of the city center, the living museum that’s roughly bounded by the Ringstrasse. But what more, exactly, is a question for another time — at the moment that centuries-old splendor is precisely what we’re concerned with, in the form of the Palais Coburg, a 19th-century neoclassical palace that’s currently doing business as an old-school top-of-the-market grand hotel.

The Coburg isn’t shy about its opulence: the entry is calculated to impress, and makes good on the promises made by the building’s ornate facade. No expense is spared in the accommodations, nor in the restaurants. The Coburg’s flagship restaurant, Silvio Nickol, has earned two MICHELIN Stars, while the Clementine im Glashaus offers modern Austrian cuisine in a beautiful greenhouse setting or on the secluded garden terrace. For an intimate drink, the wine bar serves rare offerings from the hotel’s award-winning cellar, the largest in Austria and second largest in Europe.

The Coburg has its own pool, spa and fitness center, rarity enough in this town, especially for such a small hotel. And beyond the four walls of the Palais is Vienna’s scenic and walkable city center — you’re just minutes from the Stephansplatz, and surrounded by as much opera (and shopping) as you can take.

content: The northern coast of Brazil is perhaps less well known than Rio or Bahia, but it’s not exactly a secret: the windswept dunes of Jericoacoara and the equally windswept waters of Jericoacoara Beach are famous among kitesurfers and adventuring types. You don’t have to go far, though, to get back to that undiscovered-paradise feeling. On the fringes of Preá, the next town to the east, on an unspoiled stretch of white sand, is Casana, a tiny, laid-back boutique hotel comprising little more than a handful of bungalows set just a few yards back from the beach.\n\nThe style is contemporary, but sensitive to local tradition, which means thatched roofs, plenty of wood, and up-to-date comforts like air conditioning, wi-fi, and extravagantly relaxing bathrooms. Some add plunge pools, and all sprawl out over a minimum of 80 square meters. And whether or not you’ve got your own pool, there’s always the hotel’s main pool, a beautiful black-bottomed affair that creates a mirror effect on the surface of the water. There’s a gym, a kite lounge — like a ski shop, but for kitesurfing — as well as a restaurant, a pool bar, and a beach bar, all serving upscale cocktails and creative dishes seasoned with herbs from the hotel’s own organic garden.

content:
The combination of the world’s most exciting city and the world’s most over-the-top hospitality group was always going to raise eyebrows. So what have the originators of Dubai’s fantastical Burj Al Arab cooked up for Shanghai? Just the Jumeirah Himalayas Hotel, a riotously colorful neon-lit cube atop the Himalayas Center, itself an insanely futuristic mixed-use development that’s turned Pudong into a dead ringer for one of the sets from Blade Runner, and which makes Beijing’s Olympic stadium look positively neoclassical by comparison.

What draws the Jumeirah Himalayas back from the precipice is its interiors, which, in the rooms at least, show a remarkable devotion to Chinese tradition. For all the fireworks in the exterior, and the Vegas-like excess of the public spaces, the accommodations come in rather on the tasteful end of things; they’re unflaggingly luxe in their comforts and equipment, of course, but the visual style is pure contemporary Chinese classic.

The cube of the hotel surrounds an enormous cylindrical 14-story atrium, which means that some of the interior views are as dramatic as the exterior ones. And the Jumeirah’s position in the Himalayas Center means it’s about as conveniently located as they come; in addition to the hotel’s own supply of restaurants and bars, guests will have access to a shopping mall, an art museum, and easy transport links via the maglev rail station.

The one-dimensional portrayal of Detroit as post-industrial ex-city is long out of date. Out of every bust comes a boom, eventually, and this town is definitely on the up. For a miniature version of Detroit’s renewal story, take Trumbull & Porter, a one-time Holiday Inn whose transformation brings new life to Corktown, an old Irish neighborhood just to the west of downtown.

Hometown pride reigns supreme here, driving local procurement in nearly every aspect, from the suds by Batch Brewing Company to the custom rental bikes by Detroit Bikes. Far from disavowing the area’s cradle-of-industry background, Trumbull & Porter wholeheartedly embraces the aesthetic; Patrick Thompson Design incorporated exposed conduits and bulbs, polished concrete, and whitewashed brick throughout the interior. The 144 rooms soften the effect with custom furnishings by local artisans, enlivened here and there by pastels and patterned textiles. It’s human minimalism, clean-lined and utilitarian without skimping on the creature comforts. 

You’ll be within an easy walk of the happening Michigan Avenue scene, but T & P itself is no slouch in the food and beverage department. Burroughs Lounge, situated in the lobby, takes its name from the grandfather of the literary titan, proudly forefronting an authentic pair of his period adding machines. Red Dunn Kitchen is more or less the star of the show, slinging casual New American plates and a variety of liquids to pair; in clement weather, the courtyard hosts an art showcase and beer garden with live (and, there it is again, local) music. Drink and make merry, there’s life in this city yet.

content:
We’ve remarked before on the effortlessness with which Italian hoteliers and designers combine the old and the new; even in medieval Florence it’s possible for a hotel to pay homage to the city’s history through the medium of contemporary architecture and design. Fornace Suite, set on a cobbled street on the south side of the Arno River, is just such a place, its six suites designed by the celebrated local studio Archea Associati in tribute to six Florentine artists, from Donatello and Bernini to Michelangelo himself.

There’s nothing at all antique or retro about these spaces, handsome in muted grays and unpainted wood; concrete floors provide a neutral backdrop for eye-catching contemporary furnishings, while gauzy curtains further soften that legendary Tuscan sunlight. The style is somehow at once austere and warm, and the physical comforts are first-rate.

With just six suites, of course, this isn’t exactly a full-scale grand hotel. For services like restaurants and bars you’ll have to look elsewhere. Fortunately, the immediate surroundings in Oltrarno are amply supplied with options, as well as picturesque churches, markets, and artisans’ workshops — and, just across the river, the practically endless attractions of central Florence await.

content: Most visitors come to Puymirol for its famous restaurant, Michel Trama, a fine dining landmark in the old walled village since 1979. But the hotel attached to the one-MICHELIN-Star establishment is just as impressive. Both are located in a 13th-century mansion that once belonged to the Count of Toulouse, and great care was taken to preserve many of its most charming features, from ancient terracotta tiles and rustic wooden beams to grand fireplaces and a spectacular staircase carved from oak. Architect and designer Jacques Garcia, known for his lavish interiors at hotels around Paris, brought his bold vision to the project, outfitting the historic country house with richly patterned rugs, antique furniture, sumptuous drapery, and heavy chandeliers. \n\nGarcia’s taste for the Baroque is just as evident in rooms and suites. Some are cozy and romantic, with exposed beams and framed oil paintings, while others are opulent with silk taffeta canopies, velvet loveseats, gilded mirrors, and clawfoot tubs. Suites have separate living rooms, and a few have terraces. One opens directly onto a gorgeous courtyard terrace with an outdoor pool framed by chaise longues,  illuminated after dark by the glow of decorative lanterns. Cooking classes are available with the restaurant’s chef, and the hiking trails and wineries just outside the village are easy excursions before returning for dinner.

content:
As Swiss villages go, Pontresina may not have quite the name recognition of St. Moritz, just across the valley. But it’s got one thing St. Moritz hasn’t: Hotel Schloss Pontresina. It’s a 19th-century castle, which means that in many ways it’s the best of both worlds: it’s a proper castle, with all of the capital-R Romantic atmosphere that implies, but in terms of comfort it’s every bit a modern luxury hotel rather than some drafty medieval relic.

The rooms and suites were thoroughly renovated in 2016, and they’re quintessential Alpine-contemporary luxury, with their knotty cabinetry and accents in red fabric. The best views are of the Bernina glacier, and all rooms are bathed in light from the oversized windows. Ordinary Comfort and Superior rooms are spacious enough, while the suites are downright extravagant, and while the Family Suites come with toys to keep little ones occupied, the whole hotel prides itself on its family-friendliness.

And while it’s perhaps at its best in winter, with the slopes of St. Moritz just five kilometers away, it’s a fine summer escape as well, with access to some extraordinary hiking and mountain biking. The spa is all-season as well, and the restaurant, in classic Alpine style, is more than up to the task of keeping you fueled for your adventures.

The advent of apartment-sharing apps has changed the hotel game a bit, as guests are reminded that they love living like locals — and that they love the services only a hotel can provide. It’s also brought new life to the extended-stay market; the best extended-stay apartments, like AKA Beverly Hills, combine the privacy and local flavor of an apartment rental with the luxury and style of a high-end boutique hotel.

With 88 units, it’s a sizable operation, which means it’s easier to find availability than hoping that one apartment you like is free. And its location, just off Wilshire Boulevard — so close to Spago as to have dedicated access through the lobby — means you’re right in the thick of Beverly Hills. But what’s quite possibly the most remarkable thing about AKA Beverly Hills is the apartments themselves; from one-bedroom suites to two-bedroom townhouses to the Penthouse Residences, they’re uniformly sleek, modern, and hyper-luxe.

We’re talking full kitchens with granite countertops and stainless-steel appliances, Bulgari bath products, in-suite washers and dryers, the works. Plus room service from Spago, if you don’t feel like cooking, and help with reservations if you’re going out. And residential privacy doesn’t have to mean isolation — AKA Beverly Hills has its own social life as well, headquartered on a landscaped terrace complete with fire pits and views of the distant Hollywood Hills.

content: It would be foolish for the Watergate Hotel to run away from its reputation — it was, after all, the site of what’s still the biggest scandal in American politics since Teapot Dome. So this venerable D.C. institution, fresh off nine years of closure followed by a massive renovation, is sailing straight into the wind, positioning itself as the ideal venue for hosting a (hopefully not career-ending) scandal of your own. In a town whose high-end hotels are conservative almost to a fault, the Watergate is refreshing for the fact that it’s not just luxurious, but visually decadent as well. Designer Ron Arad is responsible for the interiors, combining retro modernism with cutting-edge curves to complement architect Luigi Moretti’s vintage plan, and all the hotel’s staff, from the doormen to the housekeepers, were costumed by Mad Men designer Janie Bryant. The rooms are luxe, in a monochrome palette, a welcome departure from the college-club colors favored by other Washington hotels. If you’re lucky your balcony will face the Potomac River — and if you’re not just lucky but a bit ruthless as well, you’ll probably be in a Diplomat or Presidential suite, with acres of indoor space and, in the latter case, not one but two commanding upper-floor balconies. Kingbird is the fine-dining restaurant, Top of the Gate the rooftop bar with the 360-degree panoramic view, and the Next Whisky Bar is the place to enjoy a dram or two with your co-conspirators. Just don’t take any unnecessary risks — as your room key reminds you, at the new Watergate there’s “no need to break in.”

content: The Japanese artist and hotelier Shouya Grigg is a collector — not only of art, but of architecture. For his latest project, Shiguchi, he relocated a series of kominka, or traditional wooden farmhouses, to a quiet valley outside the ski resort of Niseko. Their A-frame structures have remained more or less the same, carefully taken apart and reassembled using an old Japanese technique wherein the hand-carved timber beams are fit together without the use of nails. But inside, they’re modern and minimalist, with private onsen baths, curated libraries, and terraces overlooking the surrounding landscape. Each is named for a natural element — chi (earth), sui (water), ka (fire), fu (wind), and ku (void or spirit) — and all showcase pieces from Grigg’s personal art collection. An elegant wood-lined spa offers hot spring-fed baths, and seasonally inspired dishes and Hokkaido wines are served with mountain views in the restaurant.

content:
If your first impression is that something looks a little bit different about Yoo2 Rio de Janeiro, rest assured, your eyes do not deceive you. This is the first hotel by the London-based Yoo Design Studio, and while it would be a big stretch to call it quintessentially English, there’s a bold, vibrant graphic sensibility — murals, street art, colorful prints — that sets it apart from the earth-toned seriousness you’ll find in many of Rio’s other high-end boutique hotels.

All the same, there’s no mistaking the fact that this is Brazil, especially in the bedrooms, where palm-tree skyscapes adorn the ceilings. There’s plentiful sunshine through wall-wide windows, and, if you’re on the right side of the hotel, views of Sugar Loaf and/or Corcovado Mountain. Themed rooms and suites add space as well as some extra design flair, as well as some of the most direct views.

Meanwhile Cariocally Restaurant makes good on its slightly unwieldy portmanteau, serving the classic cuisine of Rio de Janeiro, made from local produce and locally caught seafood, all under the direction of the highly regarded chef, Marcelo Schambeck. His seafood-based tapas dishes also accompany the cocktails at the rooftop bar, which, perhaps unsurprisingly, features the most inspiring views in the house.

content:
Please note: Rixos Flüela Davos is a seasonal hotel and is closed from mid-April through November.

Davos, one of Switzerland’s classic ski destinations, among the most elevated towns in Europe, is no stranger to the hospitality business — nor, for that matter, to the conference business. There’s room here for all sorts, including the Turkish-based Rixos group, for whom the Flüela Davos is a rare venture west of the Bosphorus. And it turns out that the Davos hospitality scene benefits from a subtle infusion of foreign flavor.

You’re here to ski, presumably, as slope access to Pischa, Rinerhorn, or Jakobshorn is almost trivially easy, all three being within walking distance. Just as important: you’re here for a familiar, traditional vision of luxury hospitality. The fireplace’s light flickers off button-studded, plush chairs, mingling with light from the chandeliers and warming your surroundings. Polished wood and elegantly fluted glasses meet the touch, while a discreetly professional staff hovers just within reach to meet any sudden needs.

Though the 49 rooms and suites partake of their fair share of parquet flooring and formal wall sconces, they also make concessions to modern technology. Credit the designers for smoothly balancing what might have been a jarring transition from gilded molding, brocaded headboards, and damask to the sterile, minimalist lines we’ve come to expect from our devices. And after balancing yourself out on the slopes, you’ll be grateful to come home to a fully equipped spa — indoor pool, jacuzzi, saunas, and massage treatments — as well as two fine-dining restaurants and a matched pair of bars, one in the lobby and the other in the mezzanine. Bottoms up.

content:
Sleeping in a modern mixed-use skyscraper might not be what you had in mind when you first thought of a trip to a tropical destination like Panama. The concept does sound a little cold, especially since the Global Hotel Panama is one of those hotels that doesn’t occupy the whole building, just the ground level and six upper floors. But hear us out. This is one of the most popular hotels in Panama City. Not because it’s terribly cozy, or for the style, which is pleasant enough. It’s in other categories that the Global Hotel Panama really delivers: excellent service, solid amenities, and location, location, location.

That location, in the Twist Tower in the downtown district of Obarrio, puts you within walking distance, or a short taxi ride, of pretty much anywhere you’d like to go in town. Convenient, indeed, especially since many travelers experience Panama City as a point of connection to somewhere else. You won’t be sorry you booked here when you arrive, overheated and exhausted, and the front desk staff offer you a flute of champagne or chilled mineral water. Things look even better when you get inside your room. The building itself is brand-new, and it looks and feels like it. Rooms and suites are spotless and state-of-the-art, smartly stocked with 40-inch LCD TVs, iPhone docking stations, Italian coffee machines, and bathrooms with walk-in showers. Floor-to-ceiling windows mean a flood of sunshine, and striking views over Panama City’s rapidly developing skyline. Suites have king-sized beds with pillow menus and marble baths with products by Salvatore Ferragamo.

Up on the twelfth floor, there’s a small outdoor swimming pool. Adjacent are the pool bar and the obligatory fitness center: choose your own adventure according to your mood and level of jet lag. You’ll find another bar on the ground level at the brasserie-style 54 East restaurant. If you’re in town for a longer than a night or two, you might take a quick course (and tasting) in Panamanian rum. But even if you’re only passing through before an early flight, you’ll want to plan ahead — you wouldn’t guess it from the outside, but the Global Hotel Panama has just sixty rooms, and they go fast.

content:
A modest little gem hiding practically in plain sight, Hôtel Square Louvois stands just across the eponymous square from the National Library, a few minutes’ walk in either direction from the Palais Garnier and the Louvre. It’s modest when compared to Paris’s grand hotels and its most exuberant boutiques, but it’s a reminder that great taste is just as valuable as a grand gesture.

Rich, sober colors dominate the interiors of this Art Deco classic, and lend a warmth and intimacy to its public spaces. The rooms carry on in the same vein, which are brought to life with accents in houndstooth textiles and oversized black-and-white photography. Even the single rooms are comfortable, with all the modern must-haves, from Bluetooth sound systems to L’Occitane bath products, and the Family suites and the split-level Saint-Anne suite edge into truly luxurious territory.

There’s a wellness area in the cellar, including a pool beneath a picturesque stone vault. A thoughtful breakfast is the extent of the kitchen’s duties, supplemented by an afternoon tea service; the location is just about as central as a Parisian hotel can get, and the number of restaurants and cafés within walking distance is practically incalculable.

content:
The town of San Ignacio is one of the capitals of rainforest tourism in Belize, and the surrounding area is home to a couple of great eco-lodges. Among the in-town options, however, there’s nothing quite like the San Ignacio Resort Hotel. First of all, the setting: though central, it’s a 17-acre riverside estate, a bona fide parcel of jungle within the city limits, with its own on-site iguana conservation project — surely not something most hotels can say.

It’s also family-owned and operated, and has been since 1976. And while that’s not always a guarantee of a superior experience, your hosts’ commitment is evident — they’ve kept the place very much up to date. The rooms range from cozy and comfortable to spacious and subtly stylish, and the better ones have views of the jungle canopy or the Macal River.

The Running W Steakhouse & Restaurant features meats from the family ranch, and the Lobby Bar is something of a local hotspot, with live music on some weekend nights. From here you’d be remiss if you didn’t explore the Belizean rainforest — while the estate and its iguana habitat are impressive, you’ll want to venture further afield as well, and the hotel is happy to arrange tours and excursions.

Headboards bear inspirational quotes against abstract pastel backgrounds; the bar is full of rock-star portraits and memorabilia, and Tag’s Café presents a kitsch version of downtown Manhattan counterculture. And underneath it all, it’s as practical and as professional as any Swiss business hotel. It might not suit everyone’s taste, but you certainly can’t accuse it of blending in.

content: If you’ve been to San Francisco at any time in the last 90 or so years you’ve noticed the Sir Francis Drake Hotel — or at least you’ve noticed its doormen, dressed in their distinctive red Beefeater uniforms, presiding over Powell Street just above Union Square. It’d be just about worth listing on Tablet solely for the Starlight Room, the penthouse bar with the 180° views of the skyline. But when you find out that Kimpton, purveyors of friendly boutique charm all across America, are also behind the Sir Francis Drake, you begin to suspect there’s much more than novelty value at play here.\n\nYou’re right, of course. (You’ve got a discerning eye for this sort of thing, if you don’t mind our saying so.) Behind the nostalgia of the doormen and the well-preserved public spaces, this is a high-functioning and not at all unstylish hotel — more classic luxury, less boutique funkiness, perhaps, than the Kimpton norm, as befits its grand dame status. The style is a mélange of Art Deco and Victorian, with noticeable modern and contemporary accents, and while the spaces aren’t over-large they’re much more than comfortable enough. The Starlight Room is enough to keep you in-house, as is Scala’s Bistro, a local Italian favorite, and Bar Drake, a classic (and less vertiginous) cocktail bar. And this being more or less the heart of San Francisco, you’re surrounded by the city’s greatest density of bars and restaurants, to say nothing of shops — though the Powell Street cable car passes right by the front door, you might well get through an entire stay here without venturing outside of walking distance.
