Please note: We are not taking reservations for this hotel at the current time.

Okay, the actual White House hasn’t been converted into luxurious extended-stay apartments. Yet. But in the meantime, two blocks away, AKA White House is just about as close as you can get to living in America’s most famous residence without winning an election. It’s not your ordinary hotel — generous square footage, full kitchens, and in-suite laundry see to that — but at the same time it’s much more than a one-off apartment share.

The one- and two-bedroom suites come with high-end comforts like plush king beds and Bulgari bath products, and the Platinum and Penthouse suites are bigger, grander, and (naturally) higher up. The look is sedate, as suits both an all-business town like D.C. and a long-stay apartment where too much extravagance can begin to grate. And while the residential atmosphere means you can be as private and self-sufficient as you like, AKA’s Resident Services Team is on hand to perform all the functions of a proper hotel concierge.

There’s a bit of in-house social life as well, courtesy of a.lounge, a capacious open-plan space that functions as a bar, lounge, workspace and informal meeting space. And located as you are in the heart of D.C., you’ve got easy access to no end of restaurants, bars, and cultural attractions.

content:
As with many cultural signifiers, “airport hotel” doesn’t mean quite the same thing in New Delhi as it does elsewhere. Rightly so: business travelers are pragmatic folks, by and large, and many come here with a full day’s transit behind them already. In any case, they’re the perfect guest — frequent, short-term stays develop nothing so much as a finely calibrated gauge for difference-making details. In this context we welcome the Roseate New Delhi to the thriving hospitality community encircling Indira Gandhi International Airport. 

The 50 rooms spread out, their full-length windows and domed ceilings working in tandem to open the interiors to the sky. The bathrooms, in marble, are no less luxurious — a rain shower does wonders to restore one’s equilibrium. The staff, subdued but hyper-competent, offers private, 24-hour service to fulfill any needs that might arise.

But why take meals in your room with two restaurants available? Kiran, regally refined in Isfahan columns, plates pan-Eurasian cuisine with an admirable focus on free-range and organic ingredients. Or try the Chinese specialties at Chi Ni (“to eat”), availing yourself of the al fresco dining option in season. Finish — or start, we’re not prudes — at Iah, the crimson, curvilinear bar space with signature cocktails, a cigar menu, and live piano to set the mood.

This being a Roseate production, a few trademarks round out the picture: a sumptuous spa with natural products, an outdoor pool, a retail outlet with accessories in traditional textiles. Reception outdoes itself to arrange for a moonlit dinner or a Bollywood-themed escapade at your request. But for the element most unlike an airplane or a board room, plant yourself in the immaculately landscaped gardens and breathe in the welcome, uncrowded silence.

content: The United States doesn’t control the whole travel business, of course, but now that the region’s great power has finally begun to come to its senses regarding the Cuban embargo, the world’s hoteliers are starting to dip their toes in this controversial corner of the Caribbean. The first full-on luxury hotel to arrive on these shores happens to be a representative of the Swiss-based Kempinski group, and the Gran Hotel Manzana Kempinski La Habana assumes a privileged position in the heart of Havana’s old city, surrounded by luxury brands that make it crystal-clear just how enormously this city is about to change.\n\nFor now, though, imagine a European luxury hotel incongruously transplanted to an emerging Caribbean city and you’ve more or less got the right idea. Its 200-plus rooms and suites are elegant and contemporary, and come with wi-fi, still a novelty here. There’s a high-end spa that feels more like Geneva than Havana, and the Manzana’s multiple restaurants and bars are a distinct upgrade over the local competitors. If you’re looking for the lost-in-time feeling, there are plenty of hotels in Cuba that are true to their original history — but if contemporary luxury is your preference, at the moment there’s only one game in town.

content:
For serious skiers, the Austrian resort village of Lech am Arlberg needs no introduction. For the rest of us — those of us who might confuse St. Anton with St. Moritz, those who wouldn’t attempt a black diamond run, let alone venture off-piste — a bit of artful name-dropping should do the trick. Lech was the preferred ski destination of Diana, Princess of Wales, as well as the former Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands. Non-royals (hallo, Tom Cruise) like it too, but you get the picture. It’s an exclusive resort, and the impossibly picturesque village is old as the hills, no pun intended: it was founded by the Swiss in the 14th century.

Needless to say, there are a few grand hotels in the Arlberg area, and more than a few luxurious chalets available for private rental. Kristiania Lech, a small hotel located at the foot of the mountains, in a relatively secluded spot just outside of town, aims to bring together the best of both. With 29 individually decorated guest rooms, it feels more like a private residence than a cookie-cutter hotel. True, some of the thematic decor, ranging from antique Chinese to French boudoir, might seem a little over-the-top for a ski trip. But that’s for you to decide, according to the helpful staff at Kristiania Lech, which is why the hotel also offers rooms and suites decorated in a classic Alpine style, plus dedicated butlers to curate your indoor and outdoor experiences. (A bath butler? Yes, please.) Standard in-room features include original artwork, flat-screen TVs, complimentary minibars, and yoga mats.

Kristiania Lech has a good spa, plus several restaurants and bars — certainly an advantage of staying in a hotel versus a private chalet, especially during a snowstorm. Otto Wagner is the most formal dining venue; there’s also a French bistro and a traditional Austrian eatery with an open fireplace, a cozy place for après-ski fondue. When it’s not freezing out, you can have lunch or coffee on the hotel’s sunny terrace. When it is, there’s an elegant lobby lounge, complete with a Steinway piano, afternoon tea service, and a martini menu.

The ski lifts, carrying you up to some of the finest runs in the world, plus magical views over the snow-covered village, are a short stroll away. The ten-minute walk isn’t much, but it can feel like it if you’re lugging ski equipment — luckily, the hotel also offers shuttle service from the front door. You’ll want to make it back to Kristiania Lech for a nightcap, at the very least: there happen to be seven thousand bottles of wine stored in the rock below the hotel, enough to impress movie stars, maybe even a royal or two.

Please note: Kristiania Lech is a seasonal hotel, and is open from December 3 through April 19.

How to get there: Kristiania Lech is located two and a half hours by train from Zürich via Langen am Arlberg, or just over two hours by car (weather permitting).

Though less lavish than some of China’s new luxury boutique hotels, it’s more than comfortable enough, and its surplus of character is the stuff lifelong memories are made of.

content:
Do not adjust your browser: despite its thoroughly French name, La Ferme de Georges is indeed located in Brazil, in the fishing village of Atins ,on the edge of the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, whose otherworldly landscape of sand dunes dotted with small lagoons is just about as far as you can get from the verdant hills of rural France. La Ferme de Georges itself, however, is an oasis, a series of little lodges surrounded by greenery and palm trees.

They’re modern in plan, yet rustic in finish, with thatched roofs and rich dark wood, and with hand-crafted furnishings alongside contemporary design pieces. The best views come from the three-bedroom Tree Lodge, which is elevated above the surrounding foliage for a 360-degree panorama, but in all honesty there’s not a bad room in the house, and all are splendidly private yet wide open to their natural surroundings.

There’s plentiful outdoor lounge space as well, some of it attached to your lodge and some of it at the central Forum, an open-air lounge with hammocks, wi-fi, and reading material. A lovely outdoor restaurant serves produce from the hotel’s organic gardens alongside other locally sourced ingredients. And the list of activities, thanks to the setting, is a long one, from kite surfing and stand-up paddling to birdwatching, multi-day treks, and much more.

content:
If there’s a unifying thread to all the Japanese hotels in Tablet’s selection, it has to be quality. Rarely, in this country, can a hotel — or anything else — get by on salesmanship alone. Craft is held in high regard here, and the result is a specific kind of boon for travelers: here, you occasionally find a hotel that’s quite simply much, much better than it needs to be. Which brings us around to the Junei Hotel Kyoto Imperial Palace West.

As may be evident from the name, it’s located just to the west of Kyoto’s impressive Imperial Palace; it’s about the same distance to the north of the picturesque Nijo Castle. The hotel’s own imposing façade hints at fortifications as well, and suggests something rather grand inside — it’s a surprise, then, to find that the Junei contains a mere eight rooms.

Those eight rooms, again, are more impressive than they need to be. They’re quite large, for one thing, and come most of the trappings of the high-end ryokan experience, from Shigaraki ceramic soaking tubs with hydrogen-enriched water to guest pajamas and Kiyomizu-style tea sets. Lavish Shidashi bento-style meals and impressive tea, sake and sweets round out the package — in some ways a stay at Junei feels like a stay at the Imperial Palace itself.

content: The Texas Hill Country, outside of Austin, is increasingly home to stylish, boutique-influenced hotels and resorts; Lucky Arrow Retreat is among the most decidedly rural of them, set on 15 acres of land a few miles outside the town of Dripping Springs. Accommodations include 10 sizeable (and comfortable) yurts, 20 modern-rustic cabins, and a handful of freestanding Porch Houses, each with a wraparound porch as well as sleeper sofas and kitchenettes — plus the Ranch House, a full-size, self-contained four-bedroom residence. Among the diversions are the bath house and pool, as well as a multitude of local adventures, and the surrounding area is home to plenty of restaurants, breweries, and wineries.

content:
Architects love China. Here the big cities are growing so fast, they’re like an R&D lab for innovations in architecture. Over here even the most traditional hotel chains have embraced a certain modernity of design, an emphasis on the aesthetic that might not go down so easily in another locale. All of this is by way of an explanation for how, for instance, a Radisson in Shanghai ends up looking as striking as the Radisson Hotel Pudong Century Park.

Given its location in Pudong, it finds itself in an environment with plenty of architectural stimulation. Once you’re inside it seems only fitting that there should be, for example, a massive sculpture of a thumb in its dramatic and colorful lobby lounge. And by the time you step off the elevator, the cloud-like white-on-white color scheme of the guest rooms seems like the most natural thing in the world.

In spite of its slightly unorthodox visual style, the Radisson at Century Park is essentially a classic luxury hotel. The rooms may be a hair less plush than some of the competition, but there’s a substantial audience which prefers this sort of energetic atmosphere to the typical overly lavish luxury style. And when it comes to the nuts and bolts, nothing’s missing — the four restaurants include an upscale classic Chinese option, the fitness center includes not just a pool but a tennis court as well, and the meeting facilities are state-of-the-art. Maybe this is just the new Shanghai standard — but if that’s the case, a lot of cities wish they could have Shanghai’s standards.

How to get there
Radisson Hotel Pudong Century Park is 30 minutes away from Pudong International Airport and 15 minutes from Maglev Station.

content: When the typically Alpine respect for health and wellness meets the Italian appetite for the good life, you can generally assume you’re in for something of a treat. This is no less true in Folgaria, a town in Trentino, home of the Dolomites — and home of Blu Hotel Natura & Spa. In winter it’s perfectly placed a quick shuttle ride from the ski lifts, in summer it’s surrounded by the hiking, biking and climbing majesty of the Alps, and in its interiors it’s devoted to the kind of refreshing, restoring relaxation for which this region of Europe has become so well known.\n\nThe architectural idiom of the Blu Hotel Natura is unquestionably the classic Alpine lodge, but this is a thorougly contemporary interpretation. Knotty blonde wood is present only in occasional accents, and the décor is light and minimalistic, with spare modern furnishings and pleasantly uncluttered layouts. There’s a wellness center, equipped with infrared and Finnish saunas, a Turkish bath, and an indoor and outdoor pool, and massages and spa treatments are available as well. Breakfast and dinner are generous affairs, in keeping with the region’s reputation for hearty fare; whatever you’re up to during the day, you can be sure you’ll be properly restored.

content: Sun Valley in Idaho is one of America’s great ski destinations, and while the postwar ski boom inspired some forgettably utilitarian architecture, there are some boutique hotels out there proving the point that contemporary design and ski-town coziness don’t have to be mutually exclusive. Hotel Ketchum, on Main Street in downtown Ketchum, is a prime example — a thorough renovation has left its interiors looking bright, sunny, and contemporary, combining modern furniture and a stylish graphic sensibility with classic rustic textures and materials of the traditional mountain lodge.\n\nIt’s clear that it’s meant to appeal to a younger audience than the average mountain lodge, and to that end it’s got a full complement of boutique-hotel services and amenities, from rooms wired with USB charging ports and 50-inch televisions to C.O. Bigelow bath products, high-end beds and linens, and a lobby lounge, re-styled as “the Hangout,” a combination breakfast room, lounge, game room, and café. There’s an outdoor pool and hot tub, as well as an on-site ski and bike shop, and a coin-op laundry for guests — an important consideration for mountain adventurers. A restaurant, a bar, and a café should be open by ski season; until then you’ll have to fuel your summer expeditions with the plentiful offerings of downtown Ketchum.

There’s more to Washington, D.C. than the grand scale and Neoclassical architecture of its official buildings. Just to the northwest of the city center is Georgetown, Washington’s oldest district, home to some exclusive residential neighborhoods, some upscale shopping and dining, and Georgetown University. It’s a warmer, more welcoming side of the nation’s capital, and the same goes for The Avery Georgetown, a warm and welcoming luxury boutique hotel — it’s smaller and more personable than the capital’s five-star business chains, and its style is a refreshing mix of the neighborhood’s historical influences and clean, contemporary boutique-hotel design.

It’s made from a pair of Federal-style buildings, whose restored exteriors blend seamlessly into the neighborhood but whose interiors are spare, bright, and stylish. Fifteen rooms means the staff is on speaking terms with every guest in the house, and while there’s nothing quite on the level of a presidential suite, you might be occasionally surprised at the loftiness of the crowd. There’s a breakfast spread that includes pastries, fruit, coffee, and tea, and a nightly reception featuring craft beers and local wines. Beyond that, you’re at the mercy of the neighborhood — thankfully Georgetown suffers no shortage of dining and drinking venues, to say nothing of shops, cafés, and picturesque sights.

content: Hua Hin, on Thailand’s gulf coast, flew under the radar for a while, as the tourism industry was focused on the islands. As a result, it’s less developed than Phuket or Koh Samui, though it’s hardly any less spectacular. This means there’s space for some truly impressive seaside hotels — among them Ananda Hua Hin, a brand-new beachfront resort whose 196 rooms, suites, and villas stand in perfect rows astride a central courtyard, lined with loungers, gardens, and pools.\n\nThe villas get front-row sea views, as well as private pools of their own, and a sort of club-level access to the Villa Lounge — as well as all the extra space and comfort that follows from having a villa all to yourself. But the rooms and suites are by no means meager; the humblest rooms still span some 33 square meters, packed with all the modern luxury-hotel comforts, and the suites double that space and add living rooms, private patios, or terraces with whirlpool tubs. To all that Ananda adds a full-service spa, no fewer than five dining and drinking venues, and a separate kids’ club and kids’ pool. Take note: for better or worse, depending on your circumstances, Ananda Hua Hin is extremely kid-friendly.

content: A glance at the exterior of the Steigenberger Frankfurter Hof tells you most of what you need to know about what it means to the city. This hotel, coming up on 150 years old, is as grand as ever, and standing as it does at the gateway to Frankfurt’s financial district it continues to play host to a substantial share of the city’s luxury customers. But anyone expecting a period piece — that is, a meticulously preserved 1876-style grand hotel to match the opulent, old-fashioned exterior — is in for a little bit of a surprise.\n\nA subtle surprise, but a surprise all the same. The Steigenberger, underneath it all, is quite up to date, a contemporary luxury hotel that pays homage to its roots with antique furniture and ornately patterned wallpaper, but is, on the whole, a modern interpretation of the original era rather than a precise reconstruction. And alongside the expected high-end in-room amenities — Nespresso machines, marble baths, the works — you’ll find the full complement of luxury-hotel services, from a well-equipped spa and wellness center to the Michelin-starred (and self-explanatory) Restaurant Français, along with a small handful of other restaurants and bars.

content:
It may not be up there with Bordeaux or Tuscany in the popular imagination, but Cyprus has a long history of wine production. Situated near the northern village of Ilgaz and surrounded by majestic mountains, Gillham Vineyard Hotel makes a strong case. It’s set on the Etel wine estate, which occupies ten acres and grows eight varieties of grapes — it almost goes without saying that vineyard tours and tastings play a significant role in the hotel’s offerings.

Of course, so do the hotel’s 31 suites. Options range from the massive Presidential Sparkling Suite to the smaller (but no less luxurious) Business Room suites. All of them offer some view of the Mediterranean Sea, the vineyard, or the surrounding Kyrenia Mountains, or some combination of the three. Suites are breezy and elegant in design, with many featuring crisp white walls and linens with dramatic pitched ceilings that show off beautiful exposed wood beams.

There’s also a lovely outdoor pool, as well as a small spa with its own indoor pool. The Chef Restaurant serves upscale Israeli-accented Mediterranean fare, and the elaborate Tapas-Wine Bar features far-ranging views of the vineyards as well as occasional live music.

content:
For reasons that we presume are obvious enough, the boutique-hotel revolution hasn’t hit Cuba just yet; quite understandably, Havana isn’t exactly a hotbed of cutting-edge modern design. Here the hotels come in various shades of nostalgic history — and there may be none quite so dedicated to the city’s 19th-century Spanish Colonial heritage as the Hotel Florida, just off the Plaza de Armas in the heart of Havana’s old quarter.

It’s nothing if not grand, its lobby lit by sunlight from the atrium above, and surrounded by the columns and arches of a traditional colonial-style arcade. Public facilities include two bars, one of them a lively piano bar with regular live performances, as well as the Floridana restaurant, an elegant, old-world dining room serving Cuban and international fare.

And for all that, the Hotel Florida has just twenty-five rooms — standard rooms and junior suites alike have traditional beamed ceilings, marble floors, bathrooms in distinctive green Cuban marble, and antique furniture and artworks. Many open onto balconies via French doors. All travel in Cuba is, to some extent, a trip back in time. It’s just that the Hotel Florida takes you farther back than most.

content: A ninety-minute drive southeast of Porto, deep in a pocket of the countryside little visited by tourists, the village of Santar is home to about a thousand residents — and a gorgeous Relais & Châteaux hotel that’s very much worth the detour. Formerly a royal residence, Valverde Santar Hotel & Spa is grand and historic, surrounded by picturesque gardens and centuries-old vineyards. A regal air remains in the hotel’s formal sitting rooms with their gilded chandeliers, original oil paintings, antique loveseats, and original hand-carved woodwork. But rooms and suites are smartly updated, both modern and quaint. The old winery was transformed into a state-of-the-art spa with a spacious indoor pool and a Turkish bath, and the mansion’s original library now serves as an atmospheric breakfast room.

The minimalist look mixes traditional Japanese and modern Scandinavian elements — tatami mats, blonde wood platform beds, dark-tiled bathrooms with soaking tubs overlooking the ocean or the bay. Some have private terraces and saunas, and all have access to the hotel’s tranquil spa, with fragranced outdoor baths and a wood-burning sauna.

content: The rugged peaks of China’s inland Yunnan province are the backdrop for the Sunyata Hotel Meili, a luxury boutique hotel built from an existing Tibetan residence in the city of Shangri-La, some 11,000 feet above sea level. It’s something of a patchwork, by design, inspired by the Japanese idea of wabi-sabi, embracing the beauty of imperfection in finishes and surfaces, even as the hotel as a whole exhibits a remarkable unity of function and form. This rough-hewn aesthetic makes the rooms, as luxurious as they are, feel humble and approachable; few of us are passing through this part of Yunnan on the way somewhere else, but hotel lovers may find the Sunyata is worth the trip on its own.

content: Just across the street from the Dartmouth Green and the rest of the college campus is Hanover Inn Dartmouth, a contemporary boutique hotel set in a historic red-brick Federal-style building that dates back to 1815. It’s here that the lively little town center meets Dartmouth College, and the list of eminent academics who’ve graced its halls is a mile long. Expect rooms that bridge the gap between the 19th-century architecture and the expectations of contemporary travelers; the restaurant, PINE, is a highlight, serving seasonal farm-to-table fare for a deeply authentic taste of New England.

Think of the Aegean and chances are you think of Greece, but that famous blue is no less stunning from the Turkish side. Alaçatı, on the Çeşme Peninsula, is a well-known seaside resort, a picturesque town set on a gently curving beach. It’s something of a magnet for windsurfers, as is the waterway on the opposite side of town that leads to Port Alaçatı. It’s here, five minutes outside of town, on a wilder stretch of coast facing a protected nature reserve, that you’ll find Biblos Beach Resort Alaçatı.

Frankly it’s a better stretch of beach, both for lounging and for windsurfing. And it’s a fantastic place for a boutique hotel. Biblos’s buildings may be made of traditional stone, but they’re modern through and through, the rooms and suites a model of understated contemporary luxury. Even the Panorama Suite, as extravagant as it is, is a model of visual restraint, with its neutral tones and industrial metallics.

The Alatia Spa, on the other hand, is as lavish as can be, with a list of facilities and treatments as long as your arm. And no fewer than three restaurants are on hand, serving everything from poolside bites to al fresco Mediterranean seafood to upscale French brasserie fare in Le Jour, a spectacular space with an expansive outdoor terrace.

content: Sri Lankan hotels are among our favorites, from the modernist beach cottages to the tea plantations of the interior. Maniumpathy, however, is something a little bit different — and a classic, at the same time. This stately home, right in the heart of one of Colombo’s most desirable neighborhoods, has belonged for five generations to a family from Jaffna, in the island’s north, and its eight suites are named for the women of the family, from Vasanthi and Anithra to Annapuranie, the 19th-century matriarch whose name graces the ground-floor master suite.\n\nIt’s the archetypal colonial-style grand residence, its interiors, though renovated, hewing closely to the original look, and furnished with vintage-style and genuine antique pieces. There’s nary a whiff of “tropical modernism” about it — this is pure traditional opulence, and while the comforts may have been updated over the course of the past century, the atmosphere remains essentially unchanged. It’s the same genteel calm you’ll enjoy in the garden and its small but lovely pool; and it’s the same genteel service you’ll enjoy throughout the hotel, where staffers typically outnumber guests, and especially at the dinner table, which specializes in Sri Lankan cooking of the Jaffna variety.

content:
Safe to say if it’s your first time in Cuba you might not be expecting something like Hotel Raquel. Built in the early 20th century in an Art Deco style that was, at the time, the height of modernity, it served as a fabric storehouse and an office building for decades, until it was closed in the 1990s in preparation for conversion into a hotel. Finally, in 2003, the newly restored Hotel Raquel made its debut, and it remains unique among Havana’s hotels for its close connection with the city’s Jewish history.

This is the old Jewish quarter, after all, which goes some way towards explaining why Hotel Raquel’s twenty-five rooms and suites all take the names of Old Testament figures, and why the restaurant, Jardín del Eden, serves classic Jewish cuisine in a country where that’s not exactly the norm, to say the least.

As for the nuts and bolts of the place, it’s a bit early to expect a proper modern luxury hotel in Havana. What you’ll find is elegant décor, plenty of details that reward the observant eye, and an atmosphere that you won’t soon forget — which is, after all, almost certainly what drew you to Cuba in the first place.

content: Oregon’s wine country is small but beautiful, and you could say the same for the Setting Inn Willamette Valley, an eight-room hotel whose stylish, contemporary interiors belie its rural setting. Platform beds, hardwood floors, and modernist-inspired furnishings set a sophisticated tone, as do details like Nespresso machines and Lather bath products. Outside, it’s pure agricultural splendor in every direction, with impressive views from the bocce court and croquet lawn — start the day with a European-style breakfast, served en suite, before venturing out for a tasting or a  winery tour or a visit to the coast.

content:
Built in the late 19th century, and then entirely rebuilt in 1911, Havana’s Hotel Telégrafo was, in its heyday a century ago, something of a legend — not just one of the top hotels in Cuba, but in all of Latin America. And now that tourism in Cuba is once again on the rise, the Telégrafo is once again setting its sights on a global audience.

They’ll love the layers of history that are on display here, from the Colonial-style brick archways of the original structure, still visible in the hotel’s inner courtyard, to the contemporary furniture and modern artworks in the surprisingly up-to-date guest rooms. With just 63 rooms and suites, it’s a modestly sized hotel, and as the room categories top out at the junior suites, it’s a fairly egalitarian one as well.

Meanwhile the Restaurant Telégrafo, situated just off that lovely inner patio, features terrace seating under the old arcade, and serves Cuban and international fare to hotel guests and Havana locals alike. There are bigger, more extravagant hotels in the capital, if that’s the sort of thing you’re after, but for a hotel that’s more charming than bombastic it would be hard to go wrong here.

content: The Hotel Nacional de Cuba has been one of Havana’s great symbols for nearly a century, and it’s had a more colorful history than most luxury hotels. Founded just before the 1933 coup, it went through something of a golden age in the Forties and Fifties — you may remember it from the second of the Godfather films. After the Revolution it went generally the way of Cuban tourism in general — which accounts for the preserved-in-amber feeling of the Nacional today. And with tourism once again on the rise, it’s possible for a whole new generation to tread the same corridors where Churchill, Hemingway, Sinatra, even Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir once walked. \n \nThere’s no mistaking the grand scale of the place, and if the fixtures and fittings aren’t exactly up to international five-star standard, it would be churlish to be surprised. Neither the boutique-hotel style revolution nor the dramatic surge in ultra-luxe hospitality have made their way to these shores yet. It’s tempting to imagine what might become of the Nacional in years to follow, but for now the key to its appeal is the feeling of watching history pass by right before your eyes.

content: Lyons-la-Forêt is designated as one of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, or the Most Beautiful Villages of France, so it’s no surprise that its oldest hotel is a picturesque landmark. Hôtel La Licorne & Spa dates back to 1610, and its timber-framed façade is quintessentially Norman in style. A cobblestoned path leads through the high-arched entryway to lush rear gardens, with umbrella-shaded café tables and a restored farmhouse that frames the quiet indoor-outdoor pool. \n\nRooms are compact, modern, and elegant, outfitted in sophisticated neutrals and framed black and white photography. Some have sleek four-poster beds or clawfoot tubs, and suites and apartments have separate living areas. Other highlights include an excellent French restaurant and a small spa with a treehouse-style treatment room.

content: The Australian-born TRIBE hotels are, with the help of Accor, a global concern, with a particularly strong presence in France. TRIBE Montpellier Gare Sud de France is exemplary: a chic and modern design-oriented hotel with just the essential splurges, so that its young (or young at heart) guests can feel a touch of luxury without blowing the budget.\n\nIts rooms are colorful and just plush enough, and come with thoughtful extras like Nespresso machines and Kevin Murphy bath products. Splurge for a sofa, or spend extra time in the Social Hub, a versatile co-working and socializing space that’s part office, part cocktail bar. There’s a grab-and-go counter for light bites and an Australian restaurant called Tribe Table, as well as a rooftop bar with a pool and views of the city. And the location, right next to the station, is as convenient as can be.

content: The Florentin resurrects Villa Speyer, a 1901 banking family mansion that spent years as Villa Kennedy before going dark in 2022. Althoff's takeover kept the villa's nine original suites intact while grafting on contemporary rooms that don't fight the heritage architecture. The central courtyard delivers the kind of removed-from-reality terrace dining that makes you forget Frankfurt's glass towers exist three bridges north. Sachsenhausen's leafy streets put museum-hopping within range, while two restaurants split duties between refined and approachable. The bar takes its spirits seriously, the cigar lounge makes no apologies, and the spa's indoor pool and treatment rooms handle the necessary decompression.

content: There’s an old school grandness to Hotel Villa Pascucci. The first sign of it is the high wrought iron gate that leads to the hotel’s private yard and elegant white façade, which hides a collection of classic rooms and suites dressed in creamy shades and Italian marble. First floor rooms also come with balconies, and views across the outdoor pool or sea.  The second pool can be found indoors, lined in floral mosaics and crowned by a frescoed ceiling, along with the spa’s hydrotherapeutic bath, a Finnish sauna, steam room and a treatment menu of massages and facials. There’s also a sports pitch for tennis, football, and basketball. Restaurant Pascucci Grand Gourmet rounds out the offering with a menu focused on Italian dishes and wines.

content: EQ Kuala Lumpur is a bold reimagining of a city classic. Rising above the site of the original Hotel Equatorial, an icon since the 1970s, the 52-story tower brings polished design, smart sustainability, and sweeping skyline views to the centre of town. Its rooms are sleek and spacious, while the wellness floor includes an infinity pool, Himalayan salt sauna, and full-service spa. Sky51, the rooftop dining and lounge space, is a destination in itself. With top-tier service, standout restaurants, and a location minutes from KLCC, EQ feels both rooted in history and ready for what is next.

content: Ho Chi Minh City’s the envy of south Vietnam, artfully straddling the line between its rich, multifaceted history and contemporary cosmopolitanism. Triangulate from the Notre Dame cathedral, the Independence palace, and the opera house and you can’t miss InterContinental Saigon. Its public spaces skew grand, though not overly ornate — credit the team for knowing when it’s enough — nodding to French colonial history without drowning in it. Rooms preserve this balance with rich earth tones and warm wood accents where they count. Rest and recharge, but don’t skimp on streetlife; this place is best perused on foot (or moped), nosing out incredible street eats as you go.

content: IHG’s Hotel Indigo line of boutique hotels is nothing if not tailored to the specific location of each hotel; Hotel Indigo Adelaide Markets takes its inspirations, both architectural and conceptual, from Adelaide Central Market, the Victorian-era covered market and food hall that is the heart of the city’s food scene. The hotel reproduces the red brick construction and the distinctive archways of the market, and also finds space for intricate tilework and accents in copper, both nods to other local traditions. Its rooms and suites are modern and warm, decorated in bold graphic prints, and its restaurants — one a modern Italian eatery, the other a rooftop raw bar — are local fixtures.

content: The Museum Hotel Antakya isn’t just located near a museum, or attached to one — it actually is a museum, a modern structure suspended by a sturdy metal frame, elevating it above the active archaeological site that was, ironically, only discovered when work on the hotel first began. It’s an unapologetically modern structure and its rooms are unapologetically contemporary-luxe to match, though the décor contains a multitude of historical references. A lavish spa and multiple high-end dining and drinking venues complete the package; simply put, it’s a very well-crafted luxury hotel in an absolutely unforgettable setting.

content: Tim Hortons co-founder and philanthropist Ron Joyce returned home to the Northumberland Shore of Nova Scotia to build Fox Harb’r Resort, a staggeringly luxurious lodging with a championship golf course and a lavish destination spa. The humblest rooms, for golfers on a pilgrimage, are still expansive and packed with high-end details like Molton Brown bath products and Frette linens; the suites, townhomes, villas, and residences lack for nothing in terms of comfort. Cape Cliff, the flagship restaurant, showcases Nova Scotia’s famous seafood; activities range from shooting and archery to sea kayaking, yacht cruises, and golf instruction for all levels of player.
